Joint Statement on Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) Sanctions
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:42:53 CET
23:42:53 KST

Joint Statement on Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) Sanctions North Korea Cyber security Joint statement On : October 29th 2026 The text of the following statement was released by Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the European Union. Throughout October and today, the European Union (EU) and the governments of Australia and the United States have implemented sanctions to target the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) use of overseas workers, malicious cyber activities, and actors involved in unlawful DPRK-Russia cooperation. Their actions represent their efforts to disrupt the DPRK’s ability to support its unlawful development of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missiles, and to counter unlawful DPRK-Russia military cooperation. These designations build on detailed reporting published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), which monitors and reports on DPRK’s non-compliance with UN Security Council resolutions in the absence of the UNSCR 1718 Committee Panel of Experts, whose mandate renewal was vetoed by Russia in 2024. The MSMT’s first and second reports outlined the DPRK’s unlawful military cooperation with Russia, along with cyber-enabled IT worker fraud, both of which serve to fund Pyongyang’s unlawful weapons programs. In September 2026, the MSMT released its third report detailing the DPRK’s deployment of overseas workers to generate revenue for its WMD and ballistic missile programs. The MSMT will continue to monitor, expose, and report on attempts to violate and evade UN sanctions by the DPRK. The MSMT and EU reaffirm our commitment to the complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the DPRK, calling on it to abandon its unlawful WMD and ballistic missile programs, and taking action to counter DPRK attempts to violate and evade UN sanctions. We continue to strongly support the implementation of all DPRK-related UN Security Council resolutions. We call on all UN Member States, and especially permanent members of the Security Council, to fully implement these resolutions.

Russian drone strike kills at least 14 at crowded railway station in Dnipro, attacks also target civilians in Chernihiv and Kremenchuk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:41:54 UTC
23:41:54 KST

A Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people at the main railway station in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday, while attacks on Chernihiv and Kremenchuk killed five more, Ukrainian officials announced. The strikes came as a localized humanitarian ceasefire continued to hold in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson Region.
Ukraine’s state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a jet-powered drone struck a platform at Dnipro’s main station as Train No. 866, a commuter service to nearby Zaporizhzhia, was preparing to depart. Despite an air raid warning and notice of an increased threat, a large number of passengers were on the platform.
Images posted by President Volodymyr Zelensky showed bodies on the ground as emergency workers carried wounded people away on stretchers. Regional authorities said at least 13 people were injured, four of them seriously, including a child.
Importantly, the ceasefire that is in effect applies only to the area around Oleshky, located on the Russian-occupied eastern bank of the Dnipro River; it is intended to allow humanitarian aid into the city and civilians to evacuate. The agreement was reached with U.S. mediation and took effect on Oct. 27. Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday that no violations had been recorded after 54 hours and that crews were clearing mines from evacuation routes ahead of planned aid deliveries.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, Russia has continued drone and missile attacks on critical infrastructure, including the railway network, increasing pressure on civilians and the economy as Ukraine faces shortages of air defense missiles.
Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians. Nevertheless, two 15-year-old girls were killed and 23 people wounded when a drone struck a busy street in the northern city of Chernihiv. And in the central city of Kremenchuk, a strike on an apartment building killed three people and wounded 15.
“Russia is deliberately targeting civilians: on trains, at stations, in residential buildings,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi wrote on Telegram. “There is no justification for this terror, and there never can be.”
Dmytro Bryzhynskyi, the head of the Chernihiv’s military administration wrote that: “Ordinary, peaceful people were attacked who were just going to work, going about their daily business, making plans for the day.”
Overall, the attacks in Dnipro, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk killed at least 19 people Thursday, according to a report by Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi.
Zelensky responded to the Dnipro attack by urging Ukraine’s international partners to increase pressure on Moscow. Earlier in October, the United States temporarily eased sanctions enforcement in order to allow for increased Russian diesel exports under an agreement between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. The European Union also removed Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list in September.
“Just how many terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and the Russian energy sector, rather than de-escalating?” Zelensky wrote on X.

Hong Kong's housing chief quits, government admits 'decades of failure' led to last year's deadly fire
Unknown

23:41:01 KST

Saadet Gökce
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Hong Kong Housing Chief Winnie Ho resigned Thursday after the government admitted that "decades of failure" contributed to a deadly 2025 fire, according to the South China Morning Post.
A scathing report by an independent committee investigating the city's deadliest blaze in decades blamed the main renovation contractor, the project consultant and an inspector for their alleged roles in the tragedy.
It also held four government agencies accountable.
The fire killed 168 people in November, making it the city's deadliest blaze in more than 70 years.
Non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets, foam boards and other flammable materials, along with openings created in escape staircases, contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the high death toll, said the report.
The committee said the Housing Bureau's Independent Checking Unit bore the greatest responsibility among the four agencies because it failed to adequately oversee renovation work at Wang Fuk Court.
The report criticized the other three agencies: the Fire Services Department, the Buildings Department and the Labor Department.
The government will introduce legislation to criminalize bid-rigging and reform the supervision of engineering and renovation contractors.
A high-level steering committee, led by the chief secretary, will oversee the implementation of the reforms.
Authorities also pledged to investigate about 50 civil servants concerning their administrative responsibilities.

29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday accused North Korea of threatening freedom across all of Europe by sending soldiers to fight against Ukraine.
After talks with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung in Seoul, Merz said Korea’s security has a bearing on Europe’s security and that Europe’s security, in turn, affects Korea's security.
“This becomes tangibly clear when, for instance, North Korean soldiers fight against Ukraine in the Donbas, thereby threatening freedom across all of Europe,” he said. “It also has consequences when, in return, Moscow supplies weapons to Pyongyang.”
Merz noted that Germany and its European partners are undertaking diplomatic efforts to find a just and lasting solution to the war between Ukraine and Russia, and thanked the South Korean leader for the country’s support for Europeans.
“I am grateful that we can continue to count on your support in this endeavor, as we know that the outcome of this war will shape the entire security architecture—both in Europe and here in Asia,” he said.
Enhanced strategic partnership
Describing South Korea as a key partner of Germany, the chancellor said both countries are democracies that value openness to the world and fair, free competition – principles that only a rules-based international order can continue to make possible.
At a time of global upheavals, he added, it is only logical to deepen the partnership, because both countries need more than ever a strong network of partners who share important interests and common values. That applies to security policy, the economy and geopolitics.
“We are therefore elevating our relations today to the level of an enhanced strategic partnership, because we share the immediate experience of what it means to live through geopolitical tensions and division,” Merz said.
South Korea marks the final leg of Merz’s three-nation tour of East Asia, which previously included visits to Singapore and Japan. The trip aims to deepen security and economic cooperation with key Indo-Pacific partners. On Friday, he is due to visit the Demilitarized Zone dividing the Korean Peninsula.

‘American psychological warfare’: Call of Duty slammed for using disaster footage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:39:28 UTC
23:39:28 KST

The latest Call of Duty game has sparked backlash over footage from South Korea’s deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush and a fictional war scenario that a local civic group has condemned as “American psychological warfare.”
Modern Warfare 4, released by Activision on October 23, introduces its campaign, centered around a fictional North Korean invasion, using seconds-long clips from the infamous Itaewon disaster.
The October 29, 2022 incident left more than 150 people dead after Halloween crowds became trapped in a narrow alley in Seoul’s nightlife district.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare is facing backlash from Koreans for allegedly using footage from the actual Itaewon crowd crush, which claimed 159 lives, in the game. They reportedly included footage of people performing CPR at the actual disaster site and recreated a similar scene in the game. Koreans are now calling for the footage to be removed and I wonder if the developers are going to do anything about it because this is absolutely insane. It has only been four years since that tragedy happened, and now people are seeing something so closely resembling that horrific incident in a video game. This is deeply insensitive to the victims, their families and everyone who was affected by the tragedy.
— kdramahotgists (@kdramahotgists) October 29, 2026
Relatives of the victims responded to the game release, which came just days before the fourth-year anniversary of the tragic event, by demanding the scenes be removed from cinematics.
In a joint statement, bereaved families and civic groups condemned the inclusion as “highly inappropriate and insensitive,” stressing that witnesses and people involved in rescue efforts continue to suffer trauma.
“If there is even a minimal sense of respect and empathy for the victims, the game developer must take corrective action immediately,” they said.
The Korea Game Users Association also demanded an explanation, apology, and replacement footage, while opposing censorship or unjustified restrictions on games.
Modern Warfare 4’s depiction of another Korean war has also drawn criticism, even before its release. Former Culture Minister Kim Sung-jae slammed the game for turning Korean society’s war trauma into entertainment.
Civic group Candlelight Action also accused it of amplifying hostility toward North Korea and called it “American psychological warfare.”
Earlier this month, President Lee Jae-myung separately condemned Ukrainian remarks suggesting an imminent clash between the two Koreas, saying they amounted to encouraging war on the peninsula.
Responding to the footage controversy, Activision told South Korean media that the archival scenes were intended to convey a fictional narrative. It denied intending to trivialize the Itaewon disaster. At the same time, the company has made no commitment to removing the footage.
However, this isn’t the first time the Modern Warfare series has sparked controversy over its in-game campaigns. Its 2009 installment, Modern Warfare 2, placed players undercover among terrorists attacking a Moscow airport. The “No Russian” mission allowed them to join in shooting unarmed civilians, provoking outrage and prompting its removal from the Russian release.
The 2019 reboot also drew accusations of anti-Russian propaganda over its “Highway of Death” storyline. It blamed Russians for an attack resembling the real-life US-led bombardment of retreating Iraqi columns in 1991 – effectively re-attributing an US war crime. Both Russian players and Western gaming publications alike criticized the sequence, while Russian streamers withdrew from promotional events.
In 2023, major Russian retailers also said they would withhold Modern Warfare III pending review over concerns that violence against Russian characters could violate local laws.
In December 2025, State Duma deputy Mikhail Delyagin similarly sought a regulatory examination of the series following complaints about its portrayal of Russia and repeated missions against Russian soldiers.

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Dozens of tons of humanitarian aid, including food, sanitary supplies, medicine and fuel, will be delivered to civilians in the town of Alyoshki, Kherson Region, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said.
US First Lady Melania Trump has confirmed that American journalists will observe the humanitarian mission.
TASS has compiled the key details of preparations for the mission.
Preparations for humanitarian mission
- Preparations for a humanitarian mission in Alyoshki began in May, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said.
- Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov noted that US First Lady Melania Trump had drawn on her extensive experience of humanitarian initiatives to help broker a ceasefire in Alyoshki as part of US peace efforts.
Ensuring humanitarian mission security
- Russian service members from Battlegroup Dnepr are clearing roads to provide safe passage to Alyoshki, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
- Troops are removing unexploded ordnance from the roads leading to the town to facilitate aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians, the ministry added.
- US First Lady Melania Trump said late on October 28 that work had begun to ensure the security of the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- In addition to clearing mines and other explosive ordnance from roads along the planned route of the humanitarian aid convoy, Russian service members are also helping civilians reach Alyoshki safely.
Foreign journalists
- Journalists from US television channel Newsmax will "witness and report firsthand" on the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki, Kirill Dmitriev, Russian special presidential envoy for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries and director general of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), said.
- US First Lady Melania Trump said later that four Newsmax journalists "will be on the ground" in Alyoshki, "embedded with Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian leaders."
- "Serving as neutral observers, they will independently record and permanently document this historic humanitarian mission," Melania Trump added.
- TASS published footage from one of its correspondents showing a plane carrying members of the humanitarian mission departing from Moscow.
- There were Russian and US journalists on board, including four Newsmax reporters and correspondents from other countries.
- Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he considered coverage of the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki by Russian journalists more important than coverage by foreign reporters.
Humanitarian aid
- The humanitarian operation currently underway in Alyoshki is aimed at providing assistance to civilians, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Russia-Africa Summit.
- Lantratova said that a large humanitarian aid convoy would be assembled to deliver food, medicine and essential supplies to those in need in Alyoshki.
- According to her, several dozen metric tons of humanitarian supplies will be delivered to residents of the town.
- The human rights commissioner added that the list of supplies had been compiled based on requests from local residents.
- The shipment primarily includes food, medicine, sanitary items, fuel and heating supplies.
- The Russian Red Cross Society (RRCS) provided humanitarian aid for the residents of Alyoshki, RRCS Chairman Pavel Savchuk said on Telegram.
- The Federation of Independent Trade Unions of Russia (FNPR) sent its first truck carrying humanitarian aid to Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, a spokesperson told TASS.
- The truck, carrying about 100 boxes containing food, sanitary items and other basic necessities, departed from the FNPR headquarters in Moscow on Thursday.
- The aid will be delivered to Alyoshki in the coming days through the FNPR office in the Southern Federal District and the Kherson Region’s trade union organization.
Meeting of Russian, Ukrainian representatives
- Representatives of Russia and Ukraine involved in the humanitarian operation in Alyoshki departed from Gomel Airport in Belarus aboard the same plane, the BelTA news agency reported.
- According to the media outlet, Russian and Ukrainian representatives first saw each other face-to-face at Gomel Airport.
- The meeting also involved Belarus, which joined the humanitarian operation.

- Minsk is providing Moscow and Kiev with the necessary comprehensive assistance while acting as guarantor of the relevant processes.

Ukrainian charged over death of Monaco royal
A Ukrainian man living in Monaco has been charged in connection with the death of Antoine de Massy, a relative of Prince Albert II, the ruler of the wealthy European principality.
The 42-year-old suspect, whose identity has not been disclosed, has reportedly lived in Monaco for three decades. Prosecutor General Stephane Thibault announced a judicial investigation on Wednesday.
According to local media, the Ukrainian national has been charged with involuntary manslaughter and failure to assist a person in danger. He denies wrongdoing and has been remanded in custody.
De Massy, 29, whose father is a first cousin of Prince Albert II, was found dead on Sunday evening after apparently falling approximately 13 meters from an elevated section of the coastal Boulevard du Larvotto into a garden behind a luxury residence.
The former competitive tennis player was reportedly last seen alive overnight Saturday into Sunday, leaving a nightclub apparently intoxicated and accompanied by another man. His family alerted authorities when he failed to attend a gathering, triggering a search that led to the discovery of his body in the secluded garden.
Thibault said CCTV footage showed the suspect accompanying de Massy along Boulevard du Larvotto. The Ukrainian national was arrested on Monday, although it remains unclear whether he was the man who reportedly left the nightclub with the victim.
Earlier this year, Monaco, known as a haven for millionaires, was rocked by a bombing targeting Ukrainian-born businessman Vadim Ermolaev, who was injured alongside members of his family.
The alleged bomber was identified as a Ukrainian woman who was later found dead in her home country, reportedly killed by her handlers. Investigators identified the suspected masterminds as an active operative of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, and an unofficial agent of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU). Both are now in Ukrainian custody.
Kiev portrayed the bombing as a profit-driven crime carried out by rogue agents. However, one suspect claimed the operation had been authorized by the Ukrainian state as a legitimate act of war against Russia.
The case resurfaced this week when former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said the Monaco bombing “echoed” an alleged Ukrainian intelligence plot against him that Austrian law enforcement had thwarted.
Kravchenko fled Ukraine for Vienna last month and was subsequently dismissed by parliament after a subordinate was accused of running a protection racket on his behalf. The Austrian authorities confirmed the arrests of suspected Ukrainian intelligence operatives in early October.

Canada to join EU network of supercomputers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:34:08 UTC
23:34:08 KST

BRUSSELS— The European Union and Canada are teaming up on compute power — a key element for training artificial intelligence models — with Canada set to join the EU's supercomputer network.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday Canada "will now become part of this network", confirming a POLITICO report from earlier this week that both sides were discussing the country's entry into the European supercomputing network.
Canada joining "enables Canadian industry, startups and researchers to access European supercomputing," von der Leyen said. "Paired with Canada's pioneering AI industry, this would allow us to develop highly competitive, innovative and safe AI systems."
Advertisement
The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an €8.2 billion budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers.
The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of €30 billion.
Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start.
“Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term ‘middle power’ cooperation plays in AI,” said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
But he added that for now “it doesn’t put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S.
“As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn’t result in massive buildouts will help,” he said.
Advertisement
Canada's engagement in the EU's supercomputer network builds further on Canada's previous partial involvement in the EU's flagship research and development program, Horizon Europe.
Horizon Europe partially funds EuroHPC.
To date, 38 countries have participated in the EU's supercomputing network: 27 EU member countries plus non-EU countries including Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Israel and Turkey.

- A Saudi Defense Ministry photo from King Khalid Air Base appears to show a Bahraini F-16 squadron pilot and a Pakistan Air Force member, analysts said.
- Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Pakistan have not commented on the image or confirmed any Bahraini deployment to the base.
A photo released by Saudi Arabia’s Defense Ministry from a visit by its top military officer to King Khalid Air Base in the kingdom’s southwest appears to show a Royal Bahraini Air Force fighter pilot and a member of the Pakistan Air Force at the base, open-source analysts at OSINTWarfare pointed out in a post.
Gen. Fayyadh Al-Ruwaili, chief of the general staff, visited military units in the southern region, units deployed along the border with Yemen and military commands in Khamis Mushait and Jazan, where he received briefings on operational missions, the Saudi Defense Ministry announced. The ministry’s statement did not mention any foreign personnel, and neither Bahrain nor Pakistan has commented on the image.
According to OSINTWarfare, the photo shows a Bahraini officer with the rank of major wearing the patch of the Royal Bahraini Air Force’s 1st Tactical Fighter Squadron, known as the Desert Falcons, on his right shoulder. The squadron flies F-16C/D fighters from Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain and is responsible for defending Bahraini airspace, and the analysts said it has not previously been publicly known to have taken part in operations abroad. A Pakistan Air Force member can be seen in the background, identifiable by his uniform, they added, though the image does not show whether the personnel are deployed to the base, how many are there or what aircraft, if any, they brought.
King Khalid Air Base sits outside Khamis Mushait in Asir province and is the main Royal Saudi Air Force hub for the southern border with Yemen, an area that has been under fire this autumn as Houthi missile and drone attacks in September struck targets in Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait and Saudi Arabia resumed its air war against the Iran-backed group.
Bahrain sent F-16s to fight alongside Saudi Arabia when it joined the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis in 2015, and on Dec. 30 that year a Royal Bahraini Air Force F-16 crashed in Jazan province while flying for the coalition, with the pilot surviving. Bahraini officials did not say at the time which squadron the aircraft belonged to.
Pakistani fighter and support aircraft arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base in the Eastern Province in April under the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement the two countries signed in September 2025, and a senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times this month that Pakistan Air Force jets are being used in strikes against Yemen’s Houthis. Analysts estimate about 8,000 Pakistani troops have deployed to the kingdom, including air force and army air defense units.
Britain said on Oct. 20 that Royal Air Force Typhoons will fly defensive patrols over Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye is preparing to send personnel under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement it signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August, pending approval by its parliament.
Saudi Arabia and Bahrain have not said whether Bahraini F-16s are operating from King Khalid Air Base or flying missions over Yemen.

29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Finnish police have launched a preliminary criminal investigation into suspected environmental damage at Google's data center construction site in Muhos, following concerns about water management and drainage practices, according to media reports on Thursday.
The Oulu Police Department is examining five investigation requests concerning the site, including one submitted by the Finnish Supervisory Agency, Finnish broadcaster Yle reported.
Police said preliminary findings pointed to "irregularities and shortcomings" in drainage and water management at the construction site, operated by Google's local subsidiary Tuike Finland.
The investigation is focused on suspected environmental damage, although additional suspected offenses could emerge as inquiries progress.
Authorities expect the investigation to continue into 2027, with additional information anticipated in December, according to the report.
The probe follows an order from the Finnish Supervisory Agency to suspend construction at Google's Muhos and Kajaani-Otanmaki projects because environmental impact assessments were not completed.
The company confirmed on Oct. 14 that it had halted preparatory work at both locations.
Regulators also found the company's water management plans insufficient to show it could adequately control environmental risks.
Tuike Finland has until Nov. 5 to submit a more detailed plan addressing drainage infrastructure, monitoring and risks associated with heavy rainfall, melting snow and potentially acidic soils.
The agency warned that failure to comply could result in enforcement action, including a conditional fine.
The projects form part of Google's €13 billion ($14.5 billion) investment in Finland.

In fall 2026, the Prague Book Tower, a fair for Russian-language tamizdat, presented Grigory Sverdlin’s book Punkt obogreva: Kak ya zanimalsya blagotvoritelnostyu v Rossii i stal vragom gosudarstva (“Warming Station: How I Did Charity Work in Russia and Became an Enemy of the State”), published by Meduza’s publishing house. Sverdlin previously headed Nochlezhka, Russia’s oldest organization helping homeless people. In 2022, he stepped down as director, left the country, and, once in exile, launched the project Idite Lesom (“Get Lost”), which helps Russians desert the army and flee the country. In Prague, Felix Sandalov and Alexey Dokuchaev, founders of the StraightForward foundation, which supported the publication of Warming Station, spoke with Grigory Sverdlin about what kind of people work in the field of charity, why it’s almost impossible for projects like Idite Lesom to find financial support, and what future awaits an organization so closely tied to the war. Meduza is publishing a lightly abridged version of this conversation.
Felix Sandalov: Grisha and I first started talking about a book — not this one, but a completely different book at the time — I think around six or seven years ago, back in our time at the Moscow publishing house Individuum. The book was conceived as a kind of field guide to the work of nonprofit organizations, since Grisha already had a great deal of experience at Nochlezhka by then. But what came out now is an entirely different [book]. In its own way, it captures the difference between charity work and civil resistance. Grisha made a real “leap of faith” and founded an entirely new organization for himself, built on new principles.
Warming Station describes a kind of seasonality in the work of charities that help homeless people. When cold weather sets in, the work grows more urgent: people die on the streets, and staff have to respond quickly — it’s a genuinely difficult period for anyone working on these projects. That was certainly true at Nochlezhka. Is there a similar seasonality to the work at Idite Lesom? And given that the media keeps stirring up talk of an impending mobilization, which Russian authorities routinely deny, are you seeing a surge in requests to Idite Lesom right now?
Grigory Sverdlin: First, let me correct you a little. You’re talking about seasonality in helping homeless people, but the real seasonality is in donations. In winter, people donate more, more often, and more willingly to help the homeless, while in summer, for obvious reasons, the issue falls out of public attention. That doesn’t mean there are fewer homeless people — they don’t go anywhere. It’s a bit easier to survive, yes, but it’s still incredibly hard.
That’s exactly the pain point and the subject of discussion in the charity community that helps people who end up on the street: raising donations is incredibly hard, and the amount of work never decreases.
As for helping people who have ended up in the Russian army, or those trying to avoid ending up there, we’re completely swamped at Idite Lesom. If you’ve written to us and have been waiting several days for a reply, I want to take this opportunity to apologize. We will definitely answer everyone.
This summer we’ve gotten about one and a half times more requests than in spring, and about three times more than last summer. Right now, about 150 to 200 people contact us every day. Many people currently in Russia are, of course, panicking about a possible mobilization this fall and thinking about how to protect themselves, their children, and their loved ones.
The number of requests from people who want to desert from the Russian army is also growing. Just two days ago, we were tallying up the numbers for August: we helped almost 150 people desert that month alone.
Sandalov: You write about all of this with such vividness and enthusiasm — you can feel how obstacles energize you, how much you enjoy finding solutions to nontrivial problems. That’s always admirable.
Tell me about your method of writing the book. You describe nearly 20 years with all the vividness of someone who lived through every event firsthand. How did you reconstruct it all? How did you transport yourself back in time? How did you reconstruct the dialogue? Did you keep some kind of diaries? Or did you [reconstruct something] from letters, or do you just have a photographic memory?
Sverdlin: Thanks for the kind words. My memory is pretty poor, so I actually did some serious “pre-research” — digging up publications that are now archival, corresponding with colleagues, and interviewing colleagues from other charities who appear in the book. It’s primarily about Nochlezhka and Idite Lesom, but of course I wanted — and I hope I managed — to paint a broader picture and talk more generally about how the charity sector sprouted up through the asphalt in Russia. It didn’t exist in Soviet times, because only the state was supposed to help. Horizontal ties weren’t welcomed. They were banned.
Alexey Dokuchaev: So who should actually be doing the helping? The state, or society and organizations like Nochlezhka?
Sverdlin: I’d rather not frame it in terms of who “should.” Overall, global experience shows that the support system works best when many charitable organizations run by enthusiasts operate alongside various state, regional, and municipal structures that are also engaged in providing help. What you end up with is a network of different charitable projects, both private and government-run, that step in when someone is in trouble.
And indeed, the ratio of private to government assistance can vary somewhat, but practice shows that private initiatives are always more empathetic and more progressive, thanks to the greater enthusiasm of the people working there, and, being less bureaucratic, [these initiatives] are able to adapt more quickly to what’s happening.
Government structures, meanwhile, will always have more stable funding and greater organizational resources. In Finland, for example, which is the world champion in helping homeless people, that’s exactly the kind of interaction between the charitable and government sectors that exists.
Sandalov: Are there organizations in other countries that, like Idite Lesom, help conscripts avoid being sent to the front? Do you have an international community that shares its pains and hopes with one another?
Sverdlin: We do have some colleagues, and I found it fascinating when, a couple of years ago, we more or less accidentally met people in America who, during the Vietnam War, did something similar to what Idite Lesom does now. They were elderly hippies by then, recounting their extensive experience.
Obviously, given the specific nature of the subject, there aren’t many such colleagues, and we can’t really exchange experience with them. With our Finnish colleagues on the subject of homelessness, we always tried to pick up tips, to bring some of Finland’s practices back to Russia. But when it comes to helping with desertion… You can’t really swap routes for crossing the Finnish border with people who help men avoid service in the Pakistani army.
Dokuchaev: Nochlezhka is, in general, an organization whose structure makes sense to all of us. With Idite Lesom, we know the name, we understand what it does. But how does the organization actually function now, and to what extent can it be built into a system? And should it be? What does systemic success look like for you, apart from the war ending? Could you get an entire regiment or division out [of combat zones] if you were given far more resources?
Sverdlin: In general, I’m a believer in sustainable structures. My professional pride is that Grisha Sverdlin isn’t in St. Petersburg, in Moscow, or at Nochlezhka anymore, and yet Nochlezhka keeps living, working, and developing. I’m very glad about that, because it’s a crucial stress test for any leader: does everything still work once they’re no longer there? With Idite Lesom, I also want to believe that we’ve managed to build that kind of system.
Idite Lesom has 10 staff members: people who receive at least some salary, myself included. There are also around 80 volunteers, though we’re constantly recruiting more. Without this professionally organized work, it wouldn’t be possible to counsel 150 to 200 people every day.
“I got a summons, what do I do?” “I want to leave Russia, can I get out?” “There’s some kind of restriction on my ‘Gosuslugi’ account. Can you explain it?” “My boyfriend was detained on the street, and they’re pressuring him to sign a contract. Help.” “I’m a conscript who’s already been forced to sign a contract, and we were told we’ll be sent to the occupied territories next week. Help, save me, what do I do?” And so on, and so on. These really are hundreds of requests every week.
To answer your question about a regiment, I feel a little awkward bragging about numbers, but I’ll say it anyway, because it’s the result of enormous work by our volunteers. We launched in September 2022. To date, we’ve counseled more than 82,000 people, and there are around 3,600 people we’ve helped desert. We’ve gotten most of them out of Russia, although in the end a fairly significant number of people decide to stay in the country, and we help them hide.
So it’s a huge amount of work, but there’s always room to grow. Just last week, we met in person with colleagues and tried to come up with new ideas for how to undermine our home country’s defense capability more effectively.
Dokuchaev: How do people find out about you? Do you work only off the requests that come in? How does someone who doesn’t read Meduza or follow your Facebook find out that if they’re sent to occupied territory tomorrow, they should write to you?
Sverdlin: Honestly, good old word of mouth works best. Besides Meduza’s readers and my Facebook, 200,000 people also follow Idite Lesom’s social media accounts. That’s a great achievement by my colleagues who handle our social media.
These people spread the information among their friends and classmates, dropping it into chat groups like those for conscripts’ mothers. I think, above all, it’s this kind of organic reach.
Second, it’s probably independent Russian journalists and bloggers, whom I’d also like to take this opportunity to thank. They write about us, which means more people find out about Idite Lesom, and more people get the chance to escape the jaws of the leviathan.
Sandalov: Several fascinating pages of Warming Station are devoted to your great lifelong passion, namely technical mountaineering. By risking your life, you get access to some of the craziest views on planet Earth. In your view, is there a connection here: do people with a propensity for all kinds of extreme activity (there’s a crude expression for it, adrenaline junkie) want to work in charitable organizations or civil resistance projects more than others? Does charity work genuinely attract that kind of crowd, or is it a coincidence?
Sverdlin: I think it’s more of a coincidence. Of course, as someone who used to work at commercial companies, I was incredibly curious when I first started out in the nonprofit world. I wanted to see what kind of people worked there and how they differed from people in business.
What I ended up seeing, first, was people with a sharper sense of justice. For most of us, I think, that sense applies to ourselves and our immediate circle, but we’re unlikely to call up the relevant city service and complain about every broken traffic light. I had a colleague, though, who would see a broken traffic light and immediately start working to get it fixed.
Second, it’s a more developed sense of empathy, one that seems to stretch to more people and more situations. I also tried to write about this in the book. You shouldn’t idealize the people who come to work in charity, because everything has a shadow side, a flip side. The amount of conflict, scandal, and manipulation I was subjected to in the charity world is something no business could even dream of.
Sandalov: Tell me about civil resistance. Over the past few years, you’ve done a lot of notable things with Idite Lesom. Probably the biggest recent one was hacking into and destroying data from Russia’s military registration database. Tell me how that changed your life.
Sverdlin: Specifically, hacking the registry — or rather, the registry developer’s systems, to be precise — didn’t change anything, because by that point we’d already been engaged in “subversive activity” for three years, and our websites had already been blocked multiple times. We had, of course, already been designated “foreign agents” by Russian authorities. I’d already been sentenced in absentia to six years. If you want details, now whenever I fly somewhere, I always check where the airline’s backup airport is, because some airlines that fly to, say, Kutaisi use Sochi as their alternate airport. If there’s some technical problem in Kutaisi, the plane will land in Sochi. And I shouldn’t be showing up in Sochi. I also almost never write about my plans, and I try not to post photos from my window — basically, I take these and other obvious security precautions.
Coming back to the organization, so far, aside from being blocked and periodic attempts to hack us, nothing major has happened. Obviously, we vet people who want to become our volunteers in multiple stages, because there’s no doubt some “comrade major” would love to get in among them. But when you’re living inside all of this, this kind of shit just feels like routine.
Hi, I’m N.
I report for Meduza from inside Russia. I could go to prison for my work. To stay safe, I have to follow strict security protocols. I know my lawyer’s phone number by heart. And, of course, my articles are published anonymously.
Working for an independent news outlet while still living in Russia feels like something out of a spy film. My friends know me by one name. My colleagues and sources know me by another. But sometimes there’s a glitch. At a close friend’s birthday party, someone I don’t know reaches out to shake my hand. “Hi, I’m Lyosha.” It takes me a few seconds to decide how to introduce myself. Do I use my real name or my pseudonym? I’m trying to figure out whether this is someone I might one day end up writing about.
What I do is journalism in exile, even though I’m not in exile myself. I have the rare opportunity to do uncensored, on-the-ground reporting in Russia. Please support Meduza so I can continue this work.
Dokuchaev: Tell me, does having this kind of work get in your way, or does it actually help you? Does it give you strength to make plans for your own life? We’re living now in pretty pleasant places, where other people don’t have a war, but we do. Still, this war will end sooner or later. Given that, it seems obvious that the best thing that could happen to Idite Lesom is for it to shut down. How do you picture [life after that]?
Sverdlin: It’s true, when I came up with this project during the mobilization in Russia, I assumed we’d be doing it for six months, maybe a year — then the war would end, and we’d all go our separate ways to other things. I was naive.
I think that for me, and for many people I’m friends with, the war has cut off any sense of a horizon ahead. I don’t know what will happen in 10 years, or even five. And for now, unfortunately, I’m not able to look that far ahead.
I have to say this is something I miss, because when I worked at Nochlezhka, my colleagues and I tried to build strategic plans. Even if we specifically wouldn’t be at Nochlezhka in 10 years, we still tried to figure out how to move toward a future with room for many different charities and government projects. We were trying to grow that mycelium. Idite Lesom, of course, is a project with no future. God willing, this project will never have a future.
Dokuchaev: A project like this really shouldn’t have a future. But the people you’ve managed to help clearly do have one. Do you keep track of what happens to the people you got out, or, conversely, the people you weren’t able to get out?
Sverdlin: We do keep track. Idite Lesom is partly a charity project, not purely civil resistance. And there’s a well-known thing in charity work: a large share of the people organizations help never come back to say thank you.
Yes, Nochlezhka’s social workers are often brought boxes of chocolates. But that’s still a tiny fraction of the boxes they’re actually owed. People who’ve been through homelessness and managed to get out of it with Nochlezhka’s help don’t look back: behind them lies a nightmare, and thank god it’s over.
It’s the same with the deserters we’ve helped get out of the Russian army. It’s often harder because we’ve never even met some of them in person. Even so, we still know where quite a lot of them are and what they’re doing. By the way, a large share of the people we help desert end up in Kazakhstan and Armenia, because those are countries where you can legally live with a Russian internal passport. I’d guess around 90% of them now live in those two countries. We stay in touch with some of these people — they write to us and share their successes in their new lives.
Sandalov: In Warming Station, you write about the complicated, ambiguous world we all live in. On one hand, the Idite Lesom initiative obviously makes sense, with a very clear goal. But there are still plenty of contradictions. I’m thinking, for instance, of accusations that you’re helping war criminals. Or, say, you write in the book yourself that American philanthropists aren’t willing to give money to help people cross the border illegally, because in their view that’s human trafficking, and charitable money can never go toward something like that. What complaints do you run into most often?
Sverdlin: As for the money issue, it’s pretty funny: when we were just starting out, we knocked on every door, obviously. And we often heard from European grant-making foundations: “What you’re doing is good, but we still support some projects in Russia — cultural or charitable ones — so we can’t get involved with such a blatantly anti-Russian project.”
American grant-making foundations really did tell us that what we’re doing is good, but under American law it counts as human trafficking, and no one will bother to sort out that we’re not smuggling live cargo across the border but Russian deserters. So we made peace with that a long time ago. Huge thanks to the people who donate to Idite Lesom, because today probably 70% to 80% of our small budget comes from donations by Russian emigres. Obviously, we stopped accepting any donations from within Russia long ago, so as not to put anyone at risk, god forbid.
When I came up with this project, I decided right away that one fewer soldier in the Russian army means one person who won’t pull the trigger and fire toward Ukraine. I still hold to that logic. Every person we’ve helped desert, or helped avoid ending up in the Russian army in the first place, is a victory, because it weakens the criminal Russian army and in that way helps Ukraine.
About 80% to 85% of the soldiers and officers we help desert never even make it to the occupied territories. They’re stationed somewhere like Sakhalin or Rostov-on-Don. When these people find out — or even before they find out — that they’re going to be sent to the front, they get in touch with us, and we start helping them desert.
We vet the people who come to us as best we can, but there’s still a small chance that a war criminal could be among them. My colleagues and I aren’t happy about that, but we understand that, yes, in theory it’s possible.
We’ve decided that we will keep doing that vetting, but we’re still not an investigative body. It’s not our job to determine who is a war criminal and who isn’t. And thank god, there are institutions whose job and resources are suited to that: the United Nations war crimes commission and so on. Basically, we’ve decided that we do what we can in this area. Beyond that, I’d like to believe that after the war, all the war criminals will be found.

Fairy chimney rockfall kills two at Turkey's Cappadocia tourist attraction after heavy rain
ANKARA, Oct 29 - Two people were killed and one other injured when rocks from a fairy chimney, a volcanic geological formation, fell after heavy rainfall in the popular Turkish resort of Cappadocia on Thursday, the local governor said.
A landslide occurred due to heavy rainfall at 3:15 p.m. (1215 GMT) and rock fragments that broke away from the fairy chimney fell onto people near the Goreme open-air museum, Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok told reporters. Rescue teams found two people dead and reached one injured person, he added.
Cappadocia, a popular tourist destination in central Turkey, is famous for its geological features called fairy chimneys.
Nationalities of the dead and injured people were not immediately clear.
Rescue teams were still searching the rubble at the scene, the governor also said. REUTERS

Belgium’s Flemish universities said Thursday they had filed a complaint against the European Commission over a lack of clear guidance on research partnerships with Israeli institutions.
The complaint was submitted to the European Ombudsman through the Flemish Interuniversity Council, which represents the universities.
The universities are seeking a common European framework outlining how human rights and international law obligations are considered in EU-funded research projects, particularly regarding cooperation with Israeli entities.
They also want clarity on whether universities could face financial penalties or compensation claims for withdrawing from partnerships over potential human rights violations.
“We have repeatedly asked the European Commission for clarification since May 2024. However, the Commission's answers remain limited to generic references to existing regulations and procedures, without concrete guidelines, criteria, or justification,” council Chairman Bernard Vanheusden said in a statement.
“As a result, universities wishing to terminate a collaboration due to the risk of human rights violations are faced with significant legal uncertainty and potential financial sanctions,” he added.
Since October 2023, Israel’s war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000, while causing widespread destruction affecting about 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure.

European Commission rejects Baltic's €500 million anti-drone request
The European Commission rejected an appeal from the Baltic defense ministers for €500 million in additional support for drone defense for the eastern flank, suggesting they borrow the money instead.
The ministers from Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania sent the request at the end of September.
The letter was classified, but Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT that the Baltic states wanted to combine drone detection, artificial intelligence and interception technology into an integrated air defence system.
However, the European Commissioner for Defense and Space, Andrius Kubilius, told LRT on Wednesday that the Commission had sent its response but could not offer the additional funding the Baltic states had sought.
"One possibility now is to make use of additional funding under the SAFE instrument. We will announce a new call in the near future, because €21 billion remained after the first call," Kubilius said.
The Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, instrument was launched last year and provides €150 billion in favourable loans for defense procurement across the EU.

Trump needs agreement that surpasses Obama's nuclear deal for deal to postpone strikes - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:27:57 UTC
23:27:57 KST

There is an ongoing flurry of diplomatic activity by Iran to try to cut some kind of interim deal that would stave off a possible new attack by US President Donald Trump on Tehran.
Some of the activity is also being pushed by US Vice President JD Vance, who has in the past been a leading voice arguing against US attacks on Iran within the Trump administration.
What is the minimum Trump needs for a new Iran nuclear deal that would get him to postpone another attack?
Note that the answer to this question is likely different from what Israel wants.
The answer is partially military but partially political and economic.
Regarding the military part, the keys are getting something that US president Barack Obama did not get in the 2015 nuclear deal and eliminating the potential for a nuclear threat over the next period of years.
At minimum, Trump needs a nuclear deal with Iran to reduce the enrichment to zero for some period of time, even if only for a few years, or to last for longer than Obama’s 10-15 years.
This accomplishment would allow him to claim a better deal, even if he did not eliminate the whole nuclear program.
Regarding eliminating the potential for a nuclear threat in the coming years (it is at least around two years away due to successful Israeli-US strikes in June 2025), Trump would need to have shipped out or diluted Iran’s stockpile of 60% highly enriched uranium, limit its enrichment capabilities regarding the several hundred centrifuges (out of around 20,000) which survived the June 2025 attacks, and restore effective inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)
He would not get all of this next week, but he would need a down payment on one or more of these items along with a timeline of a couple of months or less by which the rest of the issues would be agreed upon.
Which items would he need a down payment on?
At minimum, restoration of IAEA access and visits.
But as seen with the Islamic Republic repeatedly, access and visits can be taken away in a day.
Trump will want something now that is harder to reverse.
A time-bound commitment regarding some of the enriched uranium, some of the surviving centrifuges, or some concession relating to the Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility.
All of this would be insufficient from the Israeli perspective, because for Jerusalem, this period since June 2025 has been the once-in-50-years chance to finally end Tehran’s nuclear program.
Anything which allows Iran to enrich at some point and to keep some enriched material and centrifuges will be seen by most Israeli officials (both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main challenger Gadi Eisenkot) as wasting that once-in-a-lifetime opportunity, even if it improves security short-term.
Regardless of the terms, Israel should be investing in more effective means of dealing with Iran’s underground nuclear infrastructure, so that it is not entirely reliant on US mega bunker busters and if the US goes back to war, one hopes that it is more ready to defend Arab allies, underwater internet cables, and other sensitive targets than it was in early 2026.
Why might Trump settle for less than Israel when he also sees a nuclear Iran as a threat?
His 2026 war with Iran and the ongoing economic instability are bitterly unpopular with both Democrats and Republicans.
Trump wants to get a “win” and wants to stem the political blood loss he has suffered throughout 2026.
This motive is, in fact, why he cut a deal defined by Netanyahu and Eisenkot as “bad” in July of this year.
If Iran had stuck to the terms of that deal, which got rid of parts, but not all, of the Iran nuclear program, they would have started healing months ago.
But Tehran decided that Trump’s readiness to cut such a deal showed he was worn down. As soon as the military threat was lifted, they started violating the deal on the Strait of Hormuz.
This point raises another difference between the US and Israel.
Hormuz’s instability and being partially closed is not great for Israel, but it does not have a large impact.
For the US, the closing of the Strait has a major economic impact and is politically almost as costly as a new war because gas prices remain high.
So Trump needs a deal with Iran that will fully open the Strait and give him a horizon by which he can withdraw most American naval vessels without worrying that the Islamic Republic will then immediately violate the deal again.
Trump still may decide to attack, having lost patience with the Iranians.
But if he does cut a deal, Israel will need to pay close attention to the fine print to know exactly what holes are left open, and to convey to Washington what its red lines are, regardless of what the US signs on to.

The Tana Forum proves that Africa’s future must be forged through economic sovereignty - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:27:51 UTC
23:27:51 KST

As global powers increasingly treat the African continent as a chessboard for geopolitical maneuvering, a quiet yet profound counter-narrative is taking root in the highlands of East Africa.
The recently concluded 12th Tana High-Level Forum in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, served as a stark reminder that Africa’s destiny will neither be written in Western capitals nor dictated by foreign aid boardrooms.
Instead, it must be carved out through self-reliance, regional economic integration, and homegrown security architectures.
What made this year’s gathering stand out was not merely the high-level attendance – which brought together continental heavyweights, including the leaders of Ghana, Burundi, Mozambique, and Kenya – but the uncompromising clarity of the discourse.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s opening address cut straight to the heart of the matter: Africa can no longer afford to outsource its security and economic salvation to external actors.
From political independence to economic sovereignty
For decades, post-colonial Africa grappled with a fundamental paradox. Nations won the trappings of political sovereignty – flags, anthems, and seats at the United Nations – while remaining economically shackled to commodity-export models and international debt cycles that drained their wealth.
The discussions at the Tana Forum underscored a vital paradigm shift: Political freedom without economic sovereignty is a hollow shell.
When global supply chains fracture, and inflationary shocks ripple from Europe and Asia, the burden falls disproportionately on ordinary African households. To break this cycle, African nations must build tangible, cross-border economic interdependencies.
Ethiopia’s own trajectory offers a compelling case study.
By aggressively prioritizing domestic resource mobilization, agricultural transformation to secure food sovereignty, and major renewable energy initiatives – such as the historic completion of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) – Addis Ababa has demonstrated that self-reliance is not a slogan but a policy.
When a nation plants 56.8 billion seedlings since 2019, gets more than 90% of its electricity from renewable sources, and powers its industries with its own sweat and capital, its posture in international negotiations fundamentally changes.
Energy diplomacy and the Horn of Africa
True regional integration cannot be achieved through diplomatic communiques alone; it requires physical infrastructure and shared stakes. This is where East Africa is quietly rewriting its geopolitical script.
Through robust cross-border electricity trading via the Eastern Africa Power Pool – supplying clean energy to neighbors like Djibouti, Kenya, Sudan, and expanding footprints into Tanzania and South Sudan – Ethiopia is pioneering a new brand of “energy diplomacy.”
By binding neighboring economies together through vital resources like electricity, conflict becomes prohibitively expensive, and cooperation becomes an indispensable survival mechanism.
Furthermore, the forum rightfully placed existential issues like maritime access and regional stability under the microscope. In an era marked by shifting Red Sea security dynamics, economic integration cannot be landlocked.
Rational discussions surrounding port access and trade corridors must be framed not as zero-sum geopolitical threats but as vital catalysts for shared regional growth and stability.
The climate imperative and the road ahead
As the world looks toward upcoming global milestones – including Ethiopia’s prospective hosting of the COP32 climate summit in January 2027 – the urgency of African climate agency cannot be overstated. The continent contributes the least to global carbon emissions yet suffers the most devastating shocks to its agricultural systems.
The Tana Forum sent a unified signal: International climate finance must move past empty promises and deliver direct adaptation support to the smallholder farmers and pastoralists who anchor Africa’s food security.
Ultimately, the 12th Tana Forum proved that when African leaders gather away from the glare of traditional Western mediation, they are fully capable of diagnosing their own structural vulnerabilities and charting pragmatic solutions.
The message echoing from the shores of Lake Tana is crystal clear: Africa’s renaissance will not be handed down as charity.
It will be built by Africans – through the power of our rivers, the resilience of our economies, and an unwavering commitment to a sovereign, interconnected future.
The author is an Addis Ababa-based international relations professional and researcher specializing in Horn of Africa geopolitics.

Brothers before the ballot - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:27:35 UTC
23:27:35 KST

This week’s election in Israel is the first since October 7. It comes after three years of pain and grief.
During the campaign, each side painted its opponent as a threat to the country’s future. While this is not abnormal for an election, it certainly poses a danger for the Jewish people.
Disagreement and argumentation are part of our Jewish tradition, but demonizing and fostering hatred certainly is not.
In this past week’s Torah portion, the shepherds of Abraham and Lot quarrel over grazing land. Abraham does not wait for the disagreement to cross the line.
He goes to his nephew and says: “Let there please be no strife between you and me, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are brothers” (Genesis 13:8).
Notice what Abraham does not say. He does not tell Lot that he must think the same way. He offers to part ways: “If you go left, I will go right.” Achdut, unity, in the Torah’s first lesson on the subject, is not uniformity. Brothers can live in different places, make different choices, and still be brothers.
Our tradition is built on this. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argued for generations over hundreds of topics, some of them touching on marriage itself.
Yet the Talmud (Yevamot 14b) records that they did not refrain from marrying into one another’s families. They treated each other with affection and respect.
Israelis are divided over real questions this week: security, the draft, the place of Torah learning, the courts, and the economy. These are not trivial.
People hold their positions out of genuine conviction and love for the country and for our people.
But maybe the more important question of this election is not what we disagree on but how we treat each other while disagreeing.
The parasha continues after Lot and Abraham separate. Lot settles near Sodom, a choice the Torah clearly disapproves of. Soon after, Lot is taken captive in a regional war.
Abraham could have shrugged. Lot had made his bed. Instead, the Torah says, “Avram heard that his brother had been taken captive” (Genesis 14:14). Not his nephew, not the one who chose Sodom, but “his brother.”
Abraham arms his household and attacks the army to bring Lot home.
Whatever the result of this election, roughly half the country will wake up disappointed, many frightened. The person who voted the other way, whose party you consider a danger, is still the one who sits next to you on the bus, or in the hospital waiting room. When he is in trouble, he is still your brother.
In the summer of 2023, Israel was as divided as it had ever been. Then came Simchat Torah.
The terrorists who crossed the border did not ask anyone how they voted. They did not distinguish between religious and secular, Left and Right, kibbutznik and yeshiva student.
In the weeks that followed, neither did we.
Reservists who had marched against the government reported for duty beside those who had marched for it. Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) volunteers cooked for soldiers; secular families prayed for the hostages. For a while, the whole world saw what Jewish unity looks like.
We should not need another catastrophe to remember who we are: brothers responsible for each other. That responsibility does not pause for an election.
Settling the question of brotherhood
Unity is not a slogan; we need to pursue it actively. Especially in times of high passion, we must guard ourselves from demonization. Those we disagree with are not “traitors” or “enemies of the Jewish people.”
The person who votes differently almost always has good intentions and is trying to make Israel and the Jewish people safer, more secure, more successful. They just have a different thought process of how to attain these shared goals.
Abraham said “For we are brothers” before the land was divided, not after. He did not wait to see who got the better pasture. He settled the question of brotherhood first, so that nothing that followed could undo it.
That is the order we need this week. The Jewish people will not be decided at any polling station. We were brothers before this election, and we will be brothers after it. Let us act like it now.
The writer is the CEO of Kesher Yehudi, whose mission is to create unity between religious and secular Israelis.

Germany seeks new head of state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:27:00 UTC
23:27:00 KST

Germany seeks new head of state
October 29, 2026
Wanted: A new head of state — female, male, or other. Requirements: German citizen, entitled to vote, minimum age 40. Please apply as soon as possible! Availability starting January 30, 2027; job starts March 19, 2027.
This is not an official job posting, but Germany's federal government is indeed looking for someone to fill the nation's highest office. Having already served two terms, current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is no longer eligible for another, leaving the position open for a successor. Many feel that it is time for Germany's first-ever female head of state.
"The person should have a certain level of public recognition, be politically unbiased, capable of bringing people together, approachable and a reasonably good [public] speaker," political scientist Ursula Münch told DW.
In Germany, a federal parliamentary republic, the president serves as head of state and a representative of the country as well as someone who embodies moral authority for the nation. Unlike for instance in the US, France, or Russia, the president does not wield extensive political power or direct government affairs.
Steinmeier was nominated by his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), in 2009. However, once elected via a convention of parliamentarians and state electors, a president-elect has to suspend their party membership in order to serve in the office apolitically. This time, it is Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the power broker in the coalition government with the SPD and the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), which has the right to nominate a candidate.
Political scientist Münch says that "the three parties must agree on a person who is acceptable for all three." Since the convention that will select Steinmeier's successor is currently controlled by these three parties and their delegates, it is very likely that whoever Merz nominates will be elected.
Will Germany soon have its first female president?
"Well, I would really like it to be a woman this time. We've had 12 male federal presidents since 1949 — it's about time for a woman! But if the right man were to be nominated, I'd be fine with that too," says Münch. According to an August poll conducted by the Forsa polling institute for the RTL television network, about 74% of German respondents say they don't care whether it's a man or a woman. Another 19% explicitly want a woman, while 5% prefer a man.
Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner appears to have a good chance. She is president of the Bavarian State Parliament in Munich. Aigner is a member of the smallest party in the coalition, the Bavarian CSU, and is considered a unifying figure. She also has experience in government in Berlin, having served as agricultural minister at the federal level. She enjoys strong support within her Bavarian CSU party, whose leader Markus Söder recently said: "It would be tremendous if she became federal president."
Even members of the opposition Greens and the SPD are full of praise for Aigner's candidacy. "What are we actually waiting for? Surely Ilse Aigner has long since secured a majority across party lines?" asked SPD parliamentary group leader Matthias Miersch recently. However, Merz, who is friends with Aigner, has remained tight-lipped so far — possibly also because Aigner is not a member of Merz's party, but rather of its smaller sister party, the CSU.
Several female presidential candidates
Other potential successors from the CDU membership have also been mentioned: Bundestag President Julia Klöckner, former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer and Education Minister Karin Prien. Hesse's state premier, Boris Rhein, is also a possible candidate. In recent days, another name has been making the rounds: lawyer Ines Claus, who serves as CDU's parliamentary group leader in Hesse and deputy party chair at the federal level — and is largely unknown.
However, rumors that she would be nominated were swiftly shot down by the chancellor. Sources close to Merz emphasized that he has so far "neither made a decision nor put forward a proposal." There are "a number of suitable" options, sources added.
The president is elected every five years by the Federal Convention, which comprises all 630 members of the Bundestag and an equal number of electors who represent the state parliaments. Among them are also prominent figures from the spheres of culture, science, sports and society. The candidate who receives more than 631 votes goes on to assume office. The governing parties — the CDU/CSU and the SPD — have a combined total of 682 votes, a comfortable majority.
Presidential role key amid polarization and crisis
The office of the president is often underestimated as merely a ceremonial role. Yet, as an authority standing above the political parties, this person wields considerable political, legal and moral influence. This is especially true in times of political polarization and international crises. While the president does not govern like a chancellor, he or she represents Germany both at home and abroad.
"From a constitutional perspective, the federal president is enormously important. For example, in a political crisis, he could decide whether it makes more sense to dissolve the Bundestag or to advocate for a minority government," explains political scientist Münch. In addition, he reviews and signs laws proposed by politicians.
What happens next?
The federal chancellor and CDU chairman has an interest in an orderly process, say sources close to the government. The "first milestone" will be the meetings of the CDU Presidium and Executive Board on November 9. Until then, discussions will be held with the state chairpersons of the CDU and the CSU. Sources made it clear that the SPD and the Greens will also be consulted, "since the election of the federal president should have broad support across the democratic spectrum."
That is how political scientist Münch sees it: "I still consider the question open, with a slight edge for CSU candidate Ilse Aigner." But there could still be a real surprise, Münch adds.
This article was originally published in German.

Some European diplomats in Seoul are weighing whether they can still trust South Korea as a like-minded partner if it grows closer to Russia, the Financial Times reported on 28 October, according to South Korea’s Financial News. One European diplomat also told the FT that Seoul wants to resume trade with Russia as soon as the war ends.
As Russia presses its war against Ukraine, Kyiv’s partners count on each other to keep up the pressure on Moscow. The doubts about South Korea now come from its European partners, not only from Kyiv. The report lands eight days after Seoul said it would withdraw about half its staff from Kyiv over a dispute about two North Korean prisoners of war.
An Arctic voyage, a new adviser, and signals from Moscow
According to the FT, European diplomats saw a South Korean pilot voyage along Russia’s Arctic sea route as a sign of a tilt toward Russia, since the voyage required extensive cooperation from Moscow.
Meanwhile, on 1 October, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung appointed Song Young-gil, a six-term lawmaker and former chair of parliament’s foreign affairs committee, as his special adviser on peace diplomacy. Song once served as a special envoy to Russia, the FT noted.
On 20 October, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Rudenko said Seoul had signaled it wants to normalize relations but says full normalization can come only after a change in the geopolitical situation, which he said means the end of the war in Ukraine.
Fuel for Russia loaded at South Korean ports, but Seoul denies direct exports
The FT also cited reports of fuel shipments to Russia. A Guardian analysis published on 6 October found that more than 176,000 tons of fuel, mostly diesel, were loaded at South Korean ports in July and August. The fuel went onto seven tankers bound for Russia’s Far East, three of them under UK and EU sanctions. The Guardian said the trade does not appear to breach South Korean law.
On 8 October, South Korea’s foreign and trade ministries and customs service said no diesel, jet fuel, or gasoline had been exported to Russia through customs. They said they would examine the tankers’ routes and any divergence from their declared destinations before judging whether the law had been broken.
Ukraine’s sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said the shipments helped Russia offset refinery losses caused by Ukrainian strikes. South Korea’s presidential office called the claim inaccurate and inappropriate, saying the key facts of the transactions had not been verified.
Seoul rejects the criticism
In a statement to the FT, South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said concerns in some quarters that the country was leaning too far toward Russia were not based on fact. It added that Seoul supports international efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
Seoul cuts its Kyiv embassy staff over the POW dispute
At the same time, relations with Ukraine have deteriorated over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Zelenskyy disclosed at the UN General Assembly in September. Seoul says the disclosure broke a confidentiality understanding. Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelenskyy’s communications adviser, wrote in a Facebook comment on 25 September that “there was no such agreement.”
On 20 October, Seoul said it would withdraw roughly half its diplomatic staff from Kyiv, citing Kyiv’s failure to take “positive steps” on the POW dispute and continued Russian airstrikes, Yonhap reported. A chargé d’affaires and all consular staff will stay.
