As US midterms approach, farmers decide what to plant and how to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:25:16 UTC
23:25:16 KST

As US midterms approach, farmers decide what to plant and how to vote
In Arkansas, rising costs spurred farmer Hallie Shoffner’s long-shot Senate campaign. Will farmers back her?
When Paul McKinney, a farmer in northeast Arkansas, thinks of his son’s childhood, he remembers a small boy playing in vast fields.
To a child, a flooded rice field is “like a giant, 40-acre swimming pool”, he said.
Rice has been a staple on McKinney’s farm for four generations. Next year, however, the family plans to plant much less. Instead, they will focus on soya, a crop that is cheaper to produce.
Like farmers across the United States, McKinney is making tough decisions this year in response to higher fuel and fertiliser costs, which have skyrocketed since the start of the war on Iran.
This week, farmers also face tough choices at the polls. Democrats are expected to make gains in the midterm elections, as voters react to high prices economy-wide by switching parties or staying home.
Observers are watching farm country closely. Texas and Kansas could send Democrats to the Senate for the first time in decades. In the House of Representatives, two majority-rural districts, Wisconsin’s Third and North Carolina First, could become tipping points for Democratic control.
Still, many of the country’s most rural areas, like Arkansas, are also its most safely Republican.
That leaves an uphill battle for Democrat Hallie Shoffner, who quit farming last year to challenge Republican Senator Tom Cotton in a campaign squarely focused on rising costs.
How high costs hurt farmers
Even before the US-Israel war on Iran, high input costs were straining farmers, said Ryan Loy, an extension economist for the University of Arkansas’ Division of Agriculture.
Loy pointed to a trade war with China that began in 2018, the ongoing war in Ukraine and disruptions related to the 2025 tariffs as factors driving up input costs and disrupting markets. A drought across the US heartland, made worse by climate change, has added to the strain.
Farmers across the country are working to adapt. In Arkansas, many farmers skipped rice in favour of soya. Soya is “the least input-intensive crop, and perhaps can break even or have the shallowest loss”, Loy said.
Now Arkansas, usually the country’s top rice producer, has its lowest rice acreage since the 1970s. Many farmers hoped 2026 would bring economic recovery so they could return to rice.
Then, the war on Iran hit. With the Strait of Hormuz blocked, fertiliser costs jumped just as farmers were fertilising during the spring planting season.
Loy tracked the increase in a sample budget that he maintains for Arkansas row crop farmers. “Urea fertiliser specifically peaked about 39 percent over our budgeted amount,” Loy said. Diesel costs came in about 72 percent more than budget averaged across the planting, growing and harvesting seasons, Loy found.
Those changes represent a significant economic hit. “For our state alone, it’s an additional cost of about $343m,” Loy said.
Last week, US President Donald Trump announced an $8bn fuel relief programme for farmers, following $12bn in tariff-related aid in 2025. If the fuel relief payment were divided equally between the 50 states, it would cover less than half of the extra costs that Loy estimates Arkansas’ farmers paid this year.
McKinney, a member of the Arkansas Farm Bureau, said the announcement was welcome. Still, he hoped for longer-term solutions that would prevent “this constant battle for survival”.
For many farms, survival is indeed getting harder. Farm bankruptcies for the first three quarters of 2026 were up 19 percent compared to this time last year, according to a recent analysis by the University of Arkansas’ National Agricultural Law Center. They were up 73 percent compared to 2024.
‘We can’t keep doing this’
McKinney’s son, who grew up playing in muddy rice fields, now helps his dad farm their 24,000 acres. So does McKinney’s nephew, who this year is driving a combine.
“As has been done for us, we would love to be able to hand that down to the next generation,” said McKinney. “But you also have to think about what is going to be best for them.”
McKinney questions how long farming will provide a sustainable living. “It’s some heavy things to think about,” McKinney said.
For Shoffner, a sixth-generation Arkansas farmer, that reckoning came last year.
Higher costs, lower crop prices and the uncertainty of trade wars and tariffs “made the numbers stop working” for their 2,000-acre farm operation, Shoffner told Al Jazeera.
“I know what it feels like to work hard, make every adjustment you can, and still have to sit down with your family and say, ‘We can’t keep doing this,’” Shoffner said.
To protect her parents’ land and retirement, Shoffner closed the family’s farm. That “heartbreaking” decision helped spur her Senate run.
“I decided that if I can’t farm, I will fight,” Shoffner said.
If elected, Shoffner wants to end the war on Iran, build trade policies farmers “can actually plan around”, invest in local processing and distribution, and pass a robust Farm Bill — strategies she hopes will help farmers and rural economies more broadly.
“If we want rural communities to have a future, the people producing our food have to be able to make a living doing it.”
Cotton did not respond to a request for comment.
How will farmers vote?
Economic pain may not change farmers’ votes, however, in Arkansas or nationwide. Michael Shepherd, a political scientist at the University of Michigan, said many farmers, like many rural voters, are committed Republicans.
Committed voters tend to view the economy through a partisan lens, according to Shepherd. “Their political behaviours, their voting choices, things like that, are not particularly responsive to changes in the agricultural economy,” he said.
Some polling this year, however, did suggest the potential for movement. A poll by the Farm Journal in April found that 35 percent of farmers who “usually” vote Republican and 15 percent who “always” vote Republican were still considering how they would vote.
And September polling from Purdue showed that, for the first time this term, a majority of farmers surveyed think the country is “on the wrong track”.
Even if farmers are swayable, of course, Shoffner still may not be the one to sway them: her campaign has been far outspent by Cotton’s, an established lawmaker who has received funding from interest groups like AIPAC and leaders at companies like Anthropic and Palantir.
“If one side has a massive war chest, and the other side has very limited resources, then that game of tug of war can be won much easier than it should be,” Shepherd said.
And even if farmers do change their votes, they may not decide elections.
McKinney, who is now farming one of the Shoffner family’s former fields, said farmers represent a shrinking percentage of rural voters — their strength now is in organising, not numbers.
Still, even where candidates like Shoffner don’t win, their campaigns might signal to funders that similar races may be competitive in the future or help Democrats win down-ballot seats.
In Arkansas’ second congressional district, for example, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is betting on Democrat Chris Jones. It’s a long-shot campaign, but across the country, at least some long-shot candidates are expected to win.
“All indications are that this is gonna be one of the biggest shifts away from the president’s party that we’ve observed,” Shepherd said.

First flight with high-speed satellite internet takes off in Kazakhstan

Unknown Publisher

First flight with high-speed satellite internet takes off in Kazakhstan
Air Astana operated its first flight with high-speed satellite internet on board on October 29, 2026, flying from Almaty to Tashkent, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development.
The high-speed Wi-Fi system has been installed on an Airbus A321LR aircraft bearing the registration number EI-KGB.
The project is being carried out in partnership with SES, an international satellite communications provider, with Air Astana's own technical specialists handling the installation at the airline's maintenance facility.
Last year, the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development announced plans to expand internet access to trains and aircraft. Satellite internet is already available on trains in Kazakhstan and is now being introduced on commercial flights.
Given Kazakhstan's vast distances, reliable internet access while traveling is particularly important, allowing passengers to stay in touch with family and colleagues and access digital services throughout their journeys.
The initiative is part of the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence, declared by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, and reflects his broader vision of transforming Kazakhstan into a digital nation by bringing connectivity to areas where it was previously unavailable.
The launch of in-flight internet follows extensive cooperation between the Ministry, international satellite operators, regulatory authorities, and industry stakeholders. These efforts included negotiations, agreements on operating conditions, and the development of the necessary regulatory framework.
The Ministry also worked on legislative amendments and regulations governing non-geostationary satellite systems. Special provisions were introduced for aviation and maritime transport to remove regulatory barriers, while agreements with operators were reached to ensure compliance with Kazakhstan's legislation, including security requirements.
These efforts have laid the groundwork for expanding satellite connectivity across the transport sector and into remote and hard-to-reach areas of Kazakhstan.
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev highlighted the work behind the launch.
"Over the past year, we have worked extensively to establish the regulatory framework needed to introduce satellite internet on aircraft. Together with international partners, satellite operators, and relevant organizations, we addressed the requirements for using non-geostationary satellite systems in aviation, paving the way for the technology's rollout. Air Astana's first aircraft equipped with satellite internet is a tangible result of these efforts. We will continue expanding access to reliable, high-quality internet so that people can stay connected while traveling, whether by train or by plane," Madiyev said.
All passengers will enjoy free internet access during a promotional period lasting until January 31, 2027.
From February 1, 2027, free Wi-Fi will be available to business-class passengers and Nomad Club Gold and Diamond members. Members of all Nomad Club tiers will also have free access to messaging services, while other passengers will be able to purchase internet packages.
Air Astana will continue rolling out high-speed Wi-Fi across its Airbus A321LR fleet in phases throughout 2027.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Air Astana had launched a new international route connecting Astana and Salalah ahead of Republic Day.

Overnight into Oct. 29, Ukrainian drones attacked Russia’s Bashkortostan, hitting the Bashkir Soda Company in Sterlitamak. The strike was reported by the Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ and the independent outlet Astra, which confirmed that smoke rose over the Bashkir Soda Company as a result of the attack. Sterlitamak Mayor Emil Shaymardanov wrote on his Telegram channel that drone debris fell on the territory of one of the city’s enterprises, but assured residents that all the drones had been shot down:
“Another drone attack on Sterlitamak has been repelled. Forces of the Defense Ministry and the Combat Army Reserve shot down all 8 drones. Debris fell on the territory of one of the enterprises. Minor damage was caused, and the plant is operating normally.”
Using NASA FIRMS thermal anomaly maps, The Insider confirmed a fire at the Bashkir Soda Company — one of Russia’s largest chemical enterprises — which supplies products to the defense sector, among other customers.
Bashkir Soda Company JSC was founded in May 2013 through the merger of two large enterprises, Soda and Kaustik, and is part of the chemical holding Roskhim JSC. The company ranks first in Russia in the production of soda ash and baking soda. In addition, its website openly states that it supplies products to Russia’s military-industrial complex. In particular, the plant produces hydrochloric acid and dichloroethane, as well as terephthaloyl chloride, a unique component used in making ultra-strong materials (cables for parachute lines, space and aviation equipment, and other military products). According to the company’s website, it is the only enterprise in Russia that manufactures terephthaloyl chloride.
As Astra notes, Ukrainian drones had already attacked the Bashkir Soda Company on Aug. 27.
The Moscow Region was also subjected to a massive drone attack on the night of Oct. 28-29. According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, 613 drones flew toward Moscow and Moscow Region, of which 231 were destroyed on approach to the city. As the outlet Kommersant noted, Moscow’s Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports suspended arrivals and departures during the night. In addition, airports in Kaluga, Penza, Saratov, Yaroslavl, Nizhny Novgorod, Saransk, Samara, Ulyanovsk, Cheboksary, Kazan, Nizhnekamsk, Bugulma, Cherepovets, Kirov, Ufa, Orenburg, Izhevsk, and Perm suspended operations.

U.S. military trains on palletized SUADS anti-drone system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:21:42 UTC
23:21:42 KST

- U.S. soldiers and airmen trained on Trust Automation’s RD-SUADS, a self-powered counter-drone system that fits on a standard 463L military cargo pallet.
- RD-SUADS runs four days on its diesel generator and belongs to the SUADS family ordered under a $490 million U.S. Air Force contract.
U.S. Army soldiers and U.S. Air Force airmen at Grafenwoehr Training Area in Germany are training on the Rapidly Deployable Small-Unmanned Air Defense System, or RD-SUADS, a palletized counter-drone system built by Trust Automation of San Luis Obispo, California, as they test how training across services can sharpen the response to drone threats, U.S. Army Europe and Africa said on social media.
Photos released with the post show the troops working with the system, which the counter-drone news account Counter Unmanned Systems identified as RD-SUADS. The Army did not say which units are taking part, how long the training will run or whether the system will be fielded with units in Europe. Grafenwoehr hosted a similar effort in February, when U.S. Air Forces in Europe and Air Forces Africa ran its Joint Multi-Domain Counter Unmanned Aircraft Systems Operator Course with soldiers, airmen and Marines to assess opening the course to more services.
RD-SUADS is the air-transportable member of Trust Automation’s Small-Unmanned Air Defense System family, designed to detect, track, identify and defeat small drones at bases and deployed sites. The company built it to be shipped and set up quickly without relying on local power.
“Promoting combat agility, this C‑sUAS is a self-contained, self-powered system that fits within a 463L pallet, enabling easy transport via military aircraft. Equipped with an integrated diesel generator with standalone operational capacity for four days between refueling. Additionally, the shore power interface allows sites with power infrastructure operate the system utilizing standard DoD generator connections and base power connections,” Trust Automation said.
The 463L pallet is the standard cargo pallet used by U.S. military transport aircraft such as the C-130 and C-17, so the system can be loaded and flown in with the same handling equipment as other air cargo. The SUADS family also includes a fixed-site tower version for permanent bases and an expeditionary version sized to travel as checked baggage and fit in larger SUVs. The U.S. Department of War’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401 lists the systems in its 2026 counter-small drone quick reference guide, noting they can host several electronic warfare capabilities to defeat small drones without firing a shot.
Radar is a central sensor. In April, Echodyne said its EchoShield radar had been chosen as the primary radar for SUADS, with RD-SUADS carrying up to four of the units, after the U.S. Air Force awarded Trust Automation a $490 million contract to develop, prototype and produce counter-drone systems through 2030. That contract is an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity deal, meaning the U.S. Air Force can order systems in varying numbers and configurations over its life, and Echodyne’s radar now feeds all three SUADS versions.
The system has already been tested with the U.S. Army. Trust Automation said in October that SUADS completed a U.S. Army operational assessment during a rotation at the National Training Center at Fort Irwin, California, where it detected and engaged drones at roughly 2 to 6 km (1.2 to 3.7 miles), with coverage reaching about 7 km (4.3 miles) in favorable conditions. In that configuration, the system combined radar and electro-optical and infrared sensors with the NINJA and DroneBuster electronic attack systems.

Human trafficking victims stranded in Guinea-Bissau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:20:00 UTC
23:20:00 KST

Human trafficking victims stranded in Guinea-Bissau
October 29, 2026
This article contains descriptions of rape, exploitation and sexual assault. Reader discretion is advised.
Sadio Konimba had hoped for a better future. The 26-year-old had lost her husband and was left alone with her child in Bamako, the capital of Mali.
When an acquaintance told her about the possibility of reaching Europe via the West African nation of Guinea-Bissau, she decided to make the journey. She left her 6-year-old daughter behind with relatives for the time being.
Konimba says she was invited to the country's capital, Bissau, with the promise of work and better chances of eventually continuing on to Europe.
She was told the journey from Bamako to Bissau would cost between 100,000–125,000 CFA francs (roughly €150-€190, or $170-$210), which she paid. She had only intended to stay temporarily in Guinea-Bissau, but when she wanted to return to Mali, her money was not refunded.
"I had to pay a large sum of money," Sadio told DW, adding that instead of the prospects she had been promised, she was confronted with a very different reality.
According to Konimba's account, men from Senegal offered to repay the money she had paid if she "worked" for them. When she realized what that meant, she refused and demanded her money back. To this day, she has received nothing.
Jane, a 21-year-old woman from Sierra Leone, recounted how she was subjected to an attempted rape and other abuses at the hands of a criminal network. She told French news agency Agence France-Presse they even tried to force her into prostitution.
Sadio and Jane are among dozens of victims of a suspected human trafficking ring that was dismantled by police following an operation in Guinea-Bissau on October 21. The intervention followed complaints from victims who had reported abductions and fraud.
In a written statement to DW, the criminal investigation police said that more than five suspects had been arrested.
Trapped by fales promises
According to police, the network used a front company to lure people with promises of jobs and assistance with migration to Europe.
Around 70 people are believed to have fallen victim to the scheme. Most came from abroad, including Guinea, Mali, Cote d'Ivoire and Senegal. The suspected perpetrators allegedly charged victims between 400,000 and 700,000 CFA francs for each journey to Guinea-Bissau.
According to preliminary findings, the victims were held against their will in Bissau, subjected to pressure and forced to take part in fraudulent pyramid schemes. They were expected to recruit additional participants into the schemes through social media.
To make their operations appear legitimate, those responsible allegedly used false contact details for supposed offices in Canada, the United States and Portugal. Information from Interpol, the international police agency, helped investigators uncover the network, according to police.
Issa, a 23-year-old from Guinea, says he paid a smuggler 10 million Guinean francs (around €1,000). When he refused to recruit more people, he was allegedly threatened with death.
A growing criminal network
For Bubacar Ture, head of Guinea-Bissau's Human Rights League, the case is an alarming sign.
"As a human rights organization, we are extremely concerned about this phenomenon, which has now reached deeply troubling proportions," he told DW. In May, authorities rescued 60 foreign nationals during a similar operation.
Ture sees a link between the human trafficking problem and Guinea-Bissau's weak institutions. Criminal networks exploit these conditions to continue their activities, he said, noting that women are particularly vulnerable to human rights abuses.
The small Portuguese-speaking West African country has been plagued by political instability since independence in 1975 and is also known as a transit hub for cocaine bound for Europe.
Rescued, but still trapped far from home
A week after their rescue, the victims face a new problem: many lack the funds needed to travel back to Mali, Sierra Leone or elsewhere in West Africa.
Sadio Konimba is temporarily staying with an acquaintance in Bissau. Her friend told DW that Konimba had been deeply traumatized by what she had experienced. She had never imagined she could fall into the hands of a human trafficking network that might force her into prostitution.
Konimba herself does not want to discuss in detail what kind of work she was asked to do. Police confirm that women in such cases are often sexually exploited.
Konimba says she has managed to borrow around 75,000 CFA francs from acquaintances in recent days. But that falls short of the cost of her journey back to Bamako.
According to available information, Guinea-Bissau's migration and border authority, the Direcao-Geral de Migracao e Fronteiras (DGMF), also lacks the funds needed to finance the victims' return journeys.
Contacts have been established with the diplomatic missions of the countries concerned. But progress appears slow, and no concrete arrangements for their return have yet been announced.
Support systems falling short
Bubacar Ture criticizes the lack of protection available to victims.
"There are no public shelters for cases like these," he told DW, noting that private facilities have limited capacity, and psychological support and funding for temporary accommodation are also lacking.
The human rights advocate commends the criminal investigation police for taking action against the networks despite limited resources. At the same time, he calls for greater support.
"We make an urgent appeal to the government and international partners to provide adequate support to the judiciary, the police and the other institutions," he told DW.
For Konimba, one thing matters above all else now: returning to Bamako.
"Now I definitely want to go back to my mother and my daughter," she told DW. "Every day she asks me, 'Mom, are you coming home?' I tell her, 'I will come, I will come. Just wait a little longer.'"
But Konimba still does not have enough money for the journey. She is free, but for her, the struggle to rebuild a life with dignity has only just begun.

====================================================================================================

You Only Audition Once: Which actors came close to being cast as James Bond?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:17:41 UTC
23:17:41 KST

James Bond is one of Hollywood’s most coveted roles, and some very famous actors came close to playing 007. As we wait for the identity of the seventh actor to land the role, here's a look back at the Bonds we never got.
As you read these words, several hopefuls are waiting for the big announcement, having screen tested to become the next James Bond.
The shortlist has been revealed and we're days / weeks away from finding out which actor will succeed Daniel Craig in the iconic role. Will it be Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, or some unknown actor that will surprise everyone?
One thing is for sure: there can only be one. The rest will be ejected from the Aston Martin and their names added to a long list of would-be Bonds. These are the performers who were considered, who auditioned, and who even declined their licence to kill.
Here's a look back at those who lost out on the chance to don the famous tuxedo - with some of the screen test footage having leaked onto the internet.
Cary Grant
When it came to casting the first 007, many thought the effortlessly suave British-American star Cary Grant was the perfect fit. However, Grant went on the record and stated he was too old (58) to play Bond in Dr. No (1962). He also only wanted to do one film, and the producers were keen on holding down an actor for a multi-picture deal.
Michael Caine
It has been reported that Caine was offered the role of James Bond in 1967 after Sean Connery stepped down after You Only Live Twice. However, Sir Michael felt the role wasn’t right for him, telling The Daily Express: "I was always very much more ordinary. Bond was a glamorous, imaginative creation. I’ve always played real people."
Clint Eastwood
Failing to bag Caine following Connery's exit, another acting heavyweight was considered: Clint Eastwood. However, the Dirty Harry actor said he turned the offer down because he believed James Bond should be British. He told the Los Angeles Times: "My lawyer represented the Broccolis, and he came and said: 'They would love to have you.' But to me, that was somebody else’s gig. That’s Sean’s deal. It didn’t feel right for me to be doing it." Connery ended up coming back for Diamonds Are Forever for one last Martini.
Michael Gambon
The much-missed Irish-English thespian, best known to international audiences for his role as Albus Dumbledore in the Harry Potter film series, was approached to play James Bond for Diamonds Are Forever (1971) - following George Lazenby's solo outing in On Her Majesty's Secret Service (and before Connery agreed to one last adventure). Gambon turned it down, as he said he thought he was not good-looking enough to play the role. Funnily enough, he would go on to share the screen with Daniel Craig in 2004's Layer Cake – just before the latter was cast as Bond.
Michael Billington
British actor Michael Billington reportedly auditioned for Bond not once, not twice, but three times. He was shortlisted to replace Sean Connery for On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969), Diamonds Are Forever (1971) and Live And Let Die (1973), but was passed over every time. However, the Bond producers did cast him as KGB agent Sergei Barsov in The Spy Who Loved Me (1977) - in which he gets shot by Roger Moore's Bond in the opening ski sequence. Rough.
James Brolin
After 1981's For Your Eyes Only, Roger Moore was on the verge of retiring as 007. The Bond producers seriously considered replacing him with * gasp * an American! Josh Brolin was top of the list and screen tested to be up next in Octopussy. It nearly happened, until Moore agreed to return for two more films, before bowing out following 1985's A View To A Kill.
Sam Neill
Replacing Moore as Bond was always going to be tricky and one hot contender at the time was New Zealander Sam Neill. The actor auditioned for Cubby Broccoli, who went against director John Glen's wishes and picked Timothy Dalton instead. No shade to the much-missed Neill, but his instincts were dead on as Dalton remains one of the most underappreciated 007s - as well as the actor who paved the way for Daniel Craig's grittier iteration of Bond. Neill became a household name as Dr Alan Grant in Jurassic Park (1993) and later revealed to Den Of Geek about his Bond screen test: "It was the last time that I was bullied into doing a screen test. My agent insisted that I go and do it, [saying] it would be rude otherwise."
Mel Gibson
Another possible Moore replacement was Mel Gibson, whose star was on the rise in early 80s, having become a household name thanks to the Mad Max films. MGM reportedly wanted him to take over as Bond and offered him the role. Depending on whose version you trust, either Gibson turned it down due to length commitment, or Cubby Broccoli rejected Gibson for not being British enough. Whatever the case may be, instead of starring in 1987's The Living Daylights, Gibson cranked his career up a gear with the first Lethal Weapon film released that same year.
Liam Neeson
Following Timothy Dalton's departure and the legal woes that resulted in a Bond drought from 1989 to 1995, several names were floated for the fifth 007 actor. A courted candidate was Liam Neeson, who hadn't starred in many action movies at the time. It was later revealed in a Rolling Stone interview that his girlfriend, Natasha Richadson, told Neeson that she wouln't marry him if he'd taken the role. "My lovely wife, God rest her soul, said to me while we were shooting Nell down in the Carolinas, 'Liam, I want to tell you something: If you play James Bond, we’re not getting married.' She gave me a James Bond ultimatum, and she meant it!" Neeson tied the knot in 1994 and remained with Richardson until her death in 2009.
Sean Bean
Before he was cast opposite Pierce Brosnan in GoldenEye (1995), Sean Bean auditioned to play Bond twice. He lost out to both Timothy Dalton and Brosnan, but his screen tests were impressive enough for producers to cast him as rogue agent Alec Trevelyan.
Ralph Fiennes
Another actor who got the second-best gig... Before he played M in Skyfall, Spectre and No Time To Die, Ralph Fiennes was approached in the early 90s to succeed Timothy Dalton as Bond. In an interview with Seven Magazine, Fiennes revealed: “I don't think I felt ready to commit, and I think they were looking at Pierce. I think I would have been a terrible Bond anyway.”
Lambert Wilson
If you thought British tabloids showed their worst with the nonsensical frenzy surrounding Daniel Craig being "too blond for Bond", just imagine the uproar had the role of 007 been given to a Frenchman... Lambert Wilson was considered for the coveted part in GoldenEye (1995), but the British accent was a hurdle he couldn't clear, and the role eventually went to Pierce Brosnan.
Christian Bale
The rumour is that Barbara Broccoli courted Christian Bale for Bond after Brosnan left the role. However, the future Caped Crusader star was having none of it. According to The Daily Express, Bale said that he turned down the role as he felt Bond "was every despicable stereotype about England and British actors," adding that he'd already played a serial killer in American Psycho. Ouch.
Hugh Jackman
Following his star-making turn as Wolverine in the X-Men films, Hugh Jackman was in the running to replace Brosnan after 2002's Die Another Day. Jackman revealed he was indeed in talks to play Bond, but his shooting schedule didn't allow it. "I was about to do X-Men 2 and a call came from my agent asking if I’d be interested in Bond," he told Variety. "I just felt at the time that the scripts had become so unbelievable and crazy, and I felt like they needed to become grittier and real."
Julian McMahon
The Nip/Tuck star would have been an ideal Bond and was considered to replace Pierce Brosnan, showing that they were keen to look beyond Blighty once more. The Australian had the looks, the charisma and certainly the sophistication, but he was ultimately passed over in favour of Daniel Craig. McMahon went on to star as Doctor Doom in the Fantastic Four films and sadly died in 2025 at the age of 56.
Clive Owen
Following performances in Croupier, Godsford Park, The Bourne Identity, Closer and Sin City, Clive Owen emerged as a fan favourite to take over as Bond for Casino Royale. Considered as a frontrunner for years, Owen reportedly baulked at contractual obligations and a multi-picture deal that would have prevented him from starring in films like Inside Man and Children of Men.
Goran Višnjić
Croatian actor Goran Višnjić, best known for his role as Dr. Luka Kovač in the medical drama ER, intrigued prodcuers. The actor screen tested for Barbara Broccoli, who was impressed. But like Lambert Wilson before him, there were concerns about his accent and whether audiences would accept a non-British / non-Commonwealth actor. Shame, as the charismatic Višnjić would have brought an international dimension and flair to the character.
Michael Fassbender
Oh, the things that could have been... Michael Fassbender would have been perfect for Bond - had he not advocated for Daniel Craig during his audition! According to the Hollywood Reporter, the actor met with Barbara Broccoli and ended up vouching for his fellow actor: “I remember going into that room and meeting with her and Wilson and I think I was like, 'Daniel Craig is...' I don't know why I was promoting him. I should have been promoting myself.” A damn shame, as if we've learned anything from Inglorious Basterds, X-Men: First Class and Haywire, Fassbender has the physicality and charm required. As for his turns in Hunger, Shame and Black Bag, he's more than proven he's got the acting chops.
Henry Cavill
A then 22-year-old Cavill was very close to becoming Bond, as it was reportedly down to him and Daniel Craig for Casino Royale. Director Martin Campbell said Cavill gave a “tremendous” audition but it ultimately came down to age, as he thought the actor was too young for the role. Cavill ended up donning Superman's cape instead of the tux. Still, for many fans, he remains the Bond that got away.
Anthony Starr
Another New Zealander auditioned for the chance to be Bond in Casino Royale ... Anthony Starr, now best known for his role as Homelander on The Boys, gave a self-described "stone-faced" audition. “It is one of the worst readings of ‘Bond, James Bond’ you’ll ever see,” he shared on the Happy Sad Confused podcast last year.
Sam Worthington
Before he Na'vid up for James Cameron, the Aussie actor auditioned for Bond alongside Cavill and Craig. However, he later revealed to Variety that he couldn't nail Bond's charisma. “I could play Bond as a killer, but I couldn’t get the debonair down for the life of me,” Worthington admitted. “The suit did not fit.”
Rupert Friend
When Rupert Friend auditioned in 2005 for Casino Royale, he only had one film on his resumé: the 2004 period drama The Libertine, starring Johnny Depp and John Malkovich. The then-23-year-old sent an audition tape, and like Starr, Worthington and Cavill, ended up missing out. While Craig proved he was a worthy Bond, Friend could have been an interesting choice, as subsequent roles in shows Homeland and Anatomy of a Scandal, as well as big screen turns in The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas, The Young Victoria and The Death of Stalin showed how versatile a performer he is.
Aaron Taylor-Johnson
It's been nearly six years since the last Bond film, No Time To Die, and the post-Daniel Craig years have meant plenty of rumours surroundingthe identity of the next actor to play Bond. One name repeatedly mentioned ever since 2022 has been Aaron Taylor-Johnson. The British star known for his roles in Angus, Thongs and Perfect Snogging (a low-key masterpiece, if you haven’t seen it), Kick-Ass, the John Lennon biopic Nowhere Boy, Avengers: Age of Ultron, Nocturnal Animals and 28 Years Later was once considered the frontrunner for the seventh Bond... There were even rumours he had screen tested and that it was a done deal. Now, his name has fallen off the 007 radar – despite some clues hinting that he was still in the running. It seems - like many before him - that it wasn't meant to be, which is a shame as the 36-year-old would have made a solid Bond.
There we have it.
An exact timeline for finalizing the Bond 26 casting is not known. What we do know is that it's happening this year, as producer Amy Pascal revealed in August that "the end of the year is a good bet" for the official announcement.
Bond 26 will be directed by Canadian filmmaker and four-time Oscar nominee Denis Villeneuve and is being written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. It will be the first Bond film since Amazon took full creative control over the franchise from longtime 007 custodians Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson.
Production on the next Bond film is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028.

Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:17:35 GMT
23:17:35 KST

Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say
- Published
At least 14 people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials have said.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train headed for the southern city of Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit.
Russia's military has not publicly commented. It has repeatedly hit Ukraine's large railway network, but Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.
In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to Ukrzaliznytsia head Oleksandr Pertsovsky. He said many people were on the platform when the Russian drone struck.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform," he said.
Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit a civilian electric train.
Pictures from the Ukrainian rescue services show a large hole ripped in a platform strewn with blurred-out bodies, near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
He called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia following the incident and repeated his criticism of a controversial deal struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which eased some sanctions on Russia, allowing the US to import Russian diesel.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two girls aged 15 were killed in a Russian missile attack on the centre of Chernihiv city, in the north of the country, regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said. At least 11 others, including more children, were injured, he added.
The strikes came during efforts to uphold a fragile local ceasefire in the besieged city of Oleshky, which has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have been trapped without food, water, medicine and electricity.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Telegram that the truce was holding into a third day, and he had "set out with the Ukrainian delegation towards Oleshky" through Belarus and Russia.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has condemned Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow whilst the city hosts the Russia-Africa Summit, the Tass news agency has reported. The summit is a two-day event attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries.
The mayor of Moscow said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched overnight towards the region, most of which were shot down during their flight.
Russia's defence ministry has always denied targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
However, the dangers to passengers are very real. Attacks on Ukraine's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been hit this year, according to statistics released by Ukrzaliznytsia supplied to AFP news agency. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
There appears to have been a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure in recent weeks, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv, and a metro train hit during one of the strikes.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel's Arab parties

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alleged on Oct 29, without providing evidence, that Arab parties’ record gains in an election this week were driven in part by voter fraud, a charge rejected by Arab leaders, who accused the Premier of incitement.
The allegation represents an escalation of anti-Arab rhetoric by Netanyahu and his far-right partners after high Arab turnout in a national ballot on Oct 27 effectively blocked a smooth path to power for either him or his main Jewish rivals.
Israeli election officials said on Oct 29 that there was a probe into fraud allegations, though the election’s integrity was not “systematically compromised”.
Analysts and critics say that by stepping up attacks on Arab parties, Netanyahu may be trying to ensure his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, feels unable to even consider forming a minority government with Arab help that could oust him from power.
Netanyahu’s goal is “delegitimising any Arab-Jewish cooperation”, said Eytan Gilboa, professor of politics at Reichman University.
Election officials were expected to finish tallying votes later on Oct 29, in a tightly fought election that has produced no clear winner and is likely to be followed by weeks of protracted negotiations over a new government.
With nearly 93% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious bloc held a modest lead in seats over a bloc of right-wing and centre-left parties led by Eisenkot, with both men’s coalitions short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Parliament.
Parties representing Israel’s 21% Arab minority were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot’s bloc, with 48 seats against Netanyahu’s camp of 53, with no realistic path to power without broad Arab backing, an option Eisenkot has so far ruled out.
However, Eisenkot’s camp could also try to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside, without including them in a governing coalition.
Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of fraud; Arab parties call it incitement
Ahmad Tibi, one of the leaders of the Arab Joint List party, said Netanyahu was on an orchestrated, toxic campaign meant to undermine the election results.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told Reuters.
During and after the Oct 27 election, Netanyahu and his allies warned against rising Arab turnout, and his right-wing Likud party issued statements accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the vote”.
It demanded police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service investigate incidents of suspected election bribery and intimidation at ballot stations in Arab towns. It said it possessed evidence of such activity but has not presented it to the public.
The police say they have arrested at least seven people since Tuesday in Israel’s south, where many Arabs live, on suspicion of voter fraud. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan said they were suspected of attempting to bribe voters to cast ballots for the Arab-dominated party Ra’am, which has Islamist roots.
On Oct 29, the head of Israel’s Central Election Committee, Supreme Court jurist Noam Sohlberg, said he had asked the Shin Bet to investigate suspicions that unidentified foreign players had tried to intervene in the election.
Likud seized on Sohlberg’s request, alleging an attack on Israel’s democracy, “an Islamisation of Israel and the toppling of the right-wing in order to bring about IDF withdrawal and defeat on all fronts, foremost Iran”.
Likud said Qatar was behind the alleged election intervention, which Qatar later denied.
Ra’am head Mansour Abbas said on Oct 29 that his party was not involved in the reported suspicious conduct and urged a full investigation. He said that Netanyahu was on an incitement campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens.
“We have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimisation he is waging against Arab citizens: Nothing will come of it, because there is nothing there,” Abbas said in a statement.
In a letter sent to a parliamentarian and published by the Central Election Committee, the committee said that there was “no base for claims that there was systematic harm to the election’s integrity”.
Israeli President: ‘We must not tarnish an entire community’
After vote tallying is completed, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with party chairs and choose a candidate who he thinks has the best chance to form a government.
The coalition that last toppled Netanyahu, in 2021, relied on Abbas’ Ra’am party. But Eisenkot’s underperformance means the opposition would now need backing from the Arab-dominated Joint List, which includes an explicitly anti-Zionist party. Most Jewish leaders have shunned formal alliances with Arab parties since Israel’s founding.
Eisenkot called for an investigation that would protect election integrity but said Netanyahu was exploiting the suspicions to “spread chaos”.
He said in a statement that Netanyahu’s aim was to “challenge the official election results, in which the Israeli public voted against the government”.
Herzog said the allegations must be investigated.
“But even at a moment like this, we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy,” Herzog said in a statement. REUTERS

2 dead as ‘fairy chimney’ rock spires collapse at tourist site in Turkey’s Cappadocia
ISTANBUL – A landslide triggered by heavy rainfall caused a rock spire to collapse in Turkey’s Cappadocia tourist region on Oct 29, killing at least two people, the local governor said.
Turkey’s Cappadocia region, a magnet for tourists from around the world, is home to rock formations known as “fairy chimneys”, created by ancient volcanic activity.
“According to initial findings, two people were killed and five others injured in the incident,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on X.
“Search-and-rescue teams are continuing intensive, coordinated operations to locate any other victims who may be trapped under the debris,” he said.
The incident occurred at 3.15pm when a landslide triggered a rockfall in the town of Goreme near the open-air museum, local governor Huseyin Kok said.
The area was closed to the public following the collapse, according to reports.
Eyewitnesses reported hearing a loud noise as the rock spire near an open car parking lot fell.
Television footage showed heavy machinery digging through the rubble as rescue teams gather at the site in an effort to recover people trapped beneath the debris.
“Our search-and-rescue operations at the scene are ongoing. The government is continuing its efforts at the scene with all available resources,” Kok said.
Turkey’s culture and tourism ministry has launched restoration work in the region to help preserve the fragile rock formations from climate-related damage, natural erosion and human activity.
In 2024, another rockfall was reported in Cappadocia, although no deaths or injuries were recorded.
The Cappadocia region, a major tourist attraction known for its rock-carved underground cities and early Christian churches, is also famed for hot-air ballooning, a thriving industry that sees dozens of balloons take to the skies on clear mornings.
But concerns have been raised about safety following a series of accidents. AFP

Finland launches third Pohjanmaa-class corvette
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:14:38 UTC
23:14:38 KST

- Finland launched the third Pohjanmaa-class corvette at Rauma on Oct. 29, putting three of the four new warships in the water.
- All four corvettes are due to be completed by 2029 and will replace seven older Finnish Navy ships.
Finland launched the third of its four new Pohjanmaa-class corvettes at Rauma on Oct. 29, putting three of the Finnish Navy’s largest warships in decades in the water, the Finnish Navy said.
The ship was moved out of the construction hall at the Rauma Marine Constructions shipyard on Finland’s west coast, where fitting out will continue afloat. The Navy said all four corvettes are due to be completed by 2029 and will enter service in phases, and it has said it expects to take the ships into service between 2027 and 2029. The Navy did not say when the third ship will begin sea trials.
“The launch of the third vessel shows the progress of long-term and persistent work. This is an extensive undertaking that brings together the Navy’s future capability, domestic industrial expertise and close cooperation between different parties,” said Rear Adm. Tuomas Tiilikainen, commander of the Finnish Navy.
Construction has picked up pace across the four hulls. The first corvette, whose construction began in 2023, was launched in May 2025 and is now being fitted out. The second was launched on May 21 this year, less than a year after its keel was laid. Rauma Marine Constructions laid the keel of the third ship and started production of the fourth in January, putting all four under construction at the same time, and the fourth ship’s keel followed in July.
The corvettes are being built by RMC Defence, a subsidiary of Rauma Marine Constructions, for the Finnish Defence Forces Logistics Command under a program known as Squadron 2020. At 117 m (384 feet) long with a crew of about 70, the ships are the largest surface combatants the Finnish Navy has ordered since its coastal defense ships of the 1930s. Each is designed to stay at sea for 14 days and has a range of about 3,500 nautical miles.
The Pohjanmaa class combines several jobs that the Finnish Navy now spreads across older vessels. The four corvettes will replace seven ships: the four Rauma-class missile boats, the two Hämeenmaa-class minelayers and the minelayer Pohjanmaa, retired in 2015, whose name the new class carries. Each corvette carries anti-ship missiles, Evolved Sea Sparrow surface-to-air missiles in a vertical launcher, a 57 mm gun, torpedoes for anti-submarine warfare and rails for laying sea mines, an important task in the shallow, mine-friendly waters off Finland’s coast.
The ships also have ice-strengthened hulls so they can operate year-round in the northern Baltic, where the Gulf of Finland and the Gulf of Bothnia can freeze in winter, and they are fitted with composite ballistic armor to protect key areas. The Navy said the corvettes will give it new capability to defend Finnish waters and operate within NATO, which Finland joined in 2023.
The Navy plans to keep the Pohjanmaa class in service into the 2060s. The first ship is due to be handed over to the Navy in 2027, with all four in service by 2029.

Israeli soldier poses at damaged Lebanon church, sparking anger
A photo of an Israeli soldier smiling in front of the damaged Saint Joseph Church in the southern Lebanese village of Qaouzah has sparked widespread anger and calls to protect the 120-year-old religious site.
The image, circulated on social media on Wednesday, shows the soldier standing in front of the partially damaged church, surrounded by rubble and debris.
Much of the visible damage is to the church's roof and exterior, although the structure remains standing.
Qaouzah's mayor, Charbel Rizk, told local media that protecting the historic church would require safe access to the village, which has been cut off by Israeli military operations.
He also appealed to Pope Leo XIV and Lebanese authorities to "preserve this 120-year-old church".
"Our ancestors built the church through their hard work. The dome was already damaged during the conflict, and there is damage inside," he said, stressing the mainly Christian village's deep connection to the church.
Israel's occupation of parts of southern Lebanon has displaced civilians, while attacks on and the desecration of places of worship by Israeli soldiers have been documented across the region.
"We want to return to the village, even if we have to sleep under an olive tree or next to the church. We have had no access to the village since the beginning of the war in early March," Rizk said.
He added that the village's strategic location had left it repeatedly exposed to attacks during previous conflicts.
Vincent Gelot, director of a French Catholic organisation that has been providing supplies to isolated Christian villages in southern Lebanon, condemned attacks on religious sites following the circulation of the image.
"It is unacceptable to attack religious sanctuaries," he said, as concerns grew over the destruction of religious and cultural heritage.
However, Gelot stressed that the circumstances surrounding the damage to Saint Joseph Church remained unclear.
"We do not know when this destruction occurred or who committed it," he said, calling for an investigation to establish the facts.
He added that efforts to investigate the damage and identify those responsible had been hampered by Israeli forces preventing teams from entering the area.
Residents have also appealed to international officials to help protect their community following the circulation of the photograph.
Locals contacted Apostolic Nuncio Archbishop Paolo Borgia and US Ambassador Michael Issa, urging them to intervene to protect religious sites.
According to local media reports, around 54 families lived in Qaouzah before the latest displacement, with most forced to abandon their homes and belongings.
Parish priest Father Antonios Hanna told local media that the church held particular significance because generations of villagers had cut and carried stones to build it.
He said the building was central to the community's religious and cultural heritage.
This is not the first time photographs of Israeli soldiers at Christian religious sites in Lebanon have sparked outrage.
In May, the Israeli military launched an investigation after a photograph showing a soldier desecrating a statue of the Virgin Mary in southern Lebanon triggered international condemnation.
The image, taken in the village of Debel, showed the soldier placing a cigarette in the statue's mouth while smoking another himself.
Earlier this year, another Israeli soldier was photographed damaging a statue of Jesus in the same village. The incident followed reports that Israeli troops had bulldozed solar panels supplying electricity to the area.

Israel elections: What the record tally by Arab parties means for Zionist politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:13:23 UTC
23:13:23 KST

Arab parties, which are mostly supported by the Palestinian citizens of Israel, received a resounding victory in the October 27 election, changing the balance of power in the Knesset.
With roughly 90 percent of ballots counted as of Thursday, the two main Arab-led parties – the Joint List and Ra’am – are on track for a combined count of 19 seats.
Their total is nearly double the previous count of 10 and well above the 2020 record of 15 seats.
According to the latest tally, Netanyahu’s right-wing and ultra-Orthodox bloc is expected to win 53 seats, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot is set to bag 48 seats.
Neither Zionist bloc is expected to reach the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government in the 120-member Knesset.
The projected 19 seats give the Arab-led parties significant leverage in coalition negotiations, but they do not guarantee a place in government.
It creates an opportunity for the two Arab parties to assert their democratic credentials in a country where Palestinian Israelis have long been treated as second-class citizens.
The community, which lives in separate towns, consists of the people whose ancestors stayed put during the Nakba, the mass expulsion of over 750,000 Palestinians following the creation of Israel in 1948.
The level of discrimination against Palestinian Israelis, who now make up roughly 20 percent of the country’s population, has risen dramatically since the October 7 attacks three years ago.
Towns dominated by the Palestinian Israeli community saw a significant shift in voting patterns. Their turnout hit 80 percent, the highest in decades.
They voted in large numbers because of deep frustration with the most right-wing government in Israel’s history and its far-right ministers, who have vowed to “Judaise” parts of Israel populated by Palestinian Israelis.
Experts say Arab parties made electoral gains despite Netanyahu’s campaign strategy, which centred on delegitimisation of Arab political participation in coalition-building.
Netanyahu’s Likud party has already claimed that the election was “stolen by Arab parties” that “support terror and the elimination of the Jewish state” through bribery, threats, violence, forgeries and the use of illegal software.
Main members from both Zionist blocs have said they wouldn’t include Palestinian Israelis in a coalition.
Ferit Belder, associate professor of international relations at Istanbul’s Marmara University, tells TRT World that opposition leaders largely deferred the question until after the vote to avoid the political costs of “normalising” Arab politics in the first election after the Gaza genocide.
“Despite their electoral success, it is not guaranteed that the Arab parties will be able to translate this success into concrete gains and become part of the ‘legitimate circle of coalition-building’,” he says.
The Central Election Committee’s moves against Arab parties – left to the Supreme Court to resolve – further underscored the reluctance of Zionist parties to defend legitimate Arab participation, he adds.
Ozgur Dikmen, a scholar of Jewish politics, tells TRT World that Zionist politicians are more likely to frame the Palestinian Israeli gains as an element of insecurity and threat.
In a possible new cycle of elections, as seen between 2018 and 2022, such an “Arab threat” narrative would remain a useful tool for the right, he says.
A political force to reckon with
Numbers show the Zionist blocs’ dependence on Arab parties to reach a majority, raising the political costs of exclusion.
Gokhan Cinkara, director of Necmettin Erbakan University’s Global and Regional Studies Application and Research Centre, tells TRT World that the election results mark a significant turning point in Israeli politics.
He says the Arab parties have become a political force that can no longer be ignored.
“Anyone seeking to form a government will have to engage with the Arab parties in some way,” he says.
The two Arab parties approached the election with different strategies.
Ra’am, under Mansour Abbas, insisted on formal coalition membership to address the concerns of the Palestinian Israeli community.
Ra’am also joined the 2021 Bennett-Lapid government. Its integrationist approach and moves, such as placing former Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz on the Knesset candidate list, already positioned the party as a potential coalition partner.
The Joint List, a union of communist Hadash, secularist Ta’al, and nationalist Balad groups, offered only external support for any anti-Netanyahu government in exchange for concrete improvements: stronger action against violence and crime, better housing, and the rollback of discriminatory policies of Netanyahu’s government.
Dikmen says that the chances of “formal inclusion” of Arab parties in the coalition remain limited.
It might be slightly more possible for the Eisenkot bloc to accept a coalition supported by the Arab parties, particularly with figures such as Abbas willing to serve as supporting partners, he says.
“I do not think it would be very realistic to expect seeing a Palestinian-Israeli minister,” Dikmen says.
Belder notes that the main task for the Arab parties is to convert their Knesset seats into material improvements in the daily lives of the Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Abbas of the Ra’am party has long argued that parliamentary presence without executive power confines the parties to the “world of slogans”, Belder says.
In the Knesset, a larger and more confident Palestinian Israeli caucus can at least be expected to reshape debates on equality and minority rights, even if fundamental arguments over the character of the state remain largely unchanged.
Dikmen points out that since December 2022, the Ministry of National Security under far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir has made serious reductions in the security budget of Palestinian Israeli-majority towns, contributing to skyrocketing crime rates – one of the drivers of the high turnout.
“I think such a reaction would reflect itself in the attitudes of Palestinian members in the Knesset,” he says.
Belder anticipates that far-right efforts to undermine judicial authority and policies that harm Palestinian Israelis’ daily lives – performative home demolitions and the humiliation of residents under Ben-Gvir – can be reversed or restricted.
Settler violence in the occupied West Bank might also come under closer government scrutiny, he adds.
Cinkara notes that the Arab parties will play an important role in advancing opposition priorities, including the election of the Knesset speaker and the allocation of committee seats.
“The key challenge for the Arab parties will also be to offer their voters practical policies,” he adds.

Cornell faculty press ahead with no-confidence vote in handling of gang-rape case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:12:59 UTC
23:12:59 KST

Faculty members at Cornell University are pressing ahead with a no-confidence vote in campus leadership over its handling of a gang-rape scandal involving students at a fraternity at the Ivy League institution.
Cornell professors on Wednesday discussed, at an emotional faculty meeting, how the school’s leadership tackled a woman’s report that she was raped by at least seven male students at a fraternity house in 2024.
The Associated Press, which obtained a recording of the closed-door meeting, reported that some faculty urged patience and sought to delay the vote, while others argued that years of institutional failures required more immediate action.
Faculty will vote electronically on a proposed no-confidence resolution in Cornell’s administration through 6 November, a largely symbolic move that at least could put pressure on the university trustees that choose the university’s leadership, the AP said.
Prosecutors in New York said last month they were reopening the case after the woman, a then 20-year-old Cornell student who said she was forced to leave the university after the incident, filed a civil lawsuit naming her alleged attackers.
University leaders faced a backlash, including mass campus protests, when it was revealed that their inquiry into the woman’s original complaint resulted in only two expulsions. Others among the alleged rapists were ordered to write essays, attend workshops, or serve short suspensions as part of their punishment, following the review by Cornell, an elite, private sector university based in Ithaca, in upstate New York.
The woman accusing the men recently wrote a letter to the campus faculty senate saying she felt “unsupported and disbelieved” by Cornell’s president. And in a separate development at the weekend, a New York state judge ruled that she could continue to be identified by the pseudonym Jane Doe in the ongoing lawsuit, citing concerns for her safety.
Earlier this month, Kathy Hochul, the Democratic governor of New York state, appointed the state’s attorney general Letitia James as a special counsel to investigate the case.
At Wednesday’s faculty meeting, some faculty struggled with whether they should speak out publicly, sharing painful experiences of harassment and fears of professional retaliation, the AP said.
Beth Frances Milles, a performing arts professor, Cornell graduate and parent, pleaded for civility after describing receiving messages from women who experienced sexual assault, including former classmates.
“I understand we have to take action,” she said. “There are so many things to talk about. Please, let’s talk about it together and not sneer at each other when we disagree.”
After at least an hour of debate, members voted down an attempt to delay voting on the resolution until an independent investigation into Cornell’s handling of the sexual assault allegations was completed.
The resolution co-sponsor, Anne Marie Brady, said she was encouraged by the breadth of faculty who spoke, despite fears of retaliation. As a contingent faculty member, she said, speaking publicly carried professional risks.
“The more people who speak out, the more we protect each other,” Brady said in a phone interview after the meeting.
Music professor Ariana Kim said she unexpectedly found herself sharing her own experience of sexual harassment and bullying after hearing suggestions that faculty did not do enough to address such misconduct.
She described how the harassment affected her tenure case and how her efforts to get help from administrators, including Cornell’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, when he was provost, went nowhere.
“It’s hard to get up and do that on a number of levels,” Kim said, describing a sense of relief and pride that she had spoken.
During the meeting, economics professor Seth Sanders agreed that sexual assault was a serious problem at Cornell but said faculty did not yet know enough to judge the administration’s response.
He said about 80% of his department opposed the resolution for now, with many awaiting the independent investigation.
“I don’t think setting it up as having confidence in the administration or supporting the administration is right,” Sanders said. “I think it’s legitimate to think that you don’t know whether to have confidence because you don’t know what happened or why in the Jane Doe case.”
Wednesday’s meeting came a day after 20 female science and engineering faculty members called on Kotlikoff to resign in a letter to trustees that was obtained by AP.
The woman in the ongoing case about the fraternity incident claims she was drugged and repeatedly raped in October 2024 at a house belonging to Cornell’s since-closed chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity. All seven of the alleged attackers deny the claims against them.

‘I fear for my family’: Berlin mayoral candidate’s leaked messages expose Hamas ties, spark uproar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:11:13 UTC
23:11:13 KST

Berlin has been engulfed in political turmoil since the Sept. 20 local elections. Although the radical left-wing Die Linke party won the election, all its attempts to form a left-wing coalition with the Greens and the Social Democrats have stalled amid revelations of antisemitism within the party and ties between many of its members and radical Islamist figures and leaders of Arab crime families in the city.
A new report published Thursday morning by the German newsmagazine Der Spiegel has exposed another dimension of the relationship between Germany's radical left and extremist Islam. According to the report, Elif Eralp, Die Linke's leading candidate for Berlin governing mayor, openly acknowledged that she and her family live in fear of Hamas supporters within her party. 
The controversy began with a mistake rooted in an outdated and questionable practice in German journalism, under which interviewees insist on reviewing and revising their quotations before publication.
Eralp, who had been interviewed by Der Spiegel, also asked to review her quotes before they appeared in print. After receiving them, she returned a revised version to the magazine.
But Eralp and her aides failed to notice that the document they sent back to Der Spiegel still contained their internal correspondence discussing the changes they wanted to make. On Thursday morning, that correspondence became the magazine's lead story and a major issue on Germany's political agenda.
In the exchanges, Eralp acknowledged that she and her family were personally afraid of becoming entangled with Hamas supporters associated with the party. She even tried to remove a reference to one of them, citing police advice not to publicly identify specific crime families in Berlin.
"My husband and I don't want to name specific people. We're both afraid of these people," she wrote.
Eralp's spokeswoman explained in the correspondence that they could not delete part of the interviewer's question, only portions of Eralp's answers.
Eralp responded in what could be interpreted as considerable alarm:
"But what am I supposed to do now? It was a mistake to agree to this interview in the first place. Until now, we were talking about people involved in organized crime. Now we're talking about people with connections to Hamas. I can't put myself and my family at risk for Der Spiegel. What do we do now? Cancel the entire interview?"
The Berlin Die Linke leader continued:
"Until now, when incidents came up, including the one involving Ibrahim Ibrahim (a member of an umbrella organization associated with Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine who appeared at the party's election victory celebration in Neukölln), I condemned them in general terms. But now we're talking about condemning an individual by name."
Even the center-left joins the criticism: 'Supporters of terrorism and antisemitism are deeply entrenched in the party'
Der Spiegel's revelations triggered an uproar across Germany's political establishment.
"Berlin needs a mayor who can stand up to extremists and doesn't give the impression that they are dictating what she can say before she has even been elected," said Christopher Förster, a conservative member of Berlin's state parliament. "If she can't do that, she cannot be elected to the position."
Another member of the Berlin parliament, Burkard Dregger, said: "Anyone who gets involved with Hamas criminals and their supporters in Berlin should not be surprised when they now demand payment for their support during the campaign."
Kristin Brinker, leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) parliamentary group in Berlin, also criticized Eralp.
"If even the most senior politician no longer feels safe, how are ordinary Berliners supposed to feel? Especially considering that they don't have personal security guards to protect them," she said.
Stefan Evers, the conservative candidate for governing mayor, added in a statement to the German newspaper Bild:
"Thursday's revelations deepen the serious concerns about a left-wing government in Berlin. How is Elif Eralp supposed to protect the safety of millions of residents as mayor if she herself is afraid of the Islamist connections within her own party? The warning signs can no longer be ignored, and it is not too late to act."
Michael Müller, a former governing mayor of Berlin, said Eralp's remarks "mean that Berlin's mayor would be vulnerable to blackmail. We need to acknowledge that clearly."
Criticism also came from the left side of the political spectrum.
Martin Hikel, the center-left Social Democratic district mayor of Berlin's Neukölln borough, said: "When someone allows themselves to be constrained in this way, it only shows how deeply these forces, which glorify terrorism and antisemitism, are entrenched in the Left Party."
At midday Thursday, during the inaugural session of the city legislature, Eralp responded to the revelations and sought to contain the damage.
"I won't let anyone intimidate me. I've made that clear. It's only natural to worry about your family," she said.
Daughter of Turkish immigrants draws support from pro-Gaza voters
Eralp, 45, is the daughter of Turkish immigrants who fled their country because of political persecution. She studied law and has worked extensively on immigration, discrimination, racism, asylum seekers and equal rights, including during her time at the United Nations.
Her success story as a member of a minority group and the progressive policies she advocates led some to dub her "Berlin's Mamdani" even before the September elections, when she emerged as Die Linke's candidate for governing mayor.
One of her campaign slogans played directly on that comparison: "From New York to Berlin, the left is back."
However, as in Mamdani's case in the United States, antisemitic and anti-Israel sentiment within Die Linke has intensified considerably under Eralp, particularly among the party's younger members.
Eralp has tried unsuccessfully to contain the major controversies sparked by the behavior of some party members. But in Berlin in 2026, displays of antisemitism do not appear to be driving voters away.
Eralp has to tread carefully on issues involving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the war in Gaza. Her party has taken a clear position on the issue, formally adopting in June the claim that Israel is committing genocide.
At the same time, Eralp has spoken out against extremist incidents, including a party gathering in Neukölln that ended with participants chanting "Death to the IDF." She has also pushed for an internal investigative committee to prevent the party from being tainted by antisemitism.
On the other hand, Eralp cannot afford to abandon the party's unequivocal support for Gaza, given the importance of Muslim voters and young supporters who helped propel Die Linke upward in the polls, largely because of its anti-Israel policies.
This summer, Eralp found herself posing for campaign photographs with activists who declared that "the Palestinian liberation movement will not end until Tel Aviv is in Palestinian hands."
Earlier this month, additional details emerged about Eralp, revealing that until just a year ago, she had been a member of Rote Hilfe (Red Aid), an organization whose motto is "The ends justify the means."
The organization provides legal and financial support to people convicted of crimes, provided their actions were motivated by left-wing ideology.
Many Germans had already raised concerns about the party's ties to Arab criminal clans and its desire to reduce police funding and presence.
Now, many voters are questioning whether Eralp's past involvement with an organization that supports violence or turning a blind eye to the law in pursuit of its goals could prevent her from becoming Berlin's democratic, law-abiding leader.

Polish army will soon receive first delivery of EU-funded vests and helmets
Poland's defence company Maskpol will deliver the first batch of bullet-proof vests and helmets ordered under the EU's defence funding programme SAFE, a deputy defence minister has said.
On Wednesday, at the Maskpol Protective Equipment Company's plant in Konieczki in southern Poland, which is part of the Polish Armaments Group, Cezary Tomczyk took part in a presentation of the first batch of equipment manufactured for the Polish Army under contracts funded by the SAFE instrument. Over the coming days, tens of thousands of new helmets and vests are due to be delivered to Polish military units, including those stationed in the east of the country.
“This is the first time that equipment from the SAFE mechanism has been supplied directly to Polish Army soldiers by Maskpol,” said Tomczyk during a press conference at the factory. In his view, this is a “turning point” in the process of army modernisation.
Tomczyk announced that by the end of 2026, 17,000 KKZ-01 type vests and 20,000 HBT-02 type helmets will be delivered. He added that the total value of the contract for the supply of individual equipment for soldiers from Maskpol under the SAFE programme is PLN 1.5 billion (EUR 340 mln).
Referring to the individual soldier equipment modernisation programme Szpej, conducted since 2024, Tomczyk said an audit carried out that year showed that only about one third of Polish soldiers had equipment that was up to the highest NATO standard.
He said that the number of composite helmets in the armed forces is set to rise from 84,000 at the start of 2024 to 350,000 by the end of 2026; while the number of bulletproof vests will increase from 60,000 to 180,000.
Under the SAFE programme, the MASKPOL company will deliver to the Polish Armed Forces 300,000 HBT-02 helmets and 50,000 KKZ-01 bullet-proof vests. (PAP)

By Juliette Jabkhiro and Layli Foroudi
PARIS, Oct 29 (Reuters) - President Emmanuel Macron has accused far-right politicians including in Marine Le Pen’s National Rally of fostering an “atmosphere of racism” across France, days after a racially motivated killing in a Paris suburb.
The attack last Friday, which left one dead and seven wounded, has unleashed a bitter debate over racism in French politics and the media as the country grapples with a broad set of social grievances, months ahead of a presidential election.
“There are political movements which have led to … a kind of disinhibition of speech, an ambient racism,” Macron told YouTube influencer Hugo Decrypte in a lengthy interview released late on Wednesday.

RN lawmaker Jean-Philippe Tanguy told TF1: “It’s Macron who has run France for the past nine years. It’s on his watch that antisemitism, homophobia and hate has spread through France. He is to blame.”
‘WORDS CARRY WEIGHT’
French politicians on all sides have traded accusations of racism in the wake of the killing of 26-year-old Pengo Bossio Wangi in Trappes, a culturally diverse town 20 km (15 miles) southwest of Paris.
Anti-terrorist prosecutors said on Thursday the 39-year-old suspect, named Kevin T, acknowledged during questioning seeking victims of “African or Muslim type”. His belongings included a copy of Hitler’s book “Mein Kampf” and stickers mentioning the RN — though he said he did not support any particular party.
RN senator Edwige Diaz this week doubled down on comments by Jordan Bardella, now the party’s leader, who in 2021 called Trappes a “mini-Islamic state”. She said there was nothing wrong in that description.
“We can speak of a somewhat toxic climate in which certain people are constantly portrayed as suspicious or illegitimate,” said Zineb Alami, lawyer for Bossio Wangi’s father.
“Words carry weight,” she said.
Numerous politicians on the right, including Bardella, and media commentators have blamed the rioting and looting that took place after street protests this month on immigration, without giving evidence. At a march in memory of Bossio Wangi on Sunday, people in attendance blamed the media coverage for inciting racial hatred.
Macron’s minority centrist government also stands accused of not doing enough to tackle the spread of racist and far-right attitudes in society.
“The normalisation of the ideas of the far-right extends beyond the National Rally into the ranks of the government,” sociologist Solene Brun told Reuters.
Aurore Berge, the minister for gender equality and anti-discrimination, was urged in parliament this week to take back her comment last month that it was legitimate to discuss the “Great Replacement”, a far-right conspiracy theory that has been invoked by perpetrators of far-right attacks around the world in recent years.
In addition to the Trappes attack, far-right activists looking for confrontations with protesters were spotted across more than a dozen French cities last week, according to authorities.
