ROME, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Italy’s government will allow motorists to personalise the number plates of their vehicles, in a revenue-raising move that follows the example of the Unites States, Britain and other countries.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced the measure on Wednesday as she unveiled Italy’s 2027 budget law, the last before a general election due next year, describing the number plate initiative as a “colourful note”.

A Treasury official declined to estimate how much revenue the government expects the measure to generate.
Italian car number plates are currently made of a string of two letters, three numbers and two letters. The extent to which motorists will be allowed to stray from the standard formula is unclear.
The reform has triggered a wave of memes and jokes on social media, amid concerns that personalized license plates could open the flood-gates to insults and profanities.
One meme showed Meloni dressed up as Marie Antoniette, holding a platter of licence plates and saying, “Let them eat personalised plates” - a play on the famous phrase by the 18th century French queen “Let them eat cake”.
Some welcomed the measure, including taxi drivers, who said distinctive personalised plates could make it easier to identify legitimate operators and combat illegal services.
Opposition parties on the centre-left were less enthusiastic, saying the licence-plate initiative was a distraction from more pressing issues that budget failed to address.
“Meloni should know that Italians have already chosen their personalised plate, and it reads: ‘Meloni, go away’,” said Francesco Silvestri, a lawmaker from the Five Star Movement.

China’s Communist Party conclave on toughening discipline sees record expulsions, absences
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:09:19 CET
23:09:19 KST

BEIJING, Oct 29 (Reuters) - A Chinese Communist Party conclave on toughening internal discipline this week expelled a record number of senior officials and logged the highest ever absence rate as purges thinned its leadership ranks.
The gathering, the party’s fifth plenum since the current leadership cohort was formed in 2022, also set the 21st Party Congress for the second half of 2027 in Beijing, effectively starting proceedings for China’s tightly choreographed, twice-a-decade top reshuffle, when President Xi Jinping is expected to extend his rule for another five-year term.
The closed-door meeting of the party’s Central Committee, the largest of its top decision-making bodies, was marked by the highest rate of absences in the post-Mao era, underscoring the scale of Xi’s anti-corruption campaign and wider political shake-up.
In total, 279 full and alternate members of the leadership body attended the gathering this week, compared with the 376 originally named in 2022, a summary of the proceedings dispatched by the official Xinhua news agency showed. This means more than a quarter, or 25.8%, of the original cohort was absent, many of them due to purges.
Despite the record churn, the party portrayed itself as stronger than ever, hailing achievements it said were worthy of being “recorded forever in the history books of building Marxist political parties.”
“The main messaging for the party to its domestic and external audiences is that it must be unified,” said Kerry Brown, director of King’s College London’s Lau China Institute.
“The US will be emerging from the midterms, where the strong likelihood is yet more division and conflict,” and for Xi and his colleagues, Brown said, “the message will be: We are united, we are disciplined, and we are not like them.”
A MATTER OF SURVIVAL
Days after ascending to power in 2012, Xi told the party leadership that “if corruption is allowed to worsen unchecked, it will ultimately lead to the total collapse of the party and the state.”
He then initiated a sweeping corruption and discipline crackdown with an intensity unseen since the Mao era that has ensnared millions within China’s vast bureaucracy and has seen hundreds of top officials purged, including one-time allies and those once thought untouchable.
Xi called on the party, together with the military, to “turn the blade inward” and unleash a revolution on itself and eradicate “viruses” that corrode its health.
Thursday’s communique argued Xi’s consolidated authority had enabled the party to curb long-unchecked misconduct, resolve entrenched institutional failings, eliminate serious hidden dangers within the party, state and military, and reverse the laxity of party discipline, making it stronger through “revolutionary tempering.”
The Central Military Commission — the supreme military command — has been nearly eviscerated, with five of the seven members appointed in the 2022 reshuffle purged, leaving only Xi and vice-chair Zhang Shengmin, a discipline enforcer rather than an operational commander, in office. Zhang was unexpectedly elevated to the elite Politburo this week.
The plenum formally ratified the expulsion of 33 officials from the party, including former Politburo members Ma Xingrui and Zhang Youxia, bringing the number of sitting Politburo members ousted during the current term to three, the highest since 1980. Former senior diplomat Liu Jianchao and former industry minister Jin Zhuanglong were also among those ousted.
Xi’s public remarks suggest he regards the self-cleansing campaign as the party’s only safeguard against decay, essential for ensuring its survival and ability to rule indefinitely. Relentless self-discipline and periodic “self-revolution” for Xi offer the party a means of escaping the dynastic cycle of rise, decline and fall.
Xi “seems willing to tolerate significant short-term disruption as an investment in the party’s long-term resilience,” said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser on China at London’s Tony Blair Institute.
“It’s less about purging elite rivals, more about building a disciplined system that can sustain Xi’s political priorities across leadership cycles,” she added.
THE PARTY’S DILEMMA
After more than a decade, the campaign shows no sign of ending, with the party vowing on Thursday to keep waging the tough, protracted and all-out battle against corruption in the face of new problems and “major challenges.”
There are inherent dilemmas to party governance, said Joseph Torigian, an expert in Chinese politics at American University. “It’s necessary to keep trying to fight certain challenges that even Xi Jinping admits never go away.”
“People are always vulnerable to the sugar-coated bullets of bourgeois imperialism, so you need to continuously remind them why a sense of mission and zeal is imperative to the party’s mission.”
With few external checks on its power, the party appears reliant on campaign-style internal discipline drives to restrain the officials through whom it exercises its immense authority.
And “you need to keep having party plenums on ‘party building,’” Torigian added.
2027 LEADERSHIP RESHUFFLE
While some have speculated on a possible recalibration of Xi’s role, analysts widely expect him to secure five more years at the party’s helm next autumn.
State media have offered no hint of a loosening grip on power.
Commentaries published by the party-run People’s Daily and Xinhua in recent days have called on the party and the nation to “unite even tighter” around Xi and further uphold his status as the party’s core.
The messaging casts Xi’s consolidated authority as the most fundamental guarantee of political stability, policy continuity and China’s drive toward national rejuvenation.
“The Party is clearly going through a generational overhaul,” said King’s College London’s Brown. “But the key challenge, and the greatest unknown, is to what extent the old guard around Xi will be willing, and able, to let younger leaders assume greater power.”
The party should “improve the quality of training and selecting outstanding young cadres,” the plenum communique said.
(Reporting by Beijing Newsroom; Editing by Ros Russell and Hugh Lawson)

Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
- Published
The chaos and horror of Spain's second rail tragedy this year has been conveyed vividly by survivors of Wednesday's high-speed crash that has left at least 69 people dead.
But as Spain holds three days of mourning, revelations from leaked audio recordings of the apparent human error in a control room in the minutes before this disaster happened have given way to public disbelief and outrage, in a highly politicised climate, exactly a month before Spaniards go to the polls.
"You don't know what's happening, you don't know what has happened, you just know that you're being thrown around in a matter of seconds," said Iñaki García, 60.
He was on the stationary Iryo train that was rammed from behind by a Renfe train on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda, around 140km (87 miles) south of the capital.
"There were people injured, walking around, there were dead people," he said. "In the next carriage along there were a lot of dead people."
Recalling the horrific scenes around him, one young man told the BBC in a quivering voice: "I don't know if that's something I'll ever recover from."
Stories of tragedy have continued to emerge. A pharmacist from Urda was one of the first to reach the scene, bringing with him first aid supplies and medicine.
"One of [the passengers] was saying goodbye to his wife and children. His last words were 'God is good'," Antonio García told Spanish radio.
Similar scenes of grief played out only nine months ago in the southern village of Adamuz, when a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people.
Now, in the town of Urda, just like Adamuz, awful stories are combined with acts of kindness and solidarity.
Locals turned out to help the injured, bringing blankets, food and water to a nearby sports hall that was converted into a makeshift hospital for much of the day.
"We all started to turn out to help and we organised ourselves as best we could," said Rosa María Domínguez, a local woman, who described the scene as "a horror film".
However, the overriding sentiment that these two tragedies have generated is one of confusion and a failure to comprehend how this could have happened.
Not long ago, the speed, efficiency and safety of Spain's high-speed rail system, the largest in Europe, was the envy of its neighbours.
The Adamuz crash triggered a nationwide debate about whether the network was fit for purpose.
This latest incident intensifies pressure on the left-wing government of Pedro Sánchez, in the middle of an election campaign where his Socialist PSOE is behind the conservatives in most opinion polls.
On Wednesday night a demonstration protesting at the government's handling of the rail network saw far-right groups turn out and clash with police.
Although the main parties, other than the far-right Vox, have suspended campaigning, Sánchez has twice visited the scene of the crash and his People's Party rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo came to Urda on Thursday.
Sánchez's transport minister, Óscar Puente, made clear from the start that a computer failure followed by human error was the likely cause of the crash. By late evening, leaked audio recordings of a control-room operator talking to train drivers appeared to back that up.
Puente has long been a hate figure for the right, and with two of the worst rail tragedies in Spanish history taking place on his watch, the criticism is only going to increase.
Spain's biggest train drivers' union Semaf condemned the leak of audio recordings as irresponsible and slanted. The union had already called a strike for Thursday in a bid to ensure that "urgency to travel is never prioritised over safety".
One train driver, Vicente Almenar, told Spanish media: "They always look for the last link in the chain, where it's weakest, but here the entire procedure failed because we don't even know what our colleague was seeing on the screen," he told Spanish media.
Sánchez had not been expecting rail safety to dominate his campaign, but that now looks increasingly likely.
After two accidents and more than 100 deaths on the same high-speed line, Feijóo told reporters in Urda on Thursday: "The Spanish people need answers. They are wondering what is happening to high-speed rail in their country."
And he emphasised that politics was not about talking - it was about acting.

‘Genocide’ and ‘apartheid’: Harvard's hometown backs divestment from IDF suppliers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:07:48 UTC
23:07:48 KST

The city home to Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) moved Wednesday to promote divestment from companies supplying weapons and technology to the Israel Defense Forces.
The City Council of Cambridge, a university city of approximately 123,000 residents near Boston, narrowly approved a resolution calling on municipal employee pension funds to stop investing in companies involved in what the measure described as the "genocide, apartheid and occupation of Palestinians."
Among the companies identified were Israeli defense contractor Elbit Systems, U.S. technology company Palantir and aerospace giants Boeing, Lockheed Martin and GE Aerospace.
The vote followed a heated debate, after council members spent six hours at an earlier meeting hearing testimony from residents. When the vote was postponed at that meeting, audience members shouted, "You are all complicit in genocide" and "From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free."
The approved resolution calls on the city to develop its own list of companies that municipal pension funds could use when considering divestment. A separate proposal to extend the boycott to companies involved with the IDF through municipal procurement contracts, rather than investments alone, was also narrowly defeated.
A compromise over the BDS movement
The original proposal was introduced by City Council member Ayah Al-Zubi, a Harvard graduate. "This is the worst atrocity of our lifetimes, and we are invested in it," she said during the discussions. "I don't want blood on my hands, and none of us should."
Al-Zubi argued that while the United States imposes sanctions on countries such as China, Iran, Russia and Syria, it gives Israel a "blank check." Asked why she was singling out Israel, she replied, "I'm not making Israel look bad. I'm telling the truth."
Al-Zubi initially sought to adopt a list of approximately 100 companies compiled by the American Friends Service Committee (AFSC), a Quaker organization, which had gained support among activists affiliated with the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel.
Deputy Mayor Burhan Azeem, however, proposed a compromise: Cambridge would develop an independent list without formally adopting the BDS movement's platform. That version ultimately secured council approval.
According to Cambridge for Palestine, the activist group behind the initiative, the city's employee pension and benefits funds held approximately $24 million in investments in companies included on the original boycott list during fiscal year 2025. The group also claimed that Cambridge had spent about $4 million on contracts with companies supplying technology to the IDF and Israel Police.
The activists' list included three Israeli financial institutions, Bank Hapoalim, Bank Leumi and Israel Discount Bank, in which they estimated the municipal funds held approximately $660,000. The activists accused the banks of financing Israeli settlements.
One of the first companies on the list was Elbit Systems, which previously maintained offices in the area before leaving in 2024 following repeated pro-Palestinian demonstrations.
During one protest in 2023, nine demonstrators were arrested following clashes with police, even though the offices housed an Elbit subsidiary specializing in medical equipment development. Boycott activists portrayed the company's departure as a victory, while Elbit said the relocation was driven by business considerations.
The list also includes Palantir, the American software company that develops data analytics and artificial intelligence systems and works with security agencies, alongside major U.S. weapons manufacturers.
Broader boycott rejected over concerns for city services
The proposal to prohibit municipal procurement contracts with the targeted companies failed after Azeem, despite supporting investment divestment, voted against the broader measure.
He explained that such a restriction could undermine essential services and the city's ability to purchase equipment. During the debate, council members raised concerns that the proposed boycott could make it difficult for Cambridge to buy body cameras for its police officers.
Following the vote, pro-Palestinian activists shouted "Shame" at council members, while some left the chamber in anger.
The debate also divided the local Jewish community. Opponents warned that the resolution could fuel antisemitism and unfairly single out Israel. Jewish residents described fears about displaying their religious identity in public and incidents of harassment involving Jewish children at local schools.
Council members Denise Simmons and Patty Nolan also cited an incident in which an Israeli-owned business was vandalized with antisemitic graffiti while neighboring businesses were left untouched.
Simmons proposed applying a similar policy to companies implicated in war crimes around the world, rather than focusing on a single country.
Nolan warned that the measure was dividing the city and could attract unwanted attention from the Trump administration, which has already clashed with Harvard over allegations of discrimination and antisemitism.
Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, however, defended the initiative, saying it was about "corporate accountability and how Cambridge invests public funds," rather than religion or identity.
Jeremy Burton, executive director of the Jewish Community Relations Council of Greater Boston, criticized the resolution's use of the term "genocide." He nevertheless welcomed the council's decision to reject the broader commercial boycott and avoid formally adopting the BDS platform.
Pro-Palestinian activists celebrated the passage of the divestment resolution but expressed disappointment over the failure of the separate procurement proposal.
Harvard and MIT not covered by the decision
The controversy also reached Harvard's student newspaper, The Harvard Crimson, where an editorial supported divestment. Three members of the editorial board dissented, arguing that the City Council should focus on residents' needs rather than risk pension funds to make a political statement.
Despite the debate's proximity to two of the world's most prominent universities, neither Harvard nor MIT is a party to the decision. Both are independent institutions, and the Cambridge resolution does not apply to their investments or their relationships with Israel.
Cambridge is not the first municipality in the Boston area to consider such a move. In neighboring Somerville, residents supported a nonbinding referendum calling for divestment from companies linked to Israel.
But the Cambridge resolution carries additional symbolic significance because of the city's global reputation as a center of academia, innovation and the technology industry.

Deadly train crash deepens political crisis in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

23:07:11 KST

Deadly train crash deepens political crisis in Spain
A deadly high-speed train collision in Spain has deepened a political crisis engulfing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government ahead of next month’s general election, as opposition parties demand accountability. The disaster, which killed at least 69 people, has sparked angry protests and calls for resignations.
The collision occurred near Urda in Toledo province when a high-speed train operated by Spain’s state railway company Renfe struck a stationary train. Audio recordings obtained by El Pais suggest controllers breached safety protocols despite repeated warnings from the stationary train’s driver. It was Spain’s second major railway disaster this year, following a collision near Adamuz in January that killed 46 people.
The tragedy has become a major issue in Spain’s election campaign, with the right-wing Vox party blaming Sanchez and the left-wing Frente Amplio coalition demanding political accountability.
“Beyond technical responsibilities, we demand the assumption of political responsibilities. Out of responsibility and humanity,” Frente Amplio said in a statement on Wednesday.
The coalition, which includes parties allied with Sanchez’s government, called for an independent audit of the railway network, describing two deadly high-speed train accidents in one year as “unacceptable.”
The leader of the main opposition People’s Party, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, also demanded an immediate investigation into the state of Spain’s railways, but stopped short of calling for resignations.
“Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure, what condition the tracks and safety systems are in,” Feijoo said.
Public anger spilled onto the streets of Madrid on Wednesday, where protesters clashed with police outside the Transport Ministry while demanding the resignations of Sanchez and Transport Minister Oscar Puente. Some demonstrators hurled flares and other objects at officers, who responded with tear gas.
Vox and its affiliated trade union Solidaridad staged a separate rally in central Madrid, where protesters carried a banner reading “Corruption kills.”
Sanchez has promised a thorough investigation, calling two such disasters in one year unacceptable. He has also pledged to strengthen railway safety while standing by Puente, according to El Pais.
The tragedy has added to the Socialist-led government’s troubles following parliamentary defeats and mass protests over soaring housing costs. Sanchez called early elections after parliament rejected key housing measures in September, with the vote scheduled for November 29.

The tabloids that used Thomas Markle to attack Meghan should now reflect. I bet they won’t | Zoe Willliams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:06:57 UTC
23:06:57 KST

As the allegations mount against Thomas Markle Sr, his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, has released a statement describing her deep distress, and saying her priority is the protection of children. Is this the point at which Thomas Markle will cease to be an acceptable source for the Sussex character attacks that have become a tabloid staple? The Daily Mail and its sister paper, the Mail on Sunday, have been utterly brazen in their cultivation of the embittered Thomas Snr, using him as a weapon against his daughter since she first married into the royal family. Now, they’ll cut loose from him and describe the charges laid against him with the same outrage as everyone else. It would be institutionally impossible for them to discuss or reflect on their prior relationship with Markle without admitting a long-range and vindictive grudge against his daughter.
Markle denies all allegations against him. His son, Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jr, described in a video for the Sun the material he claims to have found on his father’s spare mobile phone, after Markle Sr had gone back to the US to have his leg amputated. Markle Jr was in the Philippines, where both men had moved in 2025. He said the material included “the most horrific video of a very young Asian girl … couldn’t have been more than 10 years old”. He almost threw up; he almost dropped the phone. His immediate fear was for what else he might be inadvertently in possession of. “I’m on the hook for this, now,” he said.
As he made contact with the FBI, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and the Pennsylvania state police, he reportedly found more and more material: “the most obscene, disgusting, lowest-of-the-low images … thousands and thousands of them.” He said he started to question every aspect of his family history, all the times his father had hastily snapped shut his laptop, “all the locked rooms in all the houses we’ve ever lived in”.
Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. In 2019, she was passed a letter alleging that he had sexually abused a child, which she says had been sent to the Metropolitan police. The Met took no action on that letter and it has been reported that they subsequently misplaced it – whether that’s because they could believe no ill of Thomas Markle, or simply because they lose things, is unknown.
But until now, the Daily Mail and the Mail on Sunday’s trust in Markle Sr and solidarity with him have been without question.
In 2018, he handed the Mail on Sunday a five-page letter that his daughter had written to him after her wedding, which he had declined to attend, citing health reasons. Meghan successfully sued Associated Newspapers for printing part of the letter, though “printing” doesn’t really encompass the torrent of coverage and insinuation they wrung from its contents. It was the start of a relationship between the newspaper and the now alleged sex offender that was so close by last year that when Thomas Markle learned about his amputation, the first person he told was Caroline Graham, the Mail on Sunday’s US editor (and previously a biographer of Queen Camilla). In photos of the pair together, the emotions are almost laughably legible: Markle looks pugnacious and triumphant, like the guy who’s managed to get public opinion on speed dial. Graham looks serene and also victorious, the first reporter on to Goose Green in the tabloids’ favourite war.
A free press is essential and sometimes it is scabrous. But is this what a free press is for? To groom an estranged parent or other former intimate of someone in public life in order to undermine the latter person’s credibility and standing, seems sadistic. That’s a large word, particularly in the context of the allegations against Thomas Markle, and I use it advisedly. One of the hideous things about family estrangement is the feeling that everyone involved has had their character besmirched. The accused fight back with counter-claims. Nobody’s probity survives unscathed (although most of us could tell that Meghan’s father was exploiting her lovelessly for attention, and probably cash, long before these charges surfaced).
A political or media enemy plundering that dynamic for an easy win, for clicks, for a vendetta, does not even have the fog of emotionality as a defence. Everybody recoils from it. When the Republican gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy, made an attack ad featuring his opponent’s mother calling her daughter, Amy Acton, a liar, most people didn’t know the history. They didn’t know that Donna Arthur had lost custody of her children decades previously, after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted on charges of child rape. People could nevertheless see how low it was to air a view that was poisonous by definition under the fig leaf of hearing from both sides.
Ramaswamy lost a major endorsement and had venue cancellations within a day of that attack ad. What the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday would have to lose to even reflect on their allegiances in this episode is impossible to guess.
- Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

ECB holds interest rates steady as rising energy prices cloud outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:05:29 UTC
23:05:29 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
The European Central Bank (ECB) left its three key interest rates unchanged on Thursday, warning that rising energy prices pose upside risks to inflation and downside risks to economic growth.
The decision keeps the benchmark deposit facility rate at 2.5%, the main refinancing operations rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending facility rate at 2.9%, the bank said in a statement.
"While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage," the Governing Council said.
"The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth," it added.
The central bank noted that financing conditions have tightened since its previous policy meeting, which is expected to weigh on both price pressures and economic expansion.
Reiterating its commitment to ensuring inflation stabilizes at its 2% medium-term target, the bank emphasized that it is not pre-committing to a specific interest rate path.
"The Governing Council remains well positioned to navigate the current elevated uncertainty," the statement said, confirming that policymakers will maintain a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach based on incoming economic and financial data.
The bank also confirmed that its asset purchase program and pandemic emergency purchase program portfolios continue to decline at a measured and predictable pace, as the Eurosystem no longer reinvests principal payments from maturing securities.

Russia Keeps S-400 Systems on Combat Readiness in Kaliningrad Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:03:24 UTC
23:03:24 KST

Russian S-400 air defense missile systems in the Kaliningrad region are in a state of constant combat readiness.
This is stated in the Baltic Sea Overwatch report, published by ICEYE.
Satellite imagery has captured launchers at an air defense position near the port of Baltiysk in the deployed position.
The raised launchers indicate that the systems are ready to launch anti-aircraft missiles, rather than simply being on standby at their positions.
The company notes that this is not a temporary measure, as satellite monitoring indicates that this deployment has been in place in the Kaliningrad region for quite some time.
Baltiysk is one of Russia’s key naval bases in the region and the home port of the Baltic Fleet.
The deployment of air defense assets near the port strengthens the air defense of Russian military infrastructure in the Kaliningrad exclave.
The 183rd Guards Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment is one of the air defense units in the Kaliningrad region, which historically was part of the Baltic Fleet’s 44th Air Defense Division.
At the same time, the ICEYE report does not specify which unit occupies the position near Baltiysk.
The Kaliningrad region is a key deployment area for Russian air defense assets in the Baltic theater. Previously, the 183rd and 1,545th Guards Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiments, armed with S-400 systems, were stationed in the region.
In November 2023, Militarnyi reported that Russia had redeployed S-400 air defense systems from the Kaliningrad region to Rostov-on-Don. At that time, according to the news report, an analysis of satellite imagery revealed the movement of components of these systems from several positions in the region.

Russia's sanctioned Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov is heading to a G20 meeting in the US, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova stated. Ukraine, meanwhile, is still waiting for Washington's sign-off on the air defense missiles it needs.
Ukraine is fighting Russia's air war while its main ally squeezes it too, from capped Starlink links to missing US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles, leaving Kyiv weaker before any talks. A new round of the US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral talks is expected in Abu Dhabi in November.
Moscow's sanctioned minister plans to argue against sanctions
Lavrov will lead the Russian delegation at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting, which the US hosts in Atlanta on 30–31 October. In his speeches, he will denounce “the use of economic ‘weapons’ to fight opponents, including sanctions,” Russia's Foreign Ministry stated. The US Treasury sanctioned Lavrov on 25 February 2022, the day after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The ministry claimed its delegation ran into American red tape over visas. Journalists in Lavrov's press pool still received US visas without movement restrictions, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
The State Department's announcement of the meeting doesn't mention Russia or say whether Lavrov got a sanctions waiver. Republican Congressman Don Bacon told RFE/RL that Russian leaders “should not be welcomed in any of these forums.” “They lead a pariah state,” he said.
Moscow's demands arrive days after its missiles hit Kyiv
Lavrov will also stress “the cornerstone importance of indivisible security” as the basis of multipolarity, the ministry stated. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has ruled out neutrality and limits on Ukraine's army.
Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv university campus, then return before dawn for the Southern Bridge again
A day before the trip was announced, Lavrov called the US-Russia diesel deal a purely business arrangement. “There were no strings attached,” he claimed.
Lavrov brings these demands days after Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv university campus and the Southern Bridge, killing a 46-year-old woman, the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office reported. Kyiv has waited almost a month for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's signature on Patriot and NASAMS missiles, Zelenskyy wrote.
Moscow keeps collecting from Washington
The visit adds to a run of US moves in Moscow's favor. This month, the US Treasury cleared Russian diesel blocked by sanctions. US President Donald Trump then waived tariffs on buyers of Russian oil. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright also said investors could buy sanctioned shadow-fleet tankers and return them to legal trade. Russia, for its part, kept striking Ukraine's energy sites during the truce Trump announced.
Russian officials are also back in G20 rooms in person. In late August, Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended a G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. It was his first in-person G20 appearance since 2022, and European officials refused to join the group photo with him. The State Department has stated that Russia is welcome at all G20 meetings, and a senior US official said Russia would be invited to the leaders' summit in Miami in December.
Western ministers used to push back at those tables. When Lavrov spoke at the G20 meeting in Johannesburg in February 2025, then-British Foreign Secretary David Lammy said he saw no appetite for peace.
In Atlanta, Obama accuses the White House of selling out Ukrainians
Former US President Barack Obama campaigned in Atlanta on 28 October, two days before Lavrov's meeting there.
“And while we're alienating key allies like Canada, the White House is bending the knee to Vladimir Putin of Russia and selling out Ukrainians who are fighting for their freedom and democracy,” Obama said.
He also likened Trump's self-enrichment in office to “what dictators in other countries do.”

Finnish news agency STT to cease operations with loss of 89 jobs
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:01:25 EET
23:01:25 KST

The Finnish News Agency STT will wind down the news and photojournalism units of its business from March next year.
The move will lead to the loss of 89 jobs at one of the oldest operating news agencies in the world.
STT announced last month that the company's board was planning to cease operations after nearly 140 years, a decision labelled "shocking" by Finland's journalism union Journalistiliitto. In a press release at the time, the agency said the restructure was prompted by long-standing losses and a challenging operating environment.
When the restructuring and redundancy talks with staff representatives were launched, the company said the status of all 95 permanent employees were included in the talks. Yle understands that six people will be offered the opportunity to continue working for the company in non-journalistic roles.
STT's Viestintäpalvelut (communication service) unit, which distributes press releases, will continue operating after March. It employs seven people, who were excluded from the restructuring negotiations.
End of an era
The impending shutdown of STT's news and photojournalism units comes after years of financial struggles.
Last year, STT's largest shareholder, Sanoma Media Finland, announced plans to significantly reduce its use of the agency's news and photo services — leading to a restructuring round and casting significant doubt over the agency's future.
The government granted STT around one million euros in state aid, but the money was not accepted by the agency as it was not deemed enough to keep it afloat.
The Helsinki-based agency was founded in 1887, and throughout its history its news and photojournalism services have been widely used by all major Finnish media outlets.
"The news is devastating," Marjaana Varmavuori, chair of the Union of Journalists in Finland, wrote in a press release. "STT is not just one media company among others. Its role in producing and distributing reliable information in Finland is irreplaceable."

Why some men don’t flex when their manhood is challenged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:00:50 UTC
23:00:50 KST

Men who blend emotional openness and progressive gender attitudes into their sense of manhood appear to be less reactive when their masculinity is called into question, according to new research published in Social Psychology Quarterly. While men often respond to gender-related insecurities by exaggerating tough, dominant attitudes, men in this experiment who more strongly endorsed a flexible masculine identity showed less of that overcompensation. The findings suggest that how men react to challenges to their gender status depends in part on how they define manhood for themselves.
In sociology and psychology, the dominant cultural ideal of manhood in a society is known as hegemonic masculinity. In the United States, this traditional standard expects men to be physically tough, emotionally guarded, self-reliant, heterosexual, dominant, and strictly avoidant of anything considered feminine. Because meeting all of these rigid standards at all times is nearly impossible, many men experience their gender status as fragile and easily challenged. When a man feels that his manhood has been doubted, he may engage in masculine overcompensation, which is the tendency to exaggerate aggressive, dominant, or traditionally macho behaviors in an effort to prove his status to himself and others.
Psychological research has repeatedly shown how easily this defensive reaction can be triggered. For example, a 2008 series of experiments demonstrated that people widely view manhood as an uncertain social status that must be earned and can be easily lost through a single unmanly act. Building on that idea, a 2013 experimental study found that men who were falsely told they scored in the feminine range on a survey about gender identity reacted by expressing greater support for war, more negative attitudes toward gay people, and stronger interest in purchasing sport utility vehicles.
When men face doubts about their manhood, the effects can be physical as well as attitudinal, and individual differences shape how strongly they react. In a study covered by PsyPost in 2017, men whose masculinity was challenged tried to display physical toughness by administering higher voltages of electric shock to their own arms, especially if they already saw themselves as highly masculine.
Most research on masculine overcompensation has assumed that all men measure themselves against a single, traditional standard of toughness and dominance. In recent years, however, sociologists have documented the rise of what they call hybrid masculinity, a gender style in which men selectively incorporate traits typically associated with women or marginalized groups into their identity.
A man practicing hybrid masculinity might openly discuss his emotions, follow a skincare routine, show physical affection to male friends, or voice support for feminism and LGBTQ+ rights. The authors of a 2014 sociological review argued that adopting these traits allows relatively privileged men to create symbolic distance between themselves and traditional macho norms while still retaining their broader social status.
If hybrid masculinity gives men a way to feel secure in their gender identity without relying on rigid toughness, it raises the question of whether these men still feel compelled to act dominant when their manhood is challenged. Justin Huft, a PhD candidate in sociology at the University of California, Riverside, designed an experiment to test whether endorsing hybrid masculinity shields men from the tendency to overcompensate. Huft also set out to create the first survey tool designed to measure hybrid masculinity in statistical research.
“While there has been interesting work done on masculine overcompensation, it has largely depicted masculinity as a monolithic identity,” Huft told PsyPost. “This is inconsistent with some other work in the masculinities literature, which depicts multiple forms of masculinity. My aim was to explore how masculine overcompensation looks when accounting for another form of masculine identity.”
To test this idea, Huft recruited 988 heterosexual adult men living in the United States through the online research platform Connect. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 83, with an average age of about 40 years, and reported an average household income between $50,000 and $59,999 per year. Roughly 65 percent of the men identified as white, 15 percent as Black, 10 percent as Asian, 8 percent as Latinx, and 2 percent as another racial background. Politically, about 46 percent described themselves as liberal, 31 percent as conservative, and 22 percent as moderate, while 54 percent reported having a religious affiliation.
Before receiving any feedback, participants rated their baseline level of traditional masculinity. They also completed Huft’s newly developed 20-item hybrid masculinity questionnaire on a 5-point scale. Statistical testing showed that the new scale captured two closely related aspects of hybrid masculinity: progressive gender attitudes, such as supporting women’s and LGBTQ+ rights or agreeing that men can wear makeup, and emotional expressiveness, such as telling others when feeling sad, showing empathy, and expressing affection toward male friends.
Participants also answered questions measuring three concepts from sociological identity theory: how important being masculine was to their overall sense of self (known as identity prominence), how frequently they thought about their masculinity in daily situations like work or social events (known as identity salience), and how much they felt close friends and family viewed their masculinity the same way they did (known as identity verification).
For the experimental manipulation, participants completed items that appeared to evaluate their masculinity and were then given false feedback on a 0 to 100 scale, where 0 represented feminine and 100 represented masculine. Men were randomly assigned to either a non-threatening group, where they were told that their answers placed them at the high end of the average male range, or a threatening group, where they were told that they scored at the high end of the average female range.
Following the feedback, participants completed a 21-item questionnaire measuring their agreement with traditional, dominant masculine norms on a scale from 1 to 7. This questionnaire assessed seven hallmarks of rigid manhood: emotional restriction, self-reliance, negative views of gay people, avoidance of femininity, placing a high priority on sex, desiring dominance as a leader, and valuing physical toughness.
Prior to receiving the false feedback, the two groups did not differ in their baseline traditional masculinity, measured with a separate questionnaire on which the sample averaged 5.08 out of 7. After the feedback was delivered, however, men who were told they scored in the average female range endorsed higher levels of rigid masculine norms, averaging 3.19 out of 7 compared to 2.97 out of 7 among men who were told they scored in the male range. That difference is small, about one-sixth of the typical spread in scores, but it indicates that the experimental threat triggered masculine overcompensation across the sample as a whole.
Huft then ran statistical regression models that controlled for baseline masculinity, identity importance, everyday awareness of masculinity, identity verification, religiosity, political conservatism, race, and household income. Even after accounting for all of those factors, receiving the masculinity-threatening feedback predicted a 0.17-point increase in dominant masculine norms in the baseline model, while scoring higher on hybrid masculinity was strongly linked to lower endorsement of those rigid norms overall.
When Huft tested how the two factors interacted, he found that hybrid masculinity moderated the impact of the threat, reducing the overcompensation effect by 0.23 points for each 1-point increase on the hybrid masculinity scale. In practical terms, men with low hybrid masculinity scores showed a larger increase in rigid, dominant attitudes after their manhood was questioned, whereas the gap between the threatened and non-threatened groups shrank toward zero among men who strongly endorsed hybrid masculinity.
Several background characteristics also predicted higher endorsement of rigid masculine norms regardless of which feedback participants received. Men who thought about their masculinity frequently in daily life, held more conservative political views, had lower household incomes, or identified as non-white tended to endorse traditional masculine norms more strongly.
The overall presence of a defensive reaction aligns with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that threats to manhood heightened support for aggressive political and foreign-policy strategies, though that earlier work focused on political aggression rather than personal masculine norms and observed the effect among liberal men rather than conservative men. In Huft’s study, by contrast, men who scored high on hybrid masculinity tended to be more politically liberal and reacted less to the threat.
The new findings also stand in tension with a study covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which did not find an increase in conservative political views, support for war, or homophobia after a masculinity threat, though that study examined broader political and social attitudes rather than the comprehensive inventory of personal masculine norms used by Huft.
Huft offers two possible explanations for the buffering pattern found in his study. Men who embrace emotional openness and progressive views may have already loosened the tie between their sense of self-worth and traditional macho ideals, making feedback about feminine traits less upsetting, or they may draw on other aspects of their identity, such as emotional maturity or humor, to feel secure without needing to act tough.
While this flexibility appears to reduce aggressive overcompensation at the individual level, Huft cautions that hybrid masculinity does not automatically dismantle gender inequality in society. Instead, sociological theory suggests that blending softer traits into manhood can allow men to present themselves as modern and progressive while quietly preserving the social privileges associated with being a man.
“Masculinity isn’t just one thing,” Huft explained. “It contains different attitudes, behaviors, and characteristics. These different constellations of masculinity cause people to perceive and experience masculinity threats differently. This, in turn, creates different sorts of responses to masculinity threats.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because men who scored high on the new hybrid masculinity scale also tended to report that being masculine was less central to their overall identity, the questionnaire cannot completely untangle whether these men were strategically blending gender traits to maintain their status or whether they simply cared less about manhood altogether. In addition, the experiment could not capture why men adopted hybrid traits in the first place, such as whether they adopted those traits preemptively, in response to past challenges to their manhood, or for unrelated reasons.
Hybrid masculinity was also measured rather than assigned, so men who scored high on it differed from low scorers in other ways. Most notably, they tended to be much more politically liberal, and the study did not test whether political views shaped how men responded to the threat. The new scale has so far been tested in only this one sample, and the study did not report whether participants believed the false feedback.
The study also focused exclusively on heterosexual, cisgender men in the United States, meaning the findings cannot be generalized to gay, bisexual, or transgender men. According to hybrid masculinity theorists, the ability to adopt feminine or non-traditional traits without facing harsh social penalties is often easiest for white, middle-class, heterosexual men, so future studies will need to test whether hybrid masculinity works the same way across different racial and socioeconomic groups.
It is also possible that for men who pride themselves on being progressive and emotionally sensitive, being told they scored as highly masculine could actually feel like a threat to their progressive self-image, prompting them to distance themselves even further from traditional manhood. Finally, future research could explore whether men whose manhood is challenged try to restore their pride in areas outside of gender altogether, such as by emphasizing their career achievements or financial status.
The study, “Hybrid Masculinity as a Buffer against Threats to Masculinity,” was authored by Justin Huft.

My sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. What can I do? | Leading questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:00:47 UTC
23:00:47 KST

My sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. No matter how high or low the stakes, she has to win. When she doesn’t, she becomes explosive with rage, and often upends the game, sweeps dice off the table, or storms off in a rage. She is otherwise a normal and lovely person, with whom I get on very well. Seeing this side of her makes me deeply uncomfortable and it feels really childish and inappropriate. Will she behave that way with me if I say or do something she doesn’t like?
I think in an effort to smooth the tension, my husband’s family always laughs and teases her about her reaction. It’s like her “special little characteristic” that everyone pretends to love. I wish there was a way to address it but everyone seems to just sweep it under the rug. My husband is aware of how I feel about this.
Recently, she’s started dating a new partner, who is absolutely lovely. When she has a big reaction after board games I can also sense him tensing up, so I know this is affecting more than just me. Ultimately, I’m worried for my sister-in-law that if she continues this behaviour, and the family continues to indulge it, she will suffer personal and professional consequences. I also don’t enjoy being around the dynamic, and think it is likely we’ll spend less time with her as a result. What can I do?
Eleanor says: I know someone who ended a relationship because their partner too gleefully teamed up with an ex to lie in a game of wink murder. I know someone who decided not to have kids with their then partner because when he played with kids, he got a kick out of really scaring them. I know someone whose friendship never recovered after one shouted the c-word in a card game.
Often it’s in the fictional that we most see the real.
It’s not that the way you behave in a game is a straightforward guide to the kind of person you are. The whole reason games are fun is that that isn’t true. Games let you experiment with being a different kind of person; they let you explore different kinds of agency. They are fun and absorbing precisely because you focus on a single goal or way of reasoning. A game is a vacation from the rules and goals of normal life, and an excursion into new ones.
But games aren’t meant to be a moral exemption to your usual self. They’re meant to let you play with and develop your usual self by putting it in unusual circumstances. Treating games as a forum for exorcising the worst parts of yourself with the petulant excuse “it’s just a game” misunderstands the whole enterprise.
So what can you do about your sister in law doing exactly that?
You’re astute to notice that the family going along with it doesn’t help. And you’re astute to notice that their laughter might be a bid to make things less awkward – not a sign that they actually enjoy it. Like how we laugh after an off-colour comment, hoping to social magic it into counting as a joke. They might hope that if they applaud, make this “her thing”, that transforms her behaviour into a fun bit – not just an adult having a tantrum.
Their approach might make things less awkward, but it doesn’t give the disruptive person evidence of how disruptive they are. As always, the more you paper over the cracks someone’s created, the less you can be surprised when they don’t notice them.
Sometimes the best way to puncture “it’s just a game” is to show people that you’re judging them in reality.
You don’t have to say “don’t do that” or “why are you so mad” while they’re heated. (In fact, if it’s a real anger management thing, it’s better not to). You can just let your sincere attitude show in a moment they presumed would be structured by the fiction. A long look without a smile or a laugh. Silence. A hint of the ick it’s giving you in real life. In the same way that laughing along is a bid to turn a tantrum into a joke, reacting as you would in other circumstances can be a bid to separate her behaviour from the game.
Awkward, yes; socially costly, yes. But as with all things, if you want her to know you’d prefer she stopped this, you have to endure the discomfort of her learning how you feel.
The boyfriend who lied in wink murder, the man who scared the kids and the friend who shouted in the card game didn’t realise that the way they acted in games would affect how people saw them in real life, until it was too late. A long look across the table now – or even a quiet word from a relative once she’s calmed down – is a much kinder way for her to find out.
The reader’s letter has been edited.

Erin Patterson is set to find out if she could face a longer prison sentence or a new trial, as Victoria’s highest court hands down its decision on two appeals regarding her triple murder case.
The court of appeal is set to rule on the two appeals from 10am on Friday, after justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd heard arguments from her legal team and prosecutors in August.
Patterson, 52, is not expected to attend the appeal decision in person.
She was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.
Patterson was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.
She has appealed against her convictions, while the director of public prosecutions appealed against Patterson’s sentence, arguing that it was manifestly inadequate.
In August, the court heard Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars.
Her lawyers argued seven grounds for her appeal, including that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.
Richard Edney, for Patterson, said the failure to properly separate the jury during their deliberations was a fundamental irregularity that had denied her a fair trial.
“What we say has occurred here in the applicant’s trial was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure of a process,” Edney told the court in August.
They also argued that the trial judge Christopher Beale erred in ruling that photos and videos related to mushrooms and found on an SD card in Patterson’s home was inadmissible, as it tended to support her evidence that she foraged for mushrooms.
During the hearings, Brendan Kissane KC, the DPP, said that even though Patterson would be aged in her 80s by the time she was eligible for parole, her sentence was still too lenient.
When asked whether a longer non-parole period would essentially damn Patterson to dying behind bars, and had “some artifice of it being life with life”, Kissane told the court: “It has its harsh aspect to it, of course, we accept that.”
“But in our submission that is not a matter that is outweighed by the seriousness of the offending.”
There are several possible outcomes to Patterson’s appeal: leave to appeal is not granted; leave to appeal is granted, but her appeal dismissed; leave to appeal is granted, her appeal upheld and a retrial ordered; or her leave to appeal is granted, the appeal upheld, and acquittal entered.
If either of the final two decisions are handed down, there will be no need to rule on the DPP’s sentence appeal.
If not, either the appeal fails, or it succeeds and Patterson is resentenced by the court of appeal.

My phone thinks my boyfriend is my ‘best friend’. It’s not alone | Patrick Lenton
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:00:46 UTC
23:00:46 KST

My boyfriend and I invented a game on our recent trip to Italy. We called it “invisible gays”, which might have been an attempt at some kind of word play around “gays” and “gaze” – but I was on holiday and feeling lazy, so I didn’t push it.
The game began when one night he took me out to a little trattoria to celebrate my birthday. It was a warm night, and fairy lights were entangled in the fragrant blooming flowers over our heads, and we drank good wine and ate bowls of perfect pasta, and there was candlelight, and it was so romantic I wouldn’t have blinked if two dogs had started smooching over a strand of spaghetti. Che bello!
We were one of four tables, all couples of various ages looking at each other with disgusting wet amorous eyes. During the evening a man selling roses approached the other tables. One young guy even bought one, presenting the blossom with a flourish to his girlfriend, earning applause from other patrons and a round of toothy photos. Caught up in the moment, my partner pulled out his wallet to buy a rose for me too, despite my wildly insincere protestations – but the rose man didn’t even clock us as a couple and wandered off into the night.
I briefly wondered if it was because my outfit wasn’t chic enough for Rome. Then I realised we were the only couple who weren’t the societal default setting of a man and a woman, having instead made the dire mistake of being two beautiful men dining together. I wonder if he thought we were some kind of complicated interracial brothers?
This continued all around Italy, with more than seven episodes of being passed over at romantic tourist traps marked on our scorecard. When I organised a fancy dinner for my boyfriend’s birthday weeks later, one of the servers said I was a “good friend” for doing so.
I’m used to the way that being in a same-sex couple can make you hyper visible or put a homophobic spotlight on you, so that it feels like every time you kiss in public it’s like Frodo putting on the One Ring, drawing the attention of the Dark Lord and his screeching Nazgûl. I’m used to muttered comments from people you walk by on the streets when you’re holding hands, or of making out with a tall guy outside a bar after our first date only for a car full of men to stop and yell slurs at us. I’m used to holding the hand of a boyfriend as we were chased down the backstreets of Newtown late at night by three silent men.
I’ve also dated enough women to know that there’s a contrast – no woman I’ve ever dated has flinched away from a kiss on the cheek and whispered: “Maybe not in public.” I’ve had men I’ve dated comment on how “openly affectionate” I am, because I haven’t had to learn to self-censor my public love languages. Women I date usually just comment on how clean my legs are and how many Gilmore Girls references I make.
Obviously being hyper visible and therefore at risk of overt and violent homophobia is worse than not being able to buy an overpriced street flower. Over the past year in Australia, hate crimes against gay and bisexual men have been making headlines. As someone who has suffered a hate crime or two, I can confirm that dealing with this should be the authorities’ priority instead of cracking down on the rose men of Rome.
But with the 10-year anniversary of the marriage equality win coming up next year, it’s worth looking at all the ways being in a same-sex relationship can still make you weirdly invisible. It’s another argument for why Mardi Gras, pride flags and Idahobit days in schools are still so necessary – because, when love between queer people goes unseen, it makes it seem as though it isn’t “normal”. And when queer identity is treated as abnormal, it fertilises the ground necessary to justify violence against queer people.
We all know the little “collections” of photos and videos our smartphones occasionally create. This can be anything from “Your trip in Italy 2026” to “Furry pals throughout the years”. It’s been a source of constant amusement to me that it sorts all the photos of my boyfriend and me into a collection called “best friends”. These are photos of two men kissing and, without oversharing, sometimes photos of two men doing things even more intimate than kissing (kayaking).
It shows you that homosexual invisibility is so hardwired into aspects of society that a phone short-circuits and decides that two men in love are just good bros. I’ve never had any of the women I’ve dated put into a folder called “best friends”. In fact, none of the women who are my actual best friends have made it into those folders either. My dog does get filed there, which, when its alongside my boyfriend, feels a little like one of those slippery slope arguments made by the Australian Christian Lobby during the plebiscite.
It seems as though we have a Goldilocks problem with queer relationship visibility: there’s too much visibility or there’s not enough. Make up your mind!
Not only do I simply want to express my love for my boyfriend publicly and without risk of violence, and for it to be recognised for what it is; I also don’t want my sexuality to be the only thing that people notice me for. I want to be noticed for my abnormally good looks and sex appeal.

How £100 vanishes in minutes: inside the ‘slot farms’ targeted in the budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:00:45 UTC
23:00:45 KST

AGC's and bookmakers line Peterborough street, some open 24 hours a day
How £100 vanishes in minutes: inside the ‘slot farms’ targeted in the budget
John Healey has hit adult gaming centres with 25% tax. Undercover footage shows how they lure customers
The last of five £20 notes disappears into the slot machine as The Verve’s Bittersweet Symphony plays over the shop’s sound system.
That’s it, £100 gone in the space of about five minutes, swallowed up by one of the many “slot farms” that dominate the shopping streets of Peterborough.
All that’s left to show for it is a free KitKat, one of the incentives staff use to tempt customers into staying a little longer and losing a little more.
It’s lunchtime on a Thursday and dozens of glassy-eyed hopefuls are having the same experience, feeding in what little cash they have and cursing as it disappears.
The same pattern is repeated across the country. Gamblers in Great Britain lost £2.7bn on slot machines last year, nearly double the annual budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which oversees the sector.
In his inaugural budget this week, the chancellor, John Healey, took direct aim at slot machines by raising “machine games duty”, the tax levied on them, from 20% to 25%. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.
But what is the reality of Britain’s booming slot machine industry and why is it in the government’s crosshairs?
What are slot machines?
The most popular machines in the UK are so-called category B3 terminals. They allow you to stake £2 every 2.5 seconds for a jackpot of up to £500. A £2 maximum stake may not sound like a lot but losses can stack up quickly. In this test, £100 is gone in just five minutes.
How £100 disappears in five minutes on high-speed B3 terminal machine
That’s one reason why each machine earns £40,000 a year on average, more than the median pay of a British worker. Slot machines are found in bookmakers, casinos and bingo halls but the venues that really pack them are adult gaming centres (AGCs), sometimes known as slot farms.
How are AGCs making their money?
They’re on pretty much every British high street, disproportionately in poorer areas. On some, such as this stretch in Peterborough, almost every shop is a bookmaker or an AGC.
By far the two biggest AGC operators are Admiral, which is owned by an Austrian billionaire, and Merkur, owned by a German billionaire. Both have targeted the UK for growth in recent years.
Why are AGCs controversial?
AGCs have their critics, including Andy Burnham, who has accused them of “targeting some of the most vulnerable in our communities”. Notable examples include when Merkur was fined £100,000 in 2025, after the Guardian revealed it had allowed an older woman with terminal cancer to rack up huge losses over two spells lasting 16 hours.
As well as the potential for rapid losses, the machines are associated with higher rates of problem gambling than products such as sports betting. Critics also point to practices apparently designed to keep punters playing and losing. For a start, the majority of venues are open 24 hours a day, while the Guardian has previously revealed that staff are paid bonuses linked to customers’ losses, undermining their incentive to intervene to prevent problem gambling.
Shops are increasingly offering a new breed of super slot machine, featuring a comfy armchair and a highly-immersive, 65-inch screen. Staff will offer drinks and snacks to keep punters playing, there are regular prize draws and “free spin” offers, and you can make cash withdrawals from your bank without leaving the shop.
Punters will sometimes play more than one machine simultaneously. Admiral has introduced a two-machine limit, which it says is designed to reduce harmful gambling.
Many are open under bingo licences, which may sound more benign to local authority planning committees. In practice, most have one bingo machine that is rarely used, if ever.
Bingo machines are not in working order and are rarely used
Can you win?
On a one-off basis, it’s possible to win up to £500. In tests across several AGC venues, the Guardian occasionally won some money, which will be donated to charity. But the machines have a fixed “return to player”, meaning that regular slot machine players will always lose. That’s why slots are a good target for a tax raid, and a valuable cash cow for companies, which like predictable sources of income. It’s also why gambling harm experts think they’re dangerous.
Will the budget tax raid change things?
Bookmakers say it will cost them money, leading to shop closures. Entain, which owns Ladbrokes, expects a £25m hit. But shares in the three listed slot machine operators – Entain, the William Hill owner Evoke and the Grosvenor Casinos owner Rank Group – rose sharply after the budget. Relieved investors had feared Healey would opt for a 40% rate.
AGCs were singled out by the chancellor, who said they and vape shops would be excluded from business rates relief, costing them a combined £10m. But AGCs appear well-placed to thrive anyway because of their low overheads and 24-hour opening. For the slot farms, it’s business as usual.
What do the slots companies say?
Neither Admiral nor Merkur responded to a request for comment. Bacta, the slot machine trade body, said its members’ venues were “among the safest places to gamble, with experienced staff on hand to identify problems and provide support to customers”.
“Player protection is central to our approach, and machines in AGCs are designed with inbuilt tools to encourage safe play, facilitate self-exclusion and help prevent problem gambling,” it said.
“Games in these venues are low-stake – costing as little as 10p a spin – and these businesses have been a longstanding part of the high street for decades, providing low-stake entertainment, local jobs and a boost to local economies. AGCs tend to open on high streets where there is already footfall, alongside other hospitality and leisure venues, and where planning and licensing permissions allow.
“Our members operate within one of the most tightly regulated licensing regimes in the world. Venues are regularly inspected, must comply with strict conditions, and can have licences refused or revoked where licensing objectives are at risk.”

Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

23:00:00 KST

A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.
The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.
“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”
The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.
The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)
Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.
Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.
“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”
According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.
“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

Russian military personnel losses in October 2026 have reached 49,040 as of October 29, marking the highest monthly figure since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The General Staff reported that the previous monthly record was registered in December 2024, when Russian forces suffered 48,670 personnel losses.
With October still underway, Russia’s average daily personnel losses have reached approximately 1,750, according to Ukrainian military estimates.
The figures also indicate a substantial increase in Russian losses over recent months. In February 2026, Russian forces sustained an estimated 26,090 personnel losses, compared with 46,230 in September and 49,040 as of October 29.
“Why this matters: The rate of Russian personnel losses exceeds the military’s ability to replenish its units. Each month of the war is becoming increasingly costly for Russia’s armed forces,” the General Staff added.
Ukrainian drone strikes have killed or wounded more than 302,000 Russian military personnel since the beginning of 2026, averaging over 1,000 casualties per day in less than ten months, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported on October 27.
March recorded the highest number of Russian personnel casualties from Ukrainian drone strikes, with 33,989 soldiers killed or wounded. April followed with 33,961 casualties, while February saw the lowest monthly total at 26,204.
Throughout the year, Ukrainian drone units have consistently inflicted tens of thousands of casualties on Russian forces each month. Monthly totals exceeded 30,000 in January, March, April, May, July, and September.
In September alone, drone strikes killed or wounded 32,739 Russian troops. During the first 25 days of October, Ukrainian forces recorded an additional 27,829 Russian personnel casualties from drone operations.
Overall, as of October 29, 2026, Russia’s estimated personnel losses since the beginning of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine had reached approximately 1,584,910, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.

Russia has around 140 Su-34 aircraft of various modifications — DIU

Russia has around 140 Su-34s and continues to produce them. Since the beginning of the invasion, 43 aircraft have been destroyed and seven more damaged.
The Russian Aerospace Forces have approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service, which are the main carriers of glide bombs and precision-guided missiles used by the enemy to attack Ukraine’s frontline regions. This was reported by the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence, reports UNN.
Details
Su-34 fighter-bombers are one of the key components of the aggressor state Russia’s strike aviation in the war against Ukraine. Their use as carriers of guided aerial bombs has enabled the occupation army to expand its ability to strike ground targets, particularly in areas of active hostilities and frontline settlements
The intelligence agency notes that, despite significant combat losses, Russia continues to produce and modernize Su-34s, attempting to maintain the size of its aircraft fleet and preserve the intensity of its missile and bomb strikes.
At the same time, the ability to further expand this capability depends on production capacity, the availability of technological components, and the ability of Russia’s defence industry to compensate for losses.
As of October 22, 2026, approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications, including modernized Su-34Ms (Su-34NVOs), are in service with the Russian Aerospace Forces
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russia has lost 43 aircraft of this type destroyed, while another seven have been damaged.
Such losses are quite substantial for the aggressor’s aircraft fleet, whose restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, significant financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation. For comparison, the number of destroyed Su-34s is equivalent to approximately 2.5–3 years of their production at estimated capacities of 14–18 aircraft annually
During Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, the role of the Su-34 in the aggressor’s strike aviation has undergone a significant transformation. At the initial stage of the invasion, these aircraft were primarily used to bomb ground targets with unguided aerial bombs, including FAB-250, FAB-500 M-62, and BetAB-500 concrete-piercing bombs.
The use of such weapons required approaching the targets, which increased the aircraft’s vulnerability to Ukrainian air defence systems.
At the same time, Su-34s began to be used as carriers of Kh-31 and Kh-59 guided air-launched missiles, as well as, in some cases, Kh-35U anti-ship missiles to strike ground targets.
We remind you
The Ukrainian Navy destroyed four Russian Su-34 bombers, while two more were damaged on the territory of Borysoglebsk airfield. This aircraft is a deeply modernized version of the basic frontline Su-34 bomber, which Russia began serial production of in 2020. Thanks to its new hardpoints, the aircraft is the main carrier of glide bombs and precision-guided missiles used by the enemy to attack Ukraine’s frontline regions.
