Authorities in Kazakhstan have removed a monument to Vladimir Lenin from the village of Kushmurun in Kostanay region as part of wider efforts to reduce Soviet-era influence across Central Asia, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported on October 29.
The monument was dismantled at the request of the regional administration after local residents collected nearly 400 signatures supporting its removal. Previous attempts to remove it in 2015 and 2022 had failed after opposition from supporters of the Soviet legacy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The initiative group supporting the demolition linked Soviet rule directly to mass famine and political repression in Kazakhstan. Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service noted that estimates of deaths during the Asharshylyk famine of the early 1930s reach as high as 2.3 million people, nearly half of Kazakhstan’s population at the time.
Some researchers have described the catastrophe as the “Kazakh Holodomor,” drawing parallels with the Holodomor in Ukraine.
Ukraine’s intelligence service stated that the removal of the Lenin monument and growing public discussion of Soviet-era repression have unsettled Russian political strategists because they challenge Moscow’s narrative of a prosperous shared Soviet past.
Russia presents itself internationally as the legal successor to the Soviet Union. The intelligence service argued that renewed attention to the individual histories of former Soviet republics, including famine, repression, and forced political control, undermines the mythology surrounding the Soviet period.
Similar de-Sovietization processes have intensified elsewhere in Central Asia, although their form differs between countries.
In Kyrgyzstan, calls for broader decommunization and derussification have grown during 2026. Uzbekistan has been described as a regional leader in this process, while Tajikistan has emphasized national identity and historical memory.
Turkmenistan has pursued its own model centered on national sovereignty within an isolationist and neutral foreign policy.
Despite those differences, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service assessed that de-Sovietization, decommunization, and derussification efforts across Central Asia share a common objective of reducing dependence on and influence from Russia.
The trend contrasts with Russian efforts to revive Soviet symbolism in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories. UNITED24 Media previously reported that Russian authorities in temporarily occupied eastern Ukrainian city of Luhansk promoted Stalin and Lenin imagery during a February 14 propaganda event, replacing traditional Valentine’s Day themes with Soviet symbols.

A majority of American voters believe Russian leader Vladimir Putin is deliberately delaying efforts to end the war in Ukraine, while nearly two-thirds support continued military assistance to Kyiv and stronger sanctions against Moscow if Russia refuses to negotiate and prolongs the war, according to the October Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll, conducted by HarrisX.
The survey, which polled 2,700 registered US voters between October 24 and 26, 2026, is part of one of the most consistent polling series tracking American public opinion on Russia’s war against Ukraine. Its regular measurements provide insight into how attitudes toward the war and potential peace negotiations evolve over time.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The latest findings show that 68% of respondents believe Putin is stalling negotiations with the United States and Western countries rather than genuinely seeking peace, up from 61% in September. Only 32% believe the Russian leader sincerely wants to end the war.
Skepticism toward Putin extends across political affiliations, with 74% of Democrats and independent or other-party voters saying he is delaying negotiations, compared with 58% of Republicans.
By contrast, 61% of Americans believe Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy genuinely wants to end the war, while 39% think he is stalling negotiations, a slight increase from 37% in September.
Support for Zelenskyy’s stated intentions is particularly strong among Democrats, with 69% believing he is genuinely seeking peace. The same view is shared by 61% of independent or other-party voters and 52% of Republicans.
Beyond perceptions of the two leaders, the poll also indicates substantial bipartisan support for maintaining pressure on Moscow if it refuses to engage in peace negotiations.
According to the findings, 64% of Americans support continuing weapons assistance to Ukraine and imposing additional sanctions on Russia if Moscow refuses to negotiate and prolongs the war.
Notably, support for these measures is nearly identical among Republicans and Democrats, with 67% of Republican voters and 66% of Democratic voters backing continued military assistance and additional economic pressure under those circumstances.
The findings highlight an area of bipartisan agreement on US policy toward Russia’s war against Ukraine despite broader political divisions in the United States.
The survey also found growing support for direct US security guarantees for Ukraine as part of a potential peace agreement involving Ukrainian territorial concessions. Some 64% of respondents supported such an arrangement, compared with 58% in September.
However, American attitudes toward economic measures targeting Russia become more complex when domestic energy costs are taken into account.
According to the poll, 61% of Americans oppose the United States purchasing Russian oil and diesel fuel while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine, while 39% support such purchases. Opposition is particularly strong among Democrats, with 73% against buying Russian oil and diesel, compared with 64% of independent or other-party voters.
Republicans were more divided, with 54% supporting purchases of Russian oil and diesel fuel and 46% opposing them.
At the same time, 63% of respondents said they prioritize lower fuel prices over restricting Russia’s ability to finance the war, revealing a contrast between opposition to Russian energy purchases and concerns about domestic energy costs.
The findings come as diplomatic efforts to arrange further negotiations between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States continue.
A proposed trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi remains dependent on confirmation from Washington, although both Kyiv and Moscow have expressed their readiness to participate, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists on October 28.
Zelenskyy explained that the timing of the talks, expected to take place in November, could be affected by Washington’s ongoing diplomatic engagement in the Middle East.

TRIPOLI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- In a workshop humming with engines in Mayah, 40 km southwest of the Libyan capital Tripoli, 25-year-old Rawan Abu Aisha is building a career uncommon for Libyan women -- turning a childhood passion for cars into a business modifying engines.
Growing up, Abu Aisha often watched her father work as a mechanic. "The workshop environment was familiar to me from childhood because I grew up watching my father work with cars," Abu Aisha told Xinhua.
"Over time, that interest became something I wanted to turn into a profession," she explained, saying the opportunity came through an entrepreneurship competition in Libya that invited participants to present innovative business ideas.
Drawing on her family background, she proposed modifying car engines to meet owners' specific needs. The idea became real when a customer agreed to an engine replacement. The project subsequently grew into a company established in 2022, whose primary business is modifying engines using its own custom-built units.
"My father's support and practical experience helped me take my first steps in this field," she said. "His encouragement gave me the confidence to develop my skills and turn an idea into a real business."
Her studies in entrepreneurship also equipped her with knowledge of business management, marketing and accounting, helping the company move beyond its technical roots toward a more structured management approach. What began as a business relying largely on customer recommendations later expanded its reach through an online presence and social media platforms.
According to Abu Aisha, the company's social media page has attracted over 50,000 followers, and demand for its services has grown so rapidly that her current team can barely keep up.
"The growing number of followers and the rising demand for our services show that there is considerable interest in what we do," she said. "Our next step is to expand the business and improve our ability to meet customers' needs."
Abu Aisha also hopes to partner with companies abroad, stressing the importance of long-term planning and continuous development.
"Building a sustainable business requires more than providing a good technical service," she said. "It also requires organized management, continuous improvement and a clear vision for the future."
While she believes social acceptance of women in the workplace has grown in recent years, Abu Aisha's greatest lesson from entrepreneurship is that young women must take initiative and pursue their ambitions, rather than let stereotypes dictate their choices.
"Women should not allow stereotypes to decide what they can or cannot do," she said. "They should be willing to try, learn and discover their abilities through practical experience."
For young women considering careers in mechanics, engineering or other nontraditional fields, her journey shows how personal interests can be turned into professional opportunities through determination, learning and hands-on experience.
"I want to continue developing the business and provide services that customers can trust," she said. "I believe that competence and expertise, rather than gender, should determine whether someone can succeed in a particular profession." ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: New study traces evolution of terrestrial animals on Qinghai-Xizang Plateau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:45 CST
22:53:45 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A new study has reconstructed the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, offering a clearer picture of how the unique fauna of Earth's "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years.
The research, led by a team from the Chengdu Institute of Biology (CIB) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, was recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
"Overall, the study deepens understanding of how mountain animal life evolves and provides a framework for studying how biodiversity forms in mountain regions worldwide," said Li Jiatang, a researcher at CIB.
Home to many species found nowhere else, the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, covering about 3.07 million square kilometers and ranging in elevation from 88 to 8,848 meters, according to the researchers.
The plateau platform, the Himalayas and the Hengduan Mountains are the plateau's three major subregions.
Scientists have long been interested in how the plateau's tectonic history and monsoon systems shaped the evolution of local biodiversity. However, earlier studies mostly looked at plants or single animal groups, leaving the overall development of the plateau's land animals poorly understood.
To fill this gap, the researchers combined time-calibrated evolutionary trees covering more than 20,000 species across invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. They then reconstructed the evolutionary history of 527 endemic terrestrial animal species on the plateau.
The study found that most of the plateau's endemic land animals did not arrive from elsewhere and then become new species. Instead, many evolved locally, splitting into new species right where they were, something scientists call in situ diversification.
The plateau was also a major receiver of species. The study found that animals moved in nearly twice as often as they moved out. The Qinghai-Xizang Plateau therefore played two roles at once: it was a place where new species formed, and a biogeographic sink that took in more species than it sent out.
The three subregions played very different roles. The Hengduan Mountains were the main source of local species formation, producing many new species. The Himalayas were both a source and a sink, producing new species locally and receiving species from elsewhere. The plateau platform produced very few new species locally, with most of its animal life coming from immigration, making it an important sink and a major receiver of species.
The researchers also examined how geology and climate shaped this evolutionary history. They found that a major climate transition about 34 million years ago marked the onset of sustained species diversification and biological exchange. However, the timing of these processes varied across the three subregions, reflecting differences in their uplift histories and monsoon systems.
The study also found a consistent "plants first, animals later" pattern. By comparing animal evolution with plant studies, the researchers identified this pattern across the plateau and its subregions. Early-colonizing plant groups created suitable ecological niches, laying the foundation for later animal immigration and diversification. ■

====================================================================================================

Antarctic sea ice loss disrupts ocean freshwater system: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:28 CST
22:53:28 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW) has rapidly become saltier and denser as Antarctic sea ice loss reduces freshwater input, potentially affecting deep-ocean warming and sea levels, according to new research.
The AAIW, a vast layer of fresh water spanning much of the Southern Hemisphere's ocean, helps store carbon, supply oxygen and drive global ocean currents. It plays a role in heat, freshwater and carbon redistribution around the planet, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of Melbourne.
The study, published in Nature Climate Change, found that Antarctic summer sea-ice melt helped maintain the AAIW from 1995 to 2015. From 2016, Antarctic sea ice declined to record lows. Between 2016 and 2024, reduced freshwater input led the water layer to become saltier, denser and deeper.
The team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of about 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, along with satellite and atmospheric datasets.
Researchers said the last time the AAIW underwent a similar shift was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica. However, that transition took thousands of years, rather than two decades.
The researchers said changes in the AAIW could affect the ocean's ability to store carbon and push more excess heat into deeper waters, meaning existing models may underestimate deep-ocean warming and miscalculate regional sea-level rise. ■

29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Finland recorded 333 drug-related deaths in 2025, its highest-ever total and a 35% increase from the previous year, Statistics Finland said Thursday.
Statistics Finland data showed that the number of drug-related deaths increased across all age groups and genders, but in particular among younger people and women.
Sixty-four people aged 15-24 died, up 60% from the previous year. Drugs accounted for one in five deaths among people in that age group, the agency said.
The highest number of drug-related deaths was among 25-34-year-olds, with 85 fatalities, up by 12 from 2024.
Deaths among women reached a record 94, compared with 50 a year earlier. Men still accounted for most fatalities.
Most drug-related deaths involved a combination of substances. Alcohol and medications, including psychiatric drugs, were often involved alongside the drug identified as the main contributor to death.
Buprenorphine, an opioid medication used to treat opioid dependence but which is also commonly abused, remained the most common substance identified in fatal accidental drug poisonings and those where intent was unclear.
Designer drugs in the synthetic opioid category have also become more common, the agency added.
Nearly one in 10 drug-related deaths was a suicide.
Helsinki recorded the highest number of deaths at 58, followed by Pirkanmaa with 30, Southwest Finland with 28 and North Ostrobothnia with 25.
Relative to population, the highest mortality rate was in the Paijat-Hame region, at 9.8 deaths per 100,000 people.

Iraq PM donates $10m to Syria's Umayyad, Sayyida Zainab mosques
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:50:47 UTC
22:50:47 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq PM donates $10m to Syria's Umayyad Mosque, Sayyida Zainab shrine in conciliatory gesture
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has donated $10 million from his personal funds to two of Damascus' most prominent religious sites, the Umayyad Mosque and the Sayyida Zainab shrine, in a symbolic gesture highlighting shared religious and historical ties as Baghdad and Damascus seek to strengthen relations.
Zaidi allocated $5 million to each site during his visit to the Syrian capital on Wednesday, according to a statement from his media office.
The visit marked the first by an Iraqi prime minister to Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024. Zaidi, a Shia Muslim, was accompanied by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and other senior officials during visits to both sites.
The choice of destinations was largely symbolic. The Umayyad Mosque is one of the most important historic Sunni Muslim sites in the region, while the Sayyida Zainab shrine is among Syria’s most prominent Shia pilgrimage destinations.
Together, the visits offered a public display of religious coexistence and Arab solidarity at a time when the two countries are seeking to move beyond years of political tension.
Zaidi prayed at both the Umayyad Mosque and later did the same at Sayyida Zainab.
Beyond its religious importance, the Umayyad Mosque, which was built in the eighth century, is associated with the political power of the Umayyad Dynasty, which had its capital in Damascus and is often associated with Sunni Islam.
The mosque itself, however, is also part of a shared Islamic heritage and has significance for Muslims from different backgrounds. Its complex includes a site traditionally associated with the head of Hussein.
The Sayyida Zainab shrine, meanwhile, is widely believed by Shia Muslims to be the burial place of Zainab bint Ali, the granddaughter of Prophet Muhammad and sister of Hussein. It has become one of the region's most important destinations for Shia pilgrims.
The shrine also became a focal point of sectarian mobilisation during Syria’s civil war. Iran-backed Shia militias that fought alongside Assad’s forces justified their intervention in the conflict by saying it was necessary to protect it from extremist Sunni groups.
The two sites' historical and religious associations make Zaidi's visits notable amid efforts to ease sectarian tensions and strengthen ties between the neighbouring countries.
'One people in two countries'
The visits came after Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said that Iraqi visitors would be welcome at the Sayyida Zainab shrine, provided appropriate security arrangements were in place.
In a recent interview with Iraqi broadcaster Dijlah TV, Sharaa said authorities had arrested people who attempted to exploit the issue to stir sectarian tensions.
He also stressed that Damascus did not view its relationship with Baghdad through a sectarian or ethnic lens, but instead sought to build on shared history, economic interests and longstanding social connections between the two populations.
Alongside the religious visits, Zaidi and Sharaa discussed economic cooperation, security coordination and regional developments.
A key issue was the proposed revival of the Iraq-Syria oil export corridor, which would allow Iraqi crude oil to reach Mediterranean markets through Syria’s port of Baniyas.
According to a statement from Zaidi’s office, the two sides discussed exporting Iraqi oil through the pipeline at a capacity of up to two million barrels per day.
Relations between the two countries have faced difficulties since Assad’s removal, particularly given the role of Iran-backed Iraqi and regional militias in supporting his government during the Syrian war.
Some Iran-aligned factions in Iraq have been wary of Syria’s new leadership. However, the government has sought to take a more pragmatic approach towards Damascus, focusing on border security, trade and regional cooperation.
During his meeting with Sharaa, al-Zaidi described Iraqis and Syrians as “one people in two countries,” stressing the need to deepen their partnership and expand bilateral cooperation.
The two leaders had previously met in September on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

Will the new Flemish road tax be beneficial for you or are you better off sticking with the old scheme?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:50:35 UTC
22:50:35 KST

From today, everyone in Flanders can check for themselves whether the planned Flemish reform of road tax will work out more favourably or not. The Flemish Government is launching a website where you can work out the difference between the old and the new tax yourself. If the new scheme works out cheaper, you can indicate straight away that you wish to switch. Anyone who does not wish to switch need not do anything.
Will the new Flemish road tax be beneficial for you or are you better off sticking with the old scheme?
In 2027, the annual road tax (JVB) in Flanders will be reformed. For most vehicles, the Flemish government will use just two parameters: the car’s weight and its CO₂ emissions. “The lighter and cleaner your car, the less you pay,” is the message. For cars with a powerful engine (over 2400 cc), you’ll pay slightly more.
Anyone who wants to check for themselves whether the new road tax will be cheaper can do so from today via the website www.vlaanderen.be/vergelijker , but it will be handy to have somebody who reads Dutch on hand. The Comparison Tool makes the reform very clear.
How does it work?
To make a comparison, all you need is your number plate and your registration date. Simply enter these details into the new Comparison Tool and you’ll immediately see a comparison between your current road tax and the new rate.
If the new rate is cheaper, you can switch to the new system straight away. If the current rate is cheaper – which may be the case, for example, for cars with a powerful engine or older cars – then you don’t need to do anything, and you’ll remain on the current rate until you buy your next car.

Healey’s budget paves way for ‘brutal’ spending review next year, warns IFS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:47:30 UTC
22:47:30 KST

John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget failed to cover a £28bn shortfall in the public finances needed to avoid a return to austerity, according to Britain’s leading tax and spending experts.
A day after his address to the Commons, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the chancellor had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking several big decisions in his debut tax and spending statement.
After his low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, the thinktank said Healey had left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms.
But as the war in the Middle East fuels a surge in inflation – raising the cost of delivering public services – the chancellor has in effect pencilled in large cuts in the run-up to the next general election.
Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.
“It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review,” she said.
With Labour having promised there would be no return to austerity, and as Andy Burnham’s government prepares for the next election, she said it appeared extremely unlikely that Healey would follow through with such cuts.
“A clear short-term risk with the chancellor’s choices is that next year – with low headroom and a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments – we see another season of damaging speculation about tax rises,” she said.
In his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock emanating from the Middle East war.
Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – allowing a hit to the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drives up the UK government’s borrowing costs.
Faced with grim forecasts for household living standards and growth in the British economy, the IFS said it was a “reasonable choice” for the chancellor to allow for a modest reduction in headroom.
However, his deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the thinktank to criticise his plans for meeting the fiscal rules, because they in effect relied on him cutting public spending or announcing tax increases that he had yet to prepare the public for.
“My concern is not that it would be impossible to deliver the implied cuts to other services – that could be done. But I’m sceptical that this government would be willing to do it,” Miller said.

The victory of Serbia’s Student List has fundamentally changed the country’s political landscape. But winning the election may prove to have been the easier part.
The movement that emerged from two years of student protests won the elections without a conventional party structure, without a clearly identifiable leader and, for much of the campaign, without revealing who would actually run the country if it won.
That ambiguity was one of its greatest political strengths. Now, however, the same ambiguity may become a problem.

Jovo Bakić, sociologist and one of the most prominent figures on the Student List, has explicitly said that a new government would not impose sanctions on Moscow. He described Russia as a historically important partner for Serbia, arguing that sanctions imposed by a small country such as Serbia would have little practical effect while carrying considerable symbolic consequences.
Academician of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts and professor at the University of Belgrade’s Faculty of Chemistry, Radomir Saičić, told RIA Novosti that the Students’ List does not plan to impose sanctions on Russia.
“As we stated in our programme, the Students’ List does not advocate imposing sanctions against Russia,” Saičić said.
He noted that Serbia itself had been subjected to sanctions and argued that such measures do not solve problems.
“Problems should be resolved through dialogue, negotiations and agreements, not sanctions,” Saičić said.
Dejan Šoškić, a candidate on the “Students Win” list, and posible new prime minister said that Serbia must develop good-neighbourly relations with Croatia, while noting that there would probably continue to be significant differences in the general perception of what happened in the 1990s, and that the Students’ List does not concern itself with that issue. In an interview with Index.hr, Šoškić announced better relations with Croatia and the European Union, while he did not answer a question about the new government’s position towards Russia.
“The Students’ List advocates full respect for the legal framework in Serbia, including international law. The legal framework in Serbia is therefore quite clear, because the Constitution states that Kosovo and Metohija is an autonomous province of Serbia. On the other hand, key documents of the international legal framework, such as United Nations Security Council Resolution 1244, also affirm this,” Šoškić said.
As for the European Union, Šoškić was less definitive.
“I believe that Serbia will certainly be in a position to fulfil the EU criteria much more easily and quickly. Whether it will join the European Union at some point after fulfilling all the conditions will depend, among other things, on whether the European Union offers Serbia full membership, as well as on whether, in a referendum at the end of that process, the citizens of Serbia decide in favour of that option,” Šoškić added.
Marta Kos’s message to the future government
It is already clear that when it comes to Serbia’s relations with Russia, the new government, just like the previous one, has no intention of aligning itself with Brussels’ policy. European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos spoke with Ilija Srdanović, the lead candidate of the Students’ List, and immediately stressed that a change of government in Belgrade does not remove the obligation to align with the EU’s foreign and security policy. Brussels has indicated that it will assess the future government’s concrete actions, including on the basis of its relations with Moscow.
Marta Kos said that “Serbia will not be able to make significant progress towards EU accession unless it aligns its foreign and security policy with Brussels, including its position on Russia and the sanctions imposed on Moscow over the war in Ukraine.”
The European Commissioner, responding to a question about whether Serbia could become an EU member without joining sanctions against Russia, said that it would be very difficult for a country that does not share the EU’s strategic foreign-policy positions to make progress.
“It will probably not be possible for a country that does not align with us on strategic interests — namely foreign and security policy, or our joint opposition to Russia, particularly in the context of Russia’s war in Ukraine — to make progress. It will be very, very difficult,” Kos said.
The official postition of the Student's list contradicts one of former President Aleksandar Vučić’s central warnings during the campaign: that a Student List victory would eventually mean a dramatic change in Serbia’s policy towards Moscow in terms of imposing sanctions.
For now, there is no indication that sanctions against Russia are about to become part of Serbia’s foreign policy. Given the response from the new authorities, we can conclude that it will be business as usual.
The Student List’s programme also retains Serbia’s policy of military neutrality and rejects NATO membership. Its position on Kosovo remains firmly opposed to Kosovo’s unilateral declaration of independence and to its membership of international organisations.
You could search with a magnifying glass for any difference in policy towards Kosovo between old and new power in Belgrade, and you would not find one. That elephant will therefore remain in the room when it comes to Serbia’s diplomatic relations with the West. We can expect tensions to ease, along with a shift away from harsh rhetoric and threats, but there will be no fundamental change.
This means that the arrival of new government in Belgrade should not automatically be interpreted as a geopolitical realignment in the traditional sense. Professor Radomir Saičić on Kosovo said:
"For us, Kosovo is a temporarily occupied territory. Russia has done more to defend Serbia’s territorial integrity in Kosovo and Metohija than this regime has. Fake patriots accuse the students of lacking patriotism, but it was not the students who signed the Brussels and Washington Agreements, nor did they accept the Franco-German plan."
A pro-European movement — but a suspicious one
The student movement is essentially a “big tent” movement, bringing together people with very different worldviews who were united by their opposition to the rule of Aleksandar Vučić and their criticism of the nature of his government, rather than an ideologically clearly defined alliance.
The more likely scenario is a complicated balancing act: closer political and economic cooperation with the European Union, while maintaining military neutrality, avoiding sanctions against Russia and preserving existing energy and diplomatic links with Moscow.
That will be difficult.
The EU is Serbia’s largest economic partner, while Russia remains important because of energy and, above all, its position on Kosovo. The Student List will therefore have to reconcile two realities that have often been presented as mutually exclusive in Serbian politics.
The Student List is very broadly pro-European. But it is not a traditional pro-EU political organisation. Its relationship with Brussels is likely to be considerably more complicated than that of a government simply seeking to accelerate Serbia’s EU accession.
The leader of the Students’ List, Dr Ilija Srdanović, spoke most openly about the European Union:
“We will remain on the path of European integration. Serbia committed itself to the European integration process back in 2000, 26 years ago. That work will continue. The process will continue. What we can certainly promise, however, is that we will not do what the previous government did: allow public support for European integration in Serbia to fall by 20 percentage points over a period of 15 years. That is the net outcome, the overall result of what the previous government did.
We will certainly bring our domestic policies fully into line with Chapters 23 and 24, on the basis of the same civilisational values: respect for the rule of law and equality, anti-corruption measures, the functioning of institutions and media freedom. These chapters are the main obstacle to further progress towards European integration.”
The students and many of their supporters are deeply suspicious of the way the European Union dealt with the previous Serbian government. For years, Brussels maintained close relations with Vučić’s administration despite growing concerns over democratic standards, media freedom, the electoral environment and the concentration of political power.
Europe has constantly sent Serbia divergent signals. From the past almost two decades the European Parliament has been highly critical, describing Serbia as a “captured state” and sharply criticizing the authorities in all of its reports. The European Commission has been more moderate, alternating between a tougher and a more conciliatory approach, while the European Council has, since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine — and even before that — effectively frozen Serbia’s European integration process. As a result, it is sometimes difficult to discern what Europe’s position towards Serbia actually is.
For many people who supported the student movement, the EU’s willingness to cooperate with the SNS government was not a sign of pragmatic diplomacy but evidence that Brussels tolerated authoritarian tendencies in Belgrade for the sake of stability.
The Western Balkans: a chance for a reset
The regional dimension could prove to be one of the areas where the new government moves fastest. The Student List has signalled that relations with Serbia’s neighbours should be relaxed and that Belgrade should return to a more predictable and less confrontational regional policy. Two issues will be particularly important.
On Bosnia and Herzegovina, the movement is expected to insist on respect for the Dayton Peace Agreement and Serbia’s obligations towards the constitutional order established by Dayton. That could mean a less interventionist approach and an attempt to reduce the political temperature between Belgrade and Sarajevo.
Given that Milorad Dodik, the de facto leader of the Bosnian Serbs, openly sided with the now-former government and maintained that position for 14 years, it is reasonable to expect that the new government in Belgrade will, at the very least, take a cool stance towards him personally.
Similarly, when it comes to Serbs in Croatia, the Erdut Agreement and the rights and political status of the Serbian minority are likely to remain an important reference point.
This could potentially represent one of the biggest changes in Serbia’s regional policy: defending the interests of Serbs outside Serbia while simultaneously trying to reduce tensions with neighbouring states.
A less confrontational Belgrade could also improve relations with Montenegro, as well as Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Serbian politics has often been perceived both in Podgorica and Sarajevo as unpredictable or excessively interventionist.
Hungary: a particularly interesting test
Relations with Hungary will be another early test.
The previous Serbian government developed an exceptionally close relationship with Viktor Orbán. That relationship was political, economic and personal, and Budapest became one of Belgrade’s most important partners inside the European Union.
The arrival of Péter Magyar changes that equation.
A Student List government is likely to have a much closer political affinity with Magyar’s European orientation than with Orbán’s model of government. That does not mean Serbia will abandon its economic relationship with Hungary. On the contrary, there are too many practical interests at stake.
But the political chemistry will almost certainly play a role.
The question is whether Belgrade will seek to build a new relationship with Budapest based less on personal ties between leaders and more on institutional cooperation between two neighbouring European states.
China: perhaps the biggest question mark
If Russia is the area where the Student List has already given relatively clear signals, China remains considerably less defined.
During the Vučić era, Chinese companies became deeply involved in Serbian infrastructure, mining, and industrial projects. Beijing has become an important economic partner, only second to the EU, and many of those investments cannot simply be cancelled by a new government.
At the same time, the Student List is likely to face pressure from parts of its electorate to scrutinise Chinese investments more closely — particularly questions concerning transparency, environmental standards, public procurement and the treatment of state-owned Chinese companies.
The most probable outcome is therefore not a dramatic break with Beijing. China’s economic presence in Serbia is simply too significant for that.
But there could be a transition from politically driven strategic partnership towards a more conventional investment relationship, in which Chinese companies are expected to compete under clearer rules and greater transparency.
The movement’s foreign-policy balance may ultimately look less like an ideological choice between East and West and more like an attempt to redefine Serbia’s relationships with Russia, China and the EU on different terms.
The problem that comes with power
Perhaps the greatest uncertainty, however, has nothing to do with Russia, China or the EU.
It is the Student List itself.
For almost a year, the movement successfully concealed its internal political architecture. At various points, speculation suggested that the rector of the University of Belgrade, Vladan Đokić, might become its political leader. In the end, he was not even a parliamentary candidate.
That episode illustrates just how effectively the students have kept their cards close to their chest.
The same caution must therefore be applied to current speculation about possible office holders.
Informal discussions have mentioned academic and professor Radomir Saičić as a possible presidential candidate, while economist Dejan Šoškić is being mentioned as a possible prime minister. But these names should be treated as political speculation rather than established decisions.
The Student List has already demonstrated that it can surprise almost everyone.
It may do so again.
From movement to government
The transformation will nevertheless have to happen quickly. The movement’s decentralised structure was an advantage during the political struggle. Once in government, however, decentralisation can become paralysis. The public will want to know who is responsible for the economy, foreign affairs, defence, the interior, the security services, education and the judiciary. And the state bureaucracy will want instructions.
This is where the Student List faces its most dangerous transition: from moral authority to political accountability. During the protests, it was enough to say what needed to change. In government, they will have to decide how. That distinction is enormous.
The first signs of change
The political earthquake is already shaking institutions beyond parliament.
On Wednesday, the public broadcaster RTS Director-General Manja Grčić resigned, just eight months after being appointed. Her resignation followed demands from parts of the RTS workforce, informal employee organisations and the Student List for changes in the management of the public broadcaster.
The students have made a radical transformation of Serbia’s media landscape one of their central demands, particularly concerning outlets that are directly or indirectly financed with public money.
But the events surrounding the private TV Informer have also demonstrated the danger of a rapid transition. On Monday night, a group of protesters entered the premises of Informer TV, one of the staunchest supporters of the former Vučić's governments. The incident escalated into a confrontation with police outside the building, and workers inside. The Student List subsequently distanced itself from the break-in and called for calm and non-violence.
This is an important distinction.
Removing political influence from the media is one thing.
Replacing one form of political pressure with another would be quite another.
The new authorities will therefore be judged not only by whom they remove, but by the rules they establish for everyone who comes afterwards.
However, these elections have demonstrated something that media experts have been pointing out for a long time: the role of the media in political developments is greatly overestimated. Compared with the authorities, the students had very limited media exposure, yet they still won a convincing victory.
This shows that the government and the opposition were operating in two parallel realities. While the role of the media cannot be entirely dismissed, the elections have demonstrated that traditional media can no longer dictate the narrative. This trend is clearly visible in the United States and many European countries, and Serbia is no exception.
There are already calls for changes at the security services, including demands for the resignation of the leadership of Serbia’s intelligence apparatus. Prosecutors have suddenly started pulling “forgotten” cases out of their drawers, and the first arrests have begun. It is highly unlikely that the institutional shake-up will end with the first resignations.
The presidential election will provide the next test
And Serbia’s political transition will not end with the parliamentary election. Presidential elections are expected before the end of the year, meaning that the Student List must soon answer another fundamental question: who represents the new Serbia?
This will force the movement to confront precisely the problem it avoided during its rise.
It will have to personalise power. A government cannot be anonymous. Someone must become prime minister. Ministers must be elected, state-owned companies need directors, the security services need new leadership and public institutions need people capable of taking responsibility for decisions. The Student List will therefore have to move with extraordinary speed from a movement into a governing structure.
The election victory was achieved by a collective movement whose greatest political asset was that it had no single face. Presidential elections and forming a new Government requires the opposite.
A prime minister must negotiate. A president must represent the country abroad. Ministers must make decisions. Somebody must ultimately accept responsibility if, or when those decisions prove unpopular.
This will be an equally difficult challenge for Vučić as opposition leader. He can no longer run for president, and his absolute dominance over the Serbian Progressive Party has meant that, over the past 14 years, no one else has been given the opportunity to emerge as the party’s number two.
That is why the coming weeks may be more important than the election itself. The Student List has already shown that it knows how to win without revealing its full strategy. Now it has to demonstrate that it knows how to govern without losing the principles that brought it to power.
The students spent a year keeping their cards hidden.
They now have to show them.
And Serbia — as well as the EU, Russia, China and the countries of the Western Balkans — will be watching every card they play.

European Defence: The E5 Aims to Build a Stronger Europe Within a Stronger NATO

Unknown Publisher

European Defence: The E5 Aims to Build a Stronger Europe Within a Stronger NATO
Meeting in Paris on Monday, 26 October, representatives of Europe’s five leading military powers reaffirmed their determination to strengthen Europe’s role in NATO’s collective defence. In response to the Russian threat, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom intend to step up their military and industrial cooperation while continuing their support for Ukraine.
Military and Industrial Cooperation to Strengthen NATO’s European Pillar
The E5 is a consultation framework bringing together the Defence Ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. At their meeting in Paris on 26 October, hosted by French Minister for the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin, the five countries reaffirmed the need for Europe to shoulder greater responsibility for its own defence while preserving its strategic partnership with the United States. “Produce more, produce faster,” Catherine Vautrin urged, calling for stronger European industrial capabilities and the development of equipment suited to both current conflicts and future threats. Achieving this ambition will require greater interoperability between armed forces, greater control over strategic technologies and closer coordination of defence investment. Also attending the meeting, EU High Representative Kaja Kallas stressed the importance of translating defence spending into tangible operational capabilities while maintaining pressure on Russia through sanctions. European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, meanwhile, emphasised the urgent need to accelerate industrial contracts and equipment deliveries, particularly through EU funding mechanisms designed to strengthen Ukraine’s capabilities.
In their joint statement, the E5 members reaffirmed their determination to build a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO, notably by increasing investment in Europe’s defence industrial capabilities.
A Stronger European Commitment to Ukraine
Support for Ukraine was also high on the agenda. “We are fully committed,” Catherine Vautrin affirmed, stressing the need to preserve European unity in the face of intimidation. In their joint statement, the five countries identified Russia as the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security, citing its ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine and the growing use of hybrid attacks. German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius shared this assessment, stating that Vladimir Putin has shown no genuine willingness to agree to a ceasefire. As Russian strikes continue to target Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and civilian population, European countries continue to provide tangible support, particularly in air defence.
For Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto, this mobilisation directly serves Europe’s security interests: “Helping Ukraine is not simply about helping another country; it is about safeguarding our own future and security.” Polish Deputy Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski, meanwhile, emphasised the need to develop more affordable air defence systems and strengthen industrial cooperation with Kyiv. NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska also stressed the importance of air defence, calling on Allies to step up their support to protect Ukrainian cities and infrastructure as winter approaches. British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting reiterated the UK’s determination to maintain economic pressure on Moscow and continue supporting Ukraine over the long term. The E5 members also reaffirmed the importance of countering Russia’s shadow fleet and their commitment to helping provide robust security guarantees for Ukraine once a ceasefire or peace agreement is in place.
A Common Response to Other Threats to European Security
Tensions in the Middle East were also discussed, particularly maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, two vital shipping routes for international trade and energy supplies.
Beyond these issues, the group plans to intensify dialogue between political and military leaders and strengthen cooperation between national defence industries. The next E5 meeting is scheduled to take place in Rome in March 2027, with the aim of continuing to translate this political alignment into tangible operational capabilities.

Ukraine prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship of the Black Sea Commission
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Ukraine prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship of the Black Sea Commission
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship of the Black Sea Commission due to its aggression and environmental damage. Kyiv called for the damage to be assessed and Russia’s participation to be limited.
The Ukrainian delegation prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship during the 47th meeting of the Commission on the Protection of the Black Sea Against Pollution. This was reported by the Ministry of Economy and Environment of Ukraine, writes UNN.
A state waging an aggressive war and harming the marine environment should not head the body responsible for its protection
In her statement, she added that the Ukrainian side is drawing attention to the significant environmental consequences of Russia’s aggression for the entire Black Sea region. Attacks on infrastructure, damage to wastewater treatment facilities, pollution of water and soil, and the destruction of protected natural areas are creating threats that extend far beyond Ukraine.
Thus, the coasts of the Black and Azov Seas, the deltas of the Danube and Dnipro rivers, as well as wetlands of international importance, are suffering from the hostilities. Pollution is spreading through the sea, and the consequences for marine ecosystems may persist for many years.
The Ukrainian delegation emphasized that Russia’s actions run counter to international law and lead to marine pollution, undermining the joint efforts of coastal states aimed at fulfilling their obligations under the Convention on the Protection of the Black Sea Against Pollution (the Bucharest Convention).
It is noted that Ukraine called on the states parties to the Convention to provide a clear assessment of the actions of the Russian Federation and their environmental consequences, support the assessment of the condition of the marine environment and the damage caused by the war, and take joint measures to prevent further pollution.
Separately, the Ukrainian side raised the issue of the possibility of applying legal and procedural mechanisms to fully terminate Russia’s participation in the work of the Convention’s bodies. The relevant initiative is to be considered by the contracting parties.

Hong Kong’s housing chief has resigned to take political responsibility for the devastating fire at Wang Fuk Court, offering condolences to the families of the victims and expressing hope that those who perished may rest in peace.

UK social media ban may lock out more than 100,000 teenagers without ID
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:45:05 UTC
22:45:05 KST

More than 100,000 British teenagers risk being locked out of social media if they do not have a passport or driving licence when an under-16 ban is introduced next year.
Ofcom, the UK’s online watchdog, said about 150,000 16- to 17-year-olds do not own a passport or driving licence, which are likely to be needed to access age-restricted platforms.
The Australia-style ban on under-16s accessing social media services, including Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, is due to come into force next spring.
The head of Ofcom, Melanie Dawes, said “motivated children” would seek to bypass the restrictions, as has happened in Australia.
On Thursday, Ofcom published an assessment of age verification measures that could underpin the ban, outlining four “highly effective” methods: checking a person’s official ID against a live selfie, a bank verifying an account holder’s age, an official digital ID service like the Young Scot card, or estimating someone’s age via a selfie.
However, the watchdog said a form of official ID would probably be needed as a “backstop” for other methods, such as facial age estimation, which could be inaccurate by several years. Ofcom said a cohort of 16- to 17-year-olds could miss out as a result.
“This means that people without a form of photo ID will likely need to take steps to obtain one to access age-restricted services,” the regulator said.
More than nine out of 10 Britons over 16 have passports or driving licences.
Facial age estimation has been a popular measure for enforcing over-18 access to pornographic websites in the UK, which have been subject to stringent age checks since last year, indicating that this method will be used by social media plaforms as well.
The UK government has not confirmed which platforms will be affected by the ban but it is expected to cover the same sites as in Australia. Those are: Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.
In March, Australia’s eSafety commissioner said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s had flouted the ban since it was imposed in December last year. A survey of 900 Australian parents found 31% said their children still had one or more social media accounts after the ban, compared with 49% before the laws.
Ofcom’s chief executive acknowledged the risk of evasion and said the ban would be a “huge cultural shift for the UK”.
“We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk,” said Dawes. “This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play.”
The government is expected to introduce regulations confirming the ban by the end of the year, with Ofcom also opening a consultation on the best age verification methods before issuing official guidance on which measures to adopt.

Polish bishop convicted for failing to promptly report child sex abuse allegations
Unknown

2026-10-29
13:45:01 UTC

In the first ruling of its kind in Poland, a Catholic bishop has been found guilty of failing to promptly inform the law enforcement authorities about allegations of child sex abuse committed by priests under his authority.
Andrzej Jeż, the bishop of Tarnów, was handed a non-custodial sentence that will require him to donate 25% of his earnings for two years to a charity that supports victims of child sexual abuse.
However, the verdict can still be appealed, and the diocese of Tarnów has already announced that it “disagrees with the court’s ruling” and that an appeal will be filed.
Pierwszy taki wyrok w Polsce. Biskup skazany za zwlekanie z powiadomieniem prokuratury o pedofilach w sutannach
Ordynariusz tarnowski bp Andrzej Jeż jest pierwszym biskupem oskarżonym o zbyt późne powiadomienie prokuratury o pedofilii w Kościele. I pierwszym, który który został…
— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 29, 2026
The case relates to alleged abuse by two priests who worked under Jeż’s authority. They can be identified only as Stanisław P. and Tomasz K. under Polish privacy law.
In 2022, prosecutors discontinued an investigation into allegations against Stanisław P. because the statute of limitations had expired, despite concluding that he had harmed at least 95 children and committed “sexual acts” against 77 of them over several decades in parishes in Poland and Ukraine.
In 2023, prosecutors decided to charge Tomasz K., who allegedly sexually abused children as early as 2018. However, they have been unable to formally present the charges to him because of his poor health, news website OKO.press reported earlier this year.
Though Jeż was not accused of complicity in the alleged abuse itself, he was charged under a 2017 law making it a criminal offence not to “immediately notify the authorities” of “credible information” about sexual abuse of minors. The offence is punishable by up to three years in prison.
Investigators say that, although an internal church probe into Stanisław P. was initiated in the 2000s and a decision to remove him from the clergy was made in 2013, Jeż only notified the prosecutor’s office in 2020. In the case of Tomasz K., the bishop notified prosecutors only in 2021.
In court, prosecutor Marcin Stępień said that Jeż’s failure to report the abuse promptly had allowed the statute of limitations to expire in the case of some of Stanisław P.’s victims.
Stępień also noted that the bishop had only come forward with the information when media coverage brought the allegations against Stanisław P. to light, reports broadcaster TVN.
A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers.
It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026
Prosecutors sought a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for three years, and a fine of 20,000 zloty (€4,550). Jeż, however, denied the allegations against him and sought an acquittal. He argued that he had reported the alleged abuse to the authorities as soon as there was credible information.
On Thursday, the court found the bishop guilty, giving him a sentence known as “restriction of liberty” (ograniczenie wolnośći), under which a convict is not imprisoned but required to do some kind of social good.
In Jeż’s case, the court ordered that 25% of his salary for two years be donated to the Empowering Children Foundation (Dajemy Dzieciom Siłę), which supports victims of child abuse. He was additionally ordered to pay 20,000 zloty to the Fund for Assistance to Victims and Post-Penitentiary Assistance.
In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”.
The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up.
The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”.
In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy.

Road safety in Bulgaria requires joint efforts beyond the police

Thursday, 29 October 2026, 14:26
Interior Minister Demerdzhiev
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Bulgaria has the highest road traffic fatality rate in the EU, according to data published by the European Commission on 29 October. Commenting on the figures today, Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said work was continuing on a comprehensive strategy to address the problem and that, in his words, its implementation had already begun.
“At present, the police are the only ones tackling road traffic accidents, whereas in countries where the situation is different, the police account for just 33% of the effort,” Demerdzhiev complained. “We are currently trying to make up for the absence of state and municipal institutions,” the minister added.
He also stressed the need to improve road infrastructure, which would help reduce the number of road accidents.

Damascus, Amman contradict each other on attack that killed civilians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:44:42 UTC
22:44:42 KST

Damascus, Amman contradict each other on attack that killed civilians
Analysts say accountability is needed to quell public outrage over killing of family in southern Syria.
Public anger in Syria has threatened to boil over following disagreements between Amman and Damascus over Jordanian attacks on the southern Syrian regions of Deraa and Suwayda on Monday evening.
Jordan said its air force had killed more than 20 ISIL (ISIS) fighters in retaliatory strikes on what it called “dens of terrorist organisations in southern Syria”, linked to suspects accused of being behind last week’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the kingdom, which was claimed by the group.
But the next day, anger mounted in Syria as images spread of a slain grandmother and her three grandchildren.
While Jordan has launched attacks on Syria in the past, including assaults that led to civilian casualties, this latest episode seems to have captured public anger.
“The anger also reflects an expectation that the authorities in Damascus should now be able to protect Syrians and demand answers when they are killed or harmed,” Navvar Saban, a researcher in security and military affairs at the Arab Center for Contemporary Syrian Studies, told Al Jazeera.
“If people feel Damascus is more concerned with protecting the relationship with the Jordanians than accountability, some of the anger could turn inward.”
Contradicting accounts
Monday’s attack reportedly came in response to the assault on a Greek Orthodox church that killed nine people and wounded at least 34 others in the village of Hamoud in the Karak governorate, about 120km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
Jordanian authorities said the attack was carried out by “extremist terrorists”.
Jordan’s King Abdullah II promised to respond with an “iron fist”.
“Jordan has absorbed many terrorist attacks before, but this one was especially brazen given the Christian church and the nature of the event being targeted,” Sean Yom, an expert on Jordan at Temple University in the United States, told Al Jazeera.
“Because of its unprecedented nature, explicitly targeting a protected Christian minority in the tribal heartland of Karak, the government instantly felt popular demands to show results from the investigation and arrest of the perpetrators. This pressure to be responsive is especially acute right now, because security and policing remain core strengths of the Jordanian state.”
Jordanian authorities arrested three men connected to the attack on the church on Monday. That evening, Jordan also launched the attack on southern Syria, which it said was carried out in coordination with authorities in Damascus.
But Damascus has contradicted that account.
The Syrian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that it had informed Jordan of its “complete reservation” over the attacks, and said they took place “without prior coordination or notification with the Syrian side”. An official described the strikes as “treacherous”.
“Both governments have something to defend politically,” Saban said. “Amman wants to show that it acted against a serious threat through legitimate security channels. On the other hand, Damascus cannot afford to appear to have approved an operation that killed Syrian families. The investigation needs to establish who communicated with whom, when, and about which target. Until then, I would avoid either assuming Syria secretly approved everything or treating the coordination as a simple misunderstanding.”
The family’s bodies were recovered after they were killed by the Jordanian strike on a tent in the village of al-Taff, in the Lajat area of northeastern Deraa province. Syria’s civil defence said three other family members were wounded in the attack.
Meanwhile, in the al-Shayah farms near Nassib, in the Deraa countryside, an 80-year-old man named Riyad Karrad was also killed by a strike. Another man named Mutlaq Abu al-Khalil, 60, was killed in Shuhayb, in Suwayda’s northern countryside.
Syrian customs authorities closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, before reopening it to passenger and commercial traffic on Wednesday.
Syrian-Jordanian relations
Jordan has launched several air strikes on Syria since 2023. It says those strikes generally target arms or drug smugglers.
Under the regime of former President Bashar al-Assad, southern Syria became the site of cross-border drug smuggling, including the stimulant captagon. Some of those operations are believed to have continued after the fall of the Assad regime. At times, the Jordanian strikes have killed civilians, such as a January 2024 attack that Human Rights Watch said killed women and children.
Since the fall of the regime in December 2024, relations between Amman and Damascus have been lukewarm, though slowly improving. Analysts say this is down to shared interests.
“Syria needs healthy trading and commercial partners like Jordan, and Jordan wants Syria to become more secure and coherent for three reasons,” Yom said.
“A strong and friendly Syria can accept more repatriated refugees from Jordan, where there are still hundreds of thousands. It can also help seal the porous border and prevent arms and drug smuggling activities along their shared frontier. And lastly, a stronger allied Syria helps Jordan resist Israel’s creeping annexation, including the West Bank as well as more parts of Syria and Lebanon. So both have mutual interests tied to their sovereignty in maintaining good relations.”
Amman was also the site of a July 2025 trilateral agreement signing between Syria, the US and Jordan aimed at resolving internal disputes over violence in Suwayda.
“Only days before the strike, the two foreign ministers were discussing a strategic partnership and preparing another meeting of their High Coordination Council that is a significant investment in the relationship,” Saban said. “My expectation is that this is a serious strain rather than a rupture. Both governments have strong reasons to keep cooperation over the border, armed groups smuggling, etc. But this incident raises an uncomfortable question for Damascus.”
For its part, Syria’s Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as a violation of the country’s sovereignty but seemed to indicate relations with Amman would continue to be strengthened. It said Damascus is coordinating with Amman to establish a joint security committee to strengthen border security and prevent similar incidents.
In the meantime, Saban said that regardless of coordination with Damascus, accountability is needed to subside public anger.
“Even if an investigation established that Damascus approved some part of the operation, that would not explain why those people were killed or remove the need for accountability,” he said. “Ultimately, the families deserve a specific answer about the strike that killed their relatives, their friends, their family. Syrians need to understand why their families got killed.”

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun on Thursday called for an end to Israeli attacks on Lebanon and reaffirmed his country’s commitment to diplomatic and negotiated solutions, Anadolu reports.

He called for “greater European support” for the Lebanese army and security institutions, describing such assistance as “a direct investment in the stability of Lebanon and the region.”

Despite the agreement, Israel has continued its attacks on southern Lebanon.
Reforms and reconstruction
On the economic front, Aoun said Lebanon was continuing to work with the International Monetary Fund to complete reforms. He expressed hope that Germany would contribute to reconstruction within a framework led by the World Bank.
He called for a shift from emergency aid to a sustainable development partnership and urged greater German private-sector investment.
Lebanon is seeking a lending program with the IMF, which requires banking, economic and financial reforms. Talks have yet to be concluded despite a series of steps taken by Lebanese authorities.

UNIFIL has been deployed in southern Lebanon since 1978 under UN Security Council resolutions to monitor the cessation of hostilities and help maintain security and stability.

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7, 2027, nearly nine months before her term ends, the bank announced on Oct. 29.
“It has been a great pride and a huge privilege to serve this institution,” Lagarde said in a video posted on X. She said she was leaving an ECB “fit for the future.”
European Council President António Costa said the process to appoint her successor would begin immediately to ensure a smooth transition.
The timing gives EU leaders an opportunity to choose the next ECB chief before France’s presidential election in spring 2027.
Former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos, general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, are seen as frontrunners.
EU leaders must also choose replacements for executive board member Isabel Schnabel, who leaves in January, and chief economist Philip Lane, whose term ends in May.
Lagarde has led the ECB since November 2019, having previously headed the International Monetary Fund and served as French finance minister. Her eight-year term was due to end in October 2027.
She did not announce her next role. She has ruled out running for the French presidency but has been linked to the chairmanship of the World Economic Forum, which hosts the annual Davos gathering.
The ECB later kept its key deposit rate at 2.5 percent, warning that rising energy prices could push inflation higher and weaken growth.
Eurozone inflation reached 3.8 percent in September, well above the bank’s 2 percent target.
Policymakers are contending with the energy shock from the Iran war, tighter financing conditions and concerns over France’s public finances.

Ex-Swiss minister Berset defends young people's right to demonstrate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:39:28 UTC
22:39:28 KST

Ex-Swiss minister Berset defends young people’s right to demonstrate
In the face of a wave of demonstrations across Europe, the Secretary General of the Council of Europe defends the right to demonstrate while strongly condemning the violence. For Alain Berset, these mobilisations reveal a deep malaise: the destruction of future prospects for an entire generation.
From France to Albania, via Italy, Spain and Portugal, for several weeks now, European youth have been taking to the streets. The list of concerns include housing that has become inaccessible, schools and public services degraded, the cost of living and precariousness, mistrust of leaders, among others. This anger does not spare Switzerland: a day of mobilisation is planned for November 20 in several cities in the country.
Symptom of a ‘living democracy’
Sometimes punctuated by violence, these demonstrations question the state of democracy on the continent. For Berset, these movements are above all the symptom of a “living democracy”.
“You have the right to express your opinions, to meet peacefully, to have demands, to see that we can have differences, to have respect for different positions, to debate them. All this is part of a living democracy,” he said on Wednesday during the Swiss public broadcaster programme RTS Forum.
+ Ex-Swiss minister Berset takes Council of Europe top job
The former Swiss minister, who took part in the Swiss Parliament’s Foreign Policy Day, said there are also limits. “When it turns violent, when movements are instrumentalised by violent groups to break or to steal, it is absolutely unacceptable,” he continues. “And it’s a real problem because it indirectly calls into question the often very legitimate motivations of the young people who are mobilising.”
Different causes, a common malaise
What strikes him most is the simultaneity of these movements in European countries with very different national contexts. “The reasons that pushed young people into the streets in France are not the same as those we see in Albania or Serbia,” he said. “On the other hand, they all refer to the same root of the problem: the lack of prospects in a world dominated by crises, wars and the feeling that we do not really know what the future will bring.”
For him, the contrast with the young people of 20 or 25 years ago is striking: they had “the impression of having in front of [them] a boulevard that was opening up to have perspectives, projects, to develop”.
Today’s young people are facing “a continent on which war is back, in Ukraine”, he regrets. Not to mention “the war in Iran”, “violations of international law almost everywhere”, “the climate crisis”, “the pandemic crisis” from which we have emerged, “artificial intelligence” which is said to destroy us, he lists. This accumulation of threats “destroys prospects” and undermines “confidence in democratic systems”.
Warning against a security drift
Faced with calls to limit the right to demonstrate, especially in France, to avoid looting and other destruction, Alain Berset warns against a security drift. “We must be very careful not to accept that our freedoms are diminished or reduced for what we think is a secure democracy,” he insists.
The Council of Europe recently called on the states concerned to respect the right to demonstrate. For Berset, the question is complex but essential: “If we had to take this reason [violence] to destroy freedom of expression, then the question that arises is: ‘What’s the next one we’re going to touch?'”
The Serbian example illustrates the ability of democracy to channel protest: after two years of “not always easy” demonstrations following the deadly collapse of a train station in Novi Sad, students “managed to win elections last Sunday”. He added that “we are now waiting to see them at work to carry out their own project for society”.
Faced with this accumulation of crises, Alain Berset formulates a wish that may come as a surprise: “We must return to something wiser, a little more boring. I miss a slightly more boring world. We could use a little more boredom.”
