Qatar denies meddling in Israeli election: 'If it were true, Qatar would own all of Israel'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:38:48 UTC
22:38:48 KST

Qatar on Thursday rejected allegations that it had attempted to influence Israel's election results by transferring money, accusing Israeli politicians and media figures of spreading disinformation to drag Doha into Israel's post-election political disputes.
"We reject the allegations made by certain Israeli politicians and their media associates, who have launched yet another disinformation campaign aimed at dragging Qatar into Israel's political disputes following this week's elections," said Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari. "They accuse us of buying Netanyahu, buying the left, and now buying the Arab vote. If all these claims were to be believed, Qatar would probably own all of Israel."
In a post on X, al-Ansari described the allegations as both "ridiculous and dangerous," saying the repeated references to Qatar reflected an excessive obsession with his country among certain Israeli political and media figures.
"Do not use Qatar as a scapegoat for political failures," he wrote. "Instead of trying to divert attention toward Qatar, they would be better off focusing on voters, improving people's daily lives and repairing the damage they have caused in the region."
Qatar also emphasized that the matter concerned Israel's internal affairs.
"Any government emerging from these elections must uphold international law and relevant United Nations resolutions, engage seriously and sincerely with the Palestinian issue, and respect the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, foremost among them the right to self-determination and an independent state along the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital," the statement said. "This requires responsibility and accountability."
Election chief orders Shin Bet investigation into suspected foreign interference
The controversy began with a letter sent by Central Elections Committee Chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg to Shin Bet Director David Zini.
"The integrity of elections is at the heart of democracy," Sohlberg wrote. Although he stressed that he was unable to assess the credibility of the suspicions, he said the allegations required a thorough investigation because they involved possible foreign actors.
"Given that these suspicions concern foreign elements, there is an obligation to investigate them properly in order to safeguard the integrity of Knesset elections, prevent illegal activity intended to undermine democratic institutions and prevent subversion," he wrote.
Sohlberg instructed Zini to make every effort to provide investigative findings within a week. "I instruct you to do everything in your power to examine these suspicions thoroughly and use the Shin Bet's authority to identify evidence that substantiates or disproves them," the justice wrote. "Only in this way can we ensure public confidence in the election and the integrity of the democratic process."
Citing the legal deadlines for filing election appeals, Sohlberg asked Zini to present any available findings within the coming week.
Yesh Atid lawmaker Vladimir Beliak subsequently demanded that the Central Elections Committee's leadership convene to review the evidence underlying Sohlberg's decision to order an investigation.
Responding on Sohlberg's behalf, acting committee Director General Dean Livne emphasized that the election itself had been conducted lawfully. "The Knesset elections were conducted in accordance with the law. The integrity of voting at polling stations was carefully protected, and to the best of our knowledge, claims of systematic violations of election integrity are baseless," Livne said.
He added that statements made by the police commissioner and Shin Bet director on Election Day and afterward supported that assessment.
Livne explained that Sohlberg had written to Zini after receiving sensitive classified intelligence in his capacity as chairman of the Central Elections Committee. "The information raised suspicions that required further examination to determine whether there was substantiated evidence," he said. "Immediately upon receiving the information, the committee chairman instructed that the investigation be expanded."
Because the investigation is ongoing and the intelligence is highly classified, Livne said there was no justification for convening a meeting of the committee's leadership.
Why wasn't the suspected interference stopped before the election?
Questions have also emerged about why the Shin Bet did not act before Israelis went to the polls.
As an intelligence agency responsible for preventing threats to national security, the Shin Bet possessed information about the possibility of unlawful money transfers before the election, two official sources connected to the case confirmed to ynet.
However, Central Elections Committee officials said the Shin Bet participated in every security assessment held in the days preceding the vote and never informed the committee of any such suspicions or intelligence. Had the information been shared, officials said, the agency would immediately have been asked to act to prevent interference in real time and protect the integrity of the election.
"The obvious question is how the service could have possessed what was allegedly solid and deeply troubling intelligence before the election, yet failed to act or launch an investigation before voting took place," one official said.
Zini initiated a meeting Wednesday with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, briefing him on the case and presenting intelligence materials and suspicions that he described as "well-founded."
Yashar! chairman Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the largest political bloc opposing Netanyahu, received a briefing on the matter from Sohlberg on Wednesday and met Zini on Thursday. "During the meeting, Eisenkot was briefed on suspicions concerning foreign involvement in Israel's elections," his office said. "Eisenkot expressed his support for the Shin Bet and law enforcement authorities in conducting a swift and transparent investigation."
Likud links two separate investigations
Meanwhile, police had arrested seven suspects by Thursday morning in a separate election bribery investigation involving envelopes associated with the Arab party Ra'am that were discovered in the Negev. Tens of thousands of shekels in cash were found in the homes of some suspects.
That investigation is separate from the suspected Qatari funding case. It is being handled by the National Fraud Investigations Unit within Lahav 433, rather than by the Shin Bet. Three suspects were arrested on Election Day, while four others were arrested Thursday and taken for questioning.
Likud, which has been running a campaign challenging the legitimacy of Arab parties, sought to connect the two investigations. The party dubbed the controversy "Ra'amgate" and alleged that the election had been stolen. "This is an earthquake. They stole the election in Israel!" Likud said in a statement.
The party described Sohlberg's remarks about suspected foreign involvement and voter bribery benefiting Arab parties as an unprecedented political shock.
"This is an attack on democracy intended to bring about a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and the overthrow of right-wing rule, leading to the IDF's withdrawal and defeat on every front, first and foremost Iran," the statement said.
However, the two investigations remain distinct, and no evidence has been publicly established connecting the alleged Qatari transfers to the separate election bribery case in the Negev.
Ra'am denies involvement: 'We have nothing to do with this'
Ra'am chairman Mansour Abbas denied that his party had any connection to either investigation.
"Ra'am welcomes the decision by Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg to investigate suspicions of improper attempts to influence the election through foreign funding," Abbas said in a statement. "Safeguarding election integrity and the rule of law is a civic and democratic obligation that we have made a central principle of our party."
Abbas insisted that Ra'am had no connection to the allegations and pledged full cooperation with law enforcement authorities. "Ra'am has nothing to do with the affair in question or with any other affair, and we declare that we will cooperate fully with all law enforcement authorities to establish the truth," he said.
Abbas also directed a personal message at Netanyahu, using his nickname, "Abu Yair," and accusing him of employing Qatari agents in his office.
"And to Abu Yair, who employs Qatari agents in his office, we have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimization he is conducting against Arab citizens: 'There will be nothing because there is nothing.' But unlike you, in our case it is the truth, not another lie."
Over the past 24 hours, Likud has submitted materials to the Central Elections Committee that it says include firsthand recordings of individuals from Arab communities admitting to bribing voters with fuel vouchers and cash.
Police, however, rejected Likud's claims Thursday morning, saying there was "no evidence whatsoever" supporting the allegation that the election had been stolen.
The Central Elections Committee has likewise emphasized that voting was conducted lawfully and that it has no evidence of systematic manipulation of the results, even as the Shin Bet continues investigating suspicions of foreign interference.

Rock collapse causes casualties at Turkish tourist hotspot – media (VIDEOS)
At least two people have been killed and another injured after rocks broke off a natural formation at a popular tourist destination in Türkiye’s Cappadocia region, local media have reported, citing provincial authorities.
The incident occurred at around 3:15 PM local time on Thursday following heavy rainfall, Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok told reporters.
The collapse took place near the entrance to the Goreme Open-Air Museum, where rocks broke off one of the region’s distinctive fairy chimney formations.
Rescue teams recovered two bodies from beneath the debris, while another person was taken to hospital with injuries, according to the governor.
Police, gendarmerie, medical personnel, and disaster response teams were dispatched to the scene, he said.
Rescuers are continuing to search the debris for anyone who might still be trapped, while the authorities have yet to release the victims’ identities or nationalities.
According to media reports, rain and wind have affected the region intermittently this week, forcing the cancellation of Cappadocia’s popular hot-air balloon tours on Wednesday and Thursday.

Rembrandt's masterpieces become tattoos in the Netherlands

13:37:29 UTC
22:37:29 KST

The Poor Man's Rembrandt Project, first launched in 2023, has returned by popular demand, bringing tattoo artists into the house where Rembrandt once lived and worked. Among those taking part is Associated Press correspondent Mike Corder, who had covered the original event without imagining he would one day get a tattoo himself. This time, he sat down with renowned Dutch tattoo artist Henk Schiffmacher, better known as Hanky Panky, to have Rembrandt's 1630 etching Self-Portrait with Beret, Wide-Eyed reproduced on his arm. After around half an hour, the young artist's wide-eyed expression was permanently etched into Corder's skin.
Schiffmacher, whose career spans more than 45 years, has tattooed celebrities including Lady Gaga and members of the Red Hot Chili Peppers. He embraces the nickname "Poor Man's Rembrandt", seeing tattooing as an art form that accompanies its owner for life.
The museum's director, Milou Halbesma, says Rembrandt's self-portraits reveal his remarkable honesty, capturing every wrinkle and imperfection, including his own.
The project brings together two very different artistic traditions, transforming centuries-old etchings into contemporary body art. As Schiffmacher finished Corder's tattoo, he welcomed him into what he jokingly called the "world of freaks". The journalist's verdict was simple: happy with the result, if a little sore. The project runs until 7 November.

Ieva Jāgere: Latvia must be among the first choices for international investment projects

Internationally recognised site selection consultants whose recommendations influence global companies’ decisions on where to locate new manufacturing facilities, technology centres and other investment projects will gather in Riga this week. On 29 October, Latvia’s capital will host the Site Selectors Guild European Conference for the first time in the Baltic States. The Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) sees the event as an important opportunity to strengthen Latvia’s position in the international competition for investment.
The Site Selectors Guild brings together internationally recognised site selection consultants who help multinational companies evaluate different countries and make investment location decisions. Eleven Guild members will visit Riga, including representatives of international consulting firms such as JLL, Newmark, BCI Global and IBM Plant Location International. Their recommendations can be decisive when companies are choosing between several countries competing for the same investment project.
“Investment does not begin with the construction of a factory. It begins with a decision about which country a company should choose for its development. And the people who have come to Riga this week play an important role in making those decisions. The fact that they have chosen to meet in Latvia is significant recognition of our country’s visibility, but making a good impression alone is not enough in the competition for investment. Companies need to know how quickly they can start operating, what support is available and who can help resolve specific issues. Latvia’s advantage lies in its ability to make decisions quickly and ensure direct cooperation with the people responsible. Our task is to make sure that the next time these consultants are looking for a location for a new factory or technology centre on behalf of their clients, Latvia is among their first choices. That is why, during the conference, LIAA will also present concrete opportunities and advantages that Latvia can offer international companies seeking to expand their operations and implement new investment projects here,” emphasises Ieva Jāgere, Director of LIAA.
Latvia’s competitiveness in attracting investment is also reflected in its results to date. In 2025, 31 investment projects with a total value of €1.01 billion were launched with LIAA’s involvement. Meanwhile, during the first nine months of 2026, the total planned value of investment projects attracted by LIAA reached €886.8 million, representing almost 90% of the agency’s €1 billion target for the year.
LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere will attend a meeting with conference participants on 28 October. During the conference, LIAA will use the opportunity to establish contacts with international consultants and present Latvia’s investment environment. Key elements of Latvia’s investment proposition include access to the European Union’s single market, a skilled workforce, the exemption of reinvested corporate profits from corporate income tax, and the opportunity for eligible investment projects to benefit from the Green Corridor initiative, which accelerates access to certain public administration services.
According to LIAA, maintaining cooperation after the conference will be particularly important to ensure that consultants have access to up-to-date information about investment opportunities in Latvia and direct contacts to facilitate future projects. This will help Latvia become involved at an early stage in the evaluation of new investment projects and compete for their implementation.
The second Site Selectors Guild European Conference will take place on 29 October at the Radisson Blu Latvija Conference & Spa Hotel in Riga. It will bring together site selection consultants and representatives of economic development organisations from Europe, North America and Asia. The conference programme will feature discussions on global investment trends, the impact of artificial intelligence on site selection, energy availability, clean technologies and the semiconductor industry.
The conference is organised by the Site Selectors Guild, with the Riga Investment and Tourism Agency (RITA) serving as the host partner.

Lagarde has headed the bank since November 1, 2019, and her term was originally scheduled to end in late October 2027.
In a video posted by the ECB chief, adhesive bandages were visible on her face. To "avoid speculation on social media," Lagarde explained that she had undergone a minor medical procedure earlier in the week, and urged others to follow medical advice and get regular skin check-ups.

Earlier, World Economic Forum (WEF) founder Klaus Schwab told the Financial Times that he had invited Lagarde to succeed him at the helm of the forum starting in early 2027. Lagarde has not yet publicly confirmed these plans.

America’s hegemonic gamble: how a third war could push Iran towards nuclear weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:33:21 UTC
22:33:21 KST

The most dangerous moment for a dominant power comes when it considers continuing a war necessary to vindicate the decision to begin it. At that point, every inadequate outcome can become an argument for a larger attack. Past costs raise the demand for victory, even as the conditions for achieving it grow more difficult. America is approaching such a point in its confrontation with Iran: a war intended to demonstrate its capacity to exercise power has become a test of that power’s credibility.
The Atlantic’s report of 22 October offers a clear account of this calculation. Drawing on conversations with officials and people familiar with the discussions, it describes a belief in US President Donald Trump’s circle that economic pressure has brought Iran to the brink and that another round of strikes could make regime change possible. The same report stresses that no final decision to resume attacks has been taken. What has returned is the expectation that one additional application of pressure will deliver a decisive result.
That expectation is a new expression of an old error: the assumption that an enemy’s vulnerability guarantees that its behaviour can be managed. Iran can suffer damage without accepting the political outcome its attacker seeks. The distance between these two possibilities is where military action becomes a hegemonic gamble.
Understanding this gamble requires attention to the function of a “manageable enemy”. In this calculation, the presence of a familiar adversary helps organise alliances, justify a military presence and establish the need for protection. Such an enemy’s value to the dominant power depends on the expectation that the scale of the threat, the costs of confrontation and the terms on which it ends can be controlled. In this picture, Iran is important enough for a confrontation with it to carry regional significance, yet is imagined to be sufficiently vulnerable that it cannot alter the rules of engagement.
The account of protection and obedience offered by Carl Schmitt, the German jurist and political theorist, helps clarify this relationship. In his analysis, the protecting power plays a role in determining the enemy and shaping political allegiance. Extending this argument to America’s regional order suggests that a claim to security leadership rests on the expectation that the leader can provide protection and contain danger. “Manageable enemy” is this essay’s own formulation; what it draws from Schmitt is the relationship between the promise of protection and political authority.
The difficulty begins when confronting the enemy makes the promised security more costly. Allies that rely on American protection also become exposed to the consequences of American policy. If military operations produce prolonged insecurity, economic disruption and the prospect of retaliation, the capacity to destroy remains intact, but the claim to control the crisis’s outcome comes into question. Hegemonic authority erodes in the gap between the two.
READ: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warn US would ‘regret’ any new attack
The experience of Iraq should have made Washington more alert to this gap. The fall of Saddam Hussein’s government did not resolve the problem of establishing a stable order favourable to the United States. In Iran’s case, even the conversion of military strikes into political collapse has encountered serious obstacles. Institutional plurality, sources of national attachment and experience of governing under pressure make it difficult to move automatically from eliminating individuals to disabling the system. A government can grow weaker while retaining the capacity to make decisions and resist.
The 12-day war of June 2025 and the US-Israeli campaign that began on 28 February, 2026 exposed this problem on different scales. Iran’s losses have been real. Yet the outcome those losses were supposed to produce – acceptance of a future determined by Washington and Tel Aviv – remains contested. The continuation of negotiations, threats and pressure itself demonstrates that military superiority has yet to produce the intended political conclusion.
A Reuters report of 27 August records the distance between the initial expectation and the resulting situation. Trump had spoken of a campaign lasting four to five weeks, yet six months later the United States was caught between increasing the pressure and finding a face-saving exit. That distance matters for understanding the next decision, because a protracted war can change what ending it means to the power that began it.
This is where the hegemonic gamble takes shape. Once a president ties his credibility to forcing Iran to retreat, an agreement that recognises Iran’s continuing freedom of action may appear to him as an admission of failure. Concern for personal credibility then becomes entangled with concern for the credibility of American threats and the confidence of allies. A specific conflict comes to bear the burden of vindicating a much broader claim to power.
This does not mean that ending the war would automatically bring down American hegemony. The danger lies in how the war’s end is interpreted. If Washington regards Tehran’s overt submission as the only acceptable outcome, it narrows its own access to exits that could preserve American power and resources. Under these conditions, a third round of major strikes can be presented as an opportunity to repair the credibility damaged by the first two.
The promise is similar each time: this will be the final application of pressure. Yet if the expected political response fails to materialise, further pressure is demanded to justify what came before. Even a desire to concentrate on larger rivals will not necessarily interrupt this cycle. A leader who has defined withdrawal from a conflict as defeat may deepen his commitment in an attempt to escape it.
Iran, meanwhile, does not remain the static target it was at the beginning of the confrontation. The experience of attack changes its perception of threats and the ways it preserves the functions of government. Replacing commanders, sustaining decision-making and drawing on different means of imposing costs are elements of an adaptive capacity that assessments based solely on the number of targets destroyed tend to overlook.
OPINION: Iran’s new military doctrine is designed to make victory meaningless
Adaptation to war, however, should not be confused with immunity from it. Organisational survival can coexist with social exhaustion, damaged infrastructure and dwindling resources. Experience teaches both sides, and the attacker can also change its methods. The argument about the difficulty of an American political victory must therefore remain grounded in the problem of converting destruction into compliance. No past experience guarantees the failure of the next round of strikes.
For Tehran, this presents a more difficult problem. The ability to endure a war does not necessarily prevent the next one from beginning. Iran may be able to deny its enemy an easy victory while still facing repeated cycles of attack, reconstruction and renewed threats. Each instance of survival imposes a further cost on society and leaves the question of future security unresolved.
Viewed in this light, a condition of neither war nor peace can gradually become intolerable. If a ceasefire is accompanied by continued economic pressure and the enduring possibility of attack, reconstruction remains vulnerable to renewed interruption. The state plans for the future, but the viability of those plans depends on its enemy’s next decision. Under these conditions, the problem of deterrence extends beyond absorbing the costs of one war to preventing its recurrence.
This is where the continuation of America’s gamble could alter Iran’s nuclear calculations. If Iranian decision-makers conclude that their existing instruments raise the costs of war without preventing its recurrence, the argument advanced by advocates of nuclear weapons gains strength. They can contend that escaping the cycle of attacks requires a different form of deterrence.
Signs of this debate are already visible. An excerpt from a Financial Times report, reproduced by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace on 20 October, describes growing calls among some hardline politicians, parliamentarians and analysts to abandon opposition to nuclear weapons and withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The report indicates a shift within part of the political debate; it does not establish that the government has taken an official decision.
If a third round of strikes also fails to produce a dependable political settlement, that argument could become stronger. For advocates of a change in nuclear policy, the latest experience would provide further evidence that a temporary halt to bombing does not secure the future. In that case, acquiring a weapon could be proposed as a means of preventing a fourth round, although there would be no guarantee that it would achieve that objective.
READ: UN nuclear watchdog chief urges Iran to grant IAEA access to verify nuclear material
A considerable distance separates this calculation from its realisation. A stronger incentive, a political decision, practical capability and a reliable deterrent are distinct stages. A Reuters report of 7 October emphasises the severe damage to facilities and the uncertainty surrounding the state of the nuclear programme. That uncertainty prevents us from treating the path to a weapon as straightforward or inevitable. An attempt to follow that path could itself increase the risk of further attacks.
Despite these limitations, the contradiction within the policy of pressure remains: operations justified as a means of preventing the weaponisation of Iran’s nuclear programme may increase the political influence of those advocating precisely that choice. Destroying capacity and strengthening incentives can happen simultaneously. Short-term military success does not, by itself, answer the long-term problem of non-proliferation.
Israel also has agency in this process. Its government may regard the rebuilding of Iran’s capabilities as a threat that must be contained again. But the United States must reckon with a wider set of consequences: the security of regional partners, economic costs and the ability to bring the conflict to an end. Treating these two sets of objectives as identical risks turning every stage of Iranian recovery into a fresh demand for American intervention.
A way out depends on changing the conditions that both sides use to justify the next round. Verifiable limits on the nuclear programme must be linked to a credible reduction in the risk of attack and a genuine opportunity for reconstruction. An agreement that offers Tehran only the promise of a pause will not weaken the argument of those advocating nuclear deterrence. Accepting that Iran has a viable economic and security future, by contrast, could change the basis of the calculation.
To preserve its power, America must be able to distinguish between ending an unsuccessful war and surrendering its global position. Insisting that only Iran’s submission can preserve American credibility is precisely what binds that credibility to an increasingly costly outcome.
The danger of a third round is that Washington returns to war to prove that its enemy can be managed, while Tehran concludes from the recurrence of war that it must permanently change the costs of attacking it. In that event, the gamble to preserve hegemony could strengthen the very nuclear incentive that the war was supposed to eliminate.
OPINION: Ending the war requires accepting Iran in the Middle East

When Philosophers Reinvent The Wheel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:33:17 UTC
22:33:17 KST

You may not believe this, but philosophers sometimes work in ignorance of research programs, bodies of literature, methodologies, and findings outside of philosophy that could be relevant to their work.
In a post at his blog, Ethan Landes (Eindhoven) shares how he recently discovered that the relatively young philosophical subfield of conceptual engineering, to which he contributes, appears to have reinvented a wheel produced 50 years ago by scholars in the field of sociolinguistics.
Neat find. But ouch.
He writes:
There is an entire literature that discusses things at a level that I (we?) all thought was unique to conceptual engineering. An entire literature the conceptual engineering literature could have drawn on for ideas and knowledge. But no one looked carefully, so we have a decade of literature of us forging our own paths.
It reminds me of the time I spent an hour fighting my way up an English hill through thick, knee-high heather, only to discover at the top that [there] had been an unmarked path 20 meters to my right the whole time.
Some degree of ignorance of other fields is a cost of disciplinary specialization for creatures who sometimes have to do things that cut into their research—like sleep, or die. Since specialization has its benefits, some ignorance is expected.
And its worth noting that philosophy is increasingly interdisciplinary, and on some measures, the most interdisciplinary field in the humanities.
Still, philosophy’s remit is about as broad as can be, so perhaps it has a greater risk of interdisciplinary ignorance leading to research which duplicates work done elsewhere, or research which would have been significantly advanced in light of awareness of very similar research already conducted outside of philosophy.
Dr. Landes gave us one example, but I’m sure there are others, both contemporary and historical. Let’s hear about them.

UAE oil spill: which beaches are closed and what tourists should know
Authorities in Sharjah, a city in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), have temporarily closed its beaches as a precaution following a tanker oil spill that affected the coastline of the neighboring emirate of Umm Al Quwain, according to the Sharjah Government Media Bureau and the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The October 28 announcement said the closure was intended to prevent pollution from reaching Sharjah’s beaches. Specialized teams and relevant authorities are taking measures to protect the coastline, while residents and visitors have been urged to follow official instructions.
UAE authorities: Our beaches are closed due to an oil spill resulting from damage to a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz. ▫️ The footage shows the coastline of the emirate of Umm al-Quwain, located 30 km from Sharjah and 120 km from the Strait of Hormuz. https://t.co/i4iRVczP0q
— Sprinter Press (@Sprinter_Press) October 24, 2026
What caused the pollution?
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirmed that the UAE’s monitoring and environmental assessment system detected marine pollution from a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain’s beaches. The ministry did not identify the vessel or specify what caused the leak in its statement.
The spill also caused odors noticed by residents in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain. The ministry said these odors posed no health risks to residents.
Specialized teams, working with local and federal authorities, immediately began containing the pollution and cordoning off affected areas. Cleanup and remediation operations are underway, alongside coastal surveys and environmental assessments to determine the extent of the impact.
🛰🇦🇪 Satellite imagery from this morning (Oct. 24th) reveals an oil spill washing ashore in the UAE. The impact is heavily visible in Al Seanneeah, located just 50km north of Dubai. https://t.co/306ZVOpY9g
— MenchOsint (@MenchOsint) October 24, 2026
Which beaches are closed?
In Umm Al Quwain, all beaches and coastal areas are temporarily closed. Restrictions will remain until technical teams complete their assessments and identify the measures needed to ensure safety and protect the marine environment.
In Ras Al Khaimah, authorities announced the closure of all public beaches on October 24 until further notice. Residents and visitors were urged to follow official instructions and avoid affected coastal areas.

In Sharjah, the October 28 announcement covers the city’s beaches. Al Hamriyah Beach had already been temporarily closed on October 23 as a precaution against pollution from the spill. The latest statement does not announce a blanket closure of beaches throughout the emirate.
Separately, Dibba Al Hisn Beach in Sharjah was closed for maintenance and improvement works. That closure was not attributed to the spill.
Several hotels and resorts in Umm Al Quwain and Ras Al Khaimah also told Gulf News that beach access and sea swimming were restricted, while pools, restaurants and other facilities continued operating. Guests should confirm the current arrangements directly with their hotel.

What should tourists do if their beach is closed?
Visitors should respect beach closures and check official updates before heading to the coast. The ministry has urged fishermen and other sea users to follow authorities’ instructions and refrain from fishing in polluted areas.
Travelers already staying at an affected property can contact their hotel to confirm which facilities remain available and ask their tour operator or booking provider about alternative accommodation or changes to travel dates.
Before accepting any changes, guests should request written confirmation of additional charges, cancellation conditions and the facilities available at an alternative property. The official statements reviewed do not announce a general refund or relocation scheme.
Those considering a beach in another emirate should check local authority notices and confirm access with the destination before traveling.

What if you come into contact with oil?
General oil-spill guidance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises avoiding areas where oil or tar is visible or can be smelled. If oil gets on the skin, wash it off with soap and water. Do not use gasoline or other solvents. Seek medical advice if a rash develops or contamination is difficult to remove. This is general guidance, rather than an advisory issued specifically for the UAE incident.
No reopening dates were provided in the closure announcements reviewed. The UAE ministry has pledged further updates and urged the public to rely on official information and avoid spreading rumors.

JD Vance contacts senior Iranian official in bid to revive peace talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:32:32 UTC
22:32:32 KST

With less than a week until the US congressional midterm elections, the Wall Street Journal has reported that JD Vance has written to Mohsen Rezaei in a bid to revive negotiations, as Trump continues to warn of possible renewed strikes again
US Vice President JD Vance has reached out to Iran's security chief in an effort to restart peace negotiations and avert another US attack on the Islamic republic, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.
Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, reportedly at the direction of US President Donald Trump, according to one of the newspaper's sources.
The outreach aims to establish whether Washington and Tehran can find enough common ground to persuade Trump to hold off on ordering what officials have described as a “short but intense” military campaign against Iran in the coming weeks.
The initiative comes despite Trump’s recent declaration that his administration was not negotiating with Iran and his repeated warnings that further military action could be imminent.
The letter and subsequent contacts between US and Iranian officials have focused on establishing a framework for potential negotiations rather than outlining a detailed peace agreement, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Axios separately reported that Vance stressed in his letter that any negotiations aimed at preventing renewed US military strikes would have to address Iran’s nuclear programme.
A US official told Axios that Vance had proposed sending the letter and that Trump had welcomed the initiative, although the official declined to specify when it was delivered.
However, Trump offered a different account on Wednesday, denying that he had instructed Vance to pursue peace negotiations with Iran. The US president said the contact was primarily aimed at facilitating the delivery of medical supplies.
“They need help with medical supplies and various things,” Trump told reporters, adding that Vance had sought his approval before proceeding.
Abbas Araghchi, Iran's foreign minister, wrote on X on Wednesday: "While our brave armed forces are fully prepared to defend the homeland, Iran is still giving diplomacy a chance to succeed."
He added: "We are still in close and continuous contact with mediators to examine ideas that could guarantee implementation of our seven-day plan even in less than a week."
The letter comes as Washington has reportedly warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible new military campaign against Iran after the US midterm elections on 3 November, according to the Wall Street Journal,
However, Trump has not made a final decision on whether to authorise further strikes, citing people briefed on the discussions.
The conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes in late February, has severely disrupted energy shipments from Gulf countries, with restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz contributing to wider economic fallout.

Western Europe is falling apart – we should prepare for what comes next
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:32:30 UTC
22:32:30 KST

Western Europe is falling apart – we should prepare for what comes next
For Russia, developments in the rest of Europe matter primarily insofar as they affect our national interests. Above all, this concerns security given that, for centuries, Russia has faced its greatest challenges from the West, and there’s little reason to assume that this historical pattern has disappeared.
Western Europe’s leading countries now stand at a crossroads, yet the choice confronting them isn’t simply between competing models of domestic development, it’s between war and peace with their neighbors, foremost among them Russia, whose size and historical role have repeatedly made it the principal obstacle to Western European expansion.
The unrest sweeping several European countries this autumn marks a new phase in the continent’s systemic crisis as it reflects the convergence of two long-term problems that much of Europe’s political establishment has proved incapable of resolving.
The first is the exhaustion of the socioeconomic model that sustained Western European prosperity throughout the Cold War and its aftermath. That model depended on Europe’s privileged position in the global economy and the absence of serious competitors beyond the Western world, but China’s rise, combined with increasingly limited resources, has undermined those advantages.
Closer economic integration with Russia, and access to its enormous natural wealth, might have offered Western Europe a final opportunity to preserve its exceptional position, but instead regional leaders allowed their own arrogance to prevent an accommodation with Moscow because they couldn’t accept that Russia wished to live peacefully with its neighbors, but on terms consistent with its own interests.
The second problem is Western Europe’s longstanding absence of genuine sovereignty.
Integration into the American-led NATO system has deprived even major powers such as Germany, France, and Britain of the freedom to pursue fundamental political change and one of the alliance’s practical functions has been to preserve the existing political order within its member states.
Any serious attempt to transform that order would require a reassessment of relations with Washington and such independence is something these European governments have long been unwilling, or unable, to contemplate.
Together, these structural weaknesses have left Western Europe’s political and economic establishments effectively paralyzed.
For nearly two decades, governments have substituted the appearance of activity for meaningful reform. Successive emergencies, involving migration, the pandemic, hostility towards Russia, and preparations for military confrontation, have allowed leaders to avoid addressing deeper problem and this helps explain the temptation to interpret today’s unrest as another exercise in political manipulation. Emmanuel Macron, for example, has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to survive the consequences of disastrous decisions through tactical maneuvering.
Yet it would be a mistake to dismiss the protests as artificial or orchestrated.
In France, the initial demonstrations were driven by schoolchildren and university students demanding more teachers and improvements to an education system suffering from declining standards, but these grievances are hardly unique to France and they reflect broader weaknesses in modern education, including funding arrangements that encourage institutions to compete for pupils rather than concentrate on teaching.
By early October, the French protests had expanded as other groups affected by Macron’s liberal economic policies joined the demonstrations. The authorities blamed the political left, while unrest escalated into rioting and looting.
Similar discontent emerged in Spain and Portugal, where soaring housing costs became the immediate trigger. Both countries have spent years occupying subordinate positions within the European Union, with little influence over its economic priorities, even as their former politicians find comfortable positions in Brussels.
Western Europe has consequently entered a period in which conventional political competition is increasingly accompanied by mass protest and the participation of young people is particularly significant.
In France, the EU’s most important military power and its only nuclear-armed member, it was students who provided the initial momentum. While much of the adult electorate has descended into political apathy under Macron, younger generations retain aspirations for a better future and their grievances are genuine. So, too, is the wider crisis that has brought people onto the streets.
There are therefore grounds to believe that public dissatisfaction may eventually bring new political forces to power, which from Russia’s perspective raises an obvious possibility in that perhaps Western Europe’s next generation of leaders will prove more reasonable on questions of security and relations with Moscow.
Such hopes, however, may be premature because they reflect less our actual experience of European politics than our desire to imagine a Western Europe capable of recovering its political judgement.
Indeed, the objective nature of the present crisis makes its possible consequences especially troubling and European history offers little reassurance that profound domestic upheaval produces peaceful relations with neighbouring countries. On the contrary, revolutionary transformations have repeatedly generated external aggression, and the French Revolution provides one example.
The upheavals of the late 18th century were followed by wars against neighboring states and, eventually, Napoleon’s attempt to dominate Europe.
The extraordinary energy released by revolution demanded an outlet, while new rulers also needed resources and opportunities for enrichment beyond their borders.
As Henry Kissinger observed in his early historical work, the internal foundations of Napoleon’s expansionism helped prevent a lasting accommodation with Russia after the disastrous campaign of 1812.
Germany offers an even more destructive precedent, where the political upheavals of the 20th century ultimately brought to power a regime whose ambitions extended far beyond Germany’s borders. The conquest of neighboring countries was followed by an attack on the Soviet Union and the most devastating war in human history.
Again, internal political transformation was accompanied by an effort to direct national energies towards external expansion and the consequences of that war fundamentally altered Europe’s position as many of its leading states lost much of their effective sovereignty and became dependent on the United States for their security.
Paradoxically, that dependence may now offer some protection against the most dangerous consequences of Europe’s internal crisis because governments that lack genuine strategic independence may also lack the freedom to embark upon adventures of their own choosing.
Nevertheless, Russia can’t base its security on the assumption that European political upheaval will produce more sensible leaders even if the temptation to hope for a peaceful transformation of Europe is understandable. Hope isn’t a strategy, and history provides ample grounds for caution.
Russia must therefore prepare not for the miracle of a Western Europe reconciled to peaceful coexistence, but for the possibility that its internal crisis will once again find expression in confrontation abroad.
Whatever political forces eventually emerge from the present turmoil, preparing for a military confrontation with our European neighbors must remain one of Russia’s central strategic priorities.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

North Korea fires some 10 ballistic missiles into Sea of Japan
North Korea fired some 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan from around Wonsan, Kangwon Province, on Thursday, the South Korean military said, JIJI Press reported.
The Japanese government said that none have fallen into the country's exclusive economic zone.
The missiles were fired around 12:30 p.m. Japan time and flew about 250 kilometers, according to the South Korean military. No damage to aircraft or ships around Japan has been confirmed.
Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a press conference in Tokyo that the missile launches by North Korea "violate U.N. Security Council resolutions and pose a serious problem to the safety of the people."
He also said that Japan lodged a protest with North Korea through the embassy route in Beijing.
Earlier, it was reported that South Korea renewed its offer Friday to hold military talks with North Korea to discuss their conflicting views on where the inter-Korean border sits, seeking to ease tensions sparked by last month's land mine blast inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).

Three regions record highest construction growth in Kazakhstan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Three regions record highest construction growth in Kazakhstan
Ulytau and Kyzylorda regions, along with the city of Shymkent, recorded the highest growth in construction activity in Kazakhstan during the first nine months of 2026, Qazinform News Agency quotes Minister of Industry and Construction Yerssaiyn Nagaspayev as saying.
According to Nagaspayev, Kazakhstan's construction volume index stood at 111.5% in the first nine months of 2026, with construction activity increasing 2.4-fold in Ulytau region, 31.5% in Kyzylorda region, and 25.4% in Shymkent.
Growth in Ulytau region was largely driven by the construction of railway lines, roads, gas pipelines, and other infrastructure facilities.
In Kyzylorda region, major projects included roads, residential buildings, a multidisciplinary hospital, and the Kyzylorda Arena sports complex. Meanwhile, Shymkent saw growth in residential and industrial construction, along with road reconstruction projects.
However, construction volumes declined in several regions, falling by 28.1% in Zhetysu region, 16% in Karaganda region, and 2% in North Kazakhstan region.
The declines were mainly due to reduced activity on certain infrastructure and industrial projects, particularly those related to gas supply, railway and road construction, and water supply systems.
However, Nagaspayev stressed that lower construction volumes do not necessarily reflect a lack of investment or construction capacity. He noted that a more accurate assessment should consider funding levels, the timelines of major projects, and the availability of construction resources.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan plans to build nearly 70 new healthcare facilities across the country.

Belarus Mastered Repair of Yak-130 Trainer&Combat Aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:32:09 UTC
22:32:09 KST

Belarusian 558th Aircraft Repair Plant in Baranavichy has begun repairing Yak-130 trainer and combat aircraft for the first time, in cooperation with the Russian developer.
The State Authority for Military Industry of the Republic of Belarus announced this on October 29.
The work is carried out depending on the technical condition of the aircraft. It includes the restoration of components, including complex onboard equipment systems.
The plant’s engineers will also repair aircraft and radio-electronic equipment, weapons and other aircraft systems.
Russia’s Yakovlev PJSC, the developer of the Yak-130, and component manufacturers have also been involved in the programme.
The State Authority for Military Industry did not specify the number of aircraft in the first batch, their ownership or the deadline for completing the work. The value of the contract has also not been disclosed.
The plant previously specialised in the repair and modernisation of Su-25, Su-27, Su-30 and MiG-29 aircraft, as well as Mi-8 and Mi-24 helicopters.
The plant is also preparing to localise the production of components and final assembly of Russian Su-25 attack aircraft. To this end, the enterprise has built more than 20,000 square metres of new production facilities.
In addition, Belarusian aircraft repair specialists are involved in restoring Russian combat aircraft. According to Ukrainian intelligence, experts from the 558th plant were sent to the Air Force Repair Plant No 121 at Kubinka, Russia, to carry out repairs.
The Yak-130 is a two-seat jet aircraft of Russian design intended for training combat aircraft pilots.
It is equipped with two engines, has nine hardpoints and can carry up to three tonnes of weapons, including aerial bombs and missiles.
Belarus received 12 Yak-130 trainer and combat aircraft from Russia in three batches of four in 2015, 2016 and 2019. One of them crashed near Baranavichy in May 2021.

Higher energy prices trigger surge in inflation now at 5.26%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:31:51 UTC
22:31:51 KST

Inflation, the figure that reflects the general rise in the price level, has risen to 5.26 per cent this month. The cost of living in Belgium has risen mainly due to the sharp increase in the price of natural gas and electricity.
Inflation in Belgium continues to rise: whilst the cost of living rose by 4.69 per cent last month, inflation has increased to 5.26 per cent this month according to the statistics agency Statbel.
Anyone following the news on energy prices knows the cause all too well: the sharp rise in energy prices is caused by the ongoing tensions in the Middle East, which have been putting pressure on gas and oil supplies to Europe for months.
Following the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, inflation saw its first significant spike in April, rising to over 4 per cent. After a slight dip in June, inflation has been on a steady upward trend again since July.
Inflation has not been this high since April. Back then, too, sky-high energy prices were to blame.
Natural gas more expensive too
Compared with a year ago, energy inflation this month stands at 33.22 per cent, compared with 24.37 per cent in September.
Electricity is 23.7 per cent more expensive than in October last year, heating oil 30.8 per cent and natural gas as much as 52.5 per cent.
In addition to price rises for natural gas, electricity and heating oil, rising rents, higher tuition fees for higher education, more expensive clothing and airfares are also driving inflation.
The sharp rise in the price of external storage devices is also striking: +48.7 per cent. As a result of the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) computer applications, high global demand has led to a shortage of hard drives and memory cards.
Trigger index not exceeded
The health index, on which any indexation of wages and benefits is based, rose from 4 per cent in September to 4.53 per cent in October. The rise is not sufficient to trigger a 2% top-up.
The last time this happened was the case was in June. As a result, benefits and the salaries of civil servants got a 2% top up in September.
According to the Planning Office’s inflation forecasts from last month, the reference index was set to be exceeded again in November. The Planning Bureau will publish new inflation forecasts on Tuesday.

Foreign residents: get organised, starting with dual nationality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:30:59 UTC
22:30:59 KST

Foreign residents: get organised, starting with dual nationality
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Eelco Keij founded the Foundation for Dutch Nationals Abroad (SNBN), which lobbies for Dutch people living overseas. A bill due before parliament in December would allow dual nationality both for them and for foreign residents who naturalise here – but the coalition agreement only backs the first part. Keij says the international community needs to organise and lobby for itself, or risk being left behind.
Foreign residents in the Netherlands need lasting political influence, and could learn from another group that once had no voice in Dutch politics: Dutch citizens abroad.
In 2011, when I became a US citizen alongside my native Dutch citizenship, I realised that most Dutch people abroad could not have dual citizenship. As my case fell under one of the exceptions, I actually could be both. I felt lucky for myself, and pity for others. This is where my second realisation came in, possibly spurred by having worked for years in lobbying, advocacy and the Dutch parliament: no one in the Dutch political system would ever stand up for people like me, living abroad.
First, I set up a debate on dual nationality, from New York, and soon after, a petition among the Dutch abroad, reaching both astonishing numbers of citizens and articles in the Dutch national press. Aiming for a longer-term strategy, I studied how other European countries treated their citizens abroad. It turned out that in some countries the diaspora had organized itself in interest organisations, like the French, Danish and Swiss abroad.
Through this research, it became clear to me that the Dutch living abroad also needed a formal vehicle to be heard in Dutch politics. Together with other concerned Dutch citizens living abroad I founded the Foundation for the Dutch Abroad (SNBN), in 2019. The SNBN is a volunteer advocacy and lobby organization – strategic by design, focused on results.
Gaining recognition 
Aware that the Dutch political scene is fragmented, coalition-based, and unpredictable, our board is mostly formed of Dutch citizens abroad who are members of different political parties. That way, while remaining non-partisan as an organisation, board members have many formal and informal contacts with different political parties. As a consequence, Dutch politicians started hearing us, and seeing us.
Our efforts contributed to the 2022 constitutional change enabling Dutch citizens abroad to participate in elections for the Dutch Senate through an electoral college. Moreover, we saw how our outreach on various occasions led to mitigation of legislation and a willingness among Dutch politicians to engage with us, having discovered a new electorate.
Currently, we are fully focused on the advancement of a bill that was introduced almost ten years ago, which lies at the very heart of our foundation: allowing Dutch citizens abroad to have dual citizenship.
But the dual citizenship bill also covers foreigners in the Netherlands. If passed in full, it would also scrap the requirement forcing them to give up their original nationality.
Spoiler: that is not going to happen. The SNBN found there is currently no political majority to support foreigners in the Netherlands in their quest for dual citizenship. Their interests are beyond our mandate. But the political end result may be favoring the Dutch abroad, without equivalent progress for foreigners residing in the Netherlands – an aspect that could be dropped from the bill.
Time to start lobbying 
To our surprise, we have not seen a visible, coordinated lobby on behalf of foreign residents in the Netherlands in the debate on dual citizenship. The bill also covers them, yet they have been largely absent from the debate. So what to do now?
Unlike in countries such as Germany, Luxembourg and Ireland, where migrant-representing organizations already exist, we have not encountered a comparable, visible lobby in this debate on behalf of foreign residents in the Netherlands.
Perhaps with a suggested blueprint of the SNBN at hand, it may well be up to someone, a foreigner residing in the Netherlands, or a group of them, to step up and say: “Let’s start working on that.” Surely there are many issues this interest organisation could work on, including citizenship and naturalisation, family reunification, political participation and voting rights. Above all, it would give foreign residents visibility with Dutch politicians.
As SNBN we can attest to one thing: an important part of lasting political influence is to embed different political streams within the organization’s structure, whether it’s volunteer staff, board members or advisory board members. With that, and the right commitment, there is a real opportunity to build lasting political influence.
Readers: your turn.

NATO allies fear Trump will delay Patriot missiles for Ukraine until after US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:30:40 UTC
22:30:40 KST

Ukraine has called on US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth to sign off on the delivery of crucial Patriot defence systems used to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. But NATO sources warn the situation is "unpredictable."
NATO allies are increasingly pessimistic that Ukraine will receive desperately needed US-made Patriot interceptor missiles before next week's US midterm elections, amid suspicions that President Donald Trump is using military aid to pressure Kyiv into concessions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said his country is still waiting for US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth to approve the transfer of additional interceptors, but NATO sources have told Euronews that the situation remains “unpredictable”, with allies unclear about whether the systems will be released and when they might arrive.
The uncertainty comes as Ukraine's air defences struggle to keep pace with Russian attacks, while US interceptor stocks are under growing pressure from the war against Iran.
Russian attacks outpace US production
Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region over the previous two weeks, highlighting the scale of Ukraine's air defence challenge.
The figures illustrate the scale of the challenge facing Ukraine as it seeks to replenish its air defence stocks.
According to separate Ukrainian estimates, the US produces around 60 to 65 Patriot interceptors a month — fewer than the number of ballistic missiles Russia has launched at Kyiv and the surrounding region in just two weeks.
That production must also meet demand from other US allies and partners worldwide, including countries in the Middle East and the Gulf.
Trump pressures Kyiv over to Russian oil strikes
The uncertainty over Patriot deliveries comes as Trump pressures Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel refineries, arguing that the attacks are driving up global energy prices and hurting American and European consumers.
“We spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it,” Trump said during a visit to his golf resort in Ireland in September.
“There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel. That's hurting the world,” he added.
The US-Israeli war on Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a key shipping route through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas supplies passed — triggered what the International Energy Agency (IEA) described as the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.
With Trump's approval ratings at record lows ahead of the November 3rd midterms, some analysts believe his demands on Ukraine, including the withholding of Patriot interceptors, are intended to demonstrate action on soaring energy prices.
He recently waived punitive sanctions on Russian oil in an attempt to ease the cost to consumers by making more supply available.
Trump "wants to be seen to be doing something about the issues that are making voters unhappy, and one of them is the price of diesel, and that particularly affects farmers and red state voters in the Midwest and the United States," said former US Ambassador to NATO, Kurt Volker.
He [Trump] thinks it'd be a "great story for him to be able to say, I've got Vladimir Putin giving us diesel, and I've got Zelensky to stop attacking the refineries, so 'I'm fighting for you'," said Volker who served until Trump's first term.
Trump "using leverage" against Ukraine
Asked whether there were any indications that the interceptors would be released to Ukraine soon, one NATO source said there was little clarity.
“It's so unpredictable,” the source said.
“Trump is using as much leverage as he has over Ukraine ahead of the midterms,” the source added.
The source suggested that Trump was also seeking to push Kyiv towards a peace deal involving territorial concessions.
Two sources said Washington was frustrated by the lack of progress towards ending Russia's war against Ukraine and wanted the conflict to end as soon as possible.
One source described the war as a “stone in the boot” for Washington, but said the US understood it needed to maintain its relationship with NATO allies, including in the context of the war in Iran.
The US is relying heavily on allies to launch strategic bombers some of which can carry two dozen 2,000lb bombs to attack Iran.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian civilians continue to die as Russia intensifies its missile campaign against the country.
NATO Secretary General, Mark Rutte has urged allies to bilaterally send their own Patriot systems given the urgent needs of Ukraine.
Greece and Spain are two countries which hold considerable stockpiles of less technically advanced PAC-2 systems, NATO sources say. But neither Athens or Madrid have heeded the call of Rutte or the alliance to hand over the interceptors.
Ukraine faces interceptor shortage
Ukraine receives US-made weapons through NATO's Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, under which allies fund purchases of American military equipment for transfer to Kyiv.
Volker says he thinks the delay may also be due to the US needing the supplies to resume heavy fighting against Iran.
"It seems to be the case that European countries have purchased Patriot missiles, the anti-missile missiles, and that they have not been delivered to Ukraine yet," he said.
"And there's no information or explanation from the Pentagon about this," Volker added. "Perhaps they intend to restart the war in Iran "and don't know how many Patriot missiles they're going to need for themselves."
Volker said the prospect of US weapons paid for by European taxpayers being withheld from Ukraine is particularly troubling for European allies, already unsettled by Washington's approach to Moscow.
Concerns have been compounded by restrictions affecting Ukraine's access to Starlink satellite internet services and by proposals floated during US-led peace talks that European governments unfreeze Russian assets.
Europeans have noted the overtures by US envoy Steve Witkoff to Russian President Vladimir Putin, describing him as a "humanitarian," as an indication that the US's allegiance is shifting in favour of Moscow.
In recent talks, the US had suggested unfreezing Russian assets mainly held in Europe and transferring them to the US for future use in Ukraine.
"Some of these proposals were very much one-sided in favour of Russia, including that Europe would unfreeze the frozen Russian assets," Volker said.
"Crazy stuff coming out of these proposals here," he said.
The uncertainty over deliveries also affects Ukraine's access to NASAMS, the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, a US-Norwegian air defence system designed to counter short- and medium-range aerial threats.
Global shortage with no quick fix
The Patriot system's PAC-3 interceptor is the most capable weapons available to Ukraine for countering ballistic missile threats, including by Russia in its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
A global shortage of PAC-3 interceptors, exacerbated by their use in the US war against Iran, is putting further pressure on supplies.
The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has reported that US inventories of Patriot and other interceptors, alongside long-range strike munitions, had been depleted by about half during the conflict in Iran.
The depletion could undermine US military readiness in potential future conflicts, particularly with China, but also with Russia or North Korea, the Washington-based think tank warned.
Replenishing interceptor stocks is costly, technically complex, and time-consuming, meaning Ukraine's supply constraints are not ending any time soon.
Patriot interceptors cost over $4 million each, while manufacturing them can take close to two years, according to the estimates cited.
A tentative US commitment to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles under licence has also stalled, despite Trump announcing the initiative at the NATO summit in Ankara in July.
Meanwhile, Germany has been given the license to produce PAC-2 interceptor missiles - the less advanced, less expensive version of the PAC-3. Its production line is due to deliver the PAC-2 units by December 2026 or January 2027 at the earliest.
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said his government has offered produce the PAC-3 in a bid to kick-start much-needed access.
With supplies stretched and no clear timeline for additional deliveries, Ukraine faces growing uncertainty over its ability to intercept Russia's continuing missile attacks.

October 30 has been declared a Day of Mourning in Chernihiv for those killed as a result of Russian strikes
Kyiv • UNN
On October 30, Chernihiv will honor four residents killed by Russian strikes on October 21, 23, and 29. Entertainment events will be prohibited.
October 30 has been declared a Day of Mourning in Chernihiv for the city’s residents who were killed as a result of Russian strikes between October 21 and 29. The Chernihiv City Council reports this, UNN writes.
On October 21, a 61-year-old man was killed as a result of a Russian strike on Chernihiv. On October 23, a 68-year-old man was killed in an attack on an enterprise. On October 29, two 15-year-old girls were killed as a result of another Russian strike on the city
On the Day of Mourning, the State Flag of Ukraine with a black ribbon will be flown at half-mast on the buildings of state authorities, local self-government bodies, enterprises, and institutions. Entertainment and concert events will also be banned in the city, as will the broadcasting of entertainment music at markets, in retail and restaurant establishments, and on public transport.

Suicide deaths in Germany surge to 27-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:30:31 UTC
22:30:31 KST

Suicide deaths in Germany surge to 27-year high
Germany has seen its highest annual suicide toll in nearly three decades, with 11,334 deaths recorded last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office. Experts suggest that the surge may be linked to a loosely regulated assisted-suicide system, which allows even healthy adults to seek help ending their lives.
The data set released earlier this month and analyzed in greater detail on Wednesday by Germany’s National Suicide Prevention Program (NaSPro) found a rise of 962 suicides, or 9.3%, in 2025, taking the annual toll to its highest level since 1998.
The total was greater than the approximately 7,677 people killed in traffic accidents, homicides, illegal-drug-related deaths and AIDS combined, the report said, adding that men accounted for 69.2% of suicides.
Since 2021, the annual total has climbed 23% though the number of suicides remains below its historical peak of 18,825 in 1981, NaSPro said.
While men accounted for most suicides, the increase was disproportionately concentrated among women, whose deaths rose 17.9%, compared with 5.8% among men. Most suicides (73.7%) also occur in the over-50 age group.
Although hanging remained the most common method of suicide (4,145), it was followed by medication (2,848 cases), which saw a striking surge compared to 2024, when it accounted for 2,002 deaths. This category alone accounted for nearly 88% of the entire annual increase.
The latest figures also point to an increase in suicide deaths among the German youth: among girls aged 15 to 19, deaths surged from 52 in 2024 to 84 in 2025, while the overall toll among teenagers rose from 188 to 208. Suicide accounted for approximately 18% of all deaths among people aged five to 24.
While the German government did not offer a definitive explanation for the dramatic increase, multiple experts linked it to the expansion of assisted suicides, which are not separately identified in official mortality statistics. Three major organizations providing such services reported 1,287 assisted deaths last year, up from 977 in 2024 and just 346 in 2021; medication is also the most common method used in assisted suicides.
Germany’s legal framework permits assisted suicide even for people who are not terminally ill or suffering from incurable conditions. Individuals willing to go this path are not required to provide any justification, and in principle, even a physically healthy young adult can legally seek assistance if the decision is voluntary, informed, and enduring. However, nobody is obliged to assist, and euthanasia performed directly by another person remains illegal.
Ulrich Hegerl, chairman of the German Depression Aid and Suicide Prevention Foundation, criticized what he described as the country’s “extreme position” on the matter, warning that “when assisted suicide becomes normalized as a service, this threshold is lowered, and the number of tragic, preventable suicides rises.”
Suicide researcher Ute Lewitzka of Goethe University Frankfurt, meanwhile, has offered another explanation, describing the surge as a crisis phenomenon. She suggested that financial hardship and uncertainty can intensify suicidal thoughts among vulnerable people, while social media could also contribute. Lewitzka also criticized what she described as Germany’s inadequate access to psychological care.

"International reserves amounted to $729.6 bln as of the close of business on October 23, 2026, having increased by $6.4 bln or by 0.9% over the week, largely due to positive revaluation," the regulator informed.
Reserves totaled $723.2 bln as of October 16.
Russia’s international reserves are highly liquid foreign assets available with the Bank of Russia and the Russian Government. They comprise foreign currency, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), a reserve position in the International Monetary Fund and monetary gold. The target level of the Central Bank for international reserves is $500 bln.
