Mission in Alyoshki and unacceptability of colonial practices: Putin’s statements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:28:13 UTC
22:28:13 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The Russian business community rejects colonial methods and conducts business with African partners on respectful terms, investing in their countries, Russian President Vladimir Putin stated at the Russia-Africa summit.
It is hardly possible to speak of socio-economic development without guaranteeing security, he noted.
Putin added that a humanitarian operation is currently underway in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region to provide assistance to the civilian population.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the head of state.
Security
It is impossible to discuss socio-economic development without guaranteeing security: "Naturally, without resolving these problems, it is impossible to speak of any kind of economic or social development. It is self-evident. Of course, the UN Security Council must devote the necessary attention to this."
Ukrainian settlement and operation in Alyoshki
A humanitarian operation is currently underway in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region to provide assistance to the civilian population: "Regarding the zone of the Russian-Ukrainian conflict: an operation is scheduled right now, over these next few days, today or tomorrow, with the support of the First Lady of the United States [Melania Trump] by the way, to provide aid specifically to the civilian population."
Ukrainian forces have mined the approaches to Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, bringing the settlement closer to a humanitarian catastrophe: "The situation had been developing for a long time."
Russia is exploring options for a peaceful settlement of the conflict in Ukraine: "We are working on this as well, just as we are addressing issues related to a peaceful settlement of the Ukrainian crisis itself."
Alignment of positions between Russia and Africa on pressing issues
Russia and Africa are natural allies in building a multipolar world system free from dictates: "Russia and Africa are united by truly strong bonds of friendship and close partnership. We are natural allies in building a multipolar and truly democratic world order. A world order free of diktat and double standards, based on respect for the norms of international law and fundamental principles of the UN Charter and, what's more, in their entirety and interrelation."
The positions of Russia and African states on the most pressing issues of global politics are similar or coincide: "We advocate for an equitable dialogue and for taking into account the interests of all states."
Russia-Africa summits bring significant added value, as they give a powerful impetus to the development of mutually beneficial ties: "Such summits offer us a valuable opportunity to exchange views on the current state of Russian-African relations and give a powerful boost to our multifaceted and mutually beneficial ties."
Development of Africa
Moscow remains interested in seeing African countries develop, protect their sovereignty, and achieve sustainable economic growth: "Russia has been and remains interested in seeing African nations protect their sovereignty, achieve steady growth, and strengthen their economies and social sectors. To address these goals, we are ready to continue working together with you across all these areas."
Africa will be able not only to feed itself but also to become a major food exporter in the future: "We are convinced that through the application of modern agricultural technologies and the proper organization of agricultural production, as you have noted, dear friends, Africa will be able in the future not only to feed itself but also to become a major exporter of various types of food products."
Economic cooperation
Russia’s trade turnover with Africa has grown 1.5-fold since the previous summit, reaching $27 bln: "The momentum is good, but the true potential of our collaboration is significantly greater, of course," Putin added.
The Russian business community rejects colonial methods and conducts business with African partners on respectful terms, investing in their countries: "Our business community always approaches cooperation with African partners with honesty, respect, and good faith, conducting business on equal terms. Rather than siphoning off profits in the spirit of the colonial practices of former imperial powers, they invest what they earn in the development of your countries’ economies, eagerly share advanced technologies and expertise, and extensively engage local subcontractors, creating new production facilities and jobs."
Many Russian companies have long been successfully carrying out large-scale investment projects in Africa: "This refers to sectors including energy and the peaceful use of nuclear power, mining and mineral extraction, industrial cooperation, logistics, and tourism."
Russian businesses in Africa demonstrate social responsibility by caring for the well-being of local employees and the local environment: "What is important, Russian businesses operate in Africa in a socially responsible manner: they look after the well-being of their employees and their families, fund and participate in the implementation of significant humanitarian programs, pay close attention to ecological and environmental issues, and show respect for internal political processes."
Moscow has established an uninterrupted channel for mutual settlements with African countries, with the ruble accounting for 85% of those transactions: "All of this helps to shield our economic exchanges from external influence and makes them more resilient to fluctuations in the global economic and political landscape."
Russian companies are interested in relocating some of their production facilities to African countries, especially in the current sanctions environment: "I won’t say anything unexpected, but this is entirely in Russia’s interests, especially in today’s environment, with numerous sanctions being applied to the Russian economy and Russian enterprises. Our companies are interested in relocating certain production facilities to African countries."
African nations already enjoy certain advantages in trade with Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), including full exemptions from customs duties: "The EAEU’s unified system of tariff preferences offers African exporters significant benefits when importing goods into the Eurasian market. Forty-seven countries on the continent are eligible for these benefits, with 32 of them enjoying completely zeroed-out customs duties."
Initiatives to introduce advanced Russian services are underway in Africa with the participation of Russian businesses: "Promising initiatives to introduce advanced Russian digital services are being actively implemented on the continent with the participation of Russian businesses."
Ensuring stability and security
Russia is doing much to help African countries maintain internal stability and security, and to strengthen their defense capabilities: "As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, our country makes a significant contribution to resolving ongoing conflicts and preventing new ones on the African continent. That said, we consistently proceed from the fundamental principle that you yourselves have proclaimed: ‘African solutions to African problems.’ Russia is doing a great deal to assist African states in maintaining internal stability and security, and in strengthening their defense and security capabilities."
Diplomatic presence
Russia’s diplomatic presence on the African continent is being expanded systematically: "I must mention the systematic steps being taken by the Russian side to expand our diplomatic presence on the continent. Since the previous summit in 2023, eight new Russian embassies have begun operations in African states, bringing the total number to 48. At the same time, a network of trade missions is being developed; there are currently only six of them, but their activities cover 16 African countries."
Botswana, Seychelles and Togo are planning to open their embassies in Moscow soon, and Russia supports their intention: "We render all necessary assistance to African diplomatic missions operating in Russia. Their number is also growing. We also know about the intention of Botswana, the Seychelles Islands and Togo to open their embassies in Moscow soon and, naturally, we support them."
Middle East
One must not lose sight of the problems facing Palestine, which continues to suffer amid developments in the Persian Gulf: "Of course, amid the events in the Persian Gulf, we must not forget the problems of Palestine, which continues to suffer."
Russia believes a definitive resolution to the Palestinian question can only be achieved through the implementation of the principle of establishing two states: "Russia supports and believes that a final resolution to the Palestinian question can only be reached through the implementation of the well-established two-state principle, which includes the creation of a fully-fledged state on Palestinian territory, a Palestinian state."
Freedom of navigation
It is important to ensure freedom of navigation in all regions of the world, as well as compliance with international maritime law: "I would like to say that the most important thing here is to ensure adherence to the fundamental norms of international maritime law and to guarantee freedom of navigation. This should apply to all regions of the world."

The building of these new 'drone ports' reflects Moscow's growing investment in long-range attack drones as a long-term strategic tool, which can be used both against Ukraine or against countries on NATO's eastern flank.
The Oct. 29 attack was the second strike on the Navlya facility, with the first being on Aug. 3, also targeting launch and storage facilities.

Can EU and India work together to secure Indo-Pacific?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:26:00 UTC
22:26:00 KST

Can EU and India work together to secure Indo-Pacific?
October 29, 2026
The European Union is vying for a larger role in Indo-Pacific security as the US finds itself on the back foot in the Eastern Hemisphere.
India is among the regional powers looking for new allies. Its rising economy and increasingly global ambitions have pushed it into new forums and partnerships, including ever closer defense ties with the European bloc.
In January this year, India and the EU signed a Security and Defense Partnership, followed by their first formal Security and Defense Dialogue in March. More meetings followed throughout the year, including the fifth Maritime Security Dialogue in Brussels last month.
However, while both sides want to boost cooperation on maritime security, working together in the Indo-Pacific remains a challenge — India and European countries simply have different defense priorities.
France a player in the Indian Ocean theater
"Europe can be a credible defense partner of India, especially in the maritime theater in general and Indo-Pacific in particular," Mohan Kumar, a former Indian ambassador to France, told DW.
But Europe's capacity to expand its role is constrained by other security crises.
"European distractions such as the conflict in Ukraine, which is of existential importance for it, do detract from this objective and can be a limiting factor," he added.
France is a notable exception, given its established military presence in the Indian Ocean.
"France, with its presence in Reunion Island and Mayotte, is already cooperating with India in the Indian Ocean theater and this cooperation can be intensified," added Kumar.
Javed Ashraf, another Indian diplomat, said that France has been "a strong, trusted and consistent security partner across the full spectrum of defense cooperation."
"What makes the partnership easier is the acceptance that the two may not always agree or be in a position to cooperate," said Ashraf.
"France also stands out for India because [France] has currently no defense cooperation with Pakistan or with China," he told DW.
EU disunited on security?
While France remains the EU's only nuclear power and maintains its strongest military force, a cooperation between Paris and New Delhi does not automatically translate into a coherent European security role across the Indo-Pacific.
"Europe as an entity has very little role in the Indo-Pacific security despite the announcement of a strategy in 2025," said Tara Kartha, a former member of India's National Security Council Secretariat.
She pointed to political differences among EU members as an obstacle to a coherent security outlook.
Those differences were on display during the EU's October 15–16 summit in Brussels, when leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine, but also signaled disagreements over funding and national priorities.
What can EU offer to India?
This could also explain why, as India's defense ties with Europe keep expanding, much of that cooperation still takes place between New Delhi and individual European nations.
Germany, Spain, Italy and Poland have all emerged as important partners.
Ashraf said Brussels could signal broader support for its member states' partnerships with India and provide access to EU-funded programs, boosting cooperation in areas such as maritime security, space, critical minerals, chips and defense technologies.
"India is also becoming an important source of defense supplies for a re-arming Europe," the diplomat said.
There may also be opportunities to share experience in emerging areas of warfare.
"India could also access drone technology in light of valuable experience gained by Europeans in Ukraine," Kumar said.
Germany, the EU's largest economy, is another important part of this relationship. Alongside France, it has become a defense partner for India, including through major equipment purchases. India could push for its relationship with Berlin to include industrial partnerships and technology development.
But experts warn that closer defense ties should not be confused with a shared strategic outlook, as European countries have their own priorities.
Russia and China as major obstacles
The differences between Brussels and New Delhi are particularly clear when it comes to Russia and China.
India still relies heavily on Russian equipment and technology, even as it seeks to diversify its defense supplies. European governments, meanwhile, have been engaged in a tense standoff with Russia since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
That creates a problem for those seeking to deepen defense industry ties.
"Buying a few big-ticket defense items, such as Rafale fighter jets from France or submarines from Germany, is one thing," said Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor of European Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi.
"However, integrating India's defense industry into the expanding European defense value chain is more challenging as long as Russia remains Europe's principal security concern," he said.
China presents a different but equally important challenge. For India, China is a rival and source of major security issues, including an ongoing border dispute. While the EU also sees China as a "systemic rival," its members differ in how they balance security concerns with their economic relationships with China.
These differences complicate attempts to develop a shared assessment of Indo-Pacific threats.
On a geopolitical level, India wants partnerships that strengthen its capabilities without requiring it to align fully with another power's strategic priorities. European governments are also weighing their regional ambitions against security demands closer to home.
Cooperation without a security umbrella
The new India-EU partnership creates a framework for closer engagement, but it does not amount to a joint security commitment.
Ashraf said the two sides could strengthen their mutual capabilities but were unlikely to exercise a visible influence on the global security order.
For now, maritime domain awareness, information-sharing, defense technology and selective industrial cooperation offer more realistic prospects than a common security role of the EU and India across the Indo-Pacific.

Police open preliminary probe into Google's data centre site activities in Muhos

15:25:05 EET
22:25:05 KST

The Oulu Police Department has opened a preliminary investigation into the activities at Google's data centre construction site in Muhos, following a request from the Finnish Supervisory Agency to look into the matter.
The department has received five requests for an investigation related to the Muhos site, all of which will be addressed in the preliminary probe.
The data centre construction work is part of the tech giant's 13 billion euro investment in Finland.
Police said the matter is being investigated under the criminal heading of suspected environmental damage. They noted that other possible charges may be clarified as the preliminary investigation proceeds.
Police said that, based on current information, there have been irregularities and shortcomings in drainage and water management at the data centre project's worksite, which is run by Google's local subsidiary Tuike Finland.
The preliminary investigation is expected to take a good deal of time, police said, adding that efforts will be made to complete the probe during 2027.
The department said that it will aim to provide more information about the matter in December.
Authority's request
In a press release issued last week, the Finnish Supervisory Agency explained that it ordered Tuike Finland to halt construction work on two data centre projects — in Muhos and Kajaani-Otanmäki — because required environmental impact assessments for both projects remained incomplete.
The company complied, confirming on 14 October that preparatory work had been suspended at both sites.
Among other issues, the authority found Tuike Finland's water management plans insufficient to prove that water-related environmental impacts can be properly controlled.
It said the firm needs to submit a detailed water management plan by 5 November, including planned structures, timelines and independent water monitoring, accounting for heavy rainfall, snowmelt, and risks from acidic black shale soils in the area.
The authority noted that if adequate action is not taken, it may pursue formal enforcement measures, including a conditional fine.

ECB holds rates at 2.5% as Lagarde announces early exit with inflation near double the target
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:24:45 UTC
22:24:45 KST

The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, hours after President Christine Lagarde said she would leave next February, months before her term ends, as France's bond market turmoil and inflation at 3.8% cloud the outlook for the eurozone.
The European Central Bank (ECB) left its key deposit rate unchanged at 2.5% on Thursday, at a meeting overshadowed by President Christine Lagarde's announcement earlier in the day that she will leave her post next February, months before her term ends.
The pause comes as a sell-off in French government bonds pushes up borrowing costs across the eurozone, while inflation runs at 3.8%, almost double the ECB's 2% target.
The decision by the Governing Council, which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro, follows two rate hikes this year, the latest in September, as energy prices linked to the Iran war drove inflation higher. The rates on its main refinancing operations and marginal lending facility also stay at 2.65% and 2.90% respectively.
In its statement, the ECB said energy prices had "continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook".
Underlying inflation has "remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage", it said, but warned that the size and duration of the energy shock were "likely to drive up inflation and lower growth".
The central bank also acknowledged that financing conditions "have tightened since the Governing Council's last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth", and repeated that it was "not pre-committing to a particular rate path".
Inflation in the eurozone rose to 3.8% in September, up from 3.2% in August, and the pause had been widely expected.
Lagarde's departure
The meeting came just hours after Lagarde said she would step down on 7 February 2027, around nine months before her eight-year term ends.
The ECB gave no reason, but reports since February have linked the timing to France's presidential election in April 2027.
"I leave this institution with a sense of a good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," Lagarde said in a separate statement.
Her exit sets off a race to lead the central bank, with Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot seen as frontrunners.
Two other seats on the ECB's six-member Executive Board, including that of chief economist Philip Lane, also open up in the first half of next year.
France in focus
The decision lands in the middle of France's political and fiscal crisis.
French 10-year borrowing costs climbed above 5% last week for the first time since 2002. On Thursday, the yield stood at around 5%, with the gap over German debt at roughly 155 basis points.
Ratings agency Moody’s kept France’s Aa3 rating unchanged last Friday, but with a negative outlook, while a divided parliament struggles to pass next year's budget.
As Euronews reported ahead of the meeting, Dutch bank ING estimated that the rise in bond yields since September had done the work of a 25 basis point hike in Germany, and closer to 50 basis points in France.
"The bond market has taken over the ECB's job," it said in a note.
Lagarde has so far poured cold water on hopes of a rescue. Speaking in Bangkok earlier this month, she said that "the primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies."
In Thursday's statement, the ECB repeated its standard line that the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), its never-used tool to buy the bonds of countries facing unjustified spikes in borrowing costs, is "available to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that pose a serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy".
It also left its balance sheet policy untouched, with its bond portfolios still shrinking as it no longer reinvests maturing debt, even though ING had expected a quiet pause in that run-down.

Poland's foreign ministry is checking reports of a fatal train crash in Spain, with no Polish casualties reported so far, ministry spokesman Maciej Wewior said on Wednesday.
Two passenger trains, including a high-speed one, collided on Wednesday morning near the Urda station in the Toledo province in central Spain, news agency EFE reported.
Spanish newspaper ABC, citing the country's Civil Defence Service, reported on Wednesday morning that at least 46 people had died in the collision on the Madrid-Andalusia route. The cause of the crash remains unknown.
In the early afternoon on Wednesday, Castilla-La Mancha regional government said the death toll increased to 64 people.
"We are checking media reports, and our consulate in Spain is active." Wewior told reporters. "As of now, there is no information about any Polish citizens being among the casualties."
Polish President Karol Nawrocki expressed his sadness about the tragic crash in a post on X on Wednesday.

"In these painful moments, Poland mourns alongside the Spanish people. Our thoughts are with those who have lost their loved ones and with everyone affected by this tragedy," he added.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reacted to the "devastating news from Spain" on X.
"I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost their loved ones and wish for a swift recovery of those injured. All Poles are with the Spanish people in this terrible time," he wrote.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski wrote on X on Wednesday that he was "deeply saddened by the tragic train accident in Spain".
"My heartfelt condolences go out to the families and loved ones of the victims. I wish all those injured a swift recovery. In these difficult moments, Poland stands in solidarity with Spain and its people. We stand with you," Sikorski wrote.
Polish Infrastructure Minister Dariusz Klimczak on Wednesday expressed his condolences to the families of those killed in the train crash. "My thoughts are also with the injured and everyone affected by this tragedy," he wrote on X.
Spain's Health Minister Monica Garcia told public radio station Cadena SER that the accident was "very serious".
Esther Padilla, a spokeswoman for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, which includes the Toledo province, confirmed that at least 10 people had died, the EFE reported.

"I am deeply shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo province," Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez wrote on X. "My condolences, solidarity and support go out to all the victims and their families."

Israeli police reject Likud claims of election fraud by Arab parties
Israel police have said there is no evidence to support claims by Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party that Arab parties "stole" the election, after parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel secured 19 seats amid a high-stakes vote that left neither Netanyahu nor his main challenger Gadi Eisenkot with enough seats to form a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
On Thursday, police rejected repeated allegations by Likud that Arab parties had committed fraud.
Likud had called for an investigation by police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency into claims of widespread voter fraud and intimidation.
A police source, cited by several Israeli media outlets, said: “Election day passed with very few irregular incidents concerning the integrity of the election, even when compared to previous elections.”
“It should be emphasised that there is no investigative- or intelligence-based supporting evidence for the claims,” the source added.
The latest comments came a day after an official from Israel’s Central Elections Committee (CEC) also dismissed the allegations.
Speaking to Israeli radio station Reshet Bet, the CEC’s acting director general, Dean Livne, said the committee conducts a comprehensive review of complaints.
In a statement, Likud claimed that “hundreds of testimonies” showed that Arab parties, including Ra’am, which participated in the 2021-2022 Israeli government, had bribed ballot committee members and multiple voters with envelopes of cash.
Likud also alleged “double voting, discrepancies between the number of envelopes and the number of voters, use of illegal voter mobilization software, and more”.
Following the election, Likud continued to insist that Arab parties had “stolen” the vote.
Haaretz reported that the party had invested millions of shekels in a system designed to “supervise” polling stations in Arab communities.
Likud’s allegations also came amid concerns over the spread of misinformation on social media.
An image shared by Netanyahu purportedly showing voters queuing at a polling station in the Palestinian-majority city of Sakhnin on Tuesday was found to have been generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence (AI), according to BBC Verify.
The image appeared to show Palestinian voters with Israeli citizenship queuing to vote after Netanyahu shared a Channel 14 report on X claiming there was “unusual congestion at polling stations in the Arab sector”.
However, BBC Verify said its analysis detected signs that the image had been generated or manipulated using AI.
Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot have both claimed a path to victory, with Eisenkot’s coalition potentially depending on Arab parties, including Ra’am and the Joint List.
The two groups are poised to secure a record number of seats and could hold the balance of power in the Knesset.
The Joint List has previously criticised Netanyahu and Likud’s allegations against Arab parties and voters, accusing them of using fearmongering tactics, including exaggerating Arab turnout in the parliamentary election and circulating AI-generated content.
The alliance has condemned the conduct, warning that it risked fuelling further hostility towards Arab communities in Israel.
“Netanyahu is afraid of high turnout in our community because he knows it will bring down his government,” it said in a statement.

European Commission: Estonia among Europe's safest countries for road deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:23:00 UTC
22:23:00 KST

European Commission: Estonia among Europe's safest countries for road deaths
Estonia saw 43 road deaths last year, placing it sixth overall among Europe's safest countries, according to final European Commission figures for 2025.
This figure, at 31 deaths per million, puts it slightly ahead of Finland, Germany and the Netherlands and significantly better than Latvia and Lithuania.
Roads in built up areas of Estonia were, however, significantly safer than those in rural areas, and while the incidence of deaths on the roads continues to fall in Estonia, it is not falling at a rate fast enough to meet a state target of half of 2019's figure by or in 2030. Also, the first half of this year saw a rise in road deaths in Estonia.
Sweden and Norway recorded 19 road deaths per million in 2025, followed by Denmark and Switzerland at 24, and Iceland at 26.
These were the only countries to post figures better than Estonia's 31 per million. Estonia was followed by Malta and Ireland at 33, Finland, Germany and the Netherlands (all 34) and Spain at 36, according to figures published on Wednesday.
Lithuania posted 138 road deaths last year, or 48 per million, while Latvia's figure was 64 per million.
The other highest rates were seen in Serbia (75 per million), Bulgaria (71), Romania (68) and Croatia (67).
Across the EU, EFTA countries and Serbia, 19,350 people died on the roads last year, or 43 per million,
The Commission said road deaths across Europe fell 3 percent on year to 2025 (580 fewer), and by 15 percent compared with 2019 (3,400 fewer road traffic deaths).
The Commission noted that, however, compared with the EU average, Estonia had a higher share of fatal road accidents on roads outside urban areas.
Between 2019 and 2025 road deaths in Estonia fell 17 percent. This, the Commission says, suggests Estonia will likely not meet its 2030 target of halving road deaths compared with 2019, though the Commission noted that annual figures can fluctuate significantly given the country's small population and low number of deaths in absolute terms.
The same data shows that in the first months of 2026 road deaths in Estonia rose sharply again, by over 10 percent. ERR reported in August that 30 people had died on Estonian roads in the first seven months of this year, four more than in the same period a year earlier.
For Europe as a whole, preliminary 2026 data show that in the first half of the year more countries saw road deaths fall by more than 5 percent compared with the same period in 2025 than saw them rise. The overall trend is therefore positive, the Commission said.

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) updated its forecast of transfers to the state budget for 2027, as of October 1, from the initial UAH 49 billion to UAH 70 billion and informed the Economy Ministry, NBU Governor Andrei Pyshnyy said at a briefing in Kyiv on Thursday.

"It is not hard for the National Bank to earn a profit, but the price for society and for the Ukrainian economy may be catastrophic. We would like a very substantive, expert and responsible discussion that does not assume that a short-term budget requirement can undermine the public good," Pyshnyy said.

Russia and India can help unlock Sierra Leone’s mineral wealth – minister (VIDEO)
The West African nation of Sierra Leone is looking to India and Russia for technology and expertise to process its mineral resources rather than remain a mere supplier to the world’s industrialized countries.
Sierra Leone wants to combine Russian mining expertise with Indian technology to develop its mineral wealth and expand domestic processing, the country’s Minister of Mines and Mineral Resources, Julius Daniel Mattai, told RT.
“Geology is not wealth,” the minister noted on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on Wednesday. He argued that mineral resources must be combined with knowledge and effective governance to generate economic benefits. Sierra Leone is seeking investment and technology for this move.
More and more African leaders are emphasizing local processing as they push to move their economies up the industrial value chain. It was also raised at the summit by African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye, who called for partnerships that would help African countries manufacture finished products, RT reported on Wednesday.
'Sierra Leone is Looking to Combine Russian Know-How With Indian Tech Talent’ - Julius Daniel Mattai, 🇸🇱's Minister of Mines & Mineral Resources ‘If we combine Russian knowledge, resilience, technology, education, with the intellectual capacity and capabilities of India, that means we have good friends,’ Julius Daniel Mattai tells RT India, on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit.
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 28, 2026
“We cannot accept a future where Africa supplies the minerals … while value addition and manufacturing take place elsewhere,” South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told the BRICS summit in New Delhi last month.
Sierra Leone is preparing to sign a memorandum of understanding with the Russian State University for Geological Prospecting covering scholarships, staff exchanges, laboratory access, and technology transfer, Mattai said.
Russia’s expertise in geological data interpretation, mineral processing, smelting and refining could support Sierra Leone’s mining industry, Mattai said. He stressed that reliable energy would be essential to expanding domestic processing and manufacturing.
Sierra Leone also expressed interest in cooperation with Russia on rare earth minerals, with Mattai saying in June that deposits containing such minerals had been identified in the country.
India already has a presence in Sierra Leone’s mining and industrial sectors. An Indian company that initially used scrap metal to produce steel has secured a mining concession and plans to extract iron ore for domestic processing, Mattai told RT.
Indian companies are also active in information technology, digitalization, artificial intelligence, and solar energy, while educational institutions have been established with Indian involvement, he added.
Bilateral trade between India and Sierra Leone reached nearly $450 million in the financial year ended March 2026, according to India’s High Commission. Indian imports from Sierra Leone include minerals, ores, and metals.

TIRANA, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Opposition lawmakers in Albania disrupted a parliament session by letting off flares on Thursday following weeks of violent anti-government protests called by students demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.
Members of the opposition Democratic Party of Albania also blocked access to the podium when a law on the Central Bank was being voted on.
“These (ruling lawmakers) are criminals and they deserve tear gas, rubber bullets, cracked skulls and broken bones, not the young people,” opposition leader Sali Berisha said during his speech before his microphone was cut off.
Other opposition members surrounded him during the speech, holding photos of protesters injured by rubber bullets. Some held aloft blue flares, the colour of their party.
Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana since mid-October and spread to other cities.
Demonstrators demanding Rama’s resignation have set fire to government buildings and banks, smashed shop windows and pulled up paving stones to throw at police.
The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful summer protests against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and won a fourth term in office last year.
On Sunday, Rama introduced new measures to curb violence, including fines of 500,000 lek ($6,200) for anyone who participates in a protest that turns violent, even if they do not personally commit acts of violence.
This week the protests were mainly peaceful, and another is planned for Saturday.
Prime Minister Rama has again called on students for dialogue and introduced new economic measures such as cheaper fuel and more money for poor families in an attempt to stop the violence in the streets.

US economy grows 3.4% in Q3, beating expectations

Gökhan Ergöçün
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
The US economy expanded at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter of 2026, accelerating from 2.2% growth in the previous quarter, and exceeding market forecasts of 3.2%.
The pickup in real gross domestic product primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending, according to an advance estimate by the Bureau of Economic Analysis on Thursday.
Those gains were partly offset by a downturn in exports, while imports increased at a faster pace than in the second quarter.
Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which combine consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, rose 4.9% in the July-September period following a 4.6% increase in the second quarter.
Price pressures eased during the quarter, with the gross domestic purchases price index rising 3% compared with a 5.6% advance in the preceding three months.
The personal consumption expenditures price index increased 2.1% in the third quarter, down sharply from a 5% increase in the second quarter.
Excluding volatile food and energy components, the core personal consumption expenditures price index rose 2.5%, slowing from 3.3% in the prior quarter.

A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:14:52 UTC
22:14:52 KST

A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- McGill University
- Summary:
- Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a brain signal that may help explain why schizophrenia produces such a wide variety of symptoms, including difficulties with perception, movement, and speech. The discovery suggests that problems that appear unrelated could actually stem from a shared disruption in how the brain processes information.
Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder that can affect how people experience the world, interact with their surroundings, and communicate with others. These symptoms are typically studied as separate features of the condition, but new research suggests they may have more in common than previously recognized.
The study, published in Science Advances, was conducted by scientists from McGill University, the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre, the University of Montreal, the Research Centre of the University of Montreal Health Centre, and the Douglas Research Centre. Their findings point to a common brain mechanism that may help explain several distinct symptoms of schizophrenia.
A Weakened Brain Signal Links Multiple Schizophrenia Symptoms
To investigate this connection, researchers examined beta-band brain activity in 25 people diagnosed with schizophrenia and 25 healthy participants. Beta-band activity refers to rhythmic patterns of electrical activity in the brain that are involved in coordinating information processing, perception, and movement.
Participants completed tasks designed to test how accurately they could judge the timing of visual and auditory information. The researchers also analyzed their speech to look for signs of disorganized thinking and communication.
The results revealed a striking pattern. People with schizophrenia showed weaker and slower beta-band activity than those in the control group. More importantly, the participants with the most pronounced abnormalities in this brain signal also tended to have greater difficulty processing the timing of sights and sounds, more disorganized speech, and more severe clinical symptoms.
These three features of schizophrenia are usually investigated independently. Finding that they were all associated with changes in the same brain signal suggests that a shared underlying process may contribute to the disorder's diverse effects.
A New Window Into How the Brain Processes Reality
"This gives us early but compelling evidence that measuring the brain's operations, especially how it builds and revises its own model of the world, may help us appreciate that there is a common thread behind the confusing array of symptoms we see in disorders like schizophrenia," said Dr. Lena Palaniyappan, senior author of the study, Professor of Psychiatry at McGill and director of the Centre of Excellence in Youth Mental Health at the Douglas Hospital.
The brain constantly uses incoming sensory information to develop and update its understanding of the surrounding environment. This process helps people interpret what they see and hear, anticipate events, and coordinate their actions. The new findings suggest that disruptions in this process could help explain why schizophrenia affects several different aspects of behavior and perception.
The researchers used high-resolution magnetoencephalography, or MEG, to measure brain activity. This imaging technique detects the tiny magnetic fields generated by electrical activity in the brain, allowing scientists to track changes in neural signals with exceptional precision. The scans were performed at the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital (The Neuro).
"What struck us was that the same weakened brain signal kept showing up wherever we looked, whether patients were processing a sound, a sight or completing a movement," said Hsi (Tiana) Wei, lead author of the study and postdoctoral scholar in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and the Douglas Research Centre. "Seeing the same pattern across these different domains suggested there may be a common underlying process linking the symptoms."
Could the Discovery Help Detect Psychosis Earlier?
Beyond providing new insight into schizophrenia, the findings could eventually help researchers identify young people who are at greater risk of developing psychosis. Psychosis involves a disruption in how someone perceives or interprets reality and can include experiences such as hallucinations or delusions.
Early identification is particularly important because the first signs of schizophrenia often appear during adolescence but may go unrecognized for an extended period.
"The very first sign of schizophrenia begins in our adolescence, but this often gets missed for a long time. If this finding is confirmed in larger samples, we may have a potentially useful method to identify who, among youth seeking help for mental health, needs extra support to prevent psychosis," Palaniyappan said.
However, the researchers emphasized that the results are preliminary. The study included only 50 participants, and additional research involving larger, independent groups will be necessary to determine how reliably the brain signal is associated with speech disturbances and overall symptom severity.
"This is a first, modest-size study, and the associations with speech and clinical severity will need to be tested in larger independent samples before we can be confident in them," Wei said.
If future studies confirm the findings, measuring beta-band activity could potentially become a useful tool for identifying people who need earlier support. Wei also suggested that the brain signal may deserve investigation as a possible target for future schizophrenia treatments.
Story Source:
Materials provided by McGill University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hsi T. Wei, Dominic Boutet, Rukun Dou, Jessica Ahrens, Nadia Zeramdini, Alban Voppel, Fernando Gonzales-Aste, Fatme Abboud, Sylvain Baillet, Lena Palaniyappan. Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (43) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh5819

Europe’s own ICE? Inside Brussels plans to triple Frontex and expand deportation powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:12:53 UTC
22:12:53 KST

The European Commission wants to triple Frontex's workforce and give it sweeping new powers to deport migrants beyond EU borders and monitor social media, prompting warnings over surveillance and fundamental rights.
The EU's border and coastguard agency, Frontex, is set to gain unprecedented powers to deport irregular migrants, monitor social media and respond to mass arrivals at EU borders under a sweeping reform proposed by the European Commission.
The overhaul would significantly expand Frontex's mandate, triple its workforce and give it a much greater role in deportations beyond EU territory.
Brussels says the changes are needed to tackle new migration challenges, including orchestrated border crossings such as the mass arrival of an estimated 80,000 people in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July.
But the proposals have already sparked controversy, with critics warning that the agency's expanded powers and budget could lead to further fundamental rights violations and intrusive surveillance.
Here are the main elements of the reform, which must still be approved by EU member states and the European Parliament.
New focus on deportations
One of the most significant changes is a shift in Frontex's focus from managing the EU's external borders towards deporting irregular migrants.
The agency will become the "central EU actor on returns", providing "support from A to Z", according to EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner.
While responsibility for returning irregular migrants to their countries of origin remains with EU countries, the agency will help by identifying the individuals to be returned, operating return flights and providing reintegration assistance through a new Return Coordination Centre.
Crucially, the agency will also be able to operate from one non-EU country to another, a major change that would allow Frontex officials to help deport migrants before they even reach Europe.
This means they will also take part in deportations from return hubs to countries of origin, as a recently approved law allows such hubs to be set up outside the EU.
Civil society organisations claim this system would be opaque and difficult to scrutinize.
“The Commission wants to turn Frontex into a deportation agency operating far beyond Europe’s borders, where abuses will be harder to expose”, Iftach Cohen, co-director of NGO Front-LEX, told Euronews.
Any cooperation with a third country will require a specific agreement with the country concerned, to be negotiated by the Commission and finally approved by the EU member states and Parliament.
“This is shameful and makes Frontex closer and closer to Donald Trump’s ICE,” Italian socialist MEP Cecilia Strada told Euronews, referring to the controversial US agency in charge of apprehending and deporting irregular migrants.
Frontex’s new tasks will be facilitated by a separate regulation to “digitalise” returns, which is set to simplify and speed up administrative procedures by sharing information among EU member states. It also sparks controversy, as organizations such as Statewatch warned of the risks of excessive data collection.
New powers to monitor social media
Frontex would also be tasked with monitoring social media to detect advertisements for people-smuggling and anticipate mass arrivals at EU borders.
An EU official acknowledged that the proposal was partly a response to July's crisis in Ceuta, when an estimated 80,000 people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave in North Africa.
“There was lots of messaging [on social media] before what happened, lots of misinformation. If we have a sort of real-time ability to see these things happening upstream, then it’s possible then to envisage reactions”, the official said.
A new internal structure called the “Online Monitoring and Response Centre” will be set up, and Frontex will also be allowed to identify illegal content, flag it to social media platforms and trigger requests to competent authorities to have it removed.
“The digital dimension is not a technical annexe to the Frontex reform, it is one of its main enablers”, said Henna Virkkunen, Commission Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty and Security.
However, national authorities remain responsible for deciding the legality of content.
Frontex will apply for “trusted flagger” status, which must be approved by national authorities. If it is granted, Frontex’s flags would be assessed as a priority and, where warranted, removed.
Critics warn that the new powers could amount to intrusive online surveillance, threatening privacy and freedom of expression.
“Social media surveillance poses serious risks to people’s data,” French Green MEP Mélissa Camara told Euronews.
Even far-right MEPs, who traditionally favour stricter border controls and expanded powers for Frontex, have raised concerns.
"We will not accept the fight against traffickers on social media becoming a pretext for monitoring citizens' opinions. We will make no concessions and we will not sign blank checks," said Susanna Ceccardi of Italy's League, signalling a potentially heated debate when the legislation reaches Parliament.
A rapid reaction force
The reform would also establish a Quick Reaction Force, another measure inspired by the Ceuta crisis.
The specialised unit could be deployed at short notice to an EU country's external border in the event of an emergency, allowing Frontex to respond more rapidly to sudden surges in arrivals.
The decision to deploy it can be taken by Frontex’s Executive Director, but only following a request from the member state concerned.
The reform leaves unchanged the subordination of Frontex officials to national authorities.
Tripling of staff
The expanded mandate would come with a substantial increase in staff, funding and equipment.
The Commission wants to triple Frontex's workforce to 30,000 officers by 2041, up from the current 10,000.
The agency’s own standing corps, in charge of patrolling the borders, will double from 3,000 to 6,000 officers, plus 7,000 officers seconded from EU states’ national police forces.
The total is completed by a new “European border and return reserve” of 17,000 officers who will remain in their home countries and be deployed only if needed.
“[Officers] in the reserve would be trained up to Frontex’s standards and made available for quick deployment. But they are still part of the national resources and will not be paid out of the Frontex budget,” an EU official said.
Frontex is allocated almost €6 billion in the current EU budget, and the Commission has proposed doubling its funding in the 2028-2034 cycle.
With the new mandate, the agency will be able to acquire, lease and co-own equipment such as drones for surveillance and AI-enabled tools, acting as a central purchasing body in joint procurement with member states. At present, it must rely on equipment provided by national forces.
The increase in personnel and resources will not be matched by a proportional increase in the number of Fundamental Rights Officers (FROs), the Frontex team that monitors respect for migrants’ rights in returns and border control operations.
The size of the FRO team is decided “on an annual basis, based on resources,” an EU official told Euronews, in a further cause for concern for NGOs.
"This proposal massively expands Frontex's powers to track, control and deport, without introducing stronger human rights safeguards," said Chiara Catelli, advocacy officer at PICUM, a Brussels-based NGO defending migrants' rights.
“All this for an agency with a track record of allegations of complicity in fundamental rights violations,” she said.

Russell Brand’s wife tells court he is ‘amazingly attentive husband’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:12:36 UTC
22:12:36 KST

Russell Brand’s wife has told a court that they previously split up over his promiscuity but that he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”.
Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand, 39, said they fell in love after meeting in 2006 but that the comedian found monogamy difficult.
“I wasn’t interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people,” she said.
Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.
Giving evidence at Southwark crown court on Wednesday, Laura told the court she met Brand at the Edinburgh festival in 2006 after his show Shame, which was “very, very, very funny”, “extremely entertaining” and sexually explicit.
She said they met in the foyer of the Assembly Rooms, where Brand complimented her friend, who had a boyfriend. Laura recalled: “And he said to me: ‘But tell me you don’t have a boyfriend,’ and I said: ‘No, I don’t.’”
Laura recalled that Brand contacted her the next day and they had oral sex. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked: “Did he want to have penetrative sex?” to which Laura replied: “I didn’t want to, but I don’t remember it even being a topic. I didn’t intend to and I don’t remember him asking.”
They began dating in September 2006 and Brand “absolutely” respected her wishes sexually, Laura said. Describing his treatment of her, she said: “Very caring, totally at my pace. I was not experienced, I had only had one partner before Russell and I felt entirely cared for, and looked after by Russell.”
But the court heard their relationship broke down over his cheating. Winter asked: “Did you become aware shortly thereafter that he was promiscuous and engaging in sexual activity with others?” Laura replied: “I was aware when I met him that he liked women and I was aware towards the latter part of that year that he was engaging with other women, yes.”
Laura said the couple split up in February 2007 because of his infidelity. “I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous. We talked about it. I did find that difficult,” she said.
Laura said she was “heartbroken” after the breakup but that the pair resumed contact as friends in summer 2007. She said she became friendly again with Brand when his marriage to the US pop star Katy Perry ended, and that they restarted their relationship in 2015, married two years later, and now have three children together.
When asked if she was aware of Brand’s promiscuity during their time apart, Laura said: “I was very aware of it and I would read about it regularly in the papers and he also told me; we talked about it.”
Both the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, and the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, objected when Winter asked Laura what her view was “as to the truth” of the criminal allegations her husband faces.
“She’s not here as an expert witness,” the judge said.
Winter then asked Laura to describe Brand, to which she replied: “Russell, my husband, is caring, he’s kind, he’s a wonderful father to our children, he’s an amazingly attentive husband.
“He’s got an eye for detail I’ve never known before. The way he treats me is to really know me, I feel very seen by him, in a way I’ve never experienced before. I love him very much.”
She continued: “We have a very frank, honest and clear relationship and marriage. It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest.”
In cross-examination, Karmy-Jones noted that Laura had been present throughout most of the trial and had taken notes. She also challenged Laura about how much contact she had had with Brand after their break up in 2007.
Laura said she had spoken to Brand after his marriage to Perry ended. “He called me after his marriage and gifted me meditation for me and my boyfriend at the time,” she said.
Brand nodded and smiled as Laura insisted that while they had not had a sexual relationship in the years before they got back together in 2015, they had spent time together by going to the theatre and watching TV box sets.
The prosecutor said that in 2017, shortly after the couple had their first child, Brand was a guest on the US talkshow, The Wendy Williams Show. She said the comedian had said of his relationship with Laura: “When we went out with each other we loved each other very much but I was in a phase where I thought the world was an amusement park made out of orgasms.”
Laura replied: “I’m not denying he said that. I probably didn’t watch it.”
Earlier, statements from two of Brand’s ex-girlfriends were read to the court, as they gave good accounts of his character. They also said he had cheated on them and they had supported him financially.
Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
The trial continues.

Details
"You can look at my quotes from January 2023, when we began working, and I said that we would do exactly what we are doing now," the head of DC Studios wrote in response to a since-deleted post.
"I said that some stories would stand alone, like the Guardians films (Clayface is exactly that), while some would be part of a larger narrative structure, which is the Superman saga. At the same time, every part of the larger story must work on its own, regardless of whether you need to watch everything else," Gunn noted.

R. Martin, and much more."
Gunn’s reference to the ‘8-10 year roadmap’ concerns a virtual Warner Bros. Discovery meeting in 2022 involving him and his co-chair, Peter Safran, where he said that they had developed an 8-10-year plan for DC’s development. Russia says it detained teenagers recruited by Ukrainian intelligence through Telegram dating bot
Russian authorities detained several young men and women in Moscow, St. Petersburg, the Leningrad region, and other regions between August and October after Ukrainian intelligence services recruited them through the Telegram dating bot Leonardo Daivinchik to carry out acts of sabotage, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee.

In one case, she said, a teenager bought flammable liquids and set fire to several gas stations. Other cases involved the arson of police department service vehicles and the arson of a transformer cabinet. All those detained face charges under Russia’s criminal statute against terrorism.
The FSB said it detained eight teenagers, ages 14 to 17, along with two adults, ages 19 and 24, in Moscow and St. Petersburg, as well as the Leningrad, Nizhny Novgorod, Omsk, Ryazan, and Sverdlovsk regions, between August and October.
In late July 2026, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) accused Pavel Durov of aiding terrorism. The agency said the Telegram founder’s messaging app had failed to remove bots used by Ukrainian intelligence services. Among other things, the agency said Ukrainian intelligence services had drawn young Russians into “sabotage and terrorist activity” through the popular Telegram dating bot Leonardo Daivinchik.

Shell rakes in $12B profit as Middle East war drives up prices
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Oil and gas giant Shell has recorded $10.8 billion in adjusted quarterly profits – double what it made in the same period last year – as war in the Middle East boosts energy prices.
Since the US and Israel began attacking Iran this year, Shell’s fuel products have risen in value, largely due to strikes on competing refineries in the region that produce petrol and diesel.
The corporation, which moved its headquarters out of The Hague to London in 2022, made record profits after Russia invaded Ukraine the same year, and has seen profits surge again since the outbreak of war with Iran.
MPs have called for a windfall tax to prevent Shell or other energy conglomerates from profiting from geopolitical conflict.
Shell’s move to London makes placing a levy on the profits harder, however, and the European Commission has also ruled out an EU-wide windfall tax, saying it’s a matter for individual nations.

Russian attacks on Ukraine driving up Poland's air-defense costs: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:09:35 UTC
22:09:35 KST

Jo Harper
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Russian attacks on western Ukraine are driving up neighboring Poland's air-defense costs even when no drones or missiles enter its airspace, Polish daily Rzeczpospolita reported Thursday.
Poland has been deploying military aircraft more frequently during Russian strikes on western Ukraine, with many missions precautionary and ending without any violation of Polish airspace, the newspaper said.
Citing Defense Ministry data, it put the average cost of flying an F-16 fighter jet at 76,859 zlotys ($19,500) per hour, including fuel and aircraft servicing.
That means keeping a pair of fighters in the air for one hour costs more than 150,000 zlotys ($38,000), while longer missions involving replacement aircraft can cost substantially more.
That figure excludes the full cost of placing Poland’s wider air-defense system on alert, including personnel, radar operations, command centers and ground-based air-defense units.
Polish military aircraft have been operating over the country almost daily in recent weeks as Russia repeatedly attacks Ukraine, including areas near the Polish border, according to Rzeczpospolita.
The newspaper described the repeated deployments as an asymmetric financial burden, arguing that Moscow can force Warsaw to incur significant costs without sending weapons into Polish airspace.
Poland is investing in additional radars, electronic warfare systems, anti-aircraft artillery and interceptor drones, but the network is not yet fully developed, the newspaper reported.

Swiss study finds cold showers are good for your health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:07:53 UTC
22:07:53 KST

Swiss study finds cold showers are good for your health
People who take cold showers are less likely to be absent from work. This is the conclusion reached by a study carried out by the University of Basel. According to the study, a daily cold shower reduces the number of days missed from work due to illness by more than 30%.
Over a period of twelve weeks, more than 700 study participants aged between 18 and 65 were asked to take as cold a shower as their shower facilities would allow, as the University of Basel announced on Thursday. To take part, participants had to be in good health and not have previously taken cold showers on a regular basis.
Compared with a control group who continued to shower as usual, the cold-showerers felt unwell on 26% fewer days on average. They were absent from work 31% less often than those who took warm showers.
Habituation effect proven
The experiment was part of a PhD thesis in which psychologist Lena Glaser at the University of Basel investigated how people can be motivated to adopt more environmentally friendly behaviour. She explored the question of whether people are more willing to change their behaviour if it can be easily integrated into their daily lives and brings them personal benefits.
She chose cold showers as an example. While these may be unpleasant at first, they can be integrated into daily life without much effort, explained Glaser. They also save energy and money.
+ The Basel researcher whose work triggered a longevity revolution
A particularly large number of participants dropped out of the experiment in the first two weeks. After that, the number of dropouts fell. “So there does seem to be a habituation effect,” Glaser was quoted as saying in the press release.
Over the course of the study, the remaining participants reported an increasing sense of physical and mental well-being. They cited feeling more alert and refreshed after showering as an immediate reward. The pride they felt at having overcome their reluctance also motivated them.
It is not known whether the participants continued to take cold showers after the twelve weeks were over.

How Israel's expanding occupation is deepening Syria's dilemma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:06:20 UTC
22:06:20 KST

Breadcrumb
How Israel's expanding occupation is deepening Syria's dilemma
Damascus - The Israeli military shot dead a developmentally disabled Syrian man last Thursday, triggering a wave of protests across the country against Israel’s continued occupation of parts of Daraa, Quneitra, and the Golan Heights.
The families of individuals detained and illegally transferred to Israel gathered outside the UN headquarters in Damascus on Friday to protest the killing of Muath Al-Baaer. Hundreds also came out to protest in Idlib, Homs, Hasakah, and Quneitra.
Anger is growing in Syria as Israel deepens its occupation in the south. Israel has occupied the Golan Heights since it captured it from Syria in the 1967 Six-Day War, unilaterally annexing the territory in 1981.
However, following the fall of Assad’s regime in 2024, Israel extended its occupation zone, deploying forces into the neighbouring Quneitra and Daraa regions. It is here that many young men have been disappearing following the Israeli military’s many night raids.
Yet, these disappearances did not begin with the fall of the regime.
In 2024, eight months before now-President Ahmed Al-Sharaa stormed into Damascus, Saddam Hassan Ahmed, 16, was arrested by Israeli forces in Quneitra. He still languishes in an Israeli prison, alongside 38 other Syrian men.
On Friday, his father, Abu Saddam, gathered with other families of the kidnapped in the shade of an apartment complex directly facing the UN headquarters. They were waiting for the protest to start, as their permit was only valid from 2pm.
Abu Saddam is the informal spokesman for the families of the kidnapped, but he insists that the decision to protest was collective.
“We came here to stand together in support of one another, as well as our sons, to stand alongside them until they are released,” he told The New Arab.
“We call on UN forces to pressure the occupying state,” he declared. “We want them to use their influence to secure the release of those detained in Israeli prisons.”
At the permitted time, a small crowd of several dozen gathered and waved the Syrian flag, chanting revolutionary slogans of unity and solidarity.
Overlooking the protest, people came out on their balconies in the upmarket apartment blocks to observe. One woman, holding a placard with her son's face on it, pointed up to them. “Why haven’t they come down to join us?” she shouted. “This is their country too.”
Whilst the turnout was relatively modest in Damascus, large crowds gathered in several other cities to protest the continued Israeli occupation.
“Protests were recorded in eight different governorates of Syria, indicating that the Israeli activities have become a national issue,” Muaz Al-Abdullah, a Middle East Research Manager at ACLED, a conflict tracking organisation, told The New Arab.
“[This is] one of the few causes that unites Syrians across different regions,” he added. “The killing of Muath Al-Baeer was the spark, not the cause.”
An entrenched occupation
Israel's occupation of southern Syria happens in the shadows; on the ground it is uncommon to even catch a glimpse of Israeli soldiers. Yet this shadow of fear looms large over the families of Quneitra.
The Israeli military has established a number of outposts on many of the region's strategic hilltops, from which they terrorise local residents. “Things are becoming more difficult,” says Abu Saddam.
“Their rhetoric has become more heated, and the attacks are increasing, especially as the elections approach.”
According to Al-Abdullah, their presence “is increasingly affecting how civilians use their land and move between villages”.
Under the rubric of creating a security zone, the Israeli military is damaging agricultural lands, confiscating livestock, and destroying woodland and homes near its bases. It has also continued developing Sufa 53 - a fortified military road and network of fortified positions - on the border between Quneitra and the occupied Golan Heights.
Analysts agree that, whilst the occupation of southern Syria is shaped by its own specificities, there are clear resemblances justified on a doctrine of security used to explain the ongoing occupations in southern Lebanon and the West Bank.
Israel also frequently establishes flying checkpoints and launches night raids to illegally detain the area’s young men - many of whom are taken into Israel and have yet to return.
For Mohanad Al-Rish, a Research Manager at COAR Global, a political consultancy firm, this practice raises “serious concerns” as a violation of the Geneva Convention, in which “the forcible transfer of protected persons from occupied territory to the territory of the occupying power is prohibited”.
The Convention requires that those accused of offences be detained within the occupied territory.
Beyond the legal implications, he recognises the “significant consequences” for civilians living in the region, who are faced with a daily sense of insecurity and declining confidence in the Syrian government’s ability to protect them.
The government's position
“I don’t believe the Syrian government has many effective options,” says Al-Rish. Syria’s fragile security environment and weak state capacity mean that any “direct confrontation would carry considerable risk,” he argues.
Israel has made clear its willingness to strike at the heart of the government. During the massacres in Suweida targeting Syria’s Druze minority in 2025, Israel bombed the Syrian Ministry of Defence building and the grounds of the Presidential Palace.
In August, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz, standing atop occupied Mount Hermon, sent a “message” to Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa stating, “When you wake up in your palace in Damascus, look up at Mt Hermon, and you will see the Israeli military.”
Due to this, Damascus continues to communicate that it does not seek military escalation and is committed to the diplomatic track, which appears to have stalled. The last known meeting in August between the head of Mossad, Roman Gofman, and Syrian Foreign Minister, Assad Al-Shaibani, seemed to offer little tangible progress.
According to Al-Abdullah, ACLED recorded 24 Israeli incursions the week of the talks, compared to 15 the week before, signalling that Tel Aviv didn’t seek to reduce tensions following the meeting.
With Syria limited to continuing to apply diplomatic pressure through international mediators, Al-Rish believes that the “political environment surrounding these negotiations is changing, [meaning] maintaining the same approach becomes increasingly difficult, particularly in the face of growing domestic frustration.”
He acknowledges that given Syria’s weak security infrastructure, the accumulation of grievance could “become increasingly difficult to contain.”
Growing anger
Although Abu Saddam and the families of the missing made clear that their anger is not directed at the government nor the UN, this recent wave of protests reflects growing frustration about the current settlement in southern Syria.
Although Damascus is clear in its intention to avoid conflict with Israel, one danger is that grievances “could be exploited by third parties, particularly Iran-backed networks,” argues Al-Rish. If people feel disillusioned with the government, they may seek retribution elsewhere.
It would seem that armed groups are active in southern Syria. The Syrian authorities have foiled several plots, most recently on 29 September, when they arrested three men in Deraa province alleging that they were establishing rocket platforms intended to “destabilise the region.”
There is a danger that Damascus may fail to foil a plot, and thus open the door to fierce Israeli retaliation and further potential escalation.
According to Al-Abdullah, “[this] has already happened.” ACLED has recorded four armed clashes between armed groups in Syria and the Israeli military since the fall of the regime. “Each time, the Israeli response was severe,” he adds.
For now, there seems little that Damascus can do other than harden its condemnation of Israeli violations, but for the families of the missing this offers little salvation. All they want is for their sons to come home.
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues

The European Commission said Thursday that EU member states share the objective of pursuing closer relations with Canada, despite reported disagreements over the proposed use of the term "associate membership" in a joint summit statement.
Speaking at the midday briefing in Brussels, spokesperson Paula Pinho said the EU remained committed to strengthening ties with Canada, adding that discussions would continue with the European Parliament, member states, and Canadian counterparts.
"As associate member of the EU, this is precisely an ever closer association of Canada to the European Union, short of full membership itself," Pinho said.
She stressed that the commission was "fully on board" with member states regarding the approach, objective, and ambition of pursuing closer association with Canada.
Pinho acknowledged that it would have been preferable for member states to have reached an agreement on the initial wording but said there was now a strong common basis for moving forward.
Her remarks came after EU member states reportedly remained divided over whether to include the term "associate membership" in a joint statement ahead of the EU-Canada summit.
Politico reported Tuesday that at least four countries opposed the wording, with Germany leading efforts to remove the term from the proposed text.
EU ambassadors failed to reach an agreement during talks Monday, while a subsequent silence procedure was also blocked after Germany and at least three other member states raised objections, according to EU diplomats cited by the outlet.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen first floated the idea of associate membership for Canada during her State of the Union address in Strasbourg last month, suggesting a closer relationship short of full EU membership.
The proposal has exposed differences among member states, with diplomats previously telling Politico that von der Leyen had not consulted national capitals before announcing the initiative.
The summit in Montreal, taking place on Thursday and Friday, is expected to focus on strengthening EU-Canada relations and expanding cooperation in trade, energy, education, and the Arctic.

Ukrainian intelligence reveals the size of Russia's Su-34 fighter-bomber fleet

Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU)
Quote: "As of 22 October 2026, the Russian Aerospace Forces had approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service, including upgraded Su-34M (Su-34NVO) aircraft."
Details: According to DIU, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed since the start of the full-scale invasion, while another seven have been damaged.
DIU noted that these losses are significant for Russia's military air fleet, as replacing the aircraft requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources and specialised industrial cooperation.
"By way of a comparison, the number of Su-34s destroyed is equivalent to approximately 2½-3 years of production based on an estimated capacity of 14-18 aircraft per year," the intelligence agency explained.
DIU said Su-34 fighter-bombers were one of the key components of Russia's strike aviation in its war against Ukraine. Their use as carriers of guided aerial bombs has enabled the Russian military to expand its ability to strike ground targets, particularly in areas of active hostilities and frontline settlements.
"Despite significant combat losses, Russia continues to produce and modernise the Su-34, attempting to maintain the size of its aircraft fleet and sustain the intensity of its missile and bomb strikes," the intelligence agency emphasised.
Meanwhile, according to DIU, Russia's ability to further expand this capability depends on production capacity, the availability of technological components and the Russian military industry's ability to compensate for its losses.
Background: In October, Russian state corporation Rostec announced that a new batch of Su-34 aircraft had been delivered to the Russian Aerospace Forces. The number of aircraft delivered was not specified.
