Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:04:04 UTC
22:04:04 KST

Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- American Academy of Neurology
- Summary:
- A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.
- Share:
Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health.
A study published in Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes.
Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages.
"Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil.
Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss.
Study Tracks Nearly 13,000 Adults for Eight Years
To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years.
At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners.
Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda.
Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes.
Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information.
Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time.
High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline
The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least.
After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group.
That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period.
Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging.
These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems.
Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes
When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants.
Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60.
The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake.
Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory.
Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol.
Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners.
Should People Rethink Artificial Sweeteners?
The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain.
"While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives."
Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes.
In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption.
The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences.
Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes.
The research was supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Science, Technology, and Innovation, and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development.

Germany holds two 19-year-olds over Bulgaria’s Starlink arson, and Sofia says they also attacked the network Ukraine fights with elsewhere in the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:03:50 UTC
22:03:50 KST

The Higher Regional Court in Düsseldorf has ordered two 19-year-old Germans held pending extradition to Bulgaria, which accuses them of setting fire to Starlink antennas at a satellite ground station near Sofia, the court and Düsseldorf prosecutors said on 29 October. The men, from Duisburg and Moers, were arrested on 23 October, German prosecutors told Reuters.
As Russia presses its war on Ukraine, Starlink keeps Ukraine’s drone units and front-line troops connected, and its ground sites in Europe have become targets. Within a month, fires and attempted fires hit Starlink sites in Poland, Bulgaria, and Lithuania, and Warsaw and Vilnius have linked them to Russia. The Bulgarian case now has its first arrests, and Sofia says the same pair struck another EU country, which would make it more than a one-off.
Sofia says the pair struck another EU country on 18 October
Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said he expected both suspects to be handed over to Bulgaria, and that the same two carried out a similar attack in another EU member state on 18 October, the state news agency BTA reported on 28 October. He did not name the country outright, but went on to cite Lithuania’s prime minister on an attempted arson there.
Overnight on 18 October, intruders tried to set fire to a Lithuanian company that stores Starlink equipment used by Ukraine, but tipped-off guards foiled the attempt. Lithuania’s prime minister called it part of Russia’s hybrid war.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the suspects had been detained in Germany several days earlier, and that disclosing their names sooner would have let them flee. The opposition wants to know whether a foreign security service warned Bulgaria at least a week before the attack, and how two 19-year-olds could enter the country and leave unnoticed. Parliament has failed three times to gather a quorum for a sitting to hear Radev and the security chiefs.
The suspects refuse a quick handover
The two did not agree to a simplified extradition, and the court will rule later on whether handing them over is admissible, according to the court’s statement carried by the dts news agency. Any extradition is to be approved only on the condition that, after a final sentence, they are offered a transfer back to Germany to serve it. Their lawyers plan to contest the Bulgarian warrant, dpa reported.
Bulgarian prosecutors say the pair crossed from Serbia as tourists on 9 October, set fire to eight antennas at the Plana teleport south of Sofia, and drove back to Serbia the same night. They were charged in absentia, a Sofia court confirmed European arrest warrants for them, and they face three to 12 years in prison if convicted.
Sofia City prosecutors announced the arrests on 27 October and said German authorities are gathering evidence for the case under a European investigation order. The pre-trial investigation continues, they said.

Over 233,000 double-envelope ballots counted in Israeli election, nearly 50% of total

Unknown Publisher

Ikrame Imane Kouachi
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
More than 233,000 double-envelope ballots, nearly 50% of the total, have been counted in Israel’s elections, Israeli media reported Thursday.
A total of 233,815 double-envelope ballots have been counted out of nearly 500,000, the daily Yedioth Ahronoth reported.
Double-envelope ballots are used by voters casting their ballots away from their registered polling stations, including soldiers, diplomats, police officers, and displaced residents.
Officials check identification details on the outer envelope to prevent duplicate voting, then separate it from the anonymous ballot before counting.
The remaining votes could change individual parties’ seat totals and the balance between the rival blocs.
The Central Elections Committee estimates that the double-envelope vote count will conclude later in the afternoon, according to the report.
After all regular ballots were counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 seats, compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and 19 for predominantly Arab parties, according to Channel 12.
Neither main bloc was projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
The Joint List was projected to secure 12 seats and the United Arab List (Ra’am) seven, giving Arab parties a record combined representation of 19 seats.
Voter turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999, according to the election committee.

Russia proposes cutting off mobile service to phones brought from abroad unless owners register them within two weeks

Russia proposes cutting off mobile service to phones brought from abroad unless owners register them within two weeks
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry has proposed cutting off cellular service to smartphones brought in from abroad starting in April 2027 if their owners fail to register them by IMEI number within two weeks, the Russian business news outlet RBC reported.
IMEI is a unique 15-digit number assigned to every mobile device during manufacturing.
The initiative, under discussion at the Digital Development Ministry, would apply to smartphones brought into Russia from abroad for personal use. Owners would have two weeks to register their phones after bringing them into the country, or carriers would disconnect the devices from the network.
“This [registering] can be done on Gosuslugi within a two-week period. If registration is not completed within the established period, such devices will not be serviced on the networks,” the ministry said.
The ministry said the measure aims to combat people who import smartphones into Russia one at a time to resell them.
The initiative will not affect phones that were working on Russian networks before April 2027.
In June, the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, passed a second set of measures aimed at fighting fraud. It calls for creating a unified IMEI database in Russia with a “blacklist” of phones that were stolen or illegally brought into the country.

The grammar of political hate? How a single word choice predicts nastier Facebook comment sections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:00:50 UTC
22:00:50 KST

Subtle grammatical choices in political social media posts are linked to how much hostility users express in the comment sections below them. A large-scale analysis of Facebook discussions published in Social Psychological and Personality Science indicates that posts referring to political groups with nouns rather than adjectives, or making sweeping generalizations about a party, tend to attract a higher proportion of prejudiced replies. Although the effect of any single post is small, the findings suggest that everyday wording habits online could gradually contribute to political division.
Hostility between opposing party supporters, which social scientists call affective polarization, has risen in the United States and several other democracies. Affective polarization refers to the tendency for citizens to view members of an opposing political party with dislike and distrust while favoring their own political group. At high levels, this animosity can lead voters to treat political rivals as enemies rather than fellow citizens, a dynamic linked to eroding trust in democratic institutions.
Sorting people into “us” versus “them” naturally creates some group bias, yet the intensity of that bias depends heavily on a psychological concept known as entitativity. Entitativity describes the extent to which an observer perceives a collection of people as a unified, tightly knit whole rather than a loose assortment of individuals. Supporting this idea, a 2018 meta-analysis of 33 samples found that the more people view an outside group as a coherent entity, the more prejudice they tend to hold toward its members. In politics, research has indicated that believing partisans are fundamentally different kinds of people was linked to greater partisan hostility, through more blame and assumed malicious intent, whereas believing political views themselves are fixed was linked to less.
“In essence, perceiving a group as entitative makes group members appear more interchangeable,” study author Carsten W. Sander, a research associate at Humboldt University of Berlin who conducted the research at Universität Hamburg with co-author Juliane Degner, a professor of social psychology there, told PsyPost. “People then generalize one member’s behavior to the whole group, retaliate against one group member for offenses committed by another, and generally show more outgroup prejudice. We reasoned that this could also fuel political polarization, understood as growing prejudice toward the political outparty.”
Because national political parties contain millions of people, citizens cannot observe an entire party firsthand and instead rely on media and conversation to judge how unified the other side is. Beyond explicit statements about a group, grammatical structures can quietly signal uniformity. One such cue is whether a writer uses a noun label, such as “Senate Republicans,” or an adjective label, such as “Republican senators.” Using a noun defines a person primarily by a single group category, whereas an adjective treats party affiliation as just one trait among many.
Controlled experiments show that these grammatical distinctions shape how people judge unfamiliar or minority groups. For instance, a 2020 study of print news readers found that articles describing an ethnic minority member with a noun rather than an adjective led readers to express slightly greater prejudice toward that entire minority group, whether the story was positive or negative.
A second cue involves generic statements, which are broad claims attributing an enduring trait to a group as an abstract whole, such as “Democrats want climate action,” rather than non-generic phrasing like “some Democrats want climate action.” In a 2010 experimental study of children and adults, participants who learned about a fictional animal category through generic statements were more likely to treat its members as sharing the same underlying nature, though the effect was weaker in children.
Most evidence on noun labels and generic phrasing comes from laboratory studies involving fictional or unfamiliar categories. Sander and Degner wanted to test whether these subtle wording differences also influence hostility toward established political groups like U.S. Democrats and Republicans in real-world online conversations. The authors noted that the relative frequency of partisan noun labels in U.S. online news has risen substantially in recent years, raising the question of how such language plays out on social media.
To examine this in a natural setting, the researchers gathered public Facebook posts and comments through the Meta Content Library. They selected Facebook because it has a diverse American user base and frequently hosts text-based political discussions. After excluding posts in which party labels referred to institutions or events rather than people (such as “the Democratic Party” or “the Republican primary”), the final sample included 45,780 posts and 769,684 direct replies written by 391,386 unique users across 3,878 pages and profiles. News media outlets contributed the largest share of posts, alongside public figures, politicians, and government officials.
To analyze hundreds of thousands of messages, the authors fine-tuned five artificial intelligence models built on transformer architectures, which are machine-learning programs that process language by evaluating how words relate in context. They trained and tested these models on thousands of human-coded examples, supplemented for two of the models with 600 synthetic posts written in matched pairs that differed in only one feature. One model classified whether a post used a party label as a noun (such as “voting Democrats”) or an adjective (such as “Democratic voters”). A second model identified whether the post made a broad generic claim about a group as a whole or a non-generic statement limited by qualifiers or referring to a single past action.
To account for other factors that might provoke angry replies, the models also tracked whether each post referred to a single individual, a subgroup (such as “House Republicans”), or the broader party, and whether the original post itself expressed hostility toward a political party. A separate model evaluated all 769,684 comments to detect partisan prejudice, defined as dislike or negativity aimed at a political group or collective target (such as “Dems are the worst” or “Idiots!”), while excluding remarks aimed only at a single person (such as “I hate Biden”). The researchers publicly registered their hypotheses and analysis plan in advance.
The researchers then used multilevel statistical models to test whether the wording of a specific post predicted the proportion of prejudiced comments below it. Comparing different posts published on the exact same Facebook page allowed the analysis to account for unmeasured differences between pages and their audiences. Across all 45,780 posts, posts using noun labels received a higher proportion of prejudiced comments than posts on the same page using adjective labels. Before controls, the odds that any given comment expressed partisan prejudice were 1.39 times higher beneath noun-label posts than beneath adjective-label posts, an odds ratio that fell to 1.15 after controlling for post prejudice and whether the target was an individual, subgroup, or whole party.
In practical terms, on a typical Facebook page where 59 percent of posts used noun labels, the model predicted that 16.7 percent of comments under a noun-label post would express partisan prejudice, compared with 14.8 percent under an adjective-label post. That is an absolute difference of 1.9 percentage points, or a relative difference of about 13 percent. By contrast, a page’s overall average use of noun labels across all its posts was not a statistically significant predictor of comment prejudice after controls were added, which the authors interpret as a sign that commenters were responding to the wording of the specific post, though they caution that comparisons between pages are vulnerable to hidden differences.
For their second main analysis, the authors tested generic language across the 26,026 posts and 437,744 comments that referred to political groups or subgroups rather than specific individuals. Posts using party labels generically drew a higher share of prejudiced replies than non-generic posts, with an odds ratio of 1.22 before adjustments and 1.20 after controlling for noun usage, post prejudice, and whether the post targeted a subgroup or the broader party.
On a typical page where 29 percent of posts were generic, the predicted probability of a prejudiced comment was 22.2 percent under generic posts versus 19.2 percent under non-generic posts, an absolute difference of 3.0 percentage points or a relative difference of roughly 16 percent. At the page level, pages that posted generic statements more often actually drew somewhat fewer prejudiced comments once other factors were accounted for, a pattern the authors attribute to other differences between pages rather than to the wording itself.
In that second analysis, noun labels continued to independently predict higher rates of prejudiced comments alongside generic phrasing, indicating that each feature was linked to online hostility on its own. Supplementary analyses also showed that these patterns held true whether posts mentioned Democrats or Republicans. Even when comparing different comments written by the exact same user across multiple posts, noun and generic labels still predicted more prejudiced replies, which the authors interpret as a sign that the language affected how users commented rather than merely attracting already hostile users.
These findings align with a study covered by PsyPost in early 2024, which found that broad generic statements about political parties led people to perceive a wider ideological gap between Democrats and Republicans than statements containing qualifiers like “some.” That earlier research measured perceived ideological divides in survey experiments, whereas the new study indicates that generic phrasing is also linked to hostile expressions in real-world social media discussions.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because the study observed existing social media activity rather than randomly assigning different wordings to readers, it cannot establish with certainty that grammatical labels directly caused the increase in prejudiced replies. In addition, the study only captured whether someone wrote a hostile comment in the moment, leaving open whether noun or generic labels create lasting attitude shifts or briefly trigger existing frustrations.
“The key caveat is that the findings are observational,” Sander explained. “Features of the post content that we didn’t control for could be driving both the labeling and the prejudiced comments, so the results shouldn’t be read as showing that labels cause prejudice.” Still, he added, “our results and earlier experimental research are consistent with that possibility.”
The automated classifiers were also imperfect. In test data, the model that detected prejudiced comments caught about 73 percent of them, and about 68 percent of the comments it flagged were truly prejudiced, so some misclassification is likely.
Another caveat is that the statistical effects of a single post’s wording are small, and subtle cues from nouns or generic statements might be overshadowed by explicit news about party infighting or unanimous votes. At the same time, the authors propose that labeling habits could spread through social networks, as one person’s phrasing influences another’s, a possibility they say still needs testing. They also argue that even if a post only briefly nudges a few users to leave hostile replies, those comments remain visible on the page, where they could give other readers an exaggerated impression of how much the opposing party dislikes them.
“The effects were small: about 15% prejudiced comments under adjective labels versus 17% under noun labels,” Sander said. “If they turn out to be causal, though, they could nevertheless matter in practice: Labeling choices by high-reach news outlets could affect very large audiences, and small effects may accumulate as people read many posts over time.”
To test whether changing how parties are labeled actually reduces online hostility, the researchers hope to evaluate these wording variations in real-world trials over extended periods. “The next step would be an experimental replication, for example in collaboration with an online news outlet that would let us randomly vary the labeling in its social media posts, as this would allow us to establish causality,” Sander noted.
Future studies could also examine whether shifting toward adjective labels, qualifiers like “some,” or person-first phrasing such as “people who voted Republican” helps cool down political comment sections. Researchers might additionally test whether describing discrete past actions, such as “Republicans voted,” rather than permanent group traits, such as “Republicans are,” tempers partisan animosity.
The study, “Constructing the Enemy: Noun and Generic Party Labels Predict Partisan Prejudice in Social Media Comments,” was authored by Carsten W. Sander and Juliane Degner.

Could Abdul El-Sayed’s plan for AI companies stave off catastrophe? | Jerel Ezell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:00:44 UTC
22:00:44 KST

The Michigan senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, occupies a strange but increasingly common place in modern American politics. He’s praised by progressives, begrudgingly tolerated by moderate Democrats and largely demonized by Republicans.
He’s also uniquely positioned to forge an all-too-elusive thread of political kinship between these perpetually-at-odds groups with his bold but contentious plan for reining in AI, called AI Under Democracy.
And it couldn’t come at a better time. According to a poll conducted this summer by NBC News, 70% of Americans said that they were more worried than excited about AI, a shocking reversal from just a couple of years ago. Another poll from Quinnipiac several weeks ago found that 73% of Americans are concerned about AI posing a threat to human existence.
AI Under Democracy was revealed several weeks before the Michigan Democratic primary. At the time, El-Sayed was still a relative underdog, a physician with threadbare political credentials and views that – it seemed – were woefully misaligned with the moderate, blue-collar sensibilities of Michiganders.
When it comes to his AI plan, and a companion proposal called AI Under Control that he released this month, that may no longer be the case. In fact, it could be a potential antidote to our ideological gridlock over the promise and peril of AI.
Back in 2023, I was invited to be a guest on Abdul El-Sayed’s podcast, America Dissected. Both Michigan natives with backgrounds in public health, El-Sayed and I commiserated over global leaders’ glaring lack of relatability and, by extension, the grating way they dismiss – and often increase –the struggles of everyday people. It all seems quite prescient now.
Barack Obama recently urged Democrats to rally around AI regulation in the midterms, but El-Sayed and many progressive Democrats have already been leading the charge.
El-Sayed’s AI ethos is deeply shaped by his history as a healthcare provider – not as a politician. His maxim for AI development is “first, do no harm,” a transposition of the Hippocratic oath into this new wild west of technology, as AI companies face pressure to balance profit against the public interest.
To this end, El-Sayed’s proposal calls for corporate divestiture from AI’s largest companies, recognizing that legacy companies such as Google, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon simply have too much controlling interest in frontier AI ventures like OpenAI and Anthropic, creating untenable friction between their revenue-generation prerogatives and our public safety.
For example, Microsoft has an estimated 27% stake in OpenAI, and Google owns 14% of Anthropic, giving each a sizable say in how the companies operate. Under El-Sayed’s proposal, the tech giants would have to divest or abandon those investments within a defined transitional period.
The plan also calls for the regulation of datacenters: slowing the volume of developments, facilitating local job creation, freezing residential utility costs, and addressing the public health and quality of life issues that datacenters produce in terms of noise and pollution. He has been especially vocal about the colossal OpenAI-Oracle datacenter being erected just outside of Ann Arbor, Michigan, where he attended the University of Michigan.
Today, there’s a groundswell of resistance towards datacenters. An August poll found that only one in 9 Americans would support the construction of a datacenter in their local community. El-Sayed’s plan dovetails with the public’s clear and growing opposition: keep AI’s footprint and its environmental and socioeconomic consequences – those known and as yet unknown – contained.
Far and away the most controversial – but essential – part of El-Sayed’s plan to thwart an AI-fueled catastrophe is his call for 50% + one of board seats (a simple majority) at influential AI companies to be publicly appointed or democratically elected. This would in theory foster transparency around AI companies’ plans and give Americans the power to veto decisions – on matters like datacenter development and biological weapons manufacturing – that could undermine the public interest.
While both Democrats and Republicans may come to support heavier regulation and moratoriums on AI, public control may be an entirely different can of worms. For many, the idea of transferring ownership of a private enterprise to a public trust smacks of socialism. And this narrative certainly feeds into the common Republican critique of El-Sayed, as well as his Republican challenger Mike Rogers’ even more aggressive attempt to tar him as a feckless communist.
However, communities across the US have long embraced public ownership of essential resources such as water, natural gas, and electricity. And according to a June report, roughly 69% of American adults support AI companies transferring 50% of their stock to public sovereign wealth fund, a pot of money used to support public interests.
This is a paradigm which Bernie Sanders, El-Sayed’s most prominent booster on Capitol Hill, has legislatively proposed. There’s a good chance that Americans will continue warming up to this idea.
It’s not a coincidence that, as we approach the midterms, feverish debates are now erupting over how – or even whether – AI’s soaring risks can now be tempered via federal policy.
Naturally, in the US, people are looking to their political leaders for answers – even though a whopping 78% of Americans disapprove of how Congressional members are handling their job and Donald Trump’s approval ratings are underwater.
Many of these politicians seem unaware of or ambivalent about the state of AI and its mushrooming perils. That’s where younger, tech-savvy candidates like El-Sayed – who has called for a pause on AI’s most potent releases, a ban on artificial superintelligence, and an AI kill switch – shine and can provide leadership and restraint as we confront a future where AI is ubiquitous.
Exhibit A of the opposite: Trump and other administration officials who have been aggressively poo-poohing demands to slow AI’s rapid ascension, saying the uproar is a “hoax” while continuing to insist on the US’s AI dominance at essentially any cost.
To be sure, some – including leaders in the White House and Silicon Valley investors beholden to the sunken cost principle – will remain bullish on AI.
But calls for regulation from everyday people on both sides of aisle should be the ultimate shot across the bow. And AI’s top plutocrats, such as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, rallying around the idea of “pacing the frontier” are a big, red flag being waved right in society’s face.
All this can be addressed through a deliberate, balanced public ownership policy.
- Jerel Ezell is executive director of the Center for AI and Everybody and an assistant professor at the University of Chicago

The high drama of volcanic wines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:00:44 UTC
22:00:44 KST

Good stories need jeopardy. Take The Princess Bride, one of my favourite films, which I recently introduced to my mildly terrified children. It’s a cult love story of high peril: Westley, believed dead, sets out to win back Buttercup (forced into marriage with another) on a quest involving pirates, duels, torture, a miracle and a battle of wits over a goblet of poisoned wine. There is struggle, magic and, ultimately, emotional reward. You’ll need to stay with me here: volcanic vines, too, tend to have a rocky journey, albeit with happy results for the drinker.
My ears perk up at the term “volcanic wine”, despite being less a style than a geological category. Volcanic soils take many forms – ash, basalt, obsidian, pumice, tuff – and interact with climate, altitude, water availability, grape variety and farming to produce wines with a very particular sense of place. Often, they have little in common with each other; a deep, rich nerello mascalese from Mount Etna’s north side bears little comparison to a light, leathery listán negro from Tenerife, say. And yet I’m sure there is something – perhaps it’s more a feeling than a taste – that I get from wines from volcanic terroirs. “It’s a hard thing to get across,” agrees importer Nic Rizzi of Modal Wines, “but they do have an extra tension.”
Tension is the word. Volcanic landscapes impose particular demands: on Etna, for instance, the vines’ roots have to negotiate thin, stony soil formed from lava flows and ashfall; on Santorini, vines grow in loose pumice, ash and volcanic sand, with little rainfall and fierce winds; while in the Canary Islands, the vines can grow in deep layers of black ash. These are difficult landscapes to farm, but, as we know, a rocky journey does make for a good story.
Rizzi imports wines made by Victoria Torres Pecis from La Palma in the Canaries, a place with “a majestic and wild energy”. There are black ash soils, vineyards above the cloud layer at 1,200m and ancient vines trained low to the ground to protect them from high winds. Farming here is labour-intensive; there are heatwaves and drought, and in 2021 a volcano erupted during harvest. “It takes a certain kind of person to put themselves through that pain and graft,” Rizzi says, “and that struggle comes through in the wine.” (Torres’ Las Machuqueras in today’s pick is a unicorn wine that sings deliciously of struggle.)
Not to get too woo-woo about it, but, for me, volcanic wines share an energy. Legends have been built around volcanoes; they hold a mystical place in our imaginations. But, in very real terms, wines from these terroirs are deeply complex – saline, herbal, savoury and mineral – with a sense of tension that keeps you coming back. Like all interesting characters, their charisma is hard won.
Volcanic wines that give you bang for your buck
M&S Etna Rosato £14 Ocado, 12%. From high, lava-terraced vineyards comes this deeply hued, mineral rosé that goes with everything
Bodega Volcanes Carménère 2024 £12.50 Majestic, 14%. Energetic autumn red from one of Chile’s 3,000 volcanoes – expect dark fruit and umami.
De Falco Fiordilava Falanghina del Vesuvio 2024 £16 The Wine Society, 13%. The name means “flower of lava”, though it’s not floral, but rather a softly mineral falanghina from the slopes of Vesuvius.
Rampazzi Bianco Andrea Occhipinti 2025 £23.50 Sip Wines, 12%. Savoury and subtly smoky Tuscan beauty from above Europe’s oldest volcanic lake.
Cave Verdier-Logel Volcanique Gamay Rouge 2024 £20 Sourcing Table, 13.5%. At once juicy and peppery, this great-value Loire gamay hails from the volcanic basalt soils of the Massif Central foothills.
Victoria Torres Pecis Las Machuqueras 2016/19 £55 Modal Wines, 12.5%. Pricey, yes, but black ash soils, very old vines, harsh conditions and tiny yields combine to create a deeply textured and salty wine

Putin’s two-war advantage over Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:00:39 UTC
22:00:39 KST

Putin's two-war advantage over Trump
U.S. President Donald Trump in Fort Myers, Florida, U.S., on Oct. 23, 2026. (Alex Wong / Getty Images)
Two wars are testing U.S. President Donald Trump's ability to shape world events — and Russia is using the situation to its advantage.
As the U.S. pushes Russia to end its invasion of Ukraine, Moscow is also involved in the war between the U.S. and Iran. Major news outlets have reported that Russia is sharing military intelligence with Tehran, even as Trump has praised Moscow for staying out of the fighting.
The contradiction was clear last week. During high-level talks in St. Petersburg, U.S. negotiators met with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. But when Trump was asked about the talks on Oct. 21, he turned to Iran.
"Trump is essentially confronted with two major wars that he has a massive political interest in ending."
"We negotiated with Russia to stop the war with Ukraine, and we have been pretty happy with Russia that they have not gotten involved with Iran," Trump told reporters.
His comments point to an opportunity for Putin. With Trump eager to end both wars, Moscow can present itself as a partner in resolving one while pursuing its own goals in the other.
"Trump is essentially confronted with two major wars that he has a massive political interest in ending," said Christian Emery, an associate professor of international politics at University College London.
"Putin is trying to exploit Trump's domestic political vulnerability to achieve his main aim: normalizing relations with the U.S. without offering any serious concessions on Ukraine," he added.
A practical partnership
Since the start of Russia’s all-out war against Ukraine, both Russia and Iran have sought to bolster bilateral ties.
In January 2025, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian visited the Kremlin to sign a long-heralded partnership deal between the two countries.
Under heavy sanctions, Iran and Russia expanded trade and shored up their positions on the global stage. Russia has also benefited from Iranian drone technology, using Shahed-type drones extensively in attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The relationship remains a practical one, says Arman Mahmoudian, a research fellow at the Global and National Security Institute and a faculty member at the University of South Florida.
Russia has reasons to keep Iran close. Tehran's presence ensures that there is at least one country with friendly ties in the Persian Gulf. It also means that the Kremlin retains influence in the Middle East, something that took a blow with the fall of Syria's former Russian-backed president, Bashar al-Assad, in December 2024.
But these are secondary concerns compared with Ukraine, says Mahmoudian. Moscow has behaved accordingly by supporting Iran with intelligence, but has not risked further damaging relations with the United States by providing large amounts of ammunition and weapons.
"This relationship between Russia and Iran is not an alliance but a partnership driven by shared interests," he says, adding that Moscow would be unlikely to prioritize Tehran over a potential rapprochement with Washington.
Tehran keeps check
Yet none of this means Tehran is entirely at Moscow's mercy. Iran, too, sees the relationship as one of mutual convenience, using its ties with Russia to maintain a foothold on the international stage.
"Russia offers Iran a platform on the international stage; every once in a while, the Russian and Iranian presidents meet. There's a lot of fanfare," says Sina Azodi, a visiting scholar and lecturer at the Institute for Middle East Studies at George Washington University.
"Is Russia going to backstab us again?"
"But I don't think that Iranians can ever trust Russia. There's always this discussion of, "' Is Russia going to backstab us again?'"
That mistrust reflects the limits of what Moscow can offer. "Putin has little or no leverage to compel the Iranians to make concessions," says Emery. "Nor can he offer the security guarantees that would ease their concerns about being attacked by the U.S. and Israel again."
For Moscow, however, the value of the relationship lies less in what it can deliver to Tehran than in what it can offer Washington. By presenting itself as a potential mediator, while demonstrating its willingness to act against Iranian interests, the Kremlin can signal that its cooperation comes at a price — and that it is prepared to trade its ties with Tehran for concessions elsewhere.
In that calculation, Iran is not necessarily a partner Russia intends to protect, but a source of leverage in a much larger negotiation. And if Moscow believes that distancing itself from Tehran could help secure U.S. concessions over Ukraine, there is little reason to expect loyalty to stand in the way.

China’s fourth aircraft carrier, widely believed to be the country’s first with a nuclear-powered system, could launch as early as next year, according to US researchers, as Beijing pursues a fleet capable of projecting naval and air power far beyond its shores.
A launch in 2027 would coincide with the centenary of the People’s Liberation Army, with the anniversary falling on August 1. Beijing has previously used major military anniversaries to showcase developments in its armed forces.
The Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) said in an updated assessment on Tuesday that satellite imagery from this month showed the warship – commonly referred to as the Type 004 – at a construction stage comparable to that of China’s third carrier, the Fujian, in May 2021, about a year before its June 2022 launch.
This suggests the Type 004 could enter the water next year. However, analysts cautioned that its larger size and potentially more complex propulsion system, as well as unforeseen issues, could put it on a different schedule from the Fujian. Beijing does not disclose construction timelines.

Bulldozers, glyphosate, white phosphorus: Israel’s destruction of South Lebanon’s olive groves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

On October 15, Israeli forces expelled residents and farmers from Azariel, an olive grove on the outskirts of Kfarshouba in South Lebanon, ordering them to return the following week if they still wished to harvest their trees. The next morning, an Israeli bulldozer, flanked by two army tanks, invaded the olive grove and uprooted the trees.
A few days before the expulsion, Chebli, a farmer from Kfarshouba, had watched an Israeli bulldozer uproot 70 olive trees belonging to his neighbor.
“I went over to him and found him crying,” he told Mondoweiss. “He spent more than 20 years plowing this land and pruning the trees, and he hadn’t even harvested them yet.”
Following the partial ceasefire agreement that was signed in June of this year, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the military would remain in what Israel calls its “security zone” in order to “continue to destroy terrorist infrastructure.” In addition to this, Israeli defense minister Israel Katz declared that Lebanese civilians will not be allowed to return south of the Litani River, leaving hundreds of thousands of people indefinitely waiting to return. For farmers and agricultural workers, this forced displacement means not only losing their homes, but also their livelihood.
Olive groves cover around 62,000 hectares of land in Lebanon – nearly a quarter of the country’s farmland – making it one of the most vital crops in the country. The autumn harvest, which peaks in October and November, yields around 19,000 to 20,000 tons of olive oil per year, according to the International Olive Council. One of the oldest olive trees in the world, estimated at 1,100 years old, reportedly resides in the northern part of the country. In Kfarshouba, Chebli’s village that is now occupied by the Israeli army, the olive trees range between 300 and 500 years old.
Across South Lebanon, farmers and residents describe a pattern of bulldozed groves, ancient trees uprooted and stolen, and Israeli troops expelling anyone who tries to reach their land. On October 11, the Lebanese Army said Israeli fire killed Ali Abdel Hassan Sweidan, a retired chief warrant officer, as he was inspecting his property in Yater, in Bint Jbeil district, during the olive harvest.
The war has also severed farmers from their markets. “Khiam alone used to buy half the South’s harvest,” Chebli said, by his own estimate, referring to the hilltop town on the Israeli border, which Israeli forces now occupy.
“The olive season is gold for people,” he said. “It lets you hold your head up.”
Beyond the Yellow Line
Israel continues to occupy a buffer zone behind what it calls the “yellow line,” an area that includes 55 to 62 towns and villages, totaling around 6 percent of Lebanese territory. The US-brokered ceasefire agreement was supposed to enforce an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, but has instead facilitated further land grabs and demolitions.
Israel expanded its occupation of the South during the latest military escalation of a protracted war that began three years ago. After the November 2024 ceasefire, Israel continued to strike Lebanon almost daily, killing 139 civilians during that time. On March 2, 2026, two days after a US-Israeli strike killed Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, Hezbollah fired rockets that the Israeli military said fell in open areas. Israel responded with a full-scale military campaign that killed at least 4,389 people in Lebanon, despite the temporary truce agreed upon in April, and the partial ceasefire agreement signed in June.
In Kfarshouba, Israeli forces have drawn a line through the farmland that no one may cross, according to Ali Salah al-Dhiyab, one of the village’s mukhtars, the elected officials who serve as village heads. Since 2024, he said, farmers have been able to reach their land only once, for a single day.
“We harvested like thieves,” he told Mondoweiss. “You don’t know how you’ll get there or how you’ll get back.”
The municipality had petitioned UNIFIL, the UN peacekeeping force in South Lebanon, and the Mechanism Committee, the US-chaired diplomatic body tasked with monitoring the ceasefire, for permission to harvest. Lebanese intelligence officials communicated Israel’s response, which allowed only 100 people and 25 cars to enter their village for one day. They also required farmers to hand over their phones and identity cards and barred the Lebanese Army and UNIFIL from accompanying them.
The municipal council rejected the offer. Kfarshouba has around 1,000 farming households, al-Dhiyab said, and families harvest their own trees.
“If you have 400 trees, you’ll pick five or ten and forget the rest,” he said. “Israel is bulldozing the land and the stones, everything. Unfortunately, half the olives are already gone.”
Al-Dhiyab said buyers were turning away oil from the South for fear of contamination. “You offer someone a tin of oil and he tells you, ‘I won’t buy it, there’s white phosphorus in it,’” he said.
Nothing left to press
For many farmers, there are no groves remaining to be turned away from. In May, while displaced with his family in Beirut, Rafik Baraka discovered that his olive trees had been destroyed by the Israeli army. He learned what had happened from satellite images on Google and from acquaintances in the Lebanese Army and UNIFIL. Some of his trees were bulldozed and burned, he said, but the eldest trees were uprooted and stolen.
“Israel changed the face of the land,” Baraka said.
The 64-year-old farmer from Rab Thalathin, a village in Marjayoun district in southern Lebanon, owned 152 trees, some of them between 100 and 200 years old. His grandfather had planted them, his father had cared for them, and he carried on the tradition. Every autumn, his family spent about 10 days in the village picking and pressing olives, making around 80 tins of oil in an average year.
This year, there was nothing to harvest.
“Our village was bulldozed completely, the houses, the cemeteries, and the olive trees,” Baraka told Mondoweiss. “They left nothing.”
The uprooting of olive trees has reached a French court. A 37-year-old French businessman of Lebanese origin, who has not been publicly named, has filed a complaint in Paris against unknown persons, accusing the Israeli military of uprooting about 600 olive trees from his family’s land in Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, an Israeli-occupied village north of the Litani River. He says some of the trees were around 500 years old, and that his family had farmed the land for 250 years.
The complaint alleges theft, destruction, and damage to property amounting to war crimes. It claims that Israeli forces took control of the area, and the trees were uprooted, roots and all, with suspicions that they were taken to Israel.
A war on all living things
The South produces around 38 percent of Lebanon’s olives, most of which have been destroyed or harmed. According to Greenpeace, Israeli attacks burned or bulldozed at least 65,000 olive trees in the 2023–2024 war alone. Officials and environmental groups have accused Israel of ecocide, with some campaigning to recognize the intentional environmental destruction as a crime under international law.
In February, Israeli aircrafts sprayed glyphosate, a weedkiller that kills plants down to the roots, over roughly 8.5 square kilometers (3.3 square miles) near the border. Lebanese authorities reported that Israeli strikes have also used white phosphorus, a chemical that ignites in air and can burn skin to the bone. Human Rights Watch said the Israeli military unlawfully fired white phosphorus over homes in the southern town of Yohmor al-Shaqif on March 3.
In addition to this, a recent study by Lebanon’s National Council for Scientific Research (CNRS) found chromium above permissible limits in about 45 percent of 134 soil samples taken in the South and the Bekaa, the fertile valley in eastern Lebanon that is the country’s main farming region, which has also been a target of Israeli airstrikes.
Sara Salloum, co-founder and president of AgriMovement, a Lebanese farming group that promotes chemical-free agriculture and local seeds, told Mondoweiss that ecocide includes “the destruction of the foundations of life and of communities’ ability to carry on living in their land.”
“Destroying productive land can prolong displacement, weaken the possibility of return, and make communities depend on aid instead of producing their own food,” Salloum said.
Similar destruction has been recorded in Palestine. In Gaza, a UN satellite analysis found that Israel’s military campaign had damaged 89 percent of orchards and trees by late September 2025, and by June 2026 only 3 percent of cropland remained both accessible and undamaged.
In the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian Authority says settlers and Israeli forces cut down or damaged more than 26,000 olive trees in the first half of 2026. In May, Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, announced plans to uproot 3,000 more to make way for settlements. Between September 25 and October 1, the Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture reported $1.75 million in losses to farmers across seven West Bank governorates.
“This is part of the pattern of systematic destruction in Lebanon, Palestine and Syria, and especially Gaza,” Salloum said. “Confronting ecocide means protecting the land and its people together.”
‘They destroyed our memories‘
For Rafik Baraka, the loss cannot be measured in tins of olive oil.
“Even if we go back and replant, we need twenty years before the tree becomes a tree that bears fruit,” he said. “They didn’t only destroy history and geography. They destroyed our memories. This tree didn’t grow by itself.”
Baraka described the harvest season like an annual festival, with families eating together under the trees and helping one another to complete the task.
“No reconstruction or rehabilitation can bring back that closeness,” he said. “The Israeli knows what he is doing. He doesn’t only want to uproot you from your land, but from your memory too.” Although Baraka’s children did not grow up as farmers, they always returned to the olive groves every year for harvest season, a tradition their father hopes will outlive this war.
“I am sure that when we are gone, they will come back and care for this land because it is part of their inheritance,” he said.

AI Foundations for Learners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Sara Davila directs students toward responsible and creative use of AI
Students today encounter AI across nearly every aspect of their learning, from search engines and writing tools to content recommendations and automated feedback. Students may rely on AI regularly without fully understanding how it works, what it produces, or what is sacrificed when there is no effort and the opportunity to reflect is lost. While these systems can support efficiency and access, they also introduce new challenges related to independence, authorship, and critical thinking. The challenge for educators lies in helping learners move from dependency and passive consumption to active, intentional creation.
Just as educators benefit from a framework to guide thoughtful use of AI, students also need structured support to develop responsible and effective practice. English language learners have distinct and unique challenges that can impact their overall interaction and satisfaction with AI tools. Language learners may rely more heavily on translation tools or prefer AI-polished and translated work over their own voice. Given how quickly AI has become embedded in everyday tools, from a WhatsApp chat to word-processing applications, providing guidance is critical to support the unique needs of language learners while building digital literacy, AI competence, and English proficiency.
The AI Competency Framework for Students
The AI Competency Framework for Students offers a way for educators to support our learners (UNESCO, 2024). Like the AI Competency Framework for Teachers (UNESCO, 2024) this is not a scripted curriculum or a checklist of digital skills but rather a lens for learning that helps students build confidence, ethics, and agency as they navigate AI-enhanced environments.
The student framework consists of four dimensions:
1. A Human-Centered Mindset
2. Responsible AI Ethics
3. AI Techniques
4. AI Systems Design
Together, these dimensions create a path for student use of AI, helping learners navigate from understanding to autonomy. As students learn to use AI thoughtfully, responsibly, and creatively, they can explore how these tools can deepen their own learning and creativity without risking opportunities for growth and reflection.
1. A Human-Centered Mindset: AI as Assistant to Learning
The foundation of AI literacy for students is the understanding that AI is a tool developed by humans to support humans’ success, not as a replacement for human knowledge, ingenuity, or innovation. When learners understand this, they can begin to use AI as a partner in the learning process without shortcutting key opportunities to gain new skills and abilities.
A key aspect of the framework is how it can help focus on the importance of reflection for learning. In practice, this mindset means guiding students to ask reflective questions like:
- Is this tool helping me practice a skill or doing the work for me?
- Am I still thinking, analyzing, and expressing my own ideas?
In some ways, the goal is to help students understand how using AI tools can impact their own sense of ownership, critical thinking, and creativity. As research has shown, when AI is introduced into learning is a key component of success: too soon and the lack of effort leads to complete disengagement, where just-in-time AI can stimulate critical thinking and creativity (Kosmyna et al., 2025). When learners think first and use AI afterward, they retain more knowledge, demonstrate greater creativity, and engage more deeply with content. Timing and intention make the difference between cognitive support and cognitive erosion.
2. Responsible AI Ethics: Learning to Make Informed Choices
As students experiment with AI, they also need to understand its ethical dimensions. Responsible use begins with three essential questions:
- Does this help me learn?
AI should extend thinking, not replace it. Students can learn to evaluate whether a tool supports skill growth or short-circuits effort.
- Am I being honest about my work?
Academic integrity must adapt to the AI era. Learners should know how to acknowledge when they’ve used an AI tool, much like citing a source. This transparency reinforces ownership and ethical behavior.
- Am I protecting my privacy?
Students should never share personal information, school details, or sensitive data with online systems. Developing digital boundaries is now as essential as learning to write a thesis statement.
Discussing these principles in the classroom helps learners turn ethical considerations into tangible questions that support learner understanding and autonomy with AI tools. Further, discussing ethical uses of AI helps learners consider academic integrity, much like understanding the difference between paraphrasing and plagiarism. By framing AI use around learning, honesty, and privacy, educators help students build habits that extend beyond the classroom and into responsible digital participation.
3. AI Techniques: Building Skill Through Purposeful Practice
The third dimension focuses on developing the practical skills to use AI effectively. This is where students learn how to communicate with AI tools and choose the right one for a given task. This includes working with generative AI models like ChatGPT or Claude, as well as identifying common forms of AI embedded in everyday technologies that often go unnoticed.
For example:
- When revising writing, a student might use an AI grammar checker to find sentence-level errors.
- When exploring a new topic, they might use a research-focused tool like Google Search or Perplexity to locate and evaluate reliable sources.
- When practicing pronunciation, they might use a speech-based AI to listen, repeat, and self-assess.
Over the last two decades, a variety of AI tools have launched, working quietly in the background to shape tasks and decisions without drawing attention. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday technologies, students must learn not only how to use visible tools but how to recognize when AI is influencing their work in less obvious ways. When a learner accepts a suggested sentence in a Word document or changes a topic based on a search result, they may not realize that AI is informing their decisions and potentially changing their intended communication. As such, helping students be selective, intentional, and aware becomes a key component of AI literacy.
4. AI Systems Design: Creating and Developing AI
The final dimension of the student framework is creative and empowering. It introduces learners to the idea that interacting with AI does not have to be a passive experience, but rather, these tools can be used to build what our learners imagine. As students learn how AI responds to input, they begin to see that they can shape how it behaves, understand its limits, and eventually use it, adapt it, or even build their own to support their own interests and personal goals.
Supporting this dimension does not require teachers to become AI developers or technical specialists. Rather, it involves helping students recognize that AI systems are not fixed tools but evolving constructions shaped by human choices, assumptions, and priorities. As students begin to understand this relationship, they move beyond interacting with AI toward thinking about how such systems are formed, how they can be questioned, and how they might one day be shaped to serve human purposes more deliberately.
To support this development, teachers can guide students with simple but powerful questions such as:
- What am I asking this tool to do, and why?
- How does the way I interact with the tool affect the result I get?
- What decisions seem to be built into this system?
- How could this tool be adapted to better support my own goals?
- If I were designing this tool, what would I change?
These questions shift attention away from the tool and back to the learner’s thinking, helping students see how their decisions shape AI outcomes. Over time, this awareness allows learners to move beyond using AI toward influencing and adapting how it is used. This reinforces a critical idea: meaningful learning comes not from the power of AI but from students’ ability to direct, evaluate, and shape the tools they work with.
From Users to Creators: A New Model of Learning
When all four dimensions come together, students transition from consuming AI output to creating with AI. Their learning pathway mirrors the development of knowledge from understanding to complex creation.
- Understand — Grasp what AI is and how it works.
- Apply — Use AI purposefully to support learning tasks.
- Create — Design new ideas, projects, or systems using AI as a tool for innovation.
This evolution turns students into collaborators in their own education. They become thinkers who use AI to test hypotheses, refine arguments, and imagine possibilities. These are all skills that prepare students for a world where human intelligence and machine intelligence will coexist.
Ultimately, the AI competency frameworks for teachers and students empower educators to guide students toward critical resilience—the ability to use AI creatively without losing their own voice or agency. The goal is to support the development of thoughtful citizens who understand AI’s limits, question its authority, and shape its future responsibly. Our role as educators is to ensure that AI enhances, not replaces, the essential processes of thinking and learning. By modeling curiosity, critical judgment, and ethical awareness, we prepare students to use these tools with intention and independence.
References
Kosmyna, N., Hauptmann, E., Yuan, Y., Situ, J., Liao, X., Beresnitzky, A., Maes, P. (2025). “Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of cognitive debt when using an AI assistant for essay writing task.” arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08872
UNESCO. (2024). AI Competency Framework for Students. Paris, France: UNESCO. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000391105
UNESCO. (2024). AI Competency Framework for Teachers. Paris, France: UNESCO. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000391104
Sara Davila, at Educating Her World, is an English language education specialist with global experience. Sara has helped educators and learning organizations reimagine English programs through evidence-based curriculum design, practical professional development, and 21st-century approaches to teaching and learning. Sara is based in Chicago, working worldwide. Learn more at saradavila.com.

Declared 38 years ago, denied since: the Algiers Declaration remains a milestone in the Palestinian struggle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:59:54 UTC
21:59:54 KST

On 15 November, 1988, in Algiers, Yasser Arafat, chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO), stood before the Palestine National Council, the PLO’s parliament-in-exile, and proclaimed the Palestinian Declaration of Independence. Drafted by the celebrated late Palestinian poet Mahmoud Darwish, the text claimed sovereignty over the territories Israel occupied in 1967 – the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem. Some 75 countries recognised the declaration within a month, and more than 90 had done so by early 1989, giving the Palestinian national movement unprecedented diplomatic momentum. Yet nearly four decades later, Palestinian statehood remains unrealised on the ground.
This historic declaration did not emerge in a vacuum but rather after a long fight against Israeli occupation. Two distinct developments forced the Palestinian liberation movement to make such an announcement. First, the eruption of the First Intifada, the popular Palestinian uprising, in December 1987 shifted the political centre of gravity to the occupied territories, compelling the PLO leadership in exile in Tunis to translate popular resistance into a concrete diplomatic platform. It was one of the rare moments in the history of the Palestinian struggle in which those living under brutal occupation forced their own will on their leadership abroad.
Second, King Hussein of Jordan’s formal severance of legal and administrative ties with the West Bank in July 1988 created a vacuum that forced the PLO to assert immediate authority. By making this move in Algiers, the PLO executed a major strategic pivot: invoking UN General Assembly Resolution 181, the 1947 partition plan, alongside UN Security Council Resolutions 242 and 338, it implicitly accepted a two-state framework, trading the historical demand for total liberation for a sovereign state on 22 per cent of historic Palestine.
This major development in the Palestinian struggle had far-reaching diplomatic consequences. First and foremost, it forced the administration of US President Ronald Reagan to open formal talks with the PLO for the very first time. Following the first official session in Tunis in December 1988, the US ambassador to Tunisia, Robert Pelletreau, described the talks as “practical” and marked by a “seriousness of purpose”.
While this dialogue did not immediately translate into official US recognition of the Palestinian right to independence and statehood, it signalled a seismic shift. It demonstrated that the US, as Israel’s primary military, financial and political patron, could no longer ignore the reality on the ground: that the Israeli occupation of Palestinian land was unsustainable, and that maintaining the status quo was both morally indefensible and politically costly.
Though no one expected an immediate breakthrough, opening a direct diplomatic channel with Washington was a major political victory for the PLO – an essential milestone that forced the international community to engage directly with the organisation, ultimately paving the way for Israel’s formal recognition of the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people under the 1993 Oslo Accords.
Yet 38 years after Yasser Arafat read those words in Algiers, no sovereign Palestinian state exists, and the horizon for achieving one seems further away than it ever has been. Israel has steadily fragmented and swallowed up the very land on which that state was proclaimed in 1988. Over nearly four decades, continuous land confiscation, state-sanctioned illegal construction and an ever-expanding infrastructure of military control have systematically carved up the West Bank and East Jerusalem.
READ: Fatah, Hamas set to meet in Cairo next week to resume Palestinian dialogue: Sources
Every day, gangs of private colonisers steal the territory designated for a future Palestinian state – armed, state-backed paramilitary networks often sanitised under the benign label of “settlers”, as though they were peaceful pioneers arriving in a land without a people. What was declared as the foundation of a sovereign nation has instead been trapped in an ongoing process of forced displacement and de facto annexation, rendering the idea of an independent Palestinian state more elusive today than at any point since the Algiers Declaration.
But as dark as the physical reality on the ground remains, the international standing of the Palestinian cause has reached a historic turning point. Three years after the onset of the devastating genocide in Gaza, the world not only possesses a deeper understanding of Palestinian suffering but has also rallied behind its struggle with unprecedented diplomatic and popular support. Western governments that once resisted statehood have been forced to align with global reality; major European powers, including the United Kingdom, France and Spain, have formally recognised the State of Palestine – a diplomatic breakthrough unthinkable just a few years ago.
Even within the United States, Palestine is no longer a distant foreign policy issue quietly buried in diplomatic corridors. As the country heads towards the crucial midterm elections on 3 November, with control of both houses of Congress up for grabs, Palestinian liberation has emerged as a central domestic campaign issue. In states such as Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed, an outspoken advocate of Palestinian rights, won the Democratic Senate nomination in August, pro-Palestine candidates are mounting formidable campaigns for Congress, proving that the call for Palestinian rights has broken through to the highest halls of Western power.
On the legal front, the Palestinian aspiration for liberation has found a powerful parallel in international courts and human rights tribunals, shifting from political declarations to binding accountability. This transformation has gathered pace in recent years: in November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued historic arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, piercing decades of systemic impunity. This followed monumental legal interventions by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
Two decades after its landmark advisory opinion of 9 July, 2004, which declared Israel’s separation wall in the occupied West Bank illegal, the ICJ issued a historic advisory opinion on 19 July, 2024, declaring Israel’s decades-long occupation fundamentally unlawful and demanding that it end as rapidly as possible. Backed by successive UN Human Rights Council reports, an overwhelming UN General Assembly vote to upgrade Palestine’s rights at the UN and a mounting international consensus, international jurisprudence has effectively unmasked the occupation as a criminal enterprise that diplomatic grace can no longer shield.
Thirty-eight years after the late Yasser Arafat stood in Algiers and declared independence, the contrast between the diplomatic vision of 1988 and the brutal reality on the ground could not be starker. Yet the Palestinian cause has broken out of the geopolitical cage that decades of cynical management and Western-backed impunity built for it. Today, unprecedented global solidarity, monumental legal reckonings and a generation refusing erasure confront the physical fragmentation of the land and the relentless theft by armed colonisers. The 1988 declaration was never merely a piece of paper; it was an enduring baseline of national identity and justice. And as the scales of international law and global conscience finally begin to tip, that foundational promise remains unyielding – and its fulfilment inevitable.
