Economic Watch: Smart, green and service-oriented: Canton Fair mirrors new momentum in China's foreign trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:59:37 CST
21:59:37 KST

GUANGZHOU, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The 140th edition of the China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, is showcasing smart, green and service-oriented products, with high-tech, customized and low-carbon debuts drawing global buyers and highlighting new opportunities for Chinese manufacturing.
Logistics robots, drink-making robots and pet-companion robots crowded the intelligent robotics area at the fair, which is being held from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4 in Guangzhou, capital of south China's Guangdong Province.
At the booth of Hangzhou Taixi Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd., buyers lined up to try out a consumer waist-assist exoskeleton. Many overseas buyers held the handrail and shuffled forward, step by step, to feel how the device relieves pressure on their lower limbs.
It is the first flagship product to integrate its human-oriented physical AI technology roadmap, said company founder Liang Linchao. The device uses waist motors and sensors to detect movement and assist lower-limb mobility. Its weight has been cut to about 2 kg, and alongside a refined appearance, algorithms and gait plans tailored to elderly people and hemiplegic patients have been added.
The cluster of cutting-edge smart equipment reflects a broader push toward industrial innovation. At this fair, 64 percent of exhibitors have integrated the industrial internet and artificial intelligence into R&D and production, and new products accounted for 23.2 percent of exhibits, marking a record high.
"At today's Canton Fair, consumer electronics are the dominant category, and tech products such as new energy storage, embodied intelligence and smart healthcare are eye-catching, with many cutting-edge Chinese-made products making their debut," said Zhang Li, an official with the Ministry of Commerce.
Nearby, several European buyers closely watched the scrolling data at DSL Tech Group's booth. The AI-POOL low-chlorine intelligent pool system uses sensor probes to collect the pool's real-time indicators such as residual chlorine, pH level, turbidity and water pressure, and automatically coordinates pumps, disinfection units and sand-filter backwash systems.
Chen Meixiang, the representative of the company, demonstrated on her phone how users can receive alerts about water quality abnormalities from thousands of miles away. The system adjusts automatically, so staff no longer need to visit regularly to take samples and mix chemicals.
"Many overseas private pools used to rely on maintenance workers visiting once a week, and water quality would easily exceed standards," Chen said. These European clients are mainly pool operation and maintenance service providers, attracted by the system's ability to cut manual maintenance costs.
These technology-driven products are also reflected in trade data. Customs statistics show that in the first three quarters of 2026, China's total imports and exports of industrial robots, electronic components, computer parts and electrical equipment exceeded 10 trillion yuan (1.49 trillion U.S. dollars), up 58.9 percent year on year, driving overall import and export growth by 11.3 percentage points.
Liu Chun, president of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, said that driven by technological innovation and industrial upgrading, high-tech and high-value-added products are gradually becoming the main growth engine of foreign trade, pushing "China's smart manufacturing" toward the high end of global industrial and value chains.
This service-oriented approach is visible at the booth of Shandong Linuo Paradigma Co., Ltd., where sales staff explained tailored plans to buyers from different continents.
"Africa lacks power and is windy and dusty, so we cut costs and provide solar water-heating systems that are easy to install and run without electricity," a staff member of the company said. "The Middle East wants high quality, so we match energy-saving products with high-standard certification, and South Asia emphasizes large capacity and durability, so we strengthen system adaptability."
The company has set up agent systems and localized service outlets in markets of Belt and Road partner countries, combining Chinese manufacturing, German-partnered technology and global service into a competitive edge.
Beyond individual products, the latest edition of the Canton Fair also features a batch of prefabricated new products, including space capsules, portable integrated kitchens and modular homestay houses. Chinese suppliers are moving from selling parts to selling whole houses, and integrated overseas expansion is supporting a new growth path.
"By launching prefabricated building solutions for cultural tourism camps, we have attracted buyers from Australia, Brazil, and Saudi Arabia among other countries, and more than 300 have reached preliminary agreements. We will continue to use project meetings to deliver full-chain services from planning to design, construction and operation," said Jia Xuehong, planning and design director of Chongqing SUNDON Prefabricated Construction and Technology Co., Ltd.
More and more foreign trade companies are shifting from simply taking orders and shipping goods to building systems and exporting supporting services. At the fair, 36.5 percent of exhibitors have started a transformation of "product plus service."
For the first time, the trade services zone covers all 10 major categories of producer services, including logistics and warehousing, industrial design, overseas operation and maintenance, cross-border investment and financing and other supporting services, building a one-stop support platform for companies expanding overseas.
Yang Jie, secretary-general of the Guangdong Industrial Design Association, said that under an industrial design and R&D approach that runs through the whole life cycle and centers on consumer pain points, more and more Chinese companies are winning favor in more markets by integrating design into the early stages of development and coordinating it with technology to deliver innovative products and solutions.
Green products are another highlight. Amid the global energy transition, green products and low-carbon technologies have become highly sought-after in international markets. At the fair, exhibitor Xiamen HiTHIUM Energy Storage Technology focused on showcasing its flagship long-duration energy storage products, presenting stable and reliable long-duration power supply solutions to overseas buyers.
Wang Pengcheng, co-founder and CEO of the company, said more and more countries and regions are advancing energy structure transition, and the company hopes that through the Canton Fair, the "Chinese solution" for long-duration energy storage can be seen by the world, so that more countries have the option of using stable, green and affordable clean power.
China is enriching global supply with quality green and smart products and helping accelerate the global green, low-carbon and digital and intelligent transition. Over the past decade, China has provided more than 80 percent of the world's photovoltaic modules and 70 percent of its wind power equipment, effectively driving down the cost of global wind and solar power generation.
Commenting on the trend, Liang Yutian, associate dean of the Institute of International and Regional Studies, Sun Yat-sen University, said the concentrated display of new energy, energy storage equipment, green home appliances and other products reflects the global green transition forming new market demand. In the future, around the digital economy, green energy, smart manufacturing and low-carbon technologies, countries can further strengthen technological cooperation, industrial coordination and standards alignment to cultivate new international growth points.
From continuous breakthroughs in hard technology to complete solutions stepping into the spotlight, and green thinking embedded in products, the innovation vitality surging at the Canton Fair illustrates how China's foreign trade keeps cultivating new advantages and deepening its links with the world. ■

Qatar denied the allegations that it interfered in Israel's elections or funded efforts to influence the results, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said on Thursday, accusing Israeli politicians and media figures of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," al-Ansari wrote.
Al-Ansari accused “certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media” of attempting to draw Qatar into Israel's domestic political disputes following the elections.
He argued that successive allegations had portrayed Doha as financially supporting opposing sides of the Israeli political spectrum, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the political left, and Arab voters.
"If these claims were to be believed, Qatar would apparently own all of Israel," he wrote.
'Qatar not scapegoat for political failures'
"These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure. Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians," he wrote.
He urged those making the accusations to focus instead on their voters, improving living conditions and addressing the consequences of their policies in the region.
Al-Ansari reiterated that Qatar does not participate in Israeli electoral politics and would reject attempts to involve the country in Israel's internal disputes.
"We reiterate that we have no involvement in Israel’s political or electoral competition," he wrote.
"These are internal Israeli matters in which we do not interfere, and we will not accept any attempt to draw Qatar into its domestic political disputes."
Incoming government should 'engage seriously with Palestinian issue'
The Qatari spokesperson also said any incoming government must engage seriously with the Palestinian issue and recognize Palestinian national rights, including the establishment of an independent Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967, lines, with east Jerusalem as its capital.
Al-Ansari stressed that Qatar would continue its diplomatic and humanitarian activities despite the allegations, including its involvement in regional mediation efforts and its support for the Palestinian people.
"We will not remain silent while Qatar’s name is exploited to serve electoral agendas or narrow political interests," he concluded.

African health ministers urge enhanced readiness, solidarity as Ebola outbreak escalates
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:59:26 CST
21:59:26 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- African health ministers on Wednesday joined the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO) for an emergency meeting, calling for enhanced continental preparedness and greater solidarity to contain the expanding multi-country Ebola outbreak.
The virtual meeting on Ebola was held amid the rapid geographical spread of the ongoing outbreak of the Bundibugyo Ebola strain. The outbreak has surpassed 10,170 confirmed cases with a mounting death toll, with four African countries affected so far, namely the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria.
Addressing the emergency meeting, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya said the Ebola outbreak has, over the past five months, grown from a national crisis into a continental health security test.
Emphasizing that "the main priority today in our continent is to stop Ebola," he stressed insecurity, complex humanitarian situations, a lack of medical countermeasures, and limited funding are compounding the crisis.
Kaseya said that the confirmed cases in the outbreaks have reached 10,172, with more than 4,932 deaths and a case fatality rate of 48.5 percent. Some 2,727 patients have recovered from the disease.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a message delivered on his behalf, stressed that "we are still facing an extremely serious and difficult outbreak."
"This outbreak in the DRC is not a single outbreak in a single place. It is many outbreaks across a vast and complex area, requiring a sustained response everywhere at the same time," he said.
He noted that recent measures taken by authorities in Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria demonstrate the continent's capacity to manage outbreaks when detected early and met with rapid responses.
Describing Kenya's response to the outbreak as a "whole-of-government and whole-of-society" approach, Patrick Amoth, director-general for health in Kenya's Ministry of Health, stressed that the country's experience also points to gaps Africa must close.
He highlighted health workforce infections, the cross-border spread of cases bypassing surveillance and contact tracing, and Africa's reliance on uncertain donated medicines amid a lack of licensed vaccines or specific therapeutics as critical gaps.
He stressed that Kenya will keep travel and trade open and will not impose restrictions beyond what international health regulations and evidence require. He further noted that the country will share data, sequences, and lessons openly.
Echoing the sentiment, Ugandan Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi noted that the country's experience shows that transmission can be interrupted when countries act early and decisively.
"Uganda was affected by this outbreak and was able to interrupt transmission within our borders," he said. "Our experience should give us hope, but should also give us a sense of responsibility."
He noted that the outbreak's international dimension requires sustained attention. "The lesson is straightforward: when a public health emergency threatens several countries, our response must also become regional and continental."
Beyond the four affected nations, 10 other countries across Africa have previously been designated as high-risk, namely South Sudan, Rwanda, Zambia, the Central African Republic, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Somalia. ■

Across China: Water-skimming motorcycle stunt puts rural county on tourist map
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:59:19 CST
21:59:19 KST

CHANGSHA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A water-skimming stunt challenge has turned a rural Chinese county into an unlikely destination for tourists and motorcycle fans, drawing nearly as many visitors during the event as its entire population.
Mayang, a county with 274,000 permanent residents in central China's Hunan Province, received 250,000 tourist arrivals when Zhang Xue rode a custom-built motorcycle across the Jinjiang River on Sunday, the latest stage in a 17-year effort to master the water.
Zhang, 39, rode 40.74 km across the river. The run, which included seven consecutive U-turns, was certified by Guinness World Records as the longest distance traveled by a modified motorcycle on open water.
In 2009, he tried to ride across the water on a rudimentary modified motorcycle and fell into the river four times, reaching no more than 20 meters.
Zhang said he never lost faith in the project, even when failure seemed routine. "Even if I failed, I would have no regrets. I enjoy the process."
Today, Zhang is better known as the founder of ZXMOTO, the motorcycle manufacturer he established in Chongqing in 2024. Its French rider Valentin Debise ended the 2026 World Supersport season as runner-up in the riders' standings, while the company finished third in the manufacturers' championship in its debut year.
The motorcycle used in Mayang, the MX450, was built on a standard frame and powertrain, and fitted with an amphibious skimming kit. A front steering sled acted as a water rudder, while the rear wheel's deep-tread tire was partially submerged in the river, generating thrust to propel the bike forward. The bike had to maintain sufficient speed to stay on the surface, making U-turns particularly risky.
"The challenge was not only technical but physical," said Deng Liansong, a research and development engineer at ZXMOTO.
Guinness World Records adjudicator Xiong Wen, who witnessed the attempt in Mayang, said the significance of the event went beyond the numbers. "It is inspiring to see one person's passion for motorcycles persist for so many years and finally be recognized by more people," she said.
Videos of the run spread quickly on Chinese short-video platforms, where related hashtags accumulated more than 2.3 billion views. Local officials said traffic at Mayang's highway toll stations rose about 21 percent as visitors arrived from other parts of Hunan, as well as from Guangdong and Chongqing.
Zhao Yazhou, a motorcycle fan from Zhengzhou in central China's Henan Province, drove 11 hours to watch the challenge. He said the experience felt far more powerful in person than on a screen.
During the event period, the county generated 125 million yuan (about 18.76 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue, according to Tian Haishan, deputy director of Mayang County's bureau of culture, tourism, radio and television. On the day of the challenge, around 80,000 people were present, he added.
Tian described the event as a high-profile example of rural cultural tourism breaking into mainstream attention. "Zhang's extreme challenge in his hometown was not just the birth of a Guinness record," he said. "It helped bring Mayang into the national spotlight."
Zhang, recently appointed as a cultural tourism ambassador for Huaihua City, used the event to promote iconic products from his home county of Mayang, which is administered by Huaihua City. His bike carried branding for Mayang's traditional brown sugar, as well as symbols of rock sugar oranges and dragon boats.
Exposure from his Superbike World Championship appearance in March helped sell out a year's inventory of the brown sugar in three days, Tian said.
Zhang said his resilience was shaped by the place where he grew up. "Different regional cultures influence a person's character," Zhang said. "My unyielding nature comes from this land. I chose to fulfill my dream here so that my hometown could be seen by the world." ■

Israel's communications law suspended as High Court examines legal challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:59:17 UTC
21:59:17 KST

The government must explain why the Broadcasting Law it passed this year should not be canceled following allegations of legislative defects, the High Court of Justice decided Thursday.
The conditional order issued gives the government and the relevant ministers and committees until January 7, 2027, to file responses.
The hearing will be before an expanded panel of nine justices.
Attorney Yaniv Goldberg, head of the Economic Division at the Movement for Quality Government in Israel, highlighted the court's reasoning behind the freeze.
"The communications minister can announce that he will not cooperate with the proceedings, but he cannot exempt himself from the rule of law. The High Court of Justice is now demanding answers to allegations of flaws in the legislative process through which the law was advanced, while suspending its entry into force," he said.
"This is an important step forward in the petitions, including the Movement's petition, against a law that changes the rules of the game in the communications market.
"A proper legislative process is intended to ensure that decisions affecting the information available to every citizen are made transparently, following professional review and genuine debate. We will continue working to overturn the law and protect media independence and the public's right to receive information free from political control."
High Court suspends Israeli communications law
This comes after the law has been frozen multiple times.
Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara asked the High Court of Justice in September to freeze the Broadcasting Law until it rules on 11 petitions challenging it.
Serious failures throughout the legislative process make the petitions exceptionally strong, the court said.
Baharav-Miara told the court that key parts of the reform reached the Knesset without the required professional review and were pushed through a committee effectively controlled by Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi.
She said the law could now trigger business and ownership changes that would be difficult to reverse if the court later strikes it down.
In July, the court temporarily froze the provisions of the broadcasting reform that were meant to take effect that summer.
Notably, most of the reform is scheduled to enter into force two years after the law’s publication.
Under the law, the search committee would be chaired by the Communications Ministry director-general and include representatives of the Regulatory Authority, Finance Ministry, and Competition Authority, as well as an academic representative.
It would recommend candidates for six public positions on the new nine-member regulatory council, who would then be appointed by the communications minister. The council’s three remaining members would be civil servants representing the Communications Ministry and the relevant government regulators.
The Knesset passed the law by a 53-48 vote in July, completing one of Karhi’s central legislative initiatives shortly before the Knesset’s dissolution.

From commitments to action: Taiwan and the world creating climate solutions together - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:59:16 UTC
21:59:16 KST

In 2026, extreme heat continued to sweep across the globe, with historically high temperatures occurring in many regions. Western Europe experienced its hottest June on record. These temperatures intensified drought and wildfires and put pressure on water resources.
This disrupted public health, energy supplies, and economic activity. Taiwan has likewise faced climate risks including extreme heat, heavy rainfall, and typhoons. Climate change has become a shared challenge with profound implications for social stability, industrial development, and national resilience.
Against this backdrop, global climate governance is moving beyond the formulation of targets and commitments toward concrete implementation. At this year’s COP31 meeting, participants will emphasize the principles of dialogue, consensus, and action while working to turn commitments into concrete, trackable results.
Even though Taiwan is not a party to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it continues to work on climate governance in the spirit of the Paris Agreement.
Having submitted its 2035 nationally determined contributions in 2025, Taiwan is now translating its emissions-reduction targets into action by many government agencies to reach a green industrial transition, resource circulation, climate adaptation, and a just transition. It is also collaborating with international partners to develop practical solutions.
Aligning with international norms while achieving concrete emissions reductions through transparent governance
Article 4 of the Paris Agreement calls on parties to progressively strengthen mitigation plans and reach nationally determined contributions.
The enhanced transparency framework laid out in Article 13 calls for consistent, trackable information to assess progress on climate actions. Aligning with these international norms, Taiwan this year formally approved its third-phase greenhouse gas reduction action programs for six sectors, covering the years 2026-2030.
These programs address energy, manufacturing, residential and commercial buildings, transportation, agriculture, and the environment, incorporating 20 flagship mitigation action plans, annual emissions targets, and 63 performance indicators. They further embed national mitigation goals into sectoral policies and allow for annual monitoring and evaluation.
Taiwan’s latest national greenhouse gas inventory also shows that net greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 were 6.59% below 2005 levels and demonstrated a decline for the third consecutive year. Over the same period, real GDP continued to grow, even as carbon dioxide emission density fell 48.59%. This indicates a gradual decoupling of economic growth from carbon emissions.
As concerns transparency, Taiwan follows recommended frameworks set by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement. It regularly publishes related documents, including nationally determined contributions, biennial transparency reports, and national inventory reports, matching international practice.
Through clear mitigation pathways, sectoral action, and transparent information, Taiwan will continue to assess its progress and turn climate commitments into measurable, trackable outcomes.
Pursuing net-zero and zero waste to enhance industrial competitiveness during the green transition
To accelerate the green industrial transition, Taiwan began collecting carbon fees this year, part of its effort to make carbon pricing a key policy instrument for the decarbonization of industry.
The collection system is linked to voluntary reduction plans and preferential rates that encourage companies to incorporate emissions reductions into their investment and operational decisions.
In the first year of collection, the carbon fee has thus far generated NT$ 4.97 billion ($154.5 million) in revenue, which goes to the Greenhouse Gas Management Fund, a dedicated fund for greenhouse gas reduction and climate change adaptation efforts. The fund offers loan credit guarantees and interest subsidies to optimize operations.
Meanwhile, the Regulations Governing Subsidies for Greenhouse Gas Reduction Technologies and Climate Change Adaptation were promulgated to support reduction technologies and adaptation measures.
Through such diverse instruments as subsidies, financing, and risk sharing, Taiwan’s framework will introduce more private capital in support of the net-zero transition.
During the next stage, a cap-and-trade system will be progressively developed. This will be called the Taiwan Emissions Trading System (TW-ETS) and will move toward a diversified carbon pricing framework in which the carbon fee and the ETS operate in parallel.
The United Kingdom recently listed Taiwan’s carbon fee as a qualifying carbon pricing scheme under its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
This will permit eligible Taiwanese products to claim carbon-price deductions in accordance with applicable rules, marking an important step in building links between Taiwan’s carbon pricing framework and international systems.
The industrial net-zero transition must extend beyond energy and carbon management to address the way resources are used.
This year, Taiwan completed amendments to the Resource Circulation Promotion Act and the Waste Disposal Act, shifting management efforts from end-of-pipe treatment toward governance across the entire product life cycle. The government has identified eight major aspects of the circular economy: food, plastics, textiles, health, construction, electronics, inorganic resources, and circular industries. At present, there are 69 publicly listed companies in the circular economy sector, which generates over NT$ 1 trillion (30b.) in total annual revenue.
This shows that the circular economy is progressively taking shape as a green industry of scale.
Taiwan continues to promote digital product passports, source plastic reduction, and reuse. Through legislation, industrial collaboration, and digital innovation, Taiwan aims to accelerate resource circulation and zero waste, reduce its reliance on virgin resources, and lower its carbon burdens.
This will enhance resource security, supply chain resilience, and green competitiveness.
Strengthening climate resilience and integrating adaptation into national planning and everyday life
Article 7 of the Paris Agreement sets out a global goal to enhance adaptive capacity, strengthen resilience, and reduce vulnerability to climate change. At COP30, participants adopted the Belém Adaptation Indicators to further advance the global goal on adaptation toward measurable and trackable action.
Taiwan continues to align with international adaptation efforts by integrating climate risk assessments into national and local governance and bolstering resilience to climate events like extreme heat and torrential rainfall.
In response to a growing heat risk, Taiwan this year used a 40° Celsius extreme-heat scenario to advance cross-ministerial adaptation strategies, strengthening preparedness and coordination for public health, energy, transportation, occupational safety, and support for vulnerable groups.
Furthermore, on the instructions of President Lai Ching-te, Taiwan established the national-level Urban Forest Promotion Committee to advance the National Green Canopy Program.
This initiative makes urban forestry an element of national resilience infrastructure and integrates lidar remote sensing, 3D digital twin technology, and microclimate data to accurately identify heat hot spots and shading gaps, thereby creating a resilient terrestrial green network that balances climate adaptation with public health.
Taiwan will draft an urban forests act that will promote professional certification for protecting trees while advancing the high-value circularity of wood.
By guiding corporate ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) resources and encouraging community adoption, Taiwan will launch local demonstration zones, bringing to bear private sector expertise and emerging technologies to enhance urban resilience against extreme climate events and natural disasters.
Realizing a just transition and mobilizing society for net-zero
The preamble to the Paris Agreement emphasizes the need to take into account the imperatives of a just transition of the workforce and the creation of decent work and quality jobs.
In recent years, the UNFCCC has furthered discussions on energy, industry, labor, and the social dimensions of the transition.
At COP30, participants advanced mechanisms related to a just transition, strengthening international cooperation, technical assistance, capacity building, and knowledge sharing so that the needs and development opportunities of different groups could be addressed during the net-zero transition.
Taiwan has made leaving no one behind a core principle of its net-zero transition, and established a basis for governance that addresses a just transition via the Climate Change Response Act.
To realize a just transition while implementing carbon reduction policies, Taiwan this year is conducting stakeholder consultations across six major sectors – energy, manufacturing, residential and commercial buildings, transportation, agriculture, and environment.
By gathering a wide scope of public opinion and having each sector review and respond to this feedback, cross-ministerial collaboration is being improved.
Subsequently, Taiwan will synthesize sectoral policies to draft a nationwide just transition action plan, crafting a national-level policy framework for a just transition and ensuring that social participation remains a vital component of net-zero policy planning and execution.
This year, Taiwan used the Greenhouse Gas Management Fund to integrate cross-sectoral capacities and support workers, industries, regions, and groups affected by the transition.
This will help advance green-collar talent development, the low-carbon transition of small and medium-sized enterprises, vulnerable groups, local participation, and transition governance.
Enhancing global partnerships to jointly craft climate solutions
Article 6 of the Paris Agreement encourages voluntary cooperation to enable higher ambition for climate action while promoting sustainable development on the basis of environmental integrity, transparency, and the avoidance of double counting.
As relevant arrangements move into the stage of implementation, international climate cooperation is expanding from policy dialogue to mitigation projects, technology cooperation, capacity building, and investment, which are important pathways for accelerating implementation of the Paris Agreement.
Taiwan is moving forward with climate diplomacy through pragmatic action. Last year, Taiwan signed a memorandum of understanding on Paris Agreement cooperation with its diplomatic ally Paraguay.
Today, the two countries are advancing 12 action plans for environmental governance, thereby implementing global climate action and substantive environmental cooperation through sharing technology and engaging in youth dialogue and exchanges on the circular economy.
As global climate governance enters a critical phase focused on practice and outcomes, Taiwan will continue to deepen global partnerships through pragmatic engagement, making concrete contributions, and sharing its experience with the net-zero transition.
Taiwan seeks international support for its meaningful participation in the UNFCCC and global climate governance efforts.
It firmly believes that achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement requires the participation of every partner with the capacity and willingness to act.
Taiwan is ready to collaborate with other nations to transform climate commitments into action and together build a more resilient, sustainable net-zero future.
The writer is the Taiwanese environment minister.

Ukraine's parliament calls on world not to recognize Russia's State Duma 'elections'

Unknown Publisher

Ukraine's parliament calls on world not to recognize Russia's State Duma 'elections'
According to an Ukrinform correspondent, 250 members of parliament voted in favor of the draft resolution, No. 16091.
"The purpose of the draft resolution is to clearly and unequivocally establish the position of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine that the elections of deputies to the ninth convocation of the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation, and the composition of the State Duma formed as a result, lack democratic and political legitimacy," the explanatory note to the draft resolution states.
Under the resolution, the Verkhovna Rada appealed to the United Nations, the European Parliament, parliamentary assemblies and governments around the world, calling on them, in particular, not to recognize the legitimacy of the Russian State Duma elections or their results; not to treat the ninth-convocation State Duma as a legitimate democratic basis for confirming the representative character of the Russian authorities; and not to recognize the credentials of newly formed Russian parliamentary delegations.
The appeal also emphasizes that the electoral process in Russia took place amid the systematic shrinking of political space, persecution of opposition politicians, and restrictions on freedom of speech and the activities of independent media and civil society.
"A separate and fundamentally important violation of international law was the Russian Federation's holding of elections to its own state authority in temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. The Russian Federation has no right under international law to extend its own 'electoral process' to the territory of the sovereign state of Ukraine or to use the results of such voting to form its state authorities," the resolution states.
As Ukrinform reported, Russia included the Ukrainian-controlled cities of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk and Sviatohirsk in the Donetsk region in one of its electoral districts so that local residents could vote in the "elections" to the State Duma.
The elections to the ninth convocation of the State Duma of the Russian Federation were held from September 18 to 20, 2026.

Estonia plans to construct 150 bunkers along its northeastern border with Russia’s Leningrad region as part of a broader Baltic defense initiative, the public broadcaster ERR reported Wednesday.
“One hundred of them will be on state land, and around 50 on municipal or private land,” Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem reportedly told lawmakers.
Herem said the government is negotiating agreements with private landowners in the northeastern county of Ida-Viru, with options ranging from compensation to long-term leases and direct property buyouts.
The installations will form the so-called Baltic Defense Line, an agreement that Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania announced in 2024 to build a series of bunkers along their borders with Russia and Belarus to defend against potential attacks.
Earlier this month, the Financial Times reported that Estonia, a nation of 1.3 million people, had pivoted toward an “active defense” strategy after studying Russia’s military tactics in Ukraine.
Under the updated doctrine, Estonia has been relocating primary combat units to towns along the border with the Leningrad region. In Narva, construction is underway for facilities that can house up to 1,000 soldiers during a crisis situation.
Kremlin officials have downplayed the Estonian troop movements near the border while asserting that Russian intelligence maintains full surveillance over NATO deployments along the frontier.

Monumental building, silver coins discovered at medieval city Rusokastro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:56:13 UTC
21:56:13 KST

Monumental building, silver coins discovered at medieval city Rusokastro
Thursday 29 October 2026 13:09
Thursday, 29 October 2026, 13:09
PHOTO Regional History Museum in Burgas
Font size
A monumental building, 7.60 metres wide and of still unknown length, has been uncovered near the inner southern fortress wall. It is the latest archaeological discovery of the year made by archaeologists from Burgas at the medieval city of Rusokastro, the Regional Historical Museum in Burgas (RIM-Burgas) has announced.
The walls are 1.1 metres thick and built of stone bonded with abundant mortar. The inner surfaces of the building’s walls are heavily coated with pink waterproof mortar. This suggests that the structure was used as a water reservoir or a storehouse for food supplies. It most likely represents the ground floor of a building located in the city’s central quarter, with a second, residential floor presumed to have stood above it.
A large number of portable archaeological finds have also been unearthed, including silver coins minted under Bulgarian Tsar Ivan Alexander, Venetian silver grosso coins known as matapanes, copper coins and many other artefacts. These are now being cleaned in the restoration workshop of the Burgas museum.
Rusokastro is included on the list of priority national sites receiving state funding to support cultural tourism in Bulgaria.

A Greek-owned container ship chartered by Israeli shipping company ZIM sank in the Black Sea after being struck by unmanned surface vessels off the coast of Bulgaria on Wednesday, Bulgarian authorities said, in the latest attack on commercial shipping amid growing concerns over the spillover effects of the Russia-Ukraine war.
The Liberian-flagged CONTSHIP JET was carrying 421 shipping containers from Haifa's Gulf Port in Israel to the Romanian port of Constanța when it was attacked while passing through Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, outside the country's territorial waters.
All 18 crew members, including 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians, were rescued and safely transported to the Bulgarian port of Varna.
The Bulgarian government said it had received advance warning of the attack, believed to be connected to the war between Russia and Ukraine, but was unable to prevent it.
Footage published by a Bulgarian news website showed one of the unmanned surface vessels approaching the container ship moments before impact.
The ship sustained severe damage in the attack and subsequently sank, according to Bulgarian authorities.
The identity of those responsible remains unclear. Initial assessments suggest the vessel was not targeted because of its connection to Israel, although investigators have yet to establish a motive.
The incident has heightened concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in the western Black Sea, where attacks involving aerial and maritime drones have become increasingly frequent.
At least six vessels have been attacked by aerial or unmanned surface drones off Bulgaria's coast this month, leaving approximately 25 people dead, according to reports. The attacks have raised fears that the conflict between Russia and Ukraine is increasingly threatening shipping routes beyond the immediate war zone.
ZIM confirmed that the damaged vessel was chartered by the company but was not part of its owned fleet.
"A small container ship carrying a limited number of containers, which ZIM charters but does not own, was struck by an unmanned surface vessel in the Black Sea," the company said in a statement.
"All crew members were safely evacuated, and the expected financial damage, according to a preliminary assessment, is minimal."
The company said it was working to secure a replacement vessel and maintain service to its customers.
"To the best of our knowledge, several similar incidents involving vessels in the area have occurred over the past month," ZIM added.
Oren Caspi, chairman of ZIM's workers' union, said the attack underscored the importance of maintaining Israeli control over the shipping company amid growing geopolitical instability.
"In a reality of boycotts and security threats, in a world of political instability, we must keep ZIM Israeli," Caspi said.
"Much remains unknown about this extraordinary attack, and we are still learning the details."
Although Bulgaria does not share a land border with Russia or Ukraine, its position on the western Black Sea places it along important commercial shipping routes connecting the region to major Russian and Ukrainian ports.
The Black Sea has become a key theater of the Russia-Ukraine war, with unmanned aerial vehicles and explosive-laden maritime drones increasingly used in attacks on naval and maritime targets.
Such incidents have become more frequent in recent months, affecting Eastern European countries and shipping corridors previously considered relatively secure.
At least 45 merchant vessels have been attacked over the past 12 months in parts of the Black Sea that had not previously been classified as high-risk areas, according to figures cited in the report.
The latest sinking highlights the growing risks facing civilian shipping in the region, where commercial vessels continue to operate amid an expanding threat from unmanned weapons.
While there is no indication that the CONTSHIP JET was targeted because of its Israeli commercial connection, the attack adds to concerns among shipping operators about the safety of Black Sea routes and the potential for further disruption to international trade.

​Pragmatic or pointless? Europe’s rift over whether to pick up the phone to Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:55:22 UTC
21:55:22 KST

The Nordic countries rarely fall out in public over foreign policy, least of all over Russia.
But a 90-minute phone call this week to Vladimir Putin by the leaders of Finland and Norway drew an unusual rebuke from their Danish and Swedish neighbours.
On Tuesday, Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, spoke with Putin, in a rare high-level conversation between the Russian leader and Ukraine’s European allies. The two Nordic leaders stressed that the call had been conducted on Ukraine’s behalf and that allies had been informed in advance.
Their neighbours were not convinced.
“I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland,” said Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, who complained that the call had not been coordinated with Copenhagen. “I honestly don’t know what they think they can achieve by this.”
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, also criticised the initiative, saying he had not been informed beforehand.
The friction offered a glimpse of the divisions threatening to complicate Europe’s attempts to establish its own channel to Moscow, as governments struggle to agree not only on whether to engage Putin but also on who should speak on their behalf.
“Instead of looking like a firmly united, homogeneous group, we see a rift,” said Arkady Moshes, director of the Russia programme at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. “By the standards of the Nordic world, it’s pretty serious.”
Since the summer, European leaders have been discussing, without much progress, whether to appoint a representative to negotiate directly with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine. The debate has grown more urgent as Donald Trump has moved closer to Moscow in recent weeks at Ukraine’s expense.
A new round of peace talks is expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month, leaving European governments anxious about being sidelined in negotiations that could shape the continent’s security for decades.
“There is an agreement overall that we need to talk to Putin, but the outreach is starting to feel like a free-for-all,” said a senior European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity. “Too many leaders believe they can be the one to get Putin to negotiate.”
Mixed messages
This year, British, French and German ambassadors have held talks with Russian officials, Emmanuel Macron’s senior diplomatic adviser has travelled to Moscow, and the office of the European Council president, António Costa, has pursued its own engagement with the Kremlin.
It is a far cry from the diplomatic isolation imposed on Putin after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when most European leaders largely shunned direct contact with the Kremlin. Stubb himself said during his 2024 presidential campaign that he would not pick up the phone if Putin called.
Analysts this week blamed some of the fallout from the Stubb/Støre call on mixed messages about what it was actually for. Initially framed as an effort to convey Ukrainian messages to Putin, the call appeared to have broader aims.
Støre later defended Norway’s decision to engage directly with Putin, citing the need to manage shared fish stocks in the Barents Sea and maintain security along the countries’ common border. Stubb, meanwhile, said the conversation was also intended to prevent misunderstandings between Russia and its Nordic neighbours.
“Stubb and Støre can’t seem to get their message straight on whether this was about Ukraine or also about their own security concerns,” said Joel Linnainmäki, a former Finnish diplomat and analyst in Helsinki.
“If it looks messy, it probably is.”
The confusion reflects a wider disagreement across Europe over how to approach Putin, even as governments remain broadly united in their support for Ukraine.
“On substance there is actually quite a good level of unity in Europe, but then there are different views on how to approach Russia, when is the right time to reopen dialogue at the highest level and who should be doing it,” said Kristi Raik, director of ICDS, a leading Estonian thinktank.
France has long advocated keeping a channel to Putin open, while Germany and Britain have been more cautious. The Baltic states and Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, fear that renewed high-level engagement could ease pressure on Moscow without securing concessions.
The question of who should lead any European outreach has proved contentious.
Xavier Bettel, Luxembourg’s foreign minister and one of the few European leaders to have maintained telephone contact with Putin after the full-scale invasion, recalled facing criticism from European colleagues for taking the initiative.
“Some colleagues told me: who is the Luxembourgish prime minister to speak to the president of Russia and the president of Ukraine? You are such a small country,” he said at a conference in Prague in May.
“That’s also a problem of the state of mind of some countries who think only France, Germany or the USA can lead discussions.”
No single EU representative
For now, no single figure has a clear mandate to negotiate on behalf of the EU’s 27 member states.
In theory, the task of speaking to Moscow could fall to Kallas. But she lacks the independent authority to negotiate on behalf of the bloc without a mandate from its member states, and there has been growing frustration in European capitals over the EU’s diplomatic service, which she leads.
Kallas, a former Estonian prime minister and one of the EU’s most vehement Kremlin critics, is also seen by many as an unlikely interlocutor for Putin. Moscow has placed her on a wanted list, while Russian officials have made clear they have little appetite for engaging with her.
Reinier van Lanschot, a Dutch member of the European parliament, has called on EU leaders to convene a summit and agree on a single representative to engage with Putin.
He said: “The EU must speak with one voice, and Ukraine must always be involved. If you take those two things into account, then I think it makes perfect sense for Europe to engage in talks.”
But he acknowledged that reaching a unanimous agreement would be difficult, with any proposed appointment potentially vulnerable to a veto by a single member state.
In the meantime, this week’s Nordic initiative could encourage more European politicians to establish their own channels to Moscow, said Linnainmäki.
“It’s inevitable that politicians around Europe will now raise the question: if the Finns and Norwegians are calling Putin, why should our country not do it?” he said.
‘Putin’s plan A’
Beyond the question of who should speak to Putin lies a more basic question: whether there is any point in Europe talking to him at all.
Raik warned that Putin might interpret Europe’s sudden interest in reopening dialogue as a sign that Ukraine and its allies were growing desperate, with Kyiv facing a difficult winter.
“My concern is that the way the Kremlin is reading this step now is that the Europeans are in trouble, the Ukrainians are in trouble,” she said. “Knowing how Putin looks at Europe, I think he’s always keen to try to use opportunities to create divisions, or at least appearances of division,.”
The Kremlin’s account of Tuesday’s conversation offered little indication of any change in Putin’s maximalist demands for ending the war.
According to the Financial Times, Putin spent part of the conversation lecturing the Nordic leaders on medieval Slavic history, repeating pseudo-historical arguments that have long been used to question Ukraine’s right to exist as an independent state.
Still, Moscow has appeared more willing to entertain European involvement in diplomacy since US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg last week.
Moshes suggested that Moscow was tiring of Trump’s unpredictability and looking to Europe as an alternative, calculating that the US midterms could leave the president politically weakened.
But Putin’s willingness to take the call should not be mistaken for a readiness to compromise, Moshes cautioned.
“It doesn’t mean we are moving anywhere towards a ceasefire, let alone peace, because it’s clear that Putin’s plan A is a military defeat of Ukraine.”
Shaun Walker contributed reporting

Ukraine National Bank cuts forecast: GDP to drop 0.4% in 2026 with 12.5% inflation, rise 0.4% in 2027 with 7.3% inflation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:54:41 EET
21:54:41 KST

The National Bank of Ukraine has substantially downgraded its forecast for gross domestic product (GDP), shifting from expectations of growth of 1.8% this year and 2.8% next year to a projected contraction of 0.4% this year, followed by a recovery of just 0.4% next year.
"According to the NBU's estimates, real GDP decreased by 0.5% y-o-y in Q3. Such dynamics were driven primarily by the consequences of the sea port blockade and Russia's attacks on production facilities and logistics. Metallurgical and ore mining enterprises suffered the greatest losses. At the same time, performance also deteriorated in other industrial sectors, trade, and agriculture," the NBU said in a press release on Thursday.
The central bank specified that the consequences of the intensification of shelling had the greatest impact on the downgrade to this year's forecast, with their negative contribution to GDP estimated at 1.9 percentage points (pp).
According to the NBU, economic activity is expected to recover next year, supported in particular by public and private investment in the defense industry, the localization of weapons production financed through the Ukraine Support Loan, and projects to restore critical infrastructure.
"If the NBU's technical assumption about the improvement in logistics in mid-2027 materializes, real GDP may grow by 0.4% next year. In 2028, economic growth will speed up to 2.2% as security risks subside," the press release said.
The nominal GDP estimate for this year has been lowered to UAH 10.01 trillion from UAH 10.065 trillion, and for next year to UAH 11.135 trillion from UAH 11.22 trillion.
As for inflation, the forecast for 2026 has been raised to 12.5% from 10.0%. According to the NBU's estimates, the consequences of shelling alone will add around 0.7 pp to annual inflation. Other important factors affecting price trends will include the effects of higher fuel prices and expanded fiscal stimulus.
The National Bank recalled that headline inflation accelerated to 10.0% year-on-year in September, while core inflation rose to 8.8%. According to the NBU's estimates, these trends continued in October. Inflation dynamics were driven primarily by the direct and indirect effects of higher fuel prices resulting from the war in the Middle East, as well as the intensification of Russian attacks on Ukraine's warehousing and logistics infrastructure. Under these conditions, inflation expectations among the public remained volatile and elevated, while those of banks and analysts deteriorated markedly.
According to the NBU's forecast, inflation will slow to 7.3% in 2027. This is expected to be supported by a projected decline in global oil prices, monetary policy measures, and a likely cooling of domestic demand and the labor market in the coming months as a result of Russian attacks.
"As before, inflation is expected to return to the 5% target in 2028. A gradual easing of the pressure on businesses' production costs and an increase in domestic supply of goods and services are important preconditions for this," the press release said.
As reported, leading investment companies have substantially downgraded their macroeconomic forecasts in recent weeks. Dragon Capital, for example, now expects Ukraine's GDP to decline by 0.5% in 2026 and by 1% in 2027, whereas before the escalation of the war in July, it had forecast growth of 1.5% and 0.5%, respectively.
Investment group ICU, which in June lowered its forecast for real GDP growth in Ukraine in 2026 to 0.8% from 1.2%, now expects GDP to contract by 0.6% this year and by 1.9% next year.
Investment company Concorde Capital forecasts a 1% contraction in Ukraine's GDP in 2026 and expects it to decline further next year.
In its October macroeconomic review, the KSE Institute lowered its forecast for Ukraine's real GDP in 2026 from growth of 1.9% to a contraction of 0.3%, and for 2027 from growth of 2.1% to a contraction of 0.6%, citing intensified Russian attacks on critical infrastructure and production facilities.
In early October, the World Bank forecast that Ukraine's GDP growth would slow to 1.2% in 2026 from 1.8% in 2025, before accelerating to 1.5% in 2027. It lowered its forecast for next year from 4%.
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), citing Russian strikes on ports and vessels in the Black Sea, lowered its forecast for Ukraine's real GDP growth in 2026 to 1.5% from 2.2%, and for 2027 to 2.5% from 4%.

HMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:54:18 UTC
21:54:18 KST

The UK’s tax authority is assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires as part of a crackdown meant to raise £500m for the public purse.
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) said it had for the first time compiled a list of billionaires who are required to pay tax in the UK, regardless of whether they formally live in the country, to tackle a “wealthy tax gap” caused by those who do not pay what they ought.
In an announcement after Wednesday’s budget, the authority said it was allocating a customer compliance manager (CCM) to each billionaire with a UK tax footprint, whose complex tax affairs are often hard for HMRC to manage.
“Billionaires can present a particular example of this, with affairs often spanning multiple taxes, entities and jurisdictions and a greater need for early and coordinated engagement,” HMRC said.
It said the managers would offer voluntary discussions to each billionaire before they filed their taxes, to “help build a shared understanding of the customers’ UK tax affairs and make subsequent engagement more focused and proportionate”.
The authority also plans to start deploying new tech to monitor wealthy individuals – defined as those with income of more than £200,000 or assets over £2m in any of the last three years – involving “advanced analytics, automated triggers and artificial intelligence (AI) to identify emerging risks earlier and target compliance activity where it will have greatest impact”.
It is part of wider efforts to tackle the wealthy tax gap, whereby rich people are failing to pay what they should if all of their assets were disclosed to the tax authority. The wealthy tax gap for 2024-25 was estimated to be worth £3.6bn, equivalent to 6% of the total tax gap across the UK’s entire tax-paying population.
The tax authority said its actions would contribute at least £500m towards a larger commitment to raise £10bn of additional tax revenues by 2030.
HMRC was grilled in July last year by MPs on the parliamentary public accounts committee over its lack of understanding of tax compliance by about 1.3 million wealthy taxpayers.
 
Adam Craggs, the head of tax, investigations and financial crime at the law firm RPC, said anyone with more than £200,000 of annual income, or net assets above £2m, should now “reflect on how clearly they understand and can evidence their UK tax position and their interaction with HMRC”.

Volkswagen logs Q3 operating loss of €5.86 billion on Porsche writedown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

VW logs €5.86 billion Q3 operating loss on Porsche writedown
October 29, 2026
The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.
The company reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September. One-off costs, not least a massive writedown in its stake in struggling sister company Porsche, explained the vast bulk of the losses.
The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.
It is pursuing a major restructuring and downsizing program, trying to bolster falling profit margins, and executives said the difficulties highlighted the urgency of this process.
"The nine-month results make one thing clear: We cannot afford to lose any time. We must act quickly and decisively," chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a video statement.
What were the main takeaways from VW's Q3 figures?
The results were the latest reminder of the pressure on VW — and the wider German and Western automotive industry — to react to increasing competition in China, high costs and practical difficulties moving towards electric car production, and unpredictable and rising tariff burdens, thanks in no small part to US President Donald Trump.
Here are some of the key Q3 figures:
- An operating loss of €5.86 billion, compared to €1.3 billion in same quarter last year
- It's the company's worst single quarterly loss since the height of the "Dieselgate" emissions scandal in 2015
- Sales revenue dipped 6.3% year-on-year, to €75.3 billion
- Deliveries to customers, unit sales, and unit production numbers all dipped by roughly 15% as the company starts to reduce production levels, trying to adjust to falling demand
And here are some of the key year-to-date 9-month figures:
- Sales revenue of €233.4 billion was broadly comparable to 2025's figure of €238.7 billion
- But vehicle unit sales, at 5.9 million, are 11% lower than 6.6 million last year — meaning the group is selling fewer cars, at higher prices
- The company's order intake for new cars rose 4% year-on-year, and by 39% for battery electric vehicles (BEVs)
- Operating profit lies at just €0.1 billion, compared with €5.4 billion a year ago
- But VW said 'special items' amounting to €8.7 billion primarily explain this massive dip
- Non-cash writedowns on Porsche assets worth €6.4 billion were the largest portion of this
How did investors respond?
VW shares were already at their lowest levels in well over 10 years prior to Thursday's announcements, after months of difficult headlines and the ongoing plans to shed tens of thousands of jobs and reduce production capacities.
Perhaps as a result of this, the stock dipped briefly as markets opened and the news was published, but then started to rally as the day progressed.
By midday in Frankfurt, VW shares had climbed by 2% compared to their prices at the start of trading on the DAX.
What are VW's downsizing plans?
CEO Oliver Blume plans to shed around 100,000 jobs across the group, which includes the Audi and Porsche brands, in the coming years though a combination of layoffs and not replacing departing or retiring personnel.
Multiple factors are contributing to this. They include increased competition from Chinese manufacturers, falling revenues in China, changeable US auto tariffs under President Donald Trump, different staffing requirements when manufacturing electric cars and difficulties moving towards making and selling more electric cars at the pace once designated by political leaders.
Up to four plants in Germany could face closure as part of the plan, which has met with considerable union resistance and could lead to strikes starting next year.
CFO Antlitz said the figures showed the urgency underlying these plans, saying the company needed to increase its profit margins by 2030 to solidify its finances.
Antlitz said the operating return on sales was only 3.8% in the first nine months of the year, even before the one-off writedowns hitting the bottom line.
"That is not enough in the long term," he said.
As part of its restructuring program, the VW Group aims to restore an operating profit margin of between 8-10% by 2030.
This year, amid one-off costs now totaling in the region of €10 billion, it expects a profit margin of no more than 1%, compared to prior forecasts in the region of 5%.

Police officers and rescue workers to see pay rises in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

Police officers and rescue workers to see pay rises in 2027
The government has allocated €7.3 million to increase the salaries of rescue workers and police officers, mainly those who are "lower-paid frontline employees," Minister of the Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said on Thursday.
Speaking at the government's weekly press conference, he said rescue workers, police officers, border guards and emergency response operators at the Emergency Response Center are set to benefit from the funding boost.
"The government has allocated €7.3 million to our area of administration for pay raises. Salaries will increase in 3,764 positions from the beginning of next year," he said. In total, almost 8,000 people work in the ministry's area of administration.
"All of them deserve fair pay for their work. But the state's financial resources are limited, and this requires clear choices," Taro said.
"We are not distributing this additional money evenly as a percentage increase, but directing it primarily to lower-paid frontline employees," he explained.
Rescue workers will receive the largest pay raise, with their salaries increasing by €140 per month, Taro said. This means the minimum salary for a rescue worker will rise by nearly 9 percent and the average salary by 8 percent.
"This will bring the average salary of rescue workers to approximately 85 percent of the Estonian average. This is a necessary step forward, but it cannot be considered sufficient," the interior minister acknowledged. The average salary was €2,092 in 2025.
Taro said the minimum salary for a police officer will rise by 4.4 percent, the average salary of a patrol police officer will rise above the Estonian average, and the minimum salary of an emergency response operator at the Emergency Response Center will rise by nearly 5 percent.
He added that SMIT technicians and customer support specialists will also receive pay raises. "The pay raise will be €90 per month," Taro said.
"The pay raise also covers the immediate supervisors of frontline employees who themselves perform operational duties. Other managers' salaries will not increase. Salaries at the Ministry of the Interior will not increase," he said.

Day of Terror: Russian Strikes Kill 17 Across Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:52:49 UTC
21:52:49 KST

Russian daytime attacks killed at least 19 people in three Ukrainian cities on Thursday, Oct. 29, striking shops in central Chernihiv, an apartment building in Kremenchuk and a railway platform in Dnipro, according to preliminary figures released by Ukrainian authorities.
In Chernihiv, north of Kyiv, a Russian strike killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded nearly two dozen people, including four children, according to local officials.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In Kremenchuk, a drone struck a multistory residential building, killing three people and injuring several others, including a six-year-old child.
14 people were killed in Dnipro. Children were among the wounded as emergency services responded to the attacks.
2 teenage girls killed in central Chernihiv
A Russian Banderol strike on central Chernihiv killed two 15-year-old girls and injured at least 11 people, including children, regional governor Vyacheslav Chaus reported on Thursday, Oct. 29.
“They were only 15 years old. The enemy killed two children,” Chaus said.
The governor said the attack took place in the middle of the day, when the streets were busy.
Businesses, homes, and cars sustained extensive damage. Emergency services were working at the scene, while authorities continued assessing the consequences and confirming casualty figures.
Apartment building struck in Kremenchuk
In Kremenchuk, Poltava region, a Russian drone hit a residential apartment building, prompting the deployment of emergency services.
‘Kherson Feels Like It Did Before the War’ – Residents Describe Oleshky During Ceasefire
The regional military administration initially reported injuries before confirming that two people had been killed. Parked vehicles also caught fire at the scene, according to regional governor Vitalii Diakivnych.
The number of injured in Kremenchuk rose to 11, including three children, local media reported, citing the regional administration.
Mayor Vitalii Maletskyi had earlier reported that a woman injured in the attack had sought assistance. Emergency crews continued dealing with the aftermath while officials assessed the damage to the residential building. The initial reports did not specify how many apartments had been affected.
Railway platform attack kills 14 in Dnipro
The strikes followed a deadly attack on a railway platform in Dnipro, where Ukrainian authorities reported 14 people killed and at least five wounded.
Four were in serious condition, including an 11-year-old boy, according to regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha.
Ukrzaliznytsia said a Russian jet-powered drone struck the platform where passenger train No. 866, traveling from Dnipro to Zaporizhzhia, was located.
People were on the platform despite a warning of heightened danger, the railway operator said. Rescuers, medical personnel, and police were dispatched to the scene, while regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said the wounded were receiving treatment.
Civilian facilities hit on successive days
Thursday’s attacks came as communities were still dealing with damage from earlier Russian strikes on civilian facilities.
In Chernihiv, a drone attack at around 4 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 28, damaged a municipal veterinary and animal sterilization center. Police reported that three women, aged 59, 40, and 18, were wounded.
One dog was killed, while another dog and three cats were injured. Investigators were collecting evidence for a war crimes investigation.
Kremenchuk has also faced repeated attacks this month. A Russian drone struck a university teaching building during the overnight assault reported on Oct. 21, injuring three people, including a 16-year-old.
The teenager was hospitalized with a concussion and blast-related injuries. A fire broke out on the building’s fifth floor before rescuers extinguished it.
