US vs China: As the world splits into AI blocs, where does Europe stand?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:51:25 UTC
21:51:25 KST

As the US and China build rival AI blocs, Europe is scrambling to reduce its dependence on both. But despite its ambitions to become a technological power in its own right, the EU still lacks the chips, infrastructure and homegrown AI models to compete on equal terms.
With the two leading AI powers, the United States and China, forming their own AI blocs, other countries are manoeuvring to harness the strengths of both groupings and avoid losing out.
Europe is trying to become a third force in AI, but sovereignty is harder to achieve than simply building a home-grown model. Its prospects depend on whether it can also secure the computing power, chips and infrastructure needed to develop and run AI at scale.
As the rivalry intensifies, experts say the window for countries to be able to choose freely between the AI superpowers may be narrowing, forcing them to at one point pick between the US-led Pax Silica, which the EU is already a part of, or the China-inspired World AI Cooperation Organization. But could Europe eventually offer an alternative?
US and China form separate AI blocs
In the artificial intelligence technology race, the United States and China have formed blocs with other nations seeking to set standards and reap AI's potential benefits.
Europe and many other countries are in a dilemma: Do they go with the US’s most advanced chips and AI technologies, or join China’s more affordable, open-source AI systems?
A European alternative
Views in Europe have changed sharply this year as fears mount over how vulnerable the European Union is to exploitation.
Trump’s forced shutdown of Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models in June, as well as the more recent switching off of Elon Musk’s military-grade satellite network Starshield in Ukraine, have raised alarm bells in European capitals.
In June, the EU unveiled its European Technological Sovereignty Package, a wide-ranging set of proposals aimed at boosting the continent’s chip production capacity, expanding data centre capacity, supporting sustainable AI, promoting open-source software and integrating data centres into the energy grid to develop sovereign AI for energy management.
The EU has already made progress in boosting chip manufacturing capacity through its Chips Act. This includes a recent €319 million state aid package for Austrian firm Infineon Technologies to develop next-generation semiconductors, as well as €5 billion in Italy and €1.6 billion in Czechia for similar projects.
Europe also has established strengths in the semiconductor supply chain, thanks to firms such as ASML, which produces advanced lithography systems needed to manufacture chips, and Soitec, which supplies semiconductor substrates used to make them.
But the bloc’s ambitions extend beyond chipmaking. The EU is also building a federated cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure that its architects say could fundamentally change the continent’s relationship with major US and Chinese technology providers.
Rather than building a single European cloud platform from scratch, the project connects existing national infrastructure into a federated network of nodes designed to operate across borders.
Yet Europe remains heavily dependent on foreign technology, particularly in AI. The EU has no dominant frontier AI model comparable to those developed by OpenAI, Anthropic or China’s DeepSeek, and has limited leverage over the companies building the technology. France’s Mistral is one of the few prominent European contenders.
The EU is also trying to rein in its €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China, driven in part by the bloc’s reliance on Beijing for critical raw materials and electrical components needed for AI infrastructure. Up to 90% of Europe’s rare earth elements come from China, according to Euronews reporting on the cost of reducing that dependence.
Beijing has since agreed to create a “green channel” to streamline and expedite licence approvals for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU, as part of an initial trade deal with the bloc.
Alongside efforts to build up its industrial capacity, Brussels has sought to position Europe as a global rule-setter for artificial intelligence.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen vowed that Europe would help write the rules for AI, positioning the bloc as a rule-setter on a par with Washington and Beijing. The EU’s AI Act, adopted in 2024, is billed by Brussels as the “world’s first comprehensive rules on artificial intelligence”.
The Act regulates AI according to a four-tier risk framework, with obligations increasing according to the risks posed by a system. While limited-risk applications such as spam filters face relatively light requirements, certain practices deemed to pose unacceptable risks, including social scoring, are prohibited.
But European companies, concerned that the rules could stifle innovation as they race to catch up with US and Chinese rivals, lobbied hard and secured a delay to rules covering high-risk systems through the AI Omnibus bill, amid a broader shift in the Commission’s political priorities following the 2024 EU elections.
Amid growing global calls for greater control over AI, von der Leyen said the EU’s rules put “Europe in the position to shape global efforts”.
She also said she would invite the main frontier labs “for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”. European firms have been more wary of slowing down, fearing this could be an attempt by US giants to lock in their dominance.
Kazakhstan among countries hoping to harness the best of both blocs
Kazakhstan, a Central Asian nation of about 21 million people, is a rare example of a country that has sought to bridge that gap.
Just three weeks after its AI minister Zhaslan Madiyev visited Washington in June to join the US. group working to strengthen AI supply chains, he headed to Shanghai for a signing ceremony making the Central Asian country a founding member of China’s initiative to shape the global AI agenda.
Being in Pax Silica means more technological partnerships, high-tech manufacturing jobs and a place in global AI supply chains. At the same time, as part of China’s World AI Cooperation Organization alongside 28 other initial founding countries including Pakistan and Russia, Kazakhstan hopes to also have a voice in setting regional and global AI standards.
“Everyone is hedging,” said Dana Masalimova, a former Kazakhstan diplomat and independent scholar and center associate at the Kathryn W. and Shelby Cullom Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies at Harvard University.
“We don’t want this binary choice,” she said.
Kazakhstan is benefiting from both US and Chinese investments, but is in a “very precarious spot,” Masalimova said.
It has rich critical mineral resources essential to AI development and has cheap electricity to power data centers, which have become politically fraught in the US.
Earlier this year, Kazakhstan’s government signed an investment deal worth up to $10 billion involving Nvidia to build a “data center valley” in the country.
Meanwhile, more Chinese companies are investing in Kazakhstan. Local officials say Chinese foreign direct investment in Kazakhstan reached a record $2.8 billion in 2025. Chinese leader Xi Jinping met with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in July to expand cooperation under China’s global infrastructure building Belt and Road initiative.
Washington’s pressure campaign versus Beijing’s courtship
Both China and the US are leveraging access to AI to increase their global influence.
President Donald Trump insisted last month that “whoever wins AI, wins.” US officials and AI companies have accused China of large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American models.
Beijing has rejected those claims and says the US is pursuing an AI monopoly while restricting China’s access to some of the world’s most cutting-edge AI chips and chipmaking machinery.
Washington has signalled that Pax Silica — with China as its implicit target — is only for the trusted.
“Countries can’t be trusted partners in Pax Silica while substantively engaging in initiatives that advance a competing vision for super intelligence,” the US State Department said, using the Trump administration’s new preferred term for AI.
For its part, Beijing touts the openness and inclusiveness of its World AI Cooperation Organization. “As both major countries in AI, China and the United States should leverage respective strengths in AI rather than guarding against each other,” the Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement. “AI should not be owned by major countries.”
The two AI powers have different messaging largely because Beijing needs to court third countries in its bid to build an alternative coalition, whereas Washington already has a powerful network of allies, said Kyle Chan, a fellow at The Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center.
That lends power to what he described as “swing countries.”
Indonesia, Singapore may also be caught between China and the US
Like Kazakhstan, Indonesia has resources vital for AI and other technologies, such as nickel and copper. It’s also seeking to make the most of both AI powers, having joined China’s World AI Cooperation Organization.
Indonesia wants to benefit from both, Mari Pangestu, the Indonesian National Economic Council’s vice chair, told reporters at a University of Hong Kong Business School event. “We should be able to be part of both, put it that way. And choose the best system.”
US AI firms are bringing investments to other countries like Singapore, where Anthropic is setting up its latest Asia office. The city-state says it is also considering joining China’s AI organization.
In Saudi Arabia, the AI startup Humain unveiled in September a platform built on an open model by a Chinese AI company. The kingdom also has a deal with Nvidia to expand AI computing with its advanced chips.
France, one of the most ambitious AI developers aside from the US and China, is attempting to go its own way with its startup Mistral, whose new model released this month outperforms some advanced Chinese models.
Japan is closely aligned with the US on strategic and security issues, including advanced semiconductors, trusted AI and standards. But it will not reject the more affordable Chinese AI models for “lower-risk applications,” said Takahiro Tsuchiya, a professor at Kyoto’s University of Foreign Studies.
Difficult to challenge the 2 leading powers
For countries which have substantial economic and military capacity but no self-developed powerful frontier AI models of their own, aligning with the US may be vital for their access to data centres and chip deals with US companies, said Anton Leicht and Sam Winter-Levy at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Essentially, their access to advanced AI systems “depends on the whims of policymakers in Washington and Beijing,” they said, while those countries may have limited influence over AI’s future.
China, meanwhile, has been closing the technology gap with the US when it comes to chipmaking and advanced AI capabilities, but it still trails top US technological capabilities, at least for now.
Also, Beijing’s open-source approach allows countries to be less reliant on the US, and China has been providing funding for developing countries to develop their own AI ecosystems, said Alberto Lemma, a research fellow at the think tank ODI Global.
To date, China has provided official sector grants and loans for projects and activities that use or enable AI technologies in at least 77 low- and middle-income countries, according to the AidData research lab at William & Mary, a public university in Virginia.
Some top recipients include Nigeria, Zambia, Ghana, Bangladesh, Senegal, Cameroon and Kenya.
Public perceptions are also changing. Recent study results from Pew Research Center have shown that people in middle-income countries are becoming more positive and trusting of China when it comes to AI and the technology’s regulation.
All things considered, many countries “don’t want to pick a side ... because there are advantages and disadvantages to each technology stack,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Most countries may eventually lack a good option since they cannot compete on building AI frontier models, but “every country in the world in some way or another is thinking about AI sovereignty,” he said. After all, “maybe no other country than the US and China can really build these very large, powerful models.”

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:51:10 UTC
21:51:10 KST

On Oct. 28, the U.S. Treasury Department imposed sanctions on 10 individuals and one organization involved in fraudulent schemes carried out by North Korean IT workers. Two Russian citizens, Vitold Obertas and Ilya Boykov, were hit with restrictions, along with eight citizens of North Korea. Washington says that the money obtained through the identified schemes was used to finance North Korea’s ballistic missile and weapons of mass destruction programs.
According to the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), North Korean IT workers get jobs at American and other foreign companies using fake documents, stolen personal data, and fictitious identities. Most of the income these workers receive is seized by North Korean authorities and sent to finance military programs. In addition, North Koreans who gain access to various corporate networks use their positions to steal confidential data and plant malicious software. Intermediaries help North Koreans move money as part of these schemes.
The Treasury named Russian national Vitold Obertas as one such intermediary. Acting on behalf of the North Korean company Amnokgang Technology Development Company (Amnokgang), which was already sanctioned by the U.S., Obertas carried out cryptocurrency conversions worth about $2 million, along with other currency transactions worth $1.25 million.
A full namesake of the sanctioned Vitold Viktorovich Obertas appears in various Russian public registries. According to RBC Companies, a person with that name was registered as an individual entrepreneur in Primorsky Territory on July 16, 2009. His main line of business was listed as fishing, but other spheres of activity included cargo handling, manufacturing of household appliances, and repair of personal and household goods. His individual entrepreneur status was terminated on Nov. 22, 2025. It is also known that Obertas headed AS-Holder LLC (liquidated in 2023) and worked at other companies connected with maritime shipping and security services.
According to OFAC, the other Russian national, Ilya Boykov, has been helping LLC Alis, which is linked to North Korea’s Chinyong Information Technology Cooperation Company. The U.S. Treasury alleges that Boykov handled cryptocurrency exchange, transaction tracking, and logistical support, and that the total amount of cryptocurrency transactions carried out with his help amounted to around $3.5 million.
Also sanctioned was the First Financial and Technical Development Center (FFTDC), an organization that, according to the U.S. Treasury, is located in Russia and controlled by North Korean authorities. The center allegedly laundered money using cryptocurrency. Six North Koreans working in Russia have earned more than $750,000 for the organization since 2025. All of them were included on the sanctions list by name.

A Russian general from Chuhuiv has been charged with ordering a strike on the Skovoroda Museum in 2022. A guard was injured and the building was destroyed.
A Russian lieutenant general is accused of ordering a missile strike on the Hryhorii Skovoroda National Literary and Memorial Museum. The Prosecutor General’s Office reports this, UNN writes.
According to the investigation, a Russian lieutenant general originally from Chuhuiv in the Kharkiv region ordered a missile strike on the Hryhorii Skovoroda National Museum. This concerns the commander of the 6th Air Force and Air Defense Army of the Russian Federation
It is noted that the general knew for certain that he was attacking not a military target but a monument of Ukrainian culture. Despite this, he issued a combat order to destroy it. The investigation established the entire chain through which the order was transmitted via the commanders of the air division and the fighter aviation regiment.
Indictments against both have already been sent to court.
On May 6, 2022, a Russian Su-35S struck an 18th-century estate with a Kh-35 anti-ship missile, where Hryhorii Skovoroda spent the last years of his life and near which he was first buried
As a result of the strike, the museum’s security guard was injured. The roof and ceilings were destroyed, and the walls and part of the exhibition were damaged. The historic building was left in a state of disrepair
The Russian lieutenant general is accused of violating the laws and customs of war, committed by prior conspiracy by a group of persons.
Prosecutors from the Prosecutor General’s Office approved the indictment. The pretrial investigation was conducted by investigators from the Main Investigative Department of the Security Service of Ukraine.
Update
As of September 2026, the actions of Russian military personnel have damaged or destroyed 2,161 sites of Ukraine’s cultural heritage. Among the damaged and destroyed sites are 104 cultural heritage sites in territories included on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Fighting rages near Yemen’s Taiz as UN urges humanitarian access
Fighting has forced more than 281,000 people from their homes in Yemen since the beginning of August, the UN said.
Fighting has escalated in Yemen, with media affiliated to government forces reporting a surge in hostilities with the Houthis on several fronts south of Taiz in southwestern Yemen.
Yemen Today TV reported on Thursday that fighting was taking place on the Al-Aqroudh and Al-Masrakh fronts, as well as in Al-Rahn village in the Sabir al-Mawadim district.
Houthi-affiliated media reported four air strikes against the city of Mocha and its port on the Red Sea, west of Taiz.
Yemeni government forces in Taiz said they repelled attacks on Al-Aqroud, as they tried to break the Houthi siege of the area.
“Our forces have carried out 749 military operations over the past 24 hours, resulting in the death or injury of 239 militants and the destruction of 117 vehicles and armoured vehicles,” Majid al-Nazili, a spokesman for Yemeni government forces, told Al Jazeera.
The Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – also advanced on Jabal Sabr on Sunday, the strategic mountain overlooking Taiz. It has become the focus of the fighting between the Iran-backed group and forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, backed by Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, flights have resumed at Aden international airport, the Anadolu news agency reported. Services were suspended on Wednesday after witnesses said a missile had landed on the Al-Nasr Camp, adjacent to the airport, where Yemeni coastguard forces and interior ministry headquarters are located.
A military source told Al Jazeera on Thursday that government forces carried out three air strikes against Houthi military gatherings and vehicles southeast of Taiz, claiming that they targeted the group’s positions and movements on the Al-Aqroud front. This comes as the Houthi group reported more than 100 air strikes targeting the capital city Sanaa, and eight other Yemeni governorates, over the past 24 hours.
The surge in fighting across multiple fronts in Yemen has worsened a spiralling humanitarian crisis.
The conflict has forced more than 281,000 people from their homes in Yemen since the beginning of August, according to the United Nations’ humanitarian agency.
The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that “time is running out” to deliver aid to the 800,000 people trapped inside the city of Taiz.
Humanitarian access has become increasingly difficult over the past three weeks, OCHA said, due to damage to a key road linking Taiz to southern governorates. Aid supplies now have to pass narrow mountain routes to reach people in need.
OCHA called on fighters not to target civilians or aid convoys. “All parties must respect international humanitarian law and allow safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access so that aid can reach people in need,” it said.
The war in Yemen has escalated sharply since the Houthis seized strategic territory from government forces along the Red Sea coast last month, prompting a counteroffensive. Saudi Arabia has since intensified its strikes on the group.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, which is aligned with Yemen’s government forces, have dealt a blow to the kingdom, the world’s biggest exporter of crude oil, disrupting its businesses, airlines and residents, and damaging its international image.

You also want to step-by-step reduce your dependence, and I think this is a very good win-win situation for both sides," said McAllister.

So, if India with its special relationship with Russia - and also India with its constructive relationship with Ukraine - can play any kind of role constructively, it would be welcome," he said, while praising Jaishankar's "constructive" role for peace.

Fans voted for individual award-winning years, allowing the same player to appear more than once among the contenders.
Organisers clarified the status of the initiative on the official Ballon d’Or website.
“Please note that this is a public vote celebrating fan passion, not an official trophy,” they stated.
Ronaldo claimed his first Ballon d’Or in 2008 after helping Manchester United win the Premier League and Champions League. He scored 42 goals across all competitions during the 2007/08 campaign. Messi’s runner-up entry recognized his 2012 triumph, when he scored 91 goals during the calendar year.
Voting ran from October 1 to 27. Under the official rules, each entry required purchasing a digital photograph for €1. Multiple votes were permitted, with a separate purchase required each time. Participants also entered a draw for two tickets to the 2027 Ballon d’Or ceremony.
Organizers disclosed that 5,009 people voted more than once, including 44 who submitted between 10 and 26 entries.
The poll does not change the players’ official award totals: Messi holds a record eight Ballons d’Or, while Ronaldo has five.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that England captain Harry Kane had won the 2026 Ballon d’Or, becoming the first Englishman to receive the award since Michael Owen in 2001.

Astronomers discover a possible new dwarf planet in Solar System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:43:22 UTC
21:43:22 KST

Astronomers discover a possible new dwarf planet in Solar System
The Vera Rubin Observatory has detected a possible new dwarf planet orbiting the Sun beyond Neptune, marking a potentially significant discovery in the outer Solar System, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Space.com.
The icy object, designated as 2026 ED138, is estimated to measure between 600 and 1,500 kilometers in diameter. According to scientists, it may be large enough for its own gravity to be sculpted into a nearly spherical body, one of the key criteria for classifying an object as a dwarf planet.
If confirmed, 2026 ED138 would join the five officially recognized dwarf planets in the Solar System: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.
The object was discovered by Matthew Holman of the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian (CfA). On October 13, he identified it while analyzing previously collected data from the Vera Rubin Observatory using a search code developed with his CfA colleague Kevin Napier.
The search revealed an object beyond Neptune’s orbit that appeared unusually bright despite its great distance from the Sun. This suggested that it could be larger than the average trans-Neptunian object.
“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said in a statement released on October 27, when the discovery was announced. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."
Located atop Cerro Pachón in northern Chile at an altitude of 2,682 meters, the Vera Rubin Observatory is equipped with an 8.4-meter primary mirror. The observatory achieved first light in April 2025 and began its main scientific program, the 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), in June 2026.
Earlier, it was reported that samples returned from the Moon’s far side suggest that uneven heating caused by Earth’s gravity helped shape its contrasting hemispheres billions of years ago.

Yemeni authorities accuse Houthis of using toxic substances

Yemeni authorities accuse Houthis of using banned toxic substances in Taiz attacks
Yemeni authorities in the country’s Taiz province accused the Houthis on Wednesday of using internationally prohibited toxic materials in their attacks, as fighting rages on between government forces and Houthi rebels.
A statement from local authorities in Taiz called for an urgent investigation into the materials used in the attacks.
It came after field reports indicating that the shelling carried out by the Houthis contained banned toxic substances.
The authorities added that similar incidents had previously been recorded, with several cases of civilians fainting and suffocating after attacks.
Meanwhile, a Houthi-run human rights group said on Thursday that a Saudi strike had hit a paint factory west of Taiz, saying that this could release toxins into the surrounding area. It added that the strike caused a fire to break out which could also contaminate nearby soil and groundwater, accusing Saudi Arabia of carrying out war crimes.
The development comes as clashes have resumed between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis on several fronts.
Taiz, which is the country’s third-largest city, has been largely besieged since the start of the month, with the Houthis taking key towns and roads around it. As a result, the price of basic goods in the city has skyrocketed, while the UN warned last week that road closures had blocked vital supplies.
Earlier this week, local media reported, citing authorities in Taiz, that Houthi sniper fire had killed five civilians and wounded five others, including children, in the villages of Hamma, al-Damna, and other nearby communities.
The Yemeni army also said on Thursday that two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis struck Aden International Airport, injuring civilians and causing some damage. Yahya Saree, the Houthi military spokesperson, also called for civilians to evacuate the airport ahead of a planned attack.
Authorities in Taiz have called for UN intervention, demanding that international bodies support investigations and hold those responsible for using potentially prohibited substances accountable.
The statement added that the Yemeni armed forces and security forces would take the necessary measures to deter attacks and protect civilians in accordance with international humanitarian law.
The siege on Taiz has prompted the internationally recognised government's Ministry of Public Health to issue a stark warning over an impending humanitarian disaster, which could kill thousands of people due to the collapse of basic medical services and a lack of vital supplies.
An official report from Taiz’s Health Office this month said that there is systematic destruction to the health infrastructure amid the conflict, noting that 256 out of 345 health facilities had been captured while 25 had sustained damage.
It also stated that at least 15 ambulances had been vandalised and looted, and that around 246,711 people lack access to basic healthcare services.
The recent spate of attacks has meant that many services have also come to a halt, including immunisation and children's health services, with 9,454 infants being affected.
The war in Yemen has flared up again last September, with pro-government forces initially launching a major offensive to retake territory in western Yemen controlled by the Houthis.
However the Houthis gained the upper hand and captured all of Yemen's west coast, near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait later that month.
They have also launched missiles and drones at energy facilities, airports, and military bases in Saudi Arabia.

TIRANA, Oct 29 - Opposition lawmakers in Albania disrupted a parliament session by letting off flares on Thursday following weeks of violent anti-government protests called by students demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.
Members of the opposition Democratic Party of Albania also blocked access to the podium when a law on the Central Bank was being voted on.
"These (ruling lawmakers) are criminals and they deserve tear gas, rubber bullets, cracked skulls and broken bones, not the young people," opposition leader Sali Berisha said during his speech before his microphone was cut off.

Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana since mid-October and spread to other cities.
Demonstrators demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings and banks, smashed shop windows and pulled up paving stones to throw at police.
The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful summer protests against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and won a fourth term in office last year.
On Sunday, Rama introduced new measures to curb violence, including fines of 500,000 lek ($6,200) for anyone who participates in a protest that turns violent, even if they do not personally commit acts of violence.
This week the protests were mainly peaceful, and another is planned for Saturday.
Prime Minister Rama has again called on students for dialogue and introduced new economic measures such as cheaper fuel and more money for poor families in an attempt to stop the violence in the streets. REUTERS

The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
Under the verdict, the former judge has also been banned from driving for ten years.
The prosecutor's office recalled that the fatal crash occurred in May 2023. According to investigators, around midnight, the judge, driving a Lexus ES350 while intoxicated, struck an on-duty serviceman of the National Guard of Ukraine at a checkpoint. The victim died at the scene.
According to an expert examination, the driver began braking immediately before the collision rather than in advance, as required by the road signs.
Using his legal knowledge and experience in handling road accident cases, the defendant refused to undergo an examination to determine his level of intoxication. During the forced collection of biological samples, he attempted to falsify the test results by providing water and saliva instead of biological material. In doing so, he sought to evade liability for driving under the influence of alcohol.
"The case has been before the court since September 2023. Throughout this period, the defendant filed numerous motions to disqualify the judge and prosecutor, and hearings were repeatedly postponed at the defense team's request. More than 50 court hearings were not held as a result of motions filed by the defense. The defense also filed more than 30 motions to disqualify the judge and prosecutor. In addition, the defendant attempted to secure his release from custody by enlisting in the military," the prosecutor's office said.
The prosecution opposed his mobilization, and the court also rejected the motion for his mobilization.
Prosecutors proved that the driver had violated traffic safety rules while intoxicated, causing the serviceman's death, an offense under Part 3 of Article 286-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
In May 2023, Oleksii Tandyr, then head of the Makariv District Court in the Kyiv region, fatally struck a National Guard serviceman at a checkpoint in Kyiv. The High Council of Justice authorized his arrest. An expert examination found that the judge had been under the influence of alcohol at the time of the crash.
The pre-trial investigation into Tandyr was completed that summer, and the case was sent to court.
The High Council of Justice subsequently dismissed Tandyr from his judicial post.
In January this year, the court allowed Tandyr to be released from the pre-trial detention center on bail set at UAH 119.88 million. The appellate court later reduced the amount to nearly UAH 20 million.
In the spring, law enforcement officers exposed a criminal organization involved in real estate fraud. Tandyr was among those implicated.

A 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals a lost world where early humans lived
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:38:53 UTC
21:38:53 KST

A 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals a lost world where early humans lived
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee
- Summary:
- A remarkably preserved elephant tooth dating back nearly 700,000 years has revealed a surprisingly lush prehistoric world where giant elephants and early humans lived side by side. Discovered in northern Israel alongside ancient stone tools, the tooth belonged to a straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Ice Age.
- Share:
A single ancient elephant tooth is offering scientists a remarkable glimpse into a world that existed nearly 700,000 years ago. Found in northern Israel, the fossil has helped researchers reconstruct a surprisingly lush prehistoric landscape filled with forests, rivers, wetlands, and abundant vegetation. This ancient environment supported enormous elephants and some of the region's earliest human populations, revealing how access to water and natural resources may have helped our ancestors survive and move between continents.
The discovery comes from Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (GBY-NBA), an archaeological site where early humans produced stone tools hundreds of thousands of years ago. Elephant remains were unearthed alongside handaxes and cleavers made from basalt, a volcanic rock. These implements belong to the Acheulian tradition, one of the oldest and most widespread stone tool technologies in human history.
The research, published in Quaternary Science Reviews, was led by Hannah Farrell (a PhD candidate at Haifa University). The team examined a large elephant molar and fragments of tusk recovered from Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (Daughters of Jacob Bridge), situated in the Jordan Rift Valley just south of today's Hula Valley. The site was excavated by Prof. Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and his colleagues.
A Giant Elephant Tooth Reveals a Lost Prehistoric World
The fossils belonged to Palaeoloxodon antiquus, commonly known as the straight-tusked elephant. This enormous prehistoric animal was among the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene, the geological period that included the most recent ice ages.
Rather than focusing only on the animal itself, the scientists treated its tooth as a record of the world in which it lived. Teeth can preserve chemical clues about an animal's diet and surroundings, allowing researchers to investigate environmental conditions from hundreds of thousands of years ago.
To uncover those clues, the team combined several scientific techniques, including CT scans, 3D reconstruction, microscopic examination of tooth wear, isotope geochemistry, and pollen analysis. CT imaging allowed them to examine the fossil's internal structure, while chemical measurements and microscopic evidence helped build a picture of the ancient habitat.
The results pointed to a remarkably persistent landscape containing woodlands, open grasslands, marshes, flowing rivers, and shallow bodies of water. Carbon isotope measurements suggested that the elephant lived in an environment with a dependable water supply. Meanwhile, pollen preserved in nearby sediments revealed a variety of wetland plants, including reeds, sedges, willow, tamarisk, and aquatic vegetation.
Together, these findings suggest that the region offered a diverse and productive environment capable of supporting both giant mammals and early human communities.
An Ancient Oasis Along a Crucial Human Migration Route
The location of this prehistoric landscape makes the discovery particularly significant. The Hula Valley lies within the Levantine Corridor, a natural passage connecting Africa and Eurasia that played an important role in the movements of ancient humans and animals.
Researchers believe the area functioned as a relatively stable ecological refuge, maintaining vital habitats and resources over long periods. Its rivers, wetlands, forests, and grasslands would have offered dependable sources of water, vegetation, and animal life for populations traveling through the region.
For early humans, access to such environments could have made the difference between surviving in an unfamiliar landscape and being unable to sustain a population. Understanding these habitats may therefore help explain how ancient human groups moved through the region and adapted to changing environmental conditions.
According to Prof. Sharon, "understanding how humans and animals responded to environmental change hundreds of thousands of years ago helps us better understand the forces that shaped our species."
The findings highlight the importance of studying ancient landscapes alongside the fossils and artifacts found within them. By reconstructing the environments that supported prehistoric life, researchers can gain a clearer understanding of the conditions that influenced early human survival and migration.
"The availability of water, vegetation, and animal resources shaped where humans and wildlife could survive," Sharon says. "The wetlands, rivers, and woodlands of the Hula Valley helped sustain life along one of the world's earliest migration corridors, offering a rare opportunity to understand the ecological conditions that supported both animals and human populations nearly 700,000 years ago."
The study brought together specialists from several Israeli universities. Farrell of the University of Haifa conducted the research using material from the site excavated by Sharon and his colleagues. Additional collaborators included Cheryl A. Makarewicz (isotope studies) and Nimrod Marom (archaeozoology) of the University of Haifa, as well as Minji Jin and Dafna Langgut (pollen studies) of Tel Aviv University.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hannah Farrell, Gonen Sharon, Minji Jin, Dafna Langgut, Cheryl A. Makarewicz, Nimrod Marom. Elephant dental remains from the Acheulian site at North Bridge Acheulian–Gesher Benot Ya\'aqov: hominin behavior and environmental implications. Quaternary Science Reviews, 2026; 392: 110277 DOI: 10.1016/j.quascirev.2026.110277

The warning came during a visit to China by 12 MEPs, who urged Beijing to build on a deal reached earlier this month to limit Chinese hybrid car exports to the EU.
The EU's trade deficit with China has reached a record €360 billion and continues to widen as low-cost Chinese imports flood the European market, threatening jobs and industries.
"The recent TIC [Trade and Investment Consultations] agreement on hybrid car imports is a good starting point in stabilising fair trade and producing benefits for people on the ground," German Socialist MEP Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament's trade committee, said after the visit.
"However, we made clear to our Chinese counterparts that we expect to see more sectors following the same approach in the future."
Under the October deal, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually over four years, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.
But restricting hybrid car imports alone will do little to reverse the growing trade imbalance.
The EU and China have entered a new phase of negotiations, with talks expected to continue until at least March 2027, when EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is due to meet his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao.
“Heavy” job losses
The issue was raised during a meeting between the MEP delegation and Wang in China, where exports have become a cornerstone of Beijing's industrial strategy.
“The Chinese export model is simply not sustainable for the EU,” French liberal MEP Pascal Canfin, the standing rapporteur on trade relations with China, also said.
Given the urgency, EU leaders mandated the European Commission at a summit earlier this month to impose unilateral quotas and tariffs on imports of chemicals and industrial machinery, two other sectors seriously threatened by Chinese competition.
While negotiations continue, the Commission is also working on a "kill-switch" that would cut China's access to the single market in the event of market distortions caused by economic pressure.
The EU is also tackling unfair Chinese trade practices through product-by-product investigations, but EU countries consider this insufficient, given that Chinese imports threaten entire sectors of EU's industry.
Last Friday, after meeting the 27 EU trade ministers, Šefčovič said that every head of state or government is “concerned” that there might be “heavy losses of jobs.”
He added: “We have to proceed not only with the traditional trade techniques, but also with a very political approach.”

Artificial intelligence was the focus of the workshop “Human-Centered AI and Societal Benefits,” held last night at Casa Italia, the headquarters of the Italian Embassy in London, and organized in collaboration with the University of Manchester and Sapiente Education. Researchers, industry experts, and representatives of civil society discussed how to develop artificial intelligence centered on people, capable of generating trust, transparency, and tangible benefits for the community. This is an issue on which Italy has already made a clear choice, becoming the first country in the European Union to adopt a national law on artificial intelligence, set to take effect in October 2025. The guiding principle is that AI should reinforce—not replace—human decision-making and responsibility, with effective human oversight at every stage.

South Korean prosecutors press for death sentence in Yoon martial law case
Former president faces renewed death penalty demand as he appeals life sentence for insurrection.
South Korean prosecutors are seeking the death penalty for former President Yoon Suk-yeol over his failed attempt to impose military rule.
The team led by special prosecutor Cho Eun-suk renewed the demand at an appeal hearing in Seoul on Thursday, arguing that Yoon’s actions threatened South Korea‘s democracy.
He was sentenced to life imprisonment in February after being convicted of leading an insurrection.
Prosecutors had previously sought the death penalty at Yoon’s original trial in January, but the court sentenced him to life imprisonment the following month.
At Thursday’s hearing at the Seoul High Court, a prosecutor said there was “no reason to hesitate” over imposing the death penalty, according to South Korea’s Yonhap news agency.
South Korea retains the death penalty but has not carried out an execution since 1997.
Prosecutors argued that this long pause should not prevent judges from sentencing Yoon to death.
Yoon declared martial law on December 3, 2024, deploying soldiers and police to the National Assembly, South Korea’s parliament.
Lawmakers overcame a security blockade to vote down the measure, forcing the government to withdraw it about six hours after it was announced.
The lower court found that Yoon had tried to stop parliament from functioning, detain political opponents and remain in control of the country for an extended period.
Yoon’s lawyers told reporters on Thursday that he had intended to warn an opposition-controlled parliament against what he considered attempts to obstruct his government, not to establish authoritarian rule.
Speaking at the Seoul High Court on October 27, Yoon also denied seeking to establish a long-term dictatorship, according to the Hankyoreh newspaper.
The crisis led parliament to impeach Yoon in December 2024. South Korea’s Constitutional Court, which decides whether to uphold impeachments, removed him from office in April 2025.
The appeals court plans two more hearings, including Yoon’s final statement on November 5.

What an eight-hour power cut taught me about food stockpiling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:35:43 UTC
21:35:43 KST

I’m writing this from the North Sea coast, where I’m in a semi-enforced lockdown at my in-laws’ house. It’s only temporary. Like most of the UK, storms Austen and Boelo hit us in quick succession, and we’ve been in and out of power cuts ever since. We were in the kitchen when the first storm hit and we slipped into an eight-hour power cut.
Of course we didn’t know it would be eight hours at the time, so you can only imagine the panic-raid lunch of all the things we worried might go off: blue cheese and cold chicken on semi-defrosted bread; fridge-cold stewed apple with warming yoghurt; and, finally, a thumb of goat’s cheese with some dark chocolate that I found in my bag. Once the rain stopped, we headed to a pub seemingly untouched by this so-called “weather bomb” and had chips. All in all, a fairly civilised array of picky bits, though I appreciate goat’s cheese and chocolate isn’t for everyone, which is why I ate them in the bathroom.
I’d already been wondering about the timing of the government’s Be Ready campaign last week, which urged us to keep enough supplies to manage for 72 hours. Maybe it wasn’t just about tapping into our autumnal urge to pickle and preserve, after all. It was only once the power went off that I actually bothered to read the National Resilience Checklist before the wifi went, too. For three days, it recommends three litres of water per person per day, as well as enough non-perishable food (tinned meat, fish and vegetables, dried fruit and nuts) to get you through.
With the next few days in mind, I did a quick inventory of my in-laws’ store cupboard. And while I enjoy capers, white marzipan, sardines, dried dates and cannellini beans in their own way, 72 hours suddenly felt like a lifetime. Spotting a pouch of Merchant Gourmet Spanish-style grains, I briefly flirted with the idea of hiding it in another cupboard for leverage, before accepting that might be a bad vibe. Had we been at home, it would have been coconut milk, Jaffa cakes and various seeds.
Despite government advice, I had planned to avoid Tesco, assuming it would be overrun by panicked locals and denuded shelves. There’s a logic to panic shopping in times of panic, but we’re not there yet, guys! If we start rapidly changing our buying habits, we risk dismantling an already precarious system that can adapt only so much. The so-called doom boom – the surge in doomsday prepping – will make things only worse; one person’s stockpile is another person’s shortage. It’s worth remembering that local community resilience matters much more than any fancy bunker planning.
Still, fear can be powerful, which is probably why I’ve made a list of things we should add to our next few shops. I’m aiming for a more “deep-pantry” method: buying two or three extra items a week max, and only what we’d want to eat tomorrow. There is something strangely relaxing about pulling together a no-cook dinner from a more prudent shopping excursion, particularly with all-year salads. Meera Sodha’s no-cook chickpea and tomato salad is a winner at mine even if there’s no power cut. I love the idea of Harumi Kurihara’s Hijiki seaweed salad because I have most of the ingredients, and in retrospect I probably could have made Anna Berrill’s sardine and celery salad this week. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’s recipe for sardine and red onion salad takes five minutes to cobble together.
Other than that, if I learned anything from those eight long hours out here, it’s the following: sweetened condensed milk can be both a pudding and a coffee whitener; got kids? Get UHT milk for cereal; most prepper-friendly meals tend to come from canned food, but think about pouches, too; think first in, first out, and place new food at the back of the cupboard or fridge, so you eat the older stuff first; think about food not as an add-on but as the whole meal (canned smoked mussels go well with canned white beans, say); and, finally, if you really want chips, make sure you have a cooking stove, and consider planting potatoes. They are weirdly easy to grow.
My week in food
Sandwich saint | It’s been over six months since Pret stopped selling its only good sandwich, the jambon beurre, due to a possible cornichon shortage. I’ve spent almost all that time perfecting my own version using ingredients from Lidl. Then, the other week, I got a tip-off that chef Pascal Wiedemann at Pompette in Oxford makes the best version, not least because every single element – baguette, ham, cornichons, butter, dijon mustard – is made in-house. It takes him three days from start to finish, and they sell it every day! I’m particularly excited by the ham, which comes from the Tamworth pigs at nearby Paddock Farm. I’m off to Oxford next week, so will report back.
Flying solo | I’m very much married with children, but have been vicariously enjoying Eli Davies’ The Spinster Cookbook. Memoirs and recipes always make the best reading, though don’t buy this if you want only recipes – the first one, about drinking vodka and “fancified” toast, doesn’t land for about 70 pages. It’s more of a manifesto for single women that follows Davies’ relationship to cooking and domesticity as a single woman in a family-size world. Imagine Katharine Whitehorn scarfing Kettle Chips over the sink, and you’re halfway there.
TV dinners | I have become quietly fascinated by the contestants’ eating habits on The Traitors. The way they balance plates of lasagne and chopped salad on their laps. The sheer quantity of toast and juice consumed at breakfast – and why no one touches the pastries (according to previous contestants, they’re stale). I did a deep dive on Reddit to find out what’s in those jars in the kitchen, and can confirm: Skittles, dried apricots, dates and Haribo gummies.

Is this play-safe budget a sign that the prime minister is planning an early election? | Larry Elliott
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:34:24 UTC
21:34:24 KST

Great hopes were invested in Andy Burnham when he became prime minister in July. He went big on the failings of 40 years of neoliberalism, emphasised the need for Britain to start making things again and promised growth in every postcode.
 
Back in the summer, John Healey’s first budget was seen as an opportunity to start delivering on these ambitions, but it has been clear for some time that it wouldn’t do so. The road to the New Jerusalem – judging by the chancellor’s “breathing space” package – will be a slow and arduous one. Healey has taken what he inherited from Rachel Reeves and performed some minor tweaks. Not so much a revolution as continuity Keir Starmer.
 
As has been the hallmark of Burnham’s first 100 days in Downing Street, there was plenty of activity in the budget but the slew of measures – almost 100 in all – was a hotchpotch and had no real semblance of a strategy being fleshed out. Not many budgets linger long in the memory and it is unlikely that Healey’s will break with this tradition.
In essence, it has bought Healey and Burnham some time. For the moment they can argue that the budget was just part one of a three-stage process, to be followed by the government’s 10-year-plan and next year’s spending review. They need to use that time wisely or the glitzy PR will cease to impress.
 
There are, of course, reasons why the chancellor played it safe. Energy prices have rocketed since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February. The consequent higher inflation has resulted in higher interest rates for mortgages, business loans and government borrowing.
 
Optimism about an early resolution to the war is fast fading. Indeed, the prospect of an intensification of the conflict after next week’s US midterm elections has led to a fresh surge in the cost of crude oil and gas in the past couple of weeks. The modest help provided in the budget to reduce energy bills will be dwarfed by the expected price increases in January. A tough winter lies ahead.
 
As the dust settles, a number of conclusions can be drawn. One is that Britain remains – as Burnham once put it – in hock to the bond markets. Healey may well have wanted to come up with a more generous energy support package, but was constrained by the fear that the financial markets would cut up rough. Ever since Liz Truss’s mini budget in 2022, governments have lived in fear of another sell off in government bonds. Healey is like a contestant in Strictly Come Dancing – he knows that the markets always have the casting vote.
 
To be fair to the chancellor, he borrowed £20bn more to invest in infrastructure spending, using the flexibility in meeting the government’s rules for the public finances provided by Reeves. That was welcome and – at first glance – didn’t appear to unsettle the markets.
 
Whether Healey’s array of minor fixes to help with cost of living pressures is enough to keep voters sweet is another matter. The economy has so far showed impressive resilience in the face of the energy shock caused by events in the Middle East, but that strength has been concentrated in the financial and business sectors of the economy, with growth in artificial intelligence particularly striking. Consumer-facing sectors – such as hospitality and housing – have been much weaker, with the most recent report on consumer confidence showing the sharpest monthly fall since the Brexit referendum in 2016.
 
That’s hardly surprising given the fact that taxes as a share of national income are on course next year to be at their highest ever level, and that spending power is being eroded by rising fuel and energy costs. In its latest report on the economy, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates that living standards will fall next year and by 2030-31 will be only 2% higher than they were before the Covid pandemic. A lost decade in other words.
 
It is against this unpropitious backdrop that many pundits – particularly in the City – have seen the lack of meat in the budget not as an indication that the government is dithering, but as a sign that Burnham is preparing the ground for an early general election. On this reading, all the big decisions – on social care, relations with the EU, and defence – have been parked until the prime minister has his own mandate.
 
The case for holding a snap poll is not just that voters seem to have taken to Burnham, although he is certainly enjoying a honeymoon period. It is also that Labour is currently benefiting from the lack of a single challenger on the right as the Conservatives and Reform slug it out, and from the problems facing both the Greens and the Liberal Democrats on the left. The polls show Labour in the lead.
 
Even so, an early election would be a colossal risk for a party with a commanding majority and two and a half years of the current parliament still to run. The OBR thinks the economy will grow more slowly in 2027 than in 2026, while living standards will actually fall before picking up in 2028 as the energy shock abates. Next week’s anticipated rise in interest rates from the Bank of England may not be the last. The prime minister is arguably at the peak of his popularity.
 
Burnham has repeatedly said that he has no plans to go to the country early, which if true will be a relief to the many Labour MPs who would almost certainly lose their seats, even now that the polls are looking more favourable. But if that is his intention, he will need to get a move on – because now is as good as it is going to get.
- Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

Why is Russia sending fighter jets and air defences to Ethiopia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:32:49 UTC
21:32:49 KST

Why is Russia sending fighter jets and air defences to Ethiopia?
Experts say Moscow is seeking arms revenue and further diplomatic influence.
Ethiopia has received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will acquire four S-400 air defence batteries, in a deal experts say strengthens Moscow’s foothold in the Horn of Africa while bolstering Addis Ababa’s military amid conflict at home and tensions with neighbouring Eritrea.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the deal in Moscow during the two-day Russia-Africa Summit.
“I value the friendly relations between Russia and Ethiopia,” Russian President Vladimir Putin said in a statement. “Russia and Ethiopia stand together in international affairs.”
Experts say the agreement builds on decades of military cooperation, offering Moscow arms revenue and diplomatic influence while allowing Ethiopia to strengthen its armed forces amid its ongoing conflict in Tigray.
Here is what we know:
What weapons is Ethiopia acquiring?
Abiy said Ethiopia had taken delivery of its first 12 Su-35s under an earlier agreement with Russia, with four S-400 batteries to follow, but did not say when the air defence systems would arrive.
The aircraft would expand an air force already equipped with Russian fighter jets. The S-400 systems would complement this existing fleet by helping the military defend itself against aerial threats, experts say.
“They would be best used against conventional air threats,” Benedict Manzin, a lead analyst on the Middle East and Africa at risk consultancy Sibylline, told Al Jazeera. “In a war with Eritrea, they could be used against Eritrea’s limited air force and drones.”
However, air defences do not provide protection against every kind of attack.
“As we have seen in Ukraine, conventional air defence systems can be overwhelmed by small, cheap drones,” he said.
Why does Russia want closer ties with Ethiopia?
The relationship predates the current competition for influence in Africa.
“Russia has been engaged in Ethiopia for decades, part of the legacy of the Cold War,” Manzin said.
The Soviet Union backed Ethiopia’s former communist government. Today’s cooperation builds on those foundations, with the two countries having signed military agreements intended to improve the Ethiopian armed forces’ capabilities through technology, knowledge and training, according to the Ethiopian News Agency.
Commercial interests also matter.
“Russia is also in the business of making money through arms sales,” Manzin said. “This is one of Russia’s primary exports to Africa.”
Weapons sales provide revenue while sustaining relationships with governments that require training, maintenance and replacement equipment. But the partnership extends beyond defence.
Abiy said his talks with Putin covered nuclear energy, health and trade, alongside bilateral and multilateral cooperation, while in a statement, Putin said bilateral trade exceeded $1.3bn in January-September, more than twice the figure for all of 2025.
He identified energy, agriculture, industry and education among potential areas for further cooperation.
Ethiopia’s size also makes it attractive to competing powers, with experts saying that because it is Africa’s second-most populous country, it offers a substantial market.
“Everyone engages a bit, and Ethiopia tries to maximise its gains,” Manzin said.
Does this mean Ethiopia is turning away from the West?
Manzin suggested Ethiopia is widening its options rather than committing exclusively to Moscow.
“African states are aware that they are a focus of geopolitical competition,” he said.
That competition gives governments room to seek weapons, investment and diplomatic backing from different partners. Ethiopia’s relationship with Russia coexists with a significant Chinese presence and continuing Western investment in the country.
“China has a huge presence in Ethiopia, and Russian arms have always been a huge factor,” Manzin said. Moscow is seeking to turn those established connections into broader influence as Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine constrain its international relationships.
Russia supplied 15 percent of African imports of major weapons in 2021–2025, behind the United States at 19 percent and China at 17 percent, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
Could the weapons be used in Tigray?
In his statement, Abiy thanked Putin for ensuring the aircraft were delivered a year ahead of schedule and said the equipment would strengthen Ethiopia’s ability to “preemptively deter aggression”.
The delivery comes amid renewed fighting in Tigray, a separate rebellion in Amhara and concerns about a possible conflict with Eritrea.
“Ethiopia is buying a lot of aircraft,” Manzin said. “The timing comes as Ethiopia is going through conflict in Tigray, with speculation about war with Eritrea.”
He cautioned against assuming the latest battlefield developments directly prompted purchases negotiated earlier.
“Aircraft are helpful regardless, as they are using aircraft and the air force heavily during any suppression,” he said.
What’s the conflict about?
Fighting between Ethiopia’s federal army and Tigrayan forces intensified in late September, in effect unravelling the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war.
Each side has blamed the other for renewed violence. Tensions grew following the formation of a seven-group alliance seeking to overthrow Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration.
Government troops and allied forces entered Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, earlier in October after Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters withdrew.
Addis Ababa subsequently installed a six-month caretaker administration, but rebel commanders have promised to continue fighting.

In an interview with Germany’s BILD newspaper, the commander of the Kommando Spezialkrafte (KSK, Special Operations Command) elite special forces unit, Brig. Gen. Andreas Kuhne, said it was now preparing for a role in support of conventional battlefield operations against Russia.
The KSK was formed in 1996, primarily to conduct hostage rescue, counter-terrorist operations, and high-risk reconnaissance beyond the capabilities of conventional military or law enforcement agencies. According to Kuhne, these operations were typically planned to be short-term, three days or less, after which the operators would return to base for “eating, showering, and doing laundry.”

While some KSK troops were deployed to Afghanistan on operations against the Taliban, those missions also followed a similar pattern. The future enemy now “sit in the east,” the commander said. “We are very specifically focused on the opponent Russia,” he added, noting that KSK is training to prepare for a potential conventional military confrontation in which it “will have to hold out in the field for much longer, potentially indefinitely.”
There have been reports that some NATO members’ special forces have already been involved in supporting Ukraine in the war that resulted from Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion which will further influence the KSK’s training.
Ukrainian Delegation Heads Toward Oleshky for Aid Mission

Training for KSK is being adapted to focus on operations in extreme cold and against Russia’s forces equipped with tanks, artillery, drones, and electronic warfare systems. It is probable that the unit will operate in advance of Germany’s conventional forces in the event of a crisis on NATO’s Eastern Flank.
Kuhne told BILD that, “if the 45th Panzerbrigade in Lithuania starts its engines in an emergency, we want to have already done our job. Within four hours we will be on the plane in Stuttgart. And then we will have everything we need with us.”
The strength of the KSK is thought to be around 1,500 personnel, a third of which are special forces operators – although Kuhne said the unit was currently operating at around 70-80 percent of its manpower levels.
The KSK re-rolling comes amid Germany attempting to increase the size of its armed forces. The deployment of the 45th Armored Brigade to Lithuania, which was formally inaugurated in May 2025, is an indication of Berlin’s commitment to NATO and in addressing the threat from Russia.
The Brigade consists of around 4,800 personnel, equipped with Leopard 2 main battle tanks, and Puma Infantry Fighting Vehicles supported by PzH 2000 155mm self-propelled howitzers.

"Volumes of international financial assistance in Q3 were smaller than expected, primarily due to Ukraine delaying the implementation of reforms. That said, in October, the parliament adopted a number of laws to unblock the financing form the EU and the IMF," the regulator said in a press release published on Thursday.
The NBU added that the pace of fulfilling commitments under support programs is expected to accelerate further, reducing uncertainty regarding sources of budget financing.

For next year, the regulator projects inflows of approximately $52 billion and $37 billion, respectively.
"Such volumes of assistance would allow financing large budget needs and maintaining international reserves at a comfortable level (more than $62 billion in 2026–2027)," the NBU said.
According to the press release, the forecast for international reserves at the end of 2028 was also lowered, to $57 billion from $70 billion.
As reported, in its July macroeconomic forecast, the regulator raised its estimate of international reserves at the end of 2026 to $69.7 billion from $64.8 billion, for 2027 to $73.7 billion from $66.5 billion, and for 2028 to $70 billion from $61.1 billion.
However, international reserves declined from July through September this year after rising by 12.1% in June. In September alone, they fell by $1.6 billion, or 3.2%, to $47.1 billion.

National Bank of Ukraine hikes key rate to 16.5% as expected, signals hold until Q2 2027
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:30:37 EET
21:30:37 KST

The Board of the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) raised its key policy rate by 0.5 percentage points (pp) to 16.5% per annum, effective October 30, due to a substantial intensification of price pressures and a deterioration in inflation expectations.
"The NBU stands ready to respond flexibly to further changes in the balance of risks, taking into account both the persistence of price pressures and potential effects of weaker economic activity," the regulator said in a press release on Thursday.
The central bank's current forecast envisages keeping the key policy rate at 16.5% through the second quarter of 2027. At the same time, the regulator will adjust monetary policy depending on how events actually unfold, particularly the impact of Russian attacks on inflation and economic activity, the statement said.
In September, headline inflation accelerated to 10% year-on-year, while core inflation rose to 8.8%, and this trend continued in October. The main factors were higher fuel prices due to the war in the Middle East and an intensification of Russian attacks on warehousing and logistics infrastructure, the NBU recalled.
The regulator raised its inflation forecast for the end of 2026 to 12.5% from 10%, and for 2027 to 7.3% from 6.9%. As before, the regulator expects inflation to return to its 5% target in 2028.
In the NBU's view, the previous tightening of interest rate policy has already supported the attractiveness of hryvnia-denominated assets: large banks have also begun raising rates on hryvnia deposits. The current decision is also intended to curb pressure on the foreign exchange market, which has intensified amid declining exports and deteriorating expectations against the backdrop of Russian attacks.
The minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee members' discussion preceding the decision to raise the key policy rate to 16.5% per annum will be published on November 9.
The next meeting of the NBU Board on monetary policy is scheduled for December 17, 2026.
As reported, after cutting the key policy rate to 15% in late January 2026, the NBU kept it at that level for three consecutive meetings before raising it by 0.5 pp three times in a row starting in July.

Denmark wants to ban ‘turbo chickens’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:30:04 UTC
21:30:04 KST

The Danish government wants to ban a fast-growing breed known as “turbo chickens,” setting up another clash with the farm sector over animal welfare.
“We can see that there are widespread problems with the welfare of turbo chickens," Danish Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen told news channel TV2 this week. "They simply grow too fast for their bodies to keep up."
The move, which would be first in the world, is the latest in a series of new restrictions for the country's farmers. The center-left coalition government, which rode to power on concerns about animal well-being in what was dubbed the "pig election" earlier this year, is now turning to poultry.
Advertisement
Madsen said he wants to ban the fast-growing chickens, known as the Ross 308 breed, at both the national and EU level. His announcement came just a day after a documentary aired with hidden-camera footage from a chicken farm. The footage showed chickens illegally getting just three hours of darkness a day to accelerate growth.
The Ross 308 breed, a widely used breed in poultry production, reaches a body weight of around 2 kilograms over just 33 days, but that can lead to injuries and trouble moving.
A broad group of parties appears to back the proposal. But questions over both the "legal and financial aspects" remain, Madsen acknowledged.
Chicken sector advocates warned that in practice, consumers would simply buy more meat from foreign farms, making it hard for Danish chicken farmers to compete. Poultry company Danpo told specialist outlet LandbrugsAvisen that it was prepared to move away from fast-growing breeds if the ban also covered imports.
But that could prove tricky on an EU level, where common rules of free movement of goods apply.
Denmark previously pushed Brussels to ban turbo chickens at the EU level in the past, and an earlier bid to ban them at the national level fizzled. Copenhagen's new effort is likely to find an ally in The Hague. The Dutch government proposed a similar national-level ban in September, which the parliament is now considering.
The European Commission plans to announce new welfare rules for chickens later this year. While it has promised a ban on cages and the practice of killing day-old male chicks, it has not announced any bans on certain breeds.

Oleh Makovetskyi will be tried for violating the laws and customs of war committed as part of a premeditated conspiracy by a group of individuals. He faces up to 15 years' imprisonment or a life sentence.
The museum in Skovorodynivka is a large memorial complex of monuments dating back to the 18th century, dedicated to the life and work of the famous Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhorii Savych Skovoroda. It was founded in 1972.

Strike on the museum in Skovorodynivka

At that time, the missile struck beneath the roof of the building, igniting a fire that engulfed the entire museum. The 35-year-old son of the museum director, who had stayed behind to guard the premises overnight, suffered injuries. He was pulled from under the rubble and taken to hospital.
Only the statue of the philosopher survived the missile strike, becoming a distinctive symbol of resilience. Later, museum staff collected shards of pottery, metal fragments and charred books.
In 2024, the Security Service of Ukraine identified who had ordered the destruction of the Skovoroda Museum. It turned out to be Ivan Panchenko, commander of the 159th Fighter Aviation Regiment of the Western Military District of the Russian Armed Forces.
