Asian Cybersecurity in the Age of AI and Quantum Computing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

It was immediately apparent to habitués of Singapore International Cyber Week (SICW) that this year’s edition – the 11th, which ran from October 12-15 – was going to be different. Just days before the opening, on October 9, Taira Masaaki, who heads the Liberal Democratic Party’s cybersecurity strategy headquarters, told an emergency party meeting that Japan was in “a state of emergency in cyberspace.” More than 20 major Japanese companies had disclosed attacks in the preceding weeks. A ransomware attack on IDC Frontier, SoftBank’s cloud subsidiary, on October 7 took down systems at 495 companies and local governments.
It is unclear whether artificial intelligence (AI) directed any of those attacks. However, what was clear was that AI was the frisson that changed – perhaps for good – the tone and tenor of discussions at the plenaries, the closed sessions, and the corridor conversations at SICW. It has perhaps altered permanently the nature of discourse at all cyber forums of equal scale and standing that aspire to similar convening power.
What follows are thoughts and takeaways on where we should go from here.
Companies With the Power of States
U.S. AI companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic were in the room this year at SICW. It would have been useful to also have had some of the large Chinese AI firms present in order to get a sense of the alternative approaches. But regardless of their country of origin, some of these firms wield the power of states, and of powerful states for that matter. Their models automate tasks, and as we have seen in 2026, that increasingly includes cyber attacks. As AI agents become increasingly autonomous, the infrastructure underpinning them becomes an increasingly attractive target for cyberattacks.
Yet the companies developing these technologies and governments see different elements of the threat. A government can monitor attacks on its own networks and critical infrastructure, whilst frontier AI labs and major cloud providers can detect patterns of malicious activity across their customers and services. Neither has the complete picture. Ransomware is a clear example of where this matters. If these different sources of intelligence can be brought together, it would make it easier to spot emerging threats and understand how attackers are operating in order to disrupt attacks before they spread.
This is also changing how governments work with industry. Traditionally, governments set cybersecurity requirements, consulted industry, and expected or legislated that companies comply. However, frontier AI presents a far more complicated problem, which changes the dynamic. The companies who develop advanced AI systems possess technical knowledge, operational experience, and insights into emerging threats that governments cannot easily replicate.
The dichotomy here lies in the fact that while governments are considering how AI companies should be regulated, they are increasingly reliant on the technology and the expertise those same companies have. This means that the companies themselves have considerable influence over the decisions governments are trying to make about them.
Australia’s 2026 cyber threat assessment, released in October, illustrates what is at stake perfectly. The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) warned that AI has been enabling malicious actors to identify vulnerabilities and carry out attacks – conduct espionage, steal money, and disrupt systems – at greater speed, scale, and sophistication. ASD Director General Abigail Bradshaw warned that frontier AI models had “redefined” the threat facing Australia, making further disruption to essential services increasingly likely.
The report pointed to emerging risks from the unintended behavior of AI agents, a problem that Australia has very publicly been managing over the past few months. Furthermore, it stated that there have been over 4,400 notifications to Australian organizations about possible malicious activity over the past year, which is an increase of almost 80 percent from 2025.
Bradshaw went on to state that ASD had been working directly with frontier AI companies, including OpenAI, to establish new early-warning protocols around emerging model capabilities and their potential misuse. These arrangements have also been shared with other AI labs and Five Eyes intelligence partners. This is significant as it demonstrates intelligence agencies need to work with AI frontier labs before new capabilities are widely deployed, rather than responding to the threats that they appear to increasingly unleash. The question is how do governments secure that cooperation while retaining independence and authority to regulate those same companies.
This is where Singapore’s approach becomes particularly interesting.
It seems likely that Singapore’s approach will (as so often is the case in these matters) be measured and shorn of histrionics – relying on the assumption that the cooperative approach can work, at least in the first instance. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo, who is at the helm of the cybersecurity portfolio, while noting the safeguards put in place by frontier AI companies, said that these were insufficient, given the risks posed by increasingly capable systems. She also told Parliament days before SICW opened that Singapore does not currently require frontier AI developers to give the government access to their models, warning that a rigid requirement could be counterproductive if it makes companies limit cooperation or information-sharing. The non-coercive approach was on view when Anthropic, in the course of opening its Singapore office, signed an MOU covering AI safety, security, and model evaluation at Cyber Week.
Filling the Quantum Gap
Amid all the talk of AI, it was easy to miss some of the deeper signals and concerns emanating from conversations at SICW.
Post-quantum cryptography was the quieter theme, perhaps because technically, it does not have a date attached to it. A quantum computer able to break today’s public-key encryption does not yet exist, but there was general agreement that that day – “Q-Day” – can be glimpsed on the horizon.
The problem here is that we do not need to reach Q-Day for the risks to eventuate. Policymakers and technical experts across the region should be considering it now, rather than assuming that their successors will carry the can. The risk to secrets is already real, because data stolen now can be stored and decrypted later. Organizations holding information that needs to remain confidential for years to come should already be planning their migration to quantum-resistant cryptography. Even after this is completed, systems will require continual monitoring and updating as the technology and subsequent threat evolves.
All this also means the need for discussions and coordination not just within but across regions. Australia has recommended that companies complete the transition by the end of 2030. Singapore has set 2031 as the target for critical infrastructure and 2035 for everyone else. At surface level these timelines appear reasonable, but international networks and supply chains do not operate within national boundaries. If one country, or one part of a network, has migrated while another has not, the security communications and data shared between them remains exposed. Therefore, industry and governments need to think beyond their own migration deadlines and consider how different timelines will impact the networks and services that connect them.
The Politics of Getting Everyone in the Room
Despite these uncertainties, there were positives that underlined SICW’s convening power. The event brought Washington, Beijing, and Moscow into the same building, alongside ASEAN’s cyber ministers, the United Nations, and, this year, senior officials from Anthropic and OpenAI. No other annual cyber convention meeting assembles all of those layers at once.
The interactions should not be sugar-coated. Officials from the EU walked out of the High-Level Panel on Diplomacy, which featured a Russian official (Dmitrii Bukin from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs), just as they had done in 2025. (Some did, however, leave staffers at the end of the room to take notes). And there were occasional sharp moments from the United States, for example when Sean Cairncross, the United States national cyber director, used the plenary to attack digital authoritarianism. Chinese officials chose not to respond directly, and it does not appear that others (including ASEAN states) shared these sentiments.
SICW is not – at least not yet – a showpiece for great power cyber grandstanding. Singapore officials may well want to keep the tone even-handed. At the same time, they may value balance, with middle and even smaller powers having a seat at the table. After all, Singapore officials repeatedly averred in and about SICW that the decisions in this realm cannot be left to the major powers and the frontier AI companies, and that cyber diplomacy has to involve all. The program reflected that, with delegations from Timor-Leste to Tuvalu.
Australia is on the same page and is playing a role in this respect. When it helped set up the Pacific Cyber Security Operational Network in 2018, the point was to give every Pacific incident responder a counterpart to call, and most of those calls now go island to island rather than through Canberra. Tuvalu shows how far the layers have joined. The Falepili Union of 2023 gave Australia a security role in a country of 11,000 people, and ground has since been broken on the Tuvalu Vaka cable, a US$56 million link delivered with Google and backed by Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Taiwan, and the United States.
What to Do Before 2027
Cyber diplomacy has enough rules. It needs more follow-through.
The common thread is that the technology now moves faster than the policy written to govern it. It would be tempting therefore to suggest that new norms are needed. But our conclusion from the week is that the region does not need a new set of rules. The norms already agreed at the United Nations and endorsed within ASEAN (in the case of the GGE, the Group of Governmental Experts, with the permanent mechanism established by the OEWG also being welcomed by the body) are adequate to the task. What is missing is implementation, and that is work small and middle powers are well placed to lead.
What is actually required is picking a small number of things the countries in the room can do together, and doing them before the next SICW. Three concrete steps follow from this year’s discussions.
First, align post-quantum migration deadlines across shared infrastructure, or at least agree which systems must migrate on the earlier timeline whoever owns them. Second, build information-sharing arrangements with the large technology firms that give governments the view of telemetry they cannot collect themselves, on terms that survive a change of chief executive. Third, agree on a common ASEAN vocabulary for AI risk that carries weight and meaning beyond the region, so that a regulator in Jakarta and a regulator in Canberra mean the same thing when they describe risk.
Singapore chairs ASEAN in 2027, which makes the next SIWC especially significant. For Australia and Singapore it is the first real test of whether small and middle powers can set a cyber agenda rather than hold a seat while others set it.
The rules are written. The next 12 months will show who is prepared to carry them out.

A week of Israel’s lockdown in Hebron: What’s happened, when will it end?
Israel is imposing a tight siege of Hebron amid raids, home demolitions and displacement.
The Israeli army is continuing its military lockdown of Hebron for the seventh consecutive day, carrying out raids and tightening restrictions in the occupied West Bank’s largest city.
Two Palestinians were injured and seven detained by Israeli forces on Thursday, according to the Wafa news agency, as Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians and their vehicles in the Ras al-Joura area, near the city’s northern entrance.
Israel has imposed a tight siege of Hebron since Friday last week, closing all entrances and exits and restricting residents’ freedom of movement and their ability to access critical services. More than 3,000 people have been forced out of the city as a number of Palestinian homes have been converted into military posts and barracks.
Meanwhile, Israeli settlers carried out attacks on Palestinian communities around Hebron. In the latest incident on Wednesday, settlers assaulted three foreign journalists, Andrey Ilyich Khrzhanovskiy, also known as Andrey X, Adele Shoko and Jasper Nathaniel. Andrey X reportedly lost consciousness, was taken to a police station and remained detained without receiving medical care.
What has happened over the past week in Hebron?
Israel’s campaign follows the killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint near the illegal Israeli settlement of Telem last week. The gunmen were later killed by Israeli forces in Hebron.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced on social media that he had ordered security forces to immediately close Hebron and “prepare for a full lockdown across all of Judea and Samaria [the Israeli term for the occupied West Bank].
“We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely,” he proclaimed.
Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for “a comprehensive military campaign in [the West Bank]… exactly as we did in Gaza”. A United Nations inquiry last year found Israel’s war on Gaza constituted a genocide.
As the siege began, Israeli forces launched a large demolition operation on dozens of Palestinian buildings. Troops also stormed the Ein Deir Bahha neighbourhood, forcing dozens of families to flee their homes at night without any belongings.
Footage showed Israeli soldiers beating and injuring Hijazi Shawer, a 70-year-old Palestinian shopkeeper and community leader.
Israeli forces also fired tear gas canisters at Al-Ahli Hospital in Hebron, causing panic among patients and staff. Hospitals are strictly protected under international humanitarian law, but the Israeli military has been known to attack hospitals throughout its genocidal war on Gaza, as well.
On Wednesday, the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society reported that at least 110 people had been detained in the Hebron governorate since the raids began, including three women and seven children.
As Israeli forces besieged Hebron, they also isolated 12 villages and hamlets in the Masafer Yatta region in the south, leaving residents and farmers cut off from urban centres and markets, and dozens of patients who require daily medical care unable to reach hospitals.
Israeli settlers uprooted more than 200 fruit trees, destroyed water wells and agricultural facilities east of Hebron, and prevented farmers from harvesting olives, Wafa reported. Hebron accounts for about 40 percent of Palestinian industrial output and 30 percent of exports.
Israeli forces on Wednesday detained a Palestinian victim of a settler assault in the Khirbet Quwaweis area of Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron. A young man and a woman were also detained in the al-Kassara area, south of Hebron, following an Israeli raid on Monday.
What have the responses to this been?
Palestinian officials have accused Netanyahu and his hard-right government of exploiting the operation to secure settler votes before Tuesday’s elections in Israel this week.
Palestinian human rights organisation Al-Haq said the siege of Hebron violates international law and amounts to an international crime. “Given the illegality of Israel’s military occupation and the illegal settler colonial apartheid regime, the entire military operation in Hebron constitutes a prohibited act of aggression,” it stated.
The Israeli NGO B’Tselem said the Israeli military’s “operation in Hebron has nothing to do with security. It is an act of collective punishment.”
UN Human Rights Chief Volker Turk said: “Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing.”
Roland Friedrich, the director of UNRWA Affairs for the occupied West Bank, said the developments brought “alarming echoes of the massive displacement witnessed in the northern occupied West Bank in early 2025, where more than 34,000 Palestine refugees from Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps remain forcibly displaced over a year later”.
Muhammed Shehada, at the Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, told Al Jazeera that the Israeli government’s use of collective punishment as a tool of deterrence against Palestinians has reached unprecedented levels.
“It’s not just about punishing the family [of an attacker], but it’s about punishing the entire community, the whole neighbourhood, the whole town and even the whole city,” he said.
Shehada argued that the genocide in Gaza had turned previously “unthinkable” policies into “core tactics”. “The Israeli government’s goal is to advance de facto annexation, ethnic cleansing in the West Bank by making life impossible,” he said.
In this context, Shehada added, collective punishment should be seen as “a terror tactic” to prevent any reaction to the unprecedented pace of ethnic cleansing and displacement of the Palestinian population.

Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:27:31 GMT

Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal
- Published
For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this coming two-day meeting in Montreal.
Thursday and Friday's summit will be closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.
The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
Von der Leyen, speaking to reporters after landing in Montreal on Wednesday, said the two sides will "start discussing how to make Canada the first associate member of the EU".
"Our ambition is to build the closest partnership we have ever had with a non-European country," she said.
Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship.
Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.
According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".
Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement last month.
The concept of "associate membership", he added, is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada.
"Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.
Lüttenberg noted, however, that neither Canada nor the EU is seeking full membership for the North American country.
Rather, both want to bring Canada "as close as possible" to the bloc without membership.
On the first day of the summit, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.
Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days.
Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months.
But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic.
Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.
And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties.
"The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit.
- What could EU associate member status mean for Canada? 
  - Published19 hours ago
- Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member' 
  - Published17 September
Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer.
US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway.
Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme.
It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.
Carney said earlier this week that the summit would "launch further formal discussions" between Canada and the EU on deepening ties and creating new opportunities for both sides.
As for what this new relationship status will be called, the prime minister said the "nomenclature" does not matter.
"What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:26:25 UTC
21:26:25 KST

NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s
NASA’s Juno spacecraft has uncovered Jupiter’s surprisingly complex defense against the solar wind, revealing physics that could help explain the power of exploding stars.
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- University of Iowa
- Summary:
- NASA’s Juno spacecraft has discovered that Jupiter uses a surprisingly complex system of powerful plasma waves and multiple shock regions to defend against the solar wind. The findings reveal major differences between Jupiter and Earth and could help scientists understand the enormous shock waves produced by exploding stars.
- Share:
NASA's Juno spacecraft has uncovered remarkable new details about how Jupiter withstands the constant stream of high-energy particles flowing from the Sun. The findings reveal that the solar system's largest planet relies on a much more complex system of plasma waves and shock regions than Earth does.
Led by scientists at the University of Iowa, the research provides the most detailed observations yet of Jupiter's bow shock, an invisible boundary where particles from the Sun encounter the planet's magnetic environment. The discovery reveals important differences in how Jupiter and Earth respond to these incoming particles.
Beyond Jupiter, the results could also help scientists understand some of the most powerful events in the universe, including the extreme shock waves associated with exploding stars.
How Jupiter Protects Itself From the Solar Wind
The Sun continuously releases a stream of electrically charged particles called the solar wind. These particles travel through space at tremendous speeds, often faster than the speed at which sound waves move through the surrounding plasma. When the solar wind approaches a planet with a magnetic field, it encounters a boundary known as the bow shock.
At Earth, this boundary plays an important protective role. It slows and heats the incoming particles, helping redirect much of the solar wind around the planet. Without this process, more harmful particles could reach Earth's atmosphere, potentially making conditions less favorable for life.
Jupiter also has a bow shock, but its enormous size, powerful magnetic field, and gaseous composition make it a particularly interesting place to study how these boundaries behave. Scientists have long wanted to understand whether Jupiter handles the solar wind differently from Earth and what those differences might reveal about other objects throughout the universe.
Scientists Discover a More Complex Defense System
Using measurements from Juno, researchers discovered that Jupiter relies on plasma waves with multiple frequencies to slow and heat incoming solar particles. These different frequencies, known as "harmonics," create a more elaborate wave pattern than the one typically observed at Earth.
The process can be compared to music. Just as several notes played together produce a richer sound than a single note, plasma waves containing multiple frequencies can interact with incoming particles in more complex ways. This allows Jupiter's bow shock to transfer energy to more particles, heating them and reducing their speed.
Earth's bow shock, by comparison, primarily uses plasma waves concentrated around a single frequency. That simpler arrangement is generally sufficient for the conditions encountered near our planet.
"Jupiter has found its own way to deal with the solar wind, through plasma waves that are stronger and exhibit richer harmonic structures," says Jayasri Joseph, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Iowa and the study's corresponding author. "That's important because if you have multiple frequencies, you can heat more particles in the solar wind and slow them down."
Jupiter Has an Extra Line of Defense
The researchers identified another striking difference in how the two planets interact with the solar wind.
Before incoming particles reach Jupiter's main bow shock, they can encounter smaller shock structures called shocklets. These additional regions help slow the solar wind before it arrives at the primary shock boundary.
Earth's bow shock, in contrast, generally serves as the main region where the incoming solar wind is slowed and redirected. Jupiter's additional shock structures reveal a more complicated process for managing the energy carried by solar particles.
"Earth does not need to take these extra steps to handle the solar wind because the impact isn't as powerful," says Bill Kurth, a research scientist in Iowa's Department of Physics and Astronomy and a coauthor of the study.
Kurth has participated in NASA's Juno mission since the spacecraft launched in 2011.
What Jupiter Can Teach Us About Exploding Stars
Although these observations focus on Jupiter, their significance could extend far beyond our solar system.
Shock waves occur throughout the universe, particularly in environments where enormous amounts of energy are released. Some of the most extreme examples are found in supernova remnants, the expanding clouds of material left behind when certain dying stars explode.
These cosmic shock waves are vastly more powerful than those encountered near Jupiter. However, the physical processes that control how energy moves through plasma share important similarities. By examining Jupiter's bow shock in unprecedented detail, scientists can investigate mechanisms that would be much harder to measure directly around distant stars.
"Because even more powerful shocks occur around astrophysical objects such as supernova remnants, Jupiter's bow shock offers a nearby natural laboratory for exploring and for understanding how nature converts enormous amounts of flow energy into heat and energetic particles," Joseph says.
Understanding these processes could improve scientific models of how shock waves transfer energy, heat particles, and shape environments across the universe.
NASA's Juno Makes Unprecedented Measurements
The breakthrough was made possible by observations Juno collected in December 2024. The NASA spacecraft has been orbiting Jupiter since July 2016, providing researchers with an extraordinary opportunity to investigate the giant planet and its surrounding environment.
A key part of the discovery came from the Juno Waves instrument, which was designed and built by physicists at the University of Iowa. The instrument measures electric and magnetic wave activity, allowing scientists to study the behavior of plasma around Jupiter.
Earlier spacecraft had detected the presence of bow shocks at outer planets, but they lacked the measurements needed to reveal the detailed structure of the plasma waves involved. Juno's observations have now provided a much clearer picture of how these waves behave at Jupiter.
The findings were published online on July 31 in Nature Communications in a study titled "Plasma wave observations from Juno spacecraft at the Jovian bow shock."
Research Team and NASA Support
Additional contributors from the University of Iowa included Allison Jaynes, an associate professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy, along with Jeremy Faden and Chris Piker, who provide research support in the same department.
The international research team also included Lynn Wilson III of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; John Connerney of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center and the Space Research Corporation; Frederic Allegrini of the Southwest Research Institute and the University of Texas-San Antonio; Rob Wilson of the University of Colorado-Boulder; Ali Sulaiman of the University of Minnesota; Scott Boltion and Robert Ebert of the Southwest Research Institute; and Barry Mauk of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory.
NASA provided funding for the research.

Materials provided by University of Iowa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- J. Joseph, W. S. Kurth, L. B. Wilson, J. E. P. Connerney, F. Allegrini, R. J. Wilson, A. H. Sulaiman, R. W. Ebert, J. B. Faden, C. W. Piker, A. N. Jaynes, B. H. Mauk, S. J. Bolton. Plasma wave observations from Juno spacecraft at the Jovian bow shock. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76223-x

Ukraine to Co-Found New International Defence Bank With Canada and European Partners
Ukraine will become a co-founder of the new Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), joining Canada and eight other countries in establishing the international institution, Canada’s Department of Finance announced on October 26.
Canadian Finance and National Revenue Minister François-Philippe Champagne confirmed that Canada, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Türkiye, and Ukraine will jointly establish the DSRB.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The participating countries are expected to sign the bank’s Articles of Agreement in Luxembourg on November 30, 2026. The DSRB will be headquartered in Canada and operate a European hub in Luxembourg.
The bank is being created to mobilize public and private capital for defense, security, and resilience projects among participating countries. Its mandate will include sovereign financing, expansion of defense-industrial capacity, critical supply chains, and eligible defense procurement.
The DSRB is also intended to address financing gaps faced by governments and defense companies, including small- and medium-sized enterprises. Financing will be available to eligible members on equal terms, regardless of their size or economic capacity.
Canada stated that the bank will seek a AAA credit rating backed by participating countries, allowing it to reduce borrowing costs, expand access to long-term financing, and attract additional commercial investment into the defense sector.
“In an increasingly uncertain and divided world, Canada is working to bring together like-minded partners to mobilize and deploy private capital in support of collective security,” Champagne stated.
Membership will remain open to other allies and close partners that share the bank’s objectives.
The November signing follows negotiations on the Articles of Agreement held in Montréal in spring 2026 and a joint declaration issued by participating countries in July. Canada expects the DSRB to become fully operational in 2027.
The new DSRB would add another financing mechanism for defense support involving Ukraine. UNITED24 Media previously reported that NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) allows allies to finance US-made weapons requested by Kyiv, with the mechanism supplying 95% of Ukraine’s Patriot missiles one year after its launch.

Russia’s Gold Reserves Hit Lowest Level Since 2019 as War Costs Drain State Finances

- Category

Russia’s Gold Reserves Hit Lowest Level Since 2019 as War Costs Drain State Finances
Russia is drawing down its gold reserves to cover a widening budget deficit, according to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) on October 28. The growing financial pressure stems from declining oil and gas revenues and rising government spending, including expenditures on the war against Ukraine.
The agency reported that Russia’s Central Bank reduced its physical holdings of monetary gold for the tenth consecutive month in September 2026. During the month, reserves fell by 6.2 metric tons to approximately 2,260 tons, their lowest level since late 2019.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Since December 2025, Russia’s gold holdings have declined by approximately 62 tons, representing a 2.7% reduction, according to the intelligence service.
The decline comes amid a broader reduction in Russia’s international reserves. As of October 9, their total value stood at approximately $723.5 billion, down $45.5 billion, or 5.9%, from the beginning of September.
Between September and October, the dollar value of Russia’s monetary gold holdings also decreased from $333.5 billion to $301.6 billion. The SZRU attributed the decline not only to the reduction in physical gold reserves but also to fluctuations in market prices and the revaluation of assets.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the Russian government has increasingly relied on accumulated reserves to address its growing budget deficit.
“Oil and gas revenues are declining, while government spending, particularly on the war against Ukraine, remains high. To cover the funding shortfall, Russia’s Ministry of Finance sells foreign currency and gold assets from the National Wealth Fund to the Central Bank in exchange for rubles. The Central Bank then conducts corresponding transactions on the domestic market using Chinese yuan and gold,” the statement read.
However, the SZRU noted that Russia’s ability to access its reserves remains constrained by international sanctions imposed following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A substantial portion of the Russian Central Bank’s foreign assets has been frozen since 2022, leaving domestically held gold and yuan-denominated assets among the more accessible resources for financial operations.
As a result, the agency emphasized that the total value of Russia’s international reserves does not accurately reflect the amount of funding immediately available to the Russian government.
While selling reserve assets allows Moscow to temporarily sustain government spending without immediately increasing borrowing or reducing expenditures, the intelligence service warned that such measures cannot replace stable sources of revenue.
If the budget deficit persists and reserves are not replenished, Russia could face increasing pressure to borrow more, raise taxes, or reduce government programs to maintain its financial commitments.
“The decline in gold reserves reflects mounting financial constraints on Russia. The war is consuming government resources, while falling revenues are forcing the Kremlin to draw on its accumulated reserves. As these reserves continue to shrink, financing current expenditures without increasing debt, raising taxes, or cutting spending will become increasingly difficult,” SZRU added.
The pressure on Russia’s finances is also reflected in the scale of its military expenditures. Russia spends more than $200 billion annually on its war against Ukraine, an amount that appears to represent the upper limit of what Moscow and its economy can currently sustain as sanctions continue to restrict additional revenue generation.
Concerns over Russia’s fiscal position have also emerged in assessments of its proposed federal budget for 2027–2029.
On October 22, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported that the draft budget contained significant discrepancies, insufficiently substantiated revenue forecasts, and substantial amounts of spending without clearly defined allocations.
Citing findings by Russia’s Accounts Chamber, the agency said that supporting documentation for $288.24 billion in expenditures, representing 77% of the publicly disclosed portion of the 2027 federal budget, was inconsistent with the draft’s financial parameters.
The documents also lacked supporting calculations for 13 revenue categories totaling $9.72 billion, raising further questions about the reliability of the government’s budget projections.

Russia at Sea, China in the Air—Japan Tracks Spy Ship and Recon Aircraft Near Its Islands
Japan tracked a Russian Navy intelligence-gathering ship moving through the Tsushima Strait while three Chinese military aircraft operated near the country’s southwestern islands, Japan’s Joint Staff said on October 28.
Between October 27 and 28, the Russian Navy intelligence ship SSV-535 Kareliya, a Meridian-class vessel, sailed southwest through the Tsushima Strait before continuing toward the East China Sea.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Soviet-designed Project 864 Meridian class is built for signals intelligence, including intercepting communications and monitoring radar emissions. The ships carry extensive antenna arrays beneath distinctive radomes and are also equipped for hydroacoustic intelligence collection.
Japan’s Maritime Self-Defense Force dispatched the minesweeper Hirashima, assigned to the 3rd Minesweeper Division at Sasebo, to monitor the Russian vessel. A P-1 maritime patrol aircraft from the 4th Air Wing at Atsugi also tracked its movement from the air.
Later on October 28, Chinese military aviation activity was detected in the same broader region.
A Chinese BZK-005 reconnaissance drone and a Y-9 intelligence aircraft flew from the East China Sea toward the Pacific, passing through the airspace corridor between Okinawa and Miyako islands. After turning over the Pacific, both aircraft returned toward mainland China along approximately the same route.
The BZK-005 is a long-endurance reconnaissance UAV capable of remaining airborne for up to 40 hours. It carries electro-optical and infrared sensors as well as synthetic-aperture radar for surveillance missions.
The Y-9 reconnaissance variant is designed for signals and electronic intelligence, using antenna arrays positioned along the fuselage to intercept communications and locate radar emitters.
A third Chinese aircraft, a maritime patrol variant of the Y-9 family, also operated in the region the same day, flying from the direction of mainland China toward waters southwest of the Danjo Islands and northwest of Okinawa.
The maritime patrol version carries a nose-mounted search radar, a magnetic anomaly detector in the tail for locating submarines, electro-optical sensors, and an internal weapons bay capable of carrying sonobuoys, torpedoes, and anti-ship missiles.
Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighters from its Southwestern Air Defense Command to monitor the Chinese aircraft.
Earlier, reports emerged that Japan scrambled fighter jets 442 times in response to Chinese and Russian aircraft during the first half of fiscal year 2026, up sharply from 265 scrambles during the same period last year.

The Verkhovna Rada supported a fine of 170,000 hryvnias for the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers for illegally registering people for military service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:23:37 EET
21:23:37 KST

The Verkhovna Rada supported a fine of 170,000 hryvnias for the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers for illegally registering people for military service
Kyiv • UNN
Members of Parliament supported a 170,000-hryvnia fine for the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers for illegally registering citizens for military service. The provision is not yet in effect.
The Verkhovna Rada, in the bill strengthening liability for organizing and using so-called drop schemes, also supported an amendment providing for a fine of 170,000 hryvnias for employees of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers for unlawfully registering citizens for military service who are not subject to such a procedure, UNN reports.
Details
On Wednesday, October 28, the Verkhovna Rada adopted a law that strengthens criminal liability for illegal transactions involving bank cards, accounts, and electronic wallets. The document provides for fines of up to 170,000 hryvnias and imprisonment for up to six years for organizing and using so-called drop schemes.
Before the second reading, Amendment No. 11 was submitted to the bill, supplementing Article 201-1 of the Code of Ukraine on Administrative Offenses with the following provision: "a violation by an official of the procedure for keeping military registration records of conscripts, persons liable for military service, or reservists, which resulted in the registration of persons who, under the law, are not subject to military registration as conscripts, persons liable for military service, or reservists, entails the imposition of a fine amounting to ten thousand non-taxable minimum incomes of citizens."
That is, liability is provided for Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers for registering persons for military service who are not subject to such registration. A fine of 170,000 hryvnias will be imposed for such a violation.
The Verkhovna Rada Committee on Law Enforcement, while preparing the bill for its second reading, rejected this amendment; however, during the vote, the lawmakers supported it, and it was included in the final version of the bill.
However, it should be noted that these provisions are not yet in force, as the document must first be signed by Verkhovna Rada Speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk and President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who may veto the law, after which the document must be published in the parliamentary newspaper "Holos Ukrainy."
The law is to enter into force on the day following the day of its publication.
We remind you
The law strengthening liability for electronic communications fraud and the activities of fraudulent "call centers," which provides for punishment of up to 12 years in prison, entered into force on Friday, September 18.

Alyssa Mcmurtry
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
The death toll from Spain’s high-speed rail disaster rose to 69 on Thursday as questions mounted over why safety systems failed to prevent a train from slamming into another that was stopped ahead.
Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of Castile-La Mancha, announced the latest death following Wednesday’s collision near Urda in Toledo province.
Of 110 people hospitalized, 60 had been discharged and 50 remained under treatment, he said. The four most seriously injured among 15 critical patients were improving, offering grounds for cautious optimism, he added.
Crews were removing wreckage and identifying victims after recovering additional human remains overnight. Garcia-Page said authorities did not expect to find more bodies beneath the carriages.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged to establish what happened and prevent another disaster.
“The entire central government is working day and night to respond to victims’ families, clarify every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety so this does not happen again,” he said at a joint news conference with Garcia-Page.
Safety failures under scrutiny
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said Wednesday that a technical failure of the LZB automatic train protection system stopped at least six trains before controllers authorized a Renfe train to resume normal speed, meaning up to 200 kilometers (124 miles) per hour.
Puente called that decision “inexplicable,” given that an Iryo train remained stationary ahead. The controller has reportedly been questioned by Spanish police.
Recordings broadcast by Spanish media captured the authorization to resume normal running. The Iryo driver also reported being unable to move about five minutes before the impact, according to the recordings.
The disaster has renewed scrutiny of safeguards when automatic protection fails.
Spain’s rail accident investigation commission warned after a 2024 incident in Cuenca that the only effective barrier against a potential collision had been a controller’s visual check that the track section was clear – something which appears to have been the case again in Wednesday’s tragedy.
That safeguard depended entirely on human judgment and could fail, the commission said, recommending technical protections, according to a report cited by Cadena SER.
Experts also questioned both infrastructure upkeep and operational decisions. Spain spent €95,860 ($106,812) per kilometer on rail maintenance in 2022, roughly half the EU average, according to European Commission figures cited by El Pais.
Meanwhile, high-speed passenger numbers reached 44.5 million last year, double the 2019 total, the newspaper reported.
Engineer Jordi Vinolas Prat told El Pais that the system itself “worked perfectly” by stopping the trains, but the crucial question was related to internal protocol and how this type of mistake was allowed to happen.
The crash comes amid campaigning for Spain’s national elections and follows January’s high-speed collision in Adamuz, which killed 46 people.
Sanchez said Wednesday that two high-speed rail disasters in one year were “unacceptable.”
Opposition leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo demanded a “complete and independent review” of the rail network and answers about warnings received over the past year. The left-wing Frente Amplio also called for an independent audit and for the transport minister to testify in the Spanish parliament.
The far-right Vox party was the only party to have continued campaigning Wednesday, with its leader Santiago Abascal blaming the disaster on Sanchez’s “corruption and ideological fanaticism.”

Mazari, who has won international recognition for speaking out against the disappearances of political activists and for defending minorities and journalists, and Chattha have drawn support from rights groups that have condemned their imprisonment.

The public prosecutor did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Mazari and Chattha have been in custody since their arrest on January 23 in a separate case over social media posts that prosecutors said were anti-state.

Spain’s deadly train crash adds new complication to Sanchez reelection campaign
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:19:28 CET

By Victoria Waldersee and Charlie Devereux
MADRID, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had hoped to ride a wave of public anger over the eviction of an octogenarian, who later died, to win reelection in a snap election, but Wednesday’s deadly train crash has dealt a serious blow to his campaign.
The accident in Toledo province killed 68 people and came just nine months after another deadly crash on the same line, leading to accusations from experts and the public of underinvestment in railway infrastructure under Sanchez’s government after years of rapid network expansion.
“If we were scared of taking trains before, now we’re even more so … Just when you think nothing else could possibly go wrong, something new happens. There needs to be major change,” Oscar, a 24-year-old who declined to give his last name, said at Madrid’s Atocha station on Wednesday.
Speaking at the accident site on Wednesday, Sanchez said the “terrible tragedy” would be investigated and pledged to address any failures that came to light.
“If we need to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so, because it is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” he said.
Sanchez, who had been trailing in most opinion polls, had appeared to be gaining some traction, with an October survey by state-run pollster CIS showing his party ahead with just weeks to go to the November 29 election.
The death of Maricarmen Abascal, who was evicted from her home of more than 70 years, sparked widespread protests across Spain, focusing political attention on a housing crisis that is cited in polls as the top priority for most Spaniards.
The outcry over Abascal, which led Sanchez to call for a snap election on October 5, was an opportunity to divert media attention from his government’s handling of a migrant crisis in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta this summer. Right-wing parties and security forces had accused the Socialists of underinvestment in border infrastructure despite repeated warnings from staff.
NO ROOM FOR ‘TRIUMPHALIST RHETORIC’
Sanchez, 54, has pitched himself as the candidate of progress instead of a return by the far right to government for the first time since the death of dictator Francisco Franco.
He has so far run a positive, upbeat campaign, giving interviews on pop culture talk shows and podcasts as his party attempts to mobilise millions of undecided left-leaning voters to the polls.
“I don’t think that triumphalist rhetoric … has any place right now and I suspect it will be a long time before we see that kind of attitude return,” said Paco Camas, public affairs director at pollster Ipsos.
This week’s crash will force a shift towards a more sombre tone, Camas said.
Sanchez’s opponents immediately called for accountability and said they would not be silenced by mourning.
“Pain does not oblige us to keep quiet. Serenity is not silence… Spaniards will ask urgent questions which deserve answers,” said Alberto Nuñez Feijoo, president of the conservative People’s Party, promising a full review of the network if he came into power.
PROTESTERS GATHER IN MADRID
On Wednesday evening, hundreds of mostly far-right demonstrators gathered in front of Spain’s Transport Ministry to call for Sanchez’s resignation, with one carrying a banner emblazoned with the words, “Spain can’t take it anymore.”
“This government has destroyed absolutely everything, including infrastructure,” said Santiago Abascal, the leader of far-right Vox at a rally on Wednesday. “We will not let them use the mourning we share, the anger, pain and indignation, to silence even for a second the condemnation of what is happening in Spain.”
Transport Minister Oscar Puente rejected allegations in a press conference on Wednesday that Spain’s railway system was dangerous, stating it was “reliable and safe … with the limits of the material itself and of human action, as is the case with any form of transport.”
NO TRUST IN RAIL SERVICES
Sanchez once touted the country’s 4,000 km (2,485 miles) high-speed rail system - the world’s second-largest after China’s - as a political asset, though it may now become a liability.
Polls in Spanish media conducted in January after the last fatal crash showed 57% perceived a worsening of rail services since Sanchez came into office and nearly 60% stated they had little or no trust in Spain’s railway system.
An investigation into the cause of that accident is still underway, according to Spain’s transport ministry, with a preliminary report identifying a fracture in the rail which appeared to have occurred prior to the derailment.
High-speed rail use, which had broken records in 2024 and 2025, fell 15% in the first half of this year compared to the same period last year, data from Spain’s competition authority showed.
Puente declined to say on Wednesday whether he would step down, stating it was “not the time” to talk about himself.
(Reporting by Victoria Waldersee, Charlie Devereux, Corina Pons, Pietro Lombardi; Writing by Victoria Waldersee; Editing by Sharon Singleton)

Pompeii cupboard opens window onto life before Vesuvius erupted
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:19:26 CET
21:19:26 KST

By Crispian Balmer
ROME, Oct 29 (Reuters) - A cupboard sealed for almost 2,000 years in Pompeii has yielded an intimate snapshot of one resident’s life before Mount Vesuvius destroyed the ancient Roman city, from make-up utensils and perfume to coins, cooking pots and childhood amulets.
The once-thriving city of Pompeii, near Naples, was buried by a volcanic eruption in AD 79, preserving buildings, objects and graffiti under metres of ash.
Archaeologists pieced together bits of the wooden cupboard from traces uncovered in a house on Via dell’Abbondanza, one of the busiest streets of ancient Pompeii, the site said in a statement.
“We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of whoever lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their daily life,” said site director Gabriel Zuchtriegel.
Among the objects stored inside was a necklace comprising at least 24 tiny objects made of bone, glass paste, earthenware and rock crystal, including images of the gods Bes and Mercury, as well as miniature hands, feet, pine cones and bunches of grapes.
Such necklaces, known as crepundia, were traditionally given to Roman children both as protective amulets and as rattles whose sounds helped adults keep track of them.
They were sometimes kept into adulthood as mementos of childhood, offering a particularly personal connection to the unknown inhabitant of the house.
PERFUME, MONEY AND MICE
Other finds tell a more prosaic story of daily life.
There were tweezers, a small glass perfume or ointment bottle and an incense burner, alongside bronze, glass and ceramic vessels and cooking pots. Lead weights in a wooden box suggested that someone in the house was involved in trade.
A small woven container held 38 bronze coins.
The fact that both money and objects with apparent sentimental value remained behind suggests the owners had no time to retrieve them after Vesuvius erupted.
“Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art. It is also a place where the most ordinary objects restore the human dimension of the past,” Zuchtriegel said.
“The value of this discovery lies in the possibility of reading together the different traces of a life: personal habits, work and memories.”
The house, in a central area of Pompeii, is tentatively associated with a man named Cornelius Maximus because of inscriptions discovered there. Its facade was first excavated in 1912, but archaeologists have only now investigated some of the rooms behind it as part of a wider restoration project.
The excavation also provided evidence that some problems of urban living have changed remarkably little in two millennia, with archaeologists finding the fragmented skeletons of two young mice inside an amphora kept on a raised storage area.
(Reporting by Crispian Balmer, editing by Alvise Armellini)

South Korea is the final stop on Merz’s week-long trip to Asia, which has also taken him to Singapore and Japan.
During the tour, he has sought to strengthen defence ties and promote closer economic cooperation among like-minded countries as a counterweight to U.S. tariff policies and China’s state-backed industrial expansion.

Police name Serbian suspects in Tefaf jewellery heist
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch police have published the names of the five Serbian people suspected of robbing the Tefaf art fair in Maastricht in 2022. The gang got away with roughly €40 million in goods, according to Europol.
The suspects, four men and one woman, are Aleksandar Cenic (50), Aleksandar Stojiljkovic (50), Dusko Dimitrijevic (50), Bratislav Stojanovic (41) and Ninoslava Jovic (41). Police believe they are in the Serbian city of Niš or near Belgrade.
The public prosecution service (OM) is offering €20,000 for tip-offs leading to the arrest of any member of the group, who have all been placed on Europol’s most wanted list and the Dutch national wanted list, the OM said on Thursday.
The Serbian government is refusing extradition requests, which is standard practice for its own citizens. Dutch police said they hope that naming them will lead to tips about their movements, so they can be traced and caught if they travel abroad.
Four of the thieves went into the art fair on June 28, 2022, smartly dressed and wearing caps and glasses to partially conceal their identities. Police later identified a woman as a fifth suspect.
They were reportedly armed with what looked like guns, and were seen smashing glass cabinets with sledgehammers and grabbing jewellery. Two of the men held bystanders back with their weapons, and the gang fled on electric scooters.
None were caught in the immediate aftermath. Some of the stolen diamonds have since been recovered in Hong Kong, Israel and Botswana.
The fair’s insurer is also offering a reward of €500,000, broadcaster NOS reported.

Nearly 1,700 people have been killed and more than 7,000 injured in Yemen since August amid a military escalation, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Thursday, Anadolu reports.
In a report, the agency recorded 1,677 deaths and 7,395 injuries during the period, including 559 casualties between Oct. 20 and 25 alone, averaging about 93 casualties a day.
Fighting continued during the reporting period in the governorates of Taiz, Lahj, and Marib, while lower casualty figures were recorded in Aden, Al-Dhalea, and Shabwa, according to the report.
The WHO said it delivered 56 trauma and emergency kits to the city of Taiz on Oct. 24, including 46 kits for trauma care and 10 for emergency health services.
The delivery also included around 30 metric tons of medical supplies for three hospitals and one health center.
READ: Yemeni army claims 239 Houthis neutralized in 749 operations over 24 hours
The agency warned that only six of 31 mobile medical teams remained operational in Marib, leaving residents struggling to access health services amid damage to health facilities and shortages of supplies.
Al-Thawra General Hospital in Taiz city came under fire on Oct. 20, leaving three soldiers and one patient injured, according to the WHO.
The agency warned that continued disruption to essential services and shortages of medicines, fuel, and water, along with inadequate waste management, were increasing the risk of infectious disease outbreaks, particularly in Taiz.
Taiz, Yemen’s most populous province, remains divided between government forces and the Houthis. Government forces control Taiz city, the provincial capital, and other parts of the province.
Since July, military escalation between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has resumed, particularly in Taiz and Lahj, killing and injuring thousands, according to UN reports.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis divided the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014. A Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

Pompeii cupboard opens window onto life before Vesuvius erupted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:11:43 UTC
21:11:43 KST

Pompeii cupboard opens window onto life before Vesuvius erupted
ROME, Oct 29 - A cupboard sealed for almost 2,000 years in Pompeii has yielded an intimate snapshot of one resident's life before Mount Vesuvius destroyed the ancient Roman city, from make-up utensils and perfume to coins, cooking pots and childhood amulets.
The once-thriving city of Pompeii, near Naples, was buried by a volcanic eruption in AD 79, preserving buildings, objects and graffiti under metres of ash.
Archaeologists pieced together bits of the wooden cupboard from traces uncovered in a house on Via dell'Abbondanza, one of the busiest streets of ancient Pompeii, the site said in a statement.
"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of whoever lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their daily life," said site director Gabriel Zuchtriegel.
Among the objects stored inside was a necklace comprising at least 24 tiny objects made of bone, glass paste, earthenware and rock crystal, including images of the gods Bes and Mercury, as well as miniature hands, feet, pine cones and bunches of grapes.
Such necklaces, known as crepundia, were traditionally given to Roman children both as protective amulets and as rattles whose sounds helped adults keep track of them.
They were sometimes kept into adulthood as mementos of childhood, offering a particularly personal connection to the unknown inhabitant of the house.
PERFUME, MONEY AND MICE
Other finds tell a more prosaic story of daily life.
There were tweezers, a small glass perfume or ointment bottle and an incense burner, alongside bronze, glass and ceramic vessels and cooking pots. Lead weights in a wooden box suggested that someone in the house was involved in trade.
A small woven container held 38 bronze coins.
The fact that both money and objects with apparent sentimental value remained behind suggests the owners had no time to retrieve them after Vesuvius erupted.
"Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art. It is also a place where the most ordinary objects restore the human dimension of the past," Zuchtriegel said.
"The value of this discovery lies in the possibility of reading together the different traces of a life: personal habits, work and memories."
The house, in a central area of Pompeii, is tentatively associated with a man named Cornelius Maximus because of inscriptions discovered there. Its facade was first excavated in 1912, but archaeologists have only now investigated some of the rooms behind it as part of a wider restoration project.
The excavation also provided evidence that some problems of urban living have changed remarkably little in two millennia, with archaeologists finding the fragmented skeletons of two young mice inside an amphora kept on a raised storage area. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Scientists can now rewire living brains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:10:31 UTC
21:10:31 KST

The human brain holds around 86 billion neurons, wired together in a vast web of hundreds of trillions of connections. These connections, bridged by structures called synapses, form circuits responsible for everything we feel, perceive and do. And they constantly shift as we grow, learn, make memories and form habits.
Neuroscientists have long sought to hack into these circuits to understand how the brain works. Just 20 years ago they developed a technique called optogenetics, which offered some of the first glimpses of these circuits in action—it uses light to turn cells, including brain cells, on and off.
The work won three scientists the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. If brain pathways were highways, optogenetics would be akin to “controlling the volume of traffic on a road network that’s already built,” says Sangkyu Lee, a neurobiologist at the Institute for Basic Science in South Korea.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Better yet, however, would be “changing the structure of the ‘road’ itself,” Lee says—by actually editing the brain’s connections. More recently, scientists have figured out how to add new connections and delete existing ones, and they have used these techniques to change animals’ behavior and even to implant memories. Ultimately, these tools could yield discoveries about the brain and potentially even treatments for psychiatric conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).
“The idea that, by manipulating brain activity, you could, in principle, make someone happy or sad, or thirsty or hungry, is incredible when you think about the ramifications,” says Don Arnold, a neurobiologist at the University of Southern California.
Making Connections
Kafui Dzirasa, a psychiatrist at Duke University, stumbled into “synaptic engineering” by accident. He had been trying to develop treatments for psychiatric conditions using brain-machine interfaces to alter neural activity. Electrodes would pick up activity in one brain region and cause a computer to stimulate another—essentially “wiring” the two regions together. But as a potential treatment for mental illness, it was impractical. So Dzirasa began contemplating other ways to connect two disparate brain regions.
“We realized that’s what a synapse does, so we thought, ‘Why don't we just create a synapse?’” he says.
Neurobiologists had already developed a way to do this in a creature with a very simple brain: the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans. It has only around 300 neurons, making it ideal for neuroscientists to study. In 2014 Ithai Rabinowitch, a neurobiologist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and his colleagues successfully altered the worms’ behavior by rewiring their neural circuits.
The team did this by creating a kind of synapse that passes electrically charged particles between two cells through special protein channels. These proteins are made by genes that are snuck into cells’ DNA using a specially programmed virus. Rabinowitch’s team inserted mouse synapse proteins into the worms, which created artificial connections that didn’t interfere with worms’ existing synapses. The researchers were able to alter a circuit governing the worms’ sense of smell, causing them to avoid an odor they previously found attractive.
This technique has since been used to study neural circuits involved in everything from defecation to learning. In one striking example, another team of researchers used it to rewire a memory. First, they trained worms to prefer a specific temperature. Then they bypassed the memory with an electrical synapse, causing the worms to move toward warmer temperatures instead. “It’s like an inception experiment, where you plant a memory by making an artificial connection,” says that study’s senior author Daniel Colón-Ramos, a cell biologist at the Yale School of Medicine.
But could this approach work in the more complex brains of mammals? As brains get bigger and more complicated, the potential for unintended connections is harder to prevent—these can wreak havoc, potentially causing death. “You need to achieve much more control and precision in an animal with billions of neurons,” Colón-Ramos says.
In a study published in May, Dzirasa, Colón-Ramos and their team proved the technique could be done in a mouse. They created synapse proteins that only connected to a specially engineered partner—not to each other or to synapse proteins that were already in the mouse’s brain. They used the tool to connect different cell types in two brain circuits, producing changes in the mice’s behavior.
Some of these behavioral changes offer hints at parallels in human brains. In a study posted to the preprint server bioRxiv last March, Dzirasa and his colleagues tested the tool in mice with a genetic mutation that caused repetitive grooming behaviors reminiscent of OCD. The researchers introduced synapses to bypass the disrupted circuit, which reduced this pathological behavior. “That’s a clear demonstration of the potential power of this in thinking about human diseases,” Dzirasa says.
Adding Subtraction
Researchers have developed other techniques for engineering new connections, too. But some situations may call for the opposite approach: deleting existing connections. For instance, PTSD can cause otherwise innocuous sights or sounds to trigger anxiety. These reactions may stem from connections formed between sensory neurons and “negative emotion” cells in the amygdala.
“It’s tantalizing to think, if you could wipe those synapses out, maybe you’d get rid of this,” Arnold says.
So far, synapse-deleting tools are much less precise than synapse-adding ones. For example, Arnold and his colleagues discovered a technique that degrades proteins that hold synapses together, deleting them from neurons en masse. Last year they expanded this into a toolkit that can delete only inhibitory or only excitatory synapses (which respectively make neurons less or more likely to fire) and that can be activated with light or chemicals.
And in a study in April, Lee and his colleagues described a slightly more precise synapse-deleting tool called Synthetic Trogocytosis, or SynTrogo, which works by recruiting astrocytes, a type of brain cell that prunes synapses naturally. Using special “lock” and “key” proteins to trigger pruning, Lee’s team was able to delete less than a third of specific cell types’ synapses in two parts of mice’s hippocampus, a brain region that is crucial for memory. The remaining connections became stronger, and the mice showed better performance than unedited animals in memory tests. This finding hints at potential applications in neurodevelopmental conditions that involve abnormal connectivity, such as schizophrenia, but also those involving memory impairment, such as dementia.
Having techniques that can delete as well as add synapses “gives much more versatility,” Colón-Ramos says. “You have a gas pedal, but now you also have brakes, so you can do much more.”
Looking ahead, Rabinowitch envisages a day when scientists can construct designer connectomes—entire brains’ worth of custom connections. “You sit by your computer and say, ‘Let’s build this brain,’” he says. “Then it spills out the list of genes you need to introduce into the organism, and you build your synthetic connectome.” Ultimately, this could produce edited animals that perform specific tasks or even artificial life, Rabinowitch says.
We are a long way from these techniques being used in humans. Optogenetics, the 20-year-old, Nobel Prize–winning technology, has only just proven itself safe in trials of human treatments.
To edit human circuits, researchers will have to figure out how to safely deliver DNA across the blood-brain barrier and into neurons. Scientists are working on brain delivery systems, but “that’s a barrier nobody’s really solved yet,” Arnold says. And no one knows how safe these new tools are. “We’re starting to test if human tissue can tolerate them,” Dzirasa says.
And perhaps more critically, researchers need to understand human brain function better before they can usefully intervene. Synaptic engineering may be just what’s needed to figure this out, however. “If you don’t know how something works, you cannot fix it,” Colón-Ramos says. “These tools will lead to the knowledge we need for any aspiration of healing.”

Trump tells allies to brace for return to Iran war after midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:10:00 UTC
21:10:00 KST

U.S. officials have warned several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for possible renewed military action against Iran after next week’s U.S. midterm elections and potential Iranian retaliation, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter.
Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by U.S. diplomats and defense officials.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon.
The White House and U.S. officials declined to comment.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month – summarily rejected by Trump – that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a cease-fire.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates Foreign Ministry issued a statement urging the sides to "exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions" and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February.
The U.S. has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate – leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
While the U.S. has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the Middle East has become more complicated.
The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the U.S.
It's unclear how soon after Election Day that the U.S. military would be ready to potentially resume strikes.
The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard – roughly 9,000 troops in all – from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the U.S. military in the region.
At the time, one U.S. official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
Late Wednesday, reports emerged that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had fired the Pentagon’s top military planner. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, according to a defense official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters. That official said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing.
Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran.
The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that's driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy.
The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress.
While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes.
During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming "in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind."
"Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?" Trump said earlier in the same address. "I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete – a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then – especially if they feel U.S. actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank.
"Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?" he said.
