Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:07:58 UTC
21:07:58 KST

Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Davis
- Summary:
- Mathematicians have uncovered what they argue is a fundamental flaw in the standard model of the universe, potentially challenging the need for dark energy. Their calculations suggest that the mathematical framework used to describe cosmic expansion is inherently unstable and that the universe could accelerate naturally under Einstein's original theory of gravity. The findings also raise surprising questions about whether our location in the universe is as ordinary as scientists have long assumed.
- Share:
Mathematicians are raising a major challenge to one of modern cosmology's most widely accepted explanations: the idea that dark energy is driving the accelerating expansion of the universe.
A study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society A presents mathematical findings that researchers at the University of California, Davis, say reveal a fundamental instability in the standard model of the expanding universe. Their calculations suggest that cosmic acceleration could emerge naturally from Einstein's equations, potentially eliminating the need to invoke mysterious dark energy.
The work challenges the Lambda-cold dark matter model, the leading framework scientists use to describe the universe's evolution since the Big Bang. The researchers reached their conclusions by studying the Einstein-Euler equations, which combine Einstein's theory of general relativity with equations describing how fluids behave. Together, these mathematical tools help scientists investigate everything from galaxies and black holes to the expansion of the cosmos.
A Hidden Instability in Our Model of the Universe
To explain the problem, Blake Temple, the study's corresponding author and a distinguished professor emeritus of mathematics at UC Davis, offered a simple comparison: a pencil balanced vertically on its tip.
"All the forces are in balance when a pencil is standing on end, so it is a 'solution of the equations,'" he said. "But it's unstable. Any breath of air and it falls away."
According to Temple, the team's mathematical analysis shows that Friedmann spacetimes, which form the foundation of conventional models of cosmic expansion, are unstable at both small and large scales in the context of the Big Bang. He described the standard solution as exceptionally unstable.
"Unstable solutions in physics and science are considered not physical," Temple said. "You'll never observe them in nature."
This instability could have far-reaching consequences. If the universe naturally evolves away from the behavior predicted by these conventional models, its accelerating expansion might not require a separate form of energy to explain it. Instead, Temple argues, the answer could already be contained within Einstein's original theory of gravity.
"The instability of all Friedmann spacetimes to accelerated expansion suggests a simpler, more natural explanation for the acceleration of the universe than dark energy," he said.
Why Scientists Believe Dark Energy Is Expanding the Universe
For nearly three decades, dark energy has been the leading explanation for one of astronomy's most puzzling discoveries: the universe is not simply expanding, but its expansion is accelerating.
The concept has roots in Einstein's groundbreaking 1915 theory of general relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of space and time. Einstein originally believed the universe was static, neither expanding nor contracting. To make his equations compatible with that assumption, he introduced a mathematical term that counteracted gravity, calling it the "cosmological constant."
That assumption changed after Edwin Hubble discovered evidence in 1929 that the universe was expanding. Einstein famously referred to his introduction of the cosmological constant as his "biggest blunder," since his original equations without the additional term could have predicted an expanding universe.
The cosmological constant returned to prominence in the 1990s, when astronomers discovered that cosmic expansion was speeding up. It became closely associated with dark energy, the name given to the unknown component thought to be responsible for this acceleration.
Today's standard cosmological framework builds on the Friedmann universe, a mathematical description in which space expands while matter remains evenly distributed across the cosmos at any given moment. This assumption of large-scale uniformity plays a central role in how scientists reconstruct the universe's history.
But Temple and his collaborators began questioning whether the underlying mathematics could remain stable, prompting them to investigate other possible explanations for the observed acceleration.
Could Einstein's Equations Explain Cosmic Acceleration?
The researchers initially considered whether a massive shockwave might help explain the universe's expansion and the unexpected acceleration associated with it.
"Our first idea was that maybe the universe was expanding because there was a shockwave, and the anomalous acceleration was the expanding wave behind that shockwave," Temple said. "Then we realized there's a family of self-similar solutions during the radiation epoch of the Big Bang, which might model that expanding wave."
In mathematics and physics, self-similar solutions describe patterns that retain their underlying structure when viewed at different scales. A familiar example is a fractal, in which similar shapes can appear at increasingly larger or smaller sizes.
The researchers identified a family of these solutions associated with the radiation-dominated period of the early universe, when radiation played a major role in determining how the cosmos evolved.
Building on their earlier work, they used a self-similar form of Einstein's equations to represent the standard cosmological model as a rest point, a mathematical state in which the system's defining variables remain unchanged. This approach allowed them to examine whether small departures from that state would disappear or grow over time.
Their analysis provided a mathematical framework for evaluating the stability of the standard model and, more broadly, Friedmann spacetimes during the matter-dominated era of the early universe, when matter became more influential than radiation.
A Mathematical Challenge to the Standard Big Bang Model
The results suggest that the conventional mathematical descriptions of the expanding universe are vulnerable to disturbances that grow rather than fade.
"We prove that, like Einstein's static model, the Friedmann spacetimes are all unstable to radial perturbation at large length scales," Temple said. "This appears to rule out the Lambda-cold dark matter model as a viable stable solution of the Einstein equations of general relativity, with or without dark energy."
Radial perturbations are disturbances that change with distance from a central point. In the researchers' mathematical framework, such changes can cause the behavior of an expanding universe to depart from the predictions of the standard Friedmann model.
"This means," he added, "that the Big Bang should generically look exactly like a Friedmann spacetime near the center of symmetry, but generically one should observe accelerations away from Friedmann far from the center."
In other words, the universe could behave much like the standard model predicts near a central region while exhibiting different expansion behavior farther away.
The researchers argue that this instability may offer a natural route to accelerated cosmic expansion without adding a cosmological constant or invoking dark energy. Their calculations indicate that the acceleration can emerge directly from the Einstein-Euler equations themselves.
The findings represent a theoretical challenge to standard cosmology rather than observational proof that dark energy is unnecessary. Establishing whether this alternative can describe the actual universe would require determining how well its predictions match astronomical observations.
Does the Universe Have a Special Location?
Beyond the dark energy question, the study also raises a more fundamental issue involving the Copernican principle.
Named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, who helped overturn the belief that Earth sits at the center of the solar system, the principle holds that our location in the universe is not fundamentally special or privileged.
This assumption has become an important part of modern cosmology, supporting the view that the universe looks broadly similar when observed from different locations on sufficiently large scales.
The researchers' alternative mathematical framework introduces a center of spherical symmetry, raising questions about where an observer would need to be located for the model to agree with observations.
Temple argues that the Copernican principle must be applied consistently when evaluating competing explanations of the universe.
"Both the Lambda-cold dark matter model and a spherically symmetric spacetime produce a special place where we must lie for the model to be physically plausible," Temple said. "If this principle rules out one, it has to rule out the other."
The work opens another avenue for investigating why the universe's expansion is accelerating. Although dark energy remains a central component of the prevailing cosmological model, the researchers contend that the mathematics of general relativity may offer a different explanation for the same phenomenon.
If further theoretical and observational work supports their interpretation, it could lead to a significant reassessment of how scientists understand cosmic expansion and the mathematical foundations of the Big Bang.
The research received funding from the United Kingdom's Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council and the American Institute of Mathematics SQuaREs Program.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Davis. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- C. Alexander, B. Temple, Z. Vogler. The instability of critical and underdense Friedmann spacetimes at the Big Bang as an alternative to dark energy. Proceedings of the Royal Society A Mathematical Physical and Engineering Science, 2026; 482 (2338) DOI: 10.1098/rspa.2025.0912

No aircraft previously operated by the Ethiopian Air Force had been observed in a similar paint scheme. However, according to Reuters, Russia’s state arms exporter Rosoboronexport told the outlet about the first batch of two Su-35 fighter jets being delivered that day.
Abiy Ahmed also announced that Ethiopia would receive four batteries of long-range S-400 SAM systems. However, the prime minister did not disclose the delivery timeline or the value of the deal.
Militarnyi previously reported that in January 2024, the Ethiopian Air Force received its first batch of Russian Su-30 fighter jets of an unknown variant. The aircraft were assigned tail numbers ‘2401’ and ‘2402.’ One theory is that Ethiopia might have acquired former Indian Su-30Ks.

Failed Belgian police digitization project cost taxpayers $155M amid mounting budget pressures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:07:08 UTC
21:07:08 KST

Melike Pala
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Belgium's failed police digitization project cost taxpayers €139.4 million ($155 million), nearly twice the amount previously disclosed by the government, according to a report by the country's Court of Audit, as the country faces mounting budgetary pressures and EU demands for fiscal consolidation.
The report cited by public broadcaster VRT on Thursday found that millions of euros were spent on software licenses that are now unusable, while also pointing to serious shortcomings in project management and the government's reliance on external IT consultants.
The total expenditure is significantly higher than the €75.8 million previously acknowledged by Interior Minister Bernard Quintin in parliament.
The i-Police project was launched in late 2021 to modernize police operations, integrate fragmented databases into a single information platform, and help law enforcement agencies identify criminal networks and security risks more efficiently.
However, Quintin terminated the €299 million contract with French IT consultancy firm Sopra Steria in December 2025, citing the absence of tangible results despite years of implementation and payments.
According to the Court of Audit, approximately €30.8 million was spent on software licenses, of which €21.6 million, or 70%, is of no use to the police today.
Some €7.3 million worth of licenses were never used, while another €14.2 million worth were used during the development phase but became unusable after the project was discontinued.
The auditors warned that the financial consequences could extend beyond the initial purchases, as maintenance, support, and renewal costs can continue for years.
The revelations come as Belgium faces growing pressure to bring its public finances under control, with its budget deficit and public debt significantly exceeding EU fiscal limits.
According to Eurostat data published on Oct. 21, Belgium's government deficit reached 5.2% of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025.
Public debt stood at 108.1% of GDP at the end of 2025, placing Belgium among the EU's most indebted member states.
Both figures exceed the EU's fiscal reference limits, which set a maximum budget deficit of 3% of GDP and public debt of 60% of GDP.
Belgium remains subject to the EU's Excessive Deficit Procedure, which requires member states to take corrective action when their public finances exceed the bloc's fiscal thresholds.

Communique of the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:06:10 CST
21:06:10 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China concluded its fifth plenary session on Thursday in Beijing with a communique issued.
The following is the full text of the communique:
Communique of the Fifth Plenary Session of
the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China
Adopted at the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee
of the Communist Party of China on October 29, 2026
The 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China convened its fifth plenary session in Beijing from October 26 to 29, 2026.
A total of 162 members and 117 alternate members of the Central Committee attended the session. Members of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and leading officials from relevant departments were present at the meeting in a non-voting capacity. Some of our primary-level colleagues and a number of experts and scholars, serving as delegates to the 20th National Party Congress, also attended the meeting in a non-voting capacity.
The Political Bureau of the Central Committee presided over the meeting. Xi Jinping, General Secretary of the Central Committee, delivered an important address.
The Central Committee heard and discussed a report on the work of the Political Bureau, presented by Xi Jinping on behalf of the Political Bureau. They also deliberated and adopted the Resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance. Xi Jinping delivered explanatory remarks on the draft Resolution.
At the session, the Central Committee fully affirmed the work of the Political Bureau since the fourth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee. It was unanimously agreed that the Political Bureau has secured progress in the following respects: earnestly implementing the guiding principles from the Party's 20th National Congress and the plenary sessions of the 20th Central Committee; adhering to the general principle of pursuing progress while ensuring stability; fully and faithfully applying the new development philosophy on all fronts; implementing the Five-Sphere Integrated Plan and the Four-Pronged Comprehensive Strategy in a coordinated way; balancing domestic and international imperatives; ensuring both development and security; delivering tangible results in high-quality economic development; advancing socialist democracy and the rule of law; improving public communication and cultural work; ensuring the people's wellbeing and promoting ecological conservation; safeguarding national security and social stability; further strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance; modernizing national defense and the armed forces; carrying out work related to Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan; and pursuing major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics. Thanks to these efforts, the 14th Five-Year Plan has been brought to a successful conclusion and the 15th Five-Year Plan period is off to a good start with new progress and results achieved in the cause of the Party and the country. It was also noted that, this year, we launched a study campaign on establishing and practicing the correct view of performance and celebrated the 105th anniversary of the Communist Party of China. These occasions have further harnessed the mighty force that stems from the entire Party and the whole nation forging ahead in unity.
Looking back on the Party's journey since its founding, the Central Committee pointed out at the session that the key to the success of the Communist Party of China in winning one victory after another lies in its pursuit of the high ideal of communism, its dedication to achieving lasting greatness for the Chinese nation, and its commitment to seeking happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the Chinese nation. During each historical period, the Party has attached great importance to its self-governance, had the courage to uphold truth and correct errors, and grown ever stronger by relying on its own efforts and the support of the people to resolve its own problems, ultimately emerging as the strong leadership core in the cause of the Party and the people. The Party advanced Party building as a great project and then a great new project in the periods of revolution, development, and reform, and it has made further progress in this regard in the new era since its 18th National Congress. During this course, the Party has found two answers to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall: the people's oversight over government and the Party's self-reform. These are the unique discoveries of the Communist Party of China, and will forever stand out in the history of Marxist parties.
Participants at the session gave a highly positive assessment of the great achievements our Party has made in exercising full and rigorous self-governance in the new era. It was unanimously agreed that the Central Committee with Comrade Xi Jinping at its core demonstrated tremendous political courage and a strong sense of responsibility in confronting the grave situation marked by weak, hollow, and watered-down Party leadership, lax, superficial, and ineffective self-supervision and self-governance, as well as some startling problems within the Party. Staying firmly committed to full and rigorous Party self-governance, the Central Committee introduced the most stringent measures and dedicated continuous efforts to tackle all these prominent issues. As a result, the problem of lax and weak self-supervision and self-governance has been addressed at the root, unhealthy tendencies that had long gone unchecked have been curbed, deep-seated problems that had plagued the Party for years have been remedied, and serious dangers hidden within the Party, the state, and the military have been removed. The Party has thus grown stronger through revolutionary tempering. The endeavors to advance full and rigorous governance over the Party in the new era have broken new ground in the self-reform of our century-old Party and brought about historic achievements and transformations in the cause of the Party and the country. The Party and the people have thus seized the historic initiative in building a great party and a great country.
It was pointed out that as the Party endeavors to supervise, govern, develop, and strengthen itself in the new era, the Central Committee with Comrade Xi Jinping at its core has put forward a series of new ideas, new thinking, and new strategies in response to the major questions of our times -- what kind of long-term governing Marxist party we should build and how we should build it, thereby giving birth to Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building. This thought has enriched and developed Marxist theory on party building, and it represents a major achievement in advancing the Party's theoretical innovation through the integration of the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and its fine traditional culture. It stands as a crystallization of the practical experience and collective wisdom of the Party and the people. TEHRAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The navy of Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) announced on Thursday that three "violating" oil tankers that sought to cross the Strait of Hormuz through the "unauthorized" route south of the waterway exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines over the past 24 hours.
In a statement on the IRGC's official news outlet Sepah News, the navy said the vessels were abandoned off the strait's southern coasts.

Iran tightened its grip on the strait on Feb. 28, barring safe passage of vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States following their joint strikes on Iranian territory.
In a separate statement on Thursday, the IRGC Navy said its electronic warfare unit managed within the preceding hours to take control of the guidance and navigation systems of a U.S. Army MQM-170 Outlaw "espionage and decoy" drone west of the strait and land it safely.
It added that the drone had been tasked with identifying Iran's air defense systems along the southern coasts, and data recovery showed it had taken off from the coast of a regional country.
In another statement on Thursday, the IRGC said its aerospace division's air defense systems shot down an MQ-1 Predator drone east of the strait within the preceding hour. It was the 14th MQ-1 intercepted by its air defense forces in recent months. ■

Feature: Myanmar's Thadingyut Festival blends faith, family, grassroots commerce
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:06:06 CST
21:06:06 KST

YANGON, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Sunlight glints off the gilded spires of the Botahtaung Pagoda against a clear, pale blue sky in downtown Yangon. Tens of thousands of devotees have gathered here to pay homage to the Buddha during the Thadingyut Festival, one of Myanmar's most cherished occasions for family reunions and religious devotion.
On the full moon day of the festival, which marks the Buddha's descent from heaven, the pagoda compound hums with the footsteps of pilgrims and visitors.
"Since the Full Moon Day of Thadingyut coincides with my daughter's birthday, our family comes to the pagoda to perform meritorious deeds," said Ei Phyu, a local resident from Yangon.
During the three-day festival, which ran from Oct. 25 to 27 this year, her family lights oil lamps at home, makes donations, and prepares rice, meals and curries to offer to Buddhist monks and share with neighbours, she said on the sidelines of a candle-lighting event held by the pagoda's Board of Trustees on the evening of the full moon day.
Devotees like Ei Phyu are part of a vast wave of worshippers gathering at sacred landmarks across Myanmar. While Botahtaung Pagoda typically welcomes 4,000 to 5,000 visitors on a standard day, daily attendance leaps to between 30,000 and 70,000 during major religious holidays, according to U Aung Myat, a member of the pagoda's Board of Trustees.
The festive spirit extends far beyond Yangon, lighting up regions like Bagan and Kyaukse with hot-air balloon releases, live music concerts, and traditional contests.
In Kyaukse Town, located in the Mandalay Region, the famed Kyaukse Elephant Dance Competition stood out as a highlight of the weekend festivities.
U Tin Aung, who has served as a judge for the competition for over two decades, emphasized the heritage behind the spectacle. He noted that the 75-year-old tradition plays a vital role in preserving local cultural identity.
The Thadingyut Festival is a time for paying respect to elders and reuniting with family members who work in different places, he said, noting that the Kyaukse elephant dance festival also reflects these values, bringing people from towns and villages together in celebration.
Beyond offering ordinary citizens a welcome respite from daily hardships, the festival serves as a vital economic engine for local governments aiming to stimulate grassroots commerce and support small entrepreneurs.
In the ancient city of Bagan, market fairs showcasing traditional foods and products from micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) were held alongside traditional balloon releases in the pagoda-dense archaeological zone, according to U Myo Min Aung, deputy director of the Hotels and Tourism Development Implementation and Training Department in Bagan.
At People's Square in Yangon, Khin Thida Tun, owner of Pyae Thanakha, sold various value-added products made from thanakha, a natural cosmetic paste made from the ground bark, wood or roots of the thanakha tree, on the sidelines of a four-day Thadingyut fair featuring live performances and an MSME market fair.
"I'm thrilled to participate as an MSME owner because it gives us a chance to promote our brand locally and network with other businesses," she said, adding that her booth welcomed roughly 100 regular customers and new visitors in a single day. ■

CANBERRA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Australia's physical energy exports, including coal, liquefied natural gas (LNG), uranium and crude oil, fell to their lowest level in 10 years in 2024-25, declining 3.1 percent overall, official data showed on Thursday.
Black coal remained Australia's largest energy export, falling 1.1 percent, while LNG exports declined 2.2 percent, according to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
Renewable energy production continued to grow, up almost 10 percent in 2024-25, following a 5-percent rise in 2023-24. Solar remained Australia's largest renewable energy source, up 11 percent, while wind production increased 15 percent, the ABS said in its latest Energy Account report.
Total household energy use increased by 0.3 percent in 2024-25, with petrol, electricity and natural gas remaining the main energy products used by Australian households, according to the ABS. ■

China Focus: AI drives digital transformation in China's primary care
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:05:51 CST
21:05:51 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China is introducing AI-powered tools in community health centers to speed up the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare, improve primary care, expand equitable access and enhance public well-being.
Artificial intelligence (AI) assistants that support voice-based consultations, automated medical records, medication-risk screening, follow-up reminders and health education are appearing in community health centers. They are becoming a key part of the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare.
The push comes as family doctors in China take on a wide range of duties, from resident registration and chronic-disease follow-up to initial screening and public-health record keeping, often burdened by heavy paperwork and limited staffing.
AI-assisted family-doctor services have been introduced in many cities and provinces this year.
In May, the Longgang District of Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province launched the "Ant Afu" app, allowing residents to check medical reports, obtain AI-assisted interpretations, sign up for family-doctor services and link family members' health information.
In Beijing's Fengtai District, the Majiapu Community Health Service Center has deployed an AI family doctor and an AI health steward. Built on large models and AI-agent technologies, the system supports chronic-disease management, wearable-device monitoring and automatic risk alerts, with high-risk cases forwarded to contracted family doctors.
In Wuxi, east China's Jiangsu Province, AI was used in a citywide cancer screening campaign. Residents completed risk self-assessments through a mobile app or an AI-powered voice questionnaire, and big-data models identified high-risk groups for follow-up screening at 49 institutions equipped with AI-assisted imaging, ultrasound and endoscopy systems.
According to the Wuxi Municipal Health Commission, the AI-enabled screening significantly improved cancer detection among high-risk groups, with liver and lung cancers detected at markedly higher rates than in the general population.
Industry insiders say the most significant shift is that AI is moving from isolated add-on tools into routine clinical workflows in some community health centers. Earlier systems often required doctors to open separate applications for image reading or diagnostic support. The newer AI systems are being integrated with hospital information systems and health-checkup platforms, so that AI prompts appear within the interfaces doctors already use.
"AI used to seem lofty and unrelated to primary care," said Nie Chunlei, vice president of the Community Health Association of China. "But now we can see it has taken root at the grassroots level."
With growing demand and expanding real-world deployments, more tech companies are entering the sector, further driving the digital upgrade of grassroots healthcare services.
Ant Group's Ant Afu health app has rolled out its "AI agent plus human doctor" model in more than 40 cities. Tens of thousands of grassroots doctors use the platform, and it had served more than 5 million residents by mid-August this year.
The push is not limited to Ant Group. JD Health, Runda Medical and others are also ramping up investment in primary-care AI, each drawing on its own strengths.
Policy support has become more explicit. In October 2025, five national agencies issued guidance identifying intelligent clinical decision support, AI-enabled family-doctor services and coordinated chronic-disease management as priority areas. The guidance sets a goal of basically achieving full coverage of AI-assisted diagnosis and treatment in primary care institutions by 2030.
Still, industry insiders caution that scaling AI across primary care requires careful adaptation. AI cannot simply be transplanted into primary care; it must be tailored to frontline needs, embedded in daily workflows and built into applications that are replicable, scalable and can be regulated -- challenges that will take time to resolve.
Sun Dehui, R&D director at the Beijing Medical Robotics Industry Innovation Center, said primary-care AI is a clear long-term direction for public health. With policy support increasingly focused on the grassroots level, the sector is poised for rapid growth in the coming years, offering significant market potential while continuing to ease the burden on frontline clinicians and benefiting residents with chronic conditions. ■

ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's government said Thursday that Aden International Airport had resumed normal operations after a temporary suspension triggered by a Houthi attack that damaged its runway a day earlier.
Transport Minister Mohsen Haidara announced the resumption during an inspection of the airport, saying technical teams had carried out urgent repairs to the section of the runway hit in the Wednesday's attack, according to a statement from the Ministry of Transport posted on social media platform X.
Haidara said flights to and from Aden were being rescheduled and airlines had been notified to resume services.
He condemned the attack on what he described as a "civilian facility" serving passengers from across Yemen.
The reopening came a day after explosions were heard near the airport in two rounds of attacks that halted operations and prompted hundreds of passengers, including patients, to leave.
Shortly before the blasts, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea issued what he called a "final" warning urging people at the airport to evacuate immediately.
Sarea claimed that a Saudi military cargo aircraft was at the airport transporting weapons, without providing evidence. The Yemeni government did not immediately respond.
The attack came amid an escalating confrontation between the Houthis and government forces supported by the Saudi-led coalition, with missile, drone and air attacks intensifying in recent days.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting the coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government. ■

"Couldn't ask for a better way to start the round," said Laopakdee. "Before it started, I knew it was going to be windy out there and it was going to be tough. Eight under wasn't on my bingo card today, but I was able to pull it off and it feels amazing."
Bai, a 20-year-old from New Zealand, carded a five-under 66 to lead a strong contingent of New Zealanders on the leaderboard. He offset three birdies with a lone bogey on his first nine and added three more birdies coming in to reach five under. Fellow New Zealanders Ryan Xie and Cooper Moore finished at four-under 67.
Joseph Cao from Hong Kong, China, the youngest player in the field at 14, was tied for sixth at two under alongside New Zealand's Yuki Miya, Australia's Kayun Mudadana, Malaysia's Nateesh Ganesh and China's Wu Qiyou.
"The wind was very strong in the afternoon, but I'm still quite happy with my score. I also stayed relatively calm when I encountered difficulties," Wu said. "This course is definitely challenging in the wind. At 69, I'm not too far behind the top three, and I think there will be plenty of opportunities to catch up over the next few days."
A 36-hole cut will be made to the top 60 and ties after Friday's second round.
The 17th edition of the championship runs from Oct. 29 to Nov. 1 on Te Arai Links' South Course, with 120 players from 39 countries and regions competing in the 72-hole stroke-play event.
The winner will earn invitations to the 2027 Masters Tournament, the 155th Open Championship and the 132nd Amateur Championship. ■

Yemen escalation kills nearly 1,700, injures over 7,000 since August: UN agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:05:05 UTC
21:05:05 KST

Mohammed Sami, Ikram Kouachi
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Nearly 1,700 people have been killed and more than 7,000 injured in Yemen since August amid a military escalation, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Thursday.
In a report, the agency recorded 1,677 deaths and 7,395 injuries during the period, including 559 casualties between Oct. 20 and 25 alone, averaging about 93 casualties a day.
Fighting continued during the reporting period in the governorates of Taiz, Lahj, and Marib, while lower casualty figures were recorded in Aden, Al-Dhalea, and Shabwa, according to the report.
The WHO said it delivered 56 trauma and emergency kits to the city of Taiz on Oct. 24, including 46 kits for trauma care and 10 for emergency health services.
The delivery also included around 30 metric tons of medical supplies for three hospitals and one health center.
The agency warned that only six of 31 mobile medical teams remained operational in Marib, leaving residents struggling to access health services amid damage to health facilities and shortages of supplies.
Al-Thawra General Hospital in Taiz city came under fire on Oct. 20, leaving three soldiers and one patient injured, according to the WHO.
The agency warned that continued disruption to essential services and shortages of medicines, fuel, and water, along with inadequate waste management, were increasing the risk of infectious disease outbreaks, particularly in Taiz.
Taiz, Yemen’s most populous province, remains divided between government forces and the Houthis. Government forces control Taiz city, the provincial capital, and other parts of the province.
Since July, military escalation between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has resumed, particularly in Taiz and Lahj, killing and injuring thousands, according to UN reports.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014. A Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

Alyoshki ceasefire, humanitarian convoy: statements by ombudswoman, Defense Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:04:00 UTC
21:04:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The compliance of Russia and Ukraine with the ceasefire, which has been in effect around the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region for 54 hours now, is allowing the servicemen to clear roads of mines and prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova reported.
Russia’s battlegroup Dnepr is clearing roads of mines and explosives to ensure the safety of the routes to Alyoshki. According to the Russian Defense Ministry, servicemen are clearing the area of unexploded ordnance to facilitate aid delivery and resident evacuations.
TASS has compiled the key information known at this time.
Compliance with ceasefire
According to Lantratova, the ceasefire declared in connection with the humanitarian mission in the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region is being fully observed, with no incidents: "The ceasefire has been in effect for 54 hours: since 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27. The parties are fully complying with their commitments, and no violations have been recorded."
The human rights commissioner noted that she is in constant contact with her Ukrainian counterpart Dmitry Lubinets, and that they are coordinating the implementation of the agreements together.
Lantratova emphasized the importance of continued compliance, as the safety of the town's residents and everyone involved in the mission depends on it.
Humanitarian aid
Lantratova reported that a large humanitarian convoy with food, medicine, and all the essentials for the residents of Alyoshki has been put together: "We have gathered all the items that the people need into this convoy, which will be delivered to those in need in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region."
The ombudswoman clarified that the list of items needed by the people in Alyoshki was compiled at the request of the residents themselves. First and foremost, the list includes food, medicine, hygiene products, fuel, and heating supplies.
She noted that preparations are underway to deliver essential supplies to those remaining in the town and to ensure a safe exit for those who wish to leave.
Ensuring safe passage for humanitarian convoy
The Russian human rights commissioner emphasized that the parties’ adherence to the ceasefire allows the servicemen to "continue clearing roads of mines and prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy."
She added that the Russian army is carrying out all the necessary engineering and technical work and that mine clearance operations are underway.
Defense Ministry’s statement
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr is clearing roads to ensure the safety of routes to Alyoshki, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
According to its statement, sections of road adjacent to the city are being cleared of explosive devices and unexploded ordnance to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians.
The ministry emphasized that servicemen from the battlegroup Dnepr discovered NATO ammunition near the bypass road leading to the town of Alyoshki.
According to the Russian army, most of the Ukrainian armed forces' mines found near Alyoshki were scattered by drones and are predominantly of Western manufacture.
The ministry noted that unexploded NATO-standard munitions pose a "particular danger" to Alyoshki residents because they "can detonate from the slightest mechanical impact."
To ensure the safety of Alyoshki’s civilians, sappers from the battlegroup Dnepr are destroying the mines on site "using a shaped charge," the Russian Defense Ministry stated.
On situation in Alyoshki
At 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27, the Russian Armed Forces declared a ceasefire in the Kherson area of the line of engagement in preparation for a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region.
Earlier, with the assistance of US First Lady Melania Trump, Russia and Ukraine agreed to a ceasefire in Alyoshki to ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid and prepare for the evacuation of the civilian population through a special safe corridor.
An independent US media organization will accompany and document the actions of Russian and Ukrainian groups throughout the process.
On September 21, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki as critical.
Ukrainian shelling and drone attacks have made it impossible to deliver food or medicine to the city.

Shadow fleet sanctions: Can the EU act if the US pulls back?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:01:00 UTC
21:01:00 KST

Russia shadow fleet sanctions: Can the EU act if the US pulls back?
October 29, 2026
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has increasingly relied on a so-called shadow fleet to bypass Western sanctions and transport its oil around the world.
Other heavily sanctioned countries, including Iran and Venezuela, have also been accused of using such vessels to export petroleum products.
These tankers often rely on deceptive practices like turning off their location transponders to evade detection and conceal the cargo's true origins or destinations.
The fleet, which consists largely of aging, uninsured and poorly maintained tankers, has raised widespread concern across the shipping industry. Yet it has expanded rapidly in recent years and now accounts for nearly 19% of global oil tanker capacity, according to estimates by financial intelligence firm S&P Global.
"The shadow fleet is a scourge," Elisabeth Braw, senior fellow at the think tank Atlantic Council, said, adding that "it is in nobody's interest" to have these ships sailing around in the world's oceans.
She pointed out that these tankers undermine the maritime order and increase the risk of accidents and environmental damage.
"Every country should use its leverage with Russia to ask it not to use the fleet," she told DW, noting that ultimately all countries suffer the consequences.
Easing sanctions to reduce freight rates?
To clamp down on the fleet and curb Russia's oil export revenues, the United States and European countries have stepped up efforts to intercept tankers accused of violating sanctions.
The Trump administration, however, is reportedly considering lifting sanctions on some shadow fleet vessels and allowing them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.
A US official told Reuters earlier this month that the move was intended to ease record-high global freight rates.
Lifting sanctions on the shadow fleet "would decrease the effectiveness of the sanctions regime overall," said Michael Carpenter, senior fellow for Transatlantic Affairs at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS). Such a move "rewards the aggressor and helps Moscow gain revenues to continue attacking Ukraine," he told DW.
"This is the exact opposite of what the US should be doing if it wants to end the war."
Carpenter, who previously served as US ambassador to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said any sanctions relief would also put the US and the EU "strategically at odds with each other, with the EU clearly backing Ukraine and the US increasingly supporting Russia's financial goals."
This view is shared by Ben Harris, vice president and director of Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution.
Lifting sanctions on shadow fleet tankers would "make it substantially easier for Russia to trade its oil at market rates," he said, pointing out that it would "improve its government finances since so much revenue is tied to energy markets."
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, however, rejected suggestions that the US was removing sanctions from shadow fleet tankers.
"We are converting dark tankers to legitimate tankers," Bloomberg quoted Wright as saying last week. "There is no removing of sanctions," he stressed, adding that the US government was working with investors who buy idle sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.
"We're going to move some of the ships from what I call the 'bad-guy fleet' to the 'good-guy fleet,'" Wright said. "They will not carry sanctioned oil anymore."
The US government has yet to unveil a detailed plan for shadow fleet tankers.
Trump's deal with Putin raises concerns
The proposal follows a deal that US President Donald Trump struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin this month to allow sales of Russian diesel onto global markets.
The agreement was seen as part of Trump's efforts to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
The US president also waived broad new sanctions on Russia authorized by a recent legislation, which targeted Moscow's energy revenues and threatened tariffs against the world's largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas.
The decision was sharply criticized by Ukraine and its European allies over concerns that it could undermine the credibility of sanctions and weaken Western economic pressure on Moscow.
Harris said that "the US sanctions carry outsized weight because of the threat [for countries and businesses] of being cut off from the US financial system."
What can the EU do?
If the US steps away from its sanctions on the shadow fleet, he argued, "the responsibility shifts to European policymakers." But they have "less effective options because of the diminished threat of severing financial ties."
Still, the expert stressed that Europe has some tools, pointing to the continent's key role in global shipping and insurance services.
"They can implement measures demanding that tankers carry legitimate and established insurance when traveling through their waters," he said, noting that it "would mean that many shadow fleet tankers could not in practice legally transport Russian oil."
Harris added that European policymakers could also pressure countries worldwide to better regulate the tankers flying their flags.
Carpenter said even if US eases some restrictions, the EU will have no choice but to continue enforcing its sanctions on these vessels.
"The vast majority of the shadow fleet traverses the Baltic Sea and exits it via the Danish Strait," he noted, adding that the EU is "uniquely positioned to board and inspect vessels moving through this key chokepoint."
But Russia has threatened to seize ships belonging to European countries in retaliation for interdicting and seizing Russian vessels suspected of being part of the shadow fleet.
And without US backing, Carpenter said, "it will be harder for EU countries to take on the burdens and risks of sanctions enforcement."
Braw echoed this view, saying that Ukraine's European allies will have to remain united and continue working closely with partners such as Japan, Australia and Canada. Nevertheless, she stressed that what they can achieve on their own "is far less than what they can achieve if the US is part of the team."
Edited by: Rob Mudge

It’s easy to see through Trump’s Ukraine ploy | Kenneth Roth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:00:42 UTC
21:00:42 KST

As the US midterms approach, Donald Trump is abandoning Ukraine’s democracy in a desperate effort to deny responsibility for worsening inflation. Yet this past weekend’s dramatic elections in Brazil and Serbia show that voters can see through such subterfuge.
There is nothing like a political party’s corrupt indifference to the plight of ordinary people to galvanize voter turnout. If US voters follow in the footsteps of their Brazilian and Serbian counterparts, a Democratic landslide is likely.
If that happens, Democrats in Congress must act quickly to rein in Trump before he does more damage to the US’s economy and global stature.
Any objective observer would see that Trump’s war of choice against Iran has inflated energy prices, because Iran predictably responded by restricting shipments in the strait of Hormuz, through which much of the Middle East’s oil and gas flows. But Trump, never one to admit error, needed a scapegoat. Enter Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
While holding off Russian troops on the front lines in the Donbas region of eastern Ukraine, Zelenskyy’s forces have been damaging the Russian economy by attacking its oil refineries. That has finally brought the war home to ordinary Russians in the form of long lines at gasoline stations. It has also disrupted oil production, putting pressure on a major source of revenue for Putin to fund his invasion.
Trump is trying to blame the inflationary surge in US gasoline and diesel prices on these attacks, even though their effect on the global market is small compared to the diminished flow through the strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, with Russia making only limited progress in eastern Ukraine despite losing hundreds of thousands of troops, Putin has taken, as is his wont, to attacking Ukrainian civilians. He has bombed their cities and attacked their energy infrastructure to deprive them of heat for their homes this coming winter.
He seems to hope that a freezing populace will pressure Zelensky to capitulate. Yet many Ukrainians remain determined to defend their country’s democracy from Putin’s dictatorship.
So Putin has turned to his ace-in-the-hole, Trump. The naive American president, with his inattention to detail, craving for flattery, and disturbing admiration for autocrats, was easily won over.
Trump has now openly sided with Russia. He has authorized the purchase of diesel fuel from Russia, financing Putin’s attacks on Ukrainian cities. The gesture will not noticeably reduce market prices before the midterms, but it allows Trump to make a nod of acknowledgment toward the affordability crisis that he normally derides.
He has waived new sanctions on Russia which had just been adopted by overwhelming Congressional majorities in the name of the late senator Lindsey Graham, a purported friend of Trump whose devotion to Ukraine’s democracy Trump now betrays.
The Trump administration suspended delivery of defensive missiles to Ukraine and early-warning intelligence of Russian attacks just as Putin was intensifying his bombing of Ukrainian cities, leaving civilian residents to their fate.
And it reportedly greenlit a decision by Trump’s buddy Elon Musk to slow Starshield, the version of the Starlink satellite internet service that Ukraine’s military depends on for its drones to defend the front line against a vastly larger Russian military.
Finally, Trump called for an “energy ceasefire”, by which he effectively meant only an end to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries (Ukraine has only one badly damaged refinery), not an end of Putin’s efforts to force Ukrainians to freeze this winter. Ukraine is attacking what are arguably legitimate military targets. Putin is committing war crimes. Yet Trump condemned only Ukraine’s attacks, not Russia’s.
The Ukrainian government would have welcomed a real energy ceasefire but rejected this selective one.
Trump claims his embrace of Putin is an effort to build a relationship with him so he will negotiate peace. But offering him enormous benefits in return for nothing won’t force him to the bargaining table. The former German chancellor Angela Merkel believed that tying Russia to Europe economically would preserve peace with Russia. Instead, Putin acquired the means to invade Ukraine.
Trump’s amateur diplomats – Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – are hardly primed to do better. Witkoff embarrassingly dubbed Putin a “humanitarian” for releasing one elderly American held in prison on concocted charges while Putin kept up the indiscriminate attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The envoys still seem to think that Putin aspires for only a chunk of Ukrainian territory rather than the destruction of Ukraine’s democracy.
Trump hopes his blame-Ukraine campaign will prevent a Republican midterm debacle. It should only reinforce voter sentiment that Trump is indifferent to their plight, that he would rather deploy smoke and mirrors than alter his corrupt, self-serving reign.
Will a Democratic midterm victory make a difference? The American presidency largely runs foreign policy, with little input from Congress. However, there are some things that the Democrats might do if they take the reins in January.
I would begin with sanctions on Russia. The latest round of sanctions won overwhelming bipartisan support, yet the legislation contained the traditional national-interest waiver that Trump invoked to ignore them.
The Democrats should re-enact the legislation without the waiver. They might even name the bill again after Graham. Outrage against Trump’s betrayal of Ukraine is widespread among Congressional members of both parties in Washington. If the legislation can secure a veto-proof two-thirds majority, Trump would be stuck with it.
That might also break his aura of being beyond restraint. A successful rectification of US policy toward Ukraine might be followed by bills that limit Trump’s tariff authority or curtail the funds he needs to keep fighting Iran – as he is considering doing after the midterms.
There is nothing normal about the current Republican Congress’s abdication of its foreign policy role to Trump’s self-promoting priorities. Ukraine is on the frontline of the global defense of democracy. The American people see that. So does Congress. Trump may be oblivious, but under Democratic leadership, Congress should take matters into its own hands.
- Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

Ketamine and MDMA treatments are linked to epigenetic changes in genes tied to brain plasticity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:00:38 UTC
21:00:38 KST

Ketamine and MDMA treatment were associated with changes in DNA methylation, a chemical modification that can influence gene activity, at genes linked to neuroplasticity and immune processes, according to a study published in Translational Psychiatry. The changes were measured in blood and saliva samples from people treated for depression or post-traumatic stress disorder.
DNA methylation is a chemical mark that can influence how easily a cell reads certain genes. It does not alter the DNA code itself. Researchers often measure methylation in blood or saliva because those samples are easier to collect than brain tissue. However, a change in blood or saliva does not necessarily mean the same change has occurred in the brain.
Ketamine and MDMA are being studied for mental health conditions, including depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Both are sometimes called psychoplastogens, compounds thought to promote neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to form and reorganize connections. They act through different mechanisms, and researchers do not yet fully understand how their effects may last beyond the treatment sessions.
Led by Moira G. Semple of Arizona State University, the researchers investigated whether either treatment was associated with methylation changes in genes considered relevant to brain health. Rather than examining the entire genome, they focused on about 2,900 genes that are particularly active in the brain or involved in signaling between nerve cells, an approach intended to make the analysis more manageable in small samples.
The researchers analyzed samples from two separate studies. The ketamine group included 20 people (average age about 40; 15 women) with moderate-to-severe depression, PTSD, or both. They received six ketamine infusions over two to three weeks, with blood samples collected before treatment and 10 days after it ended.
The MDMA group included 16 people (average age about 43; seven women) with severe PTSD who took part in a Phase 3 clinical trial of MDMA-assisted therapy. They received three MDMA doses about four weeks apart alongside psychotherapy, with saliva collected before treatment and six to eight weeks after the final session. Neither analysis included a comparison group that did not receive the drug.
In each group, no individual methylation site changed enough to remain statistically significant after correcting for the large number of sites tested. When the researchers combined results across all the sites within each gene, they identified 405 genes with statistically significant methylation changes after ketamine and 346 after MDMA.
In both groups, the changes clustered in biological pathways related to neuroplasticity, such as the structure and organization of synapses, the points where nerve cells communicate. Some pathways related to immune and stress-response signaling also emerged. Ketamine was associated with changes in genes involved in glutamate signaling, while MDMA was associated with changes in genes such as BDNF, which supports the growth and survival of nerve cells, and a dopamine transporter gene.
The two treatments overlapped only partly at the level of individual genes. Forty-seven genes changed in both groups, but only about a quarter changed in the same direction, and the sizes of the changes were not correlated. The overlap was greater at the level of broader biological pathways, and both treatments were associated with increased methylation of EFNA5, a gene that has been linked to PTSD in large genetic studies.
Some of the patterns also differed. Ketamine changes were more strongly linked to synapse-related pathways, while MDMA changes were associated with a wider range of processes, including the movement of substances across cell membranes and electrical signaling. The authors noted that these differences could reflect the treatments’ distinct effects, but could also be due to differences between the studies, such as the use of psychotherapy with MDMA, the mix of diagnoses in the ketamine group, and the different sample types and collection times.
The authors summarized the shared pattern: “Across both compounds, altered loci [locations in the genome] converged on pathways related to neuroplasticity and neuroimmune regulation.” This is evidence of treatment-associated molecular changes, not proof that these changes explain why either treatment may help patients.
Some limitations should be noted. The groups were small, neither included a comparison group, and the study did not examine whether the methylation changes were related to symptom improvement. The ketamine and MDMA participants were not compared within one trial and differed in diagnosis, treatment context, and whether blood or saliva was tested.
The study also could not show whether the methylation changes affected gene activity, and participants receiving ketamine were allowed to continue most of their medications. Smoking and ethnicity, both of which can affect methylation, were not included in the analysis. Two of the authors are employees of TruDiagnostic, an epigenetic testing company, and nonprofits led by two other authors helped fund the MDMA analyses.
The study, “Brain-targeted epigenetic effects of two emerging psychoplastogens: ketamine & MDMA,” was authored by Moira G. Semple, Sarah E. Mennenga, Ryan Smith, Varun B. Dwaraka, Baruch Rael Cahn, Joseph Tafur, David M. Rabin, Berra Yazar-Klosinski and Candace R. Lewis.

A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics
The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation
One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.
The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.
Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.
The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.
There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.
Nailing a Mars cloud’s features
Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.
The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.
The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.
While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.
The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.
“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.
Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

Russia and Ukraine have intensified drone and missile attacks in recent months, even as Moscow and Kyiv prepare to resume US-mediated peace talks next month.
At least 14 people were killed after a Russian drone struck a platform at a railway station in the central-eastern Ukrainian city of Dnipro where a train was standing, authorities said on Thursday.
"13 people were killed in a Russian attack on Dnipro. At least five more were wounded," Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha said on Telegram.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the strike as "horrific", saying Russian forces had attacked a platform "where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing".

"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform," he wrote on Facebook.

Meanwhile, more than 600 Ukrainian drones were launched towards the Moscow region overnight, most of which were shot down, according to the Russian capital's mayor, as the city hosts a Russia-Africa summit.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that "613 UAVs flew towards the Moscow region" between Wednesday night and Thursday morning.
"Most were neutralised by the Defence Ministry's air defence forces on the distant approaches. 231 drones were destroyed on the approach to Moscow," he added.

Russia has lifted gasoline sales restrictions in 15 regions as fuel supplies improve following a pause in Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Restrictions have also been fully lifted in occupied Crimea and Sevastopol, where fuel shortages had been particularly severe.
However, fuel supplies remain uneven across Russia. In the Tambov region, customers still face purchase limits, and filling portable fuel containers is prohibited.
Some areas of the Leningrad region are experiencing supply disruptions, while gas stations in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District continue to restrict sales.
Fuel availability remains limited nationwide. On Oct. 28, AI-92 gasoline was available at 42% of Russian gas stations, while AI-95 was available at 34% and diesel at 37%, according to Benzonavt, a service that tracks fuel availability using driver reports and open sources.
Higher-octane gasoline grades AI-98 and AI-100 were available at just 1% and 3% of stations, respectively.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister of Energy Alexander Novak said in mid-October that the situation was improving as refineries returned from maintenance and security measures were strengthened.
Russia’s fuel use also tends to peak in the summer, according to earlier Reuters reports, with an estimated 115,000 tons of gasoline consumed per day.
Ukraine May Return to Light Masking Over Russian Drones
The easing of restrictions comes after a pause in Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. Following calls from US President Donald Trump for Kyiv to stop striking Russian refineries, Ukraine carried out only a handful of further attacks.
The latest reported strikes targeted the Ryazan refinery on Oct. 15 and a facility in Surgut on Oct. 16.
Gasoline prices have also declined in dozens of regions. Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, recorded price drops in 57 regions during the week of Oct. 20-26. The steepest declines were reported in Kamchatka Krai, at 12.6%, and the Ivanovo region, at 11.4%.
Data from OMT Consult, cited by The Moscow Times, showed that between Oct. 19 and Oct. 26, AI-95 gasoline prices fell by 1.33 rubles to 77.51 rubles ($0.96) per liter, while AI-92 dropped by 1.54 rubles to 72.48 rubles ($0.90). Diesel prices edged down by 0.05 rubles to 82.87 rubles ($1.02) per liter.

Two citizens suspected of setting fire to Starlink satellite communication antennas in Bulgaria have been detained in Germany.

Both suspects, aged 19, were detained in Germany on October 23 under European arrest warrants. Onelives in Duisburg, while the other resides in nearby Moers.
The two suspects remain in custody in Germany. The Higher Regional Court in Düsseldorf is considering whether to extradite them to Bulgaria.
According to Bulgarian investigators, the men entered Bulgaria from Serbia on October 9 through the Kalotina bordercrossing. That evening, at around 10:25 p.m., they allegedly set fire to Starlink antennas at a satellite facility in Plana, south of Sofia.
After the attack, the suspects left Bulgaria and returned to Serbia. They were travelling in a car with German licence plates that was not registered to either of them.
The fire completely destroyed three antennas and damaged several others.
The Sofia City Prosecutor’s Office has received official confirmation of the suspects’ arrests. Both men have been charged in absentia with arson committed jointly.
If found guilty, they face prison sentences of between three and 12 years.
Earlier reports said that two German citizens, aged 20 and 21, had been arrested in Bulgaria on October 12 in connection with the case.
The attack took place at a facility in the Plana mountains near Sofia. According to initial information shared by Bulgarian MP Ivaylo Mirchev, the attackers set fire to 11 of the 17 Starlink antennas at the site. Mirchev also published a video showing the fire.
Similar attacks on Starlink infrastructure have previously been reported in Poland and Lithuania. Near Vilnius, an attempt was made to set fire to a Starlink station, while in Poland, law enforcement authorities are investigating possible links between Russian intelligence services and an act of sabotage targeting Starlink ground equipment.

Lithuania to introduce universal military conscription in 2032, president says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:55:00 UTC
20:55:00 KST

Lithuania plans to introduce universal military conscription in 2032, requiring a larger number of young people to serve in the armed forces amid security concerns, President Gitanas Nausėda said Thursday.
The State Defence Council, which comprises the country’s political and military leadership, agreed on the timeline at a meeting, Nausėda told reporters afterward.
Women would continue to be able to perform military service on a voluntary basis, he said.
Lithuania currently drafts more than 5,000 young people into the armed forces each year. Under universal conscription, the annual number would rise to about 7,500, accounting for demographic trends and the fact that some young people are deemed medically unfit for service, the president said.
Nausėda said the 2032 target would give the country time to invest in adequate accommodation for the larger number of conscripts and train enough instructors.
The authorities also need to balance conscript training with refresher training for reserve personnel to ensure both are carried out effectively, he said.
“I think implementing conscription from 2032 is optimal,” Nausėda said.
According to Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, the government wanted a quicker transition to universal conscription, but were convinced by the military to push back the date to 2032.
“You could say there is political will, but at the same time, there is the question of the military’s readiness. The military has clearly stated that they would be ready by 2032,” Sinkevičius told reporters after Thursday’s State Defence Council meeting.
The date for introducing universal conscription was discussed “at length and in detail, with lively debates” at the council, the PM said.
“Everyone agreed that this isn’t a race, nor is it a matter of setting a specific date in stone – that we must move toward universal conscription and that it is inevitable, but needs to be done when you’re prepared,” he said.
The preparations would include training some 300 instructors and building suitable facilities to house the young draftees, he added.
The council also agreed to expand the range of service options available to conscripts. These could include training as drone operators or assisting the State Border Guard Service and firefighting and rescue services, the president said.
After trying to switch to fully professional armed forces, Lithuania restored partial conscription in 2015, citing increased security threats following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014.

PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, October 29: Spanish papers discuss Wednesday's deadly train collision. The New York Times investigates whether a "safest seat" in the event of a train crash exists. Next, we look at a report about "the shocking rise of rib remodelling". We end with some photos from the Arctic and Antarctica.
Spanish papers are reacting to the devastating train crash that killed dozens of people on Wednesday. Both El Mundo and El País emphasise that it's not the first time this has happened – the last train accident in Spain was only nine months ago. El País also has a first-person story: "I travelled on this train", writes a journalist who works for the paper. He happened to be there during the crash. He already covered the Adamuz disaster in January and now he writes: "I had that feeling again of living through a nightmare". He also describes the strange calm and how he and other passengers managed to free themselves from the last carriage.
The New York Times asks the question "Is there a safest seat in a train crash?" The answer is not so simple. There's a rough consensus that it's best to sit in the middle of the train, in case of a hit from the front or the back. Some experts are even more precise, saying the best bet is sitting in the middle, in an aisle seat facing backward – that's because if the train suddenly stops, the whiplash would be less brutal and there's a smaller chance of being hit by flying objects. But experts told the paper that there are too many variables in train crashes to say for certain. This time in Spain, for example, the hit was from the back, so the safest place to sit would have been in the front of the train. But of course passengers couldn't have known in advance of the nature of the crash.
The tragedy is still very recent, but it could already have political repercussions. According to Democrata, it could harm Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's reputation before snap elections that are happening in only a month's time. The weak link among his ministers is Oscar Puente, the transport minister, who was already in post in January during the first train crash. According to the paper, he has three options: "continuity, resignation or dismissal". Puente is under fire, and not only because of the actual crashes. Some time after the previous rail disaster, he appeared in a comedy video in which he imitated a derailing train.
Next, The Guardian reports that rib remodelling surgery is on the rise. First, the patient's ribs are fractured, and then the person has to stay in a corset for three months, almost 24/7. The idea is to give the person a wasp-like waist. The Guardian spoke to people who went through it, who say it's extremely painful and feels like "being hit by a bus". One lady who did it couldn't sleep comfortably for more than a week because she was in constant pain. Although the procedure remains rare, more and more people are deciding to do it. Between 2018 and 2024, there were more than 2,300 patients, with an overall complication rate of 3.7 percent, which remains quite high for beauty procedures.
Finally, a new photography book by polar specialists Sue Flood and Ian Dawson captures the Arctic and Antarctica. The Times shows its favourite photographs that "document life at the frozen edges of the world".
You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

Russia continues to use American microchips in the production of ballistic and cruise missiles, as replacing them with Russian components has so far proven unsuccessful, Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasyuk stated.
"A very large number of American components. First and foremost, in ballistic missiles. Also in cruise missiles," he said in response to a question from an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent on whether Russia continues to use American components in its weaponry.
He added that in 2025 the Russians attempted to replace American microchips with Russian ones, but in 2026 they returned to American-manufactured microchips.
Vlasyuk noted that American components play a crucial role in Russian missiles, particularly in ensuring their precision and technical performance characteristics.
He also emphasized the need for full synchronization of sanctions against Russian arms manufacturers and more active work by law enforcement agencies to investigate and halt the supply of microelectronics to Russia.
According to Vlasyuk, foreign-made components, particularly from German companies, are also being detected in Russian missiles, pointing to the need to strengthen supply chain controls.

Kazakhstan imports more gas in nine months of 2026 than in all of 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:54:00 UTC
20:54:00 KST

ASTANA, October 29. /TASS/. Kazakhstan imported 6.4 bln cubic meters of gas in January-September 2026, compared with 4.7 bln cubic meters for the whole of 2025, with Russia among its suppliers, BES.media reported, citing a response from the country’s Energy Ministry to an inquiry.
Meanwhile, Kazakhstan’s marketable gas production declined by 10% in the first nine months of the year. According to the ministry, the country produced 17.6 bln cubic meters of marketable gas in January-September 2026.
The ministry attributed the increase in imports to rising domestic consumption. It explained that agreements with Russia provide for gas purchases in the event of a decline in domestic supplies, such as during unplanned shutdowns at major marketable gas producers in the heating season.
As BES.media noted, the ministry did not provide gas import figures for January-September 2025, making it impossible to compare purchase volumes for the corresponding periods. The ministry also declined to disclose the cost of imported gas, citing commercial confidentiality.
