“Mary Peltola has looked Alaskans in the eyes for the past year and a half and lied to them,” Sullivan wrote in a post to social media.
Lisa Murkowski calls Peltola's alleged ballot-stacking scheme 'simply wrong'
In a statement posted to social media, Lisa Murkowski, the senior Republican senator from Alaska, condemned Mary Peltola’s effort to peel votes away from her opponent, Dan Sullivan, by recruiting a candidate into the race with the same name.
But she stopped well short of Donald Trump’s calls to disqualify Peltola from the ballot or to criminally investigate her.
“While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process,” Murkowski wrote. “Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments.”
Murkowski, a moderate Republican who has broken with Trump on a number of occasions, just yesterday endorsed a Democratic candidate in the state governor’s race.
Peltola continued: “By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong. Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign – what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials.”
After rallying in Ohio yesterday, Donald Trump will head east to Rock Hill, South Carolina, to stump for an unexpectedly at-risk Republican incumbent in the deep red state.
Senator Darline Graham, the sister of the late South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, was appointed to finish out her brother’s term after his death earlier this year. She’s running to win a full term in the seat, but has found herself in a narrow race against Democratic nominee Annie Andrews.
South Carolina represents the latest in a series of typical Republican strongholds where Trump has traveled in the weeks leading up to the midterms, as the GOP fears losing races it might have normally thought of as safe wins.
Alaska governor orders investigation into Peltola campaign claims
An investigation has been launched in Alaska into whether Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign for Senate should face criminal charges or civil penalties.
Republican governor Mike Dunleavy ordered the inquiry into whether Peltola’s campaign recruited candidates to draw votes from the state’s Republican incumbent.
It follows a New York Times report claiming the Democratic candidate’s campaign was involved in recruiting a retiree named Dan J Sullivan to enter the race against senator Dan S Sullivan.
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” he said in a post on X. “Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.”
Republicans condemned the presence in the race of two candidates named Dan Sullivan – one the two-term US senator, the second a retiree living in south-eastern Alaska with scant political experience – calling the newcomer a ploy by Democrats to cost the incumbent re-election by splitting his supporters.
Peltola’s campaign has denied involvement with the other Dan Sullivan, but the NYT reports that her officials together with the party’s campaign arm, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to find other people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska, and encourage them to run.
Their reporting is based on interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager and other sources, together with documents and text messages related to the recruitment effort.
Donald Trump has demanded that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola and a rival sharing the name of Alaska’s Republican incumbent be removed from next week’s election ballot, accusing Democrats of an illegal scheme to confuse voters.
His call followed a New York Times investigation reporting that Democratic operatives seeking to defeat Republican senator Dan Sullivan had secretly recruited so-called “spoiler” candidates, including one also named Dan Sullivan, in an effort to draw votes away from the sitting senator.
“It has just been determined that the Democrats in Alaska illegally searched for, and recruited, a man named Dan Sullivan,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He accused Democrats of committing perjury by making false statements under oath in federal court, and demanded that the incumbent be allowed to run without either Peltola or the “FAKE Dan Sullivan” on the ballot.
He told reporters later that Peltola and any other alleged accomplices should be prosecuted. “To me, that’s voter fraud at the highest level,” he said.

Judge rebuffs Trump DoJ’s bid to force California to set aside 20,000 ballots
Sam Levine
A federal judge declined to order California election officials to segregate and not count ballots from people the Trump administration claimed were non-citizens, rebuffing a legally thin request from the justice department that appeared designed to cast doubt over the results of the midterms.
The ruling from US district judge David Carter, nominated to the federal bench by Bill Clinton, comes about two weeks after the justice department delivered a USB drive to election officials in Los Angeles and Sacramento that it said contained the names of 20,000 non-citizens on the state’s voter rolls. There are more than 23 million registered voters in California and non-citizen voting is extremely rare.
“This case is about the right of every American citizen to vote in a free and fair election,” Carter wrote in his Wednesday evening ruling. “Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”
“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign,” Carter continued. “But California and its people are sovereign, too.”
The justice department gave officials just 48 hours to review the list and said it would sue the state if officials did not sequester ballots from those whose citizenship it could not confirm. The department refused to provide more details about its methodology and Los Angeles officials found preliminary indicators the list was inaccurate. The justice department then sued California on 15 October to try and force the state to sequester the ballots and verify citizenship.
How did the Cheesecake Factory end up in a Maga fight over ‘elitism’?
Matthew Cantor
Around lunchtime on Tuesday, a Rolls-Royce stopped at the intersection of Beverly Drive and Dayton Way in Beverly Hills, California. Local people in athleisure walked past Balenciaga, Dior and Prada boutiques, as visitors on Hollywood bus tours ogled nearby Rodeo Drive, where Burberry and Louis Vuitton shops meet at a celebrated street corner.
Up the street, across from the upmarket Erewhon grocery store – home to $21 smoothies – a few diners sat outside an American landmark: the Cheesecake Factory.
The beloved restaurant chain began here in Beverly Hills in 1978; now it has hundreds of locations across the US and Canada. And this week, it’s become the US’s latest surreal culture-war touchstone.
It started when Barack Obama, campaigning for Democrats in Ohio, made a joke that hit Donald Trump right in the real estate. Referring to his successor’s remodeling obsession, the former president said: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”
The joke was about maximalism: Saddam had 100 palaces and loved gold plating, and the Cheesecake Factory, while affordable for many, offers swanky surroundings that a curmudgeon might describe as over the top. While the Beverly Hills restaurant has a fairly staid interior, a nearby location at Los Angeles’s Grove mall has a grand staircase, floral paintings on the ceilings and an ornate balcony.
Obama’s comments got a laugh at the rally – which surely contained many Cheesecake Factory customers – and went viral. It’s likely the former president knew he would touch a nerve, given Trump’s twin fixations on remodeling and on Obama himself.
Donald Trump and the former president Barack Obama have continued to trade barbs on the campaign trail, with less than a week to go before congressional races that could shift the balance of power in Washington.
While Donald Trump has been on a weeks-long campaign blitz that has exposed Republican concerns about losing control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, Obama had kept a relatively low public profile until the past week.
However, the former Democratic president has taken a more prominent role in recent days, delivering speeches criticizing Trump, which appear to have got under the skin of the current occupant of the White House.
“These are not serious people,” he said of Donald Trump and the Republican party, speaking at a Wednesday campaign rally in suburban Atlanta. “And we’re all paying the price for their lack of seriousness.”
Obama has offered pointed criticism of Republican candidates and Donald Trump in a style that has been unusual for the former president.
He continued to do so on Wednesday, again invoking the image of Trump’s gilded renovations of the White House and noting Trump’s strident reaction to his crack last week likening it to Saddam Hussein decorating a Cheesecake Factory.
“The Saddam Hussein thing didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said. “I mean, it’s all crazy, but this is the crazy part: they mobilized a whole government response to that joke.
“The White House even called the secretary of the treasury,” the former president continued. “The guy who is trying to figure out how to lower inflation … they told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory.”
Trump, meanwhile, defended his White House decor and said Obama left the property deteriorated.
“The White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country, and we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years,” he said at a rally in Ohio.
Thirty-five of the 100 Senate seats and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are being contested next Tuesday. Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats’ chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest for the Senate seen as very close.

Estonia's volunteer rescuers send 146th aid shipment to Ukraine
The Estonian Rescue Association (Päästeliit) has sent aid to Ukrainian rescuers, funded by donations and the Foreign Ministry, providing shelter, power and heating for over 30,000 people this winter.
The Kyiv consignment has included a minibus, two high-pressure tents with trailers, diesel heaters, power stations, lighting towers and heated blankets, enough to set up two emergency centers, Estonia's Embassy to Ukraine announced.
"This was our 146th shipment to Ukraine. Every time we hand over new equipment, we hope the situation will improve. Unfortunately, the head of Kyiv's rescue service confirmed that the situation is already worse than ever, and that the coming winter will put civilians — especially children — in an even more difficult position than last year," said Piia Kallas, head of the Estonian Rescue Association, a volunteer organization which complements the Rescue Board (Päästeamet).
Estonian Rescue Association delivered emergency tents and equipment to Ukraine's rescue services @SESU_UA. The aid will provide temporary shelter, electricity and heating for more than 30,000 people during the winter. The package was funded by @MFAestonia and donations. https://t.co/fOGAZI2tOy
— Estonia in Ukraine (@EE_Ukraine) October 28, 2026
The shipment delivered to Kyiv included a minibus, two high-pressure tents with trailers, diesel heaters, battery power stations, battery-powered lamps, lighting towers, heated blankets, folding tables and chairs, fast chargers, thermos flasks, changing mats, children's toys and play mats. With this equipment, rescuers can set up two emergency centers where residents can find temporary shelter and warmth, charge their devices and receive psychological first aid.
A second delivery reached rescuers in Rivne oblast in southeastern Ukraine, including an off-road vehicle, a generator, battery power stations, lighting towers and heaters. The generator was donated by a private donor who decided to give their equipment to those who need it most.
Since the start of the invasion in February 2022, with support from donors and partners, the Rescue Association has delivered nearly €7 million worth of rescue equipment and vehicles to Ukrainian rescuers.

Israel’s election rhetoric: What candidates said, and how they performed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:27:22 UTC
20:27:22 KST

Israel’s election rhetoric: What candidates said, and how they performed
From Netanyahu to Ben-Gvir, campaign boasts and attacks on Arab parties have been met with a deadlocked result.
Israel’s parliamentary election on Tuesday produced no clear winner, with nearly 90 percent of ballots counted and both major political blocs falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc is on course to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot is expected to secure 48 seats.
The Arab-majority parties won 19 seats, a historic high, driven by record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel of about 80 percent. That has placed the Arab parties at the centre of coalition arithmetic, even as several party leaders ruled out governing with them.
So what did the main contenders say in the run-up to and during the vote, and how did they fare? Here is a look:
Benjamin Netanyahu, Likud: Elections ‘stolen by Arab parties’
Pre-election: In the build-up to the election, Netanyahu expressed confidence, telling The Jerusalem Post on October 22, “I’m gonna have five more terms.”
On Sunday, he targeted the opposition, with Haaretz citing a broadcast on Israel’s Channel 14 that Netanyahu warned if they win, they will “give citizenship to hundreds of thousands of Palestinians”, a move that would signal the “end of the Jewish state”.
Election day: On Tuesday, he said forming a government with Arab-led parties would be “a shame and a disgrace”.
“It is forbidden – simply forbidden – to endanger Israel and to establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties,” he told supporters.
Post-election day: After the elections, Netanyahu’s Likud party took aim at Palestinian citizens of Israel who voted.
In a party statement shared by Netanyahu, it claimed the elections “were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state through serious criminal offences”. According to The Times of Israel, police and the Central Elections Committee have already dismissed these claims.
What the results show: Likud is on course for 26 seats, the largest party, with 20.65 percent of the vote. But his bloc has 53 seats, eight short of a majority.
Gadi Eisenkot, Yashar Party: ‘I do not see an Arab party that accepts my principles’
Pre-election: In a September interview with The Jerusalem Post, he dismissed the idea he would need to form a coalition with Arab parties: “I believe the majority we receive will be much larger than what the polls currently show,” adding “I do not see an Arab party that accepts my principles.”
He also said his “inner feeling is that I now have the ability to defeat Netanyahu”.
Election day: Eisenkot rallied Israelis to get rid of “the worst government Israel has known”.
However, he acknowledged how tight the race was, saying, “We are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state.”
Post-election day: On Wednesday, Eisenkot told his supporters the Israeli public “voted against” Netanyahu and promised, “to ensure that the people’s decision is translated into a Zionist government”.
What the results show: Yashar is on course for 21 seats, with 16.16 percent. His bloc has 48, 13 short of a majority, and he cannot reach 61 without the Arab-led parties.
Naftali Bennett, Together Party: ‘The October 7 government is going home’
Pre-election: In February, months before the vote, Bennett told a closed conference of party activists that he stood by his 2021 decision to govern with Ra’am, but said he would not repeat it.
He said, “We will establish a unity government under my leadership … We are going to win, and we are going to form it,” Israel National News reported.
Election day: “Netanyahu has lost, and the October 7 government is going home,” Bennett told supporters in Tel Aviv.
Post-election: In a post on X, Bennett told Israelis to “lift your heads” and said he will do everything “to establish a Zionist Alliance of Servants government”.
What the results show: Together is on course for 12 seats with 9.07 percent, narrowly behind the Joint List.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, Otzma Yehudit: Palestinians in Gaza ‘shouldn’t live’
Pre-election: In his election campaign, Ben-Gvir expressed his most genocidal views yet, saying in August that there are Palestinians in Gaza “who are not worthy of life. They shouldn’t live. They’re not even people.” He called for Israel to kill “30 to 40” people in Gaza every night.
Election day: “If you want this country to stay Jewish and Zionist, if you don’t want it to be in the hands of (Israeli Knesset members) Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi, go out and vote,” he told supporters at the entrance to the Arab city of Kafr Qasim.
What the results show: Otzma Yehudit is on course for seven seats, with 5.58 percent, less than half of the 15 he wanted.
Bezalel Smotrich, Religious Zionism-Zehut: ‘Jewish settlements will be established in Gaza’
Pre-election: In a statement he issued in August, he promised an expansion of his settlement “revolution” with a programme for the “Judaization of the Negev and the Galilee” at the expense of Palestinians, as part of his campaign.
Election day: He warned on Facebook of high turnout in communities of Palestinian citizens of Israel, claiming that failing to mobilise right-wing voters could let “terror supporters” into government.
That night, he told supporters “Jewish settlements will be established in Gaza.”
What the results show: Religious Zionism is on course for six seats, with 4.78 percent.
Yousef Jabareen, Joint List: ‘Change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership’
Pre-election: In August, he stated that only “a large and strong Joint List will work with all its might to send the Netanyahu/Ben-Gvir/Smotrich government home”, according to The Jerusalem Post.
Election day, night: In a video statement, he said Netanyahu knew “we can put an end to his bloody reign.”
Post-election: He wrote on X that his party was ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”, which he called one of “bloodshed”.
“Against a politics of supremacy, racism, and exclusion, we offer a completely different alternative. The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote.
What the results show: The Joint List is on course for 12 seats with 9.14 percent, making it the third-largest party by vote share.
Mansour Abbas, Ra’am: Netanyahu uses ‘scare tactic to mobilise right-wing voters’
Election day, night: In July, Abbas set Ra’am a goal of at least seven seats, enough, he argued, to make it the balance of power in a “government of change”.
Election day: He hit back at Netanyahu’s posts about Palestinian citizens of Israel, stating in a video that he was “lying and inciting against Ra’am, using it as a scare tactic to mobilise right-wing voters and drive them to the polls”.
What the results show: Ra’am is on course for eight seats, with 6.09 percent, beating his target of seven.
Avigdor Lieberman, Yisrael Beiteinu: ‘We will reach 61 seats’
Pre-election: On October 15, he claimed: “We will reach 61 seats or more for the change bloc.”
Election day: He urged patience, saying on Friday, “we’ll be able to talk about a much better and more optimistic picture.”
What the results show: Yisrael Beiteinu is on course for seven seats, with 5.93 percent.
Yair Lapid, Together: Netanyahu is ‘busy fear-mongering’
Pre-election: In September, he posted a statement which said, “Netanyahu ignored every warning before October 7, and now, 28 days before the election, he’s suddenly busy fear-mongering.”
Election day: He declared victory, stating, “The Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat.”
What the results show: Together, which he co-leads with Bennett, is on course for 12 seats, with 9.07 percent.

Firehawk raises $150M at $1.4B valuation to build more rocket motors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:26:16 UTC
20:26:16 KST

- Firehawk raised more than $150 million in a Series D led by Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, valuing the company above $1.4 billion.
- The funds will expand its Oklahoma propellant plant and Mississippi missile integration site to scale rocket and artillery motor production.
Dallas-based rocket propulsion firm Firehawk has raised more than $150 million in a Series D round that values the company at more than $1.4 billion, money it will use to scale up U.S. production of rocket propellant, solid rocket motors and artillery motors, the company said on social media on Oct. 28.
Private equity firm Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, co-founded by Dallas investor Kyle Bass, led the round, with new and existing investors and strategic partners also taking part. Firehawk said the round was upsized and oversubscribed, and the Dallas Morning News reported its original target was $100 million. The company did not disclose how much each investor put in.
The money will fund the build-out of Firehawk’s propellant and rocket motor plant in Lawton, Oklahoma, and its missile integration facility in Crawford, Mississippi, along with new research and development sites and more hiring, the company said in its funding announcement. Firehawk plans to produce more than 100,000 artillery motors in 2027 under a commercial agreement with General Dynamics, and its Oklahoma plant is expected to start low-rate production by mid-2027.
Firehawk was founded in 2019 by CEO Will Edwards to make hybrid rocket engines powered by 3D-printed fuel, and it now describes itself as covering the whole chain from propellant to motors to complete rounds. Its pitch is volume: the U.S. military’s appetite for rockets and missiles has outrun the small number of established solid rocket motor suppliers, and Firehawk says its patented manufacturing process can produce propellant faster and at larger scale for smaller tactical weapons.
The company broke ground on its Great Plains Arsenal rocket motor and propellant plant in Lawton in April. Its Crawford site can integrate 40,000 tactical rockets a year, and Firehawk says it plans to raise that to about 120,000 at full-rate production.
Much of that work centers on the Hydra-70, the 70 mm unguided rocket fired from U.S. Army attack helicopters and other aircraft. This summer the U.S. Army picked Firehawk as one of four new companies to build Hydra-70 rockets, alongside iRocket, Nammo Perry and Albers, with each required to deliver 24 prototype M151 rockets within 18 months. In August, Firehawk fired six Hydra-70 rockets at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, all of which worked as intended.
The Series D follows a $60 million Series C that closed in September 2025 and a strategic investment in November 2025 aimed at speeding up solid rocket motor production and integration.
Firehawk has not said how many Hydra-70 rockets or rocket motors it has delivered to the U.S. military so far, or when its Oklahoma plant will reach full-rate production.

ATHENS/SOFIA, Oct 29 (Reuters) - A Greek container ship has sunk after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria on Wednesday, the Bulgarian government said, in the latest of a series of strikes on ships in the western Black Sea this month.
It was not immediately clear who had carried out the attack, which added to growing concerns about the impact of Russia’s war in Ukraine on commercial shipping in the area.
The Liberian-flagged CONTSHIP JET, loaded with 421 containers, was badly damaged by three sea drones as it passed through Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) - but outside its territorial waters - en route from Haifa in Israel to Constanța in Romania.
The crew of 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians were all rescued and transferred safely to the Bulgarian port of Varna, Contships Management said.
At least six ships have been attacked by drones off Bulgaria this month, and about two dozen seafarers are feared dead, according to government statements.
Bulgaria, a member of the European Union and NATO, has sought assistance to bolster security off its Black Sea coast.
Bulgarian naval commander Kiril Mihaylov told national television authorities had been alerted to a possible drone attack by a French patrol aircraft, but had been unable to prevent it.
The government said that initial inspections on Thursday had found no visible traces of pollution from the ship, whose cargo included lithium-ion batteries, corrosive liquids and acids and industrial components.

German industry groups urge Berlin to join defence bank initiative

By Marc Jones and Maria Martinez
BERLIN, Oct 29 (Reuters) - German business and industry associations on Thursday urged the government to join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), saying membership was needed to close financing gaps for companies in the defence sector and protect their access to future projects.
The joint statement was signed by groups including the German Security and Defence Industry Association (BDSV), aerospace association BDLI, the chamber of commerce DIHK, engineering association VDMA, savings banks group DSGV and the Startup Association.
The proposed multilateral institution, backed by Canada, seven other NATO countries and Ukraine, would provide long-term, low-cost financing for defence, security and resilience projects.
“The geostrategic threat situation urgently requires new answers and approaches: financing for the defence sector must be secured sustainably over the long term,” said Elisabeth Hauschild, managing director of BDSV.
The associations said the bank could offer guarantees for commercial loans to small and medium-sized companies, including startups, as well as long-term loans, venture capital and equity financing for capacity expansion, innovation and critical raw materials.
“As a multilateral development bank, it provides the decisive risk buffer through guarantees and long-term financing instruments—particularly where established banks have so far been reluctant to support long-term contracts for the Mittelstand,” Hauschild said.
The DSRB, which will be based in Canada, has faced challenges securing support from larger European nations. Reuters was first to report in September last year that Britain had declined to join the project.
A spokesperson for the German finance ministry told Reuters on Monday that Germany was an observer in the negotiations on DSRB’s charter and was reviewing open questions.
Germany should participate in the bank’s founding process and join the group of founding states as soon as possible, the business associations said.
The groups warned that companies from member countries could receive preferential access to procurement projects financed by the DSRB under its planned charter rules. If Germany stayed outside the institution, its companies could be excluded from market opportunities or face a competitive disadvantage against rivals from member states, they added.

ECB President Lagarde resigns at time of mounting challenges for Europe
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:25:42 CET
20:25:42 KST

By Francesco Canepa and Balazs Koranyi
FRANKFURT, Oct 29 (Reuters) - European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde resigned on Thursday, ending months of speculation about her future just as Europe enters a period of rising economic volatility and divisive electoral politics, particularly in her native France.
Lagarde will step down on February 7, giving current European Union leaders time to pick her successor before a French presidential election that polls show far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favoured to win. Her term was due to expire next October.
The move comes as the ECB battles inflation risks from an Iran war-driven oil shock while a sharp rise in bond yields, especially in France, threatens to dampen growth.
“I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future,” Lagarde, 70, said in a short video shared on social media.
A source with direct knowledge of the matter said Lagarde, a former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund, had resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in France and globally. As ECB president, she was expected to remain neutral to safeguard the institution’s independence.
Only three months ago, Lagarde dismissed talk of an early exit, saying she could not leave the ECB with inflationary “clouds” gathering on the horizon.
FRANCE’S RIGHT-WING PARTY LAMENTS MOVE
Jean-Philippe Tanguy, charged with drafting economic policy for Le Pen’s election manifesto, told Reuters Lagarde’s move showed contempt for the rule of law: “I saw this coming. Another insult in our direction – lamentable.”
Markus Ferber, a German member of the European parliament for the centre-right European People’s Party, also said Lagarde’s early resignation sent “the wrong signal” given high inflation, nervous bond markets and looming elections.
“If the impression arises that such a departure is timed around national elections, it damages trust in an institution that must stand above any domestic political calculation,” Ferber, who sits on the parliamentary committee that will confirm Lagarde’s successor, said.
By contrast, Marcel Fratzscher, president of German think-tank DIW, said Lagarde was showing “a strong sense of responsibility towards Europe”.
“By leaving office early, Christine Lagarde gives European governments and institutions an opportunity to appoint a successor who will safeguard European values and protect the ECB’s independence,” he told Reuters.
Lagarde has not addressed such matters directly. She has said she would not be a candidate for the French presidency but would advocate for pro-European values in her home country “in whichever capacity” she deemed most efficient.
European Council President Antonio Costa said the process to find Lagarde’s successor would begin immediately.
The appointment is likely to be part of a broader package of top ECB jobs involving the executive board seat of Isabel Schnabel, who will leave in early January, and chief economist Philip Lane, due to depart in May.
COMPETENT CANDIDATES REASSURE MARKETS
The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are widely seen as frontrunners to replace Lagarde.
“The rumoured successors are both very competent, well established central bankers, so for markets, it won’t matter too much,” Piet Haines Christiansen, an economist at Danske Bank, said.
Financial markets showed little reaction to the announcement, with some analysts saying the ECB had now built a reputation that outlived any of its leaders.
“The ECB is now quite well established, the market is familiar with the way it operates,” Goldman Sachs’ head of Fixed Income Macro Investing Simon Dangoor said. “Our view is that institutional behaviour is likely to outlast Lagarde, and be quite similar, whoever takes over.”
Lagarde’s term was scheduled to run until the end of October 2027 but speculation about an early departure had been mounting for months, with the World Economic Forum seen as a likely destination. The WEF declined to comment.
RATE HIKES AND BOND TURMOIL
Lagarde’s resignation comes just as the ECB is in the middle of a rate-hiking cycle aimed at preventing an oil-price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into other prices and wages.
But it must also contend with a surge in government bond yields — especially in debt-laden France — that has pushed up borrowing costs for households and businesses and which Lagarde has said will curb growth and inflation.
Caught between persistent inflation fuelled by a renewed surge in energy costs and deteriorating financing conditions, the ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday while signalling that another increase, potentially as soon as December, remains likely.
“There is likely a low bar to another hike in December, given the likelihood of another upward revision of the ECB’s inflation forecast due to higher energy prices,” Oliver Rakau at Oxford Economics said.
The ECB is due to announce its interest rate decision at 1315 GMT on Thursday, followed by Lagarde’s regular press conference at 1345 GMT.
Money markets are currently pricing another three rate increases from the ECB by the end of next year, which would take the deposit rate to 3.25%, a level that is widely seen as restricting economic growth.
(Additional reporting by Elizabeth Pineau in Paris and Klaus Lauer in Berlin; Editing by Catherine Evans and Toby Chopra)

Who is to blame for Hong Kong’s deadly 2025 fire?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:25:33 CET
20:25:33 KST

HONG KONG, Oct 29 (Reuters) - An independent Hong Kong committee blamed a renovation contractor and consultant as well as four government departments for a deadly blaze that killed 168 people in the city last November, according to its report released to the public on Thursday.
The more than 1,000-page report by the judge-led panel detailed a series of regulatory and supervisory failings in Hong Kong’s building renovation and regulatory system that it said had contributed to the rapid spread of the fire.
KEY FINDINGS:
* Prestige Construction & Engineering Co. Ltd, the main contractor for the works, and Will Power Architects Co, the consultant for the works, were fully aware of the fire risks and ignored all complaints raised by residents.
* Prestige failed to maintain proper oversight at every level and cut corners. It also did not effectively enforce anti-smoking policies on site, despite persistent complaints.
* Prestige refused to conduct works in phases as requested by the management committee, resulting in all eight blocks being simultaneously enclosed in combustible scaffolding and materials, which contributed to the rapid spread of the fire.
* Will Power, as project consultant, failed to provide proper independent supervision of Prestige and did not intervene in key safety issues.
* Will Power approved the use of flammable foam boards and non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets, despite knowing the fire risks and initially expressing concern.
* Will Power failed to act as an independent supervisor, instead enabling or acquiescing to Prestige’s cost-cutting and unsafe practices, betraying the trust placed in it by homeowners.
* The fire was most likely started by a “glowing source…likely a cigarette”.
* No government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues, and complaints about fire hazards “fell into a vacuum”.
* Multiple government departments failed to properly investigate persistent and well-documented resident complaints about fire hazards, smoking, unsafe materials and procedural irregularities.
* The way in which the Labour Department handled complaints outlining serious safety concerns — such as smoking on site, and about fire retardancy of scaffolding nets and foam boards — was unsatisfactory.
* Hong Kong’s Independent Checking Unit (ICU) failed in its supervisory responsibilities to ensure safety. The ICU’s systemic regulatory failures and operational lapses were major contributors to the unsafe conditions that led to the fire.
* There was inadequate regulation and verification of temporary building materials (e.g., scaffolding nets, foam boards, plastic sheeting), with authorities relying on paper certificates without laboratory testing or on-site sampling, enabling the use of non-fire-retardant materials.
* There was a lack of effective communication and coordination among government departments, leading to complaints and fire safety issues being passed between departments without resolution, creating regulatory vacuums.
* The disaster involved not just violations of safety rules but also long-standing flaws in the regulatory regimes and slack enforcement attitude.
* Various unlawful and dubious practices in the large-scale building and renovation industry are acknowledged, including bid-rigging. “Some of them have triad affiliations … The committee is of the view that such a corrupt eco-system is intolerable.”
* The Competition Commission (CC) and Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) both found that bid rigging is a widespread, systemic, and long-standing practice among building maintenance contractors in Hong Kong.
* Investigations revealed that some bid-rigging operations are orchestrated by syndicates, often with triad involvement, who coordinate which contractors will win certain tenders through cover bidding, bid suppression or bid rotation.

In November 2025 Hungary signed an agreement to buy American nuclear fuel and US technology to store spent fuel at a Russian-built nuclear power plant.
Hungary is also considering replacing Russia’s Rosatom as the main contractor in the expansion of its Paks nuclear power plant and has started sounding out alternative suppliers as part of a review of the project. Magyar’s government is expected to decide on the Paks expansion later this year or early in 2027.

“They’ve run out of money,” Paul said. “That’s why they couldn’t buy fuel. They’ve even had difficulties paying the crew on the ship, which even makes it more difficult. So we’re really not expecting any money back.”
Villa Vie did not respond to emailed questions or phone calls. In a statement on Tuesday, it said it was seeking to restructure and recapitalize, but no deals had been finalised.
“That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured,” the company said, and added it was working to support those affected.

“And then when we got to Cambodia, absolutely no internet,” he said. “And the food quality began to deteriorate about three months ago, and we knew that the company was running out of money at that time.”
The Montoyas said they now planned to live off the money they had budgeted for the monthly fees and spend some time in Malaysia.
Lynn said they would miss the community aboard the ship more than the lost money.
“It’s hard to lose that money, but I also look at it as, we’ve had 17 months of going to the most amazing places and meeting the most amazing people,” she said.

Christine Lagarde: The outsider who led the ECB her way
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:25:23 CET
20:25:23 KST

By Francesco Canepa and Leigh Thomas
FRANKFURT, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Christine Lagarde’s decision to step down early as European Central Bank president ends an eventful seven years at an institution she was never expected to lead.
The former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund arrived in Frankfurt in 2019 as the first ECB chief with no formal economics training or central banking experience — prompting some market participants to label her a “credibility risk.”
In fact, she knew so little about the institution that Lagarde, 70, later said she had accepted the job thinking the presidency was a five-year mandate, rather than eight.
Yet after a tenure dominated by a pandemic, two energy shocks and the worst inflation spike in the euro zone’s history, Lagarde leaves with a record that defied the sceptics.
“Her seven years at the ECB have been, on the whole, pretty good,” said Willem Buiter, an economist and former Bank of England official, noting that the ECB managed to bring inflation back down faster than peers in Britain and the United States.
Her exit, however, threatens to be as political as her arrival.
By walking away before her eight-year term ends, Lagarde gives European Union leaders a chance to pick her successor before a French election next spring that opinion polls suggest far-right candidate Marine Le Pen will win, replacing President Emmanuel Macron.
For an institution that fiercely guards its independence from political meddling, the timing has drawn sharp criticism from central bank watchers.
“This is debasing the institution and just following the purely political calculus of the French president,” said Paul De Grauwe, a professor at the London School of Economics.
Lagarde and Macron have not addressed such criticism directly. Lagarde has said she would not be a candidate for the French presidency but would advocate for pro-European values in her home country “in whichever capacity” she deemed most efficient.
‘BETTER WITH BUTTER’
Throughout her career, Lagarde has stood apart from more technocratic colleagues through a mix of charm, consensus-building and folksy pragmatism.
Favouring plain-speaking homilies over dense economic theory, the then-IMF chief famously declared that “everything is better with butter” when discussing growth and told governments to “fix the roof while the sun is shining”.
Unorthodoxy was a hallmark of Lagarde’s career, and the subject of her upcoming autobiography “Lady First”.
A former corporate lawyer who spent years in Chicago, she entered French politics in 2005 as an outsider. Early missteps earned her the domestic moniker “Madame Lagaffe,” but she soon became one of then-President Nicolas Sarkozy’s sharpest operators, steering French banks through the 2008 crash.
She led the IMF through Europe’s debt crisis, navigating a messy Greek rescue that imposed harsh austerity, and sparked outrage in Athens when she bluntly urged suffering citizens to “pay their taxes”.
Her appetite for high-stakes bets showed again in 2018 with a record $57-billion lifeline for Argentina to back then-President Mauricio Macri. The gamble unravelled, failing to halt a currency collapse or avert a deep recession, and left the IMF bound to its most troubled debtor.
THE SPREADS CRISIS AND THE TRIBAL CLIQUE
Her occasional unfamiliarity with the nuances of central banking still peeked through.
In March 2020, as the pandemic rattled sovereign debt markets, Lagarde told a press conference the ECB was “not here to close spreads” between Italian and German borrowing costs.
The comment triggered an immediate selloff in bond markets and forced her to swiftly walk it back.
Under Lagarde’s watch, the ECB swiftly rolled out emergency bond-buying that stabilised markets as COVID-19 spread. It launched its fastest series of interest-rate hikes to bring inflation under control following Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, although it later acknowledged it had been slow to recognise the full impact of spiking energy prices.
As ECB president, she once described economists as a “tribal clique” — a provocative jab at the profession’s establishment, though she later softened the blow by saying she hoped to join the tribe.
A ‘MORE POLITICAL’ ECB PRESIDENT
Lagarde used her political skills to repair rifts. Unlike her predecessor Mario Draghi, whose top-down style embittered some hawkish northern European peers, she worked to build consensus among the euro zone’s 21 national central bank chiefs.
Her willingness to wade into politics remained evident: in January, Lagarde walked out of a World Economic Forum dinner in Davos during a speech by US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that criticised Europe, an episode that underscored fraught transatlantic relations.
Whoever succeeds her when she leaves the ECB on February 7 will face fresh challenges including strains in French bond markets ahead of next year’s election and a Middle East conflict that threatens a new bout of inflation.
Ultimately, Lagarde’s legacy may be a paradox: an outsider who showed that political diplomacy could steer a central bank through historic shocks, but whose early departure served as a final reminder of her political instincts.
“She was put there for a reason: being more political than her predecessor and, on that mission, I think she largely succeeded,” Frederik Ducrozet, head of strategy and macro research at Pictet Wealth Management, said.
(Additional reporting by Balazs Koranyi; Editing by Catherine Evans)

In Lebanese village near Israeli troops, farmers brave danger to harvest their olives

By Catherine Cartier, Emilie Madi and Raghed Waked
ZIBQIN, Lebanon Oct 29 (Reuters) - In a field overlooking a lush valley in southern Lebanon, residents of the village of Zibqin balanced on branches picking their olives while Lebanese Army soldiers stood nearby.
Zibqin is adjacent to Israel’s self-declared “security zone” in southern Lebanon, where Israeli troops have demolished dozens of villages, saying armed group Hezbollah had embedded itself in civilian infrastructure — a claim the group denies. Israeli shelling frequently strikes the valley below the olive groves despite a June ceasefire between the two sides.
As Palestinians, Israeli rights groups and the UN report increased violence and olive thefts by Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Lebanese farmers also fear for their safety, illustrating how conflict is again upending the annual harvest.
Despite the danger, Lebanese farmers are returning to fields they have tended for generations, determined to harvest a crop that is one of their main sources of income and nutrition.
Ali Bzieh, a 65-year-old farmer from Zibqin, said he had no choice but to come to the fields. “This is my land, this is my livelihood, this is a harvest we wait for from one year to the next,” he said, sitting under the branches of an olive tree. “We have an attachment to this land, to the plants, and to the crops — we don’t leave them.”
LIMITED PROTECTION
Many families came back to Zibqin after the ceasefire between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah. But the situation remains unstable, Raef Bzieh, a local official, said. “The ongoing bombing and the aggressions taking place on the outskirts of the village have of course caused worry and panic among the people.”
The danger prompted residents to ask the Lebanese Army to accompany them to their fields. But Mustafa Barakat, a 50-year-old carpenter, said that even with the army, the villagers did not feel safe. “But if the Israelis decide to cause harm, they can harm us, and the army,” he said. “They have struck the Lebanese Army more than once.”
Israeli attacks have killed 26 Lebanese soldiers in 2026, according to statements posted by the Lebanese Army on X. The Lebanese Army is not party to the conflict between Hezbollah and Israel.
In response to questions from Reuters, the Israeli military said its strikes in Lebanon are against Hezbollah and its infrastructure and are not directed at the Lebanese Army or civilians. It also said it is working to “enable the olive harvest and assist residents in carrying it out”.
Thirty-eight Israeli soldiers have been killed in southern Lebanon in 2026, according to posts on the Israeli military’s website.
WAR CHANGES HARVEST’S RHYTHMS
Barakat’s days in the olive grove used to start in the early morning and stretch until sunset. Now, he limits his time in the field to when the Lebanese Army is present.
The danger has reshaped what was once an occasion for families to gather and share the hard work of harvesting olives.
“In the past, we used to treat this (harvest) season like an outing,” he said. He used to come with his family to the fields and prepare food together. ”Now, you can’t bring children… bombing could occur, and they could get hurt,” he said.
The conflict has affected the harvest in other ways too: “We weren’t able to tend to our olive trees, so our olive trees did not yield as they usually do,” said Ali, who was displaced for several months. He said the harvest was half what it normally was.
Ali said that he hoped the situation wouldn’t escalate further and force his family to flee again. But many in Zibqin were bracing for that possibility: some residents continue to pay rent for apartments in areas further north. Others have already reserved a place to stay in the event of further escalation.
Yet as war casts its shadow over the harvest for the fourth consecutive year, the farmers refuse to abandon their fields.
“This land is our identity, it is the passport we carry,” said Barakat. “If we abandon it, we are truly left without an identity.”

As criminal networks spread in Latin America, Quito is new battleground
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:25:20 CET
20:25:20 KST

By Alexandra Valencia
QUITO, Oct 29 (Reuters) - For years, the neighborhood watch group in the working-class area of Solanda in Ecuadorean capital Quito had patrolled their nighttime streets armed with little more than whistles and sticks, on the lookout for cellphone snatching and other petty crimes.
But then they realized the criminals were changing. Members of notorious national gangs began to move into the area, and shootings, contract killings and extortion took hold. The watch suspended the patrols, fearful they might be targeted themselves. Their place was taken by heavily armed troops, sent by the national government.
Ecuador’s importance as a transit point for cocaine exports from Colombia and Peru has spiked over the last half-decade, stoking an explosion in violence and crime in the once tranquil South American country that has caught up everyone from Pacific fishermen to politicians, journalists and grandmothers forced from their homes.
President Daniel Noboa, an ally of the administration of US President Donald Trump, has responded with a widespread military, police and legislative crackdown on crime, sending soldiers into the streets and hardening sentences, among other measures. The government has notched several major captures or killings of gang leaders, but that has led to fragmentation, creating vicious internecine violence and splinter groups seeking new territory.
That now includes Quito. This historic Andean city, with its whitewashed colonial buildings, cobbled streets, and backdrop of cloudcapped volcanoes, has long been a draw for tourists and digital nomads. But it is becoming an increasing focus of criminal activity, residents, police and analysts say. Gangs are using local drug sales to gain a foothold in neighborhoods, taking advantage of the capital’s strategic location to distribute drugs to the country’s ports, from where cocaine destined mostly for Europe and the US is shipped.
“Criminal organizations have tried to establish themselves in certain neighborhoods through small-scale drug trafficking,” police Lieutenant Colonel Juan Chacon told Reuters as his team conducted a raid on an alleged drug distribution site in central Quito. “That connects them to a range of other crimes.”
Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones, all gangs which the US has designated as foreign terrorist organizations, are present in Quito, according to police.
Solanda, built as a public housing project in the 1980s, with a busy commercial district and narrow streets of modest houses, appears on a national government list of high-risk Quito areas. Residents have installed a surveillance camera system on every street corner and metal gates at entrances to side streets to prevent unknown people from entering.
“With the cameras, you can identify the criminal and avoid exposing yourself,” said Maria Eugenia Alban, a community leader in Solanda. “Now criminals are no longer acting alone, and they are armed.”
GANGS ‘TRYING TO ESTABLISH A FOOTHOLD’
The pushback from authorities has had some success. An increased security response in Solanda lowered violent death figures to just two between January and September of this year, down from 13 in the same period of 2025, according to government records.
Violent death figures in Quito overall fell in 2024 and 2025 from a high of 294 in 2023, according to Interior Ministry data, as Noboa sent soldiers onto the streets. And violence still remains below that of Ecuador’s port cities like Guayaquil and Duran.
But, the armed forces say, it is a constant battle.
“Organized crime groups are trying to establish a foothold in Quito,” Lieutenant Colonel Miguel Saavedra, head of a tactical army brigade which is responsible for controlling guns, ammunition and explosives in the capital, told Reuters at a checkpoint where his unit was checking cars for weapons. His troops were seeking to “safeguard and restore security” in the city, he added.
About 4,000 police and military personnel were deployed at entry points and along strategic corridors in Quito as part of a security plan announced by Noboa in August. The city has been under a 60-day state of emergency since September.
During the first six weeks of the plan, police arrested more than 300 people, according to national police figures. The military joined police operations to check for weapons at entrances to high-risk neighborhoods and conducted targeted patrols.
Drug seizures in Quito were up nearly 500% between January and September, compared with the same period a year before, according to police figures.
Military and police operations across Ecuador cost gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining and fuel and arms trafficking nearly $20 billion in losses between January and July, according to the Defense Ministry.
However, crackdowns in one place can prompt criminal groups to seek out more favorable territory where residents are less wary of crime, said Colonel Mario Pazmino, a former head of army intelligence and current security analyst.
He said Quito is part of the “cocaine triangle,” serving as a transit and temporary storage point for drugs coming from the Colombian coastal city of Tumaco and Putumayo province, before being transported across Ecuador along Pacific and Amazon road corridors.
The capital’s strategic position has been exploited by a growing number of criminal groups over the past year, said Tiziano Breda, an analyst at conflict-monitoring organization ACLED, although its status as a “transit point” lowers the risk of it being the focus of the sort of violent disputes between groups seen elsewhere.
“In Quito’s case, international cartels and national gangs are beginning to converge and establish themselves,” Pazmino said. “Quito is a hub city. The gangs come to protect the merchandise and look for other activities.”
(Reporting by Alexandra Valencia in Quito, additional reporting by Tito Correa, Editing by Julia Symmes Cobb and Rosalba O’Brien)

‘Survival of the fittest’: The struggle to get to university in The Gambia

‘Survival of the fittest’: The struggle to get to university in The Gambia
Students at a top university protest transport shortages, poor facilities and safety concerns, demanding better services and leadership accountability.
Faraba Banta, The Gambia – For Muhammed Lamin Jallow, a student at the University of The Gambia’s School of Arts and Sciences, getting to class has become a daily struggle.
He travels about 40 km (25 miles) from home to the Faraba Banta campus, depending on university buses, to attend lectures.
But securing a seat on the bus can be challenging.
“Sometimes, it feels like survival of the fittest,” he told Al Jazeera. “We compete as to who gets in first, who gets to sit, who gets to stand and who goes to school and who does not.”
Jallow was among hundreds of students who protested at the University of The Gambia (UTG) on Monday, taking their grievances over transportation, campus facilities and student welfare to the vice chancellor’s office.
Lectures have since resumed after the government promised improvements to campus services.
But the students have more demands. They want Vice Chancellor Herbert Robinson and the director of student affairs to resign, accusing both officials of failing to perform their duties.
While the government has announced measures to address some of the concerns, the leadership dispute remains unresolved.
Transport and basic services remain concerns
The Students’ Union says its concerns affect more than 12,000 students, many of whom depend on university buses to reach campus.
Following the protest, Higher Education Minister Professor Pierre Gomez visited the campus with university representatives and officials from the Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy.
In a statement, the Ministry of Higher Education, Research, Science and Technology said the Gambia Transport Service Company had deployed 20 buses to support student transportation.
Students have also complained of limited access to safe drinking water and affordable food, as well as unreliable internet connectivity.
In response, the ministry promised that cafeterias across the university were ready to serve students and staff, but acknowledged that additional filtration was needed to make campus water safe for drinking. Water jars and dispensers have been installed at designated points, and the National Water and Electricity Company (NAWEC) had been consulted, it said.
On internet access, the ministry said work was under way to extend connectivity to the newly constructed Schools of Agriculture and Law, with completion expected within a week.
The proposals are intended to support student access to research materials and other educational resources. However, the statement did not confirm whether the work had been completed.
The ministry said it would continue working with the university, the students’ union and other relevant stakeholders to monitor implementation.
Cafeterias and practical training facilities
The reopening of cafeterias was another demand raised by students, who had complained that their closure made it difficult to find affordable meals on campus.
Ismaila Fadera, the students’ union president, said he raised the issue with Robinson on October 20 .
Fadera quoted the vice chancellor as saying: “Mister president, I have the student interest at heart, but we must balance this against administrative processes and compliance. You know I was a student too and many of us went through that. I used to carry my own water and food in my bag to university. The students should be told the reality. Having a cafeteria is a great addition to enhance the student experience but it is not right.”
The ministry said the cafeterias were ready to serve students and staff, although it provided no details on meal prices or availability at individual facilities.
Beyond food and water, students say inadequate learning facilities are affecting their education, particularly in programmes that require practical training.
At the School of Medicine and Allied Health Sciences in Banjul, students face overcrowded classrooms, inadequate ventilation, malfunctioning electrical sockets and shortages of projectors and smartboards, according to Abubacarr Manneh, president of the University of The Gambia Medical Students Association. Manneh said medical, nursing and postgraduate nursing students share the available facilities, putting pressure on classroom space.
He also worries about shortages of practical training equipment, including a promised simulation laboratory where students could develop clinical skills.
“Practical sessions are crucial in our professional training and development for better care of our patients,” he told Al Jazeera.
The university’s journalism students have similar concerns
Sukai Fatajo, a journalism student who participated in the protest, said the school needed radio and television studios to help students develop practical skills.
“We deserve better, and our demands must be met,” she told Al Jazeera.
The students’ union has also called for functional science laboratories, improvements to facilities at the medical school and adequate staffing.
The risks of getting to class
For Kumba Leigh, a journalism student, the struggle to reach the university has also become a question of personal safety.
One morning in April, Leigh was attacked by a knife-wielding assailant in her hometown of Bakau as she walked to a bus stop. She was trying to leave home early enough to secure a seat.
The attacker threatened to kill her if she did not hand over her bag. When she resisted, he struck her on the head and shoulder, cut her bag and dislocated her right arm. A nearby shopkeeper intervened, forcing the assailant to flee.
Months later, Leigh still has pain in her arm and suffers from trauma.
“No one should have to risk their life simply to travel to school,” she told Al Jazeera, calling for stronger security and increased police patrols.

====================================================================================================

Spain train crash: What happened in the 17 minutes before the collision?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:23:59 UTC
20:23:59 KST

An IT failure halted several trains on the Madrid–Seville high-speed line, but the crash came after Adif’s control centre authorised an AVE to resume its journey. Investigators are examining what caused the collision, which killed 69 people.
The collision between a Renfe AVE and an Iryo train, which occurred on Wednesday 28 October in Urda, in the central Spanish province of Toledo, has left at least 69 dead and more than 100 injured.
The accident took place at 8:53 am, at kilometre 118 on the Madrid–Seville high-speed line, when an AVE ran into the back of an Iryo train that was stationary on the same track. It is the second major high-speed rail tragedy in Spain in less than a year, after the Adamuz (Córdoba) crash in January 2026, which claimed 46 lives.
Although there is still no definitive conclusion on the causes, the investigation is focusing on a failure in the signalling system and, in particular, on the order issued from the control centre of Adif, Spain's railway infrastructure operator, at Madrid's Atocha railway station, for the AVE to resume its journey.
What went wrong with the safety system?
The first incident was recorded at around 8:30 am, when an IT failure disrupted communications and caused the LZB safety system to fail along a roughly 63-kilometre section of the Madrid–Seville high-speed line. The system transmits information between railway infrastructure and trains to monitor traffic and maintain safe distances.
The issue affected six trains, which had to stop or adjust their speed. Among them were Iryo 6076, carrying 147 passengers, including a baby, and Renfe's AVE 2080, with 397 passengers on board. The LZB system has been in operation on the line since its opening in the 1990s and is due to be replaced by the more modern European ERTMS system.
However, the IT failure alone does not explain the accident. When the main signalling system fails, alternative procedures are in place to manage train movements. Investigators are working to establish why those safeguards failed to prevent two trains from occupying the same section of track.
What order did the AVE receive from the Atocha control centre?
This is one of the key questions in the investigation. According to a reconstruction published by the Ministry of Transport and communication recordings published by El País, at 8:36 am, an Adif controller authorised the AVE driver to resume his journey under the lineside signalling block (BSL) system.
The instruction allowed the train to continue under "normal running" conditions, even though the main signalling system had failed. The driver requested confirmation of the order, which the controller subsequently confirmed.
The distinction is crucial: under "driving on sight" rules, drivers must adjust their speed to ensure they can stop before reaching any obstacle. In these circumstances, the speed limit is 40 kilometres per hour.
By contrast, permission to resume normal running meant the AVE could travel at a significantly higher speed. Transport Minister Óscar Puente described the control centre's decision as "inexplicable" and argued that the train should never have resumed its journey under those conditions.
The decisive 17 minutes: what happened before the collision?
The reconstruction of the communications provides a timeline of events that will be crucial to the investigation:
8:30 am. A computer fault disables the LZB system, forcing several trains on the Madrid–Seville high-speed line to stop.
8:36 am. Adif's control centre in Atocha authorises AVE 2080 to resume its journey under the lineside signalling block system (BSL) and continue running normally.
8:41 am. The Iryo driver informs the control centre that her train remains stopped on the approach to Urda due to a loss of transmission. The controller also authorises her to resume her journey.
8:48 am. The Iryo driver contacts Atocha again, reporting that she is unable to restart the LZB system and that her train remains stationary. According to the recordings published by El País, the AVE is not instructed to stop.
8:53 am. The AVE collides with the rear of the Iryo train, after travelling roughly 25 kilometres since receiving authorisation to continue.
The recordings released so far raise a fundamental question: why was the AVE not ordered to slow down or stop after the control centre received the warnings from the Iryo driver?
The communications, traffic logs and black box data from both trains will be crucial in reconstructing the decisions made during those 17 minutes.
Could the accident have been avoided?
This is one of the key questions that the judicial and technical investigations will need to address. The government has initially suggested possible human error at Adif's control centre, but responsibility has not yet been determined.
Investigators will need to establish whether operating protocols were correctly followed, what information was available to staff at Atocha, and why the authorisation given to the AVE was not revised after confirmation that the Iryo train remained stationary.
They will also examine whether there were additional failures in the systems responsible for monitoring and ensuring rail safety. The cause of the accident has therefore not yet been established, and responsibility cannot be attributed to any single individual until the investigations are complete.
What happens next in the investigation?
The Court of First Instance and Preliminary Investigation No. 2 in Orgaz (Toledo) has taken over the judicial investigation, which remains confidential. Among the first measures ordered by the court is a restriction on access to a two-kilometre section of the high-speed line around the crash site.
The court has also prohibited the removal of materials and debris from the affected area without prior authorisation and ordered the seizure and preservation of the trains' black boxes.
In addition, judicial police have been instructed to collect evidence from Adif's control centre in Atocha, including communications and data relating to train movements. Meanwhile, an independent technical investigation will seek to establish the causes of the crash and make recommendations to improve rail safety.

Is von der Leyen’s ‘associate membership’ for Canada already dead?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:22:21 UTC
20:22:21 KST

The term ‘associate membership’ was dropped from the EU-Canada summit text after German pushback, in a major blow to Commission President von der Leyen. Nonetheless, the two sides are still keen to boost their partnership.
Just weeks after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen unveiled a bold new blueprint for relations with third countries, starting with Canada, the idea of “associate membership” has been quietly buried. Has her grand vision already run aground?
On Wednesday, all references to associate membership were scrubbed from the joint statement due to be adopted at this week's EU-Canada summit, following objections from several member states, led by Germany.
Instead, the text agreed by member states speaks of developing an “ever closer association” between the EU and Canada, stopping short of full membership.
"It would have been much better to have unity from member states on the initial wording, but we have a strong basis that is agreed. And we are fleshing out the details. But most importantly, we have a common approach in terms of what the objective is that we want to pursue," Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said on Thursday.
It may look like a semantic distinction, but it amounts to an embarrassing political setback for von der Leyen, who floated the idea of Canada becoming the EU's first associate member with great fanfare in September.
Arriving in Montreal for the summit, von der Leyen appeared determined to press ahead regardless.
“We have a new ambition: bringing Canada closer to us than ever before, as associate member of the EU. And we want to take our unique partnership even further,” she wrote on X.
Yet despite the wordplay, the final text leaves little doubt that the much-hyped format failed to win the support of European governments, whom von der Leyen did not consult before making her grand pitch to Canada.
Her own country, Germany, led the charge to remove the term, arguing that the substance of the new partnership should be defined before attaching a label with potential legal implications, rather than the other way round.
There is an irony here. Associate membership was proposed last May by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as a way of offering Ukraine security guarantees while it worked towards full EU membership.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejected the proposal, which was never properly discussed among EU countries. Berlin, of course, denies that this is the real reason it so vehemently opposed Canada's associate membership.
“What the EU can do is technical, is a sector-by-sector approach. The ‘associate membership’ provided a package for it; it put a label on the partnership,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Perhaps even more telling, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney never fully bought into von der Leyen’s idea, preferring the notion of an 'Alliance for the Future'.
“The President used both terms. The precise nomenclature is a question for Europe,” Carney said at a press conference after von der Leyen’s speech, when asked whether he was comfortable with “associate membership”.
Again, the semantics hide different worldviews. For Carney, the Alliance for the Future is an open concept: a group of middle powers he championed in his landmark Davos speech in January as a new framework to safeguard global stability and the rules-based order.
The EU, by contrast, does not regard itself as a middle power, as officials in Brussels are fond of reminding anyone who will listen. Associate membership was intended to place the bloc at the centre of a new international coalition of democracies – not merely as one partner among equals, but as its leader.
That is why whatever arrangement the EU strikes with Canada matters beyond bilateral relations. Other like-minded countries, such as Australia, South Korea and Japan, are watching closely for a potential blueprint for how Brussels engages with third countries.
“In the world we are living in today, which is not the easiest, this is the right response: have the courage to think out of the box, have the courage to do something new, and have the courage to set out a vision,” said an EU official, also speaking on condition of anonymity.
Von der Leyen may have overplayed her hand, promising a partnership she could not deliver because she moved too far ahead of the member states. Still, it is hard to dismiss that EU-Canada ties have never been stronger in the past few months.
From joint exploitation of critical raw materials and common stockpiling to mutual market access in strategic sectors like AI and cloud, via systematic integration in EU defence programmes and early consultation on major policy areas, the relationship is on steroids.
Bernd Lange, the German MEP who chairs the European Parliament's Committee on International Trade, said that the disagreement over terminology should not overshadow the EU's growing ties with Canada.
“Getting caught up in debate over the partnership’s name only distracts from what really matters. So call it how you want, but what matters is concrete action, not words. The momentum is there,” he wrote on X.
