Mathematicians find an infinite number of Ramanujan equations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:19:15 UTC
20:19:15 KST

The legendary mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan and Yifeng Huang, a postdoctoral researcher at Emory University, have something in common: they will not be ignored. In 1912 Ramanujan, a 24-year-old clerk at what was then the Madras Port Trust in India, began mailing pages of new, unproven formulas to mathematicians across England. One of his letters eventually reached British mathematician G. H. Hardy at the University of Cambridge, who recognized Ramanujan as a visionary, invited him to visit and helped launch his groundbreaking career.
More than a century later, Huang, while a graduate student at the University of Michigan, began e-mailing mathematicians letter after letter—more than 40 in total. He scarcely heard back.
Huang’s ideas concerned two formulas that appeared in Ramanujan’s letters and are now known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. In September 2026 Huang and a few collaborators uploaded a proof that the historic equations represent a single case of a much grander geometrical theory. In particular, the work showed that the Roger-Ramanujan identities correspond to a trefoil knot in a certain space. The trefoil, known as the shape of the familiar Celtic knot, is one of the simplest mathematical knots. And related knots, they found, reveal an infinite number of previously unknown identities.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Everything about this subject, even the original discovery, is a surprise,” says George Andrews, a mathematician at Pennsylvania State University and an expert on Ramanujan’s math. Ramanujan, Hardy and their collaborators “were all unable to prove this,” he adds. “So the things that have cropped up from knot theory were a total surprise to me.”
The Roger-Ramanujan Identities
Hardy was responsible for shaping much of early 20th century number theory. Initially skeptical when he received a letter from Ramanujan, Hardy later wrote that he recognized the letter’s author as “a mathematician of the highest quality, a man of altogether exceptional originality and power.” It was a pivotal moment.
Two of Ramanujan’s formulas were startling: they represented an infinite series of sums on one side and an infinite series of products on the other, with no visible reason for the two to agree. By 1916 British mathematician Percy MacMahon had found a way to read them. These two equations were similar to ones studied two centuries earlier by mathematician Leonhard Euler. Euler had a neat trick for sidestepping such complexity: he connected the equations to a type of counting problem known as a “partition.” A partition of a number is a way of writing it as a sum. MacMahon transformed Ramanujan’s formulas into two kinds of partitions that looked nothing alike, but whose counts always came out identical.
Here’s how one side of a Ramanujan equation was partitioned: count the number of ways to sum up to a certain value using numbers that are at least two whole numbers apart. For instance, 6 can be written as 1 + 5, 2 + 4 and 6. So there are three partitions.
On the other side, sum using only numbers that end in 1, 4, 6 or 9. For 6, the answer is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 4 and 6, which also gives three partitions.
The formulas say these two very different counts agree for every number. Before Ramanujan could prove them, he came across an obscure proof by English mathematician Leonard James Rogers in an old math journal. Thus, the equations became known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities.
“It was regarded, for most of the 20th century, as an isolated gem,” Andrews says. No one suspected it lay at the heart of a much larger theory.
In the early 1970s Andrews uncovered an infinite family of the identities. “I discovered them only to learn that [mathematician] Basil Gordon had done them first,” Andrews says, “which was a huge disappointment for me.”
The new family came to be known as the Andrews-Gordon identities.
Since then the identities have turned up in strange places: in representation theory, in the study of symmetric functions, even in physics via the “hard hexagon model,” which describes how gas atoms can settle onto a surface in a triangular pattern.
“Who would have thought that the Rogers-Ramanujan identities were related to how liquid helium behaves when poured onto a graphite plate?” Andrews says.
A Pinch to Build a Conjecture
Yifeng Huang had a hunch.
Matrices—little spreadsheets of numbers—can undergo operations such as flips and transpositions, which must be done in a certain order to get the correct result. But if the values of the matrices are chosen such that the order of operations doesn’t matter (meaning they “commute”), then the matrices behave like coordinates and can be used to describe curves. Take any smooth curve, such as the parabola y = x2, and replace y and x with pairs of matrices. A textbook-level problem might ask: How many pairs of matrices make the equation true? A math student can find the answer.
But what happens if you use a curve that isn’t so smooth—one that has a “pinch” in it, also known as a singularity? Now textbook theory breaks down. These matrix counts had neverbeen studied.
While he was still a Ph.D. student at the University of Michigan, Huang started counting matrices on pinched curves such as y2 = x3, which comes to a sharp tip when x and y equal 0. Before long, his counts reproduced a familiar formula: one side of the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. “Already this discovery is fascinating,” Huang says. “I’m wondering what is going on. It can’t be a coincidence.”
From that single example, Huang made a bold, vague guess: What if every pinched curve hid a new identity, with its matrix count collapsing into a neat formula? Hoping to discuss the idea further, Huang wrote letters to a small group of mathematicians—around five to 10 people.
University of Virginia mathematician Ken Ono received one of those letters. But thinking Huang’s idea was “crazy,” Ono dismissed it.
Another letter recipient was Alexei Oblomkov, a mathematician at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, whose work connects algebraic geometry and knot theory. “I thought it was kind of a great idea, and later we met at one of the conferences, and I liked the idea even more,” Oblomkov says.
By then, Huang and Ruofan Jiang, now a mathematician at the University of California, Berkeley, had devised a systematic way to count how many matrices make the formulas for pinched curves true.
Oblomkov brought geometry to the table. Zoom in on the pinch in y2 = x3, he advised, and surround it with a tiny sphere in four dimensions, where mathematicians say such curves naturally live. The curve pierces the sphere along a closed loop in a “trefoil” knot. Both counts lead to the classic Rogers-Ramanujan identities. What about another curve? It also led to another knot, which was hiding another family of identities. And another curve led to yet more.
The team’s ideas crystalized into the Huang-Jiang-Oblomkov (HJO) conjecture. Simply stated, pick any two numbers a and b that are greater than 1, with no common factor. The conjecture predicts that for the curve xa = yb, a count of the matrix solutions will always collapse into a Rogers-Ramanujan-type identity. This translates into infinitely many families of identities, one for every value of a. The case a = 2 is the family Andrews and Gordon found. Every larger value of a was uncharted. And each curve comes with its own knot: the trefoil for a = 2 and b = 3 and more intricately wound torus knots for the rest.
The Proof
Again, Huang began sending out e-mails—more than 40 in 2023—and gave a circuit of seminar talks.
This time, when Ono received one of Huang’s letters, he found the idea “mind-blowing,” he says. “That’s when I joined this chase.”
By then Ono had signed on to the artificial intelligence company Axiom Math as its founding mathematician. He, Huang and another Axiom mathematician, Kenny Lau, worked for seven months in tandem with AxiomProver, the company’s math-focused AI system.
Because the ideas were so new, Ono says, they couldn’t simply ask an AI model to solve the problem—there was no literature for it to learn from. Instead AxiomProver worked like a research assistant, testing a far more expansive space of ideas than would be humanly possible. It also translated the proof into Lean, a machine-friendly language for automated proof checking. In the end, the quartet made of humans and AI stitched together ideas from five different areas of math to prove the conjecture.
Ono’s take on AI in math is more hopeful than many in his field. “Everyone talks about the end of math,” he says. “But someone had to invent this structure. This is what we should be doing.”
The team members posted their HJO conjecture to the preprint server arXiv.org in August 2026. And in September, the three followed up with the conjecture’s proof.
Recast as geometry, the old identities now point toward unmapped territory, raising questions that mathematicians are eager to explore.
“We found something exciting,” Oblomkov says, “a way to extend the geometry in the case when it’s not a trefoil knot, but a so-called Hopf link—basically you have two circles tied together. So that will be the next paper.”
Oblomkov also says Fields Medalist Peter Scholze has published a few papers that take some of Huang’s ideas even further. The pinched curves xa = yb are only the beginning. The equation is, Huang says, “only the first example of a singularity I would write down.” Oblomkov agrees: “It’s just the first case, and there will be many more.”

Five things you need to know about the Trump administration’s rollback of methane regulations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:19:02 UTC
20:19:02 KST

The Trump administration has taken an axe to environmental regulations—and this week the target became methane gas emissions.
The White House plans to slash laws governing how much methane is emitted from oil and gas wells. This includes relaxing rules around flaring—or burning off excess natural gas at well sites—as well as doing away with a program that requires speedy fixes for large methane leaks. The move also lowers standards for marginal wells, which produce little oil and gas but are responsible for about half of the industry’s methane emissions.
It’s the latest bump in a regulator roller coaster for methane. Attempts to regulate emissions on a federal level began in 2015, when the Obama administration sought to bring methane under the Clean Air Act. The first Trump administration rolled back that rule change. Then, during the Biden administration, the then Democratic-controlled Congress reinstated the methane regulations and cleared the way for the Environmental Protection Agency to apply the new standards to older equipment. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act also included provisions for charges for heavy emitters and allocated money for both industry and research to help them comply with the rules.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
All of that again went out the window with the second Trump administration. As the latest changes start to take effect, here are five things you need to know about methane and the ways that these moves will affect you.
Methane is a major driver of climate change
Carbon dioxide may be more prevalent in the atmosphere, but methane is a heavy hitter, climate-wise. The gas has been responsible for about 30 percent of the rise in global temperatures since the start of the industrial revolution, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). A methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for about 12 years, while an excess carbon dioxide molecule can persist for centuries. But methane traps heat about 80 times more effectively than carbon over 20 years and about 28 times more effectively over the course of a century. In other words, it may be shorter lived, but the damage methane does while it’s in the atmosphere is greater.
Oil and gas leaks are a major source of methane
Each year, according to the IEA, about 580 million metric tons of methane enter the atmosphere. About 40 percent of this comes from natural sources such as swamp gas and volcanic emissions. The other 60 percent comes from human sources.
Agriculture is the biggest contributor to this anthropogenic portion of methane emissions, but the combination of natural gas and petroleum production, processing and transportation comes in second. These processes are responsible for 28 percent of all U.S. methane emissions, according to the EPA.
Methane regulations have done little to move the needle
With all the regulatory back-and-forth, it’s perhaps unsurprising that research into methane emissions finds little evidence that federal rules make a difference. In a recent paper in Communications Earth & Environment, Johns Hopkins University associate professor of environmental health and engineering Scot Miller and his colleagues used satellite data to track emissions independently.
“Overall,” Miller says, “you see this landscape across the U.S. where methane leaks from oil and gas facilities are declining, but it’s not necessarily due to any kind of concerted federal action.”
Methane emissions declined by about 11 percent between 2019 and 2024, but the decline was caused by technological changes in the industry and the establishment of new natural gas pipelines that can carry methane to market—without this transport system, operators often burn off natural gas at well sites.
“If [natural gas is] actually a valuable markable product, there is evidence to show that leak rates tend to go down,” Miller explains.
The new rules would loosen restrictions on the most common oil wells in the U.S.
The new changes are twofold. First, the EPA plans to eliminate the Super Emitter Program, which would have allowed third parties to monitor oil and gas operations for leaks, via satellite, for example, and alert the EPA to leaks of 100 kilograms of methane or more per hour. Operators notified by the EPA of such large leaks would then have to investigate the leaks within days.
The Super Emitter Program has actually never been in effect, so this will make little immediate difference. “This is like the nail in the coffin,” Miller says. “These rules are already not being implemented.”
The other change would affect marginal oil and gas wells. These are wells that produce 15 barrels (2,384 liters) or less of oil per day or 90,000 cubic feet (2,549 cubic meters) or less of natural gas per day over a yearlong period. These wells accounted for 7 percent of U.S. oil and gas production as of 2021, according to the EPA, but produce about 50 percent of the industry’s methane emissions. They’re also plentiful, accounting for more than 70 percent of onshore oil and gas wells.
Each marginal well produces only a little profit, so operators may not have much incentive to invest in repairs and upgrades, Miller says.
“Methane leaks from the oil and gas industry have been declining over time, but these marginal wells are arguably a stubborn outlier,” Miller says. “The regulations proposed during the Biden administration would have helped address this issue.” But they may never come to pass now.
There is broad pushback against regulating methane
Biden administration rules to regulate methane, enacted in 2023, were expected to keep 58 million tons (52.6 million metric tons) of the gas out of the atmosphere between 2024 and 2038. Their rollback is part of a broad push against methane mitigation, however. “I think, potentially, this move would make it more difficult for a future administration to reimplement emissions regulations,” Miller says.
In the European Union, a 2024 regulation would have required methane monitoring and reporting on any imported oil, natural gas and coal. But this month, the European Parliament voted to approve a three-year delay on that regulation.
In another possible blow for methane reduction, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which the Senate plans to take up in November, would bar agencies from revoking permits issued during the Trump administration to drill on public land and would make it harder for future administrations to require methane leak monitoring or limits on flaring on public land.
“It’s difficult to have an effective or a consistent federal regulatory policy if those regulations are constantly seesawing up and down,” Miller says.
Disclosure: The reporter’s spouse is employed in the oil and gas industry and owns interests in wells.

Belgium’s deputy PM wants to use ‘trade bazooka’ on US over pharma threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:17:32 UTC
20:17:32 KST

BRUSSELS — The European Union should ready its Anti-Coercion Instrument, otherwise known as its “trade bazooka,” for use against Washington over its push to raise EU drug prices, Belgium’s deputy prime minister has said.
Frank Vandenbroucke, who also serves as the country’s health minister, issued the call in a position paper published Thursday by the Egmont Institute think tank, co-authored with his deputy head of cabinet Gloria Ghéquière.
He also said the EU should be ready to suspend the tariff concessions it granted to Washington under the Turnberry trade deal from August 2025 if the U.S. imposes additional duties on European goods.
Advertisement
The Trump administration has been pressuring European governments to pay more for medicines under its “most-favored-nation” policy as it seeks to bring American drug prices into line with those in other wealthy countries.
Washington argues that Americans are unfairly shouldering the costs of pharmaceutical research and development, while Europeans reap the benefits.
The MFN policy ties American drug prices to the lowest prices charged in a basket of wealthy countries, including France, Germany and Italy. The U.S. has already concluded MFN pricing agreements with 26 pharma companies, which have agreed to benchmark the prices of drugs supplied to the U.S. Medicaid program.
The intended effect is for drugs manufacturers to either increase prices in third countries, to lower their U.S. prices, or both.
Washington is also ramping up pressure on individual member countries to pay more for their drugs. In June, the U.S. launched a so-called Section 301 investigation into Germany’s alleged “persistent underpayment” for innovative drugs. The investigation could lead to additional tariffs, exceeding the 15% ceiling agreed under Turnberry.
Capitals are banding together to counter the U.S. pressure. At an informal meeting in Dublin last week, ministers from Ireland, France, Germany, Italy, Denmark, Sweden, the Netherlands and Belgium discussed creating an EU-wide pharmaceutical task force to coordinate their response.
Advertisement
“If we don’t work together and act as a team, countries are inevitably tempted to go it alone,” French Trade Minister Nicolas Forissier told POLITICO.
In the paper, Vandenbroucke and his colleague argue that Brussels should open an ACI investigation in response to Washington’s drug pricing policy. The instrument allows the EU to impose tariffs and restrictions on services in response to foreign threats to trade if backed by a qualified majority of member countries.
“The procedure is quite heavy, but already opening an examination would have an effect of its own,” the paper argues.
The authors also highlight a clause in Pfizer’s MFN agreement requiring it to share additional revenue from higher prices outside the U.S. with the American government. “Higher foreign payments thus become a source of revenue for the American government itself,” they write.
The deputy PM questioned the underlying basis of the policy. Because the U.S. market is so lucrative compared to all the rest, drugmakers would accept withdrawing from third countries as long as it meant keeping U.S. prices high.
Vandenbroucke, an economist by training, said the net effect would likely be an extreme increase in European drug prices — or the withdrawal of drugs from the market — while producing comparatively modest price cuts in the U.S.
According to one forecast cited in the paper, prices could triple in countries used as benchmarks, while U.S. prices would fall by just 7.5% to 15%.
“The consequences would reach well beyond the medicines budget, putting pressure on the solidarity that universal insurance is designed to secure,” the authors write.

Her remarks drew criticism from those who accused Berlin of providing political cover for Israeli strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Beyond her stance on Israel, Baerbock’s tenure as Germany’s top diplomat drew criticism over a lack of diplomatic pragmatism, inconsistent foreign policy positions, and a string of high-profile verbal blunders. She also called for the protection of Palestinian civilians and stressed that Israel’s military operations were bound by international humanitarian law.

Japan's ruling bloc, DPFP agree to cut 31 lower house seats as opposition raises doubts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:16:03 CST
20:16:03 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Japan's ruling coalition and the opposition Democratic Party for the People (DPFP) on Thursday agreed on a plan to cut 31 proportional representation seats in the House of Representatives, Kyodo News reported.
The move has drawn criticism from opposition lawmakers, with some saying it would weaken parliament's oversight of the government and is meant to pave the way for revising Japan's pacifist constitution.
According to the report, the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), its junior coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party (JIP), and the DPFP will jointly draft a bill and seek its passage during the current parliamentary session, which runs through mid-December.
Because the three parties together hold a majority in both houses of the Diet, Japan's parliament, the bill is likely to pass.
Six other opposition parties oppose the plan, saying it lacks justification and that cutting proportional representation seats would favor larger parties, Kyodo News said.
A rally against the seat cuts was held in front of the National Diet in Tokyo on Wednesday evening.
Mizuho Fukushima, leader of the Social Democratic Party, suggested the move is intended to sideline forces cautious about constitutional revision and pave the way for amending the pacifist constitution.
Tetsuya Shiokawa, chair of the Japanese Communist Party's Diet affairs committee, noted that according to estimates by the LDP, the plan would increase the LDP and the JIP's combined share of lower house seats by several percentage points.
He said the move would make parliament less representative of public opinion, weaken oversight of the government, and embolden Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration to push through its policies on the strength of its seat advantage.
Japan's House of Representatives is elected through a mixed electoral system that combines both single-seat districts and proportional representation.
Of the current 465 seats in the lower house, 289 are elected from single-seat constituencies and 176 through proportional representation.
In single-seat districts, the candidate with the most votes wins. For proportional representation, voters select a party or political group, and seats are allocated according to vote share across 11 regional blocs nationwide.
The three parties' plan would cut only proportional representation seats. It also includes changes to how proportional representation seats are allocated and would allow multiple parties to compile a joint list of proportional representation candidates. ■

Israeli military firms use European subsidiaries to obscure ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:15:03 UTC
20:15:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli military firms use European subsidiaries to obscure ties and expand, report finds
Israeli military and surveillance companies linked to the genocide in Gaza are expanding into Europe through subsidiaries, acquisitions and rebrandings that obscure their origins and human rights records, according to a new report by human rights groups.
The report, entitled "European Gateway for Genocide Technology" finds that European rearmament and fragmented regulation are opening markets for technologies developed and tested against Palestinians.
Published on Thursday by the Observatory for Human Rights and Business in the Mediterranean (ODHE) and Irídia – Centre for the Defence of Human Rights, and coordinated by SUDS and the International Institute for Nonviolent Action (NOVACT), the study identifies nine routes into Europe, including NATO procurement, EU research programmes and cybersecurity hubs such as Barcelona.
The expansion comes amid rapid growth in Israel’s defence-technology industry. Citing the Israeli economic development organisation Startup Nation Central, the report says the sector comprised more than 300 start-ups in 2025, compared with 160 in 2024. Europe accounted for 54 percent of Israel’s defence export contracts in 2024, when their total value reached approximately $14.7 billion.
But overseas expansion also reflects insecurity and difficulties attracting investment within Israel, researchers said.
"Many startups and companies are in need of investment," Felip Daza, a senior researcher at ODHE, told The New Arab.
The relocation of technology workers seeking security and companies seeking capital were converging, he said, making Europe "an attracting pole for these companies".
Europe offers cover for Israeli firms
Establishing European subsidiaries and acquiring local companies can help Israeli firms access contracts and funding while distancing themselves from their human rights records, the report argues.
Carlos Bodoque, a senior researcher at ODHE, said rebranding and corporate structures could conceal companies’ connections to products used against Palestinian civilians.
"Many of these cybersecurity companies and surveillance companies participate in European funding programmes, starting with the European Defence Fund, but also Horizon, together with universities and other public institutions," he told The New Arab.
The report highlights Intracom Defence, a Greek company acquired by state-owned Israel Aerospace Industries. According to the study, Intracom participates in 15 European Defence Fund projects, seven awarded after its acquisition and the start of the genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
Germany, Cyprus and Luxembourg provide different routes into the market, through military-industrial cooperation, favourable business conditions and corporate structures, the researchers say.
Daza described Cyprus as offering a "soft landing framework", citing its proximity to Israel and flexible tax and administrative arrangements.
"Having a base in Europe facilitates access to the single market, public contracts, and research programmes," he said, outlining how a European foothold could offer legitimacy and opportunities to expand.
Barcelona becomes a cybersecurity foothold
Barcelona in Spain's autonomous Catalonia region illustrates how this expansion extends beyond traditional arms manufacturers into Europe’s technology hubs.
Bodoque pointed to figures from Catalonia’s cybersecurity agency showing more than 500 companies operating in the sector.
He highlighted the spyware company Palm Beach Networks, citing media reporting that Alexei Levin, with links to NSO Group, had interviewed prospective recruits for the company in Barcelona.
NSO manufactures Pegasus spyware, which has been implicated in surveillance targeting journalists, lawyers and human rights defenders, the report notes.
For Bodoque, the Barcelona case raises questions about whether authorities adequately scrutinise the backgrounds of people establishing security-technology businesses.
The concern, he said, was that individuals linked to companies implicated in abuses could establish new ventures without effective barriers or scrutiny of their previous activities.
Yet establishing legal responsibility across borders remains difficult.
"We know, of course, it’s their know-how, it’s their technology, but we’re talking here about different legal frameworks, and sometimes it’s very difficult to connect," Bodoque said.
The expansion of Israel-linked firms sits in contrast to widespread popular support for Palestinians. Spain recognised Palestinian statehood in May 2024, while Barcelona’s city council voted in May 2025 to sever institutional relations with the Israeli government and end its friendship agreement with Tel Aviv. The council’s measures also targeted procurement and the participation in trade fairs of companies profiting from war and occupation.
Yet Bodoque’s account raises questions about whether those commitments translate into sufficient scrutiny of the companies and individuals entering Barcelona’s technology sector.
Daza described a wider divide between European civil society and political and business interests, saying military and economic actors "speak openly about the need for Israeli technology".
Rearmament outweighs scrutiny
European rearmament and rising NATO defence spending are creating further opportunities for Israeli suppliers, while research partnerships and technology fairs help companies develop institutional relationships, the report finds.
Many produce dual-use technologies with civilian and military applications. The authors warn that systems developed in contexts of occupation and warfare can also serve border enforcement, policing and surveillance in Europe.
Oversight, however, remains divided between national jurisdictions in the EU.
"The European Union is not acting as a unique body," Daza said. "There’s a huge fragmentation at the regulatory level."
The researchers argue that this fragmentation allows commercial cooperation to continue despite companies’ human rights records and public opposition to their activities.

Ukraine’s Linza bomber drone clears path for UGV in German exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:13:13 UTC
20:13:13 KST

- Frontline Robotics’ Linza drone took part in Quantum Systems’ Forward Edge 26 exercise in Germany, working with other unmanned systems through MOSAIC UXS.
- In one scenario, a Vector drone spotted simulated enemy drones on a ground vehicle’s route and Linza struck them with payload drops.
Ukrainian drone maker Frontline Robotics flew its Linza bomber drone alongside German, Ukrainian and other unmanned air, ground and sea systems during Forward Edge 26, a two-week exercise in Germany hosted by Quantum Systems, the company said on social media.
In one deployment, Quantum Systems’ Vector reconnaissance drone spotted simulated enemy drones along the route of an unmanned ground vehicle, and Linza then attacked the targets by dropping payloads, clearing the way for the ground vehicle, Frontline Robotics said. The company said the drone completed its missions in heavy rain and dense fog, but it did not say how many sorties it flew or how many targets it hit.
All of the systems in the exercise were connected through MOSAIC UXS, Quantum Systems’ software for controlling and coordinating unmanned platforms from different manufacturers in a single operational picture. Quantum Systems said it ran Forward Edge 26 at a military training area in central Germany and wrapped it up on Oct. 22, with no crewed vehicles in the scenarios. Systems located in Ukraine, the United States and Australia were also flown remotely during the event.
The exercise was built around four scenarios: defense against an attacking force, convoy and force protection, coastal and port surveillance, and minelaying and route clearance. In the convoy scenario, laser-based counter-drone systems protected an unmanned convoy, while the maritime scenario linked aerial and sea-based systems for coastal monitoring. Industry participants included Daimler Truck, Volkswagen, XTEND, Planet and Quantum Systems’ German-Ukrainian joint ventures, Quantum Frontline Industries and Quantum Tencore Industries.
Linza, which means “lens” in Ukrainian, is a quadcopter that can drop munitions on targets, lay mines, carry a radio relay, scout and deliver small loads of supplies to frontline positions. Frontline Robotics first introduced it in 2024 and unveiled the Linza 3.0 version in February, which the company says carries up to 4 kg (8.8 pounds) over a tactical range of 15 km (9 miles), with AI-assisted visual navigation that lets it hold position over a target without relying on satellite signals. Frontline Robotics says more than 80 units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces now use the drone.
Quantum Systems and Frontline Robotics build Linza together through Quantum Frontline Industries, a joint venture whose factory outside Munich opened in February in the presence of German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and is meant to eventually produce more than 10,000 drones a year. Germany has funded joint production of the Linza under the Build with Ukraine program, and earlier this month the joint venture signed a contract to supply Linza and Zoom reconnaissance drones to Ukraine’s National Guard in 2027.
Quantum Systems’ own Vector, the reconnaissance drone that cued Linza’s strike in the exercise, has flown extensively in Ukraine, including a mission in which one aircraft survived 11 hits and kept flying. Frontline Robotics also builds the Burya remote weapon turret, which Danish company Dropla has agreed to integrate on its unmanned ground vehicles.

Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:12:43 UTC
20:12:43 KST

Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means
With five days to go before the US midterms, analysts say the war could affect how people vote.
The Pentagon has told lawmakers in the United States that the war on Iran has cost American taxpayers at least $47.1bn so far.
The estimate, disclosed last week, comes just days before the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine if US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party will maintain control of Congress for the next two years.
In a statement on Wednesday the Pentagon also said it had “successfully obligated 97.5 percent” of the funds Trump provided the department. Last July, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) outlining tax and spending plans, which came into effect earlier this year.
We take a close look at the Pentagon estimate, and what it means for the US economy and the midterm elections.
What has the Pentagon spending report revealed?
The Pentagon told Congress that the cost of the US-Israel war on Iran as of October 16 had risen to at least $47.1bn.
Congress officials shared the Pentagon’s cost estimate breakdown with The New York Times.
According to the Times and other US media reports, the Pentagon’s estimate covers the operational costs of the war and includes a projected cost of $29bn needed to replace expended munitions such as bombs, bullets and other military hardware that has been deployed in the war so far.
It also reveals that since the war started on February 28, the US Air Force has spent $7.6bn on fighter and bomber units; the US Navy has spent $1.5bn on two dozen warships and aircraft carriers; and the US Army has spent $2.1bn to sustain its troops in the Middle East.
According to the US Central Command, there are more than 50,000 American troops stationed in the Middle East, comprising personnel deployed to large, permanent bases and to smaller forward sites across the region.
Officials told the Times that the Pentagon has spent $6.1bn to replace damaged aircraft and munitions, $645m on transport and support for commandos in the region and $24.5m on “in-house medical support” for US service members.
A congressional official added that the US Transportation Command also spent $92.2m to move equipment, and the US Cyber Command spent $14m on “cyber support operations”.
The Pentagon’s estimate, however, does not include how much Washington will need to spend to repair its damaged military bases across the Middle East and also does not take into account the cost of fuel, which is needed to power ships and aircraft used in the war.
While the Pentagon has publicly acknowledged 18 US service member fatalities in the war, The Washington Post has cited six unnamed US officials stating the true death toll is at least 22. According to the official Pentagon Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) database, 865 military personnel have been wounded in the war with Iran.
What is the response?
According to an October 19 report by USA Today, five senators from the Democratic Party had written to Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, demanding that the Pentagon reveal the true cost of the war. Their letter said the Trump administration’s “ongoing efforts to hide the true cost of this war are outrageous and unacceptable”.
Trump has not commented on the latest Pentagon estimate. But the Trump administration’s war on Iran has grown increasingly unpopular with US citizens due to its impact on US and global energy costs.
Since early March, shortly after the war began, Iran has closed the critical Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf, through which about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies were shipped until then. This has sent the price of oil spiralling and caused shortages globally. In the US, diesel, which is heavily relied on by farmers and small businesses, has nearly doubled in price.
In a post on X following the latest Pentagon report, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York wrote: “For eight months, American families have been buried by the heavy cost of Trump’s disastrous war in Iran.
“Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy,” he added.
How does the Pentagon’s estimate compare with past calculations?
Estimates for the cost of the Iran war to the US have risen steadily as the war has continued.
The Pentagon’s latest estimate is higher than the $38bn the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) forecast in September.
It is also higher than the $37.5bn price tag that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gave in July this year. Hegseth confirmed this amount during a hearing before the Senate appropriations committee and added that the cost covered some operations and maintenance extending through to the end of September.
Hegseth’s July estimate was already about $8bn higher than the previous figure released by the administration of President Donald Trump in May – $29bn.
Prior to the May estimate, in late April the Pentagon’s comptroller Jules Hurst reported that the war would cost $25bn.
Meanwhile, with the war entering its ninth month and no peace deal in sight, last month the CBO said the war with Iran could cost approximately $2bn to $3bn per month for as long as it continues.
The Pentagon’s inspector general also said last month that US troops are facing “strategic inventory shortfalls” as the war continues.
But the Trump administration has denied it is running low on weapons stockpiles.
“Cowards and traitors would like to say that the United States is short of ammunition, but that is not true. We have more ammunition than we could ever imagine using. And we are producing it at levels we have never reached before,” Trump told the United Nations General Assembly in New York in September.
Trump has also repeatedly stated that the Iran war will end when he wants it to.
Last week at an election rally in Texas, according to a report by CNBC, Trump said: “Somebody asked me before, ‘When will the war in Iran end?’ I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’”
What does the rising cost of the war mean for the midterm elections?
The US-Israel war on Iran has affected the US economy through direct government spending as well as rising energy and fuel costs.
On Wednesday, the average price of a gallon of diesel in the US hit $6.35, compared with $3.75 last year, according to the American Automobile Association.
Higher fuel costs are also driving up the cost of food – with shortages of oil and gas affecting nearly every stage of the food supply chain.
Meanwhile, the country’s national debt has surpassed a record $40 trillion, two years before expected.
As a result, the war has become deeply unpopular in the US and Trump’s approval ratings have slumped to just 33 percent – the lowest they have been at any time during his two terms as president.
With five days to go before the midterms, analysts say confirmation by the Pentagon of the high cost of the war is likely to affect how people in the US vote.
Currently, the Democrats lead Republicans by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent, a gap of 8.2 percentage points, according to RealClearPolling’s national polling average.
Chris Featherstone, a political scientist from the University of York in the United Kingdom, said this is an issue that hits at two key pillars of Trump’s political rhetoric: his promise to initiate “no new wars” during his campaign for the presidency in 2024, and his emphasis on fixing the American economy.
“The spiralling cost of the conflict for the taxpayer, and the lack of a clear end point resembles the critiques Trump levelled at the war in Afghanistan in his first presidential election campaign,” he told Al Jazeera.
According to the Costs of War Project at Brown University, the war in Afghanistan, which began in 2001, cost the US an estimated $2.26 trillion to $2.3 trillion in total across multiple presidential administrations, including George W Bush, Barack Obama and Donald Trump.
“While many of Trump’s most loyal MAGA voters are likely to remain loyal to Trump in the midterms despite the cost of the Iran conflict, the more peripheral supporters seem to be drifting away from the president ahead of the midterms, and the significant impact of this conflict on cost of living appears to be a major factor,” Featherstone said.

The localized arrangement has provided humanitarian relief while preparations for wider negotiations continue.

Russian senators propose raising minimum scores on university entrance exams

Russian senators propose raising minimum scores on university entrance exams
The Federation Council, the upper house of Russia’s parliament, has recommended that Rosobrnadzor consider raising the minimum scores required on the Unified State Exam (USE) for admission to Russian universities, according to a resolution the chamber issued October 28.
The new requirements would apply to all universities “regardless of their departmental affiliation or ownership structure.”
The Federation Council also recommended eliminating distance learning for engineering and technology majors. For fields where enrollment exceeds labor-market demand, it proposed capping the number of tuition-paying slots. It also proposed revisiting the rules and criteria for admission benefits.
In addition, the senators proposed suspending the issuance of new university licenses “until amendments aimed at improving the licensing process are made to Russian law.”
During an October 14 plenary session, Federation Council speaker Valentina Matviyenko called for tightening university licensing requirements. According to her, opening a university in Russia today is easier than opening a newspaper kiosk, and “anyone who wants to can do it, literally by pressing a couple of buttons.”
Matviyenko also proposed reducing the number of tuition-paying students at Moscow universities by limiting admission for students from other regions: “Enroll as many as are needed in the necessary fields, and no more. The rest can study at home,” Matviyenko said.
In recent years, Russian authorities have increasingly encouraged students to leave school after ninth grade and enroll in vocational schools rather than universities, BBC Russia reported. Some schools have begun reducing enrollment in upper grades, and it has become harder to get into a university after vocational school: starting in 2025, students who skip the USE can only choose a similar field of study.
In 2025, the government already gained the right to allocate tuition-paying slots across the 40 most popular fields of study that, in the authorities’ view, produce too many graduates.

Belarusian Plant Supplies Russia With Machines for Processing Optics Used in Su-57, BELPOL Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:11:54 UTC
20:11:54 KST

The Belarusian Smorgon Optical Machine Tool Plant operates in the interests of Russia’s defence industry.
This is according to an investigation by the Belarusian organisation BELPOL.
It supplies these companies with machine tools for processing optical components and also upgrades existing equipment.
These include the Izmeritel plant in Smolensk, the Baspik technology centre in Vladikavkaz, and the Polyus Scientific Research Institute in Moscow.
One of the Smorgon plant’s partners, Moscow-based JSC Central Research Institute Cyclone, is involved in the production of Russian Su-57 fighter jets, according to DIU.
According to Osint Varta, it specialises in the development and production of optoelectronic devices, thermal imaging systems, OLED microdisplays, photodetectors and machine vision systems for the defence industry.
This equipment enables the production of components for optical and optoelectronic systems used in military equipment.
The Russian companies that cooperate with the Belarusian plant produce monoculars, thermal imaging devices, optical sights, rangefinders and missile seekers.
These products have military applications, meaning that the supply and modernisation of the equipment help sustain the production capabilities of Russia’s defence industry.
The Smorgon Optical Machine Tool Plant specialises in manufacturing equipment for processing optical components, including grinding, polishing and lapping machines.
Despite its cooperation with Russian military manufacturers, the plant remains free of sanctions.
Militarnyi previously reported that Belarusian companies are systematically involved in supplying Russia’s defence industry.

Lit cigarette, combustibles and ‘human fault’ led to deadly Hong Kong fire: report

A combination of a lit cigarette and an “abundant fuel” of combustible materials caused Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades, according to a long-awaited report which found the blaze would not have killed so many people, or happened at all, without “human fault”.
Eleven months after the deadly fire tore through Wang Fuk Court, killing 168 and displacing thousands, an independent committee’s report released on Thursday assigned blame to the main contractor for renovations at the housing estate, the project consultant, and inspector Wilson Ng Yeuk for their alleged roles in the tragedy.
The 1,154-page, two-volume report also singled out four government bodies for accountability: the Buildings Department, the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit, the Fire Services Department and the Labour Department.

Spanish PM pledges to establish cause of deadly train crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:11:32 UTC
20:11:32 KST

Cranes lift wrecked train carriages as rescuers search for victims following a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. (AP Photo)
Spain began three days of mourning on Oct. 29 after its second high-speed rail collision this year killed 69 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
One of Europe's deadliest train disasters this century has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain's rail network after the transport minister reported an "error" and "inexplicable circumstances" that led to the crash.
During a visit to the crash site, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faces a general election on Nov. 29, pledged to establish the cause of the crash.
"We are working day and night not only to support the victims' families, but also to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again," he said.
The collision happened in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha on Oct. 28 morning when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.
Sniffer dogs and thermal drones were deployed at the crash site a few kilometers from the village of Urda on Oct. 29 to search for bodies, the regional government said, raising the death toll to 69 from 68.
Flags flew at half-mast on public buildings with official ceremonies and public events canceled or scaled back.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said on Oct. 28 that an automatic control system went down on 69 kilometers of track, causing all trains there to be stopped.
But the control center decided to "resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable," Puente said, with the Renfe train travelling 25 kilometers before striking the Iryo.
The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it", he added.
In January, two high-speed trains collided in the southern region of Andalusia after one of them derailed and crossed onto the adjacent track, killing 46 people.
The investigation into that accident is ongoing, but the left-wing government faced heavy criticism over its management of Spain's railways.
Train drivers went on strike on Oct. 29 "to defend rail safety." The strike had been called before the Oct. 28 crash.

German industry groups urge Berlin to join defence bank initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:11:17 KST

German industry groups urge Berlin to join defence bank initiative
BERLIN, Oct 29 - German business and industry associations on Thursday urged the government to join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), saying membership was needed to close financing gaps for companies in the defence sector and protect their access to future projects.
The joint statement was signed by groups including the German Security and Defence Industry Association (BDSV), aerospace association BDLI, the chamber of commerce DIHK, engineering association VDMA, savings banks group DSGV and the Startup Association.
The proposed multilateral institution, backed by Canada, seven other NATO countries and Ukraine, would provide long-term, low-cost financing for defence, security and resilience projects.
"The geostrategic threat situation urgently requires new answers and approaches: financing for the defence sector must be secured sustainably over the long term," said Elisabeth Hauschild, managing director of BDSV.
The associations said the bank could offer guarantees for commercial loans to small and medium-sized companies, including startups, as well as long-term loans, venture capital and equity financing for capacity expansion, innovation and critical raw materials.
"As a multilateral development bank, it provides the decisive risk buffer through guarantees and long-term financing instruments—particularly where established banks have so far been reluctant to support long-term contracts for the Mittelstand," Hauschild said.
The DSRB, which will be based in Canada, has faced challenges securing support from larger European nations. Reuters was first to report in September last year that Britain had declined to join the project.
A spokesperson for the German finance ministry told Reuters on Monday that Germany was an observer in the negotiations on DSRB's charter and was reviewing open questions.
Germany should participate in the bank's founding process and join the group of founding states as soon as possible, the business associations said.
The groups warned that companies from member countries could receive preferential access to procurement projects financed by the DSRB under its planned charter rules. If Germany stayed outside the institution, its companies could be excluded from market opportunities or face a competitive disadvantage against rivals from member states, they added. REUTERS

Christine Lagarde: The outsider who led the ECB her way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:11:13 UTC
20:11:13 KST

Christine Lagarde: The outsider who led the ECB her way
FRANKFURT, Oct 29 - Christine Lagarde's decision to step down early as European Central Bank president ends an eventful seven years at an institution she was never expected to lead.
The former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund arrived in Frankfurt in 2019 as the first ECB chief with no formal economics training or central banking experience — prompting some market participants to label her a "credibility risk."
In fact, she knew so little about the institution that Lagarde, 70, later said she had accepted the job thinking the presidency was a five-year mandate, rather than eight.
Yet after a tenure dominated by a pandemic, two energy shocks and the worst inflation spike in the euro zone's history, Lagarde leaves with a record that defied the sceptics.
"Her seven years at the ECB have been, on the whole, pretty good," said Willem Buiter, an economist and former Bank of England official, noting that the ECB managed to bring inflation back down faster than peers in Britain and the United States.
Her exit, however, threatens to be as political as her arrival.
By walking away before her eight-year term ends, Lagarde gives European Union leaders a chance to pick her successor before a French election next spring that opinion polls suggest far-right candidate Marine Le Pen will win, replacing President Emmanuel Macron.
For an institution that fiercely guards its independence from political meddling, the timing has drawn sharp criticism from central bank watchers.
"This is debasing the institution and just following the purely political calculus of the French president," said Paul De Grauwe, a professor at the London School of Economics.
Lagarde and Macron have not addressed such criticism directly. Lagarde has said she would not be a candidate for the French presidency but would advocate for pro-European values in her home country "in whichever capacity" she deemed most efficient.
'BETTER WITH BUTTER'
Throughout her career, Lagarde has stood apart from more technocratic colleagues through a mix of charm, consensus-building and folksy pragmatism.
Favouring plain-speaking homilies over dense economic theory, the then-IMF chief famously declared that "everything is better with butter" when discussing growth and told governments to "fix the roof while the sun is shining".
Unorthodoxy was a hallmark of Lagarde's career, and the subject of her upcoming autobiography "Lady First".
A former corporate lawyer who spent years in Chicago, she entered French politics in 2005 as an outsider. Early missteps earned her the domestic moniker "Madame Lagaffe," but she soon became one of then-President Nicolas Sarkozy's sharpest operators, steering French banks through the 2008 crash.
She led the IMF through Europe's debt crisis, navigating a messy Greek rescue that imposed harsh austerity, and sparked outrage in Athens when she bluntly urged suffering citizens to "pay their taxes".
Her appetite for high-stakes bets showed again in 2018 with a record $57-billion lifeline for Argentina to back then-President Mauricio Macri. The gamble unravelled, failing to halt a currency collapse or avert a deep recession, and left the IMF bound to its most troubled debtor.
THE SPREADS CRISIS AND THE TRIBAL CLIQUE
Her occasional unfamiliarity with the nuances of central banking still peeked through.
In March 2020, as the pandemic rattled sovereign debt markets, Lagarde told a press conference the ECB was "not here to close spreads" between Italian and German borrowing costs.
The comment triggered an immediate selloff in bond markets and forced her to swiftly walk it back.
Under Lagarde's watch, the ECB swiftly rolled out emergency bond-buying that stabilised markets as COVID-19 spread. It launched its fastest series of interest-rate hikes to bring inflation under control following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, although it later acknowledged it had been slow to recognise the full impact of spiking energy prices.
As ECB president, she once described economists as a "tribal clique" — a provocative jab at the profession's establishment, though she later softened the blow by saying she hoped to join the tribe.
A 'MORE POLITICAL' ECB PRESIDENT
Lagarde used her political skills to repair rifts. Unlike her predecessor Mario Draghi, whose top-down style embittered some hawkish northern European peers, she worked to build consensus among the euro zone's 21 national central bank chiefs.
Her willingness to wade into politics remained evident: in January, Lagarde walked out of a World Economic Forum dinner in Davos during a speech by US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that criticised Europe, an episode that underscored fraught transatlantic relations.
Whoever succeeds her when she leaves the ECB on February 7 will face fresh challenges including strains in French bond markets ahead of next year's election and a Middle East conflict that threatens a new bout of inflation.
Ultimately, Lagarde's legacy may be a paradox: an outsider who showed that political diplomacy could steer a central bank through historic shocks, but whose early departure served as a final reminder of her political instincts.
"She was put there for a reason: being more political than her predecessor and, on that mission, I think she largely succeeded," Frederik Ducrozet, head of strategy and macro research at Pictet Wealth Management, said. REUTERS

Four more arrested in election bribery probe as Likud seeks revotes at Arab polling stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:09:20 UTC
20:09:20 KST

Police arrested four more suspects Thursday in an investigation into alleged vote-buying on behalf of the Arab Ra'am party, including three school principals from Bedouin communities in southern Israel, as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party prepared to challenge election results at polling stations where it alleges bribery and other violations occurred.
Three of the four newly arrested suspects were subsequently released to house arrest.
The arrests bring the number of people detained in the investigation to seven since Tuesday's parliamentary election. The case centers on allegations that money and other benefits were offered to voters in exchange for supporting Ra'am, an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas.
The developments come amid a separate investigation into suspected foreign interference in the election, possibly involving tens of millions of shekels from Qatar. That inquiry is being conducted by the Shin Bet domestic security agency at the request of Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, chairman of the Central Elections Committee.
The two investigations are distinct, and no connection between the suspected Qatari funding and the alleged vote-buying involving Ra'am has been established.
Likud, meanwhile, is escalating its challenge to the election results as part of a broader political campaign against cooperation with Arab parties following an inconclusive vote that left neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition with a clear parliamentary majority.
The party is preparing to seek the annulment of results at polling stations where it claims voters were bribed or prohibited methods were used to influence the vote, ynet has learned.
Cash payments, fuel vouchers and allegations of vote-buying
A Bedouin source from the Negev, familiar with political activity in the region, described what he alleged was a system used by Arab parties, particularly Ra'am, in the days leading up to the election.
According to the source, political activists visit the homes of low-income residents and offer financial assistance ranging from 200 to 300 shekels ($65 to $95), including to families affected by home demolitions and residents of unrecognized Bedouin villages.
He alleged that the payments are presented as assistance to needy families, while recipients are asked in return to support a particular party at the ballot box.
In other cases, he claimed, fuel vouchers worth 100 shekels ($32) are distributed to people who transport residents to polling stations.
The amounts can vary depending on family size, he said, with payments allegedly distributed one or two days before the election and sometimes on Election Day itself.
The source argued that some residents do not view such payments as election bribery but rather as financial assistance, particularly given the poverty and lack of basic services affecting disadvantaged Bedouin communities.
"I don't understand what all the fuss is about," he said. "We learned this from Shas, which has been doing it for years and even distributes money in synagogues."
Shas is an ultra-Orthodox Jewish political party that has long been part of Netanyahu's governing alliances.
"So why all the fuss now? Just because we're Arabs? Because we turned out to vote and became a powerful political force?" the source asked.
His allegations against Shas were not substantiated in the account.
Likud prepares legal challenge to election results
Senior Likud officials said the party intends to petition election authorities in the coming hours over polling stations where it suspects bribery or the use of prohibited methods.
"New elections must be held at these polling stations," senior party officials said.
Attorney Ilan Bombach, Likud's legal adviser and a deputy chairman of the Central Elections Committee, is preparing the petition based on material the party previously submitted to the committee.
Likud alleges that the material documents election bribery and the use of prohibited methods, including applications that tracked the identities of voters at polling stations.
The planned challenge is separate from the Shin Bet investigation into suspected foreign financing.
Likud maintains that the evidence it has already submitted is sufficient to invalidate results at certain polling stations and require voting to be repeated there.
Bombach is not alleging that ballot papers were forged or that vote totals were falsified. Instead, the petition focuses on alleged bribery, the use of prohibited election methods and the distribution of money or other benefits to voters in exchange for their support.
The party's allegations have not been established in court.
Under Israeli election law, election results can be challenged through a separate legal process. Courts may order voting to be repeated at specific polling stations if violations are established and could have affected the results.
The planned petition comes as Arab parties have emerged with potentially decisive parliamentary influence following Tuesday's election, intensifying political disputes over whether the opposition could form a government with their support.
Seven suspects detained, including three school principals
The latest arrests follow the detention of three suspects on Election Day by investigators from Lahav, the Israel Police's national investigations unit, on suspicion of election bribery and conspiracy to commit a crime.
The original suspects were identified as Ibrahim al-Gharibi, 42, from the Al-Azazmeh community; Hussein Masaudin, 63, from Segev Shalom; and Saif Abu Riaash, 38, a physician from the Al-Sana tribe.
A magistrate's court initially extended the detention of al-Gharibi and Masaudin until Sunday while ordering Abu Riaash released to house arrest.
Police appealed the physician's release, however, and his detention was subsequently extended as well.
During court proceedings, a Lahav representative said Abu Riaash had organized gatherings at private homes to encourage residents to vote for Ra'am.
"He holds meetings in people's homes to get them to vote for Ra'am, even though he is a doctor, and that is problematic," the police representative said.
Al-Gharibi is suspected of violating election law after investigators searching his home discovered cash. A search of his vehicle also uncovered envelopes bearing Arabic writing, green shirts and flags, and Ra'am ballot slips.
Masaudin, meanwhile, accused authorities of politically motivated persecution.
His defense attorney said envelopes discovered at his home bore the name of the Islamic Movement, the religious and political movement associated with Ra'am, and that each contained 1,000 shekels ($320) intended as charitable donations to low-income families.
Investigators also seized another envelope containing 12,000 shekels ($3,840). Masaudin said that money belonged to his son.
The suspects have denied wrongdoing, and the allegations remain under investigation.
'The Bedouins came out to vote because they feared for their lives'
A relative of Abu Riaash rejected suggestions that the surge in Bedouin voter turnout resulted from improper financial inducements.
Instead, he attributed the increase to anger over National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose policies toward Bedouin communities in the Negev have drawn criticism.
"The increase in voter turnout in this election is because of one thing: the failed minister who caused damage in the Negev, Ben-Gvir," the relative said.
"Of course the Bedouins came out to vote. They feared for their lives. There's also no sense of security."
The relative said his own experiences during the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack had strengthened his determination to influence the country's political direction.
"I was at the gas station in Kfar Aza on Oct. 7. I am officially recognized as a victim of a terrorist attack, so of course I want to influence this government and change it," he said. "That's how everyone is thinking."
Separate Shin Bet investigation examines suspected Qatari funding
In a parallel development, Sohlberg, who also serves as deputy chief justice of the Supreme Court, sent an unusual letter to Shin Bet Director David Zini calling for an investigation into suspected foreign funding and election bribery involving foreign actors.
The letter followed a meeting between Sohlberg and Zini on Wednesday.
The suspected interference reportedly involves an attempt by Qatar to influence Israel's election through transfers estimated at tens of millions of shekels.
The intelligence underlying the suspicions has been described as "solid," although the precise nature of the alleged payments, their intended recipients and whether any election bribery actually occurred remain unclear.
According to information obtained by ynet, the Shin Bet had possessed the intelligence for several days but waited to determine whether the suspected bribery would take place.
The agency declined to comment on the investigation.

Ukrainian officials temper Abu Dhabi talks expectations, hope for energy truce

Ukraine's Representative to the European Union and the European Atomic Energy Community Taras Kachka, commenting on the meeting scheduled for November 4 in Abu Dhabi (the United Arab Emirates) between Ukraine, Russia and the United States at the team level, said he considered it important to resume trilateral talks on ending the war in Ukraine and hoped the parties would discuss a mutual cessation of strikes on energy infrastructure.
"This is good news. Do we have any very optimistic expectations? You know that all previous attempts have not been particularly successful. But we have had some limited successes, such as the ceasefire in Oleshky or the exchange of prisoners of war. So I think one of the topics to be discussed will be energy," he said during the special event "Support Ukraine, Defend Europe," organized by the newly established Kyiv Security Forum (KSF) Office in Brussels.
At the same time, EY-Parthenon Managing Director and former Ukrainian Finance Minister (2014–2016) Natalie Jaresko said she was convinced that "we should not believe that Putin is genuinely ready to sit down at the negotiating table at this stage."
Jaresko said that she did not have high expectations for these negotiations. At the same time, if we want to try to make progress, we must take steps now to increase pressure on the Russians, push Putin into a corner and make him believe that he needs to compromise, she said, emphasizing the importance of strengthening defense, sanctions and export controls.
Ivanna Klympush-Tsyntsadze, chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Ukraine's Integration into the EU and a member of the European Solidarity parliamentary faction, also said she did not have high expectations for the meeting in Abu Dhabi. She stressed the importance of ensuring that "Europe is finally at the negotiating table, rather than somewhere on the menu of these discussions," since European security is at stake.
She said that an energy truce should be discussed as an immediate, top-priority and urgent step toward a ceasefire. But she said that she has no expectations that this will be the outcome of these negotiations.
DTEK energy holding CEO Maxim Timchenko expressed hope that U.S. President Donald Trump's call for an energy truce would "be received positively" during the meeting.
"And if not, that will give us the moral right to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries. Perhaps this is the only way they can understand that an energy truce is important not only for us but also for Russia. That is what I hope for," he said.
Head of Ukraine's Permanent Mission to NATO Alyona Hetmanchuk agreed on the need to secure an immediate ceasefire but emphasized the importance of working to strengthen Ukraine's negotiating position.
"We may now be in the best situation in terms of holding the front line and the situation on the battlefield; we are in one of the strongest positions we have been in throughout the full-scale invasion. But our vulnerability right now is our air defense, our skies. That is why we need our partners' help to strengthen our air defense capabilities. And that will automatically strengthen our negotiating position. Because without strengthening our negotiating position, unfortunately, as you know, we will be very vulnerable in these negotiations," she said.
Kurt Volker, former U.S. special representative for Ukraine (2017–2019) and a member of the Kyiv Security Forum's Security Council, also stressed that securing a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire was the foremost priority.
Putin is not condemned often enough or loudly enough for his attacks and aggression against Ukraine, and he is not called to stop often enough. It should not be expected him to agree to this, but it could be spoken out much more loudly and in a coordinated manner: stop the fire right now, he said.
Regarding the U.S. position, Volker said he was convinced that U.S. President Donald Trump was currently focused exclusively on the midterm elections and that his position on Ukraine would not change.
Ukraine's greatest hope is the American people and the U.S. Congress. There is enormous support for Ukraine in the United States among a majority of supporters of both political parties and among a majority of the population. Legislative initiatives aimed at countering President Trump have been introduced. Republican candidates running in the midterm elections are being forced to publicly disagree with President Trump on issues such as lifting sanctions against Putin because the public views this negatively. So, in the long term, Ukraine has a strong base of support in the United States, the former U.S. special representative said.
As reported, talks in Abu Dhabi (the United Arab Emirates) between Ukraine, Russia and the United States at the team level are tentatively scheduled for November 4 this year. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the goal of the talks should be to make a meeting in a trilateral format at the leaders' level possible, as well as to discuss an energy ceasefire or a ceasefire in the Black Sea. The president also stressed the need for a meeting at the level of heads of state: "We should move from technical-level negotiations to a meeting of leaders, because key issues can be resolved only at the highest level."
The special event "Support Ukraine, Defend Europe" was attended by senior officials from the European Union, NATO and Ukraine. It was dedicated to strengthening support for Ukraine and joint European security. It was the first high-level event organized by the KSF Office in the EU, which began operating in Brussels at the initiative of KSF head and former Ukrainian Prime Minister (2014–2016) Arseniy Yatsenyuk.
