Swiss railways plans CHF7 billion digital upgrade
The digitalisation of the rail infrastructure by 2045 is expected to cost CHF7 billion. This has been confirmed by Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) and the Federal Office of Transport in response to an enquiry from the Keystone-SDA news agency.
SBB’s funding requirements for the digitalisation of rail transport amount to around CHF7 billion ($8.45 billion), as the Federal Office of Transport (FOT) announced on Thursday in response to an enquiry from the Keystone-SDA news agency. The FOT and SBB have thus confirmed a report in the Swiss paper Neue Zürcher Zeitung.
The 2027 Budget Message had earmarked CHF1 billion for the digitalisation of the rail infrastructure. This would enable a “first important step”, SBB wrote, but would be far from sufficient. In their assessment, these funds would not be enough to implement all the measures commissioned by the FOT.
+ Swiss Federal Railways profits jump as passenger numbers rise
SBB is calling for the digitalisation of the network to be driven forward resolutely, but gives priority to maintaining the existing network and service provision up to 2035. Significant parts of the safety-critical infrastructure would need to be renewed. SBB estimates this would cost around CHF7 billion by 2045.
In response to an enquiry from Keystone-SDA, the FOT confirmed SBB’s funding requirements for the implementation of the digitalisation of rail transport (ERTMS). It added that the funding would be provided through various channels.

Could reports of foreign funding, voter fraud lead to new elections? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:53:56 UTC
19:53:56 KST

Israeli election results could be annulled nationwide if allegations of foreign funding and election bribery are proven to have affected the vote, although such an outcome is considered highly unlikely, according to the legal framework governing election appeals and assessments within the political establishment on Thursday.
Following the directive to investigate suspicions of foreign funding and election bribery, the question arises: what would happen if the integrity of the elections were found to be compromised?
Under Section 86 of the Knesset Elections Law, a legal mechanism allows the annulment of election results and even orders new elections throughout the country. However, the existence of suspicions, or even the discovery of irregularities, does not automatically lead to the annulment of elections.
Furthermore, the Knesset Elections Law, particularly Section 86, does not provide for "automatic disqualification" due to violations of campaign finance laws or the receipt of foreign funding.
The prevailing assessment within the political establishment is that even if the investigation produces significant findings proving election bribery, the chances of annulling the election results nationwide are slim to virtually nonexistent.
Nevertheless, the results could be invalidated and repeat elections held at specific polling stations where proven violations of the law could have affected the outcome.
However, a distinction must be made between the legal and political dimensions. Likud and the Netanyahu bloc launched an election-night campaign to delegitimize any political move involving the Joint List and Ra'am, from forming a minority government to replacing the Knesset speaker. The allegations of election bribery could serve this campaign and give it further momentum.
Under what circumstances can election results be appealed?
The law permits an appeal if the elections as a whole, or voting at a particular polling station, were not conducted legally; if the allocation of votes among candidate lists was incorrect; if Knesset seats were not allocated according to the law; or if votes cast for a particular list were obtained unlawfully.
A central requirement is that the alleged irregularity could have affected the election results.
Who can appeal, and how much time do they have?
Under the law, those entitled to appeal include members of the Central Elections Committee and regional election committees, factions in the newly elected Knesset, MKs, candidate lists that participated in the elections, candidates who appeared on those lists, and the attorney-general.
An appeal must be filed with the Jerusalem Administrative Affairs Court within 14 days of the publication of the election results.
The court may extend the deadline under special circumstances, provided that the reasons for doing so are recorded.
Can the court order new elections nationwide?
Yes. Section 86(d) explicitly states that the court may annul the elections in their entirety or at a particular polling station and order them to be held again on a date determined by the court.
Such a decision would have significant implications, but it is not the only remedy available to the court.
<strong>Can the results be corrected without holding new elections</strong>?
Yes. The law authorizes the court to recalculate the allocation of votes among candidate lists and declare the election results accordingly.
In addition, the court may declare that a particular candidate was not lawfully elected and that another candidate won the seat.
Therefore, a successful appeal does not necessarily require the annulment of the entire election.
Can the court's decision be appealed?
Yes. As a general rule, an appeal may be filed with the Supreme Court on a question of law, subject to obtaining permission from the president of the Supreme Court.
However, if the Administrative Affairs Court annuls the elections nationwide, the law allows the parties specified in the legislation to appeal to the Supreme Court as a matter of right, even if they were not parties to the original proceedings.
In such a case, the appeal will be heard by a panel of five justices or a larger panel consisting of an odd number of justices.
Would an election appeal halt the Knesset's work?
No. Section 86(h) explicitly states that an election appeal will not delay the work of the Knesset.
It further stipulates that the outcome of an appeal will not undermine the validity of decisions already made by the Knesset.
In other words, filing an appeal does not paralyze the Knesset's parliamentary activities, even if a subsequent decision changes the election results or annuls them.
Could suspicions of foreign interference lead to the annulment of the entire election?
Under Section 86 of the Knesset Elections Law, the court has the authority to annul elections nationwide or at specific polling stations and order new elections.
The law permits appeals on several grounds, including claims that votes cast for a candidate list were obtained unlawfully or that the allocation of Knesset seats does not reflect the election results.
However, annulling an election is an exceptional remedy that requires judicial review. The mere existence of suspicions is insufficient to justify canceling the elections.

The future Israel cannot ignore: Opposition must speak to the country it hopes to lead - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:53:29 UTC
19:53:29 KST

Israel’s opposition must explain how it plans to govern the country it hopes to lead. The argument over Arab political partnership after Tuesday’s election makes that question immediate, but it will remain long after the coalition negotiations end.
Democrats chairman Yair Golan’s call on Wednesday for a government formed in partnership with Arab citizens brought the issue into focus. He argued that a vote cast in Tira carries the same weight as one cast in Givat Shmuel.
Whatever one thinks of Golan’s politics, the point stands. Arab citizens cannot be approached as potential partners only when their votes become necessary, while the harder conversation about their place in the country is postponed until another election.
Thursday morning’s reports of suspected foreign interference, including alleged Qatari funding, complicate that conversation. Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg called on the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) to investigate suspected foreign financing and election bribery.
Those suspicions require investigation. Even if unlawful funding is proved, however, that would not justify treating Arab voters collectively as participants in wrongdoing. Responsibility must be established through evidence. Citizens who cast their votes lawfully are still owed a political response.
What does the next government owe its Arab citizens?
The allegations could make opposition parties less willing to consider any arrangement dependent on Arab parties, even before investigators establish what happened. But closing off a coalition option would leave the underlying question unanswered: How do those leaders intend to build a shared future with Arab citizens?
Equal citizenship does not require agreement with every party or guarantee anyone a place in government. Parties can disagree profoundly over security, national identity, and the terms of a coalition. Treating Arab participation itself as disqualifying is another matter.
The language of a “Jewish majority” becomes troubling when it suggests that some citizens’ votes confer legitimacy and others do not. Jewish history, trauma, and the need for a national home are very real. They do not make that distinction compatible with equal citizenship.
This is where the discussion needs to move beyond the next government. What is being demanded of leadership is the ability to address Israel’s present while preparing for the society it is becoming.
Security is urgent; so are war trauma, education, and the social services people need to rebuild their lives. A government cannot postpone those needs. But it also cannot keep responding to each crisis without examining what will make the next one harder to resolve.
The debate over ultra-Orthodox (haredi) conscription is an example. Who serves now matters. So does what children are learning years before they reach military age, what opportunities they will have afterward, and what they understand their responsibilities toward the wider society to be.
The Shoresh Institution’s October 2026 handbook, drawing on Education Ministry data, puts haredi children at 25% of first graders and Arabic-speaking children at another 23%. These are children already in classrooms. We do not have to wait 50 years to understand why their education matters to the country’s future.
Their communities are different, and so are the educational challenges they face. Shoresh’s warning concerns the consequences of failing to give children the skills needed to participate in a modern economy. That failure would limit their own choices and the resources available for healthcare, welfare, and defense.
Prof. Dan Ben-David has made this connection repeatedly in interviews with The Jerusalem Post. Political leaders need to act on it while those children are still in school.
They also need to recognize that neither Arab nor haredi society stands still.
Moti Leitner’s Haredi Public party, for example, campaigned on incorporating mathematics and English into haredi education and on service for those not studying Torah. Its emergence demonstrates that arguments about work, education and responsibility are taking place within haredi society, too.
Leaders outside that community should be capable of hearing those arguments without demanding that people abandon their religious identity before being taken seriously. The same willingness to listen is needed in relations with Arab citizens, whose interests extend well beyond their usefulness to a Jewish-led bloc.
The Zionist framework through which we understand the country must contend with a society that changes from generation to generation. That does not make it less legitimate. It does require us to discuss what Jewish self-determination and equal citizenship mean in the lives of the people who share this country.
The responsibility rests with leadership, but voters cannot excuse themselves entirely. Politicians also respond to what their own supporters are prepared to accept. We cannot demand long-term thinking while refusing to hear anything that unsettles our understanding of who belongs and on what terms.
We need to hold on to our own history, connection, and identity while acknowledging those of others. Otherwise, we will keep putting out fires, paying in money, in lives and in the growing distance between us.
The opposition is asking to govern Israel. It needs to explain how it intends to govern alongside citizens whose votes it may need but whose political participation it struggles to accept.

Hegseth's latest Pentagon purge ousts top military planner Sylvia
Unknown

2026-10-29

19:52:00 KST

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired the Pentagon’s top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, in the latest ouster of a senior military officer as President Donald Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran amid an eight-month war.
Hegseth removed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Sylvia is the second general officer Hegseth ousted from the post, known in military circles as the J5. He forced Sylvia's predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, to retire last October.
The defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said no immediate replacement for Sylvia is planned and no reason was given for the firing. The Atlantic earlier reported the move.
A spokesperson for the Joint Staff expressed "deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation" and wished him and his family the best.
Typically, the J5 director and staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans with both the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the U.S. President. Sylvia's firing comes as U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly proposed new military operations against Iran.
U.S. President Donald Trump has vowed to "finish the job" in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said new strikes are an option after next week's midterm elections.
U.S. officials have told several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for potential renewed military action after Tuesday's elections, as well as the possibility Iran will retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter said. They say U.S. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on new strikes.
A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands more troops are heading to the region.
Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as the commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, now offline. He also previously served as the vice director of the J5.
He is the latest of nearly two dozen general and flag officers and other military leaders Hegseth has removed or forced to retire during his tenure. The Pentagon has not publicly explained almost all of these departures. These include the civilian secretaries of the Army and Navy and some top uniformed officers for the military services.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment late Wednesday.
Hegseth said last month he ordered the military to double cuts to top officers, aiming for a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. Approximately 800 flag and general officer positions currently exist.
"I call it accountability and long overdue," Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders at Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30.
Some members of Congress criticize cuts to general officer ranks as a "purge" that will take years to rebuild.
"He's got some kind of deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military," Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who criticizes Hegseth, said last month. "He's purging a generation of great military leaders, and it will take a generation to recover from it."

Arkhangelsk Region's national park studies waste movement in White Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:51:29 UTC
19:51:29 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 29. /TASS/. Experts of the Kenozersky National Park and the Onega Pomorie National Park in the Arkhangelsk Region studied how waste spreads across the White Sea, the Kenozersky National Park told TASS. The specialists launched buoys with a GPS tracker from different locations to watch the waste movement.
"To show clearly where the waste comes from and how it gets into the water area, authors of the project "The Sea is Disturbed" together with the Marlin‑Yug Company, and specialists of the Marine Observation Systems Laboratory in Sevastopol have produced buoys with a GPS tracker. The research buoys were produced for the first time. They are similar to those used by polar explorers when they observe ice drifts. The buoys were launched six times to demonstrate to the Arkhangelsk Region's residents optional routes the waste follows in the White Sea," the national park said.
Most waste enters the White Sea from Arkhangelsk, Severodvinsk and Novodvinsk. Waste on the shore is either fishermen's waste (gear, improvised buoys and floats), or urban waste (bottles, food packages), or the waste people leave on the beach (rubber slippers), as well as "bio-loading stations from urban sewage treatment plants" (black plastic cylinders with petals).
On every buoy, the specialists left contact information as well as notes stating that it is safe and is part of the study. The buoys' routes formed into a map of six paths of a plastic bottle conditionally forgotten on the shore. The first buoy, launched at a crowded beach on the Yagry Island, was washed onto the shores of the Solza River the next morning - it has covered 21 km. A local village resident picked up the buoy. The second buoy passed 243 km and sailed to the Onega Peninsula. It was about to be picked near the town of Lopshenga, but the wind changed, and the buoy was blown back to Severodvinsk, where it was reported by people working for the local ship repair company.
The third attempt was to send a buoy from the Mudyug Island. It reached the village of Kuya, but the tide swept the buoy out into the sea 511 km from the place where it had been launched. On the 20th day of the trip, the Solovki Museum-Reserve staff found it. Further on, it was released from the Bolshoy Solovetsky Island, sailed 136 km, and was thrown onto dry land. During the second launch, the Solovetsky buoy reached the Murmansk Region and returned to the island after a week of travel. Buoy movements in real time during all the missions were available online.
"The project has helped everyone to see clearly how in a matter of days, potential waste, left on the shore, travels tens and hundreds of kilometers and ends up in unexpected places," the project's authors noted. The project's research was supported by the Presidential Nature Foundation.

RSHP designs Hetao Alpha skyscraper in Shenzhen with "striking butterfly layout"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:51:09 UTC
19:51:09 KST

RSHP designs Hetao Alpha skyscraper in Shenzhen with “striking butterfly layout”
British studio RSHP has completed a 45-storey office skyscraper in Shenzhen, China, featuring two angled wings connected by a central core.
Called Hetao Alpha, the 212-metre-tall office building comprises a 37-storey east wing and a 44-storey west wing connected by a central core. The building sits on top of a mixed-use podium.
“The naturally ventilated office tower features a striking butterfly layout with fully glazed east and west wings,” the studio said.
Cantilevered bays extended from the central concrete core on the east and west sides to form the tower’s angled wings, which have 70,410 square metres of office space.
On every 12 levels, mega trusses located on refuge and service floors provide additional structural support.
The Hetao Alpha skyscraper has a fully glazed facade that, together with open floor plates, ensures unobstructed views of the cityscape for the office workers.
Curved double-height glazing at each of the wings’ four corners captures curated viewpoints of the Shenzhen Bay Wetlands to the west and the Hong Kong Mai Po Wetlands to the south.
Lifts are located on the north and south facades in the central volume. These were also fully glazed to offer panoramic views of the surrounding landscape.
“Centred around a concrete core with suspended corner bays, the tower minimises its perimeter structure, creating slender edges and expansive double-height views, forming the distinct structural system that defines the tower’s identity,” said Marco Tessaro, associate at RSHP.
Louvred panels on the facade and vents were incorporated into the glazing to create natural ventilation throughout the building while reducing energy consumption.
This was one of the methods used to help the project achieve China’s 3-star Green Building Evaluation Standard, which is equivalent to LEED Gold.
A six-level public podium is connected to the east wing, creating a roof terrace where half of the space is reserved for greenery.
The studio added extensive vegetation, a feature wall and water elements to improve biodiversity and help create a calm environment for socialising.
“The building’s natural ventilation, green rooftop spaces, and energy-efficient facade define a truly sustainable development that reduces consumption while enhancing wellbeing for both occupants and the wider community,” said Wenchao Zhou, associate at RSHP.
Mega triangular trusses on the podium roof help transfer the load of the east wing to the building’s central core.
Another viewing platform is located on the building’s west wing, which, together with the podium roof terrace, was designed to invite public visitors and private tenants alike to engage in outdoor activities such as observing migrating birds, a popular hobby for the locals.
According to RSHP, one of the challenges of the project was combining two separate briefs from different clients to create an uplifting mixed-use development as well as an office building with a bold and coherent architectural identity.
“Taking a holistic approach to the complex brief, RSHP’s design for Hetao Alpha has created an open and welcoming destination for work, retail, and leisure that achieves a bold architectural identity with a seamless transition between public and private space,” the studio explained.
The 13,640-square-metre public podium houses sports facilities, a library, retail, and a double-height arts exhibition space.
A passageway cuts through the north and south ends of the ground floor, helping to give the podium a floating look that reduces the perceived weight of the volume.
The entrance lobby for the office building can be found inside the podium. This double-height space is supported by a series of slim columns connected to the triangular trusses above on the podium roof.
A metro station was integrated into the basement, which also has a sunken plaza with retail stores.
“Spacious, open, and welcoming, the tower and podium integrate seamlessly to form an elegant composition that maximises connectivity with the wider public realm and the park to the east,” said Richard Paul, director of RSHP.
“With glazed office wings overlooking Shenzhen’s wetlands and a public podium offering diverse activity, the development achieves a serene, flexible environment that accommodates a wide range of uses,” he continued.
Elsewhere in China, RSHP has completed a 186-metre mixed-use skyscraper in central Shanghai, as well as a vast convention centre in Zhengzhou, with 16 exhibition halls connected by a mile-long elevated walkway

What we know about Spain’s second high-speed rail tragedy this year
Officials blame a control centre order for the Wednesday crash following a critical train signalling system failure.
At least 68 people were killed and about 80 injured when a high-speed train ploughed into the back of a stationary train in central Spain on Wednesday.
The crash, just before 9am (08:00 GMT) near Urda, a town south of Madrid, is Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster in less than a year, and comes just weeks before national elections.
The authorities have blamed an “inexplicable” order given by a rail control centre that allowed one of the trains to resume normal speed following a signalling failure.
Here is what we know about the crash:
What happened and where?
The moving train was run by Renfe, Spain’s state-owned rail company. It hit the rear of a stalled train operated by Iryo, a private player which entered the country’s high-speed railway service market in 2022.
Both trains were travelling from Madrid to Seville. The Renfe train was carrying 397 people and the Iryo train 147, according to the government of Castilla-La Mancha, the central region where the crash happened.
The trains collided on a raised section of track between Urda and the neighbouring town of Los Yebenes, near the ancient city of Toledo.
Two of the Iryo train’s carriages derailed and fell down the embankment during the collision, regional officials and emergency sources quoted by Spanish newspaper El Pais said.
The toll is the highest in a European rail accident since a 2013 derailment in the northwestern Spanish city of Santiago de Compostela killed 80 people.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited the site on Wednesday and declared three days of national mourning, starting on Thursday.
He pledged to get to the bottom of the crash, saying any negligence would come to light and any system failures would be met with a strong response.
What do we know about the dead and injured?
At least 68 people were killed in the crash and about 80 were injured, 50 of them seriously and 15 critically, said Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government.
The most seriously injured people were taken to hospitals in the region and in Madrid, the capital. Others were assessed at a sports hall near the crash site, where emergency teams sorted them by the severity of their injuries before sending them home or to hospital.
Survivors treated near the scene had head wounds, facial swelling and bloodied clothing, and many were dazed, according to local media reports.
Juan Quesada, 65, who was travelling on the Renfe train to Seville for work, suffered a head injury. “A tremendous impact and so much noise, and everyone was coming at you,” he told El Pais.
A local who contributed to supplying the makeshift medical centre told the paper the scene was “like a horror movie”.
Emergency crews continue to clear the wreckage of the two trains and search for victims trapped under the rubble. Fifty-two bodies have been recovered so far.
Spain’s Civil Guard sent a disaster investigation team to the site, with evidence from the site being collected.
What caused the collision between the trains?
At about 8:30am (07:30 GMT), a computer failure knocked out LZB, the main signalling system that automatically keeps trains on the line a safe distance apart, Transport Minister Oscar Puente said.
As a result, about six trains on a 63km (39-mile) stretch stopped automatically, including the Iryo and Renfe trains. The Renfe train had been running about 25km (15.5 miles) behind the Iryo train on the same track.
Control of those trains then passed to a centre in Madrid run by Adif, the state company that manages Spain’s rail infrastructure. Its controllers had to decide when and how fast each train could move again.
At 8:36am, controllers cleared the Renfe train to resume running at its normal speed, according to the preliminary investigation by El Pais that cites train data and recordings of calls with controllers.
The Iryo train was given the same order at 8:41am but could not get moving. At 8:48am, its driver told controllers it was still stalled.
By then, the Renfe train had sped up to more than 200km/h (124mph). At 8:53am, it smashed into the stalled Iryo train.
Was human error or a signalling failure responsible?
Puente has said the crash was caused by what he called an “inexplicable” order from the control centre after the safety system failed. He said the train drivers and engineers were not to blame.
In his view, the Renfe train should never have been allowed to move while a stop signal was still showing, or should at least have been instructed to proceed slowly.
That is what Spain’s rail rules usually require. When the automatic safety system LZB goes down, trains may only move again at up to 40km/h (25mph), slow enough for the driver to spot an obstacle and stop in time.
A backup system does take over, but it detects signals only at set points along the track to determine where each train is, rather than monitoring the line continuously.
Rail engineer Jose Luis Gonzalez Vallve told the Spanish news agency EFE that the main system, which detects a train stopped ahead and can apply brakes automatically, would have prevented the crash had it been working.
According to El Pais, there was also no signal beside the track between the two trains that could have stopped the Renfe train, leaving the controllers’ instructions as the only safeguard.
The two train companies have given their own accounts. Renfe said its train moved as instructed. Sources close to Iryo told EFE its train had stopped at a signal and called controllers, as the rules require.
Adif has not yet identified the point of failure at its control centre, sources at the company told EFE.
How have train services been affected?
Adif suspended high-speed train services between Madrid and the southern region of Andalusia after the crash, although trains are still running between Madrid and the nearby city of Toledo, and between the southern cities of Malaga and Seville.
Renfe has suspended ticket sales on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed corridor until December 13, with an alternative service between Madrid and Andalusia starting from Friday.
Why has Spain suffered two deadly high-speed crashes this year?
On January 18, a high-speed train derailed near the southern town of Adamuz, in Cordoba province, and hit an oncoming train, killing 46 people. That crash also involved Renfe and Iryo trains on the same line.
Sanchez, who leads the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), said the causes of the two crashes appeared unrelated, but that two high-speed rail accidents in one year were “unacceptable for a country like Spain”.
The Madrid-Seville line is Spain’s only high-speed route still using LZB, which dates from the line’s opening in 1992 and which the government is looking to update.
Adif was awarded a 52-month contract in 2021 to replace it with the European Union’s standard signalling system, but the work is still under way.
Spain has also seen two lower-speed train crashes this year, with one person killed in each and many others injured.
What about the political fallout?
With elections just around the corner, the crash has taken on a political dimension in Spain.
On Wednesday evening, 1,500 people gathered in front of the Ministry of Transport in a protest organised by right-wing youth groups. They called on Puente to resign and clashed with police.
Sanchez has cancelled upcoming campaign rallies to deal with the crisis.
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who heads the main opposition People’s Party (PP), cancelled campaign events during the mourning period and called for a full investigation.
“This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families,” he said. The PP holds a slight lead over the ruling PSOE in polls.
By contrast, Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right opposition party Vox, has not suspended campaign activities. Instead, he has adopted fiery rhetoric in response to the incident, labelling the government “a criminal organisation” and promising to take it to court.

Israel election deadlock could shield Netanyahu from 7 October probe: report
Israel's inconclusive election results could allow Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to evade accountability for the failures surrounding the 7 October 2023 attacks, according to Israeli newspaper Haaretz.
In an analysis published on Thursday, journalist Amos Harel argued that Tuesday's election had failed to produce a decisive outcome, potentially ushering in a prolonged period of political paralysis, with no clear path towards forming a new government.
The situation favours Netanyahu, who had feared electoral defeat, more than his opponents in the so-called "bloc of change", although the prime minister cannot claim an outright victory.
Netanyahu's coalition secured 53 seats, falling short of the 61 needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Opposition parties won 48 seats, while Palestinian parties secured 19, potentially giving Netanyahu's rivals enough parliamentary support to form a government.
If rival parties fail to form a coalition, Netanyahu could remain caretaker prime minister until another election is held, prolonging his time in office despite failing to secure a majority.
Such an outcome would be damaging for Israel but not necessarily for Netanyahu, particularly as his opponents may struggle to replicate their electoral performance in another vote, Harel argued.
The opposition entered the election under favourable conditions, with four parties crossing the electoral threshold, surplus-vote agreements and high turnout among overseas voters, yet failed to secure a decisive victory.
Netanyahu's political and military decisions in recent years have been driven primarily by his determination to remain in power and avoid imprisonment, according to the analysis.
Leaving office could expose him to a possible conviction in his ongoing corruption trial, while international arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza could further restrict his movements abroad.
The analysis also higlighted Netanyahu's campaign of exploiting anti-Arab sentiment to mobilise voters during the final hours before polling stations closed.
Likud's relative success was partly driven by identity politics, hostility towards traditional elites and fear of Palestinian citizens of Israel, attitudes Netanyahu has spent years reinforcing through the media.
However, Netanyahu's opponents also contributed to the political deadlock by refusing throughout the election campaign to recognise Palestinian parties as legitimate partners in a future governing coalition.
This rejection extended even to Mansour Abbas, leader of the United Arab List (Ra'am), who has advocated greater integration of Palestinian citizens into Israeli political life.
7 October inquiry in doubt
The election outcome has also thrown opposition plans to establish a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October attacks into uncertainty.
Opposition leaders had sought to establish an investigation into the security failures that preceded the attacks, alongside plans to reverse controversial judicial overhaul legislation and remove Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana.
Netanyahu has resisted calls for an independent state commission of inquiry into the attacks, which exposed major failures in Israel's security and intelligence establishment.
Harel warned that the election deadlock could allow Netanyahu to avoid a reckoning over those failures and his government's subsequent handling of the genocidal war on Gaza.
The analysis also raised concerns that Netanyahu could seek to renew military action against Iran to encourage opposition leaders to join a national unity government.
Netanyahu has reportedly urged US President Donald Trump to approve renewed joint strikes against Tehran, potentially aimed at overthrowing the Iranian government.
Such a confrontation could pressure opposition figures, including Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman, to reconsider their election pledges not to govern alongside Netanyahu.

Kyiv residents are switching to scooters because the Southern Bridge is closed
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv residents cover the 4 km between Osokorky and Vydubychi on scooters in 10 minutes for 60–70 hryvnias. On foot, the journey takes up to an hour.
In Kyiv, local residents are using rental electric scooters and bicycles to travel between the Osokorky and Vydubychi metro stations via the Southern Bridge, which has been closed to cars following Russian strikes. A scooter ride costs 60–70 hryvnias. This was reported by the public organization "Passengers of Kyiv" on October 29, according to UNN.
Details
"Kyiv residents have increased their use of rental electric scooters between the Osokorky and Vydubychi metro stations. It is possible to cross the Southern Bridge, which is closed to cars, by electric scooter in 10 minutes, paying 60–70 hryvnias for the service. At the same time, walking this 4-kilometer distance can take up to 1 hour. Currently, on the bridge on the Vydubychi metro side, there are a couple dozen scooters belonging to Bolt and only one from Bike Now. A Bolt specialist was also working on site, replacing batteries," the post says.
In addition, according to the public organization’s observations, people have set up an improvised bicycle parking area nearby. In particular, owners leave their bicycles, locking them to parts of the fencing. Presumably, after the end of the workday, they use them to get home across the bridge.
"We spoke with some scooter users, and they were pleased with this fast and inexpensive trip. The popularity of this shuttle-like movement by scooter is also growing because of the safety of travel—as cars are not driving at high speed in the adjacent lanes. Therefore, bicycles and electric scooters are currently a convenient, fairly safe, and certainly more cost-effective way to travel between the banks of the city than taxis," the post says.
Under these circumstances, "Passengers of Kyiv" called on representatives of the Transport Department of the Kyiv City State Administration and Kyivavtodor to temporarily remove at least one section of the crash barrier, so that people who arrive by scooter would not be forced to climb over the high barriers and get dirty, and also to remove the garbage from the spiral staircase, which Kyiv residents have begun using actively.
Reminder
From October 27 to November 1, traffic on the Southern Bridge will be partially restricted while the road surface is being repaired. Traffic toward the left bank will proceed only in the first lane.

UK keeps 623 Boxer order and adds heavy wheeled recovery vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:49:21 UTC
19:49:21 KST

- The British Army will buy a heavy wheeled recovery vehicle to recover Boxers after dropping a dedicated Boxer repair and recovery variant.
- Minister Luke Pollard said the order of 623 Boxers is unchanged, with over 500 built in Britain, alongside 72 RCH 155 artillery vehicles.
The British Army will buy a heavy wheeled recovery vehicle to tow and recover damaged Boxer armored vehicles in the field, after the Ministry of Defence dropped plans for a dedicated Boxer repair and recovery variant, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard told Parliament, UK Defence Journal reported.
Pollard was answering Conservative lawmaker Ben Obese-Jecty, the member for Huntingdon, who asked how the Army would repair Boxers in the field with no repair and recovery version on order. The minister did not say which vehicle the Army will buy, how many it needs or when the purchase will be made.
“The Army will absolutely have the ability to recover and support Boxer vehicles on the battlefield, such as through the Boxer support variants and the wider force, including the Heavy Wheeled Recovery Vehicle which we will procure,” said Pollard.
The question followed the Army’s decision this month to scrap three planned Boxer variants, armored mortar, repair and recovery, and anti-tank overwatch, as part of work on the Defence Investment Plan. In an answer the day before, Pollard said the ministry had assessed the armored recovery module built by German firm Flensburger Fahrzeugbau Gesellschaft for the role and rejected it, concluding that a generic heavy wheeled recovery vehicle would be more useful and more affordable across the whole force. Until a new vehicle arrives, Boxers recover each other, with backup from the Army’s Support Vehicle (Recovery) trucks and the tracked Challenger Armoured Repair and Recovery Vehicle.
Boxer is an eight-wheeled armored vehicle built around a common drive module that accepts different mission modules, which lets one chassis serve as a troop carrier, ambulance, command post or weapons carrier. A dedicated recovery version would have carried a crane and winch on that same chassis, keeping pace with Boxer units and sharing their protection and spare parts. A wheeled recovery truck can serve every vehicle type in the Army, but generally with less armor than a vehicle built on the Boxer hull.
Pollard said the overall order has not changed.
“There has been no change to our order of 623 Boxer vehicles, of which over 500 are being built here in the UK, and we are buying 72 Boxer RCH Artillery vehicles,” said Pollard.
All 623 Mechanised Infantry Vehicle Boxers are being delivered to a common build standard at two British plants, Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land in Telford and KNDS UK in Stockport, and Team Boxer UK delivered the 100th British-built Boxer in June. Pollard said the work backs more than 1,000 British jobs. Ministers confirmed last week that a planned third batch of Boxers is no longer being pursued through the program.
The 72 artillery vehicles are separate from that total. The RCH 155 pairs a 155 mm remote-controlled howitzer turret developed by Krauss-Maffei Wegmann with the Boxer drive module already in British service, and Britain signed a nearly £1 billion contract for 72 of the guns in May. They will replace the AS90 tracked howitzers in the close support artillery role, a gap the Army has filled with Swedish-built Archer guns since giving its AS90s to Ukraine.

Indonesia haze cost Malaysia US$1.97 billion in losses: study
Cross-border smoke from forest and peatland fires forced factories to shut, emptied classrooms and killed an estimated 1,700 people
2-MIN READ2-MIN

Smoke from this year’s Indonesian forest and peatland fires has inflicted an estimated 8 billion ringgit (US$1.97 billion) in welfare losses on Malaysia, contributing to an estimated 1,700 deaths and severely disrupting manufacturing, according to a report commissioned by the country’s leading industrial group.
The study, “The 2026 Fire Season and Transboundary Haze in Malaysia”, was conducted for the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM), as reported by the Malay Mail. Drawing on satellite data, air-quality monitoring and atmospheric modelling, the assessment tracked the impact of prolonged haze from July 1 to October 22.
Short-term exposure to fine particles from the fires contributed to an estimated 1,700 premature deaths – with a 95 per cent uncertainty interval of 1,300 to 2,300 – the report found, noting the figures reflect statistical models rather than individually confirmed fatalities.

Ukraine needs EU support to develop decentralized power generation – Kachka
Ukraine's representative to the European Union, Taras Kachka, made the statement at a special event organized by the Kyiv Security Forum entitled "Support Ukraine, Defend Europe," held in Brussels on October 28, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"At the local level, we need EU support on this decentralized generation. This is the experience of Kharkiv and other cities and it is now expanding to small and big cities, including Kyiv as well. We need to have an energy system that when every particular house, multi-apartment house, could be autonomous in terms of energy supply if the grid is not working. That can help also small businesses to stay alive and the economy continue to be operating," Kachka said.
He described the Ukraine Energy Support Fund, operating within the Energy Community, as one of the most effective assistance mechanisms. The fund pools financial contributions and purchases the equipment Ukraine needs.
"We had over EUR 2 billion aggregated in this fund, and it is one of the most efficient. But every winter, we learn new lessons what we need to buy. And this always happens, because Russia is damaging more and more elements of the grids beyond what we've been able to protect. And we also invent new ways of protecting with concrete, with hiding something under the earth. It all costs," Kachka said.
At the same time, he noted that new power generation technologies, particularly in renewable energy, help maintain the balance of the energy system. These include small wind and solar power plants, batteries and energy storage systems. Ukraine is also attracting investment in these areas.
"But the bigger picture is that you need to be able to protect your energy system. So that's why anti-ballistic, anti-missile and anti-drone systems are extremely important, since you have no alternatives," Kachka said.
He said that despite the difficult circumstances, Ukraine's energy sector remains attractive to public and private investors. As examples, the diplomat cited projects supplying equipment to Ukrainian companies with support from the Danish government, interest in energy projects under the Ukraine Investment Framework, and increased involvement by the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC).
Speaking about urgent needs, he stressed the importance of increasing fuel supplies for small generators used in residential areas and ensuring that equipment reaches Ukraine promptly.

US Muslim midterm candidates face Islamophobic attacks as Democrats lead the polls
Progressive candidates in the US are leading polls ahead of next week's midterm elections, even in some historically Republican states.
Senior Republicans have responded to these pre-election predictions with Islamophobic smears. On Sunday, President Donald Trump called Democratic Senate nominee for Michigan Abdul El-Sayed a "jihadist."
While Trump's name is not on the ballot, the midterms will be the key test of the president's popularity. According to an opinion poll by Reuters and Ipsos, just 32% of Americans approve of his presidency.
The president has dismissed his poor polling figures as "fake," claiming his true approval rating is 60% in an interview with The Washington Examiner.
Most major pollsters, including YouGov, Ipsos, and Focaldata, are predicting that the Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives.
If the Democrats gain control of the House, they will have more powers to investigate Trump, amid reports that they could potentially impeach the president for a record third time.
Some Democratic candidates and elected officials are now pledging to impeach the President again, including Tennessee Congressman Steve Cohen and Oklahoma Senate candidate N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas.
However, if they take control of the House, the Democrats will have more difficulty passing laws that undo Trump's work. As president, Trump has the power to veto most bills passed by either Congress or the Senate.
The only way to push a bill through after it has been vetoed is with a two-thirds majority vote, which would be unlikely without significant Republican rebellion against Trump.
Prediction market bettors seem confident that the Democrats will take control of the Senate. The betting company Kalshi puts the probability of the Democrats winning the Senate at 64%, based on bets placed on individual seats.
Polling companies however are less sure of the Senate results, and are looking to certain races for answers.
Two key races that pollster and analysts are looking to are the race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, and between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers in Michigan.
Pollsters are narrowly predicting Democrat wins in each of those races, but they tell two very different stories about the midterms.
Michigan is usually considered a swing state, voting for Donald Trump in 2024, and Joe Biden in 2020. That should make it fairly easy for a typical Democratic candidate to win in the state, given the current political climate.
However, Abdul El-Sayed is not a typical Democratic candidate. El-Sayed is a progressive, falling to the left of the typical Democratic platform. El-Sayed's key campaign pledges are healthcare for all and changes to corporate finances.
El-Sayed has often been compared to Zohran Mamdani, the Mayor of New York, who won on a progressive platform last year. A win for El-Sayed would be considered a vote of confidence for progressive candidates outside the cosmopolitan coastal cities.
Like Mamdani, El-Sayed, whose parents are Egyptian, is Muslim. This has opened him up to Islamophobic attacks from Republicans, including Vice President J.D. Vance.
At a rally for Rodgers on Tuesday, Vance invoked recent protests in Paris which have been pinned on France's Muslim community by many on the far-right, despite protesters coming from a diverse mix of races and ethnicities.
"If sovereignty means anything to us, it means that the nation belongs to the people of America," Vance said. "When you forget that, it’s how you get Paris. And unfortunately, it’s exactly what El-Sayed wants to bring to the shores of the United States of America."
Sayed has responded to attacks from both Vance and Trump, who said on Sunday that El-Sayed would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate."
"They think that by pointing at my name and my faith, that somehow you’re going to ignore the fact that you can’t afford your gas or your groceries, can’t see a doctor," El-Sayed said at a rally this weekend.
Meanwhile, in Texas James Talarico could be the state's first Democratic senator since 1993. While Talarico has been described as a 'progressive Christian,' he has more recently rejected the dichotomy of progressive and conservative Christians.
A win for the Democrats in Texas would be a clear sign that they can flip states previously thought of as out of reach.
Election day is 3 November, but early voting has already started. The final opinion polls will be published in the next few days, but by next week the picture of how Republicans and Democrats are fairing in the polls that matter most will be clearer.

Ukraine has ample power supply as Russian strikes cut demand 10% – DTEK CEO

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

19:46:39 KST

Ukraine has a surplus of generating capacity thanks to preparations for the autumn-winter period and a decline in electricity consumption resulting from Russian occupation forces' strikes on industrial facilities, DTEK CEO Maxim Timchenko said.
"Today, we have more than enough generating capacity, partly because of what the Russians have done to our industry over the past two months: it has led to an approximately 10% drop in electricity consumption. That is a significant amount. Of course, the need for electricity will be lower than last year. From this perspective, it may improve the situation. But this is still a reduction in demand caused by destruction. These are the consequences of these attacks," Timchenko said during the special event "Support Ukraine, Defend Europe," organized in Brussels by the recently established Office of the Kyiv Security Forum (KSF).
At the same time, he said that Russian occupation forces had begun launching intensive strikes on power lines and substations, which "prevent us from transmitting the electricity generated at our power plants to the main consumers – industry and households."
"This is our key problem right now. Despite the surplus of generating capacity, electricity in Kyiv is being cut off for two, three or four hours a day. I think companies and the government have learned their lessons. My goal, and the goal of our company, is to prevent this from happening again," the DTEK CEO said.
Timchenko reported that the company had implemented 95% of what is known as first-level passive protection for energy facilities.
"As for the second level, we need to do much more, specifically build more protective structures for our high-voltage transformers and autotransformers. And returning to our main problem right now, it is electricity transmission, not generation. We are establishing appropriate backup power sources for grid infrastructure in Kyiv and other cities. All these plans, which have been announced at various levels, will be implemented by the end of the year so that we have backup capacity for heating, sewage and water supply," he said.
The company's CEO also highlighted the difference from last year in the intensity of attacks by the aggressor and the new technologies Russia is using to destroy energy infrastructure.
"This is the key challenge. We need significantly more active defense capabilities. Unfortunately, the availability of ammunition for air defense is very low today. This applies to all facilities, from high-voltage substations to power plants. And this is precisely what could undo all our efforts, everything we have accomplished over the past eight months, five months," Timchenko said.
According to him, several large-scale attacks can shut down a power plant's electricity supply. The DTEK CEO said this had happened at one of the company's plants the previous week.
"If the Russians focus on a single facility and repeat these attacks around the clock for three to four days, we will have absolutely no chance of keeping it operational," Timchenko added.
The special event "Support Ukraine, Defend Europe" was attended by senior officials from the European Union, NATO and Ukraine. It focused on strengthening support for Ukraine and overall European security. It was the first high-level event organized by the KSF Office in the EU, which began operating in Brussels at the initiative of KSF head and former Ukrainian prime minister (2014-2016) Arseniy Yatsenyuk.

He was also banned from driving vehicles for 10 years. UNN journalist reports this from the courtroom of the Sviatoshynskyi District Court of Kyiv.
Details
The court sentenced Oleksii Tandyr, who ran over and killed a serviceman of the National Guard of Ukraine at a checkpoint, to nine years in prison and banned him from driving vehicles for 10 years.
"The court has ruled to find Tandyr Oleksii Vitaliiovych guilty of committing the criminal offense provided for in Part 3 of Article 286 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine and to impose on him, under this article, a sentence of imprisonment for a term of 9 years, with deprivation of the right to drive vehicles for a term of 10 years," the judge announced.
The court's verdict may be appealed within 30 days.
Context
On the night of May 26, 2023, Judge Oleksii Tandyr, then head of the Makariv District Court of Kyiv Region, ran over and killed a National Guard serviceman at a checkpoint in the capital. The judge was detained at the scene.
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office launched an investigation under Part 3 of Article 286-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The High Council of Justice granted the motion of the deputy Prosecutor General to consent to the judge's detention. Judge Tandyr was remanded in custody.
In August, the High Council of Justice decided to dismiss Judge Oleksii Tandyr from the Makariv District Court of Kyiv Region.
In January 2026, the European Court of Human Rights found violations of European standards of liberty and security in the case of former Judge Oleksii Tandyr. The Court awarded Tandyr 2,100 euros in compensation for non-pecuniary damage and 250 euros in legal costs.

An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson is set to have his work presented in two weeks’ time at one of the most prestigious conferences in theoretical computer science. As of Monday, much of that work is “dead,” he says, after AI showed that a 27-year-old hypothesis underpinning it is wrong.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic claimed this week to have disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH). Vast swaths of theoretical computer science research on complexity and algorithm design have been built on the premise that the effort it takes to solve certain problems increases exponentially with the size of the problem.
Jonsson expects his predicament will be “very common” at the IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, where his work will be presented by one of his coauthors. “People will start the talks: ‘ETH is false, half of my paper does not work,’” he says. It’s a vexing problem, Jonsson says, “but at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.”
Researchers haven’t independently verified, let alone had time to fully understand, the AI-produced proofs, which both firms have published on GitHub in both natural language and its machine-checkable Lean format. OpenAI has asked the UC Santa Barbara computer scientists who originally proposed the hypothesis, plus an MIT academic who has refuted a version of ETH, to rally researchers to unpack the proofs. So far, this effort includes a Google form asking for volunteers and feedback, and a commitment from OpenAI to fund a conference on the topic.
UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov plans to join the effort, as he estimates the result—if confirmed—will render him “galactically wrong” and make around 50 of his published papers either “pointless” or in need of a revisit.
“It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.”
Thore Husfeldt, head of the algorithms research group at the IT University of Copenhagen, had spent most of this year thinking about one single problem in his subfield. “As far as I can tell, it’s now all irrelevant,” he tells WIRED. Having first formulated a version of the hypothesis now disproved by OpenAI, he has been writing calculations on his blackboard to figure out what other parts of his work might have become obsolete due to the “once-in-a-generation result.” Unlike the ennui that has gripped math researchers who have faced similarly field-upending proofs generated by AI models, though, Husfeldt expressed enthusiasm about the new results.
The finding is “fantastic,” he says. “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room,” he explains. “It's like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.”
For centuries, science has advanced through making hypotheses and proving them wrong. It also isn’t unusual for an academic to be scooped or have their work otherwise undercut by another research group. But AI has accelerated this, obliterating whole research programs and spooking researchers in specific fields of math and science who wonder where they stand now that machines can outperform them.
“The last few months have been really tough. It's a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people,” Husfeldt says. “That is psychologically taxing for many people,” he says, adding that his department has considered hiring an occupational psychologist because “some people are really depressed and really sad.”
Researchers have also been overwhelmed by the volume of content now being produced, thanks to AI, including slop-level results. Midway through the interview, Husfeldt receives what he suspects to be an AI-generated 17-page paper on the consequences of the ETH result from a random Gmail account. He won’t read it: “Reading math is a very big investment of cognitive time,” he says.
OpenAI has directly contributed to this; earlier this month, it dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub, to the annoyance of academics, who complain this makes it difficult to digest the results. Adding to the frustration were several documents that contained errors, reflecting what some mathematicians saw as a hasty rollout designed to juice the company’s planned initial public offering rather than moving the field forward. This time around, OpenAI’s 60-odd-page paper on ETH seems to be written better than the companies’ past publications, academics tell WIRED.
They are now scrambling to unpack the paper and find what other results they can quickly deduce from it.
If ETH is false and it doesn’t, in fact, take exponentially more time to solve problems as they become more complex, that’s “exciting,” says Victor Lagerkvist, an associate professor at Linköping. He plans to return to problems he had previously given up on under the assumption ETH was accurate.
OpenAI’s finding could also have impacts on the cryptography that underpins web security, which is based on the assumption that certain mathematical problems take an impractically long time to solve. While this particular result doesn’t directly affect cryptography, “it should definitely scare some cryptosystem designers,” says Lokshtanov.
That’s why continued human and AI-assisted work in theoretical computer science is important, Husfeldt adds: “We want the open scientific process to identify our misunderstandings about computation, in particular because lots of modern digital infrastructure is built on assumptions about computation.”
As for Linköping’s Jonsson, he plans to revisit both his own and others’ papers that hinge on ETH being true, and believes his conference paper may eventually be salvageable through another method. He’s excited to look into the details of OpenAI’s proof and see what he can learn from it and apply it to new problems. Even though it undoes the assumptions underpinning his work, having a verdict for ETH is something he could only “dream of” before, he says. “These are exciting times,” he adds. “Most people would never experience anything like this in their career.”
“I don’t care if it's a human-written proof, or it's written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.’’

Cemvision selected for €27.5 million grant to build low-emission cement plant in Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:44:56 UTC
19:44:56 KST

Swedish company Cemvision’s RE-MENT project has been selected to receive up to €27.5 million in funding from the European Union Innovation Fund to establish a commercial-scale low-emission cement plant in Ventspils, Latvia. The project is one of only two projects planned in Latvia selected for funding under this call. The Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) supported the company throughout the application preparation and funding acquisition process.
Under the RE-MENT project, Cemvision plans to establish a plant in Ventspils capable of producing up to 500,000 tonnes of cement annually with exceptionally low production emissions. The project aims to manufacture supersulphated cement (SSC), which can reduce CO₂ emissions by more than 90% compared with conventional cement production. Over its first ten years of operation, the project is expected to avoid more than 3.1 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emissions, while strengthening European industrial competitiveness and promoting the production of sustainable construction materials.
“Being selected among the projects supported by the Innovation Fund demonstrates that our technology is ready to move from the demonstration phase to industrial-scale production,” says Claes Kollberg, CEO of Cemvision. “This grant is a decisive step towards establishing our first commercial plant and demonstrating that Europe can produce the cement it needs from industrial residual materials while generating only a fraction of the emissions associated with conventional cement production. LIAA provided significant support in preparing our application, and we look forward to continuing our close cooperation with the Latvian government and local authorities to bring the plant project to fruition.”
Cemvision will now begin preparing the grant agreement with the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA). The agreement is expected to be signed between November 2026 and March 2027.
LIAA supported the company throughout the Innovation Fund application process, including organising information days in Latvia, facilitating access to expert knowledge, and providing guidance on programme requirements and funding opportunities.
“We congratulate Cemvision on securing support from the European Union Innovation Fund for the development of its plant in Ventspils. This funding reduces the project’s financial risks and helps move the planned facility towards implementation. Investments of this kind support the development of manufacturing in Latvia using innovative technologies and open up broader opportunities for our companies in European markets,” emphasises Ieva Jāgere, Director of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA).
Cemvision’s project is one of two projects in Latvia that have secured funding under this European Union Innovation Fund call. This demonstrates Latvia’s potential to develop internationally competitive industrial projects that attract foreign investment, create new manufacturing capacity and support the transition towards a climate-neutral economy.
The first Latvian company to receive support from the European Union Innovation Fund was Aerones. In 2023, the company was awarded a €4.4 million grant to scale up the production of robotic systems for repairing wind turbine blades.
“Latvia’s industrial growth requires not only new manufacturing facilities but also modern infrastructure and accessible, high-quality housing that helps companies attract employees. The renovation of existing housing stock and the construction of new factories create demand for high-quality building materials at competitive prices. Cemvision’s planned investment in Ventspils demonstrates how green technologies can become a competitive advantage for industry: lower emissions mean reduced exposure to fluctuations in CO₂ allowance prices. For Latvia, this represents an opportunity to produce modern construction materials both for domestic needs and for export. The Nordic market is strategically important for Latvia. Earlier this year, I led a Latvian business trade mission to Sweden to establish new business partnerships and encourage investment that supports the shared growth of the Baltic and Nordic region. The value of investments like this extends far beyond the factory itself – they generate orders for Latvian companies, create new jobs and bring in export revenues, strengthening the economy as a whole,” emphasises Viktors Valainis, Latvia’s Minister of Economics.
In 2027, LIAA, together with the Ministry of Climate and Energy (KEM) and the Employers’ Confederation of Latvia (LDDK), plans to organise an in-person Innovation Fund information day. The event will provide Latvian companies with information about the Fund’s financing opportunities and application requirements. The date and registration details will be announced at a later stage.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

US Delivers $7.9 Million in Demining Equipment to Ukrainian Sappers
The United States has delivered a new batch of specialized demining gear valued at $7.9 million to the State Special Transport Service of Ukraine.
According to the US Embassy in Ukraine, humanitarian landmine clearance directly aligns with American security and economic interests by creating safe conditions for US businesses to operate on Ukrainian territory, Hromadske reported on October 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new shipment is designed to help Ukrainian sappers safely and effectively clear landmines, anti-personnel mines, and unexploded munitions across contaminated areas.
Large areas of the country remain heavily contaminated with explosive remnants of war following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The State Special Transport Service works alongside other national agencies to clear hazard zones. The US government has previously funded training programs and instruction for more than 2,200 sappers serving in the unit, as reported by Hromadske.
US-trained units from the agency have already made thousands of areas safe, restoring 1,764 square kilometers of land. During these operations, specialists have identified and neutralized more than 262,000 mines and explosive items.
Almost 23% of Ukraine's territory remains contaminated—roughly 128,000 square kilometers—and full clearance is expected to take at least a decade.
Explosive devices have killed or injured more than 1,358 people since 2022, among them 380 killed, and clearing a single hectare costs at least $1,400.
The contamination keeps growing even as crews clear it. Russian forces have stepped up remote mining of Ukrainian supply routes, dropping explosive charges and magnetic mines from drones around Chasiv Yar and nearby Kostiantynivka in the Donetsk region.
Ukrainian units there must scan and clear the roads before every logistics run, often flying reconnaissance drones ahead of the movement.

Taiwan claims Pakistan briefly shut airspace to Taiwanese flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:42:00 UTC
19:42:00 KST

Taiwan on Thursday accused Pakistan of briefly closing its airspace to Taiwanese cargo and passenger flights, while pointing fingers at China of being behind the move.
"We suspect definitely China was behind this," Chen Ming-chi, a top official, said after confirming that Pakistan had closed and reopened its airspace to Taiwanese airlines.
China Airlines and EVA Air, which are both based in Taiwan, normally fly over Pakistan on their Asia-Europe route.
Last weekend, however, they began rerouting their Europe-bound flights further south over the Gulf or further north over Russia, AFP analysis of flight tracking data shows.
Some Taiwanese flights have resumed flying over Pakistan, according to the latest data.
"China Airlines and EVA received a notice from the Pakistan authorities that they will lift the ban, but only temporarily ... till the end of the winter," Chen said.
Neither airline would confirm that Pakistan had closed or reopened its airspace when contacted by AFP.
"We condemn Pakistan, and if China is behind this, I think that is a very bad practice to use its leverage over the countries in the Global South to do that," Chen said.
"I think that gets in the way of the safety of the passengers and the smooth operation of the global supply chain."
Pakistan's Defense Minister Khawaja Asif told Bloomberg News Wednesday that the airspace was closed in adherence with Beijing's "One China policy."
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Thursday that "as far as we are aware, there are no obstacles for residents of the Taiwan region to travel internationally."
China claims Taiwan as part of its territory and opposes the self-governed island's participation in international organizations and exchanges with other countries.
Chen said it was the first time a country had closed its airspace to Taiwanese commercial flights.
In April, the Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar revoked overflight permits for Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te's flight to Eswatini, Taipei's only African ally, forcing him to postpone the trip.
At the time, Taiwan blamed "intense pressure" from China for the revocation.
"China now learned that this could be an effective way to block our airspace access and therefore sort of further isolate Taiwan," Chen said.
"We see this is the discovery that they can weaponize the airspace assets."
Taiwan does not have formal diplomatic ties with Pakistan, which has close relations with China.
Chen said "many like-minded" countries had assisted Taiwan over the airspace closure.
"We are afraid that this might be a practice that spreads to other Global South countries," Chen said.
"I think that is a major concern for not only for Taiwan, but also for other countries in the region and beyond."
Pakistan and China have maintained close diplomatic and strategic relations for decades, often describing their partnership as an "all-weather friendship" that is "higher than the Himalayas, deeper than the oceans, sweeter than honey and stronger than steel."
China is Pakistan's largest trading partner and a major investor, particularly through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), and has poured tens of billions of dollars into funding massive transport, energy and infrastructure projects.

Also found were several "books, including a Quran, a Bible, and Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf", as well as stickers celebrating the far-right National Rally (RN) party.
Christen said the stickers bore slogans such as "Long live France, RN, proud to be French", but they were not produced by the party led by Marine Le Pen, who is leading opinion polls to succeed Emmanuel Macron as French president in elections next spring.
Kevin T. had told investigators that "he designed the stickers found in his home himself, and then ordered them to be manufactured via Amazon more than a year ago."
The suspect said that "he is neither a member of nor a sympathiser with any political party", Christen said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Some 13 killed when Russian drone strikes trains in central Ukraine

At least 13 people were killed and 10 others wounded Thursday when a Russian jet-powered drone struck two trains stopped at a station in central Ukraine, officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described it in a post on X as a "horrific attack” that struck passenger trains in Dnipro.
"The Russians attacked the platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing. Unfortunately, as of now, 13 people have been confirmed dead," Zelenskyy said on social media.
"Fair and decisive actions by America and Europe are needed against Russian escalation," he added.
Dnipropetrovsk Regional Gov. Oleksandr Ganzha on Telegram said: "Thirteen people were killed in a Russian attack on Dnipro. At least five more were wounded."
Dnipro mayor Borys Filatov also lamented "a tragedy" in the city, saying on social media that "a drone hit a civilian electric train."
"Many people have been killed. Lots are wounded," he said.
The state Ukrainian Railways operator said a jet-powered Russian drone had hit the Dnipro train station.
"The strike hit one of the platforms, where train No. 866 Dnipro-Zaporizhzhia was at the time," it said on Telegram.
An elevated threat level had been announced, according to the rail company's chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform," he said on Facebook.
Russia has fired drones on trains across Ukraine since the first days of its 2022 invasion – destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing several railway workers.
In September alone, passengers were evacuated from more than 5,800 Ukrainian train services due to the threat of Russian drone strikes, the national railway operator told AFP.
The country's vast train network is a vital form of transport in the country, where journeys between east and west can take 24 hours.
