US warns allies on possible Iran strikes after elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:39:55 UTC
19:39:55 KST

Breadcrumb
US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections
US officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections in the United States—as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter.
Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by US diplomats and defense officials.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical 3 November midterm elections in the United States are over.
Those threats and the fresh US urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon.
The White House and US officials declined to comment.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month—summarily rejected by Trump—that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to "exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions" and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that was launched by the US and Israel in late February.
The US has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate—leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said.
The allies have also been urged by US officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
While the US has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the region has become more tense.
The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
Meanwhile, Israel continues to strike Gaza and southern Lebanon despite alleged ceasefire agreements.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential fighting by the US.
It's unclear how soon after Election Day that the US military would be ready to potentially resume strikes.
The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard—roughly 9,000 troops in all—from San Diego to the Gulf to bolster the US military in the region.
At the time, one US official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the 3 Nov. elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran.
The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that's driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy.
The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress.
While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes.
During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming "in a couple of weeks, if you don't mind."
"Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?" Trump said earlier in the same address. "I said, 'Whenever I want it to end.' It'll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete—a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then—especially if they feel US actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank.
"Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?" he said.

Russia opened 8 new embassies in Africa since 2023, bringing total to 48: Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:39:24 UTC
19:39:24 KST

Elena Teslova
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Russia has opened eight new embassies in African countries since the previous Russia-Africa summit in 2023, bringing the total number of Russian embassies on the continent to 48, President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday.
Speaking at the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, Putin noted that African countries were also expanding their diplomatic presence in Russia.
"I'd like to mention the systematic steps taken by the Russian side to expand its diplomatic presence on the continent. Since the previous summit in 2023, eight new Russian embassies have begun work in African states, and their total number has reached 48," he said.
Putin also expressed support for plans by Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo to open embassies in Moscow.
"We also know of the intentions of Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo to open their embassies in Moscow in the near future and, naturally, we support this," he said.
Beyond diplomatic ties, Putin highlighted efforts to expand Russia's economic presence in Africa, including through a growing network of trade missions.
"So far, there are only six of them, but their activities cover 16 African countries," he said.
The president also pointed to an increase in Russian mineral fertilizer supplies to the continent, which amounted to about 1.5 million tons last year and had already exceeded 2.2 million tons this year.
Turning to financial cooperation, Putin said the ruble's share in Russian-African commercial transactions had reached up to 85%.
“The share of the ruble in Russian-African commercial transactions already stands at up to 85%. This makes it possible to protect our economic exchanges from external influence,” he said.
Putin also said Russia was interested in relocating certain production facilities to Africa amid external pressure, while emphasizing that decisions made by African governments must remain sovereign.
The third Russia-Africa summit and the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum are being held in Moscow.

Rescue teams search wreckage for survivors after train crash in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:39:03 UTC
19:39:03 KST

Rescue teams search wreckage for survivors after train crash in Spain
A canine unit and cranes have been deployed to aid search and rescue efforts following the deadly crash.
Rescuers in Spain are searching for victims and survivors a day after a train struck another from behind, killing 68 people, in the country’s second high-speed rail disaster this year.
Emergency workers and rescue teams with sniffer dogs continued to look for victims on Thursday morning, a day after the collision in Toledo province, central Spain.
Cranes were in place to help shift the carriages as police and soldiers helped to pick through the wreckage strewn down the gravel slope where at least three train carriages were derailed by the impact.
Esther Padilla, a spokeswoman for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, told TVE that teams were working “very carefully, because we still cannot say with certainty that there are no more victims trapped in the twisted wreckage”.
“A canine unit was deployed yesterday. They will go back in today to make sure that nobody else remains there,” she added.
She said 53 people remained in hospital, with 15 in critical care.
Three days of mourning have been declared for those killed in the accident.
Wednesday’s crash followed a similar fatal accident earlier this year involving the same rail companies on the same line.
In January, 46 people died when a train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going in the opposite way in southern Spain.
The collision has reopened a national debate about the safety of Spain’s high-speed rail network, the biggest in Europe and, until recently, a source of national pride.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the crash happened after several trains stopped automatically due to a signal failure.
A state-run Renfe train was then authorised to proceed at normal speed even though a stationary Iryo-operated train was ahead.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited the crash site on Wednesday. He pledged an investigation into the latest collision and promised improvements to prevent another tragedy like the two that have shaken trust in a rail system that carried 45 million travellers last year, including millions of tourists.
“It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail,” Sanchez said. “It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.”
The Spanish train drivers’ union, SEMAF, said that it does not want to speculate on the cause of the crash.
“We wish to exercise caution until we have a detailed understanding of exactly what happened, so as not to engage in speculation,” SEMAF said in a statement late on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, SEMAF said train drivers have gone ahead with a previously planned strike to push for more railway safety and structural change.

Germany news: Volkswagen posts 3rd quarter losses of nearly €6 billion amid competition from China

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:37:00 UTC
19:37:00 KST

Germany news: Merz says North Korea threatening Europe's freedom
Published October 29, 2026last updated October 29, 2026
What you need to know
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in South Korea at the end of his Asia tour
- Merz and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung deepen their countries' strategic partnership, including security and military ties
- Germany's president Steinmeier continues his trip to China, where he called for free global trade to be strengthened
- Volkswagen (VW) posts 3rd quarter losses of €5.8 billion ($6.46 bln)
- VW has been struggling to keep pace with competition from China and to transition to electric vehicles
- 8-year-old girl sustains serious injuries after wolf attack at a wildlife park in Brandenburg
Here are the main headlines from and about Germany on Thursday, October 29, 2026:
IN DEPTH: The search for President Steinmeier's successor
Several names are being floated to replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's ceremonial head of state — including some that could be the first woman to hold the post.
Read our full report here.
Ping-pong vs. politics: Steinmeier takes on German Olympian Boll
After delivering his speech at Peking University, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities to play ping-pong with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll.
In the university sports hall, the two faced each other, accompanied by two Chinese participants — a referee and the university president. Right from the start, Steinmeier downplayed his chances, and subsequently lost 1–7.
Boll, who won silver at the Beijing Olympics in 2008, is the most successful German table tennis player of all time.
He won several Olympic medals, as well as titles in World Cups and World Championships during his storied career, which saw him ranked as the number 1 player in the world in 2003, 2011 and 2018.
To this day, Boll remains one of the best-known Germans in China, where ping-pong is unofficially considered the national sport.
Boll is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.
Steinmeier calls for fair trade in China during Bejiing visit
Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Thursday called on China to reduce economic imbalances between the two countries, as well as between China and Europe.
Steinmeier, who was speaking at the renowned Peking University, also urged China to work with Germany and other European nations to strengthen the international, rules-based order and "to advocate for peace and free global trade."
The German president, who holds a largely ceremonial role, spoke of his respect for China's rapid development in its economy, technology and politics, calling China a "defining world power."
But Steinmeier added, "With greatness and power comes great responsibility."
"We are not concerned about China's rise. We are watching how China rises," he said.
"We do not want to decouple from China; on the contrary, we want to structure trade in such a way that it continues to benefit both sides." This, he said, requires fair and uniform rules.
Steinmeier was referring to the high barriers European companies face when trying to operate in the Chinese market. Since China heavily subsidizes its exports to Europe, the European market comes under pressure too quickly.
This poses "the danger of one-sided vulnerability," Steinmeier said. Europeans cannot want this for their economy, just as "China does not want it for its economy."
What did Steinmeier say about China and the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East?
He also called on China to exert more influence on Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.
According to Steinmeier, China's interests are also at stake in this war, just as they are in the Middle East. As a major trading power, China also needs free sea lanes, intact supply chains, and a secure energy supply.
"The longer these conflicts persist, the weaker the global economy as a whole becomes — and with it, one of its largest economies: China," the president said.
Steinmeier addressed future issues in which China should take a particular interest: climate change and artificial intelligence. He appealed to his hosts, saying that when it comes to AI, "we should jointly establish international guidelines so that the technology remains under human control," he said.
On the final day of his state visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership and hold talks with, among others, President Xi Jinping.
Steinmeier is making his first visit to China in eight years, as he seeks to boost bilateral ties.
Friedrich Merz accuses North Korea of threatening Europe's freedom
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday said North Korea was threatening "freedom throughout Europe" by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Merz highlighted that Russia was supplying weapons to North Korea.
The chancellor said this arrangement therefore shows how "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects Korea's security."
North Korea has boosted its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pyongyang has provided Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. It has also, according to South Korean intelligence services, sent about 15,000 soldiers to fight alongside Russian forces.
In exchange, Russia provides financial backing, military technology and security guarantees to North Korea.
Before Merz's arrival on Thursday, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, according to the South Korean military.
At the start of his visit, Merz said he hoped that Korea would eventually be unified. The peninsula has been split along the 38th parallel since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953.
Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen their two nations' strategic and security ties, which includes joint military exercises and exchange of intelligence.
The chancellor is expected to conclude his trip to South Korea with a visit to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.
WATCH: Can Germany's pivot to Asia end its reliance on China?
Germany is looking for new partners in Asia. As Chancellor Friedrich Merz travels to Singapore, Japan and South Korea, Berlin is trying to reduce its economic dependence on China while adapting to a changing global order. But can countries in the Indo-Pacific, besides China, help Germany diversify its trade and security partnerships?
This week on Berlin Briefing, DW's Giulia Saudelli speaks with DW Business Reporter Steven Beardsley and DW Chief Political Correspondent Nina Haase, who is traveling with the chancellor.
They discuss Germany's push to "de-risk" from China, growing security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, and whether middle powers can work together to shape the future global order.
Germany, South Korea upgrade ties to 'enhanced strategic partnership'
Germany and South Korea on Thursday pledged to work together on the economy, energy and security and high-tech industries, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said.
The South Korean leader made the announcement after a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Seoul.
At a joint press conference, Lee told reporters that he had asked Merz for Germany's backing in securing favorable treatment for South Korea as part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act.
The two leaders also agreed to improve bilateral ties to an "enhanced strategic partnership," Lee said.
8-year-old girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German zoo
An eight-year-old girl sustained serious injuries after she was attacked by at least one wolf at a wildlife park in Brandenburg in east Germany.
The child was brought to hospital by a rescue helicopter on Wednesday.
Local officials said a zookeeper had helped prevent other children from being attacked.
Police are investigating how and why the attack occurred, which took place during a special program for children.
Police on Thursday said their investigation was centered on a staff member who was in the enclosure with the children, a spokeswoman said.
The Teltow-Fläming district administration said the incident happened before the wildlife park's regular opening hours as part of an "Animal Keeper Day" for children.
The administration also said the attack had taken place in the polar wolf enclosure.
"While the animals in the wildlife enclosure were being watered, the wolves kept there attacked a girl and seriously injured her," the district administration said.
The zookeeper's quick action prevented "further harm to two other girls" who were also at the scene, the district added.
The park will remain closed for the time being, officials said, as authorities launch a safety review at the wildlife park, which is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin.
Police are still probing the circumstances that led to the children being inside the enclosure.
The Johannismühle Wildlife Park said it was cooperating with authorities but could not provide further details due to the open investigation.
"We deeply regret the incident, and the affected family has our full support," the park said.
The wildlife park was closed until further notice "due to technical reasons," a sign at the entrance said on Thursday.
A wolf bit a woman in a busy shopping area in Hamburg this year, in what is thought to be the first such attack since wolves were reintroduced to the country in 1998.
German Chancellor Merz says he hopes for Korean reunification
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is visiting Seoul, said at the start of his visit that he hopes North and South Korea will eventually be reunited.
The Korean Peninsula has been divided into two states since the Korean War ended in 1953.
Merz pointed to his own country's division between West and East Germany for much of the second half of the 20th century.
"Korea and Germany are united by the painful experience of division," he wrote in the guest book during his meeting with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
"I also wish for the people of Korea what we are fortunate to experience in Germany: unity in freedom."
North Korea is a largely isolated dictatorship ruled by Kim Jong Un, while the South is a democracy that has close ties with the West.
The two Koreas technically remain at war since a truce ended hostilities.
Merz is set to visit the demilitarized zone (DMZ), which divides the two countries, on Friday.
The German chancellor's visit to South Korea is the last stop on his tour of Asia this week, which has also seen him visit Japan and Singapore.
IN DEPTH: Bayern Munich coach's hospital stay highlights need for better support
Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany has just returned home from the hospital, admitting that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"
Read our full report on Kompany's health and the need for better support for coaches at the highest level of sport here.
WATCH: Why big automakers are losing China
They were once top sellers in China. Now the likes of Volkswagen, Toyota and Honda are losing ground to a new generation of Chinese carmakers. What happened?
VW reports 3rd quarter losses of €5.8 billion
Volkswagen (VW) reported third quarter losses of €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) on Thursday, as it faces rising competition from China.
Germany's biggest car maker had reported a loss of just over €1.07 billion in the same period last year.
Volkswagen, like other car makers, has struggled to keep pace with fierce competition from China, the world's biggest car market. VW has also struggled with the transition to electric vehicles and with declining demand.
Volkswagen last month warned that its 10-brand group, which includes makers such as Audi, Seat and Skoda, was facing a 10-billion-euro hit to its annual profits.
The most significant hit came from Porsche, Volkswagen's luxury sports car and SUV subsidiary. Porsche, which was once a major driver of profits for the VW group, was also one of the main factors behind VW's quarterly losses in 2025.
The luxury brand has been hit by a sales slump in China, US tariff policy and its electric vehicle strategy.
VW announced this year that it plans to cut over 100,000 jobs across the group by the end of the decade as it tries to reduce costs. It announced on Thursday that its restructuring would cost the company 31 billion euros.
The company is considering or has decided to shut down multiple German factories — including plants in Zwickau, Emden, Hanover, and Neckarsulm.
"What matters now is swift and consistent implementation," Arno Antlitz, VW's chief financial officer said in a statement. "We cannot lose any time and need to act quickly and decisively."
For more on this story, read our full report by DW's Mark Hallam.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom in Bonn on the banks of the Rhine, which is bathed in autumnal hues and fog as we near the end of October.
We open today's coverage of Germany with the news that Volkswagen's recent struggles have translated into huge losses.
The country's largest auto manufacturer, which has already announced job cuts of 100,000 by the end of the decade, reported third quarter losses of nearly 6 billion euro.
On the other side of the world, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is concluding his tour of East Asia with a visit to South Korea, while President Frank-Walter Steinmeier continues his visit to China.

He also called on China to exert more influence on Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.
According to Steinmeier, China's interests are also at stake in this war, just as they are in the Middle East. As a major trading power, China also needs free sea lanes, intact supply chains, and a secure energy supply.
"The longer these conflicts persist, the weaker the global economy as a whole becomes — and with it, one of its largest economies: China," the president said.
Steinmeier addressed future issues in which China should take a particular interest: climate change and artificial intelligence. He appealed to his hosts, saying that when it comes to AI, "we should jointly establish international guidelines so that the technology remains under human control," he said.
On the final day of his state visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership and hold talks with, among others, President Xi Jinping.
Steinmeier is making his first visit to China in eight years, as he seeks to boost bilateral ties.
Friedrich Merz accuses North Korea of threatening Europe's freedom
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday said North Korea was threatening "freedom throughout Europe" by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Merz highlighted that Russia was supplying weapons to North Korea.
The chancellor said this arrangement therefore shows how "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects Korea's security."
North Korea has boosted its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pyongyang has provided Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. It has also, according to South Korean intelligence services, sent about 15,000 soldiers to fight alongside Russian forces.
In exchange, Russia provides financial backing, military technology and security guarantees to North Korea.
Before Merz's arrival on Thursday, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, according to the South Korean military.
At the start of his visit, Merz said he hoped that Korea would eventually be unified. The peninsula has been split along the 38th parallel since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953.
Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen their two nations' strategic and security ties, which includes joint military exercises and exchange of intelligence.
The chancellor is expected to conclude his trip to South Korea with a visit to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.
WATCH: Can Germany's pivot to Asia end its reliance on China?
Germany is looking for new partners in Asia. As Chancellor Friedrich Merz travels to Singapore, Japan and South Korea, Berlin is trying to reduce its economic dependence on China while adapting to a changing global order. But can countries in the Indo-Pacific, besides China, help Germany diversify its trade and security partnerships?
This week on Berlin Briefing, DW's Giulia Saudelli speaks with DW Business Reporter Steven Beardsley and DW Chief Political Correspondent Nina Haase, who is traveling with the chancellor.
They discuss Germany's push to "de-risk" from China, growing security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, and whether middle powers can work together to shape the future global order.
Germany, South Korea upgrade ties to 'enhanced strategic partnership'
Germany and South Korea on Thursday pledged to work together on the economy, energy and security and high-tech industries, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said.
The South Korean leader made the announcement after a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Seoul.
At a joint press conference, Lee told reporters that he had asked Merz for Germany's backing in securing favorable treatment for South Korea as part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act.
The two leaders also agreed to improve bilateral ties to an "enhanced strategic partnership," Lee said.
8-year-old girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German zoo
An eight-year-old girl sustained serious injuries after she was attacked by at least one wolf at a wildlife park in Brandenburg in east Germany.
The child was brought to hospital by a rescue helicopter on Wednesday.
Local officials said a zookeeper had helped prevent other children from being attacked.
Police are investigating how and why the attack occurred, which took place during a special program for children.
Police on Thursday said their investigation was centered on a staff member who was in the enclosure with the children, a spokeswoman said.
The Teltow-Fläming district administration said the incident happened before the wildlife park's regular opening hours as part of an "Animal Keeper Day" for children.
The administration also said the attack had taken place in the polar wolf enclosure.
"While the animals in the wildlife enclosure were being watered, the wolves kept there attacked a girl and seriously injured her," the district administration said.
The zookeeper's quick action prevented "further harm to two other girls" who were also at the scene, the district added.
The park will remain closed for the time being, officials said, as authorities launch a safety review at the wildlife park, which is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin.
Police are still probing the circumstances that led to the children being inside the enclosure.
The Johannismühle Wildlife Park said it was cooperating with authorities but could not provide further details due to the open investigation.
"We deeply regret the incident, and the affected family has our full support," the park said.
The wildlife park was closed until further notice "due to technical reasons," a sign at the entrance said on Thursday.
A wolf bit a woman in a busy shopping area in Hamburg this year, in what is thought to be the first such attack since wolves were reintroduced to the country in 1998.
German Chancellor Merz says he hopes for Korean reunification
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is visiting Seoul, said at the start of his visit that he hopes North and South Korea will eventually be reunited.
The Korean Peninsula has been divided into two states since the Korean War ended in 1953.
Merz pointed to his own country's division between West and East Germany for much of the second half of the 20th century.
"Korea and Germany are united by the painful experience of division," he wrote in the guest book during his meeting with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
"I also wish for the people of Korea what we are fortunate to experience in Germany: unity in freedom."
North Korea is a largely isolated dictatorship ruled by Kim Jong Un, while the South is a democracy that has close ties with the West.
The two Koreas technically remain at war since a truce ended hostilities.
Merz is set to visit the demilitarized zone (DMZ), which divides the two countries, on Friday.
The German chancellor's visit to South Korea is the last stop on his tour of Asia this week, which has also seen him visit Japan and Singapore.

VW reports 3rd quarter losses of €5.8 billion
Volkswagen (VW) reported third quarter losses of €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) on Thursday, as it faces rising competition from China.
Germany's biggest car maker had reported a loss of just over €1.07 billion in the same period last year.
Volkswagen, like other car makers, has struggled to keep pace with fierce competition from China, the world's biggest car market. VW has also struggled with the transition to electric vehicles and with declining demand.
Volkswagen last month warned that its 10-brand group, which includes makers such as Audi, Seat and Skoda, was facing a 10-billion-euro hit to its annual profits.
The most significant hit came from Porsche, Volkswagen's luxury sports car and SUV subsidiary. Porsche, which was once a major driver of profits for the VW group, was also one of the main factors behind VW's quarterly losses in 2025.
The luxury brand has been hit by a sales slump in China, US tariff policy and its electric vehicle strategy.
VW announced this year that it plans to cut over 100,000 jobs across the group by the end of the decade as it tries to reduce costs. It announced on Thursday that its restructuring would cost the company 31 billion euros.
The company is considering or has decided to shut down multiple German factories — including plants in Zwickau, Emden, Hanover, and Neckarsulm.
"What matters now is swift and consistent implementation," Arno Antlitz, VW's chief financial officer said in a statement. "We cannot lose any time and need to act quickly and decisively."

This approach, in which we establish production hubs and use them to enter the markets of neighboring countries, will become our new strategy for localizing production and promoting our technological platforms for export," the industry and trade minister noted.

ECB President Lagarde resigns after months of speculation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:36:19 UTC
19:36:19 KST

ECB President Lagarde resigns at time of mounting challenges for Europe
FRANKFURT, Oct 29 - European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced her resignation on Thursday, ending months of speculation about her future just as Europe enters a period of rising economic volatility and divisive electoral politics.
Lagarde will step down on February 7, giving current European Union leaders time to pick a successor well before a French presidential election that polls show far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favoured to win.
The move comes as the ECB battles inflation risks from an Iran-driven oil shock while a sharp rise in bond yields, especially in France, threatens to dampen growth.
"I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," Lagarde said in a short video shared on social media.
A source with direct knowledge of the matter said Lagarde had resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally. As ECB president, she was expected to remain neutral to safeguard the institution's independence.
European Council President Antonio Costa said in a statement the process to find a successor for Lagarde would begin immediately. The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are widely seen as frontrunners.
"The rumoured successors are both very competent, well established central bankers, so for markets, it won’t matter too much," Piet Haines Christiansen, an economist at Danske Bank, said.
Financial markets did not move much after the announcement, with some analysts noting the ECB had by now built a reputation that outlived any of its leaders.
"The ECB is now quite well established, the market is familiar with the way it operates," Goldman Sachs' head of Fixed Income Macro Investing Simon Dangoor said. "Our view is that institutional behaviour is likely to outlast Lagarde, and be quite similar, whoever takes over."
Lagarde's term was scheduled to run until the end of October 2027 but speculation about an early departure had been mounting for months, with the World Economic Forum seen as a likely destination.
RATE HIKES AND BOND TURMOIL
The ECB is in the middle of a rate-hiking cycle aimed at preventing an oil-price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into other prices and wages.
But it must also contend with a surge in government bond yields — especially in debt-laden France — that has pushed up borrowing costs for households and businesses and which Lagarde has said will curb growth and inflation.
Caught between persistent inflation fuelled by a renewed surge in energy costs and deteriorating financing conditions, the ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday while signalling that another increase, potentially as soon as December, remains likely.
"There is likely a low bar to another hike in December, given the likelihood of another upward revision of the ECB's inflation forecast due to higher energy prices," Oliver Rakau at Oxford Economics said.
The ECB is due to announce its interest rate decision at 1315 GMT on Thursday, followed by Lagarde's regular press conference at 1345 GMT.
Money markets are currently pricing another three rate increases from the ECB by the end of next year, which would take the deposit rate to 3.25%, a level that is widely seen as restricting economic growth.
FRENCH TURMOIL IN FOCUS BUT NO ACTION
The more immediate challenge for policymakers may be turmoil in bond markets.
A global rise in yields, fuelled by stronger growth expectations, higher debt issuance and massive investment linked to artificial intelligence, is pushing up borrowing costs for governments, households and businesses alike.
In France, investors have become increasingly uneasy about the country's growing debt burden and uncertain fiscal outlook following this year's elections. Concerns have been amplified by suggestions from parts of the political left that debt held by the ECB could be written off.
The result has been a sharp increase in French borrowing costs. France is now paying some of the highest yields in a quarter-century to raise money on bond markets, while the premium investors demand to hold French debt over benchmark German bonds is larger than for any other euro zone country.
That has fuelled speculation that the ECB might be forced to respond, if only verbally for now.
"They've typically come up with a new tool that's customised for that specific set of circumstances," said Dangoor at Goldman Sachs.
The ECB's first line of defence would probably be flexible reinvestment of proceeds from bonds acquired during its vast asset-purchase programmes of the previous decade.
Beyond that, it could activate its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument, a scheme designed to counter what policymakers deem unjustified market pressure. REUTERS

ECB head Christine Lagarde to step down in February
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:33:00 UTC
19:33:00 KST

ECB head Christine Lagarde to step down in February
October 29, 2026
Christine Lagarde, who has headed the European Central Bank for seven years, has announced that she is stepping down prematurely from the position.
"European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde today informed the Governing Council and the president of the European Council Antonio Costa that she will step down from her position on 7 February 2027," the ECB said in a statement.
European Council President Antonio Costa said a process to find her successor would start immediately.
The announcement comes ahead of a key meeting of the bank this week that is likely to focus on France's deteriorating public finances.
No reason has so far been given for Lagarde's premature departure, but there has been speculation that she would leave early to enable EU leaders to choose her successor before French elections in the spring that could see a eurosceptic far-right victory influence the choice.
Her term, which began on November 1, 2019, would normally have ended at the end of October 2027.
Lagarde, a former French finance minister, was also head of the International Monetary Fund from 2011 to 2019.
Lagarde 'provided steady and determine stewardship' — Costa
Costa praised Lagarde's leadership during her seven-year stint at the ECB helm, a period in which the EU and the world faced great challenges.
"Through a global pandemic, a war in Europe, energy crises and inflation shocks, she has provided a steady and determined stewardship, helping to safeguard stability and the resilience of the euro area," Costa posted on social media.
"To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay, with a view to a timely decision," Costa said.
Lagarde herself has voiced satisfaction with her record.
"I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," Lagarde, a French economist, said in a short video shared on social media.
The ECB head is chosen by the leaders of the 21 eurozone countries.
ECB to decide interest rate, discuss France
The announcement of Lagarde's imminent departure comes as the ECB is to hold a meeting this week where it is expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5%, while signaling that this is likely to rise again before the end of the year.
The bank has already raised interest rates twice since June in a bid to curb inflation fueled by the energy shock caused by the Iran war.
However, Thursday's meeting is also likely to focus on the fiscal and political crisis in France, Europe's second-biggest economy.
French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, rose to their highest level in 25 years last week amid a deadlock over next year's budget.
Recent protests, at which many demonstrators were calling for more spending on public services, were also marred by considerable violence.
There has been speculation as to whether the ECB could, for the first time, use the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), a crisis-fighting tool that allows the bank to buy bonds of a eurozone member if yields rise uncontrollably and there is a risk of financial stress spreading.
However, most observers believe the problems in France do not yet meet the strict conditions stipulated for its use.

The ECB head is chosen by the leaders of the 21 eurozone countries.
ECB to decide interest rate, discuss France
The announcement of Lagarde's imminent departure comes as the ECB is to hold a meeting this week where it is expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5%, while signaling that this is likely to rise again before the end of the year.
The bank has already raised interest rates twice since June in a bid to curb inflation fueled by the energy shock caused by the Iran war.
However, Thursday's meeting is also likely to focus on the fiscal and political crisis in France, Europe's second-biggest economy.
French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, rose to their highest level in 25 years last week amid a deadlock over next year's budget.
Recent protests, at which many demonstrators were calling for more spending on public services, were also marred by considerable violence.
There has been speculation as to whether the ECB could, for the first time, use the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), a crisis-fighting tool that allows the bank to buy bonds of a eurozone member if yields rise uncontrollably and there is a risk of financial stress spreading.
However, most observers believe the problems in France do not yet meet the strict conditions stipulated for its use.
Edited by: Wesley Rahn

A senior Lloyds Banking Group executive has criticised the chancellor for linking bank tax increases to energy bill support for UK households, as he warned the government against extending the higher levy beyond March 2028.
Lloyds’s chief financial officer, William Chalmers, acknowledged that the economic environment was “challenging” but said the government should not seek to ease pressure on households at the expense of the banking sector as it provides loans that could fuel UK growth.
“Ultimately, it is important that the UK banking sector is able to deliver banking services to businesses and households and communities in a cost-effective way, in order to promote UK growth,” he said, adding that it was also important that the sector stayed internationally competitive.
“We therefore very much hope that yesterday’s tax increase is indeed a temporary measure, to help ensure the business environment remains consistent with supporting long-term investment,” Chalmers told journalists during an earnings call on Thursday morning.
The comments came less than 24 hours after the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans to double the bank surcharge, which is levied on top of corporation tax, to 6% from January. He said the increase would be “time-limited”, lasting 15 months, in order “to pay for immediate support on energy bills”.
However, Chalmers questioned the government’s decision to tie bank taxes to rising energy costs, amid concerns that doing so could open the door to an extension, or a further rise in the levy, after the 15 months expire.
“We hope this tax rate is limited,” he said. “When we look forward, what impact, if any, will energy prices have on that? Well, I don’t see an obvious linkage between energy prices and bank taxes.
“In fact, if anything, it makes it even more important that we’re able to lend into the real economy and secure growth, which is the best defence against energy price impacts that might otherwise be there on the UK economy.”
While the Treasury has promised to legislate for the 15-month tax-rise limit in the financial bill, senior bankers and industry lobbyists have privately questioned whether a further energy crisis could throw that limit out the window.
Some pointed to Spain, where a two-year windfall tax on banks, meant to alleviate cost of living pressures in 2022, was ultimately extended a further three years, and increased from 4.8% to 7% for the country’s largest banks.
“We are a major taxpayer,” Chalmers said: “We paid around £1.8bn of corporate taxes year to date, and it is important to us that we have a stable and a predictable tax regime.”
Lloyds revealed on Thursday that its third-quarter pre-tax profits almost doubled from a year earlier, from £1.2bn to £2.3bn. However, that increase largely reflected the £800m hit it took last year after setting aside another £800m for compensation relating to the motor finance scandal.
The bank’s results were also supported by a 10% rise in net interest income, which measures the difference between what it charges borrowers and what it pays to savers, showing the bank continued to benefit from higher interest rates.
Net interest income has risen across the banking industry, as inflation expectations – driven by higher fuel prices triggered by the war in the Middle East – pushed up interest rates.

Exclusive-Pentagon treating military base freezer malfunctions as suspected cyberattack, officials say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:31:54 CET
19:31:54 KST

By Raphael Satter, AJ Vicens and Phil Stewart
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The Pentagon is treating the spate of mysterious freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the United States in August as a suspected hack, according to four officials familiar with the matter.
One of the officials said the military investigators were in touch with their French counterparts about a similar cyberattack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets there earlier this month.
Reuters was not able to ascertain how far along the Pentagon’s investigation was or whether it had reached any conclusions about what happened or who might be responsible. When asked about the investigation, the Pentagon said that a unit of Cyber Command — the military’s cyber force — was “working in close coordination with interagency and law enforcement partners.” It did not elaborate.
The US Army Criminal Investigation Division said its Cyber Field Office was involved in the investigation and that it was working with French law enforcement to better understand “the refrigeration outages in Europe.”
The late August malfunctions in the United States affected at least six commissaries — on-base stores where military personnel buy their food — according to a Reuters review of the military bases’ contemporaneous Facebook posts and website updates. In at least one of the cases, the freezers did not simply stop working; the cooling units’ temperatures were cranked up overnight, yielding mounds of wilted or melted food in the morning.
The Fort Huachuca, Arizona, Facebook account explained on August 26 that its freezer “went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food. Trust us when we say it was ‘spoiled.’”
The spate of rogue freezer behavior and the possibility of cybersabotage were first reported on August 28 by a recently created blog called Signal and Silence. The involvement of military investigators and their contacts with the French were reported by the newspaper Stars and Stripes and Britain’s Daily Telegraph, respectively. The news that the investigators were treating the incident as a suspected hack is being reported here for the first time.
The French Embassy in Washington did not return a message seeking comment.
FRENCH FREEZERS FRIED
If confirmed to be a cyberattack, the refrigerator malfunctions would be another illustration of how vulnerable critical infrastructure — in this case cold storage — can be to hackers.
The French freezer cyberattack overrode the temperature controls on commercial cooling units in more than 350 establishments, leading to dramatic scenes as supermarkets’ frozen food aisles were cleared of spoiled merchandise.
The French hack involved cranking the temperature inside the units up rather than merely knocking them offline, similar to what happened in Fort Huachuca in Arizona. Some French refrigeration units had the temperature turned up so high they caught fire. The French attack’s total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, one supermarket owner estimated earlier this month.
The French cyberattack appeared to have been easy to pull off, experts previously told Reuters. The Danish firm Danfoss, whose controllers ran made many of the stricken units, said that many of the controllers were obsolete or were running outdated firmware, which could have made it easy for hackers to break in. Reuters could not establish whether Danfoss or any other brand of freezer controller were in use at the affected US bases. Danfoss did not return messages seeking comment.
CHILLING HACKS
Refrigeration plays a critical role in the distribution of fresh food and the sabotage of cold storage facilities over the internet has long been seen as a nightmare scenario, alongside the loss of electricity or water plants.
Earlier this year, the Global Food Safety Initiative, an industry body, called on food safety professionals and IT leaders to work together to ensure “robust cybersecurity” for refrigeration technology, noting that “a hacked cooling system is just as dangerous as a broken one.”
Hackers have previously sabotaged fridges and freezers both in the United States and elsewhere.
Danfoss has said that, in 2022, hackers either targeted or broke into supermarkets in Russia and Israel that were using obsolete versions of its cold storage controllers. In December of last year, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles accused a Ukrainian woman of being part of a hacker group that knocked out the refrigeration at a meatpacking facility in 2024, ruining more than 2,000 pounds of meat.
The root problem was that controllers that were initially conceived as isolated interfaces that would be serviced by an in-person technician were increasingly being connected to the internet, said Bill Moore, the chief executive of industrial cybersecurity firm Xona Systems. Concerns about online exposure were not unique to cooling systems, he said, but they could have particularly serious consequences there.
“It can definitely disrupt the supply chain for food,” he said.
(Reporting by Raphael Satter, AJ Vicens, and Phil Stewart.)

Trump confronts a new midterm battleground: South Carolina
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:31:38 CET
19:31:38 KST

By Jacob Bogage
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump will stage a campaign rally in South Carolina for the second time in two weeks on Thursday, as new polls show the Senate race between incumbent Republican Darline Graham and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews is a toss-up.
With control of Congress at stake in Tuesday’s midterm elections, some Republicans are beginning to fret that their traditional stronghold of South Carolina has become a battleground state.
The race is part of a trend that shows contests in Republican-leaning states now tilting toward Democrats in the campaign’s final days, in part because of Trump’s low ratings in opinion polls.
Republicans are fighting to retain Senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina and Maine to maintain their six-seat Senate majority. Polls show Democrats leading in each of those states.
Polls and independent analysts favor the Democrats to retake control of the House, while Senate control is considered too close to call. A Democratic victory could place limits on Trump and usher in congressional investigations of his administration over its final two years.
Republicans are newly on the defensive in once unthinkable territory. South Carolina hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since Fritz Hollings, who was first elected in 1966 and served until 2005.
Trump has also rallied in recent days in Mississippi, where the campaign between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom has tightened. Colom would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, a tenuous period of the 19th century immediately following the Civil War.
Republican political operatives have also grown concerned over the Nebraska Senate race between Republican Senator Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn.
In South Carolina, Andrews and Graham are competing for a seat once held by Graham’s brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of Trump’s foremost Republican allies and died suddenly in July.
Lindsey Graham was a key foreign policy voice in Congress and an interlocutor between Senate Republican leadership and the White House. He long counted his sister as his foremost political adviser, though polls suggest her stumbles on the campaign trail appear to have hurt her standing.
Former South Carolina elected officials have also backed Andrews in recent days. Two former governors, Republican David Beasley and Democrat Jim Hodges, endorsed Andrews in a television advertisement.
Former Republican Governor Nikki Haley, a Trump appointee during the president’s first term who challenged him for the White House in 2024, has not endorsed either candidate.
Responding to criticism of her campaign as unpolished, Graham said she was not a career politician and does not “speak politician.” Graham’s campaign has said endorsements from political figures mattered less than support from voters and from Trump.
Trump and Republicans’ focus in South Carolina and other traditional conservative strongholds has consequences far beyond those states, campaign officials say. Republicans had opportunities to challenge Democrats in Michigan and Georgia in the midterms, and also had hopes of picking off another seat in Minnesota.
But defending turf in the South has forced Republicans to divert vital resources away from those races - and sent Trump on a frenetic nationwide campaign tour through 19 states since the start of October.
He has rallies planned in Florida, Kansas and Iowa in the final days before the Tuesday vote.
(Reporting by Jacob Bogage; editing by Lincoln Feast)

Israel eyes Covenant’s low-cost Anthem cruise missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:30:52 UTC
19:30:52 KST

- Israeli Defense Ministry Director General Amir Baram visited Covenant, maker of the Anthem cruise missile, focusing on munitions independence and production capacity.
- Baram said the ministry backs both defense-tech startups and established industries, calling defense exports a critical growth engine.
Israel’s Defense Ministry Director General, retired Maj. Gen. Amir Baram, has visited Covenant, the startup behind the Anthem low-cost cruise missile, in a tour the ministry said focused on strengthening Israel’s munitions independence, expanding its production base and preserving the country’s qualitative and technological edge in the years ahead.
The ministry said on social media on Oct. 29 that the stop was part of a series of visits by Baram to leading defense companies under its strategy to strengthen Israel’s defense-tech ecosystem, in which the ministry acts as the integrating body between the Israel Defense Forces and the defense industry. It did not announce an order or agreement with Covenant.
“The Ministry’s policy is to encourage and strengthen both defense-tech companies and new startups, as well as the established industries. This balance is essential for fostering healthy competition, driving innovation and out-of-the-box thinking, maintaining our qualitative edge, and developing ‘the next surprises,'” said Baram.
“We must look ahead to an intense security decade and adapt our plans to both global changes and the evolution of the battlefield. Defense exports are a critical growth engine and an enabling tool, not only for strengthening the economy, but also for building the IDF’s force and delivering a critical mass of advanced systems to the warfighters on the front lines,” he said.
Covenant, founded in 2024 by Michael Kaufman and Ofir Dayan, kept its work secret until Sept. 9, when it unveiled Anthem and disclosed more than $250 million raised across three rounds led by Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, Lux, 8VC, Aleph and Lightspeed, Tectonic reported. The company is headquartered in Washington and runs a research, development and production site in Israel alongside factories in Texas and Germany.
Anthem is a ground-launched cruise missile that uses a solid rocket motor to get airborne and a jet engine burning heavy fuel for the cruise phase, and Covenant says it was designed from the start to be built in the thousands at a fraction of the cost of older systems such as the Tomahawk. The company has not disclosed the missile’s price, range or exact payload. Since its first flight in August 2025, Anthem has completed more than 200 test flights, including several with U.S. forces in the United States and abroad, though it has not been used in combat.
Covenant says it has booked about $150 million in orders covering qualification, development and production, along with a roughly $70 million cost-sharing agreement with the U.S. Navy’s Rapid Capabilities Office to develop a maritime version of the missile. Earlier this month, Denmark said it would buy ground-launched Anthem missiles to be built in Leipzig, Germany, where Covenant’s production line is due to open in 2027, while Germany’s Defense Ministry is also in talks with the company as it evaluates low-cost cruise missiles.
Baram’s push for munitions independence, meaning Israel can build critical weapons and components without relying on foreign supply chains, has taken him to several manufacturers this year, including loitering munition maker Uvision in July. In August he met the heads of about 20 defense-tech and startup companies, and the ministry said then that the number of defense-tech firms under its oversight had grown to 322 since the start of the war, with its orders from them reaching about $330 million, roughly double the same period a year earlier.

====================================================================================================

Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED TV: Midrange Quality, Upscale Color Accuracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Accurate color for movies, shows, and games. Affordable price for the RGB TV category. Nice low-latency gaming capability. Easy setup.
TIRED
Not as bright as some RGB models. Didn’t render some dark scenes in movies with enough contrast or clarity. Internal speakers were just average.
An array of brilliant colors is what you want from an RGB television, and on that front, the Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED delivers. After having reviewed a number of the top RGB TVs, including the flagship Hisense UR9 RGB MiniLED and offerings from Samsung and LG, I can report that this UR8 is solidly good. It provides mini RGB tech at a lower price than the impressive UR9. As long as you can accept UR8's lacking contrast and brightness capabilities—at least compared to its high-performing sibling—the television's color accuracy stands to wow you.
What makes RGB models like the Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED so interesting is that you can tweak the picture quality for more brilliant and accurate colors. While testing proved the UR9 has a brighter panel that performs at a higher caliber for movies, shows, games, and even displaying artwork, the UR8 is certainly colorful. But are the compromises of this more budget-friendly model worth the savings? That has less of a clear, black-and-white answer.
Setting Up Shop
The UR8 is a bit thicker than the UR9, but it is otherwise visually similar: They appear to have the same chassis and similarly feature a single pedestal. The stand snaps into place and requires some screws, but the assembly process is overall straightforward and quick. Installation couldn't be simpler: Just scan a QR code that connects to Google Home and move through the steps.
The left side of the TV houses all of the port inputs: an Ethernet port for reliable streaming, an optical audio port, a coaxial port, and one USB-A port for external storage or connecting an HD antenna. Like the UR9, this model supports Wi-Fi 6E for speedy and reliable streaming. For color accuracy, the UR8 meets 100 percent of the BT.2020 spec and is Pantone Validated, meaning it can showcase a broad selection of color variation.
Photograph: John Brandon
Now for the key differences in specs between the UR8 and UR9 RGB models: The UR8 is around 3,500 nits while the UR9 is 5,000 nits—a delta that made a big difference in my benchmarks, which I’ll cover in a bit. The UR8 has four HDMI 2.1 ports, while the UR9 only has three; however, the UR9 adds a USB-C port on the side for low-latency gaming, which didn't prove particularly impactful.
The UR8 also has less capable internal speakers than the UR9. It’s a 2.1.2 system (two main channels, one sub, and two height channels) compared to the 4.1.2 channel configuration on the UR9 (which adds a side channel). If you use a soundbar or an AV receiver, this won’t matter. Both models support Dolby Atmos and have an eARC passthrough audio port for surround sound.
The UR8 offers a 55-inch size, while the UR9’s smallest size is 65-inch. Otherwise, both are available in 75-inch, 85-inch, and 100-inch sizes.
Finally, the two share a remote control design, with a nicely centered Home button but a strangely hidden Mute on the lower right. I am not sure why there is a shortcut button for Kidoodle.TV, either, but I love that it’s backlit.
Diving Into the Benchmarks
Photograph: John Brandon
First, some background on micro and mini RGB televisions: Like traditional LED televisions, RGB models use LED backlights. But instead of shining white or blue lights through a color filter and LCD panel (as is the standard for an LED television), RGB TVs use red, green, and blue lights. The result is often strikingly realistic, even if you’re watching during the bright daylight.
To test the capabilities of the UR8, I watched scenes of the film Awake on Netflix that are so remarkably dark on many midrange televisions that it's nearly impossible to see what's happening. As with all RGB televisions I've tested, I could adjust the picture quality on the UR8 to help with contrast, but that function isn't a cure-all. Initially, a scene where the main character rides a bike was almost completely dark, especially while using Dolby Vision Reference mode and standard Dolby Vision modes. Switching to a custom Dolby Vision setting helped after I cranked up the brightness, but the picture still wasn’t overly clear.
Next, I watched an episode of House of the Dragon using the HBO Max app via Google Cast. During a scene with a dragon, the scales looked visible but not nearly as textured as they did when using the UR9. Whether the subtle difference is worth paying more for the higher model remains to be seen, but the differences are noticeable nonetheless.
In the movie The Creator on Fandango at Home, a beach landing looked a bit washed out and dark. During The Batman, gunfire looked bright enough in a dark hallway scene, but—similar to the aforementioned dragon scene—lacked rich detail.
The Super Mario Galaxy Movie on Peacock is tailor-made for testing colors: Stars floated around on the screen in a brilliant rainbow of colors, appearing bright and accurate, but some of them had too much blooming (aka a halo effect where bright tones bleed onto their darker surrounding colors). In all fairness, the UR9 also rendered this scene in a similar way.
Photograph: John Brandon
It’s not all bad news, though. In fact, in the movie Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 on Disney+, the RGB tech kicked into high gear. The color accuracy was ultrarealistic, showing bright blues, reds, and oranges in an opening scene. My only issue was that the contrast was not as tonally rich as it was on the UR9, and it also lacked some shadow detail. The LG Micro RGB Evo rendered this scene even brighter.
For benchmark tests using the Spears & Munsil discs, skin tones looked dimmer and less varied than the LG Micro RGB Evo or the Hisense UR9. The demo reel revealed a few other differences, too: White mist on a white mountain didn’t look as distinct as it did on the UR9, but (thanks again to the color accuracy) it did render green grass by a fence to a similar appearance as what the UR9 produced. A scene showing dark trees at night looked much clearer on the UR9 thanks to the higher nits rating. On the UR8, you could see the texture on the trees, and a red cactus and yellow flower also looked darker on the UR8.
Games People Play on RGB and More
This is a great TV for video games, as it can sense the game content, adjust for latency, and even help improve picture quality. Every time I started a game, the UR8 (similar to the UR9) automatically made key picture adjustments. Blacks looked a bit richer than expected, which was great for Resident Evil: Requiem, because it seemed the entire game took place in the dark. Here, the Hisense UR8 delivered an atmospheric look: dark and moody but not washed out. In fact, I didn’t notice much of a difference in latency compared to playing the same game on the UR9. (Indeed, Hisense reps told me the latency was roughly the same.)
Photograph: John Brandon
Senua's Saga: Hellblade II on the Xbox Series X looked vibrant on the UR8, despite its dark scenes by an ocean. Rocks in one scene reflected the ambient light in an ultrarealistic way that could make you feel as if you could pick one up. I also played NBA 2K27 with the DLSS 5 setting turned on and loved the clarity and crispness. Some players looked amazingly photorealistic, and colors popped so clearly.
Surround sound audio using the UR8's internal speakers was not as convincing as with the Hisense UR9, but the lower model still had a nice oomph during more explosive action movies.
Several features matched the caliber of the UR9, including Google Gemini suggesting movies and letting me create an AI-generated slideshow by voice. AI smoothing for motion worked well for games and movies, and both televisions did a good job adjusting for ambient light. I also loved how artwork (including a shipwreck painting) featured deep textures and luminance.
All in all, the Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED performed as expected at this price—not as bright as the UR9, but certainly just as colorful. As long as you can accept that it's not the flagship model, the UR8 color accuracy is still a major perk.
John Brandon is a contributing writer for WIRED. He reviews televisions, projectors, speakers, and other AV staples. He started writing full-time in 2001 and has been featured in Forbes, Popular Mechanics, The Telegraph, Minnesota Monthly magazine, and many other publications. He lives in Minneapolis–Saint Paul.
