A Hacker Targeted High-Stakes Poker Players With Malware That Exposed Their Cards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

In a fitting sign of the times, the hacker’s carefully laid plans were foiled by an AI agent.
It was September 25, 2026, and Alex, a professional online poker player, was using his Claude AI agent to review some play statistics. (Alex only agreed to speak with WIRED under a pseudonym to avoid any risk of reprisals from threat actors.) After Alex’s SQL database crashed and needed to be reset, the Claude agent noticed something suspicious: A program called MeshAgent was operating in the background, where it seemed to be capable of capturing Alex’s screen and even controlling his entire machine.
Thanks to the Claude agent’s report, Alex could see the program had been installed on April 24, and not by Alex himself. Alex says the agent identified 11 time-stamped events when the program had been capturing his screen based on graphic errors it caused during screen sharing instances. During all 11, Alex had been playing a session on ACR, also called Americas Cardroom, a major worldwide online poker operator.
He checked his hand histories and quickly found the most troubling info yet: The same opponent, playing under the handle OxOO, was at his table for 10 of those 11 sessions.
The handle was familiar. Alex and several friends in the high-stakes community had shared suspicions about this player’s behavior in the past. Alex checked the player’s win rate stats via a public tracking site; they were astronomically higher than the best players in the world, a statistical impossibility given the sample of hands played. In Alex’s view, it was glaringly obvious that this player was cheating.
An investigation by Alex and other members of the high-stakes community in subsequent days confirmed his fears—and then some. Alex was one of hundreds of players allegedly targeted with this type of malware by the same reported threat actor across a period of multiple years. Alex, who was the first to discover MeshAgent on his computer, claims he was “only” ripped off for around $30,000, a relatively moderate sum for the level he plays at; many of his peers weren’t so lucky.
With millions of dollars allegedly stolen across the biggest sites on the internet, the poker world is searching for answers about how the scheme was allowed to continue so long, whether major sites took the risk seriously after it was reported, and whether online poker itself has been irreversibly compromised.
Poker has never been short on cheating controversies; online poker especially so. The “superuser” method, in which a cheater gains unauthorized access to their opponents’ cards and can therefore act with perfect information against them, was one of the first to show up online.
Two major sites in online poker’s early days, Absolute Poker and Ultimate Bet, served as cautionary tales in the mid-2000s. In separate instances, superuser cheaters were able to gain insider access to the websites and bilk players for millions of dollars. (Much of the loot was refunded to players following an investigation.) Those high-profile incidents led to tightened security measures from many top poker sites.
Another minor superuser incident took place in 2013, when a Finnish high-stakes player said his laptop had been stolen from his hotel room during a European Poker Tour tournament in Barcelona. When the laptop was recovered, it had been infected with malware that allowed a hacker to view his screen remotely. And maybe the most famous superuser scandal of all took place on the live felt: In a story that made it all the way to SportsCenter, a player named Mike Postle was accused of stealing over $250,000 from livestreamed games at Stones Gambling Hall in 2018 and 2019 with the aid of what observers believed to be an alleged accomplice with access to live card data who fed information to Postle’s phone. (Postle denied the accusations, alleging it was “fake news.”)
Outside one relatively small (and quickly remedied) incident in 2023, though, the online poker world had gone years without a confirmed superuser incident—until now. And some of what’s known about this latest attempt signals a savvier threat actor than in previous scandals, plus a degree of patience not typically seen in attacks like these.
“Traditionally, when you see these types of financially motivated threat actors, they will get access to a system and then as soon as they’re on it, they’ll do a scope of what they have access to and then they’ll hit everyone all at once and dump all the wallets,” says WolfSec, a cybersecurity professional who consults with many high-stakes poker players on security measures. He was first to break the news of the MeshAgent scam on September 29, on his X account. (WolfSec agreed to speak to WIRED under the condition his real name not be used out of fears of reprisals from hackers; WIRED independently confirmed his credentials as a cybersecurity expert.)
But this hacker didn’t do any of that, despite many of these players having large cryptocurrency holdings and other investments accessible on their machines. The attacker seemed instead to be performing advanced reconnaissance. In fact, WolfSec believes the same threat actor was attempting to attack players’ machines as early as 2022 using a more basic technique; because no known funds were stolen at the time, no other action was taken once the players wiped the malware from their computers.
It appears, though, that the hacker was simply biding his time and improving his methods in preparation for an eventual strike.
Instead of targeting individual players directly, this more recent attack involved third-party software programs called IntuitiveTables and Jurojin. These programs allow professionals to play dozens of online poker hands at once. Using these popular “multi-table” tools, players can switch between live games with a keystroke, place bets or make plays with hot keys, and other actions that make it easier to play at several virtual tables at the same time. The hacker compromised both applications, WolfSec says, pushing malicious software to over a thousand estimated users.
In the case of Jurojin, the attacker gained access to the developer’s own system for software updates and was able to deliver the remote-access agent to existing users through normal, automatic updates.
The developer of Intuitive Tables was running Jurojin on their test computer, and that machine got the remote-access agent as part of Jurojin’s compromised software update. Using the agent, the attacker added malicious code to the Intuitive Tables application before the developer signed the security certificate for an updated build of the app. That version carrying the malicious code was posted to the Intuitive Tables website as a public download, and everyone who installed that version of the app unknowingly also installed a backdoor on their computer.
In both instances, the malicious code was delivered through a standard update channel or an official release, so neither the users nor their antivirus apps detected anything amiss.
The modified version of Intuitive Tables behaved exactly like the clean version, with one exception: It also checked players’ files for their usernames.
“If you were on a hard-coded list that was stored on the attacker’s infrastructure, which [the malware] reached out to and downloaded and compared your username to, then it acted as a malicious program and downloaded additional malicious files,” WolfSec says. “If you weren’t on that list, then it became the normal program and didn’t do anything malicious at all.”
The list appears to have been populated primarily with regular high-stakes players across several sites. All of the players on the list appear to have had the MeshAgent program installed covertly on their machines. The hacker was ready to pounce.
In early 2025, a couple of new players began frequenting high-stakes games—one on ACR (using the handle “JackKlompus”) and another major global site called CoinPoker (handle: “Europe”). Strangely, despite not being familiar to other regulars in these games, the players refused to identify themselves in table chats, a common request that’s typically granted by new players in high-stakes poker. The new opponents were also winning with improbable frequency. (Later, once the pros started sharing information about their games, it was pieced together that these players were the same person.)
Mike, a professional poker player who spoke to WIRED using a pseudonym due to fear of reprisals from hackers, played on both sites at the time and was at tables with the player using these handles. Mike says at first he wondered if the mystery player’s success was somehow explainable. Maybe they were doing something new that Mike and his fellow pros just hadn’t figured out.
“You could kind of excuse it” at first, Mike says. “Maybe this guy is really, really good or something.”
As the number of winning hands grew, though, Mike and several high-stakes friends became more suspicious. They initially suspected that the player was using real-time assistance via game-theory-based engines that outperform the best human players. Real-time assistance is banned across major sites, but is difficult to police perfectly and is something pros are regularly watching out for. Mike mostly stopped playing at tables with the mystery player, as a precaution.
Like WolfSec, Mike reflects on a relative level of skill and discipline employed by this player during those 2025 sessions, especially compared to other known cheaters in poker history. The account generally used standard bet sizes and played normal hand ranges. Its session-by-session play never raised too many eyebrows; only the account’s win rate over time drew scrutiny.
But in June 2026, Mike played a two-hour heads-up (one-on-one) session on a different site, ClubWPT Gold, which he’d later determine—following reviews with the website’s security team—came against the same player from the 2025 sessions. The player used a different handle to evade detection, so Mike didn’t see a reason to be extra cautious. The opponent simply steamrolled Mike, making every correct decision even in seemingly impossible spots—almost like he could see Mike’s cards. “It was very blatant,” Mike says.
Immediately after the session, Mike messaged several friends in the high-stakes world to say he thought he’d been cheated.
Turns out he was right. When word of the hack broke publicly on WolfSec’s X account, ClubWPT Gold investigated. The site banned the account Mike had played against and refunded him for his losses, says Randy Lundy, head of customer operations for ClubWPT Gold.
This alleged cheater’s presence in online circles was an open secret across the community by this point. In fact, Mario Mosböck, a poker ambassador for CoinPoker who was authorized to speak about the company’s response to the hack, says the site began investigating this player as early as 2025, banning them and refunding over $100,000 in allegedly stolen funds to affected players. (Mosböck says the return of funds was delayed several months because the alleged cheater appealed the confiscation to regulators.) The player’s simple win rate and play style statistics appeared to be evidence of malfeasance, even if the site couldn’t definitively determine how the cheating was happening.
How, then, was the same alleged cheater allowed to keep ripping off players like Alex and Mike on multiple other supposedly reputable sites more than a year later?
“They confirmed multiple times that they looked at my report, but for whatever reason they didn't act on it,” says Patrick Howard, a professional poker player and founder of the coaching company Mobius Poker.
The “they” he’s referring to is GGPoker, arguably the most well-known site in the world for non-US players. Howard says he submitted a report to the site in early September 2026, weeks before the MeshAgent hack became public, highlighting the alleged cheater’s unusual play and urging the site to investigate.
“I found multiple three- to four-standard-deviation outliers,” Howard says, and that was across a limited hand history sample sent to him by friends and clients. He sent his findings to the GGPoker team but received no response. He got a reply only after WolfSec’s public reveal of the hack on X, with the site telling him there “wasn’t conclusive evidence” to act at the time of his complaint.
Various online poker sites handled the incident differently. Players have largely praised CoinPoker for proactively banning the player based on win rate and play tendencies alone, which are accepted as definitive indicators of cheating at stakes this high and with samples this large; while ClubWPT Gold only seems to have been impacted later in the scheme, that site also appears to have acted decisively upon discovering it.
But the hacker remained active on GGPoker and ACR until late September, allegedly stealing between $1.5 million and $4 million, based on the estimates of the sources WIRED spoke to for this story.
“Players are frustrated, because they had been reporting this for a year,” says John Andress, head of game integrity for A5 Labs, a cybersecurity platform that provides anti-cheating services to ClubWPT Gold and other brands. “A few of the platforms just completely ignored them.”
This was despite signs that many feel were all too obvious.
CoinPoker says the player’s alleged true identity was known early in this process, after the company conducted a webcam security interview with them in February 2025. The name the player gave matched the handle the player later used on GGPoker, which requires players to use their real name as their handle instead of a pseudonym for certain high-stakes games. (WIRED is not naming the player because they have not been charged with any crime. The player did not respond to multiple requests for comment on this story). The CoinPoker spokesman says their team reached out to ACR with their findings as well and received no response. (Requests for comment from WIRED to ACR and GGPoker received no reply.)
To its credit, GGPoker acknowledged the incident and announced several fixes in an October 15 blog post, including banning third-party tools and adding win-rate anomaly detection. The site also says it traced the accused attacker’s funds to a Coinbase account and has asked the crypto company to restrict the account and preserve its records; it says it also provided the wallet addresses to industry watchdogs and law enforcement.
But ACR is going the opposite direction: On October 18, it emailed players claiming its security team found no compromised game outcomes or wrongdoing and will not issue any refunds—despite, in the same email, announcing a new feature to stop remote-viewing tools from capturing the images of the cards in players’ hands.
Other entities have taken concrete action: Both Jurojin and IntuitiveTables (via its Discord channel) released tools to help users detect whether the MeshAgent hack had affected their machines. AceGuardian, a research group that’s part of A5 Labs, put out an open-source “superuser detection” tool designed for use on any poker site. WolfSec says he submitted a complaint to the the Internet Crime Complaint Center, the cybercrime arm of the FBI, and has been working with players on improving machine security. The FBI, when reached for comment by WIRED, would not confirm receipt nor any details of this complaint.
But these efforts will be so successful only if the sites treat these incidents with more scrutiny and don’t just spring into action in the aftermath of major attacks.
“Ultimately, the sites have to ban the players,” Howard says. “I think they dropped the ball here.”

Your Program Needs Outcomes, Not Outputs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

The Department of War is making its acquisition leaders accountable for mission outcomes. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth set the tone in November 2025, when he announced an overhaul of defense acquisition at the National War College. He said contracting officers would be judged on mission outcomes rather than regulatory compliance, and that evaluation criteria would center on mission effectiveness over meeting specifications.
His overhaul also directed the reorganization of program executive offices into portfolio acquisition executives (PAEs), each the single accountable official for the outcomes of an entire portfolio. The strategy released with the overhaul calls for accountability measures that “prioritize outcomes rather than activity.” The Air Force completed its transition in July 2026, designating PAEs for all 17 of its acquisition portfolios.
In September 2026, the DoW CIO brought the same focus to software policy. DoW Instruction 8430.01, Accelerated Mission Software, directs enterprise reporting to focus on value stream and mission outcomes, and treats delivery metrics, like deployment frequency, as diagnostics for individual teams.
Outputs vs. outcomes
Outputs are what a team produces: features, releases, story points, reports. Outcomes are changes in user or system behavior that directly and positively impact the mission value stream. For example, an analyst now completes their task 50% faster, or a pilot now gets the data they need in seconds instead of minutes. Impact is the mission result those changes produce: the mission succeeding, lives saved, critical services reaching the people who need them.
Effort without mission impact
You’ve probably sat through some version of a program review where the team has been at it for months, if not years. They’ve closed hundreds of story points and checked off every milestone, the demos look great, and leadership hears “on track” at every checkpoint. The software makes it to production, but few operators use it, because nobody designed it around how they work. And for all of that effort, the program has made no measurable impact on the mission since the day the government signed the contract.
Unfortunately, this happens to the majority of large government software initiatives. According to the Standish Group data that GSA’s 18F cites, 87% of large government software projects fail. The Standish bar is generous: it counts a project as success when it lands on time, on budget, and with a satisfied customer, even if the mission never changed.
Bryon Kroger, a former Air Force intelligence officer who co-founded Kessel Run (the DoW’s first software factory) and now leads Rise8 as founder and CEO, described programs like these at Prodacity, Rise8’s annual training event for GovTech leaders. He was clear that the people on those programs work hard, contractors and government alike. The problem, he said, is that “the entire system is oriented around the activities and the outputs instead of the outcomes.”
Stop paying for hope
For as much as the community talks about outcomes and new directives call for them, contracts still pay for hours and features. Even firm-fixed-price contracts often pay for level of effort. The government pays the contractor for time spent and people assigned whether or not the mission improves. After delivery, programs often hand adoption to another contractor or a government team, so if the software ships and the mission doesn’t move, the government owns that problem. In general, Kroger said, “we’re buying hope.” Programs pay vendors and hope for an outcome in production that turns into mission value, and that’s a risky bet.
How to buy outcomes
In a world where outcomes are the end goal, outputs should stay off the contract. Teams rarely know exactly what to build up front, so a contract that lists outputs almost always gets them wrong. How do you buy outcomes, then?
Buying outcomes works backward from understanding the desired mission impact. Program leadership names that impact, and the government and contractor team work out which change in user or system behavior would produce it and measure where that behavior stands today. That change and its baseline go on contract, and success means that change, measured in production.
Deliver outcomes, guaranteed
An outcome on contract still needs a team built to deliver it. Kroger saw the limits of the software factory model firsthand at Kessel Run. Software factories brought agile delivery into government, but over time, bureaucracy pulled many of them back to contracts that paid for effort and metrics that counted outputs. What was missing was a model for outcomes from start to finish.
Rise8 built the Outcome Factory to keep what worked and hold every stage accountable to validated mission outcomes. For programs where the government and Rise8 each meet a set of shared commitments, Rise8 guarantees the first validated mission outcome in production within 180 days, or keeps working for free until it is.
The Rise8 Outcome Factory starts with the long-range impact a program needs, maps the current state, and finds the single bottleneck limiting that impact. Together, the Rise8 and government teams set a measurable target aimed at that constraint and continuously deliver software every week until they can validate each outcome against its baseline. When they hit the target, they find the next constraint and start again.
Ask what changed
The Department of War is working to close the gap between outputs and outcomes, from how it judges contracting officers to how it measures software. Every contract can help close this gap too, by naming the change it’s paying for.
The next time a program review says “on track,” ask: what changed for the people using the software, and by how much? If nobody can answer that, the program is still buying outputs and it may be time to start buying outcomes with the Rise8 Outcome Factory. Are you ready to scope your first mission outcome and get it to your operators within 180 days, reach out to us to scope your first mission outcome in a free working session and see if your program qualifies for the guarantee.

Montana acquires sustainable furniture maker Takt

Montana acquires sustainable furniture maker Takt
Montana has announced its buyout of fellow Danish design brand Takt, known for its solid wood furniture and pioneering approach to sustainable design.
Founded in 2019 by trained physicist and former Lego and Bang & Olufsen executive Henrik Taudorf Lorensen, Takt makes modern Scandinavian furniture from FSC-certified wood that is low-carbon, flat-pack and designed for disassembly.
Its future launches and existing catalogue, including products such as the Cross chair by British design duo Pearson Lloyd and Anderssen & Voll’s Spoke sofa, will now be sold under the collection name Takt by Montana.
Montana CEO Joakim Lassen said he hopes they will act as an understated counterpart to Montana’s existing selection of colourful modular furniture – including the Montana System storage – and bring valuable learnings about sustainability to the table.
“Takt brings experience with materials and the environment, and we are looking forward to bringing our respective experience together and taking this work even further,” he said.
Takt is known for its ambitious approach to sustainability, focused on driving down emissions primarily through the design of its products rather than operational cuts, to become net zero by 2030.
The company assesses the carbon footprint of its products throughout their entire lifecycle using the EU’s Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) single score, in a bid to bring down its emissions, and claims to be the only design brand to consistently have all of its products marked with the EU Ecolabel.
“I have a background as a scientist, so it was important to me to start measuring things,” Lorensen told Dezeen during our Carbon Revolution series. “The starting point was to get a grasp of the impact of the choices we’re making.”
Lorensen will join Montana Furniture’s board, sharing his experience and perspective on sustainability, while Takt employees will be integrated into Montana’s organisation “as far as possible”, the company said.
By gaining access to the established, international infrastructure of Montana, which has been operating since 1982, Lorensen hopes that Takt’s furniture will be able to reach a larger audience.
“The past few years have been an exciting and instructive journey for TAKT,” he said. “We have built a brand where materials and the environment have been central, and we have collaborated with a number of talented and celebrated designers. “
“Now it is time for TAKT’s next chapter, and we are delighted that it will be written together with Montana.”

Estonia plans to build about 150 bunkers in Ida-Viru County, along the border with Russia, Defense Minister Martin Herem said during a question-and-answer session in the Riigikogu, the Estonian parliament, responding to a question from lawmaker Arvo Aller.
Aller asked what national defense measures are planned for Ida-Viru County and whether the state intends to acquire private land along the Narva River to plan its actions in the border zone.
“As part of the construction of the Baltic defense zone, for example, around 150 bunkers are planned in Ida-Viru County, 100 of which will be on state land and about 50 on municipal or private land,” Herem said.

The Baltic states have steadily strengthened their defenses in recent years amid fears of aggression from Russia. Estonia installed stationary drone detection and monitoring equipment along its border, while Finland completed a 200-kilometer (124-mile) fence along its border with Russia. Lithuania is also building a barrier along its border with the Kaliningrad region.

Hong Kong leader apologises and housing minister resigns after fire investigation exposes failures
Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee apologised on Thursday for a fire that ravaged a residential tower blocks in Tai Po in November 2025, killing 168, injuring 79 and displacing thousands of others. Housing Secretary Winnie Ho resigned Wednesday for her department's failure to supervise the maintenance work. A three-month investigation into conduct will follow, alongside proposals to criminalise bid rigging in relation to the complex's US $38 million renovation contract.
Hong Kong leader John Lee apologised Thursday and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the city’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight.
The massive fire that broke out last November engulfed seven buildings in an apartment complex in a northern suburban district, killing 168 people and displacing thousands of others.
Many former residents of Wang Fuk Court have spent nearly a year waiting to see how the government will address accountability for the disaster that claimed their loved ones and their homes, which were then undergoing building maintenance work.
At the opening of the news conference, Lee and seven other top officials bowed in apology. Lee said Housing Secretary Winnie Ho “should bear political responsibility," although no personal wrongdoing was found. He said Ho had resigned Wednesday.

An independent committee found that the Housing Bureau’s independent checking unit failed in its duties supervising the maintenance work. Lee said the Buildings Department, the Fire Services Department and the Labour Department had shortcomings in supervision over fire hazards of the apartment complex.
He said a three-month investigation will be conducted into the four government agencies to determine whether staff were derelict in their duties.
Officials also proposed a series of measures, including criminalising bid rigging.
Read moreHong Kong leader orders probe into deadly blaze that killed 151
The committee's report said evidence pointed to a lighted cigarette being the cause of the fire, which started on the flat roof between two apartments on the first floor of Wang Cheong House. The committee heard substantial evidence that construction workers had smoked on site, including on the scaffolding, while a few cigarette butts and some partially burnt materials, such as cardboard boxes, were found on the flat roof.
Experts found the use of foam boards, non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets and canvases contributed to the fire’s spread, among other factors, the report said.
A majority of the deaths were caused by smoke inhalation rather than burns. The replacement of some staircase windows with movable aluminum composite panels or wooden boards for workers’ convenience allowed smoke to infiltrate residents’ escape routes. Opaque foam boards that covered the apartments’ windows blocked residents’ views, delaying evacuation. The shutdown of the fire alarm system was also a factor in the heavy death toll.

The committee said evidence clearly demonstrated that Will Power Architects Company, the consultant for the maintenance project, and Prestige Construction & Engineering Co., the main contractor on the project, had cut corners.
“There is no doubt that they are the main culprits responsible for the occurrence of the inferno and the high fatalities in the tragic incident,” the report said.

It said the evidence also revealed an array of registered contractors and building professionals who conducted no substantive work and were only asked to lend their names to “rubber-stamp” statutory forms in return for a fee. The private contractors and consultants had deceived the regulators, it said.

Among the shortcomings were the lack of proper investigations into the use of the foam boards and the fire-retardant quality of the scaffolding nets despite multiple complaints. The Independent Checking Unit should be criticised for adopting the practice of giving prenotification to consultants and contractors about site inspections, it added.
The committee's work is separate from criminal investigations in which seven people and two companies, Will Power and Prestige, were charged with offenses including manslaughter and conspiracy to defraud over the fire.

US VP Vance contacted top Iran security official: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:29:16 UTC
19:29:16 KST

U.S. Vice President JD Vance has contacted Iran’s security chief in a bid to revive peace talks that could head off a renewed American assault on the Islamic Republic, the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 28.
Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, the Journal reported, in a move that one of the newspaper’s sources said was directed by President Donald Trump.
The letter, as well as subsequent talks between U.S. and Iranian officials, focused on a possible framework for negotiations rather than specifics of a peace proposal, the Journal said.

Global warming threatens dozens of Swiss mountain huts: Experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:28:59 UTC
19:28:59 KST

Burak Bir
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Global warming is increasingly destabilizing the Swiss Alps as thawing permafrost and retreating glaciers threaten mountain infrastructure, affecting nearly half of the Swiss Alpine huts, according to media reports Thursday.
The Swiss Alpine Club (SAC) is being forced to relocate certain huts and spend millions on new facilities and protective measures, news outlet Swiss Info reported.
Cracks had been steadily spreading and widening in the Mutthorn mountain hut in the Bernese Oberland until it was closed in 2021 as it faced danger of collapsing due to thawing permafrost.
"We knew this hut probably wouldn’t last another hundred years. But the fact that it collapsed so quickly really scared us," Fabienne Notter, president of the Weissenstein section of the Swiss Alpine Club (SAC), told Swiss public broadcaster RTS.
Of the 152 SAC huts dotted across the Swiss Alps, 65 are in areas potentially threatened by thawing permafrost. Access routes are also becoming more hazardous due to rockfalls, mudslides and ground movement.
"We cannot predict what will fall or when. But one thing is certain it will collapse," said Nils Hahlen, head of natural hazards for canton of Bern.
The Aletsch Glacier is losing between four and six meters in thickness each year, forcing the staircase to be extended every two or three years.
"When there is no more meltwater left, the available water has to last until the following May," said Christoph Sager, the hut manager.
In one case, a replacement Mutthorn hut was built slightly over half a mile (900 meters) from the original site, on more stable ground in a location less exposed to avalanches.
The old hut was completely dismantled in the summer of 2025 at a cost of more than $480,000.

Financial Times refuses to correct Putin call ‘disinformation’ – media
The Financial Times has refused to correct an anonymously sourced article about a recent phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and the leaders of Norway and Finland, despite objections from both Nordic governments.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb spoke with Putin earlier this week, drawing criticism from some of Europe’s more Russia-hawkish politicians. Store has since demanded the FT retracts its reporting on teh conversation.
The British newspaper claimed that Putin spent significant time “lecturing” the Nordic leaders on “medieval Slavic history” and its relevance to the Ukraine conflict. Citing three anonymous sources described only as “familiar with the conversation,” the FT portrayed the Russian president as “fixated” on history.
Store’s government told Norwegian daily Verdens Gang (VG) that the characterization was inaccurate and that Finland had contacted the FT on behalf of both countries to challenge its account. Finnish media also covered the joint refutation, with the newspaper Helsingin Sanomat citing its own sources to dispute the British paper’s description of the call.
Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov said later in the day that the FT article is “some invented information, or rather disinformation” and that the Nordic leaders were correct to call out the publication.
The FT, however, rejected the request, telling VG that it stood by its reporting.
Its article, published on Tuesday, was written by three journalists.
One of them, American national Christopher Miller, previously worked for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, a US government-funded international broadcaster originally established with covert CIA funding to conduct anti-communist propaganda operations during the Cold War. Miller went to Ukraine in 2010 as a volunteer with the US Peace Corps.
His co-authors, Max Seddon and Henry Foy, head the FT’s bureaus in Moscow and Brussels, respectively.
Last week, the newspaper published a lengthy article by Seddon titled “The Putin whisperers,” recounting a dramatic but difficult-to-verify story of American and German nationals attempting to avert a “nuclear Armageddon” through backchannel diplomacy with Moscow.
Foy, notoriously broke a story in 2025 alleging that a plane carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had experienced suspected Russian GPS jamming. The FT journalist was himself aboard the aircraft when it landed in Bulgaria.
Key elements of the story were challenged almost immediately by flight-tracking service Flightradar24. Bulgarian authorities subsequently debunked the core claims relayed by FT.
Despite the discrepancies, the FT insisted it stood by its reporting. Foy did not respond to requests for comment from fellow journalists who questioned the account.

====================================================================================================

Can the world’s religions survive the existence of aliens?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:26:37 UTC
19:26:37 KST

One of the greatest mysteries of life is whether we are alone in the cosmos. The laws of probability suggest we aren’t, but despite centuries of searching, we have never seen any clear evidence of life beyond our planet. Still, the world’s religious leaders are already formulating how they would respond to extraterrestrial life—and some have more interesting approaches than others.
These discussions took center stage at a Capitol Hill gathering called the Disclosure Forum that took place earlier this year on a sunny day in June. A gaggle of lawmakers, retired military personnel, academics and businesspeople crowded into the Russell Senate Office Building’s Kennedy Caucus Room with me. As I listened, they spitballed ideas on how to handle what they believe are the increasingly likely chances of first contact with alien life.
Several speakers at the event stressed that a revelation that Earth has been visited by intelligent extraterrestrials would raise immediate questions about planetary defense. Others theorized hopefully that there could be enormous economic opportunities.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
There would also be enormous societal impacts: Carlos Eire, a historian and religious studies professor at Yale University, told event attendees that finding out humanity isn’t alone in the universe could shake us to our very souls—religious leaders would need to contain the fallout, he said.
Eire serves on the advisory board for the Disclosure Foundation, a nonprofit that organized the event and is dedicated to transparency around unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) and aliens.
“If disclosure reveals that there are nonhuman intelligences,” Eire told me later in an interview, “it remains to be seen who these intelligences really are and what they do, or what they’re hoping to accomplish, with human beings.”
“There won’t be a single reaction,” he adds. “For some people, it will confirm all sorts of things. For some people, it will demolish certain beliefs.”
Reactions could be split along religious lines—and some belief systems may be better equipped to deal with aliens than others, experts say.
For example, Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and other religions that originate in the Global East “have always conceived of the universe as vast, as going through many cycles of existence,” says Jeffery Long, a religious studies professor at Elizabethtown College.
Hinduism, Long tells me, has many deities, some of whom are described in religious texts as traveling through the cosmos on “vimanas”—flying chariots that could, to some, be read as akin to spaceships.
“If you start reading ancient Hindu literature and about different deities and then other species of intelligent beings, it’s very sci-fi,” Long says.
Meanwhile, the Abrahamic religions—the largest of which are Christianity, Judaism and Islam—are largely accepting of the idea that conscious life might exist that isn’t human, but none of these religions are monoliths.
The sheer scope of Christian belief systems makes attitudes to aliens among believers difficult to pin down, Eire says. Some theologians are optimistic: in his 2023 book Astrobiology and Christian Doctrine: Exploring the Implications of Life in the Universe, which received some NASA grant funding, Andrew Davison, now a divinity professor at the University of Oxford, wrote that he believes Christianity would be more “robust” in accepting alien life than some might think.
Certainly, leaders in the Roman Catholic Church have hinted at being open to extraterrestrials—the late Pope Francis once said he’d happily baptize an alien if they asked—Eire points out that within certain forms of Christianity, such as Protestantism, there can be incredible diversity in beliefs.
“There are Bible-thumping antievolutionists in parts of the U.S. that call themselves Evangelicals, and there are Evangelicals that are damn close to Catholics,” Eire says. “Predicting what Protestants will do is just impossible. The spectrum is so wide and contains so many different kinds of Christianity.”
The Abrahamic religion that may be the most open-minded about aliens, Long says, is also the oldest. Jewish scripture, while making no mention of spaceships, does include repeated mention of angels with a higher consciousness than that of humans. Even the most devout followers would perhaps be accepting of aliens because the religion’s dogma is “more about ethics and living your life here and now than it’s about ‘if you do this, you’ll go to heaven,’” Long says.
Academic explorations of how religious belief might influence attitudes to potential alien life are spotty at best, but that dearth of research could change. Aliens have become less taboo for scientists beyond astrobiology; the possibility of extraterrestrial life is no longer a punch line.
At the June Disclosure Forum, I heard more about how the White House is approaching the issue by setting up an advisory group on UAP, led by Harvard professor Avi Loeb. Loeb said at the event that he hopes the UAP Science Advisory Council will go on to publish scientific findings in reputable journals. That may include research in the field of exotheology—the study of religion and theological ideas related to alien life, Eire says.
“The academic community is readier now than it was 10 years ago for various reasons,” he says. Eire points to the Pentagon’s recent publishing of several tranches of previously classified UAP-related documents and media as a reason for this increased openness.
As to whether a kind of spiritual malaise or panic might result from aliens revealing themselves, that’s unclear. According to one recent poll, a third of Americans believe at least some UAP sightings were actual spacecraft; another poll found about half the country believes aliens probably exist. But drilling down more formally into specific religions is more murky: A 2021 poll revealed that among U.S. Christians, people who said religion was very important to them were less likely to believe that intelligent life might exist on other planets, as were those who attended religious services at least weekly. Belief in alien life also varied by denomination.
Much could also hinge on what kind of alien life is out there. While most people imagine intelligent beings that are in the best case friendly and curious like E.T., or, in the worst case, here to annihilate humanity, like in Independence Day, that’s not what most exobiologists are searching for. Instead they are on the lookout for distant exoplanets that exhibit signs of life closer to Earth’s microbes than humans.
“If there was amoebalike life on other planets, that would be a significant thing,” says Shoaib Malik, a science and religion lecturer at the University of Edinburgh and co-editor of the book Islamic Theology and Extraterrestrial Life: New Frontiers in Science and Religion. But while microscopic life would “definitely show proof of concept,” Malik adds, it wouldn’t fundamentally shake people’s faith.
“I think the real challenge really is if there’s something equivalent or something more advanced than the human being, particularly if you associate human uniqueness with rationality and spirituality,” Malik says.
Other scholars aren’t so sure. David Weintraub, a retired astronomer and author of Religions and Extraterrestrial Life: How Will We Deal With It?, says the difference between a microbe and, say, a primate is only a matter of degree.
“I think it would only make a difference to someone who does not believe in evolution, and that’s where we start drilling into the religious aspect of this,” he says. “If you accept evolution as a natural part of the way the universe works, then if you find microbial life of any sort, a possibility exists that that microbial life could evolve into intelligent life someday.”
Although there are no direct comparisons of similar evolutionary situations arising in modern history, says Paul Gutjahr, a professor at Indiana University Bloomington and author of the book Faith in Space: American Religious Belief in Extraterrestrial Life, there are many examples in human history in which religion and new knowledge of the cosmos has collided. When evolution was an emerging theory, for example, it presented a major challenge to Christianity.
“What you find is that people within that tradition find ways to adapt,” Gutjahr says. “It’s not like everybody becomes a friend of evolution, but there are there are very smart, capable and vocal people that start to think about if evolution is just the way that God worked his magic.”

ECB President Christine Lagarde to step down next February, months before her mandate ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:25:59 UTC
19:25:59 KST

Christine Lagarde will step down on 7 February 2027, around nine months before the end of her eight-year term, the European Central Bank announced on Thursday, hours before it kept interest rates on hold at 2.5%.
Christine Lagarde will leave her post as president of the European Central Bank (ECB) on 7 February 2027, the central bank announced on Thursday, around nine months before her eight-year term was due to end.
The news immediately kicks off a closely watched race for one of Europe's most powerful jobs at a time of economic stagnation and global turmoil. Her succession will be decided by the 21 countries that share the euro.
The announcement came hours before the ECB left its deposit rate unchanged at 2.5%, as turmoil in France's bond market weighs on borrowing costs across the eurozone.
Lagarde informed the ECB's Governing Council, which sets interest rates for the eurozone, and European Council President António Costa of her decision, the central bank said in a statement.
"The Governing Council thanked President Lagarde warmly and gave her a long standing ovation," it read.
In a separate public statement, Lagarde said she was leaving with a sense of a job well done and an ECB that was fit for the future.
Separately, the ECB president also "said she is stepping down before the end of her term so that she has greater freedom to express her views and to engage in non-monetary matters, because she cannot remain neutral when she sees the developments taking place in her own country and in the world," people familiar with the matter told Euronews.
"She said she can be useful as a French national, European citizen and citizen of the world," the sources added.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reacted to the news, thanking Lagarde for her service and stating that "from the pandemic to Russia's war of aggression, your steady hand has helped keep our economy stable and resilient".
European Council President António Costa also thanked Lagarde, praising her "dedication as President of the European Central Bank since November 2019".
"To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay," Costa added.
French President Emmanuel Macron expressed "deep gratitude" for Lagarde's commitment and "for the determined action she has led at the helm of the European Central Bank in service of the stability of the eurozone".
Greek Economy and Finance Minister Kyriakos Pierrakakis, who chairs the Eurogroup of eurozone finance ministers, also thanked Lagarde on their behalf, saying her time in charge had strengthened confidence in the euro and crediting her leadership through difficult economic times.
Her successor will be appointed by the European Council, which brings together EU leaders.
Under EU rules, leaders choose the ECB president by qualified majority, on a recommendation from EU finance ministers and after consulting the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council.
Why leave early?
While the ECB gave no reason, speculation about Lagarde's early departure had been building for months.
As Euronews reported, rumours first emerged in February that Lagarde planned to leave early so that French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz could oversee the choice of her successor before France's presidential election in April of next year.
Macron is barred from running for a third term, and the far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally) has been polling strongly, raising the prospect of a eurosceptic government in Paris that could complicate the appointment of a new ECB chief.
Leaving next February gives EU leaders time to settle on a name well before French voters go to the polls.
Bank of France Governor François Villeroy de Galhau announced his own early exit in February, reportedly for similar reasons. However, Lagarde had kept her plans close to her chest for months.
The departing ECB president said in February that chairing the World Economic Forum, the organisation behind the annual Davos meeting, was "one of the many options" for her future, and in July she told Euronews that she was "not a candidate for anything" dispelling speculation that she would run in the French elections.
The race to succeed Lagarde
Two names currently lead the race to succeed Lagarde.
Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of the Bank of Spain who has run the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements since 2025, was put forward by Madrid in July in Spain’s first-ever bid for the ECB presidency.
Earlier this month, he also won the backing of Spain's main opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, whose party is leading most polls ahead of next month's snap election.
His main rival is Klaas Knot, who ran the Dutch central bank from 2011 to 2025 and is seen as a former inflation hawk turned consensus-builder. Lagarde herself has praised his "rare and very necessary" ability to foster inclusivity.
Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel has also been mentioned, though Germany has never held the job.
The presidency is also only one piece of a bigger puzzle.
Isabel Schnabel, the German board member in charge of market operations, is leaving on 3 January 2027 to join the IMF, while chief economist Philip Lane's term ends shortly after on 31 May 2027.
That means half of the ECB's six-member Executive Board, which runs the central bank day to day, will change hands within five months, and the three posts are expected to be negotiated between capitals as a package.
Eurozone governments had until Wednesday to put forward candidates for Schnabel's seat, but this deadline has been extended until 27 November. The Eurogroup did not make an announcement but a spokesperson has confirmed it to media outlets.
France, Germany and Italy have long held seats on the board, while Spain wants to return after losing its place when Luis de Guindos' vice-presidency passed to Croatia's Boris Vujčić this year.
Germany is expected to push to keep the market operations portfolio.
Meanwhile, Paris is widely expected to aim for the chief economist job rather than a third French presidency. "France knows how to play the game so they are very likely not going to try for a third French ECB President," Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at Dutch bank ING, told Euronews in February.
Countries traditionally hold only one seat each, meaning a Knot presidency would also likely mean fellow Dutch board member Frank Elderson stepping aside.

Life magazine, the inspiration for &quot;The Secret Life of Walter Mitty,&quot; is being revived again
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:25:18 EET
19:25:18 KST

Life magazine, the inspiration for "The Secret Life of Walter Mitty," is being revived again
Kyiv • UNN
The iconic Life magazine will resume print publication next month as a quarterly with the backing of Karlie Kloss. The publication will also develop video, films, and events.
The iconic magazine Life, a chronicler of 20th-century America known for its visual storytelling, is being revived and will return next month in print as a quarterly, despite challenging business conditions. The New York Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
"Nearly two decades after the last edition ceased publication, Life magazine is coming back to life," the publication says.
The iconic publication, known for its red-bordered logo and commitment to visual storytelling, will begin publishing again next month as a quarterly print edition. It is returning to a fragmented media landscape that exists in a very different world from the height of the publication's popularity in the mid-20th century, before the internet, social media and artificial intelligence upended the business model of magazine publishing.
But Karlie Kloss, the model and entrepreneur who is supporting the project through her company Bedford Media, says the brand's legacy deserves to be revived and adapted for the 21st century. In addition to a website and social media presence, Life plans to expand its activities to include short films, documentaries and events.
"What made Life magazine special was its ability to bring the world closer together," Kloss said. "And it is our responsibility to preserve and protect that legacy."
The magazine's history
Life magazine was founded in 1936 by Henry Luce, the founder of Time and Fortune magazines. The cover of the first issue featured a black-and-white photograph by Margaret Bourke-White depicting the concrete Fort Peck Dam in Montana, United States, which was part of U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt's "New Deal." The issue sold out immediately.
Life magazine, which became a monument to the power of photojournalism, documented mid-20th-century American life, including World War II, the space race and the civil rights movement. It published the work of photographers such as Robert Capa, Alfred Eisenstaedt and Gordon Parks, resulting in such unforgettable images as the sailor kissing a woman in Times Square on V-J Day in 1945, as well as portraits of Marilyn Monroe and James Dean. The magazine also was the first to publish Ernest Hemingway's complete novella "The Old Man and the Sea" and commissioned Norman Mailer to cover the Apollo 11 crew's 1969 Moon landing.
The magazine's circulation peaked in the 1960s, exceeding eight million copies. But as television's popularity began to upend the magazine industry, Time Inc. discontinued the weekly magazine in 1972. Its life was revived in 1978, this time as a monthly magazine, and continued until 2000, when Time Inc. announced the end of regular publication.
The magazine played a role in the adventure film "The Secret Life of Walter Mitty" (2013), in which the protagonist - Walter Mitty (played by Ben Stiller) - works as a manager of the photo negative department at Life magazine.

Bulgarians and their descendants have left a lasting mark on the culture, social and political life, and even the architecture of South America. Little is known about many of them in Bulgaria, yet their stories deserve to be told. Twenty-three such life stories have been brought together by Aksinia Ivanova and Ivan Tsankov in their new book, Bulgarian Talents on South American Soil.
The authors have lived in Argentina since the beginning of the century, while maintaining close ties with Bulgaria. They founded the civic association Bulgarians in Argentina and launched the first Spanish-language media outlets on Bulgaria on the continent, including the losbulgaros.com.ar news portal and the online radio station My Bulgaria, among others. They have also embarked on making films and writing books about “the other Bulgaria”, the one that generations of emigrants and their children have built through their hard work and talent on the other side of the Atlantic.
Aksinia Ivanova and Ivan Tsankov are currently spending a month in Europe. Their programme included the 21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media in Budapest and the presentation of Bulgarian Talents on South American Soil in Sofia. 
Ivan Tsankov spoke about the book in the Radio Bulgaria studio, explaining how the idea came about and how the authors discovered the people whose stories it tells.
Ivan Tsankov and Aksinia Ivanova
PHOTO BTA
It all began with a meeting with a writer of Bulgarian descent from Uruguay who had moved to Argentina and contacted them to ask for information. Through their conversations with her, Aksinia and Ivan learned about her work, her renown in Uruguay and the books she had once presented to the country’s president, José Mujica. They began to wonder how many other compatriots across the ocean might have stories waiting for someone to hear them.
Seeking answers, they launched the “Discover Bulgarian Talent” campaign on their online radio station, My Bulgaria. They tracked down compatriots and people of Bulgarian origin, interviewed them and collected their biographies. Gradually, they gathered enough material for a book that brings together contemporary figures and personalities from the past.
Mario Nestoroff
PHOTO Digital edition of Bulgarian talents on South-American soil
The story of the poet Mario Nestoroff, the son of Bulgarian emigrants, made a particularly strong impression on them. Tsankov describes him as the most outstanding talent to emerge from the Bulgarian community in Argentina.
Mario Nestoroff won a national literary competition with his poem Song of Chaco. Among the members of the jury was Jorge Luis Borges. Although Nestoroff never published a book during his lifetime, his poems were turned into songs and are studied in Argentine schools. Aksinia and Ivan dedicated their documentary film A Heart Like a Bird to him. The film was screened in Sofia at the presentation of their book, marking the 90th anniversary of the poet’s birth.
In which fields have Bulgarians in South America made their most notable contributions? And what do the lives featured in Bulgarian Talents on South American Soil have in common? Ivan Tsankov explains:
Ivan Tsankov in Radio Bulgaria's studio
PHOTO Miglena Ivanova
“Most of them are writers. Literature has been strongly represented ever since the first waves of Bulgarian emigration to South America. The writer Samuil Strezov, who belonged to that very first wave, enjoyed considerable fame in his day. His first published book (Anga: Memoirs of an Emigrant (editor’s note), was even presented to literary circles in France. It aroused great interest there.
As for what these people have in common, which is what you are asking me about, yes, there is something, and we always emphasise it. These are typically Bulgarian traits which, I believe, are evident not only in literature but also in other fields that allow Bulgarian talent to flourish even on foreign soil. Despite all the difficulties of starting a new life in the New World, where, as you know, one has to fight for survival, for one’s place in society and for many other things, this talent is so distinctive that wherever Bulgarians go, it finds a way to blossom. They demonstrate what they are capable of and make a name for themselves, not only in their chosen field but also in their new community.”
Vatyo Koralsky
PHOTO Digital edition of Bulgarian talents on South-American soil
Among the stories collected by Aksinia and Ivan is that of civil engineer Vatyo Koralski, who arrived in Argentina in 1948 with a degree and only a few coins in his pocket. In Tucumán, he founded his own company, became a pioneer of high-rise residential construction in the city and was awarded the title of Distinguished Citizen.
Each emigrant finds their own path, shaped by their talents, opportunities and the hand life deals them. But how does an emigrant community earn the trust of the wider society, and how are Bulgarians in Argentina regarded more generally.
“In areas where the Bulgarian community is large, particularly the province of Chaco, which is home to the largest and oldest Bulgarian community, it enjoys a very high standing,” Ivan Tsankov explains. “Let me clarify why Bulgarians went there: it was the centre of the cotton industry. At a time when synthetic fabrics did not exist, cotton was a highly sought-after commodity, and there was a constant need for labour. That is why they settled there.
This was the first community to establish a school for its children. Its members are also known for the traditional industriousness that we know so well here in Bulgaria, as well as for their honesty. All these qualities have earned Bulgarians a high standing in the wider community.
Another factor is the talent of Bulgarians, who have made their mark not only in their professional fields, whether literature, music or painting, but also in public life. Many individuals have made significant contributions and are highly respected in their respective provinces. One example is our compatriot Omar Tsenov, who, sadly, has passed away. He was a well-known writer, religious figure, statesman and much more. A school in his hometown was named after him during his lifetime by government decree. That alone speaks volumes.”
PHOTO BTA
Readers can do more than simply read the book: they can also see and hear the people whose stories it tells. A QR code provides access to photographs, audio and video materials, including interviews recorded by Aksinia and Ivan. In this way, the names and biographies come to life through faces, voices and personal recollections.
The book is published in both Bulgarian and Spanish. The inclusion of Spanish reflects the particular nature of the Bulgarian community in Argentina, as the Radio Bulgaria guest explains:
“There is one particular aspect that I would like to clarify, something that is not widely known in Bulgaria about the Bulgarian community in Argentina. The vast majority of its members are descendants of Bulgarian immigrants. The only thing that gives away their connection to Bulgaria is their surname, ending in ‘-off’. They do not speak Bulgarian.
That is why we broadcast and write in Spanish, so that we can reach them. Otherwise, no one would pay attention to what we create if we did it in Bulgarian, even though that would be easier for us. We have even been criticised for being a Bulgarian media outlet that publishes in a foreign language. But that is the reason.”
Even when the language of their ancestors is no longer spoken at home, family stories continue to be passed down. They inspire younger generations to discover the country their families once left behind. In recent years, social media have created the impression that growing numbers of people of Bulgarian descent are reconnecting with their roots. Is this interest genuinely increasing, or is it simply becoming more visible?
PHOTO sbj-bg.eu
“I want to make it clear that interest in their roots and in Bulgaria has always existed. It has been constant,” Ivan Tsankov insists. “The people we are in contact with, who make up this community, now include descendants of immigrants in their fourth generation. Their earliest impressions came from their ancestors, their grandfathers and grandmothers, who told them about Bulgaria. They know very well what banitsa is, for example. They adore traditional Bulgarian costumes.
For them, Bulgaria is something sacred. Unfortunately, only a small proportion of them have visited Bulgaria and know the country first-hand.”
And so, as the descendants of emigrants seek to reconnect with Bulgaria, Aksinia Ivanova and Ivan Tsankov’s book gives us an opportunity to draw closer to them. It allows us to discover the people behind the names and see how their achievements have become part of life on a distant continent.
PHOTO Miglena Ivanova

Eesti 200 calls for euthanasia referendum to gather citizens' views
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:25:00 UTC
19:25:00 KST

Eesti 200 calls for euthanasia referendum to gather citizens' views
Junior coalition party Eesti 200 has proposed holding a referendum to ask citizens for their views on legalizing euthanasia at the same time as the Riigikogu elections in March 2027.
The Eesti 200 parliamentary group submitted a draft resolution on Thursday to ask eligible voters whether adults with legal capacity in Estonia should have the right to end their lives with dignity through medical assistance in the event of a serious incurable illness, the party announced.
The party's Chairman Kristina Kallas said the aim is to get guidance from citizens for future policymaking.
The draft does not establish a legal framework for assisted suicide or euthanasia. Nor would it yet decide on the possible content of such regulations.
"We do not want to provide simple answers to difficult questions with this draft. At the same time, we believe that our society is ready to discuss whether and under what conditions people should have the opportunity to end their lives with dignity through medical assistance instead of enduring incurable pain and severe suffering," Kallas said.
"That is why we propose holding a referendum alongside the Riigikogu elections in March, so that Estonia's eligible voters can express their position in principle, which would serve as democratic guidance for the next parliament. Based on the will expressed by citizens in the referendum, the next Riigikogu can begin developing regulations suitable for Estonia," she explained.
According to the draft, the ballot paper would contain the question: "Should Estonia legalize the right of an adult with legal capacity to end their life with dignity through medical assistance in the event of a serious and incurable illness?" The response options would be "yes" and "no."
Eesti 200 parliamentary group member Kadri Tali, who spoke when submitting the draft in the Riigikogu, said the European Court of Human Rights has found that a person has the right to decide to end their own life of their own free will, but states have been given the opportunity to shape their own legislation on the matter.
"I appeal to all parties to talk to your voters and members and ask for their opinions as well. Hopefully, as a result, you will find a way to support holding the referendum in the Riigikogu," she said.
"This is not a matter of party politics, but a human issue. We cannot always decide how long a person's life will be. But we can decide how much care, compassion and dignity there is in it," Tali added.

German unmanned ground vehicle gets Ukrainian SABER weapon station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:24:42 UTC
19:24:42 KST

- ARX Robotics and Roboneers completed initial integration tests of the SABER remote weapon station on the GEREON unmanned ground vehicle.
- The companies plan to integrate SABER M2 and MK 19 configurations by the end of 2026, with deliveries tailored to Ukraine’s needs.
German defense startup ARX Robotics and Ukrainian manufacturer Roboneers have completed initial integration tests of Roboneers’ SABER remote weapon station on ARX’s GEREON unmanned ground vehicle, and plan to start fitting armed versions by the end of 2026, the companies announced on Oct. 29.
The first SABER modules will be integrated in M2 and MK 19 (M) configurations, built around the .50-caliber M2 heavy machine gun and the 40 mm MK 19 automatic grenade launcher. Deliveries will follow the operational needs of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, the companies said. They did not disclose how many armed GEREONs Ukraine will receive, the value of any order, or when the first vehicles will reach frontline units.
“Modern armed forces require platforms that can adapt quickly to different missions, integrate new technologies and work seamlessly with existing systems. This is exactly what GEREON was built to deliver: modularity, interoperability and mission-readiness. Together with ROBONEERS, we demonstrate that new defence tech companies can move at the speed the theatre of combat demands – delivering capabilities where it matters most,” said Maximilian Wied, CFO and co-founder of ARX Robotics.
The pairing splits the work between the two systems. GEREON supplies mobility, electrical power and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sensors, while the SABER mount carries the weapon and handles fire support. SABER is a modular family of remotely operated weapon stations designed to take different weapons, from assault rifles to grenade launchers, so a unit can choose the armament for a mission while keeping the same ground vehicle. Until now, Roboneers has fitted SABER mainly to its own vehicles, and the integration adds the GEREON as another carrier.
“The SABER combat module is designed to adapt to the operational needs of military units, not the other way around. The integration with the GEREON UGV platform demonstrates this interoperability and shows how both companies are accelerating the deployment of urgently needed capabilities to the front lines,” said Anton Skrypnyk, CEO of ROBONEERS.
GEREON is ARX Robotics’ medium-sized unmanned ground vehicle, and the company says its fleet in Ukraine is the largest Western-built UGV fleet deployed there. The vehicles have been in Ukrainian service since early 2025, and ARX has since won a contract for several hundred GEREON units, followed in May 2026 by another order for several hundred more vehicles that expanded its Ukrainian fleet to five times its original size. The modular design lets the same vehicle switch between resupply, casualty evacuation, electronic warfare, reconnaissance, combat and counter-drone roles. ARX also builds GEREONs in Britain after its first British Army contract in April.
Roboneers says its systems have been used in more than 15,000 frontline missions since 2014. Its product line includes the Rys Pro ground vehicle alongside the SABER weapon stations.
The integration is the first concrete result of a strategic technical partnership the two companies signed on Oct. 4 in Kyiv, during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s state visit to Ukraine and in the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. That agreement covers joint development and deeper integration of their systems.
It builds on an industrial tie-up from June, when ARX and Roboneers formed ARX Industries, a joint venture to mass-produce the Rys Pro UGV at sites in Germany and Ukraine, with a target of four-digit production numbers in its first year. The companies have already delivered 30 ground vehicles to a single Ukrainian regiment, which uses them for logistics, casualty evacuation and ammunition resupply at the same time.
Most of the unmanned ground vehicles Ukraine has fielded so far carry cargo or wounded soldiers. Armed versions remain a smaller share, and the GEREON-SABER combination would give Ukrainian units a heavy machine gun or grenade launcher on a vehicle they already operate in large numbers.
The companies said integration of the M2 and MK 19 configurations is due to be completed by the end of 2026.

Taiwan economy flashes red light for record 10th straight month in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:24:36 UTC
19:24:36 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s economy flashed a red light for a record 10th consecutive month in September as AI demand continued to drive growth.
The National Development Council said Thursday that the composite economic indicator rose to 41 points, up one point from August’s revised score of 40. This marked the longest recorded streak of red lights since records began in 1984, per Liberty Times.
Taiwan uses a five-color system to gauge the health of its economy, with colors ranging from blue to red based on a composite score of 9 to 45 points. Blue (9-16 points) signals contraction, yellow-blue (17-22 points) indicates sluggish growth, green (23-31 points) represents stable growth, yellow-red (32-37 points) means the economy is warming up, and red (38-45 points) indicates an overheated or booming economy.
Of the nine components used to calculate the indicator, overtime hours in the industrial and service sectors shifted from green to yellow-red, adding one point. The change reflected sustained production activity in AI-related industries, while the leading and coincident indicators continued to rise, signaling continued economic growth.
Looking ahead, the NDC said rapid AI adoption and continued investment by global cloud service providers in AI infrastructure should boost shipments of Taiwanese electronics and information and communications technology products. AI’s spillover effects are also gradually extending to traditional industries, potentially adding to export momentum.
Investment is poised to strengthen as domestic semiconductor, memory, and substrate manufacturers increase capital spending, while foreign companies expand their operations in Taiwan. Government efforts to encourage small and medium-sized businesses to upgrade and transform their operations should also support private investment.
On the consumption front, strong corporate performance could encourage more companies to raise wages, while recovering automobile sales, holiday-related spending, and the approaching year-end shopping season should boost domestic demand. However, the NDC cautioned that geopolitical conflicts, changes in international trade policies, concerns about AI companies’ financing, and monetary policy decisions by major central banks remain key uncertainties.

Typhoon Champi causes NT$489 million in agricultural losses in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:24:20 UTC
19:24:20 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Typhoon Champi caused an estimated NT$489.14 million (US$15.4 million) in agricultural losses and damage to private facilities across Taiwan, according to the Ministry of Agriculture.
The ministry’s Department of Statistics said the losses totaled NT$398.22 million in agricultural, forestry, fishery, and livestock products, while damage to private facilities accounted for NT$90.92 million. The figures were compiled from local government and agricultural agency reports as of 11 a.m. Thursday.
Yunlin County reported the highest losses at NT$147.77 million, accounting for 30% of the national total, followed by Taitung County at NT$88.54 million, or 18%, and Taichung at NT$66.15 million, or 14%. Pingtung County reported NT$50.77 million in losses, while Miaoli County recorded NT$32.89 million.
Crop damage accounted for NT$397.88 million in losses. A total of 7,497 hectares of farmland was affected, with damage averaging 21% and an estimated 1,595 hectares rendered incapable of producing a harvest.
Garlic suffered the heaviest crop losses, with 468 hectares affected and estimated losses of NT$65.86 million. Sugar apples were the second-hardest-hit crop, with 644 hectares damaged and losses of NT$52.04 million, followed by Murcott mandarins at NT$20.93 million, bananas at NT$20.36 million, and peanuts at NT$19.58 million.
Livestock losses were estimated at NT$341,000, mainly involving chickens. Damage to private facilities totaled NT$90.92 million, including NT$5.41 million in agricultural facilities, NT$8.77 million in livestock facilities, and NT$76.74 million in fishing infrastructure.
Fishing infrastructure losses were concentrated in Pingtung, Taitung, and Hualien counties, where fishing vessels and fixed fishing nets were damaged. The ministry said the damage assessment was ongoing and that cash assistance and low-interest loans had been announced for eligible areas and affected agricultural sectors.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Nearly 800 government websites and systems have been affected by major PHP security flaws, the Administration for Cyber Security said Thursday.
PHP is a widely used programming language for building websites and web applications. The development team released security updates on Oct. 21 to address two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow attackers to execute code remotely without authentication.
ACS Director-General Tsai Fu-longe (蔡福隆) said nearly 300 government agencies had reported affected systems as of Wednesday, per CNA. The agency has required daily updates on repairs since issuing an alert last week, and 460 of the roughly 800 affected websites and systems had been patched.

Tsai also addressed the exposure of candidates’ national ID numbers on a government financial disclosure website, saying preliminary findings suggested a programming error by an outsourced contractor had caused the leak, per Liberty Times.
The Ministry of Digital Affairs will work with the Central Election Commission to complete security testing and ensure the website is secure, Tsai said.

ECB President Christine Lagarde to step down in February 2027, nine months before term ends
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down on February 7, 2027, nearly nine months before her term expires, the ECB said Thursday. Her successor will be appointed by the European Council under EU treaty rules.
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde will step down in February 2027, several months before her term expires in October next year, the Frankfurt-based institution said Thursday.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
"European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde today informed the Governing Council and the president of the European Council Antonio Costa that she will step down from her position on 7 February 2027," the ECB said in a statement.
Lagarde's departure before the end of her term opens the way for European leaders to choose a new ECB chief before French presidential elections scheduled for April, in a race where eurosceptic far-right and far-left candidates are leading in opinion polls.
Lagarde herself has ruled out standing for the presidency, telling French newspaper La Croix last month that it would "not be a good idea".Months of speculation have preceded her departure, and Lagarde has been tipped to take the helm of the World Economic Forum, which organises the annual summit of politicians and business leaders in Davos, Switzerland.
Lagarde took the helm at the ECB in November 2019, having previously led the International Monetary Fund and served as French finance minister.
Her tenure took in the Covid-19 pandemic and an inflationary wave that followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which prompted a spike in energy prices.
Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, praised Lagarde's "leadership" and said the process to name a successor would begin immediately.
"Through a global pandemic, a war in Europe, energy crises and inflation shocks, she has provided a steady and determined stewardship, helping to safeguard stability and the resilience of the euro area," Costa posted on social media.
"To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay, with a view to a timely decision," Costa said.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday praised Christine Lagarde's "European commitment" and "determined" leadership at the head of the ECB, and called for preparations for her succession to be made "in an orderly and balanced way", with European partners.
He expressed his deep gratitude to Lagarde for her action during her tenure.
