Trump demands Alaska candidates be removed over alleged ballot scheme
A New York Times investigation links Democratic operatives to a namesake candidate in Alaska’s Senate race.
US President Donald Trump has called for the removal and prosecution of two candidates in Alaska’s Senate race, accusing Democrats of orchestrating a scheme to mislead voters.
Trump’s demand on Wednesday followed a New York Times investigation into efforts by people linked to Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign to recruit candidates who could draw support from Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, including a retired teacher with the same name.
The November 3 vote could help determine control of the US Senate, Congress’s upper chamber.
In Truth Social posts on Wednesday, Trump accused Peltola and Daniel J Sullivan Jr of election fraud and called for both to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.
He described the alleged operation as “Voter Fraud at the Highest Level” and accused Democrats of lying under oath.
The Times noted that recruiting candidates to split an opponent’s vote – a practice known as ballot stacking – is generally legal and has been used by both parties in Alaska.
The two Sullivans are among four candidates in Alaska’s ranked-choice election.
Voters rank candidates by preference, with votes transferred if a first choice is eliminated. The ballot identifies the sitting senator as an incumbent Republican.
His namesake says he entered the race independently.
The Times reported that the effort began in 2025, when a Peltola aide was asked to identify Alaskans named Dan Sullivan.
Citing interviews and messages, it said Peltola advisers and officials from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which supports Democratic Senate candidates, discussed ways to reshape the ballot.
The newspaper identified Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz as a recruiter who approached potential candidates, sometimes under an assumed name.
It also reported that another Democrat withdrew after an approach from Kurtz, opening a place for Republican Gerald Heikes, who said he too had been encouraged to run.
Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, told the Times that Peltola knew about the operation but did not participate directly.
Rios later sought to withdraw her statements and the newspaper said other evidence supported its reporting.
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic campaign committee denied recruiting candidates. Her campaign said political threats from Washington would not stop her candidacy.
Senator Sullivan accused Peltola of deceiving voters on Fox News on Wednesday.
Recruiting candidates to divide an opponent’s support is generally legal, the Times noted, and both major parties have used such tactics in Alaska.
The state’s Supreme Court upheld the retired teacher’s right to stand in June.
Trump’s Justice Department, the federal government’s legal arm, sued Alaska last week, seeking to delay certification if Senator Sullivan loses and votes for his namesake could have affected the outcome.
Alaska has asked the court to dismiss the case, arguing that it lacks legal grounds.

Could suspected Qatari interference see Israel's election annulled?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:21:38 UTC
19:21:38 KST

The unusual letter sent by Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg to Shin Bet Director David Zini has already sparked controversy. It confirms a familiar concern: Qatar has sought to influence Israeli public opinion, including through activities examined in the so-called Qatargate affair, which is awaiting a decision by prosecutors on whether to file criminal charges.
At this stage, however, it is important to emphasize that the extent of any Qatari interference in Israel's parliamentary election, if such interference occurred at all, remains unclear, as does the nature of any actions taken. According to Sohlberg's letter, there are indications of possible election bribery involving a foreign state and individuals in Israel.
What does Israeli law say?
Election bribery is prohibited under Israeli law. Section 122 of the Knesset Elections Law provides for a prison sentence of up to five years for violations.
When a foreign state is involved, the possibility of prosecuting the party offering the bribe is remote. However, the law also makes accepting a bribe a criminal offense.
The provision applies to anyone who "receives or agrees to receive a bribe, for themselves or another person, in order to vote or refrain from voting, either altogether or for a particular list of candidates."
Former Knesset member Shmuel Flatto-Sharon was charged and convicted under the election bribery provision, not for directly paying voters but for promising them benefits in exchange for their support, according to a 1984 Supreme Court ruling.
In that decision, the justices explained the principle underlying the prohibition on offering benefits in exchange for votes.
"Freedom of choice means not only the physical freedom to place a ballot in the ballot box, but also, and above all, the complete freedom to go through the voting process as a free person, mentally and intellectually," the court wrote.
"Therefore, any act that restricts or eliminates, directly or indirectly, the voter's freedom of thought and ability to genuinely express their preferred course of action and worldview according to their independent judgment, whether through a benefit that undermines that freedom or through the imposition of another person's views, violates the fundamental principle of electoral integrity and independence."
The justices went on to warn that tolerating such practices would undermine the foundations of democracy.
"Such acts are therefore fundamentally unacceptable," the ruling said.
"A different or more lenient approach to this issue, acceptance of such acts and participation in them would inevitably disrupt the democratic process and distort its character, since the unavoidable result would be that those who control the money would also control public opinion and, consequently, political power, with all that entails. There can be no more serious distortion of the principles of a democratic system in an enlightened society."
From challenging election results to overturning them
If law enforcement authorities determine that the information provides sufficient grounds to open an investigation, and such an investigation is launched, the central question will be what evidence investigators uncover.
Beyond the criminal process, which could involve an investigation, indictment and trial, authorities would also need to consider whether any offenses affected the integrity of the election and, if so, to what extent.
Claims that electoral violations influenced the results, potentially warranting their annulment, would be considered separately from criminal proceedings.
Under Israel's election law, the results of a parliamentary election can be challenged through an appeal heard by the Jerusalem District Court.
Such an appeal is entirely independent of any criminal investigation or prosecution. The court can consider allegations of election bribery even if no criminal proceedings have been initiated.
Political parties and the attorney general are authorized to file such appeals.
The law generally allows just two weeks after an election to submit an appeal, although the court may extend that deadline if it provides reasons for doing so. In the current circumstances, the need to examine allegations of foreign interference could potentially justify an extension.
Under the law, a panel of three Jerusalem District Court judges would hear the appeal.
One possible argument would be that "the election as a whole or voting at a particular polling station was not conducted in accordance with the law."
Another provision allows an appeal on the grounds that "votes cast for a particular list of candidates were obtained unlawfully," provided that the alleged irregularity could have affected the election results.
This requirement is particularly significant: Establishing that an election offense occurred would not, by itself, necessarily be sufficient to overturn the results. The court would also have to consider whether the violation was capable of influencing the outcome.
If an investigation by police and the Shin Bet substantiates Sohlberg's suspicions of election bribery involving a foreign state, Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara would have to consider whether to challenge the election results and how broadly such an appeal should be framed.
Once an appeal is filed, the court would examine the evidence presented and determine whether it establishes violations of election law.
If the judges conclude that offenses were committed, they would then have to decide what consequences those violations should carry.
The Knesset Elections Law provides that "the court may annul the election in its entirety or at a particular polling station and order a new election to be held on a date it determines."
The broader the violations and the greater their impact on electoral integrity, the more extensive the remedy the court could consider.
Could Israel actually hold another election?
An Israeli court has never ordered the annulment of a nationwide parliamentary election, and such an outcome appears unlikely in this case as well.
However, if investigators uncover violations of election law, such as bribery, and those offenses can be traced to a specific geographic area or individual polling stations, the Jerusalem District Court could annul the results only in those locations.
It could then order voting to be repeated at the affected polling stations or in the relevant area, rather than requiring the entire country to return to the polls.
The distinction is important because the legal response would depend not simply on whether wrongdoing occurred, but on its scope and potential effect on the election results.
In any event, Israeli law explicitly provides that an election appeal does not suspend the work of the newly elected Knesset.
An appeal under the relevant provision does not delay parliamentary proceedings, and its outcome does not undermine the legality of decisions already made by the legislature.
That means the 26th Knesset can begin its work as scheduled, even while allegations of foreign interference are investigated and any subsequent legal challenges are considered.

Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor's eastern part may develop cargo traffic to APAC markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:21:14 UTC
19:21:14 KST

KHABAROVSK, October 29. /TASS/. The eastern part of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor may develop new cargo traffic between the European part and the Asia-Pacific countries (APAC), Director of the Eastern Center for State Planning (Vostokgosplan) Mikhail Kuznetsov told TASS.
A week earlier, the European Commission unveiled the EU's new Arctic strategy, which for the first time in more than 30 years focuses on military construction. One of its key provisions is that any equipment and technologies that the EU will create for the Arctic should have both civilian and military applications. In an earlier interview with TASS, while commenting on the EU strategy, the Eastern Center for State Planning's director emphasized that Russia should turn its historical advantages in the Arctic into competitive ones due to the growing interest of European countries in developing Arctic transport routes.
"The Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor's eastern part is nowadays of particular importance for the development of transit traffic," he said. "It connects the European part with the markets of the Asia-Pacific region and opens up opportunities for structuring fundamentally new goods flows."
Among significant sections of this eastern corridor, he highlighted Chukotka, where the port of Pevek's upgrade, the development of transshipment terminals and related infrastructures will build up the navigation reliability on eastern approaches to the Northern Sea Route. As for Yakutia, the Tiksi -Nayba hub creation, new logistics corridors, and the river transport network development will ensure a close connection between the mainland areas and the Arctic coast, thus stimulating field development and increasing the Northern Supplies Program's reliability.
"The third part is Kamchatka, Primorye (the Primorsky Region)," he continued. "Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky is one of the main ports of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor's eastern part. Vladivostok and the Vostochny Port are hubs for the integration of Arctic transportation with international routes, as well as transshipment hub ports. Additionally, those are also a base for ship repairing."
He stressed that the newly-created capacities need to be synchronized with the formation of promising goods flows. This approach ensures payback and the long-term economic feasibility of route development. "Therefore, our key task is to form a stable cargo base through integrated industrial development, expansion of domestic and export transportation, and cooperation with Asian countries. This logic is the basis and ideology of a comprehensive project to develop the Arctic and the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor."
International competition in the Arctic is similar to playing Go
The increasing international competition in the Arctic is similar to the game of Go, where strategic space exploration is of key importance. "As for the international competition in the Arctic, we may compare it rather not with chess but with the game of Go: it is not the confrontation of pieces that matters, but the strategic exploration of space. We occupy a significant part of this "Arctic board". We have great advantages in the experience of operating the Northern Sea Route. Now we need to turn them into a long-term economic benefit for both Russia and for friendly, constructive-minded countries," he said.
We are talking about creating a reliable, cost-effective transport route of global importance, he added.
"The European Union's new strategy demonstrates claims to increase participation in competition and in the Northern Sea Route's development. However, realistic economic consequences of these ambitions will be largely determined by Russia's actions and by the global interest of the Eastern countries in the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor's development," the center's director said in conclusion.

Russia Cracks Down on Dating Chatbot ‘Exploited’ by Ukrainian Intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:20:24 UTC
19:20:24 KST

Both Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) and the Investigative Committee of the Ministry of Internal Affairs reported on Thursday about widespread instances of Ukrainian intelligence agencies using social media to recruit youths to carry out sabotage activities. They specifically mentioned the popular chatbot “Dayvinchik/Leo – Dating, Chat, and New Friends” on Telegram.
The FSB said it has cracked down on the activities of young people who committed or were planning to commit “sabotage and terrorist activities” under the influence of Ukrainian spies “through deception and psychological manipulation” in several regions of Russia.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the report, 56 individuals, aged between 12 and 24, who were recruited through the bot, had been arrested since July 2025. The reports added that in August and September of this year alone eight minors – aged 14 to 17 – and two adult Russian citizens – aged 19 and 24 – were detained in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and the Leningrad, Nizhny Novgorod, Omsk, Ryazan, and Sverdlovsk Regions.
How it was done
The Moscow Times, reporting on the issue, outlined the methodology being used by Ukraine to identify those susceptible to recruitment. According to the FSB, “Ukrainian intelligence officers” posed as young men seeking romantic relationships. Once they snared an “interested,” Russian user they acquired personal information including their geolocated residency, persuaded them to transfer money to pay for restaurant reservations, and to click on “phishing links.”
Ukraine Plans Draft Reform to End Street Conscription
In the “next phase” of recruitment the target was contacted by another “Ukrainian operator” posing as a member of the FSB or Rosfinmonitoring, Russia’s official financial intelligence unit. They were informed that the transferred funds had gone to the Armed Forces of Ukrainian (AFU) and the geolocation information they had provided would be used to carry out missile and drone attacks.
The FSB says the individuals were threatened with criminal prosecution and having been “deceived and intimidated” under extreme “psychological pressure” were “coerced” into committing arson or other attacks on targeted sites – ostensibly as part of anti-terrorism security checks.
Summary of the sort of Dayvinchik-inspired “terrorist” attacks
In its Telegram announcement the Investigative Committee of Russia of the Leningrad Oblast gave examples of some of the prosecutions it was involved in.
A teenage boy living in St. Petersburg who had “met a girl” on the chatbot was threatened by someone with prosecution along with his family unless he carried out arson attacks. In response the youth purchased flammable liquid with which he set fire to two gas stations, one in the city’s Pushkin district and another in the Tosno district of the Leningrad Oblast –recording his actions on video as “proof.”
The second example was that of two “underage girls,” one of whom set fire in September to a gas station on Parashutnaya Street in St. Petersburg, and the other who set police vehicles at the Marata police station on fire but was arrested on her way to a second police station.
Thirdly the committee reported that on Thursday Oct. 1 an 18-year-old resident of Vladivostok filmed himself on his phone pouring solvent into a transformer cabinet on the Leningrad section of the Moscow Railway and set it on fire. He recorded the incident on his phone and then fled. The young man was also involved in the crime through the “Diving” chatbot on the Telegram messenger. At the request of the investigation, the court has chosen a measure of restraint in the form of detention.
The Moscow Times reported in July, that the FSB charged Telegram founder Pavel Durov with “assisting terrorist activity” by failing to remove channels, chats, and bots, including the “Dayvinchik” bot, hosted on the platform and exploited by Ukrainian intelligence agencies to inspire terrorist attacks in Russia.
Closing the stable door
On its website, the FSB warned that of the 56 arrested so far, those who have reached the age of criminal responsibility (16 years) face lengthy prison terms. It warned that no Russian citizen should disclose personal information of either themselves or others, pay for services, follow links, provide geolocation information, photograph or video buildings, structures, facilities, terrain, vehicles, equipment, or people to those met on online dating sites, including “Dayvinchik” chatbot.
It said no one from FSB, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Investigative Committee of the Prosecutor’s Office, Rosfinmonitoring, the Central Bank, or the Gosuslugi (the online platform used to access state and municipal services) uses messaging apps such as Max, Telegram, WhatsApp, or other platforms.
It added they do not conduct telephone surveys, solicit the transfer of funds to unknown bank accounts, do not confirm their official status via videoconferencing, do not conduct or request others to carry out searches, investigative actions, or special operations.
The FSB said that in the event of an attempt to obtain such information or request such action, particularly for minors, communication should be immediately ended and notified to the authorities, adding this will significantly reduce the risk of further involvement in sabotage and terrorist activities. It then provided a list of telephone numbers that could be used to report such instances.

The Russians attacked the Krok do Tvaryn (Step Towards Animals) veterinary and sterilisation centre in Chernihiv, where stray cats and dogs were spayed and neutered and provided with temporary shelter on 28 October. One dog has been killed.
Source: Chernihiv City Council; animal welfare organisation UAnimals
Details: Three people were also reported injured: a 59-year-old woman, a 40-year-old woman and an 18-year-old woman. Three cats and one dog also suffered injuries.

They suffered blast injuries and shrapnel wounds of varying severity.
The veterinary centre's premises were damaged as a result of the strike. Krok do Tvaryn reported that by the evening of 28 October, they had cleared the area of glass and debris and boarded up shattered windows with plywood. The damaged cat houses, operating theatre and administrative rooms now need repairs.
Kind-hearted people took in 101 animals for temporary fostering. Severely ill and elderly pets remained at the centre for now. Krok do Tvaryn noted that anyone ready to take in those pets is welcome to do so in a few days.
Quote from the centre: "We are in touch and ready to take the animals back if things don't work out with someone! We are grateful to everyone who responded, but we know that sometimes emotions cause us to overestimate our strength. We will be grateful for feedback and further responsible treatment!"
Krok do Tvaryn has opened a fundraiser to help with the restoration of the premises.
Background: In early October in Kyiv Oblast, the Sadyba Niushanik, a bird sanctuary in Kyiv Oblast that cares for many birds and rescues dozens of orphaned storks every year, has been hit by a Russian strike. Around 190 birds were killed.

Asia-Pacific Community: From anxiety to calm: Chinese support transforms maternal, child healthcare in western Pakistan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:19:34 CST
19:19:34 KST

By Raheela Nazir
ISLAMABAD, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- For 28-year-old Gul Bano, the birth of her fourth child brought something she had not experienced during her previous three deliveries -- a sense of calm.
Two months ago, Bano arrived at a basic health unit in the provincial capital city of Balochistan to give birth. Unlike her earlier experiences, she found herself surrounded by modern medical equipment, trained health workers, and a clean, well-equipped delivery room.
"This time, I was not afraid," Bano said, recalling the day her baby was born. "Everything was available here, and the delivery was much easier than it was a few years ago."
Among the equipment that assisted her was a vein detector, which makes it easier to locate veins, particularly when an intravenous line or blood sample is needed, as well as a vacuum extractor, making it easier for her to deliver.
For Bano, however, the difference was not only about medical equipment. She said the care she received made her feel respected and comfortable.
"My husband works as a daily-wage laborer and earns less than 5 U.S. dollars a day, hindering us as a family from affording quality healthcare. Here, everything was provided to me free of charge, even the delivery gown. The bed was clean, and the equipment was ready," she said. "I did not have to worry about anything."
Her experience reflects the changes taking place in maternal and child healthcare facilities across Balochistan. Supported by the government of China, these facilities are offering safer and more dignified childbirth services for mothers.
China has been helping the government of Balochistan in upgrading maternal and child healthcare facilities, including the improvement of 100 medical facilities across the province.
The cooperation aims to strengthen medical infrastructure, provide modern equipment, and improve services for mothers and newborns, particularly in areas where access to quality healthcare has traditionally been difficult.
For women like Bano, these improvements are not simply about new machines or renovated rooms, but can mean the difference between approaching childbirth with anxiety and facing it with confidence.
"I am very happy with the treatment I received," she said. "I thank China for helping us. My fourth child arrived not only as a new member of the family, but also as a reminder of how better healthcare can change a mother's experience at one of the most important moments of her life."
Balochistan has the highest maternal and neonatal mortality rates in Pakistan, largely because 70 percent of the population lives in remote, scattered and hard-to-reach areas, Sana Furqan, a medical practitioner at the Basic Health Unit in the Hudda locality of Quetta, told Xinhua.
"For decades, access has been the biggest barrier. This China-supported project is the first large-scale targeted intervention focused entirely on mothers and children at the primary healthcare level, bringing life-saving care to the doorstep of women in remote districts," she said.
Talking about the newly equipped healthcare facilities and renovation, Furqan said the Chinese government has supplied equipment like ultrasound machines, delivery beds, baby warmers, incubators, and essential laboratory equipment.
"This upgrade is going to bring proximity, preparedness, timeliness and continuity, which is critical to prevent deaths from postpartum hemorrhage, sepsis and birth asphyxia," she said, adding that it will also provide solar solutions, ambulances, as well as training for female staff.
"The project would have transformative impacts on the basic healthcare system of Balochistan. In the medium term, we expect a measurable reduction in maternal mortality ratio and neonatal mortality rate, and a sharp decline in preventable complications," she added.
Furqan believes the assistance is not seen as charity, but as brotherhood. "The people of Balochistan, especially its mothers, will never forget that when they needed help the most, China stood with them."
In a conversation with Xinhua, Provincial Health Minister Bakht Muhammad Kakar said that Pakistan-China cooperation in the health sector is opening a new chapter in people-centered development, turning the friendship between the two countries into tangible benefits for communities.
China has one of the most advanced, efficient, and equitable healthcare systems in the world, Kakar said, underlining that despite its own vast population, the country has achieved universal maternal and child health coverage, which is an inspiration for Pakistan.
"We want to learn from China's experience in maternal health monitoring, village doctor system, and digital health records," the health minister said. ■

China to take all necessary measures should EU impose discriminatory trade restrictions: commerce ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:19:17 CST
19:19:17 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China will take all necessary measures to safeguard its interests and the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises if the European Union (EU) insists on imposing discriminatory restrictions on Chinese products, the Ministry of Commerce said Thursday.
Ministry spokesperson Huang Ling made the remarks at a regular news conference in response to media reports that the EU is considering extending the understanding reached between China and the EU on hybrid vehicle trade to other sectors such as chemicals.
Imposing artificial barriers to normal trade may violate World Trade Organization rules and would not help improve the competitiveness of EU industries. Instead, such measures would place a heavier burden on downstream industries, pushing up inflation in the EU and undermining the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains, Huang said.
Huang said the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, held recently, made positive progress and yielded a number of agreed outcomes, showing that both sides have the willingness, ability and wisdom to properly manage their economic and trade differences through dialogue and consultation.
China has repeatedly stressed that it is a partner in addressing the problems facing the EU, rather than the source of those problems, Huang said, adding that China is willing to strengthen dialogue and consultation with the EU, continue exploring solutions to each other's economic and trade concerns, and promote upward balancing and forward progress in China-EU trade.
China firmly opposes any protectionist practices involving the abuse of trade defense instruments, Huang said. ■

An estimated 1,700 deaths, with a range of 1,300 to 2,300, were linked to short-term exposure to fine particulate matter from fire smoke between July 1 and Oct. 22, according to a report commissioned by the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM).
About 1,600 deaths were attributed to transboundary smoke. Assuming fire smoke is no more toxic than other fine particles, the estimated death toll falls to about 600.
Using standard benefit-transfer methods, the deaths represent an estimated welfare loss of 8 billion ringgit, with a range of 3 billion ringgit to 15 billion ringgit.
The haze also disrupted business operations. The FMM survey of 86 member sites, including 81 manufacturers, found that 69 percent experienced some operational impact, while 26 percent reported moderate or significant disruption, mainly due to staff absenteeism. Nearly two-thirds said they had already been affected in August or September. ■

SC disposes of Mahua Moitra's plea seeking public disclosure of AIF, FPI beneficiaries

19:17:59 KST

TMC MP Mahua Moitra approached the Supreme Court seeking public disclosure of the ultimate beneficial owners of AIFs and FPIs, but the Court dismissed her plea, citing the absence of a legal framework mandating such disclosure.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday disposed of Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra's plea seeking public disclosure of the ultimate beneficial owners and portfolio holdings of alternative investment funds (AIFs), foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) and their intermediaries, saying it could not issue directions in the absence of a legal framework mandating such disclosures.A bench of Justices BV Nagarathna, R Mahadevan and DK Upadhyaya said there was no existing legal regime requiring full public disclosure of the ultimate beneficial owners of these funds. It said the court could direct the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to ensure compliance if such a framework existed, but could not issue a mandamus without one."Had there been any legal regime and the SEBI was not following it, the court can direct for compliance but in the absence of any framework or legal regime, the court cannot issue any mandamus," it observed.The bench also questioned Moitra's decision to approach the court, suggesting that she could have raised the issue in Parliament and sought a discussion on it.Advocate Prashant Bhushan, appearing for Moitra, argued that the court could direct SEBI to ensure full disclosure of the actual beneficiaries of these funds even in the absence of a specific regulatory framework. He contended that innocent investors were being "manipulated" by investors who artificially boosted the share prices of companies.
In her public interest litigation (PIL), Moitra sought greater transparency and investor awareness in India's financial markets by making details of the ultimate beneficial owners and portfolio holdings of AIFs and FPIs publicly available.The plea noted that SEBI regulates India's securities markets and oversees the operations of AIFs and FPIs as part of its mandate.

Hebron's Palestinian families face displacement, home seizures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:17:18 UTC
19:17:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Forced displacement and homes taken deepen the crisis for Hebron's Palestinian families
Abu Raji al-Jaabari never imagined he would have to leave his home in Hebron, in the occupied southern West Bank, without knowing when he could return.
The 55-year-old father of four is among thousands of Palestinians displaced by the Israeli army's military attack on Hebron, launched on Friday following the deaths of two Israeli soldiers.
The military attack includes movement restrictions, raids and arrests across the governorate, disrupting daily life and forcing families to seek shelter elsewhere.
Al-Jaabari and his family are now staying at his brother's house in another town in Hebron governorate.
While his brother has provided them with temporary shelter, the family has had to leave behind their belongings and familiar surroundings, adjusting their daily lives to circumstances they had not anticipated.
"When we left our home, we thought of nothing but reaching a place where we could feel safe. We had no time to organise ourselves or consider everything we might need," al-Jaabari told The New Arab. "We left so much behind, not knowing whether we would return in two days, a week or even longer."
The family is managing immediate needs while awaiting a chance to return. Without a clear timeline, planning is difficult, especially as al-Jaabari worries about his property and belongings left behind.
"What worries us most is that we don't know how long this situation will last," he said. "When you leave without knowing when, or if, you will return, you cannot plan for anything. You keep thinking about your home and the things you left behind, wondering whether you will find everything as you left it."
Beyond the loss of his home, al-Jaabari said displacement has separated his family from the neighbours who were part of their everyday lives.
"Our neighbours aren't just people we happen to run into; they are part of our lives," he said. "We used to look out for one another and share the details of our daily lives. When we were forced to leave, we also lost those connections and the feeling of being among our own people."
Fatima al-Natsha has also been forced to leave her home and seek refuge with relatives in Hebron. Away from her familiar surroundings, she is trying to adapt to temporary accommodation while managing her family's daily needs.
For al-Natsha, the experience has meant reorganising family life around a temporary living arrangement while remaining unable to determine when they might return. The uncertainty surrounding their home has compounded the difficulties of adjusting to their new circumstances.
"When you are in your own home, everything is familiar. You know where you keep your belongings and how to organise your day. But when you are forced to leave, you find yourself facing an entirely different life," she told TNA.
"We manage day by day, unable to plan ahead because we don't know when we'll return home or what we'll find. We worry about where we're staying, our family's needs, and the home we left behind," she said.
Al-Natsha missed the familiar routines and faces of neighbourhood life, which she can no longer take for granted.
For al-Natsha and al-Jaabari, finding temporary shelter has offered an immediate reprieve, but it has not resolved the central question hanging over their lives: when they will be able to return home.
Thousands displaced as homes are seized
The experiences of al-Jaabari and al-Natsha reflect a broader displacement crisis across Hebron governorate.
Ola al-Qawasmi, a spokesperson for Hebron Municipality, told The New Arab that municipal records showed 780 families, comprising 4,969 people, had been displaced from their homes.
Those displaced include 336 infants under the age of two, 441 people aged 60 and above, 216 pregnant or breastfeeding women, 44 people with disabilities and 312 people with chronic illnesses, al-Qawasmi said.
She added that displaced families had sought shelter with relatives, while the municipality had opened temporary shelters in preparation for further displacement as the Israeli operation and siege continued.
Finding shelter, however, has not resolved their problems. Restrictions on movement and the closure of parts of the city have made it difficult for displaced residents to return to their homes to retrieve medicines, clothing and other essential belongings.
Fears have also grown over the seizure of residential properties and ongoing demolition and land-clearing operations.
Riyad Khamis, spokesperson for the Follow-up, Support and Relief Committee, noted that Israeli forces have taken over homes and buildings in several parts of Hebron.
"Among them is a house belonging to the al-Natsheh family in the al-Zaytoun suburb, south of the city, whose owner was arrested before the property was converted into a military barracks," he said.
The seizures raise concerns that displacement could outlast the military operation itself, particularly if homes remain in military use or sustain damage that prevents residents from returning.
The Palestinian Prisoners' Club said that the Israeli army arrested about 85 people, including a young woman, since the operation began in the governorate.
It added that more than 250 people have been detained and subjected to field interrogations.
For families with children, older people and sick relatives, displacement has created urgent needs for medicines, healthcare and basic necessities, alongside the uncertainty over when they might return.
Closures cripple Hebron's economy
The consequences of the Israeli military operation extend beyond displaced households to Hebron's economy, a major centre of Palestinian industry, commerce and production.
Movement restrictions have prevented workers from reaching their jobs and disrupted the transport of goods, deepening financial pressures on businesses and households.
Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari told TNA that restrictions shut factories and other businesses. Damage to water and sewage networks worsened living conditions and hindered recovery.
Ramallah-based political analyst Ahmed Rafiq Awad told TNA that the operation risked imposing lasting changes on Hebron, pointing to the displacement of residents and the seizure of homes, some of which have been converted into military positions.
He said these measures threaten to fragment neighbourhoods by separating residents from their homes and the social networks on which they rely.
"The factory closures and disrupted trade in Hebron, a major centre of Palestinian economic activity, are adding to the economic pressures facing the wider Palestinian economy," he added.
For displaced Palestinian families, the immediate priority is meeting their daily needs, but the future remains uncertain, particular when or even if they'll return to their homes in Hebron.

Med-IREN project studies floods, heat stress with Cyprus serving as a climate-resilience model
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:16:41 CET
19:16:41 KST

Monitoring the effects of intense
urban flooding and heatwaves to collect data that can inform the
design of nature-based solutions to address climate risks is the
aim of the activities carried out by the European Med-IREN
project in Larnaca, Cyprus.
                                    
Here the Cyprus Energy Agency, a partner in the initiative, is
working in two areas identified as particularly exposed to
climate risks: the Kalo Chorio river in the Kamares area, which
is at risk of flooding, and the Agioi Anargiroi social housing
neighbourhood, which is affected by urban heat stress.
                                    
Last week, the Cypriot city hosted a meeting of the partners of
the Med-IREN European cooperation project, which combines
nature-based expertise with engineering developments to protect
critical infrastructure from the impacts of climate change. The
meeting provided an opportunity to review the latest
developments in the project's activities in the area.
                                    
In Kamares, a flow meter will be installed in the river to
collect data on water flow during rainfall events. This
information will help improve understanding of runoff conditions
and identify the most significant rainfall and flooding events.
                                    
In the Agioi Anargiroi neighbourhood, the project will carry out
a series of measurements to map heat stress. Several instruments
will be used, including a tripod-mounted thermal comfort
monitoring device, a drone equipped with a thermal camera, and a
portable device to measure heat stress on people. The data
collected will be combined to provide a comprehensive picture of
heat conditions across the neighbourhood.
                                    
Based on the data gathered, Med-IREN aims to identify the
nature-based solutions best suited to different situations to
address the risks posed by climate change. In Larnaca, potential
options include permeable materials and rain gardens to promote
water infiltration, as well as additional vegetation and green
corridors to provide shade and reduce local temperatures.
                                    
The activities carried out in the Cypriot city could also
provide examples for other Mediterranean cities facing similar
challenges, including extreme heat, flooding, rapid urbanisation
and a shortage of green spaces.

ECB President Lagarde resigns effective Feb 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:16:31 UTC
19:16:31 KST

European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde resigns after months of speculation
- Christine Lagarde has resigned as ECB president, ending months of speculation. She will step down on Feb 7 2027, giving EU leaders time to choose a successor.
- Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos are seen as frontrunners. Her exit comes before the French presidential election, where Marine Le Pen is currently favoured.
- The ECB faces high inflation, rising bond yields and weak growth. It is expected to keep rates at 2.5% and may signal another rise in December.
AI generated
FRANKFURT – The European Central Bank (ECB) president Christine Lagarde announced her resignation on Oct 29, ending months of speculation about her future at a complex juncture for Europe and the bank.
Lagarde will step down on Feb 7, giving current European Union leaders time to pick a successor well before a French presidential election that polls show far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favourite to win.
The move comes as the ECB battles inflation risks from an Iran-driven oil shock while a sharp rise in bond yields, especially in France, threatens to dampen growth.
“I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future,” Lagarde said in a short video shared on social media.
A source with direct knowledge of the matter said Lagarde had resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally. As ECB president, she was expected to remain neutral to safeguard the institution’s independence.
European Council President Antonio Costa said in a statement the process to find a successor for Lagarde would begin immediately. The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are widely seen as front runners.
“The rumoured successors are both very competent, well established central bankers, so for markets, it won’t matter too much,” Piet Haines Christiansen, an economist at Danske Bank, said.
Financial markets did not move much after the announcement, with some analysts noting the ECB had by now built a reputation that outlived any of its leaders.
“The ECB is now quite well established, the market is familiar with the way it operates,” Goldman Sachs’ head of fixed income macro investing Simon Dangoor said. “Our view is that institutional behaviour is likely to outlast Lagarde, and be quite similar, whoever takes over.”
Lagarde’s term was scheduled to run until the end of October 2027, but speculation about an early departure had been mounting for months, with the World Economic Forum seen as a likely destination.
Rate hikes and bond turmoil
The ECB is in the middle of a rate-hiking cycle aimed at preventing an oil-price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into other prices and wages.
But it must also contend with a surge in government bond yields – especially in debt-laden France – that has pushed up borrowing costs for households and businesses and which Lagarde has said will curb growth and inflation.
Caught between persistent inflation fuelled by a renewed surge in energy costs and deteriorating financing conditions, the ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Oct 29 while signalling that another increase, potentially as soon as December, remains likely.
“There is likely a low bar to another hike in December, given the likelihood of another upward revision of the ECB’s inflation forecast due to higher energy prices,” Oliver Rakau at Oxford Economics said.
The ECB is due to announce its interest rate decision at 9.15pm on Oct 29, followed by Lagarde’s regular press conference at 9.45pm.
Money markets are currently pricing another three rate increases from the ECB by the end of 2027, which would take the deposit rate to 3.25%, a level that is widely seen as restricting economic growth.
French turmoil in focus but no action
The more immediate challenge for policymakers may be turmoil in bond markets.
A global rise in yields, fuelled by stronger growth expectations, higher debt issuance and massive investment linked to artificial intelligence, is pushing up borrowing costs for governments, households and businesses alike.
In France, investors have become increasingly uneasy about the country’s growing debt burden and uncertain fiscal outlook following the 2026 elections. Concerns have been amplified by suggestions from parts of the political left that debt held by the ECB could be written off.
The result has been a sharp increase in French borrowing costs. France is now paying some of the highest yields in a quarter-century to raise money on bond markets, while the premium investors demand to hold French debt over benchmark German bonds is larger than for any other euro zone country.
That has fuelled speculation that the ECB might be forced to respond, if only verbally for now.
“They’ve typically come up with a new tool that’s customised for that specific set of circumstances,” said Dangoor at Goldman Sachs.
The ECB’s first line of defence would probably be flexible reinvestment of proceeds from bonds acquired during its vast asset-purchase programmes of the previous decade.
Beyond that, it could activate its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument, a scheme designed to counter what policymakers deem unjustified market pressure. REUTERS

I Did Push-Ups With Snap’s Chunky AR Glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

I hadn’t expected to be doing augmented reality push-ups in the middle of the mall. Yet there I was, wearing bulky Snap Specs while facing the ground.
The Lens (what Snap calls apps on its augmented reality headset) is called Thirty Ups. It is in Halloween mode now, so when I look down, a virtual cartoon Jack-o’-lantern sits right next to where I’m supposed to start working out. I’m not trying to get jacked right now, but my goal is to see if these gigantic smart glasses will fall off when I’m staring straight down and moving up and down.
I get into position and start my workout. When I go down and back up, a little virtual circle on the ground below me starts counting up. I don’t get to 30 push-ups. I’m surrounded by people, many of whom are now staring at me, and it feels too hot outside to keep going without feeling gross. I get in 12 reps before giving up. The glasses only count 11 because it tells me I “skipped” one. Great.
The nearby Snap representative is thrilled. “You’re the first person who’s tried that one,” he says. I’m also pleasantly surprised. These glasses seem huge, but they stayed on my face just fine.
Snap announced its Specs in June. They cost $2,195 and will start to ship in the coming weeks. It took a few months for Snap to share what actual features would be available on the glasses
WIRED’s Julian Chokkattu and I both tried out Snap’s Specs last week. He got a dedicated demo with the company. I was offered one, too, but instead I happened to stumble upon the Specs First Look demo at the Westfield Century City shopping center in Los Angeles. The space has been here for just a couple of weeks.
It was a warm Sunday afternoon, and a steady stream of people came through the mall’s demo zone. Snap reps handed out Specs to anyone curious enough to register and hang out. Kids were running around, and the glasses looked especially large on their faces. When people left the demo, they got a free cup of ice cream with a small, Specs-shaped chocolate cookie.
The Specs had a dozen or so Lenses available for testing. Aside from the push-ups, the Specs let you finger paint in midair, see navigation directions overlaid on the real world, or engage with the physical environment by drawing on a notepad or analyzing text in a print book. They also have some sporty features, like one that allegedly helps with golf and another through a partnership with the NBA that guides you through shooting hoops.
You may have noticed that the glasses look pretty chunky. That’s true, but I was pleasantly surprised by how lightweight they felt and how well they stayed put. (The glasses come in two sizes, so if the small is too tight, try the larger model.) Another surprise was how well the virtual digital elements held up in bright light. I made a point of walking into direct sunlight to test out the screen. With the brightness turned all the way up, the onscreen elements were still visible. The glasses had automatically switched into “sunglasses mode” and dimmed to block the sun. The Snap rep said the lenses protect the eyes from UV rays at all times.
The problem, though, is that Snap is really trying to make the case that these glasses—or at least future, smaller iterations—are the holy grail of consumer tech. But I still don’t care to wear them in public. Walking around with the AR elements on can be distracting. Even if you turn it all off, the waveguides on the lenses still have a rainbow shimmer in your vision as you move. I wouldn’t want to wear these while driving or even walking when I really need to see where I'm going. At one point in the demo, I had to dodge a kid wearing a pair of Specs who was wildly swinging punches at something on the screen only he could see.
Most of the device features are controlled with your hands, like pinching two fingers together to open a lens or move something around. You can play Beat Saber-esque games by moving your hands around. But the controls can be finicky, and I found myself clawing at the air repeatedly to move or open something. Chokkattu tried writing in Google Docs—a demo showing the Specs as a computer you can work with anywhere—but the connected Bluetooth keyboard had a severe input lag, making typing a chore.
It also feels odd that some Specs features really just feel like advertising. A Harry Potter spell-casting experience is a fun idea, but really it just comes across as an ad for the upcoming HBO show. The Specs also have a shopping feature which lets you browse stores online. It’s a reminder that one day your augmented vision will be bombarded with pop-up ads.
I have a hard time imagining who these glasses are for. Given the price, it’s clearly aimed at developers and early adopters. But I tried the developer version of the Specs in 2024. The new glasses are much more comfortable and slightly less chonky, but the software hasn't changed much since then. Snap has shown off the same finger painting demo every time I’ve tried them, and every time it works until it doesn’t. The Specs are interesting but lack a killer feature, and Meta and Xreal both have more polished mixed-reality glasses that cost less. That’s going to make Specs a hard sell.
“We see consumer adoption as a process—the hardware, software, available experiences and price all need to develop together,” a Snap representative wrote in a statement to WIRED. “Specs bring computing into the world without pulling you out of it.”
For now, Snap’s most compelling pitch might be the free ice cream.

Russia's human rights chief Yana Lantratova said Thursday that she was traveling with a team of American journalists to the occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky as Moscow and Kyiv enforce a temporary ceasefire in the area to allow for evacuations and the delivery of humanitarian supplies to locals.
Lantratova said the four journalists were from the U.S. conservative outlet Newsmax. Her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets, was also traveling to the area around Oleshky, she added.
"We have been preparing this mission since May, thoroughly planning every stage, including the preparation of the humanitarian convoy," Lantratova wrote in a post on Telegram.
The Kremlin said that the presence of American reporters in Oleshky was "unimportant." Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told state media that "what's important to me is that Russian journalists will be there."
Neither Russia nor Ukraine has reported any violations of the ceasefire, which was brokered by the Trump administration and began on Tuesday.
Russia took control of Oleshky in the early days of its 2022 invasion. Residents of the town have faced regular shelling, as well as acute shortages of food and medicine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that demining efforts were underway in Oleshky, according to the Interfax news agency.
"We hope that today or tomorrow residents will be able to receive humanitarian aid safely and without obstruction, and that those wishing to leave will be able to do so," Peskov was quoted as saying.
The ceasefire in Oleshky also applies to its surrounding areas in the wider Kherson region.
Reuters contributed reporting.

At the historic Merion Cricket Club in Haverford, the Consul General of Italy in Philadelphia, Nico Frandi, delivered a speech dedicated to the deep bond that unites Italy and the United States. In particular, the consul referred to the American Northeast and the territory of the consular district: a solid bridge built over more than three centuries of exploration, a fruitful exchange of ideas, goods, and strategic and sector-specific alliances, but, above all, through the active contribution of the great Italian migration. The occasion also served as an opportunity to review the Consulate’s achievements over the past year, including integrated promotion and cultural and economic diplomacy, in support of Italy’s extensive presence and the many examples of excellence from the Bel Paese across this vast territory of the United States.

Bolsonaro claims to be Brazil's rightful leader after escape to US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:13:00 UTC
19:13:00 KST

Brazil’s defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro insisted Wednesday that he was the country’s rightful leader after fleeing to the United States in self-imposed exile.
His defiance on arrival in Florida signaled continued upheaval for Brazil, where leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a dramatic runoff election Sunday.
"I am the elected president and the criminals who stole Brazil's election are part of a criminal organization that has established a tyranny," Bolsonaro said in a statement published on his X account, denouncing "electoral fraud."
"I will lead the opposition from here," he said. In a subsequent statement, he revised his claim, saying he is the "leader," rather than "president."
Bolsonaro, 45, touched down earlier Wednesday on a private jet at Opa-Locka Executive Airport near Miami.
Rogerio Marinho, the leader of Bolsonaro's Liberal Party in the Senate, told reporters in Brasilia that he was in "solidarity" with the former candidate, describing him as a "political exile."
However, he distanced himself from Bolsonaro's statement and refused to back up Bolsonaro's claims of electoral fraud.
"The Liberal Party cannot make that claim," he said. "There is no evidence of that."
Flavio Bolsonaro "is an expression of the right in Brazil today ... he calls himself a leader and it's true: he's a leader," Marinho told reporters.
U.S. President Donald Trump's hard-right administration has strong links to Bolsonaro and his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest in Brazil after attempting to overturn his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
Trump reiterated his view that Brazil's election was "very strange" but told reporters he "won't get involved" in Flavio Bolsonaro's claim to the presidency.
Details of how Bolsonaro, accompanied by his wife and daughters, reached the United States are still emerging.
He is under investigation in his home country over alleged corruption and money laundering. With his current parliamentary immunity about to expire, he was ordered to surrender his passports but left anyway, reaching the United States via Argentina and Ecuador.
A police source told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, but the senator has also held Italian nationality since 2023, according to Italian documents seen by AFP.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the Bolsonaro family members were inspected and cleared "with applicable immigration laws and procedures."
The travel ban was issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who led the case against Bolsonaro's father and is fiercely criticized by the Brazilian right.
Lula, who won Sunday's election with 51.8% of the vote, called Bolsonaro's departure a "shameful" act.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration Tuesday.
But Brazilian police issued a statement Wednesday saying that he was not considered a fugitive.
There was controversy in neighboring Argentina, where opposition lawmakers demanded to know how Bolsonaro had managed to transit through the country.
While Argentinian authorities said he was carrying valid travel documents, officials have asked Cabinet chief Diego Santilli to provide details to Parliament, according to opposition lawmaker Agustin Rossi.
The most high-profile fraud case against Bolsonaro in Brazil centers on the unreleased biopic "Dark Horse," starring U.S. actor Jim Caviezel as Flavio's father, Jair.
In May, the outlet Intercept Brasil revealed audio recordings in which Flavio Bolsonaro negotiated approximately $24 million to finance the film with banker Daniel Vorcaro, who is jailed over one of Brazil's biggest fraud cases.
Before the leak, Flavio Bolsonaro had denied knowing Vorcaro or that the banker had financed the movie.
In July, the Supreme Court ordered a probe into the film's financing and whether it involved corruption, money laundering or the illegal movement of currency.
Bolsonaro acknowledged Vorcaro had funded the film but insisted it was a private business deal that was "completely legal."

What does home mean to Arab artists at Paris Art Week?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:12:01 UTC
19:12:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Where is home? Arab artists answered 'here too' at Paris Art Week 2026
"When you are a kid who grows up in a country at war, you have a problem of feeling that you belong," says Palestinian artist Aysha E Arar in the courtyard of the Monnaie de Paris, home of the art fair Asia NOW, a key fixture of Paris Art Week. "You don't feel you have a home."
The artist is still catching her breath after singing at full lung capacity in an improvised performance in the Monnaie courtyard. She was just as shaken as the viewers who witnessed the performance and vibrated with her: "I felt I had to do it, so I did it, from my heart."
The artist, who also has a show at the Paris gallery sans titre, sang verses from The Horse of Hope, a poem she wrote calling for chains and borders to be broken. "When I sing, I feel it all: the anger, the sadness, the love," she added.
This year's Paris Art Week, which ran from 19 to 25 October, unfolded amid ongoing protests and unrest, largely driven by student demonstrations over poor school conditions, teacher shortages, and overcrowded classrooms.
With the city in turmoil, one might have expected this year's edition to be postponed or cancelled. Instead, it went ahead, even as the situation on the streets continued to escalate.
Arab visibility explored
As expected, Arab artists featured prominently across several fairs, including MENART, dedicated to modern and contemporary art from the Middle East and North Africa, and AKAA, which focuses on African art. They were also represented at Asia NOW and Art Basel Paris, which closed early due to protests.
Beyond the art fairs, notable solo exhibitions by artists from the Middle East and North Africa were also on display at the Institut du Monde Arabe, the Palais de Tokyo, the Fondation Cartier and the Fondation Louis Vuitton.
Although many of these spaces are emblematic of the inextricable link between capitalism and art, it still mattered that Arab artists had the opportunity to exhibit their work in them.
This is particularly true in France, where, according to the Institut national de la statistique et des études économiques (INSEE), around 2.1 million immigrants were born in the Maghreb, alongside a further 2.4 million people whose parents immigrated from the region, not including the third generation. Together, that amounts to roughly one person in 15.
Despite this significant presence, Arabs remain underrepresented in French public life. In the media, Arabs barely exist.
People perceived as non-white accounted for about 15 percent of those seen on French television between 2013 and 2023, according to the broadcast regulator Arcom, while making up a quarter of those shown in a negative light in news and documentary programmes.
On the streets, they are watched closely. In the Défenseur des droits’ latest survey, young men perceived as Arab, North African or Black were four times more likely than the rest of the population to be stopped for an identity check, and 12 times more likely to be searched, frisked, taken to a police station or ordered to move on.
Palestine, meanwhile, remains a country whose name seems increasingly difficult for French media to say out loud, even after France recognised the State of Palestine in September 2025.
'Where is home?'
Against this backdrop, MENART's focus on home felt particularly timely this year.
Paris remains, de facto, one of Europe's most multicultural capitals. As Arab artists filled booths, walls and courtyards across the city, they helped shift the narrative towards one in which Paris could also be a home. Many came from countries ravaged by war, continuing a long history of artists finding a place in the French capital.
As MENART's founder, Laure d'Hauteville, put it, the question of home extends beyond geography. It was precisely for this reason that she asked around 100 artists from 18 countries across the Levant, the Gulf and the Maghreb, as well as their diasporas, ‘Where is home?’, while maintaining a balance between women and men.
For Aysha E Arar, the question of belonging is also deeply personal. Born in 1993 in Jaljulia, her family history traces back to 1948.
One grandfather fled to the West Bank and ended up with Palestinian papers; the other refused to leave his house and ended up with Israeli citizenship, which she inherited.
"I am Arab-Israeli, but I define myself as Palestinian," she said. "When I travel, however, my passport is Israeli, and that is very confusing," she noted.
As for MENART's presentation of ‘home’, it was described as "neither a place nor a time, but a sum of emotions, layers, tensions".
That understanding showed in the fair's range of galleries, with strong representation from the Gulf, including Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Muscat.
Dubai's Nasij gave a solo booth to Palestinian-Canadian artist Samar Hejazi, whose thread installation was titled Maw6ini, meaning ‘my homeland’.
Beyond the commercial art market, the fair described itself as "a true space for reflection and transmission."
Before the closing weekend, each fair drew its own map: the Middle East and North Africa at MENART, West Asia at Asia NOW, and Africa and its diasporas at AKAA. The market matters: a booth at Art Basel Paris is precisely how an artist from Tunis or Jeddah ends up in a Paris collection, a museum's acquisitions list, or a curator's notebook.
At the Grand Palais, Selma Feriani, director of what many consider Tunisia's leading gallery on the international art scene, was having a good fair.
"To be honest, I don't think the climate is affecting the fair," she said. She added that her artists had been "extremely well received," with works placed in both private and institutional collections.
For Selma, showing at Art Basel Paris also means maintaining cultural ties between Tunisia and France while bringing wider attention to artists from the region.
"Tunis and France have a direct link, and it’s important for us to be here and to represent our artists, but also represent artists from North Africa and the Global South," she said.
That commitment to representing different generations and artistic traditions also shaped Selma's gallery programme.
She said she tried “to bring as many artists as possible” to reflect the gallery’s programme and its DNA.
Each year, she also includes a modernist artist from one of North Africa’s different artistic schools, including the Casablanca School.
This year, the gallery displayed work by Baya, the Algerian painter, alongside contemporary pieces.
A short distance away, near Beirut-based gallery Marfa, Saudi gallery ATHR presented a similarly broad view of the region’s artistic landscape, bringing together artists from different generations.
Founded in Jeddah in 2009 and now also operating in Riyadh and AlUla, the gallery presented a 1991 work by Abdulrahman AlSoliman, born in Al-Hasa in 1954 and the first president of the Saudi Society for Fine Arts.
Alongside Abdulrahman’s work, ATHR showcased artists exploring identity and everyday cultural references in different ways.
The booth featured Palestinian-Saudi conceptual artist Ayman Yossri Daydban, who prints old Egyptian film posters and proverbs on tissue boxes, and Mohammad Alfaraj’s The Storyteller (2016), shown two weeks after his solo exhibition opened at the Fondation Louis Vuitton.
The exhibition also represented Sarah Abu Abdallah, Sara Abdu, and Emirati artist Rami Farook.
Curating perceptions
In the Gulf’s version of West Asia, the story is one of growth, and nobody tells it more insistently than Saudi Arabia.
For a decade, the country has presented itself as a safe, wealthy place where the state can build an art ecosystem from the top down: AlUla, the Diriyah biennials, residencies and Saudi artists exhibiting in Western institutions.
Collaborations with French public and private institutions are frequent. One of the clearest examples is Villa Hegra in AlUla, Saudi Arabia, part of a network of cultural institutions, much like Villa Medici in Rome, that represents France abroad.
Villa Hegra had its own exhibition at Asia NOW. Curator Basmah Felemban presented Tables Around: Six Proposals from Saudi Arabia with Gaël Charbau, her fellow artistic director at Villa Hegra.
The exhibition featured new commissions by seven Saudi women artists, centred on the table, where families and institutions talk through the changes Saudi Arabia is experiencing.
You could smell Reem Al Nasser’s piece: fresh jasmine woven using the technique employed for bridal crowns in southern Saudi Arabia, which, Basmah told The New Arab, is also used for bullets.
Zahra Bundakji made sculptures of the foil-wrapped chocolate trays left in Saudi living rooms until their contents became inedible.
Meanwhile, Reem Ali’s Her Mental Tools fitted a table fan with kitchen-knife blades, challenging the idea that a woman at home lives in a small world.
When asked whether the exhibition aimed to challenge a particular image of Saudi Arabia among French audiences, Basmah said the intention had not necessarily been to tailor the show to French eyes.
"Who am I to curate perceptions of Saudi?" she said.
And yet few understand the importance of soft power better than the Saudis, particularly after 10 October, when a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthis hit the domestic terminal of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
The airport was struck four times in five days and shut down; Dammam’s airport was hit too. Of Basmah’s seven artists, "only four were able to come through the airports that are open."
The picture of a Gulf state insulated from the wars around it, steadily building a state-led art scene, no longer holds.
In this context, Basmah was practical.
"At the end of the day, who cares about an exhibition? What’s most important is your safety and your family," she shared.
The Sumerians at the tailor
The question of home took a different turn at OFFSCREEN, the moving-image fair that had taken over the Chapelle Saint-Louis de la Salpêtrière.
There, Iraqi artist Adel Abidin approached migration and identity through the absurdity of imagining an ancient civilisation confronted with the present.
During Adel’s conversation with The New Arab, a helicopter passed overhead. It was unclear whether it was there for the hospital next door or formed part of the extensive surveillance operation by the French police.
For Adel, the question of home is also personal. Under Saddam Hussein, he could not get into art school, so he left to pursue a master’s degree in Helsinki in December 2000.
"Then I got accepted, and George Bush attacked Baghdad," he said, but he stayed, and after about 26 years, the city had become his home.
He added that home is a place where he can stay and express himself freely.
Inside, NIKA Project Space showed an installation centred on his video Unfitted (2024), which began as a joke between friends about Iraq.
"If the Sumerians will come now, and they will see the situation, they will go back and destroy their civilisation and never think of doing it," he said.
Adel took the figures from the Standard of Ur, the Sumerian artefact depicting scenes of war and peace in the British Museum, and made them "do as everybody is doing nowadays, migrating and going to a tailor, which is the touch of sarcasm here, to change their identities or their outfit."
The video never showed them dressed. "So that’s why the video is called Unfitted," he said.
On the protests, Adel was unequivocal.
"I think it’s super cool that people have the right to demonstrate and express their feelings. I’m against destruction, against burning and stealing and looting," he explained.
He believes in the power of art, even if, as he said, "It doesn’t have the magic wand," adding that every little piece matters.
Articulating the malaise
From Adel’s sardonic take on migration, the week’s highlights turned to a more intimate unease at the Palais de Tokyo.
One of the most moving exhibitions is Lebanese artist Ali Cherri’s Today is OK, running until 14 February 2027.
The Franco-Lebanese artist built the exhibition around his film La Sentinelle, which follows a French soldier through the night of 14 July, France's national holiday.
Sculptures within an immersive installation carried the film into the galleries: the guard, the preparation for conflict and what war does to bodies.
In the short film, the soldier, LeFleur, meaning ‘the flower’, is inhabited by a malaise he cannot quite name, not even when the psychiatrist at the infirmary asks him why he wants to shoot himself in the mouth.
"Just like that," he said. "Or no particular reason."
The context in which Art Week unfolded makes it hard not to think of the larger, collective malaise that twists the guts of the French people and translates into millions of slogans and battles to fight for.
Ultimately, the rage in the streets is a symptom that something is not working, and has not been working for a very long time.
The unrest had been building since late September, when lycée students across France began blockading their schools over overcrowded classes, unreplaced teachers, unsafe buildings and Parcoursup, the discriminatory university admissions platform.
Saturday 17 October marked a peak in the turmoil, as the student movement merged with protests against the cost of living, drawing around 550,000 people across France, including 110,000 in Paris.
The unrest continued the following day, as shops in Les Halles were looted, shopfront windows smashed, bins and bicycles thrown around, and cars and bikes set on fire in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Limoges.
By Monday, around 3,000 businesses had been damaged or looted, and more than 2,400 people had been arrested.
In Ali’s film, which explores Eros and Thanatos in a disturbing way, the protagonist, Sergeant LeFleur, finds a moment of comfort in a queer performer's singing, whose voice expresses rage, sadness, love, and pain.
It was the perfect mirror to Aysha E Arar’s heartfelt singing.
Just as in the streets of Paris, love, rage, violence and reason were all mixed together, all there, all demanding change.
[Cover photo: Adel Abidin’s 'Abandoned Relic', presented by NIKA Project Space at OFFSCREEN Paris 2026, reinterprets the ancient Standard of Ur, reflecting on displacement, abandoned civilisations and the negotiation of new identities. Photo credit: Ivan Erofeev.]

KYIV – A Russian drone slammed into a busy platform at a railway station in Ukraine’s Dnipro on Oct 29, killing at least 14 people in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called a “horrific” attack that demands a response from Kyiv’s allies.
The strike came as Ukraine and Russia strive to uphold a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky – under Russian occupation since 2022, and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages.
The truce was holding into its third day, both countries said, with the Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets announcing that he had “set out with the Ukrainian delegation towards Oleshky” through Belarus and Russia.
But elsewhere, Moscow continued to pummel Ukraine.
The strike at the Dnipro train station hit a platform “where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing”, Zelensky said.
By early afternoon on Oct 29, Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha said the death toll from the strike had risen to 14.
Another 14 had been wounded, he said, adding that six of them were in severe condition after suffering “multiple shrapnel wounds”, including an 11-year-old boy and a man who had “both legs amputated”.
Zelensky slammed the attack as “horrific” and insisted that “sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues”.
Images released by Ukrainian emergency services showed bodies on the platform, rescuers helping victims to safety, and two burnt-out passenger trains with their windows shattered.
French President Emmanuel Macron reacted with outrage to the attack, stressing the need for “far more than a localised ceasefire” like the one in Oleshky.
“It is intolerable that Russia continues to reject all proposals to this end, choosing instead to pursue escalation and target civilians,” he said on X.
Zelensky slams US sanctions relief for Russia
Russia has fired drones on trains across Ukraine since the first days of its 2022 invasion – destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing several railway workers.
Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted three jet-powered drones in a daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.
In the aftermath of the attack, Zelensky refreshed his criticism of a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to ease some sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel onto global markets.
“How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and the energy sector, instead of de-escalating,” he asked.
At least six others were killed across Ukraine in separate Russian attacks, according to local officials.
Two teenage girls killed in strike north of Kyiv
A strike on the city centre of Chernihiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded nearly two dozen others, including four children, the head of the city’s military administration, Dmytro Bryzhynsky, said.
A drone also slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing three and wounding several – including a six-year-old – the local governor said.
Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.
The Kremlin earlier this week vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under US mediation.
Zelensky said on Oct 28 it would be a “huge success” if the local ceasefire in Oleshky – brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump – allowed for the evacuation of stranded citizens.
Locals trapped there have resorted to hunting and eating pigeons in recent months, former residents in touch with those in the city told AFP.
Russia and Ukraine are to meet in November with US envoys, to discuss ways to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, with no firm dates set for the talks yet.
Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.
Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.
Ukraine and its allies say ceding ground to Moscow would be tantamount to a capitulation and leave Kyiv vulnerable to future Russian attacks. REUTERS

Bird flu outbreaks prompt national indoor shelter order
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Three recent outbreaks of bird flu have led agriculture secretary Silvio Erkens to order farmers to keep their poultry indoors.
Two of the outbreaks occurred in Groningen and one in Noord-Holland. Wild birds, which are currently migrating south, have also been found to carry the disease.
“It is important to limit contact between kept birds and potentially infected wild birds as much as possible,” Erkens told broadcaster NOS. “That way we are doing everything we can to prevent new outbreaks.”
Bird hobbyists don’t have to comply with the order, but they must shield their birds in aviaries or other shelters. All non-essential visitors are also banned from places where birds are kept.
Consumers
While poultry farmers are hard-hit, the price and availability of poultry have remained relatively stable.
“The prices have been high enough for the past couple of months, so they are stable for now,” says Babak Sadeghi, who owns Chris Kip in Amsterdam’s Albert Cuyp Market. “But increased transport and petrol prices have affected suppliers and deliveries.”
Bird flu has also been found in Denmark, Germany, the United Kingdom and other places.
Erkens is pushing for mandatory vaccinations of egg-laying hens against bird flu.
