‘Restored nature hits record 252 mln hectares, but still off target’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:09:18 UTC
19:09:18 KST

A helicopter from Brazil's environmental agency flies over an area of the Amazon rainforest during a wildfire-fighting operation in Autazes, Amazonas state, Brazil, Oct. 15, 2026. (AP File Photo)
Countries are restoring about 252 million hectares of nature, a record level according to a United Nations report published on Oct. 29, but this still falls short of global 2030 targets.
"This report captures the largest documented restoration effort in history," said Doreen Robinson at the U.N. Environment Program. The restored area is equivalent to the size of Argentina or Algeria.
But the report estimates the pace of restoration efforts must "triple" to meet the 2030 target of one billion, and funding will need to increase sharply, particularly from the private sector.
Nature restoration efforts recorded in 149 countries have mostly taken place on land, with 232 million hectares involved, compared with 11 million hectares of inland waters and 5.7 million hectares of marine and coastal waters.
This "lags far behind ambition in both freshwater [inland water] and marine and coastal ecosystems, yet these ecosystems are degrading at the highest rates," the report warned.
As part of the U.N. Decade on Ecosystem Restoration from 2021 to 2030, and an international agreement adopted in 2022 known as the Kunming-Montreal framework, states have committed to taking action to halt biodiversity loss and protect the planet.
In terms of restoration on land, China is far ahead of other regions, with 137 million hectares, followed by Mongolia, Kazakhstan and Ethiopia.

In Pompeii, a woman's wardrobe resurfaces with beauty items and jewels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:08:38 UTC
19:08:38 KST

Jewels, coins, tools and cosmetics: a cupboard in Cornelius Maximus's house brings to life the daily lives of Pompeii's women before Vesuvius erupted in AD 79.
The wardrobe of a woman from ancient Pompeii has come to light again. Thanks to the work of archaeologists it has been possible to recover the interior of a cabinet that held everyday items in house IX 11, 7, or the house of Cornelius Maximus, in the central area of the city buried by Vesuvius.
Looking at these objects, it is almost as if we can conjure up the life of a woman of Pompeii before the site was destroyed in AD 79. Among the finds are make-up tools(tweezers, a spatula for mixing pigments), a glass balsamarium, a perfume burner to fill the home with pleasant fragrances, a bronze lamp, alongside lead weights, probably used for a commercial activity and kept in a small wooden box of which only faint traces remain.
What was in the Pompeian woman's wardrobe
Vases and pots in bronze, glass and ceramic were also found: everyday household objects, but perhaps also heavy with memories, as in the case of an elegant little jug decorated with pine-scale motifs. There is also a necklace composed of at least 24 miniature objectsin faïence, bone, glass paste and rock crystal, all pierced for suspension and representing deities (Bes and Mercury can be identified), feet and hands, pine cones and bunches of grapes.
According to experts, such necklaces were sometimes regarded as "magical" objects used in spells and potions; in reality they are what are known as crepundia, literally 'rattles': necklaces with amulets that were given to children to protect them, but also so that they could be heard when they moved.
It was not unusual for adults to keep them too, often in small boxes or, as in this case, in cloth bags inside wardrobes, apparently as keepsakes of a childhood of which little else remained. The Roman world was characterised by a high degree of geographic mobility at all levels, from slaves to wealthy merchants, so that many people found themselves living far from relatives and parents and from the places of their childhood.
The small treasure hidden in the wardrobe
Another secret kept in the wardrobe unearthed in the excavation is a small hoard of coins: there are 38 of them, all bronze, preserved in a "cistella", a small container made of plant material using basketry techniques, the remains of which were analysed after being recovered during the dig. The presence of the coins in particular suggests that the owner or owners did not have time to recover the objects of value, whether economic or emotional.
If they were in the city at the time of the catastrophe, they will have tried to flee. If they managed to escape, they would not have returned to dig under the floors for their possessions, unlike others whose efforts have left traces revealed by recent excavations.
But perhaps they did not succeed and may be among those who, as the historian Tacitus recalls, died without heirs and whose property would have been used for the refounding of Pompeii, which ultimately never took place. These are questions destined to remain open.
The human dimension of Pompeii's past pieced back together
"Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art; it is also somewhere where the most ordinary objects restore the human dimension of the past. The value of this discovery lies in the possibility of reading together the different traces of a life: personal habits, work, memories," says the director of the Archaeological Park, Gabriel Zuchtriegel.
"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of the person who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their everyday life," the director adds.
What we know about the House of Cornelius Maximus
The excavation has helped clarify some aspects of the house in which the wardrobe was found. The facade of the dwelling, tentatively attributed to a figure named Cornelius Maximus on the basis of inscriptions now no longer visible, had already been excavated in 1912. Only now, however, has part of the rooms behind it been investigated, as part of the major restoration and accessibility project for the adjacent Insula dei Casti Amanti.
Although our knowledge of the house remains partial, some highly interesting data have emerged: on the one hand, the refined Fourth Style wall paintings in the room with the wardrobe, attributable to the workshop on Via di Castricio, indicate a certain standard of living, in line with the central position of the house, which overlooks one of the main arteries of the ancient city.
On the other hand, at the time of the eruption various works were nevertheless in progress that must have affected liveability considerably. Added to this is the discovery of at least two mouse skeletons, found inside an amphora on a mezzanine. According to analyses carried out in the park's laboratory, they probably belonged to the species Apodemus sylvaticus, also known as the "wood mouse".
Mice of this kind normally live in natural environments and gardens, from where they often invade attics and storage areas in human dwellings in search of food. The two specimens found at Pompeii were not fully mature, as indicated by the degree of development of their skeletons (117 tiny fragments). The discovery adds to evidence of the presence of rodents in other Vesuvian contexts, such as the service quarters of the suburban villa at Civita Giuliana or the sewers of Herculaneum, and offers the image of an urban society that also had to contend with unwelcome guests.

ECB President Lagarde to step down in February
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:07:45 UTC
19:07:45 KST

Christine Lagarde is pictured during the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group in Bangkok on Oct. 14, 2026. | Anthony Wallace/AFP via Getty Images
Christine Lagarde said she will step down as president of the European Central Bank on Feb. 7, creating a vacancy at the top of one of Europe’s most powerful institutions and fueling further speculation about a possible return to French politics.
An official familiar with Lagarde’s thinking, granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter, said she made her move now, almost a full year before the end of her term, to have “greater freedom to express her views and to engage in non-monetary matters, because she cannot remain neutral when she sees the developments taking place in her own country and in the world.”
The ECB said in a statement only that Lagarde had informed European Council President António Costa of the decision earlier on Thursday.
Advertisement
The announcement clears the way for a package deal among EU capitals over at least three appointments to the ECB’s six-strong Executive Board. Isabel Schnabel, head of the Bank’s markets department, is due to leave in January to take a senior role at the International Monetary Fund, while Philip Lane is due to depart the influential chief economist’s position in May.
Negotiations over the appointments are likely to be intense, given the ECB’s vital influence in international markets, and the never-ending pressure on European government finances. Former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos, who heads the Bank for International Settlements, are seen as the two frontrunners in the race for the top job. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said a decision would be taken by year-end.
The timing of the announcement means that President Emmanuel Macron will have a say in choosing Lagarde’s successor before he himself leaves office next spring. Marine Le Pen, the National Rally leader and a longtime critic of the EU, is currently well ahead in the polls to win the French presidency, and may take a radically different view about who should lead the ECB.
“The EU is trying to guard at least somewhat against the risk that right-wing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election,” said Berenberg Bank’s head of research Holger Schmieding.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard-left France Unbowed party, protested that Macron had already engineered a similar situation at the Bank of France, where François Villeroy de Galhau’s early departure “allowed Macron to install his assistant,” Emmanuel Moulin, as governor.
Speculation has long swirled that Lagarde, formerly finance minister under President Nicolas Sarkozy, may throw herself back into French politics. She has stressed the need for “a pro-European voice” in the French elections, while still being consistently coy about running herself. Thursday’s announcement comes at a time when candidates from mainstream camps in France are all losing ground to Mélenchon, who wants the ECB to “set fire” to its French debt holdings. None looks likely to make the final round of the presidential election in May.
Advertisement
Whoever follows her as ECB president will inherit an increasingly tense situation in Europe’s bond markets, where borrowing costs are hitting their highest level in years due to a cocktail of war-fueled inflation, demographics and competition from capital from Big Tech companies chasing AI-related riches.
The problems are particularly acute in France, the eurozone’s second-largest economy, which faces a political impasse and mounting pressure over its public debt.
Lagarde succeeded Mario Draghi at the ECB in 2019, after leading the International Monetary Fund and, in her time in office, has been a stalwart of the centrist mainstream that is now being squeezed by both wings of the political spectrum across Europe.
“Christine Lagarde has led the European Central Bank through difficult times,” German finance minister Lars Klingbeil said in a statement. “Under her leadership, the ECB has kept the euro stable even during crises: when the coronavirus pandemic hit Europe hard, when Russia invaded Ukraine, and most recently in the face of the economic shocks caused by the war in Iran.”
“Christine Lagarde’s tenure at the helm of the ECB has only strengthened the confidence in the European single currency,” Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis said in a statement, promising to give the council a “swift” recommendation on the succession to heads of government.
The ECB gave no details about Lagarde’s plans after leaving Frankfurt. However, she has talked to the World Economic Forum about taking over as chair, according to its founder Klaus Schwab. Reuters reported that the organizer of Davos could announce her appointment as early as this month.
“I leave this institution with a sense of good work done, and an ECB that is fit for the future,” Lagarde said in a video post on LinkedIn.
This story has been updated.Giorgio Leali contributed reporting.

Swiss stock market climbs to new all-time high

Swiss stock market climbs to new all-time high
The Swiss stock market hit a new record on Thursday. The benchmark SMI index rose briefly to just under 14,732 points during the morning, surpassing the previous high set in mid-August by a good 50 points.
On Thursday, the blue-chip stocks provided support for the SMI. Shares in the pharmaceutical group Novartis rose by 2% at around 9:50 am, those of the food giant Nestlé by 1% and those of the pharmaceutical company Roche by 0.5%. By contrast, shares in the building materials group Amrize plummeted by just over 5% following disappointing quarterly figures and a downward revision to its full-year forecast.
According to traders, the stock market rally of recent weeks is primarily due to a shift in investor sentiment. Investors are increasingly pulling money out of technology shares and investing instead in companies that are comparatively resilient to economic downturns. The Swiss stock market is benefiting particularly strongly from this, as pharmaceutical and food companies carry significant weight in the SMI.
+ How the pharma industry is adapting to a new era
In particular, the heavyweights Roche, Novartis and Nestlé have recently driven the benchmark index higher. Their products remain in demand even in economically challenging times. Encouraging financial results from various Swiss companies provided further momentum on the stock market.
The Swiss stock market is thus proving resilient despite the war in the Middle East, high oil prices and mounting inflation concerns. This is because high energy prices are fuelling inflation and thereby increasing the pressure on central banks to keep interest rates high or raise them further. This is weighing particularly heavily on technology shares. Many of these companies are valued on the stock market on the basis of high profit expectations for the future. From today’s perspective, such future profits lose value when interest rates rise.

Pentagon treating military base freezer malfunctions as suspected cyberattack, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:06:25 UTC
19:06:25 KST

Pentagon treating military base freezer malfunctions as suspected cyberattack, officials say
- The Pentagon is treating freezer failures at US military bases as a suspected cyberattack. Investigators are working with Cyber Command, law enforcement, and French counterparts.
- At least six commissaries were hit in late August. In one case at Fort Huachuca, the freezer “went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food”.
- The case raises wider fears about hacked cold storage. A similar French attack hit over 350 sites, caused major food losses, and showed outdated controllers can be easy targets.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US Pentagon is treating the spate of mysterious freezer malfunctions that spoilt food at military bases across the United States in August as a suspected hack, according to four officials familiar with the matter.
One of the officials said the military investigators were in touch with their French counterparts about a similar cyberattack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets there earlier in October.
Reuters was unable to ascertain how far along the Pentagon’s investigation was or whether it had reached any conclusions about what happened or who might be responsible.
When asked about the investigation, the Pentagon said that a unit of Cyber Command – the military’s cyber force – was “working in close coordination with interagency and law enforcement partners”. It did not elaborate.
The US Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division said its Cyber Field Office was involved in the investigation and that it was working with French law enforcement to better understand “the refrigeration outages in Europe”.
The late August malfunctions in the United States affected at least six commissaries – on-base stores where military personnel buy their food – according to a Reuters review of the military bases’ contemporaneous Facebook posts and website updates.
In at least one of the cases, the freezers did not simply stop working; the cooling units’ temperatures were cranked up overnight, yielding mounds of wilted or melted food in the morning.
The Fort Huachuca, Arizona Facebook account explained on Aug 26 that its freezer “went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food. Trust us when we say it was ‘spoiled’”.
The spate of rogue freezer behaviour and the possibility of cyber-sabotage were first reported on Aug 28 by a recently created blog called Signal and Silence.
The involvement of military investigators and their contacts with the French were reported by the newspaper Stars and Stripes and Britain’s Daily Telegraph, respectively. The news that the investigators were treating the incident as a suspected hack was first reported by Reuters.
The French Embassy in Washington said it would have no comment.
French freezers fried
If confirmed to be a cyberattack, the refrigerator malfunctions would be another illustration of how vulnerable critical infrastructure – in this case cold storage – can be to hackers.
The French freezer cyberattack overrode the temperature controls on commercial cooling units in more than 350 establishments, leading to dramatic scenes as supermarkets’ frozen food aisles were cleared of spoilt merchandise.
The French hack involved cranking the temperature inside the units up rather than merely knocking them offline, similar to what happened in Fort Huachuca in Arizona. Some French refrigeration units had the temperature turned up so high they caught fire.
The French attack’s total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, one supermarket owner estimated earlier in October.
The French cyberattack appeared to have been easy to pull off, experts previously told Reuters. The Danish firm Danfoss, whose controllers ran many of the stricken units, said that many of the devices were obsolete or were running outdated firmware, which could have made it easy for hackers to break in.
Reuters could not establish whether Danfoss or any other brand of freezer controller were in use at the affected US bases. Danfoss did not return messages seeking comment.
Chilling hacks
Refrigeration plays a critical role in the distribution of fresh food and the sabotage of cold storage facilities over the internet has long been seen as a nightmare scenario, alongside the loss of electricity or water plants.
Earlier in 2026, the Global Food Safety Initiative, an industry body, called on food safety professionals and IT leaders to work together to ensure “robust cybersecurity” for refrigeration technology, noting that “a hacked cooling system is just as dangerous as a broken one”.
Hackers have previously sabotaged fridges and freezers both in the US and elsewhere.
Danfoss has said that, in 2022, hackers either targeted or broke into supermarkets in Russia and Israel that were using obsolete versions of its cold storage controllers.
In December 2025, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles accused a Ukrainian woman of being part of a hacker group that knocked out the refrigeration at a meatpacking facility in 2024, ruining more than 900kg of meat.
The root problem was that controllers that were initially conceived as isolated interfaces that would be serviced by an in-person technician were increasingly being connected to the internet, said Bill Moore, the chief executive of industrial cybersecurity firm Xona Systems.
Concerns about online exposure were not unique to cooling systems, he said, but they could have particularly serious consequences there.
“It can definitely disrupt the supply chain for food,” he said. REUTERS

Trump confronts a new midterm battleground: South Carolina
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 - President Donald Trump will stage a campaign rally in South Carolina for the second time in two weeks on Thursday, as new polls show the Senate race between incumbent Republican Darline Graham and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews is a toss-up.
With control of Congress at stake in Tuesday's midterm elections, some Republicans are beginning to fret that their traditional stronghold of South Carolina has become a battleground state.
The race is part of a trend that shows contests in Republican-leaning states now tilting toward Democrats in the campaign's final days, in part because of Trump’s low ratings in opinion polls.
Republicans are fighting to retain Senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina and Maine to maintain their six-seat Senate majority. Polls show Democrats leading in each of those states.
Polls and independent analysts favor the Democrats to retake control of the House, while Senate control is considered too close to call. A Democratic victory could place limits on Trump and usher in congressional investigations of his administration over its final two years.
Republicans are newly on the defensive in once unthinkable territory. South Carolina hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since Fritz Hollings, who was first elected in 1966 and served until 2005.
Trump has also rallied in recent days in Mississippi, where the campaign between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom has tightened. Colom would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, a tenuous period of the 19th century immediately following the Civil War.
Republican political operatives have also grown concerned over the Nebraska Senate race between Republican Senator Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn.
In South Carolina, Andrews and Graham are competing for a seat once held by Graham's brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of Trump’s foremost Republican allies and died suddenly in July.
Lindsey Graham was a key foreign policy voice in Congress and an interlocutor between Senate Republican leadership and the White House. He long counted his sister as his foremost political adviser, though polls suggest her stumbles on the campaign trail appear to have hurt her standing.
Former South Carolina elected officials have also backed Andrews in recent days. Two former governors, Republican David Beasley and Democrat Jim Hodges, endorsed Andrews in a television advertisement.
Former Republican Governor Nikki Haley, a Trump appointee during the president’s first term who challenged him for the White House in 2024, has not endorsed either candidate.
Responding to criticism of her campaign as unpolished, Graham said she was not a career politician and does not "speak politician." Graham's campaign has said endorsements from political figures mattered less than support from voters and from Trump.
Trump and Republicans’ focus in South Carolina and other traditional conservative strongholds has consequences far beyond those states, campaign officials say. Republicans had opportunities to challenge Democrats in Michigan and Georgia in the midterms, and also had hopes of picking off another seat in Minnesota.
But defending turf in the South has forced Republicans to divert vital resources away from those races - and sent Trump on a frenetic nationwide campaign tour through 19 states since the start of October.
He has rallies planned in Florida, Kansas and Iowa in the final days before the Tuesday vote. REUTERS

Fire broke out at a nuclear facility in the United States - no contamination detected
Kyiv • UNN
A fire broke out at the Savannah River Site in South Carolina and was extinguished. One worker sustained minor injuries; no contamination was detected.
A fire occurred at the Savannah River nuclear facility in the United States; no contamination was detected after the emergency. Newsweek reports, UNN writes.
Details
Representatives of the Savannah River Site (SRS) said radiological surveys detected no contamination following a fire at the Savannah River National Laboratory on Wednesday evening, October 28, local time.
One employee sustained minor injuries and was taken to a hospital, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) told Fox News.
An emergency was declared at the facility at 5:07 p.m. local time at the site near Aiken, South Carolina, after a fire was reported at the Savannah River National Laboratory. The fire has since been extinguished, according to the latest SRS press release.
The latest social media update confirms that the emergency is "over."
As of 9:45 p.m. local time on Wednesday, October 28, the emergency had been terminated, and protective measures, including the site perimeter, had been removed.
Residents nearby had earlier been urged to monitor local television and radio broadcasts for any actions that state officials might announce.
What is known about the nuclear facility
According to the SRS website, the facility is part of the United States' national nuclear security facilities.
According to the website, it was built in the 1950s to produce materials used in nuclear weapons, primarily plutonium-239 and tritium. Five reactors were built there, along with two chemical separation plants, a heavy-water extraction plant, a tritium extraction plant, a nuclear fuel and target fabrication facility, and waste disposal facilities.

Ship reported on fire off Oman as Iran escalation fears mount
October 29, 2026
A ship on fire has been reported in the Strait of Hormuz, British maritime agency UKMTO said on Thursday.
The agency, which is run by the British Royal Navy, did not give details on the cause of the blaze or any casualties.
Iran has, however, recently stepped up its attacks on ships that it sees as using the waterway without proper authorization.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that three tankers had exploded and caught fire in the past 24 hours after hitting sea mines while using an "unauthorized" route, but it is not known if the case reported to the UKMTO is one of them.
This comes as Iran has reported shooting down another US drone east of the waterway as fears grow of a new escalation in the US-Iran war.
Iran steps up attacks in Strait of Hormuz
The UKMTO said the captain of another ship had reported the blaze onboard a vessel spotted 9 nautical miles (17 kilometers) north of the town of Khasab in Oman, which is located just off the strait.
The status of the crew is unknown, and so far no information has emerged pertaining to damage or environmental impact.
Since the Middle East war was triggered in February by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Tehran has sought to control the strait, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, and has attacked ships it considers to be unauthorized users of the waterway.
Oil exports through the waterway fell again last week, according to shipping data provider Kpler.
Attacks on ships in the strait are at the highest level since the war began, according to US-based think tank Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where the burning ship was reportedly sighted.
US drone downed
The reported ship fire comes as Iran says its forces have downed a drone near the strait, with the Tasnim news agency citing the IRGC as saying a new, advanced air defense system was used.
The report said that Iran's armed forces have destroyed 14 drones of this type and more than 50 MQ-9 Reaper drones since the war broke out.
The claims have not been independently verified, though the US Congressional Research Service says dozens of US aircraft and drones have been reported lost or damaged since the war began.
Fears of new US strikes
The latest incidents come as US President Donald Trump is widely seen to be considering fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Last week, Trump said, "we may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war. He did not, however, give any timeframe.
A third US aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are currently heading to the region.
As reports of a possible renewed escalation swirl, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly nonetheless fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia.
If confirmed, the ouster would be the latest in a series of such high-level departures under the Trump administration, with Sylvia's predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee being forced to retire last October.
According to a report in The Atlantic, no reason was given for Sylvia's departure and no replacement has been named.

Swiss researchers develop climate adaptation tools
The effects of climate change are already being felt in Switzerland, the National Centre for Climate Services (NCCS) announced on Thursday as the “NCCS-Impacts” research project drew to a close. Heat, drought and extreme weather are taking their toll on public health, agriculture and forests.
The research project provided new insights to help better assess the risks to health, the natural environment, the economy and infrastructure, and to plan adaptation to global warming in a targeted manner.
+ ETH Zurich research: Switzerland’s worst-case climate scenario now more likely
Between 2022 and 2026, over 100 researchers and experts worked on the project to develop the foundations and tools needed to address the consequences of a changing climate.
The programme’s results include, for example, a forecasting tool that predicts the influx of emergency patients into hospitals during heatwaves, and an app that assesses climate-related yield fluctuations for the agricultural sector. Fundamental research, such as new socio-economic scenarios for the future up to 2100, was also carried out.

Breaking: Russia strikes platform at Dnipro station with jet-powered drone, at least 14 dead
Editor's note: This is a developing story and will be updated regularly.
Russian forces struck a train platform at Dnipro railway station on the morning of Oct. 29, killing at least 14 people and wounding at least 14 more, authorities said.
A passenger train was preparing to depart the platform for Zaporizhzhia when the station was attacked by a Russian jet-powered drone, Ukrainian Railways wrote on social media.
According to Ukraine's Air Force, the area was attacked around 11:00 a.m. by four Russian jet-powered drones, three of which were downed by Ukrainian air defense before reaching their targets.
Despite the air raid alert and announcements of a heightened threat, people remained on the platform, Ukrainian Railways said.
Passengers were told to evacuate from the stationary train around ten minutes before the strike, with station and train staff checking each train car one by one.
At 11:29 a.m., Dnipropetrovsk Oblast governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported that medics were already at the scene of the attack, providing first aid.
"A horrific Russian attack on Dnipro train station," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media in response to the attack, "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
"How many such terrorist attacks has Russia carried out on our people after lifting sanctions on some Russian oligarchs and energy companies instead of de-escalating."
The attack on Dnipro is just the latest in Russia's escalating campaign to strike Ukraine's railway infrastructure, including the targeting of passenger trains themselves.
Russia's recent targeting of Ukrainian Railways facilities — facilitated by the use of jet-powered drones — has led to strict new rules in the event of air raid alerts, with passengers often evacuated in the middle of the countryside for hours until the all-clear is sounded.
The threat warnings also affect trains waiting at stations, where passengers are likewise told to exit the trains, though the accumulation of people waiting for their train to leave and the reluctance of some to go to a shelter often creates new safety risks.
Elsewhere across Ukraine, the cities of Chernihiv and Kremenchuk were also targeted by daytime Russian attacks.
Around noon, Russian forces struck the center of Chernihiv in northern Ukraine with Banderol cruise missiles, killing two 15-year-old girls, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
At least 24 more people were injured in the attack, including four children, city administration head Dmytro Bryzhynskyi said.
Meanwhile, in the city of Kremenchuk in Poltava Oblast, at least three people were killed and 15 injured after Russian drones struck an apartment building in a residential area, according to local authorities.

Directed by the Afghan-born Canadian filmmaker Salar Pashtoonyar, Hills and Mountains recalls how the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 upended life in the once-stable country. The story is told from the perspective of a woman whose identity Pashtoonyar has protected by using a voice actor and altering some details of her life. Born in 1969, she describes seeing the ‘peaceful and tolerant’ homeland of her childhood deteriorate into a place where parents married off their teenage daughters to keep them from starving. Ultimately, a false accusation of an affair led to her own forced marriage and shattered her family life. Pashtoonyar pairs her narration with sweeping scenes from the mountainous country, drawing out the intersections between landscape, lived experience and global history.

Army still wants an armoured mortar but currently has no route
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:58 GMT
19:00:58 KST

The Army continues to require an armoured mortar capability and is looking at alternative ways of delivering it, including through the Heavy Protected Mobility programme, which remains in its concept phase with no procurement decision taken, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress had been made in procuring an armoured mortar capability, following an earlier answer on armoured fighting vehicle finance.
Luke Pollard said: “The Army continues to require an armoured mortar capability. Alternative delivery routes, including through the Heavy Protected Mobility (PM) programme are being considered. The Heavy PM programme remains in its concept phase, and no final procurement decision has been taken.”
An armoured mortar is a heavy mortar carried inside a protected vehicle and fired from within it. A battlegroup can put high explosive onto a target within a couple of minutes of the call and then move before counter-battery fire arrives. Dismounted mortar teams can do the first part but not the second, and in a war where drones find a firing position within minutes, the ability to shoot and drive away is valuable.
An armoured mortar variant had been expected to come through the Boxer programme, and the answer that prompted this question established that funding had been removed from part of the armoured fighting vehicle portfolio. Pollard said separately that the decision reflected “a broader reprioritisation of capability investment to maximise operational effect and affordability”. The Army still needs the capability and no route to it has been settled.
Heavy Protected Mobility is the programme intended to replace the Army’s ageing protected vehicles, and a concept phase is the earliest formal stage of a procurement, well before a competition, a contract or a date.

Only about half of social science findings held up when retested, major replication project finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:33 UTC
19:00:33 KST

A large-scale international project has found that roughly half of tested scientific claims across the social and behavioral sciences hold up when independent researchers attempt to repeat the work. The research, published in Nature, indicates that the challenges of verifying published findings are not confined to a single field, but rather extend across disciplines including psychology, economics, sociology, education, business, and political science. On average, the effects observed in the replication attempts were less than half as large as those originally reported.
In scientific research, a replication attempt involves testing the exact same question as a previous study using independent data to see if the original conclusion holds true. If a scientific discovery represents a genuine regularity in human behavior, independent researchers following a similar procedure or analyzing a fresh dataset should be able to observe a similar result. Repeating past studies helps verify whether an initial finding is reliable enough to inform public policy, education, or clinical practice.
Over the past decade, large-scale verification efforts have raised questions about how often published findings hold up under scrutiny. A 2015 replication project tested 100 psychology studies and found that only about one-third produced the original results, sparking widespread discussion about research reliability. Follow-up investigations soon tested other areas of study to see if the issue was unique to psychology.
Other fields showed a similar pattern. A 2016 study of laboratory experiments in economics found that 11 out of 18 studies produced a statistically significant effect in the same direction as the original. Similarly, a 2018 investigation of social science experiments published in top-tier general science journals found that about 62 percent repeated successfully, though the strength of the findings was cut roughly in half. Together with other replication efforts, these projects suggested that across hundreds of attempts, roughly half of well-powered replications produced a statistically significant result in the same direction as the original.
Researchers have proposed several systemic explanations for why many published findings fail to repeat. Academic journals have historically favored novel, positive discoveries over inconclusive or negative results, creating a publication filter where studies that happen to overestimate an effect by chance are the ones most likely to be printed. Small sample sizes, flawed measurement tools, and flexible data analysis practices can also produce false positives. At the same time, academic culture has often discouraged verification work; for example, a 2017 study found that only about 3 percent of psychology journals explicitly welcomed replication studies, while a third implicitly discouraged them.
Most prior verification projects focused on a single academic discipline or examined relatively small groups of papers. To determine whether the patterns seen in earlier efforts apply across the broader landscape of human behavior research, a massive collaborative team led by Andrew H. Tyner of the Center for Open Science, alongside senior colleague Timothy M. Errington and corresponding author Brian A. Nosek, executive director of the Center for Open Science and a professor at the University of Virginia, launched a systematic cross-disciplinary investigation.
Nosek also coordinated the 2015 psychology project and co-authored the 2018 analysis of studies in top general science journals. The new work was conducted as part of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) program, bringing together hundreds of researchers from 31 countries.
“This project was part of a larger research program called SCORE that involved thousands of researchers around the world and began in 2019,” Nosek told PsyPost. “We were investigating whether algorithms could predict the replicability of findings to support decision-making about what research is needed next to advance knowledge.”
The researchers began by gathering a random sample of 3,900 quantitative papers published between 2009 and 2018 across 62 journals representing six major disciplines: business, economics, education, political science, psychology, and sociology. To be eligible, a paper had to use real human data, ranging from individual participants to families, businesses, or political entities, and report a positive statistical result. From a pool of 1,500 eligible papers, the team matched specific scientific claims with independent research groups who had the expertise and resources to test them.
In total, the teams completed 296 replication attempts covering 274 unique scientific claims drawn from 164 published papers across 54 journals. For 98 of the papers, researchers collected brand-new data from participants, while for 66 papers, teams analyzed existing secondary datasets that had not been used in the original research. Across the subset of studies where standard correlation metrics could be calculated, the median sample size was 206 in the original papers and 545 in the replication studies.
To ensure the tests were fair and rigorous, the replication studies were designed to have high statistical power, meaning they used large enough samples to have a median 99.6 percent chance of detecting an effect as large as the one originally reported. Whenever possible, teams used the original study materials. Before any data were collected or analyzed, each study’s design and analysis plan went through an internal peer review process, which invited feedback from the original authors, and was publicly registered in advance on the Open Science Framework to prevent researchers from altering their methods after seeing the results.
The researchers first evaluated the outcomes using the most common yardstick in social science: whether the replication study produced a statistically significant result in the same direction as the original paper. In science, statistical significance means that an observed pattern would be unlikely if there were no real effect, typically using a threshold of less than a 5 percent probability. Because some papers had multiple claims tested, the authors calculated results both by weighting claims so each paper counted equally and by counting each claim individually.
When weighted by paper, 80.8 of the 164 papers, or 49.3 percent, produced results in the same pattern that met the threshold for statistical significance. Another 40.4 percent of the papers showed a null effect, meaning the result did not reach statistical significance, while 9.7 percent actually produced a statistically significant result in the opposite direction of the original claim. When looking at the 274 unweighted claims individually, 151 claims, or 55.1 percent, succeeded by this measure, while 35.8 percent showed a null effect and 8.8 percent went in the opposite direction.
Beyond yes-or-no significance thresholds, the researchers examined the magnitude of the findings, known as the effect size. To compare studies that used different statistical models, the team converted the results of 157 papers (representing 249 claims) into a standardized correlation measure called Pearson’s r, which runs from -1 to 1, where 0 means no relationship, 1 means a perfect relationship, and negative values indicate a relationship in the opposite direction. Across the original papers, the median effect size was 0.25, whereas in the replication studies, the median effect size dropped to 0.10.
This drop from 0.25 to 0.10 represents a 58.1 percent relative reduction in the correlation and an 82.4 percent reduction in shared variance, a measure of how much one variable explains another. Overall, 80.3 percent of the replicated papers (126 of 157) and 70.3 percent of the individual claims (175 of 249) yielded smaller effect sizes than the original studies. Some of this shrinkage is expected due to a statistical phenomenon called regression to the mean: because the researchers only tested positive published results, any original studies that happened to overestimate the true effect by luck would naturally be followed by smaller, more realistic estimates upon retesting.
“The basic finding is that establishing the replicability of published results cannot be taken for granted,” Nosek said. “The main practical implication is that this research exposes greater uncertainty in the published literature than we might recognize. Establishing credibility and verifying research claims is an effortful process and our assumptions about the strength and nature of a finding are sometimes incorrect.”
When the researchers broke the results down across the six academic disciplines, they found only modest variation, and the differences between fields were not statistically significant. Weighted by paper, the success rates were 42.5 percent in economics (10.2 of 24 papers), 47.2 percent in business (17.0 of 36), 49.0 percent in psychology (28.4 of 58), 51.1 percent in sociology (9.2 of 18), 52.0 percent in political science (7.8 of 15), and 63.1 percent in education (8.2 of 13). However, some fields contributed only a handful of papers, such as 13 in education, so their individual estimates are uncertain. Similarly, the year a paper was published between 2009 and 2018 did not have a statistically significant relation to whether it held up.
The team also compared studies that gathered brand-new data against those that analyzed existing secondary datasets. Both approaches succeeded at similar rates on the basic significance metric: 47.8 percent of papers using new data held up, compared to 51.4 percent of papers using secondary data. However, when looking at effect sizes, studies using new data saw their median effect size drop from 0.28 in the original work to 0.11 in the replication, whereas secondary data studies started with smaller original effects (a median of 0.13) and dropped only slightly to 0.10.
Because scientists disagree on the best mathematical way to define a successful replication, the authors also evaluated the data using 12 additional criteria, such as checking whether the replication result fell within the original study’s margin of error, or combining both studies in a meta-analysis. Across all 13 methods, the estimated success rate ranged from 28.6 percent to 74.8 percent, with a median of 49.3 percent. The highest success rate (74.8 percent) came from combining the original and new data together in a meta-analysis, a method that leans toward success because it bakes in the original positive data, while methods that penalized replication studies for finding either smaller or larger effects than the original study produced the lowest rates.
“These findings confirm and extend existing work on replicability, such as the ‘Many Labs’ studies,” Stephanie Zellers, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Helsinki who holds a PhD in psychology and was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “Many Labs projects aim to test the replicability of specific research findings using a multisite collaborative approach. This work extends beyond this approach by comprehensively testing a wider range of research findings across behavioral and social science disciplines. The authors used a systematic, representative, and random approach to identify claims for testing, though there was some non-random selection introduced by teams choosing to start a specific replication project.”
“I am quite confident in these results and that is due in large part to the transparent and nuanced reporting,” Zellers said. “I appreciated the detailed discussion of replication metrics – these methods of comparing an original result to the replication result in order to decide if the original result replicated or not. Our choice of metric influences what the answer means, when we ask the question ‘did this study replicate?’ They all have their assumptions, strengths and limitations, and I am more confident in these results because the authors used different metrics when possible.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. A single successful replication does not mean the original finding is beyond doubt, and no two studies in the social sciences are ever identical. Shifting a study to a new year, a new group of participants, or a different cultural setting can alter the outcome for legitimate reasons that scientists do not yet fully understand.
“Failing to replicate a finding does not mean that the original finding is wrong,” Nosek emphasized. “One possibility is that the original finding is a false positive or exaggerated. Other possibilities are that we made an error in the replication study, or that unrecognized factors influenced the finding differently between the original and replication studies.”
“These findings do not mean that social and behavioral sciences are only ‘correct’ about half of the time and should not be interpreted as such,” Zellers added. “Replication is not inherently a positive thing and lack of replication is not inherently a problem. Rather we should focus on the total body of evidence for a claim and critically evaluate uncertainty in the evidence alongside the context and boundaries of the effect.” She noted that “meta-research is not a scientific ‘witch hunt’ focused on debunking some specific claim via replication, it is an essential part of science that helps us understand and evaluate a whole body of evidence for or against some claim.”
In addition, the studies tested in this project were not a purely random slice of all social science. Although the initial pool of papers was chosen randomly, the final 164 papers were those that proved practical to repeat within the project’s budget, timeline, and researcher expertise. Resource-intensive studies were less likely to be attempted, and qualitative research and papers reporting null results were excluded from the start. The mix of fields also shifted: psychology made up about 24 percent of the original sample but 35.4 percent of the completed papers, while education and political science shrank in relative share.
“I would be interested to see a project that tests replicability in a broader group of journals, broader research results like null and qualitative findings, and in different time periods of published results,” Zellers noted. “These types of studies could help us understand drivers of replicability and unreplicability.”
The authors suggest that the core issue facing the social and behavioral sciences is not necessarily a lack of replicability itself, as cutting-edge research naturally involves taking risks on uncertain ideas that may not pan out. In their view, the challenge is overconfidence: treating a single published paper as established fact rather than preliminary evidence.
“I think the authors do a reasonable job in discussing the findings without any sensationalist language about disciplines in crisis or fields being ‘built on noise,’ however I would also caution against any misinterpretation that suggests we should not be concerned about these relatively low rates of replicability,” Zellers explained. “Replication does not prove an original claim true and unreplicability does not prove an original claim false, and so we should not interpret any single replication result as good or bad without more information. That said, the overall low rate of replicability in social sciences fields is concerning because it may stem from systemic issues in scientific publishing, like publication bias toward positive results and overconfidence in published claims.”
“I was surprised that most of the research community readily accepted these findings,” Nosek remarked. “Our prior systematic replication studies generated substantial, heated debate. There are still a variety of perspectives on the implications of these results, but there was much less heated rhetoric. I think that is a sign of progress?”
Future research could use the publicly available dataset to examine what predicts whether a study holds up. Earlier work along these lines, including research covered by PsyPost in 2022, found that the political slant of psychology findings was not associated with whether they replicated.
Nosek added, “Now that we have published several systematic replication studies, many research efforts are using the outcomes to advance various research questions such as: How do you decide whether a finding has replicated successfully? (Not a trivial question!) What factors cause increases or decreases in replicability? How prevalent are each of those causes? Is there an optimal replicability rate for different research circumstances?”
“Discovery science is often high-risk high-reward, resulting both in powerful new findings and many false leads,” Zellers said of investigating optimal replicability rates. “Replication science can help us identify which leads may be dead ends, as well as understand moderators and generalizability. We need both to create robust and impactful science, especially when translating our research claims into care, policy, and practice. What is the optimal balance between discovery and replication science to make the best use of increasingly limited financial resources in research?”
The study, “Investigating the replicability of the social and behavioural sciences,” was authored by Andrew H. Tyner, Anna Lou Abatayo, Mason Daley, Samuel Field, Nicholas Fox, Noah A. Flávio Bolsonaro’s defeat is a major blow to Trump and his orange wave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:32 UTC
19:00:32 KST

For Donald Trump, Brazil’s presidential election was meant to represent the crest of the “orange wave” – a three-year surge of rightwing triumphs that has reshaped Latin American politics in the US president’s tangerine-hued image.
The far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, was supposed to claim the presidency on Sunday, bringing the region’s biggest democracy and economy into Trump’s orbit, after similar victories in Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Honduras, Ecuador and Peru – not to mention the capture of Venezuela’s government after the country was invaded in January.
But Brazilian voters had other ideas, turning out in huge numbers to vote against the pro-Trump populist and return the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to power. On Tuesday, as Lula celebrated his 81st birthday to the sound of samba in Brasília, Bolsonaro fled to Miami on a private jet.
“This is a significant blow, indisputably, to Trump’s regional strategy,” Benjamin Gedan, the director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, said of Bolsonaro’s defeat.
“[Trump] was perceived to be steamrolling over South America, having invaded Venezuela and seen close allies win elections in Argentina and Chile, in Bolivia and Colombia. That momentum had given the impression that he could determine political outcomes throughout Latin America – and he clearly enjoyed it,” added Gedan, a former White House South America adviser.
“This is a region where he was really perceived to have a successful foreign policy, and this just flies in the face of that image.”
The US setback was celebrated in China, whose rapidly growing influence in Latin America Trump has been trying to combat with his so-called “Donroe doctrine” of regional domination. “[Lula has] effectively thwarted Trump’s strategy for the region … Trump failed to bring Brazil, the largest nation in South America, under his sway,” Hu Xijin, a prominent Beijing propagandist, enthused on X.
Trump has responded to his ally’s failure by halfheartedly querying the election, which Lula won by 4.3m votes.
“I think the election was really strange … It’s so terrible to see,” he told reporters. “But I wasn’t involved,” Trump added, despite a months-long campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure apparently designed to boost Bolsonaro.
Despite Trump’s decision to offer shelter to Bolsonaro – who is facing several criminal investigations in Brazil – many observers suspect the US president is unlikely to pick a major fight with Lula over his rightwing ally’s plight.
“One of Trump’s good qualities - and I mean this sincerely, even though it sounds ironic – is that he can smell a loser, and he wants to be around winners,” said Michael Paarlberg, a former Latin America adviser to Bernie Sanders.
Paarlberg noted how Trump got along with leftist “winners” including Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – and even Lula himself. “I like Lula, I get along with him very well,” Trump said this week.
“He will certainly favour his ideological co-partisans,” Paarlberg said of Trump, “but if the stink of loserdom starts to waft over them, he will drop them.”
The “stink of loserdom” certainly wafted over Bolsonaro as he fled into Argentina on Tuesday and caught a private jet to Florida, where he briefly declared himself Brazil’s “true president-elect” before apparently changing his mind.
Brazilian social networks filled with memes mocking the far-right politician who, only hours earlier, had vowed to stay in Brazil to lead opposition to Lula.
One particularly scathing internet joke featured a photo of Bolsonaro and a parody of his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan, which was: “God, Homeland, and Family.” “Goodbye, Homeland and Family,” it said.
Speaking at his birthday party, Lula said: “This is what the Bolsonaro family is like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US.”
Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, claimed Bolsonaro’s movement – which was founded by his jailed father, former president Jair Bolsonaro – was dead in the water after Sunday’s defeat, although the losing candidate secured 59.8m votes.
“I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Amorim said, recalling how the movement had lost two successive elections to Lula, in 2022 and 2026.
Amorim predicted a more reasonable conservative movement would replace Bolsonaro’s “extremist” one and called his loss “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.
Under Lula, Amorim indicated Brazil would not join Trump’s controversial Shield of the Americas “counter-cartel coalition” – as Bolsonaro had planned to do.
But Amorim also signalled Lula would pursue pragmatic ties with Washington. “[Trump] has a certain level of pragmatism. They know Brazil isn’t just any old country. So I think we’ll seek to have proper, balanced relations without failing to defend our interests, but without being needlessly hostile, as we’ve always tried to do,” he said, recalling Lula’s good rapport with George W Bush.
Amorim attributed Trump’s questioning of Brazil’s election to “incorrect things” that “rightwing radicals from the state department” had put on his desk.
On Monday, Trump’s former chief strategist, Steve Bannon, urged Trump and secretary of state Marco Rubio to sever diplomatic and trade relations and “shut down everything with Brazil” as a result of the election supposedly being “stolen up in your face”.
Paarlberg said Trump’s remarks – criticizing the election, but emphasising his fondness of Lula – suggested he would not take Bannon’s advice.
“I read that as: ‘I will give you [Bolsonaro] moral support, but nothing else’,” Paarlberg said. “He certainly wasn’t saying: ‘I’m going to call for further tariffs, or further visa sanctions or any further actual measures to try to punish the Lula government.”
Gedan was unsure about Trump’s next move. “Anything’s possible, and I’m certain he has no idea how he’s going to approach it either,” he said.
But Gedan believed Trump and Lula could patch things up – perhaps striking a deal involving Brazil’s massive critical mineral reserves - despite Trump’s hopes of a “glorious return” for the Bolsonaros being dashed.
“There’s actually quite a bit of space for a positive relationship, if Trump does not decide to explode US-Brazil relations,” he said. “I think you absolutely could see Trump finding a way to admire Lula’s political skills.”

A new wave of electric ferries is here in the US. Some even fly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

Cutting through New York Harbor in the shadow of the Statue of Liberty, the small white boat we were riding on caught the attention of passengers aboard a nearby sightseeing ferry.
“It’s quite a curiosity at the moment,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.
His company builds fully electric hydrofoil boats. These vessels use underwater “wings” to lift their hulls above the surface as they pick up speed. By raising the boat out of the water, the design dramatically reduces drag, one of the biggest obstacles to making boats more energy-efficient.
“We’re picking up speed. We’re going for a takeoff,” Laakmann said as the boat rapidly accelerated.
The hydrofoils lifted the hull about a foot and a half above the water. Almost immediately, the ride transformed. The familiar slap of the boat pushing through waves became a smooth, almost airborne glide.
How hydrofoils make electric boats ‘viable’
The hydrofoil effect is more than a novelty. Water creates significant resistance, and overcoming it takes energy. Electrifying boats is a challenge because batteries are heavy, and that extra weight increases the power needed to move the vessel. Hydrofoils may offer a solution. By lifting much of the hull out of the water, they reduce drag, allowing a vessel to move more efficiently.
“We substantially reduce the drag that you feel and that’s really what makes electrification viable,” Laakmann said.
Vessev says its hydrofoil design cuts drag by about 66%. That greater efficiency allows the boats to carry smaller battery packs, reducing both weight and cost.
But efficiency is only part of the equation. Making a boat electric is not simply a matter of replacing a diesel engine with a motor and battery. Operators must also consider how far a vessel needs to travel, how many passengers it carries, how quickly it must recharge, and how much weight it can accommodate.
From novelty to everyday transport
Vessev operates passenger services in New Zealand and is expanding to Australia. In the US, its first service is planned for Lake Tahoe. Laakmann sees a future in which electric vessels become a routine part of public transportation, rather than a niche attraction.
“More like subways, more like buses, more like Ubers, more like taxis but on the water,” he said.
Waterways can connect communities and move passengers without adding more vehicles to crowded roads. When powered by increasingly clean electricity, electric ferries can also cut the pollution associated with diesel engines.
Transportation remains the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, according to federal environmental data. Road vehicles account for much of that pollution, but ships and other watercraft also burn fossil fuels. Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality around busy waterfronts.
Vessev is not alone in pursuing the technology. In Stockholm, commuters are already riding electric hydrofoil ferries built by the Swedish company Candela. The company says its design can reduce energy use by as much as 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. Norway has ordered 20 of its electric hydrofoil boats for coastal service.
For ferry operators, the attraction is not simply environmental. More efficient designs and advances in battery technology are opening up routes for electric boats that might once have been impractical. There is also the potential for lower operating costs as fuel prices soar.
“I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Laakmann said.
San Francisco prepares to plug in
In San Francisco, the city’s largest ferry operator carries about 3.5 million passengers a year, according to Seamus Murphy, who leads the agency. The network serves a region shaped by water, with commuters relying on boats to cross the bay and reach the city.
“We have a lot of waterfront,” Murphy said.
Yet the fleet runs entirely on fossil fuels. All 18 vessels in the system are powered by diesel. That is set to change as the agency prepares to add four battery-powered ferries over the next two years. It is part of an electric overhaul worth about half a billion dollars that also includes charging infrastructure at docks.
Unlike a car that can be plugged in at home overnight, a ferry may need to complete repeated trips on a fixed timetable. Its batteries must provide enough energy for the route, while shore-side chargers deliver enough power during the time the vessel spends at the terminal.
Making that work requires more than the right boat. Operators must coordinate vessel range, timetables and charging capacity to keep passengers moving without disrupting service. San Francisco won’t initially be using hydrofoil boats, but the agency says its new vessels will make it the first ferry operator in the United States to run high-speed, all-electric ferries.
The economics of going electric
For transit agencies, climate goals alone rarely justify a major fleet overhaul. The numbers have to add up.
Battery-powered ferries generally require a larger initial investment in vessels and charging equipment. But electric motors can be more efficient than diesel engines, and operators may save money over time on fuel and maintenance. Murphy said rising diesel costs and improvements in battery technology strengthened the case for making the switch.
“You make the upfront investment at the beginning and then you save over time and at the end of the day you’re going to have lower costs in the long term,” he said.
The financial case depends a lot on the route. Batteries remain heavy and expensive, charging infrastructure can be costly, and not every route is suited to a fully electric vessel. Long distances, tight schedules and limited opportunities to recharge can all complicate the transition.
The shift could create opportunities well beyond the water. For San Francisco’s expansion, the boats and their batteries are being built in the United States. This could create opportunities for domestic manufacturing jobs.
For Murphy, the transition is a chance to cut pollution while helping develop new business for shipbuilders and battery manufacturers.
“These jobs are going to get created in other countries and we have an ability to create them here if we manage this in the right way,” Murphy said. “We don’t want to be left behind,” he added.
- Climate Central is an independent group of scientists and communicators who research and report the facts about our changing climate and how it affects people’s lives.

Trump’s plea – ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ – deserves to backfire | Margaret Sullivan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

As he criss-crosses the nation, stumping for Republican candidates, Donald Trump keeps asking voters to use their imaginations.
“In this election, I’m asking you to pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just pretend,” he urged at a Kansas rally as he campaigned for the incumbent senator Roger Marshall and gubernatorial challenger Ty Masterson last month.
“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.
But will it work? That seems increasingly unlikely.
Given his own lack of popularity and weird behavior, it’s an egotistical notion – more appealing to himself than to voters.
After all, his approval ratings are in the basement. Gas prices are higher, on average, than at any time during the Biden years. People feel like they need to float a loan before heading to the supermarket.
In that Kansas rally, he referred to the opposition as “Dumocrats”, which is typical of the level of presidential discourse to which the nation has become accustomed.
In his rallies, he appears “increasingly detached from reality”, as one campaign analysis in the Independent put it, as he “vacillates between topics to the point where his remarks border on the nonsensical and he ends every appearance by awkwardly dancing to the Village People’s well-known gay anthem YMCA”.
Stranger still, as the Guardian’s Adam Gabbatt reported recently, Trump has been offering “unsolicited and increasingly unhinged assessments of men’s bodies” over the past few weeks.
“I examined his ass,” the president said in Kentucky, speaking about Republican senator Jon Husted. “And then I looked at his shoulders … I looked at his jawline … I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I’m still recovering.”
Trump has also been – to put it mildly – stretching the truth on the campaign trail, sometimes merely misleading in his remarks, sometimes straight-up lying.
For example, he promised a North Carolina rally that gas and oil prices would tumble soon and he claimed: “I had it down to the lowest level in years,” apparently speaking about the price of filling up a gas tank at the pump. A PolitiFact examination disputed this, noting that when Trump took office at the beginning of last year, the average gas price was $3.23 a gallon, but by late September of this year, it was $4.61.
But it’s not just what he says at rallies that may backfire on the candidates he hopes to help.
Much of what’s happened in Trump’s second term is working against Republican candidates. That includes the widespread self-dealing that, as the historian Garrett Graff wrote recently, “is so endemic and so obvious that it has broken through to voters”.
It’s also his misguided war, his rants on social media, his disparagement of longtime allies, including Canada. It’s also his obvious plan to declare the election rigged should it not go his way.
“Even Maga die-hards and GOP allies in Congress have grown weary of his erratic behavior,” as the Wall Street Journal’s Jason Riley noted.
And Democrats, including Barack Obama, are only too happy to campaign by associating Republican candidates with Trump.
These midterm elections, Obama told a crowd in Ohio, “is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration. It’s the circuit breaker in the system.”
That blast of sanity and good sense seems far more likely to resonate with potential voters than Trump’s unhinged rants and dangerous threats.
Pretend he’s on the ballot?
Maybe that’s effective with Trump’s remaining cult-like base. And maybe it will bring some of those loyalists out to vote next week if they had been thinking of sitting out this election.
But more likely, the imagined association with Trump will serve to remind most voters that Trump’s malfeasance must be rebuked and rejected. Certainly not encouraged.
- Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables

Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
Students gifted only water celery or white wormwood, choosing these fragrant plants to symbolise a pure pursuit of knowledge
While it is common for Chinese people to hold banquets for teachers upon graduation as a way of honouring them – a traditional value – in ancient China, students expressed their respect for teachers differently: by presenting them with vegetables.
The tradition began in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). On the first day of school, students wore blue gowns and brought their teachers wild vegetables they had gathered themselves. They then bowed reverently before memorial tablets honouring ancient sages. The ceremony was followed by a group dance, which also expressed the students’ respect for their teachers and their dedication to their studies.
Not just any vegetables could be presented to teachers on this day. Water celery and white wormwood were preferred because they were seen as clean, fragrant and ethereal, symbolising the students’ pure pursuit of knowledge.

Halloween Is a Chance to Rethink Your Relationship With Fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Whether you’re watching a scary movie or tiptoeing through a haunted house, Halloween can stir up spooky feelings. A gory scene may force you to cover your eyes or jump out of your seat. What drives these reactions is fear, a powerful core emotion.
Being afraid can feel like getting stuck in your own horror show—your heart pounds, your pupils dilate, and you may gasp or scream. These reactions are not under conscious control; they’re rooted in biology. Like all emotions, fear plays an important role. It helps you survive and bolt for safety.
Halloween gives you a chance to experiment with fear. It’s a time when the fright is real, but the threat is not.
As psychotherapists who specialize in Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy (AEDP), we know that being able to name and work with fear is good for health. Acknowledging your emotions makes you less likely to suppress or avoid them, drink too much, or become numb to what you’re feeling.
While these behaviors take the edge off temporarily, research shows that stuffing down your emotions can lead to mental-health concerns, such as depression and anxiety, which have become more common among U.S. children and adults in recent years.
If you’d like to safely explore your relationship with fear this Halloween season, here are five exercises we recommend.
Recognize fear in your body
Have you ever tried to outsmart fear? Perhaps you scolded yourself for being a scaredy-cat or tried to stop the feeling with logic. Messages from society and our families often promote a mind-over-matter approach, reinforcing the belief that we can think our way out of an emotion.
A healthier approach is to get out of your head and tune into your body. During a frightening moment, notice the telltale signs of alarm, like trembling hands, a racing heart, or feeling cold. These physical sensations are important messengers that clue you into what core emotions you’re experiencing.
Once you identify and name them, their intensity will likely diminish. It may sound like a small act, but research shows that putting language on your emotions can help regulate and tame distress.
Watch fear come and go
Gripping, painful emotions can seem permanent. But watching them come and go can remind your brain that even the most frightening experiences are temporary.
During a spooky scene, you may want to cover your face or turn away. Rather than immediately distracting yourself, approach the emotion with curiosity. Observe how fear builds, peaks, and eventually subsides.
Curiosity helps us embrace a sense of wonder. Research shows that a curious mindset can cultivate positive emotions and reduce worry.
Calm the scary feeling
When fright takes hold, breathing techniques like 4-7-8 breathing or box breathing can soothe your nervous system. Taking long breaths instead of shallow ones sends oxygen to your muscles, which can help relieve tension.
You can also practice what eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapists call “dual attention.” Keep your eyes glued to the frightening scene and stay with the sensations in your body as you take deep belly breaths. Research shows that belly breathing increases parasympathetic regulation of the heart through vagal pathways, helping the body settle into a calmer state.
Discover how fear makes you want to move
When a ghoul jumps out or a frightening sound catches you off guard, pay attention to what your body wants to do. Do you feel an urge to flee, freeze, duck, or reach for someone’s hand?
In AEDP, we call these “adaptive actions,” and they offer clues about how your nervous system responds to perceived danger.
All core emotions, including fear, have impulses—energy in the body that makes us want to take action. When someone responds to our emotions with shame instead of empathy, we learn to block these impulses, creating a pressure-cooker effect. This can lead to symptoms like insomnia, muscular tension, and rumination that can hurt your health.
Noticing fear’s impulses expands your emotional awareness and sets the stage for you to work through other core emotions with greater wisdom.
Notice how connection changes fear
Sharing a scary moment with another person can make it easier to tolerate. That’s because having someone by your side doesn’t just provide reassurance; it calms the amygdala, the brain’s emotional center, and helps you heal past wounds and traumas.
We recommend this experiment: Watch a horror movie alone, and then with someone you trust. Or visit a haunted house with a trusted friend or partner. Notice what happens when you share the experience.
A little emotions education goes a long way towards nurturing your well-being. By learning to stay with fear, you teach your brain that you can handle challenging emotions.
And when we know emotions aren’t something to fear, we’re better equipped to handle life’s challenges with authenticity, flexibility, and courage.

In final push, Trump rallies in red states, offering a rosy and off-script message
