Pentagon fires top military planner
The Pentagon has fired its top military strategist as Washington draws up contingency plans for a possible escalation of hostilities with Iran.
Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia has been removed from his position as director for strategy, plans, and policy (J5) on the Joint Staff, a spokesman confirmed late Wednesday, following media reports of his dismissal.
His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced into retirement a year ago amid reported friction with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine. Sylvia previously served as vice director of the J5.
The Pentagon did not explain Sylvia’s departure. His responsibilities included developing military strategies and plans to advise the chairman and the US president. He joins nearly two dozen senior military and civilian officials removed during Hegseth’s tenure.
The secretary has portrayed the dismissals as part of an effort to reduce the military’s bloated ranks of generals and make the armed forces more efficient and lethal. Critics, however, have characterized the shake-up as an ideological “purge.”
President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of renewing large-scale hostilities with Iran, including resuming the intensive bombing campaign conducted during the first 40 days of the conflict, which the US and Israel launched in late February. A potential escalation could be timed around the November midterm elections.
Military experts have widely expressed concern that another bombing campaign would fail to “finish the job,” as Trump has put it, while further increasing the conflict’s economic toll worldwide. Tehran has repeatedly warned that it is prepared to retaliate against US allies in the Gulf region if it faces renewed attacks.
Conversely, speculation has emerged that Trump could dismiss Hegseth after the midterms, when the opposition Democratic Party is expected to make gains in both chambers of Congress. Critics of the Iran war, including Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, have argued that firing the secretary could help Trump avoid a potential impeachment battle if Democrats take control of the House.
Trump’s public rhetoric remains supportive of Hegseth and his policies.

Ukrainians mostly ready for fifth wartime winter – survey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:53:25 EET
18:53:25 KST

According to a study by Comfy, 40% of respondents consider themselves fully prepared for winter, 46% have partially prepared, and only 14% are postponing preparations or do not plan them at all, the retailer's press service reported.
In mid-October, the company conducted a telephone survey among customers to find out how ready Ukrainians are for winter and potential blackouts, what equipment they already own, and what they plan to purchase.
Power banks remain the most common solution for autonomy, owned by 56% of respondents. They are followed by rechargeable flashlights and lamps (39%), power stations (37%), uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) or batteries (31%), and generators (17%). At the same time, 8% of surveyed customers do not possess any of the listed categories of equipment.
Among those planning purchases, the greatest interest is directed toward power stations, high-capacity power banks, and UPS units for routers or gas boilers. Thus, consumers are seeking solutions that will help maintain communication, lighting, and the operation of critical household appliances.
The main barrier to purchasing equipment ahead of the winter period remains price—60% of respondents planning to buy equipment cited the need to save up money for quality devices as the primary obstacle.
For the majority of respondents, the greatest discomfort during prolonged outages stems from domestic inconveniences—the lack of water, the inability to use a stove, and cold in the home. Additionally, 37% of respondents complain about the inability to work or study due to a lack of internet.
Ukrainians are also adapting their leisure activities to the new conditions: popular pastimes during outages include board games, card games, and puzzles, reading, watching movies when power is available, and spending time communicating with family.
The company noted that the survey showed Ukrainians are preparing for winter striving not only to survive outages but also to preserve their usual routine, connectivity, and ability to work.
The study was conducted by Comfy using the CATI method to find out how Ukrainians are preparing for the 2026–2027 winter season. The survey period ran from October 9 to October 24, 2026, covering all of Ukraine.
As of October 2026, the Comfy chain comprises 115 stores across 56 cities in Ukraine. According to the company, revenue for 2025 totaled UAH 55.8 billion, a 17% increase compared to 2024.
According to YouControl data, the owner of Comfy Trade LLC is Comfy Holdings Limited (100%, Cyprus), with Stanislav Ronis and Svitlana Hutsul as ultimate beneficial owners.

Israel on edge over final election results as uncertainty looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:53:00 UTC
18:53:00 KST

Israelis awaited final election results Thursday amid indications that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies nor opposition parties, including Arab-led factions, had secured a parliamentary majority.
Adding to the uncertainty, the head of the Central Elections Committee asked the Shin Bet intelligence service to investigate alleged foreign interference. The letter dated Wednesday noted alleged funding by "foreign entities against the Israeli interest," without specifics, and could not speak to the validity of the claims. It was not clear who made them. It requested findings within the week. Israeli law requires election results to be certified by Nov. 4.
Netanyahu swiftly seized on the request to the Shin Bet to assert that no party should cooperate with Arab-led ones, even though the letter said nothing about that issue. His chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, warned that political actors should not "exploit the situation" to influence the timing of the swearing-in of the next parliament, set for Nov. 10.
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of "attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public – and against the Arab public in particular."
Sami Abu Shehadeh, chair of a party on the Arab-led Joint List, called the claims a new phase of "incitement" against Arab-led groups.
The developments amplified the difficult decisions for the weeks ahead. Those include whether some Jewish and Arab parties would team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu would toss that aside and join forces with the deeply divisive prime minister.
While this plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
Final results could come as early as Thursday evening after about a half-million absentee ballots are counted from military personnel, diplomats, people in prisons and hospitals, and others. They are not expected to sway the results dramatically.
Local media projected 53 parliament seats for Netanyahu's bloc, 48 seats for opposition parties and 19 for Arab-led ones, which also want Netanyahu out.
Netanyahu's Likud, despite receiving the most votes, earlier accused Arab-led parties of stealing the election and asked the election committee to investigate. It did not provide specific evidence to support its claims. The election committee has said the number of reported irregularities in the relatively calm election was low.
Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament, the Knesset. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties that had a strong showing, as some Arab citizens broke longstanding vows never to vote in a country where they have long faced discrimination. Such an alliance would reach the 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset.
Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio he’s heard from the opposition bloc to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker and he told them the party would support the bloc’s candidate. He also urged Eisenkot to have political courage.
The Joint List has noted the "unprecedented show of strength" by Arab voters and the Jewish voters "willing to swim against the tide of racism."
There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government and that was brief.
Next week, Israel’s president will task someone with forming the next government. It has traditionally been the leader of the party with the most votes, but that’s not required.
If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, President Isaac Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step – something Eisenkot has said as well.
New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.
Israel, already divided along multiple fault lines – Jews and Arabs, secular and religious – entered the election with huge and painful issues at stake.
Those include whether the fast-growing ultra-Orthodox population should remain exempted from compulsory military service in a country where many families have seen their sons and daughters killed in three years of inconclusive wars.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has been especially polarizing, with corruption allegations hanging over him along with accusations that he delayed making deals over the war in Gaza, including to free hostages, for political gain.
While many Israelis voted with security issues first in mind, the country’s international standing is also at stake after widespread criticism over the treatment of Palestinians in Gaza and growing violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank .
For Arab citizens, who make up 20% of Israel’s population, there is cautious hope of change. "God willing, we will have something for us in the government, something that will bring us our rights," said Brosli Elias, a resident of Nazareth, one of Israel’s largest Arab cities.
Meanwhile, the threat of further strikes against Iran adds to the election uncertainty, as the Trump administration has spoken of new attacks after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Experts have said Netanyahu could seize on a renewed all-out war to press for a unity government with him in charge.
That could delay what Netanyahu has long resisted: a public inquiry into the security failures into Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas incursion that sparked Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.

Russia may use the Oleshky truce to rebuild its forces, ISW warns, as evacuees face a route through Russia and Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:51:56 UTC
18:51:56 KST

Oleshky residents who choose Ukraine are to be taken through Russia and flown to Belarus, and the ceasefire agreement does not say how they will get from there to Ukrainian-held territory, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) noted on 28 October. ISW also warned that Russia may use the truce to rebuild its forces in Kherson Oblast.
Oleshky, a town across the Dnipro from Kherson, has been occupied by Russia since February 2022, and about 2,000 people remain there, short of food and medicine. A US-brokered truce took hold on 27 October so aid can go in and residents can leave. The mission will show whether Russia lets those who choose Ukraine actually get home.
Anapa, Homiel, and then?
Pages of the agreement, signed on 23 October by Ukraine’s human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, were published by Fox News. They send the Ukrainian delegation and residents who want to go to Ukraine from Oleshky to the airport in Russia’s Anapa. From there, a Russian Defense Ministry military transport plane is to fly them to Homiel in Belarus, with the flight expected on 31 October.
The delegation includes Lubinets, two of his staff, and two Ukrainian journalists, accompanied by a representative of the Russian ombudsman’s office and of the group coordinating the mission. Russia’s Dnepr Grouping of Forces, which holds the left bank of the Dnipro, provides the escort. ISW pointed out that the pages do not explain how evacuees travel on from Belarus, and that it remains unclear whether Russia will give residents “a legitimate and duress-free choice” to return to Ukraine.
Ceasefire planned for occupied Oleshky as residents face starvation and blocked escape routes, White House announces
A route through Russia may also mean so-called filtration. People leaving occupied Mariupol in 2022 had to pass Russian screening, and many who hoped to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory were taken to Russia instead, Human Rights Watch documented. In Washington, the Congressional Ukraine Caucus welcomed the ceasefire but raised alarm over reports that Russia was keeping Oleshky residents from evacuating to Ukrainian-controlled territory, RFE/RL reported.
On 29 October, the Ukrainian delegation led by Lubinets arrived in Belarus, and the two delegations held their first in-person meeting at Homiel airport, Belarus’s state agency BelTA reported. Belarus has also joined the operation, BelTA said. Lubinets confirmed the same day that he had set off for Oleshky with the delegation to deliver aid and work on making sure people can leave safely.
Aid due on 30 October
The truce has held for 54 hours without violations, Lubinets said on 29 October. Routes are being demined, and an aid cargo is to reach Oleshky on 30 October, he added. The truce is set to last until 22:59 on 1 November. Across the river, the Kherson Oblast administration recorded no shelling and no civilian casualties over the past day.
Lantratova wrote that aid had been sent, saying residents need “food, fuel, medicine, hygiene products,” and that they would be able to leave wherever they wanted to go. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia expected residents to get aid within a day or two and those who wished to leave to be able to do so, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who brokered the truce, announced that four Newsmax journalists will work in Oleshky alongside the Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian teams. Her post quoted Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote that Russia “welcomes” the Newsmax journalists, rather than any Ukrainian official:
A pause Russia may use
On the truce’s first day, Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov inspected the Dnepr Grouping and met its commander, Colonel General Mikhail Teplinsky. The ministry said they discussed drone units. Ukrainian serviceman and analyst Volodymyr Molchanov told Radio NV that intelligence shows Russia rapidly reinforcing its forces in Oleshky, bringing in what Ukrainian drones had kept out.
Russian forces may use the limited ceasefire to reconstitute in Kherson Oblast, ISW assessed.

MLC election results: BJP wins big, but Congress and Samajwadi Party send a message from Nagpur, Varanasi
Unknown

BJP's big win in MLC elections comes with setbacks in Nagpur and Varanasi
The MLC elections across four states brought both shock and cheer for the BJP and Congress. While the Congress suffered a humiliating defeat in Karnataka, where it is in power but failed to win a single seat, the BJP faltered in two constituencies which mattered the most. One being Nagpur, which is home to the RSS headquarters, and Varanasi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's parliamentary constituency.The BJP nevertheless emerged as the largest party, winning 13 of the 28 seats contested, while its allies took the NDA's tally to 16. The alliance swept all four seats in Karnataka, won six of the 11 seats in Uttar Pradesh and secured four of the eight seats in Bihar. In Maharashtra, the ruling Mahayuti won two of the five seats, while the opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi secured three.The Congress's only victory came from Nagpur, a political stronghold of Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis and Union minister Nitin Gadkari. In Uttar Pradesh, the Samajwadi Party retained the Varanasi Teachers' constituency and was heading towards victory in the Graduates' seat, both of which it had won in 2020.
BJP-led NDA secured 16 of the 28 MLC seats across four states, while the SP won five seats in Uttar Pradesh and Congress retained Nagpur in Maharashtra.
What began as celebrations and sharp jibes at the Congress on Wednesday turned into a war of words on Thursday, as the results in Nagpur and Varanasi gave the opposition grounds to question the BJP's claims of electoral dominance.
BJP mocks Congress over 'zero' seats
As the early results came in on Wednesday, BJP leaders targeted the Congress over its poor performance, particularly in Karnataka, where the party is in power but failed to win a single seat.PM Modi took a swipe at the opposition party on X, pointing out that voting in the four states had taken place using ballot papers."Guess how many seats Congress won?" he asked.
The remark came amid the Congress's repeated allegations over electronic voting machines and its demand for a return to ballot-paper voting.BJP president Nitin Nabin also targeted the Congress, saying the party had failed to win public support despite voting being conducted using ballot papers."The people are repeatedly rejecting Congress' anarchist politics," Nabin said, adding that public trust remained with PM Modi irrespective of whether elections were conducted using EVMs or ballot papers.
BJP president Nitin Nabin targeted Congress over its poor performance in the MLC elections, pointing out that voting had taken place using ballot papers.
BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi also attacked Rahul Gandhi over his allegations of vote theft"Kamchori ki aadat chhodiye. Vote chori ka shabd apke muh se khud chhoot jayega," he said, asking the Congress leader to give up what he described as a habit of avoiding hard work.
Nagpur win gives Congress a chance to respond
Congress candidate and sitting MLC Abhijeet Wanjari defeated BJP's Sudhakar Kohale to retain the Nagpur Division Graduates' constituency after more than 40 hours of counting.Kohale had initially taken the lead before Wanjari overtook him through preferential votes.Nagpur is important for the BJP. Besides housing the RSS headquarters, it is associated with Fadnavis and Gadkari, both of whom campaigned for Kohale.The Congress had wrested the seat from the BJP in 2020, when Wanjari defeated Sandip Joshi. By retaining it in 2026, the party prevented the BJP from reclaiming a constituency it had dominated for decades.The Maharashtra Congress also targeted Fadnavis over a social media post in which he had claimed that the party had failed to win a single seat.
Congress leader Jairam Ramesh questioned the BJP's setbacks in Nagpur and Varanasi after PM Modi mocked the party's performance in the MLC elections.
Sharing a screenshot of what it said was a deleted post by Fadnavis, the party accused him of celebrating before counting was complete. The post had described the Congress's performance as a "big fat zero".The Congress said Fadnavis had been forced to delete the post after the Nagpur result and warned that the outcome was only a trailer of future political battles.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh also responded to PM Modi's remarks, questioning the BJP's losses in Nagpur and Varanasi."The Prime Minister needs to introspect, but instead, he's lecturing others! Before counting Congress's seats, I wish he'd also reflect on why the BJP lost both seats in his own parliamentary constituency of Varanasi, and how Congress managed to defeat the BJP in RSS's stronghold of Nagpur?" Ramesh said."Mr. Modi, stop the trolling," he added, accusing the government of failing to address inflation, unemployment and weak private investment.Ramesh claimed that voters in Varanasi, Nagpur, Lucknow, Prayagraj and Patna had expressed dissatisfaction with the Centre's policies.
Varanasi setback gives SP a boost ahead of 2027
The BJP's biggest setback in Uttar Pradesh came from Varanasi, where the Samajwadi Party retained the Teachers' seat and established an unassailable lead in the Graduates' constituency.The BJP retained six of the 11 seats contested in the state, while the SP won four and was heading towards a fifth.The SP had won both Varanasi seats in 2020 as well. Six years later, the BJP has failed to dislodge the party from either constituency despite its strong presence in the region.Although the two MLC constituencies cover a wider geographical area than PM Modi's Lok Sabha seat, the results carry political significance given Varanasi's association with the Prime Minister since 2014.They also come after PM Modi's victory margin in Varanasi declined from nearly 4.8 lakh votes in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections to around 1.5 lakh in 2024.Across Uttar Pradesh, the SP's tally is set to rise from three seats in 2020 to five, while the BJP has retained its tally of six.The SP had also emerged as the largest party in Uttar Pradesh in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, winning 37 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats against the BJP's 33.BJP deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya acknowledged that the party had expected a better performance."These elections are decided by highly educated and qualified voters. The BJP has repeated its previous performance, but we expected to win more seats. We will examine why we fell short," Maurya said.The SP, meanwhile, has repeatedly accused the BJP of electoral irregularities, allegations the ruling party has rejected.On polling day, Akhilesh Yadav had claimed that the BJP was attempting to influence even the MLC elections, which have a limited electorate."If the BJP can do this in MLC polls for teachers and graduate constituencies where a limited number of people cast votes, one can imagine their preparation for the assembly polls," he had said.
What do the results mean for 2027?
The NDA's overall tally shows that the BJP and its allies remain ahead in these Legislative Council contests. But the results in Nagpur and Varanasi also show that the party has struggled to regain certain seats despite its strong presence in both regions.In Uttar Pradesh, the SP and Congress are preparing to contest the 2027 assembly elections together, hoping to build on their performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls.
The alliance won 43 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats in 2024, reducing the BJP's tally from 62 in 2019 to 33. Akhilesh Yadav has said the alliance will continue in 2027, although the two parties still need to settle their seat-sharing arrangement.The MLC results, however, cannot be treated as an indication of how the state will vote in the assembly elections. These contests involve a limited electorate of registered graduates and teachers, unlike assembly polls, which are decided by a much wider voter base.For the BJP, which is seeking a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh, the challenge will be to counter the opposition's gains. For the SP-Congress alliance, the question is whether it can repeat its 2024 Lok Sabha performance when the state's 403 assembly seats go to the polls in 2027.

The Office of the Inspector General of the U.S. Department of Defense rejected a request from senators to investigate restrictions on Starlink and Starshield operations in Ukraine.
The Associated Press reported the decision, citing a response from the agency obtained by journalists.
The request for an investigation was submitted by nine U.S. senators – five Democrats and four Republicans. They called for an examination of the reasons behind the reduction in satellite communication speeds, which complicated efforts to intercept Russian strike drones.
In its response, the Inspector General told lawmakers that the U.S. Air Force would be better suited to address the matter. According to a congressional source cited by the outlet, the decision effectively amounts to a refusal to conduct an independent investigation into SpaceX’s activities.
The request sought to determine whether Pentagon officials or representatives of other agencies had issued instructions to restrict Starlink and Starshield, approved such decisions, or been informed of them in advance.
The authors of the initiative also expressed concern about the Pentagon’s dependence on SpaceX services.
Further questions arose from conflicting explanations provided by U.S. authorities and SpaceX regarding changes to the terms of satellite communications operations.
“The Trump administration and SpaceX have given conflicting explanations for the disruptions. An independent investigation is needed to determine who was responsible and prevent similar incidents in the future,” said U.S. Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen.
Elon Musk previously confirmed that SpaceX had restricted Starlink speeds in Ukraine, claiming that the restrictions were imposed because the service’s terms of use had allegedly been violated. Ukraine denied the claim. Musk also said that decisions regarding the military satellite communications system Starshield were controlled by the U.S. government.
Donald Trump denied ordering restrictions on communications in Ukraine. Meanwhile, U.S. Vice President JD Vance did not rule out the possibility that the measures had been coordinated between the White House and Elon Musk.
Amid the connectivity issues, Finnish company ICEYE, Nokia, and the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine announced plans to cooperate on space technologies, including the development of an independent satellite communications system for Ukraine.

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) units in the special military operation zone in Ukraine have received Spektr-K video receivers designed to operate at frequencies above 12 GHz, the press service of the developer, Sector JSC, reported.
It said that the device operates at frequencies that are beyond the reach of electronic warfare systems.
"Spektr-K video receivers designed to operate on ‘invincible’ frequencies have begun arriving in the special military operation zone, enabling stable signal reception in areas where electronic warfare systems are currently absent. The device consists of a proven Spektr receiver paired with an analog converter. The converter handles the lower range; together, they provide reception from 1,000 to 12,000+ MHz. It is precisely this expanded range that allows operation in areas where jammers (devices that create radio interference to block wireless communications) simply do not exist and are not currently expected to appear," the statement reads.
According to the developers, the upper limit of the reception frequency range is considerably broader than the officially stated range; however, "the exact values are being deliberately withheld." Sector also noted that before being deployed to the special military operation zone, Spektr-K was tested at the Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies.
"The device can be tuned to any arbitrary frequency, without being tied to ‘frequency grids’ or ‘standard channels.’ If a signal exists in principle, the receiver will work with it. A full scan of the band with RSSI display takes less than 12 seconds, which gives the operator a comprehensive picture of the airwaves," the press service noted. The device features a superheterodyne circuit with double conversion (splitting the signal into two intermediate frequencies), which "ensures stable operation amid interference and minimizes the impact of mirror channels."
"The receiver is versatile: it captures video signals from any analog drone - whether friendly or enemy - which also makes it an effective tool for intercepting video imagery as part of electronic intelligence systems. In addition, the device can be easily integrated into virtually any ground control station in place of the standard video receiver," Sector added.
Sector JSC is a developer and manufacturer of Russian specialized equipment for drones and unmanned aerial vehicles. The company’s products are used by both military and civilian UAV operators.

Russia Reopens Azov Sea Passage for Grain Ships Following Months of Maritime Stagnation
Russia has allowed grain vessels to exit the Sea of Azov for the first time since July, granting temporary departure clearance to ships operating out of the commercial ports of Temryuk and Kavkaz.
According to three sources familiar with the matter, permission for departure was granted on October 26 with at least one vessel already passing through the Kerch Strait into the Black Sea, Bloomberg reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ships that are fully crewed and prepared for transit are currently permitted to submit applications to secure official clearance to leave harbor.
Despite the granted clearances, commercial vessels navigating across the Black Sea remain exposed to security risks and potential strikes while en route.
However, without a formal ceasefire, granting ships permission to depart the Azov Sea provides only a partial solution to the export bottleneck. Vessels navigating across the Black Sea remain highly vulnerable to drone attacks.
“Initial market reaction was brisk to the downside,” said Bertrand Oesterle, a commodity broker and vice president with StoneX. “Few believe a reopening of ports will significantly alter the risk outlook,” Bloomberg reported.
Over the course of a week from July 6 to July 12, 2026, Ukrainian unmanned systems carried out a systematic campaign in the Sea of Azov, striking 90 Russian vessels—including tankers, tugboats, ferries, and cargo ships—before reaching a total of 105 vessels targeted within eight days.
In response to the continuous drone attacks, Russia temporarily suspended navigation through the Don–Azov Canal and stopped processing applications for passage through the Kerch Strait to protect its fleet.
The operation targeted river-sea class tankers and support ships used to deliver fuel to Crimea, transfer crude oil into the Black Sea, and sustain Russian military logistics along the occupied coastline.
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said on July 10 that they had struck 13 Russian shadow fleet vessels in a single operation. Combined with an earlier FPV drone attack conducted by the Kairos unit, Ukrainian officials say 48 Russian vessels were hit over a five-day period.

A Russian drone strike on a railway platform in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro has killed 14 people and injured over dozen others, regional authorities said.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Hanzha initially reported 13 deaths and at least five people injured. He later updated the number of wounded to 10, 13 and then 14, before confirming that the death toll had risen to 14.

Hanzha added that medical personnel were staying by the wounded’s side and doing everything possible to save their lives.
State-owned Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) said a Russian jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) struck a railway station platform where train No. 866, traveling from Dnipro to Zaporizhzhia, was located at the time.
Despite an alert warning of heightened danger, people were present on the platform, the railway operator said. Rescuers, medics. and law enforcement officers are working at the scene.
Meanwhile, local Telegram channels have already begun sharing photos from the scene.
Ukrainian Delegation Heads Toward Oleshky for Aid Mission

“A horrific Russian strike on the railway station in Dnipro. The Russians used a drone to attack the platform where a regular suburban commuter train and a scheduled passenger train were located. Unfortunately, as of now, 13 deaths have been confirmed. My condolences to the families and loved ones,” he wrote.
Zelensky stressed that Moscow had shown no signs of moving toward de-escalation, even after sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and parts of the energy sector.

“Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be weakened as long as this Russian war continues. It is time for new, stronger sanctions measures from the EU, America, and the G7,” Zelensky added.
The deadly Russian strike on Dnipro’s railway infrastructure echoes the April 2022 attack on Kramatorsk railway station in eastern Ukraine, where a missile strike killed 61 people and injured more than 160.
Around 4,000 civilians had gathered at the station to board evacuation trains as Russian forces advanced.
The station was struck at around 10:30 a.m. on April 8 by a Tochka-U missile believed to have been equipped with cluster munitions.
The station reopened in October 2022, about six months after the strike.
An investigation by the Center for Information Resilience, a nonprofit organization, concluded in October 2022 that the available evidence pointed to Russia as the likely perpetrator.
Investigators identified three possible missile launch sites in Russian-occupied territory and said the missile may have been launched from near Shakhtne, east of Donetsk.
Russia denied responsibility, claiming it did not possess the type of Tochka-U missile used in the attack and describing the strike as a Ukrainian provocation. Ukrainian prosecutors said they had evidence of Russian responsibility, while the investigation continued.

Lithuanian authorities have identified two men suspected of attempting to set fire to Starlink equipment in Vilnius earlier this month. Both men, who live in Germany, have been arrested there at Bulgaria’s request, Lithuanian law enforcement officials said Thursday.
The suspects are foreign nationals in their 20s, one holding German and Turkish citizenship and the other German and Serbian citizenship, Saulius Briginas, deputy head of the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau, told reporters.
Investigators believe the men arrived in Lithuania on the eve of the incident and left immediately after the attempted arson.
“They have no ties to Lithuania and came here to commit this crime,” Briginas said. “This was not a spontaneous crime. They knew exactly where they were going and what they intended to do, and they prepared for it in advance.”
Nėrijus Puškorius, chief prosecutor in the Organised Crime and Corruption Investigation Division of the Vilnius Regional Prosecutor’s Office, said the men face suspicions of forming an organised terrorist group to commit terrorist crimes, participating in a terrorist group, travelling for terrorist purposes and committing a terrorist act that could have had serious consequences.
The most severe penalty for forming or participating in a terrorist group is 10 to 15 years in prison, Puškorius said.
The suspects had been placed on a wanted list, and Lithuanian authorities are cooperating with law enforcement partners in Bulgaria, Poland and Germany.
“The two individuals have been detained in Germany,” Puškorius said, adding that a decision on whether they will be transferred to Lithuania would be made later.
Briginas said the suspects were also linked to arson attacks targeting Starlink equipment in Poland and Bulgaria. More people have been detained in Poland in connection with the incidents, he said.
The two men arrested in Germany are not believed to have personally set fire to Starlink equipment in Poland, but investigators suspect they were involved in that crime as well.
The attempted arson in Vilnius took place several weeks ago at premises belonging to Lithuanian company Delska, where the US company SpaceX operates and stores Starlink equipment. Lithuanian politicians have linked the incident to Russia.
Similar incidents have been investigated in Bulgaria, where several antennas used to connect to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire, and in Poland, where a fire broke out at a Starlink satellite communications station in the country’s central region in September.

US measles surge reminds of Europe’s vaccination gaps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:47:33 UTC
18:47:33 KST

The US risks losing its measles elimination status as under-vaccinated communities across Europe remain vulnerable to imported cases.
The United States is at risk of losing its measles-free status as cases surge, raising fresh concerns about the vulnerability of European communities where vaccination coverage remains below the level needed to prevent sustained transmission.
More than 4,500 cases have been reported in the US this year — roughly twice the total reported last year. A forecast published in JAMA suggests that measles could become endemic again in the US if vaccination rates fail to improve, potentially resulting in 851,300 cases, more than 170,000 hospitalisations and 2,550 deaths over 25 years.
The outbreak across the Atlantic could also signal a wider risk, Kitty Mohan, vice-president of the Standing Committee of European Doctors (CPME) and its rapporteur on vaccination, told Euronews.
“Due to international travel routes and the ease and speed at which people move across borders, combined the infectiousness of measles before the rash starts, people can travel quite far whilst infectious and so the disease can spread rapidly,” Mohan said.
Measles is among the most contagious infectious diseases. People can transmit the virus for around four days before the characteristic rash appears, meaning they may travel across borders before realising they are ill.
“15 mins face to face with someone who is infectious will mean you are likely to get measles,” Mohan said.
The US is not the only country where measles continues to circulate. The biggest outbreaks currently are in Bangladesh, with cases surpassing 65,430, Indonesia with 46,578 and Guatemala with 31,222 cases.
“Whether an imported case leads to further transmission in Europe depends primarily on immunity levels in the affected community in Europe and whether the virus reaches groups with low vaccination coverage,” the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) told Euronews.
Vaccination coverage was 92% for the first dose and 88% for the second dose — a “strong population protection,” ECDC said.
But that remains below the recommended 95% two-dose coverage needed at national and local levels to prevent sustained transmission and achieve measles elimination. National averages can also conceal areas or communities with lower vaccination coverage.
“Most measles cases occur in unvaccinated people,” the ECDC said, recommending that countries close immunity gaps, ensure both vaccine doses are administered on time, offer catch-up vaccination to eligible adolescents and adults, and maintain strong surveillance and outbreak-response systems.
The consequences extend beyond those who can choose to get vaccinated. Infants who are too young to receive the vaccine, as well as people who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons or whose immune systems cannot mount an adequate response, depend on high levels of immunity in the wider population.
“Herd immunity or maintaining vaccination rates above a threshold would protect these groups - so lower rates make them more susceptible to disease,” Mohan said.
Pockets of low coverage
The problem is not confined to countries with low national vaccination rates. Clusters of unvaccinated or under-vaccinated people can emerge within otherwise well-protected populations, creating local conditions in which outbreaks can take hold.
Coverage gaps can reflect a range of factors, including difficulties accessing vaccination services, limited information or awareness, and concerns about vaccines.
“There are traditional risk groups - such as traveller communities and some religious groups who historically have been reluctant to vaccinate,” said Mohan.
However, ECDC underlined that “the presence of a group of unvaccinated people does not automatically mean that a large outbreak will spread across the wider population,” using the Urkult festival in northern Sweden as an example. The outbreak at the festival occurred between 30 July and 2 August this year, mainly affecting unvaccinated children and adolescents. It involved 28 cases, including 12 secondary cases, but did not lead to sustained transmission in the wider population.
"The fact that there were relatively few secondary cases among those exposed at the festival is due to the high level of immunity within the population, a result of strong participation in the childhood vaccination program," said Johanna Rubin, Acting Head of the Vaccination Unit at Sweden’s public health agency.
“This once again highlights the importance of high community-level protection,” ECDC said.
For now, the risk for Europeans remains the same, ECDC said, as per its latest assessment, with the overall risk set as moderate for infants under 12 months, children aged one to five and immunocompromised people. For older unvaccinated children and adults, the risk is estimated to range from low to moderate. People with immunity from vaccination or previous infection are considered to have a low risk of measles.
ECDC surveillance data indicate fewer reported measles cases in 2026 than in 2025, although 2026 figures remain preliminary and should be interpreted with caution.
Measles is endemic in twelve European countries: Bosnia and Herzegovina, France, Georgia, Germany, Italy, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Poland, Romania, Russia, Türkiye, and Ukraine.
Romania reported most of the cases, with numbers reaching 30,692 in 2024, up from 3,371 in 2023.
Six European countries: Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan have re-established endemic measles transmission based on the number of cases in 2024 earlier this year.

Law Firm Linked to Elon Musk Started an ‘Election Integrity’ Organization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

The law firm that helped set up Elon Musk’s America PAC has created a new, nationwide “election integrity” organization aligned with Donald Trump’s false claims of election fraud, WIRED has learned.
The organization, a nonprofit called the Association of State and Local Election Officials, was established by a lawyer then at Lex Politica, the Musk-linked law firm founded by Chris Gober, who was chief counsel for America PAC in 2024 and is now running in Texas for a spot in the House of Representatives.
The board of directors, according to the nonprofit’s registration filing in Texas, boasts Florida secretary of state Cord Byrd, current and former state election officials in Georgia, a Michigan state representative, and the president of Cleta Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, a Trump administration-aligned election denial group. Byrd announced his involvement with the group—which he said won’t begin until after the election—alongside Florida governor Ron DeSantis in September, as the pair touted its mission, which aims to bring what they call “election integrity” policies down to the state and local level nationwide.
It’s not clear if Musk is involved in the organization. Until now, Musk has simply been a funder of Republican candidates and causes, and a benefactor of government contracts. Musk’s financial involvement in the midterm elections has been extensive: Musk’s America PAC is financing a sprawling canvassing operation aimed at helping Republican candidates get out the vote in November, and Musk is the single largest donor to Republican candidates this election cycle, spending more than $445 million, targeting Senate races key to maintaining a Republican majority. Since July, Musk has spent nearly as much money—$276 million—to boost Republican candidates as he did during the entire 2024 presidential election cycle. These elections are crucial for Musk. If Democrats win majorities in the House and Senate, Musk and his companies could be the subject of congressional investigations.
The link between a law firm that has worked with Musk and officials involved in purported “election integrity” activities is not surprising. For years, Musk has pushed the racist great replacement theory, which posits that minorities are systematically replacing white people in the US and in Western countries around the world. Election denialism—rooted in the unfounded theory of widespread voting by undocumented immigrants—is part of that racist theory of demographic societal change.
Musk has continually pushed election conspiracies that align with Trump’s false claims of election fraud, and this year, he’s doubled down. Musk has been a major disseminator of election misinformation this cycle, and recently boosted the false story that Texas US senate candidate James Talarico had been committed to a psychiatric facility in Ohio. America PAC has also spread inaccurate information about mail-in ballots.
The Association of State and Local Election Officials was first registered on June 17 by Michael Garcar as a nonprofit in Texas. At the time, Garcar was an attorney at Lex Politica, which was expanded after its lead lawyer, Gober, helped launch Musk’s America PAC. Gober has represented Musk’s and America PAC’s political interests in court cases in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.
On July 20, the Association of State and Local Election Officials was granted tax-exempt status by the IRS, according to an agency letter addressed to the organization at its Washington, DC, address. That address—a box in a UPS Store on Pennsylvania Avenue—is the same as the one Garcar listed on the organization’s Texas filing and belongs to Lex Politica, according to a US Supreme Court filing from one of the firm’s attorneys, Erin Hawley, wife of Senator Josh Hawley. The nonprofit’s Texas registration was first unearthed by True North Research, a Democratic-linked research group.
Garcar has since left Lex Politica and now works for Five Rings Law Group. The firm lists just two partners—both Lex Politica alums—and former Koch Industries lawyer Jenny Kim. Before launching Five Rings, Kim worked for Gober.
Garcar, Kim, and Gober did not respond to questions about Lex Politica’s ties to the Association of State and Local Election Officials.
At a September 24 press conference about the organization, Byrd and DeSantis announced their partnership with the nonprofit and said the Association of State and Local Election Officials will use Florida’s hard-line voting and election rules as a “blueprint” to enact similar policies across the country.
Byrd said the organization would “have state chapters to support, educate, and train local and state election officials on election integrity, because that’s something that the other side has been very good at.”
“They’re the ones going in and certifying and training people who run our elections, and not doing it in a way that we think comports with the law and voter trust,” Byrd said. The association “will be a national organization to promote election integrity, principles, and federal law and policy,” he added.
Under Byrd and DeSantis’ leadership, Florida has enacted rules and laws that voting rights advocates have criticized, including passing a state version of the federal SAVE Act that requires proof of citizenship at polling locations and prohibits the use of student IDs to vote beginning in 2027. “I’m very excited to head up that initiative and take what we’ve done in Florida as the blueprint, as the model for the nation, take it nationwide,” Byrd said in September.
The offices of Byrd and DeSantis did not respond to questions about their involvement with the organization.
The organization’s board is also staffed by Sharon Bemis, the president of Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, the country’s most prominent election denial organization; Julie Adams, an election denier who is both a member of the Fulton County Board of Elections in Georgia and a regional coordinator for the Election Integrity Network; Janice Johnston, who recently left the MAGA-dominated Georgia State Election Board; and Michigan state house representative Ann Bollin, who has coordinated with the Election Integrity Network.
The organization’s board members did not respond to questions for this story, though Johnston and Bollin have both previously denied being election deniers. The organization’s Texas registration contains no information about its work, and the group does not appear to have a web presence.
But the presence of Johnston and Adams on the board is telling.
In Georgia, Adams has made a name for herself by pushing Trump’s conspiracies about widespread election fraud and has sued multiple times for access to voting records with the help of the Republican National Committee. She has refused to certify results without being allowed to inspect voting records.
Johnston recently left Georgia’s State Election Board for what she said were “family and personal responsibility” reasons, and her time there was marked by turmoil, partisanship, and legal battles based on false fraud claims. Under her direction, the election board pursued specious investigations of Fulton County, supported mass voter purges championed by election denial activists, and worked to effectively eliminate voting machines.
Adams and Johnston have long targeted Fulton County for supposed fraud, and gleefully celebrated when, in January, the FBI raided an elections warehouse there, seizing tens of thousands of ballots from the 2020 election. Johnston was one of the unnamed witnesses in the FBI affidavit that preceded the raid, providing information about alleged double-counted ballots to the agency that had already been investigated and proven to have had no effect on the outcome of the 2020 election.
The Justice Department briefly fought in court to keep her name hidden from public view, but described a witness in the affidavit as “a Republican-appointed member” of the State Election Board who previously “was an obstetrician,” which identified Johnston. As the raid was being carried out, Johnston went live on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast from an SUV parked nearby.
When asked about Johnston’s presence on the board of the new Musk-linked election denial organization, Sara Tindall Ghazal, the lone Democrat on the Georgia State Election Board and Johnston’s former colleague, replied, “lol.”
“I mean this quite seriously, ‘lol.’ That’s my comment,” she tells WIRED.
And while Musk has quietly increased his political funding of Republicans, he has taken a bit of a step back from publicly discussing or posting about US politics and elections—with the exception of Talarico. His most recent post about voting is from September, when he responded to a question from Senator Mike Lee, a Republican from Utah. “Who benefits from noncitizen voting?” Lee asked on X.
“Democrats, which is why they push for open borders and noncitizen voting!” Musk responded. “Incentives explain behavior.”

By Mikhail Flores and Joe Cash
BEIJING/CEBU, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Tensions between the Philippines and China resurfaced at the close of a two-day ASEAN defence gathering on Thursday, with Beijing accusing an unnamed Philippine politician of obstructing its participation and Manila saying China had been given an opportunity to state its position.
China’s defence ministry said the “self-serving” politician had “imposed obstacles to China’s participation” in the expanded ASEAN defence ministers’ meeting in Cebu, without identifying the person.
Its spokesperson Zhang Xiaogang said at a press conference the actions ran counter to the meeting’s open and inclusive spirit, violated diplomatic norms, and undermined China’s rights as a dialogue partner.
China was represented at the meeting by a military attache in the absence of Defence Minister Dong Jun, who was likely attending a key Chinese Communist Party meeting in Beijing this week.
Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, who chaired the meetings, did not directly address the Chinese allegation of obstruction but said Beijing had been given the opportunity to present its views and that no ASEAN member raised similar concerns.
“The important fact is they were able to articulate their position on regional maritime security with little additions,” Teodoro said at his closing press conference. The Philippines has said its defence ministry sent notice to its Chinese counterpart with an invitation to join the forum.
“We allowed the exchange of views to be robust, and I think that was the important thing, the opportunity to be heard,” Teodoro said.
Relations between Beijing and Manila have soured amid repeated confrontations in the disputed South China Sea and, more recently, Chinese sanctions imposed on Teodoro.
The exchange put the spotlight back on that increasingly fraught relationship after defence officials at the annual gathering stressed practical cooperation and sought to find areas of agreement despite differences over the South China Sea and other regional security issues.
PHILIPPINES DEFENDS GROWING NETWORK OF DEFENCE PARTNERSHIPS
Washington used the gathering to reaffirm its commitment to the region, with US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday pledging the US would defend its interests and those of allies and partners while proposing greater defence cooperation with the 11-member bloc.
China claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea via a nine-dash line on its maps that cuts into parts of the exclusive economic zones of Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei and Indonesia. An international arbitral tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision Beijing rejects.
During bilateral meetings with several counterparts, including from other South China Sea claimant states, Teodoro stressed the importance of the 2016 ruling, arguing that its underlying principles were part of international law and not solely a Philippine matter.
In talks with Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, the two expressed serious concerns over the increasing scale and frequency of what they described as China’s coercive activities in disputed waters.
Teodoro also defended his country’s growing network of defence partnerships and rejected suggestions they undermined regional stability, saying the Philippines faced “unilateral and illegal claims made by China over its maritime domain.”
“If other ASEAN countries were subjected to the same kind of action in the magnitude the Philippines is experiencing, I am sure that they would resist this to the best of their ability,” Teodoro said as he reiterated the country’s commitment to peace and security.
(Reporting by Mikhail Flores in Cebu and Joe Cash in Beijing; additional reporting by Nestor Corrales in Manila, Writing by Andrew Silver in Beijing and Karen Lema in Manila; Editing by Liz Lee, Jacqueline Wong, Ros Russell and Keith Weir)

Oct 29 (Reuters) - The student-led protest movement that unseated Serbia’s longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a weekend election called on Thursday for the resignation of leading public figures and investigations into alleged corruption during Vucic’s tenure.
Candidates for the student movement ran on an anti-graft ticket, with their landslide victory heralding a new era in the Balkan country’s politics, which Vucic dominated for 12 years.
At a press conference in a park in front of the parliament building, representatives of the students demanded the resignation of police commanders, officials in the state security and military intelligence agencies, and state prosecutors.
They also called for the reopening or expediting of cases related to the dealings of Vucic’s government, including the 2024 railway station canopy collapse in Novi Sad that killed 16 people and sparked the student protest movement.
“We demand an immediate audit of the current state of public institutions, ministries, public enterprises, the EPS electric power utility, and state funds, including finances, contracts, public procurement and assumed obligations,” said Filip Ubovic, a student activist. He urged public sector employees to preserve documents and report suspicious activity during the transition of power.
Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) deny allegations of corruption and repression. But the country has slipped down international indexes that measure press freedom and corruption, and critics have complained of violent attempts to silence them.
In one high-profile case, prosecutors allege that senior government officials, including culture minister Nikola Selakovic, forged documents to unlawfully remove the protected status of the former Yugoslav Army headquarters in central Belgrade that US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner wanted to develop into a luxury hotel complex.
Selakovic denies wrongdoing. Kushner was not accused of wrongdoing and has since dropped the project.
“The Student List … urgently demands that the Supreme Public Prosecutor ensure that all public prosecutor’s offices act lawfully, impartially, and swiftly in cases that have drawn significant public attention,” said Jovan Vujicic, an assistant professor at the University of Kragujevac’s Faculty of Law who will enter parliament for the Student List.
Supreme Public Prosecutor Zagorka Dolovac on Thursday instructed chief prosecutors to submit requests to the police to prevent the destruction of official and other documents in state institutions.
VUCIC TO REVAMP PARTY DEFEATED IN ELECTION
The call came a day after the director of pro-Vucic Serbian state television RTS, Manja Grcic, resigned after discussions with union representatives, saying she was aware that among some parts of the public, her stay in office is “temporarily perceived as an obstacle to change”.
Mirjana Nikolic, a professor and the rector of the University of Arts in Belgrade who will also enter parliament, proposed a temporary management board at RTS to “ensure continuity of operations, editorial independence, and the protection of journalists”.
A few minutes earlier, Vucic, on Pink TV, which is also supportive of the previous government, condemned what he called the forced removal of Grcic. He also said he would refresh the SNS’s board, bringing in new people to two-thirds of the positions.
“We want to…examine how to change ourselves, how to be prepared for the difficult times ahead, to have…persons with knowledge and who will show genuine care for the people in the future,” Vucic said.
In its latest update on Wednesday, Serbia’s electoral commission said the Student List had secured 140 seats in the country’s 250-seat parliament, with the SNS on 104, although the result is still not finalised, meaning parliament cannot be convened.
The country is waiting to see who the students will appoint as prime minister and to other key positions.

Explainer-How could Israel break the election deadlock?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:44:02 CET
18:44:02 KST

By Maayan Lubell
JERUSALEM, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Israel’s election this week was indecisive and there is no clear winner poised to form a government. Benjamin Netanyahu remains in office as caretaker prime minister, but faces a parliament stacked with an opposition majority vying to oust him.
Here are some scenarios that could follow:
ANOTHER ELECTION
After the formal final election results are published next week, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with party representatives and then taps the candidate whom he deems to have the best chance to form a government.
If the candidate fails, another can try and if that candidate fails, the Knesset can nominate another. There is a deadline for the process of around 100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is held.
Herzog said on Wednesday that everything must be done to avoid another election and urged the parties to come with an open mind to the consultations with him.
UNITY GOVERNMENT
Netanyahu’s Likud party, emerging as the largest in the Knesset, forms a coalition that would likely include centrist and right-wing opposition parties such as Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar, the second-largest party, Avigdor Lieberman’s Israel Our Home and Naftali Bennett’s Together faction.
That grouping would secure 66 seats, a majority in the 120-seat parliament.
However, this option appears remote at this point because it would mean Netanyahu would likely have to abandon his natural political allies, the far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties. Further, the opposition parties would have to break their main election pledge to their voters: unseating Netanyahu.
Still, if neither camp is able to form a government at the end of weeks of protracted negotiations, a unity government may emerge as a last option.
Renewed fighting with Iran, or other players, could also push the sides together.
EISENKOT MINORITY GOVERNMENT
If Herzog taps Eisenkot first, he could try to form a government with Yashar’s natural allies — Together, The Democrats and Israel Our Home — propped up by Israel’s two Arab parties, even if they are not members of this government: Ra’am and the Joint List.
Eisenkot’s camp would number 48 seats, according to the latest vote tally, with the Arab parties numbering 19 seats that together reach a 67-seat majority.
But even if Eisenkot reverses his campaign pledge not to have Arab parties in government and accepts their support, it would be a hard sell to many Israelis whose attitudes toward Israel’s Arab minority have hardened further since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack.
Netanyahu has focused his campaign on delegitimizing support from Arab parties, who surged to record heights in Tuesday’s election, and for now, only The Democrats, a centre-left party, has come out publicly calling for their inclusion.
Both Arab parties have signalled that they are prepared to cooperate with Eisenkot’s camp.
Ra’am joined Bennett’s government in 2021, the first time an independent Arab party entered an Israeli coalition. That government collapsed after 18 months.
NETANYAHU FINDS A MAJORITY FOR A RIGHT-WING GOVERNMENT
Netanyahu’s coalition has fallen from its original 64 seats to 53, according to the latest election results. But Israel’s longest-serving leader is viewed as one of its most skilled politicians and he could split the opposition by peeling away members of its parties and bringing them over to his side.
He has managed to do this before, including as opposition head in the run-up to the 2022 election, which he won. But the coalition he was battling at the time had a far narrower lead and he did not need too many defectors to destabilize his political rivals.
(Reporting by Maayan Lubell; Editing by Sharon Singleton)

Top Russian official takes US journalists into besieged Ukrainian city ahead of evacuation
Italy

2026-10-29

18:44:02 KST

Oct 29 (Reuters) - Russia and Ukraine both praised US first lady Melania Trump on Thursday for helping to broker a truce around the acutely deprived Russian-held Ukrainian town of Oleshky, as efforts began to bring in food and medicines and enable hundreds to leave.
Yet any sense of wider relief in a war that began with a Russian invasion almost five years ago was rapidly dispelled by a drone strike that killed 13 people crowding onto a commuter train at the main station in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, according to local officials, where no ceasefire was in place.
The Oleshky operation aims to address a growing crisis in a town marooned inside a war zone since 2022 - but is also part of a diplomatic dance where both sides want to show US President Donald Trump that they back his peace efforts, albeit for different reasons.
Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner, said she was taking four journalists from the conservative US outlet Newsmax to the area as her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets, also headed for Oleshky.
PUTIN SAYS MOSCOW IS MAKING PEACE EFFORTS
President Vladimir Putin told a summit in Moscow that relief supplies would begin reaching civilians on Thursday and Friday, “with the support, incidentally, of the First Lady of the United States”.
Lubinets, for his part, extended Kyiv’s “special thanks” to someone who was “personally devoting her time and attention to the humanitarian mission and assistance to civilians in Oleshky”.
Trump has cast Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy as an obstacle to peace while praising Putin, who emphasised on Thursday that Russia was “working on issues relating to a possible peaceful resolution of the Ukrainian crisis itself”.
Although Russia, like Ukraine, denies targeting civilians, strikes on trains and other civilian infrastructure have become increasingly common as Ukraine’s stocks of air defence missiles have dwindled. Civilian deaths have also increased inside Russia.
On Thursday, the state rail company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a jet-powered drone had hit a platform in the Ukrainian industrial hub of Dnipro where a commuter train was preparing to depart for nearby Zaporizhzhia.
Although US-mediated peace talks are due to resume next month in Abu Dhabi after a long pause, the two sides are far apart when it comes to terms for ending the war.
But both recognise the power of Trump, who has another two years in power left regardless of the outcome of US midterm legislative elections next month, to affect the course of the conflict.
Russia still hopes that Trump can pressure Kyiv into agreeing a deal that meets many of its conditions - such as full Russian control of Ukraine’s Donbas region and a bar on Ukraine joining the transatlantic defence alliance, NATO.
Kyiv, meanwhile, wants to ensure that US intelligence sharing continues along with full access to Elon Musk’s recently disrupted battlefield communications system, Starshield, and that European-bought US military hardware, including Patriot interceptor missiles, continues to flow.
KHERSON CEASEFIRE DUE TO CONTINUE UNTIL SUNDAY
The truce applies only to Oleshky and the wider Kherson region, which has suffered years of near-daily drone and artillery attacks. Some 1,500 of the prewar population of 24,000 people are believed to live among the ruins, under regular shellfire amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Ukraine has long accused Russia of refusing to let aid in or people out. Russia says it is Ukrainian mines on the approach roads and Ukrainian shelling that have prevented the delivery of aid or the safe evacuation of residents.
By the middle of Thursday, neither Ukraine nor Russia had reported any violations of the ceasefire, which was due to last until Sunday.
“Demining is under way there, and we hope that today or tomorrow residents will be able to receive humanitarian aid safely and without obstruction, and that those wishing to leave will be able to do so,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was cited as saying by the Interfax news agency.
Residents wishing to leave and return to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government are expected to exit via Russia-controlled Crimea before crossing into southern Russia and being flown to Belarus from where they will be able to cross the border into Ukraine.

Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) has raised the country’s cyber risk level to “high,” the second-highest level on its scale, citing the deteriorating security situation and events in recent months.
Announcing the decision at a news conference on Tuesday, NSM Director Arne Christian Haugstoyl urged Norwegian businesses to strengthen their digital defenses and address known software vulnerabilities immediately.
The authority warned that the rapid development of artificial intelligence is enabling threat actors to identify and exploit security weaknesses much more efficiently.
“Businesses therefore have hours, not days or weeks, to close known vulnerabilities,” Haugstoyl said.
In a press release, NSM called on Norwegian companies to implement preventive security measures without delay and published a list of 21 recommended actions applicable to businesses across the country.
Justice and Emergency Preparedness Minister Astri Aas-Hansen also urged companies to assess their IT security and rapidly address vulnerabilities, broadcaster NRK reported.
According to Haugstoyl, successful cyber operations targeting Norwegian businesses have tripled over the past year, with several incidents resulting in serious consequences.
One publicly known case involved the municipality of Lorenskog, where a large amount of data was stolen in a breach.
The stolen information was subsequently sold on the dark web.
The elevated risk assessment underscores growing concerns about cyber threat actors' ability to exploit digital vulnerabilities, particularly as artificial intelligence accelerates their capabilities.

Russian air defense systems intercepted a record 1,214 Ukrainian drones across the country amid an overnight air barrage, the Defense Ministry said Thursday, as authorities in Ukraine said Russia killed at least 14 people in a strike on a train platform.
The total number of downed drones in Russia surpassed the previous record set on Sept. 20, when the military reported destroying more than 1,100 Ukrainian unmanned aircraft across the country and annexed Crimea during the final day of parliamentary and regional elections.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said Thursday that 613 drones were tracked in the skies above the Moscow region overnight, with around a third of them being destroyed on their approach to the Russian capital.
The Kremlin condemned the attack on Moscow, which is currently hosting more than 22 foreign leaders at the Russia-Africa summit.
In Ukraine, authorities in the Dnipro region said a Russian drone struck a train platform, killing 14 people and wounding five others. It marked one of the most deadly attacks on the southeastern region in recent months.
A separate attack on the Rivne region of northwestern Ukraine killed one person overnight.
Back in Russia, authorities in the industrial city of Sterlitamak, located in the republic of Bashkortostan, said falling drone debris caused minor damage at an industrial site.
The exiled outlet Astra said it used eyewitness footage of smoke rising above an industrial area in Sterlitamak to identify the targeted site as the Bashkir Soda Company, located 1,200 kilometers (750 miles) east of Russia’s border with Ukraine. It was previously attacked on Aug. 27.
The company is Russia’s only producer of terephthaloyl chloride, a critical chemical used to make high-strength aramid fibers found in body armor, helmets and protective military vehicle materials.
In the Perm region, Governor Dmitry Makhonin said a Ukrainian drone attack caused slight damage to an industrial facility, which he did not identify by name.
One person was killed and seven were injured in the southwestern Belgorod region, according to local officials.
Thursday’s deadly exchange of attacks in Russia and Ukraine came as negotiators from the two warring countries prepare to hold a new round of U.S.-mediated talks to end the conflict.
A renewed flurry of diplomacy, spearheaded by White House special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, has once again raised hopes that a peace agreement can be reached.
However, serious doubts remain about the extent to which either Ukraine or Russia is ready to make a compromise on what have so far been major sticking points, such as control of the eastern Donbas region and security guarantees that will satisfy both countries.
European officials have increasingly thrown themselves into the fray of diplomacy with Moscow in recent months, with the leaders of Norway and Finland earlier this week holding a call with Putin to discuss ways to de-escalate the Ukraine war.
Despite the outreach from officials in Europe, the Kremlin has stressed that it is not yet ready to have them directly involved in peace talks, which have so far been limited to meetings between Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators.
Still, Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov said Thursday that Moscow would “sooner or later need to talk to people we don’t particularly like,” referring to European leaders.

General Atomics and Saab have flown an airborne early warning radar on an uncrewed MQ-9B, the same aircraft the Royal Air Force operates as Protector, tracking fighter jets and commercial aircraft along with maritime targets at long range during months of testing, according to the companies.
The flights used a Saab LoyalEye radar carried in payload pods on a General Atomics MQ-9B operating from the company’s Desert Horizon facility in southern California, and demonstrated simultaneous tracking of several airborne and maritime targets, including multiple instrumented fighter jets acting as targets.
David Alexander, president of General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, said: “This has been one of the most highly anticipated flight tests we have performed. The level of customer interest in AEW capability on MQ-9B throughout the world is extremely high. It just makes sense.”
Carl-Johan Bergholm, head of Saab’s surveillance business area, said: “This flight test underscores Saab’s commitment to evolving airborne early warning capabilities to meet future operational needs. LoyalEye complements existing capabilities by adding flexibility, extending reach, and enabling a more efficient use of resources in demanding environments.”
Airborne early warning has always meant a large crewed aircraft, because the radar, the operators and the fuel to stay up all demanded size, and the number any air force can afford has fallen with every generation. Britain is buying three Wedgetail aircraft to replace a Sentry fleet that once numbered seven. The Royal Air Force will hold one of the smallest early warning forces of any major air arm.
Putting the radar on an uncrewed aircraft changes the arithmetic of that problem, because an MQ-9B can stay airborne far longer than a crewed jet, costs a fraction as much to buy and operate, and risks nobody if it is lost. What it cannot do is carry the battle management staff who make a Wedgetail more than a big flying radar, so the companies describe the command and control function being performed elsewhere, on the ground, on a ship or aboard an existing crewed aircraft, etc.
Protector entered Royal Air Force service at RAF Waddington this year, replacing Reaper, and ministers confirmed this month that eleven of the sixteen aircraft on order have been delivered. The type is certified to fly in civil airspace. Earlier armed drones were not, and that certification is why Protector can fly over Britain.
General Atomics is also developing a short take-off and landing version of the MQ-9B intended to operate from aircraft carriers, a configuration the Royal Navy has watched closely as it works out what flies from HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Queen Elizabeth alongside the F-35B.
Saab’s existing airborne early warning radars fly on the GlobalEye, based on the Bombardier Global 6000 business jet, which Sweden operates and which has been sold to the United Arab Emirates and ordered by Denmark.

Trump-Putin diesel deal has not lowered US fuel prices – WSJ
Average US diesel prices have risen by 7 cents since US President Donald Trump reached a deal with Russia on diesel supplies.
Source: The Wall Street Journal
Details: According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average price of a gallon of diesel in the US reached US$6.35 on Wednesday 28 October (about US$1.68 per litre), up from US$6.28 per gallon when Trump announced the deal.
On 9 October, Trump wrote that Russia was expected to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to US and global markets in October, a further 500,000 tonnes in November, and another 1 million tonnes immediately afterwards.
However, the newspaper reported that analysts remain sceptical that the deal will help bring down high diesel prices in the US and worldwide.
Experts also say Russia may be unable to export the promised volumes of diesel because of the poor condition of its oil refineries and export restrictions.
Even if Russia manages to do so, the promised volumes would cover only a fraction of the global shortfall. They amount to just over 100,000 barrels per day in October and around 125,000 barrels per day in November. In 2025, Russia was able to ship around 800,000 barrels per day.
Background:
- On 22 October, the first tanker carrying 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel set sail for New York. The vessel is expected to arrive in the US on 7 November. Two more tankers were subsequently added.
- One of the three tankers is under sanctions imposed by the EU, the UK and Canada.

Researchers develop AI tool to identify bacterial DNA in soil
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:49:12 CST
23:49:12 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Israeli researchers have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) tool that can identify bacterial DNA in tiny genetic fragments found in soil, the Hebrew University of Jerusalem said Thursday.
Researchers extract DNA from soil samples to study the microorganisms living there, but identifying the source of many genetic fragments remains difficult.
The tool, called BBERT, is an AI model designed to process highly fragmented DNA/RNA sequences as short as 100 DNA letters and learn patterns in bacterial DNA, the university said in a statement.
In their study, published in Nucleic Acids Research, the researchers showed that the tool can identify bacterial DNA, including genetic material that can't be matched to existing reference databases.
The tool helps distinguish bacterial DNA from that of other organisms and identify fragments containing protein-making instructions, they said.
In tests, BBERT distinguished bacterial from non-bacterial DNA with around 90 percent accuracy, identified protein-making fragments with 88 percent accuracy and their correct reading frames with 96 percent accuracy.
Tested on 1,969 publicly available soil DNA datasets, the tool identified many fragments that existing methods had left unclassified.
The researchers said that the tool could help uncover previously overlooked genetic information and better understand the diversity of life in soil. ■
