FRANKFURT, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The European Central Bank (ECB) announced on Thursday that it would leave its key interest rates unchanged.
The interest rates on the deposit facility, the main refinancing operations and the marginal lending facility will remain unchanged at 2.5 percent, 2.65 percent and 2.9 percent, respectively.
Rising energy prices are posing upside risks to the inflation outlook but underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far, the ECB said in a press release.
"The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth."
Inflation in the euro area surged in September to 3.8 percent from 3.2 percent in August, hitting a three-year high. The rise in inflation has been driven largely by higher energy prices, according to data released by the European Commission.
The ECB has hiked interest rates twice this year, pushing the interest rate on the deposit facility up to 2.5 percent from two percent.
The ECB insists that it is "well positioned" to navigate the current elevated uncertainty and will still continue to follow its data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determine its future monetary policy stance.
The ECB is scheduled to publish its latest edition of the staff projections in December. ■

Finnish news agency STT to end news services after 139 years
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:49:00 CST
23:49:00 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Finland's national news agency STT announced on Thursday that it will shut down its news and photo services by the end of March 2027, ending 139 years of journalistic operations amid prolonged financial difficulties.
STT's board confirmed the decision after completing legally mandated negotiations with employees. The closure is expected to eliminate 89 positions, including 68 journalism jobs. In addition, 30 fixed-term employment contracts or framework agreements will end.
STT said its news and photo services would continue operating until March 31, 2027. Its press release distribution business, which employs seven people, would remain operational.
The agency attributed the closure to years of financial losses and a lack of shareholders' commitment to sustain and develop its operations. Previous cost-cutting measures had failed to restore financial viability.
Its financial situation worsened when Sanoma, Finland's major media group and STT's principal shareholder, stopped using the agency's services at the beginning of 2026.
STT CEO Kimmo Laaksonen described the closure as "a great tragedy for Finnish society as a whole," noting that the agency would mark its 139th anniversary on Sunday.
The Finnish government had earlier pledged 1.05 million euros (about 1.17 million U.S. dollars) in financial assistance to STT. However, the funding was never disbursed, and the Ministry of Transport and Communications suspended preparations for the subsidy in September pending a decision on the agency's future.
Founded in 1887, STT is one of the world's oldest national news agencies. The closure will leave Finland among the few European countries without a national news agency.
The Union of Journalists in Finland has warned that the loss of STT could weaken access to reliable information, particularly in regional and local media, which depend heavily on the agency for national and international news coverage.
The union said regional news outlets would face higher costs or reduced news coverage as they seek alternatives to STT's services. It also warned that the closure could threaten the survival of other struggling media organizations. ■

Matevosyan noted that the core task of COP17 is to complete the first global review of progress under the KMGBF and deliver on the Yerevan Pathway, shifting global efforts from pledges to tangible action to conserve nature.
"A majority of parties have submitted their national reports, laying an objective foundation for the assessment. Available evidence shows the world is far from reaching the 2030 targets," he said, noting that the first-ever global review of collective progress towards the KMGBF in Yerevan is of critical importance because it will clarify how close the world is to achieving its goals and identify implementation gaps.
Beyond the negotiations, China took the lead in establishing the Kunming Biodiversity Fund in 2021, contributing its own resources to help developing countries strengthen their conservation capacity. Officially launched in 2024, the fund offers new opportunities and helps turn decisions made at COP meetings into tangible results, he said.
Matevosyan said China and Armenia are already cooperating on national parks and protected areas.
"I had the honor of visiting China's Botanical Garden and China's Elephant Park during the Kunming Dialogue. My team and I met many scientists and specialist protected-area managers in China. We maintain excellent contact with the Chinese delegation, which has also visited Armenia's national parks," he said.
The success of COP17 will not end on Oct. 30, as Armenia will hold the COP presidency for another two years, he said.
He welcomed the Parties' strong willingness to advance work and their request for more time for negotiations. In the final stage of the conference, the presidency aims to produce a robust, objective global review. ■

Early warning radar flown on Protector type airframe

Unknown Publisher

General Atomics and Saab have flown an airborne early warning radar on an uncrewed MQ-9B, the same aircraft the Royal Air Force operates as Protector, tracking fighter jets and commercial aircraft along with maritime targets at long range during months of testing, according to the companies.
The flights used a Saab LoyalEye radar carried in payload pods on a General Atomics MQ-9B operating from the company’s Desert Horizon facility in southern California, and demonstrated simultaneous tracking of several airborne and maritime targets, including multiple instrumented fighter jets acting as targets.
David Alexander, president of General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, said: “This has been one of the most highly anticipated flight tests we have performed. The level of customer interest in AEW capability on MQ-9B throughout the world is extremely high. It just makes sense.”
Carl-Johan Bergholm, head of Saab’s surveillance business area, said: “This flight test underscores Saab’s commitment to evolving airborne early warning capabilities to meet future operational needs. LoyalEye complements existing capabilities by adding flexibility, extending reach, and enabling a more efficient use of resources in demanding environments.”
Airborne early warning has always meant a large crewed aircraft, because the radar, the operators and the fuel to stay up all demanded size, and the number any air force can afford has fallen with every generation. Britain is buying three Wedgetail aircraft to replace a Sentry fleet that once numbered seven. The Royal Air Force will hold one of the smallest early warning forces of any major air arm.
Putting the radar on an uncrewed aircraft changes the arithmetic of that problem, because an MQ-9B can stay airborne far longer than a crewed jet, costs a fraction as much to buy and operate, and risks nobody if it is lost. What it cannot do is carry the battle management staff who make a Wedgetail more than a big flying radar, so the companies describe the command and control function being performed elsewhere, on the ground, on a ship or aboard an existing crewed aircraft, etc.
Protector entered Royal Air Force service at RAF Waddington this year, replacing Reaper, and ministers confirmed this month that eleven of the sixteen aircraft on order have been delivered. The type is certified to fly in civil airspace. Earlier armed drones were not, and that certification is why Protector can fly over Britain.
General Atomics is also developing a short take-off and landing version of the MQ-9B intended to operate from aircraft carriers, a configuration the Royal Navy has watched closely as it works out what flies from HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Queen Elizabeth alongside the F-35B.
Saab’s existing airborne early warning radars fly on the GlobalEye, based on the Bombardier Global 6000 business jet, which Sweden operates and which has been sold to the United Arab Emirates and ordered by Denmark.

Trump-Putin diesel deal has not lowered US fuel prices – WSJ
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:40:00 EET
18:40:00 KST

Trump-Putin diesel deal has not lowered US fuel prices – WSJ
Average US diesel prices have risen by 7 cents since US President Donald Trump reached a deal with Russia on diesel supplies.
Source: The Wall Street Journal
Details: According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average price of a gallon of diesel in the US reached US$6.35 on Wednesday 28 October (about US$1.68 per litre), up from US$6.28 per gallon when Trump announced the deal.
On 9 October, Trump wrote that Russia was expected to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to US and global markets in October, a further 500,000 tonnes in November, and another 1 million tonnes immediately afterwards.
However, the newspaper reported that analysts remain sceptical that the deal will help bring down high diesel prices in the US and worldwide.
Experts also say Russia may be unable to export the promised volumes of diesel because of the poor condition of its oil refineries and export restrictions.
Even if Russia manages to do so, the promised volumes would cover only a fraction of the global shortfall. They amount to just over 100,000 barrels per day in October and around 125,000 barrels per day in November. In 2025, Russia was able to ship around 800,000 barrels per day.
Background:
- On 22 October, the first tanker carrying 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel set sail for New York. The vessel is expected to arrive in the US on 7 November. Two more tankers were subsequently added.
- One of the three tankers is under sanctions imposed by the EU, the UK and Canada.

Jetten backpedals on plans to tax the royals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:38:45 UTC
18:38:45 KST

Jetten backpedals on plans to tax the royals
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Prime minister Rob Jetten is refusing to act on calls for the royal family to pay taxes, despite his party D66 having actively backed the idea for years.
The Dutch royals receive personal salaries, which is only a fraction of their overall wealth, and plans to tax them on their incomes have been debated by parliament for more than a decade.
The king, for example, will receive roughly €7.5 million from the state next year, of which €1.2 million is personal income and the rest covers staff and running costs. He pays no tax on it. In January 2024 D66 tabled a motion calling on the government to change the constitution so that the royals would pay income tax.
For the first time in history, the motion got two-thirds parliamentary support, with over 100 MPs backing it. But the successive prime ministers Mark Rutte and Dick Schoof both refused to push the plan forward.
Last December D66 also voted for a similar motion by GroenLinks-PvdA (Pro) MP Laura Bromet, asking that royals who receive an allowance pay the same taxes as everyone else.
Now Jetten appears to be doing the same. He told MPs on Wednesday that the yearly debate had become an “unproductive dynamic” and that he wants a broader review of a “future-proof monarchy” instead.
He promised the Christian Democrats (CDA) that it would not lead to a ceremonial monarchy. Ending the exemption would also require a change to the constitution, which exempts the king from tax on his allowance.
Opposition parties are furious at his backpedalling on the issue. “D66 was angry every year that the motions were not implemented. Now the party has a unique opportunity to reflect on the future of the monarchy,” Socialist (SP) MP Sandra Beckerman told NOS. “You would think that you would seize that opportunity.”
Dutch republican group Republiek, which campaigns for the abolition of the monarchy, wrote an open letter to Jetten saying “a large majority of the population indicates time and again in polls that they are in favour of the king paying taxes.”
“For twelve years now, there has been a majority in the House of Representatives in favour of abolishing the tax exemption for the royal family. Time and again, the plans failed during the implementation by the prime ministers. But now you are our prime minister.”
The letter is signed off using the campaign slogan D66 used to come to power in the current coalition: “In your own words: het kan wel” (it’s possible).
MPs will soon vote on a motion from Bromet backing Jetten’s review, and one from Beckerman telling the cabinet to act on the royal tax motions parliament has already passed.

Talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the US have been stalled since winter, and the fight now is over timing. On 27 October, Zelenskyy said Kyiv wants that round before a Putin-Trump-Xi summit, which would leave Ukraine out of the room. Putin proposed that summit, The Wall Street Journal reported. Ankara’s statement names neither track, but Ukraine sits at the table only in the first.
Ankara offers support, but no date or venue
The statement named no date or Turkish venue. In July, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said in Kyiv that the Türkiye-mediated Istanbul talks should continue in the same format. Türkiye hosted Russia-Ukraine talks in 2022 and 2025. The 2 June 2025 round in Istanbul ended with a prisoner swap deal but no ceasefire. In March, Zelenskyy named Türkiye among possible venues.
“I really don’t want this to be Yalta 2, 3, 4”: Zelenskyy fears Trump-Xi-Putin meeting could redivide world, with Ukraine on agenda
Everyone says soon, but no date is set

Trump told reporters on 28 October that a meeting with Putin and Zelenskyy would be set up soon. The Kremlin keeps its condition. Ushakov claimed on 27 October that such a contact makes the most sense after the negotiation process ends, and repeated that Zelenskyy should come to Moscow.
Another mediator does not decide which meeting comes first. Kyiv and Moscow have both confirmed Abu Dhabi, Zelenskyy said, so it now depends on the US side. Earlier this month, Trump said he waived new sanctions on Russia so as not to drive Moscow from the talks.

Taiwan semiconductor output forecast to top NT$9.1 trillion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:36:46 UTC
18:36:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The nation's semiconductor industry output is forecast to exceed NT$9.1 trillion (US$279.6 billion) this year, Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association Chair Hou Yung-ching (侯永清) said Thursday.
The figure would represent a 40.9% increase from last year, when industry output was NT$6.5 trillion. Thirty years ago, output stood at NT$180 billion, according to CTEE and Tai Sounds.
Hou said Taiwan ranks first globally in wafer manufacturing and semiconductor packaging and testing, and second in chip design. Its comprehensive industry structure and close cooperation across the supply chain have supported growth.
Rapid AI development is driving demand for related equipment, materials, and chemicals, prompting suppliers to expand production capacity. Securing land for new facilities has been a particular hurdle, Hou said.
With government assistance, the association has helped suppliers identify suitable sites for expansion. Four materials suppliers are expected to begin construction in April next year, while another seven are still completing the necessary procedures.
The association has also worked with the Industrial Technology Research Institute and chipmaker TSMC to establish a platform for equipment suppliers to test their products and better understand manufacturers' requirements. The initiative aims to help suppliers address technical gaps and develop products that meet industry needs.
Hou said the country's semiconductor industry has significant room to grow, although energy supply and other external factors remain challenges. As the sector expands, the association has added 18 international corporate members since 2023, bringing its total membership to 220, up from 57 founding members.

Taiwan's Wan Hai Lines expands Indian market presence with new route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:36:26 UTC
18:36:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wan Hai Lines Ltd. is expanding its presence in the Indian market with the launch of a new shipping service in late November.
The new service will connect markets in Vietnam, southern China, Malaysia, and western India. Container ships with capacities of 2,800 to 3,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) will operate on a 35-day rotation, according to CTEE.
Wan Hai expects the new route to complement its existing network and strengthen shipping connections across the region. The port rotation will cover Haiphong, Qinzhou, Nansha, Shekou, Port Klang, Mundra, Nhava Sheva, and Port Klang before returning to Haiphong.
The company reported consolidated revenue of NT$21.8 billion (US$669 million) in September, up 97.63% from a year earlier. Revenue for the first nine months reached NT$136.2 billion, an annual increase of 27.28%, according to UDN Money.
Wan Hai said shipping demand has recovered more strongly than in previous years following China's National Day holiday in early October, as manufacturing and shipping activities gradually resume. Cargo owners are arranging shipments earlier than usual to reduce supply chain uncertainty caused by port congestion, shipping delays, and fluctuating fuel costs.
The fourth quarter is traditionally a peak season for intra-Asia short-sea shipping. With cargo volumes continuing to grow and freight rates remaining at relatively favorable levels, Wan Hai expects its operating momentum to remain stable.

Japan and US Agree to Establish AIM-120 Missile Assembly Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:35:46 UTC
18:35:46 KST

Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and U.S.Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have agreed to establish a facility in Japan to assemble AIM-120 air-to-air missiles.
According to Nikkei, negotiations on the project have been underway since at least 2024.
Preparations for localizing AIM-120 missile production had been underway since at least September 1, 2026. On that date, Japan’s Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency published Notice No. 137, seeking a contractor to conduct research into establishing domestic production of components for these missiles.
Applications were accepted until September 30, with the research scheduled for completion by March 26, 2027.
Requirements for potential contractors included being a Japanese company and having experience in the design, production, and testing of medium-range air-to-air missiles.
One company that meets these criteria is Mitsubishi Electric, which has extensive experience in producing domestically developed air-to-air missiles of this class, including the Type 99, a Japanese counterpart to the American AIM-120.
On April 28, 2026, Mitsubishi Electric confirmed that it was in talks with Raytheon about participating in the joint production of AMRAAM missiles. At the time, the two companies were discussing the extent of Japan’s involvement in missile production.
The work will involve manufacturing circuit card assemblies. In the future, Mitsubishi Electric plans to participate in the missiles’ final assembly and checkout.
The exact location of the planned facility is currently unknown.
The construction of a facility for assembling, inspecting, and testing AIM-120 missiles is linked to two ambitious plans.
The first is Japan’s plan to procure 1,200 missiles of this type to equip its F-35A and F-35B fighter jets.
Due to certain restrictions, Japanese missiles cannot be integrated into these aircraft. As a result, Japan cannot standardize its missile arsenal using only domestically produced weapons.
The second objective is to manufacture missiles for export to the United States amid growing demand for these munitions. AIM-120 missiles are among the most widely used air-to-air missiles in the world and are equipped with active radarseekers.
They are used by numerous types of combat aircraft, as well as by NASAMS air defense systems operated by the United States and several European countries, including Ukraine. Ukraine’s NASAMS systems regularly use these missiles to repel Russian aerial attacks, creating a significant need to replenish stocks.

Brussels rejects Baltic states’ €500 million anti-drone request, suggests borrowing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:34:00 UTC
18:34:00 KST

The European Commission has responded to a request by Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia for 500 million euros to develop anti-drone defences, but has offered no new funding on the scale sought by the three Baltic states.
Defence ministers from the three countries sent a letter to the European Commission in late September requesting urgent financial support to strengthen defences against drones.
Several stray drones have entered the Baltic airspaces this year amid air attacks between Ukraine and Russia.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, Estonian Defence Minister Martin Herem and Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis sought the funding to develop an anti-drone system that could also serve as a model for other European Union countries.
The letter was classified, but Kaunas told LRT that the Baltic states wanted to combine drone detection, artificial intelligence and interception technology into an integrated air defence system.
“Air defence and anti-drone solutions are important not only for our region but for all of Europe. Lithuania has taken the lead in developing an anti-drone air defence system,” Kaunas said.
The Baltic states had hoped the European Commission would approve additional funding for regional anti-drone defences before the end of this year. The commission previously told LRT.lt that it was carefully assessing the request and took member states’ concerns very seriously.
However, Andrius Kubilius, the European commissioner for defence and space, told LRT on Wednesday that the commission had sent its response but could not offer the additional funding the Baltic states had sought.
“One possibility now is to make use of additional funding under the SAFE instrument. We will announce a new call in the near future, because 21 billion euros remained after the first call,” Kubilius said.
He added that there were few other substantial funding opportunities available through EU budget programs because the current budget period was nearing its end.
Funding for anti-drone measures may also be available through the Integrated Border Management Fund, LRT understands, although the sums involved would be far below the 500 million euros requested by the Baltic states.
SAFE loans offer an alternative
The Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, instrument, launched last year, provides 150 billion euros in favourable loans for defence procurement across the EU.
The scheme offers loans with repayment periods of up to 45 years and advance payments of up to 15%. The loans are financed through EU-level borrowing, benefiting from the bloc’s AAA credit rating.
Lithuania has been allocated access to up to 6.375 billion euros in SAFE loans. The government plans to use the funds to establish a land forces division, develop the Baltic Defence Line, strengthen air defence, purchase ammunition and military equipment, and finance other military modernisation projects.
In October, Lithuania’s Finance Ministry submitted its first request to the European Commission for a 1.06-billion-euro loan under the scheme.
If approved, the request would bring Lithuania’s total SAFE funding, including a 800-million-euro advance received in June, to 1.86 billion euros, about 29% of the country’s total allocation.

Israel election results live: Netanyahu accused of ‘ugly delegitimisation campaign’ after his claims about Arab parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:32:55 UTC
18:32:55 KST

Qatar says accusations of election interference in Israel 'ridiculous and dangerous'
Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman rejected accusations “made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media” that his country had interfered in the Israeli elections.
“We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome,” Majed al-Ansari said on X.
“They accuse Qatar of buying off Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli political left and now, in this latest campaign, the Arab vote... These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure.”
Ahmad Tibi, one of the leaders of the Arab Joint List party, said Benjamin Netanyahu was on an orchestrated, toxic campaign meant to undermine the election results.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told Reuters.
During and after Tuesday’s election, Netanyahu and his allies warned against rising Arab turnout and his right-wing Likud party issued statements accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the vote.“
It demanded police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service investigate incidents of suspected election bribery and intimidation at ballot stations in Arab towns. It said it possessed evidence of such activity but has not presented it to the public.
Abbas expresses hope for dialogue with new Israeli government
Mahmoud Abbas, the president of the Palestinian Authority, expressed hope that the Israeli election would pave the way for renewed peace talks.
“For many years now, we have been extending a hand to the Israeli side in order to achieve peace with them, so that Israel and Palestine may live in security, stability and peace,” Abbas said during a meeting with Cypriot president Nikos Christodoulides in Nicosia.
“We hope that, immediately after a new Israeli government is formed, we will be able to engage in dialogue together.”
As vote counting continues in Israel, here is a roundup of today’s key developments:
Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have amplified allegations of election fraud against parties representing Palestinian citizens in Israel. He and members of his coalition have referred the parties to Shin Bet, the country’s domestic security service, for investigation. Netanyahu’s Likud party accused the Palestinian parties of “stealing” the election and claimed, without evidence, that they received money from Qatar.
Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, rejected the allegations, saying they were “ridiculous and dangerous”. Responding to the claims, he said: “We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome.”
The Israeli president, Isaac Herzog, has come to the defence of Palestinian voters, as he urged political leaders against “tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote”. He saidShin Bet and the country’s central elections committee would investigate allegations of foreign interference “throughly”.
The central elections committee’s acting director general, Dean Livne, said there was “no basis for claims of systematic violations of election integrity”. The Israeli police also dismissed the claims, according to comments reported in Hebrew-language media, with one source quoted as saying: “Election day passed with very few irregular incidents.”
Netanyahu’s chief rival, former military chief and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, warned political opponents against exploiting allegations of foreign interference to delay the swearing-in of the next Knesset, which is set for 10 November.
The sentiment was shared by Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, who accused Netanyahu of trying to “undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimisation campaign” targeting Palestinian citizens in Israel.
So far, Netanyahu’s bloc is projected to win 53 seats, compared with 48 for the grouping led by rival Eisenkot. Palestinian parties are projected to win 19 seats, a record high.
The final tally of absentee ballots is not expected to significantly shift the results, with no grouping managing to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Qatar says accusations of election interference in Israel 'ridiculous and dangerous'
Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman rejected accusations “made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media” that his country had interfered in the Israeli elections.
“We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome,” Majed al-Ansari said on X.
“They accuse Qatar of buying off Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli political left and now, in this latest campaign, the Arab vote... These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure.”
Both Benjamin Netanyahu and his immediate challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, lack the seats in the Knesset to form a majority government. Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice.
They could forge a pact with the Arab Israeli parties, currently heading for an historic 19 seats, which would allow them to vote Netanyahu out and form a governing coalition. Or they could enter a unity government with Netanyahu, in return for a ministry or two.
Likud officials are cited in today’s Israeli press as saying Eisenkot will ultimately have no option but to throw in his lot with Netanyahu. Other observers say that would be political suicide, especially as the opposition leader vowed in the campaign he would never collaborate with the prime minister.
However, Eisenkot and key members of his bloc have also ruled out cooperation with the Arab party lists. Breaking either pledge would be costly for them.
The prime minister’s attack on the legitimacy of the Palestinian vote is designed to tip the scales, to force Eisenkot into the Netanyahu camp by increasing the political toxicity of any arrangement with Arab parties, the Joint List and Ra’am.
For its part, the Joint List has ruled out participating in an Eisenkot government because of his bloc’s support for the war in Gaza and the occupation of southern Lebanon, but it has offered to support an Eisenkot minority government with tactical voting in the new Knesset, in the shared interest of ousting Netanyahu.
Even such a transactional arrangement is hard to achieve given the state of Israeli Jewish politics. The only Zionist party that advocates cooperation with Palestinians, the Democrats, won just 6.5% of the total vote by the latest count.
The right and centre-right accounted for 66.5%, while ultra-orthodox Jewish parties won 11%.
Against that background, Eisenkot has doubled down on his determination to form a Zionist government. Such rhetoric makes the prospect of cooperation with Arab parties even more remote, but he is hoping instead to lure away conservative Jews from Likud, just as Netanyahu’s is trawling for defectors from Eisenkot’s “Change” bloc.
This is the current phase of the post-election struggle, and it is one that, for now, excludes Arab Israelis, despite their dramatically increased political strength.
The head of one of Israel’s parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel rejected allegations of electoral fraud and welcomed an investigation, saying his moderate Islamist Ra’am party had “no connection” to the matter.
“Ra’am has no connection whatsoever to the affair in question or to any other affairs, and we declare that we will fully cooperate with all law enforcement authorities to uncover the truth,” Mansour Abbas said, according to a spokesperson for his party.
Analysis: Netanyahu cries foul as Palestinian parties in Israel surge
Julian Borger
The race to form a government in Israel has begun with characteristically brass-knuckle tactics from Benjamin Netanyahu. He and other members of his coalition have referred the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, the only part of the opposition which over-performed in Tuesday’s elections, to the country’s domestic security service, the Shin Bet, for investigation.
The government’s claims centre around the allegation that Qatari funds were used illegally to buy votes and mobilise Palestinian Israeli citizens. There is so far no evidence to support the accusation. Haaretz quotes a senior police official saying there were no signs of election fraud and that Tuesday’s vote was cleaner than usual.
In Nazareth on election day, it was clear that turnout was unusually high because of anxiety and fear of what actions the extremists in Netanyahu’s government might turn their attention to Palestinian communities in Israel if they continue in power.
The only reported irregularities involved the the ruling coalition. Many of the ballots delivered to the polling station were printed only in Hebrew, while monitors from the far right used a variety of ploys to slow down the vote.
There is also a certain irony underpinning the allegations as Netanyahu is mired in a scandal over Qatari payments to his advisers in return for improving the Gulf monarchy’s image.
'We must avoid tarnishing an entire community,' says Herzog in defence of Palestinian vote
Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, has come to the defence of Palestinian voters in the Israeli election, amid accusations by Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies of alleged ballot fraud by parties representing Palestinian voters of Israel.
Herzog said he has spoken to the heads of the country’s central elections committee and Shin Bet regarding allegations of foreign interference in Tuesday’s vote, saying the issue must be “thoroughly investigated”.
“I am closely following developments in the investigation into the suspicions reported this morning,” he said in remarks published by Israeli media.
He added: “But even at a moment like this, we must avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy.”
Herzog called on party representatives ahead of impending coalition talks to reconsider their positions out of a sense of responsibility towards the country.
Once the official results are in, I will meet with representatives of all the political groups. I say this to everyone here – to the public and its leaders – ahead of next week’s consultations: keep an open mind, keep an open heart and broaden your perspective.
There is only one question that should be at the forefront of your minds: what is in the best interests of the country?”
Palestinian party leader accuses Netanyahu of laying groundwork to reject election results
A Palestinian party leader in Israel has accused Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies of undermining the legitimacy of “the clearest election results Israel has seen in decades”.
Sami Abu Shehadeh, chair of the Balad party which forms part of the Arab-led Joint List, said unsubstantiated allegations of foreign interference in the election sought to delegitimise the Palestinian vote.
What began with the illegal disqualification of Arab parties escalated into incitement against Arab parties and the Arab public. On election day, hundreds of far-right activists armed with weapons were deployed at polling stations in Arab towns in an attempt to suppress voter turnout. Now, this racist blood libel is entering its next phase, fuelled by dangerous accusations.
Netanyahu and his allies are dangerous. They are laying the groundwork to reject the clearest election results Israel has seen in decades.”
He added that Netanyahu, as “a man charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust”, was inciting against the Palestinian citizens of Israel, which make up 20% of the population.
He continued:
In any functioning democracy, those who lose an election accept responsibility and step down. In Israel, the losing side manufactures a racist blood libel and calls on the security forces to use force to overturn the people’s verdict.
We must not let the far right steal the election or drag the country into another election on the basis of fabricated, delusional accusations.
Echoing Ben-Gvir, the far-right Israeli finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has also called on Shin Bet to interrogate the leaders of parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, amid claims of alleged foreign election interference that critics say risk casting suspicion on the Arab vote.
“The suspicion of election manipulation using foreign Islamist money is a litmus test for the State of Israel,” Smotrich said on X.
“The heads of the Arab parties must be interrogated by the Shin Bet today.”
Golan accuses Netanyahu of 'ugly delegitimisation campaign' against Palestinian voters
Hot on Eisenkot’s heels, Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, has accused Benjamin Netanyahu of trying to “undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimisation campaign” targeting Palestinian citizens in Israel.
Netanyahu’s Likud party has claimed – without evidence – that parties representing these citizens have “stolen” the election and demanded the police and the Shin Bet investigate the allegations.
In a post on X, Golan said:
Netanyahu suffered a crushing democratic defeat. The public fired him, and he refuses to accept the verdict of the voters.
Now he is trying to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimisation campaign against the will of the public, and against the Arab public in particular.
Any genuine suspicion of damage to the integrity of the elections must be investigated to the end.”
Israel’s central elections committee has requested the Shin Bet to investigate alleged foreign interference, the Associated Press reported, citing claims in a letter dated Wednesday of funding by “foreign entities against the Israeli interest” but providing no details or assessment of their validity. The source of the allegations remains unclear, and the committee has requested findings within a week, ahead of the 4 November deadline for certifying election results under Israeli law.

Spanish Transport Minister Blames Train Crash That Killed 68 on ‘Inexplicable’ Error
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Spanish authorities are investigating the cause behind a high-speed train collision Wednesday morning that killed at least 68 people and injured dozens of others. The country’s transport minister suggested that a combination of “inexplicable” human error and a computer failure was likely behind the tragedy, which occurred near Urda, Toledo, more than 80 miles south of Madrid.
Transport Minister Óscar Puente said in a press conference that the state-operated Renfe train slamming into the rear of a stationary private train operated by Iryo was due to an “inexplicable” order from a command center for Spain’s trains. Puente said the center had a computer malfunction before the order.
“It was the control center, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” Puente said. He added later: “Clearly, it was a wrong decision.”
Puente said that they have identified the person who decided to let the Renfe train continue moving even though the Iryo one had already stopped, but he has not spoken to the control center operator. “This person is subject to whatever the investigation determines,” Puente said in the press conference.
The regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, where the Toledo town is, said in a social media post that 53 people are still receiving medical treatment in healthcare facilities. The number of people hospitalized reached 107 earlier in the day.
Renfe said train services between Madrid, Ciudad Real, and Andalusia have been suspended.
The Wednesday collision is now the deadliest train crash in the country since a 2013 incident in Santiago de Compostela that killed 80 people. But the latest collision follows a similarly deadly train crash in January, which involved high-speed trains operated by the same two companies. In that crash, which occurred in Adamuz, Córdoba, 46 people died and 122 sustained injuries.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who visited the crash site, announced that his government would declare three days of mourning in response and vowed an investigation. “What is unacceptable for a country like Spain is to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” Sánchez said, though he noted that it “is highly likely that the two accidents are unrelated.”
Despite the accident, Puente insisted that the Spanish rail system is “safe and comparable to that of other countries in our region.” However, while there are “very clear” regulations and protocols in place, he admitted, “failures can obviously occur.”
What happened?
The crashes involved a Renfe high-speed train bound for Seville with 393 people on board, and an Iryo train carrying 151 passengers. The Renfe train departed Madrid at 8:00 a.m. local time, while the Iryo train left a little earlier at 7:54 a.m., plying the same route.
Spain’s rail infrastructure uses the German LZB (Linienzugbeeinflussung) system, a railway safety technology that monitors train speeds and sends traffic instructions to the driver’s cab. Operations are meant to revert to manual control when the automated safety system fails.
Puente, in the press conference, said that at around 8:30 a.m., three computers on the railway network experienced a communication failure, taking the LZB control system offline along a 63 km (39 mi) stretch of the track. This automatically stopped about six trains traveling on that section, Puente said. The central command center would assume manual management of rail traffic.
By 8:36 a.m., the command center authorized the Renfe train to continue its journey “normally,” even though Puente says internal protocols dictate otherwise and that a “red signal” should have prevented the journey from resuming. The Renfe train had 25 km (15.5 mi) to travel before it struck the Iryo train, roughly 17 minutes later, at 8:53 a.m. The speed it reached before the impact is still unknown, but it could reach up to 200 km/h (124 mph) for that stretch of track.
What to know about Spanish high-speed rail
Spain is among the world leaders in investing in domestic high-speed rail infrastructure—defined as rails for trains that can travel 250 km/h (155 mph) and over, according to the European Commission’s Ninth Rail Market Monitoring report last year. The report shows that of European Union countries, Spain allocated the most to high-speed rail between 2018 and 2022, averaging €1.5 billion (around $1.67 billion) per year.
Latest data from the International Union of Railways shows that Spain has laid nearly 4,000 km (2,400 mi) of high-speed track, second only to China, which has laid more than 47,000 km (28,000 mi).
The European country only legally opened its domestic commercial high-speed passenger rail market to private competitors in December 2020, and Iryo became one of the commercial high-speed operators in Spain in 2022.
Spanish news outlet El Debate reported, citing data from the State Railway Safety Agency, that the number of “significant accidents” on the country’s rail network has increased over the years.

Liquid Glass Finally Makes Sense on the iPhone Duo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Apple rarely admits a mistake. But when it unveiled new versions of its operating systems this summer, it came close.
“With all major design updates, there’s a natural process where we take a bold leap forward, and then we continue to iterate,” said Apple's human interface designer, Shubham Kedia, during a predictably sleek keynote video. “Our team really appreciates your feedback, and we considered it deeply as we refined the new design.”
Not quite “Sorry, everyone, we messed up,” but for Apple, practically an apology tour. The subject was Liquid Glass, Apple’s most divisive interface design since at least iOS 7. Apple's Vision Pro mixed-reality headset (which itself flopped) inspired the translucent design language, and the company brought it to millions of other Apple devices.
The result was a mess—at odds with Steve Jobs’ famous line, “Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.” Liquid Glass started obsessed with gloss and effects, despite promises it would bring your content to the foreground. Yet Apple’s own press release showed interfaces with illegible text. Worse, users found constant reflections and flickering color shifts distracting, and a lack of clarity across devices hurt accessibility.
But iOS 27, alongside updates to Apple's other software platforms, signaled a shift in priorities after Kedia’s mea culpa. Kedia spoke of reincorporating design cornerstones in what was, if not quite a U-turn, then at least a rediscovery of a core principle: how it works. Instantly, interface elements across Apple devices gained greater clarity and structure, making it easier to tell apps' components from content. The most obvious change, though, was a slider.
Thinking Differently
Apple said it tuned Liquid Glass to diffuse complex content more effectively, keeping elements legible when above imagery and text. But it also acknowledged that not everyone wants the same thing—some users might prefer a more tinted look, and others “would like Liquid Glass to be even more clear.” You can now decide for yourself with the Liquid Design slider in Settings. For a company known for being opinionated, such bet-hedging was surprising but not unwelcome. Choice isn’t a bad thing, and now users had more of it.
“I immediately pushed that slider all the way to the most tinted setting, and pretty much all the legibility issues vanished,” Ben Rice McCarthy, an indie developer behind popular apps like Obscura and Indigo, tells WIRED. McCarthy has long criticized Liquid Glass. Now? Not so much.
“Liquid Glass introduced a lot of issues without adequate solutions, but this year’s operating systems solved or improved a lot of them,” McCarthy says. “There’s the adaptiveness of the interface. Buttons can grow into menus. Controls merge and divide like cells as you transition between views. Toolbars can expand and contract smoothly as the view changes size.”
Flexibility matters when resizing windows across any device. But while announcing its updates, Apple also dropped major hints that all but confirmed new hardware—it showed iPhone apps running on an iPad or a Mac could resize to a suspiciously specific shape that matched the rumored inner display dimensions of Apple’s upcoming folding phone.
Designed to Flow
When Apple showed off the iPhone Duo, everything clicked. Its passport-shaped display bucks the trend of iPhones and their rivals growing taller over the years. The Duo is wider and almost squat, and when opened, it naturally defaults to landscape, echoing the iPad Mini display.
Apple being Apple, it wanted to avoid the jarring jolt between displays that’s often evident on rival foldables, so it made content appear to move seamlessly from one screen to the other. That begins with the hardware. As Molly Anderson, Apple's vice president of Industrial Design, said at the September keynote: “To achieve this continuity, we designed iPhone Duo around a consistent aspect ratio that is the same across both displays.” But it’s the software—rooted in Liquid Glass—that sells the illusion.
The most arresting element is a fancy animation, which various folks in the Android space are now busy being “inspired” by. It reinforces the idea of a flowing interface. Meanwhile, Liquid Glass freed Apple from being prescriptive about where essential controls live. On the Duo, they sit at the side. When the phone’s closed, that frees up space for content. When it’s open, the controls stay in a consistent spot, so you never have to hunt for them. Reorient the device, and everything settles into the most appropriate place.
That’s form following function, not function being subservient to form. This device and its flexible interface don’t strictly need the Liquid Glass design language, but the two feel made for each other. Liquid Glass finally makes sense on the iPhone Duo—and with Apple’s other refinements, it’s starting to make sense elsewhere, too.
Clarity of Purpose
How much of this is happenstance is hard to say. Given Apple’s lead times, pure coincidence seems unlikely. And even if Liquid Glass wasn’t made with the Duo in mind, it adapts to it.
Liquid Glass feels more considered. It’s increasingly tuned for individual devices rather than governed by a “universal” aesthetic forced onto them all. The result is operating systems that feel solid rather than fragile, with interfaces less likely to fight content for your attention. On Macs and iPads, the Liquid Glass revamp now looks more like a love letter to Aqua—Apple's water-themed interface introduced in 2000. On the iPhone, it’s usable again. On the Duo, it’s a delight.
That’s not to say it’s perfect. “There’s some weirdness that hasn’t been fully resolved, and there needs to be a consistency to all these materials or the metaphors break down,” McCarthy says. “But overall, Liquid Glass is vastly improved.”
And it’s worth remembering that while the Duo is new, Liquid Glass is relatively young, too. As developer Steve Troughton-Smith wrote, “For some iPhone apps, even with keen developers, it will take six months to a year of work to properly support iPhone Duo. A lot of developers are still trying to finish the Liquid Glass transition they started last year.”
A useful reminder that transitions take time. But at least now, Apple’s vision looks clear.

Büro Ole Scheeren designs winding concrete gallery in South Korea "without traditional thresholds"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Büro Ole Scheeren designs winding concrete gallery in South Korea “without traditional thresholds”
Architecture studio Büro Ole Scheeren has revealed designs for the Suseong Continuum, a snaking, concrete art gallery in Daegu, South Korea.
Set to be built within the city’s Yeonhwaji park, the 364-square-metre gallery was designed specifically for showcasing digital art.
Berlin-based Büro Ole Scheeren designed the gallery as a continuous space, without any enclosed rooms and or doorways, in a bid to reflect the “flows” of digital art.
“We wanted to build a gallery without traditional thresholds: a gradient of realities that morph into one another as you gradually move through the space,” studio founder Ole Scheeren said.
“The substance of digital art is not rooted in the physical domain of distinct objects and isolated experiences… it exists in a world of overlaps and connections, where one condition potentially flows into the next.”
“Landscape, circulation and exhibition become a continuous experience,” the studio added.
The Suseong Continuum gallery was unveiled as part of this year’s Suseong International Biennale, which invites architects to realise permanent public works across Daegu.
Commissioned by the Suseong District Government, the design by Büro Ole Scheeren is expected to open for the biennale’s 2028 edition.
Once complete, visitors will access the space via a winding path, from which the gallery was designed to emerge as an extrusion.
Conceived as a “continuation of the landscape”, the gallery’s twisting volume will be partially embedded into the park’s topography and oriented toward a nearby lotus pond.
Its structure will be built using board-marked concrete to create a rough exterior texture. Inside, this textured surface will transition to smooth concrete walls for projecting media onto.
According to Büro Ole Scheeren, the gallery’s layout and materiality were designed to reflect the transition from the park’s natural landscape to the digital interiors.
“Technology is often seen as an opposite to nature,” Scheeren said. “With Suseong Continuum we wanted to explore how we can create a way of extending the way we perceive the relationship between both domains – a journey that starts in the park and that seamlessly carries you into the digital realm.”
“There is no single moment where one world ends and the other begins, it is a continuous transformation.”
“What begins as natural landscape gradually transforms into digital media,” the studio added.
Renders of the gallery’s stripped-back interior reveal its immersive exhibition spaces framed by curving walls.
A layered ceiling will run the building’s full length to conceal all lighting and technical infrastructure, which was developed by the studio in collaboration with the Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe.
“The interior unfolds as a spatial gradient in which light, sound, enclosure and immersion shift gradually along the visitor’s route,” the studio said.
“Curving walls widen into open spaces and tighten into passages; atmospheres transform rather than switch,” it added.
The design will remain on show at the Suseong International Biennale until 22 November.
In Shenzhen, China, the studio has revealed plans for skyscrapers with “waterfall” facades and its design for the Róng Museum of Arts is currently under construction.
Images by Büro Ole Scheeren

More than 29,000 double-envelope ballots, around 6% of the total, have been counted in Israel’s elections, with the Central Elections Committee expecting the count to conclude by the afternoon, Israeli media reported Thursday.
A total of 29,253 double-envelope ballots have been counted out of nearly 500,000, the daily Yedioth Ahronoth noted.
Double-envelope ballots are used by voters casting their votes away from their registered polling stations, including soldiers, diplomats, police officers, and displaced residents.
Officials check identification details on the outer envelope to prevent duplicate voting, then separate it from the anonymous ballot before counting.
The remaining votes could change individual parties’ seat totals and the balance between the rival blocs.
READ: Israel’s final election results expected Thursday evening: Election official
The Central Elections Committee estimates that the double-envelope vote count will conclude by the afternoon, according to the report.
After all regular ballots were counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 seats, compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and 19 for predominantly Arab parties, according to Channel 12.
Neither main bloc was projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
The Joint List was projected to secure 12 seats and the United Arab List (Ra’am) seven, giving Arab parties a record combined representation of 19 seats.
Voter turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999, according to the election committee.

Poland to Transfer Two MiG-29s to Ukraine in €50 Million Aid Package
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:26:53 UTC
18:26:53 KST

Poland will transfer two Soviet-era MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine in the near future as part of a new military aid package worth around €50 million ($55 million), a Polish defense official said.
Dariusz Łukowski, director of the Strategy and Defense Planning Department at Poland’s Ministry of National Defense, confirmed the transfer to Rzeczpospolita on Thursday, Oct. 29.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The decision has been made, and these two MiG-29s will be transferred,” Łukowski said when asked when Ukraine would receive the aircraft.
One of the jets has reached the end of its service life, while the other remains airworthy, according to media reports.
The package will also include 155mm and 152mm artillery ammunition, 102mm ammunition for the six-barreled cannons mounted on F-16 fighter jets, and missiles for Piorun man-portable air defense systems.
Poland’s defense ministry confirmed it is preparing the new aid package but did not disclose its full contents, citing confidentiality. The ministry said the package would depend on Poland’s national security needs and the capabilities of its armed forces.
It added that equipment being decommissioned by the Polish military could still prove useful to Ukraine.
Nawrocki backs MiG-29 swap in principle
Polish President Karol Nawrocki has also signaled that a proposed deal to transfer MiG-29s to Ukraine in exchange for Ukrainian drone technology is compatible with Warsaw’s policy.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 28, 2026
Speaking alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky in Warsaw on Dec. 19, 2025, during their first in-person meeting since Nawrocki’s August inauguration, the Polish president said the proposal did not contradict their policy.
“I want to remind you that my scope of responsibilities is to take care of the interests of Polish soldiers, especially those from Malbork, who are wondering what will happen to the MiGs,” Nawrocki said.
He called for a “strategic, symmetrical partnership” between the two countries, reflecting his insistence that Ukraine should offer greater reciprocity for Polish support.
“This exchange of MiGs for anti-drone systems does not contradict our policy. So, after resolving the formal issues, I think this issue will be resolved,” Nawrocki said, stopping short of explicitly approving the proposed swap.
MiG-29 for Ukraine’s drone know-how
In early December, Poland’s military command said it was considering transferring its remaining MiG-29s to Ukraine in exchange for access to Ukrainian drone and missile technology.
The proposed deal would involve six to eight retired MiG-29s inherited by Poland from the communist era.
Ukraine already operates around 40 MiG-29s, according to Poland’s state news agency PAP. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukraine has received 14 MiG-29s from Poland and 13 from Slovakia.
The aircraft would provide a near-term boost to Ukraine’s air force, as its pilots are already familiar with the Soviet-designed jets. Poland, meanwhile, plans to replace its MiG-29s with US-made F-16s and South Korean FA-50s.
Ukraine is also seeking to modernize its air force with Western aircraft. Zelensky has discussed potential acquisitions of Gripen fighters from Sweden and Rafale jets from France as part of a longer-term effort to build a modern air fleet.

Palestinian American Majdi Gaith runs for Berkeley City Council
Unknown

Breadcrumb
'It's OK to run': Palestinian American Majdi Gaith runs for Berkeley City Council
On a sunny afternoon in downtown Berkeley, in California campaign volunteers are going door to door to help elect Majdi Gaith for City Council.
The Palestinian American, whose family hails from the occupied West Bank, is running on a platform of affordable housing, increased social services and support for small brick-and-mortar businesses.
He is running against incumbent Igor Tregub, who came to office in a special election in 2024. Though Tregub is generally considered a progressive, many in this historically left-wing college town would like to see more progressive policies.
"I jumped into the race because our city council has been operating dysfunctionally. They don’t really listen to the needs of their residents," Gaith told The New Arab, as he was getting ready for another round of canvassing.
"I thought having a new voice on the council would be beneficial. The current city council member voted against the ceasefire resolution," he said, referring to a resolution that multiple cities made in response to Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
Gaith was born and raised in the Bay Area, and he has run Jaffa Coffee Roasters on University Avenue with his brothers since 2024. He believes running a small business has given him an important perspective for running for public office.
"Honestly, behind the register, listening to people for the past two years, people vent. They tell us the city’s not working," he said.
"I'm out canvassing for Majdi Gaith for City Council District 4 in Berkeley because we really need change in Berkeley. Our city council is working on behalf of special interests," Matt O’Brien, a 40-year resident of Berkeley, told The New Arab after knocking on doors around a week before election day.
On a typical weekend, Gaith has around 50 volunteers canvassing for him in a district of just over 15,000 residents, many of them students, who tend to be low-turnout voters.
Without polling, it is difficult to predict the outcome of the race. So far, he has reached his maximum campaign contributions (allowed by law), with the majority of donations coming from local sources, an important indicator for local elections that are often funded by outside contributions.
As a challenger to the incumbent, Gaith is considered the underdog. Moreover, as a Palestinian and a Muslim, it was perhaps predictable that the issue of Israel would take centre stage in a local election.
After Gaith said that the city council had been taken over by Zionists, he faced what his supporters described as a smear campaign of anti-Palestinian and anti-Muslim racism. In at least one instance, his opponents referred to him as a Hamas supporter. To show their solidarity, a group was formed called Berkeley Jews for Majdi, which included a local rabbi.
Earlier this month, they held a press conference on the steps of Berkeley City Hall. They addressed pushback of Gaith's criticism of Israel.
"Jews for Majdi oppose anti-Palestinian racism and its use to unfairly portray a devoted community member, small business owner, Bay Area native and Cal alum as an antisemite," they said in a written statement.
"We must stand against anti-Palestinian racism. It has no place in our community. We believe that critique of Israel is not antisemitic and covers over the harm caused by actual antisemitism that arises from white supremacy," the statement continued.

Navantia UK is increasing its commitment to recruit apprentices across its British yards from 500 to 750 by 2030, an announcement made as the Scottish Secretary and the defence industry minister visited the company’s yard at Methil in Fife, according to the company.
The apprentices will work on building three Fleet Solid Support ships for the Royal Fleet Auxiliary and will be ready to take on further projects for the Ministry of Defence.
Donato Martinez, chief executive of Navantia UK, said: “There is real momentum at Methil. We are investing in the yard, bringing in new work and recruiting more people. We also need to build the skills that will support the yard and our wider business in the years ahead.
“That is why we are increasing our nationwide commitment from 500 apprentices by 2030 to 750. It will give more young people the chance to build skilled careers in our industry and help us develop the workforce we need as the business grows.
“Methil has an important role to play in the future of UK shipbuilding. The investment being made here, the skills in the workforce and the opportunities ahead, including Programme Euston, give us a strong base to keep building from.”
Investment at Methil has reached £26.7 million since Navantia UK acquired the yard in January 2025, including a further £12 million announced this year for training facilities, machinery, infrastructure and new technology. The workforce has grown from 180 to 275 and 75 apprentices are now training at the site, including 21 who arrived this year, part of a company-wide intake of 121 joining 222 already employed across the four British yards at Methil, Arnish, Belfast and Appledore.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “The UK Government worked hard to secure the future of yards such as Methil as part of our commitment to Scotland’s industrial heartlands, and today with Navantia I’ve seen the difference that commitment has made. A busier order book, a growing workforce and a large increase in apprenticeships – this is what’s possible when government and industry work together.
“There are huge opportunities with the defence dividend that come from being part of the United Kingdom. I’m proud that the UK Government’s support for the sector is delivering skilled jobs and growth for communities right across Scotland. This is a new age of industrialisation for the UK, with Scotland at its heart.”
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Apprentices are at the heart of defence’s industrial base that keeps this country safe. These opportunities pave the way for the next generation, providing essential skills, training and experience while contributing to the security of the UK.”
Programme Euston, referred to by Martinez, is the Ministry of Defence programme for new floating docks at His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde, and the Chancellor confirmed that those docks will be built and delivered in British shipyards. The GMB union has argued that Methil should get the work.

Estonia to call all women aged 40 for breast cancer risk analysis screening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

Estonia to call all women aged 40 for breast cancer risk analysis screening
Estonia is set to become the first country in the world where people are invited to screening programs based on genetic data. Next week, all 40-year-old women will receive an invitation for genetic testing to determine their individual breast cancer risk, regardless of whether or not they have health insurance.
Until now, women have been invited to breast cancer screening after their 50th birthday, but starting next week, all 40-year-old women will receive an invitation so that each woman's risk of developing breast cancer can be calculated based on genetic data.
"If this risk is higher than usual – if the risk for these 40-year-old women is the same as it is for other women at the age of 50 – then including these women in screening earlier is justified. Starting mammography already at the age of 40," said Steven Smit, head of the biobank laboratory at the Estonian Genome Center.
Around 3,000 genetic variants are taken into account when calculating the risk. However, the study does not include BRCA gene mutations, which led actress Angelina Jolie to decide to have her breasts removed 13 years ago to prevent developing the disease.
"These are hereditary forms of cancer, which are assessed through separate tests as needed if there has been breast cancer in the family," Smit said.
There are almost 10,000 40-year-old women in Estonia, and invitations will be sent both to those who have already donated their genes to the Estonian Genome Center and to those who have not.
"The gene donors' data will not be checked automatically. The first step is still to go to the Health Portal and submit a declaration of consent there so that the data can be used in the healthcare system," said Krista Kruuv-Käo, head of preventive services at the Estonian Health Insurance Fund.
The same declaration of consent must also be completed by women whose data is not in the Estonian Genome Center. They will receive a referral to a laboratory to provide a blood sample.
It is also possible to put this service in place for other serious diseases, but the Health Insurance Fund does not consider this reasonable, as the state would not have the capacity to follow up on them.
"We are also analyzing how we could use genetic risk in the case of cardiovascular diseases to more precisely involve those people whose risks are higher in preventive measures," Kruuv-Käo said.
Currently, the Estonian Genome Center holds data on approximately one-fifth of Estonia's population, and no new gene donors are being accepted.
"The Genome Center would certainly be fully prepared for this, but at the moment there is simply no funding available for it. The Genome Center's general funding has also been reduced in recent years," Smit said.

Russia says 'battlefield situation' will determine when Ukraine peace talks begin
The start of planned trilateral negotiations between Russia, the U.S., and Ukraine on ending Moscow's war will depend on the situation on the battlefield, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Oct. 28.
The Kremlin has signaled openness to resuming trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi for the first time in more than eight months, but the sides have yet to confirm a date.
The talks come amid a renewed U.S. push to restart negotiations, which have largely stalled over the Kremlin's demands that Kyiv surrender parts of Donbas, a strategically vital region in eastern Ukraine that Russian forces have been unable to capture fully.
"We haven't sent any signals yet," Ushakov told Russian reporters regarding the exact date of the consultations, while noting that the meeting could take place in Abu Dhabi "after Nov. 4."
"That, too, will depend on the situation on the battlefield and the overall situation," he added.
Ushakov said the composition of the Russian delegation had not yet been finalized, although "the core group is in place." He also ruled out European participation in the upcoming meeting.
"There is absolutely no talk of that at this point," Ushakov said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 28 that he expects the planned trilateral negotiations to take place in mid-November, adding that Washington has yet to confirm a date.
The planned meeting follows a renewed U.S. effort to revive negotiations. Moscow has repeatedly rejected Western-backed proposals for a full and unconditional ceasefire, which Kyiv has supported, while continuing to demand that Ukraine cede Donbas.
Ukrainian officials do not expect a major breakthrough in Abu Dhabi but hope the talks will help restart regular negotiations.
The technical talks are expected to cover a potential energy and maritime ceasefire, exchanges of military and civilian captives, and the return of Ukrainian children abducted by Russia.

Selling nicotine-free vapes to under-18s banned from today, government says
Selling nicotine-free vapes to children under the age of 18 has become illegal from today, the government has said.
Children were already banned from buying vapes containing nicotine. But, under the Tobacco and Vapes Act, shops across the UK will now be banned from selling nicotine-free vapes, and nicotine pouches, to children.
In an article for the Daily Mirror welcoming the new law, Prof Sir Chris Whitty, the chief medical officer for England, said:
Vaping can be a way to help established adult smokers who are already addicted to nicotine from tobacco to swap to a less dangerous product. Vaping is considered safer than smoking, but that is a low bar. Vapes should therefore never be used by children or non-smokers.
Some children have already come to harm from bad reactions to vapes. The long-term health harms of vaping in today’s children will only become clear over time. They are however unlikely to be good; inhaling multiple, often heated, chemicals into the lungs may well do irreversible harm.
According to the Department of Health and Social Care, which has put out a new release about how the ban will operate in England, “more than a million children are estimated to have tried vaping, with more than 370,000 vaping regularly, putting them at a higher risk of developing respiratory illnesses.” Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are also implementing bans.

Healey's longterm government spending plans would require cuts government probably wouldn't accept, IFS says
Here are some more lines from Helen Miller’s presentation about the Institute for Fiscal Studies’ assessment of the budget. (See 10.45am.)
Miller said higher inflation means John Healey would need at least £17bn to avoid real-terms cuts in some government departments under the long-term spending plans. Echoing a point made by the Resolution Foundation (see 8.36am and 10.21am), she said:
The chancellor left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms. In the face of higher inflation, this means that the real-terms value of budgets has been cut. Taken at face value, and alongside the inherited plans to slow down spending growth sharply in coming years, that is a big choice. It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review. Avoiding the cuts implied by both higher inflation and tight envelopes could plausibly require a top-up of £17bn in 2030-31. That’s true even before thinking about the £11bn needed to fund defence plans.
She said she did not believe Healey would implement the future spending cuts implied by his departmental spending plans. She said:
I want to be clear that my concern is not that it would be impossible to deliver the implied cuts to other services – that could be done. But I’m sceptical that this government would be willing to do it. I’m also sceptical because I didn’t hear John Healey starting the kind of pitch-rolling that you would expect if he intended to deliver these spending plans. And I’m sceptical because history advises scepticism. When chancellors pencil in tight spending plans in the future, they tend not to deliver.
She criticised Healey for raiding the reserves to fund the defence investment plan. She explained:
I’m grumpy about how the chancellor decided to fund the relatively small hole in the defence investment plan – that’s the plan that gets defence spending to 2.7% of GDP next year and keeps it there until 2029–30. Much of it came from further cuts to the capital budgets of other government departments. Fine. Priorities change. But the rest came from raiding reserves in future years. This is worth drawing out: John Healey has now spent 25% of the capital reserve set aside for the next three years. He’s also spent 40% of the day-to-day reserve. This is categorically not what the reserves are for. Drawing down reserves is another way that the government has reduced its buffer against future shocks.
She said it was “sad” that the government was having to decide who should get energy support based on council tax bands that are based on property values 35 years ago. She said:
It is also sad that, in the time since the last energy price surge, the government hasn’t bothered to invest in the data that would have allowed a package more targeted at those most badly hit by rising energy prices. But here we are.
She said Healey was at risk of needing to put up taxes next year. She said:
I am left with the impression that the chancellor is hoping the economic forecasts improve enough that he can make good on his plan to cut borrowing without having to also make large cuts to public spending or raise taxes. I hope that happens. And it might – a re-opening of the strait of Hormuz or AI-driven productivity growth really could create sunnier skies. But, equally, things could get worse. If they do, the chancellor now has less insurance.
A clear short-term risk with the chancellor’s choices is that next year – with low headroom and a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments – we see another season of damaging speculation about tax rises.
Healey's new 'founder's relief' tax cut for entrepreneurs 'looks bonkers', says IFS
Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank, is giving a presentation summing up the IFS’s view of the budget. Arguing that it contained plenty of “bad things” as well as welcome measures, she singled out founders’ relief for particular criticism.
She said:
After years of arguing that business asset disposal relief was a bad idea – and just when I thought the relief was on its last legs – a new, similar relief has popped up. The new founders’ relief looks bonkers. It gives a lower rate of capital gains tax to a small subset of people with large gains. That will include some entrepreneurs that make investments with broader societal benefits – although most of that activity would have happened without the relief. But it will also include people that just got lucky. There are very complex rules around who gets it – rules that will incentivise people to change their behaviour in weird ways simply to be able to get the relief. I could go on. But the punchline is that this looks to me like yet another tax break for a chosen group with little economic reasoning behind it.
Tories overtake Reform UK in 'poll of polls' tracker

Different polling companies use different methods, and so the poll of polls provides a reliable overview. Other poll of poll trackers are available, but Politico’s may be the most widely read in Westminster.
