How 2020s are set to be worst decade, by far, since 1960s for rising living standards, according to Resolution Foundation
The Resolution Foundation has now published its full 48-page report on the budget. Some of its main arguments were covered earlier. (See 8.36am.)
Here are five charts from the report illustrating five of its main arguments.
1) The amount the government is spending paying interest on its debt is “high and rising”, the report says. It says:
Debt interest spending is now forecast to reach £147bn in 2029-30, £13bn more than in March. This leaves debt interest spending at 4.1 per cent of GDP in 2029-30 (and peaking marginally higher at 4.14 per cent in 2031-32, the highest on record since 1956-57) and above the total expected spend on universal credit, Housing Benefit and Child Benefit combined in that year.
2) The 2020s are set to be the worst decade, by far, for more than half a century for rising living standards, the report says.
The 2020s are on course to have the lowest growth in incomes of any decade on record when measured using Real Household Disposable Income (RHDI). RHDI is projected to rise by just 1.4 per cent in total over the decade (equivalent to £400 in 2026-27 prices), one-tenth of the growth rate achieved in the 2010s (which itself was the second-worst decade on record). Income growth this decade is set to be much weaker than GDP growth because of rising taxes and import prices.
3) Labour’s cost of living support package benefits the rich almost as much as the poor, the report says.
Taken altogether, the Government’s £4.4bn cost of living package for 2025-26 and 2026-27 is poorly targeted. As Figure 8 makes clear, support is very widely spread. The Household Energy Payment goes to up to 20 million households in England, which are dispersed across the income distribution (87 per cent of the bottom half of the income distribution and 73 per cent of the top live in Council Tax bands A-D). The VAT cut and the Fuel Duty delay are not targeted at all. Taken together, we estimate that 52 per cent of the whole cost of living package will benefit the poorest half of the income distribution this year and next, with the other 48 per cent going to the top half (equivalent to an average £158 for poorer households, compared to £144 for richer households).
4) But, overall, the tax and benefit changes since the government took power have been progressive, the report says.
We estimate that annual incomes will, on average, be £320 higher for households in the bottom quintile in 2029- 30, compared to £2,000 lower for those in the top quintile as a result of the Starmer and Burnham governments’ measures. This is largely the result of policies announced before this budget: the repeal of the two-child limit and the commitment to uprate the universal credit standard allowance at a higher rate than inflation for four years, both introduced from April 2026.
5) All government spending departments apart from defence, health and education are likely to face cuts in spending per head from the end of this decade under current plans, the report says.
Healey denies postponing difficult decisions on welfare
John Healey has denied postponing difficult decisions on the welfare system, insisting the government is making changes “now”.
Thinktanks and opposition parties have made this claim. But, when this was put to Healey in an interview on GB News, he replied:
This was a broken system. And two years ago we started putting back in place face-to-face assessments. We’ve changed terms of universal credit, so people don’t have to brand themselves as too sick to work.
So, those are changes we’re making now. But in the long run, as I’ve argued, and the prime minister has said, too, we have to bring the cost of benefits down.
Treasury says Healey hasn't committed to cutting welfare bill before election, claiming interview answer misinterpreted
John Healey is rowing back from his answer in an interview in the Today programme implying he wanted welfare spending to go down before the next general election. According to Chris Mason, the BBC’s political editor, Treasury sources are saying his words have been over-interpreted.
This relates to what Healey said in an interview with Nick Robinson for the Today programme. It was broadcast this morning, but recorded yesterday, and the BBC has written it up in a story on its website headlined: “Healey promises reduction in welfare bill before next election”.
For the record, here is the key exchange.
Robinson: Let’s take welfare if we could. £19bn up in the year ahead. That’s the entire police budget for England and Wales. That’s the entire annual defence equipment budget. And yet in your speech you said, well, we’ve got a couple of reports coming next month, then we’ll have a white paper, which in non-Westminster jargon means a consultation, then you’ll have some legislation, then you’ll have a row in the Labour party. You’re not going to make any of these cuts before the next election, are you?
Healey: Well first, I’ve said clearly, the prime minister said as well, we have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures. We do have a big report, two big reports being produced next month, that will help us map out the way that we need to change the system for the long run. We are in fact reducing and have been over the last two years the rate of increase in the welfare bill compared to the previous period – I’m afraid to say – of a broken system the Conservatives put in place. We’re bringing back and have brought back face to face assessments which they axed for instance. We’ve been changing universal credits so people aren’t branding themselves as too sick to work in order to make that system work better.
Robinson: But you’re reducing the rate of increase in welfare spending chancellor aren’t you? But the OBR’s forecast is that £1 in every £8 will be spent on welfare by 2030 or thereabouts. You’ve got to make cuts, haven’t you?
Healey: This system is unsustainable. I’ve been clear about that. The prime minister’s been clear about it ….
Robinson: Briefly, because I want to give you the chance to talk about other things – there will be cuts in welfare before the election?
Healey:There will be there will be a reduction in the benefits bill. We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progressive to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill and I feel a moral duty to deal with these youngsters who at the moment have been written off by previous governments.
The answer highlighted in bold is what gave the BBC its story. Healey paused slightly between the first “there will be” and the second “there will be” and it would be perfectly reasonable to interpret it as:
There will be. [Direct answer to Robinson’s question.] There will be a reduction in the benefits bill [etc etc – Healey expanding on the answer.]
But the Treasury is implying what he meant was:
There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill [Healey simply repeating three words as he launches into more general answer, not answering Robinson directly, but just explaining the government’s approach.]
Reasonable people could interpret is either way. But Mason said the Treasury had told him the first interpretation was not accurate, and that if Healey really wanted to commit to getting cutting the benefits bill before the general election, he would have announced that in the budget.
Given that Alan Milburn himself has said that his plans to tackle youth unemployment may require more spending upfront in return for savings later, and given that welfare reforms often take most of a decade to roll out, it does seem unlikely that Healey intended to say the benefits bill would be cut before the election.
But, as Mason pointed out on the Today programme, “correcting” this story means the Treasury is implicitly saying benefit spending won’t go down before the election – which is very helpful to the Tories and Reform UK.
Healey accused by Resolution Foundation of ‘complete failure’ to target energy bill support at those most in need
Good morning. The day after the budget is often the moment when big initiatives announced by the chancellor the day before with a flourish start to unravel as experts pore over the small print. There is not much of that happening this morning – mainly because John Healey did not have any really big initiatives up his sleeve. Compared with a normal budget, his tax and spending initiatives were mostly relatively minor. That means that the opposition parties have been struggling to find things to attack, and so instead they have resorted to criticising Healey for what he did not do: slash welfare (the Tory/Reform UK solution), or join the EU’s single market (the Lib Dems’).
Healey has given interviews to all the main broadcasters, which are playing out this morning, but they were recorded last night and they don’t have any sensational new revelations. As Rowena Mason reports, one of the top lines was Healey saying he would cut welfare spending before the election.
But there were other lines in the interviews too. I will be posting all the highlights this morning.
The two main public spending thinktanks, the Institute for Fiscal Studies and the Resolution Foundation, are both publishing reports assessing the budget this morning. The RF has issued a news release with its main findings and its assessment of the overall economic impact of the budget measures highlights three problems.
It accuses Healey of a “complete failure” to target help with energy bills at those most in need. It says:
The poorest half of households will gain £158 on average from cost of living support this year and next, just £14 more than the £144 received by the richest half – highlighting a complete failure to target help at those who need it most.
It says long-term public spending plans imply a return to austerity. It says:
Tight spending plans beyond 2028-29 imply departmental budgets will take more of the strain in the future. But if the 3% defence target is met and real health spending continues to grow at 2.6%, pencilled-in spending totals imply that funding for 13 ‘unprotected’ departments will fall to just 4.7% of GDP by 2031-32, close to the post-austerity historic low.
It says people will get poorer between now and the end of the parliament. It says:
Median real annual disposable incomes for working age households are set to grow by a paltry £600 over the course of the parliament. Worse still, those gains are already behind us. Between now (2026-27) and the end of the parliament (2028-29), typical incomes are forecast to fall in total by £1,050 (3 per cent).
This is one reason why so many people continue to think Andy Burnham will call an election next spring (before the electorate feels the full misery of getting poorer) – despite Burnham yesterday saying he would not hold one within the next 12 months.

9am: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, and Ruth Curtice, head of the Resolution Foundation, speak at an event where the RF is presenting its budget analysis.
9.30am: Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
After 11.30am: MPs resume the budget debate in the Commons.
Lunchtime:Andy Burnham is on a visit to a Rolls-Royce factory in the Midlands where he is speaking to the media.

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Ischaemic heart disease was Malaysia's leading cause of death in 2025, accounting for 18,001 deaths, or 13 percent of the total, the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) said on Thursday.
The disease was the leading cause of death among males, with 12,670 deaths, while pneumonia was the main cause of death among females, accounting for 7,684 deaths, DOSM said in a statement.
Ischaemic heart disease was also the leading cause of death among Malays and Indians, while pneumonia topped the list among Chinese and other Bumiputera communities.
Overall, Malaysia recorded 199,807 deaths in 2025, up 0.4 percent from 198,992 in 2024.
Of the total deaths last year, 138,507, or 69.3 percent, were medically certified, DOSM said. ■

China Focus: China expands foreign business access at world's largest free trade port
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:23:45 CST
18:23:45 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China has unveiled 16 measures to make it easier for foreign businesses and professionals to operate in the Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP), the world's largest FTP by area, with new policies covering energy trade, medical services and bonded business operations, according to a government circular made public Thursday.
Under the measures, foreign physicians legally licensed to practice medicine overseas may obtain permits to provide clinical diagnosis and treatment services in Hainan for up to three years, with extensions available in accordance with relevant regulations.
More convenient policies regarding work permits and stay and residence will also be introduced for foreign nationals.
The Hainan FTP, located in China's southernmost island province, launched island-wide special customs operations in December 2025, allowing freer entry of overseas goods, expanded zero-tariff coverage and more business-friendly measures as part of China's efforts to promote high-standard opening-up.
Overseas companies will be allowed to use bonded facilities at Hainan's liquefied natural gas (LNG) receiving terminals, while the FTP will be supported in conducting LNG futures delivery warehouse operations after LNG futures contracts are launched.
Other measures include promoting offshore trade, expanding the range of products eligible for bonded maintenance, facilitating the entry of eligible bonded remanufactured products into pilot free trade zones on the Chinese mainland, encouraging the use of the yuan in new forms of barter trade, and deepening the FTP's economic and trade cooperation with China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Bonded remanufactured products entering mainland pilot free trade zones will be subject to applicable import tariffs, import-related value-added tax and consumption tax. They must also meet all applicable technical requirements for equivalent new products and relevant regulations on remanufactured products, and be clearly labeled as such.
The circular also calls for improved insurance products and services in areas such as international transportation and bonded maintenance.
The latest measures come amid robust growth in Hainan's foreign trade. In the first three quarters of 2026, the province's goods imports and exports reached 285.44 billion yuan (about 42.5 billion U.S. dollars), up 49.8 percent year on year, while trade in services rose 11.7 percent to 56.95 billion yuan, according to data from Hainan's provincial commerce authorities.
Trade in maintenance and repair services more than doubled year on year to 3.31 billion yuan during the same period, according to the provincial commerce department. The trade mainly came from imports of aircraft materials and components and revenues from aircraft maintenance services.
The number of newly established foreign-invested enterprises in Hainan rose 38.6 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, according to the State Administration for Market Regulation.
The FTP measures are part of China's broader efforts to promote high-standard opening-up. The country has announced plans to further expand pilot opening-up programs in sectors such as value-added telecommunications, biotechnology and wholly foreign-owned hospitals, while taking steps to facilitate cross-border trade and investment.
The circular was jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and the General Administration of Customs. ■

17:23:37 CST
18:23:37 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have mapped genetic links to 16 diseases, identifying nearly 1,500 genes that may contribute to conditions ranging from cancer to immune and neurological disorders.
The team, from the Garvan Institute of Medical Research in collaboration with the Murdoch Children's Research Institute and the University of New South Wales in Australia, and other partners, analyzed the gene sequence and activity of more than 9 million individual immune cells from nearly 2,000 people, the largest dataset of its kind, according to a statement released Thursday by the Garvan Institute.
The three studies, published in Nature, examined how genetic variations affect gene activity, repetitive DNA sequences and chromatin accessibility, which influence whether genes can be switched on or off. The findings revealed previously unknown mechanisms linking genetic variations to disease risk.
The research could help accelerate drug development and precision medicine by identifying the genetic mechanisms underlying disease and the patients likely to respond to particular treatments. ■

China's longest metro loop line enters full operation in Wuhan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:23:06 CST
18:23:06 KST

A train runs on the Wuhan Metro Line 12 in Wuhan, central China's Hubei Province, Oct. 29, 2026. China's longest subway loop line, the Wuhan Metro Line 12, started full line operation on Thursday. The 59.9-km line has 37 stations and stretches across seven administrative districts of the city. By far, the total mileage of Wuhan Metro in operation has exceeded 581 kilometers. (Xinhua/Xiao Yijiu)
WUHAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Metro Line 12 in Wuhan, the capital of central China's Hubei Province, became fully operational on Thursday, making it China's longest metro loop line, according to the China Association of Metros.
Stretching 59.9 kilometers and serving 37 underground stations across seven urban districts of Wuhan, the line connects the Wuchang and Hankou railway hubs and offers transfers to 18 existing and planned lines. A full loop takes about 96 minutes.
The line opened in two phases. The first phase, 35.3 kilometers long, entered service on May 1 this year. With the second phase now operational, Wuhan Metro's operational length exceeds 581 kilometers, roughly the driving distance between Berlin and Munich or between Rome and Milan.
Wuhan, known as the "river city," has complex geological and hydrological conditions, which posed multiple challenges during construction. The line passes under the Yangtze River twice and the Hanjiang River once. Construction teams overcame a series of technical difficulties, including high water pressure and composite strata.
One cross-river tunnel, in particular, is approximately 4 kilometers long, with its lowest point 71.4 meters below the Yangtze River surface. The project has provided valuable experience for building super-large-diameter cross-river tunnels in China.
Wuhan, home to over 13.86 million permanent residents, is a key transport hub in China and a core city of the Yangtze River Economic Belt. The opening of Metro Line 12 is expected to further facilitate cross-river commuting.
China has issued a plan to comprehensively advance the high-quality development of integrated transport services during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the Ministry of Transport announced in July this year. The plan aims to basically establish a modern integrated transport service system by 2030.
Under the plan, China will improve connections among different modes of transport, make passenger transfers more convenient and enhance freight logistics services. ■

Türkiye celebrates 103rd Republic Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:21:16 UTC
18:21:16 KST

Esra Tekin
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Türkiye on Thursday marks the 103rd anniversary of the founding of the republic with official ceremonies, cultural events and public celebrations across the country, with the capital Ankara at the center of commemorations.
Turkish flags are hoisted at homes, workplaces, and public spaces.
Municipalities will host concerts, cultural programs and public events, while families gather in parks, squares, and other public spaces to mark the occasion.
In major cities, celebrations are set to continue through parades and fireworks later in the evening.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan visited Anitkabir, the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, the founder of the Republic of Türkiye.
On Oct. 29, 1923, Ataturk proclaimed the Republic of Türkiye, formally establishing a new political order founded on national sovereignty.
The Turkish Grand National Assembly elected him as the country's first president.
The republic emerged from the Turkish War of Independence, a struggle led by Ataturk and the national movement against foreign occupation and attempts to partition Anatolia after World War I.
The victory of the national movement paved the way for the establishment of an independent state in which political legitimacy rested with the nation rather than a hereditary ruler.
The proclamation of the republic was followed by a far-reaching program of reforms aimed at transforming Türkiye's political, legal, educational and social institutions.
Under Ataturk's leadership, the country modernized legal and educational systems, expanded public education, and adopted reforms intended to build a modern nation-state.
On this day, the Turkish nation commemorates the triumph of national independence, the principle that sovereignty belongs unconditionally to the nation, and the commitment to a republic whose institutions are grounded in reason and citizenship.

Army standing up a Deep Recce Strike Brigade
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:21:11 GMT
18:21:11 KST

The Army has approved and is implementing a Deep Recce Strike Brigade to pull intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and precision strike together at corps level, including what the department calls novel one-way effectors, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Stuart Anderson, the Conservative member for South Shropshire, asked what progress had been made on accelerating the development and deployment of the new Recce-Strike approach set out on page 111 of the Strategic Defence Review.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Army has approved and is implementing a Deep Recce Strike Brigade to provide Corps-level (HQ ARRC) integration of intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and precision strike capabilities, including novel one-way effectors. The 5th Generation Land Force programme will increase human-machine teaming, autonomy and decision advantage, further accelerating recce-strike capability across the force.”
A one-way effector is a munition that does not come back, in practice a loitering munition or an attack drone, and the phrase has become the department’s preferred term for a class of weapon that Ukraine has turned into the dominant means of killing vehicles and artillery well behind the line of contact.
The headquarters named is the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks in Gloucester, a NATO corps headquarters Britain provides and commands. The brigade’s output therefore arrives at the level where a corps commander shapes a battle, above divisional and brigade level.
The Strategic Defence Review published in June 2025 set out recce-strike as the organising idea for the future Army, describing a mix of sensors, long-range fires and autonomous systems connected by a digital targeting network. The Defence Investment Plan put £1.8 billion into that targeting web, and the Army has separately acknowledged that its existing drones cannot talk to each other, creating the Uncrewed Systems Centre to deal with that.
The 5th Generation Land Force programme covers the Army’s wider modernisation, including human-machine teaming and the mix of crewed and uncrewed platforms the service expects to field through the next decade.

Ukraine to Become Co-Founder of Defence, Security and Resilience Bank DSRB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:20:31 UTC
18:20:31 KST

Canada and eight other countries, including Ukraine, will sign the founding agreement for the Defence, Security & Resilience Bank (DSRB) in Luxembourg on November 30, 2026.
This reads in an official statement by Canadian Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne.
The DSRB will mobilise public and private capital to finance defence procurement, expand weapons production and develop critical supply chains. Both the governments of participating countries and defence industry companies will be eligible for funding.
The bank aims to secure the highest AAA credit rating, backed by financial support from its founding countries. This would allow it to raise long-term funding at lower rates and reduce the cost of financing defence projects.
A separate focus will be supporting small and medium-sized enterprises, which typically have limited access to banking services. The bank will provide financial guarantees to lenders and loans to participating countries to implement priority projects.
Ukraine is among the countries participating in the development of the DSRB’s initial policies and operating rules. In July, the Canadian government said that partner countries would determine the institution’s operating principles and mechanisms for financing defence needs.
In the same statement, Canada separately emphasised the need to accelerate the adoption of technologies proven in combat and expand industrial cooperation among participating countries. Particular attention will be given to countries facing armed aggression, namely Ukraine.
According to Reuters, the bank’s founders aim to raise around €100 billion. The funds are intended to provide concessional loans for defence projects and guarantees to financial institutions working with arms manufacturers.
The DSRB’s founding documents were agreed upon during multilateral talks in Montreal in April 2026. In July, nine countries confirmed their intention to establish the bank at the NATO summit in Ankara.
The bank is expected to become full-scale operations in 2027.
In addition to Canada and Ukraine, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania and Turkey have joined the establishment of the financial institution. Other allies and close partners that share its goals will also be able to join the bank. The DSRB’s headquarters will be in Canada, with a European hub in Luxembourg.
Meanwhile, the United Kingdom has decided not to join the DSRB. Instead, London will develop its own Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM).

New evidence links Singapore palm oil giant to Indonesian deforesters, despite denials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:20:14 UTC
18:20:14 KST

DEFORESTATION INC
New evidence links Singapore palm oil giant to Indonesian deforesters, despite denials
Two environmental groups have uncovered operational, commercial, personnel and logistical links between First Resources and Indonesian suppliers accused of forest destruction. It’s not the first time the company has obscured its supply chain.
One of the world’s largest palm oil producers allegedly misled investors and corporate customers when it denied links to Indonesian suppliers accused of deforestation, a group of environmental organizations found.
The Singapore-based First Resources group, owned by the billionaire Fangiono family, oversees more than 270,000 hectares of oil palm plantations and is currently under scrutiny as Indonesia and neighboring nations battle a toxic haze caused by illegal fires used to clear land for agriculture.
In 2024, First Resources rejected allegations by the Gecko Project, a partner of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, which had linked the conglomerate to a company now known as Kalimantan Agro Sejahtera (KAS) and palm oil firms allegedly responsible for deforestation on the island of Borneo. The findings were part of Deforestation Inc., a cross-border investigation led by ICIJ that exposed how a lightly regulated sustainability industry overlooks forest destruction and human rights violations when granting environmental certifications.
The Rainforest Action Network and the Environmental Investigation Agency have now uncovered new evidence showing that First Resources, KAS and another company appear to be part of the same corporate group, and have operational, commercial, personnel and logistical connections.
Confidential financial information and court records reveal that, despite marketing its operations as sustainable, First Resources “laundered” into its supply chain palm oil sourced from the suppliers linked to forest loss, according to the reports published today. The company sells its products to Cargill and other major food processing and trading firms.
The researchers also followed trucks and barges and found that a Fangiono-controlled bulking facility was used to offload and transport crude palm oil sourced from mills belonging to First Resources, KAS Group and FAP Agri — indicating close trade relationships. Companies’ employees interviewed by the researchers also confirmed that the firms were linked to each other, the RAN report said.
Alex Helan, a senior researcher at RAN, said the new revelations show how major players in the forestry sector use “tactics of hide and seek through corporate structures” that weaken authorities’ fight against forest destruction.
“Deforestation in Indonesia has been declining over the last decade, influenced by market expectations for deforestation-free products, together with stronger government enforcement,” Helan told ICIJ. “However, this progress is being undermined by companies using complex corporate structures to hide their continued links to deforestation.”
First Resources denied the allegations, saying it operates according to the law and “does not have coordinated, integrated, and co-mingled Crude Palm Oil (CPO) supply chains” with the Indonesian suppliers mentioned in the report.
‘Related parties’ undercut sustainability claims
First Resources first pledged to end deforestation in its supply chain in 2015. Since then, more than half of its plantations have been certified as sustainable by the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, a voluntary certification organization, according to corporate records.
Companies often use their green certification status to attract lenders, investors and clients committed to “environmental, social and governance” guidelines.
As a publicly listed company on the Singapore Stock Exchange, First Resources is also required to submit a sustainability report, in which it routinely touts its commitment to transparency and environmental standards. The report is not reviewed by an independent third-party — a loophole identified by ICIJ’s Deforestation Inc., which showed how forestry companies use certifications based on flawed audits to advertise products and operations as compliant with environmental standards, labor laws and human rights, misinforming shareholders as well as customers.
The new findings by RAN, EIA and Kaom Telepak raise questions about the company’s sustainability claims — and the RSPO’s and the Stock Exchange’s ability to hold it accountable.
According to the environmental groups, over the last decade, large-scale deforestation has continued in a number of palm oil concessions surrounding First Resources facilities operating under the name KAS Group. The company is controlled on paper by a businessman with a very limited public profile who has been described by researchers as a close associate of the Fangionos’.
The KAS Group operates across several Indonesian provinces with about 15,000 employees, 70,000 hectares of land and six palm oil mills, according to job and training adverts uncovered by the researchers. Information about its ownership is hidden behind shell companies incorporated in the British Virgin Islands, a secrecy jurisdiction.
Satellite images analyzed for the report reveal that KAS Group and FAP Agri, another palm oil producer allegedly linked to First Resources, were responsible for clearing more than 9,300 hectares of forest between 2021 to 2026, including areas inhabited by the endangered Eastern Grey Gibbons.
Last year, the RSPO found its member, First Resources, in breach of the organization’s transparency rules and suspended it temporarily. It did not, however, require the company to treat the suspect suppliers as part of the same group, and First Resources has continued to deny links to the Indonesian firms.
“The RSPO complaints panel got it wrong,” RAN’s Helan said, “and has thereby allowed apparent laundering of deforestation palm oil to take place.”
Newly uncovered records from a lawsuit filed by KAS Group in 2022 includes employees’ statements describing regular transport of KAS palm oil to First Resource operations, RAN’s report said. Internal accounting files obtained by the researchers and dated April 2024 also appear to identify the three companies – First Resources, KAS Group and FAP Agri – as “related parties” and show close trading links, the report said.
FAP Agri denied any wrongdoing in a statement to RAN. KAS Group did not reply to requests for comment.
The EIA investigation also found that South Sorong concessions sold by First Resources in 2025 and a First Resources-linked shipping company have the same ultimate owner: an entity registered in the British Virgin Islands. This raises “significant questions about whether the divestment resulted in complete separation from the assets,” EIA’s analyst Ben Melling told ICIJ.
Taken together, Melling said, the findings show that “buyers, investors and certification bodies need to step up their due diligence.”

3 in 4 pilots report dozing off or fighting sleep while flying planes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:20:00 UTC
18:20:00 KST

3 in 4 pilots report dozing off or fighting sleep while flying planes
- A European Cockpit Association (ECA) survey found 76.8% of 7,200 pilots across 32 countries had at least one cockpit “microsleep” in four weeks, raising fears about fatigue and safety.
- Only 37.2% usually report when they are too tired to fly, while 24.2% do not report it and fly anyway.
- Microsleeps are involuntary episodes of sleep lasting a few seconds. People experiencing them may appear awake, even with their eyes open, but fail to process information.
AI generated
Three in four pilots have admitted to briefly dozing off or struggling to stay awake while inside the cockpit, a European survey has found.
The report, released on Oct 26 by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), has renewed concerns about overworked and exhausted flight crews that, in turn, present an unseen risk to flying.
The ECA drew on responses from about 7,200 pilots across 32 countries.
Some 76.8% of those surveyed reported at least one cockpit “microsleep” in the previous four weeks, while 38.8% said they usually do not get enough rest to prevent fatigue from accumulating.
They cited brief and uncontrolled sleep, head nodding and fighting to keep their eyes open.
Microsleeps are involuntary episodes of sleep lasting a few seconds. People experiencing them may appear awake, even with their eyes open, but fail to process information, according to the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health.
The survey was voluntary and conducted online from Aug 4 to Sept 7.
Reporting fatigue is itself a problem, the ECA said.
Only 37.2% said they usually report themselves unfit when they are too tired to fly, while 24.2% said they do not report it and fly anyway.
“When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit,” Captain Coen George, an ECA board director, said in a statement.
‘Alarming number’
Incidents of pilots falling asleep while helming a flight have been reported in Asia.
On Jan 25, 2024, both pilots aboard a Batik Air flight from Kendari to Jakarta fell asleep during the flight, according to Indonesia’s National Transportation Safety Committee. The Airbus A320 was carrying 153 passengers and six crew members.
The captain had been resting when the first officer inadvertently fell asleep. The captain woke up about 28 minutes after the first officer’s last radio transmission, found the aircraft off its intended flight path and woke his colleague.
The plane landed safely, with no injuries or damage.
Investigators found that the first officer’s sleep before duty had been interrupted while helping care for his month-old twins.
In a statement to People magazine, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency said flight-time limits provide a safety baseline, while airlines must actively manage fatigue through reporting systems, operational measures and a culture that allows crews to raise concerns without fear of consequences.
The cockpit association’s president, Captain Tanja Harter, called for stronger oversight and protections for pilots reporting fatigue, saying the lack of meaningful progress since 2023 required action from airlines and regulators.
“Having more than three in four pilots say they reported dozing off while at work is definitely an alarming number, and the industry does need to take note of this,” Bobby Laurie, a Pennsylvania-based travel expert and former flight attendant, told Fox News Digital.
“But it’s not necessarily a warning sign that the flight that you’ve been on had a pilot or both pilots asleep,” he said.

What worker guarantees do unions and lawmakers demand to unblock EU Inc?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:18:10 UTC
18:18:10 KST

Trade unions say the Commission’s pledge that labour law is “unaffected” does not close loopholes in the flagship 28th regime. Lawmakers cannot agree on how to fix them.
The EU’s plan for a single, digital company form is stuck on a question that has split lawmakers for weeks. Whose workers’ rights apply when a company incorporates in one country but employs people in another?
The Council adopted its negotiating position on 23 October. In Parliament, the Legal Affairs Committee’s votes on EU Inc. were cancelled twice this month because political groups could not agree on employee participation. A new committee vote is scheduled for 5 November, with a plenary vote set for 12 November.
The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) argues that the Commission’s reassurance that employment law is unaffected only answers part of the problem.
Individual rights versus collective rights
Labour lawyers broadly accept that ordinary employment rights survive. Under EU conflict-of-law rules, choosing another country’s law generally cannot strip a worker of the mandatory protections of the country where they habitually work.
The gap, unions say, is in rights tied to the company itself, especially board-level worker representation. Under the Commission’s proposal, participation rights for an EU Inc. follow its registered office. Because the company can register in one country without locating its headquarters or workforce there, founders could effectively choose the participation regime when they incorporate.
“We do see that risk,” ETUC Deputy General Secretary Isabelle Schömann told Euronews, pointing to evidence from existing European companies. She says the practice is established: “We already have evidence that businesses are looking for a letterbox company.”
She cited data from the European Trade Union Institute showing that 63% of existing European Companies (SEs) are empty “shelf” entities.
What unions want
ETUC wants the safeguards written into binding articles rather than recitals, which guide interpretation but are not enforceable. Its main demands are:
- A workplace rule. Collective and participation rights should apply where employees habitually work. “European legislation is not there to downgrade existing protection for workers,” Schömann said.
- Non-regression. Where several national regimes apply, the highest level of participation should prevail.
- Workforce aggregation. Employees in branches, subsidiaries and controlled group companies should count towards national co-determination thresholds, so companies cannot split their headcount to stay below them.
- An anti-circumvention clause. This would cover artificial structures, not just “wholly artificial” arrangements.
- Data and enforcement. Labour inspectors and unions would get access to workforce data. Workers and unions could sue in the country of work, and serious abuse could lead to loss of EU Inc. status.
The loopholes unions see
The Council’s mandate adds an optional safeguard for branches. Host countries with participation rules can opt in. A foreign company whose branch workforce passes their threshold must either create a local subsidiary or grant equivalent rights. Unions say this falls short because it is optional, covers branches rather than every group structure, and could keep workers away from the parent board.
Its anti-abuse provision, allowing national authorities to act against “wholly artificial” arrangements, is case-by-case and reactive. A firm with some genuine activity in its country of registration might escape it even if it chose that country partly to avoid co-determination.
Other concerns include the speed of the process. Schömann said “48 hours is too short to allow for the preventive checks that any business has to undertake,” and warned that fast closures could leave workers unable to trace unpaid wages and social contributions.
Stock options are the other flashpoint. ETUC says they must not substitute for pay: “you can’t pay your electricity bill with it,” Schömann said. “If you want to retain talent, you have to pay those talents.” Parliament’s draft would make option plans voluntary and bar them from replacing wages or cutting social-security contributions.
Startups: ‘getting it right’
Startup groups reject the idea that they want to weaken labour protection. Simon Schaefer, CEO of the startup network Factory, signed a 15 October letter warning EU leaders that negotiations were hollowing out the proposal. His priority is preserving free choice of administrative headquarters, which he sees as what makes EU Inc. a true alternative to Delaware.
On fraud, he was direct. “We agree with every try and effort to prevent fraud,” he said. “We’re in unison with the trade unions that we do not want to abuse workers’ rights,” he added.
He argues that targeted rules, such as barring stock options from pushing pay below the minimum wage, are better than excluding entire industries. Schaefer said he is prepared to see the file delayed if it worsens. “For us, getting it right is almost more important right now than the actual speed,” he said.
What's next?
The sticking point is the fallback if management and workers cannot agree on participation. Social Democrats and Greens treat a protective default as a red line, while Renew and business-friendly lawmakers object to exporting one country’s co-determination model across borders. A compromise reported in Parliament would require companies to create a local subsidiary once they pass a host-country threshold, but that could leave the parent board untouched. If the 5 November vote goes ahead, it will show if the gap can be bridged.

How could an oil spill off UAE coast affect desalination plants?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:16:10 UTC
18:16:10 KST

Breadcrumb
How could the oil spill off the UAE coast affect desalination plants?
An oil spill off the United Arab Emirates that has prompted temporary restrictions on fishing and on access to several beaches has raised concerns over the risk of environmental contamination and questions about the potential impact on desalination plants.
What are the main environmental concerns?
The spill is coming from a vessel that shipping sources have identified as crude oil tanker Gem No.2, which they said had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, in the Ras Al Khaimah emirate.
Residents in some northern emirates had posted on social media about strange odours, but authorities said last week that those posed no health risks.
On Wednesday, authorities in Sharjah were the latest to close all beaches as a precaution.
Repeated attacks on commercial vessels since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran have heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
The incident off the UAE has also raised questions about what impact oil spills can have on desalination plants, which crowd the Emirati coastline and, just like in other Gulf countries, are a key supplier of water.
In the UAE, desalinated water accounts for more than 80% of potable water. Major plants include those at Dubai's Jebel Ali industrial port, and at Taweelah between Abu Dhabi and Dubai.
Gulf desalination plants had already come under threat from direct hits in the conflict earlier this year.
Maritime intelligence firm Windward said on Sunday that the leak was threatening the seawater intake of the Naqa'a desalination plant at the border between Umm Al Quwain and Ras Al Khaimah.
Footage verified by Reuters showed that the oil slick had reached a location in Ras Al Khaimah about 2 km away from the plant.
Water experts told Reuters that it was currently hard to assess the potential impact on desalination plants without more information on the extent of the spill. There have been no shutdowns of plants announced in the UAE so far.
The UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, Ras Al Khaimah Media Office and the Naqa'a plant did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
What's the level of risk from this spill?
Any oil spill has the potential to impact the environment, but the extent of the damage depends on the type of oil and the volume, said Simon Boxall, a senior lecturer at the University of Southampton.
Satellite technology can help identify oil slicks floating on the sea's surface but does not provide an indication of how thick that layer is, he noted.
"Crude oil in particular is a natural product. And so crude oil will break down in the marine environment, particularly in the warm waters such as the Gulf, within a matter of a few weeks," he said.
"A thicker spill obviously carries more oil, and when it hits the beaches, when it hits the marine environment, both at sea, on the seabed, and on the coast, then it has a potential to cause more damage. It will eventually break down, but that does take time."
What's the potential threat to desalination plants?
Plants need to be shut down as soon as oil gets anywhere near them to avoid contamination, said Boxall.
Nidal Hilal, director of New York University Abu Dhabi's Water Research Center, said oil spills can threaten desalination plants even when the oil does not physically reach the plant itself, with the principal vulnerability being the seawater intake, which draws raw seawater into the facility for treatment.
"For the UAE, where desalination is a cornerstone of drinking-water security, a key concern is whether the oil could reach seawater intakes and compromise the treatment process," he told Reuters.
It is important to make a distinction between a threat to water quality, a temporary shutdown of a plant, and actual physical damage to the facility, he said.
What can be done to prevent damage and how long do repairs take?
The most effective strategy is to establish several layers of protection rather than rely on a single intervention.
"For the current incident, the priorities should be to prevent oil from reaching desalination intakes, protect treatment equipment, and maintain a safe and reliable drinking-water supply," said Hilal.
Generally, recovery time depends on whether contaminated seawater entered the plant and if the incident causes persistent fouling and equipment damage, he said, listing plant design and the type and quantity of oil among factors that can also play a role.
Have similar incidents happened in the past?
Technical studies and previous incidents have shown that oil contamination can disrupt desalination operations and even damage treatment equipment, said Hilal.
A major spill in 1991 during the Gulf War ended up being one of the largest in history, leading to several desalination plant shutdowns in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait and causing extensive shoreline contamination.
"Decades on, we are still seeing problems with pollution from that particular incident," said Boxall.
However, that spill and the one in the Gulf of Mexico in 2010 were much larger, he said, noting that the UAE spill was not "anything of that scale".

The Meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) began in Türkiye's capital Ankara on Thursday as part of the organization’s 13th summit.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hosted the meeting, according to diplomatic sources.
Foreign ministers of the OTS posed for a family photo ahead of the meeting.
The summit, to be held on Thursday and Friday in Ankara, will be hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, under the theme Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.
Established in 2009, the OTS, formerly known as the Turkic Council, adopted its current name during its eighth summit held in the Turkish metropolis Istanbul in 2021.
While Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan are members, Turkmenistan, Hungary, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, and the Economic Cooperation Organization hold observer status.
The organization said on Oct. 24 that the summit would bring together the heads of state of its member states, as well as high-level representatives from observer states and its secretary general, to “discuss the current state and future prospects of cooperation within the Organization,” among other issues.
It said the heads of state are expected to review the progress achieved across the OTS’ priority areas, and that particular emphasis will be placed on “further strengthening unity and solidarity” among the Turkic states and advancing cooperation under the Turkic World Vision 2040.
It added that the summit will also mark the handover of the OTS’ chairmanship from Azerbaijan to Türkiye, and is expected to address the appointment of a new secretary general and the organization’s strategic priorities “for the forthcoming period.”
“The Heads of State are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, together with a number of decisions and documents aimed at deepening cooperation and further strengthening the institutional framework of the OTS,” it added.

Promises and Perils of Nepal’s India Pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:11:00 UTC
18:11:00 KST

After months of keeping New Delhi at arm’s length, Nepal’s Balendra Shah government is discovering both the appeal and the political risks of drawing it closer.
Formed after the March 2026 elections, the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) government did not start on the right foot with the southern neighbor. First, new Prime Minister Balendra Shah declined a one-on-one meeting with then-Indian Ambassador Naveen Shrivastava, in keeping with his policy of not meeting any foreign officials.
What rankled more with the Indians was his subsequent refusal to meet India’s Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, who was coming to Kathmandu carrying Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s formal invitation for Shah to visit India. Misri’s trip was called off. India — which continues to emphasize its “unique” relations with Nepal that are unlike its ties with any other country — saw this as a snub, and a breach of trust.
Those were not the only irritants in bilateral ties. The new government in Kathmandu started taxing goods bought by Nepali nationals in Indian border towns, hampering the business of these hubs that rely on Nepali buyers. Entry of Indian vehicles into Nepal was also restricted.
That was the state of affairs for the first five or six months of the Shah government.
But the tide seems to have turned and the government now appears keen to woo the Indians. At the forefront of this effort is Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle.
Even before the March elections, as a top RSP leader, Wagle had repeatedly visited New Delhi with a message that should his party come to power, it would go the extra mile to protect Indian interests.
Of late, Wagle seems to have gotten the government’s green light to boldly assert that the era of “anti-India nationalism” in Nepal is over and his government is ready to turn over a new leaf with the southern neighbor.
Curiously, he and his government also sound accommodative of India’s self-declared red lines. In a recent interview with The Hindu, the Nepali minister said that Nepal now accepts that India’s refusal to buy hydropower from Nepali projects with Chinese investment is a “new geopolitical reality.”
Yet the finance minister is only laying the ground for Shah’s much-awaited India visit in the third week of November. Home Minister Sudan Gurung has also contributed to this effort, outlining potential areas of bilateral cooperation in a recent op-ed. Big deals are being planned during Shah’s visit.
But for any government in Kathmandu, close relations with India come with both costs and benefits. The obvious benefit is that New Delhi pulls many strings in Kathmandu, and it can make life difficult for a Nepali prime minister it does not like. The latest overtures of his government toward India suggest Shah does not want to be one of them.
If Shah can convince New Delhi to, say, secure an additional air route for Nepal during his India trip, it will be a new feather in his bhadgaule cap — and a tangible achievement for his nationalist base back home.
Yet there are also costs of closer ties with India. Whatever Wagle says, the days of anti-India nationalism in Nepal are far from over — as is also evident in the fierce criticism of his remarks in Nepali intellectual circles. Nepalis continue to be suspicious of the oft-meddling regional hegemon that has thrice imposed crippling blockades on the landlocked country.
Shah got an overwhelming mandate, and he can afford to use some of his political capital to push through vital projects with India. But irrespective of how well Shah’s India trip goes, there will still be irritants in bilateral ties.
For instance, a major disagreement remains between Kathmandu and New Delhi on an old border dispute. After India and China unilaterally opened the Lipulekh pass — a trijunction point between the three countries — for trade earlier this year, Kathmandu swiftly dispatched diplomatic notes to New Delhi and Beijing. This issue could again flare up as both New Delhi and Beijing seem to be in a mood to overrule Nepal’s objections and give continuity to their trade through the pass.
It will be hard for the Shah government to stand firm on Lipulekh — something that is in keeping with the Nepali public sentiment — while also pursuing closer cooperation with India. If it does not handle the issue well, a “compromise” on territorial integrity to secure favorable trade terms could even be portrayed domestically as a surrender to the regional hegemon.
Then there is China. The government has signaled that closer ties with India are worth paying the price of narrowing the space for Chinese investment in Nepali hydropower.
Yet if the government pushes Beijing too far through such gestures, it will violate a central tenet of Nepali foreign policy: maintenance of a delicate balance between Beijing and New Delhi. There will thus be a strong opposition to an overt India tilt.
In the end, Shah and his ministers would do well to avoid making sweeping claims that old constraints in India-Nepal ties have disappeared or that the anti-India nationalism in Nepal has run its course. Nurturing this complicated relationship requires sustained diplomacy and setting of realistic expectations. Only then can Nepal protect its interests.

‘Scattergun’ budget will still leave Britons facing higher energy bills, says thinktank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:10:22 UTC
18:10:22 KST

John Healey delivered a “scattergun” budget that did little to boost living standards and left Britain facing “a painful second half” of the parliament, a leading economic thinktank has warned.
The Resolution Foundation said on Thursday that measures to ease household gas and electricity costs would still leave energy bills higher this year than during the last energy shock.
In a highly critical verdict on the chancellor’s efforts to provide “breathing space” for the public amid the rising prices exacerbated by the Iran war, the foundation said Healey’s budget was poorly targeted, giving the rich almost as much as the poor.
It said the subsidies to ease the rising cost of living handed the poorest half of households a gain of £158 on average this year and next, just £14 more than the £144 received by the richest half.
The thinktank’s chief executive, Ruth Curtice, said it highlighted “a complete failure to target help at those who need it most”.
In his first budget as chancellor, Healey said he would cushion the blow from rising inflation while also showing how the government planned to “rewire the economy” to boost growth.
Measures aimed at tackling soaring energy costs include the scrapping of standing charges on gas bills and energy payments of £100 for up to 20m households in council tax bands A to D.
But in its analysis of the budget, the foundation said Healey was the latest chancellor to preside over a poorly targeted energy discount scheme that has “left the UK reliant on 35-year-old property valuations to determine eligibility for support with energy bills this winter”.
Typical disposable incomes would fall by £1,050 between now and the end of the parliamentary term in 2028-29, limiting the increase over the entire five-year parliament to just £600, the foundation predicted.
Curtice said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.
“Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”
Healey said the UK was being battered by a global economic storm, with the budget watchdog – the Office for Budget Responsibility – slashing its forecast for gross domestic product growth next year.
But he promised “to steer us through the global economic storms today, to chart a new course for Britain in the years ahead, to give people fresh hope for Britain’s future”.
Curtice said: “Stepping back, this parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves, which yesterday’s budget did little to address.
“The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services – funded by huge tax rises – none of which was enough to prevent dramatic half-time substitutions in Downing Street.
“The new occupants will hope for better political fortune in the second half, but it could prove tough going against a projected £1,000 fall in disposable incomes.
“A more dramatic change of tactics may be needed, and we did not learn how the government will choose between public service ambitions and household incomes. Next year the choices will unavoidably get starker.”
Healey also included tax breaks for high street businesses as well as hiking taxes on banks and gambling.
Defending the budget measures, Andy Burnham told broadcasters: “It’s pretty bold to help 20m households with energy costs through the council tax cut this winter.
“It’s bold to lift 70,000 businesses out of business rates altogether, and that will give a real lift to high streets up and down the country.”

The 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum Was Held in Kyiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:06:38 EET
18:06:38 KST

The 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) was held in Kyiv, focusing on the performance of the Ukrainian economy amid escalating military risks. Discussions centered on how businesses can adapt to new threats, maintain production, and find resources for recovery and development.
Opening the forum, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi stated that Russia has intensified its attacks on the Ukrainian economy. According to his estimates, direct losses exceeded $7.7 billion, and more than 1 million square meters of real estate have been damaged or destroyed. By the end of the year, the Prime Minister said, the budget will fall short of planned revenues by approximately $1.5 billion.
At the same time, he emphasized that despite the consequences of the war, the economy continues to function thanks to the resilience of entrepreneurs and their teams, and support for business remains one of the government’s priorities.
“We realize how important it is right now to support Ukrainian businesses in return for this resilience, in return for this dedicated work,” said Serhiy Koretskyi.
Despite limited budgetary resources, the government is continuing its lending programs and developing mechanisms to insure against war risks. Under the “5–7–9%” program, 580 billion hryvnia in loans have already been issued since the program’s inception. 457 companies have already insured their property under the loss compensation program administered by the Export-Credit Agency, with a potential payout of over 9 billion hryvnia. The next step is a broader system of war risk insurance, to which the state plans to allocate $1 billion and attract an additional $3 billion from international partners.
Among the external challenges are the tightening of EU trade restrictions on Ukrainian exporters, particularly producers of metallurgical and agricultural products. Business representatives spoke of reduced access to the European market, while Ukraine’s representative to the EU, Taras Kachka, discussed accelerating integration into the EU’s internal market and expanding the industrial visa-free regime.
The labor shortage remains acute. Experts estimate migration losses at approximately 5 million people, while businesses are facing a shortage of skilled workers. Among possible solutions, participants discussed dual education and creating conditions to encourage Ukrainians to return by offering jobs and affordable housing.
The overall business sentiment at KIEF is cautious but business-oriented. The impact of the attacks varies by industry, but companies agree on the need to hope for the best while being prepared for various scenarios. Companies are reviewing safety protocols, setting up shelters, and developing their own response systems. In particular, Vyacheslav Klimov, co-owner of the NOVA Group, said that “Nova Poshta” has implemented its own air defense project, which has already shot down Russian drones. Companies are also developing their own fire departments.
“The top priority for Ukrainian businesses is how to adapt to the new challenges of the war and get through this winter. It’s not easy for anyone, so it’s especially important to support one another. If I need services or partners, I turn first and foremost
to Ukrainian companies. This is a matter of principle: by buying goods and services from one another, we support businesses, preserve jobs, and help our economy survive,” emphasized Vasyl Khmelnytsky, initiator of the Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) and founder of the UFuture holding company.
The business community’s main requests to the government are predictable regulations, insurance against war risks, and solutions to the labor shortage. Businesses have learned to operate amid constant threats, but the costs of security and recovery are limiting opportunities for new investments.
“We have held the KIEF both under pandemic restrictions and after the start of the full-scale invasion. This year, the question of how not only to keep businesses running during the war but also to avoid losing opportunities for development has become particularly acute. There are no ready-made solutions to all problems, so it is important to combine business expertise with the capabilities of the government and international partners,” said KMEF CEO Yuriy Pivovarov.
Title partners of the forum: UFuture, Mastercard, AEQUO, PrivatBank, Kyivstar
Forum partners: Sense Bank, NEQSOL Holding, PUMB, DTEK, Ajax Systems, Uklon, General Chereshnya, Biopharma, Eclectic Talents Group, TERWIN, CEO Club Ukraine, BALEX, Naftogaz Group.
Interfax-Ukraine is the forum’s media partner.

Photos: Aftermath of deadly Cyclone Arnab in southern India

In Pictures
Photos: Aftermath of deadly Cyclone Arnab in southern India
Cyclone Arnab has battered India’s eastern Andhra Pradesh state, killing three people and damaging homes and farmland.
Ferocious winds and torrential rain lashed India’s southeastern coast after a cyclone made landfall, killing at least three people before the storm weakened, officials said.
Cyclone Arnab hit southeastern Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday as a “very severe cyclonic storm”, with winds of 125-135km/h (77-84mph) and gusts reaching 150km/h in the early hours of Wednesday morning, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said.
Torrential rain was recorded, as much as 30 centimetres (nearly 12 inches) in parts of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states, the IMD said, with the storm weakening into a “deep depression” throughout Wednesday afternoon.
About 50,000 people were told to move to safer areas in Andhra Pradesh and another 48,000 in neighbouring Odisha.

‘Dramatic and unprecedented,’ growing calls for comprehensive investigation into suspicions of foreign intervention in Israeli elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

- i24NEWS
- Israel elections 2026
- ‘Serious suspicions,’ election committee chief orders Shin Bet to investigate foreign funding, election bribery
‘Serious suspicions,’ election committee chief orders Shin Bet to investigate foreign funding, election bribery
Sohlberg said he “cannot attest to the nature” of the suspicions but that there is a duty to investigate them. He also says the information that led to the request did not come from a political entity
Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg instructed Shin Bet head David Zini to investigate suspected foreign funding and election bribery involving foreign entities. According to a letter dated October 28, Sohlberg asked for findings, if any, within the coming week.
The letter followed a briefing in which Zini presented Sohlberg with information described as “exceptionally grave.” The allegations concern improper influence over the elections through foreign funding from outside actors working against Israeli interests.
Sohlberg noted that the information that led to the suspicions does not involve tips received from a political entity, nor is it a response to an inquiry from the Likud party, which alleges fraud and the theft of the election.
“The purity of elections is the heart of democracy,” Sohlberg wrote. “Serious suspicions have been brought before me of improper influence on the elections through foreign funding from foreign entities operating against Israeli interests.”
The committee chairman also stated that he “cannot attest to the nature of the above suspicions,” but said there was a duty to investigate them properly.
Sohlberg told Zini to “do everything in your power to investigate the matter,” and to use the Shin Bet’s powers to locate evidence substantiating the suspicions. “Only in this way can we ensure public trust in the electoral process, and the purity of the democratic process.”
Separately, Ynet reports that Sohlberg sent the letter to Zini following a meeting between them earlier in the week, and claim it may be an attempt by Qatar to influence the elections in Israel. The CEC stated that the information regarding this is “solid.”
Suggested articles
Meanwhile, several additional suspects have been arrested as part of an investigation into alleged bribery in exchange for votes for the Ra’am party.
Following the election, Likud accused Arab parties of stealing the election through bribery, threats, violence, forgery, and prohibited voter mobilization software, and said it was submitting hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to police, the Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee. Police said they have no investigative or intelligence-based evidence supporting the allegations.
According to police data, 48 complaints of fraud and impersonation had been received nationwide as of last night, compared with nearly 80 during the previous election, a decrease of about 40%.
Political reactions
Several Israeli political leaders from both sides of the political spectrum weighed in on the investigation order.
Current opposition frontrunner and Yashar Party chief Gadi Eisenkot says he is in contact with the relevant authorities and is receiving updates regarding suspicions of foreign interference in the elections. "The State of Israel must rigorously safeguard the integrity of the elections against any attempts at interference, political spin, or bias," Eisenkot said in a statement.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said the suspicion of election tampering via foreign Islamist funding “serves as a litmus test for the State of Israel.” He said the leaders of the Arab parties “must be questioned by the Shin Bet,” adding the word “today.” Smotrich also said: “The State of Israel will not be sold out to radical Islam through terror-linked funds.”

Hello Kitty firm apologises, cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China backlash
Sanrio, the company behind the hugely successful Hello Kitty franchise, has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media accused the show of "smearing China", sparking a social media backlash.
Sanrio, the Japanese company behind the popular character Hello Kitty, apologised on Thursday over its tie-up with a TV spy drama criticised as being anti-China, which had prompted the cancellation of a merchandise collaboration with the show.
It comes days after Chinese sponsors dropped football superstar Kylian Mbappé over comments calling communist leader Mao Zedong a "dictator", for which the Real Madrid forward later apologised.
Read moreReal Madrid apologises to China over Mbappé's Mao Zedong comments
In one episode of "Vivant", a drama with a wide audience in Japan, a Chinese-affiliated organisation had been depicted torturing a member of the Japanese military's unofficial spy unit.
"We have recently received feedback from various quarters regarding the collaborative merchandise with the Japanese television drama VIVANT," Sanrio said in a statement.
"We sincerely apologise for any concern this may have caused."
The project "contains expressions that are inconsistent with the Sanrio Group's corporate philosophy", it said.
Sanrio said it had "decided to cease this collaboration, as well as all subsequent projects and promotional campaigns".
Hello Kitty and other cute Sanrio characters had been depicted as characters from "Vivant" – currently in its second season – in a range of novelty merchandise items.
Read moreFrench-Saudi ‘Dragon Ball’ theme park puzzles Japanese manga fans
Before the apology, Chinese state media outlet the Global Times had accused the show of "smearing China", saying it had "sparked shock and fierce backlash on social media".
The series reflects the "anti-China narrative of the current conservative Japanese right-wing administration, catering to the trend of right-wing extremism in Japanese society", it said.
Long-frosty ties between the countries have worsened since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested last year that Japan could intervene militarily in any conflict over Taiwan.
Beijing claims self-ruled Taiwan as its territory and has vowed to bring it under control one day.
'Beauty and goodness'
The drama "is a completely fictional entertainment work", private broadcaster TBS, which created "Vivant", said in a statement to AFP.
"There is absolutely no intention to deliver messages that disparage any particular nation or hurt public sentiment," it said.
The network's president told Japanese media that TBS "does not in any way take a position that foments conflict between nations or condones the use of force or violence".
Comments posted on Chinese social media platform Weibo before Sanrio's announcement had angrily criticised the merchandise tie-up.
"Sanrio, you are a brand for conveying a message of beauty and goodness, why have you got involved with this?" one post said.
"It's disappointing," read another. "The founder has long taken part in various anti-war activities, and Sanrio was originally founded on the ideals of stopping war and cherishing peace."
Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun echoed the complaints at a regular news briefing on Thursday, following Sanrio's statement.
"This television drama once again reveals the persistent existence inside Japan of a force that seeks to use cultural products to vilify and smear China and spread anti-Chinese sentiment," he said.
"This should raise alarm amongst the international community and enlightened individuals within Japan."
The furore follows similar ire from the country over Mbappé's comments.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan pledged a “stronger and more influential” Türkiye in the coming years in a message marking the 103rd anniversary of the founding of the Turkish Republic on Oct. 29.
“Türkiye, thank God, is stronger today than it was yesterday. God willing, tomorrow it will be much stronger, enjoy greater international standing and wield considerably more influence in every field,” Erdoğan said in his Republic Day message.
He said Türkiye had made significant progress over the past 24 years in areas ranging from the defense industry and energy to transportation and diplomacy, describing these advances as milestones on the path toward a more prosperous and influential country.

Türkiye would continue working for peace and justice under the principle of “peace at home, peace in the world,” he said, referring to the motto associated with the republic’s founder, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.
Erdoğan said the Turkish people would work together to realize the government’s “Century of Türkiye” vision and carry the republic toward a brighter future.
He also paid tribute to Atatürk, his comrades-in-arms, the heroes of the Turkish War of Independence and those who died defending the country, while expressing gratitude to veterans.

Japan detected the passage of a Russian Navy reconnaissance ship and the flight of three military aircraft belonging to the People’s Republic of China near the Japanese islands.
Between October 27 and 28, the Russian intelligence-gathering ship SSV-535 Kareliya, of the Meridian class, sailed southwest through the Tsushima Strait, according to Japan’s Joint Staff of the Self-Defense Forces. The vessel then continued toward the East China Sea.
The large Project 864 Meridian-class reconnaissance ship, built during the Soviet-era and operated by Russia, is designed for electronic intelligence gathering, communications signal interception, and radar monitoring. It is equipped with antenna systems housed beneath radomes and hydroacoustic reconnaissance equipment.
Japan’s Self-Defense Forces deployed the minesweeper Hirashima, assigned to the 3rd Minesweeper Division based atSasebo, to monitor the vessel. A P-1 patrol aircraft from the 4th Air Group of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force,operating out of Atsugi Air Base, provided aerial surveillance of the ship’s movements.
On October 28, during the daytime, a Chinese BZK-005 reconnaissance unmanned aerial vehicle and a Y-9 reconnaissance aircraft flew from the East China Sea toward the Pacific Ocean.
The BZK-005 is a long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicle designed for aerial reconnaissance. It has an endurance of up to 40 hours and is equipped with electro-optical and infrared surveillance systems, as well as a synthetic aperture radar.
The specialized reconnaissance aircraft based on the Y-9 military transport aircraft is designed to conduct signals intelligence and electronic intelligence missions. It is equipped with antenna arrays along the fuselage for intercepting communications signals and determining the bearings of radar emissions.
The maritime patrol variant of the Y-9 is equipped with a search radar in the nose section, a magnetic anomaly detector in the tail boom for submarine detection, an electro-optical system, and an internal weapons bay. The bay is designed to deploy sonobuoys and launch torpedoes and anti-ship missiles.
The Chinese aircraft passed through the airspace between Okinawa and Miyako Islands. After turning over the Pacific Ocean, they returned toward mainland China along the same route.
On the same day, a Chinese patrol aircraft flew from the mainland toward the waters southwest of the Danjo Islands and then toward the waters northwest of Okinawa Island.
To monitor the Chinese aircraft, the Japan Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets under the command of its Southwestern Air Defense Force.
In August, Russia conducted high-profile missile exercises near the Southern Kuril Islands after Japan lodged a protest over Vladimir Putin’s visit to the occupied island of Iturup.

Restricted airspace now covers fifty defence sites
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:00:09 GMT
18:00:09 KST

Restricted airspace has been applied over fifty defence sites and a further one hundred and seventy are expected to follow in December, part of a wider effort to harden British military bases against drones, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Mark Pritchard, the Conservative member for The Wrekin, asked what additional support is being given to Guardian, the protective security element of Standing Joint Command, in light of increased threats to British military bases.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Defence Investment Plan provides an additional £470 million over four years for security technology and infrastructure. Restricted Airspace has been applied to 50 Defence sites, with a further 170 expected in December 2026, while £15 million has been invested in remotely piloted and counter-uncrewed aerial systems and training over the past 18 months.”
Restricted airspace makes flying a drone over a site unlawful without permission. That does not stop anyone flying, but it gives the police and the Ministry of Defence Police an offence to act on, and it removes the argument that an operator did not know where they were.
The department has set out £240 million for Project PRESAGIUM, an enhanced counter-drone system intended to detect and defeat emerging threats, and the Army is running Project Halo Shield to examine what commercially available counter-drone technology could do for site protection. The £15 million figure for remotely piloted and counter-drone systems and training over the past eighteen months is small compared with those programmes and covers work done while they are being stood up.
