Astronomers Discover a Possible New Dwarf Planet in Our Solar System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Scientists are on the verge of confirming the discovery of another member of the solar system, a potential dwarf planet. Astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile located the object, provisionally named 2026 ED138.
The prospective planet measures somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers in diameter and is located about 46 astronomical units from the sun (an astronomical unit being Earth’s approximate distance from the sun). For comparison, Pluto—which is also now considered a dwarf planet—orbits at an average distance of 40 astronomical units. Based on its location, ED138 belongs to the population of trans-Neptunian objects. According to its discoverers, it could be one of the brightest known objects of this type and also among the largest.
The difference between a planet and a dwarf planet is largely their environment. While both orbit the sun and have sufficient gravity to assume a nearly spherical shape, a planet has cleared its orbit of other bodies of comparable size. Dwarf planets, on the other hand, coexist with other objects in the region of the solar system they traverse. This is the main reason why Pluto ceased to be considered a planet in 2006 and was reclassified as a dwarf planet.
Matthew Holman, a researcher at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and a member of the observatory’s operations team, identified the object on October 13 while analyzing data collected by Rubin in 2026. A more thorough search allowed the team to locate additional observations in archived records dating back to 2016. Thanks to this set of images, the team was able to reconstruct more than a decade of the object’s trajectory.
Astronomers explain that ED138 had managed to “hide” from us because its position in the night sky is against the disk of the Milky Way, which we usually see as a thick band of millions of stars. This concentrated brightness makes it difficult to distinguish fainter objects, but the Rubin Observatory’s enormous amounts of data made it possible to identify the object amid that sea of light.
Though ED138 appears to have the right characteristics, astronomers have yet to confirm whether it is a dwarf planet. For now, astronomers know it is a trans-Neptunian object, but they need to determine its size more precisely to establish whether its own gravity is sufficient to give it a nearly spherical shape. If it meets the requirements, ED138 would join the group of five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris.
It is also not the only celestial body awaiting possible classification as a dwarf planet. Astronomers have identified dozens of objects in the outer solar system that, based on their size and other characteristics, could meet the criteria. Among the best-known candidates are Gonggong, Quaoar, Sedna, and Orcus. Experts acknowledge that the list could be even longer.
Confirming them as dwarf planets is no easy task. The enormous distance at which they lie makes it difficult to directly measure their size and mass and, above all, to determine whether their own gravity has given them a nearly spherical shape. To obtain high-resolution images of Pluto, for example, the New Horizons probe had to be sent to its vicinity—a journey that took nearly nine and a half years from its launch in 2006 to its flyby in 2015. Three years later, it reached the object Arrokoth, a small planetesimal even farther away.
The solar system is often depicted as a star surrounded by eight planets, but in reality it is a much more extensive and populous structure. In addition to planets and moons, it contains dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, and a vast number of small bodies that extend far beyond Neptune. The Kuiper Belt extends to approximately 50 astronomical units, while the scattered disk reaches nearly 1,000. Much farther out lies the Oort Cloud, a region we have never directly observed and that could extend up to about 100,000 astronomical units from the sun.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

As Latvia's 14th Saeima concluded its work on Thursday, Speaker of Parliament Daiga Mieriņa of the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) called on lawmakers to maintain respect for the Saeima and democratic values, stressing that the country is always greater than any political party, parliamentary group or parliamentary term.
In her final address to the outgoing parliament, Mieriņa acknowledged that the past four years had not been easy and had required considerable work, patience and compromise. Nevertheless, lawmakers had managed to maintain dialogue even when their opinions differed.
The Speaker recalled that during the 14th Saeima's term, parliament held 219 sittings, conducted 7,911 votes, adopted 1,060 laws and held 3,555 committee meetings.
She emphasised that the Saeima is a mirror of society, reflecting what Latvia has been and what it is today.
Mieriņa thanked lawmakers for their contributions to strengthening parliamentarism, democracy and the Latvian state, noting that every member of parliament had left their mark over the four years, whether through adopted legislation, initiatives or parliamentary debates.
She stressed that in a democracy, there are no small or large mandates, only the trust of voters granted for a limited period.
Addressing lawmakers who will continue serving in the next parliament, Mieriņa encouraged them to retain the ability to listen not only to their own voters but also to those who hold different views.
She also urged them to respect parliamentary traditions and the people on whose behalf decisions are made.
At the same time, Mieriņa noted that society is changing and a new generation is knocking on parliament's doors, bringing its own perspectives and expectations of politics.
She stressed that politicians must be willing to listen to this generation and make room for new representatives.
Mieriņa emphasised that no politician is irreplaceable, as members of parliament serve for a limited time, while Latvia, democracy and the people they serve remain.
Concluding her address, the Speaker wished lawmakers success in both their political careers and personal challenges.
She also quoted author and speaker Neale Donald Walsch, saying that a true leader is not someone who has the most followers, but someone who creates the most leaders.
Mieriņa ended her speech with the traditional Latvian wish: "May Latvia live as long as the sun!"

US reporters to monitor Russia-Ukraine truce in frontline town – Melania Trump

Alyoshki, located on the left bank of the Dnieper River, was largely cut off from essential supplies and basic services for months under a Ukrainian siege, with drone attacks and remotely laid mines hampering aid deliveries and evacuation efforts from a town where an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 civilians remained.
Russian Foreign Ministry envoy Rodion Miroshnik described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods,” accusing Ukraine of obstructing humanitarian efforts.
However, after US mediation spearheaded by the Slovenian-born US first lady, Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the area starting October 27 to allow humanitarian assistance to flow in and evacuations to proceed. As of Thursday, both Russian and Ukrainian officials reported no truce violations. The pause is scheduled to last until Sunday.

Dmitriev confirmed that Newsmax reporters will be there, adding: “Humanity and peace must prevail.”
Speaking to reporters before departing to Alyoshki, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said other foreign journalists are also expected to arrive, without providing further details.

The Russian Defense Ministry said on Thursday that most Ukrainian mines found near Alyoshki were scattered by drones, and that they are predominantly Western-made. It also released a video showing a large-scale demining effort involving remotely-controlled robots.
The Alyoshki crisis was discussed during an October 9 phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, the leaders agreed that Russia’s human rights commissioner would maintain direct contact with Melania Trump’s office. US envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently met with Putin in St. Petersburg last week to discuss proposals for ending the Ukraine conflict.

North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:58:57 UTC
17:58:57 KST

North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report says
Russian broker network recruiting North Korean labourers using student visas, Global Rights Compliance report says.
North Korean workers are being recruited into forced labour in Russia by a broker network using bogus student enrolments, according to a months-long investigation by an international law foundation.
The network brings North Koreans into Russia on student visas to skirt United Nations sanctions and labour law, as part of a state-sponsored work programme that helps fund Pyongyang’s ballistic missile development, according to the Global Rights Compliance report released on Thursday.
Operated by Russian businessman Vladimir Sokolov, labour-brokering platform KNDR.su markets North Korean workers to prospective Russian employers in agriculture, construction, industry and IT, charging a commission of 100,000-150,000 roubles ($1,240-$1,860) per placement, according to the Netherlands-based nonprofit.
In conversations with Global Rights Compliance investigators posing as prospective employers, Sokolov’s operations director, Ruslan Zhukov, said North Korean workers were enrolled in colleges they did not attend “to avoid the application of labour law”, the law foundation said.
Zhukov also described the workers being required to work 12 hours a day, six days a week, according to the report.
UN member states are prohibited from hosting North Korean workers under a 2017 UN Security Council resolution intended to deprive Pyongyang of funds for its nuclear weapons and missile programmes.
Despite UN sanctions, between 35,600 and 101,280 North Korean workers were based overseas in 2025, generating an estimated $450m-$800m for Pyongyang, according to an 11-country team that monitors sanctions enforcement.
Russia granted more than 36,000 visas to North Koreans in 2025, a fourfold increase from the previous year, almost all of which were officially for educational purposes.
Global Rights Compliance said the network also helped support Russia’s war effort in Ukraine, with Sokolov publicising at least two work sites with links to Moscow’s military-industrial complex.
Sokolov and Zhukov did not respond to requests for comment sent to Sokolov’s holding company, Black Horse, and KNDR.su.
Global Rights Compliance said Zhukov denied the report’s allegations, calling them “false, fabricated, and categorically rejected in their entirety”.
“The matter concerns exclusively students of a specialised college, sent to Russia within the framework of an intergovernmental agreement on the exchange of experience and the provision of venues for educational and industrial practical training,” a statement attributed to Zhukov said.
Lara Strangways, head of business and human rights at Global Rights Compliance, said the broker network pointed to deepening ties between North Korea and Russia.
“North Korean workers are being sent to Russian factories through a network that serves both states at once: Their labour props up Russian industry, including sites linked to the war in Ukraine, while the revenue they generate helps fund North Korea’s military programme,” Strangways said in a statement.
“What we are seeing is a clear exploitation of these workers as part of a cross-border system. If governments are serious about responding to this deepening alliance, they need to understand the role that forced labour is playing in sustaining it.”
North Korea and Russia have ramped up cooperation across various fields in recent years as Moscow became increasingly isolated on the international stage in the wake of its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Cold War-era allies ratified a landmark mutual defence treaty in 2024, with Pyongyang deploying thousands of North Korean soldiers to fight alongside Russian troops in the war on Ukraine.

The regime’s optics: Despite sanctions, Russia is advancing quantum and laser technologies for military use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:58:44 UTC
17:58:44 KST

The Insider has found that despite sanctions, Russia continues to regularly purchase advanced industrial laser equipment, allowing it to develop and manufacture its own military communications systems, lidars, target designators, and inertial navigation systems. Some purchases may also point to efforts to increase the capabilities of Russian quantum computers, which could significantly enhance the capabilities of Russian intelligence services by cracking encryption.
Cracking the world’s encryption: will Putin get a cryptographically relevant quantum computer?
The Insider has found that Russia continues to import advanced measuring instruments, components, and materials for optics and quantum electronics. The equipment being purchased — along with the research interests of the importers and end users — suggests that Russia is seeking to develop advanced laser technologies despite its continued reliance on imports for more basic laser applications.
If any country succeeds in building a “cryptographically relevant” quantum computer, and if such a machine falls into the hands of a totalitarian regime, it would significantly alter the international balance of power. Even without a quantum computer, however, mastery of advanced laser technologies would allow Russia’s military-industrial complex to develop domestic production capabilities across a range of military sectors far more quickly and effectively than it has managed to do so far.
A “cryptographically relevant” quantum computer in the hands of a totalitarian regime would significantly alter the international balance of power
Quantum computers are expected to outperform classical computers dramatically on tasks such as cracking encryption. Existing quantum computers, however, are not yet “cryptographically relevant” — meaning they remain far from being able to break the standard encryption algorithms in use at the present time. According to the latest estimates, a cryptographically relevant quantum computer capable of breaking RSA encryption with a 2,048-bit key would require at least one million physical qubits, with the number needed to break elliptic-curve cryptography with a 256-bit key estimated at around 10,000 physical qubits.
How a quantum computer works
Building a quantum computer capable of breaking modern encryption remains beyond the capabilities of even Google and IBM. IBM’s Condor quantum computer, for example, has 1,121 physical qubits based on superconducting technology. Quantum computers with around 100 qubits can be considered commercially available, in a limited sense, to major research institutions in the West.
Estimates vary on the countdown to Q-day — the point at which a cryptographically relevant quantum computer becomes available. Cloudflare, which helps secure websites around the world, cites the policies and research interests of IBM and Google to put Q-day in 2029 or 2030. In fact, the company is adjusting its own policies accordingly, transitioning to “post-quantum” protocols designed to remain resistant to the sorts of quantum attacks that could materialize in the foreseeable future.
Why photonic quantum computers require laser equipment
Russia’s most powerful quantum computers have been developed by the Lebedev Physical Institute (LPI), Rosatom, Moscow State University (MSU), and the Russian Quantum Center. The LPI–Rosatom computer has the equivalent of 70 qubits and uses ytterbium ions. MSU’s neutral-rubidium-atom computer has 72 qubits. The Russian Quantum Center’s computer uses trapped cold calcium ions and has the equivalent of 72 qubits. According to the Scientific Russia website, a 16-qubit superconducting quantum computer has been developed at the National University of Science and Technology MISIS.
The Russian Quantum Center is also involved, and in 2025, its researchers were ready to showcase a 35-qubit photonic quantum computer. The challenge now is to scale it up.
According to the Russian tax authorities’ records of fines, the work on a quantum computer for the Russian Quantum Center is being carried out by a Rosatom entity, joint venture Quantum Technologies. This conclusion is also supported by the numerous quantum computing patent applications filed by Quantum Technologies covering integrated circuit topologies for both photonic and superconducting quantum computers, as well as quantum computing algorithms and error-correction codes. Notably though, Quantum Technologies does not appear in customs records, suggesting that other organizations are handling equipment purchases on its behalf.
Such purchases are often made by subsidiaries or other companies linked through a common founder. In the case of the Russian Quantum Center, one possible candidate is its affiliated company, K2 LLC — almost all current and former K2 employees also have work experience at Quantum Technologies, including in specialized units responsible for procurement and logistics, cost accounting, reporting to federal executive authorities, support for the Committee on Quantum Technologies, and supplying equipment and consumables. This staffing structure suggests that K2 may be acting as a procurement agent for Quantum Technologies.
Advanced laser technologies — not just for quantum computers
Russian propagandists claim that Russia is now using lasers to shoot down drones; however, independent experts question the effectiveness of these systems. Whatever the case, advanced laser technologies are essential to the military-industrial complex.
Manufacturing complex-shaped components, additive manufacturing, welding and cutting, and quality control are all vital to industries such as aircraft and drone production, and all require sophisticated laser equipment. Some laser technologies, notably lidars and 3D scanners, also have direct military applications in guiding drones, artillery, and loitering munitions, as well as in reconnaissance. For years, however, Russia remained a consumer rather than a developer of laser technologies, and its own solutions were uncompetitive.
As recently as a decade ago, a trade publication reported that there were 10 Western and 100 Chinese laser specialists for every Russian one. Even during the relatively prosperous 2000s, foreign experts were critical of the capabilities of research lasers at Russian scientific centers. Industrial laser technology, meanwhile, remained largely dependent on imports, leaving many options unavalable after Western sanctions were levied in 2014. Russian-made lasers were not used at all in consumer or medical devices. Russia’s advanced laser sector was further devastated not only by neglect of science but also by the criminal prosecution of laser specialists amid the political repression of the 2020s.
Russia’s advanced laser industry collapsed not only because of the neglect of science, but also because laser specialists were prosecuted
According to data reviewed by The Insider, Russia imported $250 million worth of industrial laser equipment in 2024, excluding consumer and medical laser devices, civilian telecommunications equipment, and equipment for the entertainment industry.
The imports consisted primarily of high-power equipment: laser-cutting machines for sheet metal, pipes, other metal workpieces, and glass; machines for 3D cutting, engraving, and laser cleaning; laser welding and sintering machines; and equipment for high-precision manufacturing and measurement. The latter category included laser equipment for chip manufacturing, 3D printers, coordinate measuring machines, lidars, 3D laser scanners, rangefinders, sights, interferometers, particle-size analyzers, weld-seam inspection devices, and film-thickness gauges.
The Insider also found that Russia had imported components and assemblies in recent years to manufacture its own industrial lasers. These included blanks for active laser elements (neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnets and other crystals), lenses transparent to the relevant wavelengths, optical fibers, high-precision polishing machines, laser beam profile meters, and spectrometers. This suggests that efforts are also underway to rebuild Russia’s domestic laser industry, rather than relying solely on off-the-shelf Chinese laser equipment.
How the West is helping Putin with lasers
Russia imports predominantly sophisticated industrial laser equipment of Chinese origin, but approximately 10% is manufactured in Germany, Italy, Switzerland, Japan, the United States, and Israel. Among Western products, the most prominent suppliers by volume include Leica Geosystems (surveying scanners), Adige SPA (tube-cutting systems), Toptica Photonics AG (laboratory lasers), Stiefelmayer Lasertechnik GmbH & Co. KG (laser-cutting machines), Z-Laser GmbH (laser-cutting and welding equipment), and Sick AG (laser scanners). The leading beneficiaries of China’s laser-equipment trade include Jinan Senfeng Laser Technology, Hubei Jiuzhiyang Infrared System, Shandong Oree Laser Technology, and HSG Laser.
Supplies came almost exclusively from China, Turkey, and Israel. Individual items were shipped directly from Italy and Germany, accounting for less than 1% of the total.
Israel remains virtually the only Western country from which industrial laser equipment continued to be sold openly and directly to Russia in 2023–2025. The company that benefited in practice, regardless of its degree of involvement or awareness, was Ophir Optronics, registered in Israel but owned by the publicly traded American corporation MKS Inc. Operating in Russia under the Ophir Optronics name, the Russian company Kristalltechno LLC trades in and imports laser beam profile and spectrum analyzers.
The use of Ophir Optronics’ name, trademark, and logo in Russian commercial courts has not been challenged to date. Kristalltechno LLC has registered declarations of conformity in Russia covering a wide range of Ophir Optronics industrial cameras and their components.
On paper, the equipment is supplied by intermediaries in Turkey, Kyrgyzstan, the United Arab Emirates, China, and Hong Kong. However, customs records for some shipments identify Israel, rather than the country of the nominal supplier, as the country of dispatch.
In Russia, the equipment was most often received by Kristalltechno LLC, an established supplier to the military-industrial complex. According to 2024 data, the company did business with such Russian defense-sector enterprises as the Priborostroitelny Zavod Federal State Unitary Enterprise, the Ural Optical and Mechanical Plant (UOMZ), and the Ekran Research Institute. In effect, Kristalltechno was Ophir Optronics’ alter ego in Russia, apparently engaged in both manufacturing and resale. Curiously, according to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, Ophir Optronics has ties to Israel’s military establishment.
The Insider contacted Ophir Optronics for comment. The company responded through a representative from Kekst CNC, a reputation-management firm hired by MKS. A journalist from The Insider spoke with the representative by phone several times.
The representative issued the following statement:
“Ophir ceased working with Kristalltechno in early 2022, when the war began. We are not aware of any Ophir products being supplied to Russia through third parties. We were unaware that Kristalltechno was using our trademarks on its website and have taken steps to have them removed from the company’s website and all other marketing and sales materials. Ophir and its parent company comply with all applicable regulations governing the sale and export of our products.”
Ophir sidestepped The Insider’s question about its relationships with the companies that had exported its products to Russia, including whether they were partners, dealers, or distributors. The Insider had provided a list of these companies. Ophir also declined to explain why it had waited more than four years to check whether Kristalltechno had stopped distributing its products and using its branding. Despite repeated questions, both orally and in writing, the company also made no statement condemning either Russia’s military aggression or political repression in Russia.
Separately, a Kristalltechno employee offered a journalist from The Insider an Ophir Optronics VEGA 7Z01560 laser radiation analyzer for $5,000, with delivery in Moscow in one to two days. The journalist had inquired about the equipment’s availability from the publication’s editorial email address. The offer suggests that the device was in stock in Moscow.
A Kristalltechno LLC employee offered an Insider journalist a laser radiation analyzer for $5,000 in Moscow
The market price of the same equipment in the West is around $1,300, illustrating the additional costs that sanctions and export controls impose on Russia’s high-tech industries.
What Russia’s modern private laser industry looks like
Russia has every reason to develop its own advanced laser technologies rather than simply buying finished equipment. Two leading examples of Russian companies in this field are Special Systems Photonics LLC and Leningrad Laser Systems JSC (LLS), both based in St. Petersburg.
Special Systems Photonics is a regular supplier to Russian state organizations. In recent years, it has supplied the Lebedev Physical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences with components for an interferometric system to monitor laser-processing speed. Other supplies have included lasers, optical materials, light sources, spectrofluorometers, spectrometers, detectors, optical probe stations, microchip inspection systems, fiber-processing laser systems, alignment systems, optomechanical systems, and systems for precisely positioning nanoscale objects in quantum optics laboratories.
Special Systems.Photonics has also supplied equipment to Bureau 1440, which is developing Russia’s Rassvet satellite communications system, an alternative to OneWeb. According to commercial court records, the company works extensively with Russia’s military-industrial complex. Its counterparties include NPO GIPO JSC (under sanctions), the Kvant joint venture (under sanctions), the Defense Ministry’s 18th Central Research Institute, and the Elektropribor Central Research Institute Concern JSC (under sanctions).
In 2023–2025, Special Systems Photonics imported large quantities of optical equipment, including lasers, optical tables, lenses, optical fiber, fiber-splicing tools, fiber cleavers, electro-optic and acousto-optic laser modulators and their drivers, mirrors, prisms, acousto-optic filters, signal generators, and spectrum analyzers.
Among other items, the company imported German-made Carl Zeiss objective lenses, Rigol optical spectrum analyzers, and Thorlabs diffraction gratings. The company’s website showcases an impressive range of high-quality equipment. Alongside instruments for scientists and developers, customers can also purchase lidars for drone guidance systems.
The research published by Special Systems Photonics employees focuses on highly specialized subjects, including laser-induced emission spectroscopy, quantum precision measurement instruments, magneto-optical traps, quantum gravimeters, optical vector analyzers for measuring the characteristics of integrated optical circuits, and single-frequency fiber lasers for quantum applications. Single-frequency lasers play a key role in working with ultracold atoms, a technology that could provide one of the foundations for a quantum computer. The researchers have also worked on precision quantum measurements. Beyond its academic interest in quantum computing and quantum metrology, Special Systems Photonics explicitly advertises the supply of cold-atom quantum computers made by the Chinese company CAS COLD ATOM, including the 100-qubit HANYUAN-1 model and custom-built systems.
All of the above suggests that Special Systems Photonics LLC is deeply embedded in Russia’s high-tech quantum optics sector, acting as a systems integrator, developer, and center of expertise rather than merely a reseller of equipment to state organizations. The company’s purchasing patterns, combined with its interest in related technologies, suggest that its imports could potentially be used to develop a more powerful photonic quantum computer than any currently operating in Russia.
Leningrad Laser Systems JSC has imported semiconductor blanks, machinery for processing metals and other materials, fiber-optic amplifiers, optical splitters, multiplexers, plugs and sockets, diffraction gratings, and laser vibrometers. Most of the equipment came from Chinese manufacturers, though some devices and components were made in the West.
Among the Western equipment imported by Leningrad Laser Systems, high-quality German products stand out: spectroscopy cameras from Basler AG, adapters from SmarAct GmbH, optical components and optical connector cleaners from Schäfter+Kirchhoff GmbH, laser scanner heads from Scanlab GmbH, and precision dimensional measurement instruments from SIOS Messtechnik GmbH.
German equipment remains indispensable for a wide range of engineering applications, and Russian companies continue to procure it by every available means for military production. Leningrad Laser Systems has also purchased laser power and energy meters from Israel’s Ophir Optronics, discussed in the previous section. This makes it the second-largest seller of Ophir products on the Russian market, after the Moscow-based former distributor that continues to operate under the Israeli company’s branding.
Judging by its employees’ research publications, some of which are partly promotional, Leningrad Laser Systems is interested in radio-over-fiber technology for shipboard communications, high-power fiber laser cutting machines, ultraviolet laser cutting, optical fibers for specialized applications (including specially doped fibers), beam-profile shaping for specific tasks such as drilling holes, metrology, and wind lidars. LLS employees also devote considerable effort to promoting laser multiplexing equipment.
Research publications by Leningrad Laser Systems suggest that the company does more than handle customs paperwork: it develops, tests, and markets the relevant technologies in Russia. LLS also actively fulfills government contracts, supplying equipment such as fiber-drawing towers for manufacturing optical fiber used in fiber-optic cables, plasma research rigs, laser beam homogenizers, multispectral systems, photon counters, optical reflectometers, and optoacoustic modulators. Its customers have primarily been civilian universities and research institutions, including Moscow State University, St. Petersburg State University, KAI, and institutes of the Russian Academy of Sciences, as well as specialized institutes such as VNIIFTRI, VNIOFI, and Voenmekh.
According to court records, LLS has done business with the Ramenskoye Instrument-Making Plant JSC (under sanctions), the Ural Electromechanical Plant, and the Astron Optical-Mechanical Design Bureau, which manufactures drones and thermal imaging systems. Astron also produces laser ranging systems, while NPO GIPO JSC makes military sights, Elektropribor produces laser gyroscopes, and the Ramenskoye Instrument-Making Plant has developed a direct laser command-guidance system for guided missiles and electro-optical sighting systems for helicopters.
These companies are therefore more than intermediaries reselling Chinese or Western equipment. They are highly qualified specialists in the field, capable of testing equipment themselves and fulfilling complex contracts for both civilian research institutions and defense-industry enterprises. The Insider sent requests for comment to Special Systems Photonics and Leningrad Laser Systems but received no response.
More widespread military applications of lasers
Even at a less advanced technological level, Russia’s military-industrial complex is trying, with varying degrees of success, to keep pace in the field of laser technology. The following is a far from exhaustive list of technologies developed or deployed by Russia’s defense industry during the full-scale war. These systems are commercially available in the West and far less sophisticated than the cutting-edge research and development discussed above.
- At the Army-2022 exhibition, the Spectrum-AT Scientific and Production Center presented its Plastun system for multichannel observation of targets in optically opaque environments, equipped with a laser rangefinder and laser illuminator.
- Laser Components manufactures laser gyroscopes for military applications.
- Aviation and Marine Electronics Research and Production Company showcases laser rangefinders and target designators as part of multichannel surveillance systems for drones.
- In its report from the Army-2022 forum, the Regional Center for Laser Technologies (RCLT) showcased (at 3:46) a phased-array base fabricated by laser welding.
- The Inject Research and Production Enterprise developed an industrial laser soldering system.
- Laser cutting is used (at 2:29) at Uralvagonzavod.
- Lasergrad equipment is used to clean the K-3 submarine using lasers.
All this points to active efforts to develop these technologies and reduce Russia’s dependence on imported equipment and systems.
As The Insider has found, advanced Western laser technologies — in the form of equipment, components, and materials — continue to reach Russia. This is one of the few remaining fields in which Chinese manufacturers cannot always fully replace Western suppliers. At the top of the technological hierarchy are quantum computers (which, despite all the promises, may not become cryptographically relevant in the foreseeable future), quantum metrology, and quantum communications. Below these are more widely used, practical applications already in widespread use.
With military needs an overriding state priority and funding for civilian scientific research being cut, there is little doubt that the technologies and equipment entering Russia are intended not to advance fundamental science but to strengthen the capabilities of the military and security services.

Flora U-19s draw 2-2 with 9-man Chelsea in UEFA Youth League
Tallinn FC Flora's U-19 side drew 2:2 at home with English Premier League giants Chelsea's youth team Wednesday.
The game was the first leg of the UEFA Youth League second qualifying round, played at the A. Le Coq Arena in Tallinn.
After a sending-off, the visitors were down to 10 men early on in the second half, falling to nine players shortly before full-time after a second sending-off, but held on for the draw

Flora's equalizer came on 60 minutes, when Alamaa converted a penalty won by left-back Karel Isok.
"Before the game we said Chelsea are vulnerable on the counter-attack. For the first goal I got a good run at the center-back and took my chance. It was a good start to the game. I saw the goalkeeper dive one way and just put the ball calmly in the other corner," Alamaa told ERR after the match.
Chelsea finished with nine men: center-back Dante Waite was sent off on 55 minutes and midfielder Isaac Silva collected a second yellow on 89.
"In some ways you could feel the difference in level with players from a Premier League club's academy. They were technically very high-quality players. In midfield their players played some unbelievable passes. But if you go into duels the way we did today, we can take down anyone," Alamaa added.
The second leg takes place in London next Wednesday, November 4.

From reunification to Med deal: Türkiye-Libya relations take new turn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:56:00 UTC
17:56:00 KST

This month will likely be remembered as a key period in Turkish-Libyan relations. First, Libya’s House of Representatives approved a long-dormant memorandum of understanding on maritime jurisdiction and then came a critical meeting apparently kept under wraps for the reunification of Libya’s eastern and western administrations.
Overall, it appears that Türkiye’s diplomatic efforts are paying off, and doubly so: strengthening the country’s clout in the Mediterranean at a time its adversaries (including former ones such as Greece, with which Ankara hopes to mend ties) make their moves with new alliances and reinvigorating ties with North Africa, where post-Moammar Gadhafi Libya is still a key actor despite factions at odds.
On Oct. 20, Libya’s House of Representatives greenlit a maritime jurisdiction agreement with Türkiye, which has been awaiting approval since it was signed in 2019. Last Friday, media reports revealed that the eastern and western administrations in Libya sent delegates to Ankara for talks on a possible reunification. A senior Turkish official told Agence France-Presse (AFP) on Wednesday that talks have not produced an immediate result yet, but discussions focused on military reunification, with talks on political unity expected to follow in the future. Still, it is a beginning facilitated by Ankara, which rose to prominence in the last decade as a key power broker and mediator in its region and beyond.
Answering Daily Sabah’s questions about whether Libya’s House of Representatives’ decision cemented Türkiye’s influence in the region, Aylin Ünver Noi, professor of International Relations and vice rector of Beykoz University, said that the approval process made an important contribution.
“We are also seeing a process come to the fore that aligns with Türkiye’s interests in the region and reflects what Türkiye wants to achieve. However, there is something else worth keeping in mind. Türkiye has a policy regarding gas exploration and extraction activities in the Eastern Mediterranean and, more broadly, across the entire Mediterranean basin. It is trying to manage this process through bilateral relations, but at the same time, it has consistently maintained the same position from the very beginning. Türkiye says it is open to dialogue with all the countries that share maritime boundaries in the region,” she said.
Greece has long opposed the memorandum, fearing that Türkiye could gain greater influence in the Mediterranean. Athens views Türkiye as a historic rival, even as Ankara pursues rapprochement with Greece, and the deal could further complicate the maritime dispute between the two countries in the Aegean Sea.
Türkiye and Greece compete for rights in the vast sea. Soon after the deal was approved, Türkiye announced a navigational telex (Navtex) in the Mediterranean (a notice containing navigational and maritime safety warnings), citing work on a natural gas pipeline project between Türkiye and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) until late December. Like the France-led project, the gas pipeline will be a lifeline for the TRNC, which has been isolated from the international community, which refuses to recognize its sovereignty. The pipeline will connect Türkiye’s Mersin to the TRNC’s Girne (Kyrenia), covering a distance of about 101 kilometers (63 miles), including a 4-kilometer pipeline across land.
The Türkiye-Libya deal also drew the ire of the European Union, which counts Greece and the Greek Cypriot administration among its members.
If Ankara were able to implement the agreement, Türkiye could gain access to large, undiscovered gas deposits, but the deal covers a vast area claimed by Greece.
Noi said Türkiye sought to de-escalate tensions in the Med, with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan even offering a meeting in Antalya to resolve the issue, referring to the Turkish leader’s proposal to find a formula safeguarding the interests of every littoral country.
“This position has not changed. Türkiye continues to pursue it. In his latest statement, the president also said that Türkiye is not trying to do anything against anyone. Rather, it is working toward arrangements that would allow everyone to benefit and produce a win-win outcome,” she said, referring to the president’s remarks after a Cabinet meeting earlier this week.
“But that does not mean Türkiye would accept a situation in which some countries gain disproportionately while others are deprived of their rights. In other words, Türkiye wants these partnerships, but it also wants the process to be managed in a way that prevents any country from pursuing maximalist claims at the expense of others. Türkiye wants everyone to be included and no party to be excluded,” she added.
She said Türkiye in the past was excluded from forums on the Eastern Mediterranean. “It was treated as though it had no coastline in the Eastern Mediterranean and no legitimate rights or interests in the region. Today, however, we see that these agreements have set a different process in motion, with Türkiye also beginning to normalize bilateral relations with certain countries. But this does not mean that the president is pursuing this process against anyone. Rather, the message is that Türkiye is not doing this to target others, but to ensure that no one is allowed to undermine its rights,” she also stated.
Erdoğan on Monday underlined that opposition to the Libya memorandum, particularly by the European Union, had no legitimate basis. In his address after the Cabinet meeting, the president stressed Türkiye’s policy on the Eastern Mediterranean was very clear, and they had no intention “to score a goal against anyone.”
“We are only occupied with preserving our maritime jurisdiction, rights and interests. We advocate for a peaceful approach to resolve disputes, engaging in dialogue with all littoral countries. We expect all actors, the European Union in particular, to demonstrate the same constructive will,” Erdoğan said.
He noted that the aggressive discourse benefited no one. “Even if it means paying a price, we never hesitate in doing the right thing for Türkiye, for the Turkish nation. I remind those trying to exclude Türkiye from the Eastern Mediterranean to respect the joint will of Türkiye and Libya,” he added.
Another interest for Türkiye in Libya is ensuring political stability, as Ankara stands to gain from finding a new partner in Africa where, under the leadership of Erdoğan, it has significantly enhanced relations through its “Africa opening” policy.
Since last year, dialogue between Ankara and rival groups in Libya has increased as the country reached out to Khalifa Haftar, with whom it once had tensions. Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, who holds a prominent military position, and Turkish officials have held frequent talks in recent months.
Noi said that since the Arab Spring, Türkiye has had to contend with a situation shaped by the consequences of those uprisings. “They gave rise to problems such as civil wars and failed states in many parts of the region. This triggered a process that undermined the stability of those countries and negatively affected their relations with other nations. Countries that are divided and governed by different groups or rival leaderships also face another disadvantage: external powers can support different factions, further destabilizing these countries and undermining peace and development. From the very beginning of the Arab Spring, Türkiye has opposed the fragmentation of countries and the emergence of failed states, whether in Syria or Libya. On the contrary, it has consistently emphasized principles such as territorial integrity and independence,” she said.
“The same applies to Libya. Bringing the two opposing sides together would strengthen Libya as a unified country. This is something Türkiye wants, both in terms of regional stability and the development of its bilateral relations. However, Türkiye's role must not be destabilizing; on the contrary, its support has always been aimed at promoting stability,” she added.
Noi noted that Türkiye played a significant role in mediation efforts in recent years, and these efforts were institutionalized within the Foreign Ministry, which established a directorate-general for mediation.
“Türkiye has made considerable progress in this field, with successful initiatives in various parts of the world, including mediation efforts across the African continent. Therefore, Türkiye may have taken an important step in Libya by helping bring together groups that have been at odds within the country. Türkiye has already pursued a similar approach in Syria, as you know. It supports a unified Syria and wants groups pursuing separatist aims to be reintegrated into the country. Türkiye has never sought the division, fragmentation or weakening of its neighbors or other countries in the region. Instead, it has wanted them to remain unified, strong and capable of contributing to regional stability. This would be an important development both for bilateral relations and for the future and survival of the country concerned. That is what Türkiye hopes to achieve. We have already seen progress in this direction in recent days,” she said.

Spanish rescuers search trains in hope of finding survivors of deadly crash
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:55:15 CET
17:55:15 KST

By Guillermo Martinez and Michael Francis Gore
URDA, Spain, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Rescuers picked through mangled carriages on Thursday in a grim search for victims of Spain’s second fatal high-speed train crash this year, as the death toll rose to 69 and hopes of finding further survivors faded.
After cranes worked through the night to lift parts of the wreckage of Wednesday’s crash, emergency workers were seen carrying what appeared to be a body wrapped in a blanket from one of the trains in the central Spanish province of Toledo.
Regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said the death toll had risen to 69 people and that human remains had been found during overnight rescue efforts. Work now involved crane operations, particularly on a carriage that was still overturned.
“We do not believe there could be any more fatalities beneath that one, but I say this with caution,” he said.
UNIONS BLAME LACK OF FUNDING
Meanwhile, train drivers in Spain went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety a day after Europe’s deadliest train accident since a 2013 derailment in Spain’s Santiago de Compostela.
“We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again … It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had,” said Diego Martín of the train drivers’ union SEMAF.
“We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again. Everyone should be able to travel without the risk of suffering this kind of accident,” he added at Madrid’s Atocha railway station.
The crash, which followed another fatal accident in January involving the same rail companies on the same line, has also upended campaigning for a November 29 snap election, with the leaders of Spain’s two main parties suspending campaign events.
Spain’s government has declared three days of national mourning for those killed in the crash, which Transport Minister Oscar Puente said happened after several trains stopped due to a signal failure. A state-run Renfe train was then authorised to proceed at normal speed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, Puente said on Wednesday.
Unions have already blamed a lack of funding and will to improve safety, saying that talks after the accident in January were abandoned in April. Meanwhile, the government has said that the decision to authorise the Renfe train to continue its journey was “inexplicable”.
POPE SENDS CONDOLENCES
Pope Leo sent his condolences to the families of those killed, wished a speedy recovery to the injured and conveyed his support and comfort to all affected, the Vatican said, adding he had also encouraged rescue workers to continue their efforts.
Of those injured, authorities said 57 remained in hospital.
The crash prompted a major operation, which Spain’s interior ministry said involved the deployment of more than 800 military and police personnel, over 200 vehicles, three helicopters, a mobile command post, drones, mounted units and search dogs.
As investigations began, a judge in Toledo barred anyone not involved in emergency, security, healthcare or judicial work from the crash site with a 2-km (1.2-mile) exclusion zone in both directions along the Madrid-Seville high-speed rail line.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who travelled to Toledo to take part in a meeting to monitor and coordinate the emergency response, said authorities were working “day and night” to support the victims and their families and to “get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy”.
Meanwhile, Alberto Nuñez Feijoo, leader of the centre-right People’s Party, which is currently leading in polls, was due to visit the town of Urda, where local people rushed to help with rescue efforts in the aftermath of the crash.
FOREIGN NATIONALS AMONG CASUALTIES
Spain’s foreign ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, information available so far showed, of whom one was killed and at least seven injured.
Wednesday’s accident has added urgency to a debate about safety on Spain’s railways, Europe’s longest network and until recently a source of pride in the country.
Train drivers would go ahead with their strike to press for structural changes in railway safety, SEMAF said, adding that it was studying further action.
Renfe said the strike caused significant disruption to rail services, adding that passengers could change or cancel tickets free of charge and would be notified of affected services.

JAKARTA, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The head of Indonesia’s Nutrition Agency, which runs the country’s free meals programme, said on Thursday that his agency “desperately” needs to prevent food poisoning among the programme’s recipients.
• Sudaryono acknowledged food poisoning was still the main problem to be tackled
• A key campaign promise of President Prabowo Subianto launched in January 2025, the scheme has been marred by a series of problems, including cases of food poisoning and allegations of corruption
• As of September, at least 57,000 recipients had contracted food poisoning, government data showed
• “We desperately need to solve this immediately so that not a single child is poisoned. That is our top priority,” Sudaryono said at an event
• The rate of food poisoning per one million servings currently stood at 3.6, which was relatively high compared to 0.1 in the United States and 0.8 in Japan, he said
• He said he aimed to bring it in line with the US by strengthening oversight and allowing the agency to monitor CCTV footage from nearly 27,000 kitchens, which would improve worker supervision and hygiene standards
• All kitchens will be forced to purchase seven commodities, including rice, eggs, beef and chicken, on a market platform to be launched by the agency next month, he said
• The platform aims to ensure small farmers and fishermen benefit from the free meals programme, and not just large suppliers
• This year’s budget for the programme was cut by 44 trillion rupiah ($2.42 billion) from 268 trillion rupiah, he said
• The agency has opened 1,460 kitchens in remote areas and areas with high stunting rates, he added

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. "While the two countries on the Iberian Peninsula are trying to cope with a housing crisis and rising costs of living, their governments are engaging in increasingly extensive military cooperation with Ukraine. Behind the familiar phrase ‘support for Ukraine’ lies a far more specific reality: Spanish and Portuguese companies, together with Ukrainian manufacturers, are launching projects in the fields of missile technology, strike drones, guidance systems, and other weapons designed to strike Russia," he wrote in an article posted on the movement’s website.

Companies cooperating with Ukrainian firms include Tekever UAS, S.A., a Portuguese drone manufacturer whose AR3 and AR5 systems have been used by the Ukrainian armed forces since 2022, as well as the Spanish companies Sener Aeroespacial, S.A. and Escribano Mechanical and Engineering, S.L.U., and others.
"As a result, the political choices made by Madrid and Lisbon seem highly contradictory. On the one hand, there is condemnation of military actions in the Persian Gulf. On the other hand, these countries are being drawn into the war in Ukraine, which requires funding and cuts to social service budgets. While Spaniards are being forced to live in tents due to the housing crisis, and Portuguese authorities acknowledge the lack of affordable housing as one of the most pressing social problems, the governments of both countries are at the same time allocating state resources, industrial capacity, and technological expertise toward expanding arms production for Ukraine," he concluded.

====================================================================================================

Delhi’s De-Hyphenation Policy is Taking Shape in the South Caucasus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:52:00 UTC
17:52:00 KST

Few would have pictured Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar sharing a stage with his Azerbaijani counterpart, Jeyhun Bayramov, after Baku’s public backing of Islamabad during the India-Pakistan crisis of 2025.
Following the terrorist attack at Pahalgam on April 22, 2025, Azerbaijan was one of the few countries that did not publicly condemn the attack. After a telephone conversation with the Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on April 26, Baku issued a statement, expressing concern over the “recent tensions between India and Pakistan” and stressed the need to “refrain from unilateral actions in such a volatile situation.” Then, after India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, Azerbaijan explicitly condemned the Indian military strikes, saying they harmed civilians. It expressed solidarity with the people of Pakistan.
Against this backdrop, Jaishankar’s visit to Baku on October 23 – the first standalone visit by an Indian external affairs minister since 2018 – when he held talks with Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev and Foreign Minister Bayramov, marks an important step toward repairing strained bilateral ties.
At the joint press conference, Bayramov acknowledged that India and Azerbaijan “had different viewpoints on different issues,” before going on to describe discussions with Jaishankar as “very long and positive and fruitful.” Jaishankar echoed this sentiment, describing the discussions as “focused and forward looking” with both sides exchanging views on “various aspects” of the bilateral relationship and discussing important “regional and global developments from a strategic perspective.”
While no agreements were signed, both sides agreed to deepen cooperation in the oil and energy sector, expand trade and investment, and exchange commercial and business delegations. They also agreed to strengthen regular political consultations and exchange high-level visits. During the visit, Jaishankar reportedly raised the issue of cross-border terrorism, security, and common threats. Notably, including “cross-border terrorism” brought New Delhi’s primary security friction with Pakistan directly into the bilateral conversation, despite Islamabad’s close ties with Baku.
Jaishankar’s visit was not an isolated diplomatic gesture, but rather the latest in a series of moves to accelerate a thaw in India’s ties with Azerbaijan. Jaishankar’s visit to Baku was a follow-up to the meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Aliyev on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit at Bishkek in August-September this year.
Jaishankar’s visit was immediately preceded by a visit by the Indian Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh to Baku, where he led the Indian delegation for the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) held on October 15.
High-level diplomatic contact between New Delhi and Baku was restored in April this year, when India’s Secretary (West) Sibi George visited Baku for the 6th round of the India-Azerbaijan Foreign Office Consultations. The visit came less than a year after Baku condemned India’s military strikes on Pakistan. According to an Indian Ministry of External Affairs media release, the issues discussed included “trade, technology, tourism, pharmaceuticals, energy, culture, people to people exchanges and [the] fight against cross border terrorism.” The previous foreign office consultations were held in 2022.
According to an Indian media report, Azerbaijan resumed crude oil exports to India in September 2025, after a 10-month break caused by pricing issues that led to a halt in supplies. India-Azerbaijan bilateral trade has steadily dropped from $1,882 million in 2022 to $1,435 million in 2023, $958 million in 2024 and just $400 million in 2025. In the first 9 months of 2026, bilateral trade has already reached $600 million, Bayramov said.
It is important to understand the regional geopolitical context in which the thaw in New Delhi-Baku ties is playing out. India’s engagement in the South Caucasus has historically been weighted towards Armenia, Azerbaijan’s adversary in the decades-long Nagorno-Karabakh conflict. This has been a persistent irritant in India-Azerbaijan ties.
Meanwhile, Armenia has emerged as India’s strongest partner in the region – especially through defense cooperation – in recent years, driven largely by mutual concerns over an Azerbaijan-Pakistan-Türkiye nexus. The signing of the U.S. brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict in August 2025 paved the way for New Delhi to separate its relations with Baku from its position on the conflict, without risking derailing ties with Yerevan.
The evolving regional landscape has further accelerated this alignment. Nascent signs of rapprochement between Azerbaijan and Türkiye are evident, with the recent bilateral agreement to promote cooperation in academic engagements.
In September 2025, Armenia and Pakistan also established diplomatic relations after over 30 years of non-recognition by Islamabad. As more extra-regional actors come to play an active role in shaping the South Caucasus’ future, New Delhi is fast realizing it has more to lose by not engaging in multi-directional diplomacy with all actors.
Interestingly, Jaishankar’s visit comes at a time when Azerbaijan’s school hijab ban has strained Baku’s ties with one of its closest partners, Türkiye. After Baku announced a headscarf ban on September 21, Türkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan implicitly criticized the move at the U.N. General Assembly, calling it an assault on fundamental freedoms. The resulting criticism from Erdogan and other Türkish officials prompted a sharp response from Baku, triggering a rare diplomatic showdown between partners who describe themselves as “One Nation, Two States.”
Although Jaishankar’s visit was likely planned well in advance and unrelated to this sudden friction, the trip coincided perfectly with these shifting regional dynamics. It opens a valuable window for rapprochement, granting both nations greater geopolitical maneuvering space in light of New Delhi’s fraught relations with Ankara.
Another reason why New Delhi is looking to revive ties with Azerbaijan is to accelerate work on the International North South Transport Corridor (INSTC). Originally proposed in 2000, the project sat dormant for years until New Delhi recently signaled interest in reviving it, as an alternative to the conventional Suez Canal route amid growing vulnerability in global maritime chokepoints. Azerbaijan, which serves as the land bridge for the Western Route of the INSTC, will play a crucial role if New Delhi wants this route to become a dependable commercial artery. In this context, Baku agreeing to “closer coordination” on INSTC is a welcome development for New Delhi.
Yet, India’s ‘”de-hyphenation” policy may not automatically translate to a reset in ties. Because a formal peace treaty remains absent, the agreement between Azerbaijan and Armenia amounts to little more than a fragile truce. If the conflict persists or reignites, New Delhi will find itself increasingly intertwined in turbulent regional security dynamics.
Moreover, whether this relationship broadens or stagnates will also depend to a large extent on Baku’s willingness to accommodate New Delhi’s concerns regarding Pakistan and Kashmir.
Azerbaijan has been a consistent and vocal supporter of Pakistan’s position on the Kashmir issue, most notably at multilateral forums such as the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). Azerbaijan has consistently backed statements and communiques within the OIC and its contact group on Jammu and Kashmir, which condemned India’s actions in Kashmir.
Azerbaijan will be hosting the 2027 OIC Summit, and New Delhi will closely scrutinize how it frames the Kashmir issue in the grouping. Any overtly provocative framing is likely to adversely impact the future trajectory of India-Azerbaijan diplomatic and economic ties.
The trust deficit between the two sides is deep-rooted, and the recent rapprochement seems unlikely to bridge the big ideological differences between the two nations.
Nevertheless, engagement is a positive step, and a practical reflection of New Delhi’s ‘multi-alignment’ approach towards foreign policy.

Obama and Trump spar at rallies in Georgia and Ohio: Key takeaways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:51:30 UTC
17:51:30 KST

Obama and Trump spar at rallies in Georgia and Ohio: Key takeaways
Obama and Trump traded barbs over the Iran war, tariffs and the White House ballroom ahead of the US midterm elections.
Former US President Barack Obama and President Donald Trump held rival campaign rallies in Georgia and Ohio on Wednesday, trading criticism over the war in Iran, tariffs and the economy just five days before midterm elections.
Here are some of the key takeaways from their rallies:
Obama said the Iran war has made Americans less safe
“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions, the most important of which was to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for and nobody voted for,” Obama said during a campaign rally in Atlanta, Georgia.
The United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, targeting Tehran as well as the country’s nuclear and military facilities, and killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several high-ranking officials. Tehran responded with attacks on US military assets across the region and closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies.
Although a ceasefire was reached in April – and a memorandum of understanding was signed in June – both fell apart, while efforts to secure lasting peace have stalled over Iran’s nuclear programme, US sanctions and the reopening of the strait.
The US media has also reported that the US is low on weapons – particularly its Patriot missile interceptors.
“We have run down our stock of missiles, making us more vulnerable. And Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz where much of the world’s oil goes through to get to consumers,” Obama told supporters.
“This is the reason why the price of oil is up. This is the reason why the price of diesel is up. The price of just about everything is up,” he added.
“Contrary to the promises and statements and declarations that were made seven months ago, this war is not over.”
Obama took aim at Trump’s tariffs
Obama again criticised Trump’s trade tariffs, which he launched against global trading partners shortly after taking office in early 2025. Obama argued these have increased the cost of goods for American consumers rather than delivering the economic benefits promised by the administration.
“Economists said when you impose tariffs, consumers pay the tab,” Obama said. “And that’s exactly what happened.”
“Rather than having the tariffs bring down deficits like he said he would, we’re now running a debt to the tune of $40 trillion.”
In particular, he singled out Trump’s ongoing dispute with Canada, one of the US’s largest trading partners.
The two countries have been locked in a trade war, with Trump announcing 50 percent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts from January 2027. Canada retaliated with its own matching tariffs as talks fell apart in August.
“And the big trade war he’s waging now is that well-known evil empire, that historical adversary of the United States, Canada,” Obama said.
He also criticised Trump’s approach to US allies and Russia.
“While we’re alienating key allies like Canada, the White House is bending the knee to Vladimir Putin of Russia and selling out Ukrainians who are fighting for their freedom and democracy.”
Obama revisited his Cheesecake Factory joke
Obama again made fun of Trump’s White House renovations, saying the president appeared more concerned about a joke he made over the weekend than rising prices.
At an earlier rally, Obama had criticised Trump’s plans for a new ballroom, changes to the Rose Garden and the addition of gold decorations.
“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama joked. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, just gold everywhere.”
In Georgia, Obama returned to the joke. “The president wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison. That part didn’t bother him,” Obama said.
“But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comments.”
Obama joked that the White House had gone to great lengths to respond. “They mobilised a whole-of-government response to that joke. Not to inflation, but to that joke.”
He also talked about his own fondness for the restaurant chain.
“I lived at Chuck-E-Cheese and California Pizza Kitchen and the Cheesecake Factory. That was my jam for about a decade.”
Returning to Trump’s renovations, Obama added: “He is literally doing arts and crafts while we are fighting a war and trying to deal with out-of-control prices.”
Obama invoked Martin Luther King Jr
Obama closed his speech reflecting on American political culture, saying the country’s problems go beyond inflation, economic inequality and government policy.
“It’s not just about economics. It’s not just about prices. It’s about values,” he said. “There is a moral component to the choices we face right now.”
Obama warned that dishonesty and intimidation were undermining public life.
“We are not going to fix the system that’s broken. We’re not going to unrig our economy so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes, where people in the highest offices of the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully.”
He referenced a 1954 sermon by civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, who called on Americans to rediscover values society had abandoned.
“If we are to go forward today, we’ve got to go back and rediscover some mighty precious values that we’ve left behind,” Obama quoted King as saying.
Trump attacked Obama’s Iran nuclear deal
Trump defended his military campaign against Iran and criticised the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran reached under Barack Obama.
The deal limited how much uranium Iran could enrich and stockpile, and allowed international inspectors to monitor its nuclear facilities. Trump pulled the US out in 2018, saying the deal did not go far enough and failed to address Iran’s missile programme and activities in the region.
“I terminated Barack Hussein Obama’s JCPOA or the Iran nuclear deal, which was a road to a nuclear weapon for Iran and one of the dumbest deals I’ve ever seen in my life,” Trump said.
Trump claimed US military operations had since destroyed Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity and much of its military, including 159 naval vessels.
“We obliterated Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury,” he said.
Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Trump claimed oil shipments had increased and suggested renaming the waterway after himself. “We’re going to call it the Trump Strait,” he said.
The strait, between Iran and Oman, connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. Before the war, about a fifth of the world’s oil consumption passed through it.
Trump made rare reference to Epstein
Early in his remarks in Chillicothe, Ohio, Trump was interrupted by a protester shouting about Jeffrey Epstein.
Trump rarely brings up Epstein, his former friend, but on Wednesday he repeated claims he made last year that he threw Epstein out of his Florida club about two decades ago.
“That was a great thing I did, I must tell you,” Trump said. He added: “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago.”
Trump then accused Democrats of having ties to Epstein and using the controversy against him. “He was a Democrat,” Trump said.
Trump also claimed the protesters were being paid to disrupt his rallies, without providing evidence.
“These guys are paid protesters. Think of a guy, that guy’s probably 45, 50 years old. They give him $250.”
After he was interrupted by two more protesters, Trump returned to his remarks.
Trump said Venezuela delivered one million barrels of oil
Trump said Venezuela had delivered one million barrels of oil to the US for free following the US military operation that removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from power.
“Venezuela, they don’t like talking about, we just got a million barrels of oil delivered to us free of charge,” Trump said during his rally in Ohio.
The shipment arrived in Corpus Christi, Texas, on Tuesday, nearly 10 months after US forces abducted Maduro during a military operation on January 3 and transferred him to New York to face drug trafficking charges.
Since Maduro’s removal, Washington has been working with Venezuela’s interim government, led by Delcy Rodriguez, to gain greater access to the country’s oil reserves.
Trump described the military operation as a victory and said Washington was now working with Venezuela to expand oil production. “We had a little war with Venezuela. We finished it in one day,” he said.
“And we’re now working with them to produce millions and millions of barrels of oil a week.”
Trump defended Ramaswamy ad
The president in his speech once again defended Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy for a campaign advertisement featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, which has drawn backlash because of the abuse Acton experienced as a child.
“Vivek was treated very unfairly,” Trump said during his Ohio rally. “He had the mother of his opponent say that her daughter was a liar.”
Trump accused the media of treating Ramaswamy differently because he is a Republican.
“The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar. That she’s no good. That she lied about the opponent. How the hell is that his problem?”
Trump defended his White House renovations
After Obama mocked his plans for the White House, Trump said: “President Obama, who doesn’t understand cleanliness. Who doesn’t understand broken cracked stone and sidewalk?”
He said the White House had been in poor condition and that he had personally paid for repairs. “I fixed it very inexpensively. I paid for it myself. I fixed it.”
Because the White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country. And we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years.”
“It’s never looked more beautiful,” he said.
He also mocked Obama’s record of campaigning for Democratic presidential candidates.
“He got involved with Hillary Clinton … and he lost. He then got involved with Kamala and he lost.”
“They said Obama’s coming. I said that’s good.”

Investing in conventional weapons better than developing nuclear program of one's own – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

Investing in conventional weapons better than developing nuclear program of one's own – expert
Jim Stokes, a GLOBSEC expert and former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy (2023-2025), expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Ukraine joining NATO. That is the most credible option. NATO's deterrence has worked for more than 77 years because no state has ever attacked the Alliance. I do not usually use the word 'guarantee,' but there are benefits to being covered by extended nuclear deterrence from the United States, the United Kingdom and France," the expert said.
At the same time, he cautioned against expecting a nuclear program of one's own to provide absolute protection. Stokes, who headed the Staff Group of NATO's Nuclear Planning Group, outlined his arguments.
According to him, the decision to develop an independent nuclear capability cannot be taken lightly, as no one wants further proliferation of nuclear weapons, which are currently possessed by only a limited number of states. Political commitments, financial costs, the technical expertise and technology required, and the time and money needed to produce a certain number of nuclear weapons must all be taken into account. In addition, a country would need delivery systems, a doctrine, command-and-control procedures, and many other supporting capabilities.
"All of this requires a great deal of effort. I say this as someone who worked for a long time on countering the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction," Stokes said.
He also cited North Korea as an example of a country that has become a nuclear power. However, the expert noted, North Korea is a pariah state. Ukraine, or any other country, therefore needs to consider whether it wants to become a pariah and potentially face sanctions by withdrawing from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. "Would that really provide the security they seek?" he said.
At the same time, Stokes acknowledged that he understood those who argue that, from a national security perspective, nuclear weapons offer the ultimate guarantee of national security and sovereignty.
The expert therefore believes it would be better to devote time, money and effort to conventional defense.
"Whether you can be part of a nuclear alliance and reinforce that arrangement, as in NATO or another alliance, or whether there are other ways to obtain some form of security guarantee. There seem to be better options that would be available rather than pursuing a national nuclear weapons program," Stokes concluded.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that in exchange for giving up its nuclear weapons, Ukraine should have received a "security umbrella." He described the guarantees the country received at the time as "an unfair game and a major mistake."

Introduced and moderated by Agne Babrauskaite of the Italian Embassy in Vilnius, the roundtable featured translator Rasa Kliostoraityte-di Pasquale, chef and entrepreneur Gian Luca Demarco, Kestutis Smilgevicius, Secretary General of the Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference; and Julija Reklaite, Director of the Lithuanian Institute of Culture and former cultural attaché at the Lithuanian Embassy in Rome.
                                    
In introducing the event, the Italian Ambassador to Vilnius, Emanuele de Maigret, emphasized the importance of the initiative in the context of growth diplomacy.
                                    
“To concretely develop this year’s chosen theme, in line with the reform of the Farnesina (the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs) championed by Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, we have devised an innovative format that connects young students of Italian with representatives from various professional fields, such as literature and translation, gastronomy and the restaurant industry, the religious sector, and the arts,” said de Maigret.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The National Institutes of Applied Research said Tuesday that it worked with Material Science Service Company to use a special coating to stabilize wafers for material analysis.
Shrinking semiconductor processes are prompting manufacturers to develop high-numerical-aperture extreme ultraviolet lithography. The process uses metal oxide photoresists to produce finer circuit patterns on chip wafers.
NIAR said in a press release that the process is still under development and has high structural requirements. Wafers also need to be dissected to check for possible post-processing defects.
NIAR also said that cutting a wafer open may ruin its nanostructure and material interfaces. The team applied a thin coating before cutting for structural stability.
NIAR President Tsai Hung-yin (蔡宏營) said etching is one thing, but quality checking is just as important. The institute noted that material analysis is crucial to ensuring the wafers meet standards.
The institution said the National Center for Instrumentation Research uses atomic layer deposition (ALD) to form the coating. MSS used the center’s custom-built ALD equipment to test different materials.
MSS also announced that it will partner with NIAR on production verification. MSS Chair Liu Chi-lun (柳紀綸) said he is optimistic, as the firm has received requests from the world’s leading semiconductor equipment makers.
