Türkiye is marking the 103rd anniversary of the founding of its Republic with ceremonies in the capital and festivities across the country.
Celebrations in Ankara were set to begin with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and senior state officials visiting Anitkabir, the mausoleum of founder Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. Erdogan will lay a wreath, observe a moment of silence and sign the memorial book, then receive congratulations at the Presidential Complex.
In a video message, Erdogan said Türkiye is stronger today than yesterday and will be more powerful, prestigious and effective in every field tomorrow. He pointed to progress over the past 24 years in defence, energy, transport and diplomacy.
The Republic was declared on October 29 1923, with all 158 lawmakers present in Parliament voting in favour. Ataturk was subsequently elected the country’s first president with all 158 votes.
On Thursday, Türkiye’s senior officials also marked the anniversary.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said the government is working towards the 2053 and 2071 visions under Erdogan’s leadership, aiming to carry its gains further, while Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahceli said his party was determined to carry the Republic’s legacy into the “Century of Türkiye”.
National Intelligence Organization (MIT) chief Ibrahim Kalin said the Republic embodied Türkiye’s independence, unity and shared future, adding that MIT would continue working to protect national security and sovereignty.
Turkic leaders in Ankara
This year’s anniversary coincides with the 13th Organization of Turkic States (OTS) summit, which brings the leaders of the five member states to Ankara on October 29-30.
Erdogan will open the Bestepe National Garden with an equestrian show, then host an official dinner for visiting leaders.
Guests will be welcomed by the Mehter band and by soldiers and flags representing 16 historic Turkic states. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov will receive a state medal, and the president will present this year’s Ali Sir Nevai International Award.
The programme will also feature a concert by Türkiye’s Presidential Symphony Orchestra, a traditional dance performance organised by TURKSOY, an international organisation promoting Turkic culture, and live music by Turkish singer Kirac and Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen.
Celebrations across the country
Republic Day events are taking place across Türkiye.
The “Türkiye Pedals” initiative will bring together cyclists across all 81 provinces from October 29 to November 1, ahead of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya on November 9-20. Open to licensed athletes, cycling clubs, students, families and cycling enthusiasts, the events aim to promote cycling as a sustainable transport option and raise public awareness of the climate change.
The historic Istiklal Road is being crossed on horseback to mark the Republic’s 103rd year. Organised for the third time by the Equestrian and Culture Association, the ride follows the 95-kilometre route along which weapons and ammunition arriving at Inebolu Port were sent on to Anatolia during the War of Independence. Forty-five riders from across Türkiye are taking part in the two-day journey.
The Osmangazi-Türkiye Century Run on the Osmangazi Bridge is expected to draw around 6,000 participants, with nearly 8,000 applications received and athletes from 19 countries signed up. The event, held for the first time on October 29, features a 10-kilometre race for elite runners and a 5-kilometre public run. Kocaeli Metropolitan Municipality Mayor Tahir Buyukakin said organisers aim to make it a traditional annual event, bringing together people of different generations to mark the Republic Day.
In Corum, residents marked the day with a march carrying a 103-metre Turkish flag.
In Diyarbakir, students unfurled a 54-square-metre Turkish flag at the historic Ickale in the Sur district, in the shadow of the city’s thousands-of-years-old walls and stone structures. The event was led by the provincial education directorate, and the choreography was filmed from the air by drone.

The investigation revealed that the suspect came to the enemy's attention after posting anti-Ukrainian comments in Telegram channels.
"Following his recruitment, he communicated with the FSB via a specially created chatbot that the Russian special service uses to gather intelligence," the Ukrainian special service specified.
In addition to correcting strikes against energy facilities, the agent tracked the deployment locations of Defense Forces repair bases.
During searches of the detainee, two mobile phones were seized, one of which he attempted to destroy to conceal evidence of his work for the occupiers.
Security Service investigators served him a notice of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
The perpetrator is currently in custody without the right to bail.
Comprehensive measures were carried out by officers of the Main Directorate of the SBU in Donetsk and Luhansk regions under the procedural guidance of the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office.

New apps challenge Tallinn's official public transport website
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:24:00 UTC
17:24:00 KST

New apps challenge Tallinn's official public transport website
Public transport apps enterprising developers have come up with are growing in popularity and offer an alternative to Tallinn's official public transport website.
Unlike many European capitals, Tallinn still has no official public transport mobile app, while critics say the official site at transport.tallinn.ee is getting outdated and is not very user-friendly.
"The people who should know how best to do these things haven't done anything. This is the kind of thing that was being done in 2010, and in 2026 we really shouldn't still be dealing with something like this," said Kaspar Sanglepp, creator of the Go Now app, one of the competing products.
"To quickly see bus times, you have to go to different websites and click through a lot of things. I wanted to be able to get that information with one click," Sanglepp said.
"The visual design is 10–15 or more years old. It takes so much time just to get to the route planner," said Sander Pukk, creator of another app, called Mis? Kuhu? ("What? Where to?").
All public transport vehicles in Tallinn and Tartu send their location to the system every 10 seconds. Using this publicly available data, developers have created three different free apps. Despite not being advertised, between them they have amassed over 2,000 daily users.
The newest app on the scene, Tallinn Live, garnered 4,000 views in four days.
"Tallinn Live project, it's very simple: you just are going to the app, you are just using it. That's why it's basic, and that's why people love it," Taha Yasin Erel, creator of Tallinn Live, told "Aktuaalne kaamera".
"I got lots of, hundreds of comments, hundreds of new ideas, and I started with these ideas, and people started to like it more," Erel went on.
Most public transport stops in Tallinn are still old school in that they lack display boards and have only printed timetables. At peak times and with all the ongoing roadworks in Tallinn, there is often a difference between when a bus, trolleybus or tram is scheduled and when it actually arrives, something which apps can help with.
"Real-time information has definitely been the main thing. Many stops still don't have those display boards, so being able to see whether a bus is running late or not has been the subject of the most positive feedback," Pukk went on.
According to Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse, however, surveys show that people are satisfied with Tallinn Transport's website. The city nevertheless plans to update it.
"The Transport Department (TLT) is currently carrying out the relevant analyses, and we certainly plan to update it in the coming years to make it more user-friendly, with an app or a mobile view," Jesse said.

‘I held this woman in my arms. She died’: Spain mourns train crash victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:20:34 UTC
17:20:34 KST

‘I held this woman in my arms. She died’: Spain mourns train crash victims
Second tragedy on line in nine months raises questions about the levels of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.
Madrid, Spain – Joaquim Torres, who was travelling on a train which crashed into another on Wednesday, rushed to help his fellow passengers who had been injured.
Fighting back tears, he told Al Jazeera: “I held this woman in my arms and tried to comfort her, but she stopped breathing. She died, she died.”
One of about 500 passengers caught in the deadly crash, Torres had been travelling on a high-speed train from the capital, Madrid, to Seville in the south of the country. All seemed normal, until the huge crash just before 9am.
At least 68 people were killed and 77 others were injured.
Spain’s national train operator Renfe has launched an investigation into the disaster, which happened in a rural area between Urda and Los Yebenes, two small towns south of Toledo in central Spain.
But the disaster has renewed a national debate over whether Spain’s high-speed train network is safe, nine months after another train crash on the same line in which 46 people died and scores were injured at Adamuz, near Cordoba in southern Spain.
‘Apocalyptic’
Sebastian Herrero, a 46-year-old doctor who was on the train, described the scene after Wednesday’s collision.
“There were three train carriages from which they kept pulling people out and covering them with sheets. Bodies. It’s apocalyptic. It’s hard to imagine that anyone could still be alive in those three carriages. It’s a twisted mass of metal. It’s as if a bomb had gone off,” he told Al Jazeera.
Rescuers searched for survivors through the mangled wreckage of three carriages at the front of the train, which had smashed into a stationary locomotive.
Desperate relatives were waiting at Seville train station holding pictures of loved ones who had failed to arrive in the southern city, as Spanish TV presenters, dressed in black, reported on the tragedy.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has declared three days of national mourning, said: “All of Spain is mourning,” before adding that it is “not acceptable for a country like Spain” to have two major train disasters in one year. A judicial investigation is expected to begin shortly.
Train followed ‘inexplicable’ order
Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the deadly crash happened after a Renfe train was authorised to continue on its journey – despite an active red signal because of a stationary train on the line ahead, operated by the Italian consortium Iryo.
Puente said the red signal had been issued due to a computer communications failure which automatically stopped traffic, and an “inexplicable” order from the central command centre was given for the Renfe train to move on. He said train engineers were not to blame.
The trade union Solidarity, which is linked to Spain’s far-right Vox party, held a demonstration in Madrid on Wednesday night to demand Puente’s resignation, and riot police were dispatched.
In the wake of the crash, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the opposition conservative People’s Party, which is favourite to win the upcoming general election, told reporters: “Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure, the condition of the tracks and safety systems, what warnings were received from Adamuz and measures were taken.
“The Spanish people have a right to a complete and independent review of the entire rail network.”
‘Seats were flying through the air’
Fernando Seco, another passenger in the Renfe train bound for Seville, said the train had just resumed its journey following a brief stop when it collided with the other train.
“We felt a brutal crash. People were thrown through the air, seats were flying through the air,” he told TVE state television.
After leaving the wrecked train, he said he saw a “carriage split in half, with dead people trapped inside”.
Once news of the crash got out, volunteers rushed to the scene to offer whatever help they could give.
Jose Maria Rabadan, a resident of Urda, the closest town, said he and other volunteers brought food, water and blankets and provided transport for those affected by the crash.
“Whatever they ask of us, we will bring,” he told Radio Castilla-La Mancha.
The rail accident is likely to come as a major blow to the ruling Socialist Party, just a month before the country goes to the polls in a general election on November 29.
The government’s management of the Adamuz rail crash in January was heavily criticised by opposition politicians and raised questions about the levels of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.
Rail unions had planned a strike for Thursday to protest about what they say is a poor safety record on the Spanish network.
The tragedy also comes amid a boom in the use of high-speed trains, which has not been accompanied by necessary investment in maintenance of the high-speed network, according to European Commission data.
The number of rail accidents, including collisions and derailments, rose from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024, and surged to 69 in 2025, according to the Spanish railway safety authority (AESF).
Some 40 million people used the high-speed rail trains in 2024, almost double the figure for 2019. However, in the first half of this year, about 25 million travelled on the high-speed network, a year-on-year fall of 14 percent.
With cheaper fares compared with many other developed countries, the high-speed rail network has been seen as an achievement for Spain in recent years, with its expertise exported to Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom.
Between 2018 and 2022, Spain spent an average of about $1.67bn each year on high-speed lines, more than other countries with similar networks. However, only 16 percent of that was spent on maintenance or repairs, with the rest going on infrastructure, according to EC figures.
A safety risk
By contrast, Italy, Germany and France spent on average between 33 and 39 percent of their budgets on maintenance, even though each country has much smaller networks than the 4,000km (2,485 miles) in Spain.
Experts say the success of the Spanish high-speed network is putting safety at risk.
“The problem is that the train network has become very popular as it is cheap and accessible but the authorities have not spent enough on its maintenance in recent years,” Salvador Garcia-Ayllon, a professor at the Universidad Politecnica in Cartagena, who specialises in civil engineering, told Al Jazeera.
Following the Adamuz disaster, a preliminary investigation found a rail fracture was the cause of the crash, but an ongoing investigation by police has not been concluded. A judicial investigation is now expected.

One in two Swiss don't save enough to cover prolonged income loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:20:32 UTC
17:20:32 KST

One in two Swiss don’t save enough to cover prolonged income loss
The Swiss save money, but for many, their financial reserves are not enough to cope with a prolonged loss of income. Almost one in two people would struggle to maintain their standard of living after just three months without an income.
This is the finding of a study by the Zurich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW).
According to the survey, 82% of respondents save at least occasionally. Despite this, 15% do not have sufficient liquid reserves to maintain their standard of living in the absence of income, and a further 30% could cover their expenses for a period of between one and three months.
Overall, almost 45% of those surveyed would therefore face financial difficulties after three months without an income. At the other end of the scale, 23% have sufficient liquid savings to maintain their standard of living for over a year.
+ Median annual salary in Switzerland rose to CHF87,000 in 2025
“Saving regularly does not necessarily mean that a household is sufficiently prepared for a loss of income: it is also crucial how much cash is already available and how long it would last in an emergency,” explains Selina Lehner, an expert at ZHAW, quoted in a press release.
The main source of financial concern is the rise in fixed costs, cited by 22% of respondents. This is followed by insufficient financial security in the run-up to retirement, highlighted by 12%, and the fear of being unable to fund future wishes and goals, cited by 11%.
The rise in recurring expenses is a particularly significant problem for households with limited savings: rent, health insurance premiums and other regular outgoings can gradually erode the financial buffer available to cope with unforeseen events.
“Rising fixed costs do not place a one-off burden on households, but month after month: when liquidity is limited, they reduce the financial buffer and make it harder to absorb unexpected expenses,” observes Holger Hohgardt, another specialist at ZHAW, who is also quoted.
Difficulties are also evident in managing day-to-day expenditure: over the last twelve months, almost one in four people – 24% of those surveyed – have had to borrow money. Taxes are another source of concern: 29% say they have had difficulty paying their tax bill on time in at least one of the last five years.
As regards financial goals, 29% of respondents consider maintaining their standard of living a priority. A further 24% aim above all to avoid financial worries in their daily lives. The study also highlights a significant difference between overall satisfaction and satisfaction with personal finances: on a scale of zero to ten, satisfaction with life averages 7.2 points (out of 10), while financial satisfaction stands at 5.6 points.
According to the ZHAW, the findings of the survey – which polled 963 people in June – suggest that the ability to save does not necessarily equate to solid financial security. The immediate availability of money, particularly in the event of job loss or other interruptions to income, remains a key factor in households’ financial stability, the researchers point out.

Spain’s high-speed rail network faces scrutiny after deadly collision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:20:12 UTC
17:20:12 KST

Aysu Bicer
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Spain’s high-speed rail network is under scrutiny following a deadly collision that killed at least 68 people and injured dozens Wednesday.
Leaked audio recordings obtained by broadcaster RTVE indicate that controllers at state rail manager Adif instructed the driver of the moving train to disconnect the malfunctioning LZB safety system and resume the journey at speeds of up to 200 km/h.
"Disconnect and reconnect the LZB and resume journey under the protection of the BSL at normal speed," controllers told the driver at 8.36 am local time.
Minutes later, the driver of the Iryo train reported being unable to proceed: "I've had a loss of transmission and I'm stopped at the Urda entrance signal."
While the government pointed to human error in allowing a train onto an occupied track, RTVE, citing sources, disputed the timeline, reporting that the Iryo train had not received clearance to move before the collision.
The collision between the moving train and the stationary train occurred in central Spain, around 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of Madrid, between Mora and Orgaz.
The train traveling from Madrid to Seville struck the stationary Iryo train, sending several carriages plunging down an embankment.
The Iryo train, carrying 147 passengers, had halted on the tracks due to a computer system failure.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente cited system failure and human error as possible factors in the crash.
Survivors reported harrowing scenes of being thrown through the air, trapped in wreckage and breaking windows to escape.
The tragedy highlights vulnerabilities on the 1992 Madrid-Seville route, which still relies on the older LZB system instead of modern European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) safety technology.
It is the second fatal crash on the line in nine months, following a January accident near Cordoba that killed 46 people.

Lithuanian Farmers and Greens tie budget support to family referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:16:00 UTC
17:16:00 KST

The Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union has warned that its support for next year’s government spending bill could be affected unless parliament takes up a stalled proposal for an advisory referendum on the constitutional definition of family before approving the budget.
Aurelijus Veryga, leader of the Farmers and Greens Union (LVŽS), said Wednesday that he had raised the issue during budget negotiations with coalition partners, demanding that the referendum proposal be put on the parliament’s agenda before the budget is adopted.
The initiative is an attempt to entrench a conservative definition of family and prevent same-sex couples from claiming equal treatment.
“One of the issues important to us is that, before the budget is adopted, the question of an advisory referendum on the family issue should be brought before parliament,” Veryga told reporters after a meeting of the coalition council.
“This is one of the key issues for us. It will also be a kind of signal about how we should act,” he added.
Veryga said the issue would show whether the Farmers and Greens were being treated as a genuine coalition partner.
“We are not asking our coalition partners to vote in favour of the referendum in any particular way. We know there are differences of opinion,” he said.
However, he argued that deliberately blocking the proposal amounted to a demonstration of political will. He called for an end to what he described as “artificial obstruction” by the parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs, saying coalition partners had promised to find a solution at their previous meeting.
Veryga warned that if the referendum proposal is not placed on the parliament’s agenda, it could have a significant impact on how his party’s lawmakers vote on the budget.
“I really cannot say how my colleagues will act then. Since this is a very important issue for us, it will be assessed in the broader context,” he said.
In late September, the parliament’s Committee on State Administration and Local Authorities backed holding an advisory referendum on the constitutional definition of family alongside next year’s municipal elections.
The draft resolution was approved at its initial presentation in parliament in early April.
Under the proposal, voters would be asked whether they support explicitly stating in the Constitution that legal family relationships arise only from the marriage of a man and a woman, motherhood and fatherhood. Voters would choose between “Yes” and “No”.
Article 38 of Lithuania’s Constitution currently states that family is the foundation of society and the state and that the state protects and cares for the family, motherhood, fatherhood and childhood. It also states that marriage is concluded by the free consent of a man and a woman.
In a ruling issued in 2011, Lithuania’s Constitutional Court states that non-married couples can also constitute a family.

UK social media ban likely to require photo ID checks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:14:53 UTC
17:14:53 KST

LONDON — Enforcement of the U.K.’s upcoming social media ban for under-16s will probably require older teens to show a form of photo ID, according to the U.K.’s online safety regulator Ofcom.
In a government-commissioned report, Ofcom said it had identified just four methods that are “highly effective” at determining whether a user is 16 or over — while noting that “the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated, and some children will succeed in bypassing age checks.”
The advice comes after the U.K. government vowed to take a tougher approach than Australia to enforcing its ban — due to come into force next year — by requiring platforms to use “highly effective age assurance” to identify underage users.
Advertisement
It will inform regulations to implement the ban which ministers have said they aim to introduce to parliament this year.
Three of the methods identified by Ofcom — photo ID matching, using a digital ID service, or banking-based checks — require a passport or driving license at some stage, while the fourth, facial age estimation, may in some cases need to be followed by a supplementary check using one of the other methods because of a high margin of error at younger ages.
“This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right,” Ofcom CEO Melanie Dawes said.
While the age checks would involve processing of personal data, “available methods can be delivered in a way that protects users’ privacy and complies with data protection law,” Ofcom said.
It also said social media platforms should take steps to mitigate circumvention, like enabling users to report suspected underage accounts, and using age inference technology to spot activity from users who may be underage.
The regulator said it will consult on further guidance for platforms once regulations to implement the social media ban are laid.

‘Economic incentives are limited’: What does Russia really offer Africa?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:14:34 UTC
17:14:34 KST

‘Economic incentives are limited’: What does Russia really offer Africa?
African nations weigh political incentives as Moscow offers limited economic benefits compared with China and the West.
In 2019, I travelled to Berengo Palace, outside Bangui, to interview Russian mercenaries.
Once the home of Jean-Bedel Bokassa, the Central African Republic’s self-crowned emperor, it was now occupied by fighters from the Wagner Group. One of the first things they told me was not about the country they had come to defend, but the country they had left.
A man named Vladimir shook my hand.
“Russia is back in Africa,” he said.
Seven years later, Wagner’s founder, Yevgeny Prigozhin, is dead.
In the Sahel, Wagner has given way to Africa Corps, controlled by Russia’s Ministry of Defence. Moscow is fighting a war in Ukraine, where Africans have been recruited, some under false pretences. An investigation by Journalists for Justice documented 502 African deaths by June 2026.
In Douala, Cameroon, I met Mama Regina, her eyes bloodshot as she held back tears. Her son Moses had gone to Russia to fight. His portrait hung on the wall.
“So handsome,” she whispered. Like so many families, she is waiting for his body. Once again, Africans are mourning men lost in someone else’s war on another continent far away from home.
In grief, some have turned to a small but growing Russian Orthodox church. Its Cameroonian pastor was trained in St Petersburg. He says he is here to preach the “good news”.
Russia-Africa Summit
African leaders are gathering in Moscow for the Russia-Africa Summit. In 2019, 43 African heads of state or government attended the first summit in Sochi.
In St Petersburg in 2023, after Russia invaded Ukraine, only 17 heads of state came. Putin offered free grain to six African countries, which Russia later delivered. This year, the Kremlin expects delegations from 48 countries, including 22 heads of state.
“The economic incentives to go for the Russia summit are much more limited,” says Beverly Ochieng, a Dakar-based analyst.
Compared with United States-Africa and China-Africa summits, she says, Moscow offers fewer large investment commitments.
“The political incentives for attending are the primary reasons why these countries are there.”
For the military governments of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, Russia offers something more immediate: Support to remain in power.
France was pushed out; Russia stepped in. Yet armed groups continue to attack, and Human Rights Watch has accused Africa Corps forces in Mali of killing civilians and torturing detainees.
The Soviet Union trained generations of African officers, politicians and students during decolonisation.
Ochieng learned Russian at the embassy in Kenya. Moscow, she says, can still play the card of “we didn’t colonise you.”
But Russia is facing Western sanctions and looking for economic opportunities in its relationship with African nations.
In Mali, construction has begun on a gold refinery backed by Russia’s Yadran Group; the Malian state holds a 62-percent stake. In Guinea, Russian aluminium giant Rusal operates bauxite mines and an alumina plant. In Niger, Rosatom subsidiaries are discussing uranium projects with the government, after the takeover of a mine formerly operated by France’s Orano. A separate attempt to sell existing uranium stockpiles remains in dispute.
Earlier this month, Putin said Russia’s aim was not to “steal something from Africa” but to “develop together”.
Russia’s trade with Africa was about $28bn in 2025, compared with China’s $348bn. The European Union exchanged nearly 355 billion euros ($395bn) in goods with Africa in 2024.
Sergey Eledinov, a former Russian officer and security analyst, sees a trap in Russia’s military bargain in Africa. By securing governments, Moscow may give them room to look elsewhere. “Survival doesn’t create loyalty,” he says. “It creates options.”
Ochieng also cautions against mistaking Russian flags at demonstrations for widespread support. They do not mean “all Africans are just sitting around being pro-Russia,” she said.
For Moscow, she says, the summit is a chance to demonstrate its continued “political relevance”, even if the West increasingly regards it as a pariah state.

Russian Doctors Report Widespread Healthcare Cuts as Patients Pay for Basic Supplies
Unknown

Russian Doctors Report Widespread Healthcare Cuts as Patients Pay for Basic Supplies
More than three-quarters of Russian doctors reported cuts to healthcare spending in their regions, with shortages affecting salaries, medicines, supplies, and hospital budgets across the country, The Moscow Times reported on October 28.
The findings were based on a survey by Medvestnik involving medical workers from 74 Russian cities. Among respondents, 75.6% reported declining healthcare spending in their region, while 67.4% stated that cuts were affecting virtually everything, including consumables, wages, and medicines.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Nearly half of respondents, 46%, reported that patients receiving treatment at their institutions had been forced to buy medicines, dressings, or other medical supplies themselves during 2026.
Some doctors noted that patients were formally prohibited from purchasing medicines independently, while state-funded departments still lacked enough money to cover basic needs, The Moscow Times wrote.
The cuts come as Russian regional governments struggle with budget deficits and spending linked to recruiting contract soldiers for the war against Ukraine.
According to Russia’s Accounts Chamber , regional governments allocated 5.8% less to healthcare in the first half of 2026 than during the same period a year earlier.
Healthcare spending was reduced in 42 Russian regions, with cuts exceeding 20% in 11 of them. The sharpest reductions were recorded in the Altai Republic, where spending fell 40.6%, and the Kirov region, where it declined 39%.
The Kemerovo region cut healthcare spending by 33.2%, followed by Orenburg at 32.1%, Tver at 29%, Moscow region at 28.5%, Vologda at 27.2%, and Novosibirsk at 23.4%, according to The Moscow Times.
One of the largest reductions affected Russia’s primary healthcare modernization program, which had been intended to repair aging clinics. Funding for the program fell to less than half of the previous year’s level, while actual spending during the first six months dropped more than fivefold year on year.
The Moscow Times reported that the pressure on regional budgets has already prompted calls for further hospital consolidation. On October 16, Anatoly Artamonov, chair of the Federation Council’s Budget and Financial Markets Committee, stated that regions should consider closing underused hospitals and redirecting patients to larger medical facilities.
“Budget funds are insufficient, and we need to treat these resources carefully,” Artamonov explained.
The pressure on Russia’s regional budgets is also spreading beyond healthcare. UNITED24 Media previously reported that a district in Russia’s Irkutsk region planned to cut 37% of its administrative staff by the end of 2026 as its budget gap widened, with school guards, kindergarten staff, and municipal workers among the positions affected.

Dries Van Noten, Versace and migrants in new exhibition at BRUSK in Bruges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:13:02 UTC
17:13:02 KST

A new exhibition opens at the BRUSK arts centre in Bruges on Friday. ‘Hoogtij’ (Figuratively heyday, literally high tide) is an exhibition exploring the impact of the sea and water on people, fashion and art. On display are swimwear by leading designers including Dries Van Noten and fashion houses including Versace and Chanel, as well as sculptures, video art and installations addressing social issues such as climate change and migration.
The sea gives and takes. It is with this idea in mind that the new exhibition ‘Hoogtij’ at the BRUSK art centre aims to challenge visitors. “Bruges’ location on the North Sea has had a major impact on the city’s history. It enabled the city to flourish. Seas and oceans have also had a significant influence on artists and fashion designers, right up to the present day,” explains guest curator Karen Van Godtsenhoven.
The exhibition brings together the work of fashion designers such as Dries Van Noten and contemporary artists such as Rinus Van de Velde. And it does so across a wide range of art forms: from video to photography, sculpture and installations.
On swimsuits...
The exhibition is divided into various themes inspired by the tides of the sea. “The first section, ‘Low Tide’, represents the joy and fertile power of water as the source of human life,” explains Van Godtsenhoven. Swimsuits by designers including Versace, Chanel and Dries Van Noten, alongside Martin Parr’s beach photography, take centre stage here.
To barbed wire
In the final section of the exhibition, ‘High Tide’, current issues such as climate change and migration are addressed. According to Van Godtsenhoven, this section aims to encourage visitors to reflect on, for example, the dual role of the beach. “For some, it is a place of leisure; for others, a place of crossing, offering hope for a different and better life,” says Van Godtsenhoven.
The Palestinian artist Abdul Rahman Katanani, for example, created a wave out of barbed wire, symbolising how he experiences the sea as a life-threatening border.

Albania adopts measures to impose fines up to €5,500 on people at protests that become violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:11:15 UTC
17:11:15 KST

The measures come into force immediately, but require parliamentary approval within 45 days to remain in effect.
Albania introduced heavy fines on Wednesday for people present at demonstrations that turn violent, as the government seeks to manage daily protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama in the capital Tirana.
The fines, which can go as high as 500,000 leks (€5,500), are not limited to people directly engaged in violence and will be imposed on "anyone who chooses to remain in a crowd" that is carrying out acts of violence or looting in a public space, or that is "concealing their identity".
The average monthly salary before tax in Albania stands at €930.
The new rules also allow police to temporarily restrict gatherings in certain areas, including near schools, healthcare facilities and government buildings, if they deem that there is a risk of violence.
They also introduce penalties for inciting violence online and provide compensation for small businesses damaged during protests.
Anti-government protests ongoing since May
Albania has seen months of anti-government protests, with demonstrations in recent days escalating into clashes between protesters and security forces on the streets of Tirana.
The leaderless movement began peacefully in May, with demonstrations against a luxury hotel project in a nature reserve linked to US President Donald Trump's family.
By mid-October, the protests had expanded to include concerns over alleged corruption, shortcomings in the healthcare system and limited opportunities for young people in the country of 2.3 million people.
According to official estimates, protests since mid-October have caused more than €2 million in damage.
More than 350 people have been injured in clashes between protesters and police, who used tear gas and water cannon to disperse crowds.
Protest restrictions across Europe
On Sunday, Rama said he had drawn inspiration from a French bill passed by the upper house of parliament on Wednesday, which would hold protesters financially responsible for damage caused during demonstrations.
In France, the proposed legislation would require protesters to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused during demonstrations.
Meanwhile, in Italy, a new security decree introduces tougher penalties for violent protests, including prison sentences of four to 12 years for organising groups involved in violent demonstrations.

Child care sector faces further changes after shocking abuse exposed by Four Corners
In short:
A meeting of education ministers on Monday will consider the creation of a national childcare commission to improve planning and oversight of the sector.
Ministers will also discuss CCTV in child care following a trial involving 300 centres.
Four Corners this week aired shocking CCTV footage of a childcare worker physically assaulting a baby boy at a centre in Far North Queensland.
A proposed national childcare commission will be discussed at a meeting of education ministers next week, as the government faces renewed calls for changes following a Four Corners investigation into Australia's child care system.
Early Childhood Education Minister Jess Walsh told Senate estimates the commission could provide greater national oversight and strategic planning for the $20 billion sector, amid an oversupply of centres in some areas and shortages in others.
"We think a commission could assist with better strategic planning," she said.
Senator Walsh was also grilled about gaps in supervision rules, including why workers who have not completed their qualifications could be left alone with babies.
The questions follow Four Corners exposing shocking CCTV footage of a 13-month-old boy being smothered, kicked, hit and shaken 55 times by a trainee childcare worker, Edwina Ling, inside a Far North Queensland centre.
"Can you explain how a worker studying towards a qualification can be left alone with babies?" Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May asked.
Senator Walsh said state ministers had ordered a review of how the "working towards" rules applied and in what circumstances. She said an update would be provided next week.
"We have asked for a review into how working towards qualifications applies and in the circumstances where it may apply. That review is underway. We will be updated on it at the next education ministers meeting, and it's an important part of the work," Senator Walsh said.
"That service [Injinoo] has responsibilities to ensure that child was adequately supervised and that child was clearly not adequately supervised."
Senator Walsh said there was also broader work underway on adequate supervision in early childhood services.
She told the committee CCTV would be discussed at next week's meeting of education ministers following a trial involving 300 services.
CCTV proved critical in the Injinoo case. Ling originally denied hurting the children and told parents it was another child responsible for the cuts and bruises, but when she was told the footage showed it was her, she pleaded guilty to 82 assaults.
Senator Hodgins-May pressed Senator Walsh on the government's new funding enforcement powers, asking why Little Zak's Academy and Only About Children remain absent from the Commonwealth's enforcement list despite significant compliance histories.
"What does a large provider actually have to do before the Commonwealth intervenes?" she said, pointing to 25 staff ratio breaches last year.
Analysis of the country's 26 largest long-daycare providers found that half of Little Zak's centres had enforcement action in the past two years, the highest proportion of the 26 largest providers analysed.
For Only About Children, another big for-profit provider, the figure was 27 per cent, or one in four.
Liberal senator and Shadow Childcare Minister Matt O'Sullivan said there had been a "massive distrust and breakdown" in confidence in the child care sector and governments needed to do everything possible to rebuild that trust.
Ling was jailed in June for four years with a one-year non-parole period.
Queensland District Court Judge Dean Morzone KC described her offending as "monstrous, cruel and sadistic" and "a gross breach of trust".
The Injinoo Child Care Centre was closed after losing funding.

128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:10:47 UTC
17:10:47 KST

128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- Ohio State University
- Summary:
- Ancient ice discovered high in Tibet may be more than 128,000 years old, preserving an extraordinary record of Earth's climate that scientists previously thought had been lost. The discovery reveals a rare glimpse into the last ice age and could reshape our understanding of how glaciers survive dramatic changes in global climate.
- Share:
Deep within an ice cap in northwestern Tibet, scientists have uncovered evidence of a remarkable frozen record that may stretch back more than 128,000 years. The discovery suggests that ice high in the mountains has survived since the last ice age and could provide an extraordinary window into Earth's ancient climate.
The findings extend the known glacial record from the region by more than 100,000 years, making these the oldest ice cores ever recovered from this part of Tibet. They also offer rare evidence of how mountain glaciers endured major changes in Earth's climate.
Researchers reached their conclusions by examining ice cores collected from the Guliya Plateau in 1992 and 2015. Despite being drilled 23 years apart, the samples revealed strikingly similar patterns of oxygen isotopes, which scientists use to reconstruct past environmental conditions. The close match indicates that the ice has preserved a reliable and reproducible record of climate history.
"Reproducibility of the records within a given ice cap is extremely important," said Lonnie Thompson, lead author of the study, professor of earth sciences and senior research scientist at the Byrd Polar Research Center at The Ohio State University. "If you get an identical record a quarter of a century later, it can tell you a lot about the behavior of the ice over time."
How Scientists Dated the Ancient Tibetan Ice
Determining the age of ice that has remained frozen for tens of thousands of years is no simple task. To establish a more accurate timeline, the international research team turned to advanced dating methods involving radioactive isotopes of beryllium and chlorine.
These naturally occurring radioactive forms of elements decay at predictable rates, making them valuable tools for identifying events deep in Earth's environmental history. In this case, researchers used them to detect evidence of the Leschamp Geomagnetic Excursion, a dramatic disturbance in Earth's magnetic field that occurred more than 41,000 years ago and left distinctive chemical signatures in the ice.
The team then compared its findings with oxygen isotope records preserved in nearby Tibetan cave deposits. Together, the evidence suggests that the Guliya ice record may extend well beyond 128,000 years into the past.
"It's a really critical finding, because outside of the polar regions, this is the only ice core we have from the mountaintops that go back that far," he said. "Records out of Huascarán only go back over 30,000 years, not over 100,000, so that makes Guliya a very unique record."
The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.
A Frozen Climate Record From the Last Ice Age
Ice cores are among scientists' most valuable sources of information about ancient climates. As snow accumulates and gradually becomes compressed into ice, it can preserve chemical clues about the atmosphere and environmental conditions at the time. By examining different layers, researchers can piece together how climate changed over thousands of years.
However, interpreting these records depends on knowing when each layer formed. Without a reliable timeline, even an exceptionally well-preserved ice core can be difficult to understand.
That uncertainty had complicated earlier interpretations of the Guliya ice cap. Previous research suggested that its record reached back only to the middle of the Holocene, the geological epoch that began nearly 12,000 years ago following the last ice age.
The new evidence establishes that at least some of the ice is considerably older than the Holocene. This also has important implications for understanding whether large ice masses in Tibet persisted as the planet emerged from the last glacial period.
"If we only had Holocene-era ice in Tibet, that would mean that the big ice sheets from the last ice age didn't persist through the early Holocene," said Thompson. "But evidence shows that it did."
What the Discovery Reveals About Earth's Glacial History
The Guliya ice cap's unusual geography may help explain why it has preserved such an exceptionally old climate record. Its high elevation and surrounding terrain likely contributed to conditions that allowed ancient ice to remain in place through major environmental changes.
Beyond establishing the ice's age, researchers hope that a more precise timeline will help answer fundamental questions about the history of Earth's glaciers. Knowing when major periods of glaciation began, how long they lasted, and when the ice retreated is essential for reconstructing the planet's natural climate cycles.
"When did ice start forming on the planet and what did those natural processes of loss look like?" said Thompson. "We need to know those things, and the only way you can really demonstrate it is with accurate time scales on these records."
The revised timeline also creates new opportunities to investigate the Guliya ice cores in greater detail. Researchers plan to study additional samples to determine how other indicators of past climate and environmental conditions fit into this much longer history.
Those future analyses could reveal information that was previously overlooked or interpreted differently because scientists did not fully understand the age of the ice.
For Thompson, one of the most encouraging aspects of the discovery is how consistently the different measurements support the same interpretation.
"The big picture is that our results tell a very consistent story," he said. "If you get the science right, it's consistent. It's our understanding of what it's trying to tell us that has to catch up."
The research received support from the U.S. National Science Foundation. Ohio State co-authors include Mary Davis and Ellen Mosley-Thompson. Other contributors were Juerg Beer of the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology; Christof Vockenhuber and Marcus Christl of ETH Zurich in Switzerland; Tandong Yao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences; and Ninglian Wang and Ling Fang of Northwest University in China.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ohio State University. Original written by Tatyana Woodall. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lonnie G. Thompson, Mary E. Davis, Ellen Mosley-Thompson, Juerg Beer, Tandong Yao, Christof Vockenhuber, Ninglian Wang, Ling Fang, Marcus Christl. Additional evidence supports a timescale exceeding 100,000 years for the Guliya ice cap, Tibetan Plateau. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (40) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh2912

Switzerland looking at Barak MX, SAMP/T NG for missile defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:07:37 UTC
17:07:37 KST

Switzerland has narrowed its choice of an additional long-range ground-based air defence system to Israel’s Barak MX or the SAMP/T NG, while continuing to procure the Patriot system in parallel.
The Swiss Federal Council announcement on Wednesday came after reviewing offers from four manufacturers in France, Israel and South Korea. The decision to continue with the Barak MX and the SAMP/T NG was based on technical, military, defense, and security policy aspects.
“The Federal Council recognizes that Switzerland must strengthen its air defenses due to the deteriorating geopolitical situation. This requires ground-based air defense systems with a longer range and sufficient ammunition. Combined with shorter- and medium-range systems and fighter jets, these systems can counter the threat of long-range attacks, including ballistic missiles,” read a statement released by the council.
The Barak MX by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) has a multi-layered and multi-mission design. Its net-centric configuration allows operators to select the most effective engagement method depending on operational needs, a feature IAI says reduces costs and optimizes battlefield efficiency.
The versatile system can fire three types of missiles from the same vertical launcher, including the Barak MRAD for short-to-medium range of up to 35 kilometers, the Barak LRAD of up to 70 km., and the Barak ER, which can reach targets up to 150 km.
The system has been procured by several countries worldwide, such as Morocco, Thailand, Azerbaijan, Slovenia, and Cyprus, along with Israel’s navy and India’s naval, air, and ground forces.
The SAMP/T NG was made by a joint venture between Italy, the French firm Thales, and the MBDA European arms consortium. It was engineered to neutralize high-altitude targets such as maneuvering tactical ballistic missiles as well as cruise missiles and emerging threats.
The mobile system has next-generation active electronically scanned array (AESA) radars, modernized C2 engagement modules, and the Aster 30 Block 1 NT (New Technology) interceptor. It can protect both fixed strategic assets and deployed forces.
Europe has increasingly turned to Israeli air defense technology over the past decade, especially after Russia invaded Ukraine and the growing demand for rapid, combat‑proven systems. Several Israeli systems, including the Arrow 3, Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and Spyder, have been selected by European governments.
Patriot still on the table
In addition to the Barak and the SAMP/T NG, Bern is also continuing to eye the American Patriot system.
Militarily neutral Switzerland ordered five Patriot ground-to-air missile systems in 2022 from Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, with an expected delivery in 2026-2028. Because of the war in Ukraine, the timeline has been pushed back by at least five to seven years, as Washington intends to supply Germany with Patriot systems that were originally planned for Switzerland.
Nevertheless, Bern said it cannot afford to halt the Patriot acquisition without a replacement ready.
According to the Federal Council statement, “Abandoning the Patriot procurement without an alternative system due to the security situation remains out of the question.”
“It is crucial that Switzerland can quickly procure an additional system alongside Patriot that meets the requirements, increases the area to be protected, and reduces dependence on a single supplier or supply chain,” the statement added.
The final decision on which system to procure will be made after Switzerland’s Parliament debates the proposal by the Federal Council on the military’s financing. The proposal would see the armed forces boosted by an additional 24 billion francs, including six billion francs for an additional long-range ground-based air defense system and a portion for the additional costs of the Patriot systems.

prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
AENARA UNVEILS 1:1 MARS HABITAT AT POWERHOUSE PARRAMATTA
Commissioned for Task Eternal at the newly opened Powerhouse Parramatta, Off-World Habitat Wall Section is a full-scale architectural installation designed by space architecture studio AENARA, founded by Melodie Yashar. Opening November 7th, 2026, the exhibition presents a physical cross-section of a conceptual Mars habitat envisioned for the year 2075. Developed from a year-long feasibility study conducted alongside NASA collaborators, university researchers, and industry partners, the installation exposes the structural strata, mechanical utilities, and autonomous manufacturing techniques required to sustain human life in extreme off-world environments.
in situ resource utilization on Mars | image ©AENARA
3D PRINTED SULFUR CONCRETE SHELLS INTEGRATE LIFE-SUPPORT SYSTEMS
Engineered by studio AENARA, the structural assembly demonstrates the coordination between protective outer envelopes and interior life-support infrastructure. The wall cutaway details an autonomous construction sequence utilizing in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), featuring robotic 3D printed outer shells formed from sulfur concrete and local regolith, backing an inflatable pressure membrane, radiation shielding, and high-performance thermal insulation. Integrated conduits route systems for water filtration, atmospheric recycling, data transfer, and power delivery. Balancing critical life-support engineering with crew psychology, the interior module incorporates daylighting strategies and expanded window viewports, translating extreme-environment aerospace research into scalable construction methodologies applicable to both off-world sites and terrestrial circular construction.

Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, the Journal reported, in a move that one of the newspaper's sources said was directed by President Donald Trump.

The Journal also reported Wednesday that Washington had told several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible "short, intense military campaign" against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.
But the newspaper, citing people briefed on the conversations, said Trump had not made a final decision.
Iran's military has meanwhile warned it would retaliate more widely against any new attack, with Rezaei saying it could strike US-related infrastructure including data centers and other artificial intelligence targets.

By Liz Lee
BEIJING, Oct 29 (Reuters) - In its pursuit of economic self-sufficiency, China must not create one-sided dependence in other markets, Germany’s President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged in an address at a top-tier university in Beijing on Thursday.
Steinmeier, who will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, was objecting to the trade imbalance between China and Europe, according to his speech text for delivery at the prestigious Peking University.
“It is understandable that China wants to protect its economy against external shocks and negative influences,” he said, but pressed that China’s greater independence must not lead to dependence and vulnerability of others on China.
The European Union has called its widening trade deficit with China unsustainable, and warned last month it will use every possible means to remedy it.
Germany, along with France, has also proposed that the EU enact a new rapid-action measure against countries that harm it, with China likely in focus.
European companies have found themselves with no or little access to the Chinese market, while European markets face large amounts of state-subsidised Chinese imports as well as Beijing’s controls and limits on its raw materials exports, Steinmeier said.
Steinmeier argued that Europe was determined to keep its industrial base, and that he was confident that Brussels and Beijing would be able to find solutions through dialogue.
“We do not want a new bloc confrontation. That would not only be dangerous for international security, but would also be an economic loss for everyone,” said the German president who is on a five-day visit until Saturday.

NEW DELHI: A vitamin that helps the body process proteins and regulate important chemical reactions may offer a new clue to why young adults suffer strokes. A study by researchers in Bengaluru has found significantly lower levels of vitamin B6 in young adults who had an ischaemic stroke than in healthy people of a similar age.Ahead of World Stroke Day on October 29, the findings draw attention to a possible factor associated with stroke in young adults. The study compared 171 young adults who had suffered an ischaemic stroke, caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain, with 249 healthy controls.Median vitamin B6 levels in stroke patients were 40.9 nmol/L, compared with 65.6 nmol/L in the control group. Vitamin B6 insufficiency, defined by the researchers as levels below 30 nmol/L, was found in 12.3% of stroke patients, compared with just 0.7% of healthy controls.Vitamin B6 is found in liver, fish such as tuna and salmon, chicken, chickpeas, sunflower seeds, pistachios, potatoes, bananas and spinach.Prof Manjari Tripathi, head of the department of neurology at AIIMS, said vitamin B6 is essential for homocysteine metabolism. “Low vitamin B6 levels can impair this process, allowing homocysteine to rise. Elevated homocysteine can damage blood vessels, promote inflammation and contribute to clot formation, increasing stroke risk.
Maintaining adequate vitamin B6 levels through a balanced diet is important,” she said.The Bengaluru study adds to evidence linking vitamin B6 levels with stroke risk, but whether improving these levels can prevent strokes remains unclear. Dr Pravin Gupta, chairman, Marengo Asia international institute of neuro and spine, said the study was significant because vitamin B6 levels can be measured through a blood test. “However, this study shows an association, not proof that vitamin B6 supplements can prevent stroke. Further research is needed,” he said.The researchers, led by scientists from the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru, found that lower vitamin B6 levels were independently associated with higher odds of ischaemic stroke even after accounting for other factors. Among stroke patients, vitamin B6 levels were strongly inversely correlated with homocysteine, an amino acid associated with blood vessel health.
Published in Clinica Chimica Acta in 2026, the case-control study adds to research into factors associated with stroke among younger adults. However, it cannot establish whether low vitamin B6 contributes to stroke, results from other health or dietary factors, or reflects an underlying process. Further studies are needed to validate the findings.The results do not establish that vitamin B6 supplements can prevent stroke or that routine testing for the vitamin should be recommended for young adults.

She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. China controls key materials for Dutch chips, defence and energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:00:24 UTC
17:00:24 KST

China controls key materials for Dutch chips, defence and energy
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands is heavily dependent on China for seven of the eight raw materials most critical to its economy, according to new research by national statistics office CBS.
The CBS ranked more than 30 materials on the EU’s official list of critical raw materials by three measures: their economic importance to the Netherlands, the risk of supply disruption and the expected growth in demand.
Gallium was top, followed by rare earth metals, germanium, graphite, lithium, cobalt, niobium and silicon metal.
All of those except niobium are mainly processed in China before they’re sent to the Netherlands, either as materials or part of finished products. China handles at least 74% of global processing for each of the seven. The figure is 99% for gallium, 94% for graphite and 84% for rare earths. For niobium, the Netherlands depends mainly on Brazil.
The materials are vital to the semiconductor industry, defence and the energy transition, the CBS said. Demand is growing because of AI, electric cars, faster networks and new defence systems.
Gallium ranks highest because China controls almost all of the world’s production and uses strict export restrictions as political leverage, the CBS said. The metal is also the basis for microchips and other high-tech products made by large companies.
In 2025, the Netherlands imported €17.2 billion worth of critical raw materials from outside the EU, plus €123.9 billion worth of products that contain them – almost a third of the value of all imports from outside the EU.

Beyond the unemployment rate: The reality of finding work in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Beyond the unemployment rate: The reality of finding work in Switzerland
Switzerland’s unemployment rate remains low. Yet that doesn’t mean finding work to fit your skills is easy.
“It is not me; it is the job market. I had to tell myself that not to go crazy,” says Marta* a 40-year-old media expert from Poland. She’s been living in Switzerland since 2025 and looking for work for more than a year. She has worked in seven different countries for national television channels and international organisations but says this is the first time she has faced such a wall.
Unemployment in Switzerland is low compared to its peers though it’s been rising since 2023. In the second quarter of the year the country had an official unemployment rate of 3% — Switzerland only tracks people who have signed up or are eligible unemployment benefits.
Taking into account the active population out of work, which aligns with international norms, that figure rises to 4.9%.
This compares with 8.2% in France, 5.6% in Italy and 5% in the United Kingdom.
Officially, unemployment in Switzerland reached 2% in 2023, its lowest level in two decades.
One reason unemployment in Switzerland is lower than in other European countries is because of its specific education system focused on vocational education and training after middle school; roughly two-thirds of school children choose this track. In the dual system, apprentices spend most of the week working in a company while also attending vocational school. This gives young people work experience, employer contacts and qualifications aligned with actual vacancies, helping to reduce the difficult school-to-work transition that contributes to youth unemployment elsewhere.
But that figure tells just part of the story. Swissinfo interviewed ten people for this story. Testimonies all coincide. Regardless of age, sector or nationality, finding a job – especially as a foreigner – in Switzerland is a long and tiresome process with sometimes unwritten rules to follow.
Maria*, 37, from Portugal, holds a PhD in biochemistry. “I have been looking for a job since May 2024, so for two years now. I have sent thousands of applications and had only four interviews,” she says. When she finally secured an interview with a large pharmaceutical company, she says it did not provide feedback on why she was rejected.
“Often, it is not the rejection itself that is hardest. It is going through multiple stages of interviews and still having no idea why you were not chosen,” says Emily Rappitt, a career and hiring expert based in Switzerland.
According to the latest official data published by Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) the average unemployment duration in Switzerland is seven months and rises slightly for executive and C-suite managers.
This compares with nine months for Germany and twenty in France. In Italy, almost half of unemployed people had been looking for work for at least one year. Numbers for the UK were not available.
However, those numbers do not reflect the reality and people that Swissinfo spoke to. Finding work depends on skills, location, residency permit, market needs and sector. Recent data compiled independently by Adecco, a human resources provider, and SECO show that shortages persist in certain industries such as healthcare, IT and engineering, meaning finding jobs in these sectors is easier to find than in more generalist fields such as business administration and office professions.
Some jobs such as those in HR public affairs will be tougher for non-Swiss citizens as they require specific knowledge and familiarity of Swiss law and Swiss political institutions and stakeholders. In 2025, unemployment for foreign nationals reached 8.3% against 3.4% for Swiss nationals.
Furthermore, gender can play a role in finding a job. Data shows that motherhood is associated with lower earnings and slower career progression. Researchers describe this as a “motherhood penalty”, which remains a significant feature of the Swiss labour market. The main reason is that women in Switzerland often significantly reduce their working hours or even interrupt their careers after giving birth, while the vast majority of fathers — around 85% — work full-time.
Amina*, a Swiss citizen of Egyptian origin and has lived in Switzerland for 15 years. She is a mother of three and says motherhood and her flexibility came up in an interview. She was denied the job after a question specifically on that issue. She says she has sent hundreds of applications and received only one interview. “I feel like I am being discriminated against because of where I am from, my last name and the fact that I have children,” she says.
Amina is worried about the future. With one income, three children and no family in Switzerland to help, she says it is difficult to make ends meet. “What if my husband loses his job? I do not know what we will do then,” she says.
Vitamin B
Maxime*, 49, a French citizen who has lived in Lausanne for seven years, worked for Philip Morris in human resources and employee engagement before losing his job in April 2025. “I am applying through traditional channels, applying online, sending resumes, but I am also using the contacts I have. I try to stay up to date with courses I might need for future work. Networking plays a big part in the Swiss market,” he adds.
Networking is particularly important in Switzerland. It is commonly referred to as “Vitamin B”, with the B standing for Beziehungen, the German word for relationships. This means attending events in your sector and connecting with people who may be able to refer you for a job. Switzerland offers many events for both international and German-speaking professionals.
“Find advocates in your market: people who know your work, can spot opportunities, make introductions and talk about your value when you are not in the room. Know your own value. Not just your job title, years of experience or the companies you have worked for, but what you personally bring, what you are good at, what you have changed, solved, built or improved,” advices Emily Rappitt a career and hiring expert.
“I wish I had known this when I first arrived in Switzerland,” says Joanna Czarnecka-Herok, 37, from Poland, who moved to Zurich with her husband and is looking for a job in life sciences. “Applying without contacts does not bring much. I have applied for 200 jobs in a year and landed perhaps ten interviews, but without success.”
She has a PhD in molecular biology and says she was eventually offered a voluntary position (even though she thought it was a job interview for a paid position) despite her university degree. Her future employer argued that with a residency permit, she must be financially supported by her husband and should therefore accept the free work. Instead of looking for a job, she now offers her services as a consultant in longevity and science. “This was good for my mental health, as I stopped chasing one single job. It is still not enough to sustain myself in this country, but it is a step forward,” she says.
The difficulties that come with AI
The rise of artificial intelligence has also changed the application process. It is now possible to draft a CV and cover letter in minutes, yet the search for work can feel more challenging than it did only five years ago. “Applicant tracking systems and online recruitment already existed five years ago, but what is new is the scale of AI’s impact on applications and on how companies assess candidate fit. It is much easier for candidates today to tailor the language of an application to a job advert using AI. For HR, the challenge is therefore not only processing a higher number of applications but assessing the relevance of the match to the role,” says Katarzyna Czajka, a Senior HR Leader, who works as consultant.
Asked whether she would consider returning to Poland where the unemployment rate is also low at 3.4%, Joanna says: “I want to stay with my husband, and I have invested too much time in looking for a job and networking to give up now.”
However, some interviewees Swissinfo reached out to landed a job within six months. Sara*, 33, was born in Lebanon and grew up in Switzerland. After losing her previous role, she secured a job in media and communications at a major professional-services firm within six months, without relying on personal contacts. “I got very lucky. I know lots of people who have been looking for over a year. The reality is that it is an employers’ market right now, and there are hundreds, if not thousands, of highly qualified people looking for work. Between hiring freezes due to budget cuts and AI advances, it is rough right now,” she says.
*The people interviewed in this story spoke on conditions of anonymity.

Thawing permafrost threatens half of Swiss mountain huts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:57:26 UTC
16:57:26 KST

Thawing permafrost threatens half of Swiss mountain huts
Global warming is wreaking havoc in the Swiss Alps. Permafrost is thawing, glaciers are retreating and mountain footpaths are becoming increasingly unstable. The Swiss Alpine Club (SAC) is being forced to relocate certain huts and spend millions of francs on new facilities and protection efforts. Nearly half of its 152 mountain huts are affected.
Cracks had been steadily spreading and widening in the Mutthorn mountain hut in the Bernese Oberland. Closed since 2021, the building was in danger of collapsing due to thawing permafrost.
“We knew this hut probably wouldn’t last another hundred years. But the fact that it collapsed so quickly really scared us,” Fabienne Notter, president of the Weissenstein section of the Swiss Alpine Club (SAC), told the Swiss public broadcaster RTS.
A mountain falling apart
Permafrost acts as a natural glue, holding rock together. When it thaws, water penetrates the cracks, weakening the rock. Above the Mutthorn hut, a fissure that measured just 70 centimetres across in 2007 had widened to nearly 1.5 metres.
“We cannot predict what will fall or when. But one thing is certain it will collapse,” says Nils Hählen, head of natural hazards for canton Bern.
Of the 152 SAC huts dotted across the Swiss Alps, 65 are in areas potentially threatened by permafrost thawing. Access routes are also becoming more hazardous due to rockfalls, mudslides and ground movement.
>>Find out out more about this issue in the Temps Présent documentary “Là-haut sur la montagne, nos cabanes disparaissent” [“Up in the mountains our huts are disappearing”] (46min) broadcast by RTS on October 22, 2026.
Rebuilding at a price
A replacement Mutthorn hut has been built less than a kilometre from the original site, on more stable ground and in a location less exposed to avalanches. The old hut was completely dismantled in summer 2025 at a cost of CHF400,000 ($484,400).
The project required almost 700 helicopter flights. The new hut, inaugurated in June 2026 at a cost of CHF4 million, has drawn criticism within the SAC. But the project was approved by two-thirds of the members of the local section.
Disappearing glaciers
Visitors to the Konkordia hut in the Aletsch region of canton Valais must now climb more than 500 steps to reach it. The hut used to stand 50 metres above the glacier. Today, it rises roughly 300 metres above the ice.
The Aletsch Glacier is losing between four and six metres in thickness each year, forcing the staircase to be extended every two or three years. The latest renovation work cost around CHF50,000.
Water supplies are also becoming a scarce resource in mountain huts. The Konkordia hut collects meltwater in a 70,000-litre reservoir, enough for almost 6,000 overnight stays.
“When there is no more meltwater left, the available water has to last until the following May,” explains Christoph Sager, the hut manager.
More
A fifth of Swiss Alpine ice has vanished in five years
A financial challenge
The Trift hut was destroyed by an avalanche in 2021. The melting of the nearby glacier had altered the surrounding terrain and expanded potential avalanche release zones. The new building, which has been moved one kilometre away, cost CHF5 million.
According to the SAC, adapting its network of huts to a rapidly changing mountain environment will require CHF6-7 million annually. The organisation is looking for new sources of funding.
In the years ahead, some huts may have to be relocated, simplified, or even made mobile.
“The speed of the changes is taking us by surprise and catching up with us,” says Hanspeter Bürgi, chair of the SAC’s Hut Commission.
The SAC operates 152 huts but, as global warming transforms the Alps, that number may not remain unchanged for long.

Failed i-Police project cost the taxpayer over 139 million euros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:56:29 UTC
16:56:29 KST

I-Police, the police force’s failed digitalisation project, cost 139.4 million euros of taxpayers’ money. That is almost double the 76 million euros previously reported, according to a report by the Court of Auditors. The report states that millions have been spent on unusable software licences and that the government is structurally dependent on external consultants.
Failed i-Police project cost the taxpayer over 139 million euros
I-Police was launched at the end of 2021 to digitise police operations. As there were still no ‘tangible’ results by 2025, Interior Minister Bernard Quintin (Francophone liberal MR) pulled the plug on the project.
In the Chamber Home Affairs Committee earlier this year, Quintin had to admit that 75.8 million euros of taxpayers’ money had by then been spent on the failed project. At the time the MPs who fired off questions already suspected that the actual figure would be considerably higher.
At Parliament’s request, the Court of Auditors conducted a thorough review of the entire i-Police project. That report, published Wednesday morning, reveals that 139.4 million euros was spent on i-Police. That is almost double the amount initially reported.
Millions spent on unusable licences
The Court of Auditors, which audits the government’s finances, highlights, amongst other things, the purchase of 30 million euros worth of software licences, the vast majority of which are now unusable.
“Licences worth 21.6 million euros (70 per cent) are now of no use whatsoever to the police: licences worth 7.3 million euros were never used. Licences worth 14.2 million euros were used during the development phase, but the licences have become unusable due to the project being scrapped,” the report states.
“The analyses carried out by the police in 2024 and 2025 highlighted a significant financial risk regarding the licences,” the report continues. “After all, the costs are not limited to the initial purchase, as the costs for maintenance, support and renewal span several years.”
“These costs can become problematic if the solutions in question are not rolled out, are only partially utilised, or if the future of the project to which they belong is uncertain.”
'Quick wins'
The report also highlights the existence of two so-called ‘quick wins’ – milestones that were to be completed as pilot projects within 12 to 18 months of the project’s start. If these ‘quick wins’ were not achieved, the police could have halted the programme.
The Court of Auditors points out that no clear milestones were defined and that the police had already commissioned follow-up projects worth tens of millions of euros, even before the pilot projects had been completed and evaluated.
Structurally dependent on consultants
A third major issue concerns the use of consultants. According to the Court of Auditors, the police – and therefore the government – are structurally dependent on external consultants for critical IT functions.
The report states that “the police’s recruitment conditions were not suitable for recruiting specialised and highly qualified candidates”. “Recruitment was made even more difficult by the shortage of IT professionals in the labour market and their high-salary expectations.”
Judicial investigation
The Court of Auditors emphasises that it has merely scrutinised the case file, without making any judgements as to who is responsible for the debacle.
A judicial investigation is currently underway into the possible misappropriation of public funds and conflicts of interest in the case.
In connection with that investigation, it emerged earlier this week that the spokesperson for Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden (Flemish Christian democrat CD&V) and a spokesperson for the Brussels Public Prosecutor’s Office had been identified as suspects and are being investigated for possibly breaching professional confidentiality.
What is i-Police?
Digitising police processes, bringing together various data systems into a single information platform and thereby enabling the faster detection of risks and criminal networks: these were the ambitious objectives of the i-Police project, which was launched at the end of 2021.
The then Interior Minister, Annelies Verlinden (CD&V), signed a contract worth 299 million euros with the French IT consultancy firm Sopra Steria for this purpose. In December 2025, her successor, Quintin (MR), scrapped that colossal contract because, after years of invoicing totalling nearly 76 million euros, there had been “not a single tangible result”.
Shortly afterwards, the Brussels Public Prosecutor’s Office launched an investigation into the possible misappropriation of public funds and a conflict of interest in the case. Verlinden subsequently came under fire when it emerged that she had acted as a lawyer for Sopra Steria shortly before becoming Minister for the Interior in 2020.
