Presidential adviser: Lack of common EU position on Russia 'regrettable'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:12:00 UTC
16:12:00 KST

Presidential adviser: Lack of common EU position on Russia 'regrettable'
Europe lacks a shared plan for engaging Russia, which makes ending the war in Ukraine difficult, security adviser to the president Rainer Saks said.
Speaking to "Esimene stuudio" following Tuesday's phone call between Finland's President Alexander Stubb, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Saks said what matters most is that Ukraine is satisfied.
"I would say that if this phone call is followed by something that brings the peace process closer in a direction amenable to Ukraine, then it can be considered to have been entirely positive. If Ukraine is satisfied that the call went ahead, then this is also entirely positive. We can't say that if Ukraine next asks Romania or Turkey to do something, then everyone else will start waving their arms in offense — that really doesn't work. But the fact that there is no common position on how to engage with Russia is somewhat regrettable," Saks said.
Europe as a whole is not yet mature enough to talk to Putin, since there are no shared discussions and no clear action plan is being drawn up, Saks added.
Saks noted Stubb and Estonia's president at the time, Alar Karis, said in spring talks with Russia at some point were inevitable, but that there was no readiness then as Europe had no common understanding of how the process should work.
Saks said President Ülle Madise, who entered office last month, had no prior warning the call was going ahead; diplomats informed Kadriorg afterwards.
"My advice to the president is that we support these steps if they bring us closer to peace, and we simply need to communicate with each other more. Within Estonia, the first thing is of course for the government to ensure people are on the same wavelength in terms of both information and position," Saks said.
He disagreed with the claim that there is no point in engaging Putin whatsoever. "The question is not whether there is a point in communicating or not, but how you communicate and what it is you want to achieve. [But] there is no point in simply talking for the sake of talking — I agree with that part," he said.
Saks stressed that the concept of Europe being part of the process should not be interpreted as the EU as a whole being part of it, given the multiplicity of institutions and high-ranking figures that would entail. He said a coalition of the willing on support for Ukraine would have the initial moral obligation and right to put something common together. "Until that is done, these potential problems will keep recurring," he said.
Saks said the Finnish and Norwegian foreign ministries briefed diplomats from Estonia and other key partners, but that briefing was of limited value as the content of the meeting had already been splashed across the media in some detail.
As to the claim that Putin delivered a 70-minute monologue, Saks said the Russian president gives such monologues at all meetings, and that the time should be discounted somewhat for translation. "But it also shows that the Russian president took the time, considered it important, and delivered his monologue," he said.
When asked about Russian media attempts to present the call to in a light which gives the Kremlin the advantage, Saks said Moscow is trying to establish two things: first that Europe must eventually join talks, and second that the U.S. alone cannot pressure Ukraine. "That is of course a mistake we all make: we think Ukraine is fighting only because we support them. No — they are fighting because they want to survive, and in the end they decide most of all how long they can hold out, how motivated they are and so on," Saks concluded.
Finland and Norway initiated the 90-minute call from Helsinki in their capacity as states which border Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe. The call was prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the U.S. following last week's Oslo meeting.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) was briefed on Tuesday's call.

Mistral releases latest AI model for download, giving companies more control over their cybersecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:45:06 UTC
23:45:06 KST

The French AI company says its Large 4 model offers advanced coding and cyber-defence capabilities and can be run on an organisation’s own computers and servers.
Mistral has released the weights for its latest large flagship AI model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), nicknamed “Le Chonk”, claiming improvements in coding and cyber defence as Europe seeks to build alternatives to US and Chinese technology.
The French firm claims the model is “the best open agentic coding model in the world”, offering enterprises and governments “frontier AI cyber defence capabilities they can fully own and control” including the ability to “detect, analyse and respond to cyberthreats across code and IT infrastructure".
The release follows a preview of ML4 on 6 October. Since then, Mistral has spent the last three weeks reinforcing the model's learning, testing it with customers and partners under real-world conditions.
“ML4 OSS showcases our science team's ability to innovate at speed. Building on the ML4 Preview, the open weight version continues reinforcement learning training and delivers substantial gains with no signs of saturation," said Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral.
"In under three weeks within the same reinforcement learning run, we integrated customer feedback by introducing two additional reasoning modes, while making ML4 more efficient and customisable,” he added.
Mistral says the latest release of ML4 rivals other leading open models for coding while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average than Chinese model GLM-5.3. Its score on Terminal-Bench 4.0, which tests AI agents’ ability to perform coding tasks in a terminal, also rose from 28% to 41% following further training.
The release also comes as Europe faces growing cybersecurity threats, such as the recent PHP programming security flaw, discovered using AI, as well as the recent cyber-attacks on the Belgian and Norwegian governments.
More control over AI
Making the model’s weights available allows organisations to download and run it on their own infrastructure, rather than relying exclusively on an external provider’s hosted service.
This could be particularly useful for companies handling sensitive information, such as proprietary software code, that they do not want to share with an external AI service.
Organisations would have greater control over where the model runs and how it is integrated into their systems, although they would still need suitable hardware and expertise to operate it securely.
Mistral says organisations running ML4 on their own infrastructure would also not face the risk of a third-party provider restricting access to or disabling the model.
The move comes amid concerns about European dependence on US AI providers. In June, the Trump administration ordered Anthropic to suspend access to its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models for foreign nationals.
The restrictions were subsequently lifted for Fable 5, while access to Mythos 5 remained limited to selected organisations. The episode highlighted how decisions made outside Europe can affect access to advanced AI services.
Europe’s AI ambitions
Europe continues to lag behind the US and China in the development of large AI models and the resources needed to build them.
Mistral is one of Europe’s leading AI developers, but its reported valuation of around $24 billion (€20.9 billion) is far below those of US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic. [Insert verified, dated valuations and source.]
Mistral argues that despite the disparity in resources, “ML4 is now the best open model built in the West”.
The model was trained on 3,800 of US company Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell GPUs at Mistral’s European data centres. The company says ML4 achieves “state-of-the-art performance” while mobilising “a fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs” such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
The model’s European infrastructure could give customers greater operational control, but its reliance on Nvidia chips illustrates Europe’s continued dependence on foreign suppliers for key parts of the AI supply chain.
"Open source is essential to ensure state-of-the-art AI does not end up concentrated in the hands of a few actors," said Arthur Mensch, CEO and co-founder of Mistral.
"Other labs have raised hundreds of billions to develop equivalent capabilities; in three years, Mistral raised roughly $6 billion."
"We have taken the lead globally in compute efficiency and have widened the gap between Mistral and other labs in that area. Our approach is to deliver quality science and put the results in everyone's hands," he added.
A state-of-the-art model
ML4 has 1.05 trillion parameters in total, but activates around 52 billion, according to Mistral. This means it does not use all its parameters for every task, helping it process requests more efficiently.
The model also offers three reasoning modes — low, medium and high — allowing users to adjust the depth of reasoning to suit the task, from everyday requests to more complex problems.
Mistral says ML4 can turn 2D blueprints into usable 3D models using computer-aided design (CAD) software, analyse large volumes of data to support financial decision-making and use satellite and aerial imagery to detect wildfires, track crop health and monitor risks to power lines.
The French firm says the release of ML4 is part of a new generation of models spanning all modalities and that they plan to release more models from this generation in the coming months.
The model is now available through Mistral’s API, while its weights can be downloaded from Hugging Face.

Türkiye’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) is reworking proposals to set alimony durations using five criteria after President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan requested broader consultations, with the changes potentially missing the 13th Judicial Package.
AKP Group Chairman Abdullah Güler presented alternative proposals on alimony and divorce proceedings at a Central Executive Board meeting chaired by Erdoğan, explaining the Constitutional Court’s annulment of the indefinite alimony provision and its reasoning.
Erdoğan told officials to broaden consultations, consider the views of the parties involved and not settle for the proposals presented. “These are not technical proposals; they have many stakeholders, so work thoroughly on them,” he said. He said proposals might appear to meet expectations but could be perceived differently by the public.
The party plans talks with the Family Ministry directorate, partner institutions, academics and judicial officials, including family court judges. Revised alternatives will then be presented to Erdoğan. Party sources said the changes might not be ready for inclusion in the judicial package.
Five factors under discussion are a marriage lasting three to five years, the recipient’s social circumstances, prospects of remarriage, employment status and whether they have children. Judges would use these to determine payment periods but could still award indefinite support depending on the circumstances.
The court annulled the phrase “for an indefinite period” in Civil Code Article 175 on June 4, 2026. Published in the Official Gazette on Sept. 30, the ruling takes effect nine months later, allowing time for new legislation.
The existing provision allows a spouse facing poverty after divorce to seek support according to the other spouse’s means, provided the claimant is not more at fault. The ruling concerns payment duration, rather than abolishing alimony itself.

U.S. Navy awards $43.7M for F-35 mission data lab upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:11:04 UTC
16:11:04 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Lockheed Martin a $43.7 million modification to upgrade operating systems at F-35 reprogramming laboratory facilities through April 2030.
- F-35 cooperative program partners fund $29.7 million, with the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy each contributing about $7 million.
Lockheed Martin will upgrade the operating systems running the F-35 Lightning II reprogramming laboratories, which build the threat data the fighter needs for combat missions, under a $43.7 million contract modification the U.S. Navy announced on Oct. 28. Eighty percent of the work will take place in Eglin, Florida, and the remaining 20% in Fort Worth, Texas, with completion expected in April 2030.
F-35 cooperative program partners are paying $29,696,266 of the $43,673,774 total, or about 68%, while the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy each contribute $6,988,754 in fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds, all of it obligated at award. The Navy aircraft procurement account also funds U.S. Marine Corps aviation, and the announcement lists the U.S. Marine Corps among the services the labs support.
Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, issued the cost-plus-fixed-fee modification, designated P00025, without competition, adding new contract line items to contract N00019-22-C-0046. The announcement does not name the operating systems being replaced, the laboratories or hardware affected, or how the partner share is divided among countries.
The labs produce mission data files, the libraries of radars, missiles and aircraft that an F-35’s radar, electronic warfare suite and other sensors use to recognize and classify what they detect in a given region. The files are loaded onto each jet before flight from a portable drive.
At Eglin, U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps personnel of the 513th Electronic Warfare Squadron, part of the 350th Spectrum Warfare Wing, run the United States Reprogramming Laboratory, which produces mission data for U.S. jets and tests it on a hardware-in-the-loop line against simulated threat signals before release to the fleet. The squadron was activated at Eglin on April 23, 2010, to operate the lab, then valued at $300 million.
A 2017 U.S. Air Force account of the squadron’s work said mission data does not carry over automatically, so the squadron had to rebuild and repackage the files for each new version of the aircraft’s operating system. That refers to the software on the jet rather than the lab computers covered by the new award, but it explains why lab infrastructure gets steady funding as the F-35 moves through successive software releases.
Federal spending records show N00019-22-C-0046 began on April 29, 2022, as a base year plus five years of sustainment support for the Australia, Canada and United Kingdom Reprogramming Laboratory and surrogate encryption work for the Norway Italy Reprogramming Laboratory, all for non-U.S. participants. The public announcements do not explain what the surrogate encryption support involves. In April 2025, a $22,126,598 modification (P00014) added maintenance and sustainment of the U.S. Reprogramming Laboratory and the partner support complex for the U.S. military, non-DOD partners and Foreign Military Sales customers. A further $23,312,570 modification (P00022) in April 2026 continued that work.
Lockheed Martin first set up the Australia, Canada and United Kingdom Reprogramming Laboratory, known as ACURL, at its Fort Worth plant and moved it to Eglin under a $7.5 million modification awarded in 2018. British and Australian officials opened the lab there in February 2020, when it reached initial operating capability, and kept Canada’s name on the facility even though Ottawa had stepped back from the F-35 at the time. British and Australian staff now run the center as the reactivated 80 Squadron, which develops, verifies and validates mission data files for the three allies.
The Norway Italy Reprogramming Laboratory opened nearby on June 27, 2019, and was formally accepted on Sept. 22, 2021. Israel’s F-35 software work runs under a separate arrangement, and the U.S. Navy added $11.4 million in April for three additional software builds for Israel’s fleet.
Since N00019-22-C-0046 now sustains both the U.S. lab and the partner labs, the operating system work could cover either, and the Oct. 28 announcement describes it only as covering laboratory facilities and systems sustained for the U.S. services and the cooperative partners.
A separate $111.1 million modification to another Lockheed contract, N00019-20-C-0026, funded a minimum viable product of a Common Reprogramming Tool meant to replace the legacy programming tools used across the reprogramming labs. Lot 18 orders also bought multi-ship infrared search and track and Band 5 radar warning receiver hardware for development work at the U.S., ACURL and Norway-Italy labs. Each new sensor on the aircraft needs matching hardware and data in the labs, as will the 432 electronic warfare modification kits the U.S. Navy ordered for $991 million in May.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign said Thursday that cyberattacks using overseas IP addresses had breached a campaign server and flooded a platform with more than 70,000 fake sign-ups.
CNA reported that Shen’s campaign office said hackers targeted several campaign websites starting last Friday. The attackers exploited a security flaw to gain control of a server, created fake administrator accounts, and installed software to access the system remotely.

The campaign said it quickly required users to log in before signing up. The change blocked the automated submissions and allowed the platform to resume normal operations.
Shen said cybersecurity had always been a priority for his campaign. His office said all affected websites were operating normally and that it would continue to guard against further attacks.

Former Taiwan digital minister says AI can help bridge divides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:09:41 UTC
16:09:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Digital Affairs Minister Audrey Tang (唐鳳) said AI can help people bridge political divides and have a greater say in government decisions, the Financial Times reported Wednesday.
Speaking with Financial Times Innovation Editor John Thornhill, Tang explained how Taiwan uses technology to bring people with opposing views together. Digital platforms, she said, help officials find ideas with broad public support and turn them into policy.
Tang pointed to the country’s efforts to fight AI-generated investment scams in 2024. Fake videos featuring public figures, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳), had spread online to promote fraudulent investments.
As digital affairs minister, Tang sent text messages to 200,000 randomly selected phone numbers to seek public input. Officials then randomly selected 447 people to discuss solutions in small online groups, where AI helped summarize ideas and find areas of agreement.
Participants called for stronger checks on online advertisers and rules holding platforms responsible for losses from scam ads. Tang said more than 85% of participants supported the proposals, which helped shape laws passed within months.
Tang cited official figures showing that deepfake investment scam ads fell by more than 94% in 2025. She argued that the country had shown how public input could help fight online fraud without limiting free speech.
Tang also recalled the 2014 Sunflower Movement, a student-led protest against a proposed trade deal with China that led to the occupation of the legislature. Protesters feared the agreement would give Beijing more influence over the country, and Tang said public discussions helped people develop common proposals despite their differences.
Taiwan used a similar approach in 2015 to address disputes between taxi drivers and Uber over the ride-hailing firm’s services. Online discussions helped both sides reach agreement on proposed rules, offering an early example of how technology could help resolve disputes.
Tang said the country’s approach has drawn interest abroad, and she has visited 29 countries over the past two years to share its experience. In Germany, she has worked on a project that uses AI to help people find shared solutions to problems with transport and public services.
Tang said government action alone was not enough to make public participation work. She urged journalists, educators, and citizens to help turn shared ideas into practical solutions.

Poland is Trying to Insure Itself Against Another Yalta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:08:14 UTC
16:08:14 KST

Poland knows from bitter experience that even powerful allies cannot always be relied upon when it matters most. Now, as talk grows of a possible grand meeting between Washington, Moscow and Beijing—eerily reminiscent of the Yalta Conference—Warsaw is trying to make the prospect of abandonment more expensive.
The announcement on Tuesday of a European servicing centre for American PAC-3 Patriot interceptors fits a policy pursued by successive Polish governments, which is to draw Western troops, technology and defense industry into Poland until its security becomes a practical interest for its allies.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But America could have a great deal invested in Poland and still decide that its interests lie elsewhere. That is the dilemma behind the latest announcement.
In September 1939, Britain and France declared war on Germany but could not save Poland. Six years later, with the Red Army occupying Polish territory, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin determined Poland’s future at Yalta without a Polish representative at the table.
Of course, today’s Poland has NATO membership, stronger armed forces and American troops already on its soil. Yet its history offers the warning that powerful allies can have good reasons to defend you and still fail when their capabilities or priorities point elsewhere.
The cost of walking away
Poland beat Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the PAC-3 centre, which will repair and recertify interceptors used by European NATO countries.
US, Russia Discuss Oil Deals in Ukraine Peace Talks – FT
At present, European NATO countries have to send their PAC-3 interceptor missiles back to the United States for technical inspections and certification to ensure they remain safe and ready for use.
Polish Deputy Defence Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka says the shipping, work and return take “more than a year”. Doing that work in Poland should shorten the delay. Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden will also participate in the supply chain.
And that is where Poland gains leverage. The more Europe’s air defences depend on Polish facilities to keep their missiles operational, the more its allies have to lose if Poland’s security is threatened.
Britain signed a three-year defence plan with Warsaw on the same day, building on cooperation in drones, ammunition and the Narew air-defence system. Under an earlier MBDA agreement, Polish industry is to manufacture more than 1,000 CAMM-ER missiles.
British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting spoke of “a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO”. For Warsaw, the attraction is a web of contracts, technology and operational needs that give its allies something tangible to lose.
                                                                                                                                                                         Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin at Yalta in February 1945, where Poland's future was negotiated without its government at the table. (Photo by: Circa Images/GHI/Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)                             
President Karol Nawrocki is pursuing the military version of the same idea. He has called a National Security Council meeting for November 3 to discuss the long-sought-after permanent American base, adding to the existing US military presence.
The logic is straightforward. Poland is safer when its allies have more than a moral or legal obligation to defend it.
American troops, missile facilities and defence contracts give them something concrete to lose, whether in the unlikely event of a Russian invasion or the more plausible scenario of Washington and Moscow negotiating spheres of influence over Warsaw’s head.
The hope is that compromising Poland’s security would also damage the interests of those making the decisions. But the imbalance remains: Poland still needs America far more than America needs Poland.
The shadow of another Yalta
That imbalance matters as Moscow explores a grand bargain with Washington and Beijing.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin has proposed meeting Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during November’s APEC summit in China to discuss Ukraine. The meeting is unconfirmed, and there is no evidence that the three powers have agreed to divide Europe into spheres of influence. Still, the prospect of talks about European security without Europeans recalls an uncomfortable history.
Some commentary suggests Europe may finally be finding its way into the peace process. Putin’s adviser Yuri Ushakov said on Sunday that “it’s not enough to talk only to Kyiv”, adding that Europe had to be addressed too.
There was a catch. Ushakov did not say Moscow intended to negotiate with European governments as equals. In context, he could just as easily have been asking Washington to put pressure on them.
And an attempt on Tuesday at direct European diplomacy did little to dispel that suspicion.
                                                                                                                                                                         Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre (pictured) sought direct talks with Putin, exposing disagreements over European diplomacy. (Photo by Paula Bronstein/Getty Images)                             
Putin’s history lesson
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre initiated a call with Putin ahead of planned peace talks in Abu Dhabi possibly in the first half of November.
According to the Financial Times, the Russian president spent much of the 90-minute conversation giving them the Tucker Carlson treatment: a rambling lecture on medieval Slavic history, much like the one he delivered to the American broadcaster during his 2024 interview about the invasion of Ukraine.
There was little discussion of an immediate ceasefire and no visible concession.
“There were no surprises in the positions that Putin put forward,” Stubb acknowledged afterwards. It is difficult to see what was learnt that justified the diplomatic disruption.
Denmark and Sweden questioned the initiative. Estonia said it had been informed, without taking part in substantive coordination. And Stubb and Støre stressed that they were speaking only for their own countries.
To be fair, Ukraine was consulted and Zelenskyy welcomed the call. Direct contact can have value. But Russia wages sabotage and coercion across Europe, while European governments still struggle to agree who should speak to Moscow. Putin can deal with individual capitals without accepting a united European negotiating position.
There was a revealing irony in Stubb’s speech to the Nordic Council later that day. Small countries, he argued, should ask “in what areas others depend on us”. That could serve as a description of Poland’s industrial strategy. Yet the call exposed the difficulty of translating common European interests into a common diplomatic voice.
And that brings us back to Warsaw. An American missile centre and British production ties may make abandonment costlier but they cannot compel an American president to put Polish security ahead of a wider deal with Moscow.

U.S. Navy pays $23 million to shield warship power grids from hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:01:11 UTC
16:01:11 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Integer Technologies a $23.1 million contract to research zero trust cybersecurity for shipboard power systems.
- Integer will work with Florida State University’s Center for Advanced Power Systems, with research running through October 2030.
The U.S. Navy has awarded South Carolina-based Integer Technologies a $23.1 million contract to research how zero trust cybersecurity can protect the electrical power systems that run its warships, without slowing the split-second controls those systems depend on.
The Office of Naval Research awarded the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract for a program called Threat Resilient Integrated Defense for Enhanced Naval Technologies, or TRIDENT, the Department of War announced in its daily contract list this week. Integer is teaming with Florida State University and its Center for Advanced Power Systems, and work will take place in Columbia, South Carolina, through October 2030. The award is a science and technology effort, meaning it funds research and prototyping, and it does not put a new cybersecurity system on any ship.
The contract calls for investigations into “threat-informed” zero trust architecture frameworks tailored to the cyber-physical security needs of shipboard power systems. Zero trust is a security model that drops the old assumption that anything already inside a network can be trusted. Every user, device and command has to prove it is legitimate each time it asks for access. The Navy wants an architecture that lets a ship monitor the cyber and physical state of its power plant, change its defensive posture as threats change, and keep fighting through an attack while the electrical system keeps performing.
The funding structure is more complex than the headline figure. The contract has a 36-month base period and a 36-month option that would begin 12 months after award and run alongside the base, which is why the whole effort ends about four years from now. The Navy obligated $10.1 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds at award, enough to pay for the full base period, leaving about $13 million tied to the option. Navy research money is available for two years, so the fiscal 2026 funds expire at the end of fiscal 2027, the government’s current budget year. ONR bought the work through its long-range broad agency announcement for Navy and Marine Corps science and technology, an open solicitation that accepts proposals year-round, so the Navy could not say how many bids it received.
The problem TRIDENT is meant to study comes from how warship power has changed. Older surface combatants such as the Arleigh Burke-class destroyers use gas turbines geared directly to the propeller shafts, with separate, smaller generators for electricity. The three Zumwalt-class destroyers were the first U.S. Navy surface combatants built around an integrated power system that generates electricity for both propulsion and weapons. Two Rolls-Royce MT30 main turbine generators and two smaller auxiliary generators produce about 78 megawatts, which feeds the electric motors that turn the shafts and a shipwide grid for sensors, combat systems and hotel loads. The Navy’s planned DDG(X) next-generation destroyer is designed to use a similar integrated power system.
That architecture lets a ship shift power between propulsion and weapons on demand, which matters as electrical loads grow. L3Harris, which builds power distribution equipment for Virginia-class submarines, said this month that advanced radars, directed energy weapons and next-generation propulsion will place extraordinary demands on shipboard power. Laser weapons such as the 60-kilowatt-class HELIOS installed on USS Preble (DDG 88) in 2022 draw their “ammunition” straight from the ship’s electrical system.
It also means a single, software-managed grid now sits underneath nearly everything a warship does. Power is controlled by networked switchboards, power converters, protective relays and a machinery control system that decides how to route electricity and how to isolate a fault before it spreads. Those are operational technology systems: computers whose job is to move physical equipment. If an attacker could send false commands or corrupt the data those controllers rely on, the consequences would be physical, from tripping generators to cutting power to weapons or radars in combat.
The contract identifies two constraints that make zero trust hard to apply aboard ship. The first is latency. Integrated power systems rely on very fast control loops to protect equipment and keep the grid stable, and enterprise zero trust tools typically add checks, such as authentication, encryption and traffic inspection, that take time. A security layer that delays a protective trip or a power transfer by even a short interval could cause the damage it was meant to prevent. The second is the mix of legacy and modern equipment. Ships stay in service for decades and are upgraded in pieces, so a single power plant can contain older controllers that were never designed to authenticate commands alongside newer networked devices. The contract does not say which ship classes or systems the research will model.
Florida State’s Center for Advanced Power Systems is one of the Navy’s main university laboratories for electric ship research. Established in 2000 in Tallahassee, the center operates one of the largest real-time digital power system simulators along with 5-megawatt AC and DC test beds for power hardware-in-the-loop testing, in which real equipment is connected to a simulated ship grid so engineers can stress it under realistic conditions. Cybersecurity for power systems is one of its listed research areas, and it leads the Navy-funded Electric Ship Research and Development Consortium of universities. In June, Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the center an $88 million contract for modeling, simulation and testing of advanced shipboard electrical power and energy systems through 2031.
Integer Technologies is a small business founded in Columbia in 2021 by Duke Hartman and Josh Knight. It has built a portfolio of Navy research work focused on cyber-physical systems, often in partnership with universities. In September, ONR exercised a $10.2 million option on a separate Integer contract with Louisiana State University to develop a cyber-physical resilience framework for Navy maritime platforms, with work running through March 2030. The company was also among more than two dozen firms placed on the Navy’s $982 million multiple-award contract for its Unmanned Surface Vehicle Family of Systems in 2024.
The threat the Navy is preparing for has moved from theory to documented activity on land. In a February 2024 advisory, CISA, the National Security Agency and the FBI assessed with high confidence that Chinese state-sponsored hackers known as Volt Typhoon were pre-positioning themselves on IT networks to enable movement into operational technology and disrupt critical infrastructure in a crisis. The agencies said the group had compromised organizations in the continental United States and its territories, including Guam, a key hub for U.S. forces in the Pacific, and had kept access in some networks for at least five years.
Earlier cases showed what attacks on control systems can do. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, sabotaged Iranian uranium enrichment centrifuges by manipulating their industrial controllers while showing operators normal readings. In December 2015, a cyberattack on Ukrainian power distribution companies cut electricity to roughly 225,000 customers, the first publicly confirmed blackout caused by hackers. Both targeted fixed infrastructure on land, and a warship differs in important ways: its networks are smaller and more tightly controlled, and it often operates with limited outside connectivity. Ships still connect to shore networks in port and receive software and hardware updates from contractors during maintenance, which gives an attacker possible ways in.
The Department of the Navy has led the military services in applying the Pentagon’s 2022 zero trust strategy to enterprise IT, and its officials said in early 2025 that they were preparing zero trust standards for operational technology, the category that includes ship machinery and weapons platforms. TRIDENT is aimed at that harder category, where a security tool has to work within the timing and reliability limits of physical equipment.

US midterms: Five days to go – What the polls say as Trump, Harris campaign
With five days until the US midterms, here’s what polls show, the latest campaign news and what’s next.
With five days to go before the United States midterms, Democrats are ahead in national polls, but several Senate races remain close.
President Donald Trump, former President Barack Obama and Vice President JD Vance were out campaigning on Wednesday in Ohio, Georgia and North Carolina, as both parties fight for control of Congress.
Here’s what to know:
What do the latest polls say about the US midterms?
Democrats lead Republicans by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent, a gap of 8.2 percentage points, according to RealClearPolling’s national polling average.
But the national lead is not reflected in every Senate race.
In Texas, where Democrats haven’t won a Senate election since 1988, Democrat James Talarico leads Republican Ken Paxton with 48.5 percent to 46.7 percent, according to the poll aggregator.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has widened his lead over Republican Mike Rogers to seven percentage points, according to a Mitchell Research poll conducted for CBS Detroit.
The October 26-27 survey found El-Sayed leading Rogers 51 percent to 44 percent, up from a 4.2-point advantage earlier this month.
RealClearPolling showed a narrower race, with El-Sayed at 48 percent and Rogers at 46 percent.
Despite that lead, Democrats are continuing to campaign for support among young voters in Michigan.
“We need everybody and young people are a huge part of the coalition and could really be the difference-maker on November 3rd,” Will Lawrence, a Democratic candidate hoping to win Michigan’s 7th Congressional District from the Republicans, told Al Jazeera.
Democratic Congressman Maxwell Frost, who travelled from Florida to campaign for El-Sayed, said face-to-face conversations with voters were particularly important.
“Everyone’s seen the negative bigoted ads and Islamophobic ads, but what hasn’t happened is everyone hasn’t had person-to-person conversation about why Abdul is the right senator for Michigan,” he said.
Republicans are also trying to reach young voters, with one supporter telling Al Jazeera: “I think there’s definitely a movement that people don’t realise in Gen Z that is turning more conservative.”
Beyond Michigan, some voters told Al Jazeera they were frustrated with both parties.
“Each party wants to be in power and I think they’ll say what they think they want their voters to hear,” one voter said in Lexington, Kentucky.
Democratic strategist Joel Rubin described the midterms as a potential “protest election”, with many Democratic voters looking to limit Trump’s power.
“I think that overwhelmingly American voters who will vote Democratic are voting because they want to put a check on President Trump’s power,” he said.
Republican strategist Suhail Khan said Trump was losing support among a number of his own voters, who were frustrated by rising fuel prices, rents and mortgage costs.
“I keep voting and I’m independent, I vote both sides … I’m so frustrated and out of hope,” another voter said in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania.
Can Democrats take control of Congress?
Democrats are hoping to overturn Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress, but the Senate presents a bigger challenge.
They need a net gain of three seats in the House of Representatives and four in the Senate, where Republicans currently hold 53 of the 100 seats. Democrats hold 47, including two independents who caucus with them.
Democrats need to reach 51 seats to take control, but the path to a Senate majority is not simple.
“Even the most optimistic of Republicans will tell you that it’s going to be pretty tough for the GOP to hold on to the House of Representatives,” Al Jazeera’s Scott McLean said. “Different story when it comes to the US Senate, though.”
McLean said that even if Democrats win North Carolina and Ohio and hold on to their current seats, they would still be two seats short of the 51 needed for a majority.
Alaska and Texas could help close that gap. But Republicans are also hoping to win Michigan, where the race remains tight.
Taking control of the House of Representatives alone would still have significant consequences for Trump. If the Democrats flip the House, they can block parts of his legislative agenda and launch investigations into his administration.
They would also be able to call administration officials to testify before congressional committees, although the White House could challenge those demands.
What’s happened on the US midterm campaign trail in the past 24 hours?
Trump was in Ohio campaigning for Republican Senator Jon Husted, who is facing former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.
During the rally, Trump defended Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy following backlash over an advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton.
Ramaswamy was being treated “very unfairly”, Trump said. “How the hell is that his problem?”
Trump also spoke about Jeffrey Epstein after protesters interrupted his speech, saying he had expelled the late sex offender from his Mar-a-Lago club two decades ago.
Meanwhile, in Georgia, former President Obama joined Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms.
Obama criticised Republicans for their reaction to his recent Cheesecake Factory joke about White House renovations, saying they were more concerned about that than the rising cost of living.
“These are not serious people. They don’t have solutions to actual problems,” he said.
Vance also rallied in North Carolina, where former Governor Roy Cooper is facing Republican Michael Whatley in the Senate race.
What’s next for Trump, Democrats and Republicans?
Trump is scheduled to campaign in South Carolina on Thursday at 16:30 GMT, before heading to Florida on Friday and Kansas on Saturday.
South Carolina is among the Republican-held Senate seats Democrats are targeting, although the party faces a difficult contest in a traditionally conservative state.
In Texas, Vice President JD Vance will hold a rally in Weatherford at 17:15 GMT, with Republican candidate Ken Paxton facing a close Senate race against Democrat James Talarico.
Talarico will also be campaigning on Thursday in Dallas, at 00:00 GMT on Friday (7pm Thursday local time).
Al Jazeera’s Phil Lavelle reported from Texas that Republicans are particularly concerned about turnout in rural areas, where 21 percent of registered voters had cast their ballots, compared with 24 percent in the more heavily populated metropolitan areas.
Meanwhile, former Vice President Kamala Harris is expected to campaign in Georgia, where Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is defending his seat against Republican Mike Collins.
Georgia’s early in-person voting ends on Friday as both parties make their final push before Election Day.

Toblerone owner sues British vegan chocolate brand over chunky shape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

The owner of Toblerone is taking legal action against a tiny British vegan chocolate brand that it claims has been copying the Swiss chocolate bar’s famous chunky shape.
Mondelēz has filed papers at the high court in London accusing Catherine’s Originals of “passing off” and trademark infringement with its O’bar – a length of chocolate divided into segments each with a rounded semi-oval hump.
The 200g bars cost £9.20 for a milk or plain variety, and as much as £10.55 for more exotic flavours such as pumpkin spice or cinnamon swirl. A standard milk chocolate Toblerone can be bought for £2.50.
Catherine’s Originals, founded by the then teenager Catherine Dodd in 2021, makes its chocolate in Walberton in Sussex, England, and sells them via markets, online or by subscription.
Dodd said the shape of her bars reflected an O for Originals. “We stand firmly behind the product and identity we’ve created,” she said.
“We strongly disagree with the claim concerning O’bar and are working with our legal team to defend our position. Honestly, it’s fairly frightening for a small business we’ve put so much care and hard work into building. But being a smaller business does not mean being afraid to stand up for what we’ve created.”
The brand’s legal adviser, Stephen Lowry of Brandsmiths, added: “Our client disagrees with the claim and considers O’bar to have its own distinctive design and identity. We look forward to addressing the matter through the appropriate legal process.”
Mondelēz International, which also owns Britain’s Cadbury and Belgium’s Côte D’Or chocolate brands, said: “The iconic Toblerone shape is one of the most recognised and distinctive product designs in the UK and across the world, and has been a hallmark of the brand since 1929.
“We have a responsibility to protect our trademarks and intellectual property, which we take seriously. We have attempted to resolve this matter constructively and directly with Catherine’s Originals over several months but unfortunately have been unable to reach an agreement. We cannot comment further on ongoing legal matters.”
The budget chain Poundland was forced to delay the launch of its Twin Peaks bar in 2017, which had two humps rather than the single peaks of Toblerone, after a legal warning from Mondelēz.
The bar eventually relaunched, after Poundland modified the colour of the packaging and the shape of the bar, and is still on sale today.
Toblerone itself was forced to change its packaging in 2023 to remove the image of the Matterhorn mountain peak. That came after some of the chocolate bar’s production was moved outside Switzerland, falling foul of marketing restrictions relating to the use of Swiss iconography.

‘Looming stone towers like Maya temples’: a hike through Snowdonia’s slate country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

The vital moment comes a couple of hours into the walk. I drop down from a tussocky hill towards the village of Y Fron. There’s an abandoned slate-quarrying machine and a grassy track that suddenly emerges on the rim of a deep lake-filled crater. The water is the colour of an old bruise. Around the rim is a fence of lichen-crusty slates like gravestones. It’s a dark, brooding spectacle and totally unexpected. At that moment, I know that whoever designed this route knew what they were doing.
This is the Llwybr Llechi Eryri (Snowdonia Slate Trail), an 83-mile hike that follows a great loop around the national park, starting in Bangor and ending in Bethesda. It strings together a series of abandoned slate quarries with some of the finest riverside and mountain walking in the UK. I’m doing just three days, starting in Llanberis and heading to Betws-y-Coed via stops in Beddgelert and Llan Ffestiniog.
Beyond Y Fron village, I descend into my first quarry, and it proves to be a classic. This was once the Dorothea slate quarry, a vast abandoned complex of railways, cottages and chasms. I start exploring: tunnels, cuttings, huge looming stone towers like Maya temples, all overgrown with ash, birch and oak. What strikes me is the craftsmanship and precision in construction, each stone hand-fitted without mortar, all for workaday industrial buildings.
The quality of this slate was known from early times. Edward I is thought to have had his Welsh castles roofed with it, but industrial production began in the 1820s and peaked in the 1870s. Soon, there was a railway to Caernarfon and the area bristled with steam pumps, aerial cables and chains. The last-ever Cornish beam engine was installed to pump water from the deep pits, sucking up 10 gallons a second from 500ft down.
From here, the trail burrows eastwards into the Welsh mountains, until Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) appears on the horizon when it turns south, occasionally following the line of the Welsh Highland Railway all the way into Beddgelert, my first overnight stop. Named after a dog or a saint, depending on who you believe, this is a good base for hikers, having pubs, cafes, restaurants and outdoor gear shops.
The second day begins along a path combining the Slate Trail and the Cambrian Way, one of the grandees of the long-distance genre at 298 miles. I follow the route as it heads south along the River Glaslyn, with some spectacular sections on crags with the torrent below. We are getting along very nicely – so well, in fact, that I start to get footpath envy. When the Cambrian Way turns east, heading up the Matterhorn-shaped peak of Cnicht, I cannot resist. The weather forecast is bad, but the sun is out. If I pop over the peak, I can see how the two paths cross each other later.
Views of the Irish Sea open up as I climb, but there is an ominous black cloud approaching. As I reach the summit, a howling wind threatens to blow me off course. I face down the hailstones and get back to the Slate Trail, which now descends into Cwmorthin quarry. Not on the scale of Dorothea, Cwmorthin still seems epic today, dominated by vast heaps of spoiled stone – it took 10 tons to make 1 ton of marketable material. In the late 19th century, Cwmorthin was known locally as “the slaughterhouse” for its propensity to slay workers in fatal accidents. From here, the path runs down a desolate valley before dropping into Blaenau Ffestiniog, where I find a good cafe, Burrito Blasus, to fire me up the last miles into Llan Ffestiniog.
I stay in the Y Pengwern, a community-owned pub that has an excellent, friendly bar and basic rooms and food. Outside, a storm is buffeting the building, but the next day the rain has stopped and I begin with a rare treat: a magical trail beside the tumbling River Cynfal. Here, thunderous white spumes of water and dark powerful currents punch their way through a deep mossy gorge overhung by ancient fern-decked oaks. One of the midstream rock towers is said to have once been the “pulpit” of a magician called Huw Llwyd and, according to the 18th-century traveller and naturalist Thomas Pennant, his voice could be heard at night, ringing down the enchanted chasms.
As I climb higher, the forest dwindles and I emerge on a remote, wind-scoured upland of crags and bog. Even here, you can come across fragments of old quarry workings. In one abandoned cottage, a jacket still hangs on a nail behind the door, as if the occupant had just flounced out: “I’ve had enough. I’m off to America.” Many Welsh slate workers did head to the US, fed up with the poor pay and the repeated failure of strikes. In 1901, sympathetic workers in England sent a two-and-a-half ton Christmas pudding, which briefly lifted morale, but after violent clashes the landowner won, and many quarrymen emigrated.
I stop and brew some tea on my stove. I have not seen another soul all day, yet Yr Wyddfa, with all its crowds, is less than 10 miles away. This remote walk takes me to the top of the old tramway incline down to Rhiwbach quarry – an epic approach, descending to the old engine house. This place peaked in the 1860s, and being so isolated, the miners lived in barracks, some of which remain.
Farther down the valley, I spot peregrine falcons nesting close to a tumbling waterfall, above the little village of Cwm Penmachno. A few miles on, the church of St Tudclud contains an astonishing collection of inscribed stones, including the Carausius Stone. This is thought to be the gravestone of a commander of the Roman empire, who pulled off a coup d’etat in AD286, making himself emperor of Britain and northern Gaul for seven years before his assassination.
Approaching Betws-y-Coed, the path joins the River Conwy, first singled out as a beauty spot in the 17th century, long before the Romantic poets seized on the idea. For me, it’s the finale to this fine route, but the path continues and I’ll be back soon for more mountains of slate and spectacular riverside walking.
The trip was provided by Walkers’ Britain & Europe, which offers Hiking the Snowdonia Slate Trail as a seven-day self-guided 83-mile walk, including six nights’ accommodation, breakfast, luggage transfers, digital app with tour information and navigations, and emergency hotline from £890pp, departing daily from April to October

CEO of one of Australia's top cultural events becomes French knight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Biennale of Sydney CEO Barbara Moore appointed Chevalier of Ordre des Arts et des Lettres
The CEO of the Biennale of Sydney, Barbara Moore, has been appointed Chevalier of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, or a knight of the French Order of Arts and Letters.
"I'm pretty shocked by it," she told ABC Arts, ahead of the ceremony at Sydney Town Hall on October 29.
"It's a big deal and admittedly I have a bit of impostor syndrome. Like, I'm still young!
"But these endorsements mean a lot … they say we're doing something that's contributing in a positive way."
Moore, who moved to Australia from Canada in 2007, has been CEO of the festival since 2019.
The French Order of Arts and Letters is one of the country's highest cultural honours, awarded to someone for their contribution to arts and culture in France and around the world.
Past recipients include musicians Nick Cave and Kylie Minogue, actor Cate Blanchett, artist Tony Albert, the late film critic David Stratton, and former Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron.
"I think the point of these things is to encourage relationships and bonding," Moore said.
"I'm an untrained diplomat, where I'm just trying to bring people together and break down barriers.
"When the world is so used to shouting at each other and we're losing the art of listening, art helps us connect and learn from each other."
It is a poignant statement in a year when the biennale, curated by Hoor Al Qasimi, was subjected to community, commercial and political pressures, including the withdrawal of sponsors and accusations of antisemitism.
Asked how arts festivals like the biennale should navigate a charged political climate, Moore offered plainly: "Boldly, like warriors."
She continued: "If we operate through fear, if we're part of burning books and over-censoring, we have a problem.
"People are going to have feelings and opinions, especially in divisive times. But that doesn't mean we cancel organisations and we shut projects down.
"We have to remember what we're there for and that's to bring people together."
Taking Australian arts and culture abroad
Earlier this month, Moore was in France for the contemporary art fair Art Basel Paris, which was cut short in response to education and cost-of-living rallies that escalated into rioting.
She was there to take a group of biennale patrons to see a new exhibition by Ghanian artist Ibrahim Mahama. His work featured in the 2020 Biennale of Sydney, which was forced to close after 10 days by the COVID-19 pandemic.
His exhibition opened at the Cartier Foundation gallery, which partners with the biennale to platform First Nations artists and curators.
The partnership has inspired another celebration of Australian artists on the world stage, with Australia announced as guest of honour at next year's Art Paris contemporary art fair.
Art Paris director Guillaume Piens saw the large-scale work of First Nations artists including Kaylene Whiskey and Dylan Mooney at the newly reopened White Bay Power Station during the 2024 Biennale of Sydney.
"He'd never seen anything like that before, and he thought he wanted to bring First Nations artists to the fair," Moore said.
What that means for the place of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art on the world stage, Moore suggests, is more than its popularity with collectors.
"It's a reckoning," she said. "[People are asking:] 'How do we make the world a better place? How do we get through these tumultuous times?'
"Maybe looking at the oldest continuous living culture could be a good start, to think about how to exist on this planet and where the humanity is.
"Maybe there's some things we forgot we need to remember again."
The next Biennale of Sydney is scheduled to start on March 21, 2028, and will be led by Singaporean curator Low Kee Hong.

Where to place a money tree to attract prosperity: folk beliefs and care tips
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:57:43 EET
15:57:43 KST

Where to place a money tree to attract prosperity: folk beliefs and care tips
Kyiv • UNN
The jade plant is recommended to be placed in the southeast, but the main conditions are light, moderate watering, and the absence of drafts. Folk beliefs have no evidence.
The jade plant is often grown at home as a symbol of financial stability and prosperity. According to folk beliefs, the place chosen for this plant may have special significance. UNN explains more about where these beliefs originated, where it is best to place a money tree, and what conditions the plant requires.
Details
The money tree, also known as a jade plant, is easy to recognize by its fleshy, rounded leaves. Their shape resembles coins, which is why the plant has long been associated with the accumulation of wealth, stability, and financial growth. The jade plant gained particular popularity through the traditions of feng shui, in which certain areas of a home are associated with various spheres of life. Supporters of these beliefs consider that a properly placed plant can become a symbol of abundance and a reminder of financial goals.
The southeastern part of the home
According to popular feng shui recommendations, the money tree is most often advised to be placed in the southeastern part of a house or individual room. In Eastern practices, this direction is symbolically associated with wealth and prosperity.
To determine the appropriate area, you can use a compass to check where the southeast is located. After that, you should choose a place that corresponds not only to symbolic beliefs but also to the plant’s own needs. The jade plant is a succulent, so sufficient light and moderate watering are important for its healthy growth. If the southeastern part of the home is dark or a heating appliance is constantly operating nearby, it is better to find another place. The main principle is simple: beliefs may suggest a symbolic location, but the plant’s growing conditions should remain the priority.
Where else you can place a money tree
If the southeastern area is not suitable for growing a jade plant, there are other options mentioned in folk beliefs. For example, the living room, as this is a place where the family often gathers and guests are received. Therefore, popular recommendations on where to place a money tree associate this room with prosperity and harmony in the home.
The pot can be placed on a sturdy stand or a shelf near a window if there is enough light there.
You can also place the jade plant on a desk or in a home office.
In folk beliefs, the money tree here symbolizes professional development, new opportunities, and financial goals. The plant can become part of the workspace and a reminder of plans related to a career or one’s own business. However, it should be placed directly next to a computer or other devices only if there is enough space and light for the pot.
On the other hand, if the money tree is placed near the entrance, one widespread belief holds that it will symbolically help preserve the prosperity of the home. It is believed that in this way the plant seems to greet financial good fortune at the entrance to the house. However, a dark hallway or a drafty spot is not actually the best choice for a jade plant. If you want to place the pot near the entrance, it is better to find a well-lit area away from cold air and sudden temperature changes.
Where you should not place a jade plant
Folk beliefs advise against leaving a money tree among clutter or in untidy corners. Symbolically, disorder is associated with stagnation, which supposedly prevents prosperity. From a practical perspective, the plant also needs a place where it is convenient to care for it. Do not hide the pot in a cabinet, place it in a dark corner, or put it somewhere where it will constantly be knocked or brushed against.
Particular attention should be paid to the following conditions:
-  Lack of light. In a place that is too dark, the plant may become elongated and lose its attractive appearance. 
-  Constantly wet soil. Excessive watering can cause the roots to rot. 
-  A hot radiator. Placing the plant directly next to a heat source can create unfavorable conditions for it. 
-  Drafts and sudden temperature changes. It is better to avoid places where the jade plant is constantly exposed to such changes. 
Therefore, when choosing a place for a money tree, you should consider not only folk beliefs but also the lighting, temperature, and the opportunity to regularly check the condition of the soil.
Do coins under the pot and a red ribbon help?
Some folk traditions involve additional symbolic rituals. For example, a coin is placed under the pot with a jade plant, and the trunk is decorated with a red ribbon, with such actions associated with wishes for financial stability and increased prosperity. Another common custom is to grow the plant oneself from a small cutting. Those who believe in omens consider that this symbolically connects the money tree with the head of the household. However, these rituals belong to the realm of folk beliefs and have no proven effect on one’s financial situation. If the plant’s owners like them, they can be regarded as a personal tradition, without neglecting ordinary care. It is also important to ensure that decorative ribbons do not constrict the trunk and that coins or other small objects do not pose a danger to children or pets.
How to care for a money tree so that it remains healthy
According to folk beliefs, a lush and well-cared-for jade plant symbolizes prosperity. Of course, the plant’s health does not determine one’s income level, but proper care will help it maintain an attractive appearance. A jade plant needs a bright location, while watering should be moderate. Before watering it again, allow the soil to dry out: succulents store moisture in their leaves and do not like constantly wet soil. It is also important to use a pot with drainage holes so that excess water can escape. The plant should be repotted when this is necessary given its condition and the size of its root system, rather than merely because of folk recommendations about frequently changing pots. If the leaves fall off, this does not necessarily mean financial difficulties. The cause may be watering mistakes, insufficient light, or other unfavorable conditions.

Flight delay? These are the best and worst European airlines for making a compensation claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:57:35 UTC
15:57:35 KST

TAP Air Portugal, LOT Polish Airlines and Wizz Air were ranked the most honest airlines in Europe, according to AirAdvisor data.
Everybody hates flight delays, but the blow is definitely softened by the compensation guaranteed under EU law.
Under Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, passengers get €250 back for flights under 1,500 kilometres delayed for more than two hours, €400 for flights between 1,500 and 3,500 kilometres delayed for more than three hours, and €600 for all other flights delayed for more than four hours.
In theory, it’s great, but actually getting an airline to pay out what you’re owed isn’t always the quickest, or easiest, process in the world.
While you can make the claim yourself, you can also go through companies such as AirAdvisor which specialise in flight and baggage compensation claims.
Between January and June 2026, AirAdvisor helped make 68,283 claims from 59 airlines. Now, they’ve used this data to create a ranking by looking at the claim resolution rate as well as the number that were sent to court after being rejected or ignored.
The best European airlines for compensation claims
Based on this, the most honest airline in Europe is TAP Air Portugal, with a claim resolution rate of 88.7%, and a court referral rate of just 0.6%. The average time you’ll have to wait for your pay out is just 10 days, too.
LOT Polish Airlines came out second, with no claims sent to court, and a successful claim rate of 82.8%.
Third place went to Wizz Air, with a resolution rate of 72.4% and a court referral rate of 1.2%.
The top five was rounded out by Iberia in fourth, with a resolution rate of 67.3%, and Brussels Airlines, which had no cases sent to court.
Air France came sixth, followed by Aegean Airlines in seventh, KLM in eighth, ITA Airways in ninth, and SAS in 10th.
The worst European airlines for compensation claims
On the other end of the scale, the most difficult company to get a compensation claim sorted with is TAROM, Romania’s flag carrier, according to the AirAdvisor data.
Of 122 claims, just 3.3% have been successful to date, with 46.7% sent to court. The average time you’ll have to wait for payment is a whopping 110 days, too.
Next up is Aeroitalia, with a claim resolution rate of 0.6%. Some 28.2% of claims have been sent to court.
Third place went to Europe’s biggest airline, Ryanair. Of 991 qualified claims, just 2.1% have been successfully resolved, with 17.8% sent to court.
It should be noted that the data used comes from claims made through AirAdvisor, and so the wider claim resolution rates and number of cases sent to court will differ. Only airlines with more than 100 claims submitted were included in the ranking, amounting to 22 carriers. You can see all the data on the AirAdvisor website.

What 'Putin's strikes' tell us about Russia’s war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:53:44 UTC
15:53:44 KST

What 'Putin's strikes' tell us about Russia’s war in Ukraine
A Ukrainian firefighter extinguishes a fire at the site of a Russian drone strike in Kharkiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 28, 2026. (Sergey Bobok/AFP via Getty Images)
The Kremlin has instructed loyal Russian media to describe attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure as "Putin's strikes," and to portray them as far more effective than Ukrainian attacks on Russia, according to an Oct. 21 report by Meduza.
So far, few outlets have picked up the phrase, according to an analysis of Russian media and Telegram channels conducted by Join Ukraine, a Ukrainian organization researching Russia's military machine, for the Kyiv Independent.
But the instructions come as Russia struggles to achieve its objectives on the battlefield and has turned instead to intensifying strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure.
"The scale of destruction of civilian infrastructure does not, in itself, demonstrate Russia's strategic superiority or its ability to achieve its objectives in the war."
Russia has increased its capacity to carry out long-range attacks to undermine essential services by destroying critical infrastructure, while Ukraine faces shortages of air defense interceptors, according to Dara Massicot, a senior fellow in the Russia and Eurasia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
"In their thinking, they estimate that such destruction could cause instability and a collapse of morale to continue fighting — which would again be a misjudgment," she told the Kyiv Independent.
For Olga Yurkova, co-founder of the Ukrainian fact-checking organization StopFake, the phrase "Putin's strikes" substitutes this ability to destroy infrastructure and harm civilians for the ability to win the war, with the supposed achievement attributed personally to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"The scale of destruction of civilian infrastructure does not, in itself, demonstrate Russia's strategic superiority or its ability to achieve its objectives in the war," she said.
Selling 'Putin's strikes'
Yurkova pointed to an article published by Gazeta.ru in which "Putin's strikes" appeared in the subheading and editorial text, but not in the interviewee's direct quotes.
The article portrayed the attacks as part of Putin's carefully planned strategy and Russia's ability to carry them out as the result of his long-standing policies, turning reports of strikes into political promotion for the Russian president.
Gazeta.ru mentioned power outages and transport disruptions but framed them as a means of creating unbearable conditions for Kyiv and forcing Ukraine to accept Russian demands.
"The audience is encouraged to take pride in precisely these consequences. What is left out are the people for whom the strikes mean danger and the loss of basic necessities of life," Yurkova said.
read also
Putting Putin at the center
The phrase "Putin's strikes" was deliberately modeled on "Stalin's strikes," the Soviet-era name for ten major Soviet offensives in 1944, a political consultant working with the Kremlin told Meduza.
Yurkova said the historical reference reinforces Putin's image as a victorious military commander and places Russia's invasion of Ukraine within the Kremlin's propaganda narrative of repeating the Soviet victory over Nazism.
Samuel Greene, a professor of Russian politics at King's College London, suggested that associating Putin personally with the attacks may also reflect the Russian president's increasingly emotional response to Ukrainian strikes.
"It may be that he's trying to paint Ukraine's attacks as attacks on him, and thus Russia's attacks on Ukraine, which will become increasingly damaging as we approach the winter, as his own revenge on behalf of a Russia that he seeks to personify," Greene told the Kyiv Independent.
Another possibility, Greene said, is that the Kremlin sees Putin's personal image as a way to strengthen support for the war.
"If they think that public support for the war is softening, attaching Putin to it even more closely may be part of a strategy to boost that support."
He pointed to the recent State Duma elections, when Putin allowed the increasingly unpopular United Russia party to use his name and image in its campaign — something Greene said had not happened in more than two decades.
"From his perspective, and the perspective of his political advisers, that works. If they think that public support for the war is softening, attaching Putin to it even more closely may be part of a strategy to boost that support," Greene said.
According to the Russian Public Opinion Foundation, Putin's approval rating fell from 75% in July to 71% in early October.
Little uptake
An open-source analysis conducted for the Kyiv Independent by Join Ukraine identified eight articles across seven Russian websites containing the term between Oct. 18 and 22.
Five articles were comments or opinion pieces by members of regional associations of Russian war veterans. In some cases, the phrase appeared only in headlines or editorial text rather than in the veterans' own remarks.
The expression was even less common on Telegram. Among 61 major state media and pro-war channels monitored between Oct. 1 and 23, it appeared in only two posts, both by the same war correspondent who attributed the phrase to Ukrainians. Researchers found no mentions in another 485 regional Telegram channels.
Instead, Russian Telegram channels largely continued using established military terminology to describe the attacks, including "massive strikes," "retaliatory strikes," and "Geran," Russia's name for its Shahed-type drones.
Researchers also examined less direct references to strikes ordered or instructed by Putin, finding only a few posts per week, with no increase since August.
Anton Shirikov, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Kansas who studies authoritarian propaganda, said that individual slogans do not necessarily signal major strategic changes. The Kremlin sometimes tests narratives and abandons those that fail to generate the desired response, he said.
read also
Playing down Ukrainian attacks
The attempt to portray Russian strikes as Putin's overwhelming military success is only one part of the Kremlin's information strategy.
Previously disclosed guidelines from July show that Russian media were also instructed to downplay Ukrainian attacks on Russia. According to Meduza, outlets were encouraged to describe them as publicity stunts and attempts to intimidate the population, while shifting attention to Russian strikes on Ukraine.
A September analysis by Join Ukraine, published in the Kyiv Independent, showed how little information about the consequences of Ukrainian attacks reached Russian audiences. Of 407 posts about a Sept. 20 strike on the Moscow oil refinery, only six mentioned the facility's shutdown. Two state-run channels examined in the study repeated official statements in nine out of ten posts.
Yurkova said the guidelines seek to minimize the consequences of Ukrainian attacks and maintain the impression that Putin has the situation under control.
"Labeling these counterstrikes 'Putin's strikes,' I think, aims to convey to that public that Putin is still on top of things."
They also discourage public discontent and present unity around Putin as the solution, whereas showing Russians' anxiety could be understood as a signal to Kyiv that Ukraine's attacks are effective and could prolong the war.
"This creates a circular logic: the consequences of the war for Russians themselves become another reason to call on them to support Putin — the leader who made the decision to launch the full-scale invasion," Yurkova said.
read also
The Kremlin's two audiences
The competing narratives reflect the Kremlin's efforts to appeal to two increasingly different audiences, according to Shirikov.
One consists of committed pro-war Russians who demand military victories and more aggressive action. The other, larger audience is more politically passive, generally accepting the war as long as it does not significantly disrupt everyday life.
For the first group, propaganda emphasizes Russian military superiority and triumph over Ukraine and the West. For the second, it seeks to maintain a sense of normality, reassuring Russians that the government is managing the war effectively, supporting soldiers' families, and protecting the economy from sanctions.
But as the war continues, Shirikov said, balancing these messages is becoming increasingly difficult.
"Now, the more conformist audience is increasingly fatigued by the war, and speaking to it became more of a challenge for the Kremlin because the normalization narrative seems more and more out of touch when everyday lives are upended by the war," he said.
"Doubling down on militaristic and imperialistic slogans may only remind that more indifferent public that the war is going on, while they don't really understand why."
Russian television has consequently reduced the amount of war-related content, particularly openly pro-war messaging, in recent years, Shirikov said. Yet the Kremlin must still satisfy its most militaristic supporters.
"People in the Kremlin must be worried about how to sell the lack of progress in the war to that audience, which is why they still think they need to produce the super aggressive and confident messaging," Shirikov said. "Labeling these counterstrikes 'Putin's strikes,' I think, aims to convey to that public that Putin is still on top of things."

Chinese warships and aircraft operate around Taiwan overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:51:39 UTC
15:51:39 KST

- Taiwan detected six Chinese military aircraft, seven navy ships and one official ship around the island in the 24 hours to Oct. 29.
- Five aircraft entered Taiwan’s air defense identification zone, and four fighter and drone sorties crossed the Taiwan Strait median line.
Taiwan detected six Chinese military aircraft, seven People’s Liberation Army Navy ships and one Chinese official ship operating around the island in the 24 hours to 6 a.m. local time on Oct. 29, the Ministry of National Defense said on social media.
Five of the six aircraft sorties entered the northern, central and southwestern parts of Taiwan’s air defense identification zone, or ADIZ, a buffer area where Taipei asks approaching aircraft to identify themselves. The zone extends well beyond the island’s territorial airspace, and flights into it are not violations of Taiwanese airspace. The ministry said its forces monitored the activity and responded with combat air patrol aircraft, navy ships and coastal missile systems.
A map released with the report shows two separate groups of flights. Between 9:35 a.m. and 5:20 p.m. on Oct. 28, five sorties of fighters and drones operated along the median line of the Taiwan Strait, the informal boundary between the two sides, and four of them crossed it. A single fighter flew near the northern edge of the zone, north of Taiwan, between 1:55 p.m. and 2 p.m.
The ministry did not identify the aircraft or drone types, the classes of the seven navy ships, or what kind of government vessel the official ship was.
Chinese military aircraft and ships operate around Taiwan almost daily, and Taipei publishes a tally each morning. The figures vary widely from day to day. On busier days the ministry has reported dozens of aircraft, including one 24-hour period when 38 sorties and nine navy ships were detected and 31 aircraft crossed the median line. During large-scale exercises announced by China’s Eastern Theater Command, Taiwan has reported dozens of aircraft and vessels in a single day and put its forces on high alert.
The median line has no legal standing, but for decades both sides treated it as an unofficial dividing line that helped keep military aircraft apart in the narrow strait. Chinese aircraft now cross it routinely, and Taiwan’s ministry tracks each crossing in its daily reports.
