14:37:00 KST

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc holds lead
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 29, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- Latest vote count at 90% shows Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc holding the lead at 53 seats
- Anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot at 48 seats
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end
With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.
That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.
The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.
Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.
The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.
Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.
Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.
According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.
This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.
The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.
UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law.
"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.
"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."
Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.
He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW
Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.
"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."
Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.
"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.
Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.
WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock
Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.
Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.
GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc
Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

Why a Democratic win in US midterms could adversely affect Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:36:08 UTC
14:36:08 KST

Why a Democratic win in US midterms could adversely affect Europe
Complacency about rising far-right movements and renewed pressure on Ukraine could be the result.
The United States midterm elections appear stacked against the ruling Republicans, with polls suggesting the Democrats average an eight-point lead in the House of Representatives and the Senate. But if Democrats take one or both houses, could they affect upcoming elections in Europe?
Not fundamentally, analysts and observers have told Al Jazeera, but besides a welcome improvement in transatlantic relations, they point to two potentially adverse effects.
First, a Democratic Congress might produce complacency among Europeans regarding their own far-right movements.
Second, it might spur US President Donald Trump to raise pressure on Ukraine to make a deal it doesn’t want to make with Russia.
“If the Democrats win the House, let alone both houses, it will be read as, ‘you see democracies bounce back,’” said Catherine Fieschi, a nonresident scholar at Carnegie Europe, specialising in European far-right politics. It would introduce “the idea that these things don’t mean the advent of a fascist regime”, she said.
From her vantage point in Paris, Fieschi said she imagines a Democratic win leading to “a whole discussion about whether we should fear a Marine Le Pen election as much as some people say we should, or whether, in fact, it’s swings and roundabouts and, at some point, if people are really bad and really incompetent, then elections right the way,” she said.
French right-wing politician Marine Le Pen is currently leading the field in polling for presidential elections scheduled for April 18, with surveys indicating she has about 34 percent of the popular vote.
There is a precedent for the complacency Fieschi alludes to. In June 2025, the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), a think tank, polled Europeans following Trump’s first six months in office. Clear majorities in Western Europe said the US political system was broken. In Eastern Europe, majorities said it was working well – though they were weighted towards right-wing voters.
Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris warned against giving too much credit to the US for what Europeans think and do, however.
He said he believes European public opinion hardened against asylum and economic migration independently, but the US marked the shift by expressing it more violently, with military deportation flights and armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents sweeping American cities.
“I think there was a European about-turn on migration. We saw this in Germany, which had a welcoming attitude [to refugees] for many years, and they went to a more controlled policy. All northern European governments saw societies change,” he told Al Jazeera.
“But the US provided a change in tone, from induction and integration and benefaction to deterrence, border protection, increased returns and consequences if asylum is denied. I do think that pivot played a role in Europe,” Plevris added.
The fallout for Ukraine
Should French voters decide that the only way out is through electing Le Pen – “like some kind of strong medicine that would wake us up to what we might lose”, as Fieschi put it – they would have to contend with three controversial propositions – cutting French financial contributions to the European Union’s federal budget to pay for earlier retirement, cutting military aid to Ukraine and possibly leaving the single currency, the euro, in favour of a devalued franc.
Any one of those policy moves would be a major setback for the European project, which has coalesced around trade, money and now security. A cut in assistance to Ukraine would remove 3.5 percent of its foreign military aid, according to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine Support Tracker, which other allies would have to make up.
At the same time, “we could end up in a situation where Trump is basically clinching deals with Putin as fast as he can,” said Fieschi, referring to the US-Russian strategy to coerce Ukraine into a peace agreement that involves sacrificing its eastern Donbas region – something Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said would be a strategic error leading to renewed war, and which a majority of Ukrainians are against.
Trump has already leveraged US early warning on incoming ballistics and Starlink satellite navigation against Ukraine. He has twice echoed Russian calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced.
Compounding this renewed pressure from a beleaguered White House, Russia could intensify its “all-domain war”, which many European governments believe it is already waging against them, said Victoria Vdovychenko, a Ukraine expert at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics.
“Cognitive warfare never stopped on the European continent, and Russians are already using existing vulnerabilities to the utmost,” she told Al Jazeera. “I hope that the European partners will be staying very strong.”
What Europeans think
Trump’s abandonment of the world order the US and Europe established after World War II, his disregard for democracy and human rights, and his betrayal of Ukraine have already transformed European public opinion, observers say.
Only 31 percent of Europeans see the US as Europe’s “most trustworthy ally”, down from 51 percent in 2024, when Trump’s predecessor, Joe Biden, was in office, according to a poll for the German think tank Bertelsmann Stiftung.
Seventy-three percent of Europeans across all age groups say Europe should “go its own way” rather than continue a close cooperation with the US, up from 63 percent in 2024, and that figure includes a clear majority among those on the centre-right and right.
In this year’s Spring Eurobarometer, a regular pulse-taking conducted by the European Commission, 68 percent of respondents wanted the EU’s role in protecting Europeans from global crises and security risks to increase, while 39 percent wanted it to be a top priority.
In a June poll for the European Council on Foreign Relations, the description of the US as an “ally” fell from 22 percent in November 2024 to 11 percent across all territories polled in Eastern and Western Europe.
In a June poll for the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based think tank, 76 percent of people polled in 36 countries, of which nine were EU members, expressed no confidence in Trump, and 57 percent expressed unfavourable views of the US.
It would appear that such shifts against the US and especially Republicans, formed over two Trump terms, would be difficult to reverse in a single congressional election, especially with a Russian war ongoing in Europe.

Ukraine seeks to expand participation in special tribunal on Russian aggression, Karasevych says

Unknown Publisher

Ukraine seeks to expand participation in special tribunal on Russian aggression, Karasevych says
Oleksandr Karasevych, State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine, made this statement in comments to a Ukrinform correspondent in New York.
“Regarding the special tribunal, we are currently actively working to expand its geographic participation,” he noted.
Karasevych recalled that Ukraine already has a legal decision from the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe regarding the tribunal, which was supported by 38 states and the European Union. Now they must implement the agreement at the national level.
“This is no longer a political statement; it is now a legal factor,” the State Secretary emphasized.
He added that, at the same time, Ukraine is seeking to involve more states outside the Council of Europe in the tribunal. In particular, a Ukrainian delegation recently visited Japan to explain the importance of its participation at the political and governmental levels.
Karasevych noted that Japan, Australia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, and Canada were part of a key group of states that participated in drafting the legal mechanisms for establishing the tribunal, specifically its statute and the relevant agreement.
“They were part of the core group, meaning they participated at the technical level in developing the legal mechanisms, the statute, and the agreement. Now we need to work with them so that they also become participants,” he explained.
The State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs also pointed to two areas of work regarding Russia’s accountability: the creation of a special tribunal for the crime of aggression and a compensation mechanism to make up for the damages inflicted on Ukraine.
According to him, more states have formally joined the compensation mechanism, including those that are not members of the Council of Europe. Among them are Australia and Japan, which have joined the Register of Damages Caused by Russia’s Aggression Against Ukraine.
Karasevych recalled that a UN General Assembly resolution adopted in November 2022 served as the basis for developing the compensation mechanism.
He explained that the purpose of his visit to New York is to convey to the legal advisors of partner states—particularly those not yet involved in accountability processes—the importance of establishing mechanisms to hold Russia accountable.
“We must work with those who are not yet involved in our joint efforts, explaining to them what we are doing, why we are doing it, and why it is important not only for Ukraine but for the entire international community,” Karasevych said.
He emphasized that discussing issues of international law and accountability for aggression is particularly appropriate at UN headquarters, since states must adhere to the principles upon which the Organization is founded.
Karasevych also noted that on Tuesday, the Ukrainian delegation participated in a UN Security Council meeting dedicated to the topic “Women, Peace, and Security.” The next meeting involving Ukraine, scheduled for Thursday, will focus on maritime navigation. According to him, it is particularly important for Ukraine to ensure compliance with international maritime safety standards in the Black and Azov Seas.
As reported by Ukrinform, an event was held at the UN on Wednesday dedicated to implementing mechanisms to hold Russia accountable for its aggression against Ukraine.

Şanlıurfa museum preserves centuries-old traditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:33:33 UTC
14:33:33 KST

The Şanlıurfa Municipality purchased and restored the historic structure in 2008, and it opened as the City Museum in 2014. (AA Photo)
A nearly 900-year-old building from the era of the Crusader County of Edessa has been transformed into a city museum, safeguarding the southeastern province of Şanlıurfa’s traditional heritage for future generations.
Located at Beykapısı, along the city’s former walls, the building became known as the Mahmutoğlu family residence during the late Ottoman period but remained abandoned for many years. The Şanlıurfa Metropolitan Municipality purchased and restored the structure in 2008, and it opened as the City Museum in 2014.
The museum displays a city model, historical documents, books, photographs, traditional clothing, musical instruments, kitchen utensils and agricultural tools. Reconstructions also offer a glimpse into everyday life in Şanlıurfa in the past.
Exhibits covering traditional crafts, clothing, cuisine and family life allow visitors to explore the city’s cultural heritage.
Hamdullah Közcü, an art historian working at the museum, told Anadolu Agency that the institution reflects Şanlıurfa’s traditional lifestyle and has been attracting growing interest.
The entrance section presents chronological information about the communities that have lived in the city and its customs. Other exhibits explore traditional clothing, jewelry, accessories and local cuisine, as well as family life in homes built around courtyards, he said.
Közcü described the building as an important example of Anatolian military architecture, constructed on the Beykapısı city walls.
“Our museum has a history of nine centuries. It is one of the finest examples of Anatolian military architecture. Built on the Beykapısı walls, it also reflects the typical layout of traditional courtyard houses in Şanlıurfa, with main sections such as the selamlık (men’s quarters), harem (women’s quarters), camel house and stable,” he said.
Covering 1,500 square meters, the museum has 15 exhibition halls and receives between 25,000 and 30,000 visitors annually, Közcü said.
He added that the exhibits often evoke strong emotions among visitors, particularly those who spent their childhoods in similar courtyard houses.
“When visitors see Şanlıurfa’s cultural life, customs and past here, they become deeply emotional. Some spent their childhoods in courtyard houses like this one, so they experience very moving moments. Because they find traces of their own past, the Şanlıurfa City Museum feels more welcoming to them,” he said.

Syrian mosaic artist revives family craft after returning home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:32:54 UTC
14:32:54 KST

Basil Barini’s mosaic works have been drawing widespread attention.
The Barini family, who fled Syria’s war and sought refuge in Türkiye, are rebuilding their mosaic and natural stone art business in their homeland after years in exile, determined to preserve the craft and pass it on to future generations.
Muhammed Barini, an 85-year-old mosaic master with 50 years of experience, was forced to leave four factories behind when the war broke out and his family sought refuge in Türkiye.
The family resumed its work in Mardin, producing natural stone mosaics that reached customers across Türkiye and in several countries, including the United States.
After the fall of the Syrian regime, the Barinis returned home, only to find that all four factories they had built over five decades had been completely destroyed by bombardment.
Undeterred by the devastation, the family established a new, medium-sized workshop and began producing dozens of mosaic panels, seeking to overcome the scars of war through art.
The family members thanked the Turkish people and government for their hospitality and support, saying they had enjoyed a good life in Türkiye and completed important projects during their years there.
Barini, who has worked with domestic and foreign marble to create hundreds of pieces, said he had spent many years working in Türkiye and the United States.
After the changes in Syria, he decided to return home, believing that the craft should be revived in the land where it originated.
“We must return to our homeland. This profession and craft must come back to our land,” he said.
Barini said nothing remained of their former workshops when he returned to Syria. He has since resumed production in a rented space in the Ayn Tarma Valley.
“Everything here had been destroyed, and we had nothing left. Now we have started working again in our new workshop and repairing it. We will make our workshop better than before,” he said.
Comparing working conditions when he entered the profession 50 years ago with those of today, Barini said production had become much faster thanks to modern technologies.
“In the early years, we did everything by hand with limited resources. Today, adhesives, modern grinding systems and waterjet technology have made the production process much faster,” he said.
Describing his passion for the craft, Barini said: “I feel happy when I touch marble.”
He added that he felt unwell when he was away from his work and would continue producing art for as long as his strength allowed.
“I am very happy when I work. When I am away from my work, I cannot feel that happiness. When I do not work, I feel ill. Thanks be to God, I will continue my profession as long as I have the strength and can breathe,” he said.
‘Syria never left us’
Basil Barini, who began learning marble and mosaic art alongside his father in Damascus at the age of 10, said his family never abandoned its determination to preserve the craft despite the destruction caused by the war.
Having grown up in a profession with deep roots in Syria, Basil was also forced to leave the country after the conflict began. His family sought refuge in Türkiye, while he spent some time in Russia before reuniting with his relatives in Türkiye.
During their years in Türkiye, the family completed major domestic and international projects. Basil said they worked on a hippodrome project in Izmir and produced artworks for major U.S. and Canadian companies operating in Türkiye.
They also created custom designs tailored to Turkish tastes. Basil learned Turkish and became familiar with the country’s culture, producing numerous mosaic portraits, including those of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, which attracted considerable attention.
Reflecting on the family’s return, Basil said their hope of going home had never faded despite the hardships of war.
“The war forced us to leave our homes, but Syria never left us. It always remained in our hearts. No matter how much time passed, we dreamed of returning to our homeland. This is our country, and whatever happened, we were going to come back,” he said.
Basil said the family viewed mosaic art as more than a means of earning a living, using their works to convey social suffering and historical events to future generations.
Their panels have addressed a range of subjects, from Jerusalem and the Palestinian issue to the revolution in Syria, boats carrying migrants and the experiences of refugee children.
Basil thanked the Turkish people and government for the hospitality and support the family received during their years in Türkiye.
He said working alongside Turkish artisans had fostered close ties between the two communities.
“I am very happy to work alongside Turkish masters and to teach this art at the Damascus Museum. This profession has helped establish very beautiful and deep-rooted friendships between the Turkish and Syrian peoples,” he said.
Emphasizing the importance of passing mosaic art on to future generations, Basil said the family’s main goal was to help the craft flourish in both countries, create employment opportunities for young artisans and contribute to the economies of Türkiye and Syria.

Albanian artist Xhenetta Kadillari marveled at the mosque’s architecture, calling it a magnificent historical landmark. She described Selimiye as the defining highlight of her first trip to Edirne and expressed a strong desire to return.

Türkiye to open 10 new-generation libraries in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:32:23 UTC
14:32:23 KST

This photo shows the study area of the Rami Library in İstanbul.
Türkiye plans to open 10 new-generation libraries, digitize 20,000 manuscripts and rare works and restore 1,100 historical items in 2027 as part of efforts to expand access to knowledge and preserve the country’s cultural heritage.
A government program aims to transform libraries from facilities primarily used to store and lend books into spaces where knowledge is produced and shared and people can socialize.
Since 2018, construction has been completed on 29 new-generation library buildings, while 616 libraries have been renovated and equipped with modern facilities. Türkiye currently has more than 1,300 public libraries, with a combined indoor area exceeding 777,000 square meters and seating capacity for 160,000 people.
As of 2025, public libraries held 26.1 million books and had 7.2 million registered members, serving 39.2 million users. In 2027, authorities also plan to complete construction of 12 libraries, functionally restructure another 12 and open two new cultural centers.
The Presidency of Manuscripts Institution of Türkiye holds 811,527 manuscripts and rare printed works documenting the intellectual heritage of Islamic and Turkish-Islamic history. Since 2012, the institution has added 27,201 manuscripts and rare printed works to its collections through acquisitions. The digitization rate of materials held in manuscript libraries has reached 93 percent.
Under the 2027 program, authorities aim to create digital archives of 20,000 manuscripts and rare works and restore 1,100 items. They also plan to acquire 4,000 additional manuscripts and rare printed works through purchases and donations from public and private collections in Türkiye and abroad.
The program further envisages publishing 45 classical works from the Turkish-Islamic literary tradition, preparing detailed bibliographic records for 27,000 items and organizing 251 cultural and scientific events on manuscripts and rare works at national and international levels.

Türkiye marks republic’s 103rd anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:31:30 UTC
14:31:30 KST

Hundreds of thousands of people from across Türkiye flocked to Anıtkabir, the mausoleum of the republic’s founder, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, from the early hours of Oct. 29 to commemorate the 103rd anniversary of the founding of the Turkish Republic.
The republic was proclaimed on Oct. 29, 1923, following a nearly four-year-long War of Independence.
On the evening of Oct. 28, 1923, Ataütrk invited his close associates to a dinner at Çankaya Mansion in Ankara.
Recounting the evening in his seminal work “Nutuk,” Atatürk later recalled telling those gathered: “Tomorrow, we shall proclaim the republic.”
More than a century later, Republic Day continues to be celebrated across the country with widespread enthusiasm, featuring children’s performances, official ceremonies and receptions, as well as a host of cultural and commemorative events.
“Türkiye is not only preserving its stability at a difficult time marked by wars, conflicts and crises in our immediate neighborhood and in different parts of the world, but is also assuming responsibility for resolving disputes,” President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said in a video message marking the anniversary.
“I am pleased to state that Türkiye is stronger today than it was yesterday. God willing, tomorrow it will be much stronger, enjoy greater international standing and wield considerably more influence in every field,” he added.
Erdoğan visited Anıtkabir as part of the Republic Day commemorations and hosted a reception at the Presidential Complex in Ankara.
The Turkish Naval Forces, meanwhile, marked the occasion with visits by 29 vessels to 29 ports, where the ships will be opened to public visits.
A series of events befitting the republic’s 103-year legacy also took place in the capital, including concerts by the Mehteran, the traditional Ottoman military band; the Turkish Armed Forces Harmony and Music Band; and military band units.
Meanwhile, celebrations have been underway in cities across the country since the beginning of the week.
In Samsun, the Black Sea province where Atatürk launched the national liberation struggle in 1919, students marched on Oct. 28 carrying a Turkish flag measuring 1,919 meters in length, symbolizing the year the struggle began.
Elsewhere, 45 horse riders from across Türkiye embarked on a two-day journey along the 95-kilometer İstiklal Road, a historic route used during the War of Independence to transport weapons and ammunition from the Black Sea port of İnebolu into Anatolia.
Another major running event took place on Oct. 29 on the Osmangazi Bridge, which spans the Gulf of İzmit and connects its two shores.

Spain begins mourning period after deadly train crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:31:16 UTC
14:31:16 KST

Spain has begun three days of mourning to commemorate the 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision as hospitals continue to treat dozens of injured passengers and relatives wait for news of their loved ones.
The trains – one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo – were heading from Madrid on Wednesday to the southern region of Andalucía on the same line when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.
Officials said on Wednesday another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition.
The deadly crash came 10 months after 46 people were killed and dozens more injured when two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s large, modern high-speed rail network after the transport minister, Óscar Puente, said rear-end collisions such as Wednesday’s were “highly unlikely”, and suggested the accident could have been caused by human error under “inexplicable” circumstances.
He said the LZB signalling system, which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied, had gone down at about 8.30am local time owing to a computer malfunction. As a result, an estimated six trains had been halted along a stretch of about 63km of track, Puente added.
The task of monitoring the rail lines then fell to a 24-hour command centre in Madrid. Minutes after the computer malfunction, the centre instructed at least two of the trains to continue as normal, despite the fact that there was still a “stop signal” in place, the minister added.
“It was the control centre, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he said. “Clearly, it was a wrong decision.”
Emergency services combed the wreckage through the night to find more victims, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes. At daybreak, police once again launched drones to survey the crash site. One more body was found overnight, bringing the death toll to 69.
Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on Thursday morning that rescue teams did not think they would find any more bodies in one damaged carriage that was still overturned, but added that body parts had been found that would need to be identified.
“Yesterday we experienced a catastrophe that without a doubt has left all of Spain in shock,” said García-Page. He confirmed that 50 of the people who had been taken to hospitals in the region were still being treated.
The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, speaking during a visit to the emergency command centre in the city of Toledo, said the authorities were doing all they could to establish the cause of the crash and prevent another rail tragedy.
“I’d like to let all Spaniards know that every institution that is part of the state – from the smallest municipality to the government of Spain – is working day and night, not only to provide a response to the families of the victims, but also, of course, to uncover every last detail of this tragedy and to strengthen safety measures so that something like this never happens again.”
Meanwhile, train drivers in Spain went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety after what was Europe’s deadliest train accident since a 2013 derailment in Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain that killed 80 people.
The Guardia Civil police force has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid. The force said 64 people had been reported missing by relatives by Thursday morning.
A school in Urda, which lies about 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, has been turned into an information centre where relatives can inquire about loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who had arrived, some of them in tears.
Carmen García, a Red Cross psychologist, said “long and hard hours” lay ahead and that “every person will manage it in their own way”. She added: “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated.”
José Miguel Fernández, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims’ families.
“It is important for relatives to find their loved ones, even if they have died, because the grieving process is quicker when you have been able to say goodbye at that final moment,” he told Onda Cero radio.
Survivors have spoken of being thrown from their seats by the impact of the crash, and of trying to help the injured in the immediate aftermath.
The first victims to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia Civil officer, José Manuel Chacón. The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues.
Spanish media said missing people included a former minister for the conservative People’s party (PP) and several foreigners, who were thought to be on holiday in Spain.
The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.

Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente says a technical failure and a possible breach of safety procedures are being investigated following Wednesday’s collision between two high-speed trains that killed at least 68 people.
Speaking at a press conference, Puente said a technical fault had automatically stopped rail traffic on the affected section of track.
However, a high-speed train operated by Renfe, Spain’s national railway company, was subsequently allowed to continue despite a red signal, Reuters reported.
Puente said the authorization should never have been given and that investigators were examining who was responsible for the decision.
“The decision to resume traffic while the system had not been restored lies with the control center, and the control center made that decision to resume traffic under circumstances that from our point of view are incomprehensible,” he said, according to Reuters.
The minister’s comments suggest investigators are examining both the technical malfunction and the decision to allow trains to resume operating before the system was restored.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez also addressed the accident, promising a thorough investigation into its causes.
“If there has been any negligence, it will come to light, and if there have been errors in the safety system, it will be dealt with with the utmost firmness,” Sánchez said, according to The Guardian.
At least 68 people died when the two high-speed trains collided Wednesday morning.
The accident follows another deadly collision in January, when two high-speed trains crashed near Adamuz in the southern Spanish region of Andalusia.
That accident killed 46 people and injured more than 120 others.
Both collisions occurred this year on the railway route connecting Madrid and Seville.

Albania introduces heavy fines for protesters amid violent anti-government demonstrations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:30:47 UTC
14:30:47 KST

Albania has introduced new penalties for protesters as weeks of demonstrations demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation continue to escalate in the capital, Tirana.
On Wednesday, Rama’s government adopted measures allowing authorities to fine people who remain in crowds where violence or looting occurs, even if they are not directly involved.
Individuals who conceal their identities during demonstrations can also face penalties.
Fines can reach 500,000 Albanian lek, approximately 41,000 DKK, compared with an average monthly salary of less than 7,000 DKK.
Police have also been given powers to temporarily restrict gatherings in areas where they believe violence could occur.
The measures took effect Wednesday but require parliamentary approval within 45 days to remain in force.
Albania has experienced months of anti-government protests, initially sparked in late May by plans to construct luxury hotels in a coastal nature reserve.
The demonstrations were initially peaceful but expanded in mid-October to include concerns about suspected corruption, shortcomings in healthcare and limited opportunities for young people.
Protesters have since gathered daily in Tirana, with recent demonstrations resulting in violent confrontations with security forces.
Authorities estimate that the protests have caused damage exceeding 2 million euros since mid-October, while more than 350 people have been injured in clashes.
Rama said Sunday that the new measures were inspired by French legislation allowing protesters to be held financially responsible for damage caused during demonstrations.
The prime minister has also repeatedly blamed what he calls “foreign actors” for contributing to the unrest, accusing Iran and Russia of spreading misinformation online.

Direct flights from Copenhagen to Ilulissat cleared as Greenland airport opens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:30:41 UTC
14:30:41 KST

Travelers heading to western Greenland will no longer need to change planes in Nuuk after aviation authorities approved the opening of Ilulissat’s expanded airport on Thursday.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority granted final safety approval overnight, following inspections and a test flight.
“Following a long series of inspections and a test flight, we have approved that the airport meets the necessary level of safety required to operate a modern, international airport,” said deputy director Lars Korsholm.
The approval comes with temporary restrictions during the airport’s initial operating period. These will gradually be eased as the airport gains experience.
Korsholm said the restrictions were unlikely to affect scheduled flights, particularly outside the tourist season.
The airport’s runway has been extended from 845 meters to 2,200 meters, allowing larger aircraft to land in Ilulissat, a town on Greenland’s western coast near Disko Bay.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen had to connect through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.
Initially, Air Greenland will generally operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday, with additional weekly departures during busy periods, including Christmas and New Year.
Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.
The expansion forms part of a multibillion-krone investment in Greenland’s airports, which also includes improvements in Nuuk and a new airport near Qaqortoq in southern Greenland.
The projects aim to improve transport connections and support economic development, particularly through increased tourism.
Police announce stop-and-search zone for Copenhagen derby

PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Written Danish exam grades fall across Denmark’s upper secondary programs
Grades in written Danish have fallen across Denmark’s upper secondary education programs, according to the latest exam results released by the Education Ministry on Thursday.
At general upper secondary schools, known as stx, the average grade in A-level Danish, the highest subject level, fell from 6.8 in 2018 to 6.2 in 2026.
Across upper secondary programs, grades declined both compared with last year and over the longer term.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.

Five Danish municipalities agree to take additional Ukrainian refugees
Five municipalities in Jutland have volunteered to accommodate more Ukrainian refugees than their allocated share, offering some relief to municipalities facing pressure elsewhere in Denmark.
Haderslev, Horsens, Skive, Struer and Viborg will receive a combined 133 additional refugees, according to the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Viborg will take the largest share, with 65 additional arrivals, while Skive will accommodate 18.
Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov, from the Social Democrats, welcomed the decision, noting that Copenhagen and municipalities in its western suburbs are particularly stretched.
“It is a shared task to ensure that the Ukrainians who come to Denmark also gain a proper foothold in our local communities,” Bødskov said.
The announcement comes as the government seeks to restrict residence permits for displaced Ukrainians arriving from 14 areas it considers less affected by the war.
Parliament has already passed legislation excluding Ukrainian men aged 23 to 60 from obtaining residence under a special law, aiming to prevent them from avoiding military mobilization.
Several Jutland municipalities previously offered to accept additional refugees, citing available accommodation and demand for workers.
However, only Skive proceeded among the five municipalities that initially expressed interest.
Brønderslev requested additional funding, which Bødskov rejected, saying municipalities willing to help must operate under existing financial arrangements.
More than 47,000 Ukrainian refugees currently live in Denmark, compared with the 100,000 arrivals authorities prepared for in 2022.
Despite the lower number, Bødskov said pressure on municipalities justified tighter admission rules.
He acknowledged the difficulties involved while emphasizing Denmark’s continued military, civilian and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine.
Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.
Ukrainian embassy disputes Danish lawmaker’s claim of unanswered meeting request
A disagreement has emerged between Ukraine’s embassy in Copenhagen and independent Danish lawmaker Jacob Harris over attempts to arrange a meeting ahead of his planned talks with Russia’s ambassador.
In a written statement to Ritzau, Denmark’s news agency, the embassy said it had offered Harris two possible meeting dates but received no reply.
“We were surprised to hear these claims from Member of Parliament Jacob Harris,” the embassy said.
“After receiving an email from Jacob Harris requesting a meeting, we suggested two possible dates to him in the near future. However, we have not received any response.”
Harris maintains that he never received the embassy’s reply but said he was “glad that contact has been made”.
“Now I will write to them again with a view to arranging a meeting,” he said.
The embassy also stated that Harris had visited twice without an appointment, hoping to meet the ambassador.
On both occasions, the ambassador was attending previously scheduled events and was not at the embassy.
Harris confirmed the visits, saying he had hoped to arrange a meeting.
The disagreement follows Harris’ announcement Thursday that he plans to meet Russia’s ambassador in Copenhagen on November 10.
In a Facebook post, Harris called for “more diplomacy, more dialogue, and less war rhetoric”.
The planned meeting drew criticism from politicians across Denmark’s political spectrum.
Harris also wrote that he had repeatedly contacted Ukraine’s ambassador without receiving a response.
He now hopes to meet the Ukrainian ambassador before his scheduled meeting with Russia’s representative.
The Ukrainian embassy expressed appreciation for Danish political support and thanked the Danish public for its continued solidarity with Ukraine.
Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.
The group reported a third-quarter profit after tax of 397 million DKK.
Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”
Putin adviser says Frederiksen deserves to lose Greenland
Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian envoy involved in negotiations over the war in Ukraine and an adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin on economic and international affairs, said Tuesday that Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen deserves to lose Greenland.
Dmitriev made the comment in a post on the social media platform X, alongside a video in which Frederiksen criticized Finnish and Norwegian leaders for speaking by phone with Putin.
“She (Mette Frederiksen, ed.) deserves to lose Greenland. The warmongers will lose. Dialogue will prevail,” Dmitriev wrote.

The call received a mixed response from the countries’ allies. Frederiksen was among those who criticized the decision to speak with the Russian president.

“I think one should keep Europe together instead of going solo,” she added.

“Holding talks that risk dividing the European voice, that is risky,” he said Tuesday, according to Swedish media.
Støre later rejected the criticism, saying the talks were conducted with other countries’ knowledge.
