Our independent reporting can only be published with support from our readers.
The University of Copenhagen (KU) shut down several administrative systems Monday after another cyberattack, just days after hackers gained access to personal information belonging to approximately 525,000 people.
The university confirmed the latest attack on its website, reporting disruptions to several administrative systems and difficulties accessing university websites on Monday evening.
The previous breach exposed personal information including full names, CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers, work and private telephone numbers, and private email addresses.
The university has not provided further details about Monday’s attack.
Denmark’s Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization, Christina Egelund of Moderaterne (the Moderates), expressed serious concern about the repeated incidents.
“It is the second time in a short period, and it does not become less serious that it comes in the wake of several attacks on our universities,” she told Ritzau.
Several Danish universities, including the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and Aarhus University, have also experienced cyberattacks in recent weeks.
Egelund said the incidents highlighted the seriousness of the security situation.
“It is an attack on our knowledge institutions, which are an absolutely crucial pillar of society in Denmark,” she said.
The minister summoned leaders from Denmark’s eight universities to a meeting Monday to discuss cybersecurity.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, explained that universities hold large amounts of personal and research data, making them attractive targets.
Their public visibility also increases their exposure to cyber threats.
“That makes us potential targets for both cybercriminals, foreign states, and activist groups,” he said in an Aarhus University press release.
New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news
A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.
Editor-in-chief Michael Dyrby describes the content as AI-assisted rather than fully automated.
Human editors select stories, determine their angles, review AI-generated drafts, make revisions and choose images before publication.
“We could have made it so that AI did everything. But it doesn’t,” Dyrby said.
AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.
The aim is to produce more journalism with fewer resources while maintaining editorial control.
“We will find out,” Dyrby said, describing Projekt Y as an experiment in journalism’s future.
Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.
Its target audience is primarily adults aged 28 to around 60.
Dyrby, who graduated from the Danish School of Journalism in 1989, previously helped launch TV 2 News in the mid-2000s.
Projekt Y has received media subsidies and will also generate revenue through advertising.
Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.
“The ambition is to create a technology that is so simple that everyone can use it and create their own media outlet, and in that way help democratize the use of media,” Dyrby said.
Additional publications are planned throughout the remainder of this year and into 2027.
Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.
Danish publisher bans AI tools for work on manuscripts
Danish publisher Lindhardt og Ringhof has prohibited employees and external partners from using artificial intelligence to complete work for the company.
The ban applies to proofreaders, editors, manuscript readers and consultants, according to a letter distributed by the publisher.
“It is not permitted for any purpose to use AI tools for tasks that one as an external partner solves for Lindhardt og Ringhof,” the letter states.
Manuscripts and other documents provided by the publisher must not be uploaded to AI systems under any circumstances.
The company said even apparently harmless uses, such as asking AI to summarize a manuscript, could create legal and copyright risks.
“Texts that are uploaded into AI tools can subsequently be copied and data mined, even if the provider claims otherwise,” the publisher said.
Literary director Sune de Souza Schmidt-Madsen told Danish public broadcaster DR that Lindhardt og Ringhof was not aware of external partners already using AI for its assignments.
However, he said the publisher expected the issue to emerge eventually and wanted to establish its rules in advance.
The restrictions also apply to the publisher’s own employees, Schmidt-Madsen said.
Denmark issues safety guidance for vulnerable people after CPR data leak
The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.
The agency also recommends considering contact with police, a crisis center, the Danish Stalking Center or another specialized counseling service.
People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.
Power fault causes train delays and cancellations across Zealand
Passengers should expect longer travel times on most train services across Zealand because of a power fault at Copenhagen Central Station.
Three tracks at the station were without traction power Monday morning, DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, said.
The fault caused several cancellations and reduced services between Copenhagen Central Station and Næstved via Køge.
“Banedanmark is working on resolving the fault,” DSB wrote on X.
Banedanmark is the state agency responsible for maintaining Denmark’s railway infrastructure.
Danish traffic service P4 Trafik reported at 10:50 a.m. that trains at Copenhagen Central Station had temporarily stopped because of the missing power.
Services were expected to resume shortly, although passengers would continue to experience delays and occasional cancellations.
Copenhagen’s S-train network was not affected and continued to operate normally.
Strong winds and high water to ease as calmer weather reaches Denmark
Denmark’s week will begin with strong winds and elevated coastal water levels before calmer and sunnier conditions arrive around Thursday.
The strongest winds Monday morning were along Jutland’s west coast between Blåvandshuk and Skagen, Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Mette Zhang said.
Some areas continued to experience storm-force gusts, although the wind was expected to weaken during the day.
DMI maintained warnings for elevated water levels around the Wadden Sea, the central western coast of Jutland and parts of the Limfjord.
Water levels in the Wadden Sea reached more than three meters above normal overnight but were beginning to fall.
Western Denmark will experience the most clouds Monday, while eastern areas will have clearer conditions. Showers are expected in several places before conditions improve later in the day.
Temperatures will range from 9 to 13 degrees Celsius.
A new front will bring clouds, rain and stronger southerly winds overnight into Tuesday. Winds could reach gale force along the west coast, although less rain is expected than during the weekend.
Wednesday will bring a mixture of rain, showers and sunshine.
A high-pressure system is expected to stabilize the weather from Thursday, bringing less wind, drier conditions and more sunshine.
Fog may form overnight into Thursday and Friday. Clearer skies will also increase the risk of overnight frost, particularly heading into Saturday.
Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.
Danish Crown confirms slaughter without stunning at Polish subsidiary
Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.
The practice occurs on a limited basis at a slaughterhouse in Tarnow in southeastern Poland, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.
The method is legal in Poland but has been prohibited in Denmark since 2014, when prior stunning became mandatory.
Danish Crown said the Polish facility slaughtered 69,000 cattle in 2025. The company said only “a minority” were slaughtered using the kosher method but declined to provide a specific number.
Several animal welfare organizations criticized the company’s involvement.
Søren Kent Pedersen, a veterinarian with animal welfare organization Dyrenes Beskyttelse, described the practice as animal cruelty and accused Danish Crown of hypocrisy because the company publicly emphasizes animal welfare.
Danish Crown’s website states that “good animal welfare is the core of our business” and that the company protects animals’ well-being from farms through slaughter.
Sokolow chief executive Przemyslaw Gostkiewicz said Poland has a particular tradition of kosher slaughter that allows Jewish people to follow their dietary rules.
“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.
Danish Crown did not say whether it would continue permitting the practice.
Parents urged to check children’s electric scooters after illegal riding cases
Danish road safety authorities are urging parents to check electric scooters used by their children after police stopped underage riders and scooters capable of greatly exceeding the legal speed limit.
Riders must be at least 15 years old to use an electric scooter alone in traffic. Scooters may travel no faster than 20 kilometers per hour, and helmets are mandatory.
Children under 15 may ride in traffic only when accompanied by an adult.
The Danish Road Safety Council identified 21 reported cases between September 13 and October 13 involving children who were too young or scooters that could travel too fast.
The figure came from media coverage and police reports rather than a complete national count.
Children as young as nine were stopped, while some scooters could reach speeds of up to 90 kilometers per hour.
“Parents should take it seriously and check the rules before saying yes to an electric scooter,” council chief executive Jakob Bøving Arendt said.
Emergency departments in Odense and Svendborg have treated 811 people injured in electric scooter accidents since 2021. Twenty-five percent suffered serious injuries.
Odense University Hospital physician Jens Lauritsen said crashes can cause severe injuries even at legal speeds.
Modified scooters capable of traveling 60, 80 or 100 kilometers per hour could endanger both riders and others, he said.
Denmark to cull 27,000 turkeys after bird flu outbreak on Lolland
Danish authorities will cull 27,000 turkeys Monday after highly pathogenic avian influenza was detected in a flock in Stokkemarke on the island of Lolland.
It is Denmark’s second confirmed outbreak of the highly contagious disease within one week, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration said.
Another outbreak was identified Friday in a flock in Bøgelunde in Slagelse Municipality.
“It is therefore extra important at this time of year that everyone who keeps poultry or other birds does everything to prevent contact between their animals and wild birds,” agency veterinarian Mette Kirkeskov Sie said.
Owners should prevent wild birds from reaching their animals, drinking water and feed. The agency also recommends changing footwear before entering areas where birds are kept.
Authorities have established protection and surveillance zones around the infected flock on Lolland. Poultry owners within those areas must follow stricter disease control requirements.
The restrictions will remain until authorities complete their investigations and determine that the risk of further transmission has declined.
The agency said avian influenza only very rarely spreads to humans.
However, people should avoid touching sick, weakened or dead wild birds.
Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.
Queen Margrethe receives medal for 25 years of design work at Tivoli
Queen Margrethe has received a 25th anniversary medal recognizing her work as a costume and set designer for Copenhagen’s Tivoli Gardens.
Tivoli chief executive Susanne Mørch Koch presented the medal during a private ceremony at Fredensborg Palace.
“Queen Margrethe has had a truly exceptional significance for Tivoli’s performing arts,” Koch said.
The former Danish monarch has contributed to nine productions at Tivoli during the past 25 years.
Seven were staged at the Pantomime Theatre, while two appeared in Tivoli’s Concert Hall.
Her first production was Hans Christian Andersen’s “Love in the Dustbin” in 2001, for which she created costumes, scenery and an interpretation of the story.
“Queen Margrethe’s contribution has become part of Tivoli’s cultural heritage,” Koch said.
Margrethe has also contributed costumes and set designs to a new production of “The Nutcracker,” opening at Tivoli’s Concert Hall on November 26.
Three ballet dancers were honored during the ceremony. Tori Cooper and Allan Clausen marked 25 years at Tivoli, while Tommy Edvardsen celebrated 50 years at the Pantomime Theatre.
All three have performed in productions involving Margrethe, including “The Tinderbox,” “The Swineherd” and “Cinderella.”
Margrethe, 86, became Denmark’s monarch in 1972 and abdicated in favor of her son, King Frederik, on January 14, 2024.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Denmark delays new citizenship screening model – what it means for applicants
The expert group tasked with examining the possibilities for a screening model for citizenship applicants is facing further delays in its work.
The Ministry of Immigration and Integration writes this in a press release.
– Due to the scope and complexity of the work, we cannot manage to deliver our recommendations around the turn of the year. Instead, I expect that we will conclude our work in mid-March next year, says Henrik Thomassen, chairman of the expert group, in the press release.
The granting of citizenship in particular has taken up a significant amount of the political debate recently.
Most recently, the Danish People’s Party entered the debate because the party wants a Pakistani man removed from an upcoming bill that next year will make 2,055 foreigners Danish citizens.
DF’s citizenship spokesperson, Mikkel Bjørn, has found a Facebook post from 2016 in which the man, according to DF, supported an Islamic execution.
– The government should strip him of the opportunity to obtain citizenship. If they are not willing to do that, they must at the very least be willing to let us meet this man eye-to-eye so we can see the matter for ourselves, Mikkel Bjørn told DR on Thursday.
Last week, Liberal Alliance found a woman who, according to the party, has repeatedly praised Hamas and the former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Therefore, the party wants the person summoned for an interview with the Folketing’s Naturalisation Committee.
The central element in the debate regarding a bill granting citizenship to 2,055 new individuals has been whether they have been sufficiently investigated for anti-democratic views.
Every six months, a bill is introduced in the Folketing granting new individuals Danish citizenship after an often lengthy and comprehensive application process.
This also applied to the then SVM government.
But the latest granting of citizenship coincided with the calling of the general election held in March of this year, and the bill regarding the citizenship of the 2,055 individuals was therefore postponed.
A screening model must be created for people who apply for Danish citizenship to investigate whether they have anti-democratic views. The government announced this earlier in October.
However, the government has ultimately decided that it will introduce the bill before a screening model is ready.
The original bill had its first reading in the Folketing on 5 February, but three weeks later Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen (S) called a general election.
The expert group was established in 2025 and was initially given ten months to complete its work.

Country diary: A new chapter for the farm – we’re going organic | Andrea Meanwell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:30:23 UTC
14:30:23 KST

From 1 November we have change happening on our farm. We have decided to become an organic farm and have started the two-year conversion process with the Soil Association. We’ve always run the farm on organic principles, but now, with our small shop selling our beef, lamb and pork, we’ve decided that we will convert, prioritising soil health and biodiversity without the use of chemicals.
It has historically been tricky for hill farms to go organic because many are on commons with shared grazing and no physical boundaries between “hefts”, and with shared routes to and from the fell. Now the certifiers are keen to be flexible and adapt, so we have decided to give it a go. The process is funded by the government’s sustainable farming incentive scheme, which we were lucky to get into this year as so many farmers missed out.
Practically it will mean more record-keeping, vet permission needed for dipping sheep and longer withdrawal periods on many medicines. When we plant trees, we will need to source organic trees, or ask for a derogation if they’re not available. It will be the culmination of the change in our farming system, from the conventional upland beef and sheep farm we bought in 2018, to a regenerative model where biodiversity is considered something we produce as a public good. It would also be very unusual here – the north-west has only 2.4% of the UK’s organic land.
It’s a challenge, but it’s something we want to do as my son’s wife’s family farm has become organic and it has worked well for them. What we’re hoping to achieve for the farm is to increase biodiversity, produce quality breeding stock that can thrive outside all year without any additional inputs, produce food for local people to buy direct from the farm, and allow people to visit and understand the farmed landscape. It will be a talking point on future farm walks as well.
Our latest batch of beef will be in the farm shop for Christmas. It won’t be certified organic this year, but in future years we hope it will.

The Human Shelter Documentary Asks What Makes a Home from Japan to Uganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The Human Shelter: Expedition into What Makes a Home is an exploration of the feeling of home. Directed by Boris Bertram and funded by IKEA, the film looks at present ways of living in Norway, Iraq, the United States, Nigeria, Japan, Uganda, and Iceland, interrogating the role of home in order to project it into the future. Through imagery and personal narratives, the documentary connects the concept of home with landscape, movement and settling, time, migration and security, vulnerability, and nature. How do displaced populations create a home? When does a shelter become a home? Portraits, stories, and shelters across four continents give viewers a glimpse of an answer to these big questions in a one-hour film tour.
Over more than two years, Boris Bertram traveled to nine countries to collect place-based perspectives on creating shelters and feeling at home. Part of the aim was to build an idea of home for the future, in the face of climate change, globalization, and migration. Two realizations emerged from this process: everyone has the ability to speak poetically about home, and poetry becomes a source of empowerment. Through the cinematography of Henrik Bohn Ipsen and Adam Philp, viewers can appreciate a variety of landscapes and gain insight into challenging geographical circumstances and contexts of isolation, remote living, and city life.
The film's method was inspired by Danish poet and filmmaker Jørgen Leth's approach and what he called "the presence of coincidence." Locations are chosen to surprise the audience; every chapter has a central story, and every contributor is invited to express their feelings and thoughts on home and belonging. The film's seven chapters show the views of Sean Anderson, curator at MoMA in New York; Elle Marja Eira, a Sámi nomad and artist from Finnmark; Kim Bindsted, a professor at the HI-SEAS Mars habitat, a NASA-funded research project; Suhad, a 13-year-old poet from the UNHCR refugee camp in Kurdistan, Iraq; Johan Karlsson, a designer of refugee shelters at Better Shelter; Yuri, a female art photographer from Tokyo; Andri Snær Magnason, an Icelandic writer; and Godfrey Kato, an environmental activist from Uganda.
Related Article
Schools at the Border: How Architecture Supports Learning in Conditions of Displacement
 For me, documentary filmmaking is very much about people and about what it means to be human. Through my many journeys into conflict zones, I finally got the idea for a film exploring how we create homes on the edge of the world, where the world is most challenged by climate change, migration, and a lack of resources. And in that way, gather new knowledge about how we can create better homes in the future. ― Director Boris Bertram
Boris Bertram is a Danish filmmaker, producer, and educator based at Zentropa Film in Copenhagen. His filmography centers on conflict resolution and humanitarianism, in contexts of war, natural disaster, migration, and displacement. In addition to The Human Shelter, he has directed the award-winning films The Photographer of War, Bush, Blair and Fogh – The War Campaign, and Tankograd. His work is supported by the Danish Arts Foundation and, beyond film, includes video installations and documentary series. He is the showrunner, director, and scriptwriter of the Nordic documentary series Putin's Shadow War (2023), produced by DR, NRK, SVT, and YLE.
 It is interesting, because a shelter is our first concept of home. A physical place where, first and foremost, we as human beings need to feel safe and secure. Under extreme living conditions, the body itself can become our shelter. For example, a homeless person lying on the bare ground will often use their body to shield themselves from their surroundings and from nature, and will lie in the foetal position. ― Director Boris Bertram
The Human Shelter, an exploration of what makes a home, was screened at MoMA in New York in 2020 and presented by UN-Habitat as part of its global "Housing for All" campaign in 193 countries. Can Turkiye’s Libya breakthrough reshape Eastern Mediterranean diplomacy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:29:20 UTC
14:29:20 KST

Can Turkiye’s Libya breakthrough reshape Eastern Mediterranean diplomacy?
Ankara wins backing from former adversaries in Libya for its maritime border agreement, but competing claims present new diplomatic tests.
Istanbul, Turkiye – Once adversaries, Turkiye and the leadership of eastern Libya are now building closer political and military ties. Ankara has also repaired relations with Egypt in the past few years after previous hostility, but a maritime dispute is testing how far those reconciliations can go.
On Wednesday, Turkiye’s Ministry of National Defence renewed its offer to sign a maritime boundary agreement with Cairo, arguing that Egypt could gain more than 15,000sq km (5,790sq miles) of maritime jurisdiction – a figure that is Ankara’s estimate – compared with a potential further agreement with Greece, with which Cairo signed a partial maritime deal in 2020.
The offer came eight days after Libya’s eastern-based parliament in Tobruk reversed years of opposition and approved a maritime agreement signed between its rival, the internationally recognised government based in the Libyan capital, Tripoli, and Turkiye in 2019.
The agreement delineates maritime jurisdiction areas claimed by Turkiye and Libya in the Mediterranean, but Greece, Cyprus and Egypt argued that it infringes on their sovereign rights while Turkiye maintains that it complies with international law.
A senior Turkish official told Al Jazeera that eastern Libya’s leaders had come to recognise Ankara’s intentions.
“Turkiye is not there to use Libya for its own purposes,” the official said.
“From the very beginning, we have supported a policy of one Libya,” the official added, stressing that the country’s stability and resources should benefit all Libyans.
From confrontation to cooperation
Turkiye helped repel a 2019-2020 offensive on Tripoli by forces loyal to renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, leader of the military forces of the eastern government. Ankara has since expanded its relations with the eastern camp while maintaining ties with Tripoli.
The senior official said Turkish security personnel based in Tripoli had remained in contact with eastern Libyan forces even during the confrontation.
“There has actually been no change in our policy. Only the results it has produced have changed,” the official said.
The diplomatic outreach has been accompanied by military and intelligence contacts.
In May, Defence Minister Yasar Guler met Saddam Haftar, Khalifa Haftar’s son, and Abdulsalam al-Zoubi, a senior defence official in the Tripoli-based government.
Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin also met Saddam Haftar in Benghazi on June 23. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan followed in August, meeting both Khalifa and Saddam Haftar.
A change in Libya’s eastern parliamentary leadership also preceded the maritime vote. On October 6, lawmakers replaced Aguila Saleh as parliament speaker with Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi, who previously chaired the Libyan-Turkish parliamentary friendship committee.
Galip Dalay, a senior research fellow at Chatham House, sees Ankara’s engagement with its former adversaries as a strategic gain.
“This is not merely a pragmatic or tactical gain. It is a strategic gain for Turkiye,” he told Al Jazeera.
Dalay argued that closer relations with both Libyan camps make it harder to establish Eastern Mediterranean energy and security arrangements that exclude Turkiye.
What does eastern Libya gain?
The rapprochement also reflects political calculations within the Haftar camp.
Tarek Megerisi, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Saddam Haftar hopes Ankara’s influence could strengthen his own political prospects with many believing that he eventually wants to lead Libya.
The senior Turkish official said Ankara had made no specific political commitments to eastern Libyan officials beyond general principles and cooperation that would also benefit Libya.
Representatives of both Libyan camps held talks in Ankara on Friday about unifying their military structures, according to Libyan media reports. Differences over political oversight remain unresolved, and no final agreement has been announced.
But Anas El Gomati, director of the Sadeq Institute, cautioned that an understanding between Libya’s rival leaders would not necessarily produce an inclusive political settlement.
“An elite bargain between two camps can leave out everyone beyond them,” he said.
Egypt: The diplomatic balancing act
The Libyan eastern parliament’s reversal has also complicated Egypt’s position. Cairo has traditionally supported the eastern leadership but opposes the maritime agreement it has now endorsed.
On October 22, Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis announced discussions with Egypt on extending their partial 2020 maritime delimitation agreement eastwards towards Cyprus.
Four days later, Egypt joined Greece, Cyprus, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union in a statement at the United Nations rejecting the Turkiye-Libya accord.
Yet Cairo and Ankara have continued rebuilding their relationship.
Turkiye’s land forces commander, General Metin Tokel, arrived in Egypt on Monday for an official visit. The Turkish Defence Ministry has also announced a joint naval exercise in Alexandria from November 4 to 9.
The senior Turkish official told Al Jazeera that Ankara remained open to cooperation on maritime boundaries and energy but would defend what it considers its rights.
“Just as other countries say they will not give up the rights they recognise as their own, the same applies to Turkiye,” the official said.
Fidan has acknowledged Egypt’s concerns and discussed the possibility of cooperation with Italy. The official clarified, however, that no formal four-country negotiating mechanism between Turkiye, Libya, Italy and Egypt has been established.
El Gomati believes Cairo’s ability to influence decisions in eastern Libya has diminished.
“Egypt still has influence, but it no longer has a veto,” he said.
Megerisi, meanwhile, argued that Turkiye’s relationship with Egypt has become too important to sacrifice over the maritime dispute. He sees room for accommodation, potentially involving Italy’s energy company Eni, which has interests in Egypt and Libya.
A breakthrough with limits
Greece maintains that the maritime agreement disregards the rights of its islands, including Crete. Turkiye rejects those claims, arguing that islands should not automatically receive the same weight as mainland coastlines when mapping out maritime boundaries and exclusive economic zones.
Megerisi said the eastern Libyan parliament’s approval strengthens the agreement’s domestic legal footing but does little to resolve the wider dispute between the countries of the Eastern Mediterranean.
“I think both sides are maximalist,” he said.
The parliamentary vote gives Ankara greater political leverage, but it does not settle competing maritime claims or clear the way for offshore energy exploration.
Ankara now wants to build on its gains in Libya and improving ties with Egypt to strengthen its position in the Eastern Mediterranean. Its aim is to develop new partnerships and regional cooperation rather than remain outside arrangements shaped largely by Greece, Cyprus and Israel.
But that will require finding common ground with countries that continue to challenge Turkiye’s maritime claims.
The senior Turkish official said Ankara’s improved relationship with Cairo had opened the door to discussing those differences directly.
“We can now discuss every issue with Egypt, and we will discuss this one too,” the official said. “We do not have to seek the approval or consent of unrelated third countries.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc on Oct. 29 piled pressure on Israeli Arab leaders over unproven accusations of foreign funding, in a push to neuter parties that made strong gains after an otherwise indecisive election.

Some of Eisenkot’s likely partners have ruled out such an alliance but could change their minds to force Netanyahu from office. Another much-debated option among Israelis is a unity government with Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
In response to the new allegations, Eisenkot said he was receiving updates and promised “utmost vigilance” against election interference.

North Korea fired "around a dozen" short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, Seoul's defence ministry said, less than a week after South Korea proposed talks over a growing border row.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said its military detected "around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea", the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
"Our military has stepped up surveillance and vigilance against possible additional launches," it added in its statement.
The Japan Coast Guard separately said that "an object that appears to be a ballistic missile launched from North Korea seems to have already fallen", urging ships to be vigilant.
North Korea has tested a slew of weapons recently, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology.
Thursday's flurry of missiles comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea planted the landmines over a year ago.
Seoul accused Pyongyang of "a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement" and called for the North to return to dialogue.
No response
Pyongyang has since ridiculed South Korean President Lee Jae-myung's overture, with Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of the North's leader, dubbing it "the climax of the farce".
Last week, South Korea proposed military talks with the North to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, but Pyongyang has yet to respond.
The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war, as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
The ratcheting tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to North Korea have raised concerns that Seoul, an ally of Washington, could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving Pyongyang.
In his most recent comments, Trump seemingly downplayed the possibility of a summit while insisting his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un is "very good".
In October, North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested the two might meet this year.

By Satoshi Sugiyama and John Geddie
TOKYO, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Hello Kitty maker Sanrio has cancelled a collaboration with a Japanese TV spy show after a backlash in China, the second incident in days to highlight the tightrope foreign firms and celebrities must walk in the lucrative market.
The Wednesday announcement by Sanrio’s Chinese subsidiary came just after French soccer star Kylian Mbappe apologised for remarks about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong that saw several Chinese sponsors cut ties with him.
The hit show VIVANT, produced by Japanese broadcaster TBS and also available on Netflix, centres on Japanese spies and a terrorist organisation called Tent. The latest season, currently being aired, depicts a fictional Chinese intelligence agency capturing and torturing some of the Japanese spies.
Chinese anger over Sanrio’s range of soft toys, including Hello Kitty, dressed as spies from the show has simmered for days on social media and came to a head this week when Chinese state media ramped up the condemnation.
“We deeply apologize for the concern this has caused everyone,” Sanrio’s Chinese subsidiary said in a statement.
“Regarding this collaboration, we believe it contains expressions that are inconsistent with the corporate philosophy of the Sanrio Group. We have therefore decided to terminate this collaboration along with all subsequent projects and promotional activities.”
TBS did not have immediate comment on the cancellation.
TBS President Masamine Ryuho said at a regular press conference on Wednesday that the drama is “entirely fictional and has no intention of disparaging any specific country”, local media reported.
Relations between China and Japan have plunged since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi late last year said that a hypothetical Chinese attack on democratically ruled Taiwan could trigger a military response from Tokyo.
China has urged its citizens not to travel to Japan and throttled exports of rare earths to the country, minerals vital to the manufacturing of everything from cars to weapons.
Swathes of Japanese firms including Sanrio, however, are still reliant on the world’s second-biggest economy for sales. Sanrio booked sales of 9.8 billion yen ($62 million) in China in the first quarter, up almost 25% on the same period a year earlier.
Foreign brands have often faced public backlash in China. Dolce & Gabbana cancelled a Shanghai fashion show in 2018 after ads showed a Chinese woman struggling to eat pizza and spaghetti with chopsticks. H&M, Nike and Adidas in 2021 came under attack over comments made about labour conditions in Xinjiang.
(Reporting by Satoshi Sugiyama and John Geddie in Tokyo; Editing by Edwina Gibbs)

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung-based AerosoarX Chair Max Lo (羅正方) said Wednesday that the firm signed cooperation memorandums with US companies Rajant and SiMa.ai to develop AI-enabled drones and support local assembly in overseas markets, CNA reported.
Lo, who previously founded Tainan’s Geosat Aerospace, established AerosoarX on April 17. The company showcased a 15-inch foldable drone developed for the US Department of Defense’s Drone Dominance Program at the signing event.
Lo said the Russia-Ukraine war offered important lessons. He added that individual firms could no longer provide all-in-one solutions and should instead form strategic alliances with partners in like-minded countries to speed up development.
Lo said AerosoarX produces about 70% of its components in Taiwan and ships partially assembled drone platforms for final assembly at locations such as Rajant’s plant in Kentucky. He said this approach is more efficient and helps reduce tariff costs.
The company said the partnership combines its drone platforms with Rajant’s communications technology and SiMa.ai’s onboard AI capabilities. The three firms are targeting the Indo-Pacific, Europe, the US, and Japan.
AerosoarX works with Rajant on US military projects, supplying drone subsystems and components. Shipments began in April and May, with assembly and integration expected to be completed in November.
For Japan’s interceptor drone requirements, AerosoarX is helping replace Chinese-made components with alternatives from other countries.
Lo said Ukraine, Poland, and the Czech Republic are proving grounds for drone technologies. AerosoarX is shipping key components and systems to the front lines to ensure they meet operational requirements.
AerosoarX plans to set up production across the first island chain. It aims to ensure supply chain stability, local control over production, and a division of labor among partners.
Regarding the US Department of Defense’s Drone Dominance Program, Lo said AerosoarX had delivered nearly 1,000 drones to the US. He said shipments could reach 10,000 units if the company successfully passes the program’s third-stage evaluation in 2027.

The survey found that 45% of respondents supported Shen, compared with 41% for Chiang, a gap within the poll's margin of error. However, 48% expected Chiang to win reelection, while 35% predicted a victory for Shen, with 30 days remaining before the Nov. 28 local elections.

Meanwhile, 79% of respondents said life in Taipei was generally going well, and half approved of Chiang's performance as mayor, while 37% disapproved and 13% had no opinion.
Shen had stronger support among women and younger voters, while Chiang performed better among older age groups. Among men, 45% supported Chiang and 43% backed Shen, while Shen led Chiang by 9 percentage points among women, with 47% support.
Among voters younger than 40, Shen received 58% support, leading Chiang by 25 percentage points. Chiang led Shen by 1 percentage point among voters aged 40 to 59, with 44% support, and by 6 points among those aged 60 and older.
Among DPP supporters, 91% backed Shen, while 86% of KMT supporters backed Chiang. Among TPP supporters, 75% favored Chiang and 16% supported Shen. Among independent voters, 40% backed Shen, 33% supported Chiang, and 26% remained undecided.
On public image, 46% viewed Shen favorably and 31% unfavorably, compared with 44% and 36% for Chiang. On trustworthiness regarding major policies and personal pledges, 40% considered Chiang more consistent and trustworthy, while 39% trusted Shen more and 21% had no opinion.
Shen also led in voter perceptions of the candidates' visions for Taipei, with 44% finding his proposals more appealing, compared with 28% who favored Chiang's vision. Among voters younger than 40, nearly 60% preferred Shen's vision.
The poll was conducted Oct. 20-22 and Oct. 25, interviewing 1,115 adults registered as Taipei residents, while 264 people declined to participate. The survey had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

Anthropic warns Taiwan conflict could disrupt global AI chip supply
Unknown

05:24:44 UTC
14:24:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Anthropic has warned that a military conflict, blockade, or natural disaster affecting Taiwan could severely disrupt global supplies of advanced chips for years.
The AI company filed for an IPO with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday. Its filing identifies Taiwan’s dominance in advanced semiconductor manufacturing as a risk to its ability to secure the chips needed to develop and operate its AI systems.
Anthropic said the majority of the world’s most advanced chipmaking capacity is concentrated in Taiwan, primarily at TSMC. It warned that “any military conflict, tariffs and trade restrictions, economic coercion, blockade, natural disaster, or other incident affecting Taiwan could severely disrupt the global supply of advanced chips, with effects that could persist for years.”
The company said the nation’s concentration of advanced chip production exposes the global supply chain to earthquakes, typhoons, geopolitical tensions between Taiwan and China, and disruptions to the power grid, water supply, and other critical infrastructure. Efforts to expand advanced chipmaking capacity outside Taiwan, including in the US, remain in the early stages and may not materially reduce risks in the foreseeable future, it said.
Anthropic also disclosed that TSMC has sometimes been unable to meet market demand for chip manufacturing capacity. As a result, the company said it has “not always been able to obtain sufficient quantities of chips on a timely basis.”
The filing said any restrictions or delays affecting advanced chip supplies from Taiwan or TSMC could adversely affect Anthropic’s business, financial condition, and operating results.

Airbus chief Guillaume Faury said on Wednesday that the European plane maker could join a British-Japanese-Italian consortium to build a next generation fighter jet after the collapse of a Franco-German rival.
Airbus represented Germany and Spain in the Franco-German scheme, which failed amid disputes over the design, and Faury said that the German government was now in contact with other countries over possible partnerships.
The Airbus CEO told a media call that joining the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) with Britain, Japan and Italy was a "potential" solution, but there were others.
The three countries have already allocated more than $5.5 billion (€4.7bn) for the jet, aiming to have it in service by 2035. Canada has joined the programme as an observer.
"We are supporting and working closely with the German and the Spanish governments on the future of the next generation fighter", which must be "in Europe and for Europe", Faury said.
"Basically, at Airbus, we continue to believe in the need for a sixth-generation fighter in Europe as a cooperation programme. And we want to be part of that solution for Europe."
Faury said it would be for governments to decide, "ideally not in the too distant future".
Moves to build a Franco-German jet collapsed in June, with Dassault Aviation, which represented France, failing to agree on a design with Airbus and the German military. Dassault is now going it alone with the French state to build a jet to replace the Rafale.

Judge rejects Trump effort to block California ‘noncitizen’ ballots

05:06:23 UTC

Judge rejects Trump effort to block California ‘noncitizen’ ballots
Trump administration issues more than 100 subpoenas across 13 states as search for alleged noncitizen voters ramps up.
A United States judge has rejected a Department of Justice request to temporarily halt California from counting mail ballots from a list of 20,000 alleged noncitizens just six days before the country’s midterm elections.
US District Judge David Carter’s ruling on Wednesday came as US President Donald Trump expands efforts to search for alleged noncitizen voters, with subpoenas issued in at least 13 states.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote on Wednesday.
The judge, a 1998 appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, said the Justice Department’s last-minute request to exclude more than 20,000 ballots ran afoul of “longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections”.
The Justice Department swiftly appealed the decision to the Ninth US Circuit Court of Appeals and did not immediately respond to requests for comment by the Reuters news agency.
The Justice Department filed the lawsuit on October 15, a rare intervention in the voting process weeks before Tuesday’s election, when voters will choose which party controls Congress as well as their state and local representatives.
Escalating efforts from Trump
The decision marks the latest setback in Trump’s effort to expand the federal government’s role in elections ahead of the legislative midterms, as his Republican Party fights to retain control of both houses of Congress.
The Trump administration issued more than 100 subpoenas demanding records on tens of thousands of voters in at least 13 states, both Republican- and Democratic-leaning.
Most of the subpoenas Reuters documented were issued to state and local election officials in the past three months, though some date to the start of the year. Many were previously unreported, revealing a federal effort to identify potential noncitizen voters that is broader than publicly known.
It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in US federal elections. Legal experts say the records could be used to contest close midterm results, despite scant evidence that noncitizen voting is widespread.
‘Deeply flawed process’
Also on Wednesday, Democracy Docket, a US media platform that tracks election litigation, reported that the Department of Justice list of alleged noncitizen voters “appears to have been created using a deeply flawed process” that could disenfranchise US citizen voters beyond California.
In a court filing, a government whistleblower revealed that voters were being scrutinised nationwide, not just in California, as part of the federal government’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative” investigation, the group reported. The whistleblower warned that “the current process is knowingly sweeping known US citizens in as potentially ‘unlawful voters'”.
California has said the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust. It said the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data” and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters. Democracy Docket reported that in Los Angeles County, one in four voters on the “noncitizen” list were born in the US.

North Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles amid rising tensions with South Korea
North Korea fired around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, Seoul's defence ministry said. The North Korean capital Pyongyang has stepped up weapons tests in recent weeks despite South Korea's offer of military talks.
North Korea fired "around a dozen" short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, Seoul's defence ministry said, less than a week after South Korea proposed talks over a growing border row.
The launches follow a slew of recent weapons tests by Pyongyang, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology.
Read moreNorth Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said its military detected "around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea" – the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
The missiles flew about 250 kilometres, and "South Korea and the United States are conducting a detailed analysis of their exact specifications", Seoul's military said, adding it had stepped up surveillance of possible additional launches.
The Japan Coast Guard had earlier urged ships in the area to be vigilant.
Seoul's National Security Office meanwhile, said the launches violated UN Security Council resolutions, labelling them "serious acts that do nothing to help manage the current situation".
Thursday's missile flurry comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea planted the landmines over a year ago.
Seoul accused the North's capital Pyongyang of "a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement" and demanded an apology, something the North has mockingly dismissed.
'Show of force'
"This should be seen as a fairly high-level show of force," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, told AFP.
"North Korea is demonstrating that it has the capability to completely destroy major South Korean and US military facilities," he said.
Pyongyang was also sending a political message, Lim added, by "showing off its overwhelming military power and warning Seoul not to interfere with its efforts to fortify the border".
Last week, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, said the North would place loudspeakers on standby along the border "within days" and had put unspecified "new counter means" on alert.
Both countries have occasionally turned to loudspeakers blaring propaganda across their shared border and other psychological warfare methods.
South Korea days later proposed military talks with the North to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, but Pyongyang is yet to respond.
Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war, as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce, rather than a peace treaty.
The ratcheting tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to North Korea have raised concerns that Seoul – an ally of Washington – could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving Pyongyang.
In his most recent comments, Trump seemingly downplayed the possibility of a summit while insisting his relationship with Kim Jong-Un was "very good".
In October, North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested the two might meet this year.

NEW YORK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- A fire at a federal nuclear facility in the U.S. state of South Carolina triggered an emergency response on Wednesday, but it was later extinguished and no contamination was reported, officials said.

‘The more you earn, the less you keep’: readers react to the budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

‘Most people my age have written off buying a home’
Louie, 24, a chef living in London, says a lot of people have “written off the idea of even considering getting a property” in their 20s.
He is optimistic about the government’s new Your First Home scheme, which will enable people to buy a new-build property with a deposit of just 2.5%, supported by an interest-free equity loan.
But he says a smaller deposit alone will not be enough for him. “I’ve found hospitality wages to be far too volatile to even consider saving for a property,” he says.
As a result, he is studying an access course with plans to start a physiotherapy degree next year. He hopes that by the time he graduates and gains some experience, he will have a stable enough income and sufficient savings to put down a deposit.
He says the new scheme “should encourage a lot of young people to buy earlier” and adds: “We are moving in a good direction, but I’ll still save and wait until around late 20s to early 30s to start [thinking about buying], just due to how much it may cost me.”
Louie earns between £37,000 and £40,000 a year and shares a three-bedroom rented property with two friends. But rent and bills take up an increasingly large proportion of his income, leaving little room to save towards buying a home.
“I was always told that a third of your salary should go towards rent and bills, but it’s coming up to about half now, which is a little bit mental,” he says.
His landlord recently informed the household that their rent would increase by £200 a month in November.
He has managed to build up some savings. Since he was 18, he has put between 5% and 10% of his earnings into a stocks and shares investment account, and over the past year has also started making regular contributions to an Isa specifically for a house deposit.
“Nobody really wants to be spending all their money on rent,” he says. “But with the amount of money we make, you kind of have to. ”
‘I earned £126,000 last year – but still have nothing at the end of the month’
Graham Robinson is a business owner from Timperley, Greater Manchester, who runs the company KeySim. He earned £126,000 last year, but says that despite his six-figure income, he has virtually nothing left in his bank account at the end of each month.
Graham says he was “hoping for real help with the cost of employing people” from the budget. “Instead, the employment allowance stays at £10,500, while employers pick up the rising wage bill.”
He adds: “The minimum wage increase is welcome for workers, but the government gets the headline, businesses get the bill and the Treasury recoups some through tax and national insurance.”
The 45-year-old lives alone and shares care of his 10-year-old autistic son with his ex, covering all childcare costs himself.
“I know £126,000 sounds like an enormous amount of money, but after tax it works out at broadly £6,500 a month, and that really doesn’t go as far as people might think,” he says. “I don’t have expensive cars, I don’t go on extravagant holidays. I don’t really do anything particularly lavish, but at the end of the month it’s all gone.”
His mortgage payments have risen from about £900 a month to £1,300, while council tax, food, energy and other everyday expenses have also increased.
Normally earning approximately £100,000 a year, he has increasingly relied on additional dividends from his business to cover rising costs.
He is frustrated by the effective 60% income tax rate on earnings caused by the gradual withdrawal of the personal allowance on income over £100,000, which reaches zero when earnings reach £125,140.
“To put an extra £1,000 a month in my take-home pay, my salary would need to rise from £100,000 to £129,757 a year,” he says.
‘Our mortgage has increased by more than £600 a month’
Helen, 40, lives in south-west London with her husband and two children, aged eight and five. She is the main breadwinner, working in communications, while her husband runs his own architectural practice.
Her house is in council tax band D, which means she will get a £100 energy payment this winter. She welcomed the extra money, but found the way it was being distributed strange, based on bands rather than financial need.
She says the change offering self-employed people paternity pay was “great”, though now her children are older it would not benefit her family. She adds: “It was lovely to hear Dolly Parton’s book scheme mentioned, as encouraging education for all is key.”
Her family’s biggest monthly expense is their mortgage, which increased by more than £600 a month when interest rates rose. They have now fixed it until 2028.
Helen says frozen income tax thresholds are one of her biggest concerns, alongside getting the economy growing and the pressures facing small businesses. Her husband’s architectural practice is less than four years old and has struggled with the rising costs of building and a wider slowdown in construction.
“The challenge comes down to the price of energy; for example, the cost of steel, transporting materials and building homes,” she says. “It impacts everything we make, build and buy.”
‘I don’t know how people live on just the state pension’
Peter Pillinger, 72, is a widower from South Ribble in Lancashire whose state pension makes up about half his income. He also receives a pension from his career as a Methodist minister, a small amount from his late wife’s pension and an allowance for his work as a local councillor.
He is pleased with one of the key announcements: the scrapping of standing charges on gas bills. These are fixed daily fees that households pay regardless of how much gas they use.
“My gas bill in the summer is almost entirely standing charge,” he says. “They are regressive. Putting all the costs in the unit charge will encourage people to reduce usage and to insulate their homes.”
But he wonders why it will take until at least next spring for the change to come in. He also wants to know what the government will do “for those who need higher usage for medical reasons”.
He supports the changes to the state pension triple lock and believes pensioners who can afford to pay tax should do so. “If my income is £25,000 or approaching £30,000, why should it not be taxed? If everyone else is paying tax at that level, why should I not?”
Conversely, he is concerned about those surviving on much less. “I don’t know how people live on just the state pension,” he says.
‘Flowers are one of the first things people think to cut back on’
Danielle Walker, 37, is a self-employed florist based in Wakefield, West Yorkshire. She says rising fuel prices are squeezing her business from both sides, increasing the cost of making deliveries while also pushing up the price of the flowers she buys.
She welcomes the chancellor cancelling the planned fuel duty rise, but adds “it doesn’t undo the increases we’ve already faced or take away the pressure we’re under”.
Increasing the higher mileage rate from 25p to 35p a mile will not benefit her, she says, nor will the business rate threshold going up from £12,000 to £18,000, as she works from a studio.
Danielle has spent considerable time calculating delivery charges for different postcodes to ensure they cover her fuel costs and the time spent travelling. But she says she is increasingly having to absorb some of these costs herself.
“If I’ve quoted flowers for a wedding based on diesel being £1.40 a litre and it’s £2 by the time the wedding comes around, I’ve still got to get there. There’s only so much you can absorb for so long,” she says.
With customers already struggling financially, she feels unable to keep passing on rising costs without risking a loss of business.
“Flowers are a luxury item, and when people are feeling the pinch, they’re one of the first things people think to cut back on,” she says.
Danielle believes the government should look at the impact of fuel duty and VAT on small businesses that depend on driving, arguing that independent traders are particularly exposed to rising prices.
“Someone has to take it on the chin somewhere. I feel it’s unfair that small businesses are continually having to absorb these costs or lose customers by being honest about what delivery should cost.”
‘I am a single dad. The more you earn, the less you keep’
Jonny Roberts, 39, is a single dad from Newbury, Berkshire, with children aged 11 and eight. He works part-time at McDonald’s and as a tutor, while also studying for an online master’s degree. Between his two jobs, he works the equivalent of full-time hours. But even with support from universal credit, his income only just covers essentials.
“We had heard in the run-up [to the budget] there would be something on energy bills, and I’m sure millions of households are grateful for the extra £100 help towards that announced today,” he says. “But it was disappointing to see no announcement on whether local housing allowance [LHA] will be uprated.”
For Jonny, one of the biggest problems is the gap between the housing support available through universal credit and the reality of renting. He is entitled to the three-bedroom LHA rate, which gives him £1,200 a month towards his rent, but he pays £1,300 a month for a two-bedroom flat.
“The rent we’re paying isn’t particularly high for the area. It’s pretty much in line with the norm,” he says.
“Last year’s freeze and the cuts of prior government mean the housing element of universal credit seems to live in an alternate reality to the actual rents charged in the south of England.”
Jonny is also frustrated by the way universal credit reduces the financial rewards of taking on additional work.
For every extra pound he earns above his work allowance, his universal credit is reduced by 55p. Once income tax, national insurance and student loan repayments are taken into account, he says the amount he keeps from an additional shift can be surprisingly small.
With rent taking up the largest share of his budget, Jonny has little flexibility when other household costs rise. “I’m happy to go with less for myself to make sure I can feed all three of us,” he says.
Jonny was happy to see a “speeding up of the rollout of free breakfast clubs to an extra 2,000 schools” but adds: “It still seems a glacial pace when there are 17,000 primaries in the country.”
- Jonny takes part in Changing Realities, a collaboration involving more than 200 parents and carers living on low incomes, researchers at the University of Glasgow and Child Poverty Action Group. The project documents families’ experiences of living on a low income and brings their voices into discussions about poverty and social security policy.

====================================================================================================

Will the budget deliver ‘growth in every postcode’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

In just two years, there could be dozens of mayors preparing to spend billions of pounds as part of Andy Burnham’s mission to devolve greater powers across England.
Fresh devolution deals could also be in place following negotiations with leaders in Scotland, Wales and possibly Northern Ireland, allowing the prime minister to say at the next election that he has fulfilled a promise to rewire Britain’s political landscape with a view to giving more local control.
This was the message from John Healey’s first budget, which outlined the direction of travel and put in some milestones, including a 2028 commitment to devolve some income tax receipts to mayors of strategic authorities (MSAs). He added the commitment that next year, 20% of business rates revenues will go to mayors.
He told MPs that he was offering mayors 100% of their business rates income by the end of the decade and the ability to tax visitors who stay in hotels and B&Bs in their aream, via a new overnight visitors levy.
It would mean, Healey said: “New powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics. The biggest wave of devolution in a generation, driving good growth in every postcode delivered to the British people by this Labour government.”
However, Burnham’s signature phrase that he will bring “good growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” will face scrutiny once it becomes clear large parts of the country are excluded.
Manchester, the West Midlands and Liverpool City region head a list of 14 areas already governed by a mayor.
Healey said the 14 were on course to get enhanced deals, while ministers were in the final stages of signing 10 more agreements, creating MSAs for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay; Hertfordshire; Lancashire; Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland; Stoke and Staffordshire; Surrey; Thames Valley (Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Swindon); and Wessex.
Last month, Essex county council leaders agreed to adopt an MSA to secure about £1.2bn of funding over 10 years. Cornwall’s leaders, who secured a special devo deal under the previous Tory government, were at No 10 North last week – the hub of devolution discussions – hammering out an enhanced set of powers matched by extra money.
Yet there is concern that while these areas might come on board before next year, many others will be left out.
Jonathan Carr-West, chief executive of the Local Government Information Unit, a thinktank, said: “A rewired state needs every tier of government to play its part, and it needs every tier of government to be financially resilient.”
In his view, those areas without a mayor, or without a special devo deal like Cornwall, will begin to fall behind the rest, exacerbating regional inequality.
Next month, No 10 is due to publish the much-anticipated Rewiring the State delivery plan, which Burnham has said will contain the thrust of what he wants to achieve as prime minister.
Carr-West said the holes in Healey’s speech will need to be filled in by Burnham if there is to be some clarity about the way forward. “Today’s budget statement puts more, rather than less, pressure on that document,” he said.
One of the major barriers to progress is likely to be the stalled reorganisation of local government in England, which was due to convert county and district councils into a web of unitary authorities. Angela Rayner, the secretary of state for housing, local government and communities, suspended the plan in September.
Unitary authorities will carry out all the roles previously divided between counties and districts, from providing social services and education to overseeing parking and local business licences.
Several county councils have used judicial reviews to challenge the plans, forcing Rayner to rethink.
Kent is an example of an authority that is a long way from having an MSA, after the Reform UK-run county council objected to a government plan for a split into four unitaries. It has gone to court saying Kent should remain as a single entity, much like Cornwall.
Vince Maple, head of Medway council in Kent, accepts the dispute is a barrier to a deal at the moment, but says it was clear from Healey’s speech that local government reorganisation (LGR) will go ahead in some form and devo deals will follow.
“Government has made itself clear that LGR is going ahead. Most people accept it will happen,” he said.
Maple also heads the Key Cities Group of second-tier urban areas, which includes Gloucester, Sunderland and Salford. He said the expansion of MSAs to include a further 10 areas meant the government was getting closer to its “every postcode” target.
“Our members will be part of the conversation now in a way that they weren’t 24 hours ago,” he said.
There is also scepticism that the economic growth Burnham hopes to achieve from devolution may be slow to materialise.
In a judgment on the budget, the consultancy Oxford Economics, said: “A combination of limited detail, unaddressed challenges, and the length of time for any upside to show means that the devolution announcements will not lead us to revising our regional forecasts.”
Burnham will hope that rearranging the structure of local government will be enough at the next election to convince voters that change is beneficial, even if he cannot show a boost to economic growth.
