High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:38:54 GMT
06:38:54 KST

High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
- Published
A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.
It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.
The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the crash, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.
Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.
The crash happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid, between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz.
The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said.
He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.
The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.
Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."
One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.
Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.
Tangui Binier, 22, was on the Iryo train and told the BBC that "suitcases started flying and people were screaming" when the train finally came to a halt.
There was a lot of smoke and confusion, he said, and described seeing the train "completely flipped over" when he stepped outside.
"It was hard to witness", Binier said, adding that his father carried a girl who had a broken hip out of the wreckage.
He also described seeing dead bodies and missing limbs: "I don't know if I'll ever recover."
Spanish journalist Antonio Jiménez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened.
"I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described.
"I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."
Another passenger, 46-year-old Sebastián Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms."
"It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.
Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms.
"She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.
Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.
Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims.
"The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."
Most political parties in Spain cancelled their campaign events scheduled for Wednesday.
The exception was the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.
Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near Córdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.
The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence.
"Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the the main opposition People's Party.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."
Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".
Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain.

Russia Builds New Drone Base Near Ukraine Capable of Launching 100 Attack Drones Daily
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:38:14 UTC
06:38:14 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Builds New Drone Base Near Ukraine Capable of Launching 100 Attack Drones Daily
Russia is building a new drone launch facility near the Millerovo military airfield in the Rostov region, capable of supporting up to 100 attack drone launches per day, the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense (HUR) reported on October 28.
The facility's construction was confirmed through satellite imagery, according to Oboronka, citing an official statement by HUR. The site is located near Russia's border with Ukraine's temporarily occupied Luhansk region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The facility's configuration indicates that it is designed to prepare and launch jet-powered attack drones, likely Geran-4 and Geran-5, as well as their modifications. Preliminary estimates suggest that once construction is complete, the site will be capable of supporting up to 100 launches per day," HUR stated.
According to the intelligence directorate, satellite imagery showed no visible signs of active construction at the site in late August 2026. By mid-October, Russian forces had established launch positions and supporting infrastructure.
HUR noted that the rapid construction could be explained by the use of standardized technical solutions and the concentration of resources on relatively simple launch infrastructure.
"The construction of a new UAV launch facility just 3.5 kilometers from Millerovo airfield means that the Russians intend to use the same air defense systems protecting the airfield to defend it," HUR explained.
The facility could also benefit from existing roads, communications networks, logistics infrastructure, and technical support systems associated with the military airfield.
However, HUR emphasized that the actual launch rate would depend on the availability of drones, fuel, warheads, trained crews, operational equipment, and assigned missions.
Meanwhile, Russia is modernizing its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered attack drones, the intelligence directorate reported. The Geran-4 has a range of up to 770 kilometers and has received additional autonomous navigation capabilities, including an optical terrain-matching system.
HUR also reported that Russia has equipped the Geran-4 with a domestically produced jet engine and a new warhead designed to strike bridges and power transmission line supports.
The Geran-5 has a reported range of up to 950 kilometers. Its K5 modification is being fitted with a similar optical navigation system, potentially improving its ability to navigate without relying exclusively on satellite signals.
According to HUR, Russia currently operates at least 12 permanent attack drone launch facilities. The Millerovo site would expand this network and could form part of preparations to intensify drone strikes against Ukraine, particularly during the winter.
The Millerovo site is not an isolated expansion: the Tsymbulova drone base in the Oryol region has also been adding shelters and launchers for jet-powered drones as Russia ramps up output of the Gerans themselves.
As of early October, Russia was producing around 2,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month, though further growth hinges on turbojet engines largely supplied by China. Russian forces have also amassed roughly 10,000 piston-engine strike drones and launch both types together in successive waves to exhaust Ukrainian air defenses.
Ukraine has been developing interceptor drones in response, with a domestically produced P1-SUN JetKiller downing a Geran-5 on September 30.

F-22s, F-15s Rotate in at Kadena to Bolster Pacific Airpower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:37:22 UTC
06:37:22 KST

Squadrons of F-22 Raptors and F-15C Eagles have arrived at Kadena Air Base, Japan, for temporary deployments as the critical Pacific base awaits its permanent F-15EX fighters.
Stars & Stripes reported Oct. 27 that a squadron of F-22s from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, finished arriving Sept. 30. Another squadron of F-15s, from Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base New Orleans, La., also recently arrived, Stripes reported, citing a statement from the 18th Wing at Kadena.
The 18th Wing did not immediately respond to a query from Air & Space Forces Magazine. But independent aircraft trackers and photographs published by the military show those planes arriving at or operating from Kadena recently.
Kadena, located on Okinawa, is the U.S.’s closest air base to Taiwan and strategically vital.
The 18th Wing at Kadena flew squadrons of permanently assigned F-15C/D fighters for years. But those legacy fighters were rapidly aging, and in November 2022, the Air Force started withdrawing them. Those fighters will be replaced with 36 permanently assigned F-15EX Eagle II jets, beginning in fiscal 2027.
Until then, the service is rotating various fighters, including F-35s, F-22s, F-16s, and F-15 variants through Kadena on a temporary basis, to maintain the base’s ability to project airpower if necessary.
The first F-15EXs had been scheduled to arrive by now, but labor disputes and other challenges slowed Boeing’s deliveries and delayed plans. The first F-15EX earmarked for Kadena left Boeing’s St. Louis factory Aug. 28, and flew to Portland, Ore., for final systems integration, software updates, and other technical preparations. After that work is done, the jet will fly to Okinawa.
Photos posted by the 18th Wing on Oct. 27 show the Alaska F-22s at Tsuiki Air Base, Japan, taking part in Exercise Keen Sword 27, which aims to improve how U.S. and Japanese forces work together.
Aircraft trackers have also observed F-15 movements to Kadena in recent weeks.
Aviation enthusiast Aux OSINT on Oct. 24 and 25 posted flight tracker images on social media of KC-46 Pegasus tankers flying Coronet missions with F-15Cs from the 122nd, inbound to Kadena.
A Japan-based aviation photographer who posts online under the handle Okadna35 posted images Oct. 24 of F-15s arriving at Kadena, bearing markings of the New Orleans base’s 159th Fighter Wing, nicknamed the Bayou Militia.

An Israeli television channel reported Wednesday that a power-sharing deal is taking shape under which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would lead the next government for two years before handing power to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot in exchange for retiring from politics and receiving a full pardon in connection with his ongoing corruption cases.
Israel’s Channel 14 reported that President Isaac Herzog is currently seeking to advance the proposed arrangement, which could pave the way for the formation of the next government following Tuesday’s inconclusive parliamentary elections.

Turkish engineer creates live 3D pixel map of adopted hometown Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:36:45 UTC
06:36:45 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.
The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.
The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.
While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.
Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.
The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.
The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.
Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.
Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.
An observation deck at the top of the EU's tallest building, Varso Tower in Warsaw, has opened to the public.
Located 230m up on the tower's 53rd floor, the attraction offers a 360° panorama of Poland's capital.https://t.co/VeEapOmh4s

The result is an incredible level of explorable detail, from major landmarks, such as the communist-era Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower, the EU’s tallest building, down to the seating steps and bars along the Vistula River boulevards.
The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves.
A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium.
I turned Warsaw into a flight sim 🛩️

Speaking to Notes from Poland, Yildirim says that he moved to Poland in 2022 to pursue a job in IT before starting his own business. Initially living in Kraków, the country’s second-largest city, he then moved to Warsaw in 2025.
Asked what his own personal favourite places in the city are, Yildirim points to Warsaw’s parks, such as Skaryszewski, Pole Mokotowskie and Łazienki. His favourite neighbourhood is Saska Kępa on the right bank of the Vistula.
The software engineer adds that his project is an example of how AI can be an “amazing tool to do 90% of the job very quickly”. The remaining 10% of human input “is what keeps it from being ‘AI slop'”.
Yildirim says that, without the use of AI, the map of Warsaw he created would have needed an entire team to build over a period of months.

Costa Rica’s mega-prison receives first inmates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:36:16 UTC
06:36:16 KST

Costa Rica’s mega-prison receives first inmates
President Laura Fernandez inaugurated the $35m mega-prison built to house up to 5,100 inmates near San Jose.
A newly opened maximum-security mega-prison in Costa Rica has received its first batch of inmates. The prison was built with the help of the Salvadoran government on the outskirts of the capital, San Jose, the country’s Justice Ministry announced.
The Costa Rican Justice Ministry shared images on Tuesday of 123 inmates dressed in orange, seated with their heads shaved and bowed and their hands behind their necks.
“Costa Rica is writing a new chapter in its penitentiary history,” Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar said in a statement.
The new prison is called the High-Containment Center Against Organized Crime (CACCO) and constitutes a symbol of a new “tough on crime” approach championed by President Laura Fernandez’s administration. It has a capacity for 5,100 inmates.
The CACCO was built with the help of the Salvadoran government on the outskirts of Costa Rica’s capital, San Jose, at a cost of $35m. Fernandez inaugurated it on October 15.
“CACCO is a monument to national security, a forceful response to organized crime, and a guarantee that the state will exercise its authority without hesitation,” the statement added.
The new facility has a capacity equivalent to 20 percent of the country’s prison population and “will also help reduce overcrowding in the prison system”, according to Aguilar.
Costa Rica, long regarded as one of the safest countries in Latin America, has in recent years experienced a sharp rise in violence linked to drug trafficking and organised crime. It witnessed a record-setting 905 homicides in 2023, followed by 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025.
Authorities attribute most killings to disputes between criminal groups over drug trafficking routes and markets.
Right-wing leaders in other Latin American countries have also sought to replicate the mega-prison model.

Sumy Region Expands Underground Schooling, With 9 New Facilities Under Construction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:34:15 UTC
06:34:15 KST

Ukraine’s northeastern Sumy region is working on expanding its network of underground schools as Russian forces increasingly target civilians, with more than 4,200 Russian guided aerial bombs (KABs) launched during this year alone.
There are currently 13 functional underground schools in Sumy, with nine new facilities still under construction. Cost estimates and site plans had also been completed for another 14 facilities, head of the Sumy Regional Military Administration Oleh Hryhorov told Ukrinform in an exclusive interview on Wednesday, Oct. 28.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The process is ongoing and being scaled up as much as possible,” Hryhorov said, noting that the region was seeking international partners to help fund the construction.
Classrooms increasingly below ground
With the full-scale invasion now in its fifth year, Ukrainian authorities have continued working on giving children as normal a childhood as possible under such conditions.
When the school year began on Sept. 1, many students returned to in-person classes under new wartime rules, including restrictions on large gatherings that could put children at risk.
In the Sumy region, new underground schools are being built mainly in larger cities, where the number of students is highest.
The need is much lower in smaller communities, as some only have a single school, Hryhorov said. Of the region’s 280 schools, 225 have their own shelters. Although most are basic, more than 70 schools have radiation-proof shelters.
Putin Calls Musk a ‘Genius,’ Claims Close Cooperation as Ukraine Faces Starlink Disruptions
According to Hryhorov, such infrastructure allows the region to keep many students in physical classrooms. About 75,000 children are currently enrolled in the region’s schools, with 22 of them operating fully in person.
As most schools in other regions do as well, 193 are operating using a mix of in-person and remote classes.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022, 165 schools have been damaged in the region and 21 destroyed beyond repair, Hryhorov said.
Ukrinform reported that another underground school opened in the city of Sumy in October, able to accommodate up to 500 students.
A region under constant fire
The effort comes as Sumy, located about 20 kilometers from the frontline, (12 miles) continues facing near-daily Russian attacks.
Due to the proximity, Russian forces have increasingly begun relying on fiber-optic FPV drones, which can now reach almost 50 kilometers (31 miles) into the region. By October, more than 6,000 drone strikes of several types were recorded.
Since the beginning of the year, more than 4,200 guided aerial bombs were dropped on the region; about 500 targeted the Sumy community, including 192 that struck the regional capital itself.
The overall number of attacks is roughly the same as in 2025, Hryhorov said, although noting that their focus has changed. While Russian forces mostly struck military positions during the last year, they have concentrated on civilian infrastructure and the region’s residents in 2026.
To protect against drones, more than 450 kilometers (280 miles) of roads have been covered with anti-drone nets.
Hryhorov said each kilometer costs more than Hr. 1 million (roughly $22,000), rising to as much as Hr. 3 million ($66,000) when the work is done by private contractors.
The government has so far allocated Hr. 70 million ($1.5 million) for additional nets in Sumy, while regional authorities and local communities have provided a total of Hr. 1.35 billion ($30 billion) for overall security measures, including the netting.
Mandatory frontline evacuations
Meanwhile, in 213 settlements near the border, evacuations remain mandatory.
According to Hryhorov, more than 57,000 people, including 8,000 children, have already left. However, about 34,000 civilians still remain in the region.
Under mandatory evacuation orders, all children have been evacuated from the frontline communities.
On Oct. 22, regional authorities also extended mandatory evacuation of families with children to the entire Sloviansk community after Russian forces struck the settlements of the Donetsk region 42 times, injuring two boys.
Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s university district on Tuesday, Oct. 27, killing one person and injuring over 10, mostly students.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, Oct. 1, while more than 100 children and over 60 teachers sheltered inside. The Geran-4 drone struck the wall of a stairwell between the school’s second and third floors without detonating.
Although deliberate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are prohibited under international humanitarian law, they remain part of daily life for Ukrainian citizens.

Russia and Tanzania to launch joint space program (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:30:37 UTC

Russia and Tanzania to launch joint space program (VIDEO)
Russia and Tanzania have agreed to launch a joint space program, the Russian space agency Roscosmos has said. Moscow will assist Dodoma in establishing its own national space agency and developing the infrastructure needed for a domestic space industry.
On Wednesday, Roscosmos and Tanzania’s Ministry of Information, Communication and Information Technology signed a framework memorandum on strategic partnership and cooperation on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit. The event has brought delegations from 48 African countries to Moscow this week.
“Tanzania is planning to establish its own space agency, and we are ready to provide our colleagues with expert and methodological support,” Roscosmos Director General Dmitry Bakanov told journalists. The Russian space agency has already stepped up cooperation with Tanzanian specialists in the field, with support from the Russian presidential administration, he added.
According to Bakanov, Dodoma is particularly interested in developing its own spacecraft and launching them into orbit aboard Russian rockets. Roscosmos has confirmed that Russia will launch Tanzania’s first Earth remote-sensing satellite in March 2027.
During the summit, Russian specialists demonstrated to the Tanzanian delegation the country’s capabilities in training cosmonauts and space industry specialists, as well as conducting scientific experiments in space.
The two sides also discussed sharing Earth remote-sensing data and establishing ground stations in Tanzania to receive such data. According to Bakanov, the African nation also plans to increase the number of students studying space-related disciplines at Russian universities.
Under the agreement, Russia will assist Tanzania in developing infrastructure for its space industry, while the two countries will exchange expertise and best practices in training space specialists. They have also agreed to establish joint working groups and develop road maps covering all areas of cooperation.
Moscow has been actively supporting African nations’ space ambitions. Last year, the South African National Space Agency (SANSA) hailed Russia as a key partner in advancing its national space program. Pretoria “has received most of its support from the Russian Federation,” SANSA board chairman Patrick Ndlovu told Sputnik Africa at the time. Earlier that year, SANSA CEO Humbulani Mudau announced South Africa’s support for Russia’s proposal to establish a BRICS Space Council to strengthen space cooperation among member states.
In 2024, Zimbabwe announced plans to build its first spaceport with Russian assistance. The country also said it was in talks with Roscosmos about gaining access to Russia’s cosmonaut training system, among other areas of cooperation.

Once a nation has built cultural venues on that scale, the question shifts from how many to what kind. The answers now emerging are quieter, lighter and more deeply rooted than the icons of recent decades.

UN votes overwhelmingly against U.S. embargo on Cuba

05:26:46 CST
06:26:46 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The UN General Assembly on Wednesday adopted a resolution calling for an end to the decades-old U.S. embargo on Cuba.
The resolution was adopted with 130 votes in favor, 17 against and 25 abstentions.
It expresses concern about the continued promulgation and application of laws and regulations, including the Helms-Burton Act enacted by the United States in 1996, whose extraterritorial effects undermine the sovereignty of other states, the legitimate interests of individuals and entities under their jurisdiction, and the freedom of trade and navigation.
The resolution calls on all states to refrain from promulgating and applying such laws and measures, and urges states that have applied and continue to apply such laws and measures to take necessary steps to repeal or invalidate them as soon as possible.
The resolution also requests the UN secretary-general to prepare a report on the implementation of this resolution and to submit it to the General Assembly at its next annual session.
Wednesday's resolution marked the 34th consecutive adoption of a resolution on the necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States on Cuba. ■

Under Sanctions, Russia Turns to Africa With Plans to Relocate Industrial Production
Russia is ready to move part of its industrial enterprises to Africa, Russian leader Vladimir Putin announced on October 29, The Moscow Times reported the same day.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"This fully corresponds to Russia's interests, especially today, when numerous sanctions are being applied to the Russian economy and Russian enterprises," Putin stated at the Russia-Africa forum. He described the investment potential of Russian companies as "fairly high" and added that "there is work to be done here."
Putin stressed that investments in African countries must be "reliable and protected." Plants would then operate "regardless of the foreign policy situation," he explained.
He was responding to Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who argued that Africa must go beyond exporting raw materials and importing finished goods.
"We must develop our own industrial potential, modernize our agriculture, strengthen our energy infrastructure and logistics routes, and invest more in research and technology development," Ndayishimiye told the forum. He emphasized that Africa should become "a real market for production and sales" rather than remain a consumer market.
A day earlier, Putin told 22 African leaders, including those of Ethiopia, Zimbabwe and Mali, that Russia had achieved "impressive results" in high technology. He said Moscow was ready to share its know-how with its "African friends." Competitors "have to catch up with us in some areas and copy our developments," he emphasized.
Russian ministers and state companies have since set out their own offers. Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov announced that Russian companies were ready to manufacture goods in African countries under industrial cooperation.
"The main message we bring to Africa is: let's ensure sovereign development together," he stated. Reshetnikov proposed cooperation in pharmaceuticals and IT solutions. Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov expressed readiness to develop automobile manufacturing in partnership with African partners.
Rosatom proposed building floating nuclear power plants in coastal African countries. "As a starting step, a source such as a floating nuclear power unit could be a good entry point to both solve their tasks and join the nuclear club," a representative of the state corporation explained.
Russia's largest liquefied natural gas producer, Novatek, offered African countries its own production technology, proven on Arctic projects. Aluminum giant Rusal signed a memorandum with Ghana on a joint venture to mine and process bauxite, the raw material for aluminum.
Moscow's push into African markets follows steep losses in its traditional energy trade since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Gazprom has lost more than half of its exports outside the former Soviet Union, with Russian gas exports expected to total about 77 billion cubic meters in 2026, down from 185 billion in 2021.
Exports are projected to fall to 72 billion cubic meters by 2028 once the EU gas embargo takes effect, a level last seen in the second half of the 1980s. Efforts to offset the losses through a major new supply deal with China have stalled over pricing, leaving talks on the proposed Power of Siberia 2 pipeline suspended.

Russia Revives World War II-Era Arctic Shipping Route to Export Grain
Unknown

Russia Revives World War II-Era Arctic Shipping Route to Export Grain
Russia has begun using an Arctic maritime route dating back to World War II to export grain for the first time, Reuters reported on October 28. The move comes as Moscow seeks alternatives to traditional shipping corridors through the Black and Baltic Seas amid growing security risks stemming from its war against Ukraine.
To address these difficulties, Russia has been redirecting grain shipments from its southern agricultural regions to Baltic Sea ports, offering subsidies for rail transportation. At the same time, Moscow has begun exploring the Arctic as an alternative export corridor.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On October 28, the Murmansk Commercial Seaport and Demetra Holding, one of Russia’s largest grain trading companies, announced that the first shipment of 3,400 metric tons of grain, transported from the country’s main agricultural regions, was being loaded onto a vessel at the port.
According to Reuters, the vessel is expected to carry approximately 28,000 metric tons of wheat from Murmansk to Casablanca, Morocco.
Located nearly 2,000 kilometers north of Moscow, near Russia’s border with Norway, Murmansk offers access to international waters. The port also has historical significance, having served as a major entry point for Allied supplies delivered to the Soviet Union during World War II.
“At a time when traditional export routes are facing restrictions, Murmansk Commercial Seaport is swiftly opening up an alternative route to foreign markets for Russian farmers,” the port said in a statement.
The development comes as Russia increasingly relies on Baltic Sea ports to maintain its grain exports.
According to Reuters, Russia exported approximately 1.2 million metric tons of grain through Baltic ports in September alone, accounting for more than 60% of its total seaborne grain shipments that month.
To accommodate the growing volumes, Russian companies have been converting port terminals previously used to handle fertilizers and coal into facilities capable of processing grain exports.
Russia has permitted grain-carrying vessels to leave the Sea of Azov for the first time since July, temporarily authorizing departures from the commercial ports of Temryuk and Kavkaz.
Citing three sources familiar with the situation, Bloomberg reported that the clearance was issued on October 26, with at least one vessel having already crossed the Kerch Strait into the Black Sea.

ROME, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's cabinet on Wednesday approved a draft budget worth about 26 billion euros (29 billion U.S. dollars) for 2027, featuring tax cuts and social support measures.
The package expands the 33-percent income tax bracket to cover annual earnings of up to 55,000 euros, up from the current threshold of 50,000 euros. It also raises the income ceiling for self-employed workers to qualify for a flat-tax regime from 85,000 to 100,000 euros.
Other measures include a 5-percent flat tax rate for new hires under the age of 35 and an annual state contribution of 100 euros for each newborn until the child turns 18.
Meloni said a new levy on the profits of major banks, other lenders and insurance companies was expected to generate about 5 billion euros in revenue.
The budget is the government's final spending plan before general elections scheduled for 2027. The administration faces mounting pressure to tackle the rising cost of living, as trade unions, social organizations and student groups have staged protests in recent weeks.
Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti cited rising raw material costs and borrowing rates as key challenges. However, he said an agreement with European Union authorities allowing a temporary increase in next year's fiscal deficit would provide the government with additional room for spending.
The draft budget will now be submitted to parliament for approval by both chambers before being sent to EU authorities by the end of the year for assessment under the bloc's fiscal rules. Enditem (1 euro = 1.11 U.S. dollar)

According to Trading Economics, forecasts of colder-than-usual weather in parts of Europe and Asia could boost heating demand and intensify competition for LNG cargoes between the two regions, putting further upward pressure on natural gas prices. ■

MADRID, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Just nine months after a deadly railway accident near Adamuz in southern Spain, another high-speed train collision occurred on Wednesday on the same Madrid-Seville railway line, raising renewed concerns about the safety of Spain's high-speed rail network.
The collision between two high-speed trains near Urda station in Toledo province, central Spain, has killed at least 68 people and injured 180 more.
WHAT HAPPENED AND WHY?
At around 8:54 a.m. local time (0754 GMT) on Wednesday, a Renfe-operated AVE train carrying 378 passengers struck the rear of a stationary Iryo train with 147 passengers aboard near Urda station. Both trains were heading from Madrid to Seville, according to Spain's Ministry of Transport and railway operator Renfe.
At least 68 were killed, according to the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha. More than 180 people were reported injured, with some in critical condition.
Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente said at a press conference on Wednesday afternoon that the LZB train safety system had failed at around 8:30 a.m. due to a communication problem involving three computers, affecting a 63-km section of the railway and automatically bringing several trains to a halt.
According to Puente, Adif's control center subsequently authorized the AVE train to resume normal operations at around 8:36 a.m., despite a red signal and the presence of the stationary Iryo train ahead. The AVE traveled approximately 25 km before crashing into the Iryo at around 8:53 a.m..
Under Spanish railway safety regulations, trains must remain stopped when the LZB system fails and the track ahead is occupied. Any authorized movement must follow restricted operating procedures requiring drivers to maintain a speed that allows them to stop upon detecting an obstacle ahead.
Puente described the control center's decision as "inexplicable," while railway engineering expert Ramiro Aurin told Spanish news agency EFE that human error was the most likely explanation for the collision. However, the exact circumstances and responsibilities remain under investigation.
GOVERNMENT RESPONSE AND PUBLIC SCRUTINY
The tragedy prompted the Spanish government and several major political parties to suspend their scheduled activities on Wednesday.
During a visit to the accident site in Urda, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez stressed that rescuing victims and supporting their families remained the government's top priority. He pledged a thorough investigation into the collision, saying that any negligence or failures in railway safety systems would be addressed. "We will get to the bottom of this," Sanchez said.
The government also declared three days of national mourning from Oct. 29 to Oct. 31, while the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha activated an emergency response plan and mobilized additional rescue and medical resources. Several hospitals suspended scheduled activities to accommodate the injured, while psychological support teams were deployed to assist victims and their families.
The accident also triggered calls for accountability. Opposition People's Party (PP) leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo said Spain had the right to know what was happening with its railway infrastructure. He called for immediate government and judicial investigations, as well as a comprehensive and independent review of the country's entire railway network.
In Madrid, hundreds of demonstrators gathered outside the Ministry of Transport on Wednesday evening, demanding the resignation of the Transport Minister Puente.
Railway unions also called for stronger safety safeguards. The Independent Trade Union and Civil Servants' Central (CSIF) demanded an urgent explanation of the accident, accountability for those responsible, and greater investment in railway infrastructure and maintenance.
The Spanish train drivers' union Semaf said it would proceed with a strike scheduled for Thursday, calling for stronger railway safety guarantees and structural reforms. The union also said it was considering further action following the latest tragedy.
GROWING CONCERNS OVER RAIL SAFETY
The collision marks Spain's second major fatal high-speed rail accident this year, with a crash near Adamuz, in the southern province of Cordoba, claiming 46 lives on Jan. 18.
While investigations into both accidents remain ongoing, experts have pointed to different possible causes. Jordi Vinolas Prat, a mechanical engineering professor at Francisco de Vitoria University, told Europa Press that the Adamuz disaster appeared to be linked to railway infrastructure problems, while the latest collision raised questions about signaling systems.
Jose Trigueros, president of the Association of Civil Engineers, told Spanish national broadcaster RTVE that the latest collision was particularly concerning because high-speed rail safety systems were designed to prevent two trains from occupying the same section of track. He questioned the reliability of automated safety protections and the extent to which railway operations depended on human intervention.
Concerns over railway safety had already been raised following the Adamuz disaster. Rafael Escudero, secretary-general of the Sindicato Ferroviario railway union, told Spanish radio station Onda Cero that the union had called for an audit of renovation works on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line after the January accident. He urged a review of how the more than 700 million euros (770 million U.S. dollars) allocated to upgrading the line had been spent, while stressing that the cause of Wednesday's collision remained under investigation.
The latest tragedy has also unsettled some railway passengers. Daniel, a frequent traveler between Malaga and Madrid, told Spanish radio station Cadena SER that the accident had left him feeling angry and insecure, saying recent railway incidents had undermined his confidence in train travel.
Civil engineer Martin Perea, a transport specialist and master's program director at Universidad Europea, also warned of serious damage to the reputation of Spain's railway system, calling for a thorough investigation, support for victims and their families, and a broader reassessment of the country's high-speed rail operations. ■

====================================================================================================

U.S. Fed holds interest rate steady ahead of midterm elections
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:26:08 CST
06:26:08 KST

U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at a press conference in Washington, D.C., the United States, Oct. 28, 2026. The U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday kept its target range for the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.75 to 4 percent, less than a week ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. (Photo by Li Yuanqing/Xinhua)
NEW YORK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday kept its target range for the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.75 to 4 percent, less than a week ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
"Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little," said the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) in a statement.
Nevertheless, inflation remains elevated. In support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate, "the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent," the FOMC said.
The committee reaffirmed "its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system" and "price stability," saying the accumulation of more information will help the committee "determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
Of the 12 FOMC members, 10 voted to keep the rate unchanged, while two favored a rate hike.
"Since our policy action in September, we have started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households, much as we would expect," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at a press conference after the FOMC meeting. "Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations."
Financial conditions broadly are helping create a path toward price stability. But with the near-term inflation picture still too high, "it's our responsibility to get inflation down," Warsh said, adding that the Fed's discussion over recent days "focused mainly on the price stability side of our remit."
Warsh announced that the Fed will change its meeting schedule in coming years. The FOMC will still meet eight times a year.
"But in 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," he said, adding that he expects there will be two strategy sessions in 2028.
The change in the meeting schedule will allow the Fed time to think about "big questions," Warsh said.
Responding to a question about U.S. President Donald Trump's assertion that other board members want to see the country "do badly," Warsh said he will not respond to quotes from public officials.
Following the Fed's decision to keep the rate unchanged, major U.S. stock indexes kept steady, while U.S. bond yields and the U.S. dollar index rose slightly.
The Fed's pause is within market expectations after its first rate hike in three years in September. Chris Hodge, chief U.S. economist at Natixis, said in a research note earlier in the week that pausing would allow more time to determine whether recent high inflation readings were part of a larger trend.
"Inflation is still the No. 1 problem in the U.S. economy, and there are a lot of signs it is getting more broad-based," Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told CNBC. However, "given that it's right before an election, they won't hike in October."
U.S. midterm elections fall on Nov. 3. To avoid impacting the power held by each political party, the Fed has mostly maintained its charted course in previous election cycles, except in 1978, 1982, 2018 and 2022, when inflation ran high.
The Federal Reserve's decision to hold rates steady at the October meeting suggests its prior hawkish stance was a matter of empty showmanship, Cem Karsan, founder and CIO at Kai Wealth, told CNBC. "At the end of the day, they're trying to gain credibility." Karsan said the only way to respond to what is important is through more dovishness from the Fed.
Nevertheless, it is widely expected that a hike in December is still in the cards. ■

Casualties have been reported, along with disruptions to transport, markets and cross-border trade, limiting access to essential goods and services, said the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
On the Ethiopian side, the violence that erupted on Oct. 18 has reportedly displaced thousands of people in Oromia and Somali regions. This is in addition to the thousands of people who have reportedly crossed into Kenya, it said.
Local authorities in Kenya estimate that up to 50,000 people have crossed into the country since Thursday, amid reports of further crossings, it said.
Many of those fleeing are women and children. While some are staying with relatives and host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations, such as schools and churches. Food remains the most urgent need, alongside safe drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and health care, said the office.
"Continued insecurity has forced several partners to suspend activities," OCHA said. "The UN and its partners are preparing a joint assessment mission to areas affected by the violence as soon as security conditions permit."
It is critical to ensure the safety of the population, as well as safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access to all people in need, said the office.
The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has deployed an emergency team to Moyale and is working closely with the Kenyan government, UN agencies, the Kenya Red Cross Society and other humanitarian partners to support the national and local response, said OCHA.
The Kenya Red Cross Society is operating six health service points, screening for malnutrition and distributing relief items. Local communities have shared food and water, though their stocks are limited, said OCHA.
The UN and its humanitarian partners are working to scale up the response. UN agencies have deployed staff and are mobilizing additional supplies, including to prepare for potential further displacement. UNHCR is mobilizing emergency relief supplies, including essential household items and temporary shelter materials, to support nearly 12,000 people, with efforts under way to scale up assistance as needs grow, said OCHA. ■

Carvalho framed the announcement in the context of Portugal's ongoing energy crisis, saying that "freeing Portugal from dependence on fossil fuels is not a chimera: it is an essential condition for a better future and less dependence on third parties." ■

News Analysis: Britain's budget targets breathing space for households, businesses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:25:54 CST
06:25:54 KST

LONDON, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- British Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey on Wednesday unveiled the Budget 2026, aiming to give families and firms breathing space from rising costs through supporting measures in the fields including energy, income, housing, spending and business tax.
The government will provide 100 pounds (about 133 U.S. dollars) household energy payment for up to 20 million qualified households in England, with funding for similar support provided to the rest of the UK. Meanwhile, it will extend the value-added-tax cut on electricity bills to July 1, 2027, according to the budget.
The budget supports drivers by extending the cut to fuel duty for a further six months, while cutting prices at local, lower-powered public chargers to reduce costs for electric vehicle drivers who rely on them.
Earlier Wednesday, the Chancellor also abolished standing charges on household gas bills, a fixed daily fee added on top of a household gas bill regardless of how much gas has been used.
In response to the rising inflation, the government will remove tariffs from more than 100 products to lower import costs for everyday family spending such as baked beans and chocolate, and cut tariffs on kerosene and fertilizer to support households and farmers facing higher costs.
At the same time, the budget plans to increase the National Living Wage by 3.9 percent per hour on April 1, 2027.
Moreover, the budget provides a further 1.5 billion pounds (about 2 billion dollars) in funding for social and affordable housing, taking total capital investment over the next 10 years above 40 billion pounds (about 53 billion dollars).
On the front of business support, the budget backs England's high streets with a package that means all retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England will see their business rates either frozen in real terms, reduced or cut to zero.
On top of the extra 20 percent business rates cut for pubs and all but the largest live music venues, announced in July, this package will take around 70,000 more retail, hospitality and leisure businesses out of business rates by increasing the Small Business Rates Relief threshold.
To deal with the energy price hikes faced by enterprises, measures will be taken to support over 10,000 eligible businesses in electricity intensive Industrial Strategy sectors and the foundational sectors in their supply chains to cut electricity bills by up to 25 percent and bring electricity costs closer to other economies in Europe from April 2027.
However, due to the limited momentum of change brought by the budget, analysts believe there should be more ambitious plans from the government to increase living standard and boost business investment in the country.
"For this budget, the outcome for UK residents is really one in which Healey tinkers around the edges," John Bryson, a professor at the University of Birmingham, told Xinhua.
Since forecasts anticipate energy bills will rise again by as much as 27 percent in January, the government also needs to be thinking more long-term about how to protect households from rising energy bills not just in the short term but over a sustained period, said Caitlin Robinson, a professor at the University of Bristol.
This will require more ambitious investment in energy efficiency, low carbon heating and renewable electricity, Robinson added.
"This was a 'steady as you go' budget, sending the right signals to business, but lacking big calls that would really shift the economic dial," Shevaun Haviland, director general of the British Chambers of Commerce, said.
"Our key tests for the Chancellor were whether his plans would boost growth and ease costs for business. Many firms will have been hoping for a greater impact," she noted.
Tina McKenzie, national chair of the Federation of Small Businesses, hoped the increase in Small Business Rates Relief should have covered more businesses, such as manufacturers, small exporters, nurseries and office-based businesses which are not just on the high streets.
Eamonn O'Brien, chair of the Local Government Association, argued that no overall funding increase for local government means councils will continue to struggle to meet demand and provide services to their communities. ■

World Pasta Day has been celebrated annually on October 25 since 1995, when the first World Pasta Congress was held in Rome. This international initiative is coordinated by the International Pasta Organization, a nonprofit organization founded in Rome in 2006 that brings together pasta industry associations from 18 countries.

Ukraine's military reveals what Russia's war has cost Moscow — in dollars, arms, and lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:20:17 UTC
06:20:17 KST

Ukraine's military reveals what Russia's war has cost Moscow — in dollars, arms, and lives
The General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces published a video on Oct. 28 detailing the costs of Russia's full-scale invasion over the past four-and-a-half years.
The price of the war is measured in money, weapons, and soldiers — as well as lost opportunities to invest in Russia's future.
The military's video comes on the 1,707th day of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.
People
Russia has paid a heavy price in blood for every inch of territory occupied in Ukraine. Since Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff calculates that Russia has lost over 1,580,000 personnel.
The casualties include both killed and injured soldiers.
The sum means that Russia loses nearly a thousand people every day, according to the General Staff. Put another way, a Russian soldier dies every 90 seconds.
"This video is three minutes long," the narrator reads.
read also
Equipment
Moscow has lost over $204 billion in military equipment over the course of the war, the military reports.
This includes 12,448 tanks, 51,674 artillery systems, and 25,609 armored combat vehicles. Ukraine also counts 449 destroyed Russian aircraft, 356 helicopters, 35 vessels, and two submarines.
Russia has also lost over five thousand missiles and over 585,000 drones, the military said.
Money
Russia has spent hundreds of billions of dollars waging a war of choice against Ukraine.
In addition to losing billions in destroyed equipment, the Russian government also pays over $95 million per day in compensation for the dead and wounded.
Russia's oil industry has also taken a severe hit due to international sanctions and Ukraine's long-range strikes against refineries, pipelines, and shadow fleet tankers.
In a single year, from August 2025-2026, the industry's total losses reached $13.5 billion, according to the General Staff.
Every year since the start of the all-out invasion, the war has carved an even greater chunk out of the Russian economy. In 2022, the war in Ukraine accounted for 4% of Russia's GDP. In 2025, that number rose to 7.5%.
From spending $86 billion in 2022, Russia spent $190 billion on the war in 2025 and plans to spend another $186 billion in 2026.
In total, Russia has spent over $700 billion on the war against Ukraine.
"With this money, one could build 10,000 kilometers of modern highways, 1,000 new schools, 200 large hospitals, give a million rubles to every child born since the start of the full-scale invasion, pay double the pension to every pensioner for two years, and invest the rest of the money in science, which would be more than Russia has invested in it in the last 10 years," the video says.
The money would also be enough to fund the complete construction of five modern cities of 8-10 million people.
"But Russia chose war," the narrator says.

Israel election results: Netanyahu bloc holds lead with double envelopes after 90% of votes counted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:05:14 UTC
06:05:14 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc maintained its lead and was projected to win 53 seats in the next Knesset, while the opposition bloc was projected to win 48 seats, the Central Elections Committee said Thursday.
It said more than five million votes had been counted in Tuesday’s election.
Both blocs fell short of the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority without the support of the Arab parties, which at last count had won a record-breaking combined total of 19 seats.
The official vote count reached 97% on Thursday afternoon and excluded only double-envelope ballots.
Double-envelope ballots could still affect final election results
Those ballots allow eligible Israelis, including soldiers, hospital patients, prisoners, and certain election workers, to vote outside their designated polling stations. They could significantly affect the final election results.
According to the official vote count, Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to have 27 seats, making it once again the largest party in the Knesset. United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit were expected to have seven seats, and the Religious Zionist Party and Shas were expected to have six seats.
Most TV channel polling before the election projected Likud to receive significantly fewer seats, while the other parties in Netanayhu’s bloc were expected to gain more.
Central Elections Committee data projected the opposition bloc, comprising Yashar, B’Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu, and The Democrats, to have 48 seats.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar was projected to have 21 seats. B’Yachad, led by Naftali Bennett, was projected to have 12 seats. Yair Golan’s The Democrats was projected to have eight seats, and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu was projected to have seven seats.
Ofer Winter’s People of Israel and Yoaz Hendel’s The Reservists-Economic party were both projected to fall short of the required 3.25% threshold, potentially further complicating efforts by Netanyahu’s bloc to secure a majority.
The Joint List was projected to win 11 seats, while Ra’am was projected to win eight.
Amid the high Arab voter turnout, the Likud on Wednesday accused the Arab parties of allegedly stealing the election through widespread election fraud, bribery, intimidation, and ballot manipulation. It demanded an immediate investigation by law-enforcement authorities.
Despite the election results, the prospect of a unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot has appeared unlikely. Eisenkot has rejected serving under Netanyahu, including in a rotation government. Other opposition leaders have also ruled out joining a Netanyahu-led coalition.
The political deadlock could ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations.
By law, the president is required to consult the Knesset factions before deciding who receives the task of forming a government.
Herzog calls on politicians to keep open minds during coalition negotiations
President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday called on political leaders to approach coalition negotiations with open minds, warning that Israel must do everything possible to avoid another election.
“One thing must be understood, and I said this even before the elections: We must do everything, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said. “Therefore, I expect everyone who comes here to arrive with an open mind.”
He was referring to consultations expected to take place at the President’s Residence.
Golan confirmed on Wednesday that he would meet with “three opposition leaders” on Thursday. In a Channel 12 interview, he declined to name the leaders.
Earlier on Wednesday morning, Golan called on the opposition bloc to form a government with the Arab parties. He said Netanyahu had lost the election with some 55 seats, compared with the opposition’s 65, including the Arab parties.
“Netanyahu lost,” Golan posted on social media. “I know how to count to 120. Sixty-five is more than 55. That’s how Israeli democracy works. Period.”
“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid... We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he added.
Golan said the opposition had won a Zionist majority, saying Netanyahu “should subtract 16 seats” belonging to the haredi parties.
All the other opposition party leaders have said Arab parties being part of the government would be a red line for them, following the October 7 massacre in 2023.
Eisenkot has called for the leader of the largest party in the opposition bloc to become its candidate for prime minister, although no agreement on the arrangement has been announced within the bloc.
He declared victory for the opposition bloc on Tuesday night after exit polls showed Yashar in the lead. Later that night, Netanyahu also delivered a victory speech after polling began showing his bloc with a clear lead.
The political deadlock also raised the possibility of a minority government being formed that could win a Knesset confidence vote without holding an absolute majority of 61 seats. In that scenario, Arab parties could agree to support the opposition bloc. Members of the Arab parties have said anything possible should be done to prevent Netanyahu from remaining in office.
Objection within the opposition bloc to relying on Arab parties could complicate such an arrangement. Liberman openly rejected such an option ahead of the election.
Joint List prepared to 'pave the way,' for Netanyahu ouster, Jabareen says
On Wednesday, Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen said his party was ready to “pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government.” He had previously said he would support a minority government if a series of demands were met.
Later, in an interview with Army Radio, Joint List faction chairman MK Ahmad Tibi (Hadash-Ta’al) hinted at his willingness to sit with the opposition.
“The opposition bloc will be able to form a government if it has the courage,” he said. “We are extending a hand and are ready to help.”
The Bennett-Yair Lapid government formed in 2021 was the first in Israel’s history to include an Arab party, Ra’am, in the coalition. It was a highly controversial move. Bennett has since taken a firm stance against including any Arab faction in a future coalition.
Ra’am has sought to be seen as a viable coalition partner. Its chairman, Monsour Abbas, said in August that former Yesh Atid MK Yoav Segalovitz would be No. 2 on his list.
The move was unprecedented, as he was the first Jewish candidate to join the Islamist political party. The addition of a Jewish, Zionist candidate to the Arab party’s list has been widely seen as a way for Ra’am to be viewed as a more viable coalition partner.
Shir Perets and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Ford reports mixed third-quarter results, says 2027 earnings will be in line with this year

21:01:16 UTC
06:01:16 KST

DETROIT — Ford Motor expects earnings next year will be roughly in line with the automaker's anticipated results this year, the company said Wednesday as it reported mixed results for the third quarter.
The Detroit automaker beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations but slightly missed revenue estimates. The company has been working to stabilize production of its F-Series pickup trucks after dealing with supplier issues for much of the past year.
"This quarter's results reflect deliberate actions to improve profitability and deliver consistent financial returns," Ford CFO Sherry House told reporters during a call Wednesday.
Ford reported third-quarter adjusted free cash flow of $4.7 billion, roughly $2 billion higher than what analysts were anticipating, according to StreetAccount.
Here's how Ford performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 49 cents adjusted vs. 40 cents expected
- Automotive revenue: $46.08 billion vs. $46.24 billion expected
The Detroit automaker also narrowed its 2026 guidance to adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $10.5 billion and $11 billion, compared with a previous outlook of $10 billion to $11 billion. Ford maintained its adjusted free cash flow guidance for this year of between $6 billion and $7 billion.
House said the company expects 2027 earnings to be roughly in line with this year's results, citing several offsetting factors in production issues this year as well as rising commodity costs.
House noted a $1.3 billion tariff refund during the first quarter of this year was largely offset by additional costs from alternative aluminum sourcing that the company does not expect to have next year, leveling out the year-over-year comparison.
She also said production of its F-Series Super Duty trucks in Canada in 2027 will make up for lost production it's expecting at its F-150 factories to retool for new models.
"Next year will be the third year on our journey of increasing and improving our warranty and material cost savings, and that's getting extended to structural costs throughout the company as well in terms of savings," House said.
Ford CEO Jim Farley called 2027 a "foundational year" for the company on its way to a previously announced target of an 8% adjusted EBIT margin by 2029. The company reported a 5.4% margin during the third quarter.
Ahead of the results, Wall Street analysts were mixed about whether Ford would be able to maintain profits in 2027.
The company has multiple efforts that will add to costs next year: It's rolling out several new or redesigned models, including its next-generation EV and Canada-produced pickups, and is enhancing its energy business that it announced earlier this year.
The missed revenue for the third quarter was a result of each of the automaker's main business units – which are broken into Blue traditional operations, Pro fleet and Model e electric vehicle segments – underperforming compared with Wall Street's expectations, according to StreetAccount.
As part of its modified guidance, Ford said it now expects pre-tax earnings of its Ford Blue unit to be $5.5 billion, which is at the high end of a previous guidance.
It's also anticipating EBIT of about $7 billion for the year for Ford Pro and Ford Model e losses of about $4 billion. Its Ford Credit unit is expected to record about $2.8 billion in EBIT for 2026.
Ford's overall revenue, which includes its credit segment, was off roughly 2% compared with the third quarter of last year, to $49.5 billion.
Its net income also was off $400 million from a year earlier to $2 billion, while adjusted earnings before interest and taxes were up slightly year-over-year to $2.7 billion.
Ford's 2025 third-quarter results included $47.19 billion in automotive revenue, net income of $2.4 billion and earnings per share of 45 cents adjusted.

Saab launches space command and control platform

Unknown Publisher

21:00:56 GMT
06:00:56 KST

Saab has launched the Allied Mission System, a cloud-based platform that brings space domain awareness, mission management and command and control together so that operators can watch and respond to activity in orbit, according to the company.
The system fuses data from integrated sensors and third party assets, runs automated analysis to produce decision support, and gives operators the means to coordinate assets, task systems and manage missions. Its modular architecture lets data services, mission services and applications evolve separately, and it is built to integrate later with wider multi-domain operations.
Andy Keough, managing director of Saab Australia, said: “Almost everything we do relies on space in some way and we have designed our new AMS platform to give the user the capability to act in this highly congested and contested domain. This innovative and purpose driven technology leverages Saab’s experience delivering trusted multi-domain command and control systems and exemplifies our commitment to ongoing sovereign capability development.”
Chris Picton, the South Australian Minister for Defence and Space Industries, said: “South Australia is the home of the nation’s space industry and Saab’s AMS demonstrates the advanced technologies being developed right here in SA. As space becomes an increasingly important domain for national security, South Australian based companies like Saab are helping develop the sovereign capabilities Australia needs while creating high-skilled jobs and strengthening our defence industry.”
The platform was designed and built in Australia for deployment worldwide and will be sold as software as a service, with customers able to tailor and extend it. Saab already supplies command and control systems for sea, land and air forces across a range of countries.

In genocide-ravaged Gaza and the occupied West Bank, many Palestinians were less focused on who would win Israel's election than on whether anything would really change.
Whether the ICC-wanted Benjamin Netanyahu clings to power with his extremist allies or centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot comes out on top, few see much reason for hope in the Tuesday vote.
"We fear these elections could bring an even worse leader," said Huda al-Houli, a displaced resident of Khan Yunis in southern Gaza.
Such an outcome, she said, would only bring "more destruction and devastation" to the Palestinian territory.
Still, Houli said she hoped a more "human voice" would emerge in Israeli society and demand an end to the genocidal war, regardless of who forms the next government.
In Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, Ahmed Awad, 67, was equally sceptical.
"Whatever the result, and even if the politicians change, I don't think there will be any radical or dramatic shift in policies towards the Palestinian-Israeli conflict," he told AFP news agency.
With 85 percent of ballots counted from Tuesday's vote, Netanyahu's camp remained ahead but without a clear majority, leaving uncertainty over Israel's next government.
The first election since Gaza genocide comes after years of right-wing and far-right rule marked by Israeli carnage in Gaza and rising illegal settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
For Netanyahu, scrambling to cling to power, several paths remain open: renewing his alliance with far-right extremists, building a broader coalition or facing yet another political deadlock.
Far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir has already signalled that, if the current coalition survives, he would seek the defence portfolio and push for the expulsion of Gaza's population.
More of the same
Not everyone has given up hope.
"Whatever happens, it will surely be better than what we've lived through in recent years," said Abdallah Abu Rahma, 54, from Ramallah.
But if Netanyahu remains in office, he added, "any coalition he forms, he will continue down the same path".
Researcher Beth Oppenheim of the European Council on Foreign Relations suggested that a government led by Eisenkot, a former army chief, could rein in the influence of the pro-settlement far right.
In her assessment, such a government might also ease pressure on the Palestinian Authority and take a more flexible approach on aid and a ceasefire in Gaza.
But she warned against expecting too much.
There would be "nothing transformative", she said, and certainly no major shift on Palestinian statehood or the peace process, issues that have largely disappeared from Israeli political debate since October 2023.
A renewed Netanyahu coalition with far-right partners would likely mean more of the same, including illegal settlement expansion and impunity for settler violence, Oppenheim added.
"I think we need to have quite low expectations when it comes to seeing any major changes in policy from a different government," she said.
Fears of escalation
Palestinians would still face significant risks under a new Israeli government, warned Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine-Israel programme at the Arab Center Washington.
"There is every reason for Palestinians to be concerned," he said.
Eisenkot himself served in Israel's wartime cabinet during the Gaza genocide, Munayyer noted.
A fragile alternative coalition under constant attack from Netanyahu and the far-right could try to prove it was tough enough by taking a harder line on occupation of Palestine.
In the occupied West Bank, violence could rise if the far right loses power, with illegal Zionist settlers potentially acting out against a new government, he explained.
"It's important to understand that most settler violence in the West Bank is structural. It's not about the government in charge," Munayyer said.
"Settlers live in places that surround the Palestinian population. The Palestinian population is vulnerable to the settlers, who are armed, whereas the Palestinians overwhelmingly are not."
In Gaza, Adnan Al-Assar said he harboured few illusions.
"Whatever happens, they all follow the same overarching policy, directed against the Palestinian people." he said.
