On a day that could have ended Test careers, a few young ones flourish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:36:43 UTC
05:36:43 KST

The vague suspicion before play on day two of the Cape Town Test was that Australia — out of form, stalked by rumours of disharmony in the ranks, its batting line-up restocked and reshuffled for the umpteenth time — was one more calamitous batting collapse away from the end of an era.
The day of perfectly calm and controlled Test batting that took place instead was no less arresting, and in the context of this topsy-turvy series, far more surprising. For 90 overs, Australia batted diligently, adaptively, intelligently and at changing tempos, building a series of reassuring partnerships that put it in control of the game.
Elevated to the opening slot, Matt Renshaw looked safe as houses. Slotted into Steve Smith's number four position, Cameron Green hit a commanding half-century. Drafted in at the 11th hour, Josh Inglis was closing in on a century by stumps and had dragged Alex Carey along in his slipstream.
It all meant that Proteas attack leader Kagiso Rabada, who probably woke up feeling comfortable with the expectation it would be his day to wreak some havoc — perhaps even end some careers — went wicketless, as did too many of his mates.
Thanks to stands of 126 between Renshaw and Green and an undefeated 145 between Inglis and Carey, Australia reached 4-330 by stumps and walked away probably feeling in the box seat on a pitch offering very little assistance to the bowlers.
The weight of numbers was one thing, the problem-solving another. In two testing periods, South Africa made double-strikes and threatened to blow the game back open, only for the tourists to consolidate and rebuild.
The crunch moments came in the 18th over, when off-spinner Simon Harmer ripped out Travis Head and Marnus Labuschagne, and just before tea, when Renshaw and Green were removed by Marco Jansen in the space of a few overs.
Both times Australia took a deep breath, regrouped and pushed on in the same direction as before.
The only major negative of the day for Australia — although the many unkind souls who wish him bad luck will not view it so — was Labuschagne's duck. Out-of-form players often have a knack for attracting unplayable balls. At the moment, poor old Marnus can make almost anything look unplayable.
For a team that has not produced a single 100-run opening partnership in the past three years, Renshaw's 74 from 139 deliveries was a welcome return to normalcy at the top of the order. In a 58-run stand with Travis Head (41) to start off, the Queenslander was deferential and circumspect, showing they could be a fire and ice combination.
But it was Renshaw's union with Green, which stretched across 32 overs, that provided the most welcome glimpse of the future of this Australian team.
They were a study on contrasts: surely no batsman as big as Renshaw has ever made himself such a small target for bowlers; heavy-footed Green, on the other hand, has the awkward tendency to turn himself into a fast bowler's piñata, swaying and ducking into bouncers, and in this case wearing a few painful body blows from the shorter stuff South Africa threw at him in large doses.
In the latter sense, Green again showed he had guts. And as he got going, his fluent stroke play more than made up for the cobwebs he was destined to display after three and a half weeks without a competitive hit.
As Aiden Markram had treated Pat Cummins's bowling with disdain on day one, Green took it upon himself to take down Rabada, who has lorded it over Australia in the past.
The killer blow on that front was when Green moved into the 40s with a trio of swivel-pulls that brought six, six and four off consecutive deliveries.
Renshaw, as in his Durban epic, was more watchful and unassuming, content to press, deflect, dab, flick and generally accumulate — precisely the sort of calm, unhurried Test batting Australia has been crying out for in the past two years, and which is the bedrock of the big, defendable totals Australia will need to post when it can no longer rely on its brilliant but aging bowling unit.
As well as re-emphasising Labuschagne's redundancy, the Renshaw-Green partnership might also, in the wash-up, accelerate the conversation about how Australia tactfully moves on from the Smith and Labuschagne era.
What more is there to say about Marnus at this point? Harmer, who weeded him out this time, is a canny bowler and has proved himself a big-moment performer in this series. But geez, his wicket ball this time was not exactly a jaffa.
Labuschagne shuffled back to what might otherwise have been a half-volley, pushed at it with hard hands, his slicing bat plane again a horror story, and Markram gobbled the edge at slip.
And what Labuschagne had made look impossible in that brief and tortured innings was, by the end of the day, looking entirely straightforward thanks to Inglis and Carey, undefeated on 85 and 51 respectively.
Loose and a little too eager to play his shots earlier in the series, Carey took a leaf out of Renshaw's book with nudges, nurdles and strike rotation. Inglis, whose finger injury prevented even net sessions for most of the past two weeks, clobbered nine fours and two sixes to poleaxe a tiring Proteas attack.
Tomorrow, both or either batsmen could feasibly take the game and the series away from South Africa in the space of an hour or two. But then, we've said that before, haven't we?

RIO DE JANEIRO – Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who arrived in the United States on Oct 28, has declared himself the rightful leader of Brazil, alleging an electoral coup d’etat had been carried out by the country’s Supreme Court and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won the presidential election by more than four million votes.

He thanked Argentinian leader Javier Milei for helping him make the journey and US President Donald Trump, who had granted him and his family entry visas, for welcoming him.

Lula’s victory has been recognised by Brazil’s federal electoral court, global leaders, international observers and Bolsonaro’s own party.

Lawsuit seeks to block Trump administration effort to find noncitizen voters

Lawsuit seeks to block Trump administration effort to find noncitizen voters
WILMINGTON, Delaware, Oct 28 - A Trump administration initiative to deploy hundreds of investigators to hunt for noncitizen voters is illegally intimidating naturalized US citizens and subjecting them to possible disenfranchisement, according to a lawsuit filed by civil rights groups that seeks to end the practice.
The lawsuit filed on Wednesday in California federal court by the American Civil Liberties Union and affiliates also alleges that the administration is demanding state election officials deny ballots to certain voters based on flawed eligibility data, potentially undermining confidence in next week's midterm elections.
President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party is locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress, has repeatedly asserted that noncitizen voting is widespread in US elections, a claim that has been widely debunked.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that the administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas for records on tens of thousands of voters in at least a dozen states as part of the effort to uncover noncitizen voting.
"The administration can't keep creating political stunts to sow distrust in our elections and lay the groundwork to question results they don't like," said Theresa Lee, an attorney with the ACLU's Voting Rights Project, in a statement.
HOMELAND SECURITY AMONG DEFENDANTS
The lawsuit names as defendants the Department of Homeland Security and Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and US Citizenship and Immigration Services and Director Joseph Edlow. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In August, DHS launched the Unlawful Voter Initiative, which directed US Citizenship and Immigration Services personnel to generate lists of individuals to investigate for possibly voting without being a US citizen, as is legally required.
In the months since, the Justice Department has brought more than 100 cases accusing individuals of noncitizen voting. It has also launched a legal effort to prevent California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters that the administration alleges are noncitizens.
The ACLU lawsuit said the initiative has led to thousands of fully naturalized American citizens being subjected to improper investigations, door-to-door interrogations and potential disenfranchisement.
The groups alleged the initiative violates the Civil Rights Act and laws governing privacy and administrative procedures. The lawsuit seeks to vacate the Unlawful Voter Initiative and asks for the destruction of records that were created and maintained as part of the initiative.
Last week, a federal judge in California placed limits on the Unlawful Voter Initiative in nine states, but the plaintiffs said those restrictions expire at the end of Election Day on November 3, allowing the initiative to be used in future federal elections. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Most Servers on the Planet Are Vulnerable to This Firmware Code-Execution Flaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:30:00 UTC
05:30:00 KST

Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.
The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.
The Cat Has Left the Bag
The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.
With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.
“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”
CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.
As the official advisory puts it:
The malicious error can be delivered through a simple unicast sent from any network distance to a target device’s IP address, as long as it’s sent during the PXE boot sequence. An attacker can deliver a denial-of-service by causing the boot sequence to hang. When the attacker knows what the target firmware build is, it can plant a “counterfeit event” that executes the malicious code on the CPU in its UEFI firmware environment. The code runs in ring 0, a CPU’s most privileged execution level. Because exploits bypass attestation processes designed to cryptographically prove to remote servers that the hardware is secure, they present a key opportunity for elevating limited privileges.
Yet Another Forever Day
CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail, stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot flaws in EDK2. Following discovery of the vulnerability, researchers embarked on multiple fuzzing projects designed to surface other critical flaws in the open source code library. It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.
Other recently discovered UEFI flaws include:
- PKFail, a supply-chain failure resulting from non-production test platform keys, public for more than a decade before they were discovered, used in hundreds of device models;
- BootHole;
- Bootkit; and
- BlackLotus.
Like CVE-2026-97631, exploitation or use of these payloads is appealing because it allows attackers to infect machines early in the boot process, before TPM and other defenses load, so they can inflict maximum damage. Given the ubiquity of CVE-2026-97631, Moore said it’s likely a “forever” bug that will live on in end-of-support systems.
There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear.
“For exploiting the vulnerability itself, an attacker needs to guess specific addresses within the target system, so it’s not something that you can throw a single exploit at any target and get RCE across a diverse range of devices, but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those,” Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars.
“Unlike some of the previous, high-profile vulnerabilities like BootHole, Black Lotus, and Baton Drop, this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update, but they don’t need to deal with revocations, pk/kek/db/dbx key management updates, or making sure to update OS and provisioning media like you do with Secure Boot bypasses in the bootloader itself.”
CVE-2026-97631 doesn’t affect home and small office users, or any other users who boot their devices solely from disk drives. Instead, it applies only to organizations with machines that boot from local networks, or conceivably from Internet-connected resources. Even then, the targeted firmware must rely on EDK2, as opposed to a different reference implementation, and use the PXE functionality (which is turned on by default).
In an email, Intel said that none of its “commercial products currently under security support” are known to be affected. “Intel does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code, though it may be integrated by an OEM board vendor or system manufacturer,” the company added. It advised customers to check with their system manufacturer for specific guidance. Publicly available Intel reference code, however, makes reference to EDK2. Further, TianoCore has said that each Intel-supplied UEFI development kit “is a fully validated implementation … for a specific revision of the EDK II source.” Many other Intel documents reference EDK2 as well.
Arm, meanwhile, responded to a list of questions with: “CVE-2026-97631 is not directly applicable to Arm’s product portfolio.” Like Intel, firmware the company makes available also borrows heavily from EDK2. TianoCore has also documented Arm’s reliance on EDK2.
While it’s possible some platforms are free of EDK2 code, it’s prudent for users of all servers to investigate if CVE-2026-97631 affects them.
Questions sent to AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon—likely some of the other biggest organizations affected—went unanswered when this post went live. Without concrete answers to questions about the use of EDK2 by organizations like these, it’s impossible to say what or how devices are affected and what actions, if any, these organizations, or their users, should take. Representatives from the TianoCore Project also didn’t respond.
Some readers are likely to be unhappy at the lack of detail. Sometimes—particularly in cases involving botched disclosures that break embargoes months before they’re scheduled to lift—there’s no escaping the lack of actionable information in initial reporting.
Those affected should check with the maker of the firmware being used to boot their systems and ask for guidance. Beyond that, they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible. Firmware configurations should always enable security features such as TPM and Secure Boot whenever possible, although those defenses don’t protect against this particular threat. It’s also a good idea to monitor logs for signs of exploitation attempts.
This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.

"I know the Whitlam government tried to win a referendum on prices and income control and they failed," he says.
"The Australia public did not support them so I have questions about our price control would work to be frank."
That's despite annual inflation skyrocketing from 5.6 per cent in the March quarter to 12.5 per cent in December by the time of the referendum.
It continued to worsen, peaking at 17.7 per cent by mid-1975.

Surveillance cameras not a substitute for supervision in childcare, Walsh says
Further to our previous post, in Senate estimates, Minister for Early Childhood Education Jess Walsh says her state and territory counterparts will consider the benefits, restrictions and concerns around the use of cameras.
It comes after Four Corners obtained CCTV footage of a childcare worker assaulting three young boys in her care.

What are the CCTV rules in childcare centres?
Officials from the Department of Education have been asked about video surveillance protocols for childcare centres, after the latest Four Corners investigation exposed child-safety failures.
CCTV footage obtained by Four Corners showed a childcare worker inflicting 82 assaults on three young boys at Injinoo Childcare Centre in far north Queensland.
Childcare ministers will meet on Monday, where Education Minister Jason Clare has confirmed the episode will be discussed.
Liberal Senator Matt O'Sullivan asks department officials about cameras in childcare centres.

Department yet to find someone to conduct consent education review
The Department of Education says they have not secured an independent evaluator to review the Consent and Respectful Relationships Education (CRRE) program in schools.
In August, Education Minister Jason Clare ordered the independent review into the CRRE to assess its effectiveness and to determine whether it was appropriately resourced, following reports of sexual assaults in schools.
Fronting Senate estimates today, Assistant Secretary Pamela Banerjee said the Department had not received a response to their initial request for an independent evaluator earlier this month.
Last week, the Department republished the request for a quote.
"Following on from that, we will identify a suitable provider to undertake that evaluation," she said.
"We are working towards findings to be determined and the review to be completed by March/April next year, but it is subject to finding a suitable provider to undertake the work."
Barnajee says they will consult experts, state and territory education departments and non-government school sectors delivering the program.

Would Treasury consider modelling the impact of climate change on inflation?
That's the question put by independent MP Zali Steggall.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers takes this one. He doesn't commit to any specific modelling as was requested by Steggall but rather points to it being a concern for a number of ministers.
In his own portfolio, he points to the intergenerational report.
"The climate modelling makes it clear that the most important thing that we can do is to manage an orderly, energy transition," he says.
Chalmers continues:
"This is an area where so many of our economic challenges and opportunities come together. It is a big opportunity for Australia to get it right. But the risks are everywhere," he says.
Key Event
AFP granted control order for man convicted of planning terrorist act
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has confirmed that an interim control order was granted for Isaak el Matari, who was convicted in 2021 of plotting a terrorist attack.
The revelation came after Liberal MP Andrew Wallace asked Burke why he didn't seek a "continuing detention order to keep this dangerous terrorist off our streets".
Burke starts his answer by saying that el Matari engaged in views and planning that was "beyond contempt".
Burke said although there was a maximum sentence of life imprisonment for those crimes, he was given a non-parole period of five and a half years.
"I think we would all have similar questions about the gap between the maximum penalties we had made available and where this has landed," Burke said.
He said the Australian Federal Police had sought a control order.
"I am pleased to say they did go to court and seek a control order, and I'm pleased to advise the House that, earlier today, the court agreed to allow that interim control order," Burke said.
Government says 'significant work undertaken' to fix Centrelink regime that cut off payments
Tasmanian independent MP Andrew Wilkie has questioned what has been done to fix the Centrelink system in which people were cut off from payments.
Last year, a Commonwealth Ombudsman found almost 1,000 jobseekers had their payments cancelled over two years under a Centrelink compliance regime.
The framework is now being reinstated after the review, allowing Centrelink payment suspensions and penalties to resume.
Workplace Relations minister Amanda Rishworth says the government accepted all ombudsman recommendations and has targeted $48.8 million to strengthen the integrity of the system.
"The significant work undertaken includes IT system improvements, intensive testing, which will continue to ensure the system operates as intended," she says.
"She says a clearer complaints and review process has been introduced as well as greater mandatory training for all stuff to ensure good practices are decisions."

A moment for the bravery of Australian police officers

Last night, officers were honoured at the annual National Police Bravery Awards.
Among them were the 54 Queensland officers who responded to a shooting in Wieambilla the end of 2022.
The ambush at the rural property led to the death of Queensland Police Constables Matthew Arnold and Rachel McCrow.
He highlighted the bravery of Constable Keely Brough and Constable Randall Kirk during the incident, recalling their response.
"The response from the offenders was to set fire to the bushland, hoping to bring her out, she [Constable Brough] called 000 as she hid in the grass, at times whispering to the operator … as the offenders search close to her hiding place," he says.

Busy day in House of Representatives
It's been a busy day in the House of Reps, with a bunch of bills being pushed through in one go as the government scrambles to send its legislation to the Senate before the end of the year.
There's only a handful of sitting days left in the Upper House across two final weeks of sitting.
Of course getting it through the House of Reps, where the government enjoys a majority, is not the problem.
One of the things that has passed today is the government's gas reservation legislation.
A number of opposition and crossbench MPs tried to pass amendments to the bill but were voted down.
Labor also passed some amendments to its tax reform bills, including discretionary trusts.
Who is responsible for the drones flying around a NSW air base?
The Chief of the Air Force says it’s not yet clear who was behind drone incursions at the Williamtown air base.
The Department of Defence has confirmed NSW police have been investigating multiple unidentified drones flying around the base and the neighbouring Newcastle Airport over several days in July.
It’s not an isolated event. Officials have told Senate estimates there has been a surge in the number of drone incursions over or near military facilities in recent years.
In the 2025-26 financial year there were 204 "incident reports" involving drones, up from 141 in the 2024-25 financial year.
The year before that there were 56, and only 19 the year before.
But it's not yet clear exactly who is largely responsible.
When the Coalition frontbencher James Paterson asks whether the Williamtown incursion was the work of "a silly teenager" or "something much more nefarious". Defence officials simply say it isn't clear yet.
One-quarter of ADF personnel not medically fit to deploy
Around one in four Australian troops are currently ruled out from being deployed due to medical issues, a senior military official has revealed.
Defence Chief of Personnel, Lieutenant General Natasha Fox, has told Senate estimates that "over 75 per cent of the ADF are actually in a deployable medical military employment classification".
She says about 13 per cent of that cohort had been placed on light duties while recovering from temporary injuries.
"We have some that are temporarily downgraded, and those temporarily downgraded in a military employment classification might be for an injury that has an ongoing rehabilitation requirement ... but it's only a temporary downgrade."
Puberty blocker guidelines will be released on November 16
The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) will release its interim national treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse youth on November 16.
The review of the guidelines was originally commissioned by Health Minister Mark Butler in 2025, following Queensland imposing a freeze on access to the medications for children with gender dysphoria who were not already on them, and ordering its own review.
Prue Torrance, acting CEO of the NHMRC, has told a Senate estimates committee that the advice is being delivered in in line with a previous commitment from the Council to release specific guidance on puberty blockers earlier than the rest of the report.
"And we're confident we will make that date," she says.
Liberal Senator Anne Ruston asks Ms Torrance what the advice would contain.
"It will provide the latest evidence and suggestions on best practice for the use of puberty suppressants. It won't advise what clinical services or public funding should be. It is simply a review of the evidence, that's our role," she says.
The final guidelines are due in 2028.
When the 'ayes' don't have it
If you joined us yesterday, you might remember that Barnaby Joyce was planning to put an amendment in the House of Reps to get One Nation's superannuation policy up today.
Under that policy, Australians who pay rent or a mortgage could choose to divert a portion of their super to their take-home pay for up to three years.
We already knew this amendment from Joyce was probably doomed, given the government's overwhelming majority, but could he tempt anyone else to vote for it?
Unfortunately for One Nation, no. Joyce and his colleague David Farley made a lonely-looking pair sitting on the bench, as the only ones to vote "aye".
The Super Members Council would have welcomed this turn of events, warning that One Nation's plan to "turn super into an ATM" would "just drive up inflation" and "make Australians poorer in retirement".
Defence chief pushes back on story about US agents infiltrating Australian bases
The chief of the Defence Force says an article alleging that US security agents secretly infiltrated Australian naval bases in order to test their security was "factually incorrect".
Greens leader David Shoebridge has used Senate estimates to grill officials about the report, which said that the US Naval Criminal Investigative Service (NCIS) deployed undercover to multiple bases — including HMAS Stirling in Western Australia and HMAS Kuttabul in Sydney — to "test existing physical security measures".
Shoebridge says it appeared to be an extraordinary breach of national security.
But senior Defence officials say the exercise happened with Australia's "full knowledge and concurrence" and that the US agents testing security were accompanied by Australian personnel.
Chief of the Australian Defence Force, Admiral Mark Hammond, has labelled the reporting "factually incorrect".
"We work in partnership with the US authorities so they can understand the understand the security apparatus in place for their visiting ships," he says.
Calls to tackle racism in health care
The federal government has acknowledged there is work to be done in addressing racism in the healthcare system, after a report from the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners found around one-third of general practitioners have witnessed racism directed at patients in the last year.
The annual "health of the nation" report measures the trends and challenges in general practice in Australia.
It found GPs were often subject to racism themselves, with around one in five reporting they had experienced it from a patient. Despite the prevalence of racism in the sector, less than two-thirds of GPs reported feeling confident in addressing and challenging racism when it arises.
The federal government has told the ABC it is taking steps to improve outcomes in the health sector, with assistant minister for Indigenous health Rebecca White pointing to investments by the Commonwealth.
"A range of work is underway to address cultural safety and racism in the health system, including $14.6 million for the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care to strengthen cultural safety and address racism in the hospital system," she said in a statement.
"We know there is more work to do."

Teenager arrested over terrorism offences and plans for 3D-printed guns
A Darwin teenager is due to appear in children's court in the Northern Territory today, charged with alleged terrorism, violent extremist material and firearm manufacturing offences.
According to the AFP, the teenager is charged with collecting documents likely to facilitate a terrorist act, as well as schematics for 3D-printed guns.
The Northern Territory Joint Counter Terrorism Team (which includes the AFP, intelligence agency ASIO and the NT Police), started investigating earlier this month after getting a Crime Stoppers tip about "violent extremist material suspected to have been posted online by an Australian user".
AFP Counter Terrorism Commander Paula Hudson said authorities were becoming increasingly concerned about the "speed and scale of radicalisation", especially among young people.
"It is well-documented that terrorists and violent extremists use the online environment to radicalise vulnerable individuals, and technology is enabling this to occur at a rapidly increasing rate," she said.

ADF chief grilled over 'serious failures' of leadership that allowed war crimes to occur
The Chief of the Defence Force Mark Hammond says he has "nothing to contest" regarding a report that found Defence leadership helped create a culture that allowed alleged war crimes to occur in Afghanistan, as he repeatedly distanced himself from the decisions of his predecessors.
It comes as a secretive inquiry released this week found deep, systemic cultural problems were rife in the ADF's Special Air Service Regiment (SASR) and that the lack of intervention to correct them indicated "an absence of effective leadership at various levels".
Pressed by Greens leader David Shoebridge about a lack of accountability for senior leadership, Admiral Hammond said the issue predated his tenure.
"I have nothing to contest the findings or recommendations of the Inspector-General IDF report, which is again, it's been actioned by my predecessors," he said.
Asked directly why nobody in headquarters has been held to account, Admiral Hammond responded:
"Senator, again, you're talking about historical issues which predate my tenure. What I can state is that I agree with the findings of the IGADF.
"I reject the fact that people should be able to behave that way and get away with it. I'm absolutely in agreement. That is, there are serious failures here that need to be addressed.
"Ultimately, those recommendations have been made to my predecessors. They've been actioned."
Admiral Hammond emphasised he had taken significant action to improve command accountability across the ADF.
"What I can talk to is what has been done since the inquiry report with respect to improving command accountability across the service in the Australian Defence Force, the introduction of appointment to command certificate to provide greater accountability of commanders, and just in the last three months I've replaced the ADF Chiefs of Service Committee system within ADF Command Board system."
He told the committee that he raised the issue of command accountability with his respective service chiefs on his first day in the job.
Women in parliament band together after alleged attack on Helen Haines
Women from across the political divide, including Minister for Women Katy Gallagher, her Liberal counterpart Melissa McIntosh, Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young and independent MP Rebekha Sharkie, are launching a new group called the Network of Women in Parliament (NOW).
The purpose of the group is to "build connections, strengthen relationships" and share experiences and support each other "beyond political lines".
"The devastating [alleged] attack on our parliamentary colleague Helen Haines has further highlighted the importance of coming together in support, solidarity and friendship across political divides," NOW said in a press release.
"Helen has always demonstrated the importance of kindness, compassion and genuine connection across political divides."
"In many ways, she embodies the very spirit of what NOW hopes to achieve."
The group will be officially launched on November 24, and will also be a fundraiser for Haines's chosen charity, Save the Children.
Australians donating to that charity in Haines's name have so far raised just shy of $1.4 million.
Greens and Coalition in talks with Labor on gas reservation scheme
Both the Greens and the Coalition say they are in "good faith" discussions with the Labor government about its gas reservation scheme.
The legislation, which is due to be debated in the House of Representatives today, allow for up to 20 per cent of gas exports to be put aside for domestic use.
Greens leader David Shoebridge said his party wanted to see gas consumption reduce.
"That's critical for the climate," he told News24.
The Greens want a 25 per cent minimum tax on gas exports to provide revenue to fund schools and hospitals, and Shoebridge said his party's primary goal was that gas companies paid their "fair share".
Nationals MP Kevin Hogan said the Coalition wanted to see new gas come online and they had some "lines in the sand" they were negotiating on with the government.
But he added the Coalition supported the principle of a gas reservation scheme.

It's been 10 days since independent MP Helen Haines was critically injured after being hit by a car outside her Wangaratta electorate office.

ATO 'simply don't understand' small business

Labor accused of having 'sat on their hands' on ATO credit card ban
Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson has joined his Coalition colleague Andrew Hastie in saying the tax office should have "done better" on its credit card ban.
The government was forced to extend the acceptance of credit card payments after outcry from small businesses.
"The reason why they didn't do better is because there was no political leadership exercised here," Paterson told News24.
"Let's remember that the Albanese government took full credit for the ban on surcharges on credit cards. Let's remember that they were warned by the ATO months in advance that they intended to stop taking credit card payments, including from small business, for tax debts.
"And what did Labor do? Nothing. They sat on their hands."
The Liberal senator said Treasurer Jim Chalmers "owns every single piece of responsibility for this mess that they've now created".
Albanese should have admitted he got it wrong earlier, Paterson says
Liberal senator James Paterson says Prime Minister Anthony Albanese should have notified parliament sooner that he got it wrong when he initially claimed a $6 million non-competitive grant awarded to a golf club in his electorate was to fix sewerage problems.
Albanese was forced to admit the error in Question Time this week, after it was revealed in Senate estimates that the Commonwealth grant was for other improvements at the Marrickville Golf Club.
Instead, the NSW government stepped in to cover the costs of sewerage repairs.
"Whenever you make a false statement, as soon as you become aware of it, you are obliged to go at the earliest opportunity to correct the record. Now, he did not do so," Paterson told News24.
"We had to wait until he was asked in Question Time and it was dragged out of him in this merely mouthed half-admission that he had misled the House.
"In years gone by, this would have cost a minister their job. Under Albanese's government, there are no standards at all."
More states lobby Commonwealth to permit telehealth in VAD
Several state governments are openly defying the prime minister's stance on the use of telehealth in voluntary assisted dying care.
The ALP conference committed Labor to removing telehealth restrictions in voluntary assisted dying, but Prime Minister Anthony Albanese remains personally opposed.
State legislation permits some telehealth throughout the care process. But a Commonwealth Criminal Code provision overrides those laws, barring doctors from discussing VAD with patients by phone, video or email.
Now health ministers from South Australia, Tasmania, Western Australia, Victoria and the ACT have written to the Federal Health Minister Mark Butler, calling on the Commonwealth to amend the Criminal Code, saying it limits access for people in more remote areas.
"The choice for people in rural and remote areas is often between substantial and costly travel on multiple occasions, particularly while unwell, or have no access to choice at the end of their life," the letter states.
"The intent of the VAD legislation across the country is clear — everybody, regardless of where they live, should have equal access to VAD. That includes by telehealth where VAD is not easily or practically accessible in person."
No additional recording devices found across naval fleet
Over in Senate estimates, the Chief of Defence Force Mark Hammond has just finished giving his opening statement. He’ll be grilled by senators today about everything from defence spending to culture.
Admiral Hammond revealed that Defence conducted a snap audit of Australia's naval fleet to sweep for hidden recording devices following the discovery of a camera in a women’s bathroom aboard HMAS Leeuwin while docked in Cairns on October 11.
He said no additional devices were discovered as part of the audit.
“Ultimately our profession is one where our members must be able to rely on and trust each other in the most challenging circumstances," he said.
"In this context, the act of betrayal involving a recording device in a bathroom on HMAS Leeuwin was an appalling violation of that trust and the person responsible will be held to account."
He said his top priority was supporting those affected.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has been visiting a family business in the Canberra suburb of Fyshwick this morning.
Taylor is there to talk about the pressures on small businesses, with the backdrop of further heated inflation figures released yesterday.
"Family businesses like this one are the backbone of our economy," Taylor says.
"We need more of them, not less. Australians are seeing more pain as the price of everything continues to go up.

As an aside, he's not far from one of my favourite coffee shops ... maybe it's a sign to go get a coffee.

Inflation is a 'silent tax'
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie also says Australians should be "very concerned" about the prospect of another interest rate rise next week.
Yesterday's inflation figures showed a rise to 4.3 per cent, up from 4 per cent — numbers that firm up economists' predictions that the Reserve Bank is likely to raise rates again.

He does provide a list of things that won't be cut, though.

The PM handballs a question about a rare earths company in Perth called Northern Minerals to Resources Minister Madeleine King.

The question is posed to the prime minister in the context of grim inflation figures released yesterday that indicate a rate rise is likely next week.

Human override in aged care assessment could cost $11 billion

Bolsonaro flees Brazil for US after election defeat

Breadcrumb
Bolsonaro flees Brazil for US after election defeat
Brazil's defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Florida by private plane Wednesday after fleeing his country in defiance of a court order to surrender his passport.
Following speculation over his whereabouts, the 45-year-old disembarked the jet at Opa-Locka Executive Airport outside Miami, AFP witnessed, having flown via Argentina and Ecuador.
Bolsonaro, who lost a runoff election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday, is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption and money laundering and, with his defeat, is set to lose parliamentary immunity.
Only last week, he had seemed likely to become the next president of Brazil after coming out on top in the first round of elections, but Lula made a surprise surge to retain power.
Bolsonaro -- who travelled to the US with his wife and daughters -- had vowed that as president he would free his father Jair, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
A police source told AFP that Flavio Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, but the senator has also held Italian nationality since 2023, according to Italian documents seen by AFP.
The administration of President Donald Trump, an ally of the Bolsonaros, earlier said it would grant him and his family US visas.
The US Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the Bolsonaro family members were inspected and cleared "with applicable immigration laws and procedures."
The travel ban was issued by powerful Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who led the case against Flavio Bolsonaro's father and is a controversial figure hated by the Brazilian right.
Flavio Bolsonaro had vowed to seek the justice's impeachment if he were elected.
A 'shameful' act
Lula, who won the election with 51.8 percent of Sunday's vote, called Flavio Bolsonaro fleeing the country a "shameful" act.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration on Tuesday.
Brazil police issued a statement Wednesday saying that he was not considered a fugitive.
Following his election defeat, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transport problems that prevented some citizens from voting. But he insisted he would never flee.
Trump, speaking early Wednesday before Bolsonaro landed, repeated his accusations that the Brazilian election was rigged.
"The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible," the president said, adding that he approved of Bolsonaro's plan to travel to the US.
Argentina's opposition lawmakers on Wednesday demanded to know how Flavio Bolsonaro had managed to travel through the country to the United States.
While Argentinian authorities said he was carrying valid travel documents, officials have requested chief of cabinet Diego Santilli to provide details to parliament, according to opposition lawmaker Agustin Rossi.
Fraud cases
The most high-profile fraud case against Flavio Bolsonaro centers on the unreleased biopic "Dark Horse" starring US actor Jim Caviezel as Flavio's father Jair.
In May, the outlet Intercept Brasil revealed audio recordings in which Flavio Bolsonaro negotiated approximately $24 million to finance the film with banker Daniel Vorcaro, who is jailed over one of Brazil's biggest-ever fraud cases.
Before the leak, Flavio Bolsonaro had denied knowing Vorcaro, or that he had financed the movie.
In July, the Supreme Court ordered a probe into the financing of the film, and whether it involved corruption, money laundering or the illegal movement of currency.
Flavio Bolsonaro acknowledged Vorcaro had funded the film, but insisted it was a private business deal that was "completely legal."
In another probe, police are investigating whether Flavio Bolsonaro laundered money and moved funds out of the country in collaboration with his close friend, the lawyer Willer Tomaz.
Flavio's father Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat after losing to Lula and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later.

Apple brings touch to the Mac, reversing years-old stance on touchscreen laptop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:26:06 UTC
05:26:06 KST

Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touchscreen, which it's calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display.
Apple said the laptop has a new display, using OLED technology, that offers more brightness, better colors and wider viewing angles. It's using Apple's M5 Pro or Max chips, and Apple said Wednesday that it's lighter than Apple's current Pro laptops.
It's still an Apple laptop, and is running MacOS, not a version of the iPhone or iPad operating system. In a video, Apple showed users swiping on the screen to manipulate videos or images. It also has a glowing Apple logo on the laptop's lid.
The new laptop will go on sale Nov. 6 and the 14-inch version will start at $2,899. The 16-inch version will cost at least $3,399. Both are notable price increases from existing models.
This is Apple's third major product launch under new CEO John Ternus, signaling a faster cadence for hardware releases. It's also a major reversal for Apple, which has resisted putting touchscreens on its laptops for decades as some Windows machines gained the feature.
"Yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac," Ternus said in live remarks to media and analysts in Los Angeles.
The laptop market has been going through one of its worst slumps ever. Overall shipments are expected to be down 11% this year. Analysts say the AI-driven global market shortage of memory has contributed to higher laptop prices, which has hurt sales and demand.
In the third quarter, total PC shipments dropped 20% on a year-over-year basis, according to market researcher IDC. Apple's own shipments fell 11% during the quarter, according to the estimate.
Even Apple's not immune to rising memory prices, after then-CEO Tim Cook warned this summer that the situation around memory prices was "unsustainable." Nearly all Macs got price hikes this year. Mac Minis introduced in August got a $300 bump, for example.
The announcement caps a busy two months of product launches under Ternus.
Apple also introduced new iMac and MacBook Pro models with M6 chips this week, after price hikes to the lineup totaling several hundred dollars in June. Apple introduced an iPad Mini on Monday that starts at $699, $100 more than its predecessor.
In September, Apple released new iPhones, including its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. It also revealed a new smart speaker with a display called HomeView that uses a redesigned version of Siri to answer a broader range of questions.
The launch signifies the growing strategic importance of the Mac to Apple, despite it generating less revenue than the iPhone. In the most recent quarter, Apple reported $10.35 billion in Mac sales, or just under 10% of the company's total revenue.
But many software developers swear by the Mac, and it remains the only supported platform to develop iPhone apps. And in recent months, Apple has highlighted its chips and memory architecture to make the case that its computers are the best fit for local or edge AI that runs on a device, instead of the cloud.
Meta's AI model developer team bought hundreds of Mac Minis this year to test agents, for example. And Apple notably teamed up with Meta earlier this month to make an announcement that large, nearly frontier models can run on clusters of Macs connected with high-speed cabling, allowing developers to run agentic code without paying Anthropic or OpenAI.
Apple has had a historical resistance to touchscreen laptops. Software chief Craig Federighi said in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users.
"We make the world's best touch computer on an iPad," Ternus, then Apple's senior VP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal in 2021. "It's totally optimized for that. And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven't really felt a reason to change that."
Ternus has been working on Macs since he joined the company and was credited along with silicon chief Johny Srouji as the leader of Apple's effort to get Macs running on Apple's chips, not Intel's. Apple credited Ternus' work on Mac in its official CEO transition statement.
That may be why Ternus in his early days as CEO will be the executive to backtrack on a long-running Apple design philosophy.
Touchscreen laptops have been available on Windows machines for a long time, but they're just another feature, not a selling point behind most purchasing decisions, said Ryan Reith, IDC's vice president for worldwide device trackers.
Only 17% of notebook PCs shipped globally this year will have touchscreens, according to IDC data. Touchscreen laptops also have a slightly lower average selling price than non-touchscreen notebooks.
Hardware technology hasn't been the limiting factor for Apple merging its desktop and mobile interfaces, he added, and Apple could have been waiting to launch a touchscreen laptop until it could present a good user experience and perfect its software after attempts to make its iPad more like a laptop.
"This is really a user interface and software thing," Reith said. "It's one more thing that can draw the developers in."

From Gaza to Lebanon, war-battered Netanyahu strongholds stand by him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:25:19 UTC
05:25:19 KST

Sderot continues to vote Likud despite the October 7 massacre and three years of war. Voter turnout in the city stands at approximately 72%, compared with 76.8% nationwide. A total of 20,507 residents cast ballots out of 28,473 eligible voters, an increase of about 5,000 eligible voters compared with the previous election, when the city had 23,403 registered voters, according to data from the Central Elections Committee.
According to preliminary results, with 80.4% of the city's polling stations counted, Likud has won approximately 39.1% of the vote. That represents a decline of about 2.4 percentage points compared with the previous election, but still leaves the party with a substantial lead over its rivals. Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit is in second place with about 16.8%, while the Religious Zionist Party and Zehut alliance led by Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin is third with approximately 12.7%. Together, the three lists have secured about 69% of the votes counted so far. Parties associated with the change bloc have received a combined 17.4%, a figure similar to the previous election and about half a percentage point lower.
Since the October 7 attack, Sderot's population has grown significantly and now stands at about 40,000. New families have moved to the city, new neighborhoods have been built and the streets have filled up again after long months during which many residents were forced to evacuate their homes and stay in hotels. Yet neither the population growth nor the severe trauma the city experienced appears to have translated into a significant shift in voting patterns, at least according to the preliminary results.
Sderot, where Likud won approximately 41.5% of the vote in the previous election, continues to give the party a commanding lead. This is despite the fact that the deadly attack took place under a Likud-led government, and the city's police station was completely destroyed after terrorists barricaded themselves inside and a fierce battle erupted. Residents experienced firsthand the failure of the systems that were supposed to protect them. Nevertheless, for now, the ballot box shows no significant shift away from the party that was in power at the time of the massacre.
Further down the results, Shas has received approximately 7.2% of the vote, followed by Yashar! with about 6.4%. Yisrael Beiteinu has won roughly 5.1% and Beyachad about 4.5%. The Democrats have received just 1.4%, while United Torah Judaism, the Joint List and Ra'am have so far secured only negligible shares. These results are still partial, with some polling stations yet to be counted, meaning the figures could change.
Even compared with earlier elections, the current result is not unprecedented. During one of the election rounds that began in 2019, Likud won approximately 51.1% of the vote in Sderot. In other words, although the party has lost some support compared with the most recent election, it is still far from experiencing a collapse in the city. At the same time, the relatively high turnout suggests stronger participation among coalition supporters.
If there had been any doubt about the political leanings of the thousands of new residents who have moved to Sderot in recent years, whether motivated by Zionism, affordable housing, proximity to Sapir College or tax benefits, the current results appear to have settled the question. Their arrival has not brought about a political upheaval, and the city continues to maintain its traditional voting patterns in favor of the incumbent government.
That loyalty was also evident before the election. "Likud is in my blood," Danny Suissa, the owner of a well-known, long-established nut and snack shop in the city, told ynet about two and a half months ago. "I've been a Likud supporter since birth. There's nothing I can do about it. You can't change that. You don't trade a galloping horse for a dead one," he explained.
Suissa, who has lived in Sderot for decades, does not hesitate to criticize the country's leadership over the disaster and the many years residents spent living under security threats. "I've lived here for 71 years. For 22 years, our lives weren't normal. I blame everyone: the Shin Bet, IDF officers and the prime minister, too. Whoever made mistakes should be held accountable."
Asked how he could demand accountability from the country's leadership while voting once again for the same party, Suissa made no attempt to reconcile the contradiction. "I'm voting for them again because I'm a staunch Likud supporter. There's nothing I can do about it. It's in my blood," he concluded.
His words may not explain the choices of every Likud voter in Sderot, but they illustrate the gap between anger over what happened and enduring political loyalty. At least according to the interim results, even after October 7, Sderot continues to vote Likud.
Also in Kiryat Shmona and Shlomi: 'Residents lack nothing'
After years of prolonged evacuation and war that inflicted extensive damage and created an almost unimaginable reality for communities along the northern border, residents of the traditional Likud strongholds of Kiryat Shmona and Shlomi have remained loyal to Netanyahu. In Shlomi, support for Likud has even increased compared with the previous election.
At this stage, all regular ballots cast in the two communities have been counted. However, the count of double-envelope ballots, including those cast by thousands of evacuees who have yet to return to the north and apparently voted outside their hometowns, has not been completed.
Despite the difficult reality in Kiryat Shmona, where only about 14,000 of the city's 26,000 residents remain, voter turnout held steady and even rose slightly, from 61.1% in the election for the 25th Knesset to 62.1% in the election for the 26th Knesset. Contrary to expectations of a dramatic political shift following months of war, prolonged evacuation and the destruction of infrastructure, Likud suffered only a marginal decline and remained the city's largest party, winning 48% of the vote compared with 49.5% in 2022. These figures do not yet include the double-envelope ballots, which could alter or even increase the party's share of the vote.
A similar trend is reflected in the strength of the broader right-wing bloc, which continues to dominate local voting with 71.2% support, a moderate decline from the 75.8% won by the coalition in the previous election.
Shimon Amar, owner of the city's legendary Falafel Amar restaurant, woke up Wednesday morning stunned by the unexpected results. Over the past several decades, virtually every prominent politician, from the left to the right, has stopped at his restaurant for a meal and a photograph. Amar had been convinced that the traditionally pro-Likud city would vote differently this time.
"It surprised me," he admitted. Faced with damaged roads and a devastated city now struggling to rebuild and grow, he had been certain there would be a dramatic political shift. But that did not happen.
"I thought fewer people would support that party. I was sure there would be a change, but it simply didn't happen," he said. Speaking from the personal pain of a father of four, only one of whose children still lives in Kiryat Shmona, Amar called for the formation of a unity government, arguing that the country cannot afford another political battle. "There's no other choice. We can't have another election. We need to learn to live together. We're one country."
While Likud has so far recorded a slight decline in Kiryat Shmona, the trend in Shlomi is the opposite. In the northern town, which was also evacuated of all its residents in October 2023, voter turnout climbed to 70.9%, while support for the ruling party rose from 43.5% in the election for the 25th Knesset to 46% in the current election. The broader right-wing bloc maintained relatively stable support of around 69% to 70%.
Shlomi Council head Gabi Naaman does not share the shock expressed by Amar, political commentators or supporters of the change bloc. He says he predicted the result when he declared in advance that "what was will be." He criticizes the Israeli media, which he describes as "mostly hostile to Likud," and argues that the reality on the ground is simply "stronger than that hostility." In his view, residents felt the government had stood by them, leaving no reason to be surprised by their overwhelming support.
Naaman argues that despite the war and evacuation, the economic situation in local authorities is now considerably stronger than it was before October 7. He stresses that "residents lack nothing, and they are surrounded by funding for education and culture, as well as generous grants for businesses."
When confronted with the failures that led to the war, Naaman refuses to assign blame to Netanyahu or the outgoing government, arguing that Hezbollah and other external enemies bear sole responsibility.
"They are to blame for everything that happened here on October 7. The government and the prime minister were called upon to repair the situation when we were at rock bottom, when we were in the abyss. What the prime minister has done over these three years, well, nothing is perfect, but he pulled us out of the abyss and lifted us up. Today, security in our communities is the best in the State of Israel."
Naaman's backing for Netanyahu is unequivocal. "I have no intention of settling accounts with the government. We need to settle accounts with our enemies. We must give the prime minister strong backing so he can continue destroying them until he reaches good diplomatic agreements. In the meantime, over these three years, he has been doing the best possible job."
The contrast between the physical destruction and damage to communities in the north, the belated efforts to rebuild and finally provide the region with the tools it needs to grow, and continued political support for Netanyahu's bloc has a deeper sociological explanation. Professor Nissim Leon, head of the Department of Sociology and Anthropology at Bar-Ilan University, candidly admits that he expected Likud to suffer a "slap in the face" at the ballot box.
He attributes the unexpected results to a deeply rooted collective trauma that shapes the daily lives of northern residents, creating a post-traumatic reality fundamentally different from that experienced by people living in central Israel.
Leon argues that the emotions driving residents of a region that faced the threat of destruction from Hezbollah, compared with the emotions and motivations of the change bloc, produced a sharply polarized political dynamic.
"In the change bloc, the fuel was hatred, and in the right-wing bloc, the fuel was fear. Fear of Arabs took over the decision-making process," he said.
Leon describes a kind of "hierarchy of needs" among right-wing voters, in which security takes precedence over all other considerations.
"Citizens who experience fear tend to vote for whoever they believe will get the job done and protect their security. First comes security. Second comes faith in the party that most clearly and firmly represents their national community."
According to Leon, this emotional mechanism is so powerful and resistant to changing circumstances that it effectively eliminates the need for a traditional election campaign.
"Netanyahu could have slept through the entire election campaign, presented a last-minute warning about Arabs flocking to the polls, as we saw in reports on the morning after polling stations opened, and known that the deep-seated fear would do the work and bring the masses out to vote," he said.

Qatar awaits Tehran's response to new nuclear deal proposal, i24NEWS learns
Iran would take specific steps regarding its nuclear program and in return sanctions would be eased and some funds unfrozen, two regional diplomats told i24NEWS
Qatar is awaiting a response from Tehran, which could arrive as early as Thursday, regarding a new nuclear deal proposal, i24NEWS learned.
Under the current proposal, Iran will take specific steps regarding its nuclear program and in return sanctions would be eased and some funds unfrozen, two regional diplomats told i24NEWS.
The proposal would see the return of International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors to various nuclear sites.
On Tuesday, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi briefed members of the UN Security Council, stating that only the return of inspectors to those sites could provide an accurate picture of the status of Iran’s nuclear program.
The difficulty in negotiations between the US and Iran thus far stems from Iran's demand for the lifting of the 'siege' (economic pressure) and some relief from sanctions before addressing the nuclear issue.
The Trump administration, however, has insisted that a step toward addressing the nuclear issue must be taken as part of the very first phase.

I'm just suggesting that we shouldn't forget what we learn in our economics textbooks, that the argument for not going hard against a supply shock is real.

Westpac debriefs on latest inflation figures
Westpac has offered up some final thoughts on this week's official inflation data:
September Consumer Price Index revealed stronger-than-expected underlying price pressures, locking in a rate hike by the Reserve Bank of Australia in November.
At the same time, moderating dwelling-cost inflation offers a potential path for inflation to return to the target band in 2027. The three key takeaways from the release are:
- Underlying inflation accelerates: Trimmed Mean inflation rose 1.0 per cent in the September quarter and reached 3.7 per cent annually, above the Reserve Bank of Australia’s expectations. Annualising the quarterly result produces a 4 per cent pace, while reaching the bank's projected year end outcome would require an unusually low 0.6 per cent increase in December.
- Housing pressures moderate: Dwelling price inflation was flat in September, compared with an average 0.5 per cent increase over the preceding six months. Because dwellings carry a weight of about 11 per cent and commonly enter the Trimmed Mean, faster moderation could help reverse inflationary pressure in 2027, especially as builders increase discounts amid weaker demand.
- Upside risks remain: Services inflation stayed elevated, with market services excluding volatile components rising 4 per cent annually; administered prices also increased, including property rates and charges at 5.5 per cent, water and sewerage at 10.2 per cent, and electricity at 13 per cent. A November rate increase is therefore expected, and another cannot be ruled out, although slower growth and rising unemployment are expected to prevent a follow-up increase in our base case.

Record anonymous reports made to Fair Work
The Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) received a record 31,596 anonymous reports last year, as recoveries for underpaid workers increased 27 per cent.
As detailed in the FWO annual report:
- More than 181,000 workers had a total of $453 million in underpaid wages back-paid, an increase of about $95 million from the year before.
- Large corporates made up $217.3 million of the overall back payments, paid to more than 110,000 workers.
- In the fast food, restaurant and cafes sector the regulator recovered more than $5.6 million for 3,538 workers and commenced 16 litigations.
- In the building and construction sector, recoveries exceeded $6.8 million for 932 workers, with nearly 3,000 matters completed and 14 litigations commenced.
- In aged care, two enforceable undertakings (EUs) with major aged care providers Southern Cross Care (NSW & ACT) and Southern Cross Care (WA) delivered recoveries of more than $16 million after years of underpayments.
Fair Work Ombudsman Anna Booth applauded workplace participants for flagging potential wrongdoing.
"Anonymous reports help us identify emerging issues, detect patterns, and target education, engagement and compliance activities where they're needed most."
Ms Booth said the regulator continued to obtain strong recoveries as part of its strategic enforcement approach.
In 2025–26, FWO commenced 60 litigations and secured $2.3 million in penalties.
Notable penalties included $213,120 against the University of New South Wales over systemic record-keeping and pay-slip contraventions that hindered FWO's investigation into underpayments (the university later also signed an EU).
In another matter, against the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) and four of its Victorian officials, penalties of $171,500 reinforced the importance of compliance with workplace laws by all participants in the building and construction industry.
The workplace regulator also issued 1,392 compliance notices, recovering more than $33 million for more than 17,000 workers.
FWO handed out 791 infringement notices, sending a warning to employers to get their pay slip and record-keeping obligations in order or face the consequences (a total of $831,891 in fines).

Key Event
ASIC investigating the bankers behind failed Firmus float
Once upon a time, used car salesmen developed an expertise in the art of dressing up a lemon for sale.
Blacken up the tyres, polish the duco, chuck some sawdust in the diff and Bob’s your uncle.
This, hapless buyers were usually told, is a much-loved chariot with years of trouble-free motoring ahead of it.
While the practice has since been outlawed in used car yards, the tactics apparently live on in the high-octane world of investment banking much to the chagrin of our corporate regulator.
Appearing before a Senate estimates hearing this morning, Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) chief Sarah Court shed some light on the alleged shenanigans behind the great $44 billion Firmus float flop.
What did ASIC say?
Ms Court told senators that ASIC is casting an eye over the events leading up to the collapse, and particularly, statements from investment banks to potential buyers about the level of demand for the AI infrastructure outfit’s shares.
The ASIC chair was expressly asked about a letter from stockbroking firm Morgan Financial indicating “huge demand” for shares in the pre-float sale.
“We would certainly be looking at that as part of these inquiries,” Ms Court responded.
Morgans was one of four Joint Lead Managers (JLM) of the Initial Public Offering (IPO) and the ASIC chair indicated the regulator was delving into whether there was a reasonable basis for making such claims.
“Sometimes things can be pulled out of broader correspondence, but we have got a report that makes clear that lead managers must have a reasonable basis for investor demand," she said.
“I think it is fair to say that we are having a look at the broad range of issues that have been reported in the media, including the engaging of the JLMs."
These include whether representations about investor demand for the initial public offering from joint lead managers Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan, Bank of America and Morgans Financial had a reasonable basis, as well as potential conflicts of interest if the managers stood to be major sellers upon listing.
"I almost cannot give much more than sitting here today, suffice to say that this is a very significant event, and we understand that, and we need to look at it very carefully,” she said.

Key Event
No talk, and no action: US Fed chair Kevin Warsh's credibility problem
As we've been reporting the US Federal Reserve has kept interest rates on hold, a week out from the US midterm elections, with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh providing little, if any, justification for the inaction.
With inflation running hot, the market is now almost fully pricing in a December rate hike in the US.
I had the great pleasure of chatting with Platypus Economics' Justin Wolfers who has such a knack for explaining complex economics.
He says he didn't find Mr Warsh convincing on the need to get inflation down.
Professor Wolfers told me he's not sure who the "real" Kevin is.
"Kevin Walsh says the Fed needs to defeat inflation. He says the Fed's inflation target is 2%. And the inflation rate right now is somewhere between 3 and 4%, depending on which inflation measure you use.
"So if you say one thing, I'm going to keep inflation at 2%, the reality is it's higher than that. You don't do anything. You become awfully hard to understand..... None of us know really who the bloke is, what he believes."
He also said the new US Fed Chair needs to outline his strategy for keeping rates on hold, in the face of hot inflation.
"So he keeps saying, I'm not going to communicate with you. Well, we don't know who you are. He's all, I'm definitely going to defeat inflation, to which if you're not going to tell me, do something. And so, the problem is, how does he show his stripes? And at the moment, the truth is we're all a little confused.
You can watch my full interview with Justin Wolfers tonight on The Business at 8:44pm AEDT on the ABC News Channel.

Like I said, quite a list.
Here's some of their demands:
"Victoria’s net debt is approaching $200 billion – the highest of any state and around the same as that of NSW, Queensland and Tasmania combined. Interest alone costs $24 million a day. That’s money that can’t be spent on hospitals, schools, housing, better roads or services.

“Since we started speaking out about Victoria’s debt, I’ve been overwhelmed by the support. It has struck a chord with Victorians from every walk of life. I’ve spent my life in Victoria and I want the next generation of Victorians to have the same opportunities that my generation has enjoyed. Right now, $24 million a day is going on interest instead of the things that make this state great. Victoria doesn’t need a miracle, it needs a credible plan.”

Star twinkles as it sets up payment plan for $260m fine
Star Entertainment will not fold, despite a penalty more than double the figure its lawyers contended was unaffordable and could lead to its closure.
The penalty, to be paid in four instalments over 19 months, stems from a civil lawsuit brought by the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre (AUSTRAC) in 2022, which alleged Star entities failed to comply with anti-money-laundering and counterterrorism financing regulations.
The company said the penalty was materially in line with provisions it had already recorded.
Here's chairman Soo Kim, who came in to save the minute-to-midnight casino group when it was running out of cash to operate:
"Given that the current ownership and management team had nothing to do with the actions that gave rise to the proceedings, we commend the work of AUSTRAC and the Federal Court."
Star said it was continuing discussions with US-based private credit investment manager WhiteHawk regarding the $390 million credit facility agreed in May and remained confident the facility would stay available.
Shares resumed trading after a halt and rose as much as 9.6% to $0.143 today.
Earlier this week, Star swung to a profit for the first time in nearly a year, helped by strong performances at its Sydney and Gold Coast sites and cost-saving measures.
Star says it will live, despite massive fine
Star Entertainment has said a court-imposed penalty of $260 million for breaching anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing laws will not affect its ability to continue as a going concern.
