Retail, hospitality small business underperforming
Adding to what Dan said earlier Xero's small business data shows consumer-facing industries retail and hospitality are underperforming the national average.
The data suggests households are remaining cautious about discretionary spending.
Economist Louise Southall says major investment in infrastructure is supporting parts of the economy, but the average local café, retailer or service-based business isn't necessarily seeing those benefits.
"For most small businesses, higher costs and cautious household spending remain the bigger challenges," she says.
Small business sales growth slows
New data from accounting software firm Xero finds that Australian small business sales growth slowed in the September quarter, rising 5.2% year-on-year down from 7.3% y/y in the June quarter and below the long-term average of 7.8%.
The data comes from its latest 'small business insights' report which found despite recent interest rate hikes flowing through the small business economy, jobs growth increased to 3.9% year-on-year, up from 3.1% in the previous quarter.
Here are the top lines:
- Wage growth slides to 1.2% y/y, down from 2.3% in the June quarter and less than half the long-term average of 2.9%.
- Sales reach five-month low in September, dropping to 4.3% y/y last month following growth of 4.9% y/y in July and 6.4% y/y in August.
- Mining (+12.0% y/y), healthcare (+8.1% y/y) and construction (+7.9% y/y) led sales growth, while retail (+2.4% y/y) and hospitality (+2.7% y/y) remained subdued.
- Western Australia (+7.7% y/y) led sales growth, while Victoria (+3.8% y/y) and the Northern Territory (+3.7%) recorded the weakest results.
- Small businesses waited an average of 24.3 days to be paid, with invoices 6.9 days late on average.
Xero Economist Louise Southall said the data reflects an economy digesting the delayed effects of previous interest rate rises.
"The September quarter tells us small business conditions haven’t worsened, but they also haven’t improved," Southall said. "Rate rises typically take time to filter through to household spending, and that delayed effect is continuing to weigh on sales."
Removing pricks from the AI bubble
Maybe that headline didn't come across as intended.
What I mean to say is that early analysis of Microsoft's substantial earnings from its cloud division pours a little cold water on what's been a warming debate about an 'AI bubble' - whether the immense billions being spent on the hyper-scale build-out will return more profits than costs.
Here's Josh Gilbert, Lead Analyst for APAC at etoro:
"Microsoft has just given the AI sceptics a lot less to work with, growing faster than expected and guiding for even more to come. Azure growth accelerated to 48%, up from 42% last quarter and comfortably ahead of the 45% Wall Street had roughly pencilled in. Microsoft also put a dollar figure on the business for the first time at USD$33 billion for the quarter. Azure was always going to be the number that decided how this result was received, and it’s the clearest evidence yet that the billions Microsoft has poured into its AI build-out are turning into revenue.
"Azure also managed to hit that number despite some third-party data centre capacity arriving later than planned. With management guiding for growth of around 49% next quarter, there’s little reason to think the acceleration has peaked. Capacity has become the real battleground between the cloud giants right now, and Microsoft is proving it can scale its infrastructure quicker than the market had anticipated.
"Capex came in roughly USD$6.5 billion below street estimates, and Microsoft still delivered accelerating growth, which is exactly what investors needed to see in an earnings season where the market has shown very little patience for AI spending running ahead of revenue. CFO Amy Hood put the shortfall down to delayed capacity deliveries, so it seems more of a timing matter rather than restraint. I’d expect spending to step back up as that capacity lands.
"The AI race is no longer rewarding whoever spends the most, it’s rewarding whoever can show the receipts, and Microsoft’s are looking very healthy."
AI wobbles but Microsoft beats earnings expectations
In Australia, we've spent a fortnight in a financial whirl as neocloud Firmus pulled its float and the share price of (relative veteran) data centre operator NEXTDC cratered.
Investors have been waiting for new financial results from the behemoth operators of our digital world, and we've got some today. Here's how Reuters reported it.
Microsoft surpassed expectations for quarterly cloud revenue, signalling that its hefty AI investments were paying off at a time Wall Street grows increasingly wary of Big Tech's debt-fuelled spending.
Revenue at Microsoft's Azure cloud computing business grew 48% to US$33.17 billion in the first quarter ended September, topping Visible Alpha's estimates of $32.84 billion. Azure revenue was $29.4 billion in the prior quarter.
Last month, Microsoft decided to report Azure revenue in dollars, not just growth rates, giving a clearer picture of how its cloud business stacks up against rivals Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud.
Overall, Big Tech is expected to pump more than $700 billion this year into building data centres and securing the hardware and energy needed to develop and run AI technologies.
While faster revenue growth at these companies suggests their bets could be paying off, concerns about financing the outlay have grown over the past few weeks.
Shrinking cash flows and rising debt loads at US tech companies, including recent stress at neocloud CoreWeave, as well as record-high costs to insure Meta's debt against default have all added to market turmoil.
Investors last week sold off shares in Meta and many stocks central to the AI trade after the Facebook parent raised its annual capital spending forecast and announced plans to sell new stock to help fund that spending.
Microsoft had forecast capital expenditure of $190 billion in 2026. The tech giant also faces pressure as increasingly sophisticated agentic AI tools threaten its productivity software business.
Some analysts, however, believe that Microsoft's strong balance sheet gives it an edge over rivals as AI spending rises. According to Truist, the company's 5-year credit default swaps — a measure of perceived default risk — remain the tightest among tech giants, even as spreads have widened across much of the AI trade.
Microsoft is also the only one among hyperscalers expected to remain cash flow positive next year, compared with the cash burn expected at peers Alphabet, Amazon and Oracle among others.

Should we raise the GST?
Hi Daniel. I find Peter Costello’s statement that ‘raising the GST to fund more government spending is a bad idea’ a bit strange. Is anyone actually suggesting that ? What raising the GST could do , is reduce demand in the economy ( as the RBA is trying to do with interest rates obviously) and if any increased revenue was quarantined to pay down debt we’d have a proposal that would be politically palatable to both the states and the average voter imho.
- Phillip
Former Treasurer Peter Costello has told a podcast that he's against the idea of raising the GST.
The goods and services tax is a broad-based tax of 10% on practically every good (item) and service delivered in Australia.
There are plenty of items that are GST-free:
- most basic food
- some education courses, course materials and related excursions or field trips
- some medical, health and care services
- some menstrual products
- some medical aids and appliances
- some medicines
- some childcare services
- some religious services and charitable activities
- supplies of accommodation and meals to residents of retirement villages by certain operators
- cars for disabled people to use, when certain requirements are met
- water, sewerage and drainage
- international transport and related matters
- precious metals
- sales through duty-free shops
- grants of land by government
- farmland
- international mail
- exports
- sales of businesses as going concerns
- some telecommunications supplies
- eligible emissions units.
People who have less money spend a much higher proportion of it on things they need to simply survive: food, fuel and housing.
Because of this, most economists believe that any increase in the rate of the GST or broadening it to cover more things would have to also include a program to compensate poorer people for their increased cost of living compared to people who are wealthier.

Mulino defends tax office over credit card rollout
Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has defended the ATO, saying it was dealing with a "complex environment" when it failed to consult with small businesses over a ban on credit cards. 
The tax office admitted in Senate estimates last night that it should have talked to small businesses more before announcing its controversial ban on credit card payments.
Mulino says the tax office commissioner gave "thoughtful evidence" and argues it was always a "complex" series of reforms.
"They were negotiating with credit card companies, trying to get a better deal so that they could figure out what options were possible," he says.
"It was a complex environment ... and as the commissioner has said, in hindsight ... they could have beneficially engaged with small businesses more."
The transition period for small businesses was eventually extended to the end of the financial year, but has not been scrapped entirely.

Rare earths prove worth
Lynas Rare Earths, the biggest rare earths producer outside of China, has reported a 54.9% rise in first-quarter revenue on improved pricing, strong demand and higher production of rare earth products.
The miner said its average selling price rose 88% year-on-year to a record $102.1 per kg in the September quarter, helped by improved market pricing, increased bundling of light and heavy rare earth sales and floor-price contracts covering more than half its output.
Lynas said its Kalgoorlie operations will undergo a planned shutdown for two weeks during the second quarter of financial year 2027 as the Western Australian electricity network operator Western Power modifies its network to make the power supply more reliable.
Additionally, Lynas Malaysia will be shut down for a month in the December quarter for planned maintenance, which will result in lower production volumes during the quarter compared with the September quarter, the miner said.
The company posted gross sales revenue of $310.1 million for the quarter ended September 30, compared with $200.2 million a year earlier.

Workers shouldn’t pay higher tax rates than the wealthiest, union peak body argues
Unions are urging the Senate to pass the Federal Government’s 30% minimum tax on discretionary trusts, arguing that wage earners should not pay higher tax rates than the country’s wealthiest households.
In a submission to the Senate inquiry today, peak body the ACTU highlights that a nurse on an average full-time salary of $90,000 could pay up to $10,000 more in tax than a household receiving the same income through a discretionary trust.
It argues the tax system allows wealthy households to use discretionary trusts to minimise their tax burden by income splitting. That's the process where family members on lower tax brackets get some of the distributions of the trust.
ACTU analysis suggests the estimated compliance costs of the Federal Government’s proposed changes are just 0.1% of the annual income paid out of discretionary trusts.
The group contends that the wealthiest 10% of households own 90% of all trust assets, and that Australia has twenty times more discretionary trusts per person than the UK because the UK stopped allowing them to be used as tax loopholes.
A key sticking point has been concerns about how the tax changes will affect small businesses, but the ACTU reckons 90% of small businesses will be unaffected by the reforms.
Public submissions on the draft laws close today. The reforms are set to take effect from July 2028.
Here's new-ish ACTU Secretary, Melissa Donnelly:
“Australian workers are paying higher tax rates than some of the wealthiest families in the country because of discretionary trusts. These legal structures allow income splitting, so the wealthiest minimise their tax contribution to the public services we all rely on.
“Australian Unions urge all Senators to do the right thing for workers and close this unfair tax loophole. The wealthiest 10 per cent, those with a net worth above $2.3 million, own 90 per cent of discretionary trust assets in Australia. The vote on these laws will be a clear test for politicians on whose side they’re on: Australian workers, or the wealthiest and most powerful.
“A 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trust earnings will fix this economic distortion that is deepening inequality. Unions want our tax system to reward hard work, not the ability to pay a lawyer for a discretionary trust.
“Despite employer groups scaremongering, 90 per cent of small businesses will not be affected by the changes and 95 per cent of individual taxpayers don’t receive a single cent of trust income.
“Unions welcome the Albanese Government pursuing tax reform that puts the hard work of wage earners at the centre.”

ATO boss grilled on controversial credit card ban
The Australian Taxation Office boss has conceded the agency could've consulted small businesses better before announcing its controversial credit card ban. 
Commissioner of taxation Rob Heferen told Senate estimates last night he realised the Reserve Bank's surcharge ban would be a "real issue" for the ATO after receiving a letter from Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino about the RBA's reforms on April 28 this year.
"That brought it to a sharp head," Heferen said.
The commissioner said the tax office subsequently formulated two options: continue accepting credit card payments and request government funding, or ban credit cards and map out an appropriate transition for those impacted.
He said he first discussed the matter with Mulino on July 20, followed by a series of meetings.
Heferen said that on September 25, on advice from his senior executive, he personally decided to propose the credit card ban, and small businesses were informed on September 30—a day before it was made public.
US interest likely to climb: CBA analysis
What's next on interest rates from the US Federal Reserve?
Here's Commonwealth Bank's head of foreign exchange, international and geoeconomics Joseph Capurso:
"We expect high US inflation to persist because of a range of demand and supply influences.The Fed can not do much about supply but it can pull demand down to balance supply.
"Data centre construction and associated hardware and software spending is an important impulse to the US economy, even accounting for high import intensity of around 60%. However, we note the extra spending on fuel has absorbed the tax cuts. Nevertheless, private domestic demand is growing strongly and contributing to elevated inflation.
"Persistent supply curbs will also contribute to high inflation. The high rate of retirements and low immigration have tightened the labour market. With the unemployment rate trending down, we expect the quit rate and growth in employment costs to reverse course and turn up.
"There is some evidence that high energy prices have spilled over to higher consumer prices such as airfares. Moving in the other direction is tariffs. Tariffs pushed up US consumer goods prices by around 3% in 2025. But the Supreme Court ruling in February against tariffs imposed under emergency powers will weigh on consumer inflation in 2027.
"The bottom line is inflation is too high despite lower tariffs. Overall, we consider there is a solid case for the Fed to resume increasing the Funds rate in December. We expect a follow up hike in March 2027 to take the Funds rate to a range of 4.25% to 4.50%. The Funds rate would be what Fed members consider ‘restrictive’ to economic growth. Nevertheless, there is uncertainty about what level of the Funds rate is restrictive and estimates have been increasing for several years.
"Ultimately, the trend in consumer inflation will determine how much the Fed will increase the Funds rate. We consider there is a risk the Fed hikes a fourth time, possibly as early as January."

Don't raise GST, former treasurer Costello says
Peter Costello is Australia’s longest-serving Treasurer.
His tenure (1996 to 2007) and partnership with Prime Minister John Howard placed him as the architect of many of the settings that choices that are dominating our lives in the past few years.
These include the GST, capital gains discount, franking credits, and superannuation concessions.
In a podcast with Institute of Public Affairs chief economist Adam Creighton he warns Australia is falling behind.
“We used to lead the pack. We’re falling behind the pack.
“Our problems are nearly all self-inflicted.”
The former treasurer introduced the GST but has rejected raising it to fund more government spending.
“Increasing the GST to spend more is not a reform which will improve Australia. It is a bad idea.”
He thinks the top income tax rate in Australia is applied at too low an income, which he contends undermines incentives to work, invest and build businesses.
“It’s affecting work incentives, it’s affecting entrepreneurial incentives, it’s making it harder to get ahead. It’s killing aspiration, that’s what it’s doing.”
After the Howard era, Mr Costello served on the board of the Future Fund from 2009 until February 2024.
Most young people will know him as the chair of media company Nine Entertainment from 2016 to 2024, a stint that ended when he collided with a journalist in an airport.

The decision was expected. But the concerns are rising
So, the result of the Fed's meeting overnight was expected.
But that doesn't mean interest rates are on hold forever in the world's biggest economy.
The outcome of this week's meeting was widely expected after top Fed officials indicated they saw no rush to raise rates again following the quarter-percentage-point increase approved last month, despite inflation data in the meantime that was stronger than forecast and concerns that price pressures are broadening across the economy.
Energy costs remain high, including for diesel fuel, which is a key input for shipping, agriculture, and other industries. Inflation and the cost of living in general have been central to the political races that will determine whether Trump's Republican Party remains in control of both houses of Congress on November 3, or whether Democrats move into leadership positions and gain more robust oversight powers, including over the Fed.
Financial markets are still pricing in a couple of additional rate hikes in the coming months, though with slightly less conviction than before Fed Chair Kevin Warsh spoke.
Pricing shows about an 80% chance of a rate hike at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting, with another likely by March.
Inflation, which is currently around a percentage point above the Fed's target, has shown little progress in recent months.
The US central bank has missed its inflation target for five and a half years, a fact that has left some officials worried that businesses and households are becoming accustomed to faster price increases and may plan for them in ways that will make inflation harder to control.

Fed leaves rates unchanged as it awaits 'accumulation of more information'
The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week's mid-term elections in the nation and awaiting further data on the path of inflation.
'The Fed' as it is known is the US central bank. Our equivalent is the Reserve Bank, which will make its decision on interest rates on Tuesday.
In a 10-2 decision, the US central bank said it would maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated," upgrading its assessment of the economy, and hinting that further rate hikes may be coming depending on the performance of inflation.
Locally, a 'hot' - higher than expected - result for inflation adds weight to the likelihood of rates increasing on Melbourne Cup Day.
Here's what the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement:
"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2% goal... The Committee will deliver price stability."
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, speaking in a press conference following the end of the policy meeting, did not offer guidance on the outlook for monetary policy, but acknowledged that the central bank had not achieved price stability.
"We're working on it," he said.Warsh, who took over as head of the central bank in May, added that he does not believe "in prejudging meetings" and noted that "a lot of things can happen, so I'm not going to be able to share with you my musings about what happens when this group gets together six weeks from now."
Fed Governor Lisa Cook, currently being targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, cast her first dissent on a central bank policy decision, favouring a quarter-percentage-point rate hike. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice, also dissented in favour of the same rate increase.

No seat for Europe at Ukraine peace talks – Kremlin

No seat for Europe at Ukraine peace talks – Kremlin
European nations will not be invited to the next Russia-US-Ukraine peace talks, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Wednesday, a day after the leaders of Finland and Norway called Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Moscow agreed in principle to participate in a fourth round of trilateral talks following last week’s meeting between Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. Mid-November has been floated as a possible timeframe, with Abu Dhabi suggested as the venue.
“We have agreed that trilateral talks will resume, involving representatives from Russia, Ukraine, and the US,” Ushakov told Vesti. He stressed, however, that European representatives will not be invited.
“They can get there if they buy tickets. But no one intends to invite them to the negotiating table.”
Ushakov’s comments came a day after Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store called Putin for a conversation that reportedly lasted over an hour. The call sent a shockwave through Kiev’s staunchest backers, prompting Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen to condemn the Nordic leaders’ initiative, insisting it had not been coordinated with “European partners.”
However, neither Stubb nor Store brought any new proposals for settling the Ukraine conflict, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the call.
Ukraine’s European backers have been excluded from all three rounds of trilateral negotiations so far and have increasingly sought direct participation in the peace process. They have, however, not tempered their demands, insisting on an unconditional ceasefire – something Moscow has repeatedly rejected, arguing that a temporary freeze to the fighting would only allow Kiev to rest and rearm with Western weapons.
Russia has also accused the EU of acting as the principal side arming Ukraine and prolonging the conflict. In April, Brussels approved €90 billion ($100 billion) to Ukraine for 2026–2027, financed via capital markets. Earlier this month, Vladimir Zelensky asked for a further €70 billion to keep Ukraine’s budget and military afloat through next year.
Moscow has maintained that Europe’s financial and military support for Ukraine makes it a party to the conflict, which Russia has long described as a NATO-led proxy war.
Putin has also described Europe’s claims of a Russian threat to justify its military buildup as “political schizophrenia.”

UN votes to condemn embargo of Cuba despite US lobbying push
Unknown

2026-10-28
20:22:16 UTC

UN votes to condemn embargo of Cuba despite US lobbying push
US points to increase in abstentions in General Assembly as evidence that push to isolate Cuba is slowly succeeding.
The United Nations General Assembly has again voted in favour of a resolution condemning the United States’s economic embargo of Cuba despite a push by US officials to peel off support.
The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 countries in favour and 17 opposed, including the US and Israel. Another 25 countries abstained, including countries such as Germany and Italy, that had previously voted in favour. The General Assembly has voted to condemn the embargo annually for more than three decades.
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said in a social media post after the vote that the US was “once again isolated in its attempt to continue strangling the Cuban people”.
“Neither its most insane pretexts nor its pressures nor media circus will prevail over the force of facts and truth,” he added.
The US embargo on Cuba, part of an effort to isolate the country and squeeze its economy that has lasted more than six decades, has been widely condemned on the world stage and linked to worsening hardship on the island.
US President Donald Trump’s administration has implemented a series of additional economic restrictions, including an energy blockade, to further tighten the screws.
That economic campaign has also been accompanied by a US diplomatic push to further isolate Havana, an effort that US officials said is apparent in the uptick in countries that abstained during Wednesday’s vote. Cuban officials accused the US of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions and other penalties if they voted to condemn the embargo.
“I’m satisfied that so many countries now, including major economies like Korea, like Germany and others have shifted their position,” US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told reporters after the vote.
“Diplomacy takes time, but now that we’ve had a tripling of countries that have shifted, we expect that to only continue to grow,” he added.
Tensions between US and Cuban officials exploded on Tuesday during a General Assembly debate with both yelling at the other and engaging in an apparent shoving match.
Waltz said on Wednesday that Richard Tur de la Concepcion, a first secretary at Cuba’s UN mission, would be expelled from the country for “assaulting an American diplomat”.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the US and Cuban missions for comment but has not received a response.

Three media outlets seek full White House access in amended lawsuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:21:03 UTC
05:21:03 KST

Three media outlets that President Donald Trump banned from the White House in September, only to have a federal judge's order restore much of their access, amended their lawsuit Wednesday, seeking to regain full access to serve in a press pool for other reporters in the Oval Office and Air Force One.
The amended civil complaint against Trump says that since the judge ordered the White House to allow MS NOW, CNN and Politico journalists into the White House, the White House has blocked those outlets from performing pool functions they long have conducted.
The press pool routinely serves as a key source of information for the public about what a president does or says. In pool assignments, journalists agree to share with other media outlets information and images they obtain while acting as a pooler.
The amended complaint sets the stage for a court fight over whether a president, because of how he or she feels about how a media outlet covers them, can block access to individual media outlets or reporters from areas of the White House that other journalists have access to.
Ted Boutrous Jr., an attorney for the outlets, in a statement Wednesday said, "Despite two court orders restraining it from implementing the President's unconstitutional ban on CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, the White House has continued to violate the First Amendment and due process by excluding those news organizations from areas such as the Oval Office and Air Force One — the very locations that the President most frequently engages with the press."
"These exclusions, intended to punish and chill coverage of the administration that the President doesn't like, make it harder for the press to cover some of the most important events in the world for the benefit of the American people," Boutrous said.
The amended complaint in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C. says that Trump's original ban and "the White House's continued exclusion of Plaintiffs from certain [areas] are unlawful retaliation for protected First Amendment activity."
Those actions "brazenly" discriminate against the outlets "based on their perceived editorial viewpoint; the White House is expressly excluding CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO because the President dislikes the content of their coverage," the suit says.
Judge Tim Kelly's prior orders restoring access for the outlets did not require the White House to restore those outlets' access to the Oval Office or Air Force One.
The amended complaint notes that since his second term began in January 2025, Trump has held 121 press events aboard Air Force One or on the tarmac outside the presidential plane, and 138 events in the Oval Office, "during which he fielded no fewer than 4,700 questions from reporters."
"To be clear, Plaintiffs do not claim an unrestricted right to enter the Oval Office or travel aboard Air Force One," the new complaint says.
"But once the White House opens those spaces to selected journalists for newsgathering and reporting, the White House may not exclude Plaintiffs because it dislikes their coverage."
Since Trump announced the ban on Sept. 18, "the White House has repeatedly barred CNN from fulfilling its duties as designated television network pooler aboard Air Force One — a role CNN has fulfilled for more than four decades," the amended suit says.
MS NOW has not participated in the secondary TV pool since that date, and the White House has barred Politico "from two scheduled out-of-town print pool assignments aboard Air Force One," the suit says.
"Defendants have offered no official explanation for any of these exclusions," the amended complaint says.
"On information and belief, these exclusions reflect an unstated policy to carry out the President's directive to take his viewpoint-discriminatory and retaliatory ban 'as far as you can,'" the complaint says.
"Indeed, the President has been explicit that he intends to limit access to the Oval Office to news organizations that cover him favorably, declaring hours after this action was filed that 'publications that only write negatively . . . shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," the suit said.
The suit notes that after Kelly issued a preliminary injunction against Trump's ban in mid-October, "the White House issued a statement declaring that what it deems the 'Fake News' has 'no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office.'"
The amended complaint says the limited ban on pool access violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution.
"CNN, MS NOW, POLITICO, and their journalists have liberty and property interests in their press credentials and the access those credentials afford to the White House grounds to report on the President and his administration," the suit says. "That access has long extended to the Oval Office, Air Force One, and other fora that the White House has opened to the press for pool coverage."
"The ban, and Defendants' continued exclusion of Plaintiffs from certain White House press areas, deprives Plaintiffs of those interests without meeting the bare minimum requirements of due process: advance notice based on clear standards and an opportunity to be heard," the suit says.
The suit also said the White House is interfering with CNN's ability to perform its duties as one of five television networks that "staff, equip, and bear the costs associated with the primary television network pool upon which the American public (and the White House itself) relies for real-time television coverage of the President in the Oval Office, aboard Air Force One, and at the many other presidential events that due to size and other constraints simply cannot accommodate all members of the press corps."
Trump, when he announced the ban, said he was "sick" of what he called fiction and lies written about him, his administration, and the United States.
On Sept. 19, a day after he announced the ban, journalists from the three media outlets were denied access to the White House grounds and had their passes taken away when they showed up.
Two days later, the outlets first sued Trump, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Chief of Staff Susan Wiles, and Secret Service Director Sean Curran, seeking to regain access.
District Court Judge Tim Kelly on Sept. 23 issued a temporary restraining order mandating that the White House restore access to the outlets for at least 14 days.
Kelly, whom Trump appointed to the federal bench in 2017, said in his order that the ban appeared to flatly violate two federal appeals court rulings that require advance notice and an opportunity to be heard to journalists whose White House press passes are targeted for revocation.
The White House allowed journalists from the banned outlets in the next day.
On Oct. 13, Kelly issued a preliminary injunction, which indefinitely bars the White House from reinstituting the ban while the outlets' lawsuit continues in his court.
In issuing that injunction, Kelly again cited the appeals court decisions, but also said the outlets were likely to succeed on two First Amendment claims in their civil suit, which alleged retaliation and viewpoint discrimination.
Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

Russia building new drone launch site near Millerovo airfield in Rostov Oblast, HUR says
Russia is building a new site for operating attack drones near Millerovo airfield, close to the Ukrainian border, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) said on Oct. 28, citing satellite imagery.
The airfield is located in the village of Dolotinka in Russia's Rostov Oblast, about 20 kilometers (12 miles) east of Ukraine's Luhansk Oblast.
According to HUR, the facility's design indicates it is intended for the preparation and launch of jet-powered attack drones, likely Geran-4 and Geran-5 models and their variants.
"The construction of the facility in the Rostov Region may be part of Russia's preparations to intensify its attacks on Ukrainian territory, particularly during the winter," HUR said.
HUR estimated that once construction is complete, the site could accommodate up to 100 drone launches per day.
The site's actual operational tempo will depend on several factors, including supplies of ready-made drones, the availability of fuel and warheads, the number of trained drone crews, equipment readiness and the missions assigned by Russia, the statement read.
As of late August 2026, there were no significant signs of active construction at the site. Since then, launch positions and other infrastructure for drone operations have been established, HUR said.

Apple shows pricey touchscreen laptops, a first for the iPhone maker

Apple shows pricey touchscreen laptops, a first for the iPhone maker
- Apple launched its first touchscreen MacBooks in Los Angeles, led by CEO John Ternus, ending years of resistance to touch on laptops.
- The new MacBook Pro has an OLED display, starts at US$2,899, and goes on sale on Nov 6. Apple says it is aimed at creators and designers.
- Analysts say Apple faces a crowded market where cheaper touchscreen laptops are common. The move may help Apple reach more buyers, but success is not certain.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – Apple chief executive officer John Ternus unveiled the company’s first touchscreen MacBooks on Oct 28, abandoning a long-held aversion to the technology as it caps a burst of product launches ahead of the holiday shopping season.
Ternus took the stage at an Apple event in Los Angeles and showed a MacBook Pro model with an organic light-emitting diode (OLED) display, playing up the display’s contrast, sharpness and brightness in front of an audience of content creators and creative professionals.
He also said the company would return to a glowing logo on the back of the laptops.
“Look, we love the Mac, and it’s the reason why so many of us found our way to Apple in the first place. And the Mac has never been better, and it’s never been stronger,” Ternus said on Oct 28.
The event is part of a media blitz filled with new product launches following Ternus – a former Apple hardware veteran – taking over as the company’s new CEO.
He launched a folding iPhone, Duo, at Apple’s Silicon Valley headquarters in September and a smart home hub in New York earlier in October.
While those products will test new markets for Apple, the Los Angeles event could rekindle an old question: Should Apple put the touchscreens that it made mainstream in iPhones and iPads in its oldest product line?
Apple executives long resisted the idea, with Steve Jobs saying in 2010 that touchscreens on laptops were “ergonomically terrible” and then-CEO Tim Cook saying in 2012 that such devices would be as pleasing to users as converging a toaster and a refrigerator.
Before becoming Apple’s CEO, Ternus argued that Apple already made a touchscreen computer with its iPad line-up.
But touchscreens have been widely available for more than a decade on Windows devices, and with the iPhone nearing its two-decade anniversary, a new generation of buyers expects screens to respond to touch.
“I believe they were always wrong on pushing back on touch, and this is the long arm of reality setting in,” said Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy.
“Some things are purely inevitable.”
How will customers respond?
A key question for Apple is how customers will respond. The company has seen an uptick in Mac sales, but much of that growth has been among technology enthusiasts and businesses buying the machines to handle AI tasks on-device.
The new MacBook Pro starts at US$2,899 (S$3,700) for the 14-inch model with the M5 Pro chip, while the highest-end configuration starts at US$4,799 for the 16-inch model with the more powerful M5 Max chip. The new 16-inch model is 0.7 pounds lighter than the older, non-touchscreen model.
Apple said on Oct 28 that the new MacBook Pro is available for pre-order starting Oct 28 and would go on sale on Nov 6.
“This is going to be towards creators, towards designers, towards photographers, people that are going to leverage that high fidelity screen, and who many of whom have grown up tapping on screens, editing on tablets, on phones, etc,” said Tom Mainelli, head of IDC’s Device & Consumer Research Group.
To guard against burn-in, a common OLED flaw where images from long-running apps leave permanent marks on the screen, Apple redesigned the chassis to draw warm air away from the display and used the computing power in its M5 chips to keep the screen refreshed.
“You can expect an OLED to last as long as your typical LCD screen. Apple came out of the gate firing in terms of putting together both a very vibrant display and then adding the touch,” Mainelli said.
Still, some analysts questioned how much headway Apple can make in a market dominated by enterprise buyers, where rivals such as Lenovo, HP and Dell offer cheaper devices.
PC makers shipped 33.4 million touchscreen notebooks in 2025, up 22% from a year earlier and 16% of all notebooks shipped, according to IDC. The average selling price for the devices was around US$1,009, much lower than Apple’s products.
The cheapest touchscreen laptop Apple unveiled on Oct 28 also costs more than an entry-level iPhone, MacBook, iPad with accessories, Apple Watch and AirPods combined.
But the expanding line-up of products and prices suggests that the company is chasing budget-conscious buyers without losing its premium customers, in an early sign of how Ternus might broaden its appeal. REUTERS

'There cannot be business as usual with Russia' — Dutch minister urges Europe to step up for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:11:12 UTC
05:11:12 KST

'There cannot be business as usual with Russia' — Dutch minister urges Europe to step up for Ukraine
Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Dutch Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 28, 2026. (Handout / Tetiana Bulhakova)
Ukraine is about to enter another harsh winter as Russian attacks continue crippling critical infrastructure, even before the coldest days set in.
In an attempt to relieve Kyiv, the Dutch government on Oct. 28 outlined a package of non-military aid worth 1.2 billion euros ($1.3 billion), to be disbursed over the next three years and directed toward the country's economic recovery.
The Netherlands will also provide 40 million euros ($45 million) to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund, as well as 55 million euros ($62 million) to fund energy equipment from Dutch companies via the Netherlands Enterprise Agency.
The Kyiv Independent walked through central Kyiv with Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Netherlands' minister for foreign trade, to discuss how Europe can help Ukraine withstand mounting pressure on its energy and water infrastructure amid ongoing Russian attacks.
Sjoerdsma explained the benefits of investing in Ukraine and commented on some countries' willingness to do business with Russia as its full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues.
The minister added that the EU must play a bigger political role in discussing how Russia’s war should end.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
The Kyiv Independent: How is the Netherlands coordinating assistance to Ukraine for the upcoming tough winter?
Sjoerdsma: The support package we are bringing, 1.2 billion euros ($1.3 billion), is mainly aimed at helping Ukrainians protect and restore energy and water facilities, but also at training people to prevent damage to and protect these facilities so they keep running.
We see that the urgency of the upcoming winter is to ensure that cities, whether it's Kyiv or small villages in the east, remain livable. We understand that the Russian strategy is to try to break the spirit of the Ukrainian people, to literally put you in the cold, and we're going to do anything we can to prevent that from happening.
The Kyiv Independent: Regarding the protection of these facilities, what is the Netherlands doing to aid Ukraine?
Sjoerdsma: Obviously, we have to make sure there's protection, and that they cannot be easily destroyed. We try, as best we can, to bring completed equipment, but this obviously cannot always happen, as we sometimes require Ukrainian expertise to help install and maintain it.
We try to make sure it's not just a one-off, but instead a complete, integrated process that helps Ukrainian energy and water facilities.
The Kyiv Independent: What potential do you see in investing in Ukraine during wartime?
Sjoerdsma: If you look at Dutch companies already present in Ukraine, their expertise varies a lot. Some are obviously defense companies that help Ukraine build missiles for military use.
Then there are companies like Philips that help supply essential medical materials. And then, there are many smaller companies helping Ukraine, for example, providing bakers with materials. So anything from a very small scale to a very large scale is already present. It's both a sign of solidarity and a business opportunity.
Kyiv Independent: What do Dutch businesses gain from investing in Ukraine?
Sjoerdsma: We are learning so much from Ukraine, just to give two examples. In the field of defense, the innovative way in which Ukraine's army operates and adjusts, changes material needs, and utilizes drones. These are huge lessons for how we organize our army.
But also, Ukraine's resistance against Russia, its ability to adapt and restore certain facilities, especially critical infrastructure, at such speed and ingenuity, is also crucial to us. If there are any problems with the Dutch electrical network or other facilities, we'll definitely call Kyiv first to ask how you do things.
Additionally, the day after the war ends and reconstruction begins, it's not only our duty to help Ukraine rebuild as soon as possible, but also a huge opportunity for Dutch companies. These can be some of their biggest assignments to date: rebuilding entire hospitals, schools, ports, and whatever else will help Ukraine flourish again.
Kyiv Independent: As some countries are showing willingness to trade and do business with the Kremlin and Russian companies, what is the Netherlands' stance on this matter?
Sjoerdsma: Let me be very clear, this war can end today if Russia decides to stop its aggression against Ukraine. For the Netherlands, this scenario is really quite clear. Looking at the way Russia is treating cities, not just Kyiv, and aiming to erase your cultural heritage, it's clear what Moscow's end goal is, and we cannot allow that to happen.
"There's no talk about Ukraine without Ukraine in the driver's seat of what's happening."
We love doing business with Ukraine and don't see any reason to do business with Russia at this time. So no, there cannot be business as usual with Russia. Our prime minister at the European Council was quite clear about this.
While the Dutch are very robust in their support, we also believe that other European countries really need to step up. And this is not a cliche — your security is our security. To treat it as something Ukraine can do on its own, I think, is ridiculous.
This is a partnership. We are doing what we can, but others need to increase their support, and they need to do so as soon as possible, before winter sets in.
The Kyiv Independent: How can the European Union help prevent the West's future deals with Russia?
Sjoerdsma: Obviously, we do not condone the diesel deal between the U.S. and Russia. We feel it not only legitimizes Russia’s government but also reinforces its position.
I think it's crucial that, since the bulk of Ukraine's assistance comes from the EU, the EU is also a political player.
We must use our political influence to ensure that whenever discussions about a ceasefire or peace agreement take place, Ukraine is at the table. There's no talk about Ukraine without Ukraine in the driver's seat of what's happening.
I think Europe's role is to support Ukraine in its resistance against Russia, but also to make sure you are in a position to determine your own future. We see how Russia is trying to erase your identity and history, and we are determined to prevent that from happening.

Chipotle earnings miss estimates, but same-store sales increase for third straight quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:11:00 UTC
05:11:00 KST

Chipotle Mexican Grill on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results and said its restaurant-level operating margin shrank.
But the burrito chain saw traffic and same-store sales grow during the quarter as low-income consumers spent more, bucking industry trends, and CEO Scott Boatwright projected a strong finish to the year.
Shares of the company rose 7% in extended trading.
"Broader consumer and industry headwinds may continue, but initiatives across our recipe for growth strategy are building and giving us more tools to win in any environment," Boatwright said on the company's earnings conference call. "We are still in the early stages of this work, and it's gaining traction."
Like the broader restaurant industry, Chipotle saw trends soften in early October, although executives said its traffic has returned to growth since then. Boatwright said the company has "high confidence" in its performance for the rest of the fourth quarter.
"We feel very confident that November and December set up very well for us," Boatwright said.
Chief Financial Officer Adam Rymer said the company expects fourth-quarter same-store sales growth of about 2%.
Here's what the company reported for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 27 cents adjusted vs. 29 cents expected
- Revenue: $3.29 billion vs. $3.29 billion expected
Chipotle reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $339.9 million, or 27 cents per share, down from $382.1 million, or 29 cents per share, a year earlier. The company's restaurant-level operating margin fell from 24.5% to 23.3%.
Excluding restaurant asset impairment charges and stock-based compensation, the company earned 27 cents per share.
Net sales rose 9.6% to $3.29 billion, fueled by the chain's new restaurants. During the quarter, Chipotle opened 84 company-owned restaurants and five international locations run by licensees.
In the second half of July, Chipotle said it started to see sales pull back as diners grew concerned about consuming raw lettuce due to cyclospora, although its own supply was never tied to an outbreak. Then in August, the chain disclosed that it had temporarily pulled jalapenos from Minnesota restaurants after learning its supply was potentially linked to a salmonella outbreak.
Still, the chain was able to report same-store sales growth for its third straight quarter, shaking off last year's traffic woes.
Sales at stores open at least 13 months increased 2.1%, lifted by a 1.3% bump in average check.
For the first time this year, low-income consumers during the quarter outperformed the high-income cohort at its restaurants, Boatwright said. And discounts aren't the reason — low-income consumers spent the most in September, when promotions were at their low point during the quarter, he told analysts.
For the full year, Chipotle reiterated its previous forecast that its same-store sales will increase by a low-single-digit percentage.
Looking ahead to 2027, the company is projecting that it will open between 340 and 360 new company-owned locations in the U.S. and Canada and around 15 to 25 international restaurants.

The Peptide Rush Has Begun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:09:42 UTC
05:09:42 KST

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will not take action against licensed pharmacists who dispense certain unapproved peptides to consumers, according to a new policy published Oct. 28 in the Federal Register.
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that people inject into their bodies. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said in the past that he is a “big fan” of the unapproved drugs, whose benefits are largely scientifically unproven.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) essentially banned peptides in 2023 because of safety concerns. But an FDA committee met in July to review the evidence on peptides and recommend whether or not to take the highly unusual step of allowing pharmacies to dispense them absent scientific review. The committee was made up of new appointees who consulted with or were employed by companies that were interested in promoting or dispensing peptides; it recommended allowing specialty pharmacies to dispense six peptides, despite FDA staff advising against the move.
The new policy—which was signed by Kennedy—says that after the July meetings, HHS believed there was “significant interest” in the use of obtaining these peptides from compounding pharmacies. “Therefore, to expand and improve patient access, HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician compounding a drug product using a peptide bulk drug substance found in Appendix A,” the notice said. The policy said that it was going to be published in the Federal Register on Oct. 30. The peptides listed in Appendix A were BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500—the same ones the committee recommended allowing this summer.
A separate document posted on the HHS website says that after reviewing the recommendations of the committee that met in July, “the Secretary has determined that the policy advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety.”
The decision to allow the compounding of peptides is a boon for companies like Hims & Hers, which had reportedly been preparing to offer peptides in 2026. Analysts have said the market for peptides could be as high as $3.3 billion. Hims stock shot up 5% after the Oct. 28 announcement.
The move “represents a vital step toward eliminating the unsafe gray and black markets, restoring safe patient access through legitimate, physician-supervised care,” said Lee Rosebush, chair of the American Academy of Peptide Medicine, a new advocacy group, in a statement.
Other public-health professionals raised alarm about the decision, which they say allows compounding pharmacies to dispense these medications absent scientific evidence. “American consumers should not be treated like guinea pigs,” said Fred Mills, chief policy officer for Americans for Safe and Effective Medicines, in a statement. “It is possible to advance both patient safety and access to legitimate medicines, but this is not it.”
At the July hearings, consumer advocacy groups including the Center for Science in the Public Interest had argued that allowing peptides to skip a rigorous evidence-based FDA approval process would be unprecedented and dangerous to consumers.
Many physicians have spoken up against allowing peptides to be compounded. “The peptides under consideration here are untested and poorly characterized experimental drugs that should not be allowed in compounded products,” said Dr. Adriane Fugh-Berman, a professor of pharmacology and physiology at Georgetown University Medical Center, at the public comment portion of the July meeting, reminding the committee that two women had required emergency treatment after receiving peptides at a Las Vegas festival.
Critics also expressed concern that people were turning to compounding pharmacies for untested drugs. Compounding pharmacies are often used to fill specific prescriptions from a doctor, but in recent years, they have mass-produced drugs like GLP-1s for patients looking to save money. The peptide boom will put even more pressure on compounding pharmacies to quickly make drugs for telehealth sites, said Annie Lambert, a pharmacist and clinical program manager for compliance solutions at Wolters Kluwer Health.
"Compounding can and should play a legitimate clinical role, from hospitals to home infusion to filling gaps during drug shortages. But it is not a substitute for FDA-approved manufacturing, and that distinction is where a lot of today's risk sits,” she said in a statement. “My concern is that pharmacies rushing into this space will move to make a dollar faster rather than make sure they meet every requirement, from ingredient sourcing and facilities to staff training and sterility testing.”
Shortly after the new notice was published, a number of telehealth websites were already marketing the six peptides, each for a price of anywhere from $199 to $249 a month.

America's largest budget airline reports 71% jump in airfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:06:19 UTC
05:06:19 KST

Frontier Airlines reported a 71% increase in airfare in the third quarter as the country's largest budget airline tried to pass along an even bigger jump in jet fuel prices.
Frontier's fare revenue averaged $67.82 per passenger in the third quarter, compared with $39.74 last year. Including the budget airline's many fees, such as for checked and carry-on luggage, total revenue per passenger rose 30% on the year to $138.22.
Customers kept booking despite the higher prices. Frontier's passenger count rose 18% to more than 9.8 million people in the quarter. That's a difference of 1.5 million passengers from last year.
The company said demand remains strong, even at these higher prices, but Frontier still lost money as it took a $134 million charge tied to the return of some Airbus aircraft. Excluding that and other one-time charges, Frontier had an adjusted profit of $40 million.
Its posted a net loss of $104 million compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Its fuel bill soared 82% to $425 million.
Frontier forecast potential adjusted profit in the fourth quarter, saying it expects to post an adjusted loss of 15 cents per share to adjusted earnings of as much as 5 cents per share.
Carriers from Delta Air Lines to Frontier have said customers are mostly continuing to book flights despite higher fares, but that record jet fuel prices, their biggest cost after labor, are eroding profits.
Frontier shares rose close to 12%.
Frontier had eclipsed Spirit Airlines as the biggest discount carrier in the country even before that airline collapsed in May.

UN fact-finding mission says external actors fuel Sudan war, backs nationwide arms embargo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:02:41 UTC
05:02:41 KST

Merve Aydogan, Aysu Bicer
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan said Wednesday that foreign weapons, technology and personnel continue to fuel the war, as it urged stronger international action.
Speaking at a news conference at UN headquarters in New York, mission chair Mohamed Chande Othman said: "Our investigation found reasonable grounds to believe that external transfer of weapons, military technology, logistic support, and foreign personnel continue to sustain and intensify the conflict."
"We also found that external actors supplied both parties, and this helps sustain their military operations. The result is increasingly visible on the ground," he said.
Asked who is supplying the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the government, Othman said investigators found a cross-border network involving individuals and entities in Chad, Puntland in Somalia, southeast Libya and the United Arab Emirates, engaged in supplying weapons and training foreign fighters.
He said the mission is urging those states "to beef up their due diligence obligations" because of the direct consequences for civilians.
Stressing the distinction between governments and those operating from their territory, Othman said: "We have not yet, in terms of our evidence, linked any of the neighboring states as states. So, there’s a distinction there: individuals and entities in these states."
He said the mission is engaging with the UAE and Chad, noting that Chad denies using its territory and that the investigation into other states’ alleged roles is ongoing.
Mona Rishmawi, member of the mission, said both parties and their allies "are basically destroying a country of 56 million people."
"That’s really important to keep in mind," she said, adding that impunity from earlier conflicts is feeding the violence.
Asked about the Security Council's refusal in September and earlier this month to expand an arms embargo beyond Darfur, mission member Joy Ngozi Ezeilo said the report documents how surveillance and arbitrary detention are exposing civil society.
She said the mission’s role is to ensure "Sudanese civilians, whether women, children, or the displaced families, are not abandoned."
"This war, despite being the most atrocious war, is not getting the attraction it is supposed to get. And the international community is not responding in a way it should," said Ezeilo.
"We are for expansion of this arms embargo," she said, adding that the mission also supports extending the International Criminal Court’s mandate to all of Sudan.
The mission said civilians in the strategic city of El Obeid are exposed to grave risks as it remains partially encircled by RSF.
RSF-attributed drone strikes have also damaged schools and displacement sites, and disrupted access to healthcare, electricity and water, according to the report.
Meanwhile, security forces affiliated with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have intensified surveillance and arbitrary arrests, further restricting civilian freedoms.
“The situation in and around El-Obeid remains grave and the risk of atrocities are high,” said Othman.
“The attacks reported in Blue Nile, Abyei and near the Sudan-Egypt border reinforce what we have been warning about for months: the conflict is becoming more geographically extensive, more technologically sophisticated and increasingly dangerous for civilians,” he added.
The army and the RSF have been fighting since April 2023, when disagreements about the integration of military forces escalated into war.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, amid worsening famine and a deepening humanitarian crisis.

Hanwha signs four deals with Lithuanian firms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:00:24 GMT
05:00:24 KST

Hanwha Aerospace has signed four memoranda of understanding with Lithuanian companies covering work on its forty millimetre wheeled anti-aircraft gun, after an industry day in Vilnius that drew more than eighty participants from around thirty local firms, according to the company.
The agreements cover vehicle integration with KMT, turret shell fabrication with Cosmos Construction, integration of command and control systems with NATO networks in cooperation with Nortal, and cable manufacturing with T&G Lithuania. The event was organised with the Lithuanian Defence and Security Industries Association, which Hanwha Aerospace has now joined.
Vaidas Sabaliauskas, director of the association, said: “Lithuania is a small country, but we have a lot to offer. Our defence industry is growing very fast. We have strong companies, skilled engineers, and modern technologies. Hanwha brings great experience and advanced technology. We see great opportunities to work together in production, technology, research of new products.”
Senior Vice President Robert Park, head of air defence and missile launcher systems at Hanwha Aerospace, said: “We see Lithuania as a long-term strategic partner and recognise the strong technological capabilities and potential of its defence industry. We aim to build lasting industrial partnerships with Lithuanian companies, exploring opportunities in technology transfer, joint development and lifecycle support, while contributing to Lithuania’s ambition to become a regional hub for defence manufacturing and maintenance in the Baltic region.”
The gun at the centre of the agreements is a mobile system aimed at low-altitude threats including drones, combining automated fire control, target tracking and forty millimetre ammunition. The company also presented short, medium and long range air defence products and an integrated counter-drone approach pairing radar and electro-optical sensors with command and control systems and a range of countermeasures.
Hanwha Aerospace has moved aggressively into the European market since Poland’s large orders for its K9 howitzers and Chunmoo rocket launchers, and Lithuania borders both Belarus and the Kaliningrad exclave.

Colombia’s lower house rejects changes to pension reform articles
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:20 CET
05:00:20 KST

BOGOTA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Colombia’s lower house on Wednesday rejected changes to a package of specific articles from a pension reform bill that had been returned to the legislature by the Constitutional Court, which ordered lawmakers to remedy a procedural flaw in the bill.
In August, the Constitutional Court approved most of the 2024 pension system reform, championed by former President Gustavo Petro.
The rejection means the version of the bill approved by the Senate will stand and the court will now need to decide if the procedural flaw has been corrected.
The pension reform aims to strengthen the state-run pension administrator Colpensiones, reduce subsidies for high pensions, provide benefits to women with children, and expand coverage to protect older adults living in poverty.
The bill maintains the retirement age at 62 for men and 57 for women. The law requires all Colombians earning up to 2.3 times the monthly minimum wage — approximately 4 million pesos (about $1,300) — to make contributions to Colpensiones.
Those earning above that amount can choose a private pension fund for the surplus portion of their income.
The measure also stipulates that workers who failed to accumulate enough contribution weeks to qualify for a pension will receive aid, while those in poverty who did not contribute will receive a monthly payment of around $75.
The Petro government estimated more than 2.6 million older adults will benefit from the measures.
Men with 900 weeks of contributions and women with 750 will remain in the current system and will not be required to contribute to the state fund.
Some economic and social initiatives championed by Petro were rejected or faced difficulties gaining approval in Congress, where he lacked solid support. He left office in August and was replaced by right-wing President Abelardo De La Espriella, who has pledged to maintain some of Petro’s popular social reforms.
The reform is one of Colombia’s most significant social policy reforms in years, according to analysts, who note that it would expand the state’s role in the pension system while preserving a role for private funds—an issue that has long divided lawmakers, businesses, and unions.
(Reporting by Carlos Vargas and Nelson Bocanegra; Editing by Kylie Madry)

Early trauma may change how children’s cortisol responses relate to anxiety and behavior problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:00:04 UTC
05:00:04 KST

Early trauma may shape how children’s stress responses relate to anxiety and behavioral problems, according to a study published in Development and Psychopathology. Among youth who experienced potentially traumatic events before age 6, a smaller cortisol increase during a social stress task predicted a shift over the next two years toward externalizing symptoms rather than anxiety, while a larger increase predicted a shift toward anxiety.
Cortisol is a hormone involved in the body’s response to stress. It can rise when someone faces a challenge, such as speaking in front of an audience. Researchers can measure the total amount of cortisol released across a task, which reflects starting levels, as well as how much cortisol rises during the task. These two measures may capture different aspects of the body’s stress response.
Anxiety and externalizing problems, such as aggression, anger, or rule-breaking, often overlap in children and adolescents. Previous studies have found mixed links between cortisol and these symptoms, with some tying externalizing problems to heightened cortisol responses and others to blunted ones.
Led by Gretchen R. Perhamus of the Medical University of South Carolina, the research team examined whether a history of early trauma helped explain those varying patterns. Their predictions were guided by the adaptive calibration model, a theory proposing that the stress system adjusts to the level of threat in a child’s environment, so that the same stress response may relate to symptoms differently depending on a child’s experiences. They also considered whether cortisol was related to overall symptom levels or to which type of problem was more prominent.
The study included 189 youth ages 8 to 15 (average age about 11; 99 girls and 89 boys) from a larger community study in Charleston, South Carolina. Caregivers and youth were separately interviewed about a wide range of potentially traumatic experiences, including serious accidents, violence, abuse, neglect, separation from a caregiver, and natural disasters.
The researchers classified 107 participants as having experienced at least one such event before age 6, based on either the youth’s or the caregiver’s report, and 82 as having never experienced one at any age, based on both reports. Youth in the early trauma group came from households with lower average incomes and were less likely to be white.
During a laboratory visit, each young person gave a three-minute speech to a camera, as if auditioning for a TV show about kids their age, while a judge watched. The researchers collected saliva samples before and after the speech and during the following recovery period to measure cortisol, and usable cortisol data were available for 145 participants. The youth reported their own anxiety and externalizing symptoms at that visit and again two years later.
For youth with early trauma exposure, higher overall cortisol output during the task was linked with more externalizing symptoms at the same time, and with externalizing problems being more prominent than anxiety. Unexpectedly, higher overall cortisol output was linked with less anxiety in both groups.
Over the following two years, among youth with early trauma, a smaller cortisol increase during the task predicted a shift toward externalizing problems relative to anxiety, while a larger increase predicted a shift toward anxiety. Among youth with no trauma history, a larger cortisol increase predicted a decrease in anxiety over time.
The findings depended on which cortisol measure and symptom comparison the researchers examined. Overall cortisol output was linked to current symptoms, while the rise in cortisol was more informative about later changes in symptom patterns. Several associations among trauma-exposed youth emerged only when the researchers looked at which type of problem was more prominent, rather than at anxiety and externalizing symptoms separately.
The two groups did not differ in their cortisol responses. Among youth with early trauma, the number of early traumatic experiences did not change the links between cortisol and symptoms, although most of these youth had experienced only one or two such events.
Perhamus and colleagues summarized: “the specific pattern of findings was complex and depended on whether models examined concurrent or longitudinal associations, and whether they examined symptom domains or directionality.” In other words, the results did not point to one simple relationship between cortisol and mental health.
Some limitations should be noted. Trauma histories were reported retrospectively, and the researchers did not examine whether youth in the early-trauma group experienced additional traumatic events later in childhood or during the study. Because of the study design, the researchers could not test whether early trauma altered stress responses, which in turn shaped symptoms.
Puberty can also affect the stress system, and although the researchers accounted for pubertal development, it may still have influenced the results. The study measured cortisol without examining other parts of the body’s stress response, used broad measures of anxiety and externalizing problems, and drew on a relatively small community sample, so the authors say the findings need to be replicated.
The study, “Early trauma exposure moderates associations between cortisol reactivity and youth anxiety and externalizing symptoms,” was authored by Gretchen R. Perhamus, Rachel E. Siciliano, Tiffany Phu, Christopher T. Sege, Zachary W. Adams, Jane E. Joseph, Jason E. Chapman, Colleen A. Halliday, Colin Bowyer, Donte L. Bernard, Benjamin L. Hankin, Lisa M. McTeague and Carla Kmett Danielson.
