Five key takeaways from the UK Autumn Budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:46:45 UTC
03:46:45 KST

Five key takeaways from the UK Autumn Budget
The government says its policies are for the ‘working people of Britain’.
The United Kingdom’s government has announced its first budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister and leader of the Labour Party three months ago.
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey unveiled his Autumn Budget on Wednesday, announcing a series of policies that he said were for the “working people of Britain”, who have experienced a dramatic decline in living standards in recent years. Healey said the budget would give the country “breathing space” after years of economic stagnation fuelled by austerity, Brexit, the coronavirus pandemic, privatisation and rising energy prices.
So, what did Healey announce, and what will it mean for the average Brit?
Energy costs
Global fuel prices have soared in recent months because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has prompted Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway through which about 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) would normally transit.
In response, Healey said on Wednesday that 20 million households will receive a one-off payment of 100 British pounds ($133) towards their energy bills. People living in homes valued at 88,000 British pounds ($117,000) or less will receive the payment. The valuations are based on prices in April 1991, not current house prices.
Healey also said a temporary cut to VAT – a sales tax – will be extended until 1 July. The measure will reduce the annual price cap by 50 British pounds ($66.50).
However, James Meadway, an economist and co-director of the left-wing think tank Verdant, told Al Jazeera that these measures will not tackle the cost-of-living crisis in “any serious way”.
“There’s quite a lot of small things. These are not nothing. They’re just not approaching the scale of the problem that people are already facing and [which] is expected, according to the government’s own figures, to get worse over the next year,” Meadway said.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), an independent public body that analyses the country’s finances, said it expected no growth in real earnings next year. The body also sharply downgraded its growth forecast for 2027 to 1 percent, from 1.5 percent.
“There are forecasts out there saying that by the end of Parliament, it will be the worst Parliament for living standards in modern history. Put in those terms, what you got in this budget was nothing like enough,” Meadway added.
Defence spending
Healey said he would fund the government’s additional Defence Investment Plan, worth 15 billion British pounds ($20bn), and pledged to plug a gap of 4.7 billion British pounds ($6.2bn) by “reprioritising” budgets across other departments.
However, he did not detail how the government would meet its NATO commitment to spend 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2035, with an interim target of three percent in 2030. Instead, Healey said he would set out how these targets would be met during a spending review next year.
In response, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte welcomed the British government’s budget plan, saying it showed a “strong commitment” to defence.
“Good news on the new budget from MP John Healey with a strong commitment on defence,” wrote Rutte on X.
“The UK role in Transatlantic security is vital, and I welcome this move to put Britain on a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all NATO Allies in The Hague – to ensure we’re all investing what’s needed to remain ready and able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security,” Rutte added.
Ukraine was also on the agenda during Healey’s budget statement, with the chancellor pledging an additional 10 billion British pounds ($13.2bn) in economic and military aid for Kyiv in its war with Russia.
Salaries
The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage will both increase by 3.9 percent in April, at the start of the new tax year. The former currently sets a minimum hourly rate of 10.85 British pounds ($14.44) for workers aged 18 to 20, while the latter sets the rate at 12.71 British pounds ($16.91) for workers aged 21 and over.
Taxes on banks’ profits
To raise funds for additional support for households and businesses, the government will temporarily increase the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge from three percent to six percent. The increase will last for 15 months, ending on March 31, 2028. The surcharge is levied on top of standard corporation tax and is expected to raise 1.5 billion British pounds ($2bn).
Housing crisis
Affordable housing is a significant problem in the UK. The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) shows that 35 percent of men aged 20 to 35 were living at home with their parents last year, compared with 22 percent of women in the same age range.
To tackle this, Healey announced a new First Time Buyer savings account. Interest earned in such accounts, commonly referred to as Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs), is tax-free.
The First Time Buyer account will launch in 2029, replacing the current Lifetime ISA. The exact details of the new account are not yet clear. However, like the Lifetime ISA, it will pay savers a bonus of 25 percent on deposits of up to 4,000 British pounds ($5,320). That means savers can benefit from an annual government bonus of up to 1,000 British pounds ($1,330).
Healey also announced that the penalty for first-time buyers using funds from a Lifetime ISA to purchase a house worth more than 450,000 British pounds ($598,853) will immediately be reduced to 20 percent. That means savers will get back at least what they put in. The penalty was previously 25 percent.
A further 432 million British pounds ($574.9m) will also be spent over the next two years to reduce the number of people sleeping on the streets, a problem that Burnham has pledged to end.

Araghchi briefs cabinet on Tehran security summit, warns of risks to global energy markets
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has briefed the cabinet on the latest diplomatic developments, with a focus on a quadrilateral meeting in Tehran involving Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, emphasizing the need for regional cooperation to safeguard security, prevent escalation and protect national sovereignty.
Araghchi presented his report at Wednesday’s cabinet meeting, chaired by President Masoud Pezeshkian, outlining recent diplomatic consultations on regional and international affairs, including discussions with senior officials from neighboring and regional countries.
The report covered meetings involving a Qatari delegation, as well as consultations with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council; Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defense minister; Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of army staff; and Ibrahim Kalin, head of Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization.
According to the report, participants in the four-way discussions stressed the importance of strengthening regional cooperation, developing joint security mechanisms and preventing the further escalation of tensions and conflicts.
They also warned against the 'Israeli regime’s destabilizing policies,' including efforts to weaken regional states, expand military aggression, undermine governments and draw the United States into regional conflicts.
The senior officials underscored the need for regional countries to remain vigilant against developments that could fuel tensions and to deepen cooperation in defence of their sovereignty, stability and territorial integrity.
Regional ownership of security
In a message posted on Instagram following the Tehran meeting, Araghchi described the talks as a valuable opportunity to advance dialogue on regional peace and security and address shared threats and challenges. He said the agreement to continue consultations represented an important step forward.
Turning dialogue into lasting cooperation, the foreign minister stressed, would require agreement on common principles, confidence-building, mutual respect for national sovereignty and practical commitments.
Iran’s position, he said, was that sustainable regional security must be achieved through the participation of regional countries, without the military presence or interference of powers from outside the region.
“This approach is based on the responsibility of regional countries to determine their own destiny,” Araghchi wrote.
He also emphasized the need to counter the Israeli regime’s acts of aggression and destabilization, describing this as essential to protecting countries’ independence and sovereignty and preventing the spread of war.
Instagram message concluded with Iran’s diplomatic motto: “Our Neighbors, Our Priority.”
Energy diplomacy and Persian Gulf security
Araghchi also highlighted the energy dimension of Iran’s recent diplomatic engagements, saying the country’s energy diplomacy had advanced during the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow, where discussions addressed global gas markets and energy security.
He warned that any military adventurism initiated by Israel in the Persian Gulf could have potentially devastating consequences for international energy markets, making the prospect a serious concern for both gas-producing countries and consumers.
The foreign minister’s remarks underscored the connection between regional stability and global energy security, as well as the importance of diplomatic coordination among regional states in preventing conflicts that could disrupt international markets.

Putin invites African airlines to launch flights to Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:42:32 UTC
03:42:32 KST

Burç Eruygur, Elena Teslova
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday invited African airlines to launch flights to Russia.
Speaking at the plenary session of the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum in Moscow, Putin said Russia was ready to expand cooperation with African countries across trade, energy, pharmaceuticals, and transport.
"We also offer our African partners comprehensive solutions for building reliable logistics routes that will have a direct impact on the growth of trade and investment," he said. "Naturally, we invite African airlines to begin flights to the Russian Federation."
In addition, Russia could provide services in design, construction, and modernization of railways and roads, sea routes, transport hubs, and equip them with digital management, tracking, and customs declaration systems, he said.
Trade between Russia and Africa could exceed $50 billion in the near future, while Russia was involved in more than 30 prospective energy projects across 16 African countries, Putin added.
"Russian-African trade turnover exceeded $27 billion last year. In 2022, by the way, it was only $18 (billion). That's significant growth. True, of course, even that is not enough. I am convinced that we are capable of increasing this figure at least twofold in the very near future and definitely surpassing the $50 billion mark," he noted.
Russia also plans to localize the production of medicines and vaccines in Africa and establish laboratories and diagnostic centers, he said.
The Russian president described the growing influence of African countries on the international stage as part of a broader shift toward a more equitable multipolar world, in which the voices of the majority are increasingly heard.
Putin said Russia and African nations had jointly helped lay the foundations for a fairer international order.
The Russian leader recalled Moscow’s historical support for African liberation movements, economic development, and the formation of national armed forces.
The Russian president criticized Western efforts to push African countries into a “debt trap,” describing tariff wars and sanctions as “tools of neocolonialism.”
He also called for changes to the functioning of the IMF and the World Bank, saying their work should be reoriented toward the needs of developing economies.
The forum is held amid a two-day Russia-Africa summit, the third such summit since 2019, for which many African leaders arrived in Moscow.
Later Wednesday, Putin also met with leaders of Africa's regional organizations at the Kremlin and visited an exhibition held within the framework of the summit.

Inflation tracker: See how the price of everything has changed
By Simon Elvery, Jessica Riga and Madi Chwasta
Posted , updated 
If it feels like (almost) everything is getting more expensive, that's because it is.
Inflation has jumped, putting Australians on alert for another interest rate rise.
The consumer price index rose by 4.3 per cent in the past year, well above the Reserve Bank of Australia's target of 2 to 3 per cent.
Below, we've tracked prices across all kinds of goods and services, including food, electricity, travel and housing.
- You'll notice an increase in automotive fuel. It's higher than a year ago due to the Iran war and has surged in recent months due to the fuel excise cut being ended on August 2.
- There has been a decent rise in the price of games, toys and hobbies as the escalating cost of computer parts has been passed on to consumers.
- Electricity has also gone up in the past year, linked to the ending of various government subsidies that were introduced to help cover soaring power costs mostly caused by the war in Ukraine.

Turkic nations formalize new audit body TURKSAI in Antalya

Turkic nations formalize new audit body TURKSAI in Antalya
The Charter of the newly established Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions of the Member States of the Organization of Turkic States (TURKSAI) has been signed in Antalya, Türkiye, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Kazakhstan's Supreme Audit Chamber.
At the signing ceremony, the Kazakhstan delegation was led by Alikhan Smailov, Chairman of the Supreme Audit Chamber.
The decision to create TURKSAI was adopted in November 2025 in Istanbul at a meeting of supreme audit heads from OTS Member States — Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Türkiye, and Uzbekistan.
The new organization is designed to elevate audit cooperation across the Turkic world to a new level. It will facilitate sharing knowledge and expertise, enhancing audit practices, conducting joint audits, and implementing collaborative research projects
Practical cooperation under the umbrella of TURKSAI is already underway. Prior to the signing, audit professionals from across the region completed a knowledge exchange program on Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It covered the entire SDG audit lifecycle, from topic selection and audit question formulation to drafting recommendations and follow-up monitoring.
Seven auditors from the Supreme Audit Chamber participated in the program. The key takeaways will inform the planning and execution of future SDG audits in Kazakhstan.
Addressing the ceremony, Alikhan Smailov thanked Metin Yener, President of the Turkish Court of Accounts, for warm hospitality and organizing the events. He noted that formalizing the new body was the logical outcome of decisions adopted nearly a year ago in Istanbul.
"Today, we cement our agreements with a foundational document that defines the principles, scope, and operational procedures of TURKSAI," Smailov said. "The organization holds significant potential for practical cooperation. I am confident that signing this charter will serve as a reliable foundation for long-term partnership."
The Chairman of Kazakhstan's Supreme Audit Chamber highlighted that rapidly evolving public finances alongside emerging challenges demand upgraded audit methods and higher standards of public asset management.
"This cooperation, rooted in friendship, trust, solidarity, and the spirit of Turkic brotherhood, will allow our supreme audit institutions to jointly respond to modern challenges and make a meaningful contribution to the development of our states," he emphasized.
Following the ceremony, the delegation heads attended a symposium on the Sustainable Development Goals, focusing on the role of public auditing in advancing SDG targets and leveraging audit outcomes to improve public policy.
As reported earlier, Kazakhstan attaches importance to developing comprehensive cooperation with Türkiye and strengthening ties within the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), with the integration of the Turkic world among the country’s key foreign policy priorities, Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi said in an interview with Anadolu.

How do Israeli election results impact timing of possible new Iran war? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:38:46 UTC
03:38:46 KST

The Israeli election results seem to grant Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a better showing than expected. But they also clearly leave his bloc in the minority with no way to avoid new elections without cutting a deal with Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot.
How do those results impact a possible new conflict with Iran?
In recent weeks, Netanyahu was seriously considering renewing the conflict with Iran.
It seems that a mix of opposition by US President Donald Trump and IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir prevented Netanyahu from doing so, although it is also possible with the hard-to-pin-down prime minister that he just wanted Tehran to think he might attack to deter it from doing anything provocative.
But Zamir’s opposition was only to an attack before Israeli elections were held, and Trump’s opposition was only to an attack before the US midterm elections on November 3.
In fact, Trump has made numerous rumblings about resuming strikes on Iran soon after the US midterm elections, and in his endorsement of Netanyahu, he made reference to wanting Israel involved again as well.
If Eisenkot had won the battle of the blocs over Netanyahu, as forecast by the polls, he might have been able to start to form a government before the US midterm elections.
In such a scenario, it is doubtful that Netanyahu could have ordered a new attack against Iran.
As matters now stand, however, one of Eisenkot’s allies, Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman, will not even start serious talks about forming a government before Friday, when the final vote results are in.
At that point, Liberman must make the excruciating decision of breaking a promise: either making a deal with the Arab parties, making a deal with Netanyahu, or going to a second round of elections.
Even if Liberman moves toward forming a new government, it would just start complex negotiations about what each side would need to do to pave the way to a partnership.
Once there would be agreement on that, there is a whole separate negotiation on who gets what ministries and other jobs.
All of these issues are likely to take more than the four days between Friday and the US midterm elections, given that they usually take weeks or even months.
This means that Netanyahu will likely have the freedom to attack Iran if Trump wants to or would not stop him.
Zamir is in favor of attacking Iran under two conditions: The first has been and remains if Iran was either about to actually strike Israel; and the second was and is if Trump restarted the war first, and Israel had full backing offensively and defensively from the US for engaging in another round of conflict.
Generally, Zamir’s instinct has been that he is ready to strike Iran if it starts recovering its threat capabilities too fast, which it has not yet done, or if such a strike would be part of a well-thought-out and considered strategy to finally push Tehran into making key nuclear concessions to the US.
He was against attacking before the election so as not to undermine Election Day voting by a potential Iranian ballistic-missile counterstrike and to avoid the cloud of impropriety that an attack leading into the election might have been carried out to help Netanyahu’s chances.
Netanyahu's main obstacle would be Trump
Post-election, there is no reason to bar an attack, although Zamir also is not rushing toward an attack, given that he does not view Tehran as having gotten much closer to any growing substantial nuclear or ballistic-missile threat.
To be sure, both issues remain threats, but both have been put off by some period of years due to US-Israeli airstrikes in June 2025 and early 2026.
This means that Netanyahu’s main obstacle would be Trump.
Trump did not want to attack leading into the midterms because the Iran war is already dragging him and the Republic Party down in the polls. But post-midterms, and with him unable to run for a third term, he will be unrestrained and could follow his whim to hit Iran again.
Why might he still not?
His top advisers have been and are mostly against a return to war, and while some think a few days of war might loosen Iran up some, others think Iran’s refusal to crack since February has shown a few more intense days will not sway them either.
So, he may have little to gain, and some of his advisers have also warned that Tehran has shown it is willing to keep firing after a US ceasefire, meaning the conflict might last longer than a few days even if Trump wants to stop.
This could lead Trump to walk away from the price tag of another round and continue his long-term attempt to slowly wear down Iran economically.
In fact, this series of Trump’s dizzying switches from economic pressure to a sudden threat to go to war, to backing down back into economic pressure, happened in August, earlier in October, and at other times.
These inconsistent switches probably have also undermined the viability of his threat in the eyes of the Iranians.
Another possibility is that the Iranians finally get scared by his latest threat of force and offer a real deal on the nuclear issue. That would surely lead to a delay of an Iran attack.
But if Trump ultimately favors attacking, it could not come at a better time for Netanyahu.
If Netanyahu is involved with attacking Iran – as he holds a Jewish majority in the vote count, while Eisenkot and his camp are trying to rally together – a return to a focus on war with Iran would place the nation’s focus where Netanyahu prefers it.
Will Eisenkot and company find it harder to cut a deal with the Arab parties while Israelis have ballistic missiles raining down on them?
Might they feel more ready to cut a deal with Netanyahu if Iran has pushed out the October 7 massacre and haredim (ultra-Orthodox) serving in the IDF as the focus of the national conversation?
None of this means that Israel attacking Iran may not be justified on its own. Until Tehran makes new nuclear concessions, such an attack could be justified in theory, based on the idea of getting it to make those concessions.
And anytime the US offers to assist with cleaning house, many Israelis would say that Israel should not miss the chance to jump on board – as opposed to having to fight Iran solo at some later date.
Still, as long as Zamir is in no rush to strike Iran, Netanyahu would need to justify the attack with more than vague statements about Iran making new progress toward threatening Israel.
It is hard for him to both claim he succeeded at removing the nuclear and ballistic-missile threat in one sentence, and to then demand a new strike now, because time is running out.
How Netanyahu explains a third round of conflict, if it happens during coalition negotiations, will be crucial to the success of any attack and its legitimacy among the wider Israeli public.

With 85.6% of the vote counted, Hendel’s Reservists-Economic Party has received roughly 2.6% of the general vote, leaving them about 100,000 votes shy of the 3.25% threshold; however, Hendel is waiting on potentially higher support from double-envelope ballots, which have yet to be counted.
Winter pledges to continue fighting despite receiving no seats
People of Israel party leader Ofer Winter pledged on Wednesday to keep campaigning despite his party's projected failure to cross the electoral threshold and enter the Knesset, saying his movement remained committed to bringing new leadership to Israel.
In a statement on his Instagram account after Tuesday's election, Winter acknowledged that he failed to achieve his immediate political goal but insisted his party's campaign was only the beginning of a longer effort.
"Since October 7, a realization has taken shape within me that the people of Israel desperately need different leadership. United leadership, leadership that aspires to truth and justice, leadership that knows how to take responsibility," Winter wrote. "Unfortunately, I did not succeed. Not yet."
"Leadership that knows how to make decisions… We are here. For a long and shared journey."

US campaign to cripple Iran's economy risks falling short without global partners, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:38:17 UTC
03:38:17 KST

The United States’ Operation Economic Outcast, designed to sever the economic lifelines sustaining the Iranian regime, is falling short of its full potential without greater coordination with international partners, according to a new assessment published earlier this week by two experts from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
According to Michael Jacobson, the Mark and Wayne Levy Senior Fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, and Matthew Levitt, the Fromer-Wexler Senior Fellow and director of the institute’s Reinhard Program on Counterterrorism and Intelligence, closer coordination with allies on sanctions would strengthen Washington’s efforts to undermine the Iranian regime alongside the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Criticizing Washington for relying on targeted, limited diplomatic efforts to address Iran-linked terrorism, they argued that the results achieved so far have demonstrated the value of a more international approach.
On October 12, the US and 29 other governments issued a statement accusing Iran of orchestrating plots to destroy US air assets at RAF Fairford in the UK, following a similar statement a week earlier in which the US and eight countries in the Western Hemisphere condemned Iran’s terrorist and malign activities in the region.
In June, the US State Department and more than 20 other governments also accused Iran of being behind a series of attacks in Europe, North America, and Australia.
Jacobson and Levitt said some governments had initially been hesitant to condemn Iranian plots, including those on their own soil, because of concerns about Iranian retaliation and the fate of their nationals wrongfully detained in Iranian prisons, but they eventually did so with American support.
US sanctions against Iran-backed groups require stronger enforcement capabilities, experts warn
Washington’s efforts had also helped multiple countries in Central and South America designate or sanction the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Hezbollah, and Hamas in recent years, they wrote, adding that such measures carry symbolic weight while giving governments additional tools to counter the groups’ activities.
They cautioned that designations and sanctions must be backed by the material capabilities, skills, and knowledge needed to address the complex Iranian threat, including its sophisticated financial schemes, if they are to translate into meaningful action against the regime.
The Trump administration could use foreign assistance funding to advance these efforts, Jacobson and Levitt wrote, adding that Congress has already allocated almost $300 million to the State Department this fiscal year to strengthen partners’ counterterrorism capabilities.
Although the State Department has publicly committed some of that funding to addressing cartel and gang threats in Central America, similar support could also help countries counter Iran’s malign activities, they said.
US experts urge funding to disrupt Iranian smuggling and terror financing networks
The funding could be directed toward programs to train and equip Syrian border-security authorities to intercept Iranian and Hezbollah smuggling operations, including bulk cash transfers; help Yemeni Coast Guard officials detect and disrupt Houthi weapons and procurement networks; and improve Iraqi financial institutions’ ability to identify illicit Iranian financing schemes, Jacobson and Levitt wrote.
Other initiatives could strengthen efforts by authorities in West Africa and South America to uncover and prosecute Hezbollah’s illicit financial networks, they added.

The US goods trade deficit widened 2.1% month-on-month in September to $134.9 billion, marking its highest level since March 2025, the Commerce Department reported on Wednesday.

These Australians dug into the 'junk' of millions of cells. It could be a drug game-changer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:36:53 UTC
03:36:53 KST

IN BRIEF
- A study of 2,000 Australians found genetic clues linked to 16 diseases, including cancers and Alzheimer's disease.
- Researchers say the findings provide the "building blocks" for new and more targeted drug therapies.
Medical researchers have uncovered new clues about why some Australians develop certain diseases, as well as the "building blocks" for potential future treatments.
Researchers from the Sydney-based Garvan Institute of Medical Research and collaborators led three studies that examined the DNA of 2,000 Australians — recording each person's full genome and measuring gene activity in the 28 different types of immune cells.
Professor Joseph Powell, director of Garvan's Translational Genomics program and UNSW's Institute for Genomics and Health, said the research identified 1,500 genes linked to 16 different diseases.
"We did this for a range of different diseases that were all linked to immune function, so autoimmune diseases, cancers, and inflammatory conditions like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's," he said.
Researchers also identified how DNA variations influence gene activity.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Powell said they identified 21,000 genes and 180,000 DNA positions that act as a "dimmer switch" to control gene expression.
"This gives us the ability to identify how these DNA spots are controlling the activity of genes and then link that to disease," Powell said.
They also found DNA that "turned off" genetic activity, leading to the identification of an extra 350 disease-specific processes that acted as a "type of on-off switch mechanism".
"This is important ... because the way in which you would develop a therapy or treatment to target these is going to be different if the switch is an on-off switch compared to a dimmer switch," Powell said.
The answer in DNA 'junk'
Hope Tanudisastro, a junior medical officer and postdoctoral researcher at Garvan's Centre for Population Genomics and Murdoch Children's Research Institute, said the research also examined DNA "junk".
"A common theme in science is that we always have to challenge assumptions. We always have to look in places that have been understudied or overlooked," she said.
The team analysed DNA stutters, which are tandem repeats within a person's DNA.
While "long written off as junk", stutters could explain how someone's "immune system might be working", Tanudisastro said.
"Yet for years, most genetic studies have set [stutters] aside, and that's partly because they're very hard to read. It's like trying to count identical beads on a string where you can only see a few at a time. At some point, you lose track," she said.
The team measured repeats across the whole genome and tracked their effects in more than five million individual immune cells.
They found more than 69,000 of the repeat switches influencing the activity of genes in the immune system.
Unlocking new treatments for diseases
Tanudisastro said the research identified how changes in DNA and gene activity within "specific immune cell subtypes" can signal when disease is active.
They could now form the "building blocks" for the development of future targeted drug treatments, she said.
The study identified DNA repeats in "more than 200 genes" linked to conditions such as asthma, Crohn's disease, breast and prostate cancer, high cholesterol, and anaemia.
"These are common chronic conditions, and as our population ages, more Australians will be diagnosed with them, which means that better and more targeted therapies are all the more urgent to be discovered," she said.
Powell said the research is just the start, with further studies planned to examine more diseases.
He said the team will seek to develop "approaches for precision medicine".
"There's this well-recognised huge gap in developing new therapies for conditions that don't have active treatments, and for patients where there are treatments that just don't work," he said.
He said the "map" this research has created could help develop new treatments and identify existing treatments for a range of diseases.
"The findings could help researchers identify new targets for drugs and eventually develop treatments better suited to individual patients."

US envoy should speak based on facts, not fabricated accusations, Iran says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:36:20 UTC
03:36:20 KST

US envoy should speak based on facts, not fabricated accusations, Iran says
TEHRAN — Iran’s Ambassador and Chargé d’Affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, has urged the United States to address the facts rather than level 'fabricated accusations against Tehran,' condemning US and Israeli military attacks against Iran and calling for accountability under international law. In a separate address to the UN General Assembly, Darzi denounced unilateral sanctions as economic terrorism and demanded an end to Washington’s decades-long embargo against Cuba.
Speaking at the conclusion of a UN Security Council meeting on Iran, Darzi directly responded to remarks by US representative Mike Waltz, displaying photographs of Iranians killed in US and Israeli attacks.
 
“Let us speak based on facts, not on fabricated accusations,” the Iranian diplomat said, rejecting Washington’s allegations concerning Iran and its peaceful nuclear program.
Iran challenges Washington’s account of the conflict
Darzi said the US representative had failed to provide credible arguments or justification for 'Washington’s blatant act of aggression against Iran.' Instead, he argued, Waltz had resorted to repeated falsehoods and baseless allegations concerning Iran’s nuclear activities to obscure the facts and evade responsibility.
The Iranian envoy stressed that the United States and Israel had carried out repeated military attacks against Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities, which are under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards.
He maintained that Iran was the victim of the conflict, not its instigator, and accused Washington and Tel Aviv of committing war crimes against the Iranian people.
According to Darzi, the attacks had struck a wide range of civilian targets and essential infrastructure, including residential areas, schools, hospitals, bridges, airports, energy facilities, sports complexes, cultural heritage sites and railway infrastructure.
He described the strikes as flagrant violations of the UN Charter, international law and international humanitarian law, holding the United States and Israel responsible for the consequences of their military actions.
“No amount of propaganda can reverse the facts, erase the suffering of the Iranian people, or absolve those responsible of their international legal obligations,” Darzi said.
He emphasized that those who ordered, carried out or facilitated the attacks must be held accountable, warning against allowing those responsible to escape justice.
The Iranian diplomat also criticized Washington for seeking to portray itself as the victim while, in his account, conducting military aggression and inflicting mass civilian casualties.
He insisted that the distinction between aggressor and victim must not be reversed, arguing that the United States could not carry out attacks against Iran and then use the Security Council to present itself as the injured party.
Darzi said the United States and Israel would ultimately have to answer for their actions and the crimes he accused them of committing against the Iranian people.
Iran condemns sanctions as economic terrorism
In a separate address to the UN General Assembly during a debate on the need to end the US economic, commercial and financial embargo against Cuba, Darzi condemned unilateral sanctions as instruments of coercion that undermine national sovereignty, violate fundamental rights and obstruct economic development.
“Sanctions are examples of economic terrorism, while blockades enforced by armed force constitute acts of aggression under international law,” he said.
Darzi argued that unilateral coercive measures, including so-called autonomous sanctions, threatened multilateralism, destabilized international relations and undermined the principles enshrined in the UN Charter.
He described such measures as a form of collective punishment that imposed hardship on ordinary people, particularly women, children and older persons, while restricting access to healthcare, food and opportunities for development.
Referring to more than six decades of US sanctions and the economic blockade against Cuba, the Iranian envoy said Washington’s policies had inflicted severe suffering on the Cuban population and impeded the country's development.
He rejected the justification of tightening the embargo in the name of promoting democracy, arguing that the humanitarian consequences contradicted the stated objectives of the policy.
“No government is allowed to dictate the political future of a sovereign nation,” Darzi said, describing economic coercion as unlawful, immoral and inhumane.
He called for the immediate lifting of the embargo, full reparation for the damage inflicted on the Cuban people and accountability for those responsible for maintaining the restrictions.
Tehran links sanctions to violations of international law
Darzi said Iran’s opposition to unilateral sanctions was reinforced by its own experience of US economic coercion and military aggression. He reaffirmed Tehran’s unequivocal opposition to sanctions imposed against sovereign and independent states, including Cuba.
The Iranian envoy argued that invoking human rights to justify economic restrictions was fundamentally contradictory when those measures themselves undermined the rights to health, food, development and a dignified life.
He drew a parallel with the US president’s promise of assistance to the Iranian people, recalling the statement that “Help is on its way.” Darzi contrasted that promise with the subsequent US bombing of a primary school in Minab, which, according to the Iranian diplomat, killed 168 children aged between seven and 12.
He cited the incident as an example of the 'contradiction between Washington’s stated humanitarian commitments and its actions.'
Darzi also invoked Articles 1 and 2 of the UN Charter, emphasizing the principles of sovereign equality, international cooperation and friendly relations among nations. He cited Article 2(7) in arguing that unilateral coercive measures violate the principle of non-interference when used to force governments to change their domestic policies.
He warned that sanctions deepen international divisions, fuel confrontation and undermine peaceful coexistence, while imposing the heaviest burdens on vulnerable populations.
Concluding his address, Darzi reaffirmed Iran’s solidarity with the Cuban government and people and urged the General Assembly to press Washington to implement the numerous resolutions adopted by an overwhelming majority of member states calling for an end to the embargo.
He called for intensified international efforts to eliminate unilateral coercive measures, warning that their continuation undermined international law and reflected a failure to uphold fundamental legal and moral responsibilities.

Australia's $550 fuel hit is among world's highest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:36:15 UTC
03:36:15 KST

In brief
- Australians have paid more than $500 extra for fuel amid the global fuel crisis.
- Experts say that industry is driving Australia's reliance on diesel.
Surging fuel prices amid the war in the Middle East have cost Australians more than $500 per person on average, with the national impact of fuel price shocks exceeding $14 billion since March this year according to a report.
Australians have seen the third-highest fuel price increases compared to other countries, with individuals paying on average $546 more than usual, according to analysis from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
The analysis, which compared average fuel prices in January to February, before the disruption of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, with prices during March to October, found that price shocks had cost 169 countries, including Australia, $665 billion.
The country paying the most amid global fuel shocks was the United States, with more than $226 billion in additional costs.
Americans paid an extra $666 per person, Canadians $597, and New Zealand's motorists followed close behind Australians at $484 per person.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Senior economist at the University of Sydney Luke Hartigan said Australia's position in the top four alongside Canada, the US and New Zealand made sense, considering Australia has the highest per capita diesel usage rates in the world, driven by high use in mining and farming.
"That's why similar patterns appear in the US, Canada and New Zealand, all of which have large agricultural sectors, and Canada also has a significant mining industry," Hartigan told SBS News.
Geography was also an important factor, he said.
"Apart from New Zealand, these countries are vast, and distances between production centres and consumers are enormous."
"Moving fruit and vegetables from Queensland to Sydney, or freight from the Northern Territory to major cities, can involve distances comparable to crossing Europe."
Diesel costs blow out
Australia imports more than 90 per cent of its refined and crude oil, leaving it particularly vulnerable to fuel price shocks amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
But another issue contributing to Australia's vulnerability was its increasing use of diesel, which Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) CEO Amandine Denis-Ryan said was "really at odds" with the rest of the world.
"Between 2000 and recent years, Australia increased its diesel intensity by 33 per cent, while the world decreased it by 30 per cent, and countries like the US and Japan reduced it by 50 per cent," she told SBS News.
As the world's largest importer of diesel, Australia represents 10 per cent of the global seaborne diesel trade and is also the third-largest importer of petrol and jet fuel.
When compared with Australia's share of global GDP and population, Denis-Ryan said, "These numbers are enormous."
Diesel use has been trending upwards this century according to government figures, that show diesel comprises 44.1 per cent of transport energy use. It's the most used road and rail transport fuel and is a popular ship fuel.
"We've been shifting away from rail freight towards road freight, and we've also been shifting from underground coal mines, which mostly use electricity, to open-cut coal mines, which mostly use diesel," Denis-Ryan said.
And there are geological factors as well: "As we exhaust our best and most easily accessible mineral resources, we need more diesel for each tonne of coal produced and each tonne of ore produced," Denis-Ryan said, adding that Australia's vehicles were largely "really old and quite inefficient".
Australian households paying the price
Recent research from IEEFA assessed the link between inflation and oil shocks, and found that "in the last six inflation flare-ups in Australia since 2000, oil price shocks were a key contributor every time".
A reduction in the impact of oil price shocks on Australia's economy could provide broader economic benefits, Denis-Ryan said, noting that households would be less vulnerable to inflation if they switched to electric cars.
The CREA report found that while the US experienced enormous fuel costs, US electric vehicle (EV) drivers had seen just a $17 increase in charging costs since the start of March.
Hartigan said there has been an "enormous" uptake of EVs in Australia, starting at the height of the fuel crisis in March. Data from the National Australia Bank showed that EV loans doubled as Australians sought to dodge soaring petrol and diesel prices.
Senior economist at the left-wing thinktank the Australia Institute Matt Grudnoff said that governments could reduce or offset the upfront purchase cost of EVs.
But he said the bid to electrify Australia's roads should focus on industry.
"The public conversation tends to focus on household fuel costs because that's where people notice the impact most directly when they fill up their cars.
"But the data shows that a large share of the economic impact happens behind the scenes through freight and transport.
"Higher fuel prices increase the cost of moving goods around the country, which then contributes to inflation across the economy."
A move toward EVs
A recent report from the Climate Council found Australia paid more than twice as much as any other nation in additional diesel import costs during the global fuel crisis, putting the toll at $9 billion over six months.
Moves to renewable energy had saved Australians from some higher costs, the report found, with electric and hybrid cars cutting $1.7 billion in costs and saving the equivalent of 17.4 million litres of petrol and diesel per week.
Denis-Ryan said she hoped the fuel crisis would be a "wake-up call" for Australia, "particularly in terms of accelerating transport electrification, but also in looking at how we can slow the growth of oil use, and diesel use in particular, throughout Australia".

I never wanted to be a mum. At 31, I made that decision permanent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:35:19 UTC
03:35:19 KST

Child-free life vs child-free world? As more Australians embrace a child-free life, Insight explores the decision not to have kids, the stigma that comes with it, and the changing face of family. Watch Insight episode No Kids, No Problems? on SBS On Demand.
Since the age of 12, I was certain I did not want children. This was a conversation I made sure to have before getting engaged and married.
To me, having kids meant too much sacrifice of what I wanted to do and who I wanted to be.
I was 25 when I first started asking my doctor for a hysterectomy, a major surgery removing the uterus and often other reproductive organs, a procedure that would mean I would never become pregnant or have another period.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
I wanted the operation because my periods were becoming increasingly severe with age and drastically affecting my quality of life.
I experienced menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding) since my late teens and simple actions like sneezing or coughing often led to sudden bleeding and the passing of blood clots the size of a 50c piece — requiring urgent and frequent bathroom trips.
I avoided leaving home, knowing that I could simply shower if heavy bleeding occurred. I picked clothes that I wouldn’t mind getting stained and always kept Panadol and heat packs nearby.
Since I worked mostly as a contractor, missing work meant losing pay, so I had to push through and continue working despite my pain and discomfort.
I felt my whole reproductive system was malfunctioning and — as I didn't want kids — it would not be used for its primary function.
Because of these reasons and given my family's history of hysterectomies due to fibroids, I wanted to remove my uterus.
Being told I'd change my mind
When my doctor dismissed my request for a hysterectomy, I asked a few others — who also said no.
But they claimed I was too young or would eventually change my mind — despite it being a decision I had stuck by for over a decade.
Those physicians, who happened to be male, seemed to insist they understood me better than I knew myself.
About a year later, my gynaecologist recommended trying an IUD to help with my menorrhagia. Initially, I doubted its effectiveness and needed reassurance that it was a suitable option.
The pain I experienced after the insertion, which was done under general anaesthesia, felt like the worst period I ever had. Over-the-counter painkillers were supposed to be sufficient, but they provided no real relief.
However, the IUD did prove effective; my periods became less painful and there was a noticeable reduction in clotting.
And for the next three and a half years, my reproductive health was much easier to manage.
'White, hot, incandescent rage'
But at 30, I experienced an unintended and unwanted pregnancy after the IUD failed.
I had just come home from work on a Friday when I started cramping and bleeding at the front door. I finished my period about a week before and something just didn't feel right.
I told my then-husband we needed to go to the hospital.
Pregnancy was the last thing on my mind. I thought my IUD had maybe perforated my uterus.
A very anxious weekend
At the hospital, pregnancy was confirmed after blood and urine tests.
I felt like my body had betrayed me. I never wanted children and had followed the medical advice I'd been given by getting an IUD when I was denied a hysterectomy.
And yet I still became pregnant.
I was furious. White, hot, incandescent rage.
The hospital staff suspected I was experiencing a miscarriage at that time, but an ultrasound was needed to confirm.
And as all the sonographers had gone home for the weekend, I was told to wait until Monday for an ultrasound appointment but to return to hospital if the cramping and bleeding worsened.
That weekend I was extremely anxious.
I felt like my body had betrayed me.
Jessica Tymms
I was brought up in Queensland, where abortion was at the time illegal and wasn't legalised until 2018, four years later.
I was used to abortion being a criminal offence, so I questioned whether, in the absence of a miscarriage, access to abortion was even a possibility.
But after thorough online research, I realised I could legally get an abortion where I was living in Western Australia.
But my greatest concern during that weekend was experiencing an ectopic pregnancy, which is when a pregnancy grows outside inside the fallopian tube (or outside of the uterus) and it can be life-threatening if not diagnosed in time.
I composed a letter outlining my wishes, which I had both signed and witnessed, as I did not want any confusion about my medical decision, should I be unable to communicate that.
In it, I clarified that I did not wish to continue the pregnancy and asked the medical team to end it and put my well-being first should any complications arise.
'The 1 per cent club I never wanted to join'
At my ultrasound appointment on Monday morning, the monitor revealed nothing; the pregnancy had resolved naturally.
I felt immense relief that it was over and I would not need an abortion.
After my miscarriage, I returned to my original gynaecologist, still deeply distressed by everything that had happened.
Despite being on the most effective birth control available, I became pregnant — the so-called 1 per cent club I never wanted to join.
I no longer trusted IUDs or any less effective contraceptives. Once more, I requested a hysterectomy.
This time, with my then-husband present, the doctor took me seriously and suggested I get a second opinion, providing a referral.
Finally receiving a hysterectomy
Before the appointment with the second gynaecologist, I wrote down my reasons for wanting the surgery — determined to clearly communicate my case.
I was prepared to do anything to convince them to give me the surgery but to my surprise, they immediately agreed that I was old enough to make my own decision.
The only requirement was to wait six more months to be sure it wasn’t a reaction made in haste. That didn’t bother me — after waiting years already, another half-year felt insignificant.
After I'd recovered from the surgery, my concerns about potential contraceptive failure were alleviated and my quality of life significantly increased.
The absence of menstrual cycles eliminated major pain and discomfort — the need for pain relief medication, heat packs, and menstrual products, as well as stained clothing.
And I no longer required time away from work or urgent trips to the restroom due to symptoms like heavy bleeding or clotting.
Getting a hysterectomy made my life much easier in some ways. I've also saved so much money on not having to buy mountains of painkillers and pads.
'I have never doubted my childfree status'
It's now been almost 12 years, and I have never regretted having the surgery. Not once. Not even when I got divorced.
I knew I was doing what was right for me and I have never doubted my childfree status.
I think it would have been almost impossible for me to do all the things I wanted to do in my life — including earning three degrees, roller skating, indulging my passion for concerts — if I had children to provide and care for.
My life isn't overtaken or defined by parenthood, and I don't have to worry about the things most parents do: homework, if my kid is being bullied, or if they are the bully, school trips, after-school care, weekend sports. The list is endless.
And because I don't have the usual expenses that come with having children, I can regularly donate to seven or eight charities.
I also like that because I have a bit more time, I can do more for my family and community; looking after my niece in a pinch, helping my grandparents with their aged care and I have recently become a Justice of the Peace.
From my perspective, it remains concerning that women do not have full bodily autonomy, are often infantilised by medical professionals, and must contend with ongoing medical misogyny and bias.
I had to go through an IUD failure, a pregnancy, and a miscarriage before my doctors approved a hysterectomy.
I don't believe people should have to endure such experiences to get appropriate healthcare outcomes.

Fuel costs force US cruise ship to suspend multiyear voyage in Cambodia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:34:10 UTC
03:34:10 KST

Fuel costs force US cruise ship to suspend multiyear voyage in Cambodia
Hundreds of passengers are stranded after the ship’s three-and-a-half-year voyage is cut short due to fuel costs.
A United States cruise ship has suspended its around-the-world voyage in Cambodia, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark with no confirmed departure date.
The MV Odyssey, operated by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, arrived at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on Friday. The company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin, which historically averaged $1,800, had climbed to an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia.
The company said it tried to reduce consumption by slowing the ship and spending more time in port but could not offset the rising costs.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on Tuesday, adding that passing the full increase on to residents was not a realistic solution.
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has been curtailed since the United States-Israel war on Iran began, squeezing supplies of petroleum-based fuels and pushing up prices, particularly in Southeast Asia.
The ship was carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, and 156 crew members, Cambodian officials said. Some passengers said they received only seven hours notice to disembark and had to arrange their own accommodation.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from the US state of Wyoming who boarded the ship 17 months ago, said they had expected to live at sea for years. They said the company had already struggled with itinerary changes, unreliable internet and declining food quality.
“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” Lynn Montoya said, alleging mismanagement and unpaid crew members.
Other passengers said they hoped a new company or a resident-led effort could save the venture.
Carol Larson, 69, who bought her cabin for $120,000 in instalments, said she did not regret taking the risk despite the suspension.
“I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said.
The ship set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024 on a voyage originally planned to last three and a half years. Built in 1993, the ship was purchased by Villa Vie Residences in 2023 and offered cabins for long-term living with lifetime-vessel suites initially priced from about $230,000.
Cambodian officials said the ship was expected to refuel and leave on Saturday although the operator had not publicly confirmed a departure date.

IDF expands West Bank operations with counterterrorism raids as Hebron offensive continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:32:47 UTC
03:32:47 KST

The IDF is expanding its operations in the West Bank. Alongside an ongoing operation in the southern city of Hebron, the military has launched a targeted counterterrorism operation farther north, involving raids in eight villages and the city of Nablus.
The two operations are being conducted under separate divisional commands: the 98th Division in the Hebron area and the Judea and Samaria Division in the northern West Bank. According to IDF assessments, the northern operation is expected to be relatively short and focused, unlike the prolonged operation in Hebron, which has sparked disagreements between military commanders and the political leadership.
Over the past 72 hours, IDF troops have operated in the area under the Samaria Regional Brigade as part of the new operation. On Wednesday morning, they demolished the homes of Zakaria Muhammad Abd Daoud and Ibrahim Abd al-Karim Abd Daoud in the village of Beita. According to the IDF, the two carried out three explosive-device attacks in 2024 and 2025, two of which wounded members of the security forces.
Meanwhile, in the village of Yasid, soldiers from the Duvdevan undercover commando unit, acting on intelligence provided by the Shin Bet security agency, arrested a suspected terrorist accused of trafficking in explosive devices and weapons and transferring them to a terrorist cell. Undercover Border Police officers from the Judea and Samaria district arrested another wanted suspect in the village. He is suspected of manufacturing explosives and weapons, trafficking in arms and planning an attack.
As part of the operation, security forces also demolished 12 memorials commemorating terrorists, which the IDF said were associated with attacks and incitement to terrorism. The military noted that operations against incitement are conducted routinely under previously approved operational plans.
In addition, troops searched approximately 300 locations, arrested eight wanted suspects and located and confiscated weapons.
Hebron operation continues despite military concerns
While the operation in  the northern West Bank proceeds, IDF forces continue operating in Hebron, where troops from the 98th Division were deployed following Friday's deadly attack, which killed Staff Sergeant Ron Yonatan Roytman and Sergeant Yuval Shai Svilem. Three additional soldiers were lightly wounded. During searches in the city, troops located and confiscated weapons and equipment including an M16 rifle, knives and a military vest.
In addition, undercover Yamam Border Police officers operating in the Judea and Samaria district, guided by Shin Bet intelligence, conducted overnight raids in several villages within the Judea Regional Brigade's area of responsibility. They arrested six wanted suspects, including Hamas terrorist operatives, suspected of involvement in terrorist activity, including planning attacks and advancing terrorist operations.
The operation in Hebron has continued despite limited operational achievements so far. Thousands of Palestinians have left their homes during the military activity, and IDF officials also have raised legal concerns about keeping residents away from their homes for extended periods, particularly given the relatively limited quantity of weapons discovered to date.
A disagreement emerged between senior IDF commanders and the political leadership over whether the operation should continue. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir believed the military should consider ending the operation, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz demanded that it continue, citing, among other considerations, deterrence and the need to locate the weapons used by the attackers. The political leadership's position prevailed, and the operation is continuing.
The Central Command's primary objective remains preventing the spread of attacks carried out by lone terrorists and local terrorist cells, prompting extensive counterterrorism activity across the region.
Another operation, this time within the IDF
Alongside the two military operations in the West Bank, the IDF is preparing another initiative, this time within its own ranks: a nationwide effort to recover weapons and military equipment removed from the army and retained by active-duty soldiers and reservists.
Between November 1 and 12, the IDF's Technology and Logistics Directorate will conduct an equipment-return campaign, opening approximately 65 collection points at military bases across Israel. Under the initiative, soldiers and reservists will be able to return military equipment taken during their service without identifying themselves and without facing prosecution for unlawfully removing, possessing or carrying the items.
Items eligible for return include firearms, night-vision devices, communications equipment, uniforms, ceramic body armor, helmets, tactical vests, medical supplies and other military gear.
According to IDF officials, the initiative was developed partly in response to needs identified among troops. Many reservists still possess military equipment accumulated during periods of service and are being asked to return it to the army.
The campaign is intended to make returning the equipment straightforward, without criminal proceedings or identification requirements, while bringing weapons and other military property held outside the military system back under IDF control.
Thus, even as the IDF expands its counterterrorism operations in the West Bank, it is also addressing the issue of weapons and equipment that remain in soldiers' possession after their service, seeking to ensure that military property is returned to the army's control.

Robert Pattinson is on the hunt for predators in gripping new thriller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Robert Pattinson is on the hunt for predators in A24's gripping new thriller Primetime
Nothing whips pop-culture media into a reliable frenzy quite like panic over paedophilia, a phenomenon too often fuelled by sensationalism — the inexhaustible pursuit of clicks and ratings — rather than any desire for actual justice.
It's an argument that can certainly be applied to television's mid-aughts smash To Catch a Predator, a fraught but compelling synthesis of reality TV and police sting which lured online offenders into real-world traps, using youthful adult actors to play their underage victims.
The NBC show, which ran from 2004 to 2007, was a runaway success. Audiences hooted and hollered at what Jimmy Kimmel quipped had become "Punk'd for paedophiles", while host Chris Hansen was transformed into a national celebrity: America's square-jawed superhero dad taking out society's trash.
From A24's latest golden boy Lance Oppenheim (co-director, with Nathan Fielder, of their forthcoming Elizabeth Holmes documentary), the electrifying new thriller Primetime mainlines that cultural moment, plunging us into the behind-the-scenes drama of the hit show and the demons that drove its host's apparent lust for ratings.
We first see Hansen — played with slick, sadistic relish by Robert Pattinson — practising his lines ahead of the show. "You can see how this looks, right?", he repeats like a mantra, his reptilian lips curled around the famous gotcha catchphrase. Moments later he's descending the stairs of a rented home like Norma Desmond, ready for what turns out to be a very unflattering close up.
In Primetime's sweaty, hyper-saturated imagery, pores loom large on sickly-tinted skin, capillaries threaten to burst, and colours bleed to abstract excess. We could be in one of the late action director Tony Scott's gaudy, surrealistic thrillers — think Man On Fire, or Domino.
It's less a fever dream of 2006 than a dispatch from hell, sound-tracked to Fergie and shot by cinematographer David Bolen on a kaleidoscope of cameras, including vintage digital video and, at one point, a medical endoscope. The effect is period piece as half-remembered fantasy, media reconstituted for a generation nostalgic for the CRT TVs of their childhood.
The blown-out style captures the manic energy of the moment.
Buoyed by To Catch a Predator's rapid rise in popularity, the network moves the show into a primetime Wednesday night slot. Hansen soon becomes obsessed with bagging the ultimate paedophile, the 'whale' that will win him the ratings war against the show Lost.
"We need the spectacular," he tells his gun producer Andy (the always great Merritt Wever), as though he's picking the NBA draft for paedophiles. "The best of the best."
Hansen has plenty to prove. None of his NBC colleagues consider him a real journalist, and the network only seems to tolerate his show on account of its rabble-rousing popularity. Worse, he's being blackmailed by the National Enquirer, who have papped him an extra-marital tryst.
Meanwhile, the show's new recruit Dan (Skyler Gisondo), an aspiring young SoCal actor, wrestles with the challenge of playing a 'decoy' — the adults cast as the show's jailbait. "You have to find ways to protect yourself," advises fellow decoy Del (Phoebe Bridgers), who can shape-shift between teenage girl and skater boy like some kind of Orlando in cargo shorts.
It all comes to a head when the production lands their would-be ultimate ratings ticket: Texas assistant district attorney Bill Conradt (Bill and Ted's Alex Winter), whose suicide — and the subsequent fallout — would indirectly lead to the show's 2008 cancellation.
For all of its nerve-rattling, deliberately stylised intensity, it would be easy to dismiss Primetime as a little glib, even crass — a deeply troubling and complicated mass-media episode run through an A24 aesthetic filter. And by the time Pattinson is throwing Taxi Driver-style Travis Bickle shapes in a mirror, or buried in a tricked-out homage to 2001's stargate, it can feel like a film in thrall to its own excess.
The real-life Hansen, who had nothing to do with the production, has dismissed the film as a hit piece that paints him as a delusional narcissist while failing to focus on his crusade to save victims.
He's not wrong, but Primetime doesn't aspire to be an accurate portrayal of its subject.
In the movie's telling, Hansen and his travelling circus, as a Dallas news reporter once called them, are symbols of a culture's collective, and potentially dangerous, obsession — sensationalism disguised as moral mandate, and worse, an active obstruction to justice.
It's a film designed to provoke, to slip between fact and fiction, to derange its audience by immersing them in the media and the madness.
"We're cleansing the world of an ancient evil," Hansen declares at one point, a line that Pattinson practically squeezes from between his teeth, seething and savouring its mythic hyperbole. (Between this and The Drama, the man is having a very good year.)
The scene is ridiculous, even comical, and yet it cuts right to the core of a society hell-bent on protecting its innocent, even as it routinely sexualises them and sanctions their systemic abuse.
Whatever its shortcomings, Primetime reminds us what happens when that gets lost in the noise and bluster.
Primetime is in cinemas now.

Indigenous culinary school serving up talent to top restaurants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Indigenous culinary school serving up talent to top restaurants
Allan Miller remembers the tantalising smell of his grandmother cooking in the kitchen.
"Growing up, it was a lot of the women in the kitchen, but I was always around," he said.
"I always asked: 'Can I have a go?' And they never let me play around with the knives … they'd hold me, stir the food and I just loved it."
Mr Miller did not realise it at the time, but those special moments planted the seed for becoming a successful chef, taking out the Hunter Culinary Association first-year apprentice competition.
The proud Dhungutti and Wonnarua man is one of 11 First Nations graduates of the 2026 National Indigenous Culinary Institute's (NICI) commercial cookery apprenticeship, which carves out a pathway for talented cooks to become qualified chefs.
"It's kind of just like a cherry on top for me," he said.
"I've done all the work now … so it is a really good feeling just to have my hard work recognised by the people around me and by the organisation that helped me actually secure my job."
One of the highlights of his career so far has been creating a special menu using Indigenous ingredients.
"It's just putting a piece of me on the plate," he said.
"It's a good feeling, especially if [customers] enjoy it."
A cohort of restaurant critics and renowned chefs, including Neil Perry, Matt Moran, Luke Mangan, Guillaume Brahimi, Jill Dupliex and Terry Durack, established the program in 2012.
The institute's CEO Nathan Lovett said the group was on a mission to increase the number of Indigenous chefs in high-end restaurants.
"They developed a pathway program that could help develop skills, knowledge and understanding … so that people from our communities had an opportunity to get into employment working in the very best restaurants in the country," Mr Lovett said.
Since its inception, more than 100 Indigenous chefs have completed their apprenticeship — this year marks the biggest group of graduates yet.
"It is a huge testament to the apprentices who have stuck with it because for the 11 who got through, there's probably 20 or 30 who haven't," Mr Lovett said.
"Those qualified chefs go on to be more than just a chef in their restaurant.
"They're becoming leaders, becoming mentors for more apprentices coming behind them, which is a really significant part of our program now."
The class of 2026 and their guests were treated to a special long lunch designed by NICI alumni chef Kilijah Grentell with support from Aria's executive chef, Tom Gorringe.
Ms Grentell, who is now a demi-chef at Chiswick, designed the menu using native ingredients.
She says it brings her great pride seeing prestigious kitchens showcasing native ingredients on their menus.
"We have some great food and ingredients that I used when I was sometimes in the kitchen with mum," she said.
"Then seeing some of the stuff that I ate as a kid coming to a well-known restaurant … it's like full circle.
"We're trying to show that we do have food that is available, like native food, and we're trying to let that shine."
Alumni clinches GoodFood gong
Luke Bourke is also passionate about bringing Indigenous culture into world-class kitchens.
It is something he learned through NICI and has experimented with ingredients over the past decade, working in some of Australia's most illustrious kitchens.
Currently the head chef at Felon's Seafood on Manly Wharf, this week Mr Bourke became the second Indigenous chef to receive a Sydney Morning Herald Good Food hat.
"It was super exciting for me as a head chef of my first restaurant and for the Indigenous community," he said.
"To lead the way is something I'm passionate about and to show the next generation they can do it."
One of the most popular items on the menu is his wood-fired calamari with finger lime salsa.
"To put [calamari] with a native ingredient, people are blown away. It's been very well received and it's probably one of our signature dishes,"
he said.
"A lot of people come in and try it for the first time, but then they're bringing their friends and having it again."
The proud Palawa man started his journey through the National Indigenous Culinary Institute and went from the suburbs of western Sydney to the fine dining scenes of Rockpool Bar & Grill, owned by iconic Australian chef Neil Perry AM.
"Walking into a big marble bank, seeing a huge wood fire grill, all the chefs working so hard, it was definitely daunting to walk into, but then also so inspiring," he said.
Mr Bourke's inspiration and love for cooking also stem from his family.
"Nana used to work at a poultry farm, and on Dad's side — Grandma — she used to be into baking and competitions … so that sparked it from an early age," he said.
"Having an older sister, she's two years older than us, she jumped in the kitchen first, and me and my twin brother followed."
He credits part of his success to NICI and the support they provided him during challenging times.
"When you wake up and go to work, you don't see the sun, and then after work, it's quite a mental challenge as well not being able to go out and have a lifestyle," Mr Bourke explained.
"So having people there and also the 24-hour counselling that NICI provides, just to have someone to chat to … is definitely a great thing to have."
Allen Miller, who is filling in as sous-chef at Little Fish restaurant in Newcastle, wants to see more Indigenous chefs in the kitchen to support the next generation coming through.
"I feel like it's important to have that connection, especially in the kitchen [so] you know someone you can go to if times are getting tough," he said.
"My former sous-chef Adrian Rendall … I definitely look up to him. I had very hard times, and he was there to support me, and that's who I aspire to be like."
