I Put a Bunch of AI Agents in Charge of a Fantasy Soccer Team. They’re Not Better Than Humans—Yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

I have consulted my AI-powered crystal ball, and it’s telling me that frontier models are going to get a lot better at making predictions in the near future. Just ask my Premier League fantasy team.
A few weeks ago, I deployed a small horde of AI agents to craft and manage an experimental roster. Given the proliferation of AI agents into pretty much every aspect of our lives, I wanted to know if a swarm of bots could put together a winning team.
I first looked at the potential for AI here a few years ago, playing around with a tool from the UK’s Turing Institute that selected teams after modeling previous fantasy league data. Its suggestions were remarkably bonkers—it didn’t incorporate real-world information, like a player’s injury or a team’s change in management.
This time, while on a flight to visit family, I asked Codex for help. First, I fed the model a couple of relevant research papers. Then, I asked it to build a harness—instructions and code that guides different agents through various steps—that would check recent news and run a model to make predictions.
It quickly came up with a setup that seemed to collate and analyze way more information than I ever would have. And yet I was surprised by how dumb the initial team suggestions were. Leaving Erling Haaland on the bench? Really, Codex?
I then asked Codex to create a team of agents that did different things: several that read news and blog posts; others that analyzed recent results; more that ran models; and a bunch that critiqued suggestions. This seemed to significantly improve the suggestions. I tried increasing the number of agents to more than 100, hoping this would make the system smarter still, but it didn’t change much besides running up my API bill.
Still, the improvement from a few years ago was striking. According to Haifeng Xu, a computer scientist at the University of Chicago who studies the uses of AI in market situations, newer models may be even better at making predictions because they’re able to consume and analyze huge amounts of real-world information, and they’re able to orchestrate more complex systems for their guesses.
“AI is just getting smarter in understanding the world—I feel like that's the fundamental reason they’re improving,” Xu tells me.
Late last year, Xu was marveling at the growing popularity of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. He wondered how the best commercial models might fare on those markets, so alongside several colleagues, he began testing their forecasting skills.
They had models guess, for example, who would win the NBA Championship and who President Trump would meet with.
“Very quickly we started to realize that models did really well,” Xu tells me. The models were sometimes able to do better than the average person without any special instructions or guidance, he says. In their testing, GPT-5 was the best at making predictions, followed by Grok 4, Claude Sonnet, Gemini, and Llama.
The team went on to develop Prophet Arena, a benchmark that measures a model’s ability to make predictions. It’s one of a number of benchmarks designed to test AI’s future-gazing capabilities; another, Prediction Arena, from researchers at Harvard University and a company called Arcada Labs, recently gave frontier models $10,000 to wager on prediction markets over 57 days. The models consistently lost money in their experiment, but the researchers saw evidence of them improving consistently over time.
Xu tells me that AI can most effectively make predictions using a custom harness, and notes that having agents with unique tasks—reading the news, collecting other data, and analyzing the whole system, for instance—seems to be the most effective approach.
Interestingly, AI still often lags behind very skilled experts known as superforecasters. Xu explains that, although humans cannot consume as much information, their understanding of the real world—that is, of the dynamics behind a news story—is deeper.
That said, there’s growing evidence that the human superforecaster’s edge is eroding. A contest called the Metaculus Cup recently showed that AI can sometimes beat even the best human predictors. And a benchmark called ForecastBench could provide further evidence that AI can match human skills when the results of an ongoing contest conclude soon. In fact, I think we can expect the big labs to turn their attention to future-gazing as a powerful new way to measure progress in machine intelligence.
All of these predictive experiments seem to suggest that, like math, coding, and law, industries predicated on trading may soon be upended by AI. Perhaps the best human traders will take on a new kind of role: supervising and orchestrating AI agents capable of divining the future far better than they can.
For the time being, my AI’s suggestions still don’t seem all that impressive. Its team hasn’t outscored the average over the past weeks. I certainly won’t be using any of its suggestions in my own selections.
But AI will no doubt get better, perhaps making it all too easy to dominate fantasy league pretty soon. I’m kind of hoping it won’t, though, as it would spoil the fun of trying to earn bragging rights by winning all by yourself.
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Ukraine's west under attack: how Belarus is helping Russia to wage its war
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:30:00 EET
03:30:00 KST

Ukraine's west under attack: how Belarus is helping Russia to wage its war
Autumn 2026 has seen Russia step up its attacks on Ukraine's west. In August it was rare for jet-powered drones to reach the west, but by October the attacks had become massive and were happening several times a day. On 18-19 October, the Ukrainian Air Force downed 36 Geran-2 and Geran-4 jet-powered drones in five western oblasts: Rivne, Khmelnytskyi, Ternopil, Volyn and Lviv.
The Russians receive a vital boost from signal repeaters located in Belarus, which has effectively become a corridor for Russian drones heading for Ukraine's west, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. These relay stations amplify the signal for UAVs while they are en route.
Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for the State Border Guard Service, told Ukrainska Pravda that boosting signals isn't the only way the regime of self-proclaimed Belarusian president Alexander Lukashenko is helping Russia. Russian drones quite often fly into Belarusian territory too.
"They can enter from Chernihiv Oblast, travel through Belarusian territory, then reenter Ukraine within the boundaries of Kyiv and Zhytomyr Oblasts," Demchenko explained.
But even greater danger is looming, as Russia is keen to deploy ballistic missile systems on Belarusian territory as well. If missiles are launched from there, the whole of Ukraine's west will be under threat, as ballistic missiles could reach Lviv or Ivano-Frankivsk, for example, within minutes.
Will Lukashenko dare to openly join the war by permitting the launch of ballistics from Belarusian territory? And is it realistic to jam the signals of the relay systems that are helping Russian drones? Ukrainska Pravda took a closer look.
Belarusian signal repeaters: not a new story
This isn't the first time Ukraine has documented the use of signal repeaters in Belarus. In June 2026, Zelenskyy said that four relay stations in Belarus' Homiel (Gomel) and Brest oblasts were adjusting Shahed drone strikes on Ukrainians.
Zelenskyy issued an ultimatum to Lukashenko, giving him a week to turn the relay systems off or Ukraine would do it itself. Following these threats, Belarus switched off the signal boosters. It's just a few minutes away from
In September, after a three-month pause, the signal boosters started working again. Demchenko explained that it isn't worth looking for any hidden motives behind the relay systems' reactivation – quite simply, Belarus is incapable of standing up to pressure from Russia.
For Russia, the signal repeaters are an essential component in their attacks, as its forces have been unable to freely use Starlink satellite communication terminals on strike assets since the beginning of 2026. Ukraine had appealed to SpaceX because Russian drones had begun using Starlink terminals for guidance during attacks, and the US company set about disconnecting unverified terminals.
Russia is working on developing its own network, Rassvet, which could become an alternative to American satellite systems, but for now it is too soon to talk about full-scale deployment. The system is still being tested, so the relay stations have been vital to Russia in the execution of its attacks.
How do signal repeaters work?
Aviation expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi explained to UP that relays operate on a fairly simple principle. The base is an ordinary mobile telecommunications mast, which looks no different from civilian infrastructure from the outside. It is fitted with digital equipment for transmitting and receiving radio signals, as well as high-gain antennas directed towards Ukrainian airspace.
The structure is connected to a stationary power supply and also works on fibre optics. As a result, communication is established between strike groups of drones and ground control stations. The signal can cover territory to a depth of up to 140 km.
Khrapchynskyi explained that the network functions in such a way that a drone in the air is not the end user – it relays the signal to other drones. The mast on the border transmits a signal 100-140 km to the first drone, which can then transmit the signal for a further 50-70 km to another drone.
"Once a multi-hop aerial chain is set up, a strike group can advance 200 km deep into Ukrainian territory – up to 300 km if conditions are favourable," he said.
If the volumes of data being transmitted are small, a single ground-based relay system is capable of serving and maintaining up to 50 drones in the network simultaneously. But if a target needs to be confirmed, or manual guidance is required, the situation is quite different. In that mode, one base station can serve 1-3 drones at a time at most.
"This technical factor explains the shift in Russian tactics that we've been observing recently: the enemy is increasingly splitting massive raids into small, compact waves," Khrapchynskyi said.
Relay stations work the same way for both classic drones and high-speed jet-powered types. Khrapchynskyi notes that cheap drones often cover the main strike echelon with their radio field.
Where are they and how much do they cost?
The Russians position relay stations as close as possible to the border with Ukraine to ensure the signal remains stable. There must be no serious obstacles in the line of sight between the antenna and the receiver. The closer the station is to Ukrainian territory, the less of an impact terrain and woods will have on signal quality.
Photographs taken on 9 April at the opening of a new Belarusian border outpost in the village of Hdzień give proof of the stations' location. Khrapchynskyi spotted a mast with a large amount of antenna equipment in the images posted. The outpost is just 1.8 km away from the Ukrainian border – about 100 km away from the centre of Kyiv as the crow flies.
In addition to Hdzień, there are relay stations in at least four other Belarusian settlements in Homiel Oblast, according to the eRadar monitoring Telegram channel:
- Chojniki – a town approximately 45 km from the border
- Machnavičy – a village about 35-40 km from the border
- Dzierbinka – a village about 8-10 km from the border
- Buda-Safijeŭka – a village less than 5 km from the border
Given the sensitivity of the topic, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine declined to provide UP with information on the actual number of relays located in Belarus, so this data has not been officially confirmed.
Khrapchynskyi estimates that it costs up to US$20,000 on average to equip one base mast. To establish a signal along the main flight routes, Russia needs to deploy about 18-22 stations of that type.
"From a financial point of view, this is a dirt-cheap solution for Russia and Belarus," he said. "There's no need for expensive military tech here – the system is built on commercial dual-use solutions, mostly Chinese-made."
Can Ukraine counter this?
If Ukraine were to physically destroy masts on Belarusian territory, it could be falling right into Moscow's trap. A direct strike would provide the Kremlin with the perfect excuse to finally drag the Belarusian army into open combat operations.
Khrapchynskyi believes the best way of dealing with the problem may be to attempt to jam the connection between the Belarusian masts and Russian drones using electronic warfare.
Ballistic missiles: not a new story 2.0
At the start of the full-scale invasion, Russia stationed between 24 and 36 launchers in Belarus. According to Belaruski Hajun, an independent Belarusian military monitoring media outlet, in 2022 at least 721 missiles were fired on Ukraine from Belarusian territory, using Iskander systems, older Tochka-U tactical missile systems, and S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft systems.
Back then, Kyiv and Zhytomyr oblasts, as well as Ukraine's north-western regions, came under heavy attacks from the direction of Belarus. Ukraine's problem was its complete lack of Patriot or SAMP/T air defence systems, meaning that any Iskander launch meant an almost guaranteed strike. In 2026 Russia's objective is somewhat different: to stretch Ukraine's scarce air defence systems, for which there is a shortage of interceptor missiles, Khrapchynskyi noted.
A Russian Iskander-M battalion comprising four self-propelled launchers is still permanently stationed in Belarus. There are also Soviet-era ballistic systems – 36 Tochka-U launchers armed with modified missiles.
And Belarus plans to scale up its missile infrastructure even further: journalists from Skhemy (Schemes), a Radio Liberty project, have documented preparations for such plans. As early as September 2025, satellite imagery showed that three permanent specialised hangars had been built at the 465th Missile Brigade's base in Asipovichy (Osipovichi), Belarus.
"Each of these hangars is designed to house a full battalion set of 12-13 special vehicles: four launchers, four transporter-loader vehicles, and command and support equipment. In total, this site can routinely accommodate a full-fledged missile brigade – up to 12 launchers and nearly 40 pieces of support equipment," Khrapchynskyi said.
What missiles could be launched?
If Russia carries out its plans, various types of weaponry will be deployed from Belarusian territory, depending on specific combat missions. For strikes on critical infrastructure and logistics hubs in Ukraine's west, Khrapchynskyi believes the Russians may use the upgraded Iskander-1000 missile, which has a range of up to 550 km. They also have North Korean KN-23 missiles in service, which have a range of over 600 km.
"The Russians don't even need to move these ground launchers right up to our border and expose them to strikes," Khrapchynskyi said. "They can just operate from deep within Belarusian territory, targeting Lviv or Volyn oblasts with a flight time of two to three minutes."
If state-of-the-art missiles with ranges of 500-600 km are launched from Belarus' Brest and Homiel oblasts, it won't be just the closest targets like Lutsk and Rivne that will be under threat, but also Lviv, Ternopil, Ivano-Frankivsk and Khmelnytskyi – essentially the entire western rear right up to the foothills of the Carpathians, Khrapchynskyi said.
The missiles' flight time to these oblasts, if launched, would be extremely short:
- Lutsk and Rivne – up to 1½-2 minutes
- Lviv, Ternopil or Ivano-Frankivsk – up to 2½-3½ minutes
"For civilians, the air-raid siren will sound at almost the same time as the explosions or a few dozen seconds before impact, which completely eliminates the usual time buffer that the western regions have had when attacked by cruise missiles or Shahed drones," said Khrapchynskyi.
Is it realistic to expect help from our partners?
Ukraine's air defence system would be under extreme pressure in such a scenario, Khrapchynskyi explained. Assistance from allies (when available) in terms of intelligence sharing is already instantaneous – a satellite detects the thermal plume of a missile's engine within seconds of its launch and reports it immediately – so we can't expect this process to become any faster.
The only partner assistance that would be truly effective is the deployment of additional missile defence systems on Ukrainian territory.
Clearly the US Aegis Ashore missile defence base which opened in November 2024 in Redzikowo, Poland, would be a lifeline for Ukraine. However, it is part of NATO's missile defence system and therefore depends on the Alliance's political decisions, Khrapchynskyi stressed.
What should we expect from Lukashenko?
For now, the scenario of ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine from Belarusian territory is still a potential rather than an inevitable development. It all depends on whether Lukashenko bows to Russian pressure and drags Belarus into an open war.
Igar Tyshkevich, an expert on Belarus and Russia, suggested in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda that Lukashenko may comply with the Kremlin's demands if his negotiating track with the US and Poland fails. In September, the self-styled Belarusian president met with US President Donald Trump's special envoy, John Coale. They agreed on the release of 25 Belarusian political prisoners in exchange for the lifting of US sanctions against two Belarusian companies. Meanwhile, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski recently said he believes it is possible to "unfreeze" Poland's relations with Belarus.
There are currently no signs of any deadlock in efforts to mend relations with the West, so it would not at all be in Lukashenko's interests to launch missiles from his territory.
"He really loves power – his own power," Tyshkevich said. "There is only one condition on which this formula could be broken: if he suddenly decides that being the president of an independent (or at least relatively independent) country is less advantageous than being a governor in Russia. Or if there's a coup d'état in Belarus that brings overt Moscow appointees to power – in that case the probability would increase significantly."
Still, some Belarusians are not so sure about the firmness of Lukashenko's position. For instance, Belarusian journalist Kseniya Halubovich told Ukrainska Pravda that it might not be so easy for the self-proclaimed president to say no to Putin.
"If Russia decides to use Belarusian territory for a provocation or to launch ballistic missiles, Minsk's ability to say no to Moscow will be very limited," said Halubovich.
The track record of Belarus's cooperation with – or rather dependence on – Russia shows that this is indeed the case. The Belarusian defence industry has worked in Russia's interests throughout the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Between February 2022 and August 2025, Russia received at least US$1.2 billion worth of weaponry from the Lukashenko regime, the Belarusian Investigative Center has noted.
Belarusians risk becoming hostages to Putin's pressure on Lukashenko. If the self-styled president allows ballistic missiles to be launched from Belarusian territory, the geography of the war could expand to include another country. In that case, Belarusians would very likely be facing retaliatory strikes, just as Russia is right now.
Tetiana Kryvishyn, Natalia Bodnar, Ukrainska Pravda

Pathways to power: What happens next after Israel's election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28

Breadcrumb
Pathways to power: What happens next after Israel's election?
Almost 24 hours after the polls closed, it has become clear that Israel's high-stakes election has ended in a stalemate.
Neither of the two opposing blocs has enough seats to form a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, with Netanyahu's far-right coalition leading with 53 seats to the opposition bloc's 48.
The final tally won't be known until Friday, when the hundreds of thousands of "double envelope" votes are counted, and the official result won't be published until next week.
But with almost 90% of the votes now in, the two blocs' options are becoming clearer. Though Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot have both staked a claim to victory, they will both face an uphill struggle if they are to form the country's 38th government.
Here are three potential paths ahead following yesterday's inconclusive vote.
Netanyahu remains in power
Despite seeing his bloc shrink compared to the 2022 election, Netanyahu's Likud is poised to remain the largest party in the Knesset and his bloc closer to a majority than the opposition.
With 86% of the vote now in, the Likud-far-right-Haredi alliance is eight seats short of a majority, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc requires another 13.
That doesn't necessarily mean Netanyahu has the upper hand.
His options for coalition-building are as narrow as Eisenkot's, and hinge on being able to break his rival's alliance and bring some of the opposition to the other side of the aisle.
Addressing supporters, Netanyahu claimed his coalition had won a "decisive majority" and called for the formation of a "national right-wing government" - a statement that was interpreted in some quarters as an overture to the right-wing members of Eisenkot's coalition.
Avigdor Lieberman's ultranationalist Yisrael Beiteinu and the pro-settler Naftali Bennett align with Netanyahu on key issues, including ensuring Jewish supremacy at home, annexing much of the occupied West Bank, and maintaining a permanent war footing abroad.
But defection is likely to remain a distant prospect. Both have staked out staunchly anti-Netanyahu positions on the campaign trail and have ruled out entering any form of government with him.
They are also firmly opposed to ultra-Orthodox Jews' exemption from military service, which would likely continue under a new Netanyahu government. This is particularly true for the aggressively secular Lieberman, who is dead against working with Haredi parties Shas and United Torah Judaism.
There has also been speculation about whether Netanyahu could try to form a unity government with Eisenkot in a last-ditch bid to remain in power.
President Isaac Herzog - who will soon decide which of the leaders stands the best chance of forming a government - has voiced support for a unity government, though both leaders have until now flatly rejected the idea.
To get Eisenkot on board, Netanyahu could ditch his far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies, though this is unlikely to be enough to convince the Yashar leader to serve in government led by a man he has so sharply criticised.
Since the polls closed, Eisenkot has not tempered his language about the incumbent prime minister, accusing him of "division and incitement" and maintaining a "culture of lies".
Netanyahu ousted by an Arab-backed government
Eisenkot's coalition is currently on course to win 48 seats in the Knesset, five fewer than Netanyahu and 13 shy of an overall majority.
This means that his path to government runs directly through the Arab parties, which are poised to win a record number of seats and hold the balance of power.
Between them, the conservative Ra'am and the leftist/nationalist Joint List are projected to win 19 seats, meaning Eisenkot will not be able to form an administration without their support.
Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas has indicated he would be willing to enter government with the former general, in a repeat of his agreement with Naftali Bennett in 2021.
The problem for Eisenkot is that the math is not likely to add up, even after bringing Ra'am inside the tent. With the Islamist party on course to get seven seats in the Knesset, an alliance would still leave him six seats short of a majority.
That leaves the possibility of cooperating with the Joint List, which has offered to support a minority government led by Eisenkot, should it agree to several conditions, including committing to establishing a Palestinian state.
The group's leader, Yousef Jabareen, appealed to the opposition to start talks, saying it is offering a clear path to ousting Netanyahu and the far-right from power.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," he told Israeli media on Wednesday.
He articulated the choice facing Eisenkot and his partners in stark terms: "It is either continued racism, continued exclusion and continued supremacy, or genuine Jewish-Arab partnership."
Ahmad Tibi, who leads Ta'al, one of the three parties in the Joint List, said the key question coming out of the election is whether the opposition will be "brave enough" to break the taboo of working with Arab parties in order to block Netanyahu's return.
While both Palestinian-led groups clearly want to work with the Jewish-Israeli opposition, it is far less clear whether the feeling is mutual. For most of them, it is likely to be quite the opposite.
Aside from Yair Golan's centrist Democrats, the instincts of most of the opposition will be to refuse working with Arab parties and avoid reckoning with the new Palestinian agency expressed at the ballot box. Even if Eisenkot were to accept the Joint List's support, getting his hawkish partners on board would be a big ask.
Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh – who was banned from running in the election – said that racism among Jewish-Israeli leaders would block Arab parties from helping to unseat the current far-right government.
“When someone who is a candidate to be a prime minister says he does not want to sit with 20% of the population … this is racism," he told The New Arab.
Another election
If both sides fail to form a government, Israelis would be forced to return to the polls for another election.
The second vote would need to be held within 90 days of the Knesset being dissolved, keeping Netanyahu and his cabinet in power in a caretaker capacity.
A new election, coming after potentially weeks of coalition talks, would push the country into a protracted period of uncertainty, with no guarantees that a new vote would resolve the deadlock.
It would recall the years of instability between 2019 and 2022, when four separate elections were held. The gridlock was brought to an end four years ago when Netanyahu entered government with the extreme-right.
President Herzog on Wednesday appealed to political leaders to do everything they can to avoid a rerun of the election and urged them to "keep an open mind" in coalition discussions.
Netanyahu may calculate that a fresh election is his best option, especially with US president Donald Trump threatening to resume the war on Iran following the 3 November midterms.
Matthew Hoare is a journalist at The New Arab

Zagreb is celebrating the 800th anniversary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:28:48 CET
03:28:48 KST

To commemorate the eighth centenary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi, the Italian Embassy in Croatia organized the conference “The Relevance of St. Francis: From Coexistence to Communion and Fraternity’ in Zagreb, in collaboration with the Croatian Catholic University, which hosted the event, and with the Apostolic Nunciature. The conference was followed by a concert by the Ensemble Micrologus-Giullari di Dio, organized by the Italian Cultural Institute, which offered a musical journey dedicated to the Canticle of the Creatures and the ancient melodies of the Italian lauda tradition. The conference proceedings were opened by the Italian Ambassador to Croatia, Paolo Trichilo; by Monsignor Marco Malizia, Ecclesiastical Advisor to the Vice President of the Council of Ministers and Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, the Honorable Antonio Tajani, by the Apostolic Nuncio, Monsignor Leopoldo Girelli, and by the Rector of the Catholic University of Croatia, Prof. Željko Tanjić. Prof. Fra Lorenzo Turchi of the Pontifical Antonianum University in Rome served as the keynote speaker, engaging in a discussion with two Croatian professors from the universities of Split and Zagreb—both members of the Franciscan Order— on the Christian experience of St. Francis and how it can offer criteria for discernment in understanding certain dynamics of the present. The event drew a large audience and was attended by several civil and religious authorities, including Cardinal Emeritus of Zagreb Josip Bozanić, Ivan Mašina, Advisor to the Croatian Minister of Foreign Affairs; and, representing the Ministry of Culture, Šime Jerčić, Director General of the Office of the Commission for Relations with Religious Communities. In his opening remarks, Ambassador Trichilo highlighted the attention given to St. Francis by Italian institutions and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as evidenced by the establishment of the national holiday on October 4 and the organization of dedicated events by the diplomatic corps. St. Francis, the Ambassador emphasized, is a pivotal historical figure for Italian, European, and universal spirituality and culture. His message continues to be a source of inspiration that prompts us to reflect on the future and offers spiritual and ethical guidance for navigating the modern world. He then highlighted how the initiative takes on particular significance in Croatia, given the country’s Catholic tradition. Bishop Malizia conveyed greetings from Minister Tajani, expressing the minister’s satisfaction that the diplomatic network had accepted the invitation to promote initiatives on St. Francis and to focus on a spiritual and human witness capable of speaking to peoples, cultures, and traditions, and to contribute to the promotion of dialogue, peace, and fraternity. He also noted that Italy considers intercultural and interreligious dialogue an essential component of its international vision, emphasizing the important role played by cultural institutions, religious communities, and diplomacy—all united by the responsibility to safeguard peace through mutual understanding, respect, and cooperation. Bishop Malizia then expressed his appreciation for the conference, which represents not only a tribute to St. Francis but also a concrete opportunity to rediscover what unites us and to promote a culture of listening, solidarity, and peace.

Leader to students: Arm yourselves with knowledge and faith to build Islamic-Iranian Civilization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:27:32 UTC

Leader to students: Arm yourselves with knowledge and faith to build Islamic-Iranian Civilization
TEHRAN — Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei has called on university students to equip themselves with knowledge, faith and self-purification to contribute to the strength of Iran and the march toward an Islamic-Iranian Civilization.
In a reply issued on Oct. 28, 2026, to letters from a group of university students, the Leader thanked them for their kindness and said their letters reflect a resolute determination and sense of responsibility for building the future.
The full text of the reply is as follows:
In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful
Salam to my dear children,

Google announced its latest artificial intelligence (AI) model, Gemini 4 Carbon, on Wednesday, claiming significant gains in coding, autonomous agent tasks and cybersecurity defense.  
Unveiled just two weeks after the launch of its Gemini 4 Argon model, the company described Carbon in a blog post as its strongest frontier model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.
Google attributed the rapid release timeline to its researchers and AI models "working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster."  
The company claimed that Gemini 4 Carbon ranks first on the updated version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 59.

Addressing safety and alignment, Google claimed that internal testing showed Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately half compared to Argon, stating methodological caveats directly rather than fabricating missing evidence.
The company also claimed the model retrieves relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to users when facing ambiguity, while reducing task overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% during multi-step workflows.
Google said Gemini 4 Carbon will first become available to cybersecurity defenders this week before rolling out more broadly to developers, businesses and consumers.
The company plans to offer introductory pricing of $2 per 1 million input tokens and $10 per 1 million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted by 95%, before standard pricing rises to $4 per 1 million input tokens and $20 per 1 million output tokens.

TMoCA exhibition to explore how ‘Iran’ is presented and conceptualized in artworks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:22:55 UTC
03:22:55 KST

TMoCA exhibition to explore how ‘Iran’ is presented and conceptualized in artworks
TEHRAN – The exhibition “In Search of Iran: In the Collection of the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art” will open on Saturday afternoon at the museum.
It explores how “Iran” is presented and conceptualized through the lens of various artists among the works kept in the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art (TMoCA), Mehr reported.
The exhibition addresses the national significance of the TMoCA collection within the history of contemporary Iranian art by examining the diverse ways artists experience and interpret “Iran.”
The exhibition statement reads: “We do not ask which work is ‘more Iranian’; rather, we ask how Iran has been the subject of seeing and representation, and how it persists within the modes of seeing and creating. The inquiry into Iranian identity in this exhibition begins with the distinct experiences of artists—experiences that are sometimes explicitly the subject of the work, and sometimes manifest in the style of expression and construction. Belonging to Iran can be accompanied by the memory of a place, daily life, migration, or a sense of loss, taking on different forms in the works of each artist”.
“The exhibition ‘In Search of Iran’ invites the viewer to re-examine their own conception of Iran when encountering these works. In these pieces, soil sometimes becomes the very material of the work, writing turns into a way of seeing, and objects preserve the traces of life and human memory. The presence of familiar symbols does not predetermine the meaning of the work, nor does their absence necessarily signify a disconnection from the Iranian experience”.
“The seven sections of the exhibition, each guided by a specific question, offer parallel paths for the viewer to interpret the works. These paths do not follow a chronological sequence of art history; instead, the visual and conceptual connections between the pieces allow for a confrontation with diverse interpretations. In this view, no single landscape, face, or motif serves as the sole representative of the Iranian experience."
The exhibition will feature over one hundred works from the Iranian Modern Art collection, including pieces by artists such as Sohrab Sepehri, Parviz Tanavoli, Parviz Kalantari, Hossein Zenderoudi, Farah Osouli, Reza Mafi, Mohammad Ehsaei, Bahman Mohassess, and others. It will be open to the public from Sunday, through mid-December.
Established in 1977, the museum has more than 4,000 items that include 19th- and 20th-century world-class Iranian, European, and American paintings, prints, drawings, and sculptures. Being the biggest collection of Western art in the Eastern world, it includes works from almost all artistic periods and movements.
The museum was designed by Iranian architect Kamran Diba, who employed elements from traditional Persian architecture. The building itself can be regarded as an example of contemporary art, in the style of an underground Guggenheim Museum.
Most of the museum area is located underground, with a circular walkway that spirals downwards, with galleries branching outwards. Western sculptures by artists such as Ernst, Giacometti, Magritte, and Moore can be found in the museum's gardens.

UN experts 'appalled' by violence against student protesters, mass arrests in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:22:28 UTC
03:22:28 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
UN experts on Wednesday condemned violence against student protesters and mass arrests across France, describing serious injuries among minors and the detention of thousands of demonstrators as "unacceptable."
"We are appalled by the level of violence suffered by pupils and students demonstrating across France to demand what is long overdue: a functioning education system, decent material conditions for education, appropriate school and university timetables and territorial and social equality in access to quality education, in particular," the experts said in a statement.
The protests began among high school students in mid-September before spreading to universities, with demonstrators demanding better educational conditions, adequate resources and equal access to quality education.
Despite government efforts to engage with students in October, the experts said authorities prioritized security measures over addressing the protesters' underlying grievances.
"The serious and, in some cases, irreversible injuries sustained by underage demonstrators during law enforcement operations are unacceptable and unjustifiable," they said.
The experts also expressed concern over the arrests and detention of several thousand people, predominantly minors, describing the scale of the detentions as disproportionate and potentially discouraging peaceful protests.
They also condemned acts of violence that injured police officers and damaged buildings and businesses, calling for investigations and accountability.
"We regret that police officers have been injured, and that numerous buildings have been damaged and shops vandalised," they said.
"We condemn these acts of violence. Measures are needed to investigate them and bring perpetrators to justice."
The experts urged French authorities to review policing practices "in order to enable demonstrators to express their concerns and to facilitate a peaceful resolution of social conflicts."
They said they remained in contact with French authorities over the situation.

Hoorakhsh Studios to produce “Shahnameh” animated series
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:22:10 UTC
03:22:10 KST

Hoorakhsh Studios to produce “Shahnameh” animated series
TEHRAN – Production of the animated series “Shahnameh,” directed and produced by Ashkan Rahgozar, has commenced at Hoorakhsh Studios, utilizing artificial intelligence and 2D animation techniques.
Following his feature-length animated film “The Last Fiction” and the writing and production of seven graphic novels based on the stories of the “Shahnameh,” Ashkan Rahgozar has once again turned to this epic work by Ferdowsi, ILNA reported.
Aiming to adapt all the stories of Ferdowsi’s “Shahnameh” from beginning to end, the series is scheduled to be produced and broadcast simultaneously over a span of approximately ten years.
The animated series “Shahnameh” will be produced in both Persian and English, with international streaming platforms in mind.
Each season will consist of 8 to 12 episodes, with each episode estimated to run between 15 and 20 minutes.
The first season of the series, titled “The First King,” narrates the reign of Keyumars, a legendary figure from Iranian mythical history, appearing in both the Avesta and the “Shahnameh”.
“Shahnameh” is Hoorakhsh Studio’s first major, independent animated series. The studio’s portfolio includes two feature-length animated films, over 11 short animations, more than 10 music videos, the publication of 11 graphic novels, and the design and development of five video games.
The “Shahnameh” (Book of Kings) is a long epic poem written by the Persian poet Ferdowsi between c. 977 and 1010 CE and is the national epic of Greater Iran. Consisting of some 50,000 distichs or couplets (two-line verses), the “Shahnameh” is one of the world's longest epic poems, and the longest epic poem created by a single author.
It tells of the mainly mythical but, to some extent, historical past of Iran from the creation of the world until the Muslim conquest in the seventh century. Iran, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Tajikistan, and the greater region influenced by Persian culture such as Armenia, Dagestan, Georgia, Turkey, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan celebrate this national epic. It took Ferdowsi 33 years to complete the Shahnameh in its entirety.
The work is of central importance in Persian culture and the Persian language. It is regarded as a literary masterpiece and is the definitive work of the ethno-national cultural identity of Iran.
Ferdowsi (940 – 1025) is celebrated as one of the most influential figures of Persian literature and one of the greatest in the history of literature.

‘Narration of Resistance’ Caravan highlights Sistan-Baluchestan’s cultural riches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

03:21:19 KST

‘Narration of Resistance’ Caravan highlights Sistan-Baluchestan’s cultural riches
TEHRAN – A group of Iranian cultural, religious, media and sports personalities has traveled to Sistan-Baluchestan province as part of a program titled “Narration of the Resistance of the Brave,” aimed at showcasing the region’s cultural diversity, social solidarity and local capabilities.
The caravan, which arrived in the southeastern province on October 25, has organized a series of cultural, Quranic, media and sports activities across several cities, bringing its participants into contact with local residents, community figures, businesses and institutions.
According to reports by Persian media, the program seeks to present a broader picture of life in Sistan-Baluchestan, highlighting its cultural traditions, religious life, scientific and medical facilities, economic activities and the coexistence of its diverse communities.
Among the prominent figures accompanying the caravan are Hojjatoleslam Alireza Panahian, cultural activist Hossein Yekta, writer Vahid Yaminpour, television presenter Raheleh Aminian, travel documentarian Javad Gharai, television host Iman Qiasi, religious program presenter Najmeddin Shariati, singer Hamed Homayoun and several former Iranian footballers.
The initiative combines public gatherings and face-to-face encounters with television production and visits to local institutions, using familiar public figures to draw attention to a province whose cultural and social realities are often less visible in national media coverage.
Quranic gatherings emphasize religious and social ties
Quranic programs have formed a major part of the caravan’s activities, with gatherings involving nationally recognized reciters in Zahedan and Iranshahr.
These events brought residents together around Quran recitation and religious programming, highlighting the role of shared religious traditions in strengthening social connections across the province.
The caravan also included members of the television program “Mahfel,” a Quran-focused show that features reciters and participants from Iran and other countries. The team met with border guards at the country’s frontier.
The visit offered an opportunity to highlight the work of border personnel and their role in protecting Iran’s borders, while bringing media figures into direct contact with those serving in remote areas.
Hossein Yekta also visited Imam Hussein Mosque in Zahedan, where he met residents, including members of the local Sunni community. During the visit, he recalled the late Molavi Rigi, describing him as a figure associated with service to the people and the Quran.
The encounters reflect one of the main themes of the caravan’s program: presenting religious identity and community engagement as common elements connecting residents across different backgrounds.
Visits showcase medical and scientific capabilities
Beyond religious and cultural activities, the caravan has sought to introduce visitors to the province’s medical and scientific infrastructure.
Television presenter Peyman Talebi and Yekta visited Al-Zahra Ophthalmology Hospital in Zahedan, drawing attention to the specialized medical services available in the provincial capital. Media personality Raheleh Aminian also highlighted the province’s medical capabilities in her coverage of the visit.
The program extended to the region’s scientific and technological sector, with Yekta visiting Zahedan Science and Technology Park. The visit focused on the work of researchers, young innovators and technology-oriented businesses, presenting another dimension of the province beyond its geographical location and traditional economic activities.
Such visits are intended to bring greater visibility to local institutions and professionals and to encourage a more comprehensive understanding of the province’s development potential.
Markets and local traditions take center stage
The caravan’s activities have also included visits to Zahedan’s commercial districts, where participants met shopkeepers and residents and observed everyday economic and social life.
These visits provided opportunities to introduce local trades, culinary traditions and the social character of the city’s marketplaces.
Together, the market visits and cultural encounters offered a window into the everyday lives of residents, placing local customs, food, occupations and social interactions alongside the province’s religious and institutional activities.
Television and sports bring programs closer to local audiences
A major feature of the initiative has been the production and presentation of television programs from locations across the province.
Among the activities was the “El Clasico” football program in the Karimabad neighborhood of Zahedan, featuring national television presenters.
The neighborhood event brought sports-related entertainment into a local setting, allowing residents to interact directly with television personalities.
The children’s program “Mal Mal” was also scheduled in Zabol and Zahak, while “Samte Khoda,” a religious television program presented by Shariati, featured Panahian in a public gathering in Zabol.
A football match between a team of former Iranian football stars and a selection representing Sistan-Baluchestan was also announced as part of the program.
The participation of former players, including Nikbakht Vahedi, Mohsen Mosalman, Mohammad Ansari, Mohsen Bengar, Mohsen Khalili, Mehdi Amirabadi, Adel Kolahkaj and Ali Shiri, added a sporting dimension to the caravan’s activities.
A broader portrait of southeastern Iran
Sistan-Baluchestan occupies a strategically important position in southeastern Iran, bordering Pakistan and Afghanistan. Its geographical location, diverse landscapes and distinctive cultural traditions give it significance in Iran’s social, economic and regional life.
The province is home to communities with varied cultural and religious traditions, including both Sunni and Shiite Muslims. Its Balochi heritage, traditional clothing, handicrafts, cuisine and local customs form an important part of Iran’s broader cultural landscape.
At the same time, the province faces development challenges, making the visibility of its educational, medical, scientific and economic institutions an important part of discussions about its future. Visits to hospitals, technology centers, markets and community spaces can help introduce these dimensions to audiences beyond the region.
The “Narration of the Resistance of the Brave” caravan brings these themes together through a mix of public engagement and media production. Rather than concentrating on a single event or institution, its activities span religious gatherings, neighborhood programs, cultural encounters, scientific visits and sporting events.
The initiative’s organizers have emphasized resistance, solidarity and the province’s capabilities as central themes. Its coverage of everyday life and local traditions also places the experiences of residents at the heart of the program.
As the caravan continues its activities across Sistan-Baluchestan, the combination of familiar media figures and local encounters is intended to draw wider attention to the province’s people, cultural identity and institutional capacities, presenting a multifaceted view of one of Iran’s most distinctive regions.

The unit told Militarnyi about the mission.
Integrating AI is intended to reduce the workload on operators and minimize the impact of human factors during missions.
With the new system, the vehicle completed 93% of a 20-kilometer route fully autonomously. The operator took control only for a 1.4-kilometer section.

Before the mission, a specialized system travels along the route and scans the terrain using lidar. The collected laser pulses are used to create a 3D model of the terrain.
As the vehicle moves, its cameras recognize the road, road edges and obstacles in real time. The AI makes its own maneuvering decisions, while the operator can adjust the route and set speeds for individual sections.
Using artificial intelligence reduces UGVs’ dependence on a continuous communications link, including Starlink.
Andrii “Matematyк” Kopach, commander of the Lava Regiment’s UGV battalion, said the system changes the operator’s role from driver to dispatcher. The operator intervenes only when necessary, with the ultimate goal of allowing one operator to supervise several vehicles.
Apex AI is developing the software for the project. Specialists from the Lava Regiment helped define the technical requirements and conduct field tests of the platform.
The next stage in the technology’s development will be its use in evacuation missions. Widespread deployment of such systems would allow personnel to carry out more missions.
Militarnyi previously reported that Khartiia engineers had converted a U.S. M113 armored personnel carrier into an uncrewed platform for mine clearance and logistics.
That vehicle is also equipped with video cameras that transmit live footage to the operator’s screen to monitor its movement.

UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Wednesday called sanctions imposed on UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese “not acceptable.”
“You can agree or disagree with someone, but you should never ever sanction them,” said Turk in response to a question from Anadolu at a news conference in New York.

Pakistan’s Artificial Intelligence Warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:19:00 UTC
03:19:00 KST

For the first time in its volatile history, Pakistan topped the Global Terrorism Index this year, recording 1,045 terror incidents and 1,139 related deaths in 2025. The fatalities have risen further in 2026, with the third quarter of the ongoing year showing an 83 percent hike in terrorism-linked deaths as compared to the second quarter.
This surge comes amid external security woes. Last year, Pakistan and India came the closest that they have to a full-fledged war since the turn of the century, and reportedly to the brink of nuclear war. Pakistan is also engaged in persistent cross-border clashes with Afghanistan. Meanwhile, the ongoing Iran-U.S. war is reconfiguring militancy in Balochistan, after Islamabad and Tehran exchanged drone and missile strikes on each other’s territories in 2024.
Faced with these multipronged challenges, Pakistan has gradually incorporated artificial intelligence (AI) into its security strategy.
Last year, Pakistan unveiled its National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2025 to regulate AI usage. Pakistan’s military forces have already deployed AI to enhance their capabilities through research units, such as the Army Center of Emerging Technologies and the Pakistan Air Force-run Center for Artificial Intelligence and Computing (CENTAIC).
Pakistan has also unveiled a gamut of AI-enabled military weapons, including equipment manufactured by the state-owned Global Industrial & Defense Solutions (GIDS). These include unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs), such as Shahpar-II, and the Spider Anti-UAV system. Pakistan and India used numerous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in the 2025 clashes, with Islamabad deploying YIHA-III drones manufactured by the Turkish defense contractor Baykar in addition to Shahpar-II.
Drones are being extensively used along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border according to Pakistan Army sources. “We are facing the double threat – from the Afghan Taliban, and local terrorist groups – and we are countering these by using drones for surveilling and also for striking targets, especially in remote areas,” an official working with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s newly formed Police UAV Division told The Diplomat.
Military sources reveal that Pakistan is also close to deploying robots. “Law enforcement authorities already have robots in bomb disposal units. Robots are also performing reconnaissance tasks, including in border areas. Now we are working on using robots to lead clearance operations, along with transporting ammunition and supplies in military operations in [Khyber] Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan,” said a senior officer.
The security agencies have already run drills with Chinese robotic wolves. There are plans to produce similar machines indigenously, as well as humanoid and bipedal robots.
“To keep pace with India, and to nullify terrorist groups, we are always integrating new technologies in military and law enforcement agencies. However, the biggest challenge is developing our capacity due to the lack of resources and the economic challenges,” Lieutenant General Talat Masood, a former secretary of Pakistan’s Ministry of Defense Production, told The Diplomat. In this regard, Pakistan continues to benefit from Chinese architectural support for CENTAIC. Beijing is also helping Islamabad use facial recognition technology, as Pakistani security agencies gradually expand its deployment to sensitive areas, including border checkpoints and terror hotspots.
Along with fortifying security capacities, however, the Pakistani state is also using these AI-powered technologies to maintain the military establishment’s stranglehold and quell any regional or political dissent. The Diplomat has learned that the military’s media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), is allocating resources for “narrative building.” In addition to producing various forms of media, the ISPR also employs tech professionals to engage in countering what the establishment deems to be “anti-state propaganda,” a misnomer for critiques of the armed forces, the country’s military leadership, and their policies.
“A good chunk of money is going into algorithmic filtering and monitoring, and tools are being used to erase social media anonymity and target individuals accordingly. Many professionals in the IT sector and the media industry are working on these projects,” revealed a senior digital media professional working at one of Pakistan’s largest media houses.
The investment to “counter anti-state propaganda” has significantly increased following the ouster of former premier Imran Khan in 2022. The ensuing anti-army sentiment has meant that Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, and its activists, have especially been under the gun. However, the same digital tools are being wielded to suppress dissidents in Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Pakistan-administered Kashmir.
Similarly, Pakistani citizens are vulnerable to Islamist persecution, with digital blasphemy laws still providing allowance for the use of modern technology to fatally impose antediluvian punishments. This is in stark contrast with the image of moderation and reform that the Pakistani governments wants to show in front of the global audiences, especially as part of its recent role as the mediator between the U.S. and Iran.
A lack of transparency allows the state and the military establishment to deploy technology and AI beyond the realms of the already loosely defined “national security.” The National Security Policy 2022-2026 “has no mention of Artificial Intelligence,” said security analyst Abdullah Khan, the managing director of the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. “How can we deliberate over its pros and cons, when there is no official declaration of how these technologies are being used?”
Lieutenant General Talat Masood, the former Ministry of Defense Production secretary, said that transparency can only be ensured, and any overreach into the domain into fundamental rights can only be nullified, by having credible checks on the abuse of power. “The command needs to be held by a representative civilian government, which would require a revamp of the state’s power structure, so that the military and civilian can keep charge of their respective domains,” he said.
Those who defend the state’s position argue that compromising on certain freedoms is part and parcel of counterterror policymaking, especially when the situation is as grave as the one Pakistan faces today. But critics maintain that any compromises need to be justified with successful outcomes of technology and AI incorporation. So far, that hasn’t happened.
“All terror trends have increased over the past five years. There are hardly any counterterror successes for us to gauge,” said Khan of the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. “[The state] is currently in the responsive mode, whereas militants are in the offensive mode” when it comes to using technology.
“We need to change that, and enhance our own capacities beyond intelligence gathering and monitoring. When it comes to actual incorporation of technology in counterterror operations, we are still at the infancy stage,” he added.
As technology impacts the state’s role as a guarantor of its citizens’ security and freedom, it is evident that Pakistan is struggling on both fronts. And it is likely to stay that way, as long as the omnipotent military establishment continues to arbitrarily impose its whims.

Russian President Vladimir Putin "wanted very much" for U.S. First Lady Melania Trump to mediate the ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, Marc Beckman, her exclusive senior adviser, told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 28.
"President Putin wanted very much for her to participate and also wrote a formal letter explaining that she… would be recognized as the exclusive intermediary from Russia," Beckman said.
Beckman said the Russian military proposed moving the ceasefire forward by two days and expanding its geographic scope beyond Oleshky into other parts of Kherson Oblast to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and evacuation preparations. Ukraine agreed to the proposal.
He described the changes as a sign of good faith, saying both sides had cooperated in implementing the agreement so far. "Their actions will speak for themselves ultimately, but what we've seen so far is tremendous cooperation from both sides," he said, adding that both parties had upheld the ceasefire's terms to date.
But concerns have been raised about Russia's true motives in agreeing to the ceasefire, as well as its agreement to allowing Trump to mediate it.
"They know exactly what they are doing," John Foreman, CBE, a former UK defense attache in both Kyiv and Moscow, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Allowing Melania to take the credit bolsters their credentials to the MAGA base as peacemakers before the midterms," he added.
Oleshky, which had a pre-war population of around 24,000, has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
The ceasefire — announced by the White House on Oct. 23 as being mediated by Trump and soon confirmed by Ukraine and Russia — is in its second day as of Oct. 28, and is expected to last into early November, as aid is brought in, key roads are demined, and residents are evacuated.
read also
The Trump-mediated ceasefire comes after international attention to the plight of civilians trapped under Russian occupation.
Earlier this month Pope Leo called Putin and requested a ceasefire. Putin responded by blaming Ukraine for the situation.
Beckman said that as well as the Vatican, "both sides were unable to bring in the United Nations, and… the Red Cross" as mediators.
Ukraine has also warned that Russia could exploit the evacuation for propaganda purposes.
Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 25. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has warned that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos.
"Key Russian media figures are already starting to spread the narrative that Russia is 'rescuing' the residents that it has been terrorizing," Peter Pomerantsev, executive editor of The Reckoning Project, wrote in an op-ed for the Kyiv Independent.
On the Ukrainian side, Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary commissioner for human rights, is expected to arrive in Oleshky within the next 36 hours and lead the effort on the ground, Beckman said.
Beckman said Russian and Ukrainian representatives met in person in Belarus to sign the ceasefire agreement.
Representatives from both Russia and Ukraine had independently asked him to keep certain details of the ceasefire agreement confidential, citing the sensitivity of the information. He declined to disclose those details, saying both sides had emphasized the need for discretion.

Analysis-Israel’s election gives survivor Netanyahu a path to keep power
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:17:26 CET
03:17:26 KST

By Samia Nakhoul
DUBAI, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pulled ahead on Wednesday as votes were counted in Israel’s election, but the loss of a parliamentary majority leaves his path to another term dependent on drawing rivals into a coalition.
With the turnout in Tuesday’s election at a record high and nearly 86% of votes tallied, Israel’s three main broadcasters put Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties on course to win 53 seats in parliament, with the opposition bloc of rival Gadi Eisenkot trailing on 48.
Both remained short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, or parliament, while parties representing Arab Israelis were projected to win 19 seats.
“Maybe it’s hard to say it or to see it, but he’s the winner,” said former Netanyahu adviser Aviv Bushinsky, describing the prime minister’s comeback as a political “resurrection.”
The paradox, Bushinsky said, is that an election that denied Netanyahu a majority in parliament may have restored his political primacy.
Despite the fallout from the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel and criticism of the security failures on his watch that the attacks exposed, Netanyahu won the support of an unexpectedly clear majority of Israeli Jews and has emerged at the head of the largest bloc.
Netanyahu’s achievement was less to win than to survive, said Danny Citrinowicz, a regional analyst and former Israeli military intelligence officer.
Netanyahu’s bloc lost seats and fell short of the 61 needed to govern alone, but Eisenkot’s camp also lacked a viable route to power without the support of Arab parties.
“He won by not losing,” Citrinowicz said. “He managed to survive,” added Citrinowicz.
ARAB ISRAELIS MAKE GAINS
Netanyahu will stay on as caretaker prime minister while Israel’s president decides whom to ask to form a government. Despite not having a parliamentary majority, he retains the power of incumbency and a path to form a coalition government.
The election’s biggest disruption came from Israel’s Arab electorate, whose unprecedentedly high turnout handed Arab parties potentially decisive influence over what comes next.
Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by citizenship, Arab Israelis — who make up 21% of the population — could now hold the balance of power between the rival blocs.
“The Arabs have never been in a position where they held this much power,” said Dennis Ross, a former US Middle East peace negotiator.
Netanyahu’s opponents face a difficult route to removing him. Assembling a government would likely require direct or indirect support from Arab parties, a prospect that could prove difficult for potential right-wing partners such as Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman.
That leaves two broad paths — a broader unity government led by Netanyahu or another election, Israeli political analysts say.
Bushinsky sees a unity government as the most realistic option, particularly if US President Donald Trump presses Netanyahu to bring rivals into government and sideline far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
The United States is Israel’s most important ally, and Trump could use his public backing for Netanyahu as leverage to push for a broader coalition, Bushinsky said.
Failing that, Israel could remain politically deadlocked and return to the polls, a move which several political analysts said could further strengthen Netanyahu rather than change the outcome of the election.
The stalemate, Citrinowicz said, leaves Netanyahu better placed than Eisenkot to be prime minister. With another election unappealing to most parties, he said he saw a Netanyahu-led unity government — potentially bringing in Eisenkot or Bennett — as the most plausible way out.
IRAN LOOMS OVER THE FIGHT FOR POWER
Since the October 7 attacks, Israel has fought wars against Hamas in Gaza and against Hezbollah in Lebanon, and launched joint attacks with the US on Iran.
In a post-election speech to cheering supporters, Netanyahu called for a “strong right-wing national government” and cast Israel’s military gains as a historic opportunity to eliminate the Iranian threat.
“Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all. But ulterior motives must not divert us from this sacred mission,” he said.
Trump, who had urged Israelis to keep Netanyahu in power so the two leaders could “finish the job” in Iran, said the prime minister had done “very well” and credited his own endorsement with helping him.
“It might be winning or tie. The tie is sort of considered a win in that case because it’s a big chess match,” Trump said.
A more consequential question may be whether Netanyahu, fighting to remain in office, again turns to Israel’s security challenges, above all Iran, to reshape the political equation.
A renewed confrontation with Tehran could strengthen his calls for national unity, though any escalation would depend heavily on Washington.
Eisenkot, 66, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, sought to claim that mandate by framing the election as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership.
In a message to Israel’s security chiefs and public servants, Eisenkot said Netanyahu now headed a transitional government that had lost public confidence. “Stand strong and firm against any attempt to challenge you,” he said.
Netanyahu entered the election burdened by a long-running corruption trial, resistance to an independent inquiry into the Hamas attack, escalating settler violence in the occupied West Bank and a bitter battle over military service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews.
(Writing by Samia Nakhoul; Editing by Alex Richardson and Timothy Heritage)

In Ukraine’s Kherson, brief ceasefire brings rare respite
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:16:45 CET
03:16:45 KST

By Yurii Kovalenko
KHERSON, Ukraine, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Years of near-daily Russian drone and artillery attacks have turned the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson into a battered urban landscape where death is never far away.
On Wednesday, however, the residents who remain ventured cautiously into sun-drenched streets after a US-brokered ceasefire around the nearby frontline town of Oleshky put a temporary pause to the aerial threat.
“Honestly, I can’t put it into words,” kiosk owner Oleksandra Kosenko told Reuters during a visit on Wednesday. “If it stays this way, it would be really wonderful.”
Ukraine said on Wednesday that the six-day ceasefire, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, was holding, providing a rare moment of relief in the fifth year of grinding war.
The pause in fighting is aimed at paving the way for humanitarian relief for Oleshky, where residents face acute shortages of food and medicine.
CRITICAL RESPITE
For Kherson, a regional capital across the Dnipro River from Oleshky, the ceasefire - which took effect early on Tuesday - brings a brief window of respite.
Since Ukrainian troops recaptured the city from Russian occupation in November 2022, Moscow’s forces stationed on the opposite bank have shelled it regularly and hunted residents with deadly drones, officials say. Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
As the attacks continued, residents fled and businesses closed, making daily life increasingly dangerous.
The city still functions, with buses ferrying people around and shops and cafes serving customers. But the scars of the war are plain to see. Some buildings are in ruins, the pavements are largely empty and anti-drone nets are draped over the main roads.
On Wednesday, residents walked their dogs without glancing toward the sky. Elderly men sipped coffee on a bench without the din of distant explosions.
“Kherson, which was constantly under fire, literally came to life,” said Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, on the Telegram messaging app.
“People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire.”
Kosenko, the kiosk owner, said she had seen a near-doubling in the number of clients: around 50 in total. She was relieved to no longer be dashing for cover on the way to work.
ATMOSPHERE OF TENSION
On Tuesday, top Ukrainian officials described the ceasefire as a major de-escalation that could build confidence for future agreements.
Yet beneath the relief, Kosenko and others expressed wariness that fighting could erupt again at any moment. Many residents approached by Reuters declined to speak, appearing tense.
Anti-personnel mines dropped by the Russians still pose a danger even when hostilities are paused.
Battles are also raging elsewhere along the 1,200-km (750 mile) front line, where Russia remains intent on capturing the parts of the eastern Donetsk region still outside its control.
Moscow is also continuing its bombing campaign of Ukrainian cities, which has damaged critical infrastructure including in Kherson.
Locals like Olha Chyupikova, who lived through Russia’s occupation of her city, said they had learned to prepare for the worst.
“The Russians have proven that they can’t be trusted,” said the 52-year-old municipal worker.
“So I think everyone subconsciously feels like there could be some sort of provocation at any moment.”
(Writing by Dan PeleschukEditing by Ros Russell)

WINDHOEK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Namibian and Chinese universities plan to expand vocational training in Namibia through Zheng He College, which is expected to begin enrolling students and offering classes in 2027, a university official said Wednesday.
Zheng He College is a vocational education cooperation platform jointly developed by China's Nantong Vocational University and Namibia's Welwitchia University.
The college, housed in a standalone building in Namibia's capital city of Windhoek, will initially offer programs in mechanical manufacturing and automation, and construction engineering technology in the first quarter of 2027, said Amon Haufiku, director of technical and vocational education and training (TVET) at Welwitchia University.
The formal cooperation framework was established on Nov. 27, 2025, when Welwitchia University, Nantong Vocational University and Nami Prefabricated Housing, a local company, signed a tripartite cooperation agreement to promote technical and vocational education and practical training.
Haufiku said the planned programs at Zheng He College would broaden access to technical training in Namibia.
"This will allow Namibian students to access similar technical training locally, while benefiting from the expertise and experience of our Chinese partners," he said.
"As the partnership develops, we also envision student exchanges that will enable students to study in both Namibia and China, deepening cultural understanding, academic cooperation, and practical skills development."
The initiative follows commitments made during Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah's state visit to China in July, during which the two countries reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in education, technical skills training and technology.
During the visit, the two countries also signed a memorandum of understanding on TVET cooperation to promote exchanges and collaboration between their vocational education institutions. ■

Ukraine Auctions Russian Propagandist’s Kyiv Apartment for $190,000 to Fund Reconstruction
Ukraine has auctioned a confiscated apartment belonging to Russian propagandist and designer Artemy Lebedev in central Kyiv for more than $190,000, with the proceeds designated for the country’s reconstruction.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s State Property Fund on October 28, the property was sold through an online auction for 8.01 million hryvnias (approximately $190,000), exceeding its starting price of 7.07 million hryvnias (approximately $168,000).
The 193.2-square-meter (2,080-square-foot) apartment is located on Saksahanskoho Street in Kyiv’s historic center. It occupies two levels of the top floor of a six-story building and includes three rooms, office spaces, a kitchen, two bathrooms, three balconies, and utility areas.
Two bidders participated in the auction, raising the final price by 936,150 hryvnias (approximately $22,000). The property was transferred to Ukrainian state ownership following a ruling by the High Anti-Corruption Court as part of sanctions imposed against Lebedev.
Under the auction terms, the winning bidder must complete payment within 25 working days after the auction protocol is issued and settle outstanding utility bills before the purchase agreement can be finalized.
The State Property Fund confirmed that proceeds from the sale of sanctioned Russian assets are directed to Ukraine’s Fund for the Liquidation of the Consequences of Armed Aggression, which finances reconstruction efforts.
Lebedev, a Russian designer and blogger known for his pro-Kremlin positions, has faced legal action in Ukraine over his activities during Russia’s full-scale invasion.
In June 2022, he illegally entered the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, where he filmed a report for Kremlin-aligned media about Russia’s seizure of the facility. Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) subsequently notified him of suspicion of justifying Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine.

Russia Loses More Troops in a Month in Ukraine Than USSR Lost in 10 Years in Afghanistan, Stubb Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:15:11 UTC
03:15:11 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Loses More Troops in a Month in Ukraine Than USSR Lost in 10 Years in Afghanistan, Stubb Says
Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated that Russia’s offensive in eastern Ukraine would take years to achieve its objectives at the current pace, addressing the UN Security Council on September 23.
Stubb argued that drone warfare has effectively frozen much of the frontline.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking on behalf of the five Nordic countries, Stubb stated that Russian forces had captured roughly 900 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this year, while Ukraine had retaken around 800 square kilometers.
“So the line of contact is basically not moving,” Stubb stated.
At that pace, he warned, Russia would need years to seize the rest of Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Stubb also stated that roughly 25,000 soldiers are being killed each month as both sides fight across a frontline that has shifted only marginally.
He compared the monthly losses with the Soviet war in Afghanistan, noting that the USSR lost roughly 18,000 troops over the entire decade-long conflict.
“This, in my mind, is a waste of life,” Stubb stated. “So the continuation of this war is a lose-lose.”
The Finnish president attributed much of the battlefield stalemate to drones, unmanned systems, and near-constant surveillance.
“We haven’t seen anything like this previously,” Stubb noted.
He described stretches of the frontline as roughly 20-kilometer-wide “death zones,” where exposed troops and vehicles face an extremely high likelihood of being detected and attacked.
“We’re seeing unmanned vehicles, we’re seeing death zones of roughly 20 kilometers to which you cannot enter, because with a 95 percent certainty, you’re going to be wiped out,” Stubb stated.
He argued that this environment helps explain why neither side has been able to achieve a decisive breakthrough despite heavy losses.
Stubb also accused Russia of systematically targeting Ukrainian civilians, civilian infrastructure, and humanitarian operations in an attempt to intimidate the population and weaken resistance.
“The aim is to instill fear and wear down Ukraine,” he stated.
The Finnish president called for an unconditional ceasefire, or at minimum limited arrangements covering areas such as energy infrastructure and grain exports, before negotiations on security, territory, justice, and a permanent settlement.
“There has to become a time when the killing stops,” Stubb stated.
Hours after the UN Security Council meeting, Stubb and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a new defense agreement focused on drones, technology transfers, expertise, and joint industrial projects.
“This is not simply a contract or an agreement on the sale and purchase of drones,” Zelenskyy stated. “This is about security—our shared security and joint production.”
Finland has increasingly framed its defense relationship with Ukraine as a two-way exchange, with Helsinki seeking to draw on Ukrainian battlefield experience as it develops its own military capabilities.
“That is exactly why we began saying that this is not a one-way street where we simply provide something to you,” Stubb stated. “On the contrary, it is a two-way process in which we learn from you.”
“By learning from Ukraine’s experience, we are strengthening our own capabilities,” he added.
Zelenskyy previously reported that Ukraine carried out three major offensive operations in 2026, including Operation Vivaldi in the Donetsk region and Operation VELES near Kupiansk, where Ukrainian troops traveled more than 15 kilometers underground before emerging behind Russian positions.

Caretaker role could limit Netanyahu but not rule out Iran war
