“Canberra was very cold, and I’m not just talking about the weather,” former ambassador to Australia Amir Maimon said on Wednesday as he sat alongside Australian Ambassador to Israel Neil Hawkins.
Maimon was speaking at the President’s Residence at a farewell reception hosted by President Isaac Herzog in honor of Jeremy Leibler, the outgoing president of the Zionist Federation of Australia, who is stepping down after eight years at the helm.
Among those present were Jewish Agency chairman Doron Almog; Moriah Ben-David, director of the Israel office of the ZFA; representatives of Australian Zionist organizations who earlier in the week had attended meetings of the Jewish Agency’s Board of Governors; Paul Israel, the executive director of the Israel Australia Chamber of Commerce; and a large three-generation contingent of the Israeli and Australian branches of the Leibler clan.
Jeremy Leibler’s father, Mark Leibler, who headed the ZFA for 10 years and who in 2024 was awarded the President’s Medal of Honor, Israel’s highest civilian award, was among the many Leiblers who attended.
In reference to the wave of antisemitism that overtook Australia after October 7, Maiman said that Jeremy Leibler had been a source of wisdom. “It was a most challenging period for the Jewish community of Australia and the State of Israel,” Maimon recalled.
Lauding Leibler's courage
Reactions to statements from Jerusalem were also troubling, he acknowledged. Implying that the Australian government was far from friendly, Maimon credited Jeremy Leibler with successfully negotiating with the authorities to ensure that Herzog would receive a warm welcome on his state visit to Australia in February of this year. “As a result, it was a very successful visit.”
Almog, in lauding Leibler’s courage, said, “I saw you. I heard you when you said: ‘We’re not going anywhere. We’re here to stay.’”
Almog and other speakers also referred to Leibler’s love for the Jewish people and the State of Israel. Most speakers characterized Leibler as a proud Australian Jew standing tall with courage and urged him to continue to inspire.
Michal Herzog, the president’s wife, who had accompanied him on his state visit, recalled her own first visit to Australia 40 years ago, in November 1986, when she joined her in-laws for her father-in-law, then-president Chaim Herzog’s historic state visit to the island continent. It was the first visit so far south by a president of Israel.
“We feel very close to the Australian Jewish community, and we feel especially close in times of crisis,” she said.
Herzog enthused over the “immense leadership qualities” which he attributed to Jeremy Leibler. “You say what you mean,” he said. “You were very clear about bringing me to Australia. It was very impressive... You are truly an asset to the Jewish people. We know Leiblers from all sides, an incredible family.”
Israel's security and the solidarity of the Jewish people
Herzog added that people such as Jeremy Leibler are needed in the president’s Voice of the People initiative.
In response, Leibler said that he had truly begun to realize how much Israel’s security and existence rely on the solidarity of the Jewish people. He also emphasized the importance of learning how to communicate with the people with whom you disagree.
In one of his final appearances as president of the ZFA, Leibler will be among the speakers at The Jerusalem Post Conference in Sydney on November 19, as will his father. Michal Herzog will also be among the speakers, albeit via video.
The incoming president of the ZFA is David Gold, a former global chairman of the World Union of Jewish Students, and currently the president of the Mount Scopus College Foundation.
Herzog met Gold in January 2023, at a gala reunion of Mount Scopus students, teachers and old collegians living in Israel. Herzog’s father visited Mount Scopus College in 1986.

Antisemitism in Czech Republic surges over 400% since 2020, European human rights report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:24:45 UTC
02:24:45 KST

A new human rights monitoring report published has formally confirmed a massive, unprecedented surge in antisemitism across Czechia following the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war in October 2023.
The evaluation was conducted by the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance, an independent human rights monitoring body of the Council of Europe specializing in questions relating to racism, intolerance, and discrimination across the continent’s member states.
The report covers the findings of its seventh monitoring cycle for Czechia, drawing on a country visit conducted in November 2025 and documentary analysis up to March 2026. The Council of Europe is an international human rights organization comprising 46 member states, while its anti-racism commission evaluates the situation in each country approximately every five years to issue policy proposals and recommendations.
According to the report, hatred targeting Jewish individuals and Ukrainians represents a stark shift from the commission’s previous monitoring cycle in 2019, when neither group experienced such elevated degrees of hate.
While hostile rhetoric against Muslims has dropped below previously recorded levels, general xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment persist in public discourse, though the Vietnamese community in Czechia remains largely untouched by such public hostility.
Citing data compiled by the Federation of Jewish Communities in the Czech Republic, the report notes that antisemitic incidents climbed sharply from 874 cases in 2020 and 1,128 in 2021 to 2,277 in 2022.
That figure surged to 4,328 in 2023 and reached 4,694 in 2024. The report highlights the significant escalation of incidents after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks.
The vast majority of these incidents involved online hate speech, frequently holding the local Jewish community collectively responsible for actions of the Israeli government. Additionally, cases of Holocaust denial and distortion rose by 47% in 2024 as compared to the previous year.
Antisemitic assaults, attacks on Jewish property rise sharply in Czech Republic
Physical violence remained relatively rare, with two antisemitic attacks recorded between 2020 and 2023. However, four cases of physical assault against individuals perceived to be Jewish were documented in 2024 within the context of the Middle East conflict, alongside 12 recorded cases of attacks and desecration targeting Jewish property.
Targeted incidents directed against specific persons, properties, or institutions jumped from 24 total in 2022 to 32 in the brief period following October 7 through the end of 2023, culminating in 118 targeted incidents during 2024.
The commission highlighted a severe new dimension of hate crime involving an attempted arson attack on a synagogue in the city of Brno in January 2024, where an explosive device failed to detonate.
Subsequent international investigations led to the arrests of five individuals aged 13 to 18 who had been radicalized online and promoted jihadist terrorism. Two of the suspects were charged with inciting hatred and attempting a terrorist attack targeting Jewish people and property.
Czech Republic adopts new strategy to combat antisemitism, protect minority rights
The report also outlined broader human rights challenges evaluated within the country, including ongoing issues of de facto segregation and bullying affecting Roma children in schools, systemic obstacles faced by Roma in housing and healthcare, and persistent hate speech targeting LGBT+ individuals and Ukrainian refugees.
To address these issues, the commission’s report called on Czech authorities to implement targeted anti-bullying strategies in schools, ensure adequate numbers of Roma teaching assistants and healthcare mediators, improve school guidance methodologies, eliminate discrimination in the private housing market, and broaden the strategic state security approach to hate crimes to include dedicated victim support.
The report noted positive steps taken by the government since the previous evaluation, including the creation of the Office of the Government Commissioner for Roma Minority Affairs in 2022 and the adoption of the Strategy for Combating Antisemitism in the Czech Republic for 2025-2030 by government resolution in October 2025.
Developed to align with European Union guidelines, the strategy establishes objectives to ensure Jewish community safety, combat antisemitic hatred, and enhance Holocaust education while formally incorporating the working definition of antisemitism established by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), which the Czech Parliament adopted in January 2019.

Israel's election produced only one result - so why is everyone claiming victory? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:24:21 UTC
02:24:21 KST

The Israeli public went out on Tuesday and voted en masse. But its message was garbled, so garbled that both sides, and the various parties within them, found a way to claim victory.
How? Sometimes by changing the yardstick. Each party claimed to have won among those who, by its own political reckoning, count.
For Benjamin Netanyahu, that meant those who support Israel as a Jewish state. For Naftali Bennett and Gadi Eisenkot, the emphasis was on those who serve and support conscription. Yair Golan widened the circle, counting the Arab parties alongside the Jewish opposition parties to declare that the Israeli democratic majority had prevailed.
The electorate had delivered one result. The leaders supplied different definitions of victory.
All this emerged as the party leaders confronted results that gave them reasons both to celebrate and to worry. With neither bloc commanding a clear parliamentary majority, each found a constituency within which the outcome could be presented as a victory of sorts.
What does victory look like for Netanyahu?
For Netanyahu, it was a victory among those who support Israel as a Jewish state, a definition that encompasses his haredi and far-right partners.
“Likud is the biggest party in Israel,” he told supporters in his election-night speech. “The right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public, among the Jewish public and all those who support the Jewish state. That is what has become clear. A decisive majority.”
The denominator matters. By this reckoning, the Jewish parties in the change bloc count, as do all his own partners, including Shas and United Torah Judaism. The Arab parties fall outside the circle.
Whatever the final parliamentary arithmetic, Netanyahu was claiming a majority among the public he considered the relevant measure of victory.
The haredi parties belong in that calculation. They resist conscription, but support Israel’s Jewish character. Their votes count toward the majority Netanyahu was claiming.
Bennett measured the result differently.
“The alliance of those who serve defeated the alliance of draft evaders,” he declared.
Here was a different explanation of who had won and who had lost. Netanyahu’s emphasis was on support for the Jewish state. Bennett’s was on sharing the burden of defending it.
The haredi parties could fit comfortably inside Netanyahu’s definition while standing on the losing side of Bennett’s. Their resistance to conscription was precisely what made them the target of his victory claim.
Bennett went on to pledge a “Zionist government of the alliance of those who serve.” But before describing the government he wanted, he had already supplied his reading of the election: the public carrying the burden had prevailed over the political forces perpetuating its unequal distribution.
Eisenkot offered a closely related interpretation.
He said Netanyahu faced a larger, stronger Zionist majority and pledged to establish a Zionist government committed to conscription.
Eisenkot calls for universal military service
Like Bennett, Eisenkot presented the result as a victory for the public demanding that the burden of military service be shared. The haredi parties counted toward Netanyahu’s claimed mandate. In Bennett and Eisenkot’s reckoning, they stood on the losing side.
Liberman’s speech fit the pattern less neatly. He did not offer the same clear declaration of victory among a particular public. Instead, he appealed to a political tradition he argued Netanyahu had betrayed.
“Those loyal to the path of Trumpeldor, Jabotinsky and Herzl,” he said, should “raise the banner of revolt within Likud.”
His reference point was the Zionist national camp. Likud voters and members still belonged to it; Netanyahu, in Liberman’s telling, had led it astray. His appeal was to people whose political loyalties he wanted to separate from their loyalty to the prime minister.
Golan took the broadest view of the electorate.
In his election-night speech, he invoked “the Israeli, democratic majority.” By Wednesday morning, he had made the arithmetic behind that description explicit, counting the Arab parties alongside the Jewish opposition parties.
Arab votes, he argued, carry the same weight as Jewish votes. If the parties opposing the outgoing coalition together held a majority, then that was the majority against which the result, and victory, should be measured.
Here was the clearest contrast with Netanyahu. Netanyahu claimed victory among those who support Israel as a Jewish state, leaving the Arab parties outside his calculation. Golan included them and reached the opposite conclusion.
He also challenged the framing of his prospective partners. Where Bennett and Eisenkot emphasized service and Zionism, Golan emphasized equal citizenship. Arab voters did not need to pass an additional test for their votes to count toward the majority he said had demanded a change of government.
Israelis voted in the same election. Their leaders emerged claiming victory among different electorates. Now the question is how, and whether, those differing definitions of victory can produce a government.

Court orders house arrest for security coordinator charged with shooting Palestinian woman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:24:11 UTC
02:24:11 KST

The Jerusalem District Court has ordered house arrest for a West Bank settlement security coordinator charged with shooting at a Palestinian couple’s car and seriously wounding the woman, rejecting prosecutors’ request to keep him behind bars pending trial.
Pinchas (Hasi) Ran, 37, the security coordinator for the area near Itamar, was ordered to be transferred to house arrest in the Golan Heights. Judge Elad Persky cited his lack of a criminal record and military service and found that prosecutors had not identified a concrete risk that he would interfere with the proceedings after the indictment.
Ran faces charges of causing serious injury with aggravated intent and obstruction of justice in an indictment filed on Friday.
Ran allegedly stopped passersby and checked their ID cards without legal authority
According to the indictment, Ran entered the Palestinian village of Akraba near Nablus on September 18 - outside his assigned area - while traveling in a Ranger off-road vehicle with an armed career soldier. Prosecutors allege that military officials had previously warned him, following several unusual incidents, to remain within his jurisdiction and comply with procedures, particularly the rules governing the use of firearms.
Inside the village, Ran allegedly stopped passersby and checked their identity cards without legal authority. He then called on the driver of a Mazda carrying a married couple to stop.
The indictment says the driver accelerated because he feared violence after observing that the men were not soldiers and that one of them was masked. After the car passed the Ranger, prosecutors allege, Ran fired at least three shots at the departing vehicle, intending to hit it and its occupants.
Two bullets struck the car and the woman, identified in the indictment as Aseel Bani Jaber. One entered her upper back and lodged in her lung near her heart; another struck near her buttock. She underwent surgery to remove the bullets and remained hospitalized for several days.
Prosecutors further allege that Ran returned to the scene and searched for cartridge cases to obstruct a possible judicial proceeding. Later, when security officials asked him about a shooting in the area, he allegedly denied having heard about it or having been present.
Ran disputes prosecutors' account of events
Ran disputes that account. According to Honenu, the legal aid organization representing him, a vehicle without license plates drove toward him and his companion in what they perceived as an attempted ramming. The organization says the two jumped aside and that Ran then fired into the air to make the vehicle stop.
The defense submitted letters from commanders describing Ran’s reserve service and conduct during combat. One former battalion commander explicitly stated that he was not addressing the allegations, whose details he did not know, but offering his assessment of Ran’s character. The letters also described his return to service after his brother was killed on October 7, 2023.
Ran’s lawyer, Nati Rom, welcomed the house-arrest decision and urged prosecutors to reconsider the case.
A preliminary hearing is scheduled for November 12.

France launches probe into calls to kill Muslims on X

Breadcrumb
France launches probe into calls to kill Muslims on X
French prosecutors have opened a criminal investigation into death threats against Muslims and racist hate speech broadcast during a live discussion on social media platform X, according to French media reports on Tuesday.
The investigation follows an X Spaces discussion in which participants allegedly called for violence against Muslims and immigrants, prompting La France Insoumise (LFI) politician Thomas Portes to alert authorities to the threats last week.
Portes shared excerpts of the discussion, highlighting racist remarks including "this is not the country of Arabs".
Other participants reportedly urged listeners to "take advantage of street prayers because they're all gathered together" and said they "need to target a small neighbourhood and make it French". Some allegedly discussed killing people.
"I am immediately referring the matter to the Prosecutor of the Republic of Paris [Laure Beccuau]," Portes said.
According to French media reports, the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office referred the case to police after becoming aware of the threats targeting Muslims and immigrants.
Prosecutors reportedly launched an investigation into suspected public incitement to hatred or violence based on origin or religion, direct online incitement to commit a terrorist act, and public calls to commit violent crimes.
The New Arab has approached the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office for comment and could not independently verify whether Portes' complaint directly prompted the investigation.
The investigation comes days after a series of racially motivated attacks in Trappes and nearby La Verrière, outside Paris, last week.
A gunman killed one person and wounded five others, including a 12-year-old girl, in shootings that officials said may have constituted an Islamophobic "terrorist crime".
Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh said the person killed was "of African origin", while one of the wounded, who was in critical condition, was "of North African origin".
Following the attacks, the French Council of the Muslim Faith condemned the "consequences of hate speech, stigmatisation and scapegoating", renewing its warnings about the dangers of rhetoric targeting Muslim communities.
The incidents have heightened concerns over growing anti-Muslim hostility in France, where far-right political figures have increasingly targeted Muslims and immigrants in their rhetoric.
French Muslim organisations have repeatedly condemned anti-Muslim rhetoric and policies promoted by far-right politicians.
Marine Le Pen, a leading figure in the far-right National Rally party, has previously proposed fining women who wear the headscarf in public spaces.

Documents
Details
As seen in the Security Defence Review, the Army are at heightened readiness due to a new era of threat. This has placed greater demands on the Defence Training Estate across the UK, which is being used for training more regularly and at shorter notice.
As such, the firing time notifications published on Gov.UK have been standardised to show the daily timings for when live-firing is permitted on the UK DTE. This is a change from the previous method of showing when training bookings had been made in advance.
This to ensure safety of all users, as it is not possible to change Gov.UK notifications at short notice. Broadly, the only guaranteed safe times for access are before or after the firing times provided on this page, however there may be exceptional circumstances where extensions have been requested.
If you wish to use the DTE for recreation, please always refer to onsite safety warning signals to understand if the site is safe to access before doing so.
Your safety
Danger - When warning signals are displayed, regardless of the timings, do not cross the range boundary.
Warning signals are red flags by day and red lamps by night; range boundaries are marked by red and white poles.
Red flags and red lamps indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries.
Do not enter the danger area when in use, this could result in loss of life.
Do not touch any military debris, it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) via 07717542336 or the police.

Press freedom groups demand EU transparency over Gaza amid Ombudsman investigation
The European Ombudsman has launched an investigation into the European Commission’s refusal to release 17 documents concerning EU-funded infrastructure projects in Gaza, telling The New Arab on Wednesday that the inquiry was under way as the Commission confirmed it had received the request.
The inquiry was prompted by a complaint from the online newspaper EUobserver, which requested the records as part of an investigation into the extent of destruction caused by Israeli attacks on EU-funded infrastructure in the war-torn Palestinian territory.
The European Ombudsman launched the inquiry on October 14 after the Commission refused to disclose the documents.
"The complainant made the access request to the Commission in February. In June, the Commission refused access to all 17 documents that it had identified as falling within the scope of the request on protection of data, international relations, and commercial interests grounds," a spokesperson for the European Ombudsman told The New Arab.
"The complainant in July asked the Commission to review its initial decision and then turned to the Ombudsman in September when they did not receive a reply from the Commission."
The European Ombudsman stated that it has since asked the European Commission to respond to EUobserver by 4 November at the latest, as European Ombudswoman Teresa Anjinho will examine the requested documents herself if the response is unsatisfactory.
Fifteen media and press freedom organisations have also urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to improve transparency amid the investigation.
In an open letter published on Wednesday, organisations including the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), the European Federation of Journalists (EFJ) and the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) called on the EU chief to address what they described as a “silent crisis” that has hindered journalists’ efforts to obtain information needed to scrutinise matters of public interest.
The open letter, backed by the 15 organisations, criticised lengthy delays, questionable refusals and extensive redactions that can render disclosed documents largely meaningless.
The signatories also alleged that the Commission sometimes fails to retain and properly archive important records.
"The European Commission’s reputation for safeguarding EU democratic values is in peril," the letter read. "At a time when democratic norms are under attack around the world, now is the time to uphold these values."
The letter, spearheaded by CPJ’s EU deputy advocacy director, Tom Gibson, called for the repeal of the European Commission’s internal procedural rules introduced in December 2024, which the signatories said had made access to documents more difficult.
Their demands also included a renewed action plan to improve journalists’ access to information, including implementing the European Ombudsman’s recommendations and rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union.
In addition, the signatories called for the Commission to strengthen procedures for registering and archiving documents.
PEN International, one of the signatories to the open letter, told The New Arab that "restrictions on access to information can leave critical questions about decisions concerning Gaza and the use of European public funds unanswered".
It continued: "Delays, excessive redactions and withheld documents make it harder for journalists to establish how decisions were made, how public money is being spent and who should be held accountable".
PEN International further warned that restrictions on access to such material meant that "public debate risks being shaped by official accounts that cannot be independently scrutinised, weakening citizens’ ability to question decisions made in their name".
It added: "We are calling on the Commission to uphold its legal obligations and ensure that access to documents works in practice, not just in principle."
In a July report, EUobserver highlighted concerns over the Commission’s lack of transparency as it aimed to investigate documents relating to EU funding for Gaza's physical infrastructure projects such as water supply, stormwater management, sanitation and renewable energy projects.
However, concerns have mounted that many of the projects have since been destroyed during Israel’s devastating military campaign in Gaza.
The report also questioned the Commission’s refusal to disclose the records amid reports that direct losses resulting from Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza had exceeded $80 billion across 15 vital sectors, according to the territory’s Government Media Office.
The destruction has extended beyond buildings and facilities to roads, water and electricity supplies, telecommunications and sewage networks, as well as economic infrastructure and public services.
Speaking to The New Arab earlier this month, Gaza's Government Media Office director-general Smail al-Thawabta highlighted that over 95% of Gaza’s population now relies entirely on humanitarian aid and community kitchens to meet basic needs.
Meanwhile, EUobserver reported that losses suffered by EU-funded projects in Gaza were estimated at approximately €155 million alone.
The European Commission has responded to the claims, with a spokesperson telling The New Arab on Wednesday that it had received the European Ombudsman's inquiry.
Addressing the criticism, the Commission stressed that it is "one of the most transparent institutions in the world".
"We take this responsibility extremely seriously. Every year we receive more than 7,000 access to documents requests. That's 30 per working day on average. This is more than any other EU institutions," the Commission spokesperson told The New Arab.
"We process them all," they added.
"How long a request takes to be processed depends on several factors: the scale and scope of the request, the type of documents or the internal consultations needed to retrieve them."
Amid growing scrutiny of the European Commission, von der Leyen has also faced criticism over her handling of Israel’s actions in Gaza.
Rights groups, including Amnesty International, have condemned her failure to implement proposals made last year to suspend the trade component of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and impose sanctions on Israeli ministers and settlers.
Despite the lack of action, mass protests have taken place across Europe, condemning EU-Israel ties and accusing the bloc of complicity in the Gaza genocide.
"These failures come with consequences: not only for her own credibility and that of the EU, but most of all for the lives of millions displaced, killed or wounded in Palestine and across the region," Amnesty International said in a September statement.
"Von der Leyen should use this year’s address to remedy that, by firstly making good on last year’s proposals, then by ensuring the EU joins the ranks of those banning trade with Israel’s illegal settlements."

“A Failure of Expectation Calibration”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:17:57 UTC
02:17:57 KST

A team of researchers conducted a three-year study of philosophers’ judgments about the philosophical capabilities of generative artificial intelligence. Their finding: “As participants became more familiar with generative AI and increasingly recognized its formal competence, they simultaneously sharpened the boundaries they drew around what they regarded as genuinely philosophical thinking.”
The study, “Can Intelligent User Interfaces Engage in Philosophical Discussions?: A Longitudinal Mixed-Methods Study of Philosophers’ Judgments” was published earlier this year in the Joint Proceedings of the ACM Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI) Workshops 2026.
It was a small study in which the participants, 16 philosophy scholars, were asked to “assess anonymized philosophical responses and to reflect on the role of generative AI in philosophical discussion.” They were interviewed over the three year period about whether and how their attitudes about generative AI in philosophical discussion changed. That was the qualitative part of the study. The quantitative part involved the subjects rating their familiarity with generative AI and registering their evaluation of the philosophical capabilities of generative AI.
The authors, Yibo Meng (Tsinghua University), Bingyi Liu (University of Michigan), Lyumanshan Ye (Shanghai Jiao Tong University), and Yan Guan (Tsinghua University), summarize and discuss what they learned:
The qualitative findings reveal a longitudinal shift that is not merely attitudinal, but philosophical in nature. Over three years of sustained engagement, participants moved from initial resistance, through instrumental acceptance, to a principled critique of generative AI grounded in questions of understanding, embodiment, and responsibility. Importantly, this trajectory does not reflect growing pessimism about the technology’s performance. Rather, it reflects a deepening reflection on the nature of philosophical activity itself. As participants became more familiar with generative AI and increasingly recognized its formal competence, they simultaneously sharpened the boundaries they drew around what they regarded as genuinely philosophical thinking.
At the same time, the quantitative findings complicate this trajectory. Although participants consistently denied generative AI philosophical standing in their interviews, blind evaluations indicate that they nonetheless attributed to AI forms of originality typically associated with human philosophical work. From a human–AI interaction perspective, this divergence reflects a failure of expectation calibration, whereby stable normative beliefs are not updated in line with evaluative performance as system capability improves.
One possible interpretation of this: what’s going on is defensive goalpost-moving and stubborn inconsistency. In other words: philosophers are people, too. The authors suggest a less cynical alternative: that the study “prompted renewed attention to those dimensions of philosophy that participants regarded as irreducibly human—such as embodied experience, value-laden judgment, historical situatedness, and the willingness to question one’s own conceptual frameworks,” and thus served as “an occasion for [the] rearticulation” of philosophy.
Perhaps a little from column A and a little from column B?
The full study is here.
(via David Strohmaier)

AI generated
WASHINGTON – With Israel's election yielding no clear winner, US President Donald Trump could face prolonged uncertainty over who will lead Washington's closest Middle East ally as he confronts challenges from Iran and Gaza across the region.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc secured the most seats in Israel’s Parliament but still lost its parliamentary majority on Oct 27 despite Trump having endorsed him against a rival alliance of parties led by hawkish former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
While Netanyahu seemed to be in a stronger position, neither side was projected to have an outright path to form a new government after Israel’s first election since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The stage appeared to be set for a period of painstaking coalition bargaining – or possibly another election – while Netanyahu remains in power in a caretaker capacity.
The outcome will have implications for US-Israel relations, which have been dominated by the joint fight against Iran, stalled Gaza peace efforts and signs of eroding US public support for Israel.
The uncertainty comes at a sensitive moment for Trump, when he and Netanyahu have threatened to join in another round of attacks against Iran.
“Israeli politics can be messy,” said Aaron David Miller, a former Middle East adviser in Democratic and Republican administrations. From the US perspective, he said, “it would be good to get some clarity, but that’s easier said than done”.
Which outcome would Trump prefer?
Netanyahu – a consummate political survivor who has had a close but sometimes turbulent relationship with Trump dating back decades – may have survived again. He is the longest-serving Israeli prime minister and the only one whom the US President has ever worked with.
Eisenkot, who projected an image as a political outsider and security-minded former general during the campaign, has seen his governing chances dimmed but not extinguished. He is not known to have ever met Trump.
Some analysts say the creation of a broad unity government keeping Netanyahu in power might serve Trump’s interest in a politically stable Israeli partner. But neither side has shown a willingness to take that path.

What does the election mean for the war with Iran?
Topping the list is how Trump might engage with Israel in the war against Iran, which has rocked the Middle East. Trump, in his Oct 18 endorsement, insisted he wanted Netanyahu to remain in power to help him soon “finish the job” against Iran. The President said overnight that Netanyahu, who outperformed pre-election polls, had done “very well” and that his backing had boosted the Israeli leader.

Jonathan Panikoff, a former deputy US national intelligence officer on the Middle East, said any future Israeli leadership would likely be on the same page as Trump if he decides to escalate from the current stalemate with Israel’s regional arch-foe.
“It’s hard to imagine any real daylight between them on that point,” said Panikoff, who is now at the Atlantic Council think-tank in Washington.
Where Netanyahu and many Israelis have sometimes differed with Trump is when he has offered concessions in now-stalled negotiations with the Islamic Republic.
What are the implications for Gaza peace efforts?
No matter how Israel’s next government shapes up, there is little reason to believe there will be any sweeping shift in tough policies towards the Palestinians.
This doesn’t bode well for breaking the diplomatic deadlock between Israel and Hamas and fully implementing Trump’s Gaza peace plan following the war there. Israel, in response to the militants’ deadly cross-border attack, levelled much of the enclave and killed tens of thousands of Palestinians.
Administration officials have privately expressed frustration over what they see as intransigence by Netanyahu, who has insisted that Hamas must first disarm.
Eisenkot, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, stressed his military credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically during the election campaign. He has vowed to break with Netanyahu’s far-right coalition allies, but not with the hawkish approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack.
Like Netanyahu, Eisenkot opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas’ military wing must be destroyed.
But he has pledged to prevent violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, which Netanyahu’s government has been accused of tolerating. Settler attacks have drawn criticism in recent weeks from US officials worried the territory could become another Middle East flashpoint.
What about Israel’s growing isolation?
Even as Israel’s political climate is expected to remain unsettled for some time, Trump may have to contend with what opinion polls project could be the Democrats’ takeover of one or both chambers of Congress in the midterms.
That could mean increased pressure from Democrats, whose support for Israel plunged over its conduct in the Gaza war, to curb billions of dollars in US aid and weapons supplies.
Some members of Trump’s MAGA base have also become increasingly critical of Israel, accusing it of having misled Trump – who campaigned for a second term on a promise to avoid foreign military interventions – into believing Iran could easily be defeated.

The Inside Story of Why Apple Finally Brought a Touch Display to the Mac
Unknown

2026-10-28

It’s a bright day in Cupertino. Apple’s new CEO strolls to an outdoor seating area within the company’s otherworldly ring-shaped headquarters and pulls up a chair. An employee notes the angle and asks if he minds the sun. John Ternus doesn’t mind at all.
Nearly two months into his tenure, he’s been busy. While the tech world buzzes about AI agents and the upcoming IPO of a company reporting spectacular losses, Ternus’ leadership of a ridiculously profitable firm has so far been defined by a sequence of significant launches—the long-awaited foldable iPhone, a household device that can control digital appliances, new Mac Minis, and AirPods. Intentionally or not, all that activity sends a message that, even as AI dominates the public imagination, hardware products still rule.
Ternus doesn’t endorse that take, but he doesn’t object when I suggest it. “We’ve been working on these products for quite some time,” he says. “It feels like everyone here is just kind of riding high right now, enjoying it.”
I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.
Ternus beams. “Who knew?”
We are referring to the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display that Apple is releasing today at an event in Los Angeles. It’s got a mighty M5 Pro or M5 Max chip and a show-stopping tandem OLED screen. (A tandem screen has multiple light-emitting layers, producing more dramatic contrasts.) But its most conspicuous feature is one that’s been deeply woven into iPhones, iPads, and even Apple Watches for years but not Apple’s laptops: a touch display. After years of resistance, a Mac screen has finally gone digital. As in fingers.
This turnaround is a big deal to Apple fans. Ternus shrugs off the drama. “The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”
Ternus and Apple want to make sure that the Mac faithful don’t panic that the 42-year-old franchise is losing its identity to Apple’s gangbusters mobile products. “We needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”
Apple has a long history of refusing to implement certain desirable features, only to pivot when it feels the time is right. Steve Jobs once proclaimed iPods would never do video, until they did. He also once said “no one’s going to buy” a jumbo-size phone—and then Apple released a supersized iPhone 6. Then there was that time Jobs declared styluses inappropriate for tablets. Now the Apple Pencil works with iPads and the brand-new Duo.
The 2026 MacBook Pro instantly qualifies as the canonical example of this switcheroo. Apple executives had been on record regarding touch on PCs as a misbegotten idea. Never mind that just about every PC maker not headquartered in Cupertino has implemented touch on their laptops. And customers of Microsoft, Dell, Acer, Lenovo, and HP have snapped them up. Clearly, people wanted touch on their laptop displays. Even toddlers knew it—put some rug rats in front of a computer and their little arms shoot straight to the screen in futile attempts to swipe and scroll as they do on their iPads. People were baffled why Apple—the pioneer in touch displays since the iPhone—was so steadfast in its rejection.
In 2015, while doing a story about a new iMac, I pressed Phil Schiller, then the senior vice president of worldwide product marketing, on this very question. Usually, top Apple executives field such queries with cryptic remarks. In this case, Schiller began a filibuster. “I’m going to get a little bit philosophical,” he said, then launched into what I later described as the Grand Unified Theory of Apple Hardware.
He explained that every Apple hardware product—the Watch, iPad, iMac, MacBook—is basically a computer and a piece of glass. Each one has a specific function. And each one has an interface appropriate to the hardware. Multitouch is fine for products like the iPhone, he said—but not the Macintosh. He provided two reasons: ergonomics and the software interface.
“From the ergonomic standpoint, we have studied this pretty extensively, and we believe that on a desktop scenario, where you have a fixed keyboard, having to reach up to do touch interfaces is uncomfortable,” he told me.
As for the interface, Schiller argued that Apple’s two main operating systems were built on different design principles. The iPhone and iPad’s iOS was multitouch from the get-go, and didn’t use macOS conventions that require precision, such as cursors and tiny boxes to close windows. “These two worlds are different on purpose, and that’s a good thing—we can optimize around the best experience for each of those and not try to mesh them together into a least-common-denominator experience,” he told me.
A year later, when Apple introduced a MacBook Pro with the ill-fated “touch bar”—a dynamic strip of virtual function keys above the keyboard’s top row—Schiller doubled down on the view that touch should never find its way into a Mac display. He said that such a move would mean totally redesigning the menu bar for fingers, and that would clash with the experience of pointer devices like a touchpad or mouse. “You can’t optimize for both,” he said.
To double-check this assumption, Apple conducted user tests with touchscreens on Mac. “What the heck, we could be wrong,” Schiller told me then. “We’ve absolutely come away with the belief that it isn’t the right thing to do. Our instincts were correct.”
When I met with Apple executives Johny Srouji and Greg Joswiak this week to discuss the touchscreen MacBook Pro, you bet I invoked Schiller’s list of concerns. (Apple’s reps chose not to make Schiller, who now holds the title of “Apple Fellow,” available for an interview. In fact, they laughed when I asked.) It wasn’t only Schiller drawing a red line. In 2021, Ternus told journalist Joanna Stern, “The Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven’t really felt a reason to change that.”
“Ten years is a very, very long time,” says Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer. “Many things have changed, whether it's the display technology, the custom silicon, et cetera.” Eventually, he told me, the confluence of chips, display tech, and software architecture “met our bar.” “I like my engineers to be gated by physics, not imagination or timelines,” he says.
Joswiak, who holds Schiller’s old title of SVP of worldwide marketing, concedes that touch was overdue, at least for users with sophisticated needs. Its pro customers—engineers, scientists, software developers, and media creators—were impatient with Apple for its failure to let them interact directly with the screen. “Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone,” Joswiak says. “So this is something that they’re natural with. There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.”
Between the lines, Srouji and Joswiak seem to consider their competitors’ touchscreen implementations shabby and lazy. The Apple ethos, as every one of its executives will happily explain to anyone who asks, is an expectation of quality that’s sky-high. “If you’re working on something easy, you’re wasting your time,” says Srouji, who has been at Apple since 2008 and has pretty much driven its innovation by spearheading the company’s charge to custom-build silicon.
“The easy things, I want to outsource,” he continues. “So the custom silicon is hard. The touch is hard. The display is hard. Everything we build is hard.” This swaggering philosophy dates from the Steve Jobs days and, in 2026, stands in contrast to the endgame of the ascendant AI industry, which hopes to turn over the toughest parts of industrial production to superintelligent entities.
Srouji presents Mac touch as a suite of innovations, starting with that screen that Ternus described as the Mac’s best ever. It also involves custom silicon and a rearchitected thermal system to prevent the display from feeling hot when people pinch, stretch, and swipe on it. Srouji contends that current touchscreen laptops suffer from “wobble” when fingers make contact with the display; to minimize this effect, Apple has redesigned the hinge on the MacBook Pro screen to stabilize it.
When I get a demo of the 16-inch version (as with previous Pros, it’s also available in a 14-inch version), I see what they mean about the display. It’s noticeably dense and bright, and the obsidian blacks are the deepest I’ve seen on a computer screen. In part because the OLED screen doesn’t require backlighting, this MacBook weighs less than its predecessor.
As a pair of Apple managers take the MacBook through its paces, I see how Apple has addressed some of Schiller’s decade-old concerns, like having to redesign the menu bar for fingers. While it looks the same, when you move a finger over a menu item, it expands to allow you to select your choice with precision. Some of the objects on the screen, like the traffic-light buttons that close or hide windows, also get bigger when you touch them.
They show me how the touch tech can handle precision tasks, like color grading in the video editing software DaVinci Resolve, or tweaking a soundtrack on Logic Pro, Apple’s high-end audio workstation. One innovation, not just for pros, is a new gesture to pull down the “Dynamic Island,” that black oval hosting ongoing tasks that has made its way to Mac from iPhone. An expanded version floats on the screen like a widget, enabling easy access to Siri responses and Spotlight search.
But what about greasy fingers messing up the screen? I was told that the new display has an anti-reflective outer coating that will require no more cleaning than your normal non-interactive screen.
Apple clearly hopes that the MacBook Pro launch puts an exclamation point on the burst of product announcements that Apple customers are still absorbing. For the foldable Duo, some customers are impatiently waiting for delivery dates that stretch into January. (Lines were long at Apple stores last Friday, when the device went on sale, and Joswiak personally greeted those who queued up at Apple’s Fifth Avenue store in New York City.)
I ask Srouji whether Apple is making a statement with its armada of new products, maybe as a way to say that in a year dominated by AI obsession, Apple is still here. He responds much as his new boss did, contending that Apple is simply sticking to its game plan. “We’re here to build the most amazing products in the world, and we want to ship them when we believe it’s ready and complete,” says Srouji. “That’s the statement we’re making. I think everyone knows we’re here.”
While longtime users will be happy to hear that a Macintosh now has a touchscreen, those with limited budgets will be disappointed. Apple’s current stance—that touch-on-a-Mac display is most appropriate to the “pro” crowd—rationalizes an astronomical price tag: The new MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. Financial analyst Neil Cybart, who got an early MacBook Pro briefing, thinks that serious professionals will pay up. “People are in search of value, and that means going for products that leverage technology to improve what they’re doing,” he says.
When I ask Ternus about the timeline, or even the possibility, of seeing touch displays on less exorbitantly priced MacBook Airs and iMacs, he shakes his head. “You’ve been doing this a long time,” he says. “You know I will never tell you anything about our future.”
I don’t know why I bothered to ask. If Ternus said that touch would never happen on a MacBook Air, who would believe him? I’d be back at The Ring a year later, hearing that Apple had finally figured out a way to do it right.

The UN World Food Program (WFP) chief Luke Lindberg said Wednesday that the hunger situation in the Gaza Strip is "unacceptable" as he pledged to defend his staff against attacks. 
Speaking at a news conference at UN headquarters in New York, Lindberg said that "there is a very serious need" in Gaza, citing funding cuts as a major constraint on the agency's work. 
Asked how he would address Israeli troops firing on WFP convoys, given his White House connections, Lindberg said staff security is "the number one concern for me." 
"I will absolutely stand up for our employees, no matter where on Earth they are located," he said. 
He added that "if anywhere in the world there are people attacking humanitarians, I will absolutely do what I can to protect them from violence against them and their families." 
Outlining his priorities, Lindberg said: "First and foremost, it is protecting and empowering our staff members. Humanitarians have been killed all over the world in the past two years, at unprecedented levels, and it’s unacceptable." 
"Over 700 people in the last few years have been killed trying to save other people’s lives, and nobody should lose their life trying to save somebody else’s," he added. 
Asked about the WFP's partnership with the US, which backed his candidacy, Lindberg said the "United States plays a critical role. It is the largest funder for the World Food Program." 
"When I was nominated for this role by the United States, President (Donald) Trump personally called me," he said. "I have a great relationship with many members of the Trump administration." 
Lindberg stressed the need for broader donor support. "There is no one nation, no one entity that can do this alone. We have to do it together," he added.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Wednesday that France expects the next UN chief to reform and strengthen the world body.
“What we expect from a future secretary-general is that he can reform the United Nations to strengthen it, and certainly not discredit it in order to better bury it,” Barrot told the French Senate.
Barrot said France would not accept efforts by major powers to weaken or paralyze the UN, which he described as an organization founded to serve peace, development and human rights.
He said international cooperation and multilateralism were essential to protecting people from threats including war, AI, climate change and pandemics.
France, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, was making efforts to reform the organization and make it more legitimate and representative, he said.
Barrot also cited a French initiative to limit the use of veto powers by permanent Security Council members, saying it aimed to help protect civilians in Sudan, Ukraine, the Gaza Strip and Iran when they are targeted.

Israeli opposition seeks Arab party talks to oust Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:10:04 UTC
02:10:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli opposition seeks talks with Arab parties to oust Netanyahu
Israel's opposition has approached Arab parties to discuss cooperation on forming a new government, following an election in which high turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel helped deny Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a parliamentary majority.
Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Arab Movement for Change and a member of the Knesset, revealed that opposition parties had contacted Arab political leaders to coordinate efforts to replace the current Knesset speaker and explore future cooperation.
Tibi said Arab parties were not seeking ministerial portfolios in the next government but intended to use their parliamentary strength to end Netanyahu's rule.
He credited the surge in Palestinian voter turnout with preventing Netanyahu from securing the majority needed to form a government, opening the door to an alternative that could end the far-right coalition's grip on power.
The Joint List would support an opposition-backed candidate to replace the Knesset speaker, Tibi said, while condemning politicians who refuse to cooperate with Arab parties.
"Whoever insists on not forming alliances with Arab parties will lose power," he said, describing attempts to portray Arab votes as illegitimate as racist.
Arab parties offer Eisenkot parliamentary support
According to Israeli public broadcaster Kan, Tibi confirmed that the Joint List was negotiating with the opposition's "change camp" to facilitate the formation of a new government without formally joining the coalition.
"I want to do everything I can in the Knesset to pave the way for the announcement of a government," he said. "We will probably not be an integral part of this government, but there are other arrangements and possibilities."
Sources familiar with the discussions said the Joint List had offered opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot a parliamentary "safety net", similar to the arrangement under which Arab lawmakers supported Yitzhak Rabin's government in 1992.
Such an arrangement could allow Arab parties to support a government from outside the coalition without accepting ministerial positions.
The sources said contacts with Eisenkot's camp had continued over recent days and remained ongoing.
Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen also called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to remove Netanyahu from power.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government must engage in dialogue with us and pave the way for the change that the public in Israel is seeking," Jabareen told Israeli media.
Netanyahu incites against Arab voters
The developments follow an election campaign in which Netanyahu repeatedly warned supporters about rising turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu shared photographs and videos focusing on Arab lawmaker Ahmad Tibi and high turnout in Arab communities.
In one post on X, Netanyahu shared an image purportedly showing voters outside a polling station in Rahat, a predominantly Arab city in southern Israel.
"This is what is happening today in Rahat. You cannot stay at home; go out immediately and vote Likud. We are fighting for our homeland," he wrote.
Meanwhile, Democrats leader Yair Golan suggested that Arab parties should be included in opposition efforts to form a new government.
"Every member of the Knesset elected through the legal process is a legitimate part of our political system," Golan said.
However, far-right Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman rejected cooperation with Arab parties, instead calling for a rebellion within Likud against Netanyahu.
Lieberman accused Netanyahu of destroying the nationalist camp, saying the prime minister had behaved "like the head of a criminal organisation".

Sudan war and inflation leave families struggling to survive in Khartoum

Unknown Publisher

02:09:05 KST

Sudan war and inflation leave families struggling to survive in Khartoum
Soaring food prices and shrinking incomes force families in Sudan’s capital to borrow money and skip meals.
Khartoum, Sudan – Rasha Abdelaziz Musa works every day for seven hours selling tea. But by the time she finishes for the day at 10pm, she’s still unsure if she has enough to feed her four children.
Musa, 39, is doing her best, but her earnings are increasingly no longer enough to cover soaring food prices in the Sudanese capital.
Her husband, a member of the Sudanese military, has spent more than eight months on the front lines of the country’s war, in which the military has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since 2023. Musa has not heard from him for months, and he has sent no money.
In his absence, Musa has been left to provide for their children, who attend kindergarten, primary and secondary school.
Musa told Al Jazeera that feeding her family costs about 40,000 Sudanese pounds per day ($4 at the parallel-market exchange rate) before accounting for rent, household essentials and other expenses.
Some of the family staples are ful medames, a dish of stewed fava beans, or lentils. When lentils are too expensive, Musa serves taamiya, or falafel, sandwiches.
Prices regularly change, and Musa often ends the day in debt to the traders she gets her food from.
Large families struggle
Musa is not alone in struggling to cover her family’s daily expenses.
Ahmed Youssef, 61, supports a family of 12 through his work in a butcher’s shop and as an occasional intermediary in livestock sales. He can earn 90,000 to 140,000 pounds ($9 to $14) when a deal succeeds, but that income is irregular.
He told Al Jazeera that his household spends more than 100,000 Sudanese pounds ($10) daily and his income is no longer enough to support the family.
“One income is no longer enough to cover the family’s needs, and sometimes my older children have to work to help meet expenses,” Youssef told Al Jazeera.
Ali Fadil supports a family of 10. Without a permanent job, he goes to the market each morning to look for work. Some days, the 57-year-old earns enough to buy food, but on other days, he finds no work at all. And yet his daily expenses still reach about 70,000 pounds ($7), with rising prices adding to the financial pressure he faces.
“Sometimes I skip meals so I can pay for school fees or medical costs,” he said. “I also borrow money to meet other obligations.”
Food prices rise as Sudanese pound weakens
A survey of four local markets in the Khartoum State area by Al Jazeera last week found that prices for several essential foods had risen sharply within days, making it increasingly difficult for families to plan their spending.
A kilogramme (2.2.lb) of sugar cost about 10,000 pounds ($1), up from 9,000 pounds ($0.90) two days earlier. A litre (1 quart) of cooking oil rose to 25,000 pounds ($2.50) from 20,000 pounds ($2) while a loaf of bread costs 500 pounds ($0.05), compared with 300 pounds ($0.03) a week earlier.
Lentils cost about 10,000 pounds ($1) per kilogramme, up from 8,000 pounds ($0.80), and rice was priced at 13,000 pounds ($1.30) per kilogramme, up from 10,000 pounds ($1). Powdered milk reached 70,000 pounds ($7) per kilogramme, up from 60,000 ($6) two days earlier.
The Sudanese pound has also continued to weaken. According to exchange rates monitored by Al Jazeera, $1 was trading at 10,050 Sudanese pounds on the parallel market on Friday, compared with 9,500 the previous day.
Food inflation adds to pressure on households
Official figures offer further evidence of the rising cost of living, particularly in Khartoum and other urban areas.
According to Sudan’s Central Bureau of Statistics, prices across the country were 28 percent higher in September than a year earlier, up from 26 percent in August. Prices rose by 7.5 percent in September alone, more than double the increase recorded the previous month.
Food prices have risen even faster. Across Sudan, food and beverages cost nearly 37 percent more in September than a year earlier, up from an annual increase of about 21 percent in August. In September alone, food prices jumped by more than 17 percent.
The situation was particularly severe in Khartoum State, where prices were nearly 60 percent higher than a year earlier. Prices rose by more than 15 percent in September alone, following an increase of nearly 9 percent in August.
That sharp increase comes as the capital region struggles to recover from widespread destruction caused by the war. Although displaced residents have begun returning and businesses are gradually reopening since the military recaptured the state from the RSF last year, damaged infrastructure and rising transport costs continue to constrain the availability of goods.
The return of residents has also increased demand for essential supplies, further driving up prices. In September, fuel shortages hit the capital as consumption rose faster than supplies could be replenished.
Urban areas have generally been hit harder than rural communities. Food prices in towns and cities were 55 percent higher than a year earlier, up from about 40 percent in August. Overall, prices in urban areas rose by 40 percent over the past year, compared with about 21 percent in rural areas.
The war is the main driver of these increases, disrupting livelihoods and supply chains. According to the World Bank, Sudan’s economy shrank by an estimated 29 percent in 2023 and a further 14 percent in 2024 as the war devastated businesses, disrupted agricultural production and eliminated jobs.
The conflict has also forced millions of people from their homes with nearly 8.9 million people still internally displaced as of April, according to the International Organization for Migration.
War destroys livelihoods
Journalist and economic affairs specialist Khalid Teks said Sudan’s economic deterioration began long before the war. Falling oil production after South Sudan’s secession in 2011 worsened conditions as did the depreciation of the pound, cash shortages, international isolation, political conflict and corruption in the years preceding the removal of President Omar al-Bashir in 2019.
Teks said political instability during the power transition undermined Sudan’s economic performance, and deep reforms were not implemented before war broke out in 2023. The conflict devastated infrastructure and productive sectors, depleted savings and disrupted economic activity. The climate has also been a factor. Strong agricultural production in 2024 was followed by concern over limited rainfall this year and possible food shortages after the harvest begins in November.
Teks told Al Jazeera that families increasingly deplete their savings and sell their possessions to cover everyday expenses.
He also pointed to disruptions to remittance channels, which many Sudanese households rely on for financial support.
Teks called for easier humanitarian access, an end to the war, direct support for vulnerable households and low-interest loans for small businesses and craft enterprises.
“The government needs to provide direct support through dedicated funds and the Zakat Chamber, facilitate humanitarian organisations and offer affordable loans for small businesses and vocational activities,” Teks said. “This could help reopen markets and workshops and expand microfinance.

K. Budrys: mokslas, technologijos ir inovacijos lemia valstybių įtaką šiandienos pasaulyje
Unknown

Meloni says no attack on magistrates, defended work of the State
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:05:32 CET
02:05:32 KST

Premier Giorgia Meloni on Wednesday
said she had not attacked magistrates when branding as
"shameful" a decision by a Milanese preliminary investigations
judge (GIP) to order the release of Youssef Siher, a 30-year-old
Italian researcher and freelance journalist with Moroccan roots
who has been accused of being the creator of the "October 17
Movement" social media channels set up after the shocking
rioting and looting that took place in Milan on the weekend of
October 17-18.
                                    
Magistrates union ANM condemned her remarks saying they had been
"intemperate" and "unseemly".
                                    
"I have seen the responses from the National Association of
Magistrates (ANM). I will say something simple: I do not view
what I said as an attack; I view it as a defense—a defense of
the work carried out by all those who serve the State, who
labored with immense dedication to ensure that what we witnessed
on October 17th would not happen again. And it did not happen
again; it is regrettable that such work is now being undermined.
                                    
"Therefore, I do not believe that my comments were 'unseemly,'
as I have read. Frankly, I think 'unseemly' is something else
entirely—like chanting, 'Whoever doesn't jump is [against]
Meloni (referring to some left-wing magistrates, ed.).'
"That is neither my tone nor my method. However, I have a duty
to defend the work I saw so many people carry out this past
weekend, because we want to protect decent people from violence,
devastation, and destruction—from the things we have witnessed.
                                    
"That is what I said, and that is what I reiterate," she added.

Russia-Africa Summit: Putin’s key proposals on trade, technology and Western finance alternatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:05:09 UTC
02:05:09 KST

Russia-Africa Summit: Putin’s key proposals on trade, technology and Western finance alternatives
Russia and Africa can expand trade and share technology while reducing dependence on Western financial systems, President Vladimir Putin said at the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum in Moscow on Wednesday.
The event forms part of the third Russia-Africa summit, bringing delegations from 48 African countries to Moscow on October 28–29.
Speaking alongside Burundian President and African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye, Putin proposed closer banking links, called for bilateral trade to at least double, and offered Russian expertise in energy, agriculture, healthcare, and artificial intelligence.
Here are the key takeaways from the speeches and opening-day announcements.
An alternative to Western financial dependence
Putin urged Russian and African banks to expand direct ties, open branches in each other’s markets and strengthen payments in national currencies.
He proposed greater use of alternatives for exchanging payment information, including the Bank of Russia’s financial messaging system and the pan-African payments system. These arrangements would lower transaction costs and protect settlements from “politicized interference” by unfriendly countries, Putin said.
He argued that countries that don’t have their own financial systems end up relying on Western infrastructure, which ultimately limits their sovereignty.
Breaking out of ‘debt bondage’
Western countries are resisting the emergence of a multipolar world because they remain accustomed to colonial thinking and “growing fabulously rich at others’ expense,” Putin argued.
He accused them of using sanctions, tariffs, economic pressure, and interference to preserve their influence, including attempts to push African countries back into “debt bondage” through predatory lending.
Servicing such debts diverts resources from long-term development, Putin argued, calling for reforms of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank and a stronger African role in their decisions.
Doubling trade despite sanctions
Russia-Africa trade exceeded $27 billion last year, compared with $18 billion in 2022, Putin said, calling for the figure to at least double and surpass $50 billion in the near future.
He added that neither unprecedented restrictions against Russia nor Western pressure on African partners have been able to stop economic relations between the two from developing and expressed appreciation for this “firm and principled position of our African friends.”
Putin stated that Russian businesses support local processing, employment and tax revenues rather than engaging in “predatory, neocolonial exploitation” of Africa’s natural resources and people. Their investments also support healthcare, education, and environmental projects, he said.
Energy, transport and food security
Russia and African partners are implementing more than 30 energy projects in 16 countries, Putin said, describing affordable and reliable power as essential to industrial development and better living standards.
He offered cooperation on hydropower, including modernizing existing plants and supplying remote communities, alongside other energy technologies.
Russia’s Rosatom and Togo’s Energy Ministry signed a memorandum on nuclear energy cooperation. Rosatom chief Aleksey Likhachev said this could include floating nuclear power plants to supply electricity to the West African country.
Putin also stated that Russia had exported 13 million tons of agricultural products to Africa in the first nine months of 2026 with more than 40 African countries receiving Russian grain and fertilizers.
However, he stressed that Africa has the potential to feed itself, noting that Moscow is offering seeds, machinery, agricultural technology, storage, and processing infrastructure to help develop that capacity.
Transport proposals also include railways, roads, shipping routes, and logistics hubs, Putin said, inviting African airlines to begin flights to Russia.
Russian and Mozambican ministers also signed a road cooperation memorandum and discussed a possible direct shipping route.
Sharing technology and fighting epidemics
Technological independence has become an essential part of sovereignty, Putin argued, pointing to AI, cybersecurity, personal data, and digital infrastructure. Russia is ready to share its expertise, including digital public services and medical technologies, he added.
Putin also announced that Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for African countries would be extended through 2029.
Under the program, eight countries have already received 15 mobile laboratories and around 450 African specialists have been trained. Russian doctors continue to assist against infections including cholera and the outbreak of a new Ebola strain that began in the spring, he said.
Further cooperation could include local production of medicines and vaccines, diagnostic centers, and digital healthcare services.
Scholarships, youth exchanges and media links
Around 40,000 African citizens are studying at Russian universities, Putin said, with enrollment increasing by half since 2020. Scholarship places have nearly tripled over the same period, reaching 5,500 for the 2026–2027 academic year.
The president proposed to establish a Russia-African Youth Union to coordinate further exchanges between youth organizations. He also called for Russian news agencies and broadcasters to expand their presence across Africa and said that Moscow would welcome more African correspondents working in Russia.
A three-year cooperation plan
In his closing remarks, Putin stressed that discussions between senior officials alone are insufficient, which is why this year’s forum has been designed to be more accessible and focused on practical opportunities.
He invited participants to an exhibition presenting Russian technologies and proposals for joint projects, saying Moscow is ready to share its achievements with African partners.
Putin said that leaders also intend to adopt a Russia-Africa partnership action plan for 2027–2029 when the summit concludes on Thursday,
Africa wants industry, not just resource exports
During the plenary session, Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye said that Africa wants a greater role in the global economy and partnerships that help transform its resources into prosperity for its population.
“We do not want to remain merely exporters of natural resources and then import finished goods,” he said, calling for African participation throughout production and trade.
The African Union chair urged investment in local processing, technology transfers, and training, alongside energy, agriculture, transport, and infrastructure.
He also called for diversified trade, payment systems, and logistical routes connecting Africa with Russia and BRICS.

Meeting of the US, China and Russia: Zelenskyy fears &quot;Yalta 2.0&quot; - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:01:50 EET
02:01:50 KST

Meeting of the US, China and Russia: Zelenskyy fears "Yalta 2.0" - media
Kyiv • UNN
The President of Ukraine warned against a new division of spheres of influence between the US, China and Russia. He considers the format most beneficial to Moscow.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy fears an attempt to establish a new division of spheres of influence as a result of the upcoming meeting between the United States, China and Russia, similar to what happened as a result of the 1945 Yalta Conference. This is reported by Rapporteur, according to UNN.
Details
While speaking with journalists, he emphasized that he would not want a repetition of the scenario he called "Yalta 2, 3, 4." According to him, the world today is different from what it was during World War II.
Today we have a different world, a fragmented world that is very different from the world of World War II, both before and after it. A completely different technological world. Therefore, I think it is impossible simply to carry out such a redistribution among the three (the United States, Russia and China — Ed.). Although Russia wants this very much
He added that the Russians are most interested in this meeting, as they consider it an advantage for themselves. At the same time, according to him, China is the least interested in it.
I simply do not see any benefit for China, and I clearly see the advantage of this format for Russia
Context
U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff proposed that Russia hold a trilateral meeting with China's participation next month to discuss a plan to end the war in Ukraine.
The proposal is for U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to meet and reach a settlement regarding Ukraine.
Oleksii Buriachenko, president of the International Institute for Security Studies, said in a comment to UNN that only the Kremlin is interested in the potential trilateral talks between Russia, the United States and China. In particular, this would be aimed at raising the possibility of resolving Russia's war against Ukraine without the participation of Kyiv and Europe. Instead, other issues remain priorities for the United States and China.
To remind you
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin's aide, Yury Ushakov, said that representatives of European countries would not participate in the trilateral technical talks between Ukraine, the United States and Russia, which are scheduled to take place next month.

Erdogan offers condolences to Spain over deadly train crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:01:29 UTC
02:01:29 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has extended condolences to Spain over a train crash that killed at least 68 people and injured over 100 others.
“I wholeheartedly share, on behalf of my country and nation, the grief of those who lost their loved ones, and I send Türkiye’s messages of unity and solidarity to the people and government of Spain,” Erdogan said on the Turkish social media platform NSosyal on Wednesday.
He also wished a speedy recovery to those injured in the accident.
Three-day mourning
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Spain would observe three days of mourning after the tragedy.
"All of Spain is in mourning," Sanchez said from the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, adding that it was "not acceptable for a country like Spain" to suffer two such disasters in the same year.
"We will get to the bottom of this. If there has been negligence, it will be known," he said.
Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of Castile-La Mancha, warned that the death toll could rise further.
Puente said an IT failure at around 8.30 am local time (0730 GMT) affected a roughly 60-kilometre (37-mile) stretch of railway, disrupting the automatic safety system and leaving six trains stopped in the affected area.
Rail traffic was subsequently managed by infrastructure operator Adif’s control centre, which authorised a train behind a stationary Iryo train to resume its journey “as normal” at around 8.36 am local time (0736 GMT), he said.

Netanyahu eyes former allies as Likud pushes for talks with Bennett and Liberman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:00:32 UTC
02:00:32 KST

Encouraged by the emerging election results, which indicate that his Likud party will remain the largest in the next Knesset, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu turned his attention Wednesday morning to his next steps, planning his political moves and formulating a strategy for the days ahead.
Unlike in previous elections, Netanyahu did not speak with his political allies on exit poll night or the following day. Instead, he dealt with other matters, analyzed the results and showed no urgency to contact his partners. His only message to the leaders of his bloc came publicly, during his election-night speech, when he assured them they would be part of any political move he undertakes.
Why has Netanyahu remained silent for so long, breaking with his usual practice of calling his allies immediately after the exit polls? The likely explanation lies in his desire to preserve room for political maneuvering, as well as the need to formulate his next moves quickly to compel President Isaac Herzog to grant him the mandate to form a government, while preventing the rival change bloc from taking unilateral steps against him.
At this stage, Netanyahu is focusing his efforts on whether he can persuade a party from the opposing bloc to cooperate with him and avert another election. Senior Likud ministers attending the election-night gathering at the International Convention Center in Jerusalem were already arguing that the party should seek partnerships with Avigdor Liberman and Naftali Bennett, two right-wing figures in the rival bloc.
The prevailing assessment is that Liberman would refuse to serve under Netanyahu under any circumstances, and that Bennett would do the same. However, public opinion and mounting pressure could prove decisive. In the coming days, intermediaries, likely acting on Netanyahu's behalf, are expected to approach members of the opposing bloc to explore the possibility of cooperation and determine whether an alternative government could be formed.
The focus of both the pressure and the potentially attractive offers will be two of Netanyahu's former political partners. At the same time, he is expected to launch a broad public campaign against the change bloc and its intention to gain control of the Knesset speakership and parliamentary apparatus with the support of Arab parties.
The change bloc is preparing for the possibility that Netanyahu will stop at nothing, mounting an aggressive campaign against anyone who cooperates with its parliamentary initiatives. He is also already considering ways to drive a wedge between members of the opposing bloc and persuade some to abstain if those measures are brought before the Knesset plenum for a vote.
