Sweden orders four Bofors naval gun systems
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:00:22 GMT
02:00:22 KST

BAE Systems has won a contract from the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration for four Bofors 57Mk3 naval gun systems along with 57mm 3P ammunition, according to the company.
Stefan Löfström, marketing and sales director at BAE Systems Bofors, said: “This contract reinforces our long-standing role as a trusted partner to the Swedish armed forces and FMV, and our commitment to supporting the Swedish Navy with world-class capability. It demonstrates Sweden’s absolute confidence in the Bofors 57Mk3 and its advanced 3P ammunition as key capabilities for Sweden’s maritime defence.”
The 57Mk3 is a multirole gun built for air defence, anti-surface warfare and naval fire support. Paired with the programmable 3P round, which is pre-fragmented and proximity fused, it can engage drones, aircraft, missiles and surface targets.
The gun is made at the Bofors site in Karlskoga, which BAE Systems acquired through its purchase of United Defense in 2005, and the 57mm family is in service with the Swedish, Finnish, Canadian, Mexican and United States navies. The American variant is designated the Mk 110 and arms the Littoral Combat Ship and the Constellation class frigates.

Tokayev Proposes Dipping Into National Fund to Turn Kazakhstan into a ‘Big Construction Site’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

“Kazakhstan must turn into one big construction site,” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proclaimed in his October 28 national address, proposing that the government dip into the National Fund, to the tune of 6.5 trillion tenge (approximately $14.4 billion at the current exchange rate) to fund projects through 2029.
That represents more than 21 percent of the National Fund, a sovereign wealth fund created in 2000 and supplied by tax revenues from oil and gas companies. RFE/RL reported that the fund currently holds around $66.7 billion. Tokayev’s new ambition scraps a previous goal, stated in 2022 in the wake of the Qandy Qantar events as part of his “Fair Kazakhstan” pitch, to increase the National Fund’s assets to $100 billion by 2030.
From 2026 through the first two months of 2027, Tokayev said in his recent speech, 1.5 trillion tenge ($3.3 billion) would be allocated for social projects.
“I am confident that no one will object if we call this initiative a ‘People’s Construction Project,’” Tokayev said. In his subsequent remarks, he wandered through a smorgasbord of initiatives, mentioning a handful of specific efforts already underway, and spoke more generally about a huge range of ambitions.
“Particular focus should be placed on developing logistics infrastructure,” he said. Here Tokayev spoke at length about the importance of logistics – from roads to rail to air transport – in furthering Kazakhstan’s development.
Tokayev mentioned the Bakhty-Ayagoz rail line, which runs from Ayagoz in eastern Kazakhstan to the Chinese border and is expected to be completed by the end of 2027. He noted the start of construction in August of the the Aral-Caspian Highway, which “will shorten the route along the Trans-Caspian Corridor by approximately 1,000 kilometers, reducing cargo delivery time to three days.”
Tokayev took time to put special emphasis on the quality of roads – a perennial complaint in Kazakhstan – and criticize “executive bodies at the center and locally” who have treated the issue like a football.
“They kicked the issue around and did everything possible to drown the problem in an impassable swamp,” Tokayev, who has been president of Kazakhstan since 2019, said.
After discussing the importance of developing air corridors – “huge profits are literally flying past our country” – Tokayev shifted to energy. He stated the ambition for Kazakhstan to achieve a “sustainable energy surplus” by 2029, on the back of a full range of energy sources, from “clean coal” to renewables like solar. Nuclear power, he said, is of “fundamental importance,” praising as the “correct decision” the approval of a referendum on the topic in 2024. That referendum took place under heavy government pressure on critics of nuclear power.
Closely related is the hot topic of critical minerals. On that, Tokayev cautioned that “new businesses should not create obstacles for existing businesses in the local area.” He specifically referenced Qarmet, which until 2023 was known as ArcelorMittal Temirtau. That year it was acquired by the the Qazaqstan Investment Corporation. Tokayev obliqued referenced similar production facilities to those operated by Qarmet as being planned in three other regions with the help of presumably foreign investors. “It is obvious that the benefits of such inappropriate decisions are questionable,” he said, without clarifying.
“It is obvious that the role of the government in this matter needs to be significantly strengthened.”
That may raise red flags for potential investors, as it suggests a heavy government hand in managing the pathways investments take. A 2025 report from the U.S. Department of State on Kazakhstan’s investment climate noted “significant progress,” but also pointed to ongoing restrictions on foreign ownership in certain sectors – notably “a 20 percent ceiling on foreign ownership of media outlets and a 49 percent limit on domestic and international air transportation services” – while also stating that “foreign companies sometimes experience difficulties with licensing, taxation, and legal disputes due to bureaucratic hurdles and inconsistent regulatory enforcement.”
Later in his speech, Tokayev pontificated on the necessity of attracting global and domestic companies, once again criticizing “individual departments and individuals” for taking “chaotic and uncoordinated” actions. “Therefore, investment policy management should be concentrated in a single center,” Tokayev said. Centralization has its benefits, but it also concentrates both wealth and risk.
The speech went on to touch on subjects as varied as tax policy and education, ending with orders to reform the public administration system. “Civil servants must serve as models of competence,” Tokayev said. “Unfortunately, we are not seeing this yet.”

kengo kuma’s brick towers frame open-air pools at copenhagen’s upcoming bathhouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:55:25 UTC
01:55:25 KST

kengo kuma’s brick towers frame open-air pools at copenhagen’s upcoming bathhouse
swimmers can float beneath the open sky between brick towers at copenhagen's public bathhouse, set to open on december 5th, 2026.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
soon to open on copenhagen’s paper island
Kengo Kuma & Associates‘ KAI Water Culture House is set to open on December 5th, 2026, on Copenhagen‘s Papirøen (Paper Island). Bringing ten swimming pools to the city’s harborfront, the 5,800-square-meter spa introduces a new place for swimming and bathing along a waterfront that has gradually shifted from industrial use toward public recreation.
The building is recognizable at once by its five irregular brick towers, which rise above a continuous band of glass at ground level. Their sloping walls form a clustered silhouette along the quay, with spaces between the volumes opening toward the sky. From the harbor, the heavy masonry appears to hover over the transparent base. This lends the building an unusual sense of lightness, even with its monolithic presence.
five brick towers shaped around the water below
The towers in Copenhagen take their forms from the swimming pools beneath them, with each volume responding to its interior layout. Approximately 300,000 handmade bricks cover the angular surfaces, their varying gray tones relating to the city’s surrounding harbor architecture. The masonry is laid in a stepped pattern that gives the sloping walls a textured finish, particularly where the surfaces catch the changing daylight.
Across the brick facades, 403 windows of different sizes create small openings toward the city. Some bring daylight deep into the bathing areas, while others frame views across the harbor. Inside, the walls rise above the water at steep angles, creating tall bathing chambers where the enclosed architecture feels almost geological. The architects led by Kengo Kuma shape the building’s tallest volume, known as the Culture Tower, to house spaces for cultural activities and community gatherings.
an outdoor swimming pool sits between the towers
Perhaps the most unusual part of KAI is its Valley Pool, an open-air swimming basin positioned on the first floor between the five brick towers. Here, visitors can swim surrounded by the textured masonry, with the sky visible directly overhead. The arrangement creates a sheltered bathing space that remains exposed to Copenhagen’s changing weather, allowing swimmers to experience rain and even snowfall from the water.
On the same level, a heated outdoor onsen overlooks Copenhagen Harbour, drawing on Japanese bathing traditions while taking advantage of the waterfront setting. Both outdoor pools are designed for year-round use, supported by a ground-source heat pump system connected to ten boreholes extending 250 meters below ground. The architecture makes these contrasting experiences possible within the same building, moving between enclosed brick interiors and pools open to the elements.
from indoor swimming to the harbor
At ground level, KAI contains a 25-meter fitness pool alongside a teaching pool and three smaller pools for children. Upstairs, warmer bathing areas are joined by a cold plunge pool, while saunas and a steam bath provide additional facilities. The transparent lower level opens views toward the surrounding waterfront, connecting the swimming spaces visually with the harbor beyond.
Outside, a timber boardwalk will lead to designated harbor swimming and dipping areas overlooking the Royal Danish Playhouse and Opera Park. These public bathing facilities are expected to open in early 2027, following the building’s December inauguration. The project itself began with a city-led ideas competition in 2015, when Copenhagen residents submitted 160 proposals for the future of Paper Island, most of them calling for a public swimming facility.
Kengo Kuma & Associates won the subsequent architectural competition in 2017, working with Cornelius Vöge Atelier for Architecture during the early design stages and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects through detailed design and construction. Nearly a decade later, the project brings that original public request to the harbor’s edge.
project info:
project: KAI Water Culture House
location: Papirøen (Paper Island), Copenhagen, Denmark
lead architect: Kengo Kuma & Associates
early design collaboration: Cornelius Vöge Atelier for Architecture
executive architect: Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects
client: Paper Island Water Culture House Foundation
main contractor: MT Højgaard
area: 5,800 sqm
opening date: December 5th, 2026
photography: © Rasmus Hjortshøj | @rasmus_hjortshoj

Canada-EU summit: What do both sides want, and what’s at stake?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:54:51 UTC
01:54:51 KST

Canada-EU summit: What do both sides want, and what’s at stake?
The EU has proposed to make Canada its first associate member amid tensions over US tariffs.
Canada is set to host a summit with the European Union to bolster bilateral strategic and economic ties as its relations with its southern neighbour, the United States, are in sharp decline.
The summit is scheduled for October 29 to 30 in Canada’s French-speaking city of Montreal, and is expected to focus on closer cooperation on trade, technology, defence, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, research and financial services.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the move.
What is the summit, and why is it happening now?
This will be the 21st Canada-EU summit and is expected to build on the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force in 2017. It eliminates duties on up to 99 percent of all imported goods between the two sides, according to the European Council.
“In Montreal, we will take our partnership to the next level by launching our ‘Alliance for the Future’ to deepen our political, economic and institutional ties even further,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, who will be attending the summit along with Carney and von der Leyen. They are expected to issue a joint statement.
The deepening Canada-EU alignment seems fuelled by US President Donald Trump’s policies, which imposed hefty tariffs on both Canadian and European exports to the US and pushed Canada to look for ways to reduce its economic dependence on the US. Before Trump’s tariffs whipsawed relations, Canada sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to the US.
In August, trade talks between Ottawa and Washington, DC, broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
What do Canada and Europe want from each other?
Both sides are seeking opportunities that will open more options beyond the world’s largest economy.
“The opportunity is clear. The EU brings market power, research depth, and manufacturing strength. Canada brings abundant energy, critical minerals, world-class capabilities in space, artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum, and one of the world’s strongest banking systems,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
The summit will give the two sides a chance to turn these “complementary strengths into concrete benefits for our peoples,” the statement added.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a think tank in Ottawa, Canada, sees benefits and challenges.
“These fields could be beneficial for both sides, and we are likely to see specific announcements during the summit on these sectors,” she told Al Jazeera.
“The main challenge is how quickly the political momentum can turn into specific deals and projects to deliver specific economic results,” she added.
The EU describes Canada as “the only non-European country” taking part in Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s 150 billion-euro ($167bn) loan programme that supports and expedites defence procurement by EU member states.
The EU concluded its agreement with Canada, allowing it to participate under SAFE, in February, and it gives Canadian firms preferential access and treatment in defence procurements financed by the SAFE Instrument.
Could Canada become an associate member of the EU?
Last month, von der Leyen proposed that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member, suggesting a deeper relationship spanning trade, technology, defence and economic security.
Carney later welcomed the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.
However, the term “associate member” does not currently exist in EU treaties or its standard enlargement framework, according to the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), a Brussels-based think tank.
“The term does not actually matter; what is important is the practical deepening of the relationship and the actual results, no matter what the final term is,” Nadjibulla said.
Is it an anti-American alliance?
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said in her address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg last month, which Carney attended, making him the first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address.
Nadjibulla agrees.
“I do not see that as an anti-US coalition. It is rather about diversification of economic and defence partnerships and building resilience for Canada. It is a continuation of Canadian Prime Minister Carney’s policies to create opportunities. A deeper alliance with Europe is essential to this agenda,” she said.
“President Trump will likely not appreciate this, but it is about Canada having more choices in an unpredictable world,” she added.
Bob Rae, former premier of Ontario and Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2020 to 2025, told Al Jazeera that “President Trump does not control our policy. We have been having long and productive relations with the Europeans for hundreds of years, but Trump chose to treat Canada in a way that does not respect our sovereignty”.
He added that “engaging in conversations with the EU is perfectly normal and is not directed at the US”.
Trump has threatened the European Union with new tariffs over its proposal to make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member”, suggesting the move could be considered hostile to the US.
“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, in September.
Trump dismissed the prospect of Canada joining the EU as “laughable” and called the US’s northern neighbour a “terrible trade partner”.

Italy approves 2027 budget bill with newborn fund, energy cost measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:52:18 UTC
01:52:18 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's Cabinet approved the country's 2027 budget bill on Wednesday, including a fund for newborns and measures to reduce electricity and gas costs for households and businesses, local media reported.
The budget provides for a state contribution of €100 ($116) annually for each newborn from 2027 until the child turns 18, according to government sources, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
The contribution will be paid into a pension savings fund.
The measure was proposed by Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti.
The Cabinet also approved a decree aimed at reducing electricity and gas costs for households and businesses.
The measure sets a price cap of €58.9 ($68.5) per megawatt-hour, with an application period of 12 to 18 months.
Other measures on the Cabinet's agenda included a legislative decree to reform the craft sector and another to reorganize regulations governing outdoor seating areas.
The budget bill is part of the government's planned €23.5 billion package of measures for 2027, according to the draft budgetary plan previously submitted to the European Commission and the Italian parliament.

Reservists Party's last shot at Knesset: military ballots could upend election results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:51:33 UTC
01:51:33 KST

As the hours pass, it appears that the only party still below the electoral threshold with a possible path into the Knesset is the joint Reservists-Economic Party list led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha.
With 85.6% of votes counted, nearly 128,000 ballots have been cast for the list, which runs under the Hebrew ballot letters "די" (Dalet-Yod). That means the party needs approximately 57,500 additional votes to cross the electoral threshold, estimated at around 185,000 votes.
The chances of the two candidates crossing the threshold are slim, but difficult to assess precisely. While Hendel and Zelekha have so far received only about 2.6% of the general vote, their support could be higher among the double-envelope ballots, which include votes cast by soldiers and other eligible voters outside their regular polling stations.
One reason is that Zionist parties traditionally receive stronger support in these ballots. Another is Hendel's direct appeal to military reservists.
In a ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth poll of reservists published on August 21, Hendel, who was then allied with Hili Tropper, received support equivalent to nine Knesset seats, representing more than 5% of respondents. Although that survey offers little indication of his current standing, it may suggest that the support Hendel sought to cultivate among reservists does exist.
Another ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth survey, published on October 9 among first-time voters ages 18 to 22, gave Hendel and Zelekha six seats, equivalent to 3.68% of the vote. Because this demographic is also relevant to the double-envelope count, the findings provide another indication that the list could receive a higher share of the remaining votes.
If Hendel and Zelekha secure approximately 12% of the votes still outstanding, they are expected to cross the electoral threshold. That remains a significant hurdle given their relatively weak performance among the general electorate, but the possibility cannot be ruled out entirely. All television exit polls had projected that their joint list would fail to enter the Knesset.
If the Reservists-Economic Party manages to overcome the odds and cross the threshold, the parties currently positioned to lose seats, based on the count of 93% of regular polling stations and before the double-envelope ballots are counted, are Shas, Beyachad, the Joint List and Yashar!.
Politically, that would reduce Eisenkot's bloc to 46 seats and leave Netanyahu's bloc with 52. The Arab parties would hold 18 seats, although that figure could also decline as the double-envelope ballots are counted.
Hendel and Zelekha have deliberately avoided aligning themselves with either political bloc. The Reservists Party chairman told ynet Tuesday that he wanted a Zionist government, one that would depend on neither ultra-Orthodox nor Arab parties. He also said he did not want Netanyahu to remain prime minister.
During the election campaign, Hendel said he would support whichever bloc won the largest number of Zionist votes. Because he does not consider the ultra-Orthodox parties Zionist, that position could lead him to recommend Eisenkot to form the next government. In any event, without support from the Arab parties, such a recommendation would have limited practical significance.
Conversely, if Hendel and Zelekha join Netanyahu, he would need just five additional seats to reach a 61-member Knesset majority. That would likely trigger intense efforts to persuade lawmakers from the change bloc to defect. The change bloc, however, could still rely on the Arab parties to defeat the government.
Hendel said Tuesday evening that he was waiting for the double-envelope ballots to be counted. "By the end of the week, we'll know the results from the IDF polling stations," he said. "We saw incredible momentum. Let's see the actual results. In any case, we fought very, very hard, and we are fighters who work hard. We will fulfill our ambitions for the State of Israel and the Jewish people. Nobody here is giving up."

US sways more countries to oppose UN resolution condemning its Cuba embargo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:51:19 UTC
01:51:19 KST

Cuba wins UN vote against US embargo with weakest backing in 30 years
- The UN General Assembly passed a resolution calling for an end to the US embargo on Cuba, with 130 votes for, 17 against and 25 abstentions.
- Support for Cuba was the weakest in 30 years, as US pressure, sanctions and an oil blockade added to the island’s economic crisis.
- The vote followed a heated UN row, with Cuban and US officials trading insults and accusing each other of lies, coercion and corruption.
AI generated
NEW YORK - The UN General Assembly on Oct 28 adopted a new resolution calling for an end to the US embargo against Cuba, although support for the communist-ruled island fell to its lowest level in three decades.
Nearly every year since 1992 similar resolutions have been put to a vote and passed, but support for the measure in 2026 was markedly lower.
The resolution, which has called for lifting the economic, trade and financial embargo against the island, received 130 votes in favour, with 17 against and 25 abstentions.
It was the lowest level of support since 1995.
The debate for 2026, however, is taking place amid a major new pressure campaign by Washington against Cuba, including an oil blockade and broad sanctions that have severely crippled Cuba’s economy.
In recent weeks, Havana accused Washington of mounting a diplomatic offensive to pressure countries into withdrawing their support for the Cuban resolution.
“The world has once again spoken out overwhelmingly against the blockade, even despite the most blatant pressure and blackmail from the US to change the course of this vote,” Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel said in a celebratory post on X on Oct 28, later adding that the US engages in “gangster-like coercion.”
Speaking in New York, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez accused Washington of seeking to “determine the nation’s destiny” and “seize” its wealth.
In the minutes before the vote, US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz denied that Cuba was under a blockade and said “the plight of the Cuban people is exclusively the fault of this corrupt communist regime.”
“The reality is, today as we speak, there is no ring of US Navy warships around Cuba. Their ports are open. In recent months, data shows that shipments have arrived,” from around the world, he added.
The vote came a day after a dramatic shouting match on the floor of the UN General Assembly that at one point saw Rodriguez approach Waltz and shout, “You are a liar!” as Waltz shouted for him to back away.
Amid the interruptions, the chair briefly suspended the session and instructed both countries’ representatives to return to their places.
In his speech arguing against the resolution on Oct 27, Waltz held up pictures of Cuban leaders past and present, including Diaz-Canel, wearing luxury watches, prompting the Cuban delegation to repeatedly smack their desk in protest and interrupt.
Waltz later held up a satellite images and detailed luxury estates, boats and holidays that he claimed the Castro family and Cuban officials enjoy.
“The regime can never find enough fuel for Cuban ambulances. They can never find enough fuel for Cuban buses. But when the Castro family, the elites that are sitting at that table, want to go yachting, suddenly, it’s no problem.” Waltz said.
Speaking on Fox News on Oct 28 after the vote, Waltz said that the previous day’s debate, “got a little spicy.” AFP

How US midterms could fracture bipartisan support for Israel

Breadcrumb
How US midterms could fracture bipartisan support for Israel
Washington, DC - Across the United States, many candidates who support Palestinian human rights are set to score wins in the country's midterm elections in November, reflecting a big shift in US public opinion on Israel amid the war on Gaza.
The House of Representatives will likely see an influx of progressive Democrats critical of Israel who won primaries against pro-Israel opponents.
And two Senate candidates - Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine - who have accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza are locked in close races that could see them clinch seats in the upper chamber of Congress.
Abdelhalim Abdelrahman, communication director for American Muslims for Palestine (AMP), says US voters are starting to make the connection between foreign and domestic policy.
Progressive candidates have "done an excellent job exploring the intersection between the genocide in Gaza and Israel's broader destabilising conduct in the Middle East with the affordability crisis in America", Abdelrahman told The New Arab.
Since the start of the war on Gaza, the US government has provided Israel with more than $21 billion in military aid at a time when Americans are struggling with skyrocketing inflation.
The war on Iran, which the US launched jointly with Israel, put further strain on the cost of living and pushed energy prices to record highs.
"Every single day Americans are waking up to videos and pictures of the Israeli government bombing civilian infrastructure, killing Palestinian children, spreading crimes across the Middle East," Abdelrahman said.
"Meanwhile, the average American cannot afford rent. The average American has seen their wages stagnate. This funding of the Israeli government has cost the American people tons of money."
Dwindling support for Israel
Public opinion in the US has been turning against Israel for years, polls show - a trend that was accelerated by the well-documented Israeli atrocities in Gaza over the past three years.
A Pew Research Center survey in July suggested that 63 percent of US adults have unfavourable views of the Israeli government.
"The American people have come to their own conclusions that it's a great moral hazard to this country to have a government that wilfully ignores the will of the American people," said Abdelrahman.
"Now more Americans sympathise with Palestinians. Now more Americans are calling for arms embargoes and sanctions on Israel."
During the primary season, pro-Palestine progressives won House races in districts from New York to California through Michigan and Colorado.
In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani's victory last year ushered in what appears to be a new era of progressive politics in the largest city in the US. Candidates backed by the mayor won three major House contests, ousting two staunchly pro-Israel incumbent Democrats.
Darializa Avila Chevalier - who participated in the encampment against the war on Gaza at Columbia University - defeated Adriano Espaillat.
Brad Lander, an Israel critic, won his primary against Congressman Daniel Goldman, who has been one of the most uncompromising pro-Israel Democrats.
Separately, Mamdani-backed state legislator Claire Valdez won the contest for an open US House seat.
All three are running in safe Democratic seats; they are all but certain to win in the general elections on 3 November.
In Pennsylvania, State Representative Chris Rabb, a vocal opponent of Israeli policies, also won the primary in a safe Democratic district. In Colorado, progressive candidate Melat Kiros beat incumbent Diana DeGette.
Several similar storylines played out across the country, setting the stage for the most pro-Palestine Congress in US history that will take office next year to chisel a sizable gap in the near-unanimous bipartisan support that Israel has enjoyed on Capitol Hill for decades.
AIPAC 'is on its heels'
These victories came despite tens of billions of dollars spent by pro-Israel groups - spearheaded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) - to defeat candidates who support Palestinian rights.
Usamah Andrabi, spokesperson for Justice Democrats, a leading left-wing group that backed many of the pro-Palestine candidates that won this year, said overcoming AIPAC's spending took years of organising and building awareness about the role of the pro-Israel lobby group.
In 2024, AIPAC spent record amounts of money in primaries and successfully toppled two Justice Democrats-backed incumbents - House members Cori Bush and Jamal Bowman.
Andrabi said it took multiple election cycles to turn AIPAC's endorsement into "a toxic kiss of death" for Democratic campaigns.
"We suffered some really terrible losses, but this lobby is on its heels," Andrabi said.
AIPAC has been trying to conceal its spending on behalf of candidates by funnelling money to subsidiaries with generic-sounding names, known as shell PACs - a tactic that Andrabi said shows the unpopularity of the pro-Israel group.
Andrabi told The New Arab that the rise of numerous progressive candidates across the country was a product of the anger of Democratic voters after President Donald Trump won in 2024.
"Democratic voters woke up in 2025 realising that the Democratic establishment was wholly unfit and unprepared to defend our communities against Republican extremism and fascism," he said.
Andrabi added that while Gaza may not have been a top priority for all voters, support for Israel featured heavily in many contests because candidates were able to draw a line between foreign wars and domestic issues.
"It's not that every single district and every single voter in this country, the most important issue on their mind is, 'How do we end the genocide in Gaza?' But our candidates were connecting the dots, like Darializa did, who led with the slogan of 'babies, not bombs,'" Andrabi said.
"Why are we spending billions of dollars bombing hospitals and schools and killing babies abroad when the same government is defunding our schools and our jobs and our hospitals at home, and we can't afford to put a roof over our head or food on the table?"
The progressive newcomers will increase the number of legislators in Washington who are willing to push for a break from unconditional support for Israel in US policy. However, the contingency remains a minority within the Democratic caucus.
But Andrabi said the progressive bloc will have a "monumental impact" in the next Congress by highlighting where the Democratic base stands.
As Democratic voters sour on Israel, some lawmakers who have avoided criticising the US ally throughout their years-long careers have backed measures to hold the Israeli government accountable for its abuses over the past year.
Last month, 46 out of 47 Democrats in the Senate voted for a bill to compel the State Department to investigate increasing Israeli violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killing of US citizens.
Abdelrahman, of AMP, said he hopes the next Congress upholds Washington's own laws prohibiting aid to human rights abusers.
"Previous administrations and previous iterations of the American Congress have sidestepped justice and accountability for the sake of protecting Israel, and what we hope to see is that the status quo is broken," he said.
Ali Harb is a journalist based in Washington, DC. His work focuses on US foreign policy, elections, and Arab American communities

Budget package is worth approximately 26 million euros says Meloni
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:50:28 CET
01:50:28 KST

The 2027 budget package is worth a total of approximately 26 billion euros, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni stated during a press conference following the cabinet meeting at which the bill was approved. 
She said that the abolition of road tax for most Italians gas been made structural; saying that those who dismissed it as an election-time handout are proven wrong. 
She said it applies to approximately 70% of vehicles currently on the road. 
In the budget, "we are making the vehicle tax relief structural, just as we had approved during one of our final cabinet meetings. 
"This means no road tax for small-to-medium-powered cars—up to 80 kilowatts—or for motorcycles. 
We are talking about roughly 70% of the vehicles currently on the road. 
"Many tried to downplay this measure, claiming it was merely an election-time handout—partly because it was initially set to apply only in 2027—but they will now be proven wrong; they will see in black and white exactly what we had stated all along: the measure is structural and permanent. 
"At least for as long as the center-right is in government—because, as it turns out, the center-left actually likes road tax." In the budget, she added, "we are raising the threshold for the second personal income tax (IRPEF) bracket to 55,000 euros per year." "If we could have, we would have done much more," she added. 
Meloni said the IRPEF cuts would provide a benefit of 500 euros per year. 
With previous measures regarding the personal income tax (IRPEF), the State has foregone "approximately 21 billion euros. 
Now, we are taking another step forward: we are raising the threshold for the second tax bracket—taxed at 33%—up to 55,000 euros. 
"The maximum benefit is 500 euros per year. Some might say that is still not enough—we would have liked to do more—but this must be considered alongside the steps taken previously." Meloni also said that the government would provide air conditioning for all schools, using a portion of energy-related flexibility funds. 
"We have decided to use a portion of the energy-related flexibility resources to equip all schools with air conditioning units and heat pumps, making our classrooms more comfortable. It would have been better if, in the past, resources had been invested in this—rather than in desks with wheels." She also said that the 'agreed-rent' tax rate would drop to 5%, or 1% if renting to those under 35. 
"The problem of rental housing affects all of Europe, and Italy is no exception—which is why we have launched a housing plan. 
"As part of the budget, we have included a measure whereby the flat-rate tax on 'agreed-rent' [regulated-rate] leases will drop to 5%, and to 1% for those who rent to young people up to the age of 35." Meloni also said that the budget earmarks 3.4 billion to boost the National Health Fund. 
"This budget law, like all those before it, allocates significant resources to increase the National Health Fund. 
"We are boosting it by 3.4 billion, bringing the total to 146.3 billion by 2027—another record. 
"A portion of this increase is specifically earmarked for raising the salaries of emergency room doctors, who serve on the front lines—the very place where citizens experience the public healthcare system's response on a daily basis." Meloni said five billion of the budget funds would come from banks and the Tobin tax was to increase. 
Regarding the funding measures, "about 5 billion or more will come from the financial sector"—specifically from banks and insurance companies—with a "90,000-euro exemption threshold" for cooperative banks ('popolariì) and smaller institutions, alongside an increase in the Tobin tax. 
She said the budget is not directed against anyone and she thought banks and insurance companies would understand this, even though there had been no prior deal with them. 
"There was no room to reach a prior agreement" with the financial sector—a sector I would like to thank. "I believe that banks and insurance companies also understand the situation and share" the need to "lend a hand." She emphasized that "this budget is not directed against anyone; rather, in a complex time, we have asked those with fewer difficulties to lend a hand. The State is setting a good example by implementing cuts to ministries, amounting to approximately 1 billion."

Israel's election had no clear winner: What happens next? Aluf Benn and Esther Solomon explain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:49:14 UTC
01:49:14 KST

The main lesson of Israel's election on Tuesday was that "the October 7 war did not change Israeli society," said Haaretz editor-in-chief Aluf Benn, speaking on a special post-election edition of the Haaretz Podcast.
Despite the turbulence of the past four years, he said, "at the moment of truth, people clung to the tribal loyalties, to the feeling of identity, of belonging" rather than reacting critically to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's many missteps and failures, he explained.
Together with Haaretz senior analyst Esther Solomon and podcast host Allison Kaplan Sommer, Benn analyzed the complicated coalition wrangling that will determine who steers Israel into the future, after a vote in which there was a clear majority of Israeli citizens voting against Netanyahu, but with an opposition divided between Jewish Zionist parties and Arab majority parties.
Solomon hailed the record turnout in Arab communities, noting that "the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who have had an internal debate for many, many years about whether to participate in Israeli politics or not, made a historic decision this time around to participate, and in incredible numbers, and that has changed the complexion of the Knesset."
Benn and Solomon weighed post-election scenarios, assuming the Jewish opposition parties would reject partnering with the Arab parties, which could lead to new elections or a unity government including both coalition and opposition Jewish parties.
Both are, in Benn's words, "very bad options" for the bloc headed by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot. Another election is unlikely to improve the opposition's position and could well leave it worse off, while Netanyahu has a problematic track record when it comes to reaching out across the political divide.
"The idea of Netanyahu in a national unity government where there is some kind of equal division of power and labor is just absolutely ludicrous," noted Solomon. The prime minister, she emphasized, "is a person who won't share, as they say in playgroup. He made agreements for rotating prime ministerships in the past, and then just threw it all into the trash can. This is not the kind of person that he is, and his agenda does not work cohabiting with anyone who would call themselves, you know, a liberal Democrat." This leaves Israel with "very bad options, because in both cases, Netanyahu is in power, regardless of how you call it."

Elon Musk ‘a real genius’ – Putin
Russian President Vladimir Putin has praised US entrepreneur Elon Musk as a “real genius” while hailing the launch of Russia’s Starlink rival, Rassvet.
Putin made the remarks on Wednesday while touring an exhibition of Russian technological innovations, where Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev briefed him on Rassvet (“Dawn”), a domestically developed satellite internet system designed to compete with Musk’s SpaceX network.
“Elon Musk is a genius, a real genius,” Putin said, noting that the American entrepreneur has more than 5,000 satellites in orbit.
Russia was “proud” to have begun building its own satellite network “independently,” he added.
Moscow also maintains “close contact with American partners,” including Musk, to prevent interference between satellites, according to the Russian president.
Both sides value this cooperation and continue working closely despite political issues, with Russia’s space agency Roscosmos and other companies involved, he said.
According to Shadayev, the Rassvet constellation already has more than 30 satellites in orbit.
Developed by Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, part of IKS Holding, the network began with experimental satellite launches in 2023 and 2024. Another 32 spacecraft were launched in 2026, with plans to expand the constellation to 292 satellites by the end of 2027 and around 900 by 2035.
“We have only taken the first step. But what matters is that it has been taken,” Putin said. “Now we need to move from quality to quantity,” he added.

Possible new dwarf planet identified orbiting beyond Pluto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:46:04 UTC
01:46:04 KST

Possible new dwarf planet identified orbiting beyond Pluto
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 - Scientists using a Chile-based telescope have identified an icy object orbiting beyond Pluto that may join our solar system's small roster of dwarf planets.
Researchers said the candidate, named 2026 ED138, has a diameter estimated at between roughly 370 and 930 miles (600 and 1,500 km) and is orbiting about 46 times farther from the sun than Earth. By way of comparison, Pluto orbits at an average of about 40 times farther from the sun than Earth.
The object was spotted using the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory, on the summit of the Cerro Pachón mountain in central Chile. The telescope is a joint initiative of the US National Science Foundation and US Department of Energy.
Further observations are needed to confirm that the object is a dwarf planet.
If confirmed, 2026 ED138 would join five other dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union, the global authority on classifying celestial bodies. Those are Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake, all of which orbit beyond the outermost planet Neptune, and Ceres, located in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
Based on the current data, 2026 ED138 would be among the largest of the dwarf planets.
"For me, what this demonstrates is that many exciting discoveries remain to be made with the Rubin Observatory and other telescopes," said astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard & Smithsonian, who first spotted 2026 ED138.
Pluto long was considered the solar system's ninth and outermost planet, but was reclassified by the International Astronomical Union as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it did not meet the organization's formal definition of a planet. Pluto and the new dwarf planet candidate reside in a frigid region of the solar system populated by various icy bodies.
There are still questions about the size and composition of 2026 ED138. To be considered a dwarf planet, an object must possess sufficient mass for its own gravity to pull it into a round shape. 2026 ED138 appears to have sufficient mass for that, but more observations are needed.
"The main thing we need to do is to establish the physical size of 2026 ED138," Holman said.
"When we observe with Rubin, we are seeing the sun's light reflected from the object," Holman said. "A smaller, more reflective object would show the same amount of light as a larger, less reflective object. Fortunately, by looking at longer wavelengths, with an observatory like ALMA, we can detect the light emitted by the object itself," which is helpful in measuring an object's size.
ALMA, or the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, is a powerful telescope also based in Chile.
The discovery was announced at a scientific meeting in Spokane, Washington. REUTERS

A massive line of stitches running across the back of Captain Smit Machchhar’s head has brought the severity of the Indian pilot’s injuries into focus as he received a prestigious UAE honour for his role in thwarting the mid-air cockpit attack.Far-right UK leader Tommy Robinson shared a photograph of the scar on social media, praising Machchhar for his bravery. “Not all heroes wear capes. Some wear battle scars. Hero Indian Captain Smit Machchhar. The world salutes you,” Robinson wrote.
The Indian captain and his fellow flydubai crew members were conferred the First Class Order of Zayed II by UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in recognition of their efforts to protect passengers during the September 30 incident aboard flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv.The medals were presented by Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum at a presidential reception. Machchhar was seriously injured when his co-pilot allegedly attacked him with a crash axe and stabbed him inside the cockpit. The aircraft, carrying more than 170 people, reportedly plunged nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds during the incident.
Despite being covered in blood and severely wounded, Machchhar managed to release the cockpit door lock, allowing passengers and crew members to overpower the co-pilot. Two other flydubai pilots who were travelling on board then took control of the aircraft and landed it safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

Bank of Canada raises interest rates for the first time in three years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:44:44 UTC
01:44:44 KST

Bank of Canada raises interest rates for the first time in three years
The central bank increased key rate by a quarter point as soaring energy prices push up inflation.
The Bank of Canada (BoC) has raised its key interest rate for the first time in more than three years and warned that further increases might be needed to prevent soaring energy costs from fueling broader inflation.
Wednesday’s quarter-point hike to 2.5 percent was widely expected, while the bank also ramped up its inflation forecast for 2027 to 3.1 percent from the 2 percent it had predicted in July. Growth this year is set to be 1 percent, higher than the 0.7 percent seen in July.
“With the outlook for inflation substantially higher and the economy showing resilience, an increase in the policy rate is needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalised inflation,” BoC governor Tiff Macklem said.
“There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, we will proceed carefully,” he added.
The annual inflation rate hit 3.2 percent in September, above the bank’s 1 to 3 percent target range, and was driven almost solely by higher energy and energy-related transportation costs.
Macklem said inflation was expected to end the year at 3.5 percent and stay at around 3 percent for most of 2027, before returning close to the 2 percent target by the middle of 2028.
“Governing Council agreed that risks to inflation had increased and there was less scope for monetary accommodation,” Macklem said.
The rate hike was the first since July 2023.
“We don’t expect that core measures of inflation will accelerate as much as the bank fears, particularly if global energy prices ease a little, and as a result we don’t think that the policy rate will need to move above 2.75 percent,” said Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Capital Markets.
Money markets are pricing in another 25 basis point rate cut in January and see the benchmark rate going up to 3.25 percent by December next year.
Past experience suggests that businesses will increase the cost of products and services in line with changing costs over the next year, increasing overall inflation, Macklem said.
“The combination of higher energy prices and pass-through increases the persistence of inflation,” he said, although he added that there are lingering uncertainties such as the trade rift with the United States and a faster resolution of the conflict in the Middle East.
Economists who opposed a rise said core inflation, which strips out the cost of volatile items, is still hovering at about 2 percent. They also say a rate hike could impede modest economic recovery, given US trade tensions and a weak job market.
Macklem said new US tariffs would slow the economy in the fourth quarter, but expressed confidence that growth should pick up again in 2027 as consumer spending continues, exports pick up and business investment strengthens.
After a robust annualised growth of 3.3 percent in the second quarter, the economy is likely to slow to 2 percent in the third quarter and further down to 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter, the BoC’s new monetary policy report projected.
The report, however, upgraded its gross domestic product (GDP) forecast for next year and the year after to 2 percent from 1.8 percent for both 2027 and 2028, as predicted in July.
Macklem said this additional growth would help absorb the slack, or its unused capacity, in the economy.
The BoC’s next rate decision is on December 9.

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The death toll from a collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain rose to at least 68 on Wednesday, as Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged a thorough investigation into the disaster.
Speaking at the crash site in Urda, Toledo, Sanchez said authorities would determine the cause of the accident and take action if wrongdoing was uncovered, Spanish news agency EFE reported.
"We will get to the bottom of this. If there has been negligence, it will be known," he said.
Sanchez announced three days of national mourning from Oct. 29 to 31, saying it was "unacceptable for a country like Spain" to experience two high-speed rail accidents in a single year.
He referred to another train crash in Adamuz, Cordoba, in January.
The prime minister said preliminary indications suggested the two accidents had different causes, but stressed that determining this was the responsibility of independent investigators and judicial authorities.
He pledged decisive measures to restore public confidence in Spain's railway system if safety shortcomings were identified.
Meanwhile, opposition People's Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo demanded "immediate" government and judicial investigations, insisting they be conducted "with all available resources and without interference."
Feijoo said Spain "has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," calling for a comprehensive, independent review of the country's entire railway network.
He declined to discuss political responsibility for the disaster, saying it was not the day to do so.
A minute of silence will be held at 8 pm local time (1900GMT) on Wednesday at town halls across Spain to honor the victims, according to the Spanish Federation of Municipalities and Provinces, which organized the tribute.

Likud claims election ‘stolen,’ demands probe into alleged voting fraud
Party says it is submitting hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to police, Shin Bet and election officials over alleged irregularities at Arab polling stations.
Likud has alleged widespread fraud at Arab polling stations in Israel’s election, claiming the vote was “stolen” and demanding an immediate investigation by law enforcement and electoral authorities.
In a statement, the party accused Arab parties of bribery, intimidation, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited voter-mobilization software.
Likud said it was submitting hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to the Israel Police, the Shin Bet security agency and the Central Elections Committee.
Among its allegations, the party claimed that thousands of envelopes contained cash alongside ballots for the Ra’am party. It also alleged threats against polling station officials, multiple voters entering voting booths together, voting under false identities and discrepancies between the number of ballot envelopes and recorded voters.
The statement did not identify the polling stations involved or specify how many votes were allegedly affected.
Likud called on police and the Shin Bet to investigate and bring anyone responsible for criminal offenses to justice. It also demanded that the Central Elections Committee urgently examine the allegations, arguing that the purported violations had compromised the integrity of the vote and its outcome.
The party described the alleged misconduct as a “grave assault on Israeli democracy” and citizens’ voting rights.

Ethiopia clashes drive 50,000 people into Kenya: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

Nearly 50,000 people have fled southern Ethiopia into neighboring Kenya amid fighting that erupted last week, the United Nations said Wednesday, citing figures provided by local authorities.
The figure represents a sharp jump from the 36,000 recorded on Tuesday by UNHCR, the U.N. refugee agency, in the wake of clashes between the armies of southern Ethiopia's Somali and Oromia regions.
"According to local authorities, up to an estimated 50,000 people have crossed into Kenya," said Fatima Mohammed-Cole, the UNHCR representative for Kenya.
That number could quickly change given the situation on the ground, with fresh crossings being recorded, Mohammed-Cole warned.
The unrest was sparked on Oct. 20 after a Somali regional flag was hoisted in Moyale, a city jointly administered between Somali and Oromia. Several people have died in clashes, sources told AFP on Saturday.
Many of those who had fled were women and children, Mohammed-Cole said.
"While some are staying with relatives and host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations like schools and churches," she added.
UNHCR has sent an emergency team to the region and is working with the Kenyan government, alongside other humanitarian organisations such as the Red Cross, to provide aid to those displaced.
Ethiopia, Africa's second most populous country at some 130 million people, is the scene of various armed conflicts across its vast territory.
The borderlands of its various regions, whose tracing dates back to 1991, are often the source of clashes.
For several years, the federal government has been locked in conflict with rebel movements in the Oromia and Amhara regions, the country's most populous.
After months of tensions, fighting has also broken out again in the northern Tigray region, already the scene of a devastating war from 2020 to 2022.
Diplomatic disagreements with neighbouring Eritrea have likewise led to fears of another conflict between the fractious Horn of Africa neighbors.

Unknown

16:42:06 UTC
01:42:06 KST

Ethiopian online influencers are pushing for their government to invade neighboring Eritrea and seize access to the sea, following its success against rebel and Eritrean forces in the past few weeks.
The Ethiopian army has advanced right up to the border after repelling an offensive by rebels in the northern Tigray State who were supported by Eritrean troops.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has repeatedly said that securing a base on the Red Sea is a vital national objective for Ethiopia, which lost its coastline when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.
Photo: EPA
Some online influencers say that the opportunity to invade has arrived.
“The time for military action to secure access to the sea and end the Eritrean regime security threat is now for Ethiopia,” said Jawar Mohammed, a political activist who recently launched the “Now or Never” campaign on social media.
Jawar has more than 3.5 million Facebook followers and 1.3 million on TikTok, and thousands of Ethiopians have amplified his campaign, some sharing artificial intelligence (AI)-generated images of themselves in Ethiopian military uniforms as a mark of support.
Jawar, 40, was once the leader of a protest movement that helped propel Abiy to power in 2018, but fell out with the prime minister over what he sees as an increasing shift to “one-man rule,” and was jailed for two years before fleeing the country.
Despite years of criticizing Abiy’s government from an undisclosed new location in Europe, the fighting has brought Jawar back to the government’s side.
“The Ethiopian government currently holds a military and technological advantage, supported by a highly motivated force capable of advancing its strategic goal of securing sea access,” Jawar said, adding that delays could give Eritrea time to improve its defenses.
Eliyas Kebede, 25, from Addis Ababa, also spends hours every day online, posting and creating AI-generated content to support the idea of invading Eritrea, including altered maps that show the Eritrean port of Assab as part of Ethiopia.
“I see myself as someone who tries to defend his country’s narrative,” Kebede told reporters.
He said he would like to see the “Ethiopian army advance to Asmara, oust the Eritrean government, and negotiate access to Assab.”
Not everyone agrees with his approach.
“You are a warmonger, recklessly paving the way for mass deaths,” one Facebook commenter said under an image Eliyas created of a large crowd of Eritreans warmly welcoming the Ethiopian army to Assab.
Eliyas says he does not feel guilty “at all.”
“I believe my use of AI has been somewhat successful in boosting the morale of Ethiopian army supporters,” he said.
With Ethiopia and Eritrea reinforcing troop deployments along their border, the international community has expressed mounting concern about the risk of a new war.
Ethiopia has one of the harshest media climates in the world — ranked 148th out of 180 countries and regions in the Press Freedom Index by Reporters Without Borders — so many young Ethiopians rely heavily on social media for news.
Kjetil Tronvoll, a Horn of Africa specialist at Oslo New University College, said the online campaign would not sway the government’s decision on whether to invade.
However, it can “rally the diaspora and local communities around the need for regime change in Eritrea,” Tronvoll told reporters.
Yaya Beshir, a prominent online activist who has backed the campaign from Australia, posts regularly about invading Eritrea to more than 740,000 Facebook followers.
Beshir said that forcibly seizing Eritrea’s Assab port could trigger a regional security crisis, but is unconcerned.
“Ethiopia initially prioritized a peaceful solution, but after those efforts failed, it has now turned to military means,” Yaya said.

Lai outlines goals to European group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:42:04 UTC
01:42:04 KST

Taiwan will continue to counter sabotage targeting undersea Internet cables, as well as China-directed transnational repression in collaboration with the democratic world, President William Lai (賴清德) told European lawmakers at the Presidential Office in Taipei yesterday.
The nation is a trustworthy partner to the world’s alliance of democracies and will stand steadfast in the global fight against transnational repression, Lai told a meeting with a Formosa Club delegation headed by Latvian member of the European Parliament Rihards Kols.
The Formosa Club is an inter-parliamentary group of pro-Taiwan European legislators.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan thanks the Formosa Club’s members for their support in words and action that have aided the nation and improved solidarity among liberal democracies, Lai said.
The club has repeatedly issued statements urging greater cooperation between the Legislative Yuan and the European Parliament, and support for Taiwan’s quest to participate in international frameworks, Lai said.
The European lawmakers have also expressed concern over China’s hegemonic expansion, as well as emphasized the importance of peace in the Taiwan Strait to the Indo-Pacific region and Europe, he said.
Peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region are crucial to the European economy, Lai said.
The Russian invasion of Ukraine and tensions in the Taiwan Strait are reminders that democracies must build partnerships with like-minded countries to safeguard peace, he said.
Taiwan remains committed to bolstering its defense industrial base and self-defense capabilities, and cooperating with Europe to forge secure supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors and drones, he said.
The Formosa Club’s members, who represent a diverse political spectrum, are united in their support of Taiwan, said Kols, who handed Lai the club’s joint annual resolution.
The statement was signed by more than 30 lawmakers from across Europe and issued at the annual meeting of the Formosa Club in Taipei on Saturday last week.
Europe’s support for Taiwan is a consensus that transcends party divides and will endure changes in government, Kols said.
While Taiwan and other democratic societies might have different histories and responsibilities, they nonetheless “share an interest in a world where threats do not decide whom we meet, how we trade or how our people choose their future,” he said.
The resolution was offered in this spirit, reflecting a “friendship built over time” and a “clear understanding that Europe and Taiwan have much to contribute to each other’s security,” he said.
The Baltic countries and Taiwan share a determination to control their destinies and be free of interference from hegemonic powers on their doorsteps, he said.
The resolution this year emphasizes cooperation between Taiwan and Europe to establish trustworthy supply chains in strategic industries, secure undersea cables from malicious attacks and oppose unilateral changes to the cross-strait “status quo,” he said.
The club reaffirms its support for Taipei’s bid to meaningfully participate in the proceedings of international organizations and furthering the mutually beneficial friendship between Taiwan and Europe, he said.

Chances ahead in asset guidance: PwC Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:42:03 UTC
01:42:03 KST

The Asia-Pacific region’s expanding asset management market offers Taiwan’s financial firms an opportunity to attract more wealthy clients and regional capital, but stronger investment expertise and service capabilities would be essential to compete, PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) Taiwan said in a report yesterday.
Assets under management in the region are projected to rise to US$34.5 trillion by 2030 from US$23.2 trillion in 2024, while industry revenue is expected to increase by US$47 billion, the report said.
Total client assets are forecast to reach US$154.3 trillion by 2030, up from US$107.2 trillion in 2024, and assets of high-net-worth people and mass-affluent clients are projected to reach US$52.4 trillion and US$70.1 trillion respectively, the report said.
Photo: Ge You-hao, Taipei Times
As Taiwan aims to capitalize on the opportunity by developing its capital markets and financial services into a regional wealth management hub, the government’s Asian asset management center initiative has helped increase assets under management across Taiwan’s financial industry by NT$15.24 trillion to NT$47.8 trillion (US$470.1 billion to US$1.474 trillion), exceeding its original four-year growth target of NT$14 trillion ahead of schedule, PwC Taiwan said.
As of the end of August, 26 banks had been approved to provide wealth management services to high-net-worth clients, managing NT$3.11 trillion in assets, the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) said.
The asset management special zone in Kaohsiung, which allows financial institutions to test new services, had attracted 58 institutions by the end of June. Participating banks served 6,214 wealthy clients and managed NT$728.1 billion, with pilot programs covering family offices and cross-border services, the commission’s data showed.
Taiwan’s asset management market is forecast to grow at a compound annual rate of 15.9 percent through 2030, said Jassie Chen (陳麗媛), cohead of PwC Taiwan’s Asian asset management center office.
The FSC has opened the door to private equity and private credit, and is considering easing restrictions on some offshore funds. It is also planning to overhaul real-estate investment trusts, shifting toward a fund-based structure and allowing for potential investments in infrastructure, data centers, renewable energy and healthcare facilities.
The government is also promoting exchange-traded funds and Taiwan Individual Savings Accounts to deepen capital market participation.
However, a larger market will not guarantee regional competitiveness, said Kuo Po-ju (郭柏如), financial services operations leader at PwC Taiwan.
“Market growth does not mean all players will benefit equally,” Kuo said.
Firms must improve their investment expertise, technology, talent and compliance capabilities to compete on service quality rather than price, she said.

Film chronicles Lin Chih-chieh’s basketball journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:42:02 UTC
01:42:02 KST

A new documentary about retired basketball star Lin Chih-chieh premiered in Taipei on Tuesday, tracing his journey from a young player who twice walked away from the sport to become an athlete widely admired for his discipline and longevity.
Titled The Beast, which is also Lin’s nickname, the film follows Lin’s career with Taiwan Beer, China’s Zhejiang Guangsha Lions, the Taiwanese national team and the Taipei Fubon Braves, while exploring the change in his approach to the game.
Widely considered the greatest Taiwanese basketball player, Lin retired in June following the Braves’ 107-81 defeat to the Taoyuan Pauian Pilots in Game 7 of the P.League+ Finals, drawing to a close an illustrious career that spanned more than two decades.
Photo: CNA
No other Taiwanese player has matched the longevity of Lin’s career, sports broadcaster Marc Tien says in the documentary.
That was not always easy to foresee.
The film recounted how Lin left the sport in high school and again in college before finding his way back to the game.
During his early years with Taiwan Beer in the semi-professional Super Basketball League (SBL), there was a period when he rarely turned up at the court before noon, sports journalist Huang Chi-jen says in the film.
Former Taiwan Beer captain Hsu Hao-cheng, who was responsible for driving Lin to the court, describes having a “love-hate relationship” with his teammate.
Lin says in the documentary that his move to China’s professional league was a turning point.
In unfamiliar surroundings and with few outlets for his emotions, he turned to training, he said.
When he returned to Taiwan during the offseason a year later, former Taiwan Beer teammates said he had become a different person.
Lin joined Taiwan Beer in 2003, moved to Zhejiang Guangsha in 2009 and returned to Taiwan to play for the Braves in 2019.
A member of Taiwan’s “Golden Generation,” Lin won two SBL titles with Taiwan Beer in 2007 and 2008, and three consecutive P.League+ championships with the Braves from 2021 to 2023.
Lin said the film brought back memories of teammates and different stages of his career.
“There are difficult times and low points, but you have to believe in yourself and be willing to face challenges,” he said.
Planning for the documentary began in late 2024 and the production team interviewed more than 50 people, including family members, coaches and former teammates, the Braves said.
The documentary is to debut on streaming platform MyVideo early next month before becoming available on the Braves’ YouTube channel after the team’s home-opening week. Lin’s No. 12 jersey is to be retired at a ceremony on Nov. 14.

Flavio Bolsonaro departs from Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:42:01 UTC
01:42:01 KST

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who was defeated in Brazil’s presidential election at the weekend, was on his way to Ecuador after fleeing Brazil, Argentina’s government said yesterday.
Bolsonaro, who lost the runoff election to Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday, entered Argentina on Tuesday night before boarding a flight to Ecuador, the Argentine National Directorate of Migration said on X.
The 45-year-old entered Argentina “with valid travel documents and no legal impediment,” the agency said, despite a court order banning his exit.
Photo: AFP
Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters boarded “a private flight operated by the company Baires Fly S.A. bound for the city of Guayaquil, Ecuador,” it said.
Data from the Flightradar24 Web site showed that the flight took off just after midnight yesterday from the Argentine town of Puerto Iguazu in the country’s northeast.
Baires Fly did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US media citing anonymous sources had earlier reported that Bolsonaro had arrived in the US on Tuesday.
The US Department of State and US President Donald Trump said that they backed issuing visas to Bolsonaro and his family, but did not confirm their travel plans.
The Brazilian Supreme Court banned Bolsonaro from leaving the country and ordered him to hand over his passports.
He is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity.
Bolsonaro has not acknowledged his electoral defeat, citing a decision by the court to extend polling hours.
Trump said that he approved of Bolsonaro entering the US.
“Well, I would approve,” Trump told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews on his return from a campaign trip to Texas, adding that he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina.

Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan’s efforts to create a ‘Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:42:01 UTC
01:42:01 KST

Much attention is being paid to increasing security ties between Taiwan and the Philippines, and rightfully so. The stakes are potentially existential, as explored in “ Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines need to face the common threat from Beijing” (Sept. 12, page 12).
Getting less attention is that across the board the relationship is growing stronger, and both sides appear to be planning to put more of their eggs in each other’s baskets.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) in August last year confirmed plans to open a second Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) representative office in Cebu Province.
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration
Meanwhile, the Philippines representative office, Manila Economic and Cultural Office (MECO), earlier this month opened its largest overseas Filipino worker (OFW) service center in Taipei, with plans for establishing two more in central and southern Taiwan over the next two years. It is only the third such overseas service center the Philippines has opened. MECO has maintained a strong presence in Taiwan for years with representative offices in Taipei, Taichung and Kaohsiung.
These are just the latest significant moves, but they are part of a pattern of rapidly increasing ties and mutually reinforcing interest that could have long-lasting positive implications.
GOING SOUTH
In the democratic era, Taiwanese interest in the Philippines as a way to reduce reliance on China is not new. In the 1990s, President Lee Teng-hui (李登輝) launched the “go south” policy, encouraging investment in Southeast Asia, but with only modest success in the Philippines. In 2016, one of Lee’s top trade advisors, Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文), was elected president and launched a similar New Southbound Policy, with similar results.
The election of Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr as president in 2022 brought a positive change on the Philippines side towards relations with Taiwan, which has since been matched by a similar eagerness on the Taiwanese side under Foreign Minister Lin after he was appointed in 2024 by President William Lai (賴清德).
Marcos issued a memorandum in April last year easing decades-old restrictions on official exchanges with Taiwan. This quietly opened the door for higher-level, though still unofficial, contacts between the two sides.
This change quickly bore fruit; in August, Lin led a delegation of investors to the Philippines in a “private capacity” on his regular, non-diplomatic passport. Since the two sides severed diplomatic ties in 1975, this is only the second known trip by a Taiwanese foreign minister after then-minister Chang Hsiao-yen (章孝嚴) took a “vacation” to the Philippines in 1997.
This is part of a larger context. Reportedly, American investors were also in the delegation. Just the month prior to this trip, Lin had also visited Japan. Improved relations between Taiwan and the Philippines is part of a broader integration push in the region that includes the US and Japan into a more cohesive grouping of mutually supported interests.
Lin explicitly tied his efforts to those nations, saying on Facebook: “we are actively promoting the ‘Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor,’ linking it with the US-Japan-Philippines ‘Luzon Economic Corridor’ to build more resilient supply chains together.”
In the same post he added: “I have also taken note of the recent announcement by the US and the Philippines that they will work together to establish a 4,000-acre ‘Economic Security Zone’ to strengthen supply chain security and industrial development. In my view, the US possesses world-leading technological capabilities, Taiwan has a comprehensive manufacturing base and the Philippines has abundant land and a high-quality workforce.”
That development is part of the US-led Pax Silica initiative which, according to the State Department, “hails a new economic security consensus ensuring aligned partners build the AI ecosystem of tomorrow — from energy and critical minerals to high-end manufacturing and models.”
That statement lists 25 signatories, which of course does not include China, and rather forlornly Taiwan sits at the bottom listed as a “Non-Signatory Participant” with an asterisk noting that “Taiwan has endorsed the Pax Silica declaration principles via the Joint Statement on the Pax Silica Declaration and US-Taiwan Economic Security Cooperation.”
Such is Taiwan’s international standing that, despite being a key player in the “AI ecosystem of tomorrow,” it participates only through a separate endorsement rather than as a signatory.
DESTINATION: PHILIPPINES
Lin’s “Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor” remains ill-defined, but two things jump out. One is the addition of a Cebu office, and the other is his comment about “abundant land and a high-quality workforce.”
Cebu is far from Luzon geographically, but its central location makes it a major hub for domestic shipping and inter-island logistics. It is possible that Lin’s strategic calculation is to use his economic corridor plan to extend the US-Japan-Philippines efforts geographically in a way that is both complementary, but separate enough that it highlights Taiwan’s importance.
Taiwan lacks land and is increasingly desperate for a “high-quality workforce,” so, unsurprisingly, Lin sees the opportunities.
Quietly, but increasingly, Taiwan’s entire manufacturing ecosystem has grown reliant on Filipino talent. Contrary to expectations, this is happening at every level, from the lowest-tech to the highest.
The National Immigration Agency’s August report lists 214,806 Filipinos in Taiwan. The majority work in manufacturing, often starting at low-level positions. However, over time they become essential skilled technicians and managers, able to communicate in Mandarin, English and Tagalog.
Lin is likely counting on this for his “Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor.” Many Taiwanese investors already have a solid base of well-trained Filipino experts who know how to run their factory floors and manage the business.
Though exact numbers are not available, older estimates put the number of Filipinos working in white-collar high-tech positions in the low thousands, but this number is likely higher today. When I used to live near the Central Taiwan Science Park, it was not uncommon to run into Filipino engineers and technicians.
Crucially, more are being trained and prepared for just such roles. According to a July press release from the Ministry of Education, the number of Filipino students in Taiwan rose 78.7 percent between 2022 and last year, reaching 5,536. They are primarily studying engineering, information and communication technology (ICT), manufacturing, business management and medical and health sciences.
The AI ecosystem and supply chains stretch across the planet. A Filipino engineer or ICT expert trained in Taiwan, with Mandarin skills and excellent English is worth their weight in gold both locally, and even more so if they want to expand into the Philippines or English-speaking nations such as the US.
Much of China’s manufacturing dominance was originally built on Taiwanese expertise and capital, but once trained and capitalized, China favored local competitors over the Taiwanese investors. Taiwanese investment helped Malaysia develop into a significant mid-tier player in the semiconductor industry, and continues to fuel Vietnam’s growth in manufacturing.
Lin’s “Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor” has potential. Taiwan has the know-how, abundant capital, a desperate need for cheap land, energy and water and access to significant Filipino human capital to make it all work. With a presence in Manila in Luzon and future presence in the key logistics node of Cebu, Taiwan will be well positioned to facilitate investment expansion.
However, much depends on the Philippines making itself a desirable investment destination. Reviews vary widely in their assessment. In 2018 the US News & World Report named the Philippines as the “best country to invest in,” and CEO Magazineranked it seventh out of the top 10 best countries in 2020. Less positively, the Philippines ranked 95th out of 190 countries in the 2020 World Bank Report on Doing Business, though that was a jump of 29 spots from the year prior.
Ramped up interest by the US and Japan in investing in the Philippines could help smooth the way. Their financial and diplomatic muscle could pressure the Philippines to continue to make positive changes in its investment environment.
Donovan’s Deep Dives is a regular column by Courtney Donovan Smith (石東文) who writes in-depth analysis on everything about Taiwan’s political scene and geopolitics. Donovan is also the central Taiwan correspondent at ICRT FM100 Radio News, co-publisher of Compass Magazine, co-founder Taiwan Report (report.tw) and former chair of the Taichung American Chamber of Commerce. Follow him on X: @donovan_smith.
