Lawyers for ‘King of the South’ Try to Chip Away at U.S. Drug Trafficking Case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:09:00 UTC
01:09:00 KST

Attorneys for alleged South American drug trafficker Sebastián Marset have asked a federal judge to halt the search of a potentially pivotal cellular phone until the U.S. government explains how it took control of the device from Bolivia.
Marset, a Uruguayan national and self-proclaimed “King of the South,” was arrested in March in a pre-dawn raid in Santa Cruz, Bolivia. Soon after his arrest, he was expelled to Peru and then whisked to the U.S. where he faces money laundering, drug trafficking and narco terrorism charges.
Law enforcement officers in Bolivia seized three phones from the house where they arrested Marset. However, it has emerged that they seized a fourth phone from an adjacent house.
Defense lawyers say in their motion — dated October 23 — that “it is impossible” for them to “be certain as to the timing of the search and whether it was done at the behest of the DEA [Drug Enforcement Administration] or was otherwise valid under Bolivian law.”
They argue that they weren’t notified about the fourth phone, which was a potential key piece of evidence for months, hampering their efforts and raising questions about the integrity of the operation.
The phone was sent to the DEA in mid-April, but didn’t appear in any court documentation shared with the defense team until late July.
“No contemporaneous report of the chain of custody appears to have been prepared,” Marset’s defense team wrote to U.S. District Judge Rossie Alston Jr., who presides in the Eastern District of Virginia.
The DEA confirmed to the defense team, the filing said, that it had extracted data from the phone without a court order. The agent "theorized that the search did not require a court order because the defendant had previously ‘consented’ to the search of his other devices."
The lead prosecutor did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication. The DEA said it “does not comment on allegations.”
The prosecution has alleged that the four phones were used by Marset to access cryptocurrency accounts.
Crypto accounts have featured prominently in pre-trial disputes. Marset’s legal team alleges that DEA agents tried to trick his elderly mother into handing over passphrases for accounts that hold his digital currency, and later asked him to “donate” his $4 million in crypto assets.
“A seizure does not require asking the detainee’s mother for a photo of a notebook containing access phrases, which are used to move funds, not to secure them. Such contradictions warrant an explanation, which has yet to be provided,” Santiago Moratorio, Marset’s Uruguayan attorney, told OCCRP.
In a September court proceeding, the lead DEA agent denied the allegation that they had asked for a donation.
The Marset case is being closely watched across South America because of his connections to Colombia, and allegations that he had protection in Paraguay and Bolivia where more than a dozen officials were recently detained under suspicion that they had ties to Marset.
The State Department recently revoked visas for 12 Bolivian government, police, and political figures. It cited the need to defend against corruption and narco-trafficking, and said another unidentified nine Bolivians would be denied visas.
Marset’s lawyers argue that the initial charge of money laundering is invalid because it involved a single wire transfer between Portugal and China that did not involve the servers of a U.S. bank. The lawyers say Marset never trafficked drugs to the U.S. and the narco terror groups cited in court were not designated as such at the time of his dealing with them.
In pre-trial conferences, Marset’s defense team has challenged several elements of the case, trying to get the judge to strike down portions of the indictments and weaken the prosecution. Alston has said he would rule on these motions by November 6.

Israeli soldier visiting UK faces war crimes complaint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:06:17 UTC
01:06:17 KST

Israeli soldier visiting UK faces war crimes complaint
The Hind Rajab Foundation files complaint against an active Israeli soldier, escalating its global accountability campaign.
The Hind Rajab Foundation has filed a criminal complaint in the United Kingdom against Lidor Dafna, an Israeli reservist believed to be visiting the country, over alleged war crimes committed during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Dafna, who served in the 603rd Combat Engineering Battalion, is accused of participating in the demolition of a flour-producing facility in May 2025 at a time when Israel’s blockade of Gaza was leading to widespread starvation.
The foundation said footage posted by Dafna on social media shows an Israeli military bulldozer demolishing wheat silos in southern Gaza.
The filing is the latest move by the Brussels-based organisation, named after Hind Rajab, a five-year-old girl killed alongside her relatives when Israeli forces fired on their vehicle in Gaza City in January 2024.
By transforming self-published digital content into evidence for criminal complaints, the foundation is testing whether legal systems in other countries may be used to hold Israeli soldiers accountable for alleged crimes.
Natacha Bracq, head of litigation at the foundation, explained the urgency of the UK filing to Al Jazeera.
“If the authorities let him leave, he [Dafna] will go back and commit more crimes. When a state waves a suspect through its airport, knowing what is documented, it is breaching its obligations to prevent and punish genocide.”
A Counter Terrorism Policing spokesperson told Al Jazeera that its war crimes team has received 250 referrals “relating to the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict since 7 October, 2023”.
They would not comment on specific cases.
“At this time, there is no UK-based investigation into any matters relating to this particular conflict,” they said. “In addition, and as part of the UK’s international obligations, information provided to CTP relating to alleged war crimes or crimes against humanity may also be passed to the International Criminal Court (ICC), where relevant and appropriate in order to aid any of their ongoing investigations. A small number of referrals received by CTP since 7 October, 2023, relating to the Israel-Hamas conflict have been passed across to the ICC.”
For the families of victims in Gaza, the pursuit of justice through international channels is a response to the failure of internal Israeli accountability mechanisms.
Speaking from Gaza, the 45-year-old grandmother and namesake of Hind dismissed internal Israeli military investigations.
“The occupation [Israel] claims that it opens criminal justice or an investigation for their soldiers, [but] we are certainly not very interested in this topic,” she stated. “They just justify their positions to the world, … but actually on the ground, I don’t think anything happens.”
The foundation’s broader goal resonates deeply with families seeking justice for children killed during the war.
“Hind is not the first child in Gaza. Hind means surely there are many crimes like hers and more,” her grandmother added. “We support anyone who speaks in the name of childhood [and always supports] the Palestinian child.”
Turning social media posts into evidence
The Hind Rajab Foundation’s methodology relies heavily on material published by Israeli soldiers themselves.
“Our starting point is simple: Israeli soldiers documented their own crimes. They’ve posted tens of thousands of photos and videos from Gaza and Lebanon on TikTok, Instagram, X and Telegram, often with their faces and names attached,” Bracq said.
This digital footprint requires rigorous processing to become potentially admissible in legal cases.
“Our collection and analysis follow the Berkeley Protocol on Digital Open Source Investigations. Then the real work starts: verification. We geolocate every frame against satellite imagery, matching buildings, roads, water towers, destruction patterns,” Bracq said, noting that investigators then cross-reference military sources to tie a suspect to a documented act.
The Berkeley Protocol, developed by the Human Rights Center at the University of California in Berkeley and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, sets out standards for collecting, verifying, analysing and preserving digital material.
Khaled al-Shouli, an international lawyer registered with the Jordanian Bar Association who represents Palestinian victims before the International Criminal Court (ICC), said social media material could be valuable evidence.
“Its value does not decrease simply because it is a post on the internet, nor does it become decisive simply because it has spread,” al-Shouli said.
He stressed, however, that answering fundamental questions about the source, time and place is essential.
“The crucial difference is the transition from proving the occurrence of the crime to proving the responsibility of a specific person for it as the appearance of a soldier in a place does not alone prove his commission of the crime,” he said.
Legal action across borders
The foundation’s complaints have prompted authorities in several countries to question Israeli military personnel.
Bracq pointed to a significant breakthrough in Belgium, where a complaint filed by the foundation led federal police to detain and question two Israeli soldiers. Both were subsequently released.
“That arrest matters beyond the two individuals involved. It demonstrated that universal jurisdiction is not a theoretical instrument but one that puts suspects in a police station within hours, and the Belgian federal prosecutor has since referred the case onward to the International Criminal Court,” she stated.
Similar actions have disrupted travel for an Israeli in North America. In Canada, former combat soldier Guy Hochman was detained and interrogated for six hours at Toronto Pearson Airport after a complaint was filed accusing him of war crimes and incitement to genocide. He later said his Canadian visa had been revoked.
“These are ruptures in a system of impunity: the moment Israelis calculate that travelling abroad carries a real legal risk,” Bracq emphasised.
Al-Shouli clarified the legal architecture supporting these moves, distinguishing between national courts and the ICC.
“The Palestinian case relies on a set of matters that fall under the category of territorial jurisdiction over crimes committed in the Palestinian territories and not on absolute universal jurisdiction,” he noted. “This distinction is important because the multiplicity of paths expands the opportunities for accountability and does not leave it hostage to one institution.”
Limits of legal action
A Hind Rajab Foundation complaint in Brazil highlighted both the potential and the limitations of filing cases against Israelis in the courts of other countries.
In January 2025, Brazilian authorities issued an urgent order to arrest and investigate an Israeli soldier accused of planting explosives and systematically demolishing entire civilian neighbourhoods in Gaza.
While the case attracted international attention, al-Shouli cautioned against overstating its significance. Although a Brazilian judge ordered an investigation after the foundation’s complaint, the Israeli soldier left the country with the assistance of Israeli authorities before he could be detained or questioned.
The case, he explained, highlighted “the gap between opening an investigation and the ability to secure the suspect’s attendance to the justice of the court in practice”.
Political climates heavily influence these legal instruments. Bracq acknowledged that “political will does determine whether a warrant is executed” but countered that “international crimes carry no statute of limitations.” She noted that relentless documentation ensures “no future window of opportunity finds the evidence missing.”
Al-Shouli viewed government transitions pragmatically. “Changing governments opens practical windows for accountability through improving judicial cooperation,” he noted. “But we prefer to describe them as windows to activate the law, not as loopholes in it.”
Expanding the targets
The foundation is actively expanding its legal efforts beyond individual soldiers to companies and individuals involved in supplying weapons to Israel.
“Our focus has already expanded well beyond front-line soldiers because the strategy must evolve with the genocide itself and with our evidence,” Bracq stated. “We now target the suppliers of the tools of the crime, including companies involved in producing weapons for Israel.”
She cited a recent criminal complaint in Poland against a state-owned TNT producer. “No one gets impunity, from the trigger-puller to the decision-maker to the supplier,” she declared.
For the legal teams, managing the expectations of devastated families remains paramount.
“My professional responsibility begins with not selling false hopes and fake hopes to the victims. It is not permissible for me to tell a family that lost its children that depositing a file has restored its right,” al-Shouli stated. “What we ask for is not sympathy alone but rights that can be proven, claimed and accounted for, and justice will be done.”
“Universal jurisdiction is our instrument, not our objective. Our objective is justice and accountability,” Bracq concluded.
“The generation that posted their own atrocities online now has to live with the knowledge that those posts are forever evidence and that a complaint may be waiting in the next country whose border they cross.”

Global cyber incidents hit record high in 1st half of 2026: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:03:18 UTC
01:03:18 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
 Serious cyber incidents worldwide reached a record high in the first half of 2026, with researchers warning that artificial intelligence could further increase the scale and speed of attacks, ANSA reported Wednesday, citing Italy’s information security association Clusit.
The association’s updated 2026 report, presented in Verona, recorded 4,911 serious incidents globally in January-June, up 71% from the same period last year and 105% from the preceding six months.
The figure represented 93% of all incidents recorded in 2025, with an average of 819 incidents per month.
In Italy, known incidents fell to 245 from 280 in the first half of 2025, accounting for about 5% of the global total. However, incidents classified as having “high” severity rose by nearly 20 percentage points to 57% of the country’s total.
Manufacturing became Italy’s hardest-hit sector as financially motivated cybercrime against businesses increased and hacktivism, hacking intended to advance political, social, or ideological causes, declined.
Malware accounted for 43% of incidents in Italy, compared with 22.7% in 2025.
Clusit researchers said improved security procedures and defenses following Italian cybersecurity legislation and the EU's NIS2 rules could partly explain the decline in hacktivism.
The report also highlighted early signs of “agentic hacking,” in which AI agents perform attack tasks with increasing autonomy.
Researchers warned that coordinated groups of AI agents could eventually carry out fully automated attacks, adapting their strategies and combining techniques to exploit vulnerabilities in organizations’ systems.
They called for clearer responsibilities, adaptive governance and defenses capable of responding rapidly and automatically to AI-driven threats.
“The data tells us that the nature of risk is changing,” Clusit President Anna Vaccarelli said.
She urged organizations to treat cybersecurity as essential to business continuity and a shared responsibility supporting national resilience.

Davina Hayles, MSF head of mission in Haiti

Dolores Huerta, US labor leader and force for human rights, dies at 96
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:01:04 UTC
01:01:04 KST

Dolores Huerta, US labor leader and force for human rights, dies at 96
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 - Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers (UFW) with Cesar Chavez and fought legislators and powerful growers in the US to improve the lives of a previously powerless constituency, died on Wednesday at the age of 96, her family said in a statement.
Huerta was one of the foremost women in US labor history, serving the UFW as chief negotiator, strike organizer, lobbyist and reformer during its heyday in the 1960s and '70s in California's agriculture-rich Central Valley.
Thanks to the contracts the UFW negotiated, farmworkers won job security, healthcare, retirement plans, a credit union and job-specific benefits such as guaranteed rest periods, toilets in the fields, clean drinking water and protection from pesticides.
Huerta was credited with giving the UFW its slogan "Si, se puede," the loose translation of which, "Yes, we can," was later used by Barack Obama during his successful 2008 presidential campaign.
She remained a regular on the college lecture circuit into her 90s, speaking out against the immigration policies of President Donald Trump. During elections she traveled the country, endorsing candidates and registering voters.
UFW co-founder Chavez, who died in 1993 and was the face of the organization, was a seventh-grade dropout and former grape picker with a man-of-the-soil appeal who espoused the non-violent philosophies of Gandhi and Martin Luther King, with a nod to Emiliano Zapata, a leader of Mexico's peasant revolution in the early 20th century.
But Chavez had a dark side. In 2026, Huerta was one of a number of women who came forward with accounts of how they had been sexually assaulted by him, in some cases when they were minors. Huerta said that he had pressured her into having sex one time, and another time raped her. Both encounters resulted in pregnancies, and Huerta said she arranged for the babies to be raised by others.
OUT OF THE SPOTLIGHT
While Chavez was recruiting, going on well-publicized hunger strikes and being embraced by liberal lawmakers and celebrities, the diminutive, college-educated Huerta handled negotiating with growers, lobbying legislators and other business for the UFW.
She was arrested more than 20 times, subjected to death threats and other harassment. She suffered broken ribs and a damaged spleen when beaten by baton-wielding San Francisco police in a 1988 protest against the policies of George H.W. Bush during his presidential campaign.
In an interview with PBS in 2012, before the assault accusations against Chavez came to light, Huerta said she had been fine with him taking the spotlight as she wanted to focus on helping people rather than gaining fame.
"He said, 'One of us is going to have to be the spokesperson. Are you all right if I'm the spokesperson?' Of course, I said yes."
STANDING UP
Huerta was born in Dawson, New Mexico, to a Mexican immigrant family, and spent much of her youth in Stockton, California, after her parents divorced. Her father was a miner, laborer, union activist and state lawmaker; her mother raised three children while buying and running a hotel for low-income people in Stockton.
Huerta's mother instilled a spirit of activism in her daughter. Huerta was into her second marriage when she became a schoolteacher, but that career did not last long.
"I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said. "I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children."
She registered voters in Stockton and founded the Agricultural Workers Association before meeting Chavez and joining him in starting the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. In 1965 they began a series of strikes and boycotts that would last five years against various California grape growers and eventually spread to lettuce growers.
During that period the organization evolved into the United Farm Workers and picked up support from King and New York Senator Robert F. Kennedy. Not eating a grape — unless it had a union label — became a political statement in the United States.
The boycotts and strikes sometimes became contentious. In addition to industry opposition, the UFW found itself up against California Governor Ronald Reagan, who denounced the UFW as immoral and made a point of eating grapes on television.
COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
One by one, growers began signing contracts with the UFW and in 1975 Huerta's work also helped bring about another victory — passage of the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act, the first law in the US that gave farmworkers collective bargaining rights.
Huerta said that being a woman gave her an edge at the negotiating table with growers.
"They really didn't know how to respond because they couldn't do the usual forceful type of thing," she told PBS. "And when you would bring up to them and show them the conditions that the workers were working under, and they were kind of embarrassed, actually."
In 2012, Obama presented Huerta with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the country's highest civilian award.
Her life was the basis of the award-winning film "Dolores" that was shown at the Sundance Film Festival in 2017.
While the UFW's influence abated, Huerta's activism did not. In 2002 she established the Dolores Huerta Foundation for community activism with her daughter Camila Chavez as its executive director. She pushed for changes in immigration laws, voter registration, women's rights and Obama's healthcare reform.
Huerta, who said she remained close to the two children she had with Chavez, also had two children from her first marriage, five from her second and four from a long-term relationship with Richard Chavez, brother of Cesar and another key UFW figure, who died in 2011. REUTERS

A coalition of former civil servants who worked in the Biden administration and resigned over Gaza genocide has called on candidates for the 2028 US presidential election to pledge that they will bar any former officials responsible for enabling Israel's genocide from serving in future administrations.
In an open letter on Wednesday, they urged prospective contenders to sign an explicit commitment refusing to hire, promote, or appoint any political appointees who acted as architects, defenders, or key enablers of unconditional military and diplomatic support for Israel in its genocide of Palestinians.
"Senior Biden administration officials who were architects of the Gaza policy are now actively white-washing their own roles in enabling genocide," the letter said, accusing the US officials of violating US and international law by providing American weapons to Israel in the latter’s indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks in Gaza.
"The result: tens of thousands of Palestinians were killed; the remaining population was deliberately starved and displaced; and the entire territory was decimated. When faced with the opportunity to stand up in defense of our laws, they not only stayed silent, but worked resolutely in pursuit of illegal and wrongful ends in violation of both US and international law," it added.
The letter highlighted that internal warnings from thousands of US civil servants began as early as October 2023, urging the Biden administration to abide by federal statutes governing arms transfers and to call for an immediate ceasefire.
"The senior officials who turned a blind eye to the facts, lied to the American public, actively repressed internal dissent, and enabled America’s material support for Israel’s genocide have no business holding positions of influence in any future administration. They should not be welcomed in any institution from which they may exert influence over the formulation of foreign policy, or the education of America’s next generation of leaders," the former officials demanded.
The letter comes as a new UN inquiry says Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the occupied West Bank, while continuing to commit "genocide" against Palestinians in besieged Gaza despite US-brokered truce.
The commission said that Israel had committed "genocide" in Gaza and that top Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu incited these acts.
Since 2023, Israel's military has uprooted nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people in its genocide, according to Gaza's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
However, experts and studies indicate that the death toll is an undercount, with the actual figure potentially reaching 200,000 in Gaza, 60 percent of which remains under Israeli occupation.
The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Israel also faces a genocide case at the International Court of Justice for its war on the enclave.
Washington allocates $3.8 billion in annual military funding to its long-standing ally Israel.
Since October 2023, the US has spent more than $22 billion supporting Israel's actions in Gaza and neighbouring countries.
Since 1946, the US has provided over $310 billion in military and economic assistance to Israel, adjusted for inflation, according to the American think tank, Council on Foreign Relations.
Acknowledge US complicity
Addressing the chronic absence of accountability within the foreign policy establishment, the signatories warned that many former officials are already positioning themselves to re-enter government institutions, policy think tanks, and academic bodies to shape future American diplomacy.
"We must ensure these officials can never again wield power in the name of the American people," the signatories demanded, calling on candidates for the 2028 presidential nomination to commit to not hire any administration official directly responsible for enabling Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
The proposed pledge requires aspiring presidential nominees to acknowledge Washington's complicity in facilitating civilian casualties through weapons supplies, diplomatic protection, and the suppression of debate, while ensuring that those directly responsible for enabling the genocide in Gaza are permanently excluded from future policymaking.
The signatories of the letter said they support ongoing efforts to identify officials from the former administration whose actions amount to complicity in violations of US and international law.
"We also expect that former officials who do not fit into this category, and who aspire to return to government, will be able to honestly account for their own roles in the administration's Gaza policy," they said.

Falklands defences robust despite ice ship gap

Britain’s military presence in the South Atlantic is at the appropriate level for the defence of the Falkland Islands, and the absence of an ice patrol ship does not change that, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what assessment has been made of the potential impact on Argentine posture in the region of having no ice patrol ship available.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Ministry of Defence is committed to maintaining a defensive military presence in the South Atlantic to ensure the protection of the Falkland Islands and South Atlantic Islands. Our defences in the South Atlantic are robust, consisting of air, land, and maritime forces with a strong permanent presence on the Falkland Islands. I am confident that our military presence is at the appropriate level for the defence of the Islands, and we keep this under constant review.”
British forces in the South Atlantic are based around Mount Pleasant Complex on East Falkland, where Typhoons of 1435 Flight hold quick reaction alert, supported by a Voyager tanker, an A400M and Sky Sabre ground based air defence. A River class offshore patrol vessel is forward deployed to the region and the islands are garrisoned by a roulement infantry company.
HMS Protector carries out survey and inspection work under the Antarctic Treaty and has no combat role, though her presence has long been part of the pattern of British activity in the South Atlantic. She last deployed south in the 2024-25 season and will miss a second consecutive Antarctic season this year.

Diets high in fat and sugar are linked to impulsiveness in people with borderline personality disorder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

A study of adults with borderline personality disorder in the Chicago area found that those who ate more foods high in both saturated fat and added sugar tended to report greater motor impulsiveness, a tendency to act without thinking. Higher saturated fat intake was also linked to more risk-taking on a gambling task, but diet was not associated with the overall severity of borderline personality disorder symptoms. The paper was published in Nutritional Psychiatry.
Borderline personality disorder, or BPD, is a mental health condition characterized by intense emotions, unstable relationships, difficulties with self-image, and impulsive behavior. People with BPD often struggle to regulate their emotions and may engage in risky behaviors, such as excessive spending, substance misuse, or binge eating. Although specialized psychotherapy can help, about half of adults with BPD do not respond to it, highlighting the need for additional approaches.
One potentially important but largely overlooked factor is nutrition. Research has linked diets high in saturated fat and added sugar, which are common in processed foods, to greater impulsivity. Such foods may also influence the brain’s reward system and inflammatory processes, potentially affecting how people experience and manage emotions.
At the same time, people may turn to highly palatable foods in response to stress or negative emotions, suggesting that the relationship between diet and psychological functioning could work in both directions. Research on diet in BPD is limited, but one study found that women with BPD ate fewer omega-3 fatty acids and fewer foods typical of a Mediterranean diet than healthy controls. In two clinical trials, omega-3 supplements combined with the medication valproic acid appeared to reduce some BPD symptoms, particularly anger.
Study authors Sophie Boutouis and Jon E. Grant of the University of Chicago wanted to examine the relationship between saturated fat and added sugar consumption and BPD symptoms, as well as differences in diet across demographic groups. They hypothesized that higher intake of saturated fat and added sugar would be associated with more severe BPD symptoms, more co-occurring psychiatric disorders, poorer decision-making, and greater impulsivity.
The participants were adults from the Chicago area who enrolled in a clinical trial testing the antipsychotic lumateperone as a treatment for BPD. To take part, they had to be between 18 and 65 years old, have a primary diagnosis of BPD, and have symptoms above a set severity threshold; people with schizophrenia, bipolar I disorder, or moderate or severe substance use disorders were excluded. The analysis used data collected at the trial’s first visit, before treatment began.
Of 60 eligible participants, 57 completed the diet questionnaire and were included in the analysis. Their average age was 32, about 72% were women, and about half identified as white.
Participants reported how often they had eaten various foods high in saturated fat and added sugar over the past year using the Dietary Fat and Free Sugar – Short Questionnaire, which produces separate scores for foods high in saturated fat, foods high in added sugar, and foods high in both. They also completed the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale and the Cambridge Gambling Task, a computerized test of decision-making in which risk-taking is measured by how many points participants bet. Clinicians assessed co-occurring psychiatric disorders and suicidal thoughts using the Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview and rated the severity of BPD symptoms over the past week.
After accounting for age, race, depression, and suicidal thoughts, participants who ate more saturated fat tended to bet more on the gambling task, indicating greater risk-taking. After accounting for age, those who ate more foods high in both saturated fat and added sugar tended to report greater motor impulsiveness. Added sugar intake on its own was not linked to any of the impulsivity, decision-making, or symptom measures.
Contrary to the main hypothesis, diet was not associated with the overall severity of BPD symptoms, other aspects of impulsivity, or other aspects of decision-making. The authors note that diet was measured over the past year while symptom severity was measured over the past week, which may help explain why no link emerged.
The researchers also found demographic differences. Black participants reported eating more saturated fat than participants from several other groups, and people who ate more foods high in both fat and sugar tended to be older. Participants without depression or recent suicidal thoughts reported eating more saturated fat than those with these conditions, and those with a substance use disorder reported eating less added sugar.
“Saturated fat and added sugar consumption in the past year may be associated with domains related to BPD (i.e., impulsivity, risk-taking behavior). As causality cannot be inferred due to the cross-sectional design of this study, future research should examine whether improvements in nutrition may lead to reductions in BPD symptoms,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of BPD. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on a relatively small group of participants seeking treatment in a clinical trial, and results in other groups may differ. The study also did not examine participants’ medication or psychotherapy status, and, as the authors noted, its cross-sectional design does not allow causal inferences.
Because of this, it remains unknown whether high intake of fat and sugar contributes to impulsiveness or whether impulsiveness leads people to eat more of these foods. Other factors not measured in the study, such as body mass index or physical activity, could also play a role. Diet was self-reported over a full year, which can be difficult to recall accurately, and participants may have underreported unhealthy foods.
The paper, “Associations between dietary fat and sugar intake and impulsivity in adults with borderline personality disorder,” was authored by Sophie Boutouis and Jon E. Grant.

Saab and GA-ASI successfully flight test LoyalEye AEW capability on MQ-9B
Saab and General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI) have successfully flight tested an unmanned airborne early warning (AEW) capability, integrating Saab's LoyalEye airborne early warning radar with the MQ-9B remotely piloted aircraft system.
Conducted during a flight at GA-ASI's Desert Horizon Flight Operations Facility in Southern California, the activity validated the performance of the integrated system, including its ability to detect, track, and classify airborne targets from an unmanned platform. Stakeholders attended the flight test and observed the capability in real time within a representative operational scenario, highlighting the progress made in the system's development.
The flight test is part of an evaluation programme that began with the system's first flight in May 2026, underscoring the rapid progress of the capability.
"This flight test marks an important milestone in the development of unmanned airborne early warning capabilities. LoyalEye is designed to complement existing AEW&C solutions by providing additional flexibility and persistence, and today's flight validates the capability in a representative operational scenario", says Carl-Johan Bergholm, head of Saab’s business area Surveillance.
“This has been one of the most highly anticipated flight tests we have performed,” said GA-ASI President David R. Alexander. “The level of customer interest in AEW capability on MQ-9B throughout the world is extremely high. It just makes sense.”
LoyalEye on MQ-9B can operate independently or alongside manned AEW&C platforms. An unmanned AEW capability will be able to surveil large areas with persistent surveillance in operating environments where endurance, geographic reach, and reduced aircrew exposure are critical.

The mid-terms and democracy, a new national park, and political hamburgers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

The mid-terms and democracy, a new national park, and political hamburgers
Welcome to our press review of events in the United States. Every Wednesday we look at how the Swiss media have reported and reacted to three major stories in the US – in politics, finance and science.
Whenever I visit the United States, I always look forward to meals in diners and burger bars – a tasty, messy burger is tough to find in Switzerland, and if you do manage to find one, it could well cost more than CHF30 ($35). But are the days of cheap(er) US burgers over? With supply of beef low and demand as high as ever, prices are going up – with potential political consequences.
Help us improve the press review
As a reader of our weekly press review, your feedback is important to us. Please take two minutes to answer a short survey and help us improve our journalism. This survey is anonymous and all data is confidential.
👉 [Take the surveyExternal link]
Ahead of next week’s mid-term elections, American democracy is suffering a historic setback under Donald Trump, according to the Tribune de Genève.
How is American democracy faring in the run-up to the mid-terms on November 3? “Very badly,” the Tribune de Genève wrote on Tuesday, citing several independent research institutes. “According to V-Dem’s flagship report on democracy, the US has recorded its sharpest decline in history this year. Its score has fallen back to 1965 levels – a time when Martin Luther King Jr was marching in the streets and voting rights for minorities had only just been established.”
A particular problem is the lack of effective checks on the executive by Congress and the judiciary. “During Donald Trump’s second term, power has become concentrated in the hands of the president, who is increasingly governing by executive order,” the Geneva newspaper wrote. “The Republican-dominated Congress offers him little resistance. It has largely ceded its oversight and budgetary powers to the administration. The Supreme Court, too, often rules in favour of the president.”
Beyond this weakening of the checks and balances, the Tribune de Genève said Trump was exacerbating the drift towards autocracy through numerous other measures, such as attacks on the rule of law, a purge of the administration, and attacks on freedom of expression, including a crackdown on protests.
“As a result, an increasing number of Americans believe that their democracy is no longer a good model for other countries,” it wrote. “According to polls by the Pew Research Center, 69% say they are dissatisfied with the way democracy works in their country. Many have lost confidence in their political leaders.”
This frustration with the state of democracy and its institutions is currently fuelling mobilisation, according to the Tribune de Genève. “Forecasts predict a high turnout on November 3, which is likely to benefit the Democrats in particular. Nearly one in two Americans explicitly regard their vote as a vote against Trump.”
The newspaper concluded that, traditionally, mid-term elections serve as a referendum on the incumbent president, but political scientists see the upcoming election as a decisive turning point for the future of American democracy. “These elections will show whether moderate political forces are regaining influence or whether the dismantling of democratic structures is continuing and may become impossible to halt.”
“Americans can barely afford their hamburgers anymore” was the concerning headline in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ), which went on a road trip around Wyoming to explain why burgers have become political.
“Even on this overcast day in Torrington, a small town of 6,000 residents, near-record prices are being fetched once again,” the NZZ wrote from a cattle auction. “Light calves weighing up to 300kg are particularly sought after. A high-quality young Angus steer, hand-castrated and fully vaccinated, can bring in $2,500 (CHF2,050). But basically everything’s selling well.”
It’s clear why prices are high: cattle stocks are at a historic low. The drought, in particular, has taken its toll, the NZZ said, explaining that herds in the US have not been this small for almost 80 years.
“But the shortage of cattle isn’t just driving up prices; for Americans, it strikes at the very core of daily life. The nation needs meat. Fast food. After all, the hamburger is practically a staple food in this country. The culinary embodiment of the American Dream: while in 19th-century Europe meat was a privilege of the upper classes, cattle farming was booming in the US. For just a few cents, a burger soon filled every worker’s stomach. But today, by no means can everyone afford it so easily.”
As a result, burgers have become a political issue. Ahead of the mid-term elections on November 3, affordability is the dominant issue. “Most of the talk centres on petrol prices, which are a cause for concern among voters. But at least some Republicans are willing to give the president a pass on that issue – if the war in Iran is having an impact at the petrol pump, it is, after all, directed against a tyrannical regime which, in their view, also threatens the US, the ‘Great Satan’. When it comes to the Big Mac, however, that’s where their understanding ends.”
Donald Trump knows this, the NZZ explained, which is why he has relaxed the import regulations on beef, signing an executive order temporarily suspending tariffs on so-called lean beef trimmings – the stuff used to make minced beef – for certain quantities. In other words, cheap lean beef from Brazil, for example, is intended to drive down prices.
The measure, which Trump decided on in August, is valid for 90 days. “In other words, pretty much until the mid-term elections are over. The calculation is obvious. Whether it will work is another matter.”
A new national park has been created in the United States – so why are conservationists not happy?
Last week Chiricahua Park in southeastern Arizona became the 64th protected area in the US to be designated a national park. But, as Le Temps reported on Thursday, the announcement has drawn mostly criticism from the environmentalist community, which condemns it as a public relations exercise divorced from the realities on the ground.
“This new status will showcase one of Arizona’s gems, enabling us to welcome more visitors and boost the local economy,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. “This is a victory for all those who have campaigned to protect this place so that our children and grandchildren can enjoy it,” said Arizona’s Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in a rare show of bipartisan support.
The United States now has a 64th national park, “but the champagne is remaining in the fridge for conservationists”, Le Temps wrote. There are two reasons for this, it explained. First, nothing’s really changed. “Covering 49km2, Chiricahua National Park is the fourth-smallest in the country. Its designation as a national park has not been accompanied by an expansion of its area; the level of nature conservation protection previously afforded to the area remains the same, and no additional funding has been allocated for its management – despite the expected influx of more tourists. It’s therefore not a significant environmental breakthrough.”
Second, Trump-era policies remain in place. Christina Hazard, legal director of the National Parks Conservation Association, an independent organisation dedicated to protecting national parks, said that for these sites to be properly maintained, “the new US national park needs the National Park Service’s (NPS) staffing levels and funding to be restored”. Le Temps pointed out that since Donald Trump’s return to the White House, thousands of NPS staff have lost their jobs and, across the country, infrastructure is suffering while the administration prioritises projects such as the controversial refurbishment of a public golf course in Washington, D.C. or, still in the capital, the botched project involving the Reflecting Pool (see previous press review).
“Arizona’s national parks are on the brink of collapse, but instead of investing limited resources in visitor safety and other park needs, Secretary Burgum is overseeing the refurbishment of the president’s projects in Washington,” said the National Association of American Park Rangers. “It’s inexcusable that he is touting the creation of a new national park while refusing to look after the sites his department has been responsible for managing for over a century.”

Dua Lipa's literary takeover at London Literature Festival 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:59:30 UTC
00:59:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Dua Lipa is making reading cool again at this year's London Literature Festival
Pop star, activist, skincare entrepreneur and founder of an editorial platform (among her many ventures), Dua Lipa has long championed manifestation, from writing down her goals and using her song Training Season to manifest her ideal partner to mapping out major career milestones, including headlining Glastonbury.
Now, she is turning her attention to literature, taking on the role of curator for this year's 19th London Literature Festival at the Southbank Centre, one of London's leading arts and cultural venues, and cementing her status as a literary goddess of our time.
The festival brings together established literary names and emerging writers for conversations, readings, and events that explore the stories and ideas shaping our lives.
Generously supported by Bukhman Philanthropies, this year’s edition also coincides with the Southbank Centre’s 75th anniversary.
Running until 1 November, the festival has already offered plenty to get stuck into. From conversations with literary icons to poetry confronting the realities of our time and powerful personal testimony, The New Arab looks at some of the standout moments and ideas that have stayed with us so far.
Literary icons, intimate conversations and the power of poetry
For one day only, Dua made an appearance at the festival, taking to the stage alongside some of the most celebrated names in literature.
First up was British novelist Zadie Smith, whose debut novel, White Teeth, was published when she was just 24 and went on to become one of the most celebrated novels of the new millennium.
The programme also featured American singer and writer Patti Smith, who discussed her memoir, Bread of Angels. She spoke about her family and early interest in art, recalling how seeing a Picasso painting at the age of 12 and leaving the church after being told there was no place for art helped shape the independent spirit that has remained a defining part of her life and work.
Dua also welcomed Mustafa Ahmed, known as Mustafa the Poet, to the stage to discuss Nour, a project created with WePresent that brings together poetry, photography, interviews and visual art. Made freely available in 2025, the project explores themes of faith, love, grief and everyday rituals.
During the conversation, Dua revealed that Mustafa officiated her wedding to Callum Turner and wrote a poem for the couple. She described the gesture as meaningful and dedicated Noor Hindi’s Ode to Friendship to him.
Their discussion also touched on friendship and the importance of allowing the people we love the freedom to change and grow.
Special guest readings from poets Victoria Chang and Safia Elhillo added to the programme’s celebration of poetry.
A celebration of British Somali poetry
The focus on poetry continued beyond Dua’s appearance with A Celebration of British Somali Poetry, which brought together five poets to explore identity, migration and belonging. Among them was Samatar Elmi, who shared The Genocide Will Not Be Televised, a poem that combines historical references with raw, contemporary outrage.
Samatar recited the poem, which includes the lines: “The genocide will not be televised. The genocide will not be brought to you by Newsnight, Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. Piers Morgan will not ask if you condemn Hamas twice a day and thrice on Sundays. There will be no need to learn that if you place a gun to a parrot’s head, it squawks: ‘Israel has a right to defend itself,’ ‘Israel has a right to defend itself,’ in [a hundred and sixteen] languages, because the genocide will not be televised.”
Nadia Murad on survival and reclaiming her life
From poetry confronting the reporting of violence, the festival moved to personal testimony.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Nadia Murad sat down with BBC journalist Lyse Doucet to discuss surviving Islamic State group (IS) captivity in Iraq, becoming a leading voice for survivors of sexual violence and reclaiming her life beyond her past.
As Nadia put it, "Survival isn’t the same as finding peace. It’s an ongoing negotiation with memory." She also reflected on the expectations she faced early in her activism, when people pressured her to put her work before her own hopes of building a new life. "Are you supposed to suppress the part of myself that loved makeup and hair?" she asked.
Nadia also spoke about her mother, who was killed by IS, and the price women have to pay during violence and conflict.
Reflecting on how public conversations often focus on the numbers of soldiers and men killed, she said: "You know, the world focuses so much on how many soldiers are recovering or how many men were killed. It’s always about the numbers and the destruction.
"But there is always a specific price that women pay. My mother was killed because she was a woman, and they felt she was a threat to them. They thought that if she survived, she would rebuild that house or build a new one and bring the family together."
To end, Nadia reflected on how she met her now-husband, Abid Shamdeen, who was working as her translator at the time.
Describing him as the "love of her life, who gives me hope every day," she also shared a touching story from her latest book, I Choose My Beginning: A Story of Courage and Activism.
When Abid asked if there was one thing she wanted to do for herself, Nadia admitted that she felt self-conscious about her teeth. He never judged her for it. Instead, he eventually told her, "Nadia, I found you an orthodontist." Before she knew it, she had braces, "like a teenager."
Ta-Nehisi Coates and Tareq Baconi on Palestine and freedom
The festival also turned to questions of freedom and justice, as authors Ta-Nehisi Coates and Tareq Baconi joined journalist Nesrine Malik to discuss Palestine, decolonisation and their books, The Message and What Now: On Palestine, Freedom, and Our Global Future.
Tareq argued: "People who have and continue to colonise Palestine, there is no way in which the ‘us’ and the ‘them’, this colonial relationship, can coexist. Zionism means Palestinian extermination, so if we are committed to Palestinian life, we have to confront Zionism for what it is: this racist ideology that has no place in our world."
Ta-Nehisi, meanwhile, discussed how American slavery's need for expansion ultimately contributed to its own undoing, suggesting that oppressive systems can be driven by an insatiable appetite for more land and control.
He also pointed to Zionism's emphasis on maintaining a Jewish demographic majority as evidence of its exclusionary character, arguing that such a "project" cannot be separated from questions of racism.
Rama Duwaji brings the festival theme to the screen
Beyond the festival’s live events, a campaign film featuring words by Dua and animation by Syrian artist Rama Duwaji brings this year’s theme, Read the World Differently, to life on the Piccadilly Lights billboard and at the Southbank Centre.
One standout piece of writing on screen was an excerpt from Sufiyaan Salam’s Merky Books New Writers’ Prize-winning debut novel, Wimmy Road Boyz, which was also featured on Dua’s Service95 platform. The story follows three British-Pakistani friends on a chaotic night drive down Manchester’s Curry Mile.
A book swap for readers
For festivalgoers looking to take a little literary inspiration home, the festival’s book swap offers the chance to exchange books and leave recommendations for fellow readers.
It is a simple way to keep the conversation going beyond the stage, with each book offering the chance to discover a new favourite or see a familiar story in a new light.
And if there is one thing Dua’s own love life suggests, it is that a shared love of books can be a pretty good conversation starter.
The singer and Callum reportedly first bonded at a party in Los Angeles after discovering they were both reading Hernán Díaz’s Trust, having each just finished the first chapter when Callum joked, "So we’re on the same page."
The London Literature Festival runs until 1 November 2026, with events still to come

A group of former US government officials who resigned because of Washington’s policy in the Gaza Strip has urged candidates seeking the 2028 presidential nomination to pledge not to appoint officials they said enabled Israel's genocide in the enclave.
“Senior Biden Administration officials who were architects of the Gaza policy are now actively white-washing their own roles in enabling genocide,” Gaza Resignees said in a statement signed by 12 former officials.
“They violated U.S. and international law by providing U.S. weapons while Israel indiscriminately and disproportionately attacked civilians and civilian infrastructure, and as Israel arbitrarily blocked humanitarian assistance to Gaza,” it said.
The signatories include former State Department officials Josh Paul, Annelle Sheline and Stacy Gilbert, former diplomats Hala Rharrit and Mike Casey, former White House official Anna Del Castillo and former USAID senior adviser Alexander Smith. Also among them are former Army officer and Defense Intelligence Agency official Harrison Mann, former Air Force Maj. Riley Livermore, former Navy Lt. Cmdr. Hani Z. Nofal and former political appointees Tariq Habash of the Education Department and Lily Greenberg Call of the Interior Department.
“Not even two years since the end of their disastrous time in office, many of these same officials appear to be pursuing a path back into the halls of power,” they said.
“The most basic level of accountability, the most minimal level of consequences, is to ensure that those who have wreaked so much harm from within the highest levels of our Government cannot return to it,” according to the statement.
The group said that “Gaza has become a litmus test for the credibility of American politicians and the viability, in particular, of Democratic candidates.”
The pledge asks candidates to acknowledge US “complicity” in Israel's genocide in Gaza. It also asks them to exclude any past or present political appointee who was “an architect, leader, defender, or key enabler” of the policy.
In a video released with the statement, the former officials took turns reading the call over images of former Secretary of State Antony Blinken, who now sits on the board of directors of the Center for American Progress, a Washington think tank.
“We have watched as elite institutions have welcomed these officials,” said Mann, as the video showed former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk, who is now with venture capital firm Lux Capital and a CNN commentator. It also showed former National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan and former USAID Administrator Samantha Power, who both joined Harvard Kennedy School after leaving office.
“We have watched as these officials have tried to launder their bloody reputations,” Paul said, with Rharrit adding, “and prepare to re-enter the halls of power.”
“And we say, enough,” the former officials said in the video. “Enough with the culture of impunity in Washington. Enough with policies that break our laws and defy our values.”
“They have blood on their hands,” they added.
Top Biden administration officials at that time acknowledged civilian suffering in Gaza but defended Israel’s right to defend itself following the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack.
US-made weapons were photographed several times in Israeli strikes in Gaza, although US authorities have declined to confirm this.
Since October 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, mostly women and children, and wounded over 175,000, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. It has also caused widespread destruction affecting around 90% of the territory’s civilian infrastructure.
More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in the Gaza Strip since an October 2025 ceasefire went into effect.

Elena Dudum's Palestinian memoir confronts identity and erasure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:57:55 UTC
00:57:55 KST

Breadcrumb
They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful: Elena Dudum's memoir asks what it means to inherit a homeland
At its core, every coming-of-age memoir asks: How do I convince the world that I exist? However, Elena Dudum’s memoir They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful (Atria/One Signal) complicates this simple idea by asking: How do I prove my existence when the world is committed to destroying the evidence?
Unlike traditional coming-of-age memoir that simply deals with the trials of childhood, adolescence, and young adulthood, this memoir is dedicated to the process of coming into consciousness in the face of outright denial.
A Palestinian Christian raised in San Francisco, in some ways Elena’s upbringing follows the prototypical footprint for any diasporic Arab American — her grandparents came to America and built lives.
However, the particulars of her story stand out — her Palestinian-born grandparents married American-born Arabs, and contrary to post 9/11 American popular conception, she is not Muslim.
Instead, she was heavily involved in her Palestinian Christian community as a child. She moved through adolescence and young adulthood in proximity to privilege, privately educated and rubbing elbows with San Francisco's elite.
However, the truth is that although she was in the right rooms, people viewed her differently.
A third grader in 2001, she pulled her teacher aside: "I told Miss Crane that my cousin and I would not share where our family was from… We would tell people we were from Guatemala."
The fact of their origins, uttered in hushed tones. Disguised and distorted, for fear that true disclosure would mutate into misunderstood hatred.
Whether it was classmates' parents, a friend's boyfriend at the bar, or even the college administration, Elena Dudum constantly had to push against the idea of her identity rather than its reality.
A scene that stands out: Her own sense of self, punctured as an eight-year-old, when a friend's father driving her asks, "Where’s your family from again?" This inspired a grown man to ask a child whether or not she supports Israel. The first of a lifetime of questions ended with the resolute thought, "You guys anti-Semitic or something?"
From a young age, she is forced to understand that her identity is immediately challenged. Her family, a threat.
But she didn't understand this alone. Her father, forever frenzied with the need to educate his children, through private education and lectures on the way to school, armed them with the phrase: "You would be attributing to me a prejudice to which I do not subscribe."
A legacy of proof
This memoir, of course, follows the coming-of-age canon by having a parent to push against, but what I admire most is that this father-daughter relationship is unsentimental and deeply unresolved.
Are family dynamics ever truly resolved? So many memoirs pretend they can be. But Elena does not stray from truth: the difficulty of her father, and the identity of being Palestinian.
From childhood to adulthood, her father's lecturing is consistent. But his command and ferocity deplete her (and him) over time, her willingness to listen as a child arms her for the revelations she finds on her own as an adult.
How do you not lose your mind when trying to prove something you know exists? Elena writes, "Now he scours the web for one-hundred-year-old magazines about Palestine: LIFE, National Geographic, even The Illustrated London News, the world’s first graphic weekly news magazine. For years, he would reference these mysterious documents but show them to nobody. ‘I have proof,’ he would say, ‘that Palestine exists.’"
He has the archive. The difficulty lies in his inability to trust, even when his own daughter tries to access what he has hoarded as precious truth.
The lack of sentimentality comes down to this fact: this book is about inheriting a mission, whether she wanted to or not.
Each chapter starts with an epigraph from her father's archive: A quote from a 1946 issue of Life Magazine, describing the beauty, bounty, and existence of Palestine.
As much as he tries to keep her from it — growing belligerent and paranoid at the request — the epigraphs nod to one simple fact: she has inherited his mission, his collection.
She doesn't want to inherit this mission; her very existence forces her to.
Refusing to be erased
Elena’s memoir looks hard at who gets cast as actor and who as victim in narratives of atrocity, and how American institutions and everyday language shape that framing.
Her writing is clear and cogent: it points to the syntax and grammar of oppression, as well as the deliberate silence it produces.
What I find most palpable in this text is the question of how language can erase, displacing blame and reframing crime as power.
But it's not simply syntax and grammar; it's a lifetime series of silences. She takes her reader through her experience as an undergraduate at Barnard and a graduate student at Columbia, both institutions I also attended.
However, I did not embody the very identity that those institutions deny, villainise, and deliberately silence. She takes us through her discussions with the president of Barnard after their banner was removed from Barnard Hall after one single day (which I witnessed firsthand).
Elena goes against her father's advice, fearing for her safety. She speaks up, but to no avail: "I resented him for instilling a fear in me just as much as he instilled a fire."
As a graduate student at Columbia, Elena audits a course called The Creation of Israel. After sitting in class, agitated by the rage she witnessed her father embody, she can’t help but push back on every claim backed by studied evidence and stats, and the professor ultimately asks her not to participate.
But Elena knows better. Her family’s orange grove, remembered by her grandfather, whom she calls Siddi. She imagines Siddi as a child, sitting in a tree with ripe fruit in his palm.
The gold jewellery on her wrist, all her Taita carried away with her during the Nakba. In her genome, through generational word of mouth: she remembers. Her family’s name, engraved above a doorway in Palestine. Her family’s history, still standing in Ramallah.
When asking her father the very question she grapples with most: "When did I know I was Palestinian?" Her father replies, "‘It’s not because I’m Palestinian that I’m like this,’ he says. I can’t see him, but I know he’s shaking his head. ‘It’s just who I am."'
Ultimately, Elena’s personal narrative is the counter-archive: her life, testimony. She braids memoir with archival fragments; the form itself treats family memory as resistance. She knows the rage, the denial, the sheer fight, foisted upon her and her father: "Here I am, Palestinian in your wake."
Those who witness her and her memoir in entirety hold her rage and pick up the mantle. She is no longer alone in the fight for posterity, for truth. No one can ignore this memoir, or the power of rage-inducing truth.
Paulina Pinsky is a Los Angeles-based writer, author, writing coach, educator, podcaster and performer. She is the co-author of the teen guide to consent, It Doesn’t Have to Be Awkward: Dealing with Relationships, Consent, and Other Hard-to-Talk-About Stuff
Follow her on Instagram: @paulina_pinsky

UK Chancellor pledges 3% GDP on defence spending by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:56:25 UTC
00:56:25 KST

Breadcrumb
UK Chancellor pledges 3% GDP on defence spending by 2030, plans to meet NATO targets by 2035
The UK will increase defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, Chancellor John Healey has announced in the Autumn budget on Wednesday.
The Chancellor said this was part of the UK's plan to meet NATO's defence spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035.
US President Donald Trump has pressured European members of NATO to spend least 3.5% of GDP on core defence requirements after several members of the military alliance failed to meet the previous defence spending target of 2% of GDP.
As well as spending on military forces, NATO counts spending on police forces who are trained in military tactics, and can be deployed abroad as part of military operations, as defence expenditure.
Healey said he will set out the details on how he will meet the defence targets next year.
He also announced an increase in private investment in defence.
Healey previously served as Defence Secretary in Kier Starmer's Cabinet, before resigning in June over the former Prime Minister's defence investment plan, which he said "falls well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time."
Healey's resignation is widely considered one of the key factors behind the end of Starmer's premiership earlier this year.
In 2025, while Defence Secretary, Healey said the UK is in "in a new era of threat," citing the previous US-Israeli war on Iran, and Russia's war on Ukraine.
"As the threat grows, Britain must step up," he said in the same speech in Parliament.
In his budget announcement on Wednesday, he repeatedly cited the war in the Middle East as a leading cause of the UK's high cost of living, especially due to rising energy costs.
"These are the global economic storms we face'" Healey said, "we must choose the course we steer through them."
Healey also announced a £100 winter energy payment for millions of households in the lowest council tax bands.
The Chancellor also announced an extension of the five pence cut to fuel duty until July 2027.
Duty for motor fuels was temporarily cut in 2022 after fuel costs spiked following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Healey announced that the measures to ease energy bills will be funded by a temporary 3% increase in taxes for banks. The rise will be on top of the 25% corporate tax rate they currently pay.
Healey also announced an end to gas standing charges from next year in a bid to help households with energy prices which rose after the US and Israel's February invasion of Iran.
Currently, households pay a fixed yearly fee on top of their household gas bill, regardless of their usage. Scrapping the standing charge will shift that payment onto the unit rates.
That means around 60% household that use less gas will save money, while those that use the most gas will see their bills increase.
The move will not cost the Government any money. Rather, it will shift some of the burden for energy bills from lower income households to those on higher incomes.

Real Madrid has issued an apology to China over Kylian Mbappe’s controversial remarks about the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong, after the Spanish football club’s initial response failed to quell anger in China.

UN General Assembly backs resolution calling for end to US embargo on Cuba
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:53:54 UTC
00:53:54 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The UN General Assembly on Wednesday adopted a resolution calling for an end to the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the US against Cuba.
A total of 130 countries, including Türkiye, voted in favor of the draft resolution calling for the lifting of the embargo on Cuba. Seventeen countries, including the US, Israel, Ukraine, Argentina, and the United Arab Emirates, voted against it, while 25 countries abstained from voting.
Addressing the assembly before the vote, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla said the embargo was having a direct impact on the daily lives of Cubans, particularly through shortages of fuel, medicines, food and other essential goods.
“Cuba is not a threat. The blockade is a threat,” Rodriguez said, arguing that the measures were being used as a form of economic pressure against the Cuban population.”
“We are not talking about numbers. We are talking about human lives,” Rodriguez said, adding that the effects of the embargo could be felt “at the dining table of Cuban families” and by patients in hospitals.
US Representative Mike Waltz rejected Havana's characterization of the sanctions, arguing that Cuba's economic difficulties were primarily the result of the policies of its own government.
Draft resolutions adopted by the UN General Assembly since 2012 have called on the US to end the embargo.
The UN General Assembly resolution is non-binding and serves as a recommendation, reflecting the position of the international community. The US embargo against Cuba was first introduced in 1960, and its scope was expanded further in subsequent years.

Netanyahu's Likud accuses Arab parties of election fraud, demands police probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:52:58 UTC
00:52:58 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party accused the Arab political parties Wednesday of stealing the country's parliamentary elections through alleged bribery, intimidation and ballot fraud, demanding an immediate investigation by police and domestic intelligence authorities.
The accusations came after a sharp increase in Arab voter turnout helped Arab parties make significant electoral gains, potentially giving them greater influence over the formation of the next government.
In a sharply worded post on X, Likud alleged that Arab parties had committed serious criminal offenses to manipulate the results of Tuesday's election, including distributing cash to voters, threatening election officials and using prohibited software to mobilize supporters.
"The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the destruction of the Jewish state through serious criminal offenses involving bribery, threats, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters," the party said
The party said it had collected evidence of irregularities at numerous polling stations in Arab communities and would submit the material to law enforcement authorities.
Likud said it was transferring hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to the Israel Police, the Shin Bet domestic security agency and the Central Elections Committee.
Among the alleged evidence, the party cited thousands of envelopes containing cash and ballot slips for Ra'am, an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas, as well as reports of threats and violence against polling station officials.
It also alleged that multiple voters had entered voting booths together, that some people had voted under more than one identity and that discrepancies had been discovered between the number of ballot envelopes and the number of registered voters who cast ballots.
Likud further accused unnamed political operatives of using prohibited voter-mobilization software.
"We demand that the police and Shin Bet conduct a thorough investigation into the theft of the elections by the Arab parties and bring the perpetrators to justice," the statement said.
The party also demanded immediate action from the Central Elections Committee, arguing that the alleged offenses had severely compromised the integrity of the election and its results.
"This is a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens," Likud said. "Law enforcement agencies must act firmly and immediately."
Three arrested in suspected vote-buying scheme
The allegations followed the arrest Tuesday of three men from Bedouin communities in southern Israel on suspicion of attempting to bribe voters into supporting Ra'am.
Police said officers searched the suspects' homes in the Negev desert and seized envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash, along with ballot slips and other materials believed to be connected to the suspected offenses.
Investigators suspect the money was intended for distribution to voters in exchange for supporting Ra'am. The investigation is ongoing. 
According to media reports, the suspects included a doctor, a transportation driver and another political activist. All three denied wrongdoing.
A court released the doctor despite police objections, while the detention of the other two suspects was extended by five days. The doctor's lawyer said his client had organized meetings to encourage support for Ra'am but had no involvement in bribery. The driver's attorney said the cash found at his home was intended to cover transportation expenses. 
Ra'am rejected the accusations and alleged that the arrests were politically motivated attempts to suppress Arab voter turnout.
The party said its activists had been arrested at their homes before polling stations opened, rather than while attempting to influence voters. It also accused authorities of unfairly targeting the party and reported missing or damaged Ra'am ballot slips in several Arab communities. 
The arrests establish that police are investigating suspected election bribery, but do not establish Likud's broader allegations of coordinated fraud across Arab polling stations.
Arab parties make electoral gains
The dispute comes amid a significant increase in Arab political participation, which has strengthened the representation of predominantly Arab parties in the Knesset and complicated coalition calculations.
In preliminary results Wednesday, the predominantly Arab Joint List was projected to win 12 seats, while Ra'am was projected to secure seven, giving the two parties a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The Joint List brings together Arab political factions, while Ra'am, formally known as the United Arab List, is an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas and associated with the southern branch of the Islamic Movement.
Although both parties draw much of their support from Arab citizens of Israel, they differ in their political approaches. Abbas has pursued a more pragmatic strategy of negotiating with Jewish-led parties to secure funding and policy commitments for Arab communities.
Ra'am made history in 2021 when it joined the governing coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, becoming the first independent Arab party to formally participate in a governing coalition.
During the latest campaign, Abbas signaled his willingness to join another government if it committed to addressing violent crime, home demolitions, discrimination and other issues affecting Arab citizens.
The stronger showing by Arab parties has become particularly consequential because neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc nor the rival pro-change bloc led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot has secured a clear parliamentary majority.
The results have fueled debate over whether the opposition could form a government with support from Arab lawmakers, a prospect Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly rejected.
