Are GCC countries looking for a regional security pact with Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:51:14 UTC
23:51:14 KST

Are GCC countries looking for a regional security pact with Iran?
Observers say diverging views are unlikely to turn current diplomatic efforts into a lasting infrastructure.
Gulf countries have stepped up diplomacy with Iran in a bid to de-escalate tensions across the Middle East, amid fears of renewed US strikes on Tehran and intensifying hostilities between Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
The three nations that signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August – Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye – and diplomats from Qatar met with high-ranking Iranian officials on Monday in an effort to prevent the resumption of all-out war.
Underscoring the high stakes, the meeting in Tehran was attended by Saudi Minister of Defence Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, just days after Iran-aligned Houthi fighters struck Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities.
Meanwhile, during a diplomatic visit to the United Kingdom’s University of Cambridge on Monday, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi called for a regional security framework, including a “non-aggression pact”, between the Gulf countries and Iran under which the United States would no longer be the primary provider of security.
While Gulf countries appear determined to avoid another round of conflict – which has already restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupted global oil and gas supplies and wreaked havoc on energy facilities and infrastructure in Gulf states – questions remain over whether a regional agreement is possible and where it would leave relations between the US and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
Regional security or de-escalation?
On Friday, US President Donald Trump repeated warnings that Washington may carry out another military operation against Iran as rising fuel prices weigh on the US midterm elections scheduled for November 3. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Iran would respond more forcefully to any renewed US military action, stoking fears of an even wider escalation.
While this week’s talks in Tehran mark the first high-level contact between Iran and the Mecca mutual defence pact nations since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, reports suggest they have stopped short of landing an agreement.
Reuters reported that Qatari mediators presented Iran with a draft deal on Sunday, which Tehran was expected to respond to by the end of the week. On Wednesday, the news agency quoted Iranian officials as saying Qatar had put forward ideas that were unacceptable and that Tehran would show no flexibility regarding the nuclear issue.
Khaled Batarfi, a Saudi political analyst and academic, said the visit to Tehran indicated that Saudi Arabia was willing to give Iran a “last warning” and “submit to the region’s concerns”, but that Iran has so far refused.
“The gap is [wide] and what makes it worse is that there is no trust,” Batarfi told Al Jazeera.
Observers say diverging views are unlikely to turn the current diplomatic efforts into a lasting infrastructure. “It’s really hard to see a regional security framework coming out in the coming months or even years,” Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, an associate fellow at Chatham House in London, told Al Jazeera.
“What we are seeing is more small groups, flexible groups of countries that are taking the lead in trying to reach either bilateral or multilateral solutions,” the analyst said. “A regional security framework would need the same vision for the region, which is not necessarily shared… among the GCC countries themselves.”
Challenges ahead
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye share concerns that a prolonged confrontation between Iran and the US could further destabilise the region.
“The main obstacle remains the fundamental disagreement between Tehran and Washington over the sequence of commitments,” Azizi told Al Jazeera. “The US wants Iranian concessions, particularly on the nuclear issue, while Tehran insists that its conditions for ending the war must be met first.”
“Regional mediation could help bridge this gap, possibly through an interim arrangement, but the willingness of regional actors to facilitate an agreement does not necessarily mean that the two principal parties are prepared to make the necessary compromises,” he added.
As for a new security order, Azizi said regional countries do not share a common understanding of what it should look like and what role the US – which has so far been the GCC’s main security partner – would have left to play.
Iran has long advocated for a regional security architecture that would reduce or eliminate the US military presence. “Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, however, remain deeply integrated into the US security system, and there is little indication that they intend to abandon it,” Azizi said.
“The recent war has certainly raised questions about the reliability of American security guarantees, but this has encouraged these countries to diversify their security partnerships rather than fundamentally redefine their strategic alignments.”

2026-10-28

Aysu Biçer, Burç Eruygur
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
- Budget includes winter energy payments, higher bank taxes, plans to meet NATO defense spending commitments
- Kyiv welcomes additional financial, military support
The UK announced a £100 ($133) winter energy payment for 20 million households in England and £10 billion ($13.3 billion) in additional support for Ukraine, Treasury chief John Healey said Wednesday.
The measures form part of Healey's first budget, which also includes changes to bank taxation, local government financing and defense spending.
The energy payment will be available to households in council tax bands A to D, which generally cover lower-value residential properties.
Funding will also be allocated to the devolved governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to introduce similar support.
Healey announced measures to increase financial powers for local authorities and regional mayors, describing "fiscal devolution" as a key part of his budget plans.
Under the proposals, local authorities will retain business rates locally by the end of the decade, while mayors will receive a share of income tax revenue from 2028.
The government also confirmed a 3.9% increase in the minimum wage for workers aged 18 to 20, with a smaller increase for younger workers than for other age groups.
The budget includes an additional 3% on the bank surcharge, a tax paid by banks, which Healey described as "time-limited." The increase is smaller than previously expected. 
Defense and aid for Ukraine
Turning to defense, Healey said the UK's defense budget was £14 billion higher than in the final year of the Conservative government.
He said the government would set out in next year's spending review how it plans to meet the UK's NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense by 2035.
A new defense finance task force will examine ways to achieve the target, while the government will seek to increase private investment in defense, including through public-private partnerships.
On Ukraine, Healey announced £10 billion in additional economic and military support following a telephone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy earlier in the day.
Healey said he and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham informed Zelenskyy of the support package during the call.
"He told us 'you've made my day,'" Healey said.
The package includes £500 million in urgent military funding for Ukraine this winter.
Britain will stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes," the UK Treasury chief said. 
Zelenskyy welcomes additional support
Zelenskyy welcomed the announcement and said that the aid package included £7 billion in economic support for Kyiv over the next three years and another £3 billion in British export support.
In a statement on US social media company X, Zelenskyy described his phone call with Burnham as "great."
He said the export support would be allocated "primarily for the supply of much-needed weapons that will strengthen our protection of lives."
Zelenskyy said the additional funding was separate from the annual assistance London already provides to Ukraine.
He described the decision as a "truly strong" and "very timely" step that came "right as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone to deal with the problems Russia is so eager to escalate."
"Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realizing that it must end this war of its own making," Zelenskyy said.
He added that he and Burnham also discussed sanctions policy.
"I am grateful to Britain, to Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his team, and to every person around the world who understands that standing with Ukraine is the right thing to do – that it means being on the right side of history," he said.

Putin, whom Western critics accuse of trying to leverage Africa’s colonial past to Moscow’s benefit, did not name the countries he had in mind.
But he spoke of what he called “active attempts by Western countries” to drive Africans back into debt bondage and to force them to accept much-needed financial resources on predatory terms, which he said slowed their long-term development.
RUSSIA READY TO SHARE

“This is completely different from what we had with imperialist France,” he told Russia’s state RT television channel.
Putin told the summit that Russia championed greater African influence in the IMF and World Bank, was ready to embark on joint transport and agricultural infrastructure projects and that Moscow stood ready to supply grain and fertiliser to more African countries.

Thomas Hill Green
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:48:01 UTC
23:48:01 KST

[Revised entry by David Brink on October 28, 2026.
Changes to: Bibliography]
Thomas Hill Green (1836 – 82) is widely regarded as the founding and most influential figure in the tradition of British idealism that flourished in England, especially Oxford, and Scotland, especially Glasgow and Edinburgh, in the second half of the nineteenth century and early in the twentieth century (see, e.g., Mander 2011). Green’s idealism was systematic, embracing metaphysics and epistemology, ethical theory, political philosophy, and philosophy of history and religion. In metaphysics and epistemology, Green reflected the influence of Immanuel Kant, criticizing the British empiricist legacy of John Locke and David Hume. Green argued that empirical knowledge is the workmanship of the human mind, that reality depends on thought and cannot transcend it, and that the possibility of objectivity requires the existence of a single corporate or divine consciousness of which individual minds are proper parts. The only defensible form of idealism, Green thought, is absolute idealism, in which all aspects of reality are operations of a single consciousness. In ethics, Green embraced a form of perfectionism that identifies the human good with self-realization and the perfection of our nature as moral persons and agents. But self-realization must reflect the way in which individuals participate in associations and communities and, as a result, must reflect the demand that individuals pursue a common good. In articulating this conception of perfectionism, Green sees himself as synthesizing the best elements in two different ethical traditions – Greek eudaimonism and Kantian rationalism. Green’s perfectionist ethics influence his politics. He provides the philosophical foundations for a new progressive form of liberalism that transcends the laissez-faire liberalism characteristic of some strands in nineteenth century British liberalism. The state has a duty to promote the common good, and individual rights are constrained by the common good. This gives the state not just negative duties to refrain from interfering with the freedoms and opportunities of its citizens but also positive duties to provide resources and opportunities for individual self-realization. The ethical and political demand for self-realization, Green thinks, is freedom, properly understood. He believes that moral and political progress in history consists in the gradual and increasingly more adequate realization of the values of perfection, the common good, and freedom. Because Green identifies God with the metaphysical, ethical, and political principles in human nature, he sees God as immanent in the progressive developments in human history. 1. A Russian jet-powered drone hit a platform at Dnipro's railway station on 29 October, killing more than a dozen people waiting by a train, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha reported. An air alert was on, but many passengers had not left the platform. The strike came hours after another overnight Russian drone barrage across Ukraine.
Russia's air war on Ukraine leans more and more on jet-powered drones, and Ukraine's air defenses have stopped nearly 60% of the Geran-4 type over the past three months. Rail is among Russia's main targets: by late August, its strikes had damaged 492 locomotives as Moscow tried to cut Ukraine's export corridors, and in September Russia struck a passenger train near the Polish border. Civilians waiting for transport keep paying the price, and this month a Russian bomb killed 30 bus passengers in Kramatorsk.
One drone reached the platform
Around 11:00, Russia sent four jet-powered attack drones toward Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, the Air Force said. Air defenses destroyed three. The fourth hit a platform where a train stood, the state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said.

Climate change to cut rice, maize, sugarcane output in Southeast Asia: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:48:22 CST
23:48:22 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Climate change is projected to reduce production of key crops across Southeast Asia, with rice, maize and sugarcane facing declines, according to a study released on Thursday by the Singapore Food Agency and the National University of Singapore.
The ASEAN Agri Climate Impact Twenty study projects average rice production to decline by 3 to 5 percent between 2025 and 2044, while maize output could fall by 5 to 6 percent and sugarcane production by 1 to 4 percent.
In contrast, cassava production is projected to increase by 16 percent, while soybean output could rise by 11 to 13 percent.
"More favorable average projections for some crops do not mean that they are free from climate-related risks. Production could still be affected by variability in climate conditions in any particular year including extreme heat, heavy rainfall or drought in an unfavorable year," the report said.
Very strong El Niño events could reduce average crop production across the region by up to about 10 percent, the study found. Rice and rain-fed farming systems are generally more vulnerable to such events.
Overall, Southeast Asia is expected to experience rising temperatures, more frequent and prolonged heat waves, and increasingly variable rainfall, potentially disrupting water availability, planting schedules and crop yields. ■

Feature: Chinese hospital ship brings relief to Ghanaians
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:48:22 CST
23:48:22 KST

by Justice Lee Adoboe
ACCRA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- For nearly a year, Eugene Amartey Annan, a young Ghanaian engineer, has endured the pain of living with a hernia. This condition occurs when an internal organ or tissue pushes through a weak spot or opening in the surrounding muscle or tissue wall, most commonly in the abdomen, groin and testicles.
The condition became severe to the point that Annan found it difficult to work, with the cost of treatment for a local Ghanaian worker quite prohibitive.
But a change came when the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark arrived in Ghana's eastern port of Tema on Oct. 23 for a friendly visit and medical mission, the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the West African country.
On Monday, the medical team successfully operated on Annan in the theatre.
Speaking with Xinhua at the recovery ward on the military hospital vessel, Annan added that although he felt a little pain the day after the surgery, some pain relievers given to him had made the pain subside, and he was hoping to be discharged soon.
Annan lauded the medical workers on the vessel for their efficiency and professionalism, thanking them for the free medical care. "They pamper us so well that any illness will vanish. They are bringing China to Ghana."
Meanwhile, Sophia Annan, mother of the 45-year-old engineer, who came in to attend to her son at the recovery ward, also had a taste of the benevolent and efficient medical service provided by the personnel on board the vessel, who treated her hypertensive condition and eye problem free of charge.
"Whatever you ask them, they have the patience to answer you. The service provided here is free and we didn't pay anything," Sophia Annan said.
She added that the military medical personnel from China handled the patients with utmost care and empathy, serving them with food, toiletries, and dental care products.
Besides Annan and his mother, thousands of Ghanaians also received free medical care from the medical personnel on board the Auspicious Ark. Among these was Kingsford Adjei, 30, a student of the University of Cape Coast, who underwent surgery on board the huge Chinese naval hospital ship to correct a fracture sustained during a football game in January.
Adjei had to discontinue treatment due to the high cost of surgery, and had to discontinue his part-time job and depend solely on his mother for upkeep. But on Monday, medical personnel onboard the Chinese Navy hospital ship carried out free surgery on his right leg, and he was recovering in the ward when Xinhua visited.
"Right now, everything is successful; I'll go back to school again and do everything by myself. Thank you. They shouldn't stop. They should keep on doing it. Maybe there are people who didn't receive the opportunity now. Therefore, if they keep on coming, many people will benefit," he pleaded.
Moreover, many others also visited with gynaecological issues, dental issues, and everyday health issues, such as fevers, among others.
Among other visitors were those who also reported to the ophthalmology unit of the floating hospital, where they received treatment and care for age-old eye problems. Among these was Nicolas Senam Nanevie, a 48-year-old Ghanaian teacher, who had suffered eye problems with blurred eyesight since childhood, with spectacles hardly improving his condition.
Nanevie was diagnosed with glaucoma, which he was told was not fully developed for surgery, and he had been applying eye drops for temporary relief. However, when the 48-year-old teacher visited the Chinese naval hospital ship on Sunday, he was booked for surgery on Monday.
"I've been asked to visit a local eye clinic after 10 days to have the stitches removed. I am so happy and grateful," Nanevie told Xinhua.
Huang Zhen, an ophthalmologist at the eye center on the navy hospital ship, told Xinhua that an average of 200 people have visited the center daily with different eye problems since the ship arrived in Ghana last Friday.
"Most of the eye problems they came with are presbyopia, cataract, glaucoma, and others. Many patients need cataract and glaucoma surgeries, and this time we have many cataracts and glaucoma," Huang said.
She praised the Ghanaian volunteers working with the Chinese medical personnel for their efficiency and support. ■

Mistral releases latest AI model for download, giving companies more control over their cybersecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:45:06 UTC
23:45:06 KST

The French AI company says its Large 4 model offers advanced coding and cyber-defence capabilities and can be run on an organisation’s own computers and servers.
Mistral has released the weights for its latest large flagship AI model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), nicknamed “Le Chonk”, claiming improvements in coding and cyber defence as Europe seeks to build alternatives to US and Chinese technology.
The French firm claims the model is “the best open agentic coding model in the world”, offering enterprises and governments “frontier AI cyber defence capabilities they can fully own and control” including the ability to “detect, analyse and respond to cyberthreats across code and IT infrastructure".
The release follows a preview of ML4 on 6 October. Since then, Mistral has spent the last three weeks reinforcing the model's learning, testing it with customers and partners under real-world conditions.
“ML4 OSS showcases our science team's ability to innovate at speed. Building on the ML4 Preview, the open weight version continues reinforcement learning training and delivers substantial gains with no signs of saturation," said Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral.
"In under three weeks within the same reinforcement learning run, we integrated customer feedback by introducing two additional reasoning modes, while making ML4 more efficient and customisable,” he added.
Mistral says the latest release of ML4 rivals other leading open models for coding while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average than Chinese model GLM-5.3. Its score on Terminal-Bench 4.0, which tests AI agents’ ability to perform coding tasks in a terminal, also rose from 28% to 41% following further training.
The release also comes as Europe faces growing cybersecurity threats, such as the recent PHP programming security flaw, discovered using AI, as well as the recent cyber-attacks on the Belgian and Norwegian governments.
More control over AI
Making the model’s weights available allows organisations to download and run it on their own infrastructure, rather than relying exclusively on an external provider’s hosted service.
This could be particularly useful for companies handling sensitive information, such as proprietary software code, that they do not want to share with an external AI service.
Organisations would have greater control over where the model runs and how it is integrated into their systems, although they would still need suitable hardware and expertise to operate it securely.
Mistral says organisations running ML4 on their own infrastructure would also not face the risk of a third-party provider restricting access to or disabling the model.
The move comes amid concerns about European dependence on US AI providers. In June, the Trump administration ordered Anthropic to suspend access to its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models for foreign nationals.
The restrictions were subsequently lifted for Fable 5, while access to Mythos 5 remained limited to selected organisations. The episode highlighted how decisions made outside Europe can affect access to advanced AI services.
Europe’s AI ambitions
Europe continues to lag behind the US and China in the development of large AI models and the resources needed to build them.
Mistral is one of Europe’s leading AI developers, but its reported valuation of around $24 billion (€20.9 billion) is far below those of US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic. [Insert verified, dated valuations and source.]
Mistral argues that despite the disparity in resources, “ML4 is now the best open model built in the West”.
The model was trained on 3,800 of US company Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell GPUs at Mistral’s European data centres. The company says ML4 achieves “state-of-the-art performance” while mobilising “a fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs” such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
The model’s European infrastructure could give customers greater operational control, but its reliance on Nvidia chips illustrates Europe’s continued dependence on foreign suppliers for key parts of the AI supply chain.
"Open source is essential to ensure state-of-the-art AI does not end up concentrated in the hands of a few actors," said Arthur Mensch, CEO and co-founder of Mistral.
"Other labs have raised hundreds of billions to develop equivalent capabilities; in three years, Mistral raised roughly $6 billion."
"We have taken the lead globally in compute efficiency and have widened the gap between Mistral and other labs in that area. Our approach is to deliver quality science and put the results in everyone's hands," he added.
A state-of-the-art model
ML4 has 1.05 trillion parameters in total, but activates around 52 billion, according to Mistral. This means it does not use all its parameters for every task, helping it process requests more efficiently.
The model also offers three reasoning modes — low, medium and high — allowing users to adjust the depth of reasoning to suit the task, from everyday requests to more complex problems.
Mistral says ML4 can turn 2D blueprints into usable 3D models using computer-aided design (CAD) software, analyse large volumes of data to support financial decision-making and use satellite and aerial imagery to detect wildfires, track crop health and monitor risks to power lines.
The French firm says the release of ML4 is part of a new generation of models spanning all modalities and that they plan to release more models from this generation in the coming months.
The model is now available through Mistral’s API, while its weights can be downloaded from Hugging Face.

Joint Statement on Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) Sanctions
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:42:53 CET
23:42:53 KST

Joint Statement on Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) Sanctions North Korea Cyber security Joint statement On : October 29th 2026 The text of the following statement was released by Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the European Union. Throughout October and today, the European Union (EU) and the governments of Australia and the United States have implemented sanctions to target the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) use of overseas workers, malicious cyber activities, and actors involved in unlawful DPRK-Russia cooperation. Their actions represent their efforts to disrupt the DPRK’s ability to support its unlawful development of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missiles, and to counter unlawful DPRK-Russia military cooperation. These designations build on detailed reporting published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), which monitors and reports on DPRK’s non-compliance with UN Security Council resolutions in the absence of the UNSCR 1718 Committee Panel of Experts, whose mandate renewal was vetoed by Russia in 2024. The MSMT’s first and second reports outlined the DPRK’s unlawful military cooperation with Russia, along with cyber-enabled IT worker fraud, both of which serve to fund Pyongyang’s unlawful weapons programs. In September 2026, the MSMT released its third report detailing the DPRK’s deployment of overseas workers to generate revenue for its WMD and ballistic missile programs. The MSMT will continue to monitor, expose, and report on attempts to violate and evade UN sanctions by the DPRK. The MSMT and EU reaffirm our commitment to the complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the DPRK, calling on it to abandon its unlawful WMD and ballistic missile programs, and taking action to counter DPRK attempts to violate and evade UN sanctions. We continue to strongly support the implementation of all DPRK-related UN Security Council resolutions. We call on all UN Member States, and especially permanent members of the Security Council, to fully implement these resolutions.

Ukrainian charged over death of Monaco royal
A Ukrainian man living in Monaco has been charged in connection with the death of Antoine de Massy, a relative of Prince Albert II, the ruler of the wealthy European principality.
The 42-year-old suspect, whose identity has not been disclosed, has reportedly lived in Monaco for three decades. Prosecutor General Stephane Thibault announced a judicial investigation on Wednesday.
According to local media, the Ukrainian national has been charged with involuntary manslaughter and failure to assist a person in danger. He denies wrongdoing and has been remanded in custody.
De Massy, 29, whose father is a first cousin of Prince Albert II, was found dead on Sunday evening after apparently falling approximately 13 meters from an elevated section of the coastal Boulevard du Larvotto into a garden behind a luxury residence.
The former competitive tennis player was reportedly last seen alive overnight Saturday into Sunday, leaving a nightclub apparently intoxicated and accompanied by another man. His family alerted authorities when he failed to attend a gathering, triggering a search that led to the discovery of his body in the secluded garden.
Thibault said CCTV footage showed the suspect accompanying de Massy along Boulevard du Larvotto. The Ukrainian national was arrested on Monday, although it remains unclear whether he was the man who reportedly left the nightclub with the victim.
Earlier this year, Monaco, known as a haven for millionaires, was rocked by a bombing targeting Ukrainian-born businessman Vadim Ermolaev, who was injured alongside members of his family.
The alleged bomber was identified as a Ukrainian woman who was later found dead in her home country, reportedly killed by her handlers. Investigators identified the suspected masterminds as an active operative of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, and an unofficial agent of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU). Both are now in Ukrainian custody.
Kiev portrayed the bombing as a profit-driven crime carried out by rogue agents. However, one suspect claimed the operation had been authorized by the Ukrainian state as a legitimate act of war against Russia.
The case resurfaced this week when former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said the Monaco bombing “echoed” an alleged Ukrainian intelligence plot against him that Austrian law enforcement had thwarted.
Kravchenko fled Ukraine for Vienna last month and was subsequently dismissed by parliament after a subordinate was accused of running a protection racket on his behalf. The Austrian authorities confirmed the arrests of suspected Ukrainian intelligence operatives in early October.

Canada to join EU network of supercomputers

14:34:08 UTC
23:34:08 KST

BRUSSELS— The European Union and Canada are teaming up on compute power — a key element for training artificial intelligence models — with Canada set to join the EU's supercomputer network.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday Canada "will now become part of this network", confirming a POLITICO report from earlier this week that both sides were discussing the country's entry into the European supercomputing network.
Canada joining "enables Canadian industry, startups and researchers to access European supercomputing," von der Leyen said. "Paired with Canada's pioneering AI industry, this would allow us to develop highly competitive, innovative and safe AI systems."
Advertisement
The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an €8.2 billion budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers.
The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of €30 billion.
Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start.
“Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term ‘middle power’ cooperation plays in AI,” said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
But he added that for now “it doesn’t put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S.
“As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn’t result in massive buildouts will help,” he said.
Advertisement
Canada's engagement in the EU's supercomputer network builds further on Canada's previous partial involvement in the EU's flagship research and development program, Horizon Europe.
Horizon Europe partially funds EuroHPC.
To date, 38 countries have participated in the EU's supercomputing network: 27 EU member countries plus non-EU countries including Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Israel and Turkey.

- A Saudi Defense Ministry photo from King Khalid Air Base appears to show a Bahraini F-16 squadron pilot and a Pakistan Air Force member, analysts said.
- Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Pakistan have not commented on the image or confirmed any Bahraini deployment to the base.
A photo released by Saudi Arabia’s Defense Ministry from a visit by its top military officer to King Khalid Air Base in the kingdom’s southwest appears to show a Royal Bahraini Air Force fighter pilot and a member of the Pakistan Air Force at the base, open-source analysts at OSINTWarfare pointed out in a post.
Gen. Fayyadh Al-Ruwaili, chief of the general staff, visited military units in the southern region, units deployed along the border with Yemen and military commands in Khamis Mushait and Jazan, where he received briefings on operational missions, the Saudi Defense Ministry announced. The ministry’s statement did not mention any foreign personnel, and neither Bahrain nor Pakistan has commented on the image.
According to OSINTWarfare, the photo shows a Bahraini officer with the rank of major wearing the patch of the Royal Bahraini Air Force’s 1st Tactical Fighter Squadron, known as the Desert Falcons, on his right shoulder. The squadron flies F-16C/D fighters from Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain and is responsible for defending Bahraini airspace, and the analysts said it has not previously been publicly known to have taken part in operations abroad. A Pakistan Air Force member can be seen in the background, identifiable by his uniform, they added, though the image does not show whether the personnel are deployed to the base, how many are there or what aircraft, if any, they brought.
King Khalid Air Base sits outside Khamis Mushait in Asir province and is the main Royal Saudi Air Force hub for the southern border with Yemen, an area that has been under fire this autumn as Houthi missile and drone attacks in September struck targets in Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait and Saudi Arabia resumed its air war against the Iran-backed group.
Bahrain sent F-16s to fight alongside Saudi Arabia when it joined the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis in 2015, and on Dec. 30 that year a Royal Bahraini Air Force F-16 crashed in Jazan province while flying for the coalition, with the pilot surviving. Bahraini officials did not say at the time which squadron the aircraft belonged to.
Pakistani fighter and support aircraft arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base in the Eastern Province in April under the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement the two countries signed in September 2025, and a senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times this month that Pakistan Air Force jets are being used in strikes against Yemen’s Houthis. Analysts estimate about 8,000 Pakistani troops have deployed to the kingdom, including air force and army air defense units.
Britain said on Oct. 20 that Royal Air Force Typhoons will fly defensive patrols over Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye is preparing to send personnel under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement it signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August, pending approval by its parliament.
Saudi Arabia and Bahrain have not said whether Bahraini F-16s are operating from King Khalid Air Base or flying missions over Yemen.

Finnish police have launched a preliminary criminal investigation into suspected environmental damage at Google's data center construction site in Muhos, following concerns about water management and drainage practices, according to media reports on Thursday.
The Oulu Police Department is examining five investigation requests concerning the site, including one submitted by the Finnish Supervisory Agency, Finnish broadcaster Yle reported.
Police said preliminary findings pointed to "irregularities and shortcomings" in drainage and water management at the construction site, operated by Google's local subsidiary Tuike Finland.
The investigation is focused on suspected environmental damage, although additional suspected offenses could emerge as inquiries progress.
Authorities expect the investigation to continue into 2027, with additional information anticipated in December, according to the report.
The probe follows an order from the Finnish Supervisory Agency to suspend construction at Google's Muhos and Kajaani-Otanmaki projects because environmental impact assessments were not completed.
The company confirmed on Oct. 14 that it had halted preparatory work at both locations.
Regulators also found the company's water management plans insufficient to show it could adequately control environmental risks.
Tuike Finland has until Nov. 5 to submit a more detailed plan addressing drainage infrastructure, monitoring and risks associated with heavy rainfall, melting snow and potentially acidic soils.
The agency warned that failure to comply could result in enforcement action, including a conditional fine.
The projects form part of Google's €13 billion ($14.5 billion) investment in Finland.

‘I hope this project has no future’: Grigory Sverdlin on helping Russian soldiers desert and building an organization he hopes will one day be unnecessary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:32:11 UTC
23:32:11 KST

‘I hope this project has no future’: Grigory Sverdlin on helping Russian soldiers desert and building an organization he hopes will one day be unnecessary
In fall 2026, the Prague Book Tower, a fair for Russian-language tamizdat, presented Grigory Sverdlin’s book Punkt obogreva: Kak ya zanimalsya blagotvoritelnostyu v Rossii i stal vragom gosudarstva (“Warming Station: How I Did Charity Work in Russia and Became an Enemy of the State”), published by Meduza’s publishing house. Sverdlin previously headed Nochlezhka, Russia’s oldest organization helping homeless people. In 2022, he stepped down as director, left the country, and, once in exile, launched the project Idite Lesom (“Get Lost”), which helps Russians desert the army and flee the country. In Prague, Felix Sandalov and Alexey Dokuchaev, founders of the StraightForward foundation, which supported the publication of Warming Station, spoke with Grigory Sverdlin about what kind of people work in the field of charity, why it’s almost impossible for projects like Idite Lesom to find financial support, and what future awaits an organization so closely tied to the war. Meduza is publishing a lightly abridged version of this conversation.
Felix Sandalov: Grisha and I first started talking about a book — not this one, but a completely different book at the time — I think around six or seven years ago, back in our time at the Moscow publishing house Individuum. The book was conceived as a kind of field guide to the work of nonprofit organizations, since Grisha already had a great deal of experience at Nochlezhka by then. But what came out now is an entirely different [book]. In its own way, it captures the difference between charity work and civil resistance. Grisha made a real “leap of faith” and founded an entirely new organization for himself, built on new principles.
Warming Station describes a kind of seasonality in the work of charities that help homeless people. When cold weather sets in, the work grows more urgent: people die on the streets, and staff have to respond quickly — it’s a genuinely difficult period for anyone working on these projects. That was certainly true at Nochlezhka. Is there a similar seasonality to the work at Idite Lesom? And given that the media keeps stirring up talk of an impending mobilization, which Russian authorities routinely deny, are you seeing a surge in requests to Idite Lesom right now?
Grigory Sverdlin: First, let me correct you a little. You’re talking about seasonality in helping homeless people, but the real seasonality is in donations. In winter, people donate more, more often, and more willingly to help the homeless, while in summer, for obvious reasons, the issue falls out of public attention. That doesn’t mean there are fewer homeless people — they don’t go anywhere. It’s a bit easier to survive, yes, but it’s still incredibly hard.
That’s exactly the pain point and the subject of discussion in the charity community that helps people who end up on the street: raising donations is incredibly hard, and the amount of work never decreases.
As for helping people who have ended up in the Russian army, or those trying to avoid ending up there, we’re completely swamped at Idite Lesom. If you’ve written to us and have been waiting several days for a reply, I want to take this opportunity to apologize. We will definitely answer everyone.
This summer we’ve gotten about one and a half times more requests than in spring, and about three times more than last summer. Right now, about 150 to 200 people contact us every day. Many people currently in Russia are, of course, panicking about a possible mobilization this fall and thinking about how to protect themselves, their children, and their loved ones.
The number of requests from people who want to desert from the Russian army is also growing. Just two days ago, we were tallying up the numbers for August: we helped almost 150 people desert that month alone.
Sandalov: You write about all of this with such vividness and enthusiasm — you can feel how obstacles energize you, how much you enjoy finding solutions to nontrivial problems. That’s always admirable.
Tell me about your method of writing the book. You describe nearly 20 years with all the vividness of someone who lived through every event firsthand. How did you reconstruct it all? How did you transport yourself back in time? How did you reconstruct the dialogue? Did you keep some kind of diaries? Or did you [reconstruct something] from letters, or do you just have a photographic memory?
Sverdlin: Thanks for the kind words. My memory is pretty poor, so I actually did some serious “pre-research” — digging up publications that are now archival, corresponding with colleagues, and interviewing colleagues from other charities who appear in the book. It’s primarily about Nochlezhka and Idite Lesom, but of course I wanted — and I hope I managed — to paint a broader picture and talk more generally about how the charity sector sprouted up through the asphalt in Russia. It didn’t exist in Soviet times, because only the state was supposed to help. Horizontal ties weren’t welcomed. They were banned.
Alexey Dokuchaev: So who should actually be doing the helping? The state, or society and organizations like Nochlezhka?
Sverdlin: I’d rather not frame it in terms of who “should.” Overall, global experience shows that the support system works best when many charitable organizations run by enthusiasts operate alongside various state, regional, and municipal structures that are also engaged in providing help. What you end up with is a network of different charitable projects, both private and government-run, that step in when someone is in trouble.
And indeed, the ratio of private to government assistance can vary somewhat, but practice shows that private initiatives are always more empathetic and more progressive, thanks to the greater enthusiasm of the people working there, and, being less bureaucratic, [these initiatives] are able to adapt more quickly to what’s happening.
Government structures, meanwhile, will always have more stable funding and greater organizational resources. In Finland, for example, which is the world champion in helping homeless people, that’s exactly the kind of interaction between the charitable and government sectors that exists.
Sandalov: Are there organizations in other countries that, like Idite Lesom, help conscripts avoid being sent to the front? Do you have an international community that shares its pains and hopes with one another?
Sverdlin: We do have some colleagues, and I found it fascinating when, a couple of years ago, we more or less accidentally met people in America who, during the Vietnam War, did something similar to what Idite Lesom does now. They were elderly hippies by then, recounting their extensive experience.
Obviously, given the specific nature of the subject, there aren’t many such colleagues, and we can’t really exchange experience with them. With our Finnish colleagues on the subject of homelessness, we always tried to pick up tips, to bring some of Finland’s practices back to Russia. But when it comes to helping with desertion… You can’t really swap routes for crossing the Finnish border with people who help men avoid service in the Pakistani army.
Dokuchaev: Nochlezhka is, in general, an organization whose structure makes sense to all of us. With Idite Lesom, we know the name, we understand what it does. But how does the organization actually function now, and to what extent can it be built into a system? And should it be? What does systemic success look like for you, apart from the war ending? Could you get an entire regiment or division out [of combat zones] if you were given far more resources?
Sverdlin: In general, I’m a believer in sustainable structures. My professional pride is that Grisha Sverdlin isn’t in St. Petersburg, in Moscow, or at Nochlezhka anymore, and yet Nochlezhka keeps living, working, and developing. I’m very glad about that, because it’s a crucial stress test for any leader: does everything still work once they’re no longer there? With Idite Lesom, I also want to believe that we’ve managed to build that kind of system.
Idite Lesom has 10 staff members: people who receive at least some salary, myself included. There are also around 80 volunteers, though we’re constantly recruiting more. Without this professionally organized work, it wouldn’t be possible to counsel 150 to 200 people every day.
“I got a summons, what do I do?” “I want to leave Russia, can I get out?” “There’s some kind of restriction on my ‘Gosuslugi’ account. Can you explain it?” “My boyfriend was detained on the street, and they’re pressuring him to sign a contract. Help.” “I’m a conscript who’s already been forced to sign a contract, and we were told we’ll be sent to the occupied territories next week. Help, save me, what do I do?” And so on, and so on. These really are hundreds of requests every week.
To answer your question about a regiment, I feel a little awkward bragging about numbers, but I’ll say it anyway, because it’s the result of enormous work by our volunteers. We launched in September 2022. To date, we’ve counseled more than 82,000 people, and there are around 3,600 people we’ve helped desert. We’ve gotten most of them out of Russia, although in the end a fairly significant number of people decide to stay in the country, and we help them hide.
So it’s a huge amount of work, but there’s always room to grow. Just last week, we met in person with colleagues and tried to come up with new ideas for how to undermine our home country’s defense capability more effectively.
Dokuchaev: How do people find out about you? Do you work only off the requests that come in? How does someone who doesn’t read Meduza or follow your Facebook find out that if they’re sent to occupied territory tomorrow, they should write to you?
Sverdlin: Honestly, good old word of mouth works best. Besides Meduza’s readers and my Facebook, 200,000 people also follow Idite Lesom’s social media accounts. That’s a great achievement by my colleagues who handle our social media.
These people spread the information among their friends and classmates, dropping it into chat groups like those for conscripts’ mothers. I think, above all, it’s this kind of organic reach.
Second, it’s probably independent Russian journalists and bloggers, whom I’d also like to take this opportunity to thank. They write about us, which means more people find out about Idite Lesom, and more people get the chance to escape the jaws of the leviathan.
Sandalov: Several fascinating pages of Warming Station are devoted to your great lifelong passion, namely technical mountaineering. By risking your life, you get access to some of the craziest views on planet Earth. In your view, is there a connection here: do people with a propensity for all kinds of extreme activity (there’s a crude expression for it, adrenaline junkie) want to work in charitable organizations or civil resistance projects more than others? Does charity work genuinely attract that kind of crowd, or is it a coincidence?
Sverdlin: I think it’s more of a coincidence. Of course, as someone who used to work at commercial companies, I was incredibly curious when I first started out in the nonprofit world. I wanted to see what kind of people worked there and how they differed from people in business.
What I ended up seeing, first, was people with a sharper sense of justice. For most of us, I think, that sense applies to ourselves and our immediate circle, but we’re unlikely to call up the relevant city service and complain about every broken traffic light. I had a colleague, though, who would see a broken traffic light and immediately start working to get it fixed.
Second, it’s a more developed sense of empathy, one that seems to stretch to more people and more situations. I also tried to write about this in the book. You shouldn’t idealize the people who come to work in charity, because everything has a shadow side, a flip side. The amount of conflict, scandal, and manipulation I was subjected to in the charity world is something no business could even dream of.
Sandalov: Tell me about civil resistance. Over the past few years, you’ve done a lot of notable things with Idite Lesom. Probably the biggest recent one was hacking into and destroying data from Russia’s military registration database. Tell me how that changed your life.
Sverdlin: Specifically, hacking the registry — or rather, the registry developer’s systems, to be precise — didn’t change anything, because by that point we’d already been engaged in “subversive activity” for three years, and our websites had already been blocked multiple times. We had, of course, already been designated “foreign agents” by Russian authorities. I’d already been sentenced in absentia to six years. If you want details, now whenever I fly somewhere, I always check where the airline’s backup airport is, because some airlines that fly to, say, Kutaisi use Sochi as their alternate airport. If there’s some technical problem in Kutaisi, the plane will land in Sochi. And I shouldn’t be showing up in Sochi. I also almost never write about my plans, and I try not to post photos from my window — basically, I take these and other obvious security precautions.
Coming back to the organization, so far, aside from being blocked and periodic attempts to hack us, nothing major has happened. Obviously, we vet people who want to become our volunteers in multiple stages, because there’s no doubt some “comrade major” would love to get in among them. But when you’re living inside all of this, this kind of shit just feels like routine.
Hi, I’m N.
I report for Meduza from inside Russia. I could go to prison for my work. To stay safe, I have to follow strict security protocols. I know my lawyer’s phone number by heart. And, of course, my articles are published anonymously.
Working for an independent news outlet while still living in Russia feels like something out of a spy film. My friends know me by one name. My colleagues and sources know me by another. But sometimes there’s a glitch. At a close friend’s birthday party, someone I don’t know reaches out to shake my hand. “Hi, I’m Lyosha.” It takes me a few seconds to decide how to introduce myself. Do I use my real name or my pseudonym? I’m trying to figure out whether this is someone I might one day end up writing about.
What I do is journalism in exile, even though I’m not in exile myself. I have the rare opportunity to do uncensored, on-the-ground reporting in Russia. Please support Meduza so I can continue this work.
Dokuchaev: Tell me, does having this kind of work get in your way, or does it actually help you? Does it give you strength to make plans for your own life? We’re living now in pretty pleasant places, where other people don’t have a war, but we do. Still, this war will end sooner or later. Given that, it seems obvious that the best thing that could happen to Idite Lesom is for it to shut down. How do you picture [life after that]?
Sverdlin: It’s true, when I came up with this project during the mobilization in Russia, I assumed we’d be doing it for six months, maybe a year — then the war would end, and we’d all go our separate ways to other things. I was naive.
I think that for me, and for many people I’m friends with, the war has cut off any sense of a horizon ahead. I don’t know what will happen in 10 years, or even five. And for now, unfortunately, I’m not able to look that far ahead.
I have to say this is something I miss, because when I worked at Nochlezhka, my colleagues and I tried to build strategic plans. Even if we specifically wouldn’t be at Nochlezhka in 10 years, we still tried to figure out how to move toward a future with room for many different charities and government projects. We were trying to grow that mycelium. Idite Lesom, of course, is a project with no future. God willing, this project will never have a future.
Dokuchaev: A project like this really shouldn’t have a future. But the people you’ve managed to help clearly do have one. Do you keep track of what happens to the people you got out, or, conversely, the people you weren’t able to get out?
Sverdlin: We do keep track. Idite Lesom is partly a charity project, not purely civil resistance. And there’s a well-known thing in charity work: a large share of the people organizations help never come back to say thank you.
Yes, Nochlezhka’s social workers are often brought boxes of chocolates. But that’s still a tiny fraction of the boxes they’re actually owed. People who’ve been through homelessness and managed to get out of it with Nochlezhka’s help don’t look back: behind them lies a nightmare, and thank god it’s over.
It’s the same with the deserters we’ve helped get out of the Russian army. It’s often harder because we’ve never even met some of them in person. Even so, we still know where quite a lot of them are and what they’re doing. By the way, a large share of the people we help desert end up in Kazakhstan and Armenia, because those are countries where you can legally live with a Russian internal passport. I’d guess around 90% of them now live in those two countries. We stay in touch with some of these people — they write to us and share their successes in their new lives.
Sandalov: In Warming Station, you write about the complicated, ambiguous world we all live in. On one hand, the Idite Lesom initiative obviously makes sense, with a very clear goal. But there are still plenty of contradictions. I’m thinking, for instance, of accusations that you’re helping war criminals. Or, say, you write in the book yourself that American philanthropists aren’t willing to give money to help people cross the border illegally, because in their view that’s human trafficking, and charitable money can never go toward something like that. What complaints do you run into most often?
Sverdlin: As for the money issue, it’s pretty funny: when we were just starting out, we knocked on every door, obviously. And we often heard from European grant-making foundations: “What you’re doing is good, but we still support some projects in Russia — cultural or charitable ones — so we can’t get involved with such a blatantly anti-Russian project.”
American grant-making foundations really did tell us that what we’re doing is good, but under American law it counts as human trafficking, and no one will bother to sort out that we’re not smuggling live cargo across the border but Russian deserters. So we made peace with that a long time ago. Huge thanks to the people who donate to Idite Lesom, because today probably 70% to 80% of our small budget comes from donations by Russian emigres. Obviously, we stopped accepting any donations from within Russia long ago, so as not to put anyone at risk, god forbid.
When I came up with this project, I decided right away that one fewer soldier in the Russian army means one person who won’t pull the trigger and fire toward Ukraine. I still hold to that logic. Every person we’ve helped desert, or helped avoid ending up in the Russian army in the first place, is a victory, because it weakens the criminal Russian army and in that way helps Ukraine.
About 80% to 85% of the soldiers and officers we help desert never even make it to the occupied territories. They’re stationed somewhere like Sakhalin or Rostov-on-Don. When these people find out — or even before they find out — that they’re going to be sent to the front, they get in touch with us, and we start helping them desert.
We vet the people who come to us as best we can, but there’s still a small chance that a war criminal could be among them. My colleagues and I aren’t happy about that, but we understand that, yes, in theory it’s possible.
We’ve decided that we will keep doing that vetting, but we’re still not an investigative body. It’s not our job to determine who is a war criminal and who isn’t. And thank god, there are institutions whose job and resources are suited to that: the United Nations war crimes commission and so on. Basically, we’ve decided that we do what we can in this area. Beyond that, I’d like to believe that after the war, all the war criminals will be found.

Flash: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:32:00 UTC
23:32:00 KST

Flash: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot missiles
According to a Ukrinform correspondent, this was stated during a briefing by Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a special advisor to the President.
“Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the world produces ‘Patriots’ to counter them. In other words, this balance looks very strange. If we add North Korean missiles to this, and the missiles produced by Iran, then we realize that global production of anti-ballistic missiles—such as the PAC-3, for example—needs to be increased. But there are currently problems and limitations, and while the Pentagon is trying to increase these production volumes, it’s difficult to do so,” Beskrestnov noted.
He noted that Ukraine could obtain licenses to manufacture anti-ballistic missiles, but the problem lies in the backlog for their components.
To address the shortage of anti-ballistic missiles, Ukraine is requesting that missiles be provided on loan, which it would later return once it begins domestic production; however, due to the unstable global situation, European partners are unwilling to agree to such a move. For its part, the U.S., which has a sufficient supply of PAC-3s, is very limited in how many it is willing to provide.
“These missiles are in the United States, and there’s a stockpile there—some say 3,000, others 4,000; there are 5,000 missiles in the U.S.—and to protect Kyiv, for example, where the ‘Patriot’ system is deployed, through the winter, we need about 4–5% of the U.S. stockpile. That’s a very small portion. And we’re asking the U.S.: ‘Give us this, because the Russians will destroy our infrastructure,’ but this requires a political decision. A decision from the U.S. government. They could give us these missiles—it wouldn’t affect their own defense, because, as I’ve already said, it’s literally 4 percent. But they won’t. We’re receiving a very small number, and we see what’s happening now. I actually believe this is our number one problem,” Beskrestnov noted.
According to the adviser, the situation on the front lines is currently stable, and Ukraine will be able to withstand the enemy even in the event of additional mobilization in Russia. At the same time, the biggest problem today is urban warfare and the enemy’s intention to completely destroy Ukraine’s economic potential.
“Even if they mobilize an additional 300,000 people, that solves nothing. We’ll simply produce more FPVs and field more crews to attack the Russians. We’re already facing the problem that our troops aren’t meeting their targets because there simply aren’t that many Russians to begin with. It sounds very strange, but it’s true. In other words, we understand that the war has changed,” the adviser noted.
According to him, the enemy is destroying infrastructure, bridges, and warehouses in order to cripple Ukraine’s economy.
Beskrestnov emphasized that the enemy is currently stockpiling missiles and “Shahed” drones to continue attacking critical infrastructure. Kyiv will be the primary target, as the capital is a symbolic city for the Russian occupiers.
“Kyiv is a symbolic place for our enemy. They understand that the government is here, and they understand that the international community is watching Kyiv. That is why they want to attack Kyiv specifically,” the adviser emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine currently needs an aid package consisting of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles from Europe and several other countries; subsequently, the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program will become operational, and contracts with Germany for the procurement of the relevant interceptors will take effect.

Human trafficking victims stranded in Guinea-Bissau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:20:00 UTC
23:20:00 KST

Human trafficking victims stranded in Guinea-Bissau
October 29, 2026
This article contains descriptions of rape, exploitation and sexual assault. Reader discretion is advised.
Sadio Konimba had hoped for a better future. The 26-year-old had lost her husband and was left alone with her child in Bamako, the capital of Mali.
When an acquaintance told her about the possibility of reaching Europe via the West African nation of Guinea-Bissau, she decided to make the journey. She left her 6-year-old daughter behind with relatives for the time being.
Konimba says she was invited to the country's capital, Bissau, with the promise of work and better chances of eventually continuing on to Europe.
She was told the journey from Bamako to Bissau would cost between 100,000–125,000 CFA francs (roughly €150-€190, or $170-$210), which she paid. She had only intended to stay temporarily in Guinea-Bissau, but when she wanted to return to Mali, her money was not refunded.
"I had to pay a large sum of money," Sadio told DW, adding that instead of the prospects she had been promised, she was confronted with a very different reality.
According to Konimba's account, men from Senegal offered to repay the money she had paid if she "worked" for them. When she realized what that meant, she refused and demanded her money back. To this day, she has received nothing.
Jane, a 21-year-old woman from Sierra Leone, recounted how she was subjected to an attempted rape and other abuses at the hands of a criminal network. She told French news agency Agence France-Presse they even tried to force her into prostitution.
Sadio and Jane are among dozens of victims of a suspected human trafficking ring that was dismantled by police following an operation in Guinea-Bissau on October 21. The intervention followed complaints from victims who had reported abductions and fraud.
In a written statement to DW, the criminal investigation police said that more than five suspects had been arrested.
Trapped by fales promises
According to police, the network used a front company to lure people with promises of jobs and assistance with migration to Europe.
Around 70 people are believed to have fallen victim to the scheme. Most came from abroad, including Guinea, Mali, Cote d'Ivoire and Senegal. The suspected perpetrators allegedly charged victims between 400,000 and 700,000 CFA francs for each journey to Guinea-Bissau.
According to preliminary findings, the victims were held against their will in Bissau, subjected to pressure and forced to take part in fraudulent pyramid schemes. They were expected to recruit additional participants into the schemes through social media.
To make their operations appear legitimate, those responsible allegedly used false contact details for supposed offices in Canada, the United States and Portugal. Information from Interpol, the international police agency, helped investigators uncover the network, according to police.
Issa, a 23-year-old from Guinea, says he paid a smuggler 10 million Guinean francs (around €1,000). When he refused to recruit more people, he was allegedly threatened with death.
A growing criminal network
For Bubacar Ture, head of the Guinean League of Human Rights, the case is an alarming sign.
"As a human rights organization, we are extremely concerned about this phenomenon, which has now reached deeply troubling proportions," he told DW. In May, authorities rescued 60 foreign nationals during a similar operation.
Ture sees a link between the human trafficking problem and Guinea-Bissau's weak institutions. Criminal networks exploit these conditions to continue their activities, he said, noting that women are particularly vulnerable to human rights abuses.
The small Portuguese-speaking West African country has been plagued by political instability since independence in 1975 and is also known as a transit hub for cocaine bound for Europe.
Rescued, but still trapped far from home
A week after their rescue, the victims face a new problem: many lack the funds needed to travel back to Mali, Sierra Leone or elsewhere in West Africa.
Sadio Konimba is temporarily staying with an acquaintance in Bissau. Her friend told DW that Konimba had been deeply traumatized by what she had experienced. She had never imagined she could fall into the hands of a human trafficking network that might force her into prostitution.
Konimba herself does not want to discuss in detail what kind of work she was asked to do. Police confirm that women in such cases are often sexually exploited.
Konimba says she has managed to borrow around 75,000 CFA francs from acquaintances in recent days. But that falls short of the cost of her journey back to Bamako.
According to available information, Guinea-Bissau's migration and border authority, the Direcao-Geral de Migracao e Fronteiras (DGMF), also lacks the funds needed to finance the victims' return journeys.
Contacts have been established with the diplomatic missions of the countries concerned. But progress appears slow, and no concrete arrangements for their return have yet been announced.
Support systems falling short
Bubacar Ture criticizes the lack of protection available to victims.
"There are no public shelters for cases like these," he told DW, noting that private facilities have limited capacity, and psychological support and funding for temporary accommodation are also lacking.
The human rights advocate commends the criminal investigation police for taking action against the networks despite limited resources. At the same time, he calls for greater support.
"We make an urgent appeal to the government and international partners to provide adequate support to the judiciary, the police and the other institutions," he told DW.
For Konimba, one thing matters above all else now: returning to Bamako.
"Now I definitely want to go back to my mother and my daughter," she told DW. "Every day she asks me, 'Mom, are you coming home?' I tell her, 'I will come, I will come. Just wait a little longer.'"
But Konimba still does not have enough money for the journey. She is free, but for her, the struggle to rebuild a life with dignity has only just begun.
