====================================================================================================

You Only Audition Once: Which actors came close to being cast as James Bond?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:17:41 UTC
23:17:41 KST

James Bond is one of Hollywood’s most coveted roles, and some very famous actors came close to playing 007. As we wait for the identity of the seventh actor to land the role, here's a look back at the Bonds we never got.
As you read these words, several hopefuls are waiting for the big announcement, having screen tested to become the next James Bond.
The shortlist has been revealed and we're days / weeks away from finding out which actor will succeed Daniel Craig in the iconic role. Will it be Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, or some unknown actor that will surprise everyone?
One thing is for sure: there can only be one. The rest will be ejected from the Aston Martin and their names added to a long list of would-be Bonds. These are the performers who were considered, who auditioned, and who even declined their licence to kill.
Here's a look back at those who lost out on the chance to don the famous tuxedo - with some of the screen test footage having leaked onto the internet.
Cary Grant
When it came to casting the first 007, many thought the effortlessly suave British-American star Cary Grant was the perfect fit. However, Grant went on the record and stated he was too old (58) to play Bond in Dr. No (1962). He also only wanted to do one film, and the producers were keen on holding down an actor for a multi-picture deal.
Michael Caine
It has been reported that Caine was offered the role of James Bond in 1967 after Sean Connery stepped down after You Only Live Twice. However, Sir Michael felt the role wasn’t right for him, telling The Daily Express: "I was always very much more ordinary. Bond was a glamorous, imaginative creation. I’ve always played real people."
Clint Eastwood
Failing to bag Caine following Connery's exit, another acting heavyweight was considered: Clint Eastwood. However, the Dirty Harry actor said he turned the offer down because he believed James Bond should be British. He told the Los Angeles Times: "My lawyer represented the Broccolis, and he came and said: 'They would love to have you.' But to me, that was somebody else’s gig. That’s Sean’s deal. It didn’t feel right for me to be doing it." Connery ended up coming back for Diamonds Are Forever for one last Martini.
Michael Gambon
The much-missed Irish-English thespian, best known to international audiences for his role as Albus Dumbledore in the Harry Potter film series, was approached to play James Bond for Diamonds Are Forever (1971) - following George Lazenby's solo outing in On Her Majesty's Secret Service (and before Connery agreed to one last adventure). Gambon turned it down, as he said he thought he was not good-looking enough to play the role. Funnily enough, he would go on to share the screen with Daniel Craig in 2004's Layer Cake – just before the latter was cast as Bond.
Michael Billington
British actor Michael Billington reportedly auditioned for Bond not once, not twice, but three times. He was shortlisted to replace Sean Connery for On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969), Diamonds Are Forever (1971) and Live And Let Die (1973), but was passed over every time. However, the Bond producers did cast him as KGB agent Sergei Barsov in The Spy Who Loved Me (1977) - in which he gets shot by Roger Moore's Bond in the opening ski sequence. Rough.
James Brolin
After 1981's For Your Eyes Only, Roger Moore was on the verge of retiring as 007. The Bond producers seriously considered replacing him with * gasp * an American! Josh Brolin was top of the list and screen tested to be up next in Octopussy. It nearly happened, until Moore agreed to return for two more films, before bowing out following 1985's A View To A Kill.
Sam Neill
Replacing Moore as Bond was always going to be tricky and one hot contender at the time was New Zealander Sam Neill. The actor auditioned for Cubby Broccoli, who went against director John Glen's wishes and picked Timothy Dalton instead. No shade to the much-missed Neill, but his instincts were dead on as Dalton remains one of the most underappreciated 007s - as well as the actor who paved the way for Daniel Craig's grittier iteration of Bond. Neill became a household name as Dr Alan Grant in Jurassic Park (1993) and later revealed to Den Of Geek about his Bond screen test: "It was the last time that I was bullied into doing a screen test. My agent insisted that I go and do it, [saying] it would be rude otherwise."
Mel Gibson
Another possible Moore replacement was Mel Gibson, whose star was on the rise in early 80s, having become a household name thanks to the Mad Max films. MGM reportedly wanted him to take over as Bond and offered him the role. Depending on whose version you trust, either Gibson turned it down due to length commitment, or Cubby Broccoli rejected Gibson for not being British enough. Whatever the case may be, instead of starring in 1987's The Living Daylights, Gibson cranked his career up a gear with the first Lethal Weapon film released that same year.
Liam Neeson
Following Timothy Dalton's departure and the legal woes that resulted in a Bond drought from 1989 to 1995, several names were floated for the fifth 007 actor. A courted candidate was Liam Neeson, who hadn't starred in many action movies at the time. It was later revealed in a Rolling Stone interview that his girlfriend, Natasha Richadson, told Neeson that she wouln't marry him if he'd taken the role. "My lovely wife, God rest her soul, said to me while we were shooting Nell down in the Carolinas, 'Liam, I want to tell you something: If you play James Bond, we’re not getting married.' She gave me a James Bond ultimatum, and she meant it!" Neeson tied the knot in 1994 and remained with Richardson until her death in 2009.
Sean Bean
Before he was cast opposite Pierce Brosnan in GoldenEye (1995), Sean Bean auditioned to play Bond twice. He lost out to both Timothy Dalton and Brosnan, but his screen tests were impressive enough for producers to cast him as rogue agent Alec Trevelyan.
Ralph Fiennes
Another actor who got the second-best gig... Before he played M in Skyfall, Spectre and No Time To Die, Ralph Fiennes was approached in the early 90s to succeed Timothy Dalton as Bond. In an interview with Seven Magazine, Fiennes revealed: “I don't think I felt ready to commit, and I think they were looking at Pierce. I think I would have been a terrible Bond anyway.”
Lambert Wilson
If you thought British tabloids showed their worst with the nonsensical frenzy surrounding Daniel Craig being "too blond for Bond", just imagine the uproar had the role of 007 been given to a Frenchman... Lambert Wilson was considered for the coveted part in GoldenEye (1995), but the British accent was a hurdle he couldn't clear, and the role eventually went to Pierce Brosnan.
Christian Bale
The rumour is that Barbara Broccoli courted Christian Bale for Bond after Brosnan left the role. However, the future Caped Crusader star was having none of it. According to The Daily Express, Bale said that he turned down the role as he felt Bond "was every despicable stereotype about England and British actors," adding that he'd already played a serial killer in American Psycho. Ouch.
Hugh Jackman
Following his star-making turn as Wolverine in the X-Men films, Hugh Jackman was in the running to replace Brosnan after 2002's Die Another Day. Jackman revealed he was indeed in talks to play Bond, but his shooting schedule didn't allow it. "I was about to do X-Men 2 and a call came from my agent asking if I’d be interested in Bond," he told Variety. "I just felt at the time that the scripts had become so unbelievable and crazy, and I felt like they needed to become grittier and real."
Julian McMahon
The Nip/Tuck star would have been an ideal Bond and was considered to replace Pierce Brosnan, showing that they were keen to look beyond Blighty once more. The Australian had the looks, the charisma and certainly the sophistication, but he was ultimately passed over in favour of Daniel Craig. McMahon went on to star as Doctor Doom in the Fantastic Four films and sadly died in 2025 at the age of 56.
Clive Owen
Following performances in Croupier, Godsford Park, The Bourne Identity, Closer and Sin City, Clive Owen emerged as a fan favourite to take over as Bond for Casino Royale. Considered as a frontrunner for years, Owen reportedly baulked at contractual obligations and a multi-picture deal that would have prevented him from starring in films like Inside Man and Children of Men.
Goran Višnjić
Croatian actor Goran Višnjić, best known for his role as Dr. Luka Kovač in the medical drama ER, intrigued prodcuers. The actor screen tested for Barbara Broccoli, who was impressed. But like Lambert Wilson before him, there were concerns about his accent and whether audiences would accept a non-British / non-Commonwealth actor. Shame, as the charismatic Višnjić would have brought an international dimension and flair to the character.
Michael Fassbender
Oh, the things that could have been... Michael Fassbender would have been perfect for Bond - had he not advocated for Daniel Craig during his audition! According to the Hollywood Reporter, the actor met with Barbara Broccoli and ended up vouching for his fellow actor: “I remember going into that room and meeting with her and Wilson and I think I was like, 'Daniel Craig is...' I don't know why I was promoting him. I should have been promoting myself.” A damn shame, as if we've learned anything from Inglorious Basterds, X-Men: First Class and Haywire, Fassbender has the physicality and charm required. As for his turns in Hunger, Shame and Black Bag, he's more than proven he's got the acting chops.
Henry Cavill
A then 22-year-old Cavill was very close to becoming Bond, as it was reportedly down to him and Daniel Craig for Casino Royale. Director Martin Campbell said Cavill gave a “tremendous” audition but it ultimately came down to age, as he thought the actor was too young for the role. Cavill ended up donning Superman's cape instead of the tux. Still, for many fans, he remains the Bond that got away.
Anthony Starr
Another New Zealander auditioned for the chance to be Bond in Casino Royale ... Anthony Starr, now best known for his role as Homelander on The Boys, gave a self-described "stone-faced" audition. “It is one of the worst readings of ‘Bond, James Bond’ you’ll ever see,” he shared on the Happy Sad Confused podcast last year.
Sam Worthington
Before he Na'vid up for James Cameron, the Aussie actor auditioned for Bond alongside Cavill and Craig. However, he later revealed to Variety that he couldn't nail Bond's charisma. “I could play Bond as a killer, but I couldn’t get the debonair down for the life of me,” Worthington admitted. “The suit did not fit.”
Rupert Friend
When Rupert Friend auditioned in 2005 for Casino Royale, he only had one film on his resumé: the 2004 period drama The Libertine, starring Johnny Depp and John Malkovich. The then-23-year-old sent an audition tape, and like Starr, Worthington and Cavill, ended up missing out. While Craig proved he was a worthy Bond, Friend could have been an interesting choice, as subsequent roles in shows Homeland and Anatomy of a Scandal, as well as big screen turns in The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas, The Young Victoria and The Death of Stalin showed how versatile a performer he is.
Aaron Taylor-Johnson
It's been nearly six years since the last Bond film, No Time To Die, and the post-Daniel Craig years have meant plenty of rumours surroundingthe identity of the next actor to play Bond. One name repeatedly mentioned ever since 2022 has been Aaron Taylor-Johnson. The British star known for his roles in Angus, Thongs and Perfect Snogging (a low-key masterpiece, if you haven’t seen it), Kick-Ass, the John Lennon biopic Nowhere Boy, Avengers: Age of Ultron, Nocturnal Animals and 28 Years Later was once considered the frontrunner for the seventh Bond... There were even rumours he had screen tested and that it was a done deal. Now, his name has fallen off the 007 radar – despite some clues hinting that he was still in the running. It seems - like many before him - that it wasn't meant to be, which is a shame as the 36-year-old would have made a solid Bond.
There we have it.
An exact timeline for finalizing the Bond 26 casting is not known. What we do know is that it's happening this year, as producer Amy Pascal revealed in August that "the end of the year is a good bet" for the official announcement.
Bond 26 will be directed by Canadian filmmaker and four-time Oscar nominee Denis Villeneuve and is being written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. It will be the first Bond film since Amazon took full creative control over the franchise from longtime 007 custodians Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson.
Production on the next Bond film is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028.

Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:17:35 GMT
23:17:35 KST

Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say
- Published
At least 14 people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials have said.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train headed for the southern city of Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit.
Russia's military has not publicly commented. It has repeatedly hit Ukraine's large railway network, but Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.
In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to Ukrzaliznytsia head Oleksandr Pertsovsky. He said many people were on the platform when the Russian drone struck.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform," he said.
Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit a civilian electric train.
Pictures from the Ukrainian rescue services show a large hole ripped in a platform strewn with blurred-out bodies, near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
He called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia following the incident and repeated his criticism of a controversial deal struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which eased some sanctions on Russia, allowing the US to import Russian diesel.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two girls aged 15 were killed in a Russian missile attack on the centre of Chernihiv city, in the north of the country, regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said. At least 11 others, including more children, were injured, he added.
The strikes came during efforts to uphold a fragile local ceasefire in the besieged city of Oleshky, which has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have been trapped without food, water, medicine and electricity.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Telegram that the truce was holding into a third day, and he had "set out with the Ukrainian delegation towards Oleshky" through Belarus and Russia.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has condemned Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow whilst the city hosts the Russia-Africa Summit, the Tass news agency has reported. The summit is a two-day event attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries.
The mayor of Moscow said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched overnight towards the region, most of which were shot down during their flight.
Russia's defence ministry has always denied targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
However, the dangers to passengers are very real. Attacks on Ukraine's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been hit this year, according to statistics released by Ukrzaliznytsia supplied to AFP news agency. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
There appears to have been a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure in recent weeks, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv, and a metro train hit during one of the strikes.

“And let’s be really clear: it’s Reform UK that had a problem at their conference with bundling female journalists and members out of their hall. So, we’ll take no lessons from them on this.”
The Lib Dem MP involved in the incident is believed to be Caroline Voaden, who posted on social media: “We both know that’s not true Nigel don’t we?
“I’m still waiting for the apology you were required to write to me … Though I won’t hold my breath.”
A Reform source told the Telegraph they disputed the Lib Dem characterisation, saying: “It’s not true at all – it was the Lib Dem MPs being aggressive towards Nigel. This is typical Lib Dem dishonesty in an attempt to stay relevant.”
When asked for a response to the accusations, Robert Jenrick, Reform’s shadow chancellor, said: “You know what? I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates.
“The thing about Reform politicians is, yeah, we love parliament, the institution of parliament. I go there every day. I speak in parliament. I represent my constituents.
“But I’m much more interested about, actually, the issues, trying to change this country, getting out and about outside of the bubble. And I’m not interested in even responding, dignifying the nonsense that Daisy Cooper is talking about there.”
Reform has been approached for comment.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel's Arab parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:16:18 UTC
23:16:18 KST

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alleged on Oct 29, without providing evidence, that Arab parties’ record gains in an election this week were driven in part by voter fraud, a charge rejected by Arab leaders, who accused him of incitement.
The allegation represents an escalation of anti-Arab rhetoric by Netanyahu and his far-right partners after high Arab turnout in a national ballot on Oct 27 effectively blocked a smooth path to power for either him or his main Jewish rivals.
Israeli election officials said on Oct 29 that there was a probe into fraud allegations, though the election’s integrity was not “systematically compromised”.
Analysts and critics say that by stepping up attacks on Arab parties, Netanyahu may be trying to ensure his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, feels unable to even consider forming a minority government with Arab help that could oust him from power.
Netanyahu’s goal is “delegitimising any Arab-Jewish cooperation”, said Eytan Gilboa, professor of politics at Reichman University.
Election officials were expected to finish tallying votes later on Oct 29, in a tightly fought election that has produced no clear winner and is likely to be followed by weeks of protracted negotiations over a new government.
With nearly 93% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious bloc held a modest lead in seats over a bloc of right-wing and centre-left parties led by Eisenkot, with both men’s coalitions short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Parliament.
Parties representing Israel’s 21% Arab minority were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot’s bloc, with 48 seats against Netanyahu’s camp of 53, with no realistic path to power without broad Arab backing, an option Eisenkot has so far ruled out.
However, Eisenkot’s camp could also try to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside, without including them in a governing coalition.
Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of fraud; Arab parties call it incitement
Ahmad Tibi, one of the leaders of the Arab Joint List party, said Netanyahu was on an orchestrated, toxic campaign meant to undermine the election results.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told Reuters.
During and after the Oct 27 election, Netanyahu and his allies warned against rising Arab turnout, and his right-wing Likud party issued statements accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the vote”.
It demanded police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service investigate incidents of suspected election bribery and intimidation at ballot stations in Arab towns. It said it possessed evidence of such activity but has not presented it to the public.
The police say they have arrested at least seven people since Tuesday in Israel’s south, where many Arabs live, on suspicion of voter fraud. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan said they were suspected of attempting to bribe voters to cast ballots for the Arab-dominated party Ra’am, which has Islamist roots.
On Oct 29, the head of Israel’s Central Election Committee, Supreme Court jurist Noam Sohlberg, said he had asked the Shin Bet to investigate suspicions that unidentified foreign players had tried to intervene in the election.
Likud seized on Sohlberg’s request, alleging an attack on Israel’s democracy, “an Islamisation of Israel and the toppling of the right-wing in order to bring about IDF withdrawal and defeat on all fronts, foremost Iran”.
Likud said Qatar was behind the alleged election intervention, which Qatar later denied.
Ra’am head Mansour Abbas said on Oct 29 that his party was not involved in the reported suspicious conduct and urged a full investigation. He said that Netanyahu was on an incitement campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens.
“We have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimisation he is waging against Arab citizens: Nothing will come of it, because there is nothing there,” Abbas said in a statement.
In a letter sent to a parliamentarian and published by the Central Election Committee, the committee said that there was “no base for claims that there was systematic harm to the election’s integrity”.
Israeli President: ‘We must not tarnish an entire community’
After vote tallying is completed, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with party chairs and choose a candidate who he thinks has the best chance to form a government.
The coalition that last toppled Netanyahu, in 2021, relied on Abbas’ Ra’am party. But Eisenkot’s underperformance means the opposition would now need backing from the Arab-dominated Joint List, which includes an explicitly anti-Zionist party. Most Jewish leaders have shunned formal alliances with Arab parties since Israel’s founding.
Eisenkot called for an investigation that would protect election integrity but said Netanyahu was exploiting the suspicions to “spread chaos”.
He said in a statement that Netanyahu’s aim was to “challenge the official election results, in which the Israeli public voted against the government”.
Herzog said the allegations must be investigated.
“But even at a moment like this, we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy,” Herzog said in a statement. REUTERS

2 dead in rock spire collapse at tourist site in Turkey’s Cappadocia

2 dead as ‘fairy chimney’ rock spires collapse at tourist site in Turkey’s Cappadocia
ISTANBUL – A landslide triggered by heavy rainfall caused a rock spire to collapse in Turkey’s Cappadocia tourist region on Oct 29, killing at least two people, the local governor said.
Turkey’s Cappadocia region, a magnet for tourists from around the world, is home to rock formations known as “fairy chimneys”, created by ancient volcanic activity.
“According to initial findings, two people were killed and five others injured in the incident,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on X.
“Search-and-rescue teams are continuing intensive, coordinated operations to locate any other victims who may be trapped under the debris,” he said.
The incident occurred at 3.15pm when a landslide triggered a rockfall in the town of Goreme near the open-air museum, local governor Huseyin Kok said.
The area was closed to the public following the collapse, according to reports.
Eyewitnesses reported hearing a loud noise as the rock spire near an open car parking lot fell.
Television footage showed heavy machinery digging through the rubble as rescue teams gather at the site in an effort to recover people trapped beneath the debris.
“Our search-and-rescue operations at the scene are ongoing. The government is continuing its efforts at the scene with all available resources,” Kok said.
Turkey’s culture and tourism ministry has launched restoration work in the region to help preserve the fragile rock formations from climate-related damage, natural erosion and human activity.
In 2024, another rockfall was reported in Cappadocia, although no deaths or injuries were recorded.
The Cappadocia region, a major tourist attraction known for its rock-carved underground cities and early Christian churches, is also famed for hot-air ballooning, a thriving industry that sees dozens of balloons take to the skies on clear mornings.
But concerns have been raised about safety following a series of accidents. AFP

The tabloids that used Thomas Markle to attack Meghan should now reflect. I bet they won’t | Zoe Willliams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:06:57 UTC
23:06:57 KST

As the allegations mount against Thomas Markle Sr, his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, has released a statement describing her deep distress, and saying her priority is the protection of children. Is this the point at which Thomas Markle will cease to be an acceptable source for the Sussex character attacks that have become a tabloid staple? The Daily Mail and its sister paper, the Mail on Sunday, have been utterly brazen in their cultivation of the embittered Thomas Snr, using him as a weapon against his daughter since she first married into the royal family. Now, they’ll cut loose from him and describe the charges laid against him with the same outrage as everyone else. It would be institutionally impossible for them to discuss or reflect on their prior relationship with Markle without admitting a long-range and vindictive grudge against his daughter.
Markle denies all allegations against him. His son, Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jr, described in a video for the Sun the material he claims to have found on his father’s spare mobile phone, after Markle Sr had gone back to the US to have his leg amputated. Markle Jr was in the Philippines, where both men had moved in 2025. He said the material included “the most horrific video of a very young Asian girl … couldn’t have been more than 10 years old”. He almost threw up; he almost dropped the phone. His immediate fear was for what else he might be inadvertently in possession of. “I’m on the hook for this, now,” he said.
As he made contact with the FBI, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and the Pennsylvania state police, he reportedly found more and more material: “the most obscene, disgusting, lowest-of-the-low images … thousands and thousands of them.” He said he started to question every aspect of his family history, all the times his father had hastily snapped shut his laptop, “all the locked rooms in all the houses we’ve ever lived in”.
Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. In 2019, she was passed a letter alleging that he had sexually abused a child, which she says had been sent to the Metropolitan police. The Met took no action on that letter and it has been reported that they subsequently misplaced it – whether that’s because they could believe no ill of Thomas Markle, or simply because they lose things, is unknown.
But until now, the Daily Mail and the Mail on Sunday’s trust in Markle Sr and solidarity with him have been without question.
In 2018, he handed the Mail on Sunday a five-page letter that his daughter had written to him after her wedding, which he had declined to attend, citing health reasons. Meghan successfully sued Associated Newspapers for printing part of the letter, though “printing” doesn’t really encompass the torrent of coverage and insinuation they wrung from its contents. It was the start of a relationship between the newspaper and the now alleged sex offender that was so close by last year that when Thomas Markle learned about his amputation, the first person he told was Caroline Graham, the Mail on Sunday’s US editor (and previously a biographer of Queen Camilla). In photos of the pair together, the emotions are almost laughably legible: Markle looks pugnacious and triumphant, like the guy who’s managed to get public opinion on speed dial. Graham looks serene and also victorious, the first reporter on to Goose Green in the tabloids’ favourite war.
A free press is essential and sometimes it is scabrous. But is this what a free press is for? To groom an estranged parent or other former intimate of someone in public life in order to undermine the latter person’s credibility and standing, seems sadistic. That’s a large word, particularly in the context of the allegations against Thomas Markle, and I use it advisedly. One of the hideous things about family estrangement is the feeling that everyone involved has had their character besmirched. The accused fight back with counter-claims. Nobody’s probity survives unscathed (although most of us could tell that Meghan’s father was exploiting her lovelessly for attention, and probably cash, long before these charges surfaced).
A political or media enemy plundering that dynamic for an easy win, for clicks, for a vendetta, does not even have the fog of emotionality as a defence. Everybody recoils from it. When the Republican gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy, made an attack ad featuring his opponent’s mother calling her daughter, Amy Acton, a liar, most people didn’t know the history. They didn’t know that Donna Arthur had lost custody of her children decades previously, after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted on charges of child rape. People could nevertheless see how low it was to air a view that was poisonous by definition under the fig leaf of hearing from both sides.
Ramaswamy lost a major endorsement and had venue cancellations within a day of that attack ad. What the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday would have to lose to even reflect on their allegiances in this episode is impossible to guess.
- Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

ECB holds interest rates steady as rising energy prices cloud outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:05:29 UTC
23:05:29 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
The European Central Bank (ECB) left its three key interest rates unchanged on Thursday, warning that rising energy prices pose upside risks to inflation and downside risks to economic growth.
The decision keeps the benchmark deposit facility rate at 2.5%, the main refinancing operations rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending facility rate at 2.9%, the bank said in a statement.
"While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage," the Governing Council said.
"The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth," it added.
The central bank noted that financing conditions have tightened since its previous policy meeting, which is expected to weigh on both price pressures and economic expansion.
Reiterating its commitment to ensuring inflation stabilizes at its 2% medium-term target, the bank emphasized that it is not pre-committing to a specific interest rate path.
"The Governing Council remains well positioned to navigate the current elevated uncertainty," the statement said, confirming that policymakers will maintain a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach based on incoming economic and financial data.
The bank also confirmed that its asset purchase program and pandemic emergency purchase program portfolios continue to decline at a measured and predictable pace, as the Eurosystem no longer reinvests principal payments from maturing securities.

Russia Keeps S-400 Systems on Combat Readiness in Kaliningrad Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:03:24 UTC
23:03:24 KST

Russian S-400 air defense missile systems in the Kaliningrad region are in a state of constant combat readiness.
This is stated in the Baltic Sea Overwatch report, published by ICEYE.
Satellite imagery has captured launchers at an air defense position near the port of Baltiysk in the deployed position.
The raised launchers indicate that the systems are ready to launch anti-aircraft missiles, rather than simply being on standby at their positions.
The company notes that this is not a temporary measure, as satellite monitoring indicates that this deployment has been in place in the Kaliningrad region for quite some time.
Baltiysk is one of Russia’s key naval bases in the region and the home port of the Baltic Fleet.
The deployment of air defense assets near the port strengthens the air defense of Russian military infrastructure in the Kaliningrad exclave.
The 183rd Guards Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment is one of the air defense units in the Kaliningrad region, which historically was part of the Baltic Fleet’s 44th Air Defense Division.
At the same time, the ICEYE report does not specify which unit occupies the position near Baltiysk.
The Kaliningrad region is a key deployment area for Russian air defense assets in the Baltic theater. Previously, the 183rd and 1,545th Guards Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiments, armed with S-400 systems, were stationed in the region.
In November 2023, Militarnyi reported that Russia had redeployed S-400 air defense systems from the Kaliningrad region to Rostov-on-Don. At that time, according to the news report, an analysis of satellite imagery revealed the movement of components of these systems from several positions in the region.

Russia's sanctioned Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov is heading to a G20 meeting in the US, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova stated. Ukraine is fighting Russia's air war while its main ally squeezes it too, from capped Starlink links to missing US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles, leaving Kyiv weaker before any talks. A new round of the US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral talks is expected in Abu Dhabi in November.
Moscow's sanctioned minister plans to argue against sanctions
Lavrov will lead the Russian delegation at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting, which the US hosts in Atlanta on 30–31 October. In his speeches, he will denounce “the use of economic ‘weapons’ to fight opponents, including sanctions,” Russia's Foreign Ministry stated. The US Treasury sanctioned Lavrov on 25 February 2022, the day after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The ministry claimed its delegation ran into American red tape over visas. Journalists in Lavrov's press pool still received US visas without movement restrictions, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
The State Department's announcement of the meeting doesn't mention Russia or say whether Lavrov got a sanctions waiver. Republican Congressman Don Bacon told RFE/RL that Russian leaders “should not be welcomed in any of these forums.” “They lead a pariah state,” he said.
Moscow's demands arrive days after its missiles hit Kyiv
Lavrov will also stress “the cornerstone importance of indivisible security” as the basis of multipolarity, the ministry stated. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has ruled out neutrality and limits on Ukraine's army.
Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv university campus, then return before dawn for the Southern Bridge again

Kyiv has waited almost a month for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's signature on Patriot and NASAMS missiles, Zelenskyy wrote.
Moscow keeps collecting from Washington

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright also said investors could buy sanctioned shadow-fleet tankers and return them to legal trade. Russia, for its part, kept striking Ukraine's energy sites during the truce Trump announced.
Russian officials are also back in G20 rooms in person. In late August, Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended a G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. It was his first in-person G20 appearance since 2022, and European officials refused to join the group photo with him. The State Department has stated that Russia is welcome at all G20 meetings, and a senior US official said Russia would be invited to the leaders' summit in Miami in December.
Western ministers used to push back at those tables. When Lavrov spoke at the G20 meeting in Johannesburg in February 2025, then-British Foreign Secretary David Lammy said he saw no appetite for peace.
In Atlanta, Obama accuses the White House of selling out Ukrainians
Former US President Barack Obama campaigned in Atlanta on 28 October, two days before Lavrov's meeting there.
“And while we're alienating key allies like Canada, the White House is bending the knee to Vladimir Putin of Russia and selling out Ukrainians who are fighting for their freedom and democracy,” Obama said.
He also likened Trump's self-enrichment in office to “what dictators in other countries do.”

Finnish news agency STT to cease operations with loss of 89 jobs
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:01:25 EET
23:01:25 KST

The Finnish News Agency STT will wind down the news and photojournalism units of its business from March next year.
The move will lead to the loss of 89 jobs at one of the oldest operating news agencies in the world.
STT announced last month that the company's board was planning to cease operations after nearly 140 years, a decision labelled "shocking" by Finland's journalism union Journalistiliitto. In a press release at the time, the agency said the restructure was prompted by long-standing losses and a challenging operating environment.
When the restructuring and redundancy talks with staff representatives were launched, the company said the status of all 95 permanent employees were included in the talks. Yle understands that six people will be offered the opportunity to continue working for the company in non-journalistic roles.
STT's Viestintäpalvelut (communication service) unit, which distributes press releases, will continue operating after March. It employs seven people, who were excluded from the restructuring negotiations.
End of an era
The impending shutdown of STT's news and photojournalism units comes after years of financial struggles.
Last year, STT's largest shareholder, Sanoma Media Finland, announced plans to significantly reduce its use of the agency's news and photo services — leading to a restructuring round and casting significant doubt over the agency's future.
The government granted STT around one million euros in state aid, but the money was not accepted by the agency as it was not deemed enough to keep it afloat.
The Helsinki-based agency was founded in 1887, and throughout its history its news and photojournalism services have been widely used by all major Finnish media outlets.
"The news is devastating," Marjaana Varmavuori, chair of the Union of Journalists in Finland, wrote in a press release. "STT is not just one media company among others. Its role in producing and distributing reliable information in Finland is irreplaceable."

88 pct of businesses starting to adopt tokenized money: DBS survey
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:56 CST
22:53:56 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A recent survey found that 88 percent of businesses were already deploying or piloting tokenized money use cases, DBS said on Wednesday.
The report surveyed 422 business leaders across 11 markets. The findings come as "businesses rewire business operations, treasury operations and financial management toolkits amid volatility and trade fragmentation," said DBS.
Among the expected benefits of tokenized money, 72 percent of respondents cited improved auditability and traceability, while 71 percent expected real-time cross-border payments. Other benefits included stronger internal controls and governance, and better treasury liquidity management.
Stablecoins were the most widely adopted tokenized instruments, used by 63 percent of respondents, followed by tokenized deposits at 53 percent and tokenized money market funds at 52 percent.
Meanwhile, 78 percent of businesses had diversified their reliance on traditional settlement currencies by gaining exposure to multiple currencies to support trade across different markets.
Only 2 percent were not considering alternative currencies, highlighting "a broader shift towards a more diverse monetary system in the future," said DBS. ■

Feature: Revving up dreams, Libyan woman builds career in engine modification
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:55 CST
22:53:55 KST

TRIPOLI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- In a workshop humming with engines in Mayah, 40 km southwest of the Libyan capital Tripoli, 25-year-old Rawan Abu Aisha is building a career uncommon for Libyan women -- turning a childhood passion for cars into a business modifying engines.
Growing up, Abu Aisha often watched her father work as a mechanic. "The workshop environment was familiar to me from childhood because I grew up watching my father work with cars," Abu Aisha told Xinhua.
"Over time, that interest became something I wanted to turn into a profession," she explained, saying the opportunity came through an entrepreneurship competition in Libya that invited participants to present innovative business ideas.
Drawing on her family background, she proposed modifying car engines to meet owners' specific needs. The idea became real when a customer agreed to an engine replacement. The project subsequently grew into a company established in 2022, whose primary business is modifying engines using its own custom-built units.
"My father's support and practical experience helped me take my first steps in this field," she said. "His encouragement gave me the confidence to develop my skills and turn an idea into a real business."
Her studies in entrepreneurship also equipped her with knowledge of business management, marketing and accounting, helping the company move beyond its technical roots toward a more structured management approach. What began as a business relying largely on customer recommendations later expanded its reach through an online presence and social media platforms.
According to Abu Aisha, the company's social media page has attracted over 50,000 followers, and demand for its services has grown so rapidly that her current team can barely keep up.
"The growing number of followers and the rising demand for our services show that there is considerable interest in what we do," she said. "Our next step is to expand the business and improve our ability to meet customers' needs."
Abu Aisha also hopes to partner with companies abroad, stressing the importance of long-term planning and continuous development.
"Building a sustainable business requires more than providing a good technical service," she said. "It also requires organized management, continuous improvement and a clear vision for the future."
While she believes social acceptance of women in the workplace has grown in recent years, Abu Aisha's greatest lesson from entrepreneurship is that young women must take initiative and pursue their ambitions, rather than let stereotypes dictate their choices.
"Women should not allow stereotypes to decide what they can or cannot do," she said. "They should be willing to try, learn and discover their abilities through practical experience."
For young women considering careers in mechanics, engineering or other nontraditional fields, her journey shows how personal interests can be turned into professional opportunities through determination, learning and hands-on experience.
"I want to continue developing the business and provide services that customers can trust," she said. "I believe that competence and expertise, rather than gender, should determine whether someone can succeed in a particular profession." ■

Across China: New study traces evolution of terrestrial animals on Qinghai-Xizang Plateau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:45 CST
22:53:45 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A new study has reconstructed the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, offering a clearer picture of how the unique fauna of Earth's "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years.
The research, led by a team from the Chengdu Institute of Biology (CIB) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, was recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
"Overall, the study deepens understanding of how mountain animal life evolves and provides a framework for studying how biodiversity forms in mountain regions worldwide," said Li Jiatang, a researcher at CIB.
Home to many species found nowhere else, the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, covering about 3.07 million square kilometers and ranging in elevation from 88 to 8,848 meters, according to the researchers.
The plateau platform, the Himalayas and the Hengduan Mountains are the plateau's three major subregions.
Scientists have long been interested in how the plateau's tectonic history and monsoon systems shaped the evolution of local biodiversity. However, earlier studies mostly looked at plants or single animal groups, leaving the overall development of the plateau's land animals poorly understood.
To fill this gap, the researchers combined time-calibrated evolutionary trees covering more than 20,000 species across invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. They then reconstructed the evolutionary history of 527 endemic terrestrial animal species on the plateau.
The study found that most of the plateau's endemic land animals did not arrive from elsewhere and then become new species. Instead, many evolved locally, splitting into new species right where they were, something scientists call in situ diversification.
The plateau was also a major receiver of species. The study found that animals moved in nearly twice as often as they moved out. The Qinghai-Xizang Plateau therefore played two roles at once: it was a place where new species formed, and a biogeographic sink that took in more species than it sent out.
The three subregions played very different roles. The Hengduan Mountains were the main source of local species formation, producing many new species. The Himalayas were both a source and a sink, producing new species locally and receiving species from elsewhere. The plateau platform produced very few new species locally, with most of its animal life coming from immigration, making it an important sink and a major receiver of species.
The researchers also examined how geology and climate shaped this evolutionary history. They found that a major climate transition about 34 million years ago marked the onset of sustained species diversification and biological exchange. However, the timing of these processes varied across the three subregions, reflecting differences in their uplift histories and monsoon systems.
The study also found a consistent "plants first, animals later" pattern. By comparing animal evolution with plant studies, the researchers identified this pattern across the plateau and its subregions. Early-colonizing plant groups created suitable ecological niches, laying the foundation for later animal immigration and diversification. ■

   This initiative, rather than merely discussing inclusion, offered a concrete demonstration of it, highlighting professional skills, creativity, and talent in an international setting. The message conveyed is clear: inclusion means creating opportunities so that everyone can participate, contribute, and demonstrate their abilities. The point of the initiative is that people with disabilities are not merely beneficiaries of inclusion policies, but active participants in professional, social, and cultural life. Organized to mark the 160th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Italy and Japan, the initiative strengthens the dialogue between the two countries on inclusion, employment, and social participation, involving institutions, businesses, the cultural sector, and people with disabilities. 
   “Inclusion, the affirmation of every person’s dignity, and the recognition of the extraordinary talents that initiatives like this bring to light are issues of the utmost importance, on which we will continue to deepen our collaboration with Japan,” emphasized Ambassador Vattani. “It is about removing cultural—not just physical—barriers to every person’s full participation in society, by promoting a direct experience made up of shared moments and opportunities, such as this one, in which everyone can express their abilities, including through work, music, and creativity.” The culinary program was coordinated by chefs Alessandro Circiello and Fabrizio Facchini.
                                    
“We can learn from everyone, but above all, everyone can cook—because when you teach them how to make a dish or explain a recipe, they can then execute it perfectly,” says Circiello, a chef, author, and television personality who holds positions within the Italian Chefs Federation. “We’re giving special young people the chance to step up: I see so much enthusiasm, so much determination, so much drive—sometimes more than in many other young people coming out of hospitality schools.” 
   For Facchini, a chef and entrepreneur based in New York, in collaboration with the Ministry for People with Disabilities, “bringing these projects to the world means showing how cooking, hospitality, and the promotion of Italian products can create concrete opportunities, especially for workplace inclusion.” The best part is seeing the pride these young people feel while they work, the satisfaction of putting their skills to use, contributing, and feeling like they’re making a difference. WINDHOEK, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has heightened disease surveillance and strengthened preparedness at points of entry following the spread of Ebola disease across several countries, although no suspected or confirmed cases have been reported in the country, the health ministry said.
In a public health update issued Wednesday evening, the Ministry of Health and Social Services said it was strengthening preparedness and improving healthcare workers' capacity to detect, report and respond to potential Ebola cases.
The measures follow the spread of an outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus, with cases reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Kenya and Nigeria, raising concerns about cross-border transmission.
The absence of specific vaccines and treatments underscores the importance of early detection, effective surveillance and prompt medical care, the ministry noted.
It urged the public to practice good hand hygiene, avoid contact with suspected or confirmed cases and seek immediate medical attention if symptoms develop following possible exposure. People with relevant travel or contact histories were advised to inform healthcare personnel.
It also urged the public to remain calm and rely on official communications from the ministry, the World Health Organization and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for accurate information.
The Bundibugyo virus outbreak was declared in the DRC on May 15, 2026, after cases were detected in Ituri and North Kivu provinces. As of Oct. 26, the DRC, Kenya and Nigeria had reported a combined 10,151 confirmed cases, including 4,930 deaths, according to data from the World Health Organization. ■

He called for “greater European support” for the Lebanese army and security institutions, describing such assistance as “a direct investment in the stability of Lebanon and the region.”

READ: Israeli airstrikes, artillery shelling hit southern Lebanon amid intensified drone activity
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued its attacks on southern Lebanon.
Reforms and reconstruction
On the economic front, Aoun said Lebanon was continuing to work with the International Monetary Fund to complete reforms. He expressed hope that Germany would contribute to reconstruction within a framework led by the World Bank.
He called for a shift from emergency aid to a sustainable development partnership and urged greater German private-sector investment.
Lebanon is seeking a lending program with the IMF, which requires banking, economic and financial reforms. Talks have yet to be concluded despite a series of steps taken by Lebanese authorities.

UNIFIL has been deployed in southern Lebanon since 1978 under UN Security Council resolutions to monitor the cessation of hostilities and help maintain security and stability.

According to the portal, Earth observation satellites are used to monitor agricultural production, forests, water resources, mineral deposits and environmental changes.

Ex-Swiss minister Berset defends young people's right to demonstrate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:39:28 UTC
22:39:28 KST

Ex-Swiss minister Berset defends young people’s right to demonstrate
In the face of a wave of demonstrations across Europe, the Secretary General of the Council of Europe defends the right to demonstrate while strongly condemning the violence. For Alain Berset, these mobilisations reveal a deep malaise: the destruction of future prospects for an entire generation.
From France to Albania, via Italy, Spain and Portugal, for several weeks now, European youth have been taking to the streets. The list of concerns include housing that has become inaccessible, schools and public services degraded, the cost of living and precariousness, mistrust of leaders, among others. This anger does not spare Switzerland: a day of mobilisation is planned for November 20 in several cities in the country.
Symptom of a ‘living democracy’
Sometimes punctuated by violence, these demonstrations question the state of democracy on the continent. For Berset, these movements are above all the symptom of a “living democracy”.
“You have the right to express your opinions, to meet peacefully, to have demands, to see that we can have differences, to have respect for different positions, to debate them. All this is part of a living democracy,” he said on Wednesday during the Swiss public broadcaster programme RTS Forum.
+ Ex-Swiss minister Berset takes Council of Europe top job
The former Swiss minister, who took part in the Swiss Parliament’s Foreign Policy Day, said there are also limits. “When it turns violent, when movements are instrumentalised by violent groups to break or to steal, it is absolutely unacceptable,” he continues. “And it’s a real problem because it indirectly calls into question the often very legitimate motivations of the young people who are mobilising.”
Different causes, a common malaise
What strikes him most is the simultaneity of these movements in European countries with very different national contexts. “The reasons that pushed young people into the streets in France are not the same as those we see in Albania or Serbia,” he said. “On the other hand, they all refer to the same root of the problem: the lack of prospects in a world dominated by crises, wars and the feeling that we do not really know what the future will bring.”
For him, the contrast with the young people of 20 or 25 years ago is striking: they had “the impression of having in front of [them] a boulevard that was opening up to have perspectives, projects, to develop”.
Today’s young people are facing “a continent on which war is back, in Ukraine”, he regrets. Not to mention “the war in Iran”, “violations of international law almost everywhere”, “the climate crisis”, “the pandemic crisis” from which we have emerged, “artificial intelligence” which is said to destroy us, he lists. This accumulation of threats “destroys prospects” and undermines “confidence in democratic systems”.
Warning against a security drift
Faced with calls to limit the right to demonstrate, especially in France, to avoid looting and other destruction, Alain Berset warns against a security drift. “We must be very careful not to accept that our freedoms are diminished or reduced for what we think is a secure democracy,” he insists.
The Council of Europe recently called on the states concerned to respect the right to demonstrate. For Berset, the question is complex but essential: “If we had to take this reason [violence] to destroy freedom of expression, then the question that arises is: ‘What’s the next one we’re going to touch?'”
The Serbian example illustrates the ability of democracy to channel protest: after two years of “not always easy” demonstrations following the deadly collapse of a train station in Novi Sad, students “managed to win elections last Sunday”. He added that “we are now waiting to see them at work to carry out their own project for society”.
Faced with this accumulation of crises, Alain Berset formulates a wish that may come as a surprise: “We must return to something wiser, a little more boring. I miss a slightly more boring world. We could use a little more boredom.”

Qatar denies meddling in Israeli election: 'If it were true, Qatar would own all of Israel'

Qatar on Thursday rejected allegations that it had attempted to influence Israel's election results by transferring money, accusing Israeli politicians and media figures of spreading disinformation to drag Doha into Israel's post-election political disputes.
"We reject the allegations made by certain Israeli politicians and their media associates, who have launched yet another disinformation campaign aimed at dragging Qatar into Israel's political disputes following this week's elections," said Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari. "They accuse us of buying Netanyahu, buying the left, and now buying the Arab vote. If all these claims were to be believed, Qatar would probably own all of Israel."
In a post on X, al-Ansari described the allegations as both "ridiculous and dangerous," saying the repeated references to Qatar reflected an excessive obsession with his country among certain Israeli political and media figures.
"Do not use Qatar as a scapegoat for political failures," he wrote. "Instead of trying to divert attention toward Qatar, they would be better off focusing on voters, improving people's daily lives and repairing the damage they have caused in the region."
Qatar also emphasized that the matter concerned Israel's internal affairs.
"Any government emerging from these elections must uphold international law and relevant United Nations resolutions, engage seriously and sincerely with the Palestinian issue, and respect the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, foremost among them the right to self-determination and an independent state along the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital," the statement said. "This requires responsibility and accountability."
Election chief orders Shin Bet investigation into suspected foreign interference
The controversy began with a letter sent by Central Elections Committee Chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg to Shin Bet Director David Zini.
"The integrity of elections is at the heart of democracy," Sohlberg wrote. Although he stressed that he was unable to assess the credibility of the suspicions, he said the allegations required a thorough investigation because they involved possible foreign actors.
"Given that these suspicions concern foreign elements, there is an obligation to investigate them properly in order to safeguard the integrity of Knesset elections, prevent illegal activity intended to undermine democratic institutions and prevent subversion," he wrote.
Sohlberg instructed Zini to make every effort to provide investigative findings within a week. "I instruct you to do everything in your power to examine these suspicions thoroughly and use the Shin Bet's authority to identify evidence that substantiates or disproves them," the justice wrote. "Only in this way can we ensure public confidence in the election and the integrity of the democratic process."
Citing the legal deadlines for filing election appeals, Sohlberg asked Zini to present any available findings within the coming week.
Yesh Atid lawmaker Vladimir Beliak subsequently demanded that the Central Elections Committee's leadership convene to review the evidence underlying Sohlberg's decision to order an investigation.
Responding on Sohlberg's behalf, acting committee Director General Dean Livne emphasized that the election itself had been conducted lawfully. "The Knesset elections were conducted in accordance with the law. The integrity of voting at polling stations was carefully protected, and to the best of our knowledge, claims of systematic violations of election integrity are baseless," Livne said.
He added that statements made by the police commissioner and Shin Bet director on Election Day and afterward supported that assessment.
Livne explained that Sohlberg had written to Zini after receiving sensitive classified intelligence in his capacity as chairman of the Central Elections Committee. "The information raised suspicions that required further examination to determine whether there was substantiated evidence," he said. "Immediately upon receiving the information, the committee chairman instructed that the investigation be expanded."
Because the investigation is ongoing and the intelligence is highly classified, Livne said there was no justification for convening a meeting of the committee's leadership.
Why wasn't the suspected interference stopped before the election?
Questions have also emerged about why the Shin Bet did not act before Israelis went to the polls.
As an intelligence agency responsible for preventing threats to national security, the Shin Bet possessed information about the possibility of unlawful money transfers before the election, two official sources connected to the case confirmed to ynet.
However, Central Elections Committee officials said the Shin Bet participated in every security assessment held in the days preceding the vote and never informed the committee of any such suspicions or intelligence. Had the information been shared, officials said, the agency would immediately have been asked to act to prevent interference in real time and protect the integrity of the election.
"The obvious question is how the service could have possessed what was allegedly solid and deeply troubling intelligence before the election, yet failed to act or launch an investigation before voting took place," one official said.
Zini initiated a meeting Wednesday with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, briefing him on the case and presenting intelligence materials and suspicions that he described as "well-founded."
Yashar! chairman Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the largest political bloc opposing Netanyahu, received a briefing on the matter from Sohlberg on Wednesday and met Zini on Thursday. "During the meeting, Eisenkot was briefed on suspicions concerning foreign involvement in Israel's elections," his office said. "Eisenkot expressed his support for the Shin Bet and law enforcement authorities in conducting a swift and transparent investigation."
Likud links two separate investigations
Meanwhile, police had arrested seven suspects by Thursday morning in a separate election bribery investigation involving envelopes associated with the Arab party Ra'am that were discovered in the Negev. Tens of thousands of shekels in cash were found in the homes of some suspects.
That investigation is separate from the suspected Qatari funding case. It is being handled by the National Fraud Investigations Unit within Lahav 433, rather than by the Shin Bet. Three suspects were arrested on Election Day, while four others were arrested Thursday and taken for questioning.
Likud, which has been running a campaign challenging the legitimacy of Arab parties, sought to connect the two investigations. The party dubbed the controversy "Ra'amgate" and alleged that the election had been stolen. "This is an earthquake. They stole the election in Israel!" Likud said in a statement.
The party described Sohlberg's remarks about suspected foreign involvement and voter bribery benefiting Arab parties as an unprecedented political shock.
"This is an attack on democracy intended to bring about a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and the overthrow of right-wing rule, leading to the IDF's withdrawal and defeat on every front, first and foremost Iran," the statement said.
However, the two investigations remain distinct, and no evidence has been publicly established connecting the alleged Qatari transfers to the separate election bribery case in the Negev.
Ra'am denies involvement: 'We have nothing to do with this'
Ra'am chairman Mansour Abbas denied that his party had any connection to either investigation.
"Ra'am welcomes the decision by Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg to investigate suspicions of improper attempts to influence the election through foreign funding," Abbas said in a statement. "Safeguarding election integrity and the rule of law is a civic and democratic obligation that we have made a central principle of our party."
Abbas insisted that Ra'am had no connection to the allegations and pledged full cooperation with law enforcement authorities. "Ra'am has nothing to do with the affair in question or with any other affair, and we declare that we will cooperate fully with all law enforcement authorities to establish the truth," he said.
Abbas also directed a personal message at Netanyahu, using his nickname, "Abu Yair," and accusing him of employing Qatari agents in his office.
"And to Abu Yair, who employs Qatari agents in his office, we have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimization he is conducting against Arab citizens: 'There will be nothing because there is nothing.' But unlike you, in our case it is the truth, not another lie."
Over the past 24 hours, Likud has submitted materials to the Central Elections Committee that it says include firsthand recordings of individuals from Arab communities admitting to bribing voters with fuel vouchers and cash.
Police, however, rejected Likud's claims Thursday morning, saying there was "no evidence whatsoever" supporting the allegation that the election had been stolen.
The Central Elections Committee has likewise emphasized that voting was conducted lawfully and that it has no evidence of systematic manipulation of the results, even as the Shin Bet continues investigating suspicions of foreign interference.

The incident occurred at around 3:15 PM local time on Thursday following heavy rainfall, Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok told reporters.
The collapse took place near the entrance to the Goreme Open-Air Museum, where rocks broke off one of the region’s distinctive fairy chimney formations.
Rescue teams recovered two bodies from beneath the debris, while another person was taken to hospital with injuries, according to the governor.
Police, gendarmerie, medical personnel, and disaster response teams were dispatched to the scene, he said.

NATO allies fear Trump will delay Patriot missiles for Ukraine until after US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:30:40 UTC
22:30:40 KST

Ukraine has called on US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth to sign off on the delivery of crucial Patriot defence systems used to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. But NATO sources warn the situation is "unpredictable."
NATO allies are increasingly pessimistic that Ukraine will receive desperately needed US-made Patriot interceptor missiles before next week's US midterm elections, amid suspicions that President Donald Trump is using military aid to pressure Kyiv into concessions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said his country is still waiting for US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth to approve the transfer of additional interceptors, but NATO sources have told Euronews that the situation remains “unpredictable”, with allies unclear about whether the systems will be released and when they might arrive.
The uncertainty comes as Ukraine's air defences struggle to keep pace with Russian attacks, while US interceptor stocks are under growing pressure from the war against Iran.
Russian attacks outpace US production
Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region over the previous two weeks, highlighting the scale of Ukraine's air defence challenge.
The figures illustrate the scale of the challenge facing Ukraine as it seeks to replenish its air defence stocks.
According to separate Ukrainian estimates, the US produces around 60 to 65 Patriot interceptors a month — fewer than the number of ballistic missiles Russia has launched at Kyiv and the surrounding region in just two weeks.
That production must also meet demand from other US allies and partners worldwide, including countries in the Middle East and the Gulf.
Trump pressures Kyiv over to Russian oil strikes
The uncertainty over Patriot deliveries comes as Trump pressures Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel refineries, arguing that the attacks are driving up global energy prices and hurting American and European consumers.
“We spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it,” Trump said during a visit to his golf resort in Ireland in September.
“There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel. That's hurting the world,” he added.
The US-Israeli war on Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a key shipping route through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas supplies passed — triggered what the International Energy Agency (IEA) described as the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.
With Trump's approval ratings at record lows ahead of the November 3rd midterms, some analysts believe his demands on Ukraine, including the withholding of Patriot interceptors, are intended to demonstrate action on soaring energy prices.
He recently waived punitive sanctions on Russian oil in an attempt to ease the cost to consumers by making more supply available.
Trump "wants to be seen to be doing something about the issues that are making voters unhappy, and one of them is the price of diesel, and that particularly affects farmers and red state voters in the Midwest and the United States," said former US Ambassador to NATO, Kurt Volker.
He [Trump] thinks it'd be a "great story for him to be able to say, I've got Vladimir Putin giving us diesel, and I've got Zelensky to stop attacking the refineries, so 'I'm fighting for you'," said Volker who served until Trump's first term.
Trump "using leverage" against Ukraine
Asked whether there were any indications that the interceptors would be released to Ukraine soon, one NATO source said there was little clarity.
“It's so unpredictable,” the source said.
“Trump is using as much leverage as he has over Ukraine ahead of the midterms,” the source added.
The source suggested that Trump was also seeking to push Kyiv towards a peace deal involving territorial concessions.
Two sources said Washington was frustrated by the lack of progress towards ending Russia's war against Ukraine and wanted the conflict to end as soon as possible.
One source described the war as a “stone in the boot” for Washington, but said the US understood it needed to maintain its relationship with NATO allies, including in the context of the war in Iran.
The US is relying heavily on allies to launch strategic bombers some of which can carry two dozen 2,000lb bombs to attack Iran.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian civilians continue to die as Russia intensifies its missile campaign against the country.
NATO Secretary General, Mark Rutte has urged allies to bilaterally send their own Patriot systems given the urgent needs of Ukraine.
Greece and Spain are two countries which hold considerable stockpiles of less technically advanced PAC-2 systems, NATO sources say. But neither Athens or Madrid have heeded the call of Rutte or the alliance to hand over the interceptors.
Ukraine faces interceptor shortage
Ukraine receives US-made weapons through NATO's Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, under which allies fund purchases of American military equipment for transfer to Kyiv.
Volker says he thinks the delay may also be due to the US needing the supplies to resume heavy fighting against Iran.
"It seems to be the case that European countries have purchased Patriot missiles, the anti-missile missiles, and that they have not been delivered to Ukraine yet," he said.
"And there's no information or explanation from the Pentagon about this," Volker added. "Perhaps they intend to restart the war in Iran "and don't know how many Patriot missiles they're going to need for themselves."
Volker said the prospect of US weapons paid for by European taxpayers being withheld from Ukraine is particularly troubling for European allies, already unsettled by Washington's approach to Moscow.
Concerns have been compounded by restrictions affecting Ukraine's access to Starlink satellite internet services and by proposals floated during US-led peace talks that European governments unfreeze Russian assets.
Europeans have noted the overtures by US envoy Steve Witkoff to Russian President Vladimir Putin, describing him as a "humanitarian," as an indication that the US's allegiance is shifting in favour of Moscow.
In recent talks, the US had suggested unfreezing Russian assets mainly held in Europe and transferring them to the US for future use in Ukraine.
"Some of these proposals were very much one-sided in favour of Russia, including that Europe would unfreeze the frozen Russian assets," Volker said.
"Crazy stuff coming out of these proposals here," he said.
The uncertainty over deliveries also affects Ukraine's access to NASAMS, the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, a US-Norwegian air defence system designed to counter short- and medium-range aerial threats.
Global shortage with no quick fix
The Patriot system's PAC-3 interceptor is the most capable weapons available to Ukraine for countering ballistic missile threats, including by Russia in its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
A global shortage of PAC-3 interceptors, exacerbated by their use in the US war against Iran, is putting further pressure on supplies.
The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has reported that US inventories of Patriot and other interceptors, alongside long-range strike munitions, had been depleted by about half during the conflict in Iran.
The depletion could undermine US military readiness in potential future conflicts, particularly with China, but also with Russia or North Korea, the Washington-based think tank warned.
Replenishing interceptor stocks is costly, technically complex, and time-consuming, meaning Ukraine's supply constraints are not ending any time soon.
Patriot interceptors cost over $4 million each, while manufacturing them can take close to two years, according to the estimates cited.
A tentative US commitment to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles under licence has also stalled, despite Trump announcing the initiative at the NATO summit in Ankara in July.
Meanwhile, Germany has been given the license to produce PAC-2 interceptor missiles - the less advanced, less expensive version of the PAC-3. Its production line is due to deliver the PAC-2 units by December 2026 or January 2027 at the earliest.
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said his government has offered produce the PAC-3 in a bid to kick-start much-needed access.
With supplies stretched and no clear timeline for additional deliveries, Ukraine faces growing uncertainty over its ability to intercept Russia's continuing missile attacks.
