How two high-speed trains collided in central Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:50:00 UTC
20:50:00 KST

Two high-speed trains collided just before 9 am on Oct 28 in Spain, killing at least 68 people and leaving more than 50 injured. Rail services between Madrid and the southern Andalusia region have been suspended. It is Spain’s deadliest train crash since 2013.
An Iryo express train had stopped at a red signal when it was struck by a Renfe high-speed train between the towns of Los Yebenes and Urda, near Toledo, about 118km south of Madrid by rail. The trains were both heading south from Madrid to Seville.
The crash is the second collision between high-speed trains on the same line in nine months. An accident between trains operated by the same two companies killed 46 people in January. Iryo is a private high-speed rail operator, while Renfe is owned by the Spanish government.
Addressing reporters in Madrid, Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said a computer malfunction had automatically stopped all traffic on part of the line. Puente said the fatal train crash occurred after the central command centre erroneously told the Renfe train to restart, without any speed restrictions.
Authorities said there were 147 passengers on the Iryo train, and 397 were on the Renfe train.
Prior to the crashes in 2026, Spain’s last major rail disaster occurred in 2013, when 80 people were killed and 145 injured after a high-speed train veered off the track on a sharp bend as it approached the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

mcdonald’s recycles happy meal toys into wireless mouse shaped like french fries

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:49:50 UTC
20:49:50 KST

mcdonald’s recycles happy meal toys into wireless mouse shaped like french fries
developed with lenovo, this french fry-shaped wireless mouse brings a familiar red carton to the desktop, giving recycled toy plastic a new day job.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
MCDONALD’S AND LENOVO PUT FRENCH FRIES ON THE DESKTOP
McDonald’s China is giving its fries a place beside the keyboard. Developed with Lenovo, the brand’s French fry-shaped wireless mouse translates its familiar red carton and yellow contents into a computer accessory, incorporating plastic recovered from old Happy Meal toys. The collaboration brings together two recognizable features of the fast-food experience: the packaging that holds lunch and the small plastic object that tends to outlast it. This time, the latter gets something useful to do.
The design keeps the visual shorthand intact. A red lower shell carries the Golden Arches, while molded yellow fries rise across the top, giving the mouse an uneven silhouette that departs from the anonymous curves of conventional office hardware. The food reference determines the object’s shape as well as its colors, turning a piece of takeaway packaging into something intended to stay on the desk.
RECYCLED HAPPY MEAL TOYS FORM THE MOUSE’S PLASTIC SHELL
According to the product information, more than 60% of the exterior casing is made from recycled plastic sourced from collected Happy Meal toys. Lenovo describes a process involving sorting, shredding, purification, and material modification to produce recycled ABS suitable for manufacturing. The toys lose their original forms along the way: their material returns to production, eventually taking on another distinctly McDonald’s identity.
The collaboration sits within McDonald’s China’s Reimagine Good Things initiative, launched in 2021 to explore new uses for recovered materials. Previous products have included trays and flowerpots, extending the program into everyday objects. Here, the shift from toy to computer accessory also changes the intended user and setting. Something once handed out with a children’s meal reappears among the equipment of adult working life, retaining a little of its former playfulness.
WIRELESS CONNECTIVITY HIDES BENEATH THE FRENCH FRY SHAPE
Behind the sculpted fries, the mouse offers Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless connectivity, quiet-click buttons, and three adjustable sensitivity settings. A 380mAh rechargeable battery powers the device. Its accompanying carrying pouch unfolds into a mouse pad, allowing the accessory’s protective cover to become part of the desktop setup. The specifications give the novelty object a practical role, although its distinctive outline alone says little about comfort over a full working day.
This limited release places the mouse between functional equipment and branded collectible, with its appeal resting on an immediately legible transformation. A carton normally associated with a brief stop for food becomes an object designed for repeated use. Whether that makes answering emails more appetizing is another matter.
project info:
name: French fry-shaped wireless mouse
brands: McDonald’s and Lenovo | @mcdonalds and @lenovo
location: China

Finland to Acquire German RGW 110 Anti-Tank Grenade Launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:34:41 UTC
20:34:41 KST

Finland will purchase RGW 110 shoulder-fired anti-tank grenade launchers from German company Dynamit Nobel Defence for €84.5 million.
The Finnish Army press service announced the procurement.
Deliveries of the weapons and training equipment will begin in 2027. The number of grenade launchers ordered has not been disclosed.
“Main battle tanks will continue to pose a threat on the battlefield. The new system is designed to destroy them at close range,” said Colonel Ari Mure, Inspector of Infantry of the Finnish Army.
The new system will replace the French-made APILAS anti-tank weapons, which the Finnish Army has been using since the 1980s.
One of the main selection criteria was the munition’s ability to defeat explosive reactive armor and penetrate the main armor of modern tanks. Tests were conducted against targets with characteristics closely resembling those of actual combat vehicles.
Following the tests, the Finnish military and the manufacturer further improved the warhead. The assessment of the weapon system also took into account lessons learned from the war in Ukraine.
The Finnish Army noted that disposable weapon systems allow multiple soldiers to engage a single target simultaneously from different positions. The absence of complex aiming equipment also simplifies personnel training and operation.
The RGW 110 is a single-use, 110 mm anti-tank grenade launcher equipped with a tandem shaped-charge warhead. It is designed to be fired from the shoulder, and the launch tube is discarded after use.
The stated effective range is up to 800 meters. The grenade launcher belongs to the RGW family, which also includes lighter 60 mm and 90 mm models.
Militarnyi previously reported that in 2022, Ukraine purchased 2,900 RGW 90 Matador grenade launchers directly from Dynamite Nobel Defence.
In February 2024, Ukrainian Defense Industry signed a cooperation agreement with the German manufacturer. The two parties subsequently began exploring the possibility of localizing the production of Panzerfaust 3 grenade launchers in Ukraine.

Finland's state-owned gambling firm Veikkaus has announced that it is expanding its business into Denmark with a new betting brand called Viabet.

Ukraine: 13 killed in Russian drone strike on crowded Dnipro train station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:33:00 UTC
20:33:00 KST

Ukraine: 14 killed in Russian drone strike on train station
October 29, 2026
The death toll from a Russian drone attack on a passenger train which was stopped at a station in Dnipro in eastern Ukraine on Thursday morning has risen to 14, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed.
According to Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia, a jet-powered drone struck a crowded platform on which people were waiting to board a regional train to Zaporizhzhia, about a two-hour journey to the south.
"Despite an increased threat warning, people were on the platform," the company said.
Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three drones in the daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.
In images circulating on social media, bodies could be seen strewn across a train station platform, with police officers kneeling beside them.
"Russia is deliberately hunting civilians: on trains, at stations, in residential buildings," Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said. "There is no justification for this terror, and there never can be."
Dnipro city mayor Borys Filatov also confirmed the incident, which he called a "tragedy."
Zelenskyy issues veiled Trump criticism after 'horrific' attack
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack "horrific" and demanded international action from Kyiv's allies.
"Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues," he said.
"How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating?" he asked, referring to a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin which saw some sanctions on Russia eased and the release of Russian diesel stocks onto global markets.
French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his "deep concern" that Russia continues to "opt for escalation" by targeting civilians.
"In this context, we must aim for much more than a localized ceasefire — such as the one recently negotiated for Oleshky," the French president said on social media, describing Moscow’s rejection of "all proposals to that end" as "intolerable."
"Together, we must redouble our efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace and bring Russia to the negotiating table," he said.
"These are deliberate strikes against civilians, brazen in their cruelty, and the Russians are carrying them out right as the humanitarian operation in Oleshky is unfolding," continued Zelenskyy.
"Russia's signals are clear – they want the war to continue, and everyone around the world must still work very hard to achieve major de-escalation through strong steps and appropriate pressure on the aggressor."
How Russia targets Ukrainian trains
Russia has been targeting Ukrainian trains and stations since day one of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing railway workers and passengers.
Faced with an increasing number of Russian drone attacks, Ukrainian trains began large-scale passenger evacuations this year — often while trains are already mid-journey.
In September alone, more than 5,800 trains had to be evacuated due to the threat of strikes, Ukrzaliznytsia told the AFP news agency.
Most evacuations take place in regions near the front line, in the south and east of the country: in Odesa, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia.
When a potential Russian strike is detected, the train comes to a halt and passengers are required to leave their carriages and wait at a safe distance until the danger has passed.
With commercial air travel in Ukraine shut down due to the war, the country's vast railway network has become essential for transporting people and goods, as well as for entering and leaving Ukraine.
Ukraine: More Russian attacks
Also on Thursday, authorities reported at least five other fatalities resulting from other Russian attacks across Ukraine.
A strike on the city center of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded more than a dozen, according to the head of the city's military administration.
Elsewhere, a drone slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing two and wounding several — including a six-year-old.
Edited by: Wesley Rahn

Watch: Fuel crisis strands 200 passengers aboard luxury cruise ship Odyssey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:31:36 UTC
20:31:36 KST

Around 200 passengers have been left stranded in Cambodia after a cruise ship offering residents the chance to live at sea for years suspended operations because of soaring fuel costs.
The 200-metre MV Odyssey departed Belfast in October 2024 on a continuous voyage around the world. Passengers could buy or rent cabins, with some selling their possessions to fund life at sea and paying up to $120,000 for a cabin.
Its US-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said rising fuel costs had placed its business model under unsustainable financial pressure.
The company said it was working with passengers to arrange temporary accommodation while exploring options to secure its financial future. The ship is docked in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, with no confirmed departure date.
According to the operator, monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia have risen to as much as $8,000, up from $1,800. The company attributed the pressure to extraordinary increases in fuel costs following the war involving Iran.

As criminal networks spread in Latin America, Quito is new battleground
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:25:20 CET
20:25:20 KST

By Alexandra Valencia
QUITO, Oct 29 (Reuters) - For years, the neighborhood watch group in the working-class area of Solanda in Ecuadorean capital Quito had patrolled their nighttime streets armed with little more than whistles and sticks, on the lookout for cellphone snatching and other petty crimes.
But then they realized the criminals were changing. Members of notorious national gangs began to move into the area, and shootings, contract killings and extortion took hold. The watch suspended the patrols, fearful they might be targeted themselves. Their place was taken by heavily armed troops, sent by the national government.
Ecuador’s importance as a transit point for cocaine exports from Colombia and Peru has spiked over the last half-decade, stoking an explosion in violence and crime in the once tranquil South American country that has caught up everyone from Pacific fishermen to politicians, journalists and grandmothers forced from their homes.
President Daniel Noboa, an ally of the administration of US President Donald Trump, has responded with a widespread military, police and legislative crackdown on crime, sending soldiers into the streets and hardening sentences, among other measures. The government has notched several major captures or killings of gang leaders, but that has led to fragmentation, creating vicious internecine violence and splinter groups seeking new territory.
That now includes Quito. This historic Andean city, with its whitewashed colonial buildings, cobbled streets, and backdrop of cloudcapped volcanoes, has long been a draw for tourists and digital nomads. But it is becoming an increasing focus of criminal activity, residents, police and analysts say. Gangs are using local drug sales to gain a foothold in neighborhoods, taking advantage of the capital’s strategic location to distribute drugs to the country’s ports, from where cocaine destined mostly for Europe and the US is shipped.
“Criminal organizations have tried to establish themselves in certain neighborhoods through small-scale drug trafficking,” police Lieutenant Colonel Juan Chacon told Reuters as his team conducted a raid on an alleged drug distribution site in central Quito. “That connects them to a range of other crimes.”
Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones, all gangs which the US has designated as foreign terrorist organizations, are present in Quito, according to police.
Solanda, built as a public housing project in the 1980s, with a busy commercial district and narrow streets of modest houses, appears on a national government list of high-risk Quito areas. Residents have installed a surveillance camera system on every street corner and metal gates at entrances to side streets to prevent unknown people from entering.
“With the cameras, you can identify the criminal and avoid exposing yourself,” said Maria Eugenia Alban, a community leader in Solanda. “Now criminals are no longer acting alone, and they are armed.”
GANGS ‘TRYING TO ESTABLISH A FOOTHOLD’
The pushback from authorities has had some success. An increased security response in Solanda lowered violent death figures to just two between January and September of this year, down from 13 in the same period of 2025, according to government records.
Violent death figures in Quito overall fell in 2024 and 2025 from a high of 294 in 2023, according to Interior Ministry data, as Noboa sent soldiers onto the streets. And violence still remains below that of Ecuador’s port cities like Guayaquil and Duran.
But, the armed forces say, it is a constant battle.
“Organized crime groups are trying to establish a foothold in Quito,” Lieutenant Colonel Miguel Saavedra, head of a tactical army brigade which is responsible for controlling guns, ammunition and explosives in the capital, told Reuters at a checkpoint where his unit was checking cars for weapons. His troops were seeking to “safeguard and restore security” in the city, he added.
About 4,000 police and military personnel were deployed at entry points and along strategic corridors in Quito as part of a security plan announced by Noboa in August. The city has been under a 60-day state of emergency since September.
During the first six weeks of the plan, police arrested more than 300 people, according to national police figures. The military joined police operations to check for weapons at entrances to high-risk neighborhoods and conducted targeted patrols.
Drug seizures in Quito were up nearly 500% between January and September, compared with the same period a year before, according to police figures.
Military and police operations across Ecuador cost gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining and fuel and arms trafficking nearly $20 billion in losses between January and July, according to the Defense Ministry.
However, crackdowns in one place can prompt criminal groups to seek out more favorable territory where residents are less wary of crime, said Colonel Mario Pazmino, a former head of army intelligence and current security analyst.
He said Quito is part of the “cocaine triangle,” serving as a transit and temporary storage point for drugs coming from the Colombian coastal city of Tumaco and Putumayo province, before being transported across Ecuador along Pacific and Amazon road corridors.
The capital’s strategic position has been exploited by a growing number of criminal groups over the past year, said Tiziano Breda, an analyst at conflict-monitoring organization ACLED, although its status as a “transit point” lowers the risk of it being the focus of the sort of violent disputes between groups seen elsewhere.
“In Quito’s case, international cartels and national gangs are beginning to converge and establish themselves,” Pazmino said. “Quito is a hub city. The gangs come to protect the merchandise and look for other activities.”
(Reporting by Alexandra Valencia in Quito, additional reporting by Tito Correa, Editing by Julia Symmes Cobb and Rosalba O’Brien)

‘Survival of the fittest’: The struggle to get to university in The Gambia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:25:16 UTC
20:25:16 KST

‘Survival of the fittest’: The struggle to get to university in The Gambia
Students at a top university protest transport shortages, poor facilities and safety concerns, demanding better services and leadership accountability.
Faraba Banta, The Gambia – For Muhammed Lamin Jallow, a student at the University of The Gambia’s School of Arts and Sciences, getting to class has become a daily struggle.
He travels about 40 km (25 miles) from home to the Faraba Banta campus, depending on university buses, to attend lectures.
But securing a seat on the bus can be challenging.
“Sometimes, it feels like survival of the fittest,” he told Al Jazeera. “We compete as to who gets in first, who gets to sit, who gets to stand and who goes to school and who does not.”
Jallow was among hundreds of students who protested at the University of The Gambia (UTG) on Monday, taking their grievances over transportation, campus facilities and student welfare to the vice chancellor’s office.
Lectures have since resumed after the government promised improvements to campus services.
But the students have more demands. They want Vice Chancellor Herbert Robinson and the director of student affairs to resign, accusing both officials of failing to perform their duties.
While the government has announced measures to address some of the concerns, the leadership dispute remains unresolved.
Transport and basic services remain concerns
The Students’ Union says its concerns affect more than 12,000 students, many of whom depend on university buses to reach campus.
Following the protest, Higher Education Minister Professor Pierre Gomez visited the campus with university representatives and officials from the Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy.
In a statement, the Ministry of Higher Education, Research, Science and Technology said the Gambia Transport Service Company had deployed 20 buses to support student transportation.
Students have also complained of limited access to safe drinking water and affordable food, as well as unreliable internet connectivity.
In response, the ministry promised that cafeterias across the university were ready to serve students and staff, but acknowledged that additional filtration was needed to make campus water safe for drinking. Water jars and dispensers have been installed at designated points, and the National Water and Electricity Company (NAWEC) had been consulted, it said.
On internet access, the ministry said work was under way to extend connectivity to the newly constructed Schools of Agriculture and Law, with completion expected within a week.
The proposals are intended to support student access to research materials and other educational resources. However, the statement did not confirm whether the work had been completed.
The ministry said it would continue working with the university, the students’ union and other relevant stakeholders to monitor implementation.
Cafeterias and practical training facilities
The reopening of cafeterias was another demand raised by students, who had complained that their closure made it difficult to find affordable meals on campus.
Ismaila Fadera, the students’ union president, said he raised the issue with Robinson on October 20 .
Fadera quoted the vice chancellor as saying: “Mister president, I have the student interest at heart, but we must balance this against administrative processes and compliance. You know I was a student too and many of us went through that. I used to carry my own water and food in my bag to university. The students should be told the reality. Having a cafeteria is a great addition to enhance the student experience but it is not right.”
The ministry said the cafeterias were ready to serve students and staff, although it provided no details on meal prices or availability at individual facilities.
Beyond food and water, students say inadequate learning facilities are affecting their education, particularly in programmes that require practical training.
At the School of Medicine and Allied Health Sciences in Banjul, students face overcrowded classrooms, inadequate ventilation, malfunctioning electrical sockets and shortages of projectors and smartboards, according to Abubacarr Manneh, president of the University of The Gambia Medical Students Association. Manneh said medical, nursing and postgraduate nursing students share the available facilities, putting pressure on classroom space.
He also worries about shortages of practical training equipment, including a promised simulation laboratory where students could develop clinical skills.
“Practical sessions are crucial in our professional training and development for better care of our patients,” he told Al Jazeera.
The university’s journalism students have similar concerns
Sukai Fatajo, a journalism student who participated in the protest, said the school needed radio and television studios to help students develop practical skills.
“We deserve better, and our demands must be met,” she told Al Jazeera.
The students’ union has also called for functional science laboratories, improvements to facilities at the medical school and adequate staffing.
The risks of getting to class
For Kumba Leigh, a journalism student, the struggle to reach the university has also become a question of personal safety.
One morning in April, Leigh was attacked by a knife-wielding assailant in her hometown of Bakau as she walked to a bus stop. She was trying to leave home early enough to secure a seat.
The attacker threatened to kill her if she did not hand over her bag. When she resisted, he struck her on the head and shoulder, cut her bag and dislocated her right arm. A nearby shopkeeper intervened, forcing the assailant to flee.
Months later, Leigh still has pain in her arm and suffers from trauma.
“No one should have to risk their life simply to travel to school,” she told Al Jazeera, calling for stronger security and increased police patrols.

Spain train crash: What happened in the 17 minutes before the collision?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:23:59 UTC
20:23:59 KST

An IT failure halted several trains on the Madrid–Seville high-speed line, but the crash came after Adif’s control centre authorised an AVE to resume its journey. Investigators are examining what caused the collision, which killed 69 people.
The collision between a Renfe AVE and an Iryo train, which occurred on Wednesday 28 October in Urda, in the central Spanish province of Toledo, has left at least 69 dead and more than 100 injured.
The accident took place at 8:53 am, at kilometre 118 on the Madrid–Seville high-speed line, when an AVE ran into the back of an Iryo train that was stationary on the same track. It is the second major high-speed rail tragedy in Spain in less than a year, after the Adamuz (Córdoba) crash in January 2026, which claimed 46 lives.
Although there is still no definitive conclusion on the causes, the investigation is focusing on a failure in the signalling system and, in particular, on the order issued from the control centre of Adif, Spain's railway infrastructure operator, at Madrid's Atocha railway station, for the AVE to resume its journey.
What went wrong with the safety system?
The first incident was recorded at around 8:30 am, when an IT failure disrupted communications and caused the LZB safety system to fail along a roughly 63-kilometre section of the Madrid–Seville high-speed line. The system transmits information between railway infrastructure and trains to monitor traffic and maintain safe distances.
The issue affected six trains, which had to stop or adjust their speed. Among them were Iryo 6076, carrying 147 passengers, including a baby, and Renfe's AVE 2080, with 397 passengers on board. The LZB system has been in operation on the line since its opening in the 1990s and is due to be replaced by the more modern European ERTMS system.
However, the IT failure alone does not explain the accident. When the main signalling system fails, alternative procedures are in place to manage train movements. Investigators are working to establish why those safeguards failed to prevent two trains from occupying the same section of track.
What order did the AVE receive from the Atocha control centre?
This is one of the key questions in the investigation. According to a reconstruction published by the Ministry of Transport and communication recordings published by El País, at 8:36 am, an Adif controller authorised the AVE driver to resume his journey under the lineside signalling block (BSL) system.
The instruction allowed the train to continue under "normal running" conditions, even though the main signalling system had failed. The driver requested confirmation of the order, which the controller subsequently confirmed.
The distinction is crucial: under "driving on sight" rules, drivers must adjust their speed to ensure they can stop before reaching any obstacle. In these circumstances, the speed limit is 40 kilometres per hour.
By contrast, permission to resume normal running meant the AVE could travel at a significantly higher speed. Transport Minister Óscar Puente described the control centre's decision as "inexplicable" and argued that the train should never have resumed its journey under those conditions.
The decisive 17 minutes: what happened before the collision?
The reconstruction of the communications provides a timeline of events that will be crucial to the investigation:
8:30 am. A computer fault disables the LZB system, forcing several trains on the Madrid–Seville high-speed line to stop.
8:36 am. Adif's control centre in Atocha authorises AVE 2080 to resume its journey under the lineside signalling block system (BSL) and continue running normally.
8:41 am. The Iryo driver informs the control centre that her train remains stopped on the approach to Urda due to a loss of transmission. The controller also authorises her to resume her journey.
8:48 am. The Iryo driver contacts Atocha again, reporting that she is unable to restart the LZB system and that her train remains stationary. According to the recordings published by El País, the AVE is not instructed to stop.
8:53 am. The AVE collides with the rear of the Iryo train, after travelling roughly 25 kilometres since receiving authorisation to continue.
The recordings released so far raise a fundamental question: why was the AVE not ordered to slow down or stop after the control centre received the warnings from the Iryo driver?
The communications, traffic logs and black box data from both trains will be crucial in reconstructing the decisions made during those 17 minutes.
Could the accident have been avoided?
This is one of the key questions that the judicial and technical investigations will need to address. The government has initially suggested possible human error at Adif's control centre, but responsibility has not yet been determined.
Investigators will need to establish whether operating protocols were correctly followed, what information was available to staff at Atocha, and why the authorisation given to the AVE was not revised after confirmation that the Iryo train remained stationary.
They will also examine whether there were additional failures in the systems responsible for monitoring and ensuring rail safety. The cause of the accident has therefore not yet been established, and responsibility cannot be attributed to any single individual until the investigations are complete.
What happens next in the investigation?
The Court of First Instance and Preliminary Investigation No. 2 in Orgaz (Toledo) has taken over the judicial investigation, which remains confidential. Among the first measures ordered by the court is a restriction on access to a two-kilometre section of the high-speed line around the crash site.
The court has also prohibited the removal of materials and debris from the affected area without prior authorisation and ordered the seizure and preservation of the trains' black boxes.
In addition, judicial police have been instructed to collect evidence from Adif's control centre in Atocha, including communications and data relating to train movements. Meanwhile, an independent technical investigation will seek to establish the causes of the crash and make recommendations to improve rail safety.

Is von der Leyen’s ‘associate membership’ for Canada already dead?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:22:21 UTC
20:22:21 KST

The term ‘associate membership’ was dropped from the EU-Canada summit text after German pushback, in a major blow to Commission President von der Leyen. Nonetheless, the two sides are still keen to boost their partnership.
Just weeks after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen unveiled a bold new blueprint for relations with third countries, starting with Canada, the idea of “associate membership” has been quietly buried. Has her grand vision already run aground?
On Wednesday, all references to associate membership were scrubbed from the joint statement due to be adopted at this week's EU-Canada summit, following objections from several member states, led by Germany.
Instead, the text agreed by member states speaks of developing an “ever closer association” between the EU and Canada, stopping short of full membership.
"It would have been much better to have unity from member states on the initial wording, but we have a strong basis that is agreed. And we are fleshing out the details. But most importantly, we have a common approach in terms of what the objective is that we want to pursue," Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said on Thursday.
It may look like a semantic distinction, but it amounts to an embarrassing political setback for von der Leyen, who floated the idea of Canada becoming the EU's first associate member with great fanfare in September.
Arriving in Montreal for the summit, von der Leyen appeared determined to press ahead regardless.
“We have a new ambition: bringing Canada closer to us than ever before, as associate member of the EU. And we want to take our unique partnership even further,” she wrote on X.
Yet despite the wordplay, the final text leaves little doubt that the much-hyped format failed to win the support of European governments, whom von der Leyen did not consult before making her grand pitch to Canada.
Her own country, Germany, led the charge to remove the term, arguing that the substance of the new partnership should be defined before attaching a label with potential legal implications, rather than the other way round.
There is an irony here. Associate membership was proposed last May by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as a way of offering Ukraine security guarantees while it worked towards full EU membership.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejected the proposal, which was never properly discussed among EU countries. Berlin, of course, denies that this is the real reason it so vehemently opposed Canada's associate membership.
“What the EU can do is technical, is a sector-by-sector approach. The ‘associate membership’ provided a package for it; it put a label on the partnership,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Perhaps even more telling, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney never fully bought into von der Leyen’s idea, preferring the notion of an 'Alliance for the Future'.
“The President used both terms. The precise nomenclature is a question for Europe,” Carney said at a press conference after von der Leyen’s speech, when asked whether he was comfortable with “associate membership”.
Again, the semantics hide different worldviews. For Carney, the Alliance for the Future is an open concept: a group of middle powers he championed in his landmark Davos speech in January as a new framework to safeguard global stability and the rules-based order.
The EU, by contrast, does not regard itself as a middle power, as officials in Brussels are fond of reminding anyone who will listen. Associate membership was intended to place the bloc at the centre of a new international coalition of democracies – not merely as one partner among equals, but as its leader.
That is why whatever arrangement the EU strikes with Canada matters beyond bilateral relations. Other like-minded countries, such as Australia, South Korea and Japan, are watching closely for a potential blueprint for how Brussels engages with third countries.
“In the world we are living in today, which is not the easiest, this is the right response: have the courage to think out of the box, have the courage to do something new, and have the courage to set out a vision,” said an EU official, also speaking on condition of anonymity.
Von der Leyen may have overplayed her hand, promising a partnership she could not deliver because she moved too far ahead of the member states. Still, it is hard to dismiss that EU-Canada ties have never been stronger in the past few months.
From joint exploitation of critical raw materials and common stockpiling to mutual market access in strategic sectors like AI and cloud, via systematic integration in EU defence programmes and early consultation on major policy areas, the relationship is on steroids.
Bernd Lange, the German MEP who chairs the European Parliament's Committee on International Trade, said that the disagreement over terminology should not overshadow the EU's growing ties with Canada.
“Getting caught up in debate over the partnership’s name only distracts from what really matters. So call it how you want, but what matters is concrete action, not words. The momentum is there,” he wrote on X.

Israeli military firms use European subsidiaries to obscure ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:15:03 UTC
20:15:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli military firms use European subsidiaries to obscure ties and expand, report finds
Israeli military and surveillance companies linked to the genocide in Gaza are expanding into Europe through subsidiaries, acquisitions and rebrandings that obscure their origins and human rights records, according to a new report by human rights groups.
The report, entitled "European Gateway for Genocide Technology" finds that European rearmament and fragmented regulation are opening markets for technologies developed and tested against Palestinians.
Published on Thursday by the Observatory for Human Rights and Business in the Mediterranean (ODHE) and Irídia – Centre for the Defence of Human Rights, and coordinated by SUDS and the International Institute for Nonviolent Action (NOVACT), the study identifies nine routes into Europe, including NATO procurement, EU research programmes and cybersecurity hubs such as Barcelona.
The expansion comes amid rapid growth in Israel’s defence-technology industry. Citing the Israeli economic development organisation Startup Nation Central, the report says the sector comprised more than 300 start-ups in 2025, compared with 160 in 2024. Europe accounted for 54 percent of Israel’s defence export contracts in 2024, when their total value reached approximately $14.7 billion.
But overseas expansion also reflects insecurity and difficulties attracting investment within Israel, researchers said.
"Many startups and companies are in need of investment," Felip Daza, a senior researcher at ODHE, told The New Arab.
The relocation of technology workers seeking security and companies seeking capital were converging, he said, making Europe "an attracting pole for these companies".
Europe offers cover for Israeli firms
Establishing European subsidiaries and acquiring local companies can help Israeli firms access contracts and funding while distancing themselves from their human rights records, the report argues.
Carlos Bodoque, a senior researcher at ODHE, said rebranding and corporate structures could conceal companies’ connections to products used against Palestinian civilians.
"Many of these cybersecurity companies and surveillance companies participate in European funding programmes, starting with the European Defence Fund, but also Horizon, together with universities and other public institutions," he told The New Arab.
The report highlights Intracom Defence, a Greek company acquired by state-owned Israel Aerospace Industries. According to the study, Intracom participates in 15 European Defence Fund projects, seven awarded after its acquisition and the start of the genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
Germany, Cyprus and Luxembourg provide different routes into the market, through military-industrial cooperation, favourable business conditions and corporate structures, the researchers say.
Daza described Cyprus as offering a "soft landing framework", citing its proximity to Israel and flexible tax and administrative arrangements.
"Having a base in Europe facilitates access to the single market, public contracts, and research programmes," he said, outlining how a European foothold could offer legitimacy and opportunities to expand.
Barcelona becomes a cybersecurity foothold
Barcelona in Spain's autonomous Catalonia region illustrates how this expansion extends beyond traditional arms manufacturers into Europe’s technology hubs.
Bodoque pointed to figures from Catalonia’s cybersecurity agency showing more than 500 companies operating in the sector.
He highlighted the spyware company Palm Beach Networks, citing media reporting that Alexei Levin, with links to NSO Group, had interviewed prospective recruits for the company in Barcelona.
NSO manufactures Pegasus spyware, which has been implicated in surveillance targeting journalists, lawyers and human rights defenders, the report notes.
For Bodoque, the Barcelona case raises questions about whether authorities adequately scrutinise the backgrounds of people establishing security-technology businesses.
The concern, he said, was that individuals linked to companies implicated in abuses could establish new ventures without effective barriers or scrutiny of their previous activities.
Yet establishing legal responsibility across borders remains difficult.
"We know, of course, it’s their know-how, it’s their technology, but we’re talking here about different legal frameworks, and sometimes it’s very difficult to connect," Bodoque said.
The expansion of Israel-linked firms sits in contrast to widespread popular support for Palestinians. Spain recognised Palestinian statehood in May 2024, while Barcelona’s city council voted in May 2025 to sever institutional relations with the Israeli government and end its friendship agreement with Tel Aviv. The council’s measures also targeted procurement and the participation in trade fairs of companies profiting from war and occupation.
Yet Bodoque’s account raises questions about whether those commitments translate into sufficient scrutiny of the companies and individuals entering Barcelona’s technology sector.
Daza described a wider divide between European civil society and political and business interests, saying military and economic actors "speak openly about the need for Israeli technology".
Rearmament outweighs scrutiny
European rearmament and rising NATO defence spending are creating further opportunities for Israeli suppliers, while research partnerships and technology fairs help companies develop institutional relationships, the report finds.
Many produce dual-use technologies with civilian and military applications. The authors warn that systems developed in contexts of occupation and warfare can also serve border enforcement, policing and surveillance in Europe.
Oversight, however, remains divided between national jurisdictions in the EU.
"The European Union is not acting as a unique body," Daza said. "There’s a huge fragmentation at the regulatory level."
The researchers argue that this fragmentation allows commercial cooperation to continue despite companies’ human rights records and public opposition to their activities.

- Frontline Robotics’ Linza drone took part in Quantum Systems’ Forward Edge 26 exercise in Germany, working with other unmanned systems through MOSAIC UXS.
- In one scenario, a Vector drone spotted simulated enemy drones on a ground vehicle’s route and Linza struck them with payload drops.
Ukrainian drone maker Frontline Robotics flew its Linza bomber drone alongside German, Ukrainian and other unmanned air, ground and sea systems during Forward Edge 26, a two-week exercise in Germany hosted by Quantum Systems, the company said on social media.
In one deployment, Quantum Systems’ Vector reconnaissance drone spotted simulated enemy drones along the route of an unmanned ground vehicle, and Linza then attacked the targets by dropping payloads, clearing the way for the ground vehicle, Frontline Robotics said. The company said the drone completed its missions in heavy rain and dense fog, but it did not say how many sorties it flew or how many targets it hit.
All of the systems in the exercise were connected through MOSAIC UXS, Quantum Systems’ software for controlling and coordinating unmanned platforms from different manufacturers in a single operational picture. Quantum Systems said it ran Forward Edge 26 at a military training area in central Germany and wrapped it up on Oct. 22, with no crewed vehicles in the scenarios. Systems located in Ukraine, the United States and Australia were also flown remotely during the event.
The exercise was built around four scenarios: defense against an attacking force, convoy and force protection, coastal and port surveillance, and minelaying and route clearance. In the convoy scenario, laser-based counter-drone systems protected an unmanned convoy, while the maritime scenario linked aerial and sea-based systems for coastal monitoring. Industry participants included Daimler Truck, Volkswagen, XTEND, Planet and Quantum Systems’ German-Ukrainian joint ventures, Quantum Frontline Industries and Quantum Tencore Industries.
Linza, which means “lens” in Ukrainian, is a quadcopter that can drop munitions on targets, lay mines, carry a radio relay, scout and deliver small loads of supplies to frontline positions. Frontline Robotics first introduced it in 2024 and unveiled the Linza 3.0 version in February, which the company says carries up to 4 kg (8.8 pounds) over a tactical range of 15 km (9 miles), with AI-assisted visual navigation that lets it hold position over a target without relying on satellite signals. Frontline Robotics says more than 80 units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces now use the drone.
Quantum Systems and Frontline Robotics build Linza together through Quantum Frontline Industries, a joint venture whose factory outside Munich opened in February in the presence of German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and is meant to eventually produce more than 10,000 drones a year. Germany has funded joint production of the Linza under the Build with Ukraine program, and earlier this month the joint venture signed a contract to supply Linza and Zoom reconnaissance drones to Ukraine’s National Guard in 2027.
Quantum Systems’ own Vector, the reconnaissance drone that cued Linza’s strike in the exercise, has flown extensively in Ukraine, including a mission in which one aircraft survived 11 hits and kept flying. Frontline Robotics also builds the Burya remote weapon turret, which Danish company Dropla has agreed to integrate on its unmanned ground vehicles.

Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:12:43 UTC
20:12:43 KST

Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means
With five days to go before the US midterms, analysts say the war could affect how people vote.
The Pentagon has told lawmakers in the United States that the war on Iran has cost American taxpayers at least $47.1bn so far.
The estimate, disclosed last week, comes just days before the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine if US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party will maintain control of Congress for the next two years.
In a statement on Wednesday the Pentagon also said it had “successfully obligated 97.5 percent” of the funds Trump provided the department. Last July, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) outlining tax and spending plans, which came into effect earlier this year.
We take a close look at the Pentagon estimate, and what it means for the US economy and the midterm elections.
What has the Pentagon spending report revealed?
The Pentagon told Congress that the cost of the US-Israel war on Iran as of October 16 had risen to at least $47.1bn.
Congress officials shared the Pentagon’s cost estimate breakdown with The New York Times.
According to the Times and other US media reports, the Pentagon’s estimate covers the operational costs of the war and includes a projected cost of $29bn needed to replace expended munitions such as bombs, bullets and other military hardware that has been deployed in the war so far.
It also reveals that since the war started on February 28, the US Air Force has spent $7.6bn on fighter and bomber units; the US Navy has spent $1.5bn on two dozen warships and aircraft carriers; and the US Army has spent $2.1bn to sustain its troops in the Middle East.
According to the US Central Command, there are more than 50,000 American troops stationed in the Middle East, comprising personnel deployed to large, permanent bases and to smaller forward sites across the region.
Officials told the Times that the Pentagon has spent $6.1bn to replace damaged aircraft and munitions, $645m on transport and support for commandos in the region and $24.5m on “in-house medical support” for US service members.
A congressional official added that the US Transportation Command also spent $92.2m to move equipment, and the US Cyber Command spent $14m on “cyber support operations”.
The Pentagon’s estimate, however, does not include how much Washington will need to spend to repair its damaged military bases across the Middle East and also does not take into account the cost of fuel, which is needed to power ships and aircraft used in the war.
While the Pentagon has publicly acknowledged 18 US service member fatalities in the war, The Washington Post has cited six unnamed US officials stating the true death toll is at least 22. According to the official Pentagon Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) database, 865 military personnel have been wounded in the war with Iran.
What is the response?
According to an October 19 report by USA Today, five senators from the Democratic Party had written to Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, demanding that the Pentagon reveal the true cost of the war. Their letter said the Trump administration’s “ongoing efforts to hide the true cost of this war are outrageous and unacceptable”.
Trump has not commented on the latest Pentagon estimate. But the Trump administration’s war on Iran has grown increasingly unpopular with US citizens due to its impact on US and global energy costs.
Since early March, shortly after the war began, Iran has closed the critical Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf, through which about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies were shipped until then. This has sent the price of oil spiralling and caused shortages globally. In the US, diesel, which is heavily relied on by farmers and small businesses, has nearly doubled in price.
In a post on X following the latest Pentagon report, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York wrote: “For eight months, American families have been buried by the heavy cost of Trump’s disastrous war in Iran.
“Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy,” he added.
How does the Pentagon’s estimate compare with past calculations?
Estimates for the cost of the Iran war to the US have risen steadily as the war has continued.
The Pentagon’s latest estimate is higher than the $38bn the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) forecast in September.
It is also higher than the $37.5bn price tag that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gave in July this year. Hegseth confirmed this amount during a hearing before the Senate appropriations committee and added that the cost covered some operations and maintenance extending through to the end of September.
Hegseth’s July estimate was already about $8bn higher than the previous figure released by the administration of President Donald Trump in May – $29bn.
Prior to the May estimate, in late April the Pentagon’s comptroller Jules Hurst reported that the war would cost $25bn.
Meanwhile, with the war entering its ninth month and no peace deal in sight, last month the CBO said the war with Iran could cost approximately $2bn to $3bn per month for as long as it continues.
The Pentagon’s inspector general also said last month that US troops are facing “strategic inventory shortfalls” as the war continues.
But the Trump administration has denied it is running low on weapons stockpiles.
“Cowards and traitors would like to say that the United States is short of ammunition, but that is not true. We have more ammunition than we could ever imagine using. And we are producing it at levels we have never reached before,” Trump told the United Nations General Assembly in New York in September.
Trump has also repeatedly stated that the Iran war will end when he wants it to.
Last week at an election rally in Texas, according to a report by CNBC, Trump said: “Somebody asked me before, ‘When will the war in Iran end?’ I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’”
What does the rising cost of the war mean for the midterm elections?
The US-Israel war on Iran has affected the US economy through direct government spending as well as rising energy and fuel costs.
On Wednesday, the average price of a gallon of diesel in the US hit $6.35, compared with $3.75 last year, according to the American Automobile Association.
Higher fuel costs are also driving up the cost of food – with shortages of oil and gas affecting nearly every stage of the food supply chain.
Meanwhile, the country’s national debt has surpassed a record $40 trillion, two years before expected.
As a result, the war has become deeply unpopular in the US and Trump’s approval ratings have slumped to just 33 percent – the lowest they have been at any time during his two terms as president.
With five days to go before the midterms, analysts say confirmation by the Pentagon of the high cost of the war is likely to affect how people in the US vote.
Currently, the Democrats lead Republicans by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent, a gap of 8.2 percentage points, according to RealClearPolling’s national polling average.
Chris Featherstone, a political scientist from the University of York in the United Kingdom, said this is an issue that hits at two key pillars of Trump’s political rhetoric: his promise to initiate “no new wars” during his campaign for the presidency in 2024, and his emphasis on fixing the American economy.
“The spiralling cost of the conflict for the taxpayer, and the lack of a clear end point resembles the critiques Trump levelled at the war in Afghanistan in his first presidential election campaign,” he told Al Jazeera.
According to the Costs of War Project at Brown University, the war in Afghanistan, which began in 2001, cost the US an estimated $2.26 trillion to $2.3 trillion in total across multiple presidential administrations, including George W Bush, Barack Obama and Donald Trump.
“While many of Trump’s most loyal MAGA voters are likely to remain loyal to Trump in the midterms despite the cost of the Iran conflict, the more peripheral supporters seem to be drifting away from the president ahead of the midterms, and the significant impact of this conflict on cost of living appears to be a major factor,” Featherstone said.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan told US President Donald Trump on Wednesday, Oct. 28, that Ankara was ready to help revive diplomacy between Ukraine and Russia to bring the war to an end.
Turkey’s presidential communications directorate announced the offer in a readout of their telephone conversation.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Türkiye stands ready to contribute to the efforts exerted to revive the diplomatic process between Ukraine and Russia,” the statement said.
The leaders also discussed bilateral relations and developments in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen, where Erdogan advocated diplomatic solutions.
Trump congratulated Erdogan and the Turkish people ahead of Republic Day, which Turkey marks on Oct. 29.
Kyiv prepares for possible November negotiations
Erdogan’s offer comes as Ukraine, Russia, and the US prepare for another round of negotiations, with Abu Dhabi under consideration as the venue.
On Wednesday, Oct. 28, President Volodymyr Zelensky said he hoped the meeting would take place between Nov. 6 and Nov. 10.
Kyiv was still awaiting confirmation from Washington, and Zelensky said the location could change depending on developments in the Middle East.
The planned discussions would involve negotiating teams and could prepare the ground for a subsequent meeting between national leaders.
Ukraine’s proposed agenda includes de-escalation around energy infrastructure and at sea, prisoner exchanges, the release of Ukrainian civilians held in Russia, and the return of Ukrainian children.
Støre Rejects FT Report That Putin Spent 90-Minute Call Giving History Lecture
Zelensky has said the most sensitive questions, particularly territory and security guarantees, require talks at the leadership level. No date for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin has been agreed.
Turkey has already offered to host talks
Ankara previously offered Istanbul as a venue for negotiations involving Ukraine, the US, and Russia.
During an April 4 meeting with Zelensky in Istanbul, Erdogan reaffirmed Turkey’s willingness to support a sustainable peace. Zelensky subsequently said Ukraine was ready to attend talks there and participate in a leadership-level meeting in any format.
The leaders also agreed to deepen security cooperation, including projects involving Ukrainian expertise, technology, and battlefield experience.
However, Wednesday’s readout did not announce a new negotiating venue or a specific Turkish role in the upcoming round.
Ukraine presses for European participation
Kyiv has also insisted that European countries should help shape peace negotiations, arguing that the outcome will affect security across the continent.
The diplomatic push follows a Tuesday, Oct. 27 telephone conversation between Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
Finland and Norway coordinated the initiative with Ukraine and briefed Zelensky afterward. According to Kyiv, the Nordic leaders urged Putin to take concrete de-escalatory steps.
The contacts followed consultations in Oslo involving Zelensky, European partners, and US envoy Steve Witkoff, who subsequently met Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
Zelensky has stressed that European involvement should extend beyond individual countries and that no partner should be excluded from decisions affecting European security.
Limited truce brings relief as energy attacks continue
Efforts to revive broader negotiations have produced mixed results on ceasefires.
In The Hague, Zelensky said the proposed energy ceasefire had failed because Russia continued attacking Ukrainian energy facilities after Kyiv supported Trump’s proposal.
He contrasted that with initial progress under the separate humanitarian ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky, which began on Tuesday, Oct. 27 to facilitate aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Zelensky welcomed the respite for residents but said the mission’s success would ultimately depend on civilians being able to leave safely.
The localized arrangement has provided humanitarian relief while preparations for wider negotiations continue.

Russian senators propose raising minimum scores on university entrance exams

Russian senators propose raising minimum scores on university entrance exams
The Federation Council, the upper house of Russia’s parliament, has recommended that Rosobrnadzor consider raising the minimum scores required on the Unified State Exam (USE) for admission to Russian universities, according to a resolution the chamber issued October 28.
The new requirements would apply to all universities “regardless of their departmental affiliation or ownership structure.”
The Federation Council also recommended eliminating distance learning for engineering and technology majors. For fields where enrollment exceeds labor-market demand, it proposed capping the number of tuition-paying slots. It also proposed revisiting the rules and criteria for admission benefits.
In addition, the senators proposed suspending the issuance of new university licenses “until amendments aimed at improving the licensing process are made to Russian law.”
During an October 14 plenary session, Federation Council speaker Valentina Matviyenko called for tightening university licensing requirements. According to her, opening a university in Russia today is easier than opening a newspaper kiosk, and “anyone who wants to can do it, literally by pressing a couple of buttons.”
Matviyenko also proposed reducing the number of tuition-paying students at Moscow universities by limiting admission for students from other regions: “Enroll as many as are needed in the necessary fields, and no more. The rest can study at home,” Matviyenko said.
In recent years, Russian authorities have increasingly encouraged students to leave school after ninth grade and enroll in vocational schools rather than universities, BBC Russia reported. Some schools have begun reducing enrollment in upper grades, and it has become harder to get into a university after vocational school: starting in 2025, students who skip the USE can only choose a similar field of study.
In 2025, the government already gained the right to allocate tuition-paying slots across the 40 most popular fields of study that, in the authorities’ view, produce too many graduates.

Poland to transfer two more MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine
That is according to Dariusz Lukowski, director of the Department of Strategy and Defense Planning at Poland's Ministry of National Defense, Ukrinform reports, citing Rzeczpospolita.
According to Lukowski, the decision has already been made, and the transfer will take place "in the near future."

In addition to the aircraft, Poland will provide Ukraine with 155 mm and 152 mm artillery ammunition, 20×102 mm ammunition for the aircraft cannons of F-16 fighter jets, and Polish-made missiles for Piorun short-range man-portable air defense systems.

Rzeczpospolita notes that Poland has already transferred 14 MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine in 2022-2023.
The news oultet also reports that Poland is to provide Ukraine with five more PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles for Patriot systems as part of a U.S.-led international initiative in cooperation with NATO. Earlier this year, Warsaw had already transferred five such missiles.
In September, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said that Poland was preparing its largest military aid package for Ukraine and had no intention of reducing its support amid Russian attacks.

Belarusian Plant Supplies Russia With Machines for Processing Optics Used in Su-57, BELPOL Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:11:54 UTC
20:11:54 KST

The Belarusian Smorgon Optical Machine Tool Plant operates in the interests of Russia’s defence industry.
This is according to an investigation by the Belarusian organisation BELPOL.
It supplies these companies with machine tools for processing optical components and also upgrades existing equipment.
These include the Izmeritel plant in Smolensk, the Baspik technology centre in Vladikavkaz, and the Polyus Scientific Research Institute in Moscow.
One of the Smorgon plant’s partners, Moscow-based JSC Central Research Institute Cyclone, is involved in the production of Russian Su-57 fighter jets, according to DIU.
According to Osint Varta, it specialises in the development and production of optoelectronic devices, thermal imaging systems, OLED microdisplays, photodetectors and machine vision systems for the defence industry.
This equipment enables the production of components for optical and optoelectronic systems used in military equipment.
The Russian companies that cooperate with the Belarusian plant produce monoculars, thermal imaging devices, optical sights, rangefinders and missile seekers.
These products have military applications, meaning that the supply and modernisation of the equipment help sustain the production capabilities of Russia’s defence industry.
The Smorgon Optical Machine Tool Plant specialises in manufacturing equipment for processing optical components, including grinding, polishing and lapping machines.
Despite its cooperation with Russian military manufacturers, the plant remains free of sanctions.
Militarnyi previously reported that Belarusian companies are systematically involved in supplying Russia’s defence industry.

Protest at India university where no students’ union vote held for 20 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:05:18 UTC
20:05:18 KST

Protest at India university where no students’ union vote held for 20 years
Jamia Millia Islamia campus in India’s capital has seen weeks of protests, with several students on a hunger strike to demand immediate election.
New Delhi, India – Today is the 18th day of an indefinite hunger strike for Ebin Basil, a third-year student of law at Jamia Millia Islamia, a prominent Muslim university on the southeastern edge of the Indian capital.
Basil, 23, has been fasting since October 12 for the restoration of the university’s students’ union, which has been suspended for the past 20 years.
Surrounded by dozens of friends and supporters, he remains resolute as his frail body lies on a mat inside the university’s political science department building. “Till my last breath, I will be fighting,” he told Al Jazeera.
Basil is among five hunger strikers at the core of the protest, which has seen hundreds of Jamia students congregating in the grounds surrounding a statue of iconic Urdu-Persian poet Mirza Ghalib, near the university’s main entrance. Several other students who initially joined the hunger strike have withdrawn over health concerns.
The protest began this month with students holding night vigils and calling for the students’ union election. On October 16, the university suspended Basil for a year and banned two other hunger strikers from the campus. By the night of October 17, nearly 200 protesters had returned to the grounds, and their demonstrations continued.
On October 24, the entrance gates to the university were barricaded, classes moved online, and students in halls of residence were pressured to leave. Armed police and paramilitary forces were stationed outside the gate, and a ban on gatherings of more than four people was imposed on campus.
On Monday, the university administration announced that elections would be held within 15 days of the approval of a draft union constitution to be prepared according to the guidelines of the University Grants Commission, the body that controls India’s state universities.
Jamia has set a December 20 deadline for a committee to draft the union constitution and to hold elections within 15 days of the draft’s approval. But no deadline for approval has been set, prompting the students to reject the university’s offer as “too slow”.
“It is a very vague point,” Basil told Al Jazeera.
‘Important centres of resistance’
Jamia Millia Islamia’s relationship with student democracy has been marked by long interruptions.
Established in 1920 – Thursday is its 106th anniversary – Jamia was granted federal university status in 1988 and had its minority status formally recognised by the National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions in 2011.
The first student union election at Jamia was held in 1981. Elections were discontinued in 1997 amid campus unrest and resumed in 2005. But that union was dissolved the following year, with the university administration blaming an alleged attack on the vice-chancellor.
Since then, several attempts have been made to revive the union, including a high court petition in 2011 and a student hunger strike in 2017. Meanwhile, to ease the pressure, the university allowed elected department-level student bodies that did not have influence over the whole campus.
As the current protest drags on, Basil’s health continues to deteriorate. He has lost 7kg and can barely walk unaided. Blood tests show his sodium and glucose levels are low.
“My condition is very bad. I am not even able to walk on my own right now,” he said, adding that his mental health was also suffering.
Around him, the campus has turned into a fortress, with hundreds of police and paramilitary personnel guarding its gates. Classes and exams have been moved online and the university has been closed until January 13, with students in university accommodation asked to vacate their rooms.
“They have closed the university gates completely and built a wall in front of them,” Basil said.
Jamia students say an elected union would give them a collective voice to raise concerns over conditions in halls of residence, canteens, fee increases, and restrictions imposed by the university administration on joining the youth-led antigovernment protests being held across the country.
“If a union comes, the students will have power, and the administration will not have the arbitrary power it has now,” Basil said.
M K Nausheen Farook, a second-year master’s student in disaster management, agrees.
“We are continuing this protest because we have not got a proper election date. We do not trust the Jamia administration,” said the 23-year-old student from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, accusing the authorities of acting at the behest of the federal government controlled by the right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which is known for its anti-Muslim policies.
Farook also alleged that women residents in university accommodation were being pressured to leave after classes went online.
Mantasha Irfan, a master’s student of peace and conflict studies and member of the left-wing All India Students’ Association (AISA), said the protesters are facing immediate difficulties due to the administration’s crackdown.
“They have cut off our basic supplies. There is just one functioning toilet for hundreds of student protesters. There is no water or electricity,” she told Al Jazeera. “Even women students who are menstruating do not have access to sanitary pads, and they are not allowing people to bring them in.”
Irfan, 23, said the demand for a union must also be understood through Jamia’s history of political mobilisation around issues affecting the Muslim community.
“Whenever something has happened to Muslims, Jamia and AMU have been at the forefront of the struggle and important centres of resistance,” she said.
AMU refers to Aligarh Muslim University, India’s largest minority institution, located about 120km (74 miles) away in Uttar Pradesh state.
‘To discourage emergence of Muslim leaders’
The situation at AMU is no different.
After weeks of similar protests, which included a 19-day hunger strike by a number of students, authorities at AMU announced this month that students’ union elections would be held on November 5.
The AMU election would come eight years after the last students’ union was formed there, forcing many to question why Muslim institutions continue to be denied a representative body, while other prominent universities known for student activism, such as Jawaharlal Nehru University and Delhi University, continue to elect student bodies every year.
Apoorvanand, professor of Hindi at Delhi University, who goes by a single name, told Al Jazeera that Jamia and AMU occupy a distinct position because of their Muslim minority character.
“The government and university administrations are unwilling to encourage independent thinking among Muslim students or the emergence of Muslim leaders,” he said.
Apoorvanand said students across India are feeling increasingly suffocated by the “erosion of democratic spaces” on the campuses. “They are now prepared to go to any extent to ensure that democratic spaces are restored, including at Jamia Millia Islamia,” he said.
Jamia authorities say they are trying to end the standoff.
Spokeswoman Saima Saeed told Al Jazeera that their administration is “the first in 20 years” to accept the students’ demand for a union. She said the proposed constitution requires careful examination of court orders, government recommendations and the university’s statutes, adding that Jamia’s “bona fide students and employees are its primary and genuine stakeholders”.
Meanwhile, many students find themselves caught in the ongoing standoff, as they hope to return to in-person classes.
Hera Sarfaraz, a first-year master’s student in business administration, told Al Jazeera that ordinary students are suffering. They want the university administration and the protesters to resolve the issue amicably and allow academic life to resume.
“We want our regular classes back and do not want to miss out on in-person learning by being confined to online classes. This limits our exposure to university life,” she said.

Estonian unicorn Pipedrive announces 'major' restructuring, office closures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:05:00 UTC
20:05:00 KST

Estonian unicorn Pipedrive announces 'major' restructuring, office closures
Estonian-founded customer relationship management (CRM) software firm Pipedrive is to significantly downsize, the company announced Thursday.
ERR has obtained a letter to employees from Pipedrive CEO Paulo Cunha , in which he writes that the company is significantly reducing its size in all its locations — which means fewer teams, management layers and locations. Cunha said the changes affect most of Pipedrive's current jobs and roles, adding the company will be speaking to every employee individually over the next two days, to explain whether their job is at risk and what will happen next.
Äripäev also reported Pipedrive is to make structural changes which will significantly reduce its size both in Estonia and in other countries it has a presence in.
Pipedrive marketing chief Mariliis Beger would not confirm to Äripäev whether the Tallinn and Tartu offices will remain open, stating: "We can't say at the moment, because different employment laws apply in different countries."
The group currently employs nearly 800 people, around half of them in Estonia.
In his letter, Cunha said the aim is to turn into a company which brings new solutions to market faster, understands its customers more deeply and succeeds through product strength. He said the goal is more time for work requiring depth and fewer obstacles to doing it — "in many ways a company that operates like the startup we started out as."
Pipedrive says it intends to remain product-focused and continue investing in its core CRM aspects, with a sharper focus on quality and reliability. Alongside that, it says it is building an AI-driven sales system for teams which records sales conversations, keeps data current, recommends next steps and handles routine tasks so salespeople can spend more time selling.
The company states it also wants to reduce its dependence on paid search advertising, cut management layers and meeting frequencies, and consolidate into fewer locations, so that most core teams are located in the same office.
"Small businesses' habits and expectations around buying software are evolving quickly," Cunha continued, adding that continuing to deliver value to customers requires changing how software is built and sold, and how the company operates.
He said more small businesses are asking artificial intelligence (AI) for software recommendations, that free web traffic driving the company's growth has fallen sharply, and that paid traffic to replace it costs more.
Cunha wrote that recent product updates had taught the company it needs to move faster: "We invested more in product and marketing, reorganized product development, changed our ways of working and significantly reduced operating costs." But he said those steps alone were not enough: "To build a company that matches our vision, we need a smaller and simpler organisation, focused on fewer priorities and more strongly product-centered."
He added that the layoffs do not mean AI is being used to cut costs or to replace people — AI has simply changed what customers want and how they find the product.
According to Äripäev, Pipedrive is closing its Portuguese office. It still operates in Tallinn, Tartu, New York, Prague, Florida, London, Berlin and Dublin.
Founded in 2010 by Ragnar Sass, Timo Rein, Martin Henk, Urmas Purde and Martin Tajur, Pipedrive became one of Estonia's 10 unicorn firms (a privately held startup valued at US$1 billion or more) around a decade later.

‘Operation Chargeback’ payment scam probe dealt court blow

The court in Koblenz, where the first charges in the Operation Chargeback case were filed, has now told prosecutors more investigations are needed as a “central hypothesis” may no longer be valid.

Hullemann, Weigand and others have been in detention for more than a year now. They have denied the allegation.
The Koblenz court didn’t immediately reply to an e-mail seeking comment.
In 2025, prosecutors disclosed a global probe when they raided more than 60 locations and arrested some 20 individuals as part of the investigation.
They allege that networks of criminals defrauded people across the globe of more than 300 million euros by obtaining their credit card data and signing them up for fake porn, dating or other sites, with four German payment firms handling the illicit transactions.

Ukraine's General Staff reports record Russian losses of over 49,000 in October

Developing Su-57, designers faced conflicting requirements — Sukhoi Design Bureau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:03:28 UTC
20:03:28 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. When developing the Su-57 fighter jet, designers at the Sukhoi Design Bureau had to take into account conflicting requirements regarding radar visibility, aerodynamics, and structural strength, Director of the Sukhoi Design Bureau Mikhail Strelets said in an interview published by the United Aircraft Corporation (UAC, part of Rostec).
"To achieve the Su-57’s high performance characteristics, we had to solve a number of complex design and organizational challenges. We ensured the aircraft’s high performance while balancing the conflicting requirements of stealth, aerodynamics, and structural strength by seeking optimal design solutions," he said.
According to Strelets, the Su-57’s key features are its multifunctionality and stealth capabilities, which provide a tactical advantage. The key design solutions that made this possible include low observability combined with high flight performance and a multifunctional suite of onboard equipment, as well as the ability to operate covertly against both airborne and ground-based enemy targets.

So it does take a little bit of planning to try and work it out. And for 15 slots last year, we had 54 people volunteer. So again, it was very hard to narrow it down to those 15 engineers, and then we have six on reserve. So there's 21 people that have the opportunity to go away. However, with 54, there's a lot of disappointed people on the squadron, but we encourage them to put their names down for PR or aircraft guard so they at least get to go away with a team and start to understand how we work, and then we always encourage them to put their names down the following year, and hopefully their experience levels are a bit higher and they get selected for Eng.
AS1 Chris Keen: Brilliant. So the big one then, which I've asked Tom and Aidan, I asked them what their highlights were for this season, but let's slightly change it for you because you've been around a lot longer, 10 years. So what highlights have you had over that time?
