What does home mean to Arab artists at Paris Art Week?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:12:01 UTC
19:12:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Where is home? Arab artists answered 'here too' at Paris Art Week 2026
"When you are a kid who grows up in a country at war, you have a problem of feeling that you belong," says Palestinian artist Aysha E Arar in the courtyard of the Monnaie de Paris, home of the art fair Asia NOW, a key fixture of Paris Art Week. "You don't feel you have a home."
The artist is still catching her breath after singing at full lung capacity in an improvised performance in the Monnaie courtyard. She was just as shaken as the viewers who witnessed the performance and vibrated with her: "I felt I had to do it, so I did it, from my heart."
The artist, who also has a show at the Paris gallery sans titre, sang verses from The Horse of Hope, a poem she wrote calling for chains and borders to be broken. "When I sing, I feel it all: the anger, the sadness, the love," she added.
This year's Paris Art Week, which ran from 19 to 25 October, unfolded amid ongoing protests and unrest, largely driven by student demonstrations over poor school conditions, teacher shortages, and overcrowded classrooms.
With the city in turmoil, one might have expected this year's edition to be postponed or cancelled. Instead, it went ahead, even as the situation on the streets continued to escalate.
Arab visibility explored
As expected, Arab artists featured prominently across several fairs, including MENART, dedicated to modern and contemporary art from the Middle East and North Africa, and AKAA, which focuses on African art. They were also represented at Asia NOW and Art Basel Paris, which closed early due to protests.
Beyond the art fairs, notable solo exhibitions by artists from the Middle East and North Africa were also on display at the Institut du Monde Arabe, the Palais de Tokyo, the Fondation Cartier and the Fondation Louis Vuitton.
Although many of these spaces are emblematic of the inextricable link between capitalism and art, it still mattered that Arab artists had the opportunity to exhibit their work in them.
This is particularly true in France, where, according to the Institut national de la statistique et des études économiques (INSEE), around 2.1 million immigrants were born in the Maghreb, alongside a further 2.4 million people whose parents immigrated from the region, not including the third generation. Together, that amounts to roughly one person in 15.
Despite this significant presence, Arabs remain underrepresented in French public life. In the media, Arabs barely exist.
People perceived as non-white accounted for about 15 percent of those seen on French television between 2013 and 2023, according to the broadcast regulator Arcom, while making up a quarter of those shown in a negative light in news and documentary programmes.
On the streets, they are watched closely. In the Défenseur des droits’ latest survey, young men perceived as Arab, North African or Black were four times more likely than the rest of the population to be stopped for an identity check, and 12 times more likely to be searched, frisked, taken to a police station or ordered to move on.
Palestine, meanwhile, remains a country whose name seems increasingly difficult for French media to say out loud, even after France recognised the State of Palestine in September 2025.
'Where is home?'
Against this backdrop, MENART's focus on home felt particularly timely this year.
Paris remains, de facto, one of Europe's most multicultural capitals. As Arab artists filled booths, walls and courtyards across the city, they helped shift the narrative towards one in which Paris could also be a home. Many came from countries ravaged by war, continuing a long history of artists finding a place in the French capital.
As MENART's founder, Laure d'Hauteville, put it, the question of home extends beyond geography. It was precisely for this reason that she asked around 100 artists from 18 countries across the Levant, the Gulf and the Maghreb, as well as their diasporas, ‘Where is home?’, while maintaining a balance between women and men.
For Aysha E Arar, the question of belonging is also deeply personal. Born in 1993 in Jaljulia, her family history traces back to 1948.
One grandfather fled to the West Bank and ended up with Palestinian papers; the other refused to leave his house and ended up with Israeli citizenship, which she inherited.
"I am Arab-Israeli, but I define myself as Palestinian," she said. "When I travel, however, my passport is Israeli, and that is very confusing," she noted.
As for MENART's presentation of ‘home’, it was described as "neither a place nor a time, but a sum of emotions, layers, tensions".
That understanding showed in the fair's range of galleries, with strong representation from the Gulf, including Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Muscat.
Dubai's Nasij gave a solo booth to Palestinian-Canadian artist Samar Hejazi, whose thread installation was titled Maw6ini, meaning ‘my homeland’.
Beyond the commercial art market, the fair described itself as "a true space for reflection and transmission."
Before the closing weekend, each fair drew its own map: the Middle East and North Africa at MENART, West Asia at Asia NOW, and Africa and its diasporas at AKAA. The market matters: a booth at Art Basel Paris is precisely how an artist from Tunis or Jeddah ends up in a Paris collection, a museum's acquisitions list, or a curator's notebook.
At the Grand Palais, Selma Feriani, director of what many consider Tunisia's leading gallery on the international art scene, was having a good fair.
"To be honest, I don't think the climate is affecting the fair," she said. She added that her artists had been "extremely well received," with works placed in both private and institutional collections.
For Selma, showing at Art Basel Paris also means maintaining cultural ties between Tunisia and France while bringing wider attention to artists from the region.
"Tunis and France have a direct link, and it’s important for us to be here and to represent our artists, but also represent artists from North Africa and the Global South," she said.
That commitment to representing different generations and artistic traditions also shaped Selma's gallery programme.
She said she tried “to bring as many artists as possible” to reflect the gallery’s programme and its DNA.
Each year, she also includes a modernist artist from one of North Africa’s different artistic schools, including the Casablanca School.
This year, the gallery displayed work by Baya, the Algerian painter, alongside contemporary pieces.
A short distance away, near Beirut-based gallery Marfa, Saudi gallery ATHR presented a similarly broad view of the region’s artistic landscape, bringing together artists from different generations.
Founded in Jeddah in 2009 and now also operating in Riyadh and AlUla, the gallery presented a 1991 work by Abdulrahman AlSoliman, born in Al-Hasa in 1954 and the first president of the Saudi Society for Fine Arts.
Alongside Abdulrahman’s work, ATHR showcased artists exploring identity and everyday cultural references in different ways.
The booth featured Palestinian-Saudi conceptual artist Ayman Yossri Daydban, who prints old Egyptian film posters and proverbs on tissue boxes, and Mohammad Alfaraj’s The Storyteller (2016), shown two weeks after his solo exhibition opened at the Fondation Louis Vuitton.
The exhibition also represented Sarah Abu Abdallah, Sara Abdu, and Emirati artist Rami Farook.
Curating perceptions
In the Gulf’s version of West Asia, the story is one of growth, and nobody tells it more insistently than Saudi Arabia.
For a decade, the country has presented itself as a safe, wealthy place where the state can build an art ecosystem from the top down: AlUla, the Diriyah biennials, residencies and Saudi artists exhibiting in Western institutions.
Collaborations with French public and private institutions are frequent. One of the clearest examples is Villa Hegra in AlUla, Saudi Arabia, part of a network of cultural institutions, much like Villa Medici in Rome, that represents France abroad.
Villa Hegra had its own exhibition at Asia NOW. Curator Basmah Felemban presented Tables Around: Six Proposals from Saudi Arabia with Gaël Charbau, her fellow artistic director at Villa Hegra.
The exhibition featured new commissions by seven Saudi women artists, centred on the table, where families and institutions talk through the changes Saudi Arabia is experiencing.
You could smell Reem Al Nasser’s piece: fresh jasmine woven using the technique employed for bridal crowns in southern Saudi Arabia, which, Basmah told The New Arab, is also used for bullets.
Zahra Bundakji made sculptures of the foil-wrapped chocolate trays left in Saudi living rooms until their contents became inedible.
Meanwhile, Reem Ali’s Her Mental Tools fitted a table fan with kitchen-knife blades, challenging the idea that a woman at home lives in a small world.
When asked whether the exhibition aimed to challenge a particular image of Saudi Arabia among French audiences, Basmah said the intention had not necessarily been to tailor the show to French eyes.
"Who am I to curate perceptions of Saudi?" she said.
And yet few understand the importance of soft power better than the Saudis, particularly after 10 October, when a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthis hit the domestic terminal of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
The airport was struck four times in five days and shut down; Dammam’s airport was hit too. Of Basmah’s seven artists, "only four were able to come through the airports that are open."
The picture of a Gulf state insulated from the wars around it, steadily building a state-led art scene, no longer holds.
In this context, Basmah was practical.
"At the end of the day, who cares about an exhibition? What’s most important is your safety and your family," she shared.
The Sumerians at the tailor
The question of home took a different turn at OFFSCREEN, the moving-image fair that had taken over the Chapelle Saint-Louis de la Salpêtrière.
There, Iraqi artist Adel Abidin approached migration and identity through the absurdity of imagining an ancient civilisation confronted with the present.
During Adel’s conversation with The New Arab, a helicopter passed overhead. It was unclear whether it was there for the hospital next door or formed part of the extensive surveillance operation by the French police.
For Adel, the question of home is also personal. Under Saddam Hussein, he could not get into art school, so he left to pursue a master’s degree in Helsinki in December 2000.
"Then I got accepted, and George Bush attacked Baghdad," he said, but he stayed, and after about 26 years, the city had become his home.
He added that home is a place where he can stay and express himself freely.
Inside, NIKA Project Space showed an installation centred on his video Unfitted (2024), which began as a joke between friends about Iraq.
"If the Sumerians will come now, and they will see the situation, they will go back and destroy their civilisation and never think of doing it," he said.
Adel took the figures from the Standard of Ur, the Sumerian artefact depicting scenes of war and peace in the British Museum, and made them "do as everybody is doing nowadays, migrating and going to a tailor, which is the touch of sarcasm here, to change their identities or their outfit."
The video never showed them dressed. "So that’s why the video is called Unfitted," he said.
On the protests, Adel was unequivocal.
"I think it’s super cool that people have the right to demonstrate and express their feelings. I’m against destruction, against burning and stealing and looting," he explained.
He believes in the power of art, even if, as he said, "It doesn’t have the magic wand," adding that every little piece matters.
Articulating the malaise
From Adel’s sardonic take on migration, the week’s highlights turned to a more intimate unease at the Palais de Tokyo.
One of the most moving exhibitions is Lebanese artist Ali Cherri’s Today is OK, running until 14 February 2027.
The Franco-Lebanese artist built the exhibition around his film La Sentinelle, which follows a French soldier through the night of 14 July, France's national holiday.
Sculptures within an immersive installation carried the film into the galleries: the guard, the preparation for conflict and what war does to bodies.
In the short film, the soldier, LeFleur, meaning ‘the flower’, is inhabited by a malaise he cannot quite name, not even when the psychiatrist at the infirmary asks him why he wants to shoot himself in the mouth.
"Just like that," he said. "Or no particular reason."
The context in which Art Week unfolded makes it hard not to think of the larger, collective malaise that twists the guts of the French people and translates into millions of slogans and battles to fight for.
Ultimately, the rage in the streets is a symptom that something is not working, and has not been working for a very long time.
The unrest had been building since late September, when lycée students across France began blockading their schools over overcrowded classes, unreplaced teachers, unsafe buildings and Parcoursup, the discriminatory university admissions platform.
Saturday 17 October marked a peak in the turmoil, as the student movement merged with protests against the cost of living, drawing around 550,000 people across France, including 110,000 in Paris.
The unrest continued the following day, as shops in Les Halles were looted, shopfront windows smashed, bins and bicycles thrown around, and cars and bikes set on fire in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Limoges.
By Monday, around 3,000 businesses had been damaged or looted, and more than 2,400 people had been arrested.
In Ali’s film, which explores Eros and Thanatos in a disturbing way, the protagonist, Sergeant LeFleur, finds a moment of comfort in a queer performer's singing, whose voice expresses rage, sadness, love, and pain.
It was the perfect mirror to Aysha E Arar’s heartfelt singing.
Just as in the streets of Paris, love, rage, violence and reason were all mixed together, all there, all demanding change.
[Cover photo: Adel Abidin’s 'Abandoned Relic', presented by NIKA Project Space at OFFSCREEN Paris 2026, reinterprets the ancient Standard of Ur, reflecting on displacement, abandoned civilisations and the negotiation of new identities. Photo credit: Ivan Erofeev.]

KYIV – A Russian drone slammed into a busy platform at a railway station in Ukraine’s Dnipro on Oct 29, killing at least 14 people in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called a “horrific” attack that demands a response from Kyiv’s allies.
The strike came as Ukraine and Russia strive to uphold a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky – under Russian occupation since 2022, and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages.
The truce was holding into its third day, both countries said, with the Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets announcing that he had “set out with the Ukrainian delegation towards Oleshky” through Belarus and Russia.
But elsewhere, Moscow continued to pummel Ukraine.
The strike at the Dnipro train station hit a platform “where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing”, Zelensky said.
By early afternoon on Oct 29, Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha said the death toll from the strike had risen to 14.
Another 14 had been wounded, he said, adding that six of them were in severe condition after suffering “multiple shrapnel wounds”, including an 11-year-old boy and a man who had “both legs amputated”.
Zelensky slammed the attack as “horrific” and insisted that “sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues”.
Images released by Ukrainian emergency services showed bodies on the platform, rescuers helping victims to safety, and two burnt-out passenger trains with their windows shattered.
French President Emmanuel Macron reacted with outrage to the attack, stressing the need for “far more than a localised ceasefire” like the one in Oleshky.
“It is intolerable that Russia continues to reject all proposals to this end, choosing instead to pursue escalation and target civilians,” he said on X.
Zelensky slams US sanctions relief for Russia
Russia has fired drones on trains across Ukraine since the first days of its 2022 invasion – destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing several railway workers.
Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted three jet-powered drones in a daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.
In the aftermath of the attack, Zelensky refreshed his criticism of a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to ease some sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel onto global markets.
“How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and the energy sector, instead of de-escalating,” he asked.
At least six others were killed across Ukraine in separate Russian attacks, according to local officials.
Two teenage girls killed in strike north of Kyiv
A strike on the city centre of Chernihiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded nearly two dozen others, including four children, the head of the city’s military administration, Dmytro Bryzhynsky, said.
A drone also slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing three and wounding several – including a six-year-old – the local governor said.
Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.
The Kremlin earlier this week vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under US mediation.
Zelensky said on Oct 28 it would be a “huge success” if the local ceasefire in Oleshky – brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump – allowed for the evacuation of stranded citizens.
Locals trapped there have resorted to hunting and eating pigeons in recent months, former residents in touch with those in the city told AFP.
Russia and Ukraine are to meet in November with US envoys, to discuss ways to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, with no firm dates set for the talks yet.
Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.
Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.
Ukraine and its allies say ceding ground to Moscow would be tantamount to a capitulation and leave Kyiv vulnerable to future Russian attacks. REUTERS

Bird flu outbreaks prompt national indoor shelter order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:09:18 UTC
19:09:18 KST

Bird flu outbreaks prompt national indoor shelter order
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Three recent outbreaks of bird flu have led agriculture secretary Silvio Erkens to order farmers to keep their poultry indoors.
Two of the outbreaks occurred in Groningen and one in Noord-Holland. Wild birds, which are currently migrating south, have also been found to carry the disease.
“It is important to limit contact between kept birds and potentially infected wild birds as much as possible,” Erkens told broadcaster NOS. “That way we are doing everything we can to prevent new outbreaks.”
Bird hobbyists don’t have to comply with the order, but they must shield their birds in aviaries or other shelters. All non-essential visitors are also banned from places where birds are kept.
Consumers
While poultry farmers are hard-hit, the price and availability of poultry have remained relatively stable.
“The prices have been high enough for the past couple of months, so they are stable for now,” says Babak Sadeghi, who owns Chris Kip in Amsterdam’s Albert Cuyp Market. “But increased transport and petrol prices have affected suppliers and deliveries.”
Bird flu has also been found in Denmark, Germany, the United Kingdom and other places.
Erkens is pushing for mandatory vaccinations of egg-laying hens against bird flu.

‘Restored nature hits record 252 mln hectares, but still off target’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:09:18 UTC
19:09:18 KST

A helicopter from Brazil's environmental agency flies over an area of the Amazon rainforest during a wildfire-fighting operation in Autazes, Amazonas state, Brazil, Oct. 15, 2026. (AP File Photo)
Countries are restoring about 252 million hectares of nature, a record level according to a United Nations report published on Oct. 29, but this still falls short of global 2030 targets.
"This report captures the largest documented restoration effort in history," said Doreen Robinson at the U.N. Environment Program. The restored area is equivalent to the size of Argentina or Algeria.
But the report estimates the pace of restoration efforts must "triple" to meet the 2030 target of one billion, and funding will need to increase sharply, particularly from the private sector.
Nature restoration efforts recorded in 149 countries have mostly taken place on land, with 232 million hectares involved, compared with 11 million hectares of inland waters and 5.7 million hectares of marine and coastal waters.
This "lags far behind ambition in both freshwater [inland water] and marine and coastal ecosystems, yet these ecosystems are degrading at the highest rates," the report warned.
As part of the U.N. Decade on Ecosystem Restoration from 2021 to 2030, and an international agreement adopted in 2022 known as the Kunming-Montreal framework, states have committed to taking action to halt biodiversity loss and protect the planet.
In terms of restoration on land, China is far ahead of other regions, with 137 million hectares, followed by Mongolia, Kazakhstan and Ethiopia.

Trump’s plea – ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ – deserves to backfire | Margaret Sullivan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

As he criss-crosses the nation, stumping for Republican candidates, Donald Trump keeps asking voters to use their imaginations.
“In this election, I’m asking you to pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just pretend,” he urged at a Kansas rally as he campaigned for the incumbent senator Roger Marshall and gubernatorial challenger Ty Masterson last month.
“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.
But will it work? That seems increasingly unlikely.
Given his own lack of popularity and weird behavior, it’s an egotistical notion – more appealing to himself than to voters.
After all, his approval ratings are in the basement. Gas prices are higher, on average, than at any time during the Biden years. People feel like they need to float a loan before heading to the supermarket.
In that Kansas rally, he referred to the opposition as “Dumocrats”, which is typical of the level of presidential discourse to which the nation has become accustomed.
In his rallies, he appears “increasingly detached from reality”, as one campaign analysis in the Independent put it, as he “vacillates between topics to the point where his remarks border on the nonsensical and he ends every appearance by awkwardly dancing to the Village People’s well-known gay anthem YMCA”.
Stranger still, as the Guardian’s Adam Gabbatt reported recently, Trump has been offering “unsolicited and increasingly unhinged assessments of men’s bodies” over the past few weeks.
“I examined his ass,” the president said in Kentucky, speaking about Republican senator Jon Husted. “And then I looked at his shoulders … I looked at his jawline … I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I’m still recovering.”
Trump has also been – to put it mildly – stretching the truth on the campaign trail, sometimes merely misleading in his remarks, sometimes straight-up lying.
For example, he promised a North Carolina rally that gas and oil prices would tumble soon and he claimed: “I had it down to the lowest level in years,” apparently speaking about the price of filling up a gas tank at the pump. A PolitiFact examination disputed this, noting that when Trump took office at the beginning of last year, the average gas price was $3.23 a gallon, but by late September of this year, it was $4.61.
But it’s not just what he says at rallies that may backfire on the candidates he hopes to help.
Much of what’s happened in Trump’s second term is working against Republican candidates. That includes the widespread self-dealing that, as the historian Garrett Graff wrote recently, “is so endemic and so obvious that it has broken through to voters”.
It’s also his misguided war, his rants on social media, his disparagement of longtime allies, including Canada. It’s also his obvious plan to declare the election rigged should it not go his way.
“Even Maga die-hards and GOP allies in Congress have grown weary of his erratic behavior,” as the Wall Street Journal’s Jason Riley noted.
And Democrats, including Barack Obama, are only too happy to campaign by associating Republican candidates with Trump.
These midterm elections, Obama told a crowd in Ohio, “is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration. It’s the circuit breaker in the system.”
That blast of sanity and good sense seems far more likely to resonate with potential voters than Trump’s unhinged rants and dangerous threats.
Pretend he’s on the ballot?
Maybe that’s effective with Trump’s remaining cult-like base. And maybe it will bring some of those loyalists out to vote next week if they had been thinking of sitting out this election.
But more likely, the imagined association with Trump will serve to remind most voters that Trump’s malfeasance must be rebuked and rejected. Certainly not encouraged.
- Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:21 UTC
19:00:21 KST

Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
Students gifted only water celery or white wormwood, choosing these fragrant plants to symbolise a pure pursuit of knowledge
While it is common for Chinese people to hold banquets for teachers upon graduation as a way of honouring them – a traditional value – in ancient China, students expressed their respect for teachers differently: by presenting them with vegetables.
The tradition began in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). On the first day of school, students wore blue gowns and brought their teachers wild vegetables they had gathered themselves. They then bowed reverently before memorial tablets honouring ancient sages. The ceremony was followed by a group dance, which also expressed the students’ respect for their teachers and their dedication to their studies.
Not just any vegetables could be presented to teachers on this day. Water celery and white wormwood were preferred because they were seen as clean, fragrant and ethereal, symbolising the students’ pure pursuit of knowledge.

Halloween Is a Chance to Rethink Your Relationship With Fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Whether you’re watching a scary movie or tiptoeing through a haunted house, Halloween can stir up spooky feelings. A gory scene may force you to cover your eyes or jump out of your seat. What drives these reactions is fear, a powerful core emotion.
Being afraid can feel like getting stuck in your own horror show—your heart pounds, your pupils dilate, and you may gasp or scream. These reactions are not under conscious control; they’re rooted in biology. Like all emotions, fear plays an important role. It helps you survive and bolt for safety.
Halloween gives you a chance to experiment with fear. It’s a time when the fright is real, but the threat is not.
As psychotherapists who specialize in Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy (AEDP), we know that being able to name and work with fear is good for health. Acknowledging your emotions makes you less likely to suppress or avoid them, drink too much, or become numb to what you’re feeling.
While these behaviors take the edge off temporarily, research shows that stuffing down your emotions can lead to mental-health concerns, such as depression and anxiety, which have become more common among U.S. children and adults in recent years.
If you’d like to safely explore your relationship with fear this Halloween season, here are five exercises we recommend.
Recognize fear in your body
Have you ever tried to outsmart fear? Perhaps you scolded yourself for being a scaredy-cat or tried to stop the feeling with logic. Messages from society and our families often promote a mind-over-matter approach, reinforcing the belief that we can think our way out of an emotion.
A healthier approach is to get out of your head and tune into your body. During a frightening moment, notice the telltale signs of alarm, like trembling hands, a racing heart, or feeling cold. These physical sensations are important messengers that clue you into what core emotions you’re experiencing.
Once you identify and name them, their intensity will likely diminish. It may sound like a small act, but research shows that putting language on your emotions can help regulate and tame distress.
Watch fear come and go
Gripping, painful emotions can seem permanent. But watching them come and go can remind your brain that even the most frightening experiences are temporary.
During a spooky scene, you may want to cover your face or turn away. Rather than immediately distracting yourself, approach the emotion with curiosity. Observe how fear builds, peaks, and eventually subsides.
Curiosity helps us embrace a sense of wonder. Research shows that a curious mindset can cultivate positive emotions and reduce worry.
Calm the scary feeling
When fright takes hold, breathing techniques like 4-7-8 breathing or box breathing can soothe your nervous system. Taking long breaths instead of shallow ones sends oxygen to your muscles, which can help relieve tension.
You can also practice what eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapists call “dual attention.” Keep your eyes glued to the frightening scene and stay with the sensations in your body as you take deep belly breaths. Research shows that belly breathing increases parasympathetic regulation of the heart through vagal pathways, helping the body settle into a calmer state.
Discover how fear makes you want to move
When a ghoul jumps out or a frightening sound catches you off guard, pay attention to what your body wants to do. Do you feel an urge to flee, freeze, duck, or reach for someone’s hand?
In AEDP, we call these “adaptive actions,” and they offer clues about how your nervous system responds to perceived danger.
All core emotions, including fear, have impulses—energy in the body that makes us want to take action. When someone responds to our emotions with shame instead of empathy, we learn to block these impulses, creating a pressure-cooker effect. This can lead to symptoms like insomnia, muscular tension, and rumination that can hurt your health.
Noticing fear’s impulses expands your emotional awareness and sets the stage for you to work through other core emotions with greater wisdom.
Notice how connection changes fear
Sharing a scary moment with another person can make it easier to tolerate. That’s because having someone by your side doesn’t just provide reassurance; it calms the amygdala, the brain’s emotional center, and helps you heal past wounds and traumas.
We recommend this experiment: Watch a horror movie alone, and then with someone you trust. Or visit a haunted house with a trusted friend or partner. Notice what happens when you share the experience.
A little emotions education goes a long way towards nurturing your well-being. By learning to stay with fear, you teach your brain that you can handle challenging emotions.
And when we know emotions aren’t something to fear, we’re better equipped to handle life’s challenges with authenticity, flexibility, and courage.

Press review: Slovakia seeks EU role in Ukraine talks as Trump faces midterm uncertainty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The upcoming Putin-Xi-Trump summit in China is expected to focus on arms control, regional conflicts, and the future of international security; Slovakia is pushing for a greater EU role in Ukraine peace talks, including appointing an envoy for dialogue with Russia; and Republicans face possible defeat in the US midterms, raising concerns that Trump may refuse to accept the results. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Kommersant: Russia, China, US summit could help shape new world order, establish rules of engagement
The meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and US President Donald Trump, expected to take place on November 18-19 on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, will be a historic event regardless of its outcome - no comparable gathering has ever taken place. Kommersant asked leading Russian experts to share their views on which substantive issues might define the agenda of this unprecedented meeting.
Fyodor Lukyanov, editor-in-chief of Russia in Global Affairs magazine and chairman of the Presidium of the Council on Foreign and Defense Policy, believes that the meeting in Shenzhen will be primarily symbolic in nature, "but its significance should not be underestimated." "The demonstration that the world’s three largest countries, which differ considerably in both their means of exerting global influence and their respective interests, are capable of discussing global issues in a trilateral format would send a clear signal. It would mark the emergence of a particularly significant format in an increasingly chaotic and fragmented world," he told the newspaper.
"A fundamental achievement of a potential trilateral meeting would be an agreement on the principles of predictable conduct toward one another and the restoration of a sense of stability in international relations. However, whether the United States will be in a position to provide guarantees of its own predictable behavior remains an open question," Andrey Sushentsov, dean of the Faculty of International Relations at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO) and a Candidate of Political Sciences, told Kommersant.
Dmitry Trenin, president of the Russian International Affairs Council and research director of the Institute of World Military Economy and Strategy at the National Research University Higher School of Economics, noted that comparisons with the "Big Three," which convened in Tehran, Yalta, and Potsdam between 1943 and 1945, are "inappropriate." "Nevertheless, the planned meeting of the leaders of Russia, China, and the United States in Shenzhen is a tangible indication that three leading powers hold sway over the geopolitical, military, and, to some extent, technological dimensions of today’s world. The summit on Chinese soil represents a step toward building a new world order architecture," he added.
"The three leaders have no shortage of issues to discuss. First, holding the APEC forum in China’s technology hub of Shenzhen will bring a substantial economic component to the agenda. Second, Donald Trump will almost certainly seek to prioritize the future of arms control following the expiration of the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty. Third, the heads of state cannot avoid addressing regional conflicts, including Ukraine. Moscow hopes to discuss the framework of European security directly among the major powers, without the participation of Brussels or Kiev," Natalia Tsvetkova, acting director of the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Kommersant.
Izvestia: Slovakia urges greater EU role in Ukraine peace talks
Slovakia supports appointing a European Union representative for the Ukrainian settlement process, Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar told Izvestia. According to him, the candidate for this role should be acceptable to both sides of the conflict as well as to countries actively involved in peace initiatives. Bratislava believes that the EU must take a more active role in the peace process and in dialogue with Russia.
"Since the very beginning of the war in Ukraine, the current government of the Slovak Republic has maintained that there is no military solution to this conflict and that lasting peace cannot be achieved without diplomatic dialogue involving all parties. At the same time, we believe it is important for the European Union to play a more active role in the peace process and in dialogue with Russia if it wishes to preserve its natural position and defend its own interests, including its vision of a pan-European security architecture," the minister told Izvestia.
According to him, "the sooner negotiations begin, the sooner further human suffering and destruction can be prevented."
"We therefore believe that discussing the participation of an EU representative in peace negotiations is entirely appropriate. We fully support this idea and have advocated it from the outset. We support a candidate who would be acceptable to both parties to the conflict and to countries actively contributing to peace efforts," he added.
Media reports have identified Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store as potential negotiators, both of whom spoke by phone with Vladimir Putin this week. However, they contacted Moscow on behalf of their respective countries rather than the EU as a whole. This lack of coordination at the European level has already drawn sharp criticism from some countries, Izvestia noted.
The principal obstacle facing Brussels remains the absence of a unified position on the Ukrainian crisis. Against this backdrop, the EU is considering an alternative approach, as Member of the European Parliament Fernand Kartheiser previously told Izvestia. Rather than appointing a single special representative, it could establish a full negotiating team, he said.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Trump’s potential refusal to accept Republican defeat emerges as key uncertainty in US midterms
US House Speaker Mike Johnson, a prominent figure in the Republican Party, has made a highly ambiguous remark. He said Republicans would cede power if they lost the November 3 elections, but expressed hope that it would not come to that. In effect, Johnson, speaking on behalf of his party, has implicitly, if not explicitly, backed Donald Trump’s position, Nezavisimaya Gazeta writes. Trump said he would recognize the election results only if the vote was fair, while simultaneously raising the possibility of electoral fraud by Democrats. Increasingly, the central uncertainty surrounding the elections is not who will win, but whether Trump will accept the results.
As the congressional elections draw closer, opinion polls are showing an increasingly unfavorable outlook for Republicans. According to the surveys, President Trump’s party, which currently holds majorities in both chambers of Congress, is almost certain to lose control of the House of Representatives and is also likely to cede the Senate to the Democratic Party.
"Trump is engaged in an extraordinarily high-stakes gamble. The stakes are enormous - quite literally, it is all or nothing. The prospect of having to fend off investigations and possibly an impeachment attempt if Democrats win is not even the most important consideration. Trump will probably find some way out of that predicament, as he has done before. The real issue is that he has Napoleonic ambitions. He wants to leave his mark on history, reshape the world, and accomplish something on a global scale. But if Democrats secure a majority in Congress, those ambitions will effectively be curtailed," Vladimir Vasilyev, chief research fellow at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta.
Trump could pursue a wide range of options after November 3, he added. Vasilyev also outlined the most extreme scenario, which currently appears unlikely but cannot be ruled out entirely.
This would involve an attempt to undermine the foundations of American democracy by declaring a state of emergency to delay the start of the new Congress’s term. Such a move would constitute a desperate gamble, but Trump has repeatedly demonstrated that he is not afraid of taking risks.
Izvestia: Ukraine-South Korea diplomatic dispute may threaten arms supplies
A major crisis is deepening in relations between Ukraine and South Korea. Seoul has announced the recall of eight members of its embassy staff in Kiev and threatened to sever diplomatic relations entirely. Experts told Izvestia the dispute is undermining Vladimir Zelensky’s hopes of securing additional weapons.
The disagreements between the two countries surfaced in late September. At the time, Vladimir Zelensky, addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York, announced that two North Korean servicemen who had been captured by Ukrainian forces during the fighting in the Kursk Region had been handed over to Seoul.
The Ukrainian leadership, whether intentionally or inadvertently, has undermined the position of President Lee Jae Myung, according to Alexander Zhebin, leading research fellow at the Center for Korean Studies of the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences. Kiev denies the existence of secret agreements, effectively accusing the South Korean leader of lying.
"Why are the Ukrainians acting this way? Apparently, they either consider short-term political gains more important or are simply being excessively irresponsible. Nevertheless, I do not expect diplomatic relations to be severed. That would be an extremely serious step, one that often precedes war, and there is no indication of anything resembling a war in this case," the expert explained.
He also suggested that Seoul may have deliberately inflated the controversy to distance itself from the Ukrainian conflict, thereby gaining a strong justification for refusing to supply Kiev with weapons.
Political analyst Alexander Semchenko believes the current dispute is unlikely to have a significant impact on Ukraine’s position. He is convinced that Zelensky, who is acting against the wishes of US President Donald Trump, is even less concerned about South Korea’s grievances.
"He apparently believes that Seoul will be compelled to continue supporting Kiev under any circumstances because there is a common political will in the West to do so, and South Korea will be unable to resist it," the analyst told the newspaper.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Africa’s surging energy demand opens new opportunities for Russian oil, gas companies
African countries could surpass India and China in oil, gas and refined petroleum product demand growth, according to long-term forecasts by major consulting and analytical organizations, including OPEC, S&P Global, Wood Mackenzie and the International Energy Agency (IEA), Rossiyskaya Gazeta writes.
Africa’s share of global oil demand is projected to rise from 4.5% this year to 7.8% by 2045-2050, while its share of global gas demand is expected to increase from 4% to 7.5%. In addition, African countries are set to increase their share of the global market as producers of raw materials, including crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG).
This growth will be driven by three main factors: rapid population growth, urbanization, and the continent’s still relatively low levels of per capita energy consumption, Viktoria Trifonova, senior analyst at the Yakov and Partners analytical center, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta.
Meanwhile, Oleg Abelev, head of the analytical department at the Rikom-Trust investment company, noted that many African countries remain entirely dependent on imported fuel due to limited domestic oil refining capacity.
As Vasily Kutyin, director of analytics at Ingo Bank, pointed out, Africa accounts for 7% of global gas reserves. However, 70% of these reserves are located in deepwater offshore areas, while up to 30 bln cubic meters of associated petroleum gas are flared annually. For Russian companies, this translates into demand not so much for "raw materials in their pure form" as for technologies related to extraction, the monetization of associated gas, and the development of LNG infrastructure.
Africa’s oil and gas industry has enormous growth potential, but the operating environment for investors remains challenging, Abelev agreed.

I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

I am scheduled to die on August 10, 2060, at the age of 74.
So says my iPhone screen, where Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that predicts life expectancy based on your medical habits and lifestyle, has produced an image of a smiling grim reaper to celebrate my expiration date. There he was one September morning, looking especially thrilled about the reveal, gesturing with a peace sign as he reclined in a doughnut-shaped pool inflatable under that giant number: 74.
I have never resented getting older, but I suppose that’s younger than I’d like to be when my time is up. In the last four years—years that brought the passing of my grandmother and aunt within 18 months—I’ve become hyperaware of how finite my days are. Since turning 40 in January, I’ve also experienced daily reminders of aging: inexplicable pains that rotate between my back, neck, and hips. Spiritually, I feel young; physically, my body screams otherwise. Aging is natural, but I had a creeping suspicion I could buy myself more time.
Our collective obsession with life extension has given rise to a multitrillion-dollar longevity industry, bolstered by wannabe prophets like Bryan Johnson. Threats like climate change and AI doomerism only seem to have intensified existential fears, even as LLMs promise a new era of personalized medicine to address any health issue. Track enough pieces of data, the thinking goes, and algorithms can help you hack your own demise.
All of which led me to Death Clock, an app launched in 2024 aimed at tracking users’ health habits in an attempt to prolong their lives. In February, the company announced a new feature that lets you order biomarker panels. For a $69 subscription, you can get a basic blood panel that measures things like cholesterol, blood sugars, inflammation, vitamin D, and blood and organ health. There are also nine additional tests—assessing everything from hormones and micronutrients to your thyroid—that, altogether, cost $780. I opted for the routine blood panel and added the “stress” test ($29). Maybe some new insight could help me get a handle on it.
In an attempt to be more than another morbid countdown gimmick, Death Clock says it’s trained its AI on 1,200 longevity studies, actuarial data from life insurance companies, and life expectancy tables. Based on your results, its algorithms create a detailed prevention plan intended to help extend the time you have left.
Frankly, I was skeptical that anything meaningful would actually come from this. I was also, I can admit, a little fearful that I’d learn something I didn’t want to, a fact that might dissolve the little sanity I had left in a year that had already brought its share of unexpected problems.
After filling out an initial health questionnaire, a notification buzzed, forewarning my demise. There are three ways I will likely perish, it said: cardiovascular disease, a sleep disorder, or cancer (it doesn’t specify which type). This means, according to the app, I have already “completed” more than half of my existence on this mortal plane. A few days later, when I noted that my family has a mild history of diabetes, the app updated my age of death from 74 to 73.
And just like that, I lost a year.
I know I won’t live to be 100; people in my family generally croak in their early eighties. But was it possible to extend my lifespan by 10, even 15 years, with a hyperpersonalized plan? “You have two paths,” a message from the app exclaimed. “We are here to help you achieve the longer one.” I made an appointment with Quest Diagnostics, one of the two labs the company has partnered with, and willingly gave Death Clock my blood.
There’s no shortage of products that aim to reshape our relationship to our bodies. My inbox overflows with emails from longevity zealots pitching the latest anti-aging fads: salmon sperm scalp injections, a platelet-rich plasma treatment “Hailey Bieber swears by.” It’s almost too much, this urge to cheat the natural order of time.
“That’s a fool errand,” Death Clock CEO Brent Franson tells me one afternoon. He says advocates like Johnson—whose mantra “Don’t Die” reads more like a rejected Nike slogan than a wellness-oriented affirmation—“have to be really careful about inferring immortality when you have something to sell. That’s a dangerous place to be. The reality is we’re all going to die. It’s a question of when.”
Over Zoom, all I can think about is what Franson is trying to sell me.
The longevity market is projected to reach $8 trillion by 2030, meaning the future of health care may be shaped less by traditional treatment and more by personalized AI health services. With Doctronic, a HIPAA-compliant platform that works like a personal AI doctor, people can refill prescriptions without the need to see a human physician, while apps like Superpower and Lifeforce (similar to Death Clock) offer membership-based health insights and clinician-reviewed recommendations. Twin Health purports to create an AI replica, whatever that means, of a person’s metabolism. All of it is meant to help us live a little longer, though it’s unclear exactly how and at what cost.
Mike Ludkovski, a professor of statistics and applied probability at UC Santa Barbara whose research focuses on longevity analysis, says mortality awareness platforms like Death Clock “sell the illusion that individual lifespan is a linear process” that can be hacked. A 2024 Aging Cell study likewise suggested that an aging clock shouldn’t be treated as a measure of someone’s overall biological age. “Ultimately, individual-level triggers precipitating death are inherently random and will never be truly forecastable,” Ludkovski says.
I ask Franson if we’re actually getting healthier or just growing more anxious about being unhealthy. “I think both,” he says. “There’s a very unhealthy obsession with self-optimization—tracking everything, trying to control everything.”
Wasn’t Death Clock, in part, also guilty of that?
When the blood panels returned a week after I gave my sample, the results were mostly what my doctor had warned me about earlier this year. I’ve got borderline high cholesterol and blood sugar levels “creeping toward prediabetic range.” Shockingly, I have “optimal liver health” and normal cortisol levels. Videos from so-called wellness influencers had convinced me that a string of recent sleepless nights were the result of high cortisol, but, it turns out, the algorithm isn’t always right.
Based on my results, the app kept feeding me more tasks. Increase my vitamin D3! Schedule a DEXA scan for bone density! Discuss a prostate-specific antigen screening with a specialist! Despite Franson’s claim that he wants Death Clock to eventually be a replacement for primary care physicians, the app kept nudging me to discuss my results with a doctor.
Ultimately, I started to realize, tracking health data can only do so much. There is a belief, says Gretchen Terry-Leonard, author of Your Second Prime: Does Aging Suck, or Do We Suck at Aging?, that being able to measure something means it can also be managed. Death doesn’t work that way, she says, “so the measuring starts to serve a different need: the need to feel less afraid.”
Terry-Leonard is also the cofounder of the Center for Deeply Human Leadership, an independent research institute studying AI’s effect on brain health. She’s skeptical that consumer-facing longevity apps can lead to positive behavioral shifts on their own. “Facts don’t change minds,” she says. People understand that certain activities are unhealthy, but they do them anyway.
Keeping death in view is one of the oldest practices we have, and what seems to matter is whether a person feels they have the personal agency to make the necessary adjustments in their life. Researchers who study how thoughts of death shape health choices find that people move toward healthier behavior when they also have the confidence and resources to act, which not everyone does. “And without those,” Terry-Leonard tells me, “the anxiety tends to go into protecting how we feel about ourselves rather than into our health.”
While researching her book, Terry-Leonard found that older adults with more positive attitudes about aging lived an average of seven and a half years longer than those with negative outlooks. An app with a death countdown “can quietly teach us that aging is loss,” hindering longevity rather than promoting it.
In the month that I used Death Clock, this was the fact I couldn’t completely escape. I became a meticulous steward of my bodily functions, logging “daily habits” with the verve of an accountant manically calculating numbers just before tax deadline. In a single day I added 5.8 years to my life by earmarking that I’d completed at least 30 minutes of strength training, abstained from alcohol, brushed and flossed my teeth, gotten consistent sleep, spent time in the sauna, and drank more than eight glasses of water. But even as I labored to improve my death date, the clock was always there, counting down. It was an albatross that moved in a single, uniform direction: tick, tick, tick. Time became a burden I was being forced to optimize.
It makes sense that people are preoccupied with the very thing they are trying to escape. The need for control is addictive. But instead of assuaging my anxieties and questions about the great beyond, Death Clock only seemed to amplify them.
As the image of the life I want to build sharpens in my mind, a life that has already unfolded in deliciously unforeseen ways, I realize it has less to do with how I will make things happen and has everything to do with who I want them to happen with. Life isn’t about adding more time, but making it count when we can. I silenced Death Clock’s notifications on my phone and texted a friend: “Let’s meet at 7.”

Reencle Essential Review: Same Scraps, Lower Price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

There’s a new Reencle composter in town, and of all the features I thought I might miss from the trailblazing original Reencle Prime, I didn't think it would be the auto-close lid.
The overly sensitive opening sensor annoyed me at first, but I ended up not giving the Prime’s lid another thought during my nearly 1.5 years of use. In hindsight, this is a testament to its convenience. It even has a setting for it to auto-open. Walk over to the receptacle, it opens; dump your scraps in, it closes. Buttons and lids remain clean and untouched by dirty, slimy hands.
Reencle’s brand-new, lower-cost unit, the Essential, is pretty much the same as the Prime (which is still available), with a few small tweaks—updated looks, a larger shovel, and a lid you have to manually close and a button you have to press to open. The button and lid already dirty after only three weeks, but my family consistently forgets to push the lid closed, having grown used to the auto-close lids of both our trash can and our old Prime. At least a few days a week, I will be caught off guard by a constant beeping—the Essential letting us know its lid is still open.
Aside from that, the Essential delivers the same user-friendly, close-to-compost-producing experience as its older sibling, but for $150 less.
Compost in Progress
You may have heard of kitchen composters before, whether the Lomi, FoodCycler, or the original Reencle Prime. It’s a compelling fantasy: Food scraps go in the bin, and out comes ready-to-use compost.
Unfortunately, for all of these machines, it’s just that: a fantasy. Many of them (like Lomi and FoodCycler) simply grind and dry the scraps to create a material that looks kind of like dirt. Sure, it’s odorless and shelf-stable, but if you want to use it in your garden, you’ll need to mix it into potting soil at a very low ratio—like 1:10, or even 1:20 if you’re processing a lot of meat and dairy.
Reencle, meanwhile, actually uses thermophilic bacteria (including Bacillus and Actinomycetes) to break down the waste, resulting in a biologically active material that, while not ready-to-use compost, is at least part of the way there. There are a couple of other machines that also do this, and I’ve tried them, but they’re bulkier, pricier, and louder than Reencle—don’t discount the noise-polluting effects of an audible fan running 24/7, especially if you live in a small space. (Reencle’s large-capacity Gravity model was—and remains—the only food recycler/composter I’ve ever tested that was truly silent at all times.)

In final push, Trump rallies in red states, offering a rosy and off-script message

- Trump is rallying in Mississippi, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina and Kansas — longtime Republican strongholds where the party now worries its own voters may stay home.
- During off-script riffs, Trump complimented a male Republican senator’s rear end and attacked a Democratic candidate as a supporter of ‘jihadists.’
WASHINGTON — In the final days before an election that will decide control of Congress, President Trump’s closing argument — buoyant, digressive and characteristically off-script — is at times running headlong into the economic anxieties of the voters Republicans most need.
With a war in Iran driving up gas prices for Americans, Trump is boasting to supporters that the conflict is making the country rich. At a rally in Georgia, he said his aides had urged him not to brag about the billions of dollars the United States was earning on oil from the war, since Americans are “paying a little higher” in costs because of it. But he did it anyway.
“I said, I don’t give a damn,” Trump said. “We are making a freaking fortune. Our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time. And those pump prices are going to come down.”
The moment underscores the gamble at the core of Trump’s final pitch to voters. With polls showing an overwhelming majority of Americans unhappy with the economy, the president is offering a portrait of national prosperity that many voters do not recognize, and pairing it with jokes and digressions that can seem to make light of their struggles.
Tuesday’s results will be the clearest test yet of whether that message still moves his base, or whether the president has become a liability for a party at risk of losing Congress in part because of his sinking popularity.
Signs of GOP anxiety are reflected in where Trump is spending his final days campaigning. Rather than courting swing voters in battleground states, he is leading rallies in Mississippi, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina and Kansas — states that have long been Republican strongholds but where the party now worries its voters may stay home.
Still, the president is insisting to voters that the country is succeeding, and he is making the election a referendum on his agenda.
“The world is falling apart, and we are doing better than we’ve ever done,” he told a crowd in Mississippi on Monday. The next day, during a stop in Texas, he joked that the $5,000 he has promised Americans if Republicans win would not be enough for his supporters to eat a meal at Mar-a-Lago, his private club in Palm Beach, Fla.
Michigan’s Senate race has become a battle over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. He is embracing his role as a Republican target, while consistently promoting a progressive agenda to address voters’ economic worries.
“You will be my guest at Mar-a-Lago. The problem is that for $5,000 the most you’ll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert,” Trump said, laughing. “I’m not even sure you could buy that.”
Democrats have criticized the president’s remarks, calling them dismissive of voters’ concerns. Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) said Trump boasting that the country was making money out of the Iran war was a “fitting” slogan for Trump’s White House.
Trump’s personal oil and gas holdings are now estimated to be worth between $22.5 million and $81.6 million, up from $12.6 million to $46 million at the end of last year, according to a report released this week by congressional Democrats.
Joe Gruters, the chairman of the Republican National Committee, rejected the idea that the president has dismissed voters’ financial pain.
“The president, I think, shows empathy about what we’re going through, and he is fighting like hell,” Gruters said in an interview.

But that message can be overshadowed with the off-script riffs that have long defined Trump’s rallies. During a rally in Ohio, while praising Sen. Jon Husted, Trump detoured into remarks about the Republican senator’s backside as well as rapper Nicki Minaj’s.

At a separate rally, Trump turned his attention to Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, saying that if elected, El-Sayed should be forced to pass through a metal detector before entering the U.S. Senate chamber.
“Anyone with that record of support for jihadists would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane,” Trump said of El-Sayed. “They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate.”
In those moments, the message is aimed squarely at his base, which over the last decade has celebrated his unfiltered style. And it is that base, more than swing voters, that Trump has spent his precious time courting in the final stretch of the campaign.
On Monday, Trump rallied supporters in Mississippi, a state he carried by 23 points two years ago. On Tuesday, he went to Texas for the fourth time this month to make the case for Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee trying to stave off what could be the first statewide Democratic victory there in three decades. Then on Wednesday, Trump was in Ohio for the third time this month, playing defense in a state he has won every time he’s been on the ballot. And on Saturday, Trump is heading to Kansas, a state that has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932.
Gruters said the red state swing reflects the need to get Republicans to the polls.
“You can’t take anything for granted. You have to fight hard in every single state, and remind people why they need to go vote,” he said. “This is a turnout, turnout, turnout race. And we’re doing everything we can as a party.”
Trump is rallying in Republican strongholds such as Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama, betting that his presence will be enough to energize voters who might be thinking of sitting out the election.
Don Haider-Markel, a political science professor at the University of Kansas, said it is still surprising to see the party deploy the president in Republican strongholds so close to the election.
“It really reflects, not just the tilt toward Democrats, but also the lack of enthusiasm among Republican voters for this election,” Haider-Markel said.
Republicans outnumber Democrats in Kansas, but there is a possibility that Democrats can win if Republicans stay home, he said. One of the biggest assets the party has to mobilize the MAGA base is having Trump talk to them in person, he argued. But so far, it is unclear whether his closing message will resonate.
“I don’t think that he’s really speaking to the issues that voters care about, but I don’t think he’s coming to change people’s minds,” Haider-Markel said. “He’s looking for lines that get him applause and praise.”
In rally after rally, Trump has turned the event into a show about himself. In Iowa, congressional candidate Joe Mitchell presented Trump with a “man of the century” certificate. In Texas, Trump bemoaned that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize last year. And in several events, he has shown the crowd a video of a CNN analyst saying that among GOP voters, Trump is more popular than Ronald Reagan or Abraham Lincoln.
But in the end, he also tried to appeal to his base with nostalgia.
“We’ve been doing this together for 11 years, and there’s never been anything like it and there probably never will be anything like it again politically or otherwise,” he said. “So let’s go out and do what we do best and that is win on Nov. 3. We gotta win!”

Social media stars are getting paid to take sides in California's billionaire tax battle

California’s billionaire tax battle is playing out on Instagram—with paid influencers
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- As Californians weigh a ballot on a billionaire tax, campaigns are paying social media creators—from parents to foodies—to sway voters.
- Opponents have raised more than $350 million to fight the tax and back measures that could block it, and some of that is going to sponsored posts in voters’ social media feeds.
- California requires paid political posts to be disclosed, but creators’ endorsements can blur belief and compensation—and leave some voters with sharply different versions of the debate.
As California decides whether to slap billionaires with a special tax, the Golden State’s swarm of social media stars is chiming in — and increasingly getting paid to influence voters.
Unlikely influencers, from foodies to mothers to retirees, are weighing in on Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on the assets of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires and on other ballot measures created to cancel it.
Campaigns try to team up with and sometimes compensate key content creators, as their endorsements often hit harder than traditional political ads.
Between cheery Instagram videos about budget-friendly trips to a playground, a Halloween house and zoo with her kids, Bartley Chavez posted a video opposing Proposition 40 to her more than 47,500 followers.
“Look, I’m all for trying new things. A new recipe? Sure. A crazy haircut? Go for it. A quirky movie with the kids. Why not? But when we’re talking about California jobs, our family’s financial future, and the state’s economy, that’s not something I want to experiment with,” she says in the October video.
The video’s caption states the campaign opposing Proposition 40 paid her to post.
Getting political online does come with risks. In the video’s comments, one Instagram user said they unfollowed Chavez’s account, and another called her a “sell out.” Others backed her position. Chavez didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Los Angeles author and political influencer Leigh McGowan has built an audience of more than 3.5 million followers on different platforms with her no-nonsense takes on politics and other issues. She was already a supporter of the wealth tax when the Proposition 40 campaign started to pay for some of her posts.
“No one is punishing the rich. They are doing just fine,” she said in a sponsored video on Instagram. “We are simply asking them to pay an outstanding one-time tax that’ll help the rest of us.”
Campaigns have been paying attention to influencers as younger people turn to them for news, said McGowan, who’s known for pontificating from her kitchen. Many people distrust traditional media and want regular people to break down complex topics.
“We don’t know who to believe anymore, and there are just so many lies out there,” McGowan said in an interview. “The people who take the time to say authentically this is what they believe in, that’s who people believe.
More than $351 million in political donations has been poured into a high-stakes contest about a proposed wealth tax on the November ballot, making it one of the most costly campaigns in California history.
In California, political ad spending in the 2026 election cycle is projected to approach $1 billion, more than any other state, according to political advertising intelligence firm AdImpact. Roughly $114 million is expected to go to digital platforms such as Facebook, Google, Snapchat and X.
The campaign opposing Proposition 40 has plenty of money to spend on political messaging in what’s become one of the most expensive ballot fights in California’s history. Billionaires such as Google co-founder Sergey Brin have donated millions to Building a Better California, a group funding ads against the wealth tax proposal. More than $350 million has been contributed to fight the billionaire tax and support two propositions — 41 and 42 — that could block it.
Campaign finance forms show how much groups spend on digital media, but they don’t say how much of that goes to influencers. While the data are limited, campaign leaders and other experts say social media stars are playing a bigger role in how brands and political movements advertise.
“Any modern campaign that wants to win needs to be active in spaces where voters get information — and that’s exactly what the No on 40 coalition is doing,” said Evan Westrup, a spokesman for the coalition opposing Proposition 40.
Some political influencers broadcast their views independently or talk to campaigns without compensation. Others are paid a few hundred dollars or even up to $30,000 per post, according to an October report from the Center for Democracy & Technology and the Communication Technology Research Lab at the University of Pittsburgh.
The $293 million spent by California billionaires to oppose Proposition 40 is about 0.07% of their estimated wealth.
Influencers will post content for political campaigns to make money, but “genuine belief in political issues or candidates can — and often does — coexist with compensation,” the report said.
One Los Angeles influencer, The Speech Prof, who has more than 1.7 million combined followers on Instagram and TikTok, said he refused money to stop the billionaire tax.
The creator, also known as Professor Chesko, talks about everything from parenting and misogyny to politics. In September, he posted a viral video in which he says he rejected a large amount of money to oppose the billionaire tax.
This month, he posted a new video backing the billionaire tax, noting that the Proposition 40 campaign paid him to make the content. “It’s not nearly as much, but they’re a healthcare union and not corporate oligarchs. Plus I already said where I stand for free,” he said in the October video.
Professor Chesko didn’t respond to a request for comment.
The storm of new voices chiming in on the political debate, delivered through people’s personalized social media feeds, could be causing confusion, said Ramesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at UCLA.
“If I’m seeing a completely different reality than you, whether it’s through influencers, AI or social media microtargeting,” he said. “Then it’s impossible to have a common basis for making decisions or choices.”
While the anti-billionaire tax war chest is much bigger, groups behind the tax say they’re still winning on social media.
“Despite being heavily outspent, the Prop. 40 campaign has been beating the billionaires on social media content and impact,” said Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for the SEIU-UHW, the healthcare union backing the billionaire tax.
She said influencers support the tax even when they’re not paid because they understand that “California needs functioning hospitals and emergency rooms, not more tax breaks for billionaires.”
Some sponsored influencers are avoiding direct criticism of the billionaire tax and instead signaling support for a ballot measure that could nullify Proposition 40 even if voters approve it.
Proposition 42 prohibits new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings,” but it conflicts with the billionaire tax proposal. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law.
Karen Clay-Fenderson, a Los Angeles mom and retired teacher with more than 120,000 Instagram followers, has posted videos about Proposition 42.
“I did my research on 42, and I did see something about the billionaire tax. But I want to keep my retirement and my life savings. I don’t want that taxed,” she said in an interview.
She disclosed that the Proposition 42 campaign paid her for the videos, but didn’t go so far as to tell people how to vote.
“They understand that we have influence, and people listen to what we have to say,” she said. “That’s why I’m very cautious. This is what I’m doing, but you need to make your choice.”
The influencer said Steyer’s campaign committee failed to notify her of her disclosure requirements, as required by law.
In California, influencers must disclose that they are being paid by a political campaign. In September, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation that would penalize influencers who failed to disclose that they were paid to post political content. Influencers could face fines of up to $5,000 per post.
Social media platforms also have their own rules. Instagram allows paid political ads, but TikTok doesn’t — though enforcement has been an issue.
Nathan Click, a spokesperson for Proposition 42, said their partners disclose they are paid and follow all campaign laws.
“Creators play an important role in the political conversation,” he said. “And campaigns across the country partner with them to ensure their audiences understand what’s at stake in the election.”
