The physics of getting fired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
21 minute listen
The senior partner didn’t waste any time. ‘I’m sorry, Zahaan,’ he said, ‘your services are no longer required at the firm.’ We sometimes called him the Burger King behind his back, because he ate a Whopper Meal at his desk every day. I’d never spoken to him before, and now I never would again.
It was the summer of 2001. I was fresh out of university and nine months into my first job as a management consultant in London. My parents had allowed me to move back into my old room, where I routinely collapsed after getting home from the office well after midnight. Professional life was punishing, but I gave it my all. For a brief time, I felt like I was flying: at my first performance review, I was told I had ‘partner potential’.
But then I got a phone call, telling me that one of the senior American partners wanted to meet me. That was unusual; but then again, I’d been working so hard and getting such good feedback, I figured it couldn’t be anything too bad. I was directed to an office on the first floor, several levels below where I usually sat.
After he fired me, my ears buzzed and my chest tightened; I don’t remember much else, except being told that I shouldn’t even return to my desk. It became apparent that the location of the meeting had been chosen because it would allow me to take a single flight of stairs down to the ground floor. No one would need to see me, and I wouldn’t need to speak to anyone.
The decision felt cruel and unfair. But more than anything, it seemed to violate the laws that for many years had been my way of making sense of the world: the laws of physics. Cause and effect, action and reaction. What followed was an unlikely journey – one in which the equations I thought I’d left behind at university became, unexpectedly, a companion through the messiest parts of life.
Before work, before university, I attended a competitive and prestigious all-boys school in London. While I’ll be forever grateful for the opportunities my education afforded me, life still felt tough for me as a lonely and anxious teenager. The school’s social currency was confidence, quick comebacks, and an effortless cool I never quite mastered. I often felt like I was watching from the edges, trying to decode the rules of a game that everyone else grasped intuitively.
The only thing that got me through was physics. The most fundamental of the sciences, physics represented a world that was perfectly ordered. It offered structure, rules and predictability. There was no social speculation; I could just work hard and try to figure things out. Problems and solutions, equations and outcomes. It didn’t matter how popular I was – what mattered was whether I understood the system. Slowly, the chaos of the world developed a sense of form and structure.
That clarity stayed with me, through school and into university. I read physics at Oxford, convinced for a long time that I wanted to become a scientist. It wasn’t always easy; there were late nights, bitter struggles with problem sets, moments I wondered if I’d ever get it. But when it clicked, it was wonderful: entropy, quantum mechanics, cosmology, all those deep, strange laws that govern the Universe. Physics seemed like it had a purpose, and I thought we’d go the distance.
But at some point in my final year at university, things started to change. Physics still fascinated me, but I found myself drawn to other subjects too – politics, economics, business. I wanted to understand not just how the Universe worked, but how people did. So after graduating, I decided to leave physics behind and see where those other interests would take me.
For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist
As it turns out, when I stepped away from physics, many others did too. In the years after I left university at the turn of the millennium, physics began to fade from view in the English classroom. In 2006, physics A-level entries (post-16 qualifications in the UK) were down 37 per cent from where they were in 1991. The absolute numbers have since rebounded – but not for everyone. Today, the gender gap remains stark: only 23 per cent of A-level physics entries in 2026 came from girls, a figure that hasn’t budged much in decades. And more than half of GCSE physics classes in England (taken by 14- to 16-year-olds) are taught by a non-specialist, with a shortage of some 3,500 physics teachers nationally.
Research looking at why students choose or reject physics has found that it’s seen as abstract, difficult, and disconnected from real life – a perception that’s remained steady, even as enrolment has recovered. Meanwhile, newer fields – computer science, behavioural economics, even data journalism – have felt more immediate, more applicable. They speak the language of now.
What’s strange is that this perception problem has happened at the same historical moment in which physics has begun popping up in other surprising places.
Dominic Cummings, the strategist behind Brexit and later Boris Johnson’s chief adviser, gave physics a fair share of the credit for the success of his campaigns. In one of his highly popular newsletters, he paraphrased the theoretical physicist Richard Feynman: ‘The most important thing is not to fool yourself and you are the easiest person to fool.’ Then there’s Elon Musk, who credits the success of his many business ventures to physics and ‘first-principles thinking’: discard convention, start from fundamental truths. And for decades, the legendary investor Charlie Munger made the same case in finance, saying that the ‘logic and power’ of physics had helped him enormously.
For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist, praised by public figures whose decisions affect millions of lives. But look closer, and the picture is more complicated.
In the first instance, billionaires and political operatives make for awkward ambassadors; Cummings, Musk and Munger might be brilliant, but they’re also extremely divisive. But more than who they are, what interests me is how they’re putting physics to work – whether they’re truly thinking with the discipline, or just brandishing it for rhetorical effect. Is ‘physics’ simply a shorthand for cutting through complexity, for stripping down problems to their most basic parts? Or does it genuinely offer something distinctive that other sciences and ways of thinking cannot?
Philosophers call the first approach ‘reductionism’: the idea that if you break any system into small enough components and trace them far enough, you eventually arrive at physics. That view can be powerful, and explains why so many people find it attractive.
It’s also been spectacularly successful. When 19th-century physicists showed that heat was simply the motion of atoms – that temperature, seemingly its own phenomenon, was actually just particles bouncing faster – an entire science collapsed into physics. Years later, that same approach helped particle physicists break matter into smaller and smaller pieces until arriving at something apparently irreducible. From the reductionist instinct came quarks, leptons and the Higgs boson. Their catalogue blueprint, the Standard Model, remains one of the greatest intellectual achievements in human history.
But reductionism has its limits. Take politics: a radical reductionist might say that this too comes down to physics, because politics is about the behaviour of groups of people; groups are made of individual people; people are made of atoms; atoms are governed by physics. But does this mean that we could predict the outcome of, say, a national election by studying the behaviour of individual atoms inside the brains of every registered voter? Unlikely. Putting aside issues of practicality, what would be the point? Economists already have economics. Psychologists already have psychology. Politicians have political theory. Physics has value only if it’s additive and illuminating.
For me, the real value of physics had never been as a cudgel for smashing things up into their smallest bits, but as a framework for navigating systems – for recognising patterns, probing assumptions, and testing whether the models we rely on actually work as they’re meant to. We see this way of thinking throughout the history of science. When cholera swept through Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow didn’t know its cause. But he mapped the cases, identified the pattern, and traced the outbreak to a single water pump on Broad Street. The founder of what we now know as epidemiology, Snow worked by constructing and interrogating mental models of the world, probing their assumptions, and following the data wherever they led.
The question, then, is not simply whether physics can be borrowed as rhetoric, but whether it really helps us to see the world more clearly, in ways that complement and benefit other disciplines. That, at least, was what stayed with me after I stopped studying it formally. Not equations or textbooks, but a way of thinking that I found myself reaching for when my world was falling apart.
Getting fired was one of those moments. I had worked so hard, yet somehow I’d still failed. Everything I understood about cause and effect told me this shouldn’t have happened. But here I was, after months of working flat out, with nothing to show for it.
An infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance
While some might have turned to therapy or career counselling, I turned back to physics to try to move on. The immediate cause was clear enough. The dot-com bubble had burst, sending ripples across the global economy that eventually reached my desk. Belts tightened, and the harsh rule in such circumstances tends to be last in, first out.
The dot-com bust was not the first nor last time something like this would happen. In 2008 came the subprime mortgage crisis; in 2011, the eurozone crashed; in 2013, the rupee tanked; in 2015, there was turbulence on the Chinese stock market; and in 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic. All these crises had two things in common. First, almost no one saw them coming – at least not precisely when or where or how. Second, they weren’t triggered by some enormous dramatic collapse, but by small, seemingly innocuous failures that cascaded into something far larger. For example, it just took a few small incidents that might otherwise have passed unnoticed – like the failure of a local mortgage lender in Southern California – to precipitate the subprime mortgage crisis.
All these events are examples of what physicists might call chaotic systems – deterministic in theory, but in practice so sensitive to initial conditions that tiny variations can spiral into radically different outcomes. A well-known example is the ‘three-body problem’, popularised by Liu Cixin’s 2008 novel of the same name and a 2024 Netflix adaptation. If you have two planets orbiting each other, you can write down neat equations to predict their paths forever. But add a third planet, and suddenly the maths explodes into unpredictability. The three bodies are still governed by clear laws, but an infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance.
The mathematician Edward Lorenz discovered something similar in 1961 when running weather simulations. His first attempt entered starting values rounded to six decimal places. His second try was rounded only to three. Yet the results diverged so dramatically that he initially suspected it was a computer fault. In fact, tiny differences in initial conditions had cascaded into entirely different weather systems. The atmosphere, like the economy, like a career, was deterministic in principle and unpredictable in practice.
As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do
Understanding the crash was one thing, but physics also helped me think about what came next. I had believed that inputs led to proportional outcomes; logically, in that world, the way to get ahead was to work as hard as possible. But physics teaches that chaotic systems play by different rules. They call instead for surge capacity, an extra buffer that allows them to absorb shocks. Without it, even small failures can lead to total collapse.
Think of a power grid. Most of the time it hums along without problem. But during an unexpected surge, such as a heatwave when millions of air conditioners are switched on at once, the system can overload and shut down. To prevent this, engineers design grids with slack in the system and extra capacity to handle unexpected spikes. Without it, a minor disruption can cascade into a blackout.
That was my mistake. As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do. We optimise everything from our schedules to our to-do lists – convinced that if we just push a bit harder, we’ll be fine. But the more we operate at our limits, the more fragile we become.
Physics provides a different lesson. Rather than relentlessly maximising, resilience is about building the capacity to withstand outlier events when they come. That might mean time slack, leaving space in our lives to recover rather than scheduling every minute. It might mean career slack, developing new skills, side projects and networks, rather than relying on a single path. Surge capacity might not prevent a crisis, but it sure helps survive one.
After my brief and bruising spell in consulting, I joined the civil service and spent most of the rest of my 20s working in government. I loved the sense of purpose, the colleagues and the privilege of shaping policy. Yet, if I’m honest, I still carried a small canker of resentment and jealousy towards my former consulting colleagues.
Compared with the UK national average, I know I was paid well as a civil servant. But with friends on six-figure salaries, it felt like I was failing at something. They could afford nicer clothes, cars and apartments. And then there was the magic trick of turning money into more money by buying assets, further widening the gap between their bank balances and mine. What stung wasn’t the inequality itself, but the perceived unfairness of the circumstances. I felt like I’d worked just as hard and still fallen behind. That distinction between inequality and unfairness became important to me.
Psychologists have shown that we’re wired to make this distinction from a very young age. In one Yale study, children were asked to split 10 coins between two people based on their performance on a task. When the two people performed equally, the children split the coins five-five – equal and fair. When one person did better, the children split the coins six-four – unequal but still fair. The interesting result happened when the children were told that both people had performed equally, but they now had to split 11 coins. With no way to maintain fairness, what could the children do? They decided to simply throw away one coin. Time and again, the children prioritised fairness.
People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged
This distinction is also evident in physics. Inequality, in the literal sense of unevenness, is built into the fabric of the Universe. In the very beginning, the cosmos was smooth and equal, a uniform fog. Only when tiny imperfections appeared – quantum fluctuations that allowed matter to clump in some places more than others – did galaxies, stars and planets emerge. Without that inequality, there would have been no structure, no possibility of life. In that sense, inequality is not always a flaw. Sometimes it is the condition for growth and diversity.
We see the same principle in natural systems. Rivers branch into unequal tributaries. Lungs and blood vessels evolve into networks with a few large arteries feeding many smaller ones. That inequality of size isn’t corruption or greed, but a kind of efficiency. It allows flow. Yet when the flow is blocked, like when a river silts up or a vessel clogs, the system fails. The problem, in other words, is not inequality itself, but unfairness: the obstruction of flow, the stacking of rules, the blocking of opportunity.
I think this is true in human systems, too. A society where some are richer than others may be tolerable, even healthy, so long as opportunities and resources can still move freely. But a society where opportunity is blocked, where the rules are stacked, where unfairness rules – people reject that instinctively. Just as I did when I looked at my friends’ consulting careers and wondered why I’d been cast out. Physics, then, suggests that a lack of justice is the real problem, rather than inequality per se. People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged.
Suddenly I saw this dynamic about fairness everywhere I looked. The financial crisis of 2007-08 wasn’t just about banks making risky bets, but about the perception that ordinary people paid the price while bankers walked away with bonuses intact. The eurozone crisis wasn’t just about debt, but about southern European countries being squeezed by rules they hadn’t set. The Occupy protests, the Arab Spring, Brexit, Donald Trump – all, in their different ways, were rebellions against unfairness.
Looking at the world through a physicist’s lens, these moments resemble phase transitions. You can heat water gradually and nothing seems to change – until you reach a critical threshold, a boiling point, and suddenly the whole system transforms from liquid to gas. Human societies, too, can bear strain for a while. But once unfairness feels systemic, the pressure builds until the system flips.
Small wonder, then, that in an age of tumult and transition, physics has found new admirers – especially among those who want to catalyse radical change, for better or worse. Musk speaks of first principles, Cummings of complexity. Their examples show how the tools of physics can shape thinking far beyond the laboratory. But in their hands, physics can feel more like a weapon than a framework, a way of bulldozing nuance in the name of clarity. For the rest of us, the challenge is not simply to borrow the garb and glamour of physics, but to carry forward its mindset – one that values humility as much as boldness, and curiosity as much as certainty.
That, I think, is where physics can still make its greatest contribution. Not by giving us ready-made answers or comforting illusions of inevitability, but by training us to question ourselves and live with the resulting uncertainty. Public discourse is saturated with physics, yet we need a deeper grounding in what it really teaches us about how to ask better questions, to test our own blind spots, and to admit what we don’t know. That need feels more urgent as new technologies only increase the temptation to reach for shortcuts.
We need artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both
So what would it take to embed this shift? My journey with physics began when I was a teenager, and that’s where I believe we need to start now. Too often, we present physics to young people as dry and technical. We teach them equations but not frameworks, facts without wonder. We rarely tell them that physics can help with the messiest parts of life, bound up as they are with uncertainty, resilience, decision-making.
In the UK, we make things worse by forcing students to choose just three or four subjects to study for the final two years of school. In practice, this often forces a split between being on the ‘science’ track or the ‘arts’ track. That false binary deprives us of exactly the kind of multidisciplinary thinkers we need: artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both.
When I visit schools now, I try to show physics as a kind of superpower. I want young people to feel that physics is something they can use, not something that excludes them. More than anything, I want them to feel it’s theirs.
I started this essay as a young man being shown the door by a superior. I ended it somewhere else entirely, with physics as a way of making sense of the messiest parts of life. But, really, what I’ve been edging up to is a story about how certain hardwon habits of mind can help us find meaning in the messiness and unpredictability of reality. For those of us who are not professional scientists, maybe the real task isn’t to love physics uncritically, or wield it carelessly, but to use it wisely. Physics shouldn’t be a shortcut to rock-solid certainty, so much as a way to live more humanely without it.

Quebec premier boycotts Mark Carney’s EU summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:59:42 UTC
18:59:42 KST

In a letter to European leaders, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon warns that agreements running counter to Quebec’s interests “will simply not be implemented.”
Quebec’s separatist premier says that he will boycott the EU-Canada summit that opens in Montreal on Thursday, warning European leaders that deals struck there without his government’s consent may not be applied in the country’s second-biggest province.
Paul St-Pierre Plamondon confirmed his absence late Wednesday in an open letter to the European delegation, which he posted on X. His announcement followed two days of public sparring with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney over Ottawa’s refusal to let him address the summit.
“This dynamic creates uncertainty as to the application of the agreements you could negotiate during the summit,” he wrote in French.
Advertisement
In the letter, St-Pierre Plamondon says Ottawa has “decided to sideline Quebec” from the talks. He says this leaves his government with “neither a chair at the negotiating table nor the opportunity to speak,” even though the summit is on Quebec soil.
Under Canada’s federal system, he argued, the provinces implement international agreements that fall within their powers. Without Quebec’s consent, a deal that runs against its interests “will simply not be implemented,” he wrote. He also accused Ottawa of withholding “critical information” on the negotiations.
He offered to meet European leaders “in the near future, in a more opportune context.” He will send Quebec’s chief diplomat, Pascal Paradis, to the summit in his place.
Carney said Wednesday his office had offered the premier the honor of welcoming the Commission president to Montreal, and a seat at the head table. “I hope he will reconsider,” he said. On Tuesday, the prime minister had accused St-Pierre Plamondon of choosing to “leave an empty chair again.”
The row has soured the upbeat mood around the summit, which Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa have billed as a milestone. Leaders will launch an “Alliance for the Future,” a framework for shared prosperity and economic security.
St-Pierre Plamondon’s letter says many of its topics fall under Quebec’s responsibility, including health, education and natural resources.
Advertisement
The premier has also pursued his own contacts with European leaders.
He spoke by phone with French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday, and said the two had agreed on a possible meeting in France in the coming weeks.
At working level, ties have held so far, and officials describe the relationship as constructive.
Hélène Drainville, Quebec’s delegate general in Brussels, told POLITICO last week that Quebec was in talks with the European Investment Bank and the Commission, and that “all the signals are green.”
Carney, Costa and von der Leyen are due to hold a joint press conference on Friday.

A Russian drone strike on a railway platform in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro has killed 14 people and injured over dozen others, regional authorities said.
Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration (OVA), initially reported an attack on a transport infrastructure facility, saying emergency services were working at the scene.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Hanzha initially reported 13 deaths and at least five people injured. He later updated the number of wounded to 10, 13 and then 14, before confirming that the death toll had risen to 14.
In his latest Telegram update at 1:52 p.m., Hanzha wrote:
“Six are in critical condition, including an 11-year-old boy. All have sustained multiple shrapnel wounds. A 40-year-old man has had both legs amputated.”
Hanzha added that medical personnel were staying by the wounded’s side and doing everything possible to save their lives.
State-owned Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) said a Russian jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) struck a railway station platform where train No. 866, traveling from Dnipro to Zaporizhzhia, was located at the time.
Despite an alert warning of heightened danger, people were present on the platform, the railway operator said. Rescuers, medics. and law enforcement officers are working at the scene.
Meanwhile, local Telegram channels have already begun sharing photos from the scene.
Ukrainian Delegation Heads Toward Oleshky for Aid Mission
President Volodymyr Zelensky also responded to the strike in a post on Telegram.
“A horrific Russian strike on the railway station in Dnipro. The Russians used a drone to attack the platform where a regular suburban commuter train and a scheduled passenger train were located. Unfortunately, as of now, 13 deaths have been confirmed. My condolences to the families and loved ones,” he wrote.
Zelensky stressed that Moscow had shown no signs of moving toward de-escalation, even after sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and parts of the energy sector.
“How many such terrorist strikes has Russia launched against our people – even after sanctions were lifted from certain Russian oligarchs and the energy sector – instead of moving toward de-escalation?” he wrote.
He said Ukraine expects a firm response from the United States and Europe to Russia’s escalation.
“Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be weakened as long as this Russian war continues. It is time for new, stronger sanctions measures from the EU, America, and the G7,” Zelensky added.
The deadly Russian strike on Dnipro’s railway infrastructure echoes the April 2022 attack on Kramatorsk railway station in eastern Ukraine, where a missile strike killed 61 people and injured more than 160.
Around 4,000 civilians had gathered at the station to board evacuation trains as Russian forces advanced.
The station was struck at around 10:30 a.m. on April 8 by a Tochka-U missile believed to have been equipped with cluster munitions.
The station reopened in October 2022, about six months after the strike.
An investigation by the Center for Information Resilience, a nonprofit organization, concluded in October 2022 that the available evidence pointed to Russia as the likely perpetrator.
Investigators identified three possible missile launch sites in Russian-occupied territory and said the missile may have been launched from near Shakhtne, east of Donetsk.
Russia denied responsibility, claiming it did not possess the type of Tochka-U missile used in the attack and describing the strike as a Ukrainian provocation. Ukrainian prosecutors said they had evidence of Russian responsibility, while the investigation continued.

Two German citizens arrested over suspected Starlink equipment arson attempt in Vilnius

18:48:00 KST

Lithuanian authorities have identified two men suspected of attempting to set fire to Starlink equipment in Vilnius earlier this month. Both men, who live in Germany, have been arrested there at Bulgaria’s request, Lithuanian law enforcement officials said Thursday.
The suspects are foreign nationals in their 20s, one holding German and Turkish citizenship and the other German and Serbian citizenship, Saulius Briginas, deputy head of the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau, told reporters.
Investigators believe the men arrived in Lithuania on the eve of the incident and left immediately after the attempted arson.
“They have no ties to Lithuania and came here to commit this crime,” Briginas said. “This was not a spontaneous crime. They knew exactly where they were going and what they intended to do, and they prepared for it in advance.”
Nėrijus Puškorius, chief prosecutor in the Organised Crime and Corruption Investigation Division of the Vilnius Regional Prosecutor’s Office, said the men face suspicions of forming an organised terrorist group to commit terrorist crimes, participating in a terrorist group, travelling for terrorist purposes and committing a terrorist act that could have had serious consequences.
The most severe penalty for forming or participating in a terrorist group is 10 to 15 years in prison, Puškorius said.
The suspects had been placed on a wanted list, and Lithuanian authorities are cooperating with law enforcement partners in Bulgaria, Poland and Germany.
“The two individuals have been detained in Germany,” Puškorius said, adding that a decision on whether they will be transferred to Lithuania would be made later.
Briginas said the suspects were also linked to arson attacks targeting Starlink equipment in Poland and Bulgaria. More people have been detained in Poland in connection with the incidents, he said.
The two men arrested in Germany are not believed to have personally set fire to Starlink equipment in Poland, but investigators suspect they were involved in that crime as well.
The attempted arson in Vilnius took place several weeks ago at premises belonging to Lithuanian company Delska, where the US company SpaceX operates and stores Starlink equipment. Lithuanian politicians have linked the incident to Russia.
Similar incidents have been investigated in Bulgaria, where several antennas used to connect to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire, and in Poland, where a fire broke out at a Starlink satellite communications station in the country’s central region in September.

US measles surge reminds of Europe’s vaccination gaps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:47:33 UTC
18:47:33 KST

The US risks losing its measles elimination status as under-vaccinated communities across Europe remain vulnerable to imported cases.
The United States is at risk of losing its measles-free status as cases surge, raising fresh concerns about the vulnerability of European communities where vaccination coverage remains below the level needed to prevent sustained transmission.
More than 4,500 cases have been reported in the US this year — roughly twice the total reported last year. A forecast published in JAMA suggests that measles could become endemic again in the US if vaccination rates fail to improve, potentially resulting in 851,300 cases, more than 170,000 hospitalisations and 2,550 deaths over 25 years.
The outbreak across the Atlantic could also signal a wider risk, Kitty Mohan, vice-president of the Standing Committee of European Doctors (CPME) and its rapporteur on vaccination, told Euronews.
“Due to international travel routes and the ease and speed at which people move across borders, combined the infectiousness of measles before the rash starts, people can travel quite far whilst infectious and so the disease can spread rapidly,” Mohan said.
Measles is among the most contagious infectious diseases. People can transmit the virus for around four days before the characteristic rash appears, meaning they may travel across borders before realising they are ill.
“15 mins face to face with someone who is infectious will mean you are likely to get measles,” Mohan said.
The US is not the only country where measles continues to circulate. The biggest outbreaks currently are in Bangladesh, with cases surpassing 65,430, Indonesia with 46,578 and Guatemala with 31,222 cases.
“Whether an imported case leads to further transmission in Europe depends primarily on immunity levels in the affected community in Europe and whether the virus reaches groups with low vaccination coverage,” the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) told Euronews.
Vaccination coverage was 92% for the first dose and 88% for the second dose — a “strong population protection,” ECDC said.
But that remains below the recommended 95% two-dose coverage needed at national and local levels to prevent sustained transmission and achieve measles elimination. National averages can also conceal areas or communities with lower vaccination coverage.
“Most measles cases occur in unvaccinated people,” the ECDC said, recommending that countries close immunity gaps, ensure both vaccine doses are administered on time, offer catch-up vaccination to eligible adolescents and adults, and maintain strong surveillance and outbreak-response systems.
The consequences extend beyond those who can choose to get vaccinated. Infants who are too young to receive the vaccine, as well as people who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons or whose immune systems cannot mount an adequate response, depend on high levels of immunity in the wider population.
“Herd immunity or maintaining vaccination rates above a threshold would protect these groups - so lower rates make them more susceptible to disease,” Mohan said.
Pockets of low coverage
The problem is not confined to countries with low national vaccination rates. Clusters of unvaccinated or under-vaccinated people can emerge within otherwise well-protected populations, creating local conditions in which outbreaks can take hold.
Coverage gaps can reflect a range of factors, including difficulties accessing vaccination services, limited information or awareness, and concerns about vaccines.
“There are traditional risk groups - such as traveller communities and some religious groups who historically have been reluctant to vaccinate,” said Mohan.
However, ECDC underlined that “the presence of a group of unvaccinated people does not automatically mean that a large outbreak will spread across the wider population,” using the Urkult festival in northern Sweden as an example. The outbreak at the festival occurred between 30 July and 2 August this year, mainly affecting unvaccinated children and adolescents. It involved 28 cases, including 12 secondary cases, but did not lead to sustained transmission in the wider population.
"The fact that there were relatively few secondary cases among those exposed at the festival is due to the high level of immunity within the population, a result of strong participation in the childhood vaccination program," said Johanna Rubin, Acting Head of the Vaccination Unit at Sweden’s public health agency.
“This once again highlights the importance of high community-level protection,” ECDC said.
For now, the risk for Europeans remains the same, ECDC said, as per its latest assessment, with the overall risk set as moderate for infants under 12 months, children aged one to five and immunocompromised people. For older unvaccinated children and adults, the risk is estimated to range from low to moderate. People with immunity from vaccination or previous infection are considered to have a low risk of measles.
ECDC surveillance data indicate fewer reported measles cases in 2026 than in 2025, although 2026 figures remain preliminary and should be interpreted with caution.
Measles is endemic in twelve European countries: Bosnia and Herzegovina, France, Georgia, Germany, Italy, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Poland, Romania, Russia, Türkiye, and Ukraine.
Romania reported most of the cases, with numbers reaching 30,692 in 2024, up from 3,371 in 2023.
Six European countries: Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan have re-established endemic measles transmission based on the number of cases in 2024 earlier this year.

Cargo owners are arranging shipments earlier than usual to reduce supply chain uncertainty caused by port congestion, shipping delays, and fluctuating fuel costs.
The fourth quarter is traditionally a peak season for intra-Asia short-sea shipping. With cargo volumes continuing to grow and freight rates remaining at relatively favorable levels, Wan Hai expects its operating momentum to remain stable.

Japan and US Agree to Establish AIM-120 Missile Assembly Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:35:46 UTC
18:35:46 KST

Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and U.S.Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have agreed to establish a facility in Japan to assemble AIM-120 air-to-air missiles.
According to Nikkei, negotiations on the project have been underway since at least 2024.
Preparations for localizing AIM-120 missile production had been underway since at least September 1, 2026. On that date, Japan’s Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency published Notice No. 137, seeking a contractor to conduct research into establishing domestic production of components for these missiles.
Applications were accepted until September 30, with the research scheduled for completion by March 26, 2027.
Requirements for potential contractors included being a Japanese company and having experience in the design, production, and testing of medium-range air-to-air missiles.
One company that meets these criteria is Mitsubishi Electric, which has extensive experience in producing domestically developed air-to-air missiles of this class, including the Type 99, a Japanese counterpart to the American AIM-120.
On April 28, 2026, Mitsubishi Electric confirmed that it was in talks with Raytheon about participating in the joint production of AMRAAM missiles. At the time, the two companies were discussing the extent of Japan’s involvement in missile production.
The work will involve manufacturing circuit card assemblies. In the future, Mitsubishi Electric plans to participate in the missiles’ final assembly and checkout.
The exact location of the planned facility is currently unknown.
The construction of a facility for assembling, inspecting, and testing AIM-120 missiles is linked to two ambitious plans.
The first is Japan’s plan to procure 1,200 missiles of this type to equip its F-35A and F-35B fighter jets.
Due to certain restrictions, Japanese missiles cannot be integrated into these aircraft. As a result, Japan cannot standardize its missile arsenal using only domestically produced weapons.
The second objective is to manufacture missiles for export to the United States amid growing demand for these munitions. AIM-120 missiles are among the most widely used air-to-air missiles in the world and are equipped with active radarseekers.
They are used by numerous types of combat aircraft, as well as by NASAMS air defense systems operated by the United States and several European countries, including Ukraine. Ukraine’s NASAMS systems regularly use these missiles to repel Russian aerial attacks, creating a significant need to replenish stocks.

18:34:00 KST

The European Commission has responded to a request by Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia for 500 million euros to develop anti-drone defences, but has offered no new funding on the scale sought by the three Baltic states.
Defence ministers from the three countries sent a letter to the European Commission in late September requesting urgent financial support to strengthen defences against drones.
Several stray drones have entered the Baltic airspaces this year amid air attacks between Ukraine and Russia.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, Estonian Defence Minister Martin Herem and Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis sought the funding to develop an anti-drone system that could also serve as a model for other European Union countries.
The letter was classified, but Kaunas told LRT that the Baltic states wanted to combine drone detection, artificial intelligence and interception technology into an integrated air defence system.
“Air defence and anti-drone solutions are important not only for our region but for all of Europe. Lithuania has taken the lead in developing an anti-drone air defence system,” Kaunas said.
The Baltic states had hoped the European Commission would approve additional funding for regional anti-drone defences before the end of this year. The commission previously told LRT.lt that it was carefully assessing the request and took member states’ concerns very seriously.
However, Andrius Kubilius, the European commissioner for defence and space, told LRT on Wednesday that the commission had sent its response but could not offer the additional funding the Baltic states had sought.
“One possibility now is to make use of additional funding under the SAFE instrument. We will announce a new call in the near future, because 21 billion euros remained after the first call,” Kubilius said.
He added that there were few other substantial funding opportunities available through EU budget programs because the current budget period was nearing its end.
Funding for anti-drone measures may also be available through the Integrated Border Management Fund, LRT understands, although the sums involved would be far below the 500 million euros requested by the Baltic states.
SAFE loans offer an alternative
The Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, instrument, launched last year, provides 150 billion euros in favourable loans for defence procurement across the EU.
The scheme offers loans with repayment periods of up to 45 years and advance payments of up to 15%. The loans are financed through EU-level borrowing, benefiting from the bloc’s AAA credit rating.
Lithuania has been allocated access to up to 6.375 billion euros in SAFE loans. The government plans to use the funds to establish a land forces division, develop the Baltic Defence Line, strengthen air defence, purchase ammunition and military equipment, and finance other military modernisation projects.
In October, Lithuania’s Finance Ministry submitted its first request to the European Commission for a 1.06-billion-euro loan under the scheme.
If approved, the request would bring Lithuania’s total SAFE funding, including a 800-million-euro advance received in June, to 1.86 billion euros, about 29% of the country’s total allocation.

Qatar says accusations of election interference in Israel 'ridiculous and dangerous'

Both Benjamin Netanyahu and his immediate challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, lack the seats in the Knesset to form a majority government. Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice.

The right and centre-right accounted for 66.5%, while ultra-orthodox Jewish parties won 11%.
Against that background, Eisenkot has doubled down on his determination to form a Zionist government. Such rhetoric makes the prospect of cooperation with Arab parties even more remote, but he is hoping instead to lure away conservative Jews from Likud, just as Netanyahu’s is trawling for defectors from Eisenkot’s “Change” bloc.
This is the current phase of the post-election struggle, and it is one that, for now, excludes Arab Israelis, despite their dramatically increased political strength.

Explainer-How could Israel break the election deadlock?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

18:32:03 KST

Explainer-How could Israel break the election deadlock?
JERUSALEM, Oct 29 - Israel's election this week was indecisive and there is no clear winner poised to form a government. Benjamin Netanyahu remains in office as caretaker prime minister, but faces a parliament stacked with an opposition majority vying to oust him.
Here are some scenarios that could follow:
ANOTHER ELECTION
After the formal final election results are published next week, Israel's President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with party representatives and then taps the candidate whom he deems to have the best chance to form a government.
If the candidate fails, another can try and if that candidate fails, the Knesset can nominate another. There is a deadline for the process of around 100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is held.
Herzog said on Wednesday that everything must be done to avoid another election and urged the parties to come with an open mind to the consultations with him.
UNITY GOVERNMENT
Netanyahu's Likud party, emerging as the largest in the Knesset, forms a coalition that would likely include centrist and right-wing opposition parties such as Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, the second-largest party, Avigdor Lieberman's Israel Our Home and Naftali Bennett's Together faction.
That grouping would secure 66 seats, a majority in the 120-seat parliament.
However, this option appears remote at this point because it would mean Netanyahu would likely have to abandon his natural political allies, the far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties. Further, the opposition parties would have to break their main election pledge to their voters: unseating Netanyahu.
Still, if neither camp is able to form a government at the end of weeks of protracted negotiations, a unity government may emerge as a last option.
Renewed fighting with Iran, or other players, could also push the sides together.
EISENKOT MINORITY GOVERNMENT
If Herzog taps Eisenkot first, he could try to form a government with Yashar's natural allies — Together, The Democrats and Israel Our Home — propped up by Israel's two Arab parties, even if they are not members of this government: Ra'am and the Joint List.
Eisenkot's camp would number 48 seats, according to the latest vote tally, with the Arab parties numbering 19 seats that together reach a 67-seat majority.
But even if Eisenkot reverses his campaign pledge not to have Arab parties in government and accepts their support, it would be a hard sell to many Israelis whose attitudes toward Israel's Arab minority have hardened further since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack.
Netanyahu has focused his campaign on delegitimizing support from Arab parties, who surged to record heights in Tuesday's election, and for now, only The Democrats, a centre-left party, has come out publicly calling for their inclusion.
Both Arab parties have signalled that they are prepared to cooperate with Eisenkot's camp.
Ra'am joined Bennett's government in 2021, the first time an independent Arab party entered an Israeli coalition. That government collapsed after 18 months.
NETANYAHU FINDS A MAJORITY FOR A RIGHT-WING GOVERNMENT
Netanyahu's coalition has fallen from its original 64 seats to 53, according to the latest election results. But Israel's longest-serving leader is viewed as one of its most skilled politicians and he could split the opposition by peeling away members of its parties and bringing them over to his side.
He has managed to do this before, including as opposition head in the run-up to the 2022 election, which he won. But the coalition he was battling at the time had a far narrower lead and he did not need too many defectors to destabilize his political rivals. REUTERS

Here are the main headlines from and about Germany on Thursday, October 29, 2026:
Wadephul visits Panama ahead of G20 in Atlanta
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul landed in Panama on Wednesday evening for a visit.
After his arrival at Panama City airport, Wadephul handed over humanitarian supplies to his Panamanian counterpart Javier Martinez-Acha Vasquez.
The aid shipment is made up of about 20 tons of supplies. Panama was hit by a powerful earthquake this month.
The supplies include water filters, blankets, tarpaulins, cots and kitchen sets worth over €150,000 ($167,000).
More than 5,000 people are still being housed in emergency shelters, weeks after the magnitude-7.7 quake on October 9, which resulted in injuries and damaged hundreds of buildings.
Wadephul also thanked the Central American country for maintaining the Panama Canal "so responsibly and ensuring it is fit for the future, as well as more generally focusing on preserving balance in the region."
Restrictions on other sea routes due to the conflict in the Middle East has meant that the Panama Canal is more important to global trade than ever.
Wadephul is due to hold talks on Thursday with Martinez-Acha Vasquez and President Jose Raul Mulino.
Wadephul will travel to the US state of Georgia for the G20 summit in Atlanta on Friday and Saturday.
IN DEPTH: The search for President Steinmeier's successor
Several names are being floated to replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's ceremonial head of state — including some that could be the first woman to hold the post.
Read our full report here.
Ping-pong vs. politics: Steinmeier takes on German Olympian Boll
After delivering his speech at Peking University, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities to play ping-pong with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll.
In the university sports hall, the two faced each other, accompanied by two Chinese participants — a referee and the university president. Right from the start, Steinmeier downplayed his chances, and subsequently lost 1–7.
Boll, who won silver at the Beijing Olympics in 2008, is the most successful German table tennis player of all time.
He won several Olympic medals, as well as titles in World Cups and World Championships during his storied career, which saw him ranked as the number 1 player in the world in 2003, 2011 and 2018.
To this day, Boll remains one of the best-known Germans in China, where ping-pong is unofficially considered the national sport.
Boll is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.
Steinmeier calls for fair trade in China during Bejiing visit
Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Thursday called on China to reduce economic imbalances between the two countries, as well as between China and Europe.
Steinmeier, who was speaking at the renowned Peking University, also urged China to work with Germany and other European nations to strengthen the international, rules-based order and "to advocate for peace and free global trade."
The German president, who holds a largely ceremonial role, spoke of his respect for China's rapid development in its economy, technology and politics, calling China a "defining world power."
But Steinmeier added, "With greatness and power comes great responsibility."
"We are not concerned about China's rise. We are watching how China rises," he said.
"We do not want to decouple from China; on the contrary, we want to structure trade in such a way that it continues to benefit both sides." This, he said, requires fair and uniform rules.
Steinmeier was referring to the high barriers European companies face when trying to operate in the Chinese market. Since China heavily subsidizes its exports to Europe, the European market comes under pressure too quickly.
This poses "the danger of one-sided vulnerability," Steinmeier said. Europeans cannot want this for their economy, just as "China does not want it for its economy."
What did Steinmeier say about China and the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East?
He also called on China to exert more influence on Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.
According to Steinmeier, China's interests are also at stake in this war, just as they are in the Middle East. As a major trading power, China also needs free sea lanes, intact supply chains, and a secure energy supply.
"The longer these conflicts persist, the weaker the global economy as a whole becomes — and with it, one of its largest economies: China," the president said.
Steinmeier addressed future issues in which China should take a particular interest: climate change and artificial intelligence. He appealed to his hosts, saying that when it comes to AI, "we should jointly establish international guidelines so that the technology remains under human control," he said.
On the final day of his state visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership and hold talks with, among others, President Xi Jinping.
Steinmeier is making his first visit to China in eight years, as he seeks to boost bilateral ties.
Friedrich Merz accuses North Korea of threatening Europe's freedom
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday said North Korea was threatening "freedom throughout Europe" by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Merz highlighted that Russia was supplying weapons to North Korea.
The chancellor said this arrangement therefore shows how "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects Korea's security."
North Korea has boosted its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pyongyang has provided Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. It has also, according to South Korean intelligence services, sent about 15,000 soldiers to fight alongside Russian forces.
In exchange, Russia provides financial backing, military technology and security guarantees to North Korea.
Before Merz's arrival on Thursday, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, according to the South Korean military.
At the start of his visit, Merz said he hoped that Korea would eventually be unified. The peninsula has been split along the 38th parallel since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953.
Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen their two nations' strategic and security ties, which includes joint military exercises and exchange of intelligence.
The chancellor is expected to conclude his trip to South Korea with a visit to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.
WATCH: Can Germany's pivot to Asia end its reliance on China?
Germany is looking for new partners in Asia. As Chancellor Friedrich Merz travels to Singapore, Japan and South Korea, Berlin is trying to reduce its economic dependence on China while adapting to a changing global order. But can countries in the Indo-Pacific, besides China, help Germany diversify its trade and security partnerships?
This week on Berlin Briefing, DW's Giulia Saudelli speaks with DW Business Reporter Steven Beardsley and DW Chief Political Correspondent Nina Haase, who is traveling with the chancellor.
They discuss Germany's push to "de-risk" from China, growing security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, and whether middle powers can work together to shape the future global order.
Germany, South Korea upgrade ties to 'enhanced strategic partnership'
Germany and South Korea on Thursday pledged to work together on the economy, energy and security and high-tech industries, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said.
The South Korean leader made the announcement after a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Seoul.
At a joint press conference, Lee told reporters that he had asked Merz for Germany's backing in securing favorable treatment for South Korea as part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act.
The two leaders also agreed to improve bilateral ties to an "enhanced strategic partnership," Lee said.
8-year-old girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German zoo
An eight-year-old girl sustained serious injuries after she was attacked by at least one wolf at a wildlife park in Brandenburg in east Germany.
The child was brought to hospital by a rescue helicopter on Wednesday.
Local officials said a zookeeper had helped prevent other children from being attacked.
Police are investigating how and why the attack occurred, which took place during a special program for children.
Police on Thursday said their investigation was centered on a staff member who was in the enclosure with the children, a spokeswoman said.
The Teltow-Fläming district administration said the incident happened before the wildlife park's regular opening hours as part of an "Animal Keeper Day" for children.
The administration also said the attack had taken place in the polar wolf enclosure.
"While the animals in the wildlife enclosure were being watered, the wolves kept there attacked a girl and seriously injured her," the district administration said.
The zookeeper's quick action prevented "further harm to two other girls" who were also at the scene, the district added.
The park will remain closed for the time being, officials said, as authorities launch a safety review at the wildlife park, which is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin.
Police are still probing the circumstances that led to the children being inside the enclosure.
The Johannismühle Wildlife Park said it was cooperating with authorities but could not provide further details due to the open investigation.
"We deeply regret the incident, and the affected family has our full support," the park said.
The wildlife park was closed until further notice "due to technical reasons," a sign at the entrance said on Thursday.
A wolf bit a woman in a busy shopping area in Hamburg this year, in what is thought to be the first such attack since wolves were reintroduced to the country in 1998.
German Chancellor Merz says he hopes for Korean reunification
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is visiting Seoul, said at the start of his visit that he hopes North and South Korea will eventually be reunited.
The Korean Peninsula has been divided into two states since the Korean War ended in 1953.
Merz pointed to his own country's division between West and East Germany for much of the second half of the 20th century.
"Korea and Germany are united by the painful experience of division," he wrote in the guest book during his meeting with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
"I also wish for the people of Korea what we are fortunate to experience in Germany: unity in freedom."

EU delays national social media rules for children to push bloc-wide approach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:48:30 UTC
23:48:30 KST

Melike Pala
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
The European Commission has decided to postpone for 12 months draft national laws that overlap with its proposed EU-wide rules on children's access to social media, a spokesperson said on Thursday.
The decision aims to ensure consistent protection for minors across all EU member states through harmonized rules, Thomas Regnier told reporters in Brussels.
"We have a very clear proposal that we have put on the table, whereby we're introducing a gradual approach and safety by design obligations for all online services," he said, referring to the proposed European Union Kids Act.
He said the commission had decided to postpone for 12 months national draft legislation overlapping with the future EU-wide rules.
The move is intended to prevent different national age limits and regulatory requirements from creating a fragmented internal market, making it difficult for online platforms to comply with rules across the 27-member bloc, he added.
"Our proposal harmonizes the rules to make sure that all children across the EU receive equal levels of protection, because a European problem requires a united European response," Regnier said.
Asked whether the decision would also affect other member states that had notified the commission of their national legislation, Regnier said work on those laws was ongoing but would not change the commission's position against fragmentation.
He noted, however, that there were legal and procedural differences between national initiatives, citing France and Greece as examples.
According to Regnier, France and Greece had notified their legislation before the commission presented its own proposal, and the relevant standstill periods had already elapsed, distinguishing their cases from Austria's and subsequent notifications by other member states.
Last month, the commission proposed a gradual approach to restricting children's access to social media, including a ban for children under 13 and limited access for those under 15 under parental supervision.

ECB warns prolonged energy shock to drive up inflation, lower growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:46:16 UTC
23:46:16 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
The European Central Bank warned on Thursday that the growing scale and duration of the energy shock are likely to push up inflation and dampen economic growth across the eurozone.
Speaking at a news conference in Frankfurt alongside Vice-President Boris Vujcic, ECB President Christine Lagarde said policymakers decided to keep key interest rates unchanged while remaining ready to respond to elevated economic uncertainty.
"Energy prices have continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook," Lagarde said.
"The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth," she added.
Headline inflation in the single currency bloc climbed to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, driven by an 18.9% jump in energy costs as diesel and gasoline prices touched new peaks, Lagarde noted.
Inflation excluding energy edged up to 2.3% from 2.1%, food inflation rose to 1.3% from 1.1% and services inflation reached 3.2%, while goods inflation eased slightly to 1.1%.
Lagarde said energy prices have exceeded the baseline path projected by ECB staff in September, which will likely keep headline inflation well above the bank's 2% target over the coming quarters.
Wage pressures remain moderate, with compensation per employee rising 3.3% in the second quarter, while negotiated wage growth is projected to average 2.6% in the first nine months of 2027.
Despite the energy drag, incoming data shows the eurozone economy continued to expand in the third quarter, supported by a recovery in services, artificial intelligence-related business investment and government spending on defense and infrastructure.
The unemployment rate held at 6.4% in August, while productivity has gradually improved, Lagarde said.
However, risks to economic growth remain tilted to the downside, primarily due to the Middle East conflict and the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine.
"Continued disruption of energy supplies could cause energy prices to rise further and for longer than currently expected," Lagarde warned, adding that tighter financing conditions and renewed trade tensions could further weaken investment and exports.
On financing conditions, Lagarde noted that interest rates have broadly moved higher while stock prices have fallen.
Bank lending rates for firms stood at 3.8% in August, while the cost of market-based debt rose to 4.1% and corporate loan demand declined due to higher borrowing costs.
Mortgage rates rose to 3.6% in August, leading to a substantial drop in household demand for home loans.
Lagarde called for temporary, targeted and tailored fiscal measures in response to the energy shock and urged European Union policymakers to finalize the legal framework for the digital euro as quickly as possible.
Reaffirming the central bank's medium-term 2% inflation target, Lagarde stressed that future rate decisions will follow a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach without pre-committing to a specific interest rate path.

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Ischaemic heart disease was Malaysia's leading cause of death in 2025, accounting for 18,001 deaths, or 13 percent of the total, the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) said on Thursday.
The disease was the leading cause of death among males, with 12,670 deaths, while pneumonia was the main cause of death among females, accounting for 7,684 deaths, DOSM said in a statement.

China Focus: China expands foreign business access at world's largest free trade port
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:23:45 CST
18:23:45 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China has unveiled 16 measures to make it easier for foreign businesses and professionals to operate in the Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP), the world's largest FTP by area, with new policies covering energy trade, medical services and bonded business operations, according to a government circular made public Thursday.
Under the measures, foreign physicians legally licensed to practice medicine overseas may obtain permits to provide clinical diagnosis and treatment services in Hainan for up to three years, with extensions available in accordance with relevant regulations.
More convenient policies regarding work permits and stay and residence will also be introduced for foreign nationals.
The Hainan FTP, located in China's southernmost island province, launched island-wide special customs operations in December 2025, allowing freer entry of overseas goods, expanded zero-tariff coverage and more business-friendly measures as part of China's efforts to promote high-standard opening-up.
Overseas companies will be allowed to use bonded facilities at Hainan's liquefied natural gas (LNG) receiving terminals, while the FTP will be supported in conducting LNG futures delivery warehouse operations after LNG futures contracts are launched.
Other measures include promoting offshore trade, expanding the range of products eligible for bonded maintenance, facilitating the entry of eligible bonded remanufactured products into pilot free trade zones on the Chinese mainland, encouraging the use of the yuan in new forms of barter trade, and deepening the FTP's economic and trade cooperation with China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Bonded remanufactured products entering mainland pilot free trade zones will be subject to applicable import tariffs, import-related value-added tax and consumption tax. They must also meet all applicable technical requirements for equivalent new products and relevant regulations on remanufactured products, and be clearly labeled as such.
The circular also calls for improved insurance products and services in areas such as international transportation and bonded maintenance.
The latest measures come amid robust growth in Hainan's foreign trade. In the first three quarters of 2026, the province's goods imports and exports reached 285.44 billion yuan (about 42.5 billion U.S. dollars), up 49.8 percent year on year, while trade in services rose 11.7 percent to 56.95 billion yuan, according to data from Hainan's provincial commerce authorities.
Trade in maintenance and repair services more than doubled year on year to 3.31 billion yuan during the same period, according to the provincial commerce department. The trade mainly came from imports of aircraft materials and components and revenues from aircraft maintenance services.
The number of newly established foreign-invested enterprises in Hainan rose 38.6 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, according to the State Administration for Market Regulation.
The FTP measures are part of China's broader efforts to promote high-standard opening-up. The country has announced plans to further expand pilot opening-up programs in sectors such as value-added telecommunications, biotechnology and wholly foreign-owned hospitals, while taking steps to facilitate cross-border trade and investment.
The circular was jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and the General Administration of Customs. ■

SYDNEY, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have mapped genetic links to 16 diseases, identifying nearly 1,500 genes that may contribute to conditions ranging from cancer to immune and neurological disorders.
The team, from the Garvan Institute of Medical Research in collaboration with the Murdoch Children's Research Institute and the University of New South Wales in Australia, and other partners, analyzed the gene sequence and activity of more than 9 million individual immune cells from nearly 2,000 people, the largest dataset of its kind, according to a statement released Thursday by the Garvan Institute.
The three studies, published in Nature, examined how genetic variations affect gene activity, repetitive DNA sequences and chromatin accessibility, which influence whether genes can be switched on or off. The findings revealed previously unknown mechanisms linking genetic variations to disease risk.
The research could help accelerate drug development and precision medicine by identifying the genetic mechanisms underlying disease and the patients likely to respond to particular treatments. ■

====================================================================================================

How could an oil spill off UAE coast affect desalination plants?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:16:10 UTC
18:16:10 KST

Breadcrumb
How could the oil spill off the UAE coast affect desalination plants?
An oil spill off the United Arab Emirates that has prompted temporary restrictions on fishing and on access to several beaches has raised concerns over the risk of environmental contamination and questions about the potential impact on desalination plants.
What are the main environmental concerns?
The spill is coming from a vessel that shipping sources have identified as crude oil tanker Gem No.2, which they said had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, in the Ras Al Khaimah emirate.
Residents in some northern emirates had posted on social media about strange odours, but authorities said last week that those posed no health risks.
On Wednesday, authorities in Sharjah were the latest to close all beaches as a precaution.
Repeated attacks on commercial vessels since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran have heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
The incident off the UAE has also raised questions about what impact oil spills can have on desalination plants, which crowd the Emirati coastline and, just like in other Gulf countries, are a key supplier of water.
In the UAE, desalinated water accounts for more than 80% of potable water. Major plants include those at Dubai's Jebel Ali industrial port, and at Taweelah between Abu Dhabi and Dubai.
Gulf desalination plants had already come under threat from direct hits in the conflict earlier this year.
Maritime intelligence firm Windward said on Sunday that the leak was threatening the seawater intake of the Naqa'a desalination plant at the border between Umm Al Quwain and Ras Al Khaimah.
Footage verified by Reuters showed that the oil slick had reached a location in Ras Al Khaimah about 2 km away from the plant.
Water experts told Reuters that it was currently hard to assess the potential impact on desalination plants without more information on the extent of the spill. There have been no shutdowns of plants announced in the UAE so far.
The UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, Ras Al Khaimah Media Office and the Naqa'a plant did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
What's the level of risk from this spill?
Any oil spill has the potential to impact the environment, but the extent of the damage depends on the type of oil and the volume, said Simon Boxall, a senior lecturer at the University of Southampton.
Satellite technology can help identify oil slicks floating on the sea's surface but does not provide an indication of how thick that layer is, he noted.
"Crude oil in particular is a natural product. And so crude oil will break down in the marine environment, particularly in the warm waters such as the Gulf, within a matter of a few weeks," he said.
"A thicker spill obviously carries more oil, and when it hits the beaches, when it hits the marine environment, both at sea, on the seabed, and on the coast, then it has a potential to cause more damage. It will eventually break down, but that does take time."
What's the potential threat to desalination plants?
Plants need to be shut down as soon as oil gets anywhere near them to avoid contamination, said Boxall.
Nidal Hilal, director of New York University Abu Dhabi's Water Research Center, said oil spills can threaten desalination plants even when the oil does not physically reach the plant itself, with the principal vulnerability being the seawater intake, which draws raw seawater into the facility for treatment.
"For the UAE, where desalination is a cornerstone of drinking-water security, a key concern is whether the oil could reach seawater intakes and compromise the treatment process," he told Reuters.
It is important to make a distinction between a threat to water quality, a temporary shutdown of a plant, and actual physical damage to the facility, he said.
What can be done to prevent damage and how long do repairs take?
The most effective strategy is to establish several layers of protection rather than rely on a single intervention.
"For the current incident, the priorities should be to prevent oil from reaching desalination intakes, protect treatment equipment, and maintain a safe and reliable drinking-water supply," said Hilal.
Generally, recovery time depends on whether contaminated seawater entered the plant and if the incident causes persistent fouling and equipment damage, he said, listing plant design and the type and quantity of oil among factors that can also play a role.
Have similar incidents happened in the past?
Technical studies and previous incidents have shown that oil contamination can disrupt desalination operations and even damage treatment equipment, said Hilal.
A major spill in 1991 during the Gulf War ended up being one of the largest in history, leading to several desalination plant shutdowns in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait and causing extensive shoreline contamination.
"Decades on, we are still seeing problems with pollution from that particular incident," said Boxall.
However, that spill and the one in the Gulf of Mexico in 2010 were much larger, he said, noting that the UAE spill was not "anything of that scale".

Chain of failures: 5 key takeaways from report on Tai Po blaze
John Lee announces housing chief’s exit, setting up body to assist homeowners in renovation projects and criminalising bid-rigging
A long-awaited report on the Wang Fuk Court fire released by Hong Kong authorities on Thursday set out how a chain of systemic failures across the government and the construction sector led to the deaths of 168 people.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu alongside top officials announced an array of decisions, ranging from the resignation of the housing chief and setting up a new body to assist homeowners in renovation projects to criminalising bid-rigging that was regarded by officials as “the source of the problem”.
Here are the key takeaways from the report by a judge-led independent committee and a government press conference on the findings.
1. Who will be held accountable for the tragedy?
The report by the committee led by Judge David Lok Kai-hong found that unscrupulous contractors, consultants and professionals from the private sector were “the main culprits” of the tragedy.

Organization of Turkic States foreign ministers meeting begins in Ankara
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:11:24 UTC
18:11:24 KST

Sercan Irkin and Esra Tekin
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
The Meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) began in Türkiye's capital Ankara on Thursday as part of the organization’s 13th summit.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hosted the meeting, according to diplomatic sources.
Foreign ministers of the OTS posed for a family photo ahead of the meeting.
The summit, to be held on Thursday and Friday in Ankara, will be hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, under the theme Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.
Established in 2009, the OTS, formerly known as the Turkic Council, adopted its current name during its eighth summit held in the Turkish metropolis Istanbul in 2021.
While Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan are members, Turkmenistan, Hungary, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, and the Economic Cooperation Organization hold observer status.
The organization said on Oct. 24 that the summit would bring together the heads of state of its member states, as well as high-level representatives from observer states and its secretary general, to “discuss the current state and future prospects of cooperation within the Organization,” among other issues.
It said the heads of state are expected to review the progress achieved across the OTS’ priority areas, and that particular emphasis will be placed on “further strengthening unity and solidarity” among the Turkic states and advancing cooperation under the Turkic World Vision 2040.
It added that the summit will also mark the handover of the OTS’ chairmanship from Azerbaijan to Türkiye, and is expected to address the appointment of a new secretary general and the organization’s strategic priorities “for the forthcoming period.”
“The Heads of State are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, together with a number of decisions and documents aimed at deepening cooperation and further strengthening the institutional framework of the OTS,” it added.

"The number of those injured has risen to four," he said.
