Promises and Perils of Nepal’s India Pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:11:00 UTC
18:11:00 KST

After months of keeping New Delhi at arm’s length, Nepal’s Balendra Shah government is discovering both the appeal and the political risks of drawing it closer.
Formed after the March 2026 elections, the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) government did not start on the right foot with the southern neighbor. First, new Prime Minister Balendra Shah declined a one-on-one meeting with then-Indian Ambassador Naveen Shrivastava, in keeping with his policy of not meeting any foreign officials.
What rankled more with the Indians was his subsequent refusal to meet India’s Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, who was coming to Kathmandu carrying Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s formal invitation for Shah to visit India. Misri’s trip was called off. India — which continues to emphasize its “unique” relations with Nepal that are unlike its ties with any other country — saw this as a snub, and a breach of trust.
Those were not the only irritants in bilateral ties. The new government in Kathmandu started taxing goods bought by Nepali nationals in Indian border towns, hampering the business of these hubs that rely on Nepali buyers. Entry of Indian vehicles into Nepal was also restricted.
That was the state of affairs for the first five or six months of the Shah government.
But the tide seems to have turned and the government now appears keen to woo the Indians. At the forefront of this effort is Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle.
Even before the March elections, as a top RSP leader, Wagle had repeatedly visited New Delhi with a message that should his party come to power, it would go the extra mile to protect Indian interests.
Of late, Wagle seems to have gotten the government’s green light to boldly assert that the era of “anti-India nationalism” in Nepal is over and his government is ready to turn over a new leaf with the southern neighbor.
Curiously, he and his government also sound accommodative of India’s self-declared red lines. In a recent interview with The Hindu, the Nepali minister said that Nepal now accepts that India’s refusal to buy hydropower from Nepali projects with Chinese investment is a “new geopolitical reality.”
Yet the finance minister is only laying the ground for Shah’s much-awaited India visit in the third week of November. Home Minister Sudan Gurung has also contributed to this effort, outlining potential areas of bilateral cooperation in a recent op-ed. Big deals are being planned during Shah’s visit.
But for any government in Kathmandu, close relations with India come with both costs and benefits. The obvious benefit is that New Delhi pulls many strings in Kathmandu, and it can make life difficult for a Nepali prime minister it does not like. The latest overtures of his government toward India suggest Shah does not want to be one of them.
If Shah can convince New Delhi to, say, secure an additional air route for Nepal during his India trip, it will be a new feather in his bhadgaule cap — and a tangible achievement for his nationalist base back home.
Yet there are also costs of closer ties with India. Whatever Wagle says, the days of anti-India nationalism in Nepal are far from over — as is also evident in the fierce criticism of his remarks in Nepali intellectual circles. Nepalis continue to be suspicious of the oft-meddling regional hegemon that has thrice imposed crippling blockades on the landlocked country.
Shah got an overwhelming mandate, and he can afford to use some of his political capital to push through vital projects with India. But irrespective of how well Shah’s India trip goes, there will still be irritants in bilateral ties.
For instance, a major disagreement remains between Kathmandu and New Delhi on an old border dispute. After India and China unilaterally opened the Lipulekh pass — a trijunction point between the three countries — for trade earlier this year, Kathmandu swiftly dispatched diplomatic notes to New Delhi and Beijing. This issue could again flare up as both New Delhi and Beijing seem to be in a mood to overrule Nepal’s objections and give continuity to their trade through the pass.
It will be hard for the Shah government to stand firm on Lipulekh — something that is in keeping with the Nepali public sentiment — while also pursuing closer cooperation with India. If it does not handle the issue well, a “compromise” on territorial integrity to secure favorable trade terms could even be portrayed domestically as a surrender to the regional hegemon.
Then there is China. The government has signaled that closer ties with India are worth paying the price of narrowing the space for Chinese investment in Nepali hydropower.
Yet if the government pushes Beijing too far through such gestures, it will violate a central tenet of Nepali foreign policy: maintenance of a delicate balance between Beijing and New Delhi. There will thus be a strong opposition to an overt India tilt.
In the end, Shah and his ministers would do well to avoid making sweeping claims that old constraints in India-Nepal ties have disappeared or that the anti-India nationalism in Nepal has run its course. Nurturing this complicated relationship requires sustained diplomacy and setting of realistic expectations. Only then can Nepal protect its interests.

Over 135,000 displaced in Yemen’s Taiz province in 2 months: Minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:10:59 UTC
18:10:59 KST

More than 135,000 people were displaced in Yemen’s southwestern Taiz province over a roughly two-month period, a minister said Wednesday, citing government figures that also recorded 79 civilian deaths and 206 injuries, Anadolu reports.
Social Affairs and Labor Minister Mukhtar Omar Saleh Al-Yafei presented the figures at a government news conference in the temporary capital Aden, according to Yemen’s SABA news agency.
The figures cover Aug. 10 to Oct. 15, a period of military escalation and a siege that the government accuses the Houthi group of imposing on parts of the province.
Al-Yafei said field monitoring recorded the displacement of 19,600 families comprising 135,587 people, including 52,979 children.
The ministry documented 494 violations against civilians during the same period, including the killings and injuries. Damage was reported to 56 residential buildings, 12 educational facilities, eight health facilities and 10 roads and bridges, along with other property and public services.
READ: 1,574 killed, 6,939 injured in Yemen escalation since August: WHO
The minister called for a broader humanitarian response to address funding shortfalls and gaps in essential services.
Taiz Governor Nabil Shamsan said more than 1.3 million people lived in six districts affected by the siege, while shelling had damaged or destroyed about 676 homes.
He warned that services at 12 hospitals and 18 health centers were under threat. In Houthi-controlled districts, 120 health facilities had stopped operating entirely and another 66 were only partially functioning, disrupting care for more than 186,000 children under five and nearly 23,000 pregnant women.
Taiz, Yemen’s most populous province, remains divided between government forces and the Houthis. Government forces control Taiz city, the provincial capital, and other parts of the province.
Since July, a military escalation between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has resumed, particularly in Taiz and Lahj, killing and injuring thousands, according to UN reports.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014. A Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

Norwegian prime minister denies Putin lectured him and Finnish president on medieval Slavs during call
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre denied a Financial Times report that said Vladimir Putin recounted the history of the Slavs during a call with him and Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
“We asked the Financial Times to correct this because it isn’t true. And they will correct it, because we took part in the conversation,” Støre said in an interview with the Norwegian newspaper VG.
VG asked the Financial Times for comment. The paper said it would not make any changes. “We stand by our journalism,” an FT representative said.
A day earlier, the Financial Times reported that Putin gave Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister a lecture on the history of the Slavs in the Middle Ages during an October 27 call. According to the paper, Putin spent much of the conversation on what the Kremlin calls the “initial reasons for the conflict” rather than addressing key questions about ending the war in Ukraine.
Later, Støre offered a different account of the conversation on the NRK program Politisk kvarter, saying Putin spoke about the situation in Europe after 2014.
Putin has made similar lengthy digressions into Russian history in other conversations, including his 2024 interview with American journalist Tucker Carlson and his meeting with Donald Trump in Alaska.

Restricted airspace now covers fifty defence sites
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:00:09 GMT
18:00:09 KST

Restricted airspace has been applied over fifty defence sites and a further one hundred and seventy are expected to follow in December, part of a wider effort to harden British military bases against drones, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Mark Pritchard, the Conservative member for The Wrekin, asked what additional support is being given to Guardian, the protective security element of Standing Joint Command, in light of increased threats to British military bases.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Defence Investment Plan provides an additional £470 million over four years for security technology and infrastructure. Restricted Airspace has been applied to 50 Defence sites, with a further 170 expected in December 2026, while £15 million has been invested in remotely piloted and counter-uncrewed aerial systems and training over the past 18 months.”
Restricted airspace makes flying a drone over a site unlawful without permission. That does not stop anyone flying, but it gives the police and the Ministry of Defence Police an offence to act on, and it removes the argument that an operator did not know where they were.
The department has set out £240 million for Project PRESAGIUM, an enhanced counter-drone system intended to detect and defeat emerging threats, and the Army is running Project Halo Shield to examine what commercially available counter-drone technology could do for site protection. The £15 million figure for remotely piloted and counter-drone systems and training over the past eighteen months is small compared with those programmes and covers work done while they are being stood up.

Astronomers Discover a Possible New Dwarf Planet in Our Solar System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Scientists are on the verge of confirming the discovery of another member of the solar system, a potential dwarf planet. Astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile located the object, provisionally named 2026 ED138.
The prospective planet measures somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers in diameter and is located about 46 astronomical units from the sun (an astronomical unit being Earth’s approximate distance from the sun). For comparison, Pluto—which is also now considered a dwarf planet—orbits at an average distance of 40 astronomical units. Based on its location, ED138 belongs to the population of trans-Neptunian objects. According to its discoverers, it could be one of the brightest known objects of this type and also among the largest.
The difference between a planet and a dwarf planet is largely their environment. While both orbit the sun and have sufficient gravity to assume a nearly spherical shape, a planet has cleared its orbit of other bodies of comparable size. Dwarf planets, on the other hand, coexist with other objects in the region of the solar system they traverse. This is the main reason why Pluto ceased to be considered a planet in 2006 and was reclassified as a dwarf planet.
Matthew Holman, a researcher at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and a member of the observatory’s operations team, identified the object on October 13 while analyzing data collected by Rubin in 2026. A more thorough search allowed the team to locate additional observations in archived records dating back to 2016. Thanks to this set of images, the team was able to reconstruct more than a decade of the object’s trajectory.
Astronomers explain that ED138 had managed to “hide” from us because its position in the night sky is against the disk of the Milky Way, which we usually see as a thick band of millions of stars. This concentrated brightness makes it difficult to distinguish fainter objects, but the Rubin Observatory’s enormous amounts of data made it possible to identify the object amid that sea of light.
Though ED138 appears to have the right characteristics, astronomers have yet to confirm whether it is a dwarf planet. For now, astronomers know it is a trans-Neptunian object, but they need to determine its size more precisely to establish whether its own gravity is sufficient to give it a nearly spherical shape. If it meets the requirements, ED138 would join the group of five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris.
It is also not the only celestial body awaiting possible classification as a dwarf planet. Astronomers have identified dozens of objects in the outer solar system that, based on their size and other characteristics, could meet the criteria. Among the best-known candidates are Gonggong, Quaoar, Sedna, and Orcus. Experts acknowledge that the list could be even longer.
Confirming them as dwarf planets is no easy task. The enormous distance at which they lie makes it difficult to directly measure their size and mass and, above all, to determine whether their own gravity has given them a nearly spherical shape. To obtain high-resolution images of Pluto, for example, the New Horizons probe had to be sent to its vicinity—a journey that took nearly nine and a half years from its launch in 2006 to its flyby in 2015. Three years later, it reached the object Arrokoth, a small planetesimal even farther away.
The solar system is often depicted as a star surrounded by eight planets, but in reality it is a much more extensive and populous structure. In addition to planets and moons, it contains dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, and a vast number of small bodies that extend far beyond Neptune. The Kuiper Belt extends to approximately 50 astronomical units, while the scattered disk reaches nearly 1,000. Much farther out lies the Oort Cloud, a region we have never directly observed and that could extend up to about 100,000 astronomical units from the sun.

"No politician is irreplaceable" – Mieriņa delivers a significant message as Latvia's 14th Saeima concludes its work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:59:56 UTC
17:59:56 KST

As Latvia's 14th Saeima concluded its work on Thursday, Speaker of Parliament Daiga Mieriņa of the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) called on lawmakers to maintain respect for the Saeima and democratic values, stressing that the country is always greater than any political party, parliamentary group or parliamentary term.
In her final address to the outgoing parliament, Mieriņa acknowledged that the past four years had not been easy and had required considerable work, patience and compromise. Nevertheless, lawmakers had managed to maintain dialogue even when their opinions differed.
The Speaker recalled that during the 14th Saeima's term, parliament held 219 sittings, conducted 7,911 votes, adopted 1,060 laws and held 3,555 committee meetings.
She emphasised that the Saeima is a mirror of society, reflecting what Latvia has been and what it is today.
Mieriņa thanked lawmakers for their contributions to strengthening parliamentarism, democracy and the Latvian state, noting that every member of parliament had left their mark over the four years, whether through adopted legislation, initiatives or parliamentary debates.
She stressed that in a democracy, there are no small or large mandates, only the trust of voters granted for a limited period.
Addressing lawmakers who will continue serving in the next parliament, Mieriņa encouraged them to retain the ability to listen not only to their own voters but also to those who hold different views.
She also urged them to respect parliamentary traditions and the people on whose behalf decisions are made.
At the same time, Mieriņa noted that society is changing and a new generation is knocking on parliament's doors, bringing its own perspectives and expectations of politics.
She stressed that politicians must be willing to listen to this generation and make room for new representatives.
Mieriņa emphasised that no politician is irreplaceable, as members of parliament serve for a limited time, while Latvia, democracy and the people they serve remain.
Concluding her address, the Speaker wished lawmakers success in both their political careers and personal challenges.
She also quoted author and speaker Neale Donald Walsch, saying that a true leader is not someone who has the most followers, but someone who creates the most leaders.
Mieriņa ended her speech with the traditional Latvian wish: "May Latvia live as long as the sun!"

Russia Uses Fake ATESH Accounts and Messaging Bots to Expose Resistance Helpers
Russian special services are impersonating members of the ATESH movement to track down individuals attempting to assist resistance efforts during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Accounts posing as ATESH have recently appeared in chat groups belonging to other movements, including Freedom of Russia, urging users to contact a specific automated messaging bot.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Representatives of ATESH clarified that these messages are deceptive traps set up by Russian security forces to expose potential helpers.
The partisans noted that the group does not use automated bots. One fake account discovered in chat rooms was @Svysnoy_Ateshhbot, which closely mimics their actual contact handle but includes a slight spelling error.
ATESH stated that their only official contact account is @Svyaznoy_Atesh.
On October 21, 2026, agents of the ATESH partisan movement sabotaged Russian military communications around IXcellerate, one of Moscow’s largest commercial data centers, in an effort to disrupt air-defense coordination and help Ukrainian drones reach their targets.
The group stated that they were disabling enemy channels, disrupting command and control, and assisting UAVs in reaching their targets.
ATESH claimed that Russia’s Defense Ministry used infrastructure connected to the facility for military communications and air-defense command systems, effectively embedding military traffic within civilian server networks.

US reporters to monitor Russia-Ukraine truce in frontline town – Melania Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:59:04 UTC
17:59:04 KST

US reporters to monitor Russia-Ukraine truce in frontline town – Melania Trump
American journalists will observe a humanitarian mission under a Russia-Ukraine truce in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Kherson Region, Russia, US First Lady Melania Trump has said. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has confirmed that the reporters are expected there, and that demining operations are already underway.
Alyoshki, located on the left bank of the Dnieper River, was largely cut off from essential supplies and basic services for months under a Ukrainian siege, with drone attacks and remotely laid mines hampering aid deliveries and evacuation efforts from a town where an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 civilians remained.
Russian Foreign Ministry envoy Rodion Miroshnik described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods,” accusing Ukraine of obstructing humanitarian efforts.
However, after US mediation spearheaded by the Slovenian-born US first lady, Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the area starting October 27 to allow humanitarian assistance to flow in and evacuations to proceed. As of Thursday, both Russian and Ukrainian officials reported no truce violations. The pause is scheduled to last until Sunday.
Writing on X on Wednesday, Trump said four American journalists from conservative US outlet Newsmax will arrive in Alyoshki and accompany Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian leaders. “Serving as neutral observers, they will independently record and permanently document this historic humanitarian mission,” she said.
Dmitriev confirmed that Newsmax reporters will be there, adding: “Humanity and peace must prevail.”
Speaking to reporters before departing to Alyoshki, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said other foreign journalists are also expected to arrive, without providing further details.
Both Trump and Lantratova confirmed that Russia and Ukraine have begun clearing mines to secure aid routes. “It is now crucial to make the roads safe so that people can leave the town,” Lantratova said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said on Thursday that most Ukrainian mines found near Alyoshki were scattered by drones, and that they are predominantly Western-made. It also released a video showing a large-scale demining effort involving remotely-controlled robots.
The Alyoshki crisis was discussed during an October 9 phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, the leaders agreed that Russia’s human rights commissioner would maintain direct contact with Melania Trump’s office. US envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently met with Putin in St. Petersburg last week to discuss proposals for ending the Ukraine conflict.

North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:58:57 UTC
17:58:57 KST

North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report says
Russian broker network recruiting North Korean labourers using student visas, Global Rights Compliance report says.
North Korean workers are being recruited into forced labour in Russia by a broker network using bogus student enrolments, according to a months-long investigation by an international law foundation.
The network brings North Koreans into Russia on student visas to skirt United Nations sanctions and labour law, as part of a state-sponsored work programme that helps fund Pyongyang’s ballistic missile development, according to the Global Rights Compliance report released on Thursday.
Operated by Russian businessman Vladimir Sokolov, labour-brokering platform KNDR.su markets North Korean workers to prospective Russian employers in agriculture, construction, industry and IT, charging a commission of 100,000-150,000 roubles ($1,240-$1,860) per placement, according to the Netherlands-based nonprofit.
In conversations with Global Rights Compliance investigators posing as prospective employers, Sokolov’s operations director, Ruslan Zhukov, said North Korean workers were enrolled in colleges they did not attend “to avoid the application of labour law”, the law foundation said.
Zhukov also described the workers being required to work 12 hours a day, six days a week, according to the report.
UN member states are prohibited from hosting North Korean workers under a 2017 UN Security Council resolution intended to deprive Pyongyang of funds for its nuclear weapons and missile programmes.
Despite UN sanctions, between 35,600 and 101,280 North Korean workers were based overseas in 2025, generating an estimated $450m-$800m for Pyongyang, according to an 11-country team that monitors sanctions enforcement.
Russia granted more than 36,000 visas to North Koreans in 2025, a fourfold increase from the previous year, almost all of which were officially for educational purposes.
Global Rights Compliance said the network also helped support Russia’s war effort in Ukraine, with Sokolov publicising at least two work sites with links to Moscow’s military-industrial complex.
Sokolov and Zhukov did not respond to requests for comment sent to Sokolov’s holding company, Black Horse, and KNDR.su.
Global Rights Compliance said Zhukov denied the report’s allegations, calling them “false, fabricated, and categorically rejected in their entirety”.
“The matter concerns exclusively students of a specialised college, sent to Russia within the framework of an intergovernmental agreement on the exchange of experience and the provision of venues for educational and industrial practical training,” a statement attributed to Zhukov said.
Lara Strangways, head of business and human rights at Global Rights Compliance, said the broker network pointed to deepening ties between North Korea and Russia.
“North Korean workers are being sent to Russian factories through a network that serves both states at once: Their labour props up Russian industry, including sites linked to the war in Ukraine, while the revenue they generate helps fund North Korea’s military programme,” Strangways said in a statement.
“What we are seeing is a clear exploitation of these workers as part of a cross-border system. If governments are serious about responding to this deepening alliance, they need to understand the role that forced labour is playing in sustaining it.”
North Korea and Russia have ramped up cooperation across various fields in recent years as Moscow became increasingly isolated on the international stage in the wake of its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Cold War-era allies ratified a landmark mutual defence treaty in 2024, with Pyongyang deploying thousands of North Korean soldiers to fight alongside Russian troops in the war on Ukraine.

The regime’s optics: Despite sanctions, Russia is advancing quantum and laser technologies for military use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:58:44 UTC
17:58:44 KST

The Insider has found that despite sanctions, Russia continues to regularly purchase advanced industrial laser equipment, allowing it to develop and manufacture its own military communications systems, lidars, target designators, and inertial navigation systems. Some purchases may also point to efforts to increase the capabilities of Russian quantum computers, which could significantly enhance the capabilities of Russian intelligence services by cracking encryption.
Cracking the world’s encryption: will Putin get a cryptographically relevant quantum computer?
The Insider has found that Russia continues to import advanced measuring instruments, components, and materials for optics and quantum electronics. The equipment being purchased — along with the research interests of the importers and end users — suggests that Russia is seeking to develop advanced laser technologies despite its continued reliance on imports for more basic laser applications.
If any country succeeds in building a “cryptographically relevant” quantum computer, and if such a machine falls into the hands of a totalitarian regime, it would significantly alter the international balance of power. Even without a quantum computer, however, mastery of advanced laser technologies would allow Russia’s military-industrial complex to develop domestic production capabilities across a range of military sectors far more quickly and effectively than it has managed to do so far.
A “cryptographically relevant” quantum computer in the hands of a totalitarian regime would significantly alter the international balance of power
Quantum computers are expected to outperform classical computers dramatically on tasks such as cracking encryption. Existing quantum computers, however, are not yet “cryptographically relevant” — meaning they remain far from being able to break the standard encryption algorithms in use at the present time. According to the latest estimates, a cryptographically relevant quantum computer capable of breaking RSA encryption with a 2,048-bit key would require at least one million physical qubits, with the number needed to break elliptic-curve cryptography with a 256-bit key estimated at around 10,000 physical qubits.
How a quantum computer works
Building a quantum computer capable of breaking modern encryption remains beyond the capabilities of even Google and IBM. IBM’s Condor quantum computer, for example, has 1,121 physical qubits based on superconducting technology. Quantum computers with around 100 qubits can be considered commercially available, in a limited sense, to major research institutions in the West.
Estimates vary on the countdown to Q-day — the point at which a cryptographically relevant quantum computer becomes available. Cloudflare, which helps secure websites around the world, cites the policies and research interests of IBM and Google to put Q-day in 2029 or 2030. In fact, the company is adjusting its own policies accordingly, transitioning to “post-quantum” protocols designed to remain resistant to the sorts of quantum attacks that could materialize in the foreseeable future.
Why photonic quantum computers require laser equipment
Russia’s most powerful quantum computers have been developed by the Lebedev Physical Institute (LPI), Rosatom, Moscow State University (MSU), and the Russian Quantum Center. The LPI–Rosatom computer has the equivalent of 70 qubits and uses ytterbium ions. MSU’s neutral-rubidium-atom computer has 72 qubits. The Russian Quantum Center’s computer uses trapped cold calcium ions and has the equivalent of 72 qubits. According to the Scientific Russia website, a 16-qubit superconducting quantum computer has been developed at the National University of Science and Technology MISIS.
The Russian Quantum Center is also involved, and in 2025, its researchers were ready to showcase a 35-qubit photonic quantum computer. The challenge now is to scale it up.
According to the Russian tax authorities’ records of fines, the work on a quantum computer for the Russian Quantum Center is being carried out by a Rosatom entity, joint venture Quantum Technologies. This conclusion is also supported by the numerous quantum computing patent applications filed by Quantum Technologies covering integrated circuit topologies for both photonic and superconducting quantum computers, as well as quantum computing algorithms and error-correction codes. Notably though, Quantum Technologies does not appear in customs records, suggesting that other organizations are handling equipment purchases on its behalf.
Such purchases are often made by subsidiaries or other companies linked through a common founder. In the case of the Russian Quantum Center, one possible candidate is its affiliated company, K2 LLC — almost all current and former K2 employees also have work experience at Quantum Technologies, including in specialized units responsible for procurement and logistics, cost accounting, reporting to federal executive authorities, support for the Committee on Quantum Technologies, and supplying equipment and consumables. This staffing structure suggests that K2 may be acting as a procurement agent for Quantum Technologies.
Advanced laser technologies — not just for quantum computers
Russian propagandists claim that Russia is now using lasers to shoot down drones; however, independent experts question the effectiveness of these systems. Whatever the case, advanced laser technologies are essential to the military-industrial complex.
Manufacturing complex-shaped components, additive manufacturing, welding and cutting, and quality control are all vital to industries such as aircraft and drone production, and all require sophisticated laser equipment. Some laser technologies, notably lidars and 3D scanners, also have direct military applications in guiding drones, artillery, and loitering munitions, as well as in reconnaissance. For years, however, Russia remained a consumer rather than a developer of laser technologies, and its own solutions were uncompetitive.
As recently as a decade ago, a trade publication reported that there were 10 Western and 100 Chinese laser specialists for every Russian one. Even during the relatively prosperous 2000s, foreign experts were critical of the capabilities of research lasers at Russian scientific centers. Industrial laser technology, meanwhile, remained largely dependent on imports, leaving many options unavalable after Western sanctions were levied in 2014. Russian-made lasers were not used at all in consumer or medical devices. Russia’s advanced laser sector was further devastated not only by neglect of science but also by the criminal prosecution of laser specialists amid the political repression of the 2020s.
Russia’s advanced laser industry collapsed not only because of the neglect of science, but also because laser specialists were prosecuted
According to data reviewed by The Insider, Russia imported $250 million worth of industrial laser equipment in 2024, excluding consumer and medical laser devices, civilian telecommunications equipment, and equipment for the entertainment industry.
The imports consisted primarily of high-power equipment: laser-cutting machines for sheet metal, pipes, other metal workpieces, and glass; machines for 3D cutting, engraving, and laser cleaning; laser welding and sintering machines; and equipment for high-precision manufacturing and measurement. The latter category included laser equipment for chip manufacturing, 3D printers, coordinate measuring machines, lidars, 3D laser scanners, rangefinders, sights, interferometers, particle-size analyzers, weld-seam inspection devices, and film-thickness gauges.
The Insider also found that Russia had imported components and assemblies in recent years to manufacture its own industrial lasers. These included blanks for active laser elements (neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnets and other crystals), lenses transparent to the relevant wavelengths, optical fibers, high-precision polishing machines, laser beam profile meters, and spectrometers. This suggests that efforts are also underway to rebuild Russia’s domestic laser industry, rather than relying solely on off-the-shelf Chinese laser equipment.
How the West is helping Putin with lasers
Russia imports predominantly sophisticated industrial laser equipment of Chinese origin, but approximately 10% is manufactured in Germany, Italy, Switzerland, Japan, the United States, and Israel. Among Western products, the most prominent suppliers by volume include Leica Geosystems (surveying scanners), Adige SPA (tube-cutting systems), Toptica Photonics AG (laboratory lasers), Stiefelmayer Lasertechnik GmbH & Co. KG (laser-cutting machines), Z-Laser GmbH (laser-cutting and welding equipment), and Sick AG (laser scanners). The leading beneficiaries of China’s laser-equipment trade include Jinan Senfeng Laser Technology, Hubei Jiuzhiyang Infrared System, Shandong Oree Laser Technology, and HSG Laser.
Supplies came almost exclusively from China, Turkey, and Israel. Individual items were shipped directly from Italy and Germany, accounting for less than 1% of the total.
Israel remains virtually the only Western country from which industrial laser equipment continued to be sold openly and directly to Russia in 2023–2025. The company that benefited in practice, regardless of its degree of involvement or awareness, was Ophir Optronics, registered in Israel but owned by the publicly traded American corporation MKS Inc. Operating in Russia under the Ophir Optronics name, the Russian company Kristalltechno LLC trades in and imports laser beam profile and spectrum analyzers.
The use of Ophir Optronics’ name, trademark, and logo in Russian commercial courts has not been challenged to date. Kristalltechno LLC has registered declarations of conformity in Russia covering a wide range of Ophir Optronics industrial cameras and their components.
On paper, the equipment is supplied by intermediaries in Turkey, Kyrgyzstan, the United Arab Emirates, China, and Hong Kong. However, customs records for some shipments identify Israel, rather than the country of the nominal supplier, as the country of dispatch.
In Russia, the equipment was most often received by Kristalltechno LLC, an established supplier to the military-industrial complex. According to 2024 data, the company did business with such Russian defense-sector enterprises as the Priborostroitelny Zavod Federal State Unitary Enterprise, the Ural Optical and Mechanical Plant (UOMZ), and the Ekran Research Institute. In effect, Kristalltechno was Ophir Optronics’ alter ego in Russia, apparently engaged in both manufacturing and resale. Curiously, according to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, Ophir Optronics has ties to Israel’s military establishment.
The Insider contacted Ophir Optronics for comment. The company responded through a representative from Kekst CNC, a reputation-management firm hired by MKS. A journalist from The Insider spoke with the representative by phone several times.
The representative issued the following statement:
“Ophir ceased working with Kristalltechno in early 2022, when the war began. We are not aware of any Ophir products being supplied to Russia through third parties. We were unaware that Kristalltechno was using our trademarks on its website and have taken steps to have them removed from the company’s website and all other marketing and sales materials. Ophir and its parent company comply with all applicable regulations governing the sale and export of our products.”
Ophir sidestepped The Insider’s question about its relationships with the companies that had exported its products to Russia, including whether they were partners, dealers, or distributors. The Insider had provided a list of these companies. Ophir also declined to explain why it had waited more than four years to check whether Kristalltechno had stopped distributing its products and using its branding. Despite repeated questions, both orally and in writing, the company also made no statement condemning either Russia’s military aggression or political repression in Russia.
Separately, a Kristalltechno employee offered a journalist from The Insider an Ophir Optronics VEGA 7Z01560 laser radiation analyzer for $5,000, with delivery in Moscow in one to two days. The journalist had inquired about the equipment’s availability from the publication’s editorial email address. The offer suggests that the device was in stock in Moscow.
A Kristalltechno LLC employee offered an Insider journalist a laser radiation analyzer for $5,000 in Moscow
The market price of the same equipment in the West is around $1,300, illustrating the additional costs that sanctions and export controls impose on Russia’s high-tech industries.
What Russia’s modern private laser industry looks like
Russia has every reason to develop its own advanced laser technologies rather than simply buying finished equipment. Two leading examples of Russian companies in this field are Special Systems Photonics LLC and Leningrad Laser Systems JSC (LLS), both based in St. Petersburg.
Special Systems Photonics is a regular supplier to Russian state organizations. In recent years, it has supplied the Lebedev Physical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences with components for an interferometric system to monitor laser-processing speed. Other supplies have included lasers, optical materials, light sources, spectrofluorometers, spectrometers, detectors, optical probe stations, microchip inspection systems, fiber-processing laser systems, alignment systems, optomechanical systems, and systems for precisely positioning nanoscale objects in quantum optics laboratories.
Special Systems.Photonics has also supplied equipment to Bureau 1440, which is developing Russia’s Rassvet satellite communications system, an alternative to OneWeb. According to commercial court records, the company works extensively with Russia’s military-industrial complex. Its counterparties include NPO GIPO JSC (under sanctions), the Kvant joint venture (under sanctions), the Defense Ministry’s 18th Central Research Institute, and the Elektropribor Central Research Institute Concern JSC (under sanctions).
In 2023–2025, Special Systems Photonics imported large quantities of optical equipment, including lasers, optical tables, lenses, optical fiber, fiber-splicing tools, fiber cleavers, electro-optic and acousto-optic laser modulators and their drivers, mirrors, prisms, acousto-optic filters, signal generators, and spectrum analyzers.
Among other items, the company imported German-made Carl Zeiss objective lenses, Rigol optical spectrum analyzers, and Thorlabs diffraction gratings. The company’s website showcases an impressive range of high-quality equipment. Alongside instruments for scientists and developers, customers can also purchase lidars for drone guidance systems.
The research published by Special Systems Photonics employees focuses on highly specialized subjects, including laser-induced emission spectroscopy, quantum precision measurement instruments, magneto-optical traps, quantum gravimeters, optical vector analyzers for measuring the characteristics of integrated optical circuits, and single-frequency fiber lasers for quantum applications. Single-frequency lasers play a key role in working with ultracold atoms, a technology that could provide one of the foundations for a quantum computer. The researchers have also worked on precision quantum measurements. Beyond its academic interest in quantum computing and quantum metrology, Special Systems Photonics explicitly advertises the supply of cold-atom quantum computers made by the Chinese company CAS COLD ATOM, including the 100-qubit HANYUAN-1 model and custom-built systems.
All of the above suggests that Special Systems Photonics LLC is deeply embedded in Russia’s high-tech quantum optics sector, acting as a systems integrator, developer, and center of expertise rather than merely a reseller of equipment to state organizations. The company’s purchasing patterns, combined with its interest in related technologies, suggest that its imports could potentially be used to develop a more powerful photonic quantum computer than any currently operating in Russia.
Leningrad Laser Systems JSC has imported semiconductor blanks, machinery for processing metals and other materials, fiber-optic amplifiers, optical splitters, multiplexers, plugs and sockets, diffraction gratings, and laser vibrometers. Most of the equipment came from Chinese manufacturers, though some devices and components were made in the West.
Among the Western equipment imported by Leningrad Laser Systems, high-quality German products stand out: spectroscopy cameras from Basler AG, adapters from SmarAct GmbH, optical components and optical connector cleaners from Schäfter+Kirchhoff GmbH, laser scanner heads from Scanlab GmbH, and precision dimensional measurement instruments from SIOS Messtechnik GmbH.
German equipment remains indispensable for a wide range of engineering applications, and Russian companies continue to procure it by every available means for military production. Leningrad Laser Systems has also purchased laser power and energy meters from Israel’s Ophir Optronics, discussed in the previous section. This makes it the second-largest seller of Ophir products on the Russian market, after the Moscow-based former distributor that continues to operate under the Israeli company’s branding.
Judging by its employees’ research publications, some of which are partly promotional, Leningrad Laser Systems is interested in radio-over-fiber technology for shipboard communications, high-power fiber laser cutting machines, ultraviolet laser cutting, optical fibers for specialized applications (including specially doped fibers), beam-profile shaping for specific tasks such as drilling holes, metrology, and wind lidars. LLS employees also devote considerable effort to promoting laser multiplexing equipment.
Research publications by Leningrad Laser Systems suggest that the company does more than handle customs paperwork: it develops, tests, and markets the relevant technologies in Russia. LLS also actively fulfills government contracts, supplying equipment such as fiber-drawing towers for manufacturing optical fiber used in fiber-optic cables, plasma research rigs, laser beam homogenizers, multispectral systems, photon counters, optical reflectometers, and optoacoustic modulators. Its customers have primarily been civilian universities and research institutions, including Moscow State University, St. Petersburg State University, KAI, and institutes of the Russian Academy of Sciences, as well as specialized institutes such as VNIIFTRI, VNIOFI, and Voenmekh.
According to court records, LLS has done business with the Ramenskoye Instrument-Making Plant JSC (under sanctions), the Ural Electromechanical Plant, and the Astron Optical-Mechanical Design Bureau, which manufactures drones and thermal imaging systems. Astron also produces laser ranging systems, while NPO GIPO JSC makes military sights, Elektropribor produces laser gyroscopes, and the Ramenskoye Instrument-Making Plant has developed a direct laser command-guidance system for guided missiles and electro-optical sighting systems for helicopters.
These companies are therefore more than intermediaries reselling Chinese or Western equipment. They are highly qualified specialists in the field, capable of testing equipment themselves and fulfilling complex contracts for both civilian research institutions and defense-industry enterprises. The Insider sent requests for comment to Special Systems Photonics and Leningrad Laser Systems but received no response.
More widespread military applications of lasers
Even at a less advanced technological level, Russia’s military-industrial complex is trying, with varying degrees of success, to keep pace in the field of laser technology. The following is a far from exhaustive list of technologies developed or deployed by Russia’s defense industry during the full-scale war. These systems are commercially available in the West and far less sophisticated than the cutting-edge research and development discussed above.
- At the Army-2022 exhibition, the Spectrum-AT Scientific and Production Center presented its Plastun system for multichannel observation of targets in optically opaque environments, equipped with a laser rangefinder and laser illuminator.
- Laser Components manufactures laser gyroscopes for military applications.
- Aviation and Marine Electronics Research and Production Company showcases laser rangefinders and target designators as part of multichannel surveillance systems for drones.
- In its report from the Army-2022 forum, the Regional Center for Laser Technologies (RCLT) showcased (at 3:46) a phased-array base fabricated by laser welding.
- The Inject Research and Production Enterprise developed an industrial laser soldering system.
- Laser cutting is used (at 2:29) at Uralvagonzavod.
- Lasergrad equipment is used to clean the K-3 submarine using lasers.
All this points to active efforts to develop these technologies and reduce Russia’s dependence on imported equipment and systems.
As The Insider has found, advanced Western laser technologies — in the form of equipment, components, and materials — continue to reach Russia. This is one of the few remaining fields in which Chinese manufacturers cannot always fully replace Western suppliers. At the top of the technological hierarchy are quantum computers (which, despite all the promises, may not become cryptographically relevant in the foreseeable future), quantum metrology, and quantum communications. Below these are more widely used, practical applications already in widespread use.
With military needs an overriding state priority and funding for civilian scientific research being cut, there is little doubt that the technologies and equipment entering Russia are intended not to advance fundamental science but to strengthen the capabilities of the military and security services.

Flora U-19s draw 2-2 with 9-man Chelsea in UEFA Youth League
Tallinn FC Flora's U-19 side drew 2:2 at home with English Premier League giants Chelsea's youth team Wednesday.
The game was the first leg of the UEFA Youth League second qualifying round, played at the A. Le Coq Arena in Tallinn.
After a sending-off, the visitors were down to 10 men early on in the second half, falling to nine players shortly before full-time after a second sending-off, but held on for the draw
Midfielder Sander Alamaa put Flora ahead in the fourth minute, but Chelsea striker Jashayde Greenwood equalized a quarter of an hour later and then Chizaram Ezenwata put the visitors in front shortly before half-time. Flora's equalizer came on 60 minutes, when Alamaa converted a penalty won by left-back Karel Isok.
"Before the game we said Chelsea are vulnerable on the counter-attack. For the first goal I got a good run at the center-back and took my chance. It was a good start to the game. For the second goal I'm not sure it was a penalty, but at least it was given our way. I saw the goalkeeper dive one way and just put the ball calmly in the other corner," Alamaa told ERR after the match.
Chelsea finished with nine men: center-back Dante Waite was sent off on 55 minutes and midfielder Isaac Silva collected a second yellow on 89.
"In some ways you could feel the difference in level with players from a Premier League club's academy. They were technically very high-quality players. In midfield their players played some unbelievable passes. But if you go into duels the way we did today, we can take down anyone," Alamaa added.
The second leg takes place in London next Wednesday, November 4.

Storms Austen and Boelo leave cliffs up to 1.2 metres high on the Flemish coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:47:00 UTC
17:47:00 KST

Following autumn storms Austen and Boelo, cliffs have formed along the coast. On the beaches of the resorts of Blankenberge and Middelkerke, these cliffs are up to 1.2 metres high. The Maritime and Coastal Services Agency (MDK) is pulling them down using machinery. In Knokke-Heist, its was local council workers that levelled the cliffs.
Storms Austen and Boelo leave cliffs up to 1.2 metres high on the Flemish coast
The first autumn storm, Austen, swept across Belgium on Friday 23 October. The Royal Meteorological Institute (RMI) issued a code orange warning for gusts of up to 100 kilometres per hour. A day later, storm Boelo also swept across Belgium. A code yellow warning for wind was issued for the coast.
The effects of the storms are particularly clear on the beaches of Blankenberge and Middelkerke. There, experts identified cliffs up to 1.2 metres high, stretching over hundreds of metres. These are steep, almost vertical walls of sand. They form when waves wash away sand at the high-water mark during a storm.
Higher than 1 metre
The cliffs can be dangerous. They are not always clearly visible, meaning walkers could easily experience a nasty fall. “Sometimes the beach recovers naturally, thanks to the tides. If the cliffs are higher than 1 metre, we have to level them out with a machine,” explains Dries Derudder of the Maritime Services and Coast Agency(MDK). “That is now only the case in Blankenberge and Middelkerke.”
‘The cliffs will be levelled on Thursday or Friday at the latest, so that everything is safe in the run-up to the autumn half-term.’
Cliffs had also formed on the beach in Knokke-Heist. The largest were up to 2 metres high. There local council workers demolished the cliffs. “We’ve created a sort of passageway from the soft sand to the wet sand,” explains Bert De Brabandere, the alderman responsible for beaches. “People can walk there safely. In time, the water will wash away the cliffs.”

- The accident has renewed concern about rail safety after a signal failure, and train drivers kept their strike for more investment. Union SEMAF said it would not speculate until the cause is clear.
AI generated
URDA, Spain – Rescuers picked through mangled carriages on Oct 29 in a grim search for victims of Spain’s second fatal high-speed train crash in 2026, as the death toll rose to 69 and hopes of finding further survivors faded.
After cranes worked through the night to lift parts of the wreckage of the Oct 28 crash, emergency workers were seen carrying what appeared to be a body wrapped in a blanket from one of the trains in the central Spanish province of Toledo.
Regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said the death toll had risen to 69 people and that human remains had been found during overnight rescue efforts. Work now involved crane operations, particularly on a carriage that was still overturned.
“We do not believe there could be any more fatalities beneath that one, but I say this with caution,” he said.
Unions blame lack of funding
Meanwhile, train drivers in Spain went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety after what is Europe’s deadliest train accident since a 2013 derailment in Spain’s Santiago de Compostela.
“We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again... It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had,” said Diego Martin of the train drivers’ union SEMAF.
“We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again. Everyone should be able to travel without the risk of suffering this kind of accident,” he added at Madrid’s Atocha railway station.
The crash, which followed another fatal accident in January involving the same rail companies on the same line, has also upended campaigning for a Nov 29 snap election, with the leaders of Spain’s two main parties suspending campaign events.
Spain’s government has declared three days of national mourning for those killed in the crash, which Transport Minister Oscar Puente said happened after several trains stopped due to a signal failure.
A state-run Renfe train was then authorised to proceed at normal speed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, Puente said on Oct 28.
Unions have already blamed a lack of funding and will to improve safety, saying that talks after the accident in January were abandoned in April.
Meanwhile, the government has said that the decision to authorise the Renfe train to continue its journey was “inexplicable”.
Pope sends condolences
Pope Leo sent his condolences to the families of those killed, wished a speedy recovery to the injured and conveyed his support and comfort to all affected, the Vatican said, adding he had also encouraged rescue workers to continue their efforts.
Of those injured, the authorities said 57 remained in hospital.
The crash prompted a major operation, which Spain’s interior ministry said involved the deployment of more than 800 military and police personnel, over 200 vehicles, three helicopters, a mobile command post, drones, mounted units and search dogs.
As investigations began, a judge in Toledo barred anyone not involved in emergency, security, healthcare or judicial work from the crash site with a 2km exclusion zone in both directions along the Madrid-Seville high-speed rail line.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who travelled to Toledo to take part in a meeting to monitor and coordinate the emergency response, said the authorities were working “day and night” to support the victims and their families and to “get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy”.
Meanwhile, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the centre-right People’s Party, which is currently leading in polls, was due to visit the town of Urda, where local people rushed to help with rescue efforts in the aftermath of the crash.
Foreign nationals among casualties
Spain’s Foreign Ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, information available so far showed, of whom one was killed and at least seven injured.
The Oct 28 accident has added urgency to a debate about safety on Spain’s railways, Europe’s longest network and until recently a source of pride in the country.
Train drivers would go ahead with their strike to press for structural changes in railway safety, SEMAF said, adding that it was studying further action.

Australia considering Iron Dome's Tamir interceptor for missile defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:44:54 UTC
17:44:54 KST

Australia is considering looking at Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense system as it works to build its first land-based ballistic missile shield.
According to local media, Australia’s Defense Ministry has approached Washington regarding cost and delivery timelines for the US Marine Corps’ Medium Range Intercept Capability, which uses the SkyHunter, a US-built version of the Iron Dome’s Tamir interceptors.
It is also looking at the Patriot and Aegis missile defense systems. Bids from Norway’s Kongsberg and South Korea’s Hanwha are also expected.
Canberra is looking for a medium-range missile defense system as Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles has called the current geopolitical situation “The most complex and threatening strategic circumstances” since World War II.
The Australian reported that a tender issued by the country’s Defense Ministry in mid-October wants a “proven” off-the-shelf system selected by the end of next year, followed by a live-firing during Exercise Talisman Sabre by 2029. According to the report, the planned system will not be fully operational until the middle of the 2030s.
Highly critical of Israel
Australia has been heavily critical of Israel’s war in Gaza. Canberra does not supply weapons to Israel, and its purchase of Israeli defence products continues to come under political scrutiny.
But while Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has insisted that the country does “not sell arms to Israel,” Defense Industry Minister Pat Conroy has defended the country’s use of Israeli military systems.
“We make no apology for getting the best possible equipment for the Australian Defence Force,” he said at the Indo-Pacific Maritime Exposition last year.
Environment Minister Murray Watt has also supported the decision to look at Israeli technology, telling the committee on Thursday that "the government will always seek to deliver the most suitable military technology.”
Integral part of Israel’s missile defense array
Initially designed to shoot down short-range rockets, the Iron Dome has become an integral component of Israel's multi-layered defense array over the last 15 years.
The system’s modular architecture enables seamless integration with additional defense layers, and it can operate independently or as part of Israel’s broader air defense network that includes the Arrow (Arrow 2 and Arrow 3) system, which intercepts ballistic missiles outside of the Earth’s atmosphere, and the David’s Sling missile defense system, which is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles, medium- to long-range rockets, and cruise missiles fired at ranges between 40 and 300 kilometers.
Iron Dome took part in a long series of conflicts and operations, from Operation Protective Edge, Operation Guardian of the Walls, Operation Breaking Dawn, Operation Shield and Arrow, Operation Swords of Iron, and Operations Rising and Roaring Lion, where it served alongside the Arrow and David’s Sling as a central pillar in the protection of Israel’s home front.
Each round of fighting was followed by a new wave of software updates, radar refinements, and interceptor improvements.
The system’s radar has been upgraded to track more targets simultaneously, its algorithms have become faster and more selective, and its interceptors were refined to handle longer ranges and more demanding engagement profiles.
Yet, despite its successes, the Iron Dome is not infallible.
Israeli officials have consistently noted that no air‑defense system can guarantee complete protection. Some rockets inevitably penetrate the system’s defenses, underscoring the importance of measures such as early warning sirens and reinforced shelters.
Nevertheless, the system’s high interception rate has significantly reduced casualties and property damage during periods of conflict, altering both military calculations and civilian life in Israel.

AI could accelerate quantum computing breakthrough, Bank of America strategist says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:44:32 UTC
17:44:32 KST

The combination of artificial intelligence and quantum computing could accelerate advances in both technologies, potentially transforming industries ranging from healthcare to finance, according to senior Bank of America global strategist Haim Israel.
Israel, who heads the bank’s global thematic research team and is the most senior Israeli there, said advances in AI are helping researchers overcome longstanding technical challenges in quantum computing, while quantum technology could eventually address some of the processing limitations holding back AI development.
“We spent the last couple of years talking about AI, and while quantum was always there, it was in the background,” Israel told The Jerusalem Post. “But in the last two to three years, AI has allowed us to have a breakthrough.”
The bank estimates that the quantum computing industry, which has already surpassed $1 billion in annual revenue, could grow to approximately $15 billion by the end of the decade and $80 billion by 2035.
At the same time, the timeline for so-called Q-Day, the point at which quantum computers should become capable of breaking widely used encryption methods, is moving closer. According to Israel, Bank of America has brought its estimate forward to 2030.
Quantum computers operate differently from conventional computers, which process information using bits represented as either zero or one. Quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits. They exploit quantum-mechanical properties such as superposition to perform certain calculations in ways that are impractical for conventional systems.
The technology has long faced a central obstacle: qubits are highly sensitive to their surroundings, making them difficult to control and prone to errors. And unreliable results have limited the ability to scale quantum systems and use them for practical applications.
Israel said AI was helping researchers improve control over quantum systems and reduce error rates, marking a significant step toward more reliable machines.
“2022 was the inflection point with qubits going up and errors going down,” he said.
The relationship between the two technologies could become increasingly important as AI models grow in size and complexity. Training and operating advanced AI systems requires substantial computing resources, while quantum computers could eventually accelerate particular calculations that are difficult or expensive for conventional machines.
“AI helped build quantum, and quantum is bringing AI to the next level,” Israel said.
Israel said the industry was approaching an early development stage comparable to the period before the widespread adoption of ChatGPT brought generative AI to mainstream attention.
“We are before the ChatGPT moment of quantum,” he said.
Although quantum computing is at an early stage, Israel said the sector already has an established ecosystem of hardware and software developers, alongside start-ups working on encryption and related technologies. He said the industry was better positioned than AI had been at a comparable stage, although its commercial structure would be different.
But rather than becoming a widely distributed technology used by billions of people like AI, quantum computing is likely to remain concentrated in a relatively small number of highly specialized systems, he said.
Its potential applications span healthcare, financial services, chemicals, energy, industrial production, and logistics, where complex calculations could help companies improve efficiency, optimize processes, and accelerate research.
No regulation or intervention
Israel said the pace of development was raising questions about whether governments, regulators, and institutions were keeping up with the technology.
“There is not a lot of regulation, or government intervention,” he said, adding that responsibility for how these technologies are used ultimately rests with the people and institutions developing them.
He compared the issue to nuclear energy, which can be used to generate electricity but also produce weapons.
He said companies were already developing internal safeguards and best practices, while governments faced the challenge of responding to technologies advancing faster than existing regulatory frameworks.
For now, significant technical and commercial hurdles remain before quantum computing can deliver on its broadest promises. But as AI helps researchers improve quantum hardware and software, the two technologies are increasingly being developed in tandem, with potential consequences for scientific research, industrial productivity, and global cybersecurity.
“The technology is parve. It's a question of what we do with it,” Israel said. “If we use it in the right way, everything will change for the better. It’s up to us.”

Three Swiss brands among world’s 100 most valuable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:33:18 UTC
17:33:18 KST

Three Swiss brands among world’s 100 most valuable
Three Swiss brands have made it into the world’s top 100 most valuable brands. Zurich Insurance, Nescafé and Nestlé feature in this year’s ranking by the brand consultancy Interbrand.
Zurich Insurance comes out on top, ranking 58th with an estimated brand value of $15 billion (CHF12.42 billion), according to the “Best Global Brands” report published on Thursday. This also makes Zurich the highest-ranked of the four new entrants in this year’s ranking.
The other two Swiss brands are part of the Nestlé Group. Nescafé ranks 70th with a brand value of $12.1 billion. Compared with the previous year, the value of the coffee brand has fallen by 6%. The Nestlé corporate brand ranks 84th with a value of $9.7 billion. Its value remained unchanged year-on-year.
Luxury watchmakers are missing
It is striking that not a single Swiss luxury watchmaker features in the top 100. Well-known brands such as Rolex, Omega, Tag Heuer, Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet have not made it into the ranking. This is despite the fact that several international luxury brands, such as Hermès, Louis Vuitton, Chanel and Cartier, are represented.
The report does not explain why these Swiss export products – arguably the best known – are missing from the ranking. However, one of the requirements for inclusion is the availability of sufficient publicly accessible financial data. This could pose a particular hurdle for privately owned watch manufacturers.
That said, another Swiss brand could be added in future. The sports footwear manufacturer On is listed by Interbrand among the ten so-called “Brands to Watch”. This watch list features brands that the consultants believe have the potential to rise into the top 100 in future.
Apple remains the most valuable brand
According to Interbrand, the combined value of the top 100 brands has risen by 8.1% to a record total of around $3.9 trillion. The value of 68 brands increased compared with the previous year.
Apple remains at the top with a brand value of around $515 billion. Microsoft follows in second place with just under $444 billion, followed by Google with just over $389 billion.
The remaining places among the ten most valuable brands are occupied by Amazon, Samsung, Nvidia, Instagram, Coca-Cola, Toyota and YouTube.

According to the publication, the enterprise is part of the Roskhim holding company, which holds a controlling stake (57.43%). At the same time, the complex is included in the Russian Ministry of Industry and Trade’s closed registry of defense enterprises.

This is a critically important compound for the production of synthetic ballistic fibers, high-strength polymers, and aramid materials, according to the report.
It is used to manufacture body armor, helmets, and armor components for military equipment and aircraft.
Prior to this, drones had already attacked the BSC on August 27. Smoke was also seen rising above the facility at that time. Authorities did not comment on the attack.

Search teams have found an unidentified man’s body off Silivri, Istanbul, 56 days after the freighter Tuğberk İmamoğlu sank with 10 crew in a Sea of Marmara collision.
Forensic Medicine Institute tests will establish his identity, cause of death and any crew link, prosecutors said. Captain Yaşar Kayhan’s body was found 5 kilometers from the collision site on Sept. 14 and identified on Sept. 15. Nine others remain missing.

ALSU’s captain Ahmet Erarslan and third officer Murat Evciman were remanded on Sept. 3. A preliminary report cited failures of supervision and collision avoidance, respectively. Four other suspects face judicial supervision.

European Union backtracks on Canada becoming ‘associate member’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:31:09 UTC
17:31:09 KST

European Union backtracks on Canada becoming ‘associate member’
German Chancellor Merz and other EU leaders reportedly pushed for the term to be removed from a joint draft Canada-EU statement.
The European Union has dropped the idea that Canada should become an “associate member” of the bloc, according to media reports.
In a joint draft Canada-EU statement, the terms “associate member” and “associated membership” have been removed, the German news agency dpa and the Reuters news agency reported on Thursday, adding that officials planned to make the statement public on Friday.
The reports come as the EU-Canada summit in Montreal, hosted by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, is expected to start later on Thursday.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen raised the prospect of Canada becoming the 27-nation EU’s first “associate member”, a striking overture as both seek to pivot away from the United States under President Donald Trump.
However, Reuters and dpa report that von der Leyen’s suggestion of associate membership has been a divisive issue in negotiations among EU countries over the summit declaration, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and several other leaders of fellow member nations pushing for the terms to be removed from the draft, citing diplomats.
The statement now calls for an “ever closer association” between Canada and the EU, and includes a joint initiative to improve international connectivity between Europe, Canada and Asia through “new subsea cable infrastructure”.
It also proposes conducting a joint feasibility study on Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and enabling young Canadians and Europeans to work across the Atlantic.
Deeper ties to Europe are an important part of Carney’s strategy to reduce Canada’s economic and security reliance on the US since Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods. Still, Canada’s efforts to draw closer to the EU risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the US continue.
Trump previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable” and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act”, the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.
Carney has aimed to deepen ties with the EU, Canada’s second-largest trading partner, since trade relations with the US, Ottawa’s largest economic partner, have been hampered under Trump.
The Canadian leader told reporters on Tuesday that the summit would be the launch of formal negotiations between the EU and Canada that would take another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China strongly condemns and firmly opposes the United States' decision to add three Chinese entities to the so-called "Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List," a spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce said Thursday.
There is no forced labor in China, and people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang enjoy freedom and equality in employment, with their labor rights and interests effectively protected by law, the spokesperson said in response to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's announcement that it had added three Chinese entities to the list.
The U.S. measures have no factual basis, the spokesperson said, accusing the U.S. side of persistently manipulating human rights issues to pursue unilateral protectionism and bullying under the guise of human rights protection.
The spokesperson noted that the United States had recently added a large number of Chinese entities to the same list. China had lodged solemn representations with the U.S. side and taken resolute countermeasures.
Disregarding China's firm opposition, the United States has continued to impose new sanctions, this time targeting Chinese biomedical technology companies, the spokesperson said.
Such actions run counter to the consensus reached by the two heads of state, seriously undermine the stability of China-U.S. economic and trade relations, and are contrary to humanitarian principles, the spokesperson added.
The spokesperson urged the United States to immediately stop its political manipulation and smear campaigns, and cease its unjustified suppression of Chinese companies, adding that China will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its own interests. ■

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Overnight, air defense forces shot down 1,214 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
The attempt by the Ukrainian armed forces to attack Moscow with drones, carried out on Wednesday evening and overnight, was one of the largest of the year so far, according to TASS estimates based on figures published by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin on his Max channel.
Debris from the UAVs fell on the grounds of a factory in Sterlitamak, Bashkortostan. Minor damage was reported, and the plant is operating normally.
TASS has compiled the key details regarding the aftermath.
Scale
- Alert air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions last night, according to the Defense Ministry.
- The ministry reported that enemy UAVs were shot down over the Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Kaluga, Tula, Smolensk, Lipetsk, Voronezh, Tver, Oryol, Ryazan, Vladimir, Samara, Saratov, Penza, and Rostov Regions, the Moscow Region, the Republic of Bashkortostan, and the Republic of Udmurtia.
- An attempted drone attack on Moscow by the Ukrainian armed forces, carried out on Wednesday evening and overnight, was one of the largest of the year so far, according to TASS estimates based on data published by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin on his Max channel.
- According to the mayor, between 8:30 p.m. Moscow time (5:30 p.m. GMT) on October 28 and 7:00 a.m. Moscow time (4:00 a.m. GMT) on October 29, a total of 613 enemy UAVs were heading toward the Moscow Region.
- Most were neutralized by the Defense Ministry’s air defense forces at a distance, while 231 drones were destroyed on approach to Moscow, he specified.
- Air defense forces destroyed 170 Ukrainian drones over the Kaluga Region, Governor Vladislav Shapsha reported on Max.
- Air defenses destroyed 42 Ukrainian drones over the Tula Region overnight, Governor Dmitry Milyayev wrote on his Max channel.

- Air defense forces destroyed four drones over the Ulyanovsk Region, Governor Alexey Russkikh wrote on his Max channel.
Consequences
- Debris from the UAVs fell on the grounds of a facility in Sterlitamak, Bashkortostan, according to a report by Mayor Emil Shaimardanov on Telegram.
- Minor damage was reported.
- The plant is operating normally.
Airport operations
- Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) reported that temporary restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures - necessary to ensure flight safety - had been imposed at Moscow’s Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports.
- These restrictions have now been lifted.
- Two planes flying from Istanbul to Moscow turned back in mid-flight and returned due to safety restrictions at Vnukovo Airport in Moscow, a source in air traffic control services told TASS.
- In addition, restrictions were imposed at airports in Bugulma, Izhevsk, Kazan, Kaluga, Kirov, Nizhnekamsk, Orenburg, Penza, Perm, Samara, Saransk, Saratov, Ulyanovsk, Ufa, Cheboksary, Chelyabinsk, Cherepovets, and Yaroslavl.

17:20:42 KST

A group of former U.S. officials who resigned over the Biden administration's support for Israel's war on Gaza urged Democratic presidential hopefuls Wednesday to condemn Washington's role in the conflict and exclude officials responsible for the policy from future administrations.
Twelve former officials who stepped down between late 2023 and mid-2024 over former President Joe Biden's handling of the Gaza war issued a joint statement calling on candidates seeking the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028 to distance themselves from his administration's policies.
"We call on candidates for the 2028 Presidential Nomination to commit to not hire any administration official directly responsible for enabling Israel's military actions in Gaza," the group said.
The former officials also demanded that prospective candidates acknowledge what they described as Washington's complicity in Israel's "genocide" in Gaza.
A video accompanying the statement featured images of senior Biden administration figures, including former Secretary of State Antony Blinken and former national security adviser Jake Sullivan, highlighting officials associated with U.S. policy toward Israel during the conflict.
The appeal comes as divisions over U.S. support for Israel continue to shape debate within the Democratic Party ahead of the 2028 presidential race.
Biden's administration faced sustained criticism from progressive lawmakers, activists and human rights advocates over its continued military assistance and diplomatic backing for Israel despite mounting Palestinian civilian casualties and widespread destruction in Gaza.
Prominent progressive Democrats, including U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, have opposed Washington's support for Israeli military operations in Gaza and Lebanon, as well as the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Their criticism has also focused on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close political ties with Republicans, amid growing divisions within the Democratic Party over relations with Israel.
Several international human rights organizations, legal experts and United Nations investigations have concluded that Israel's military campaign in Gaza constitutes genocide.
Blinken and Sullivan previously voiced concerns over civilian deaths in Gaza, although the Biden administration continued providing military and diplomatic support to Israel throughout the conflict.
The former officials' intervention adds to pressure on prospective Democratic presidential candidates to clarify their positions on U.S. military assistance to Israel and the role of senior Biden-era policymakers in any future administration.
