‘I held this woman in my arms. She died’: Spain mourns train crash victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:20:34 UTC
17:20:34 KST

‘I held this woman in my arms. She died’: Spain mourns train crash victims
Second tragedy on line in nine months raises questions about the levels of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.
Madrid, Spain – Joaquim Torres, who was travelling on a train which crashed into another on Wednesday, rushed to help his fellow passengers who had been injured.
Fighting back tears, he told Al Jazeera: “I held this woman in my arms and tried to comfort her, but she stopped breathing. She died, she died.”
One of about 500 passengers caught in the deadly crash, Torres had been travelling on a high-speed train from the capital, Madrid, to Seville in the south of the country. All seemed normal, until the huge crash just before 9am.
At least 68 people were killed and 77 others were injured.
Spain’s national train operator Renfe has launched an investigation into the disaster, which happened in a rural area between Urda and Los Yebenes, two small towns south of Toledo in central Spain.
But the disaster has renewed a national debate over whether Spain’s high-speed train network is safe, nine months after another train crash on the same line in which 46 people died and scores were injured at Adamuz, near Cordoba in southern Spain.
‘Apocalyptic’
Sebastian Herrero, a 46-year-old doctor who was on the train, described the scene after Wednesday’s collision.
“There were three train carriages from which they kept pulling people out and covering them with sheets. Bodies. It’s apocalyptic. It’s hard to imagine that anyone could still be alive in those three carriages. It’s a twisted mass of metal. It’s as if a bomb had gone off,” he told Al Jazeera.
Rescuers searched for survivors through the mangled wreckage of three carriages at the front of the train, which had smashed into a stationary locomotive.
Desperate relatives were waiting at Seville train station holding pictures of loved ones who had failed to arrive in the southern city, as Spanish TV presenters, dressed in black, reported on the tragedy.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has declared three days of national mourning, said: “All of Spain is mourning,” before adding that it is “not acceptable for a country like Spain” to have two major train disasters in one year. A judicial investigation is expected to begin shortly.
Train followed ‘inexplicable’ order
Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the deadly crash happened after a Renfe train was authorised to continue on its journey – despite an active red signal because of a stationary train on the line ahead, operated by the Italian consortium Iryo.
Puente said the red signal had been issued due to a computer communications failure which automatically stopped traffic, and an “inexplicable” order from the central command centre was given for the Renfe train to move on. He said train engineers were not to blame.
The trade union Solidarity, which is linked to Spain’s far-right Vox party, held a demonstration in Madrid on Wednesday night to demand Puente’s resignation, and riot police were dispatched.
In the wake of the crash, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the opposition conservative People’s Party, which is favourite to win the upcoming general election, told reporters: “Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure, the condition of the tracks and safety systems, what warnings were received from Adamuz and measures were taken.
“The Spanish people have a right to a complete and independent review of the entire rail network.”
‘Seats were flying through the air’
Fernando Seco, another passenger in the Renfe train bound for Seville, said the train had just resumed its journey following a brief stop when it collided with the other train.
“We felt a brutal crash. People were thrown through the air, seats were flying through the air,” he told TVE state television.
After leaving the wrecked train, he said he saw a “carriage split in half, with dead people trapped inside”.
Once news of the crash got out, volunteers rushed to the scene to offer whatever help they could give.
Jose Maria Rabadan, a resident of Urda, the closest town, said he and other volunteers brought food, water and blankets and provided transport for those affected by the crash.
“Whatever they ask of us, we will bring,” he told Radio Castilla-La Mancha.
The rail accident is likely to come as a major blow to the ruling Socialist Party, just a month before the country goes to the polls in a general election on November 29.
The government’s management of the Adamuz rail crash in January was heavily criticised by opposition politicians and raised questions about the levels of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.
Rail unions had planned a strike for Thursday to protest about what they say is a poor safety record on the Spanish network.
The tragedy also comes amid a boom in the use of high-speed trains, which has not been accompanied by necessary investment in maintenance of the high-speed network, according to European Commission data.
The number of rail accidents, including collisions and derailments, rose from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024, and surged to 69 in 2025, according to the Spanish railway safety authority (AESF).
Some 40 million people used the high-speed rail trains in 2024, almost double the figure for 2019. However, in the first half of this year, about 25 million travelled on the high-speed network, a year-on-year fall of 14 percent.
With cheaper fares compared with many other developed countries, the high-speed rail network has been seen as an achievement for Spain in recent years, with its expertise exported to Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom.
Between 2018 and 2022, Spain spent an average of about $1.67bn each year on high-speed lines, more than other countries with similar networks. However, only 16 percent of that was spent on maintenance or repairs, with the rest going on infrastructure, according to EC figures.
A safety risk
By contrast, Italy, Germany and France spent on average between 33 and 39 percent of their budgets on maintenance, even though each country has much smaller networks than the 4,000km (2,485 miles) in Spain.
Experts say the success of the Spanish high-speed network is putting safety at risk.
“The problem is that the train network has become very popular as it is cheap and accessible but the authorities have not spent enough on its maintenance in recent years,” Salvador Garcia-Ayllon, a professor at the Universidad Politecnica in Cartagena, who specialises in civil engineering, told Al Jazeera.
Following the Adamuz disaster, a preliminary investigation found a rail fracture was the cause of the crash, but an ongoing investigation by police has not been concluded. A judicial investigation is now expected.

One in two Swiss don't save enough to cover prolonged income loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:20:32 UTC
17:20:32 KST

One in two Swiss don’t save enough to cover prolonged income loss
The Swiss save money, but for many, their financial reserves are not enough to cope with a prolonged loss of income. Almost one in two people would struggle to maintain their standard of living after just three months without an income.
This is the finding of a study by the Zurich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW).
According to the survey, 82% of respondents save at least occasionally. Despite this, 15% do not have sufficient liquid reserves to maintain their standard of living in the absence of income, and a further 30% could cover their expenses for a period of between one and three months.
Overall, almost 45% of those surveyed would therefore face financial difficulties after three months without an income. At the other end of the scale, 23% have sufficient liquid savings to maintain their standard of living for over a year.
+ Median annual salary in Switzerland rose to CHF87,000 in 2025
“Saving regularly does not necessarily mean that a household is sufficiently prepared for a loss of income: it is also crucial how much cash is already available and how long it would last in an emergency,” explains Selina Lehner, an expert at ZHAW, quoted in a press release.
The main source of financial concern is the rise in fixed costs, cited by 22% of respondents. This is followed by insufficient financial security in the run-up to retirement, highlighted by 12%, and the fear of being unable to fund future wishes and goals, cited by 11%.
The rise in recurring expenses is a particularly significant problem for households with limited savings: rent, health insurance premiums and other regular outgoings can gradually erode the financial buffer available to cope with unforeseen events.
“Rising fixed costs do not place a one-off burden on households, but month after month: when liquidity is limited, they reduce the financial buffer and make it harder to absorb unexpected expenses,” observes Holger Hohgardt, another specialist at ZHAW, who is also quoted.
Difficulties are also evident in managing day-to-day expenditure: over the last twelve months, almost one in four people – 24% of those surveyed – have had to borrow money. Taxes are another source of concern: 29% say they have had difficulty paying their tax bill on time in at least one of the last five years.
As regards financial goals, 29% of respondents consider maintaining their standard of living a priority. A further 24% aim above all to avoid financial worries in their daily lives. The study also highlights a significant difference between overall satisfaction and satisfaction with personal finances: on a scale of zero to ten, satisfaction with life averages 7.2 points (out of 10), while financial satisfaction stands at 5.6 points.
According to the ZHAW, the findings of the survey – which polled 963 people in June – suggest that the ability to save does not necessarily equate to solid financial security. The immediate availability of money, particularly in the event of job loss or other interruptions to income, remains a key factor in households’ financial stability, the researchers point out.

Spain’s high-speed rail network faces scrutiny after deadly collision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:20:12 UTC
17:20:12 KST

Aysu Bicer
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Spain’s high-speed rail network is under scrutiny following a deadly collision that killed at least 68 people and injured dozens Wednesday.
Leaked audio recordings obtained by broadcaster RTVE indicate that controllers at state rail manager Adif instructed the driver of the moving train to disconnect the malfunctioning LZB safety system and resume the journey at speeds of up to 200 km/h.
"Disconnect and reconnect the LZB and resume journey under the protection of the BSL at normal speed," controllers told the driver at 8.36 am local time.
Minutes later, the driver of the Iryo train reported being unable to proceed: "I've had a loss of transmission and I'm stopped at the Urda entrance signal."
While the government pointed to human error in allowing a train onto an occupied track, RTVE, citing sources, disputed the timeline, reporting that the Iryo train had not received clearance to move before the collision.
The collision between the moving train and the stationary train occurred in central Spain, around 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of Madrid, between Mora and Orgaz.
The train traveling from Madrid to Seville struck the stationary Iryo train, sending several carriages plunging down an embankment.
The Iryo train, carrying 147 passengers, had halted on the tracks due to a computer system failure.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente cited system failure and human error as possible factors in the crash.
Survivors reported harrowing scenes of being thrown through the air, trapped in wreckage and breaking windows to escape.
The tragedy highlights vulnerabilities on the 1992 Madrid-Seville route, which still relies on the older LZB system instead of modern European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) safety technology.
It is the second fatal crash on the line in nine months, following a January accident near Cordoba that killed 46 people.

Lithuanian Farmers and Greens tie budget support to family referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:16:00 UTC
17:16:00 KST

The Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union has warned that its support for next year’s government spending bill could be affected unless parliament takes up a stalled proposal for an advisory referendum on the constitutional definition of family before approving the budget.
Aurelijus Veryga, leader of the Farmers and Greens Union (LVŽS), said Wednesday that he had raised the issue during budget negotiations with coalition partners, demanding that the referendum proposal be put on the parliament’s agenda before the budget is adopted.
The initiative is an attempt to entrench a conservative definition of family and prevent same-sex couples from claiming equal treatment.
“One of the issues important to us is that, before the budget is adopted, the question of an advisory referendum on the family issue should be brought before parliament,” Veryga told reporters after a meeting of the coalition council.
“This is one of the key issues for us. It will also be a kind of signal about how we should act,” he added.
Veryga said the issue would show whether the Farmers and Greens were being treated as a genuine coalition partner.
“We are not asking our coalition partners to vote in favour of the referendum in any particular way. We know there are differences of opinion,” he said.
However, he argued that deliberately blocking the proposal amounted to a demonstration of political will. He called for an end to what he described as “artificial obstruction” by the parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs, saying coalition partners had promised to find a solution at their previous meeting.
Veryga warned that if the referendum proposal is not placed on the parliament’s agenda, it could have a significant impact on how his party’s lawmakers vote on the budget.
“I really cannot say how my colleagues will act then. Since this is a very important issue for us, it will be assessed in the broader context,” he said.
In late September, the parliament’s Committee on State Administration and Local Authorities backed holding an advisory referendum on the constitutional definition of family alongside next year’s municipal elections.
The draft resolution was approved at its initial presentation in parliament in early April.
Under the proposal, voters would be asked whether they support explicitly stating in the Constitution that legal family relationships arise only from the marriage of a man and a woman, motherhood and fatherhood. Voters would choose between “Yes” and “No”.
Article 38 of Lithuania’s Constitution currently states that family is the foundation of society and the state and that the state protects and cares for the family, motherhood, fatherhood and childhood. It also states that marriage is concluded by the free consent of a man and a woman.
In a ruling issued in 2011, Lithuania’s Constitutional Court states that non-married couples can also constitute a family.

UK social media ban likely to require photo ID checks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:14:53 UTC
17:14:53 KST

LONDON — Enforcement of the U.K.’s upcoming social media ban for under-16s will probably require older teens to show a form of photo ID, according to the U.K.’s online safety regulator Ofcom.
In a government-commissioned report, Ofcom said it had identified just four methods that are “highly effective” at determining whether a user is 16 or over — while noting that “the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated, and some children will succeed in bypassing age checks.”
The advice comes after the U.K. government vowed to take a tougher approach than Australia to enforcing its ban — due to come into force next year — by requiring platforms to use “highly effective age assurance” to identify underage users.
Advertisement
It will inform regulations to implement the ban which ministers have said they aim to introduce to parliament this year.
Three of the methods identified by Ofcom — photo ID matching, using a digital ID service, or banking-based checks — require a passport or driving license at some stage, while the fourth, facial age estimation, may in some cases need to be followed by a supplementary check using one of the other methods because of a high margin of error at younger ages.
“This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right,” Ofcom CEO Melanie Dawes said.
While the age checks would involve processing of personal data, “available methods can be delivered in a way that protects users’ privacy and complies with data protection law,” Ofcom said.
It also said social media platforms should take steps to mitigate circumvention, like enabling users to report suspected underage accounts, and using age inference technology to spot activity from users who may be underage.
The regulator said it will consult on further guidance for platforms once regulations to implement the social media ban are laid.

Reader Q&A: Our money and economics correspondents answer your Budget 2026 questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:00:27 UTC
17:00:27 KST

Hilary and Heather are live
Hilary and Heather are online now answering your 2026 budget questions
The 2026 budget has been revealed; how will it affect you personally, will it change the country and has chancellor John Healey done enough to prepare for the challenges ahead? Our money and economics editors Hilary Osborne and Heather Stewart are on line now answering your questions
Sign up or sign in to join the discussion. Post your questions in the comments below.
DrJWCC asks: For those of us who live out in the wilds, who are not on mains gas (as in, LPG tanks) will we benefit from standing charge removal? I’m assuming not.
 Hilary says: I’m afraid the standing charge removal will not help you, but some of the other measures will hopefully reduce your overall energy bills. The extension of the VAT cut on energy will be for everyone, so that’s about £50 off your annual costs. If you live in council tax bands A-D you will get the £100 payment in January. And there are some measures targeted at people who are not on mains gas. Tariffs on kerosene are being scrapped for two years, which should reduce costs for those who rely on heating oil, and the boiler upgrade scheme was left untouched. The scheme offers £9,000 to homeowners in England and Wales who want to install a heatpump.
Guardiangirl66 asks: Why are governments so stubbornly opposed to lifting the basic tax threshold? They adjust them to fit some people affected by fiscal drag but not others, which can’t be cheap to implement and it isn’t fair either.
Tax thresholds need to be universally applied in each band, and be simple and crystal clear. Some tapering is overdue to avoid cliff edges and high marginal tax rates but it must be for everyone.
 Heather says: If you mean the basic rate threshold, it did rise repeatedly from 2010-2020, starting under the Conservative/LibDem coalition, to 44% of average earnings - but yes it’s been frozen for quite a while since, so it kicks in at about 34% of average earnings now. I think the Labour objection to raising it further would be that it’s not a very progressive way of making a tax cut, because it’s set so high already (£12,570) that the lowest earners already don’t pay tax and so wouldn’t benefit from further rises. Completely agree re complicated tweaks to the system, though - the simpler and clearer it is, the better.
southlondon1 asks: Is there anything in this budget for young working people? I’m 27, renting a 1 bed with my partner in London, and barely earn enough money to save £50 a month, let alone save for a house. I feel like yet again the government are leaving out people like me who are nowhere near buying a house, have no children (and couldn’t afford it anyway) and our rent costs half our salary. £100 doesn’t really provide any breathing space.
 Hilary says: The main measure for young renters was the Your First Home scheme, which will mean you can think about buying a property when you have a deposit of 2.5%, but in London if you can only save £50 a month that is likely to feel a long way off. Unfortunately there was not much else that’s immediately going to help you.
The thresholds for student loan repayments and income tax remain the same, so if you get a pay rise you will see your take home pay go up by less than had these risen in line with inflation. The £100 energy payment comes alongside the removal of VAT on your electricity bills, and the planned removal of the standing charge on gas, so that’s a bit more money you will keep. However, with energy prices looking set to rise in January it’s likely you will still see your bills rise.
CordTrousers asks: Diesel is still at £1.99 a litre at our local station. That means inflation is going to remain elevated, as it feeds through to more everyday commodities there is going to be building pressure for wage increases ... Which will fuel inflation some more. After the midterms, it looks likely Trump will renew his attacks on Iran. A light touch budget like this then, feels a temporary measure. Really there’s nothing the UK can do but tighten its belt when we have such a constraint on fuel supply, is there?
 Heather says: You’re absolutely right that as an energy-importing country, it’s just a fact that a crisis like the one we’re going through makes us poorer. So I think John Healey’s message that the government can’t completely insulate consumers, but want to do a bit to help, is probably the right one. But whether he’s done enough remains to be seen - inflation is set to rise further, as you say, and the Bank of England is likely to raise interest rates next week, so that £100 cost of living payment might not look so generous by the New Year. Obviously the government is hoping the Iran conflict will subside, which might allow oil prices to fall, and the economy to bounce back (GDP growth was actually pretty strong in the first half of this year). Time will tell.
Yesterday Chancellor John Healey gave his maiden budget under Andy Burnham’s leadership, announcing measures to cut energy bills funded by a windfall tax on banks. He characterised his plan as “a budget built on fiscal discipline” fit to face “global economic storms” that are driving up up energy prices.
Does Healey’s budget represent a break with the past, or is the lower-than-expected tax on banks just another example of tinkering around the edges by another Chancellor fenced in by self-imposed fiscal rules?
Hilary Osborne, the Guardian’s money and consumer editor will be joining economics editor Heather Stewart from 3pm (GMT) today to answer your questions on the outlook for our economy.

Poland hands Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:55:07 UTC
16:55:07 KST

- Poland will soon transfer two MiG-29 fighters to Ukraine in a new aid package worth about €50 million, Rzeczpospolita reported.
- One jet has reached the end of its service life and may be used for spare parts, while the other is still flying.
Poland will soon hand Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets as part of a new military aid package worth about €50 million (about $56 million), Polish daily Rzeczpospolita reported on Oct. 29, in a story quickly picked up by Ukrainian defense outlet Milarnyi.
Reserve Lt. Gen. Dariusz Łukowski, director of the Polish Defense Ministry’s Strategy and Defense Planning Department, confirmed the transfer to the newspaper and said the decision had been made, without giving a date beyond “in the near future.” Only one of the two jets is still flying. The other has reached the end of its service life, and Rzeczpospolita reported that Ukraine may use it as a source of spare parts.
The rest of the package is mostly munitions. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland will also send 155 mm and 152 mm artillery shells, 20 mm rounds for the six-barrel cannon fitted to F-16 fighters, which Ukrainian pilots use to shoot down Russian drones, and missiles for the Piorun shoulder-fired air defense system built by Polish manufacturer Mesko. Ukrainian defense officials had said in September that the Polish donation would be worth €50 million and would include air defense equipment. Poland’s Defense Ministry declined to detail the contents, saying only that the package draws on equipment being retired by the Polish armed forces or no longer needed.
The two aircraft are a small addition to a fleet Poland has been feeding since the early part of the war. Poland began openly handing over MiG-29s in March 2023, and by that May then-Defense Minister Mariusz Błaszczak said Ukraine had received 10 of them, Militarnyi reported. In total, Poland has given Ukraine 14 MiG-29s, Militarnyi said. Rzeczpospolita reported the same figure, adding that the jets were sent in 2022 and 2023 in varying technical condition and with little publicity.
A further transfer has been discussed for more than two years. In July 2024, Poland’s security agreement with Ukraine included a pledge to consider sending at least one more MiG-29 squadron, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Warsaw could not simply give up jets still flying air policing missions unless allies supplied replacements. At the time, the Polish Air Force still had 14 MiG-29s: 11 single-seat MiG-29As and three two-seat MiG-29UB trainers.
In late 2025, the two governments began talks on the last Polish MiG-29s. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the handover would benefit Poland because Warsaw would receive Ukrainian drone and missile technology in return. That exchange has not happened. As of mid-June 2026, Poland’s deputy defense minister said no aircraft from that batch had been delivered, and Rzeczpospolita reported the technology transfer stalled at the political level after Ukraine’s president named a military unit after heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a wartime nationalist force whose legacy is deeply contested in Poland.
Poland can spare the jets because their missions are moving to newer aircraft. The MiG-29 has kept a shrinking quick reaction alert role over the Baltic, and Rzeczpospolita reported that its tasks are now handled by Polish F-16s and the first 12 South Korean-built FA-50 light fighters, which reached full operational readiness in 2026.
For Ukraine, every additional airframe matters. The Ukrainian Air Force still relies heavily on the Soviet-designed MiG-29, which it has kept flying through deliveries from Poland, Slovakia and Bulgaria and through cannibalizing retired jets for parts, while losing aircraft to Russian strikes on airfields and in the air.
The new package also follows a separate Polish contribution of Patriot interceptors. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland has given Ukraine 10 PAC-3 MSE missiles in total, five earlier this year and five more through an international donation led by the United States with NATO. Kosiniak-Kamysz said in July that Poland’s donations to Ukraine since 2022 were worth about 16.45 billion zlotys, most of them delivered in 2022 and 2023, and the ministry later declassified the full list of transferred equipment.

How to stop the US-Israel war on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:54:51 UTC

How to stop the US-Israel war on Iran
Arab states must reject Israeli hegemony and build a regional security framework independent of Washington.
The war that Israel and the United States launched against Iran on February 28 is in a lull, not at an end. Major combat has paused, diplomacy has stalled and both sides are preparing for the next round. To understand why the fighting will soon resume, we need to understand the motivations of the two governments that started it. Neither of them wants peace. Israel’s leadership seeks domination over the Middle East, and the United States seeks to preserve its domination over the world. Simply to state these aims is to underscore that both governments are operating in a world of delusion.
Israel’s political leadership is consumed by the belief that Israel’s survival depends on its military supremacy over the Arab world and on the permanent subjugation or elimination of the Palestinian people. This belief is a form of collective madness, yet it is the doctrine that governs Israeli policy. Israel’s leaders cannot accept that peace is within reach. In the Arab Peace Initiative of 2002, the Arab states offered Israel full normalisation in return for a Palestinian state on the 1967 borders, and that offer still stands. Peace cannot be built on genocide in Gaza or on hatred of the Palestinian people and the drive to remove them from their land. Yet that is the path Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has chosen, and he now campaigns on it openly, with his “national religious” allies, including Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who twist religion in the service of hatred and killing.
The United States is consumed by its declining power. Iran has been a target for more than 70 years. In 1953, the CIA and British intelligence overthrew Iran’s elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, after he nationalised Iran’s oil. The United States then installed the shah and backed his police state until the Iranian people overthrew it in 1979. The US has never forgiven Iran for escaping from US domination. The US backed Saddam Hussein’s deadly war against Iran in the 1980s, and followed with four decades of economic warfare, covert operations, cyberattacks and assassinations. Trump tore up the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018, bombed Iran’s nuclear sites in June 2025, and then, in February of this year, joined Israel in open war, killing Iran’s supreme leader in the opening strikes.
Washington’s fixation on Iran is in the service of American hegemony. In The Grand Chessboard (1997), Zbigniew Brzezinski named Iran one of five “geopolitical pivots,” states that matter less for their own power than for where they sit. Iran commands the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Brzezinski wrote that an “antihegemonic” coalition of China, Russia and Iran could emerge “only if the United States is shortsighted enough to antagonize China and Iran simultaneously.” Well, yes, Washington has been that shortsighted and reckless.
The signs that the war will restart are not hidden. This week, War Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Israel to discuss renewed joint strikes, and Israeli sources report that the plans target Iran’s petrochemical facilities and nuclear sites. The White House has promised that the United States will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections, which is another way of announcing a timetable for war. The US naval blockade of Iran’s ports has passed its 100th day. Trump rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day ceasefire in September, even though Tehran says the offer remains on the table.
Israel’s October 27 election adds fuel to the fire. On October 18, Trump endorsed Netanyahu, saying the United States would “finish the job” against Iran only with Netanyahu in charge. On October 21, at a rally in Dimona (home to the reactor where Israel secretly built its own nuclear arsenal), Netanyahu declared that the only way to end the Iranian threat is to overthrow the regime and said he had issued that directive to the army, Mossad and the security services.
Iran has understandably drawn its own conclusions. Its commanders have announced a new offensive doctrine that includes preemptive strikes and attacks on bases in neighbouring countries used for operations against Iran, and they warn that renewed attacks would bring a global energy crisis. Attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz reached a new peak this month.
This is the reality that the Arab world, especially the Gulf countries, now faces. The US bases across the Gulf did not bring security in this war. They turned their host nations into targets. The US-Israeli strategy of divide and conquer, which cast Iran as the region’s permanent enemy and invited the Arab states to shelter under American power while accepting Israeli hegemony, has brought war to the region, economic loss to the Gulf, and mass killings in Palestine and Lebanon.
The only way to stop this madness is for the Arab world to tell the United States that enough is enough. The Arab states should declare that they will never accept Israeli hegemony, that there must be a sovereign State of Palestine and that the region’s security will come from regional cooperation rather than from Washington. The solution could be two states, as in the Arab Peace Initiative, or one binational democratic state, or a confederation. What matters is that Israeli Jews and Palestinian Arabs, each about eight million people, live in peace, safety and self-determination. What is not possible is the perpetuation of Israel’s brutal apartheid state.
The beginnings are visible. Qatar has called for a regional dialogue among the Gulf Cooperation Council states, Turkiye and Pakistan, and Qatar, Pakistan and Oman have kept the channels of mediation with Tehran open throughout the war. These efforts should grow into a standing regional security framework that includes Iran, the Gulf states, Egypt, Turkiye, Iraq and Pakistan, built on mutual non-aggression, freedom of navigation, and a zone free of nuclear weapons that must eventually include Israel.
The Arab states have far more leverage than they recognise. If Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and their neighbours announced that their territory and airspace will not be used for another war on Iran, and that normalisation with Israel is off the table until a Palestinian state exists, the calculations in Washington and Tel Aviv would have to change quickly. And the American people, who hate the war on Iran and side with Palestine, would cheer.
The era of US-led divide and conquer, with Iran cast as the permanent enemy of the Arab world, is over, even if Washington and Tel Aviv refuse to admit it. The Arab states should say so openly now before the next round of war begins, and in doing so, open the way to a region that provides for its own security and peace.

Healey vows to cut welfare bill before next election with ‘tough’ approach to young people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:54:05 UTC
16:54:05 KST

John Healey had said there will be a reduction in the welfare bill before the next election, with a “tough” approach to young people who do not accept support to get a job or training.
The chancellor was repeatedly pressed on the issue in broadcast interviews after documents from the Office for Budget Responsibility suggested sickness and disability benefits would cost £100bn a year before the end of the decade.
Healey delivered a budget on Wednesday with small giveaways for most households such as £100 off energy bills to help ease the cost of living. But he deferred some difficult decisions on how defence spending at 3% of national income would be paid for and did not set out any changes to welfare – both of which are likely to be addressed at the spending review.
Speaking after the budget, Healey told BBC Radio 4’s Today: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.”
He echoed the words of Andy Burnham when he said there would be no “crude cuts” after Keir Starmer’s attempts to cut disability benefits were stopped by Labour MPs.
But he said the welfare system was “unsustainable” and that the government would set out changes after two big reports on how it could be overhauled: the Milburn review of young people and work and the Timms review of the disability benefit system.
Healey added: “We will expect, as we’ve done before, that (young people) take up the offers … and that’s the way that we can bring welfare bills down in the long term.”
Asked whether there would be a cut to the overall welfare bill before the next election, the chancellor said: “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill. We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.”
The chancellor told Good Morning Britain that the model would be based on previous Labour governments having more conditions on welfare payments for young people. “We did this when the last Labour government was first elected at the end of the 90s. We had huge youth unemployment then. In our area of South Yorkshire it was one in five.
“We did exactly the same there. Tough on those who weren’t prepared to take up the offer, but also real support and advice that said to the young people then, as we must do now: ‘You have real potential.”
The Office for Budget Responsibility said total welfare spending would grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March.
Downing Street later insisted the chancellor had not set out a timeframe for reducing the benefits bill before the next election.
 
“The chancellor is completely in line with what the prime minister has said over the last few months that the welfare bill needs to come down and we are not setting an arbitrary target or timetable on that,” the prime minister’s spokesman said.
 
“Both the prime minister and the chancellor have been crystal clear that the welfare bill needs to come down, and that we need to do that in a progressive and sustainable way and not through crude cuts which push people into hardship and puts pressure on the system elsewhere.”
In his post-budget interviews, Healey explained the choices he had made to give households some “breathing space”, paid for by higher taxes on banks and landlords.
But he said the single best thing for UK economic policy would be peace in the Middle East and Ukraine. Asked by Sky News if he was frustrated by Donald Trump’s international actions, Healey said: “President Trump is probably the one man that can bring those parties together.
“That’s why I will always work with him, if that’s what he’s pursuing. And I think it’s why the British government now is doing what we can to bring those parties together. We want to reopen the strait of Hormuz, and we absolutely want to see an end to the Russian invasion of Ukraine.”
Meanwhile, a leading economic thinktank said Healey had delivered a “scattergun” budget that did little to address Britain’s economic challenges. The Resolution Foundation said measures aimed at easing household costs would not prevent energy bills from jumping above levels seen during the last energy shock.
Measures announced in the budget aimed at tackling soaring energy costs include the scrapping of standing charges on gas bills and energy payments of £100 for up to 20m households in council tax bands A to D.
But in its analysis of the budget, the Resolution Foundation said typical annual energy bills were expected to reach £1,750 after government support in 2026-27.
That compares with £1,685 paid during the 2022-23 energy price jump after Russia invaded Ukraine.
Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the thinktank, said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.
“Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”

Slovakia to Receive Second Barak MX Air Defense Battery by End of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:52:36 UTC
16:52:36 KST

Slovakia will receive its second Israeli-made Barak MX air defense battery by the end of 2026, according to Slovak Defence Minister Robert Kaliňák, as reported by Future Army.
The first battery arrived in Slovakia in spring 2026.
The third battery is expected to be delivered in 2027.
Slovakia has ordered a total of six Barak MXbatteries, all of which are expected to be delivered by 2030. The new systems will replace the country’s Soviet-era Kub surface-to-air missile systems.
The procurement of Barak MX systems is being carried out under an intergovernmental agreement and a contract with Israel Aerospace Industries, an Israeli state-owned company. The agreement covers the delivery of launchers, missiles, radar systems, command posts, as well as logistics support and specialist training.
The development of the Barak family began in Israel in the 1980s, led by Israel Aerospace Industries in cooperation with Rafael. The initial Barak 1 variant was developed as a short-range naval air defense system to protect warships against anti-ship missiles.
Over time, the concept evolved into land-based variants, leading to the modern, modular Barak MX family of air defense systems.
The system comprises a command-and-control unit and a radar station equipped with an active electronically scanned array (AESA).
The Barak MX can use three types of surface-to-air missiles with different engagement ranges. The short-range BARAKMRAD has a range of up to 35 km, the medium-range BARAK LRAD up to 70 km, and the long-range BARAK ER can engage targets at distances of up to 150 km.
The system is capable of intercepting and destroying a wide range of targets, including aircraft, helicopters, unmanned aerial vehicles, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles.
As previously reported, the Slovak Air Force would resume protecting the country’s airspace with its own forces in the coming days, using American-made F-16 Block 70 fighter jets.

Pauline Hanson accuses Anthony Albanese of trying to divide One Nation with staffing offer
In short:
One Nation has accused Anthony Albanese of political meddling after one of its MPs rejected an unsolicited offer of a $200,000 staffer.
The dispute has intensified scrutiny of the prime minister's power to allocate parliamentary resources.
What's next?
Pauline Hanson says the current system is "grubby" and wants an independent body to set staffing levels.
One Nation has accused Anthony Albanese of trying to use his power to set parliament staffing levels to divide the party after the prime minister offered new MP David Farley extra resources.
The Farrer MP received a letter from Mr Albanese this week authorising him to hire an additional staffer on a $200,000 salary package, an "unsolicited" offer that Mr Farley has rejected.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has criticised the offer as an attempt by Labor to "exert undue political influence" and split her party, which is in the middle of a broader staffing dispute with Mr Albanese.
"We won't be bought or divided by this prime minister,"
Senator Hanson said.
Staffing levels have emerged as a significant point of contention between some crossbenchers and Mr Albanese, who has ignored calls to increase the resources provided to some independents and One Nation.
All parliamentarians are granted five electorate officers, but the power to decide additional personal staff levels is held by the prime minister.
It is understood the extra staff position offered to Mr Farley was the same as the allocation provided to fellow One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce when he quit the Nationals and moved to the crossbench.
Both parliamentarians are in the lower house and have geographically large regional electorates.
Hanson says staffing power 'open to abuse'
In statement today, Senator Hanson said the staff offer made to Mr Farley showed the system was "grubby".
"This is the type of politics that Australians are sick of," she said.
Senator Hanson has repeatedly asked Mr Albanese to let her hire more staff since One Nation achieved minor party status in the wake of Mr Joyce's defection.
"For months, One Nation has been fighting for fair, transparent and objective allocation of staffing for parliamentarians," she said.
Senator Hanson has called for staffing levels to be determined by an independent body.
"While this power has always been open to abuse, it has, in our view, been weaponised to an unprecedented extent under this Labor government and this prime minister," she said.
Senator apologises for 'clumsy' Haines comment
Earlier this week, independent West Australian senator Fatima Payman revealed she had apologised to Indi MP Helen Haines for her "clumsy wording" in relation to a staffing stoush with Labor.
During a Senate estimates hearing on Monday night, Senator Payman suggested Mr Albanese was waiting for her to suffer an attack similar to Ms Haines before he would grant extra staff.
Senator Payman refused to withdraw the comment at the time, which was described by Special Minister of State Don Farrell as an "outrageous statement".
But yesterday, Senator Payman confirmed she had contacted Ms Haines, who is in hospital recovering from a double amputation after an alleged attack last week, to clarify her remarks.
"I have apologised for my clumsy wording on Monday night, and I have conveyed those apologies directly to Dr Haines and her staff," Senator Payman said.
She maintained her need for additional staff, noting the "toll" on her current team of staff.
Crossbench unites in staffing push
Last month, Senator Hanson, Senator Payman and independent Fowler MP Dai Le teamed up to criticise what they described as "unfair" staffing double standards for some crossbenchers.
The trio called on Mr Albanese to provide a "fair" number of staff and later moved a motion attempting to strip him of the personal power to decide personnel allocations.
Data from May this year showed Senator Payman was the only independent in parliament who did not have any additional personal staff allocated.
Ms Le had one extra staff member, as did independent Bradfield MP Nicolette Boele and United Australia Party senator Ralph Babet.
The remainder of the crossbench independents have two personal staff, except Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie, who has three.
The Greens, who have one MP and 10 senators, have 15 personal staff.
One Nation, which has two MPs and four senators, has five additional staff.

Federal judge denies Trump administration request to block 20,000 California ballots over voters' questioned citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:49:48 UTC
16:49:48 KST

Darren Lyn
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
A federal judge on Wednesday denied the Donald Trump administration's request to block 20,000 California ballots cast by voters whose US citizenship is being questioned.
"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," US District Judge David Carter wrote in his ruling. "The federal government seeks to segregate and exclude over 20,000 ballots. This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections."
Carter ruled that the Trump administration's allegations were "not credible" and that intervening just days before the Nov. 3 midterm elections would both violate federal voting laws and wreak havoc during the elections.
"If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process," Carter said. "Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve."
"The Government’s Application for Temporary Restraining Order is DENIED."
Carter added that allowing the Trump administration's unprecedented request would likely lead to the disenfranchisement of legitimate voters and foster future political meddling in elections.
"Constitutional rights and our democracy are at stake. The public interest favors their protection," said Carter. "Individuals who have met the requirements of California’s voter registration laws must not be deprived of a core right merely because of unfounded allegations stemming from a procedure rife with uncertainty and errors."
Carter explained in his ruling that there are already federal laws in place to prosecute individuals who vote illegally, adding that California had already established rules "to cancel the voter registrations of any individuals proven ineligible."
"The Executive Branch cannot replace the remedy Congress carefully enacted with its own unlawful and unconstitutional solution instead," said Carter. "Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred."
"If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," he concluded. "This Court declines to be a party to such process."
Carter’s ruling was the second to deny the Trump administration a temporary restraining order against the state of California and Los Angeles County this week, after a three-judge panel of the US 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday denied the government’s emergency request in a separate order, according to media reports.

Madeira: scientists study how marine protection is restoring ocean life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:49:47 UTC
16:49:47 KST

Nearly 200 scientists are studying the marine environment off Madeira's Desertas Islands.
A ray glides over the seabed off the Desertas Islands in Madeira. The footage is being analysed by scientists trying to understand how marine protection is affecting ocean life.
Juan Mayorga, a marine biologist with National Geographic’s Pristine Seas initiative, is part of an expedition bringing together around 200 scientists to study the archipelago’s marine environment.
"It’s a good day when we see animals like this," says the Colombian researcher, who studies underwater images to measure the impact of marine protection.
The scientists, on board around 15 vessels, are surveying marine life across the archipelago, assessing the health of its ecosystems and exploring how they can better withstand climate change.
"As we protect this place, year after year, the fish get bigger and produce more and more offspring. That’s protection working," stresses marine biologist Juan Mayorga, who works for the marine conservation initiative run by the National Geographic Society.
Underwater cameras and DNA sampling help map progress
The flagship of the expedition is the 70-metre sailing ship Santa Maria Manuela, which has brought researchers from different parts of the world to the Desertas Islands, a group of three uninhabited rocky islets about 40 kilometres southeast of Madeira.
Aboard vessels such as the Santa Maria Manuela, the team uses baited underwater cameras mounted on metal frames to attract and film fish at depths of between 40 and 50 metres.
The aim is to compare two areas: the southern side of the Desertas Islands, where fishing is completely banned, and the northern side, where it is still allowed in some zones.
"We’re going to put these cameras in these protected marine areas and then also in zones where there is fishing, and we’re going to compare the two," explains Jennifer Caselle, a researcher at the Marine Science Institute at the University of California, Santa Barbara.
The research goes beyond images. The scientists also collect water samples to identify traces of fish DNA from species that may escape the cameras.
On the Desertas Islands, they also measure rock temperatures in the intertidal zone to study the effects of heat on marine organisms and help understand how biodiversity may change as the planet warms.
Studying the response to global warming
Rui Seabra, a 44-year-old researcher from the University of Porto, attaches temperature sensors to rocks exposed at low tide along a small cove.
He wants to understand how crustaceans and sponges behave in sunny and shaded areas, information that could help scientists predict how marine biodiversity will respond to rising temperatures.
"We need to understand how biodiversity will be redistributed, which species will migrate where, what conditions exist here, how they will change and which species we expect to find here in the future," he explains.
The expedition comes at a time when the urgency of protecting marine ecosystems is high on the international agenda.
Emanuel Gonçalves, the expedition leader and scientific director of the Oceano Azul Foundation, acknowledges the importance of international meetings such as the 17th COP on biodiversity (COP17), taking place in Yerevan, Armenia, in setting political priorities.
However, he points out that fieldwork cannot wait for political decisions. "That’s what science is telling us as well. This emergency for action does not allow us to sit back and wait for decisions that sometimes take decades to be made," he says.
Madeira has long been a pioneer in marine conservation. The archipelago includes the main island of Madeira, the beach destination of Porto Santo, the Desertas Islands and the remote Selvagens Islands.
In 1971 the authorities created a reserve around the Selvagens Islands to protect Cory’s shearwaters, seabirds found around Madeira and other Atlantic islands.
Expanded in 2022, the reserve now covers around 2,600 square kilometres, making it the largest marine protected area in the North Atlantic.
Another reserve set up around the Desertas Islands in the early 1990s helped a colony of Mediterranean monk seals, one of Europe’s most endangered marine mammals, grow from just eight animals to 31.

Elections chief Sohlberg orders Shin Bet probe into suspected election interference

07:49:40 UTC

The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) is investigating suspicions that foreign entities, potentially including Qatar and Turkey, funneled money into Israel to influence voting in Arab communities, following a directive from Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg to investigate suspected foreign funding and election bribery.
The investigation will not delay publication of the final election results, a Central Elections Committee source told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday. The source said it would also not prevent President Isaac Herzog from selecting a party leader to begin the coalition-building process.
Asked whether the investigation could lead to another election, the source said it was “far too early for such a question.”
“First, we need to examine whether there was any impact and whether it affects the distribution of Knesset seats at all,” he said.
Notably, N12 News reported that the Shin Bet had intelligence information about potential illegal money transfers, but did not inform the CEC, including Solberg.
The report noted that Zini presented information to the CEC that was "extraordinary in its seriousness," on Wednesday night.
Qatar's Spokesperson for the Foreign Affairs Ministry released a statement categorically denying allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections.
Likud lawyer to 'Post': Party looking into all irregularities at suspected polling places
Separately, a Likud lawyer told the Post that the party intends to seek the invalidation of results at polling stations where it suspects irregularities.
The foreign-funding inquiry, a police investigation into suspected bribery involving Ra’am voting slips, and any legal challenge to election results are distinct proceedings. None of the allegations amounts to a finding that the election results were altered unlawfully.
Israeli media have identified Qatar and Turkey as possible sources of the suspected funding. Channel 13 reported that investigators were examining whether money had passed through currency exchangers and local institutions along routes previously used to transfer terrorist funds, allegedly to encourage voting in Arab communities through unlawful means.
The source, recipients and use of the money remain under investigation. Encouraging voter participation is not, by itself, evidence of election bribery.
Why did the CEC tell the Shin Bet to investigate Qatari influence in the elections?
In his letter, dated Wednesday and made public Thursday, Sohlberg described the suspicions brought before him as serious but expressly said he could not assess their merits. He instructed Zini to use the agency’s powers to obtain evidence that would substantiate or refute them and requested any available findings during the coming week, citing the timetable for election appeals.
The letter did not identify particular countries or political parties.
The investigation was already underway before Tuesday’s vote. During a visit to the Central Elections Committee on Tuesday, Shin Bet chief David Zini publicly described the election as secure and properly supervised.
“There are challenges, and there are those trying to cause harm,” he said, adding that the authorities were succeeding under Sohlberg’s and the police’s leadership.
On Wednesday, Zini presented information to Sohlberg, who subsequently sent the instruction to investigate.
Zini also met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday evening and presented information concerning suspected foreign interference. The meeting was initiated by Zini.
In the separate police case involving suspected payments for votes for Ra’am, investigators announced further arrests on Thursday.
Police said four additional men had been arrested on suspicion of involvement in election bribery and were being questioned by Lahav 433’s National Fraud Squad. Their arrests followed those of three residents of southern Israel on Tuesday morning, Election Day, after which the case was transferred to the unit.
Police had reported finding cash and Ra’am voting slips during searches. Thursday’s statement did not identify a connection between that case and the suspected foreign funding.
Separately, police rejected Likud’s broader claim that the election was stolen. In a statement reported on Thursday morning, police said Election Day had seen relatively few election-integrity incidents and that they had no investigative or intelligence support for the allegations put to them.
Police also said they would investigate suspected criminal offenses and bring those responsible to justice.
Likud alleged on Wednesday that Arab parties had “stolen” the election through bribery, intimidation, fraud and other offenses. It said it was submitting hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to police, the Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee.
On Thursday, following publication of Sohlberg’s letter, Likud argued that Zionist parties must not cooperate with Ra’am or the Joint List to replace the Knesset speaker or form a government, alleging that votes had been bought.
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh rejected the accusations as a “racist blood libel,” accusing Netanyahu and his allies of preparing the ground to reject the election results and warning against another election on the basis of false allegations.
Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot called for all complaints to be examined thoroughly while warning that political actors must not exploit the situation to affect the swearing-in date of the 26th Knesset.
Democrats chairman Yair Golan said genuine suspicions of election misconduct must be investigated, but accused Netanyahu of trying to delegitimize the electorate’s decision, particularly Arab voters.
Democrats MK Naama Lazimi accused Likud of creating its own version of the January 6 storming of the US Capitol and urged opposition leaders to remain focused on replacing Netanyahu. She also called for another vote on declaring Qatar an enemy state.
An investigation into suspected offenses does not itself overturn election results. Section 86 of the Knesset Elections Law provides a separate court procedure for challenging them, with no automatic cancellation triggered by suspicions or the discovery of unlawful funding.
The law allows challenges on grounds including elections conducted unlawfully nationwide or at a particular polling station, incorrect allocation of votes between lists, unlawful allocation of seats, or votes obtained illegally. A central requirement is that the alleged irregularity could have affected the election results.
An election appeal must be filed with the Jerusalem District Court, sitting as a court for administrative affairs, within 14 days of publication of the results. The court may extend the deadline in special circumstances, giving reasons for doing so. A three-judge panel hears the case.
Those entitled to appeal include participating candidate lists and their candidates, Knesset members, factions of the newly elected Knesset, members of the central and regional election committees, and the attorney-general.
The court can annul the election nationwide or at a particular polling station and order a new vote. A rerun is not the only possible remedy: it can also correct the allocation of votes between lists and declare the results accordingly, or determine that one candidate was elected instead of another.
A further appeal to the Supreme Court on a legal question generally requires permission from its president and must be filed within 30 days of the judgment.
If the lower court annuls the election nationwide, those entitled to bring an election appeal may appeal to the Supreme Court as of right, even if they were not parties to the original proceeding. The case must be heard by five judges or a larger odd-numbered panel.
The law expressly states that an election appeal does not suspend the Knesset’s work. Its outcome also does not invalidate decisions the Knesset has already taken.
Sarah Ben-Nun, Shir Perets, and Amichai Stein contributed to this report.

Threshold to lose only home over unpaid utility bills rises past UAH 430,000 – Ukraine Justice Ministry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:39:16 EET
16:39:16 KST

Since October 23, Ukraine has had a higher threshold for utility debt above which a person's only home may be seized: instead of UAH 170,000, the threshold is now more than UAH 430,000, the Ministry of Justice reported.
"So, for your only home to be taken away, you would have to make quite an effort to accumulate utility debt. There are literally only a handful of such utility debtors. In other words, in 99.999% of cases, a person's only home will not be seized over utility debt. I want to reassure people on this point," the ministry quoted Andriy Haichenko, deputy justice minister for enforcement service, as saying.
The relevant provisions are stipulated in Law No. 4833-IX. According to the Ministry of Justice's calculations, if monthly utility bills amount to UAH 6,000, it would take six years of nonpayment to accumulate debt of this size. At the same time, even exceeding this amount does not mean that a home will automatically be seized.
The law also guarantees additional protection for the only homes of military personnel. It provides separate safeguards during enforcement proceedings for debtors with utility bills in areas of active hostilities and temporarily occupied territories.

El Salvador pledges more than 2,000 soldiers as Haiti delays elections
El Salvador troops to support rescue mission to find four UN-backed soldiers who disappeared after ambush.
El Salvador plans to send more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti to search for four missing Salvadoran aviation technicians and fight armed gangs, as the Caribbean country postpones its elections again.
El Salvador‘s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the deployment on Wednesday, the same day Haiti’s electoral authorities moved the first round of presidential and parliamentary elections from December 13 to July 18, 2027.
The delay is another setback to restoring elected government in a country where gang violence has made preparations for voting dangerous.
The four Salvadorans disappeared on October 18 after armed men ambushed their vehicle in Croix-des-Bouquets, east of the capital, Port-au-Prince.
They were serving with an international security mission supporting Haitian police.
President Nayib Bukele has already sent troops to help find them.
In an October 21 post on X, written in Haitian Creole, he threatened to destroy Haiti’s gangs if they did not release the missing personnel.
Bukele spoke by telephone with Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime on Wednesday.
Fils-Aime’s office said they had agreed to strengthen cooperation on rescue efforts and security operations.
It remains unclear whether the additional Salvadoran troops will join the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force, a multinational mission assisting Haitian police against gangs, or operate separately.
Foreign troops have served in Haiti under UN-backed security arrangements since 2024, partly to create safer conditions for elections.
Haiti’s nine-member Provisional Electoral Council, which organises elections, also scheduled a second round of voting and local polls for October 4, 2027.
It extended deadlines for candidates to register and introduced online voter registration.
Fewer than 900,000 people had registered by Wednesday, the Miami Herald reported, out of 6.5 million Haitians holding the identification cards needed to enrol.
Gang-controlled roads make it difficult to reach registration centres, while violence has forced many people from their homes.
Haiti has held no elections since 2016 and its last president, Jovenel Moise, was assassinated in 2021. Successive transitional authorities have delayed a return to voting, citing insecurity.
An international food security assessment released on Wednesday found that 5.94 million Haitians face acute hunger, including 1.8 million in emergency conditions, as violence disrupts farming and food deliveries.
The number facing acute hunger is projected to rise to 6.35 million by mid-2027.

Kazakh PM orders measures to curb inflation, support business and attract investment
Kazakhstan's Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov has outlined a series of measures to curb inflation, stabilize food prices, improve budget efficiency and strengthen the investment climate following the President’s state-of-the-nation address on October 28, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
Government to curb inflation and stabilize prices
The Ministry of National Economy, together with the National Bank and other government agencies, must develop measures by November 20 to improve coordination between fiscal and monetary policies, reduce inflation and increase real household incomes.
Regional authorities have been instructed to monitor food price stabilization measures weekly, while the Ministry of Trade must strengthen controls on retail markups for socially significant food products. The Ministries of Trade and Agriculture must also ensure sufficient food reserves for the winter and expand direct supplies.
Digital budget management and business development
Bektenov instructed the Ministries of Finance, National Economy and Artificial Intelligence to expand the use of digital tools and AI in budget procedures. The measures should enable automated checks, identify inefficient spending and allow real-time monitoring of budget transactions.
The government must also prepare a development plan for medium-sized businesses by the end of the year. It will focus on helping small businesses grow, improving access to long-term financing, attracting private investment, modernizing production and increasing labor productivity.
Three-year moratorium on inspections under consideration
The government will discuss introducing a three-year moratorium on inspections of micro and small businesses starting January 1, 2027. The proposal will be considered with the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs, the business ombudsman and Qurultay members.
Bektenov said the initiative aims to reduce administrative burdens and prevent excessive government interference in business activities. Proposals must be submitted to the government within two weeks.
Investment management reforms
The Ministries of National Economy and Foreign Affairs, together with the Baiterek holding, must submit proposals within 10 days to establish a unified investment management system.
The Ministry of National Economy is expected to identify a central decision-making body, clarify the responsibilities of all participants and improve coordination with investors.
Earlier, PM Bektenov called for a clear action plan to implement the President’s address.

Chinese AI model raises cybersecurity concerns in new tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:36:12 UTC
16:36:12 KST

Chinese AI model raises cybersecurity concerns in new tests
The researchers evaluated GLM-5.3, an open-weight model developed by Zhipu AI, using CyScenarioBench, a benchmark designed to test AI models on multi-stage cyber operations. The tests measure whether a model can coordinate several dependent steps to achieve an attack's objective.
GLM-5.3 completed 3 of the 13 scenarios at least once, the strongest result recorded by Irregular for an open-weight model. The researchers also reported that the model did not refuse any of the offensive tasks tested.
In the successful scenarios, the model gained access to internal services, established alternative connections within simulated networks and coordinated operations across multiple machines. It also automated remote desktop interactions and created or repaired scripts and tools to retrieve target data.
However, leading closed AI models have demonstrated higher success rates in separate evaluations. According to Irregular, these models completed 9 of 10 and 12 of 12 scenarios in their respective tests.
A separate evaluation revealed another concern. GLM-5.3 repeatedly produced correct answers while violating explicit task instructions.
In tests designed to assess its ability to find vulnerabilities in open-source code, researchers found that code reconstructed from memory contributed to roughly 80% of the successful runs they examined. Although this did not violate the instructions in those tests, it raised questions about whether the model had actually discovered the vulnerabilities or relied on previously learned code.
In a separate evaluation, researchers explicitly instructed the model not to reproduce code from memory. It nevertheless repeatedly reproduced memorized code verbatim to reach correct answers.
Irregular described this behavior as a form of reward hacking, in which a model achieves the expected result while bypassing a constraint intended to guide its behavior.
The researchers warned that evaluations focused solely on correct answers could overestimate a model's reliability. Rewarding such results during training could also reinforce instruction violations.
They recommended that organizations assess both task performance and compliance with restrictions before granting AI models broader access or greater autonomy.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that an OpenAI research model accessed a cryptocurrency wallet using a publicly known recovery phrase.

Kazakhstan to add 13.3 GW of new power capacity by 2029
Kazakhstan plans to bring 13.3 gigawatts (GW) of new power generation capacity online by 2029, Vice Minister of Energy Bakytzhan Ilyas said during a Government's meeting, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to Ilyas, the planned expansion will include 7.4 GW from conventional energy sources and another 5.9 GW from renewables.
Once completed, the projects are expected to give Kazakhstan 20% more power generation capacity than it needs to meet domestic demand.
However, several major projects are facing delays, putting some of the country's near-term capacity expansion plans behind schedule.
The modernization of Almaty Combined Heat and Power Plant No. 3, with a capacity of 544 MW, is running behind schedule, while the 926 MW gas-fired power plant in Turkistan is also facing delays, with only 190 MW expected to come online this year.
As a result, Kazakhstan is expected to bring just 1.27 GW of new power generation capacity online in 2026, less than half of the originally planned 2.66 GW.
Meanwhile, the country will begin preparing seven-year electricity supply and demand forecasts this year, taking into account the growing energy needs of major investment projects, including data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
If new power plants are commissioned on schedule, electricity generation is projected to reach 134.1 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 2027, against expected consumption of 132.8 billion kWh, resulting in a surplus of 1.3 billion kWh.
Electricity generation is expected to rise further to 143.4 billion kWh in 2028.
Earlier, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan might achieve a sustained electricity surplus by 2029.

Finance ministry increases 2027 growth prediction, warns of continued inflation and currency risks
The Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review.
The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.

Several leaders from India's opposition alliance, the INDIA bloc, have finalized the "public impeachment" proceedings they intend to carry out against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the controversial revision of voter lists.

'RSS Friends' registers in US to bolster outreach
A group of "well-wishers" of the India-based Rashtriya Sayamsevak Sangh (RSS) has registered with the US Department of Justice as a foreign agent of the right-wing Hindu nationalist group, news agency Press Trust of India reported on Thursday.
The RSS is a 101-year-old organization with millions of followers across India. It presents itself as the guardian of Hindu values, while critics widely classify it as a paramilitary organization. Under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who has deep roots in the RSS, its influence reaches to the highest levels of political power. The Group is the ideological parent of India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.
'RSS Friends,' which provided a Georgia address for itself, listed a Delhi branch of RSS in India as its "foreign principal."
The group said its proposed activities are primarily informational, educational, public-relations and community-engagement activities.
"RSS Friends does not have a written employment, consulting, lobbying, public-relations, or agency agreement with RSS containing specified deliverables, compensation, or detailed operational instructions," the group said, adding that the lack of contract did not mean the connection did not exist.
The registration of RSS Friends was submitted two days before RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's outreach program at New York's Madison Square Garden on August 29. The controversial appearance is believed to be part of the RSS' global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.
What else do we know about RSS Friends?
The group's website describes itself as a "dedicated well-wisher organization" seeking to address misrepresentation of RSS by US media or other "politically motivated actors."
Its social media, too, largely covered Bhagwat's NYC Event and has since been inactive.
IN PICTURES: Cyclone Arnab's trail of destruction:
Cyclone Arnab damages homes and farmlands in eastern India
Cyclone Arnab on Wednesday battered Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, damaging homes, farmland and electricity infrastructure, authorities said.
The cyclone made a prolonged landfall early Wednesday as a "very severe cyclonic storm" in the union territory of Puducherry and southeastern state of Andhra Pradesh.
At least three people were killed even as the storm weakened while moving inland. Two women were electrocuted in separate incidents in the port city of Visakhapatnam, while another person was killed when a tree fell in East Godavari district, officials said.
Andhra Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu later said 14 of the state's districts were badly affected, requesting urgent assistance from the central government.
The cyclone damaged 79,000 acres of crops and dozens of homes. The worst hit area was the state's fertile Konaseema district where banana and coconut plantations suffered extensively.
While the eastern state of Odisha seemed to be less impacted initially, heavy rains and winds lashed several districts there on Wednesday evening. State authorities reported landslides, uprooted trees and damaged homes and infrastructure, but zero casualties.
On Thursday morning, Indian Home Minister Amit Shah reiterated the central government's support to the impacted states.
"In the wake of Cyclone Arnab, spoke with the Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry, Odisha and Chhattisgarh and assured them of every assistance to mitigate the hardship of the people in the face of the disaster," he wrote in a post on X, adding that disaster relief teams were continuing operations on a "war footing."
'Cockroaches' back opposition-led rally against election chief
Indian youth-led political pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has decided to back the opposition bloc's upcoming November 1 rally, marking a shift in protest strategy.
The CJP said India's election commission has undermined people's right to choose their leaders through the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which allegedly deleted over 130 million names from voter lists across the country.
Election authorities said the list includes people who have died, moved away or were appearing on lists more than once, but critics argue the massive number is also likely to include a large number of eligible voters.
The CJP, several student organizations and opposition parties — with Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi at the helm — have been protesting against the revisions and alleged irregularities purported by India's election chief for over a month now.
What else did the CJP say?
"Gyanesh Kumar has lost the trust required to oversee free and fair elections. His resignation is therefore necessary to restore the credibility and independence of the Election Commission," the CJP said in a statement published on X by founder Abhijeet Dipke.
"Our constitution gave every adult citizen the right to vote. It is our responsibility to ensure that no eligible citizen is deprived of that. The Cockroach Janta Party will therefore support all organizations fighting for free and fair election in our country," it said.
Dipke's caption read: "The Cockroach Janta Party extends its support to the INDIA Bloc's November 1 rally. Nation above all!"
The CJP and Gandhi's Indian National Congress have been running parallel campaigns so far with similar demands. However, they have not expressed direct support or held joint rallies before this, possibly in an effort not to alienate people who may relate to one group but not to the other.
However, the CJP now has limited choices. Its leaders were detained and arrested while protesting earlier this month and made to sign a peace bond which prohibits them from calling for mass protests in central Delhi. Lending their support to someone else's call for protest could be the loophole they needed.

Festive voyages: Europe’s top Christmas market river cruises to book in 2026
