Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:19:59 UTC
16:19:59 KST

Choose between a sailing along the Main, the Danube or the Rhine, getting your fix of mulled wine and roasted chestnuts on the way.
One of the best parts about the holiday season are the Christmas markets. Mulled wine, roasted chestnuts, and lots and lots of sweet treats… what’s not to love?
There are plenty to choose in Europe, from the classics to lesser-known gems. But there’s no reason you have to limit yourself to just one.
We’ve previously covered the best ones you can reach by train, and now we’re taking a look at the ones you can visit via river cruise.
There are three popular options in Europe: Rivers cruise voyages along the Main, the Danube, and the Rhine.
Here’s what you need to know about each.
On the Main
Christmas markets, or Christkindlmarket, were first started in Germany, so if you’re looking for a classic experience it makes sense to book a trip along the Main.
Uniworld operates cruises between Nuremberg and Frankfurt. You’ll start at Germany’s largest Christmas market in Nuremberg before sampling Bamberg, Rothenburg and Würzburg’s festivities as well as Wiesbaden’s “twinkling star” market, finishing up in Frankfurt.
On the Danube
If you want to tick off a German Christmas market but don’t want to limit yourself to one country, you could book a river cruise along the Danube, taking in Austria and Hungary as well.
AmaWaterways has a river cruise package that takes in five Christmas markets: Nuremberg, Regensburg and Passau in Germany, plus Vienna and Budapest, the capitals of Austria and Hungary.
Scenic Cruises has a similar option, although you’ll start in Prague and transfer to Budapest by coach before stopping in Slovakia’s capital Bratislava, Vienna, Dürnstein, Melk and Passau, ending in Regensburg.
On the Rhine
For a four-country Christmas market river cruise, book yourself a sailing along the Rhine.
Avalon Waterways’ offering starts in the Dutch capital Amsterdam, passes by Cologne, Rüdesheim, Mainz and Heidelberg in Germany, Strasbourg in France, then Breisach in the Black Forest, before finally ending in Basel in Switzerland.
Viking River Cruises also has a Christmas on the Rhine cruise from Amsterdam to Basel, but stops include Dordrecht, Cologne, Koblenz, Rüdesheim, Mannheim, Speyer, Strasbourg and Breisach.

Police reject Netanyahu party's claims of widespread election fraud in Arab communities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:19:37 UTC
16:19:37 KST

The head of the Central Elections Committee on Thursday asked the Shin Bet domestic security agency to investigate serious allegations of foreign interference in Tuesday's parliamentary election, including suspected overseas funding and election bribery involving foreign actors.
Supreme Court Deputy Chief Justice Noam Sohlberg sent an unusual letter to Shin Bet Director David Zini urging him to use the agency's investigative powers to determine whether foreign entities had attempted to improperly influence the election. Sohlberg sent the letter to Zini following a meeting between the two on Wednesday.
The suspected foreign interference appears to involve Qatar funneling tens of millions of shekels to influence Israel's election, with Central Elections Committee officials describing the intelligence as "solid."
The Shin Bet had reportedly possessed the intelligence for several days but waited to see whether the suspected vote-buying would actually take place. The agency declined to comment on the ongoing investigation.
"The integrity of elections is the heart of democracy. Take integrity away from democracy, and you deprive it of its vitality," Sohlberg wrote.
He said allegations had been brought to his attention suggesting that foreign actors working against Israeli interests may have sought to influence the election through financial means.
"Serious suspicions have been brought before me concerning improper influence on the elections through foreign funding provided by external actors operating against Israeli interests," he wrote.
Sohlberg acknowledged that he could not independently assess the credibility of the allegations but stressed that their potential implications warranted a thorough investigation.
"I cannot attest to the substance of these suspicions," he wrote. "However, given that they concern foreign actors, there is an obligation to investigate them properly to safeguard the integrity of Knesset elections and prevent unlawful activity intended to undermine the democratic system and subversive activity."
The judge instructed Zini to make every effort to establish whether the allegations were supported by evidence, or whether they could be disproved.
"I ask you to do everything in your power to get to the bottom of these suspicions and to use the powers of the Israel Security Agency to uncover evidence that would substantiate or refute them," Sohlberg wrote, using the Shin Bet's formal name
"Only in this way can we ensure public confidence in the electoral process and the integrity of the democratic process."
Sohlberg also requested that the agency report its findings, if any, within the coming week, citing legal deadlines for challenging election results.
"In light of the statutory deadlines for filing election appeals, I ask that you make every effort to present me with findings, insofar as there are any, within the next week," he wrote.
The letter comes amid growing political controversy over the election results after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party accused Arab political parties Wednesday of stealing the vote through widespread criminal activity.
Likud alleged that Arab parties supporting terrorism and the destruction of the Jewish state had manipulated the results through serious criminal offenses, including vote-buying, threats against election officials, fraudulent voting and the use of prohibited software to mobilize supporters.
The party said it had submitted evidence of suspected irregularities to police, Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee and demanded an investigation.
Sohlberg's letter did not identify the foreign actors allegedly involved, specify the source of the suspected funding or establish a connection between the allegations of foreign interference and Likud's claims against Arab political parties.
Likud described the suspected foreign interference as a political earthquake, accusing foreign actors of stealing Israel's election to help Arab parties gain power.
"Ra'amgate is an earthquake. Israel's election was stolen!" the party said in a statement. "Justice Sohlberg's remarks about foreign actors interfering in the election and bribing voters to support Arab parties represent an unprecedented political shock."
Likud characterized the alleged interference as "an attack on democracy" aimed at enabling foreign control of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and the removal of the right-wing government.
"The goal is to bring about foreign control of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and the overthrow of right-wing rule in order to force an Israeli military withdrawal and defeat on all fronts, first and foremost against Iran," the statement said.
The party argued that the allegations should rule out any cooperation between Jewish-led Zionist parties and the predominantly Arab Ra'am and Joint List factions.
"Now that it has become clear that foreign actors attempted to take control of the Knesset, no Zionist party can be allowed to cooperate with Ra'am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker using votes bought with cash or establish a government that would endanger Israel," Likud said. "We demand immediate action using every means available to the Shin Bet and police to investigate these crimes," the statement concluded.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the Shin Bet to investigate Arab party leaders. "The suspicion of election manipulation using foreign Islamist money is a test for the State of Israel," he wrote on X. "The leaders of the Arab parties must be questioned by the Shin Bet today. The State of Israel will not be sold to radical Islam with terror money."
Avigdor Liberman, leader of the opposition Yisrael Beytenu party, also weighed in, describing Sohlberg's letter as "a dramatic and unprecedented development."
"I call on law enforcement authorities to act swiftly to establish the truth as soon as possible," Liberman wrote.
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar! party, is in contact with the relevant authorities and is receiving updates on allegations of foreign interference in Israel's election, his office said in a statement.
"Israel must safeguard the integrity of its elections against any attempts at interference, political spin or manipulation, and thoroughly investigate every complaint," the statement said.
"At the same time, political actors must not be allowed to exploit the situation to influence the timing of the 26th Knesset's swearing-in."
Police, however, have rejected claims of widespread election fraud, saying there was no investigative or intelligence evidence to support the allegations and that election-related irregularities had declined significantly compared with the previous vote.
"Election Day passed with a small number of exceptional incidents involving election integrity, including in comparison with previous elections," police said. "It should be emphasized that there is no investigative or intelligence evidence supporting the allegations raised in your inquiry."
The dispute comes after a surge in Arab voter turnout helped predominantly Arab parties make significant electoral gains, potentially giving them a decisive role in determining the next government. Neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc nor the rival bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot emerged from the election with a clear majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
In a sharply worded statement posted on X, Likud accused Arab political parties of orchestrating widespread electoral fraud.
"The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the destruction of the Jewish state through serious criminal offenses involving bribery, threats, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters," the party said.
Likud said it had collected hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence from polling stations in Arab communities and was transferring the material to police, the Shin Bet domestic security agency and the Central Elections Committee.
The party cited what it described as thousands of envelopes containing cash alongside ballot slips for Ra'am, an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas. It also alleged threats and violence against polling station officials, multiple voters entering voting booths together, people casting ballots under more than one identity and discrepancies between the number of ballot envelopes and registered voters.
Likud further accused unnamed political operatives of using prohibited voter-mobilization software.
"We demand that the police and Shin Bet conduct a thorough investigation into the theft of the elections by the Arab parties and bring the perpetrators to justice," the party said.
It also demanded immediate action from the Central Elections Committee, arguing that the alleged offenses had compromised the legitimacy of the election results.
"This is a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens," Likud said. "Law enforcement agencies must act firmly and immediately."
Police, however, said their assessment did not support allegations of widespread irregularities.
"We are not aware of any exceptional incidents concerning election integrity," a police official said. "In fact, during the current election, the number of incidents related to election integrity fell by nearly 40% compared with the previous election."
Likud says authorities ignored 1,183 complaints
Despite the police assessment, Likud officials insisted that their allegations had not received adequate scrutiny.
Sagi Keizler, the party's election integrity director for the Arab sector, said Likud had submitted 1,183 complaints to the Central Elections Committee on Election Day, including descriptions of individual incidents and telephone numbers for polling station officials who could corroborate the allegations.
According to Keizler, the complaints included 38 cases of suspected bribery, 25 allegations of improper police intervention, 66 reports of violence or threats, 115 suspected instances of double voting and 408 complaints involving the extraction of voter information.
The categories he identified accounted for 652 complaints. He did not provide a breakdown of the remaining 531.
"These are the complaint figures we submitted to the Central Elections Committee on Election Day itself, including details of the incidents and telephone numbers of committee members who can testify about the complaints," Keizler said.
He also accused police and election authorities of failing to contact witnesses identified by the party.
"Neither the police nor the Elections Committee called a single witness," Keizler said. "Apparently, the conclusion had already been reached in advance."
Police cast doubt on suspected vote-buying case
The suspects, residents of the Bedouin communities of Segev Shalom and Ar'ara in the Negev desert, were detained during an operation by the Southern District's Central Unit.
Police said searches of their homes uncovered envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash, along with ballot slips and other materials suspected of being connected to election offenses. Some envelopes reportedly bore Ra'am's logo.
Investigators initially suspected that the money was intended for distribution to voters in exchange for supporting the party.
The suspects reportedly included a doctor, a transportation driver and another political activist. All three denied wrongdoing.
A court subsequently released the doctor despite police objections, while extending the detention of the other two suspects by five days.
The doctor's attorney said his client had organized meetings to encourage support for Ra'am but had not participated in bribery. The driver's lawyer maintained that the cash discovered at his home was intended to cover transportation expenses.
Another suspect said money found in envelopes was intended as charitable donations for needy families on behalf of the Islamic Movement, the religious and political movement associated with Ra'am.
Police said that although the investigation remains open, investigators have not uncovered significant evidence of wrongdoing and expect the case to be closed. However, several additional suspects were arrested on Thursday.
Ra'am has rejected the allegations, accusing authorities of politically motivated arrests intended to suppress Arab voter turnout.
The party said its activists were detained at their homes before polling stations opened, rather than while attempting to influence voters. It also accused authorities of selectively targeting its members and reported that Ra'am ballot slips had been removed or damaged at polling stations in several Arab communities.
Police have not alleged that Ra'am's leadership was involved in the suspected bribery scheme.
The arrests prompted a criminal investigation into specific allegations of vote-buying but have not substantiated Likud's broader claims of coordinated fraud across Arab polling stations.
Shin Bet chief praises election safeguards
Police were not the only Israeli security authorities to express confidence in the integrity of the election.
During a visit Tuesday to the Central Elections Committee's command center, Zini said the voting process was secure and properly supervised.
"Elections in Israel are secure, properly conducted and supervised in an inspiring manner," Zini said.
"There are challenges, and there are those who try to undermine the process, but under the leadership of Justice Sohlberg and the Israel Police, we are succeeding," he added.
Arab parties' gains complicate coalition negotiations
The allegations have emerged against the backdrop of a politically inconclusive election in which increased participation by Arab citizens helped strengthen the parliamentary representation of predominantly Arab parties.
Preliminary results Wednesday projected that the Joint List, an alliance of Arab political factions led by Yousef Jabareen, would win 11-12 seats, while Ra'am would secure seven to eight. Together, the two parties were expected to hold 18-19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The gains could prove decisive because neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious allies nor the parties seeking to replace him have secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
The results have raised the possibility that opposition parties could seek to form a government with the support of Arab lawmakers, either through a formal coalition agreement or outside parliamentary backing.
Netanyahu and his political allies have repeatedly rejected such arrangements, portraying reliance on Arab parties as a threat to the country's security and political stability.
Ra'am, formally known as the United Arab List, is associated with the southern branch of the Islamic Movement. Under Abbas, the party has pursued a pragmatic approach to parliamentary politics, seeking agreements with Jewish-led parties in exchange for commitments to address longstanding problems affecting Arab communities.
In 2021, Ra'am became the first independent Arab party to formally join a governing coalition when it entered the government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
During the latest election campaign, Abbas indicated that he would consider participating in another government if it committed to addressing violent crime, home demolitions, discrimination and other issues affecting Arab citizens of Israel.
The Joint List, meanwhile, represents a separate alliance of Arab political factions with a different approach to participation in Israeli national politics.

U.S. Air Force plans long-term ASARS-2 support for the U-2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:19:31 UTC
16:19:31 KST

- The U.S. Air Force is seeking companies able to repair and sustain the U-2’s ASARS-2 imaging radar, with industry responses due Nov. 18.
- The notice states the government does not own or have access to the ASARS-2 sensor data.
The U.S. Air Force is looking for companies that can repair and sustain the Advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar System-2, or ASARS-2, the imaging radar carried by the U-2 Dragon Lady spy plane, even as the service asks Congress to retire its last U-2s by the end of fiscal 2027.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s U-2 program office posted the request for information on the federal government’s contracting website on Oct. 22 and amended it on Oct. 28, moving the response deadline from Nov. 13 to Nov. 18 at 3 p.m. Eastern. The notice is market research rather than a solicitation, and it gives no contract value, quantity or period of performance.
Under the contract logistics support the Air Force describes, a contractor would provide engineering support, repair spare assets and resolve system failures on the radar and its ground support equipment. Depot maintenance support teams would handle mission software updates, engineering for parts that are no longer manufactured, engineering change proposals, configuration management, technical manuals, specialized in-plant repair, calibration and integration with other ASARS-related systems on the U-2. The work also carries cybersecurity requirements under NIST SP 800-171 and SP 800-53, Intelligence Community Directive 503 and the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification process.
“The Government does not own or have access to the data for the ASARS-2 sensor,” the notice says.
The Air Force has classified the radar as a noncommercial item and has not yet decided what security clearance the work will require or how much of it would be performed outside the continental United States.
Data rights matter here because Raytheon, now part of RTX, has supplied ASARS for the U-2 since the early 1980s, and federal procurement records list the company as the holder of Air Force engineering and sustainment orders for the ASARS-2A version under contract FA8528-20-D-0023. A new supplier without access to the design data would have to show it can still repair and qualify the components.
The notice describes the radar’s job as producing near-real-time, high-resolution, long-range imagery of the ground day or night and in any weather. Synthetic aperture radar builds a detailed, map-like picture from radar returns as the aircraft moves, so clouds and darkness do not block it. Flying above 21,300 meters (70,000 feet), the U-2 can point the radar deep into territory it is not flying over.
The radar has gone through several versions. The baseline ASARS-2 entered service in the 1980s, and the Air Force received the first ASARS-2A as its replacement in 2001. In 2019, Raytheon said the newer ASARS-2B, built around an active electronically scanned array antenna, doubles the surveillance range of the ASARS-2A while keeping its mapping and imagery resolution. The Air Force’s fiscal 2021 budget request said the 2B replaces the 2A’s front-end components, which had become hard to support because parts were going out of production. The new notice refers only to ASARS-2 and does not say which versions the sustainment work would cover.
ASARS-2B is also slated to fly beyond the U-2: a Pentagon budget reprogramming document confirmed that the radar is part of the sensor suite for the U.S. Army’s High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System (HADES) intelligence business jets.
The notice lands in the middle of a long fight over the U-2’s future. In its fiscal 2027 budget, the Air Force proposed retiring its remaining U-2s by the end of the fiscal year, as part of a plan to divest 149 aircraft. Congress has blocked earlier retirement attempts, and House appropriators’ fiscal 2026 defense bill barred the service from divesting more than eight U-2s. The fleet is still flying: in January, maintainers at Beale Air Force Base, California, launched U-2s under simulated attack during Exercise Dragon Shield.

South Korea suspected of rapprochement with Russia amid the war - FT

South Korea suspected of rapprochement with Russia amid the war - FT
Kyiv • UNN
The voyage of a Korean container ship along the Northern Sea Route has alarmed European diplomats. Seoul denies rapprochement with Moscow and fuel exports.
South Korea's "tilt" toward Russia worries European allies. This is reported by the Financial Times, writes UNN.
Details
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung enthusiastically welcomed the crew of the PanStar Acro container ship, which had returned from an Arctic voyage. Praising the crew's "courage and sense of responsibility" in "distant seas," Lee promised to "respond with unwavering action and open a new path for the Republic of Korea."
European diplomats in Seoul were less inspired. Sailing the Northern Sea Route, which runs along Russia's Arctic coast, shortens travel time to Europe via the Suez Canal by 10 days, but requires significant cooperation from Moscow.
The voyage, the first of its kind in South Korean history and completed this month, has become a symbol of what European officials view as Seoul's diplomatic and commercial rapprochement with Moscow, even as the Kremlin deepens its partnership with North Korea and continues its war against Ukraine, the publication writes.
These concerns intensified following reports this month that more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, were shipped from South Korea to Russia in July and August, including on tankers subject to sanctions by the United Kingdom and the EU, the publication notes.
Seoul's relations with Moscow have led some European diplomats to question whether South Korea—which they regard as a "like-minded" democracy with shared economic and security interests—remains a reliable partner
"[South Koreans] are not actually 'like-minded,'" said one European diplomat from Seoul. "Their position is that the war [in Ukraine] will not last forever, and they want to restore business relations with Russia as soon as possible once it ends."
Some observers say these concerns have intensified under Lee, who took office in June 2025. Mason Richey, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies in Seoul, said that South Korean-Russian relations have been "quietly improving" since last autumn.
In a statement to the Financial Times, South Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said: "The concerns of some circles that South Korea is leaning too heavily toward Russia are contrary to the facts.
As a responsible member of the international community, the South Korean government supports and participates in global efforts aimed at ending the war in Ukraine and restoring peace."
South Korea's national security official denied reports of diesel fuel, gasoline, and aviation fuel exports to Russia, adding that the authorities were investigating whether false information about the destinations had been declared.
Meanwhile, the publication writes, Seoul's relations with Kyiv have deteriorated following a dispute over information released last month concerning the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war from Ukraine to South Korea.

Humanitarian cargo for the residents of occupied Oleshky is planned to be delivered to the city on October 30, with route demining for the mission currently underway, Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets reported.
"The ceasefire has already been in effect for 54 hours. It began on October 27 at 03:00 Kyiv time. The parties are fully abiding by the agreed arrangements; no violations of the ceasefire regime have been recorded," he wrote on Telegram.
According to the Ombudsman, demining is proceeding successfully, while the humanitarian shipment is being assembled in parallel.
Lubinets noted that compliance with the agreements became possible, in particular, thanks to constant communication with Russian Ombudsman Yana Lantratova. He separately thanked First Lady of the United States Melania Trump, who is personally paying attention to the humanitarian mission.
"Our task is to deliver humanitarian aid to the people remaining in the city and ensure the possibility of safe departure for civilians," Lubinets emphasized.
As reported, according to Fox News, the humanitarian operation in Oleshky was agreed upon through the mediation of Melania Trump. The agreement was signed on October 23 by Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets and Russian Ombudsman Yana Lantratova. The ceasefire in the Oleshky area took effect on Tuesday, and the mission will last about a week.
Four American journalists from the Newsmax outlet will be present directly in occupied Oleshky to document the humanitarian mission, U.S First Lady Melania Trump reported.

U.S. Navy pays $23 million to shield warship power grids from hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:01:11 UTC
16:01:11 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Integer Technologies a $23.1 million contract to research zero trust cybersecurity for shipboard power systems.
- Integer will work with Florida State University’s Center for Advanced Power Systems, with research running through October 2030.
The U.S. Navy has awarded South Carolina-based Integer Technologies a $23.1 million contract to research how zero trust cybersecurity can protect the electrical power systems that run its warships, without slowing the split-second controls those systems depend on.
The Office of Naval Research awarded the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract for a program called Threat Resilient Integrated Defense for Enhanced Naval Technologies, or TRIDENT, the Department of War announced in its daily contract list this week. Integer is teaming with Florida State University and its Center for Advanced Power Systems, and work will take place in Columbia, South Carolina, through October 2030. The award is a science and technology effort, meaning it funds research and prototyping, and it does not put a new cybersecurity system on any ship.
The contract calls for investigations into “threat-informed” zero trust architecture frameworks tailored to the cyber-physical security needs of shipboard power systems. Zero trust is a security model that drops the old assumption that anything already inside a network can be trusted. Every user, device and command has to prove it is legitimate each time it asks for access. The Navy wants an architecture that lets a ship monitor the cyber and physical state of its power plant, change its defensive posture as threats change, and keep fighting through an attack while the electrical system keeps performing.
The funding structure is more complex than the headline figure. The contract has a 36-month base period and a 36-month option that would begin 12 months after award and run alongside the base, which is why the whole effort ends about four years from now. The Navy obligated $10.1 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds at award, enough to pay for the full base period, leaving about $13 million tied to the option. Navy research money is available for two years, so the fiscal 2026 funds expire at the end of fiscal 2027, the government’s current budget year. ONR bought the work through its long-range broad agency announcement for Navy and Marine Corps science and technology, an open solicitation that accepts proposals year-round, so the Navy could not say how many bids it received.
The problem TRIDENT is meant to study comes from how warship power has changed. Older surface combatants such as the Arleigh Burke-class destroyers use gas turbines geared directly to the propeller shafts, with separate, smaller generators for electricity. The three Zumwalt-class destroyers were the first U.S. Navy surface combatants built around an integrated power system that generates electricity for both propulsion and weapons. Two Rolls-Royce MT30 main turbine generators and two smaller auxiliary generators produce about 78 megawatts, which feeds the electric motors that turn the shafts and a shipwide grid for sensors, combat systems and hotel loads. The Navy’s planned DDG(X) next-generation destroyer is designed to use a similar integrated power system.
That architecture lets a ship shift power between propulsion and weapons on demand, which matters as electrical loads grow. L3Harris, which builds power distribution equipment for Virginia-class submarines, said this month that advanced radars, directed energy weapons and next-generation propulsion will place extraordinary demands on shipboard power. Laser weapons such as the 60-kilowatt-class HELIOS installed on USS Preble (DDG 88) in 2022 draw their “ammunition” straight from the ship’s electrical system.
It also means a single, software-managed grid now sits underneath nearly everything a warship does. Power is controlled by networked switchboards, power converters, protective relays and a machinery control system that decides how to route electricity and how to isolate a fault before it spreads. Those are operational technology systems: computers whose job is to move physical equipment. If an attacker could send false commands or corrupt the data those controllers rely on, the consequences would be physical, from tripping generators to cutting power to weapons or radars in combat.
The contract identifies two constraints that make zero trust hard to apply aboard ship. The first is latency. Integrated power systems rely on very fast control loops to protect equipment and keep the grid stable, and enterprise zero trust tools typically add checks, such as authentication, encryption and traffic inspection, that take time. A security layer that delays a protective trip or a power transfer by even a short interval could cause the damage it was meant to prevent. The second is the mix of legacy and modern equipment. Ships stay in service for decades and are upgraded in pieces, so a single power plant can contain older controllers that were never designed to authenticate commands alongside newer networked devices. The contract does not say which ship classes or systems the research will model.
Florida State’s Center for Advanced Power Systems is one of the Navy’s main university laboratories for electric ship research. Established in 2000 in Tallahassee, the center operates one of the largest real-time digital power system simulators along with 5-megawatt AC and DC test beds for power hardware-in-the-loop testing, in which real equipment is connected to a simulated ship grid so engineers can stress it under realistic conditions. Cybersecurity for power systems is one of its listed research areas, and it leads the Navy-funded Electric Ship Research and Development Consortium of universities. In June, Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the center an $88 million contract for modeling, simulation and testing of advanced shipboard electrical power and energy systems through 2031.
Integer Technologies is a small business founded in Columbia in 2021 by Duke Hartman and Josh Knight. It has built a portfolio of Navy research work focused on cyber-physical systems, often in partnership with universities. In September, ONR exercised a $10.2 million option on a separate Integer contract with Louisiana State University to develop a cyber-physical resilience framework for Navy maritime platforms, with work running through March 2030. The company was also among more than two dozen firms placed on the Navy’s $982 million multiple-award contract for its Unmanned Surface Vehicle Family of Systems in 2024.
The threat the Navy is preparing for has moved from theory to documented activity on land. In a February 2024 advisory, CISA, the National Security Agency and the FBI assessed with high confidence that Chinese state-sponsored hackers known as Volt Typhoon were pre-positioning themselves on IT networks to enable movement into operational technology and disrupt critical infrastructure in a crisis. The agencies said the group had compromised organizations in the continental United States and its territories, including Guam, a key hub for U.S. forces in the Pacific, and had kept access in some networks for at least five years.
Earlier cases showed what attacks on control systems can do. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, sabotaged Iranian uranium enrichment centrifuges by manipulating their industrial controllers while showing operators normal readings. In December 2015, a cyberattack on Ukrainian power distribution companies cut electricity to roughly 225,000 customers, the first publicly confirmed blackout caused by hackers. Both targeted fixed infrastructure on land, and a warship differs in important ways: its networks are smaller and more tightly controlled, and it often operates with limited outside connectivity. Ships still connect to shore networks in port and receive software and hardware updates from contractors during maintenance, which gives an attacker possible ways in.
The Department of the Navy has led the military services in applying the Pentagon’s 2022 zero trust strategy to enterprise IT, and its officials said in early 2025 that they were preparing zero trust standards for operational technology, the category that includes ship machinery and weapons platforms. TRIDENT is aimed at that harder category, where a security tool has to work within the timing and reliability limits of physical equipment.

US midterms: Five days to go – What the polls say as Trump, Harris campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US midterms: Five days to go – What the polls say as Trump, Harris campaign
With five days until the US midterms, here’s what polls show, the latest campaign news and what’s next.
With five days to go before the United States midterms, Democrats are ahead in national polls, but several Senate races remain close.
President Donald Trump, former President Barack Obama and Vice President JD Vance were out campaigning on Wednesday in Ohio, Georgia and North Carolina, as both parties fight for control of Congress.
Here’s what to know:
What do the latest polls say about the US midterms?
Democrats lead Republicans by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent, a gap of 8.2 percentage points, according to RealClearPolling’s national polling average.
But the national lead is not reflected in every Senate race.
In Texas, where Democrats haven’t won a Senate election since 1988, Democrat James Talarico leads Republican Ken Paxton with 48.5 percent to 46.7 percent, according to the poll aggregator.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has widened his lead over Republican Mike Rogers to seven percentage points, according to a Mitchell Research poll conducted for CBS Detroit.
The October 26-27 survey found El-Sayed leading Rogers 51 percent to 44 percent, up from a 4.2-point advantage earlier this month.
RealClearPolling showed a narrower race, with El-Sayed at 48 percent and Rogers at 46 percent.
Despite that lead, Democrats are continuing to campaign for support among young voters in Michigan.
“We need everybody and young people are a huge part of the coalition and could really be the difference-maker on November 3rd,” Will Lawrence, a Democratic candidate hoping to win Michigan’s 7th Congressional District from the Republicans, told Al Jazeera.
Democratic Congressman Maxwell Frost, who travelled from Florida to campaign for El-Sayed, said face-to-face conversations with voters were particularly important.
“Everyone’s seen the negative bigoted ads and Islamophobic ads, but what hasn’t happened is everyone hasn’t had person-to-person conversation about why Abdul is the right senator for Michigan,” he said.
Republicans are also trying to reach young voters, with one supporter telling Al Jazeera: “I think there’s definitely a movement that people don’t realise in Gen Z that is turning more conservative.”
Beyond Michigan, some voters told Al Jazeera they were frustrated with both parties.
“Each party wants to be in power and I think they’ll say what they think they want their voters to hear,” one voter said in Lexington, Kentucky.
Democratic strategist Joel Rubin described the midterms as a potential “protest election”, with many Democratic voters looking to limit Trump’s power.
“I think that overwhelmingly American voters who will vote Democratic are voting because they want to put a check on President Trump’s power,” he said.
Republican strategist Suhail Khan said Trump was losing support among a number of his own voters, who were frustrated by rising fuel prices, rents and mortgage costs.
“I keep voting and I’m independent, I vote both sides … I’m so frustrated and out of hope,” another voter said in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania.
Can Democrats take control of Congress?
Democrats are hoping to overturn Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress, but the Senate presents a bigger challenge.
They need a net gain of three seats in the House of Representatives and four in the Senate, where Republicans currently hold 53 of the 100 seats. Democrats hold 47, including two independents who caucus with them.
Democrats need to reach 51 seats to take control, but the path to a Senate majority is not simple.
“Even the most optimistic of Republicans will tell you that it’s going to be pretty tough for the GOP to hold on to the House of Representatives,” Al Jazeera’s Scott McLean said. “Different story when it comes to the US Senate, though.”
McLean said that even if Democrats win North Carolina and Ohio and hold on to their current seats, they would still be two seats short of the 51 needed for a majority.
Alaska and Texas could help close that gap. But Republicans are also hoping to win Michigan, where the race remains tight.
Taking control of the House of Representatives alone would still have significant consequences for Trump. If the Democrats flip the House, they can block parts of his legislative agenda and launch investigations into his administration.
They would also be able to call administration officials to testify before congressional committees, although the White House could challenge those demands.
What’s happened on the US midterm campaign trail in the past 24 hours?
Trump was in Ohio campaigning for Republican Senator Jon Husted, who is facing former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.
During the rally, Trump defended Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy following backlash over an advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton.
Ramaswamy was being treated “very unfairly”, Trump said. “How the hell is that his problem?”
Trump also spoke about Jeffrey Epstein after protesters interrupted his speech, saying he had expelled the late sex offender from his Mar-a-Lago club two decades ago.
Meanwhile, in Georgia, former President Obama joined Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms.
Obama criticised Republicans for their reaction to his recent Cheesecake Factory joke about White House renovations, saying they were more concerned about that than the rising cost of living.
“These are not serious people. They don’t have solutions to actual problems,” he said.
Vance also rallied in North Carolina, where former Governor Roy Cooper is facing Republican Michael Whatley in the Senate race.
What’s next for Trump, Democrats and Republicans?
Trump is scheduled to campaign in South Carolina on Thursday at 16:30 GMT, before heading to Florida on Friday and Kansas on Saturday.
South Carolina is among the Republican-held Senate seats Democrats are targeting, although the party faces a difficult contest in a traditionally conservative state.
In Texas, Vice President JD Vance will hold a rally in Weatherford at 17:15 GMT, with Republican candidate Ken Paxton facing a close Senate race against Democrat James Talarico.
Talarico will also be campaigning on Thursday in Dallas, at 00:00 GMT on Friday (7pm Thursday local time).
Al Jazeera’s Phil Lavelle reported from Texas that Republicans are particularly concerned about turnout in rural areas, where 21 percent of registered voters had cast their ballots, compared with 24 percent in the more heavily populated metropolitan areas.
Meanwhile, former Vice President Kamala Harris is expected to campaign in Georgia, where Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is defending his seat against Republican Mike Collins.
Georgia’s early in-person voting ends on Friday as both parties make their final push before Election Day.

Ahead of European markets opening, Asian shares and US futures were mixed on Thursday morning, weighed down by some big technology stocks after Google parent Alphabet’s earnings were lower than expected.
The latest round of US technology giants’ earnings have shaken markets riding on high expectations from investors due to the global craze for artificial intelligence.
Shares of Google parent company Alphabet Inc. fell about 10% in after-hours trading. The California-based technology giant posted quarterly revenues that disappointed investors, raising questions over whether it can generate enough sales to justify its huge investments in AI.

Benchmark US crude fell 1.3% to $101.46 per barrel.

Two Fed officials were in favour of a hike, and a rate hike in December is likely since inflation remains too high, analysts said.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged less than 0.1% higher, to 23,101.86. The Shanghai Composite index shed 0.9% to 3,647.12.
Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.5% to 8,888.50.

‘Looming stone towers like Maya temples’: a hike through Snowdonia’s slate country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

The vital moment comes a couple of hours into the walk. I drop down from a tussocky hill towards the village of Y Fron. There’s an abandoned slate-quarrying machine and a grassy track that suddenly emerges on the rim of a deep lake-filled crater. The water is the colour of an old bruise. Around the rim is a fence of lichen-crusty slates like gravestones. It’s a dark, brooding spectacle and totally unexpected. At that moment, I know that whoever designed this route knew what they were doing.
This is the Llwybr Llechi Eryri (Snowdonia Slate Trail), an 83-mile hike that follows a great loop around the national park, starting in Bangor and ending in Bethesda. It strings together a series of abandoned slate quarries with some of the finest riverside and mountain walking in the UK. I’m doing just three days, starting in Llanberis and heading to Betws-y-Coed via stops in Beddgelert and Llan Ffestiniog.
Beyond Y Fron village, I descend into my first quarry, and it proves to be a classic. This was once the Dorothea slate quarry, a vast abandoned complex of railways, cottages and chasms. I start exploring: tunnels, cuttings, huge looming stone towers like Maya temples, all overgrown with ash, birch and oak. What strikes me is the craftsmanship and precision in construction, each stone hand-fitted without mortar, all for workaday industrial buildings.
The quality of this slate was known from early times. Edward I is thought to have had his Welsh castles roofed with it, but industrial production began in the 1820s and peaked in the 1870s. Soon, there was a railway to Caernarfon and the area bristled with steam pumps, aerial cables and chains. The last-ever Cornish beam engine was installed to pump water from the deep pits, sucking up 10 gallons a second from 500ft down.
From here, the trail burrows eastwards into the Welsh mountains, until Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) appears on the horizon when it turns south, occasionally following the line of the Welsh Highland Railway all the way into Beddgelert, my first overnight stop. Named after a dog or a saint, depending on who you believe, this is a good base for hikers, having pubs, cafes, restaurants and outdoor gear shops.
The second day begins along a path combining the Slate Trail and the Cambrian Way, one of the grandees of the long-distance genre at 298 miles. I follow the route as it heads south along the River Glaslyn, with some spectacular sections on crags with the torrent below. We are getting along very nicely – so well, in fact, that I start to get footpath envy. When the Cambrian Way turns east, heading up the Matterhorn-shaped peak of Cnicht, I cannot resist. The weather forecast is bad, but the sun is out. If I pop over the peak, I can see how the two paths cross each other later.
Views of the Irish Sea open up as I climb, but there is an ominous black cloud approaching. As I reach the summit, a howling wind threatens to blow me off course. I face down the hailstones and get back to the Slate Trail, which now descends into Cwmorthin quarry. Not on the scale of Dorothea, Cwmorthin still seems epic today, dominated by vast heaps of spoiled stone – it took 10 tons to make 1 ton of marketable material. In the late 19th century, Cwmorthin was known locally as “the slaughterhouse” for its propensity to slay workers in fatal accidents. From here, the path runs down a desolate valley before dropping into Blaenau Ffestiniog, where I find a good cafe, Burrito Blasus, to fire me up the last miles into Llan Ffestiniog.
I stay in the Y Pengwern, a community-owned pub that has an excellent, friendly bar and basic rooms and food. Outside, a storm is buffeting the building, but the next day the rain has stopped and I begin with a rare treat: a magical trail beside the tumbling River Cynfal. Here, thunderous white spumes of water and dark powerful currents punch their way through a deep mossy gorge overhung by ancient fern-decked oaks. One of the midstream rock towers is said to have once been the “pulpit” of a magician called Huw Llwyd and, according to the 18th-century traveller and naturalist Thomas Pennant, his voice could be heard at night, ringing down the enchanted chasms.
As I climb higher, the forest dwindles and I emerge on a remote, wind-scoured upland of crags and bog. Even here, you can come across fragments of old quarry workings. In one abandoned cottage, a jacket still hangs on a nail behind the door, as if the occupant had just flounced out: “I’ve had enough. I’m off to America.” Many Welsh slate workers did head to the US, fed up with the poor pay and the repeated failure of strikes. In 1901, sympathetic workers in England sent a two-and-a-half ton Christmas pudding, which briefly lifted morale, but after violent clashes the landowner won, and many quarrymen emigrated.
I stop and brew some tea on my stove. I have not seen another soul all day, yet Yr Wyddfa, with all its crowds, is less than 10 miles away. This remote walk takes me to the top of the old tramway incline down to Rhiwbach quarry – an epic approach, descending to the old engine house. This place peaked in the 1860s, and being so isolated, the miners lived in barracks, some of which remain.
Farther down the valley, I spot peregrine falcons nesting close to a tumbling waterfall, above the little village of Cwm Penmachno. A few miles on, the church of St Tudclud contains an astonishing collection of inscribed stones, including the Carausius Stone. This is thought to be the gravestone of a commander of the Roman empire, who pulled off a coup d’etat in AD286, making himself emperor of Britain and northern Gaul for seven years before his assassination.
Approaching Betws-y-Coed, the path joins the River Conwy, first singled out as a beauty spot in the 17th century, long before the Romantic poets seized on the idea. For me, it’s the finale to this fine route, but the path continues and I’ll be back soon for more mountains of slate and spectacular riverside walking.
The trip was provided by Walkers’ Britain & Europe, which offers Hiking the Snowdonia Slate Trail as a seven-day self-guided 83-mile walk, including six nights’ accommodation, breakfast, luggage transfers, digital app with tour information and navigations, and emergency hotline from £890pp, departing daily from April to October

‘Just come in’: 30 years of Maggie’s cancer care centres – in pictures

‘Just come in’: 30 years of Maggie’s cancer care centres – in pictures
A new photography exhibition marks 30 years of Maggie’s centres, which offer free practical, emotional and social support to people affected by cancer. Inspired by the phrase ‘just come in’ – the ethos at the centre of every Maggie’s – photographer Tabitha Jussa’s images document the everyday moments of comfort, conversation and pause that unfold within the centres
Maggie’s centre in Wirral. Tabitha Jussa created each large photograph using a large-format camera fixed in one position. Shot on film and digitally layered, each image brings together many moments recorded over the course of an hourPhotograph: Tabitha Jussa
Maggie’s Dundee. The centres offer free practical, emotional and social support to people affected by cancer in calm, non-institutional buildings that welcome visitors and provide a humane atmospherePhotograph: Tabitha Jussa
A Maggie’s centre in Southampton. The photography display explores thresholds – entrances, doorways and transitional spaces – and the experience of arriving at Maggie’s centresPhotograph: Tabitha Jussa
Oldham Maggie’s centre. The images show how architecture can communicate care and empathy, and how crossing a threshold can be the first step towards receiving supportPhotograph: Tabitha Jussa
Dundee, from the Incidental series. Alongside the Together series, Jussa made this series of analogue film photographs capturing the quieter details of each centrePhotograph: Tabitha Jussa
Maggie’s centre in Edinburgh: silver gelatin black and white prints. Selected 35mm film photographs were developed using a coffee-based developer and then printed by hand in the darkroom, where light is projected through the negative onto light-sensitive paper before being developed into a physical printPhotograph: Tabitha Jussa
Maggie’s Edinburgh: cyanotypecreated with foraged flora. Using a 19th-century photographic process, Jussa gathered plants from centre gardens and placed them on light-sensitive handmade paper exposed to sunlight, creating delicate blue silhouettesPhotograph: Tabitha Jussa

Singapore import, export prices rise on higher oil costs

2026-10-29
14:51:00 CST
15:51:00 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's import and export prices rose at a faster pace in September, driven mainly by higher oil and petroleum product prices, official data showed on Thursday.
The Import Price Index (IPI) increased 4.7 percent month on month in September, accelerating from 1.6 percent in August and marking its third consecutive monthly gain, the Department of Statistics said in a statement.
The oil index surged 16.1 percent, compared with the 4.8 percent increase in August, while the non-oil index rose 0.2 percent.
Year on year, the IPI climbed 19.9 percent, up from 15.5 percent in August. The oil index jumped 78.5 percent, while the non-oil index rose 4.4 percent.
Meanwhile, the Export Price Index (EPI) rose 3.6 percent month on month, compared with 1.9 percent in August. Its oil index increased 12.7 percent, while the non-oil index rose 0.9 percent.
Year on year, the EPI gained 19.4 percent, up from 15.2 percent in August. The oil index surged 69.9 percent, while the non-oil index increased 8.3 percent.
The increases in the non-oil indices were mainly driven by higher prices of electrical machinery apparatus, including electronic integrated circuits, the department said. ■

Restored nature hits record 252 million hectares, but still off target: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:50:00 UTC
15:50:00 KST

Restored nature hits record 252 million hectares, but still off target: UN
PARIS – Countries are restoring about 252 million hectares of nature, a record level according to a United Nations report published on Oct 29, but this still falls short of global 2030 targets.
“This report captures the largest documented restoration effort in history,” said Doreen Robinson at the UN Environment Programme in Nairobi at a press conference.
The restored area is equivalent to the size of Argentina or Algeria.
But the report estimates the pace of restoration efforts must “triple” to meet the 2030 target of one billion, and funding will need to increase sharply, particularly from the private sector.
Nature restoration efforts recorded in 149 countries have mostly taken place on land, with 232 million hectares involved, compared with 11 million hectares of inland waters and 5.7 million hectares of marine and coastal waters.
This “lags far behind ambition in both freshwater (inland water) and marine and coastal ecosystems, yet these ecosystems are degrading at the highest rates”, the report warned.
As part of the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration from 2021 to 2030, and an international agreement adopted in 2022 known as the Kunming-Montreal framework, states have committed to taking action to halt biodiversity loss and protect the planet.
The Kunming-Montreal framework aims to protect 30% of terrestrial and marine areas by the end of the decade.
Beyond nature restoration, which can include measures such as replanting trees, the process has also boosted employment with one million related jobs created and a goal of reaching 32 million by 2030.
In terms of restoration on land, China is far ahead of other regions, with 137 million hectares, followed by Mongolia, Kazakhstan and Ethiopia.
The report was published during the key biodiversity COP17 summit in Armenia running until the end of the week. AFP

Türkiye hosts 13th OTS summit to further ‘unity in language, thought, deed’
Unknown

2026-10-29

15:49:06 KST

- Leaders’ summit to be held Friday, with a meeting of Organization of Turkic States Council of Foreign Ministers to take place Thursday
- Experts tell Anadolu that summit is expected to bring results related to economy, transport
Türkiye is set to host the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) to further “unity in language, thought, and deed” among its member states.
The summit, to be held on Thursday and Friday in the Turkish capital Ankara, will be hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, under the theme Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.
Established in 2009, the OTS, formerly known as the Turkic Council, adopted its current name during its eighth summit held in the Turkish metropolis Istanbul in 2021.
While Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan are members, Turkmenistan, Hungary, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, and the Economic Cooperation Organization hold observer status.
The organization said on Oct. 24 that the summit will bring together the heads of state of its member states, as well as high-level representatives from observer states and its secretary general, to “discuss the current state and future prospects of cooperation within the Organization,” among other issues.
It said in a statement that the heads of state are expected to review the progress achieved across the OTS’ priority areas, and that particular emphasis will be placed on “further strengthening unity and solidarity” among the Turkic states and advancing cooperation under the Turkic World Vision 2040.
It added that the summit will also mark Türkiye’s assumption of the OTS’ chairmanship from Azerbaijan, and is expected to address the appointment of a new secretary general and the organization’s strategic priorities “for the forthcoming period.”
“The Heads of State are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, together with a number of decisions and documents aimed at deepening cooperation and further strengthening the institutional framework of the OTS,” it added.
The leaders’ summit will be held Friday, and a meeting of the organization's Council of Foreign Ministers will take place on Thursday.
 
‘Unity in deed’
Turan Gafarli, a non-resident fellow at the Baku-based Topchubashov Center, defined support among Turkic states and bolstering their political solidarity as the significant aspect of the Ankara summit.
Noting that they are living through a period in which the world faces “increasing uncertainty,” Gafarli told Anadolu that the Turkic world is evolving into a political structure that is “developing the capacity to act in unison in the face of international developments.”
“Naturally, this is a long-term process. Yet, the true meaning of brotherhood is not just coming together during good times, but standing by one another during difficult ones,” he said, noting his belief that the summit in Türkiye will further solidify the “atmosphere of trust built to date.”
Gafarli highlighted the term of unity used in the summit’s theme as “highly significant,” as well as expressed belief that the summit will give momentum to developments particularly in the realms of economic relations, transport corridors, and political coordination.
He stated the growing strategic importance of the Middle Corridor presented a “historic opportunity” for the Turkic states to become more closely interconnected economically, but that this requires a number of steps, including bolstering trade between member states.
“Furthermore, it is essential that the Turkic states engage in closer consultation on international issues and advocate more robustly for their shared interests,” he also said, adding he believes Türkiye’s chairmanship could bring fresh dynamism in this context.
Meanwhile, Shairbek Dzhuraev, the president of the Crossroads Central Asia research institute based in Bishkek, shared the belief that tangible progress has been observed most evidently in the economic sphere, underlining transport and transit in particular.
“The development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route depends on the harmonization of tariffs and the simplification of customs procedures. In this context, results can be measured by the time and cost involved in transporting goods,” Dzhuraev said.
Dzhuraev further underlined digitalization as a second promising area, which he defined as the focus of the organization’s informal summit held in Turkistan in southern Kazakhstan in May.
“The most substantial outcome of the Ankara summit would be the establishment of concrete timelines and mechanisms for implementing decisions already reached – particularly those concerning transport and trade,” he stated.
As part of the OTS Ankara summit, sports is also an area where unity is expected to be shown “in deed.”
During a news conference in Ankara ahead of the summit, Kursad Zorlu, the Justice and Development (AK) Party's deputy chair in charge of relations with Turkic states, said the event includes plans for players from Turkic states to be classified as domestic rather than foreign in one another’s leagues, saying the initiative would foster a football ecosystem across the Turkic world.

"The Federal Security Service, together with the Interior Ministry and the Investigative Committee, continues to document instances of Ukrainian special services using the popular Dayvinchik/Leo match bot on Telegram to recruit Russian citizens into sabotage and terrorist activities through deception and psychological manipulation," the statement said.
"In August and September 2026 alone, eight minors (aged 14 to 17) and two adult Russian citizens (aged 19 and 24) were detained in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and the Leningrad, Nizhny Novgorod, Omsk, Ryazan, and Sverdlovsk Regions for either plotting or carrying out arson attacks on law enforcement vehicles, gas stations, and energy and transport infrastructure facilities on the orders of Ukrainian special services, as well as for acting as couriers to transfer funds obtained from defrauded citizens to cryptocurrency exchange points," the press office noted. Since July 2025, 56 Russians aged 12 to 24 have been detained in various regions of Russia. They used the Telegram Dayvinchik/Leo match bot and committed crimes under the psychological influence of Ukrainian intelligence agencies, the FSB emphasized.
According to the press office, "Ukrainian intelligence officers posed as young people to make online contact with Russian users via the Telegram match bot. During these conversations, which were intended to develop romantic relationships, the Russian users sent their geolocation data, paid for restaurant reservations in advance, and clicked on phishing links," the statement said. The users were then contacted by impostors posing as representatives of the FSB or Russia’s financial watchdog Rosfinmonitoring, who threatened that the funds they had sent had allegedly been transferred to Ukrainian military accounts and that the geolocation data provided would be used to launch missile strikes or drone attacks.
"After that, the deceived and intimidated citizens, who were unable to critically assess the situation due to psychological pressure, were coerced, under the threat of criminal prosecution, into committing arson to test the anti-terrorism security of the targeted facilities and into participating in other pseudo-operational activities," the FSB noted.
As a result, the deceived teenagers and young adults became defendants in criminal cases involving terrorism, attempted terrorism, or intentional destruction or damage to property. Those who have reached the age of criminal responsibility have been charged. Given the severity of the crimes, they face lengthy prison terms, the press office added.

Afghanistan opium production jumps fivefold as farmers find ways round Taliban ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:45:16 UTC
15:45:16 KST

Afghanistan opium production jumps fivefold as farmers find ways round Taliban ban
Opium production in Afghanistan has risen fivefold in a year. According to a UN survey released on Thursday, it’s the first significant increase since the Taliban banned poppy cultivation in 2022.
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) found that the area planted with opium poppy grew by 330 per cent, to more than 43,000 hectares, up from about 10,000 hectares in 2025.
Estimated production rose by 400 per cent, from about 300 tonnes to just under 1,500 tonnes.
Both figures remain well below levels before the ban, when some 232,000 hectares were under cultivation.
For decades, Afghanistan was the world’s biggest source of illicit opium. Before the ban, it accounted for around 80 per cent of global supply.
The Taliban seized power in August 2021. In April 2022, they outlawed poppy cultivation and all narcotics, citing religious grounds.
Hidden in cereal fields
The de facto authorities say they eradicated 22,000 hectares of poppy this year. But UNODC said many farmers appear to have adapted to evade enforcement. Some are hiding small plots within cereal fields or inside walled compounds. Others are planting and harvesting at staggered intervals to avoid detection.
“The fourfold increase in opium poppy cultivation shows the difficulty in sustaining decreases in illicit opium cultivation when poor farmers have no alternatives to feed their families,” said UNODC Executive Director Monica Juma.
She urged the de facto authorities and the international community to work together to support farming communities, by investing in livelihoods, farm infrastructure and access to markets.
Shift to the northeast
Cultivation spread to 16 of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces, five more than last year. Three in every four hectares were in the northeast, now firmly the country’s main growing area. Before the ban, most poppy was grown in the southwest.
Prices dipped from $570 a kilogramme last year to $500 but remain far above pre-ban levels of under $100. UNODC said large regional price differences may encourage trafficking from the northeast to the southwest.
Stockpiles running low
The survey said traffickers in the region appear to have relied on opium stockpiles to keep supplies moving since the ban.
But recent seizure data suggest those stocks are running down. The 2026 World Drug Report also found early signs that heroin supplies in Europe are falling.
With demand holding up and prices high, shrinking supplies could push cultivation in Afghanistan higher still.
“International cooperation is needed to investigate and dismantle transnational drug trafficking networks both in Afghanistan and the rest of the world,” Ms. Juma said.
UNODC said continued monitoring would show whether this year’s jump is temporary or the start of a resurgence in opium and heroin production.

Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, elder statesman of Mexican left, dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:26:14 UTC
15:26:14 KST

Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, elder statesman of Mexican left, dies at 92
MEXICO CITY, Oct 28 - Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, an icon of the Mexican left who took up the banner of the disenfranchised in the 1980s to force changes in the political system despite never winning the presidency himself, has died at 92, the government said on Wednesday.
The first elected mayor of Mexico City, and the son of President Lazaro Cardenas, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas shook Mexico's ruling establishment to its foundations when he ran for the top job in 1988 before losing a hotly disputed election.
That election pitted Cardenas against young technocrat Carlos Salinas, candidate of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, which had dominated Mexico since 1929.
With the two running neck-and-neck on election night, the government suddenly announced the system counting the votes had crashed.
After it came back online, Salinas was declared the winner, although many analysts and Cardenas himself believed the PRI had rigged the vote to retain its hold on power.
The contest was a watershed in Mexico, leading to political reform that strengthened the opposition. Two presidential elections later, in 2000, the PRI was finally ousted.
"His role in Mexico's contemporary history is fundamental," said President Claudia Sheinbaum, hailing Cardenas' impact on Mexican politics.
"In 1988, he led a peaceful democratic movement that channeled the desire for change of millions of Mexicans," she said on social media, alluding to his supporters' belief that he was the rightful winner of the disputed presidential election.
"That historic election, in which he should have been recognized as president, marked the beginning of the democratic transformation."
Cardenas ran unsuccessfully for president twice more, fronting a leftist ticket for the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), which he helped found after breaking with the PRI in 1987. He finished third in 1994 and 2000.
Between those bids, the tall, soft-spoken Cardenas became mayor of Mexico City in 1997, beginning a long run for the PRD at the helm of the capital.
The PRD’s power waned after Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who followed in Cardenas’ footsteps as Mexico City mayor, split from it to found his own Morena party, which became the main force of the Mexican left and propelled him to the presidency.
But Cardenas' early backing of the PRD marked a turning point in Mexican politics following decades of PRI domination.
It was Cardenas who finally galvanised leftist opposition to the PRI, said historian Lorenzo Meyer, adding, "And he had the capacity to mobilise."
Cardenas paved the way for subsequent leftist challenges to the highest office, campaigning in remote villages never before visited by presidential candidates.
In later years, he emerged as an occasional critic of Lopez Obrador, a polarizing, often abrasive figure who succeeded him as the standard-bearer of the left and captured the top job in 2018.
Lopez Obrador raised huge protests when he too was denied victory in a bitterly contested presidential election in 2006, and again cried foul six years later. But the dignified Cardenas remained the left's spiritual leader for many Mexicans.
Cardenas believed free market economics would not save Mexico from economic malaise, favoring a more state-centric model, similar to that later embraced by Lopez Obrador.
COALITION BUILDER
Cardenas was born in Mexico City on May 1, 1934, the first year of his father's six-year term. A champion of land reform who nationalized the oil industry in 1938, Lazaro Cardenas was one of the most popular presidents in Mexican history.
Ironically, the late president's success helped fortify the PRI, whose legitimacy his son later challenged.
Cardenas earned an engineering degree in 1957, then spent two years in France, West Germany and Italy on a fellowship.
After returning to Mexico, he began a career as a planner and hydraulic engineer, and entered politics in 1976 as a senator for his home state of Michoacan.
As PRI governor for Michoacan from 1980 to 1986, Cardenas was seen by some as too aloof to be a compelling administrator, but his reputation for honesty stood apart from the party’s growing association with graft in the minds of many Mexicans.
Michoacan became a bastion of the PRD, and Cardenas' son, called Lazaro like his grandfather, also served as governor.
The younger Lazaro later took up senior roles under Lopez Obrador and Sheinbaum, preserving the Mexican left’s historic ties with the family.
The challenge to the PRI by Cardenas began in late 1986 when he helped form the Democratic Current within the party.
The Current led calls for the PRI to adopt a more democratic means of selecting its presidential candidate, but these were ignored and leading members left the party in 1987.
"The PRI leadership has stopped our campaign for more open procedures within the party, but we will continue the struggle for true democracy in Mexico," Cardenas said at the time.
Impressed by his coalition-building skills, newspaper El Financiero once described Cardenas as the sole candidate "who can gather leftist militants, neoliberals, and even ecologists." REUTERS

'Inexplicable'
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said on Wednesday that an automatic control system went down on 69 kilometres (43 miles) of track, causing all trains there to be stopped.
But the control centre decided to "resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable," Puente said, with the Renfe train travelling 25 kilometres before striking the Iryo.
The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it", he added.
Read moreRail safety questioned after Spain suffers second fatal high-speed train crash in a year
In January, two high-speed trains collided in the southern region of Andalusia after one of them derailed and crossed onto the adjacent track, killing 46 people.
The investigation into that accident is ongoing, but the left-wing government faced heavy criticism over its management of Spain's railways.
The latest disaster comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on November 29.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Europe’s wealth gap: Older households eight times richer than young ones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:25:02 UTC
15:25:02 KST

Europe’s wealth gap: Older households eight times richer than young ones
As protests over living costs and programme cuts spread across Europe, under-35s hold 2.8 percent of household wealth.
Student protests that began in September in France have spread to more than 11 European countries as anger rises over high rents and fuel prices and cuts to public services.
Many young protesters said they no longer expect to be better off than their parents, and household wealth data show a wide gap between generations.
Across the eurozone and two other European countries, households headed by someone under 35 have a median net wealth of about 25,000 euros ($27,870) while those headed by 55- to 64-year-olds are worth about 208,000 euros ($231,882), more than eight times as much, according to the European Central Bank’s (ECB’s) 2023 Household Finance and Consumption Survey.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera compares wealth by age groups across 22 European countries and looks at how much more expensive life has become since 2000.
Where is the wealth gap widest?
The Household Finance and Consumption Survey, run by the ECB and national central banks since 2010, tracks household wealth and debt in the eurozone, the Czech Republic and Hungary.
It measures net wealth, which includes property, cars, valuables and savings, minus debts. Under-35s hold just 2.8 percent of all household wealth in the 22 countries while 55- to 64-year-olds hold the largest share at 24 percent.
In Finland, under-35s hold 0.8 percent of household wealth, the lowest share of any country surveyed, while over-55s hold more than 71 percent. Young people’s shares are also small in Ireland (1.4 percent), Austria (1.6 percent), Greece (1.8 percent) and Germany (2 percent).
Rising housing costs mean many young people cannot afford what their parents or grandparents could.
Wealth is more evenly spread in Central and Eastern Europe. In Lithuania, under-35s hold 13.2 percent, against 15.9 percent for 55- to 64-year-olds. Their share is 12.3 percent in Croatia, 10.1 percent in Slovakia and 9.8 percent in Estonia. Malta, at 11.1 percent, is the exception outside the two regions.
The graphic below shows how household wealth is split between age groups in each country surveyed.
“What we’ve seen is actually a very strong increase in housing prices both in terms of the rental market as well as the ownership market,” Evelyn Astor of the European Social Observatory told Al Jazeera’s Counting the Cost programme.
“All of this is also reinforcing a sense of inequality because ultimately ordinary families are struggling to pay their rents or be able to purchase their homes whereas wealthy people with capital are able to make rather significant investments in the European housing market,” she said.
How much more expensive is it than 2000?
Prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, energy, transport and household bills, have risen by 67.2 percent in the eurozone, Hungary and the Czech Republic since 2000.
Of the countries in our chart, Hungary has seen the steepest rise with prices more than tripling, according to Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency. Its harmonised index of consumer prices is the EU’s official measure of how much everyday goods and services cost.
The chart below shows how consumer prices have changed in each country since 2000 with prices in 2000 set at 100 on the index.
Eastern European countries have seen the sharpest increases – particularly since 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began – because many relied heavily on Russian energy supplies.
Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average until 2022 when annual inflation in the EU hit 9.2 percent.
The surge was driven mainly by energy costs. Inflation has since eased, but the price rises of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine have not reversed.
