Taliban’s poppy ban falters as Afghan farmers say they can’t feed their children
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:19:46 CET
15:19:46 KST

By Mohammad Yunus Yawar , Sayed Hassib and Ahmad Masih Noori
BABA YUSUF, Afghanistan, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Carpets still hang on the walls of Mohammad Dawood’s home in a northern Afghanistan village, and ornate mirrors still catch the light, relics of the years when a single poppy harvest could carry his family through the year.
But the 28-year-old says he now spends his days bent over cotton and wheat in fields that barely provide a living.
“We were doing well,” he said in an interview in his home in the Baba Yusuf village of Balkh province. “Now, my children are malnourished.”
In years gone by, Afghanistan’s poppy fields produced about 80% of the world’s opium, used in the manufacture of morphine as well as in illegal drugs like heroin.
Four years ago, the Taliban began enforcing an opium ban so strict that poppy all but vanished from Afghanistan’s fields. But now their Supreme Leader’s edict is beginning to fray, worn down by a practical problem: legal crops no longer pay and many Afghan farmers say they are struggling to feed their children.
Some are turning back to poppy, and cultivation rose sharply this year, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime reported on Thursday, in a reversal that could reshape heroin markets as far away as Europe.
Many farmers “don’t have any other choice than to go back to poppy cultivation,” Polleak Ok Serei, UNODC’s country representative for Afghanistan, told Reuters.
Dawood said he is still complying with the ban. But on a bad day, he makes one-fortieth of what he used to make with poppy, he said.
Not all of his neighbours are complying. Balkh, which UNODC found to be poppy-free last year, is growing poppy again this year, the agency reported, although few farmers would dare admit it amid continued Taliban scrutiny.
Cultivation across Afghanistan more than quadrupled this year from 2025 to an estimated 43,300 hectares, according to satellite imagery analysed by the UN. Farmers now hide the poppies from Taliban officials inside cereal fields and behind mud walls.
Cultivation is still only at about a quarter of the 177,000 hectares planted in 2021, the year before the ban was imposed by the Taliban.
But opium sales in Afghanistan generated an estimated $525 million this year, the highest figure since 2018 with the exception of 2022 when the Taliban’s ban made prices skyrocket, UNODC said.
The Taliban rejected the report’s findings, saying actual cultivation was about half the UN estimate and that poppy eradication efforts continued.
The Taliban-run Interior Ministry did not respond to a request for comment by Reuters.
FALLING FARM INCOMES AND CHILD MALNUTRITION
In the country’s farmlands, aid groups say, the economic pressure has become severe.
The toll is increasingly visible among children. UN agencies warned this month that 10 out of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces had critical levels of child malnutrition this year and the number could climb to 14 in 2027.
Despite better harvests, they said, high costs and low crop prices are squeezing poorer farmers and limiting families’ access to food.
Foreign aid cuts and the Taliban’s international isolation over their crackdown on women’s rights have also played a significant role, diplomats say. But at the Alam Khil health center in Balkh, doctors and patients primarily blamed declining farm income for the growing number of severe malnutrition cases the clinic treats.
Outside the clinic, Tahira, whose husband grows cotton, waited for treatment with one of her four children, 7-month-old Benjamin, who was suffering from fever and diarrhea.
“The doctors say he is malnourished,” she said, adding that the family was barely making ends meet. “Our lives used to be good.”
The clinic is surrounded by cotton fields, where white tufts still waited to be picked.
Salima Mohammadi, a nutrition nurse at the clinic, said many families had struggled to find another crop that could support them since poppy disappeared from local fields.
“People own farmland,” she said, “but agricultural yields decrease year after year.”
INTERNATIONAL FALLOUT
What happens in fields like these will have repercussions far beyond Afghanistan. A full return to poppy production would have major implications for global drug markets, analysts say.
“Combine this with the active trafficking networks within the country and the resilient smuggling operations to get the opiates out of the country, and you have a very bleak prediction for the future,” said Paddy Ginn, an analyst with the Geneva-based Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.
Until the ban, the crop from the country’s poppy fields fuelled health crises across the world, corruption along the trafficking routes that carried it to Europe as heroin and deadly clashes between counter-narcotics forces and smugglers.
After 2022, pre-ban stockpiles initially cushioned the global shortage and blunted price spikes in Europe, giving Afghan farmers less reason to openly defy the ban. But UNODC warned on Thursday that those stockpiles may be running out, strengthening the incentive to plant again.
The Taliban regard the ban as one of their signature achievements and have cited it in their efforts to win international legitimacy.
But Taliban officials themselves have publicly acknowledged the challenges in recent years. Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban’s foreign minister, said at a meeting this month that “support for alternative livelihoods for farmers” was crucial to “ensure the continuation and strengthening of this campaign.”
But UNODC’s Ok Serei said there “was not enough support for alternative livelihoods” either from the Taliban government or the international community.
DROUGHT, WHEAT AND COTTON PRICES SQUEEZE FARMERS
The Taliban’s first ban, in 2000, collapsed about a year later, when US-led forces drove them from power after the September 11, 2001, attacks.
The current ban has lasted far longer, but the farmers expected to uphold it face harsher conditions than a generation ago. Recurring droughts have shrunk rivers and canals.
Drought has choked off much of the fresh water in the fields around Baba Yusuf, said Gul Nazar, a 56-year-old landowner, leaving well water so briny that it damages crops.
Legal alternatives have faltered, too. Wheat barely covers its costs, farmers in Baba Yusuf said. Cotton prices have fallen by about two-thirds amid a sudden nationwide glut, Gul Nazar said, a slump he partly blames on Pakistan’s closure of the border late last year, which cut off a key buyer.
Higher-value crops promoted by aid groups, such as orchard fruit or nuts, take years to establish and depend on reliable water and open export routes.
More than four in five households in Balkh and two nearby provinces reported in a UNODC survey last year that they had replaced none or only part of their lost poppy income.
Gul Nazar said he would not grow poppy again if his family’s living conditions improved. But if they grew worse, he said, he could not promise the same.
“When a person becomes hungry,” he said, “they will do anything.”
(Writing by Rick Noack; Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan)

BHUBANESWAR, India, Oct 29 (Reuters) - At least six people were killed and power supply in several areas along India’s eastern coast remained disrupted on Thursday, one day after Cyclone Arnab barrelled through the region, bringing heavy rain and gusty winds, officials said.

More than 180,000 people had been evacuated in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha ahead of the cyclone’s arrival.
Some schools were closed and some train and flight services cancelled.
Arnab formed over the Bay of Bengal, a major region for tropical cyclones that has spawned deadly storms on India’s east coast.

'It's just cold and silent': Ragnar Jónasson and Yrsa Sigurðardóttir on the rise of Icelandic Noir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:16:52 UTC
15:16:52 KST

As crime fiction continues to dominate Iceland's book charts, two of its best selling authors — Ragnar Jónasson and Yrsa Sigurðardóttir — sat down with Euronews Culture to discuss why one of the safest countries in the world is so drawn to literary darkness.
In an age of overwhelming uncertainty and anxiety, people continue to seek solace in the dark and gritty worlds of crime fiction.
One of the best selling literary genres across Europe, crime fiction has become especially popular in the United Kingdom and Nordic countries — a recent survey by Storytel Group found that crime and thrillers ranked as the most popular audiobook genres in Sweden, Norway, Finland and Poland.
This will come as no surprise to most, with Nordic Noir a pillar of the genre; known for its atmospheric bleakness, complex characters, and slow-burn procedural thrills — many of which have been turned into popular TV series. But under its umbrella exists Icelandic Noir, a subset of stories that derive their psychological suspense from the country's uniquely isolated geography.
Ragnar Jónasson and Yrsa Sigurðardóttir are often referred to as the King and Queen of this particular genre — one that has become a astonishing phenomenon amongst residents of one of the safest places in the world.
Jónasson, who started out translating the novels of legendary British crime author Agatha Christie, has written eight standalone books alongside two hugely popular series: Dark Iceland and Hulda. The latter was later adapted into The Darkness TV series, starring Lena Olin and directed by Lasse Hallström.
Sigurðardóttir, a civil engineer who began her writing career with children's fiction, has authored 5 standalone crime novels and three major series, including Black Ice, Þóra Guðmundsdóttir and Freyja and Huldar. Two have been made into feature films: Ég man þig (2017) and Kuldi (2023).
Both have sold millions of copies around the world, won multiple awards, and jointly founded the prestigious Iceland Noir festival (alongside author Quentin Bates) in 2013.
At this year's edition of the festival in November, more details will be revealed about an upcoming book they've collaborated on (more on that below).
While recently appearing at London's Taste of Iceland Festival, Euronews Culture sat down with Jónasson and Sigurðardóttir to discuss the unique characteristics of Icelandic Noir, their upcoming projects — and why you should always kill the good guys in crime fiction.
If you had to describe Iceland as a character in a few words, what would it be?
Yrsa Sigurðardóttir (YS): It's just cold and silent.
Ragnar Jónasson (RJ): It's like a tiger, in a way. Beautiful, strong, but it can also be harsh and cruel.
What is it that separates Icelandic Noir from broader Nordic Noir?
RJ: We have this island mentality and we have this pretty awful weather all year long, which I think makes our stories a little bit darker, and a little bit more linked to nature and the elements. We have this big island with a small population, so there's just a different tone to the whole thing. We don't have a big metropolis.
YS: Like Ragnar mentioned, the population is small, so the degrees of separation between people is quite low, meaning that the stories often revolve around more interpersonal things than, for example, syndicated crime or something that we don't have much of. But also, when you have places where everybody knows everybody, reputation is something that matters a lot to people, and people will take desperate measures to keep their reputation intact, which is very often used in Icelandic crime fiction as well.
Despite being one of the safest countries in the world, crime novels have become the most popular literary genre in Iceland. Why do you think this is?
YS: I think the Icelandic reader is really no different from elsewhere, and so crime fiction is a popular genre the world over. It offers the reader the promise that this crime will be solved and justice will be served, in most cases. And that's something that you can't rely on in the real world. So, it's escapism. It also offers the writer and the reader a very good opportunity to test characters. It's a fun way of writing about people, really. So crime fiction does revolve, of course, around the crime, but mostly around character.
RJ: We also have a lot of writing and literature in our DNA. And if we go back to the Icelandic sagas from the Middle Ages, some of those were also thrillers in a way. They dealt with revenge and killings and honour and law and legal battles. And just, you know, people fighting for their position. And these are thrilling stories with a lot of crime drama. We basically started writing crime fiction a long, long time ago, and it's just sort of re-emerged this century as a very popular way of telling stories in Iceland.
You both have very diverse and different backgrounds — Yrsa in civil engineering and authoring children's books, Ragnar in law, reporting and translation. What is it that drew you to writing crime fiction?
YS: I started writing children's books, which were humour based, but then it's just more tiring trying to be funny. It's hard to be fun all the time. So I wanted to write for a more mature audience. And it was really easy to decide to write crime and horror because that's what I enjoy reading.
RJ: I started with the golden age stories of Agatha Christie and her contemporaries as a teenager. I fell in love with that way of telling stories and the puzzles that they presented. And before I went to law school and university, I studied maths at college, and there is something about these types of old puzzles that, in a way, presented like maths problems. These are challenges to the reader. And then, later on, I read Scandinavian noir. In a way, I've tried to merge these two worlds into one in what I write.
You've mentioned how important characters are to crime fiction, but how do you go about developing such complex yet compelling ones?
RJ: When I read crime fiction, the story is very important, but the characters are most important, especially with a series of books, because if you like the characters, you want to come back and you want to know more. And the crime story sort of becomes secondary. And I think that is a very important lesson for anyone who's writing books to learn is that you need to want your readers to come back, not possibly to a series, but to the book. If it's a single standalone book, you want the readers to want to finish the book because they like the characters or they dislike them or they just draw them in for whatever reason. Characters don't have to be likeable. They just have to interesting. They have to be three-dimensional in a way. So, I think that is a good starting point for any crime story, is to create your protagonists.
YS: It's also about keeping characters true to what they're supposed to be like. People don't change overnight. Because most characters in crime stories are in sort of desperate situations, you have to put a lot of thought into how they would react to that in the other scene. Also, I would recommend people who are aspiring writers of crime to 'kill' good people. Nobody cares about bad people. Kill good people, that's much more interesting.
Ragnar, your 2015 novel Dimma (The Darkness) was adapted into a TV series in 2024. What was the process like of translating your words into on-screen action?
RJ: It was unreal to see my character and my scenes come alive and I tried to be on set as much as I could just to experience this and learn and see how it's done. We filmed it in Iceland in winter in a very cold climate, so it was a very memorable experience just being so cold, watching all these fantastic and talented people do their job. I think the most memorable day was [shooting for] a scene in the book where a man is run over by a car. They actually hit a man with a car and they had to do it I think three times to get it right. And at that point I thought to myself, oh my God, I should not have written that scene. I felt so sorry for the poor guy, but he was a stunt man and did it beautifully well and was unharmed.
What changes have you witnessed in the Icelandic literature scene in recent years?
RJ: People keep writing in Iceland as they've always done. They are writing more crime fiction in the past 10 to 20 years than ever before. But also a big change in the last decade or so is that Icelandic fiction is being translated much more and published more widely. If you're writing in Iceland now, the chances of writing for a bigger audience are much better than they used to be. And that goes for probably all Icelandic culture. There is an appetite for Icelandic music or cinema or books at this point, which is wonderful.
Do you have concerns about how artificial intelligence (AI) is infiltrating and impacting the arts?
YS: Yes and no. I mean, AI, it rehashes what's already been done and I think it will become bigger and then it will wind down. I remember when the first drawings came out that AI did and they just looked amazing. But then when you've seen a number of them, they become so soulless somehow. There's something missing that would not be missing if it was done by an actual artist. It's the same with AI written stories. I think people realise the difference between an actual human writing a story and a written story that's, like I said, rehashing something that's already been done.
RJ: The word in Icelandic for culture is menning, and menning is derived from the word human. So, by definition, culture comes from humans and I strongly believe that culture will always be created by humans. And so I think we don't need to worry too much. There would always be an appetite for human-made art.
You have both been working on an upcoming book together, the title and release date of which are yet to be revealed. How did this collaboration come about, and what was the process of it like?
RJ: We've known each other for a long time. We set up a book festival called Iceland Noir in Reykjavik over 10 years ago, and we keep doing that every year now as our contribution to the cultural life of Reykjavik. And throughout this time, we've always thought maybe we should do a book together because we know each other so well. Finally, last year, we had this idea for a very Icelandic Thriller set in a cave and partly set in the Icelandic highlands. We've finally written that book, which will be out next year.
YS: [The process] was so non-confrontational, it was so easy. Ragnar and I, we agree on, I think, almost everything. I don't think we've ever had an argument. We just sort of set the broad strokes and then we went to work and it was really a nice experience. We each came up with our own storyline and then we merged it together. And I think it brings out the best of both of our work, and our strength as writers.
You mentioned the Iceland Noir festival that you set up together, which has become one of the most exciting and prestigious crime fiction festivals in Europe. Could you tell us more about that?
YS: It's a four-day festival [in November]. Even though it's a very small, intimate festival, it's all in English. Our ticket holders, the majority, come from abroad — or about half of them. And we seem to punch above our weight when it comes to the talent that we have appearing. So we've been extremely lucky with managing to get really big and important good authors to appear at our festival. And I really recommend it for book lovers to check out.
RJ: It started out as a crime fiction festival and there was no crime fiction festival in Iceland at that time, and then once we had a lot of crime authors come over we thought we will expand this and we'll include actors and screenwriters and poets and all sorts of creative artists. This year we're doing an Agatha Christie day because it's 50 years since she died this year. So Christie's great-grandson is coming along with her publisher, Lucy Foley, the author who's writing the new Miss Marple book. We have Lee Child coming. We have UK rapper Tinie Tempah coming, so it's all sorts of art forms.
YS: Yeah, and a Japanese manga author. We're embracing storytelling from all sorts of genres and also other media than novels.
The 2026 edition of Iceland Noir will take place from 11 - 14 November across various venues in Reykjavik, Iceland. Find out more here.

Neighbour of new Montenegro embassy in London sues council over impact on mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

It is not a classic neighbour-from-hell dispute, what with the protagonist inviting everyone over for evening drinks and canapés. But the sudden conversion of a five-bedroom family home in Pimlico, central London, into the embassy of Montenegro has triggered a neighbourhood row that has gone all the way to the desk of a high court judge.
The first stirrings of trouble came when one resident argued in a submission to the council this spring that the new embassy’s “flagpole and rather tacky-looking flag stick out like a sore thumb” among Cambridge Street’s Grade II-listed homes.
A second person, who described Montenegro’s red flag with gold border as “gaudy”, suggested the embassy was “out of keeping with the quietly dignified” whitewash late-Regency frontages designed by Thomas Cubitt.
Some of those critics, frustrated by the lack of planning application before the installation of the embassy flagpole and plaque, were somewhat placated when drinks were put on by the chargé d’affaires of the west Balkans state. “Perhaps it would have been diplomatic to have done that at the start,” one resident commented drily.
But the party did not convince everyone, and an involuntary nextdoor neighbour to the embassy has now taken matters to the courts.
Diana Simpson, 35, an Ivy league graduate who lives with her parents on Cambridge Street, is suing Westminster city council. She is applying for judicial review and potential damages on the grounds that when the embassy did belatedly seek planning permission for its change of use and flagpole, the local authority failed to take into account the impact on her mental health of the arrival next door of Montenegro, a country that has been involved in recent scrapes with Russia.
Simpson, the daughter of a former US diplomat who has lived on the street for more than three decades, is in receipt of disability benefits after being diagnosed with clinical anxiety, long Covid and a functional neurological disorder. So unsettling has the arrival of the embassy been to Simpson that her nights are regularly affected, she claims in her statement of grounds.
She alleges: “I frequently feel the need to sleep in an alternative to my lifelong bedroom, to gain some marginal relief; sometimes pre-emptively, sometimes in the middle of the night when I cannot reason with my activated primal ‘fear’ brain response (for example, upon hearing a creak, and immediately fearing an intruder accessing my room from the embassy, despite knowing the possibility is very slim and that this response is mostly irrational).”
Citing breaches of the human rights and equality acts, Simpson has said she had considered whether it “remains tenable for me to continue to live in this house, which I had anticipated having the option of living in for the rest of my life”, adding that leaving would wrench her from a “local tight-knit community”.
Simpson told the Guardian she was confident in her case, which alleges the council failed to take into account her conditions, acted irrationally and delivered a flawed public consultation by having a closed mind to objections after the Foreign Office gave its permission.
In its defence statement, Westminster city council denies the allegations and writes: “There is no plausible interference with the claimant’s home or her private and family life.” The council is seeking a summary judgment without a hearing.
A spokesperson for Westminster City Council said: “Councils are legally required to take decisions in line with existing planning policy. It would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage.”
The case in front of Mr Justice Mould for consideration is perhaps unusual but it has highlighted a more common clash between smaller countries – as they move their embassies due to rent hikes or landlords selling up – and the residents of some of London’s more affluent streets.
The US has its London home in an intimidating purpose-built 12-storey cube structure south of the Thames. But for most of the major nations the natural home is Belgravia or perhaps South Kensington, Knightsbridge and Mayfair. There is a tendency for the lower-tier states to want to be close to these luminaries but spend not quite the same sums on rent.
It is for that reason that Montenegro has alighted in Pimlico, near Victoria coach station, and the Turkmenistan embassy has recently opened in another adapted family home on Victoria Road, in Kensington but a telling 1.4 miles from the splendours of France’s home opposite the Natural History Museum.
The move by Turkmenistan has led to some rancour, too. “I cannot understand the lack of courtesy afforded to immediate neighbours,” submitted one local to a Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea consultation. “I will find out if anything untoward has taken place and, if so, further newspaper action might be necessary.”
The correspondent added of the house in which the embassy is now located, which is owned by Tengku Fahad, 32, the Eton-educated son of the late king of Malaysia, that another location should be found for Turkmenistan, a former Soviet republic in central Asia.
“I was quite happy with the late king of Malaysia [who] lived there and I believe the property is still owned by his son,” she wrote. “We had a family living there for four years who left a while ago for tax reasons but the house has not long been vacant … I have no doubt that they are very pleasant people but, however you bill it, I for one don’t feel totally safe and the idea that there be signage and a flag up leaves me speechless.”
When approached at her home, the complainant, who asked not to be named, said the Turkmens had turned out to be “actually quite quiet” and there had been no problems “so far”.
Risks of such local hostility and scrutiny appear to have led some nations to go another way. North Korea has for two decades had an embassy in something of a place of exile in a seven-bedroom 1920s home off the A406 in Ealing, west London.
Colin Flood, a retired solicitor who lives two doors down, said they never heard a peep from them. A workman renovating the house next to the North Korean delegation added: “They are lovely people – we tidied up their greenery at the front and hope to get more work. Lovely people.”

Rachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

About 30 kilometres south of Naples, the town of Gragnano is surrounded by the Monti Lattari mountain range – the limestone backbone of the Sorrento peninsula. Historically, a series of natural springs fed into a larger stream called Vernotico, which flowed down the mountainside, passing through what was at the time the small village of Gragnano.
The natural slope of the terrain was fortuitous, because it allowed for the construction of a sequence of mills, which started in around 1263. During a visit to Gragnano last month, local historian Giuseppe Di Massa explained how it all worked; how gravity drove the flow of water from one mill to the next, in order to power vertical millstones – a system created for the inconsistent flow. The valley, with its clever water system, became known as the valley of the mills; its role milling grain, which arrived at the nearby port of Castellammare di Stabia, a vital operation to Naples and surrounding towns.
The activity of the 30 mills peaked during the 18th century, but another industry was growing, one that harnessed another natural aspect of the town: its climate. The temperature, humidity and sea breeze were ideal conditions for drying pasta.
Often in strings hung over wooden frames, pasta was dried in the streets of Gragnano, then moved inside when necessary; the skill of the pasta makers and their ability to harness the weather every bit as important as the weather itself. And the industry grew. According to the city of Gragnano website, by 1859 there were 81 pasta factories, requiring ever increasing amounts of hard durum wheat for their pasta, while the mills produced soft wheat. The mills ceased operations in the 1950s, and were largely abandoned until renovation projects turned some of them into small museums.
What has continued to grow in Gragnano, though, is the tradition and art of pasta making; now with its own Indicazione Geografica Protetta, which protects its quality (provenance of wheat, how it is extruded, how long it is dried) and connection with the region. These days, 23 producers – from tiny to vast, 15 of which make up a consortium – make more than 100,000 tonnes of pasta annually in carefully controlled conditions – conditions very different from the open streets, but requiring just as much skill. I returned to Rome with bags of pasta from seven different makers – Di Martino, Faella, Garofolo, Liguori, Afeltra, Antiche Tradizioni di Gragnano, Ducato di alfalfi – all of which pleased me with their nutty scent, porous texture and resilience in the pan.
I also came back from Gragnano with a recipe devised for the town’s Mondopasta festival this year by chef Astou Ndiaye. Born in Dakar and now living with her family in Milan, Ndiaye’s cooking draws both on her heritage and her home. For her beautiful Senegalese ragu, the meat (I used lamb) is marinated in an aromatic blend of vegetables, coriander and cloves before being braised for a stew soft enough to be pasta sauce. I used candele (hollow tubes) made by Garfalo, which I broke into short lengths. It’s a dish that sums up the spirit of pasta di Gragnano, I think; rooted in both Gragnano and Dakar, and at home anywhere.
Pasta with Senegalese-inspired lamb ragu
Serves 4
1 stick celery, trimmed
 
1 small red pepper, trimmed, deseeded and cut into strips
 
1 shallot, peeled
 
1 small bunch coriander
  
2 garlic cloves, peeled
 
3 cloves
  
Salt
  
600g boned lamb shoulder, cubed
 
Olive oil
  
1 large onion, peeled and diced
 
1 tsp paprika
  
1 tsp garam masala
  
400-500g pasta (broken candele, maccheroni, mezze maniche)
Working in a food processor, pulse the celery, red pepper, shallot, coriander, garlic, cloves and a pinch of salt into a rough mixture. Put half the mixture into a bowl, add the meat, then toss so all the chunks are coated. Cover and leave to sit for two to 24 hours (if it’s three hours or more, put it in the fridge).
Working in a large, heavy-based pan, warm four teaspoons of olive oil. Working in batches, brown the marinated meat, then lift out on to a plate.
Add the diced onions to the empty pan, along with the remaining blended mixture and marinade, paprika and garam masala, and stir well, adding more water if it seems too dry. Add the meat, stir again, then add 300ml water. Bring to a simmer, then cover for two hours. By the end of cooking, the meat should be extremely tender and falling apart in just a little thick gravy.
In a separate pot, cook the pasta in salted boiling water according to the packet instructions. Meanwhile, put half of the ragu into the bottom of a warm serving bowl. Lift the cooked, drained pasta on top, toss, adding more ragu as needed, then toss again.

From sex ‘obsession’ to losing friends, key takeaways from Russell Brand’s testimony at trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:23 UTC
15:00:23 KST

Russell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court on Wednesday to give evidence in his trial. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters
From sex ‘obsession’ to losing friends, key takeaways from Russell Brand’s testimony at trial
Comedian told jurors he now believed it was wrong to have used his fame for sex and said his life had been consumed by the allegations
Russell Brand was in the witness box for more than four hours on Wednesday at his trial at Southwark crown court. He denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
Six alleged victims say the comedian switched suddenly after appearing charming and forced them into sexual activity in a toilet, a hotel room, workplace corridors and his bedroom, acting as if nothing had happened after the attacks.
Here are the key themes and passages from Brand’s court appearance.
1. Obsession with sex
Brand said in evidence that he had an “obsession” with sex when he was younger, but denied setting himself a “goal” to sleep with 5,000 women.
He said: “I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man and with regard to the latter, with women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond-reckless philandering and idiocy.”
Brand’s former friend, Mark Pinheiro, previously told the trial that Brand had boasted on a car journey to the Labour party conference in Bournemouth about his techniques for “pulling” women and allegedly revealed an ambition to sleep with 5,000 women.
Riel Karmy-Jones KC, prosecuting, asked Brand: “Is it a goal you may have had?” Brand said: “I don’t agree, I don’t recall the conversation you are referring to.”
Brand also suggested a reported conversation in 1999 about never leaving an interaction with a woman without a “conquest” was a riff on a Woody Allen joke.
A court sketch of Riel Karmy-Jones KC cross-examining Russell Brand in the dock. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA
2. ‘Wrong’ to use fame for sex
Brand told jurors he now believed it was “wrong” of him to use his fame for sex. He said: “As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access which I agree with you was wrong.”
One of Brand’s alleged victims says she was raped after she met him at one of his Hammersmith Apollo standup performances in 2009.
The court heard he stored her name next to the letter T, which he said stood for “tart”. Asked what he meant by the word “tart”, he replied: “That was what I used to denote casual hook-ups.” He told jurors the woman had not said “no” or told him to stop as they were having sex.
Another allegation is that Brand sexually assaulted a Channel 4 worker in 2009 during a recording session, after she had been forced by members of his entourage to give him a massage. Brand agreed that, while he says he cannot remember that day, it would have been “petulant and childish” to refuse to continue the recording without first receiving a massage.
Asked if he had found thrusting his head into her lap funny, Brand replied: “I don’t remember. I don’t think it’s funny now.”
3. Consent
In his evidence Brand recalled only consensual encounters and told the court that “consent is more important than sex itself”.
The prosecution claimed he had constructed his evidence in response to the allegations. Karmy-Jones accused Brand of staying silent on the accusations in his police interviews so that he “forged” his account around the evidence.
“Were you waiting to see all that evidence before you gave your account?” she asked. Brand replied: “I was doing my best to participate.”
Court sketch of Russell Brand being questioned by his barrister, Ian Winter KC. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA
4. Blamed the media
Brand blamed the media for his public fall from grace after reporting of sexual misconduct allegations in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and news stories. Asked about the impact of the Dispatches programme, Brand said: “It was devastating.”
Brand told the court that after the programme and the articles he was unable to stay with his son at Great Ormond Street hospital in London when he was having surgery. “Due to material that had been published in the public eye they had to bar my attendance and presence,” Brand said.
He added: “My entire life has been consumed by these allegations.”
5. Shunned by friends
Brand told the court he had been unable to persuade any friend or acquaintance to give evidence on his behalf. The defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked him: “Will they touch you with a bargepole?” Brand replied: “No.”
Brand described the last few years as “deeply traumatic” and told the court that focusing on the allegations and trying to remember incidents from his past had damaged his personal life.

What’s trending for winter travel? Tripadvisor reveals its top European destinations and experiences

From snowy escapes to festive breaks, these are Europe’s trending winter destinations and experiences for a chilly getaway.
Looking for some winter holiday inspiration? A new travel index has revealed which European destinations and experiences will be trending this chilly season.
Tripadvisor’s latest study has analysed searches made by travellers in the UK between 1 August 2026 and 31 October 2026, for getaways between 1 November 2026 and 28 February 2027.
Rather than warm winter holidays, its research found that cold weather destinations are on the hotlist, with festive Christmas market towns and Alpine locations topping the list across the continent.
“It’s interesting to see such a strong trend towards cold weather escapes among Brits this winter, with travellers swapping sunloungers for snow boots," Aarushi Kumar, Associate Director of Research & Insights at Tripadvisor Group, said.
“Arctic hideaways, Alpine towns and cosy Christmas market cities taking the top spots just shows that travellers are looking to lean into the colder season rather than escape it.”
Top 10 trending winter destinations in Europe
The trending European winter destinations, according to the Tripadvisor Travel Index:
- 1. Strasbourg, France
- 2. Tromsø, Norway
- 3. Ghent, Belgium
- 4. Saariselka, Finland
- 5. Chamonix, France
- 6. Zakopane, Poland
- 7. Bruges, Belgium
- 8. Nuremberg, Germany
- 9. Salzburg, Austria
- 10. Riga, Latvia
Winter experiences in Europe you won’t want to miss
Topping Tripadvisor’s trending European destinations is Strasbourg in France. It’s famed for its Christmas market, where lights and wooden chalets set the festive scene. This year, the market will run for four weeks starting 27 November.
Alongside the market, Tripadvisor also recommends visiting the Cathedral of our Lady of Strasbourg – a masterpiece of Gothic architecture, stained glass windows and the must-see astronomical clock.
For Northern Lights chasers, book an excursion to Tromsø in Norway. To get prime views of the atmospheric phenomenon, hop on a minibus or boat tour. Visitors should also add reindeer sledding and fjord fishing to their Tromsø itineraries.
Rounding up the index’s top three trending winter destinations, Ghent in Belgium offers a host of cultural and historical experiences. A stop by a key monument like the Castle of the Counts is a must. This medieval attraction stands as Flanders’ only remaining castle from that era with a moat and largely intact defence system.
Here are some of the other experiences to try in the trending destinations this winter:
Saariselka, Finland
• Scenic snowmobile riding
• Go on a husky safari
• Photography experiences to capture the Northern Lights
Chamonix, France
• A trip to the Mont Blanc resort town and scaling Aiguille du Midi
• Go ski touring
• Visit the new Musée du Mont-Blanc
Zakopane, Poland
• Visit Zakopane’s thermal springs
• Stroll along the pedestrianised Krupówki Street
• Take in the views aboard the Gubałówka funicular railway
Bruges, Belgium
• Climb the Belfort medieval bell tower for sweeping views of the city
• Take a walking tour, with a canal cruise and chocolate tasting experience included
• Put on your skates and go ice skating at Koning Albert I-park
Nuremberg, Germany
• Experience a German holiday tradition at Nuremberg Christmas Market
• Visit Kaiserburg Nürnberg medieval castle overlooking the old town
• Go snowhiking
Salzburg, Austria
• Salzburg Christmas Market
• A visit to the Salzburg Cathedral – a 17th-century Baroque landmark
• Attend Winterfest in Volksgarten
Riga, Latvia
• A walking tour around Riga’s old town
• Sightseeing on a canal boat trip
• Snow experiences, like husky sledding

Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
Custom-designed furniture by Derya Arpac, Lærke Ryom, Kasper Kyster and Daniel Schofield sets the scene for this unconventional bookstore in the Danish capital.
Simone Book Services is a Copenhagen shop specialising in rare and independent books and magazines, but it can also be an exhibition gallery, a listening space, or a venue for book launches and other informal gatherings.
Turkish-born architect Arpac oversaw the intentionally “un-Scandinavian” interior, which includes modular shelves made from aluminium and cherry wood, mobile book trolleys and a counter dressed in leather.
The concept for the store was born out of conversations between Arpac, who works for furniture brand &Tradition, and founders Tugce Kayar Subay and Ibo Subay, a married couple with backgrounds in fashion media and marketing.
The Subays had amassed such an impressive collection of art, design and fashion literature that they launched a “literary branding” business in February 2026, curating libraries for exhibitions, offices and brand spaces.
Simone gives the couple a physical platform for this business and allows it to evolve further. It showcases their curation of books and magazines, but also furniture and objects related to reading culture.
“Tugce is the book nerd, and I’m the design nerd; we came up with this idea of combining our passions,” Arpac told Dezeen.
“We wanted to create a space where people would come and be inspired.”
Arpac’s own contribution to the space is a system of wall-mounted shelves crafted from cherry, a red-hued hardwood that offers a different aesthetic to traditional Scandinavian timbers like oak, ash or pine.
“The shelving appears to extend and climb through the space, almost like scaffolding or the structural skeleton of a building,” she said.
The leather-wrapped counter was designed by Ryom, who specialises in alternative methods of upholstery. Similar to the Garments chairs she developed for The Mindcraft Project, the bar’s edges feature zippers that open up to reveal storage areas.
Kyster developed a shelving system made from folded sheets of unpolished aluminium, intended for displaying magazines. The system is modular, so more panels could be added in future.
For seating, Schofield crafted a bench out of sheets of black-pigmented MDF that slots neatly into the store’s corner. It’s joined by mobile book trolleys made from the same material, encouraging visitors to move books around the space.
In addition to the four designers, artist Staffan Sundström was invited to create paintings for the bookstore. He contributed three pieces for the store opening, although the display will change as works are sold.
The store also includes an area dubbed “the red room”, a David Lynch-inspired space featuring red walls and matching floor-to-ceiling curtains. This 20-square-metre space offers scope for small-scale events and exhibitions.
Since opening, Simone has hosted various events, including a book launch for photographer Lasse Dearman, a curated library for sports brand ASICS and a pop-up for fashion label Bonnetje Recut.
Future ambitions include the launch of “reading objects”, including everything from bookmarks and paperweights to lighting and shelving.
Photography by Armin Tehran and Hampus Berndtson

====================================================================================================

‘There’s nothing scary about it’: Life goes on in Lithuania s troops patrol Russia border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Life in Lithuania’s southwestern town of Vištytis remains undisturbed. Local residents are not troubled either by the threat posed by Russia or by the Lithuanian troops deployed along the border with the Kaliningrad region, who are helping border guards patrol the area.
The military has been assisting the border guards since early October. Around 100 troops are expected to continue doing so until mid-November.
Government officials describe the decision as a precautionary measure in response to the possibility of a new wave of mobilisation in Russia. However, the authorities stress that the threat level along the border has not increased.
“[Potential deserters] will try to cross the state border illegally, both on land and on water. That is why we have stepped up surveillance on land, on water and in the air. As we say here, along the green border, the blue border and in the air,” Rimantas Kundreckis, commander of the Vištytis border guard post, told BNS.
The deployment of troops is estimated to have almost doubled the frequency of patrols along the border with the Kaliningrad region.
The Lithuanian-Russian state border, including the boundary of territorial waters, stretches for almost 300km. It runs through plains, forests and bodies of water.
“There’s nothing particularly scary about it, despite what I read in so many places these days,” Sandra told BNS as she hurried home carrying an armful of groceries.
She is one of just a few hundred residents of Vištytis, in the Vilkaviškis district. Most locals spend the gloomier days of autumn indoors, leaving the town’s central square looking almost deserted, with only the occasional person hurrying toward a nearby shop.
“Nothing has really changed here. You can just see that there are more patrols, but nothing else is happening. The only difference is that the military has arrived, and we see the occasional military vehicle,” the 31-year-old woman said.
She said she was not afraid of the worsening security situation in the region. Nor was her daily life being disrupted by the soldiers recently seen alongside the border guards.
“Life is normal. Everything is just as it was before. There’s no special preparation going on, with people stocking up on supplies or preparing shelters. We’re just living our lives, like everyone else in Lithuania,” Sandra said.
The state border runs through a lake
In Vištytis, a lake separates Lithuania from the Kaliningrad region.
Bright red posts protruding from the water mark the point up to which people who have provided their details to border guards are permitted to sail. Another line of yellow posts, 50 metres beyond them, marks the end of Lithuanian territory.
From the pier where border guard patrol boats moor, you can see a Russian flag flying high just a few hundred metres away.
The lake is monitored by cameras and patrolled by a border guard boat. According to Kundreckis, enhanced surveillance of the lake has helped reduce the number of accidental border crossings.
Previously, people who went out on the water to fish or relax sometimes failed to notice that they were approaching Russian territory. Border guards can now warn them of a potential violation in advance, either by calling them using the contact details they have provided or by approaching them in an official patrol boat.
Accompanying officers on a patrol of Lake Vištytis offers a practical demonstration of how border controls work. When the patrol boat spots another boat, it slows down. Officers observe the person on board and assess the distance from the marked boundary before continuing on their way without making contact.
Such checks are part of the officers’ daily duties.
The most recent border violation recorded by the Vištytis post occurred at the beginning of the year, when two Russian citizens entered Lithuania by walking across the frozen lake. Around 10 similar violations are typically recorded each year.
‘Invaluable experience’
Among those contributing to the border protection mission are troops from the Second Territorial Unit of the Darius and Girėnas National Defence Volunteer Forces (KASP).
Company commander Leonas Ruzgas sees the deployment as an opportunity not only to contribute to the country’s security but also to help soldiers develop their skills.
He was among the first to arrive at the border.
“Border guards have quite a few technological innovations and systems that we do not use, [...] because our work does not require them. So it is good to see how much our border protection has improved, share experience and learn from them,” Ruzgas said.
The commander of the Vištytis border guard post agreed. He said the deployment offered opportunities for professional development not only for officers and soldiers serving on the ground, but also for their commanders.
“The practical experience is truly invaluable. You cannot get it anywhere else, really,” Kundreckis said. “If Day X [war] were to come and the military had to take up a position here, both ordinary soldiers and commanders would already be familiar with the specifics of the area.”
Troops are rotated along the border approximately every four to five days. Different soldiers are usually sent each time, although those who wish to return can do so.
According to Ruzgas, incoming troops adapt to the duty schedules of State Border Guard Service (VSAT) officers, and their powers are largely the same.
Kundreckis said the soldiers assisting the border guards had also brought equipment that was “being successfully used to monitor both land areas and airspace”.
The post commander said he had not noticed any signs of a potential threat, describing activity on the other side of the border as routine daily operations.
“Whether it is a coincidence or not, there has been an increase in military fighter jet flights near the state border. Explosions could be heard somewhere at the training ground towards Kudirkos Naumiestis, and their helicopters have also been flying near the state border more frequently,” the commander said.
‘I was born with the Russians’
Virginijus Dapkus, who owns a farm near Vištytis, told BNS that the authorities’ heightened attention to security made him laugh.
“I was born with the Russians, grew up with the Russians and have dealings with the Russians. I know them very well, and what our authorities, our government, are saying makes me laugh. It is just scaremongering, and they have their own objectives,” Dapkus said as he prepared to go fishing.
He said he felt perfectly comfortable in Vištytis, although he was saddened by the fact that fishing was no longer permitted on the other side of the lake. According to him, the catch now is “like night and day” compared with what it used to be.
“When we were together with the Russians, we used to fish only on the Russian side. Now we fish in a swamp on the Lithuanian side. That is what we call it – the swamp,” he said.
Pranas Stankevičius, a 93-year-old former deportee, also used to fish in Lake Vištytis.
“I used to fish on the lake, but now we are no longer allowed to. You cannot put out a fishing net; they can see everything now. Everything is very restricted,” the pensioner complained.
The elderly man, who was repairing his car in the street, said he had previously enjoyed travelling to Kaliningrad, where he traded goods with others. Nevertheless, he said he understood the current border controls.
“It is not that bad. A border is a border. What can you do? We belong to Lithuania, so let them guard the border,” he said.

“The practical experience is truly invaluable. You cannot get it anywhere else, really,” Kundreckis said. “If Day X [war] were to come and the military had to take up a position here, both ordinary soldiers and commanders would already be familiar with the specifics of the area.”
Troops are rotated along the border approximately every four to five days. Different soldiers are usually sent each time, although those who wish to return can do so.
According to Ruzgas, incoming troops adapt to the duty schedules of State Border Guard Service (VSAT) officers, and their powers are largely the same.
Kundreckis said the soldiers assisting the border guards had also brought equipment that was “being successfully used to monitor both land areas and airspace”.
The post commander said he had not noticed any signs of a potential threat, describing activity on the other side of the border as routine daily operations.
“Whether it is a coincidence or not, there has been an increase in military fighter jet flights near the state border. Explosions could be heard somewhere at the training ground towards Kudirkos Naumiestis, and their helicopters have also been flying near the state border more frequently,” the commander said.
‘I was born with the Russians’
Virginijus Dapkus, who owns a farm near Vištytis, told BNS that the authorities’ heightened attention to security made him laugh.
“I was born with the Russians, grew up with the Russians and have dealings with the Russians. I know them very well, and what our authorities, our government, are saying makes me laugh. It is just scaremongering, and they have their own objectives,” Dapkus said as he prepared to go fishing.
He said he felt perfectly comfortable in Vištytis, although he was saddened by the fact that fishing was no longer permitted on the other side of the lake. According to him, the catch now is “like night and day” compared with what it used to be.
“When we were together with the Russians, we used to fish only on the Russian side. Now we fish in a swamp on the Lithuanian side. That is what we call it – the swamp,” he said.
Pranas Stankevičius, a 93-year-old former deportee, also used to fish in Lake Vištytis.
“I used to fish on the lake, but now we are no longer allowed to. You cannot put out a fishing net; they can see everything now. Everything is very restricted,” the pensioner complained.
The elderly man, who was repairing his car in the street, said he had previously enjoyed travelling to Kaliningrad, where he traded goods with others. Nevertheless, he said he understood the current border controls.
“It is not that bad. A border is a border. What can you do? We belong to Lithuania, so let them guard the border,” he said.

Cambodia: Politically connected security companies enabled slavery and rape in scamming compounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:58:00 UTC
14:58:00 KST

- Five private security companies identified where guards committed or facilitated abuses
- Members of political elite, military and police linked to security companies at multiple scam compounds
- Accountability lacking despite government crackdown
Cambodian private security companies connected to the country’s military, police and powerful business networks have helped sustain a scamming industry built on trafficking, forced labour, torture and slavery, Amnesty International said in a new report published today.
Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia identifies five private security companies that provided services at scamming compounds – and details their links to members of Cambodia’s military, police and business elites. Amnesty also identified multiple members of the military and police who worked as security guards, trained or supervised guards at more than 20 compounds.
“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“This report demonstrates Cambodian corporate actors’ direct involvement in scamming compounds. Our findings also begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny.
“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”
Guards central to confinement and abuse
Building on its previous investigations that exposed slavery, human trafficking, rape, forced labour and torture inside Cambodia’s scamming compounds, and documented the failures of the government’s subsequent crackdown, Amnesty’s latest investigation examines the security infrastructure that allowed the compounds to confine and control trafficked people and forced them to scam people globally.
Between January 2023 and September 2026, Amnesty International interviewed 151 scamming compound survivors and reviewed records concerning more than 400 additional victims. Researchers identified 86 compounds, visiting 82 of them, and found security guards at every compound.
In this latest report, Amnesty identifies the private business companies responsible for guarding the compounds and abusing the victims. We also geolocated videos from more than 200 security guards’ TikTok accounts to 23 compounds across Cambodia until August 2026. The new evidence collected by Amnesty links more than 20 members of the military and police to the private security companies that guard scamming compounds and to at least 22 of the 86 compounds.
When guards escort trafficked people to punishment rooms or stand watch during rape and torture, they are enabling abuses
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
Amnesty’s report also connects various prominent business and political figures to these security companies – including a former bank CEO, a property developer and the son of a former deputy prime minister.
Survivors consistently described guards as responsible for preventing escape, while many reported guards beating people who attempted to flee. Survivors also described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.
At the compound Park 8, also known as PV01, “Maia”, a woman from Cameroon, said guards restrained her on arrival and later took her to a dark room where managers raped her while guards stood outside. “Gabe”, a Ugandan survivor at the same compound, described being chained above basins of water, beaten for hours and shocked with an electric baton.
Most of the 151 survivors interviewed said guards carried or had immediate access to electric shock batons. Several reported seeing guards or other people carrying firearms.
“When guards escort trafficked people to punishment rooms or stand watch during rape and torture, they are enabling these abuses – and so too are the supposedly legitimate corporate actors who employ them,” Agnès Callamard said.
“Investigations must assess and follow responsibility from the lowest ranks all the way upwards to the companies, including the managers and owners who recruited, deployed and controlled security guards at scamming compounds.”
Five companies linked to at least 23 compounds
Amnesty International identified five private companies that guarded compounds where serious human rights abuses were documented. Three had links to Cambodian authorities.
Leap Somnang had the largest footprint of the companies identified and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo. All said its guards stopped them leaving compounds under threat of violence, while several described guards participating in beatings, electric shocks and keeping the victims in prolonged isolation.
Security Response, a company with close links to the Panda Bank and Huione corporate network, was linked to five compounds, including Park 8 (PV01).
ZD Security, formerly BIC Security, was linked to two compounds in Botum Sakor, including Long Bay (BS04), where survivors described torture and other ill-treatment, forced labour, unlawful confinement and violence against people trying to leave.
Dara Security was linked to two compounds in Sihanoukville, while Best Security was linked to a Bavet compound where Amnesty documented human trafficking, forced labour and child labour.
Amnesty’s report finds that at least three high-ranking military and police officers had links to compounds, strongly indicating involvement with the industry:
- The company Leap Somnang is controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chairman while also being a Colonel in the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces.
- Amnesty’s analysis showed phone numbers for Deputy Police Chief Lay Channy listed on an advertisement for Best Security. Channy was involved in the crackdown in Bavet, where Best Security guarded a compound.
- Brigadier General Tek Bunthoeun has a direct, and potentially controlling, interest in the property development comprising the BM02 compound, where Amnesty documented torture, confinement and forced labour.
Amnesty also identified multiple prominent figures with apparent business connections to compounds, without making any finding as to their personal responsibility for the abuses documented in the report. Amnesty International wrote to each corporate actor and individual identified in this report, and the full responses received are included in the report.
Links to military and police demand investigation
Amnesty International analysed official uniforms, insignia, identification numbers, public records and social-media timelines to help pinpoint precisely where and when military and police personnel were present at compounds.
In three compounds, apparent active military personnel were seen training, leading or supervising guards. In other cases, Amnesty identified apparent state personnel carrying firearms or occupying guard positions.
“The evidence suggests military and police involvement in a number of scamming compounds that helps explain how abuses at these sites persisted despite years of public reporting and repeated law-enforcement operations,” Agnès Callamard said.
Closure without accountability
Following a government crackdown launched in July 2025, large-scale scamming compound operations currently appear to be dormant. However, Amnesty International is unaware of investigations into the five security companies profiled in the report, their owners and managers or the wider commercial and state connections documented.
Prior to the publication of Amnesty’s report, Cambodian authorities responded on 15 October noting that 77 police officers had been disciplined in connection with scamming compounds.
Meanwhile, in response to Amnesty’s findings, Sophat Ban denied holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an advisor to the company owner”.
Best Security denied Lay Channy had any control over the company despite acknowledging that his phone number appeared on a company sign. Security Response denied all allegations made in Amnesty’s report, and Best Security responded that it “has no history of providing services at location BA06” and said would consider “legal action if someone has stolen (the) company’s uniform.”
Amnesty International is calling on the Cambodian authorities to establish prompt, independent and adequately resourced investigations into private security companies connected to compounds; investigate apparent serving military and police personnel involved in compound security; suspend company licences while credible allegations of serious abuse are investigated; and ensure victims have access to effective remedies and reparations.
Many of the abuses documented could constitute serious crimes under international law and Cambodian law. This includes by security guards who participated in abuses, as well as managers, executives and directors of the security companies who were aware of them.
“Even if scamming compounds are dormant at the time of publishing this report, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Agnès Callamard said.
“Largely in response to international outcry over the scamming compounds, the Cambodian authorities have announced a range of crackdown measures. But a crackdown measured only in raids, arrests and deportations risks leaving the architects and enablers untouched. Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”

Vietnam to restructure state capital in major enterprises

HANOI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam has approved a plan to restructure state capital in 21 enterprises from 2026 to 2030, including adjusting state ownership in three major banks to 65 percent, local media VnEconomy reported on Thursday.
Under the plan recently approved by Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang, state ownership in Joint Stock Commercial Bank for Investment and Development of Vietnam and Joint Stock Commercial Bank for Foreign Trade of Vietnam will be reduced from 76.73 percent and 74.8 percent, respectively, to 65 percent, according to the report.
The state stake in the Vietnam Joint Stock Commercial Bank for Industry and Trade will rise from 64.46 percent to 65 percent.
Meanwhile, the state will continue to hold 100 percent ownership in the Vietnam Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development and nine enterprises, including Vietnam National Industry-Energy Group, Vietnam Electricity, Vietnam Coal-Mineral Industry Group and Vietnam Railways Corporation, according to the government portal.
The plan also targets raising state ownership in Vietnam Airlines JSC from 39.29 percent to 86.42 percent, while reducing the state's stakes in Vietnam Maritime Corporation from over 99.46 percent to 65 percent and Vietnam Rubber Group from 96.77 percent to 75 percent. ■

Election night reckoning: pollsters confront their biggest misses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:43:46 UTC
14:43:46 KST

At 10 p.m. Tuesday, as polls closed in Israel's election, all six television news channels released their exit polls. Not all painted the same picture. Channel 12 News, Channel 13 News and Kan 11 projected 50 seats for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc, while i24NEWS projected 55, Channel 16 projected 53 and Channel 14 projected 60. There were also differences in the projected strength of individual parties.
As in every election, the exit polls were updated throughout the night as actual results from sampled polling stations came in. Most of the projections eventually moved closer to what are now the preliminary official results.
The differences between the channels are only part of the story. Polls published in the days and weeks leading up to the election sometimes presented a different picture from the exit polls.
One of the most striking examples is Likud. In Channel 13's final preelection poll, published Oct. 23, the party was projected to win just 19 seats. In the channel's initial exit poll, that figure rose to 25, and an overnight update put it at 27. According to the latest official count, Likud stands at 26 seats.
Now, with vote counting still underway, questions are emerging about the gaps between the forecasts, pollsters' ability to identify changes in voting patterns and the professional lessons to be drawn from the election.
In interviews with ynet, two pollsters who were at the center of election night described what they saw in the data, what surprised them and their initial conclusions.
'Likud's strength was something we didn't see in the polls'
Shmuel Rosner, Channel 13's pollster, acknowledged that Likud's strong showing was the biggest surprise for him. Although preelection polls identified several major trends, he said, they failed to reflect the governing party's strength.
"Some things surprised me, and others less so. The main surprise was Likud's strength, something we didn't see in the polls but which appeared fairly early in the exit polls and continued to grow throughout the evening."
And when the actual results began to emerge, were there other surprises?
"Apart from the surprise over Likud, which requires us to think about how it happened and why we didn't see it, we also didn't expect the bloc with a certain advantage to be the coalition bloc rather than the opposition.
"At the same time, some things weren't surprising. For example, we had been seeing for some time that turnout among Arab voters would be high and that the Arab parties would win many seats. We also consistently saw that neither bloc would probably reach 61 seats and that the ultra-Orthodox parties were weakening. Those were things we identified."
What is the professional lesson from this election? Will you do anything differently next time?
"It's still a little early to say what lessons we'll draw. First, we need to understand whether something happened and what it was, and then try to apply the professional lessons accordingly.
"This isn't just about an election campaign. I conduct polls regularly, so obviously, after an event like this, both I and the team I work with need to examine it and understand what happened. We need to try to figure out, as best we can, what went wrong and what we can improve.
"I've only done this once so far, and I'm not sure I'll do it again, so we'll wait and see."
'I was very, very confident in the numbers'
Tzuriel Sharon, founder and owner of the Direct Polls research institute, which conducted the preelection surveys and exit poll for i24NEWS, said he was not surprised by the results of his projection.
According to Sharon, the figures were consistent with trends he had identified throughout the campaign, and his confidence in those assessments had grown in recent weeks.
What went through your mind when the exit polls were released?
"Anticipation. Certainly when you see everyone else's numbers. On the other hand, I was very, very confident in the numbers."
What gave you that confidence?
"The numbers were very consistent with what I had been seeing throughout the entire period. I felt I had a handle on what was happening, that I understood the system, the election, Israeli sociology and the dynamics of Israeli public sentiment.
"I felt very confident in my understanding of the situation throughout the election campaign, and that feeling became much stronger in recent weeks."
How do you explain the large differences between the channels' exit polls?
"First of all, that's a question you should ask them. I believe I have the No. 1 polling system in Israel in terms of technology. I've invested enormous resources in it and its development, particularly over the past year.
"That was partly because of the election, but not only. It was also because of very large commercial clients working with the company.
"Beyond that, I wasn't living in echo chambers. I was very connected to Israeli public sentiment in all its forms. I was highly focused and insulated from background noise. In other words, I understood the mindset of voters across all the different sectors that ultimately make up the political landscape. In that respect, I felt very confident."
One of the main surprises Sharon identified was the high turnout among Arab voters. He said its scale surprised even those who had anticipated significant gains for the Arab parties.
"We knew the Arab sector would probably turn out. Conservative estimates spoke of 14 seats, while the higher estimates were already talking about 15. I think the numbers astonished everyone, and I'm inclined to believe these are figures we won't see again in future elections."
How much did the high turnout affect the exit polls?
"It affects the weight you assign to different population groups. That's something a pollster needs to know how to handle in real time. It shouldn't surprise you once you have the turnout figures.
"In preelection polls, you can estimate turnout. Here, you receive the actual figures and updates from the Central Elections Committee throughout the day."
'Don't throw the baby out with the bathwater'
Sharon also addressed questions about the reliability of polling following the discrepancies between the channels.
He said the results should not be taken as an indictment of the entire polling industry, although he expects the episode to have consequences for the media as well.
After a night like this, the public could lose faith in polls.
"I hope the Israeli public will look at Direct Polls' surveys, because here's a company that has proven itself.
"I don't think we should throw the baby out with the bathwater. It's not as though this entire industry has gone bankrupt. But there are four players who will need to do some soul-searching.
"I expect this episode to have consequences in the short term and perhaps over the longer term as well, not only for the polling industry but also for the media industry."
Still, is there anything you personally would do differently?
"You can always streamline processes and improve them. You learn from everything. There are things we tried that didn't work, and there are things we tried that turned out to be tremendous successes. It's a process of trial and error."
Sharon, like the other pollsters, has completed his work on this election campaign. But with the results failing to deliver a decisive victory to either side, the question immediately arises: Could another polling season be just around the corner, with another election?
Sharon, at least, believes not.
"I don't think we'll go to a second round. I expect we'll see a government with a different composition from the current one.
"Even if I'm going against everyone's predictions here, you saw that I went against everyone during the election campaign, too. I'm not afraid of that."
What do you think was the main message voters sent in this election?
"I think the public has spoken. Netanyahu received a yellow card from voters over his partnership with the ultra-Orthodox parties, and the center-left received a yellow card over its willingness to sit with the Arab parties.
"The public has made it very clear what kind of government it wants to see, and the politicians will have to act."

Russia’s nighttime attacks on Ukraine: explosions in Kharkiv, strikes on Dnipropetrovsk region, and one person killed in Rivne region
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked Ukraine with drones: explosions were heard in Kharkiv, while Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions suffered damage. A man was killed in Rivne region.
During the night of October 29, Russian forces attacked a number of regions of Ukraine with drones. Explosions were heard in Kharkiv, while Dnipropetrovsk and other regions came under attack. There were fatalities and injuries as a result of the attacks. This was reported by representatives of the regional military administrations, local authorities, and the police, UNN writes.
Details
In Dnipropetrovsk region, the Russians attacked three districts with drones nearly 20 times. An enterprise was damaged in Dnipro, and a 35-year-old man was injured. In Nikopol district, Nikopol, the Marhanets, Chervonohryhorivka, and Myrove communities came under attack. An administrative building, infrastructure, and a high-rise building were damaged.
At least three strikes by Russian drones were recorded in Kharkiv overnight. According to Mayor Ihor Terekhov, at around 03:17, the enemy attacked the Kholodnohirskyi district, where a fire broke out.
Later, a drone struck in the Saltivskyi district. According to updated information, an educational institution was hit. At around 07:20, an attack on the Industrialnyi district was also recorded. The consequences are being clarified.
The day before, on October 28, a 60-year-old man was killed in a Russian strike on Kharkiv's Osnovianskyi district. Three other men, aged 41, 46, and 56, were hospitalized. A 48-year-old woman also required medical assistance.
In Zaporizhzhia region, Russian forces launched 849 strikes on 44 settlements in the region over the course of the day. In particular, 20 airstrikes were recorded against a number of settlements, including Komyshuvakha, Zarichne, Veselianka, Vilniansk, and others.
In Rivne region, a Russian drone attacked a civilian enterprise in Sarny district. A 42-year-old man was killed in the strike.
According to the police, vehicles on and near the enterprise's premises, as well as neighboring houses, were damaged. Rescuers extinguished the fire, while bomb disposal experts recovered fragments of the enemy drone.
