Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc holds lead with nearly 90% of votes counted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:37:00 UTC
14:37:00 KST

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc holds lead
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 29, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- Latest vote count at 90% shows Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc holding the lead at 53 seats
- Anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot at 48 seats
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end
With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.
That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.
The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.
Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.
The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.
Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.
Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.
According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.
This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.
The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.
UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law.
"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.
"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."
Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.
He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW
Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.
"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."
Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.
"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.
Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.
WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock
Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.
Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.
GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc
Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

Why a Democratic win in US midterms could adversely affect Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:36:08 UTC
14:36:08 KST

Why a Democratic win in US midterms could adversely affect Europe
Complacency about rising far-right movements and renewed pressure on Ukraine could be the result.
The United States midterm elections appear stacked against the ruling Republicans, with polls suggesting the Democrats average an eight-point lead in the House of Representatives and the Senate. But if Democrats take one or both houses, could they affect upcoming elections in Europe?
Not fundamentally, analysts and observers have told Al Jazeera, but besides a welcome improvement in transatlantic relations, they point to two potentially adverse effects.
First, a Democratic Congress might produce complacency among Europeans regarding their own far-right movements.
Second, it might spur US President Donald Trump to raise pressure on Ukraine to make a deal it doesn’t want to make with Russia.
“If the Democrats win the House, let alone both houses, it will be read as, ‘you see democracies bounce back,’” said Catherine Fieschi, a nonresident scholar at Carnegie Europe, specialising in European far-right politics. It would introduce “the idea that these things don’t mean the advent of a fascist regime”, she said.
From her vantage point in Paris, Fieschi said she imagines a Democratic win leading to “a whole discussion about whether we should fear a Marine Le Pen election as much as some people say we should, or whether, in fact, it’s swings and roundabouts and, at some point, if people are really bad and really incompetent, then elections right the way,” she said.
French right-wing politician Marine Le Pen is currently leading the field in polling for presidential elections scheduled for April 18, with surveys indicating she has about 34 percent of the popular vote.
There is a precedent for the complacency Fieschi alludes to. In June 2025, the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), a think tank, polled Europeans following Trump’s first six months in office. Clear majorities in Western Europe said the US political system was broken. In Eastern Europe, majorities said it was working well – though they were weighted towards right-wing voters.
Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris warned against giving too much credit to the US for what Europeans think and do, however.
He said he believes European public opinion hardened against asylum and economic migration independently, but the US marked the shift by expressing it more violently, with military deportation flights and armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents sweeping American cities.
“I think there was a European about-turn on migration. We saw this in Germany, which had a welcoming attitude [to refugees] for many years, and they went to a more controlled policy. All northern European governments saw societies change,” he told Al Jazeera.
“But the US provided a change in tone, from induction and integration and benefaction to deterrence, border protection, increased returns and consequences if asylum is denied. I do think that pivot played a role in Europe,” Plevris added.
The fallout for Ukraine
Should French voters decide that the only way out is through electing Le Pen – “like some kind of strong medicine that would wake us up to what we might lose”, as Fieschi put it – they would have to contend with three controversial propositions – cutting French financial contributions to the European Union’s federal budget to pay for earlier retirement, cutting military aid to Ukraine and possibly leaving the single currency, the euro, in favour of a devalued franc.
Any one of those policy moves would be a major setback for the European project, which has coalesced around trade, money and now security. A cut in assistance to Ukraine would remove 3.5 percent of its foreign military aid, according to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine Support Tracker, which other allies would have to make up.
At the same time, “we could end up in a situation where Trump is basically clinching deals with Putin as fast as he can,” said Fieschi, referring to the US-Russian strategy to coerce Ukraine into a peace agreement that involves sacrificing its eastern Donbas region – something Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said would be a strategic error leading to renewed war, and which a majority of Ukrainians are against.
Trump has already leveraged US early warning on incoming ballistics and Starlink satellite navigation against Ukraine. He has twice echoed Russian calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced.
Compounding this renewed pressure from a beleaguered White House, Russia could intensify its “all-domain war”, which many European governments believe it is already waging against them, said Victoria Vdovychenko, a Ukraine expert at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics.
“Cognitive warfare never stopped on the European continent, and Russians are already using existing vulnerabilities to the utmost,” she told Al Jazeera. “I hope that the European partners will be staying very strong.”
What Europeans think
Trump’s abandonment of the world order the US and Europe established after World War II, his disregard for democracy and human rights, and his betrayal of Ukraine have already transformed European public opinion, observers say.
Only 31 percent of Europeans see the US as Europe’s “most trustworthy ally”, down from 51 percent in 2024, when Trump’s predecessor, Joe Biden, was in office, according to a poll for the German think tank Bertelsmann Stiftung.
Seventy-three percent of Europeans across all age groups say Europe should “go its own way” rather than continue a close cooperation with the US, up from 63 percent in 2024, and that figure includes a clear majority among those on the centre-right and right.
In this year’s Spring Eurobarometer, a regular pulse-taking conducted by the European Commission, 68 percent of respondents wanted the EU’s role in protecting Europeans from global crises and security risks to increase, while 39 percent wanted it to be a top priority.
In a June poll for the European Council on Foreign Relations, the description of the US as an “ally” fell from 22 percent in November 2024 to 11 percent across all territories polled in Eastern and Western Europe.
In a June poll for the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based think tank, 76 percent of people polled in 36 countries, of which nine were EU members, expressed no confidence in Trump, and 57 percent expressed unfavourable views of the US.
It would appear that such shifts against the US and especially Republicans, formed over two Trump terms, would be difficult to reverse in a single congressional election, especially with a Russian war ongoing in Europe.

Ukraine seeks to expand participation in special tribunal on Russian aggression, Karasevych says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:36:00 UTC
14:36:00 KST

Ukraine seeks to expand participation in special tribunal on Russian aggression, Karasevych says
Oleksandr Karasevych, State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine, made this statement in comments to a Ukrinform correspondent in New York.
“Regarding the special tribunal, we are currently actively working to expand its geographic participation,” he noted.
Karasevych recalled that Ukraine already has a legal decision from the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe regarding the tribunal, which was supported by 38 states and the European Union. Now they must implement the agreement at the national level.
“This is no longer a political statement; it is now a legal factor,” the State Secretary emphasized.
He added that, at the same time, Ukraine is seeking to involve more states outside the Council of Europe in the tribunal. In particular, a Ukrainian delegation recently visited Japan to explain the importance of its participation at the political and governmental levels.
Karasevych noted that Japan, Australia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, and Canada were part of a key group of states that participated in drafting the legal mechanisms for establishing the tribunal, specifically its statute and the relevant agreement.
“They were part of the core group, meaning they participated at the technical level in developing the legal mechanisms, the statute, and the agreement. Now we need to work with them so that they also become participants,” he explained.
The State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs also pointed to two areas of work regarding Russia’s accountability: the creation of a special tribunal for the crime of aggression and a compensation mechanism to make up for the damages inflicted on Ukraine.
According to him, more states have formally joined the compensation mechanism, including those that are not members of the Council of Europe. Among them are Australia and Japan, which have joined the Register of Damages Caused by Russia’s Aggression Against Ukraine.
Karasevych recalled that a UN General Assembly resolution adopted in November 2022 served as the basis for developing the compensation mechanism.
He explained that the purpose of his visit to New York is to convey to the legal advisors of partner states—particularly those not yet involved in accountability processes—the importance of establishing mechanisms to hold Russia accountable.
“We must work with those who are not yet involved in our joint efforts, explaining to them what we are doing, why we are doing it, and why it is important not only for Ukraine but for the entire international community,” Karasevych said.
He emphasized that discussing issues of international law and accountability for aggression is particularly appropriate at UN headquarters, since states must adhere to the principles upon which the Organization is founded.
Karasevych also noted that on Tuesday, the Ukrainian delegation participated in a UN Security Council meeting dedicated to the topic “Women, Peace, and Security.” The next meeting involving Ukraine, scheduled for Thursday, will focus on maritime navigation. According to him, it is particularly important for Ukraine to ensure compliance with international maritime safety standards in the Black and Azov Seas.
As reported by Ukrinform, an event was held at the UN on Wednesday dedicated to implementing mechanisms to hold Russia accountable for its aggression against Ukraine.

Hello Kitty maker Sanrio cuts ties with TV spy show after China backlash
Italy

14:25:53 KST

By Satoshi Sugiyama and John Geddie
TOKYO, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Hello Kitty maker Sanrio has cancelled a collaboration with a Japanese TV spy show after a backlash in China, the second incident in days to highlight the tightrope foreign firms and celebrities must walk in the lucrative market.
The Wednesday announcement by Sanrio’s Chinese subsidiary came just after French soccer star Kylian Mbappe apologised for remarks about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong that saw several Chinese sponsors cut ties with him.
The hit show VIVANT, produced by Japanese broadcaster TBS and also available on Netflix, centres on Japanese spies and a terrorist organisation called Tent. The latest season, currently being aired, depicts a fictional Chinese intelligence agency capturing and torturing some of the Japanese spies.
Chinese anger over Sanrio’s range of soft toys, including Hello Kitty, dressed as spies from the show has simmered for days on social media and came to a head this week when Chinese state media ramped up the condemnation.
“We deeply apologize for the concern this has caused everyone,” Sanrio’s Chinese subsidiary said in a statement.
“Regarding this collaboration, we believe it contains expressions that are inconsistent with the corporate philosophy of the Sanrio Group. We have therefore decided to terminate this collaboration along with all subsequent projects and promotional activities.”
TBS did not have immediate comment on the cancellation.
TBS President Masamine Ryuho said at a regular press conference on Wednesday that the drama is “entirely fictional and has no intention of disparaging any specific country”, local media reported.
Relations between China and Japan have plunged since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi late last year said that a hypothetical Chinese attack on democratically ruled Taiwan could trigger a military response from Tokyo.
China has urged its citizens not to travel to Japan and throttled exports of rare earths to the country, minerals vital to the manufacturing of everything from cars to weapons.
Swathes of Japanese firms including Sanrio, however, are still reliant on the world’s second-biggest economy for sales. Sanrio booked sales of 9.8 billion yen ($62 million) in China in the first quarter, up almost 25% on the same period a year earlier.
Foreign brands have often faced public backlash in China. Dolce & Gabbana cancelled a Shanghai fashion show in 2018 after ads showed a Chinese woman struggling to eat pizza and spaghetti with chopsticks. H&M, Nike and Adidas in 2021 came under attack over comments made about labour conditions in Xinjiang.
(Reporting by Satoshi Sugiyama and John Geddie in Tokyo; Editing by Edwina Gibbs)

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung-based AerosoarX Chair Max Lo (羅正方) said Wednesday that the firm signed cooperation memorandums with US companies Rajant and SiMa.ai to develop AI-enabled drones and support local assembly in overseas markets, CNA reported.

The company said the partnership combines its drone platforms with Rajant’s communications technology and SiMa.ai’s onboard AI capabilities. The three firms are targeting the Indo-Pacific, Europe, the US, and Japan.
AerosoarX works with Rajant on US military projects, supplying drone subsystems and components. Shipments began in April and May, with assembly and integration expected to be completed in November.
For Japan’s interceptor drone requirements, AerosoarX is helping replace Chinese-made components with alternatives from other countries.
Lo said Ukraine, Poland, and the Czech Republic are proving grounds for drone technologies. AerosoarX is shipping key components and systems to the front lines to ensure they meet operational requirements.
AerosoarX plans to set up production across the first island chain. It aims to ensure supply chain stability, local control over production, and a division of labor among partners.
Regarding the US Department of Defense’s Drone Dominance Program, Lo said AerosoarX had delivered nearly 1,000 drones to the US. He said shipments could reach 10,000 units if the company successfully passes the program’s third-stage evaluation in 2027.

Among voters younger than 40, Shen received 58% support, leading Chiang by 25 percentage points. Chiang led Shen by 1 percentage point among voters aged 40 to 59, with 44% support, and by 6 points among those aged 60 and older.
Among DPP supporters, 91% backed Shen, while 86% of KMT supporters backed Chiang. Among TPP supporters, 75% favored Chiang and 16% supported Shen. Among independent voters, 40% backed Shen, 33% supported Chiang, and 26% remained undecided.
On public image, 46% viewed Shen favorably and 31% unfavorably, compared with 44% and 36% for Chiang. On trustworthiness regarding major policies and personal pledges, 40% considered Chiang more consistent and trustworthy, while 39% trusted Shen more and 21% had no opinion.
Shen also led in voter perceptions of the candidates' visions for Taipei, with 44% finding his proposals more appealing, compared with 28% who favored Chiang's vision. Among voters younger than 40, nearly 60% preferred Shen's vision.
The poll was conducted Oct. 20-22 and Oct. 25, interviewing 1,115 adults registered as Taipei residents, while 264 people declined to participate. The survey had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

Anthropic also disclosed that TSMC has sometimes been unable to meet market demand for chip manufacturing capacity. As a result, the company said it has “not always been able to obtain sufficient quantities of chips on a timely basis.”
The filing said any restrictions or delays affecting advanced chip supplies from Taiwan or TSMC could adversely affect Anthropic’s business, financial condition, and operating results.

‘There has to be a bolder shift’: retail and hospitality businesses assess relief in budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

“It is like letting the tyres down and then handing you a pump,” says James Nye, assessing the relief handed to businesses in John Healey’s first budget as chancellor.
The managing director of Norfolk’s Anglian Country Inns argues that the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but added more labour costs for already burdened companies.
Nye, who employs 500 people at the height of the season at its 10 venues across Norfolk and Hertfordshire, was among those business owners watching Healey carefully on Wednesday, after two previous Labour budgets under Rachel Reeves had loaded extra costs on to businesses.
Healey aimed to help high street operators by removing the business rates burden from more small businesses and limiting the rise in the minimum wage for younger workers.
The chancellor put a lid on increases to business rates, so they will only rise in line with inflation for two years, and clamped down on VAT dodging by online sellers, among other measures intended to help high streets. However, some businesses argued Andy Burnham’s chancellor could have gone further.
Pets Corner, family-owned retailer
Dean Richmond, the owner of the Pets Corner chain, says the chancellor has not fixed the “fundamental problem” that its costs are rising faster than it can increase sales.
The family-owned business, founded by Richmond’s parents in 1968, now employs 1,200 people and has 159 stores. He does not expect to get much benefit from the increase in the threshold at which business rates begin to be paid.
“It’s a bit ‘moving the deckchairs on the Titanic’ on rates. There has to be a bolder shift if the government is going to help offline retail,” Richmond says.
He welcomed the move to ensure that online marketplaces such as Amazon collect VAT from more sellers, but was disappointed that Healey did not bring forward the end of tax breaks for online sellers, such as Shein and Temu, importing cheaper items from overseas.
“It feels like the world’s against us. When offline retailers all but disappear the world will miss us,” he says.
While he says Reeves’s budgets had been “really damaging, this is safe but isn’t going to change anything”.
“It is not a good news budget with the minimum wage going up,” he says, on top of the previous changes to employers’ national insurance contributions (NICs) and big increases in the minimum wage for employers.
Richmond says the business, based in Crawley in Sussex, had been forced to make “pretty drastic cuts” to the number of people it employed and to reduce bonus incentives, and had shifted to hiring older, more experienced people as there was less incentive to hire new starters.
Herdy, independent retailer and brand
Spencer Hannah is the co-founder and owner of Herdy, which has five shops in Cumbria and sells its cartoon sheep-branded homewares and clothing online and to other retailers in the UK and overseas.
“The chancellor’s key narrative was that he wanted to support British businesses doing business with Britain and we applaud and support that,” says Hannah, whose business employs 28 people directly.
But Hannah says the budget lacked the “seismic difference” to help UK retailers and their local suppliers. He welcomed relief on business rates for smaller shops but says that was “not counterbalancing what’s happened in the last two years”.
“Like everybody else running small and medium-sized enterprises, life has got slowly harder over the last two budgets and some poor choices have been made by the [last] leadership in government.”
He says increases in national insurance contributions, the minimum wage and other costs such as rent and energy have weighed on the business directly, but the “most frustrating thing” has been the impact of the higher costs for his domestic suppliers. He has been forced to ditch some of them, such as its mug manufacturer in Stoke, and look abroad.
Anglian Country Inns, pub and hotel operator
Nye says the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but against a very tough backdrop.
He welcomes help on business rates for smaller venues but says this is unlikely to assist Anglian directly. He was disappointed that the chancellor had yet again put up the legal minimum wage from April, which will more than offset the rates change for most.
A failure to cut VAT for hospitality businesses or cut national insurance contributions for younger workers were further disappointments.
Nye hopes that Healey’s support for household energy bills “might help consumer confidence”, but added: “We were expecting a little bit more to offset the massive tax increases hospitality has faced.”
“We are being crippled by taxes as a sector and the cumulative tax burden is horrific. We pay 83% as a percentage of our profits in tax,” Nye says.
“I don’t mind paying people more, but we’re then being taxed on it because the NICs threshold hasn’t changed, and the rate of NICs has gone up, so every time that the national minimum wage goes up, we’re paying more and more in tax.
“The cost of going out is getting more and more expensive. My biggest fear is that hospitality starts becoming a luxury rather than a convenience.”

Thames Water creditors to vote on emergency £2.4bn loan as cash runs low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

A group of creditors to troubled Thames Water are poised to vote on whether to grant an emergency £2.4bn loan to keep the company afloat, as campaigners raise concerns it could add £40 to each household’s bills in interest alone.
A consortium of creditors, called London & Valley Water, will vote on Thursday on whether to increase a funding facility for the debt-laden utility company to £5.4bn to keep it operating to autumn 2027.
The company’s class A creditors, which include BlackRock, Elliott Management and Silver Point Capital, last year granted it a £3bn loan at a 9.75% interest rate.
This month, Thames Water said it needed a further £2.4bn cash injection because it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its extensive debt pile before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”.
Thames Water has previously said that customers will not be on the hook for the interest on the £3bn loan, but it has almost run out of money and not paid down the debt.
Analysis by the campaign group We Own It showed that the £2.4bn loan, if it is granted on the same terms and added to bills, would cost £40 per household in interest alone, and £454 per household if the entire loan amount was included. London & Valley Water insisted it would not be added to bills.
Andy Burnham is now deciding whether to allow a takeover deal by the water company’s creditors, which would entail writing off fines and reducing environmental commitments. He is also mulling whether to nationalise the company or take another form of state control.
Some Labour politicians and environmental campaigners have said Burnham should instead put Thames Water into special administration, a form of temporary government control while a new buyer is sought.
Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “Since privatisation, £11.9bn has been extracted from Thames Water. They have already had more than enough of our money. If they cannot survive without yet another excruciatingly expensive bailout, this government must let them go bust and bring them into special administration, followed by permanent public ownership.”
The utility company serves 16 million customers in London and the Thames Valley. It has been on the brink of collapse for several years after it became overwhelmed by a debt pile that is now about £20bn. Its shareholders walked away in 2024, leaving the company under the effective control of its creditors while they work out a deal to avoid bankruptcy.
In 2025, Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat MP for Witney, along with campaigners and junior creditors, unsuccessfully took the water company to court over the £3bn loan.
On the proposed £2.4bn loan, he said: “The creditors will likely hand Thames Water yet another massively overpriced rescue loan, which customers will end up having to pay for.
“This is just another short-term fix, paid for by customers and taxpayers. The government has had more than two years to make up its mind. It’s time it did so. Put Thames Water into special administration now.”
The creditors have approved 15 previous consent requests from Thames Water. The company said this month it had so far drawn £2.65bn of the £3bn available under the “super senior” facility.
Prof Dieter Helm, an economist at the University of Oxford, doubted that a turnaround of Thames Water could be “properly funded” and said further loans were merely postponing an “inevitable” special administration.
He said: “The future investment programme for the turnaround will not be properly funded. Thames – and indeed much of the rest of the industry – is caught between a political rock and a political hard place.”
Conquest added: “During a cost of living crisis, this government cannot continue to reward Thames Water’s failures at our expense.”
Burnham has been looking at ways to take control of Thames Water in an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control. He has urged his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a list of policies for the utility company.
One option under consideration is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.
A Thames Water spokesperson said: “Additional liquidity from creditors will enable the investment to continue uninterrupted while the business seeks a recapitalisation. Customer bills are set by Ofwat, and this funding does not add any costs for households.”
A spokesperson for the London & Valley Water consortium said: “No customer bills will be used to pay for the costs of Thames Water’s rescue financing. These costs are borne entirely by the class A creditors.
“Creditors have stepped in to provide the billions of pounds of private capital needed to ensure Thames Water’s record infrastructure investment programme can continue, avoiding the need for any government financial support or taxpayer funding.”

Creative project reimagines history from First Nations perspective
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Address to the Nations reimagines history from Indigenous perspective
In the alternate timeline imagined by Address to the Nations, colonisation didn't happen in Australia, and the country is guided by a Ministry of Elders who oversee a democratic system of government.
The project is the brainchild of Yorta Yorta/Wurundjeri actor, writer, producer and director Tony Briggs, best known for creating and writing the musical comedy film, The Sapphires, and his close friend, award-winning artist, curator, producer and writer David Pledger.
To tell the story, which stretches over 300 years, Briggs and Pledger have begun building a portfolio with an art series, TV show, theatre production and video game part of the offering.
They've established the collaborative practice Tomorrow's Pasts under the moniker briggsnpledger and have built a universe that borrows from genres such as alternate futurism, counter-factual storytelling and science fiction to create an alternate Australian history as a way to imagine a better future.
"What if you could travel back in time? What would you do? We had many conversations over a long period of time around that very question," Briggs told PM.
"One of the things that kept popping up was, well, we think we'd like to sort of warn people of the mistakes.
"We can prompt you, [but] you have to find these mistakes for yourself and collect information and come forward and hopefully you come forward with the correct answers for humanity, if you like, [for] all of us, not just a certain sector of the community."
As part of the story, in 2063, the Ministry of Elders, which governs the Great Southern Nations (Australia in our current timeline) sends a message stick 300 years into the past to warn First Nations peoples about the arrival of outsiders (called The Accelerationists) and the potential for race-based conflicts.
The information sent into the past allows for the development of technology, giving First Nations peoples the power to keep control over their lands, regardless of the ambitions of outsiders.
The title of the project invokes the addresses the First Ministers (prime ministers in our timeline) deliver to the country.
Three out of the 10 addresses have so far been recorded. These are set in 1940, 1981 and 2022.
"1940 sets up what's about to happen, which is a race-based civil war in which Aboriginal Australia and its allies [are] contested by a group of [domestic] techno-fascists called the Accelerationists," Pledger told PM.
"Our First Minister in 1981 announces the beginning of the race-based civil war and over the subsequent 40 years there is a contest between Aboriginal Australians [and] allies, and the Accelerationists for sovereignty of the country."
Pledger says technology has a different trajectory in the alternate timeline.
"You have various changes in leadership, and the most significant one is the one that leads us up to the 2022 Address to the Nations, in which a young woman, Alinta Maris, who's a kind of tech genius, who has created HapTik Media and Blockchain over the preceding 20 years, in 2022, she develops non-lethal warfare, which brings the war to an end."
Audiences excited about project
The visual art series was launched in June and has been shown at special screenings in Canberra and Melbourne and will next year be programmed into Australia's premier Indigenous-led film festival, the Birrarangga Film Festival.
Founder and CEO of Indigital Mikaela Jade described the work as "incredible".
"We all have the agency and autonomy to be able to help create this future and I think this is a great catalyst for conversations," she said.
Author and historian Margo Ngawa Neale picked up on the close friendship between Briggs and Pledger.
"What I really like about it is the fact that it is Black and white working together as the only way we're going to move forward,"
she said.
"And these two fellas, their relationship is in fact in itself a model for what Address to the Nations can be."
Impossible choice between friendship and community
Briggs and Pledger first worked together about 25 years ago on the multimedia theatre production K, which Pledger wrote and directed and Briggs starred in.
They became fast friends, and their bond sparked the initial idea for Address to the Nations.
"When David and I first started talking about this idea, it was at the height of the Black Lives Matter movement and a question popped up around having to make a choice," Briggs said.
"What if either of us had to make a choice between our friendships based on our race, based on the colour of our skin, if we were forced to do it?
"And both of us, we both said, well, the first priority will be our families, number one.
"So, we talked around all of that and we sort of imagined the worst being forced upon us and it just sort of kind of cracked open this interesting conversation."
Ultimately, the two agreed they would fight to maintain their close friendship because, as Pledger says, they are like family.
"Family's not just about blood," Pledger said.
"Family's about an extension of the sorts of relationships that you can call familial at least.
"So, it gets very sticky with that kind of question because where's the friendship stop and the family begin?
"And I think that's one of the things where we found so interesting in these sort of discussions is the threshold keeps moving and hopefully it dissolves."

C Next Designers EMEA brings together over 250 professionals for design conference in Almería
For the ninth edition of the C Next Designers design conference, Spanish brand Cosentino brought together designers from Europe, Africa and the Middle East for three days of talks focused on “design as a driver of change”.
The event was held from 13 to 16 October in venues across Almería, Spain and included talks by designers such as Ron Arad, Karim Rashid and design studio Studiopepe.
It is the fourth iteration of the event held in Spain and the ninth worldwide.
This year’s conference focused on the theme Design to Transform, which champions “design as a force capable of reshaping society and adding value to it”, according to the team.
The first day opened with a welcome at the Cabo Gata Beach Hotel.
On Wednesday, the event moved to Cosentino’s industrial park in Cantoria, where Cosentino CEO Pilar Cosentino gave opening remarks.
Architect and designer Ron Arad then spoke with Cosentino commercial director for Europe, Jorge Lope about his career and collaborations with the brand, before the day ended with a guided tour of Cosentino’s facilities, including a local natural stone warehouse.
The day also featured the presentation of the latest product innovations by Valentín Tijeras, global vice president of product.
The second day took place at the Almería Science and Technology Park (PITA) and included presentations by brands Novara, Jung, Speho, TECE and Gaggenau.
Karim Rashid and Studiopepe then gave keynote speeches, which were a highlight of the day.
Dezeen editorial director (special projects) Max Fraser also moderated two panels as part of the event.
The first, held with Dornbracht, focused on hyper-personalisation as a creative tool and featured C’est Ici Design founder Monica Arango, founder of Black Architecture Danko Lekic and head of global channel management at Dornbracht Sascha Bialoian.
The second panel examined how design is changing our everyday habits, and featured Fran Silvestre Arquitectos founder Fran Silvestre, ZHA associate director Bidisha Sinha and founder of AS Architect Ayşin Sevgi Karakurt Macit.
Studio Haus closed the panels, and the event concluded with a gala dinner in the Cloister of Almería Cathedral, which was informed by the Dekton Artik Nodes collection, a new Cosentino material.
Cosentino previously launched Nara, a beige-toned porcelain surface designed to celebrate natural stone and Éclos, which was designed to be free of crystalline silica.
Last year’s C Next Designers conference featured talks by Sabine Marcelis and Peter Ippolito or Nini Andrade Silva.
To learn more about C Next Designers, visit the conference’s website.

Russia Uses North Korean Forced Labor to Sustain War Against Ukraine, Investigation Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:59:09 UTC
13:59:09 KST

A Russian recruitment network backed by North Korean officials is supplying workers to factories supporting Moscow’s war against Ukraine, using forced labor to sustain Russian production while channeling much of the workers’ earnings to Pyongyang, according to a new investigation published on Thursday, Oct. 29.
The investigation by The Hague-based human rights organization Global Rights Compliance (GRC) uncovered a network of Russian brokers bringing North Korean nationals into Russia on student visas to circumvent UN sanctions prohibiting their employment.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Some workers were placed at factories producing supplies for Russia’s military, including military food rations, according to the findings.
Investigators documented workers facing 12-hour shifts, as few as two days off per month, and threats of punishment against themselves or their families if they tried to escape.
The findings expose another dimension of the growing partnership between Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, whose government has already supplied Moscow with troops and ammunition for its war in Ukraine.
False student arrangements
The investigation identified a network linked to Moscow businessman Vladimir Sokolov and his Black Horse group of companies, which operates an online platform connecting Russian employers with North Korean workers.
North Koreans entered Russia on student visas, ostensibly to enroll at educational institutions, before being assigned to employers.
Moscow Hit by Massive Drone Attack as Airports Restrict Flights
Brokers received commissions of up to 150,000 rubles ($1,860) per worker, according to the investigation.
GRC researchers used publicly available records, facial recognition technology, and undercover inquiries, posing as prospective employers to document how the operation functioned.
The investigation also identified North Korean embassy officials in Moscow inspecting potential employment sites, indicating direct involvement by Pyongyang in arranging the placements.
One advertisement assured prospective employers that workers would not attempt to flee.
The network’s operations included placements at industrial production facilities, including a factory producing military rations used by Russian forces.
Forced labor finances North Korea’s weapons programs
The investigation found that much of the money paid for North Korean workers’ labor was diverted to the North Korean state rather than reaching the workers themselves.
The arrangement benefits both governments: Russia gains access to a tightly controlled workforce as it struggles to sustain wartime production, while Pyongyang receives foreign currency that can support its weapons programs.
GRC legal adviser Elise Lauriot Prevost said the findings exposed the convergence of two governments’ military interests, linking North Korea’s overseas forced-labor system to Russia’s growing wartime labor demands.
Lead investigator Dyland Carter said workers received little, if any, of the money employers paid for their services, with the proceeds flowing instead to the North Korean government.
The latest findings build on earlier GRC research published in March, which documented systematic exploitation of North Korean workers at Russian construction sites.
Based on interviews with 21 workers across three Russian cities, that investigation found conditions including shifts of up to 16 hours, passport confiscation, physical abuse, and mandatory payments to the North Korean government.
Some workers reported earning as little as $10 per month, while others faced escalating state-imposed quotas that trapped them in debt.
The researchers identified all 11 of the International Labour Organization’s indicators of forced labor in the workers’ testimonies.
Moscow and Pyongyang deepen wartime partnership
North Korea has become an important military partner for Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Pyongyang has supplied weapons and ammunition to Russian forces, while South Korean intelligence estimates that more than 10,000 North Korean troops have been deployed to fight alongside Russian forces since 2024.
The two countries signed a strategic partnership treaty in June 2024 that includes mutual defense commitments.
The forced-labor network shows how their cooperation extends beyond weapons transfers and battlefield operations to industrial production and financial support.
The arrangement operates despite UN Security Council sanctions adopted in 2017, which prohibited member states from hiring North Korean workers abroad and required their repatriation by the end of 2019.

US Army Pacific readying for potential Chinese invasion of Taiwan next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:29:56 UTC
13:29:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US Army Pacific has made preparations for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan next year, its commander, General Ronald Clark, said Tuesday.
The threat posed by the Davidson window is “still valid,” Clark said during the TechNet Indo-Pacific conference in Honolulu, Stars and Stripes reported. The Davidson window refers to then-US Indo-Pacific Command chief Admiral Philip Davidson’s assessment in 2021 that China would have the military capability to invade Taiwan by 2027.
However, an annual Office of the Director of National Intelligence report said the threat to Taiwan was not imminent, per Stars and Stripes. “Chinese leaders do not currently plan to execute an invasion of Taiwan in 2027, nor do they have a fixed timeline for achieving unification,” the report said.
Clark described the Davidson window as “a period of time for which we’re snapping the chalk line to say we need to be ready by this date.” “So, we’ve embarked upon a strategic approach to setting the theater that we refer to as ‘Army Ready Forward’,” he said.
Under this plan, Army Pacific has rotated troops, equipment, and supplies through islands west of the International Date Line, closer to China, Clark said.
The biggest challenge is balancing “exquisite high-end systems and affordable, mass-producible alternatives,” especially for autonomous systems, he said.

Taiwan High Speed Rail adds 40 trains for local elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:29:53 UTC
13:29:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan High Speed Rail will add 40 trains from Nov. 27 to 30 to meet demand during local elections, CNA reported Wednesday.
Voters will head to the polls on Nov. 28 to elect mayors, county magistrates, and other local officials. THSR will add 18 southbound and 22 northbound trains, bringing the total to 718 over four days.
Tickets go on sale at 12 a.m. Friday through the THSR website, mobile app, and participating convenience stores. Station ticket counters and vending machines will also sell tickets during operating hours.
THSR expects heavy southbound travel on Nov. 27 as people return home to vote. To ease crowding, it will run nine evening trains with 11 non-reserved cars each, allowing passengers to board without booking a seat.
Two to three southbound trains will depart from Nangang or Taipei each hour during the four-hour evening rush period beginning at 5 p.m. These trains will stop at every station through Taichung.
THSR advised passengers to book reserved seats early and collect their tickets before arriving at stations. Those without reservations should check station displays, as the number of non-reserved cars will vary from two to 11 per train.

- Australia is considering buying interceptors linked to Israel's Iron Dome to bolster air defences.

Australia is considering purchasing missile interceptors developed for Israel's Iron Dome as it seeks to rapidly build an air defence shield, officials said on Thursday.
Citing rapid changes in warfare seen in Ukraine and the Middle East, defence officials told a parliamentary committee that Australia wanted to have a ground-based missile defence system by the "early 2030s".
Discussions are being held over the availability of the US Patriot missile defence system and interceptor missiles developed by Israeli company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems for the Iron Dome, recently used in a new US Marines system and jointly manufactured with US company Raytheon.
Truck-mounted medium-range interceptors were tested by the US Marines in the Pacific territory of Guam in June during a regional war game in which Australia also took part.
Australia does not supply weapons to Israel and its purchase of Israeli defence products has come under political scrutiny.

Mexico’s Sheinbaum calls France’s Le Pen ‘misinformed’ over ‘Mexicanization’ remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:25:36 UTC
13:25:36 KST

Jorge Antonio Gonzalez Rocha
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum responded Wednesday to remarks made by French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen during a rally, where she warned that she would not allow the “Mexicanization” of France due to the presence of drug cartels.
“She is misinformed because the ‘Mexicanization’ that should be brought to the whole world is that of the values of Mexico's culture. Of honesty, of love, of solidarity, of fraternity, which are much needed in the entire world today,” Sheinbaum said during her morning briefing.
Le Pen, a prominent figure in France’s far-right National Rally (RN) party and a member of the French National Assembly, launched her campaign over the weekend with a strong message on security policy following the US’s approach of classifying Mexican drug cartels as terrorist organizations and pledging a hardline stance against organized crime.
“We will not allow France to slide into Mexicanization through the presence of cartels. We will eradicate these criminal organizations without hesitation, treating them as terrorists,” she said.
According to the latest security report by the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol), the presence and influence of Latin American criminal groups in the European Union have grown, particularly in drug trafficking, with the groups forming alliances with local European mafias.
Although Le Pen referred to insecurity in Mexico and organized crime as a driving force behind violence in the country, the Europol report does not mention Mexican cartels. Instead, it cites Colombian organizations such as the Clan del Golfo, Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Ecuador’s Los Lobos cartel.
However, Mexican criminal organizations, including the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and the Sinaloa Cartel, have been reported operating in France in recent months. The latter has been linked to a methamphetamine laboratory dismantled last year by the French Gendarmerie.
The term “Mexicanization” has been used by French politicians for years to refer to acts of violence in France. In 2024, French Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau used the term to warn of a growing wave of violence in the country following a shooting at a restaurant.
The use of the term sparked widespread indignation among Mexican officials, prompting a response from the Mexican Embassy in France.
“The use of this expression not only stigmatizes and stereotypes Mexico but also revictimizes Mexican families affected by violence. It also disregards the significant efforts made by the Mexican government to address violence in certain parts of its territory and undermines cooperation among members of the international community, including Mexico and France, to combat the scourge of drug trafficking and its deplorable consequences around the world,” it said.

Evolving Scope of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:21:00 UTC
13:21:00 KST

On October 25, Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Chinese Ambassador Jiang Zaidong in Islamabad to review progress on the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).
According to a statement issued by Pakistan’s Foreign Office, the discussions centered on advancing trade, investment, regional connectivity, agricultural modernization, and people-to-people exchanges. Dar also stressed the need for sustained high-level engagements to advance what the Pakistani officials describe as a “Pakistan-China Community of Shared Future in the New Era.” The meeting comes as both countries seek to fast-track the second phase of CPEC.
It appears to be part of the two countries’ ongoing effort to accelerate CPEC-related work and clarify the project’s second phase.
Phase one of the project is known for largely delivering energy projects, roads, and basic connectivity infrastructure. Phase two, on the other hand, is expected to emphasize industrial cooperation, mining, critical minerals, agriculture, and technology. Moreover, information sharing and people-to-people exchanges, long described as pillars of the corridor’s long-term vision, along with opening the mineral sector, are increasingly framed as part of the second phase.
On the ground, the path being taken to accelerate the second phase already looks different from the large-scale infrastructure focus that defined the early years of development.
Pakistan and China recently launched the China-Pakistan Information Corridor (CPIC), to counter what officials have called “misleading narratives,” expand cultural exchanges, and strengthen think tank cooperation.
From the Pakistani and Chinese perspectives, such narratives have often portrayed CPEC as little more than a debt burden or a strategic liability rather than a development partnership. The new information corridor, it seems, is intended to present a more coordinated account of the relationship. Moreover, a closer think tank engagement could, in principle, help policymakers in both countries better align priorities and reduce the informational friction that has occasionally complicated implementation. In that sense, CPIC seems linked to the practical needs of CPEC rather than standing apart from them.
In his address to inaugurate CPIC, Pakistan’s Information Minister Ataullah Tarar captured the intended shift when he observed that the first phase of CPEC connected lands, while the next would “connect our minds.” He said the information corridor will act as a bridge between the peoples of the two countries.
Arguably, this renewed emphasis on information sharing and narrative alignment is based on the fact that public perceptions and policy coordination matter as much as physical infrastructure at this stage.
Whether the issue of misinformation has undermined cooperation in the past remains open to debate. However, the decision to institutionalize fact-checking mechanisms and joint media working groups suggests that both countries now treat the issue as one that needs addressing now rather than deferred as a secondary concern.
Pakistan and China are also focusing on mapping, regulating, and opening Pakistan’s mineral sector, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province. CPEC’s phase two is expected to prioritize industrial cooperation, mining, and the excavation of critical minerals as well. Special economic zones, which are being set up, are more likely to succeed if the industries located in them can process local resources rather than simply assemble or package imported inputs.
In this regard, Rashakai Special Economic Zone (RSEZ) in KP offers a useful illustration of such cooperation between Pakistan and China. The project is operated through a joint venture involving the China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Economic Zone and Management Company. The SEZ was designed from the outset around value-addition industries, with mineral processing listed among its core designated sectors.
Provincial authorities in KP have recently intensified this message, particularly on mineral extraction and refining in the province. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi recently said that the province’s mineral resources would be extracted and sold to promote economic prosperity. He urged foreign companies to invest through joint ventures.
The timing of Kundi’s statement is particularly notable. The renewed emphasis on mineral governance comes amid a recent provincial leadership change in KP following the imposition of governor’s rule, which has shifted administrative authority from the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)-led provincial government to the federal government. Under this arrangement, Islamabad could now exercise more influence over provincial regulatory affairs, including strategic mineral assets.
This administrative shift has temporarily softened long-standing frictions between the federal and provincial governments over resource management and joint investment frameworks.
These developments point to a CPEC phase that appears to be less about infrastructure and more about information coordination, industrial networks, and the organized development of Pakistan’s mineral base.
Similarly, the approach of Pakistan and China in the second phase is different from the first phase as it appears to rest on the idea that closer policy alignment and people-to-people understanding will make the economic partnership under CPEC more viable over the long run.

A South Korean court on Thursday rejected a lawsuit by dozens of Tesla owners seeking full refunds for money paid for Full Self-Driving (FSD) driver-assistance software, ruling that the carmaker had not breached its contractual obligations.
The Seoul Central District Court ruled against the 88 plaintiffs, finding that the FSD option did not promise fully autonomous driving without human intervention and that Tesla had already provided some of the functions included in the package.
The court said Tesla’s obligation to deliver additional features depended on technological advances and regulatory approvals, adding that buyers had been aware that some functions could take considerable time to become available.

New Zealand construction costs steady despite sharp rise in diesel prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:13:40 CST
13:13:40 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand construction costs remained relatively steady in October despite a sharp rise in diesel prices, with average construction trade rates increasing just 0.1 percent over the past month, industry data showed on Thursday.
Diesel prices rose an average of 19 percent from the previous month and were 76.2 percent higher than in February. Fuel-intensive construction activities saw more noticeable increases, with excavation costs rising 3.9 percent, while piling and demolition costs both increased 0.6 percent, according to the latest Quotable Value (QV) CostBuilder monthly construction cost update.
The update recorded more than 7,000 data changes across major New Zealand cities including Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Dunedin, Hamilton and Palmerston North.
Other price rises included processed timber products, up 6.2 percent, medium-density fiberboard, up 2.8 percent, reinforcing, up 2.7 percent, and roofing and cladding, up 1.6 percent, it showed.
However, some costs declined, including adhesives and sealants, down 4.2 percent, kitchen-related costs, down 1.2 percent, and structural timber, down 0.2 percent, statistics showed.
Rising fuel costs had not translated into broad-based construction cost inflation, as increases and decreases across different products and trades largely offset each other, QV CostBuilder quantity surveyor Martin Bisset said in a statement.
Bisset advised those budgeting for construction work to continue allowing for cost fluctuations, particularly in fuel-sensitive areas. ■

Interview: CPC's discipline efforts offer reference for world, says Russian communist party leader

MOSCOW, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The efforts of the Communist Party of China (CPC) to strengthen Party discipline and improve governance offer valuable insights for political parties around the world, Dmitry Novikov, deputy chairman of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), told Xinhua.
The fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the CPC opened in Beijing on Monday, with a draft decision on some major issues concerning strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance for consideration.
Novikov, also first deputy chairman of the Russian State Duma Committee on International Affairs and deputy chairman of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, said the CPC strives to advance the interests of the people. Against this backdrop, the CPC's practice of self-reform merits close attention and offers a valuable reference for political parties with similar goals, he said.
"A disciplined Party means a strong, rapidly developing country and a cohesive society that is not torn apart by internal divisions. It means hope and a point of reference for all the peoples of the Global South," Novikov said.
He added that the CPC's emphasis on self-reform carries great significance, as it enables the Party to root out undesirable practices and address potential risks at an early stage.
Novikov stressed that strengthening self-discipline and internal oversight is not an end in itself for the CPC. Rather, the Party's fundamental task is to strengthen ties between governance and society, thereby consolidating public trust in state institutions.
"Power must be exercised to serve the people, rather than for personal gain or corporate interests. The CPC's experience is undoubtedly of historical importance. All political parties that claim to represent working people must study the practices of Chinese communists and adapt them to their respective national conditions," he said.
Novikov said that China's development is closely connected with global trends and that its goals are not at odds with the interests of people in other countries, noting that they are rooted in the principles of equality in international relations, cooperation, peaceful coexistence and the fair settlement of conflicts.
Novikov added that the CPRF closely follows the CPC's experience in Party building. "We are convinced that the uncompromising fight against bureaucracy, opportunism and complacency offers an important example for our comrades in other countries," he said.
"Politics can and must be clean, responsible and result-driven. The CPC's experience proves this. That is precisely why it has drawn worldwide attention," Novikov said. ■

Are the midterms the beginning of the end of the Trump political project?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:43:48 UTC
12:43:48 KST

Are the US midterms the beginning of the end of the Trump political project?
When Donald Trump won the 2024 US election against Kamala Harris, he pulled together a coalition of voters that don't have much history voting Republican.
Working class and lower income voters helped deliver him key swing states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, while Hispanic voters helped turn the sun belt states of Arizona and Nevada red.
Research from Pew found that Trump voters were markedly more racially and ethnically diverse in 2024 (20 per cent non-white) than they were in 2020 (14 per cent) and 2016 (10 per cent).
Virtually all demographic groups swung to Trump in 2024, but a New York Times analysis concluded the biggest shifts were among young Black and Hispanic voters.
At the time of that election, strategists wondered if Trump had catalysed a political realignment in the country that would continue to work in Republicans' favour.
But converting irregular voters into reliable members of the Republican base is not easy.
Two years on, as the cost of living bites, they don't appear to have stuck around, and the Hispanic voters that swung behind Trump have either swung right back to the Democrats, or are choosing to sit this election out.
The Republican Party appears almost certain to lose control of the House of Representatives in next week's midterm elections. Democrats also lead in polls in more than enough Senate races to be able to take control of that chamber as well (although many of those leads are within the margin of error).
Among the list of prizes that Democrats are hoping to pick up next week, the state of Texas glistens seductively.
Democrats haven't won a senate seat in the state since 1988, but this year, their candidate James Talarico is leading Republican candidate Ken Paxton in polling.
Republicans appear to be vulnerable in deep red states, and in recent weeks Trump has held rallies in Kansas, Iowa, Oklahoma and Alabama. That is not the strategy of a party that's feeling confident.
Donald Trump isn't on the ballot this year, but at rallies he has repeatedly asked voters to "pretend" he is.
"They say that Trump does great when he's on the ballot, but when he's not on the ballot … his people don't come and they don't vote for senators, congressmen," he said at a rally in South Carolina in August.
Loading...
Part of the Trump campaign's strategy in 2024 was to increase turnout rates among people who would usually stay home. Among the group of people who voted in that election but not in 2020, Pew estimated Trump had a 12 percentage point lead over Harris.
High turnout helped him two years ago. This year, it may be part of his undoing.
Trump wants voters to be thinking about him when they consider voting, because last time that drove lots of people to the polls.
The trouble is that, in 2026, the president is very unpopular.
Nobody's ever seen a president so disliked
American politicians are, as a general rule, held in much lower regard now than they used to be. But amidst an unpopular bunch, Donald Trump is reaching new depths.
YouGov and the Economist have been regularly tracking views on US presidents by asking voters whether they approve or disapprove of the job the leader is doing.
In his first term, Trump was into net negative territory effectively from the moment he took office. President Biden was in the negatives within seven months.
But in his second term, Trump has plummeted. A week out from polling day, the Economist recorded a net approval rating of -27, with 34 per cent of voters approving of the job he's doing and 61 per cent disapproving.
That is a lower net approval rating than any other president has recorded just before their midterm elections since World War II.
Given the president's party nearly always goes backwards in the House of Representatives, and that the Republicans only need to lose three seats to lose control of the House, it's not hard to see why forecasters are tipping a Democrat win.
If the midterms go as poorly for Republicans as opinion polls suggest, it could threaten Trump's command of the public's attention, as well as his authority over his party.
While he'll be in office for another two years, there's always an election around the corner in the US, and once the midterms are behind us attention will start to shift to the 2028 presidential election.
The results of these midterm elections will be an important moment in defining Trump's political legacy, as candidates start to position themselves for potential runs.
The current president regularly backs his preferred candidates in Republican primaries, and he believes his endorsement carries weight.
But will Republicans in the future be keen to embrace the Trump political project, or will they be keeping their distance the moment he's seen as a lame duck president?
