desert-inspired sensory playground brings kid’s perspective to downtown el paso
designed by miguel mendoza for the chalk the block festival, desert playgola combines recycled timber, iridescent curtains, and desert-inspired sculptures in an interactive public installation.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
DESERT PLAYGOLA BRINGS CHILD-SIZED EXPLORATION TO EL PASO
What does a city look like from just 95 centimeters above the ground? In downtown El Paso, Nómada Estudio Urbano explores this question through Desert Playgola, a temporary pavilion that transforms a traditional pergola into an interactive playground. Designed by Miguel Mendoza for the Chalk the Block public art festival, held on October 3–4, 2026, the installation combines desert-inspired sculptures, iridescent curtains, and recycled materials to create an environment where children can move, touch, and discover at their own pace. Commissioned by the City of El Paso through its Museums & Cultural Affairs Department (MCAD), the project occupies a pedestrian area along W Main Drive, turning an ordinary stretch of the city into a place for unexpected encounters.
The design takes inspiration from Urban95, an initiative by the Van Leer Foundation that encourages architects and urban planners to experience cities from the approximate height of a three-year-old child. Rather than treating children as miniature adults, the approach considers how scale, accessibility, and sensory experiences influence their relationship with public space. For Nómada Estudio Urbano, this perspective becomes the starting point for an environment without predetermined routes or activities. The name Desert Playgola combines ‘play’ and ‘pergola,’ reflecting a structure that offers shelter while leaving room for curiosity, imagination, and a little improvisation.
TIMBER STRUCTURE AND SCULPTURES CREATE A PLAYFUL LANDSCAPE
The pavilion is built around a timber framework supported by concrete block bases, with hanging iridescent curtains and colorful figures made from medium-density fiberboard (MDF). Recycled wooden pallets form a series of raised platforms covered in artificial turf, introducing changes in height and texture across the installation. Freestanding sculptures resembling prickly pear cacti are assembled from interlocking MDF pieces, bringing elements of the surrounding landscape within children’s reach. Together, these components transform the familiar pergola into a small terrain of passages, surfaces, and objects that invite visitors to explore rather than simply walk through.
The Chihuahuan Desert provides the project’s visual vocabulary, with references to prickly pears, ocotillo plants, and the region’s distinctive topography. Some of the hanging elements come together to form a face, giving Desert Playgola an almost character-like presence along the street. From a distance, the installation appears as a colorful figure occupying the urban landscape; up close, its individual parts become objects to navigate and interact with. This shift between recognizable imagery and abstract forms allows the pavilion to operate simultaneously as a piece of public art, a sheltered gathering place, and an informal playground.
SENSORY PLAY REIMAGINES THE CITY FROM 95 CENTIMETERS
Movement, light, and touch play an equally important role in the experience. Wind animates the iridescent curtains, sunlight projects shifting shadows across the ground, and artificial lighting transforms the pavilion’s appearance after dark. Children can pass between hanging elements, climb onto low platforms, examine different textures, or simply find a place to pause. There is no prescribed sequence to follow, and the installation accommodates different ways of engaging with its materials and spaces. The result is a playground that offers possibilities rather than instructions, allowing its youngest visitors to decide what happens next.
Positioned beside La Nube, El Paso’s interactive museum, Desert Playgola extends the idea of playful learning into the surrounding public realm. Its temporary presence during Chalk the Block introduces a different rhythm to the pedestrian route, encouraging visitors of different ages to stop, explore, and share the same space. For Nómada Estudio Urbano, the project reflects a broader interest in making cities more responsive to children’s experiences without separating them from everyday urban life. The studio summarizes its approach with a simple premise: a city that plays is a city that cares. In this case, it begins by bringing the city a little closer to the ground.

By Bo Erickson and Nandita Bose
CHILLICOTHE, Ohio/MORROW, Georgia, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Neither man is on the ballot but Republican President Donald Trump and Democratic former President Barack Obama took prominent roles on the campaign trail on Wednesday, with less than a week to go before congressional races that could shift the balance of power in Washington.
While Trump has been on a weeks-long campaign blitz that has underlined Republican concerns about losing control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, Obama had kept a relatively low public profile until the past week, during which he has delivered blistering speeches criticizing Trump.
Thirty-five of the 100 Senate seats and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are being contested next Tuesday. Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats’ chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest for the Senate seen as very close.
On Wednesday, Obama appeared in Morrow, Georgia, near Atlanta, where he urged voters to support Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who faces a challenge from Representative Mike Collins, a Republican.
While delivering the standard Democratic critique of Trump for imposing tariffs and going to war in Iran, Obama also said America’s values were on the ballot, as he recalled the vision of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., who is buried in Atlanta.
“There is a moral component to the choices we face right now,” Obama said.
“We are not going to fix the system that’s broken, we’re not going to unrig our economy, so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes, where people in the highest offices of the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully, if we continue to have a culture where money is deemed the only measure of our worth,” Obama said.
Trump’s public approval rating has fallen to a near record low, with Americans increasingly sour on the high cost of living and the Iran war, but he remains an animating force in the party and has campaigned hard to increase Republican turnout.
Americans have been voting for weeks, with 40 million ballots already cast, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million Americans voted early in the last midterm elections in 2022.
Addressing a rally inside a modest college gymnasium in the Ohio town of Chillicothe, the president appeared with Senator Jon Husted of Ohio as he faces a challenge from Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown.
Trump attacked Brown for supporting immigration policies the president said had overwhelmed Springfield, Ohio, with Haitian migrants. “The town went to hell,” he said.
Trump spread false claims during the 2024 presidential campaign that Haitian immigrants in Springfield were eating cats and dogs, allegations local officials repeatedly said were untrue.
TRUMP FACES PROTESTERS
Enthusiastic crowds have cheered Trump at rallies throughout the campaign, but hundreds of protesters lined Trump’s motorcade route in rural Chillicothe, raising banners that read, “Republican against Trump,” “Grab them by the ballot” and “GOP: Guardians of pedophiles.”
During the rally, protesters interrupted Trump several times, including at least one who shouted about deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
“I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” Trump said in response.
Trump and Epstein socialized in the 1990s and early 2000s, but Trump has said they later had a falling out and that he barred Epstein from Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s private club in Palm Beach, Florida.
Justice Department releases from the Epstein files have included references to Trump, as well as many other prominent figures. The department has cautioned that some materials contain allegations that were unverified or uncorroborated.
Protesters have interrupted Trump at virtually all his recent rallies. He typically accuses them of being paid protesters as they are carted off by security.
In Cleveland on Saturday, Obama poked fun at Trump’s taste in interior decorating, saying, “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” a chain of casual dining restaurants.
Trump defended his White House decor and said Obama left the property deteriorated.
“The White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country, and we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years,” Trump said in Ohio.
ALASKA, MICHIGAN RACES
Democrats will need to pick up seats in traditionally Republican-leaning states such as Ohio, Iowa or Alaska to overcome the current 53-47 Republican majority in the Senate.
The New York Times reported that aides to Mary Peltola, the Senate Democratic nominee in Alaska, worked with the campaign’s lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats’ campaign arm to recruit two candidates who are on the ballot and could siphon votes from incumbent Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan.
Representatives for Peltola did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
“Mary Peltola should resign from the race. I think she should be criminally prosecuted for what she did,” Trump told reporters before departing for Ohio.
In Michigan, where Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Gary Peters, both campaigns are relying on high-profile allies to energize supporters and boost turnout.
Rogers spent the day campaigning with Senator Ted Cruz of Texas on a four-stop bus tour culminating in Imlay City, a small community northeast of Detroit. El-Sayed, meanwhile, was scheduled to join Peters and fellow Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin for an evening canvassing rally in Downriver, southwest of Detroit.

Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:39:27 UTC
12:39:27 KST

Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
- Date:
- October 28, 2026
- Source:
- Vienna University of Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have defied a long-standing rule of laser physics by generating X-rays with much higher energies than conventional theory predicts. The surprising discovery reveals how two electrons working together can overcome a previously accepted limit, opening new possibilities for quantum research.
- Share:
Scientists have pushed X-ray generation beyond a long-accepted limit in laser physics, revealing a surprising quantum effect that conventional theory does not account for. By directing powerful ultraviolet lasers at helium atoms, researchers produced X-rays with substantially higher energies than the standard model predicts. The breakthrough depends on an unusual interaction between two electrons that allows them to release their energy together.
The discovery comes from a collaboration between TU Wien and the University of California San Diego and builds on research that helped establish the field of attosecond physics. Laser techniques developed at TU Wien in the 1990s contributed to advances recognized by the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics.
For decades, scientists have understood that directing laser light at certain atoms can cause them to emit extremely short pulses of much higher-frequency light, including X-rays. However, the established theory predicts a maximum energy for these emissions based on the properties of the incoming laser. Beyond this boundary, known as the energy cutoff, X-ray production becomes extremely weak.
The new experiment demonstrates that this familiar limit can be exceeded when two electrons interact in a particular way. The findings were published in Nature Photonics.
How Lasers Generate Powerful X-Ray Pulses
"The mechanism behind short X-ray pulses has been well known for a long time," says Prof. Tenio Popmintchev from the Institute of Photonics at TU Wien. "The laser tears a single electron away from the atom. The electron is then accelerated in the laser's electric field until it eventually collides with the atom again. The energy it loses in the process is emitted in the form of light."
During this process, the laser's electric field drives the freed electron away from its parent atom before bringing it back. When the electron returns and releases its energy, it generates light at frequencies far higher than those of the original laser beam.
Nobel laureate Ferenc Krausz used this mechanism in pioneering experiments during the 1990s. Tenio Popmintchev and his colleagues now work at the same TU Wien institute where Krausz conducted his earlier research, but their latest experiment has pushed the process beyond its previously understood boundaries.
"It can be shown that when the electron returns to its atom, it generates a whole range of different frequencies with roughly equal intensity," says Dimitar Popmintchev, postdoc in Tenio Popmintchev's team at TU Wien. "But there is an upper limit. Frequencies above this limit are much weaker; it is simply not possible to exceed a certain maximum frequency."
That prediction describes the conventional process involving a single electron. The researchers wanted to find out whether the outcome would change if two electrons participated instead.
Two Electrons Break the Expected X-Ray Energy Limit
To investigate, the team used intense ultraviolet (UV) laser pulses to interact with helium atoms. Unlike the usual process involving one electron, the experiment allowed both of helium's electrons to be removed in succession.
The first electron was released and accelerated by the laser field, followed by the second. Although the electrons were freed at different moments, their behavior remained connected through quantum correlations. This relationship means their motions cannot be treated as entirely independent.
By carefully controlling the ultraviolet laser pulses, the researchers could arrange for both electrons to return to the atom simultaneously.
"Using UV driving pulses, we can arrange for both electrons to return to the atom at exactly the same time," says Dimitar Popmintchev. "The energy of two electrons is then released all at once. And when more energy is available, a single higher-energy X-ray photon with higher frequency can also be generated."
This coordinated release of energy makes it possible to produce X-ray photons that exceed the conventional energy cutoff. Rather than relying on the energy of a single returning electron, the process draws on the combined energy of two interacting electrons.
An Unexpected X-Ray Signal Confirms the Discovery
The researchers found clear experimental evidence that the two-electron process was producing unusually energetic X-rays.
When they examined the spectrum of the emitted coherent radiation, they identified a second region of sustained emission at much higher photon energies than the standard theory predicts. This additional region, known as a plateau, was weaker than the primary emission but extended well beyond the previously established energy range.
The unexpected signal appeared only when the researchers used helium. Similar experiments involving argon and neon did not produce the same behavior in their outer electrons.
This difference provides important evidence for the proposed explanation. Helium has particularly strong correlations between its two electrons, allowing them to interact in ways that make the simultaneous release of energy possible. The outer electrons of argon and neon did not demonstrate the same effect under the experimental conditions.
A New Window Into Quantum Physics
Beyond producing higher-energy X-rays, the discovery could give scientists a powerful new way to investigate how electrons interact inside atoms and other materials.
The unusual coherent X-ray emission could serve as a highly sensitive spectroscopic "sensor" for electron-electron correlations. By studying the shape of the emitted spectrum, its maximum energy, and how it changes with the polarization of the laser light, researchers could gain information about the behavior of interacting electrons on extraordinarily short timescales.
These interactions occur over attoseconds, with one attosecond equal to one billionth of a billionth of a second. Observing processes at such speeds is essential for understanding how electrons move and influence one another in quantum systems.
Eventually, the same principle might be extended beyond individual helium atoms to molecules and solid materials in which electrons interact strongly.
The technique behind the discovery, known as high-harmonic generation, originally helped make attosecond physics possible. Now, researchers are finding that it can also reveal the complex behavior of multiple interacting quantum particles.
These insights could contribute to research on quantum computing and help scientists understand and design advanced nanomaterials with carefully controlled properties.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Vienna University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Siyang Wang, Jieyu Yan, Alba de las Heras, Sirius Song, Aleksander Prodanov, Zhihan Wu, Luis Plaja, Dimitar Popmintchev, Tenio Popmintchev. Correlated electrons extend X-ray high-harmonic generation beyond the single-electron limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (9): 1092 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01976-2

New York passes law restricting children’s use of AI chatbots

New York passes law restricting children’s use of AI chatbots
- New York passed a law on 28 October to limit minors’ use of AI chatbots that act as companions. Operators must verify ages and block chatbot traits that seem human or emotional.
- The law stops chatbots from making children think they are “human, alive, or experiences human emotions”, or that they have a “personal relationship” or “authority figure role”. Governor Kathy Hochul said it would stop chatbots acting like “friends, boyfriends and girlfriends”.
- The move is one of the toughest in the US and has split opinion. Tech:NYC called the wording “vague”, while Common Sense Media said it is “the strongest kids’ AI safety bill in the country”.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The governor of New York state signed a new law on Oct 28 preventing minors from using AI chatbots that act as companions, in one of the broadest moves yet for restricting consumer-facing models.
The law requires chatbot operators, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, to verify the ages of users and restrict the use of certain traits by the artificial intelligence interface if the user is under 18.
If used by a minor, chatbots would not be able to produce any content that could leave its user to believe it “is human, alive, or experiences human emotions”, the law states.
It also cannot generate outputs that makes the user think it “has a personal relationship, professional relationship, or an authority figure role”, nor can it frame the content it produces as being a “personal opinion”.
“No longer will minors have access to chatbots that pretend to be their friends, boyfriends and girlfriends,” New York Governor Kathy Hochul said at a signing ceremony on Oct 28.
“No longer will chatbots be able to keep sensitive information about a minor’s emotional and physical health,” Hochul added.
Other US states including California have also passed laws restricting chatbots, but the law signed by Hochul imposes some of the broadest language in regulating the tech, prompting backlash from AI companies.
Tech:NYC, a tech industry advocacy group for the sector in New York, criticised the “vague language” of the law.
“Keeping kids safe online should not mean cutting them off from tools that help them learn and prepare for careers,” the group said in a statement.
AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to an AFP request for comment on the law.
Common Sense Media, a non-profit advocacy group that provides guidelines for parents about media suitability for children, celebrated the bill’s passage, calling it “the strongest kids’ AI safety bill in the country”.
“AI companies offer chatbots with features that are dangerous, and even deadly, for kids and teens... Now, those harmful features will be outlawed in New York,” Common Sense Media chief executive Jim Steyer said in a statement. AFP

From infrastructure to AI: President Tokayev’s vision for Kazakhstan in a changing world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:18:25 UTC
12:18:25 KST

From infrastructure to AI: President Tokayev’s vision for Kazakhstan in a changing world
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's October 28 state-of-the-nation address outlined a new phase in Kazakhstan's development, combining a 6.5 trillion tenge infrastructure program with plans to strengthen energy security, develop artificial intelligence and raise living standards, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The address came as governments around the world reassess supply chains, energy needs and the infrastructure required for technological growth. For Kazakhstan, these changes present an opportunity to use its geographic position, natural resources and financial reserves to build a more diversified economy. They also place greater demands on the state, which must translate investment into productive businesses and better public services.
The speech marked a shift in emphasis within Tokayev's reform agenda. Following years of political and institutional changes, including the adoption of a new Constitution approved by 87.15% of voters in March, the President concentrated on what those institutions are expected to deliver.
Infrastructure as an economic strategy
The centerpiece was the People's Construction program, under which approximately 6.5 trillion tenge will be allocated from the National Fund through 2029 to modernize social, transport and engineering infrastructure. Some 1.5 trillion tenge is intended for projects during the remainder of 2026 and the first two months of 2027. Initial plans include around 70 healthcare facilities and nearly 50 education, sports and cultural facilities, along with improvements to utilities and transport networks. Tokayev proposed designating 2027 the Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction.
Kazakhstan's priorities reflect a wider international return to infrastructure investment. In 2021, the United States enacted the $1.2 trillion Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, including approximately $550 billion in new federal investment in transport, energy and communications. The programs differ considerably in scale and financing, but both recognize that productivity and technological competitiveness depend on reliable physical infrastructure.
Tokayev's initiative has a particularly strong domestic industrial component. He instructed that National Fund money should not be spent on imports, calling instead for greater use of Kazakhstan-made construction materials, metal structures and equipment, with local small and medium-sized enterprises involved in implementation. This could allow investment to generate demand beyond the construction industry, provided domestic suppliers can deliver the required quality and capacity.
The President also stressed that facilities must reflect the needs of individual regions. This is an important consideration for a program of such magnitude: economic returns will depend not only on how much is built, but on whether the new infrastructure is useful, affordable to operate and completed on schedule.
Energy security in the age of AI
One of the address's strongest economic connections was between artificial intelligence and electricity. Digital competitiveness is often discussed in terms of software and talent, yet data centers and advanced computing also require dependable energy supplies, communications networks and substantial capital investment.
Tokayev said Kazakhstan's annual generation of 123 billion kilowatt-hours was insufficient for its industrial and digital ambitions. He called for a sustainable electricity surplus by 2029, an updated energy balance through 2035 and accelerated development of new generating capacity. Construction of the Balkhash nuclear power plant could begin in 2027, while preparations for the proposed Moyinkum facility are expected to advance. The President also raised the possibility of a strategic uranium reserve and stressed the importance of developing domestic nuclear expertise.
He pointed to two supercomputers already launched, a third expected by year-end and the new fiber-optic connection across the Caspian Sea. These projects bring together two sides of technological development: the computational infrastructure needed for AI and the international connectivity needed to make it useful.
The address went beyond infrastructure to consider who benefits from digitalization. Tokayev called for a simplified legal regime for digital employment and pilot projects enabling rural producers to sell through online platforms. If the measures broaden access to markets and employment, digitalization could become a source of income rather than merely a more convenient way to obtain services.
Investment confidence and effective governance
Tokayev also placed considerable emphasis on the institutions that shape investment decisions. His proposals on taxation, business inspections and commercial justice share a central objective: make the rules more predictable while allowing the government to respond to practical difficulties.
Discussing the new Tax Code, the President said it was "not dogma" and directed officials to correct problematic provisions without subjecting businesses to continual rule changes. He also proposed considering a three-year moratorium on inspections of micro and small businesses from January 2027. The proposed pause, not yet enacted, would accompany efforts to strengthen digital oversight and reduce unnecessary administrative pressure.
The announcement concerning Alatau was particularly relevant to Kazakhstan's international investment ambitions. Tokayev proposed establishing an investment court based on the English common law model to hear commercial disputes, with other cases related to the city's special legal regime assigned to a civil court. The government must submit the necessary legislative amendments to the Kurultai by the end of January 2027.
The proposal addresses a consideration that financial incentives alone cannot resolve: investors need confidence that contracts will be upheld and commercial disputes decided predictably. Kazakhstan already operates a common law-based court at the Astana International Financial Centre, giving it relevant institutional experience. Applying a comparable approach in Alatau would build on an established legal framework rather than introduce an entirely unfamiliar model. Its effectiveness will depend on judicial independence, consistent judgments and their enforcement.
More broadly, Tokayev instructed the Presidential Administration to prepare a public administration reform plan by June 2027, emphasizing digital tools and clearer responsibilities. The emphasis on implementation links the country's institutional modernization with the practical requirements of economic development.
Growth that reaches households
The economic agenda included measures with direct implications for household incomes. Tokayev instructed the government to raise the minimum wage from 85,000 to 110,000 tenge on January 1, 2027, potentially benefiting nearly 1.8 million people. He also called for salary increases of up to 40% for eligible primary healthcare workers based on continuous service, affecting more than 77,000 professionals.
The President nevertheless identified inflation as a threat to living standards and called for closer coordination between the government and the National Bank. That warning matters alongside a construction program large enough to increase demand for labor, materials and financing. Higher nominal incomes and new facilities will have a greater effect if prices remain under control.
Kazakhstan enters this investment cycle with significant financial assets. According to figures cited in the address, gold and foreign exchange reserves together with National Fund assets exceed $130 billion. Tokayev argued that public resources should help attract private capital rather than replace it, and urged commercial banks to expand long-term lending to productive businesses. The challenge is to turn this financial capacity into sustainable growth without placing excessive pressure on the budget.
Kazakhstan's place in global supply chains
The international dimension of the address extended beyond technology. Tokayev called for Kazakhstan to move from serving mainly as a transit corridor between China and Europe toward operating logistics companies, consolidation hubs and digital freight systems. Capturing more value from transport would make geographic advantages more useful to the domestic economy.
A similar approach shaped his proposals on critical minerals. The President called for modern geological exploration, a national system for managing strategic metal reserves and partnerships connecting Kazakhstan to more advanced manufacturing. In agriculture, he emphasized better irrigation, long-term finance, modern processing and opportunities for applying AI.
These priorities fit Kazakhstan's multivector economic approach: maintain relations with different markets while building capabilities at home. For a middle power, resilience depends not only on maintaining diverse international partnerships but also on developing the infrastructure, industries and expertise that make those partnerships economically valuable.
From priorities to results
The address set several near-term checkpoints. An initial list of infrastructure projects is due by the end of 2026, Alatau's legislative amendments by January 2027 and the public administration reform plan by June 2027. Larger construction and energy goals extend through 2029.
The proposals are ambitious and interconnected. Better electricity supply would support industry and AI, more dependable commercial institutions could encourage investment, and infrastructure spending could stimulate domestic production while expanding public services. The results will depend on how effectively government agencies, businesses and financial institutions coordinate their work.
Tokayev's 2026 address thus places Kazakhstan's domestic development within a changing global economy. Its distinctive feature is the attempt to bring infrastructure, technological modernization, investment confidence and household well-being into one economic agenda. The measure of that approach will be whether these policies translate into lasting gains in productivity, competitiveness and living standards.

KazMunayGas and Exolum join forces to develop aviation fuel infrastructure in Kazakhstan

KazMunayGas and Exolum join forces to develop aviation fuel infrastructure in Kazakhstan
Kazakhstan’s national oil and gas company KazMunayGas (KMG) and international aviation fuel infrastructure group Exolum have agreed to cooperate on the development and modernization of aviation fuel facilities across Kazakhstan, Qazinform News Agency cites the press service of KMG.
The agreement was discussed during a meeting in Astana between KMG Management Board Chairman Askhat Khassenov and Ivan Muiño, Senior Vice President for Aviation at Exolum.
The talks focused on opportunities to expand aviation fuel infrastructure as part of Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to strengthen its transport, logistics and transit potential.
Following the meeting, KMG, KazMunayGas-Aero and Exolum Aviation signed a tripartite agreement outlining the key terms of their strategic cooperation. The document provides for the involvement of international investment, advanced technologies and industry expertise to develop aviation fuel infrastructure at airports across Kazakhstan.
For Exolum, entering the Kazakhstani market will mark the first stage of its expansion into the Eurasian region.
Under the proposed cooperation, the sides are considering the construction of aircraft refueling complexes and specialized aviation fuel storage facilities, as well as the modernization of existing infrastructure. The new and upgraded facilities will be designed to handle Jet A-1 aviation fuel in accordance with Joint Inspection Group (JIG) requirements for quality, safety and operational standards.
KMG will contribute its knowledge of the domestic market, coordinate engagement with aviation industry stakeholders and help identify and develop promising projects.
Cooperation with one of the major international companies in the sector will help accelerate technological modernization, introduce advanced practices in fuel infrastructure management and create conditions for further growth in international air transport through Kazakhstan, said Khassenov.
He also emphasized the importance of transferring Exolum’s expertise and technologies to Kazakhstani specialists, developing local workforce skills and introducing modern approaches to the operation of fuel facilities.
The companies will conduct a comprehensive economic assessment in the coming period. Based on its findings, they will determine specific projects, investment volumes, the allocation of responsibilities and the next stages of cooperation.

Activists accuse Israeli settlers of assault in occupied West Bank
Video footage posted online showed several men, some of them armed, beating Nathaniel and Andrey X.
Russian activist Adele Shoko has said that Israeli settlers attacked her alongside two of her colleagues in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, in the Masafer Yatta area of the occupied West Bank, according to social media posts.
Shoko said on social media platform X that she, US journalist Jasper Nathaniel, and Israeli-Russian activist Andrey X were beaten and threatened by armed settlers who stole equipment and personal items.

The assault follows an October 16 incident in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, where masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, setting trees on fire and throwing stones using slingshots.

Trump and Obama trade barbs in closing week of US midterm election

Trump and Obama trade barbs in closing week of US midterm elections
CHILLICOTHE, Ohio/MORROW, Georgia – Neither man is on the ballot but US Republican President Donald Trump and Democratic former president Barack Obama took prominent roles on the campaign trail on Oct 28, with less than a week to go before congressional races that could shift the balance of power in Washington.
While Trump has been on a weeks-long campaign blitz that has underlined Republican concerns about losing control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, Obama had kept a relatively low public profile until the past week, during which he has delivered blistering speeches criticising Trump.
Thirty-five of the 100 Senate seats and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are being contested on Nov 3. Non-partisan analysts generally favour Democrats’ chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest for the Senate seen as very close.
On Oct 28, Obama appeared in Morrow, Georgia, near Atlanta, where he urged voters to support Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who is challenged by Republican Representative Mike Collins.
While delivering the standard Democratic critique of Trump for imposing tariffs and going to war in Iran, Obama also said America’s values were on the ballot, as he recalled the vision of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, who is buried in Atlanta.
“There is a moral component to the choices we face right now,” he said. “We are not going to fix the system that’s broken, we’re not going to unrig our economy, so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes, where people in the highest offices of the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully, if we continue to have a culture where money is deemed the only measure of our worth.”
Trump’s public approval rating has fallen to a near record low, with Americans increasingly sour on the high cost of living and the Iran war, but he remains an animating force in the party and has campaigned hard to increase Republican turnout. Americans have been voting for weeks, with 40 million ballots already cast, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million Americans voted early in the last midterm elections in 2022.
Addressing a rally inside a modest college gymnasium in the Ohio town of Chillicothe, the President appeared with Senator Jon Husted of Ohio as he faces a challenge from Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown. He attacked Brown for supporting immigration policies that the President said had overwhelmed Springfield, Ohio, with Haitian migrants. “The town went to hell,” he said.
Trump spread false claims during the 2024 presidential campaign that Haitian immigrants in Springfield were eating cats and dogs, allegations that local officials repeatedly said were untrue.
Trump faces protesters
Enthusiastic crowds have cheered Trump at rallies throughout the campaign, but hundreds of protesters lined his motorcade route in rural Chillicothe, raising banners saying “Republican against Trump”, “Grab them by the ballot” and “GOP: Guardians of paedophiles”.
During the rally, protesters interrupted him several times, including at least one who shouted about the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” Trump said in response.
Trump and Epstein socialised in the 1990s and early 2000s, but Trump has said they later had a falling out and that he barred Epstein from Mar-a-Lago, the President’s private club in Palm Beach, Florida.
Justice Department releases from the Epstein files have included references to Trump and many other prominent figures. The department has cautioned that some materials contain allegations that were unverified or uncorroborated.
Protesters have interrupted Trump at virtually all his recent rallies. He typically accuses them of being paid protesters as they are carted off by security.
In Cleveland on Oct 24, Obama poked fun at Trump’s taste in interior decorating, saying: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory”, a chain of casual dining restaurants.
Trump defended his White House decor and said Obama left the property deteriorated. “The White House, I think, is the No. 1 symbol of our country, and we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years,” he said in Ohio.
Alaska, Michigan races
Democrats will need to pick up seats in traditionally Republican-leaning states like Ohio, Iowa or Alaska to overcome the current 53-47 Republican majority in the Senate.
The New York Times reported that aides to Mary Peltola, the Senate Democratic nominee in Alaska, worked with the campaign’s lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats’ campaign arm to recruit two candidates who are on the ballot and could siphon votes from incumbent Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan.
Representatives for Peltola did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
“Mary Peltola should resign from the race. I think she should be criminally prosecuted for what she did,” Trump told reporters before departing for Ohio.
In Michigan, where Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Gary Peters, both campaigns are relying on high-profile allies to energise supporters and boost turnout.
Rogers spent the day campaigning with Senator Ted Cruz of Texas on a four-stop bus tour culminating in Imlay City, a small community north-east of Detroit. El-Sayed, meanwhile, was scheduled to join Peters and fellow Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin for an evening canvassing rally in Downriver, south-west of Detroit. REUTERS

‘Feels like we’ve gone backwards’: Indonesia’s choking haze provides spark for wider protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:09:29 UTC
12:09:29 KST

As almost 2m hectares has gone up in smoke in Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, enveloping the region in a thick dystopian haze, 33-year-old university researcher Nurul Amalia has grown increasingly exasperated.
“The government claims to be continuously increasing the number of personnel to extinguish it. But we have yet to see any significant progress,” she says.
“People in Kalimantan continue to report toxic air conditions, and now we hear news of firefighters losing their lives,” she adds, of four volunteers killed fighting fires this month.
On Wednesday, Amalia joined hundreds in Jakarta protesting against the government, the second demonstration in a week. Chief among their demands was that President Prabowo Subianto declare the fires a national disaster.
The demand is just one on a list of grievances amid brewing anger in the world’s third-largest democracy, where analysts say a confluence of policy blunders, economic stress and a government seen as increasingly out of touch is sending Indonesia into a period of volatility unseen for decades.
Civil society groups have criticised the Prabowo presidency for wasteful government programs, increasing militarisation and centralisation of power, deepening patronage, attacks on the press, and what they say is a weakened judiciary.
The government communications agency said in a statement on Wednesday that it welcomed the aspirations of student protesters as part of an effort to nurture democracy, and that concerns raised about the environment, economy and legal reform were being addressed.
Some 70,000 firefighting personnel, it added, had been sent to fire-hit regions, and it was investigating corporations and individuals allegedly involved in starting the fires.
Prabowo marked two years in power this month, but some who voted for him say the country is, at best, stagnating.
“Not only has there been no progress,” says Ika Anastasia, a PR professional and Jakartan mother of three, “it actually feels like we’ve gone backwards.
“In my 32 years, I think this government is probably the worst,” says Aryana, a private-sector employee. “The problems keep coming one after another, and before one is solved, another appears.”
President’s approval rating sinks
Prabowo, a former military general and the ex-son-in-law of former dictator Suharto, ran in 2024 on a platform of continuity, cuddly vibes and a multibillion-dollar free meals program intended to target malnutrition.
Yet the flagship policy has been riddled with controversy.
In June this year the head of the national nutrition agency responsible for rolling out the program was arrested on allegations of corruption. Since it began, thousands of schoolchildren have been inadvertently poisoned after eating tainted meals. Among their complaints have been maggots and glass in their rice.
“This current government is strong at agenda setting in public policy, but it is very weak at delivery,” says Yanuar Nugroho, a former presidential staffer for Prabowo’s predecessor and a visiting fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS Yusof Ishak Institute.
“Never have I seen the situation like this,” he adds. “I think this is the worst and the most messy.”
In a statement on Wednesday, the government said it would strengthen supervision and involve local government in implementing the free meals program, with many children, pregnant women and lactating mothers benefiting from it.
But a poll this month by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting showed that about 62% of Indonesians now oppose it.
The same poll gave Prabowo an approval rating of 44.5%, the lowest of any Indonesian president since polling started 20 years ago.
“It’s just a horrific result. It shows that Prabowo has lost the country,” says Kevin O’Rourke, a longtime Indonesia analyst.
“I think that it’s the programs that he’s put out are failing, and those are things that people see in their communities,” he says, referring to the free meals and a costly village cooperatives program.
Economically, Indonesia is looking a bit wobbly too.
This year the Indonesian rupiah sank to record lows against the US dollar, while the country is up to its third finance minister in two years. In recent weeks footage has shown people forming snaking lines for fuel in Bali, Sulawesi and Kalimantan.
And, in what could be a major setback for south-east Asia’s biggest economy, this month global index provider MSCI threatened to downgrade Indonesia to “standalone market” status over unclear share ownership and suspected coordinated trading.
The government pointed out the economy had grown 5.29% in the second quarter of this year and poverty had fallen by 8%, while it had accelerated market reforms to address the issues raised by the MSCI.
Some analysts say the MSCI, which is not a regulator, may have gone too far.
The president was pugilistic in his response.
“Our country continues to face all sorts of disturbances, including the MSCI. They are trying to intimidate us,” he told his cabinet. “I simply want to tell MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will never back down.”
Amid the turbulence, analysts say Prabowo has developed a reputation for being stubborn, and reluctant to accept advice. The government disputed this claim, saying Prabowo holds continuous dialogue with various stakeholders.
“I can sense on the one hand, he is detached from the reality,” observes Yanuar Nugroho. “On the other hand, he has very, very strong ideas of him as like a saviour.”
So far demonstrations have been small, but the complaints are adding up.
“There is a lot of uncertainty at the moment and we’ve seen there is a lot of potential for demonstration,” says Kennedy Muslim, an analyst from Indonesian pollster Indikator. “What it needs is a trigger, but that couldn’t be predicted.”
Indonesia is now in a situation unprecedented since its reform era began after Suharto stepped down in 1998, says O’Rourke, noting that in previous administrations there were flaws but more democratic openness, independent institutions and checks and balances.
“In the past, actors always had to respect democracy and the rules of the elections and the rights of opponents in parliament. None of that exists now,” he says.
“Prabowo has a free hand. And so it’s very ugly and very unpredictable, volatile.”

Pakistan reverses decision, restores airspace access for Taiwan airlines

2026-10-29
02:44:33 UTC
11:44:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Pakistan has reversed its decision to deny Taiwanese airlines access to its airspace, restoring overflight rights for China Airlines and EVA Air, Bloomberg reported Wednesday evening.
According to documents reviewed by Bloomberg, Pakistan’s Civil Aviation Authority approved the two airlines to use Pakistani airspace from Oct. 28 through March 27, 2027.
The reversal came just hours after Pakistan Defense Minister Khawaja Asif, who also oversees aviation, told Bloomberg that the country’s aviation sector follows the “one China policy,” citing it as the reason for denying Taiwanese carriers permission to fly over Pakistan.
An earlier Bloomberg report described Pakistan as the first country to take such a measure against Taiwanese airlines.
Data from flight-tracking service Flightradar24 showed that China Airlines and EVA Air had not flown over Pakistani airspace since Sunday morning. At least 10 flights operated by the two carriers between Asia and Europe had instead flown over Russia during that period, per CNA.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs strongly condemned Pakistan’s earlier decision and remarks, accusing Islamabad of following Beijing’s narrative, disregarding reality, denigrating Taiwan’s sovereignty, and politicizing and weaponizing airspace.
The ministry said it would remain in close contact with the Ministry of Transportation and Communications. It also said it respects Taiwanese airlines’ decisions to select the most efficient routes based on flight safety, travel time, and cost, per UDN.
China Airlines and EVA Air declined to comment on Pakistan’s earlier restriction. Taiwan’s Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) said it had never prohibited airlines from flying over Russian airspace.
Transportation Minister Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) said Wednesday that airlines submit their own applications to use Russian airspace. The CAA manages flight origins and destinations, while respecting airlines’ applications to use individual countries’ airspace.
Chen said the fact that some airlines had begun flying over Russia indicated that their applications had been approved, adding that the CAA respects the carriers’ routing arrangements.

Michelin-starred Amaze blends heritage and modern technique
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:44:30 UTC
11:44:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Michelin-starred Chinese restaurant Amaze, winner of Taiwan’s inaugural Michelin Opening of the Year Award, has launched its autumn seasonal menu, “The Full Circle.”
Since opening in 2024, Amaze has earned acclaim for modern Chinese cuisine and refined hospitality. Executive Chef Yang Guang-zong (楊光宗), Chef Huang Jun-ren (黃俊仁), and Sous Chef Chou Chin-hua (周金樺) blend Jiangnan and Zhejiang culinary techniques with Western approaches to reinterpret classic regional dishes.
The menu’s title references the Chinese concept of roundness, symbolizing completeness, reunion, and harmony. Every dish, from appetizers to dessert, subtly incorporates circular visual motifs.
The meal opens with “shrimp and tea,” a variation on classic Longjing shrimp that layers tea aromas using tea powder and fried tea leaves.
Another starter, “smoked egg, scallop, and pepper,” features Sichongxi red-yolk duck eggs smoked with Ruby Black Tea, served over raw Hokkaido scallops with seared tiger-skin pepper sauce and lemon aiyu jelly.
Yang designed several dishes around personal memories and regional traditions. “Caviar and bean puree” pairs Italian caviar with snow vegetable puree, replacing fava beans with edamame and lotus seeds.
“Prawn and fruit” draws inspiration from Taiwanese pineapple shrimp balls, adding coconut for Southeast Asian flavor.
For the main course, “roast duck and seasonal vegetables” features Changhua Rose Duck aged for 15 to 20 days and roasted in the Peking duck style. It is served with basil-spinach wrappers alongside fig, mustard, and pan-seared foie gras.
The centerpiece main course, “wealthy chicken,” adapts traditional Jiangnan beggar’s chicken. Inspired by the Taiwanese practice of using Jiadong leaves in restorative home cooking, the kitchen wraps the chicken with abalone and dried scallops before encasing it in a salt crust, which guests crack open at the table.
To close the meal, Yang offers a radish-based dish inspired by memories of watching his mother-in-law make Hakka rice cakes.
The nostalgic taste once moved a regular guest to tears, stirring up childhood memories, Yang said.
“When a dish carries not just flavor, but culture, memory, and blessings, it becomes a bridge connecting human emotions,” Yang said.
Amaze launches its autumn seasonal menu, “The Full Circle.” (Taiwan News, Lyla Liu video)

Regulators say latest Fukushima discharge will not affect Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:43:49 UTC
11:43:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The latest round of treated wastewater discharge from Japan’s Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant will have no impact on Taiwan, the Nuclear Safety Commission said Tuesday.
In a press release, the NSC said the plant began releasing a new batch of wastewater on Monday, scheduled to run for 19 days. Japan began discharging treated wastewater containing tritium from the tsunami-disabled plant in August 2023.
Japan’s treatment process reduces most radionuclides in the wastewater to below regulatory limits, but tritium cannot be filtered out and is instead diluted with seawater before discharge, according to Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry.
The NSC said that tritium levels in waters around Taiwan are forecast to “remain below the minimum detectable level of monitoring instruments,” citing Central Weather Administration forecasts. Based on analysis by the Tokyo Electric Power Company, levels of radionuclides other than tritium also met regulatory standards.
The commission added that the recently discharged wastewater is expected to affect mainly waters off Japan’s east coast due to tidal movements.
The NSC monitors seawater radiation in cooperation with other government agencies, and it said that no abnormalities so far have been detected.
Real-time updates on how the wastewater is dispersing is available on the CWA’s website.

“It is clear that we need to push Putin to take the negotiations seriously,” Jetten said, arguing that Russia was suffering mounting military losses and economic pressure from international sanctions.
“The only way forward for Europeans, but also for Americans and others, is to put more sanctions on the Russian regime instead of less,” he said.
“So buying Russian energy is a very stupid idea,” Jetten added.
The Dutch leader said Europe had demonstrated since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine that it could substantially reduce its dependence on Russian fossil fuels.
“I can assure you that there is no European leader willing to buy Russian gas in the next few years,” he said.
Jetten insisted that economic pressure should continue until Moscow ends its invasion.
“What we want is Russia to stop this war, and as long as they don’t, we will hit them hard in their pockets with sanctions.”
Russia Uses North Korean Forced Labor to Sustain War Against Ukraine, Investigation Finds
US explores restoring energy ties with Russia
Jetten’s remarks come amid reports that Washington is exploring renewed energy cooperation with Moscow as part of negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.
As Kyiv Post reported on Wednesday, citing the Financial Times, US and Russian officials have discussed the possible return of American energy companies to Russia, including joint oil production projects on Sakhalin and renewed Russian crude exports to Europe through the Druzhba pipeline.
Other proposals reportedly include restoring Russian gas supplies to Europe and potentially reviving the Nord Stream pipeline system.
The reported discussions involve economic incentives that Moscow could receive under a peace settlement, although no final agreements have been announced.
US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have been involved in negotiations with Russian and Ukrainian officials.
Europe has already moved to ban Russian gas
The EU adopted binding legislation in January 2026 to permanently phase out Russian natural gas imports.
Under the timetable, long-term Russian liquefied natural gas contracts are to end from January 2027, with remaining pipeline imports phased out by November 2027 at the latest.
The measures form part of the EU’s REPowerEU strategy, designed to eliminate dependence on Russian energy and prevent Moscow from using energy supplies as political leverage.
Russian gas has not entirely disappeared from the European market. Some EU countries continue receiving Russian liquefied natural gas under existing contracts, but the bloc has committed to ending those purchases.

Kalshi, co-founders hit with criminal charges in US state of Utah

Kalshi, cofounders hit with criminal charges in US state of Utah
The charges come after a federal judge ruled that Utah could enforce its anti-gambling laws against prediction markets.
The US state of Utah has announced criminal charges against popular prediction market Kalshi and its two cofounders, accusing the platform and its executives of illegally promoting online gambling.
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed the charges against Kalshi, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara on Wednesday, a day after US President Donald Trump’s administration sued the state to block its civil enforcement actions against the platform.
According to the criminal complaint filed in a Salt Lake City court, Kalshi facilitated an undercover law enforcement officer’s wagers on sports events, including games in the NFL.
The charges come after a federal judge in August ruled that Utah was entitled to enforce its stringent anti-gambling laws against online prediction markets, following a legal bid by Kalshi to block enforcement of the law.
The criminal complaint accuses the defendants of 12 counts of online gambling promotion, one count of general gambling promotion and one count of pattern of unlawful activity.
Kalshi and Brown’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Utah has some of the strictest prohibitions against gambling in the US, with its state constitution explicitly barring lawmakers from legalising the activity.
The charges mark an escalation in a showdown between US states and the Trump administration over the regulation of prediction markets.
On Tuesday, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed a lawsuit seeking to block Utah’s enforcement actions against prediction markets, arguing that the platforms fall under federal jurisdiction.
The regulator announced the move after Utah last week filed a civil lawsuit accusing Kalshi of facilitating betting on sports, elections, politics and other outcomes in violation of anti-gambling laws.
Dozens of US states, led by both Republican and Democratic administrations, have argued that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission does not have the authority to regulate prediction markets.
Last month, the state of New Jersey asked the US Supreme Court to rule on whether state or federal authorities have jurisdiction over sports betting on prediction market platforms.

"It will also depend on the situation on the battlefield and the situation in general. You can see the situation now in the Middle East. It just doesn't allow us to hold it in the near future. Supreme Court removes October 30 deadline for additions to Delhi electoral roll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:00:02 UTC
11:00:02 KST

Supreme Court asked the Election Commission not to stop adding names to Delhi's electoral rolls by the October 30 deadline
NEW DELHI: In a relief to over 43 lakh voters excluded from Delhi’s draft electoral rolls for ‘permanently shifting out’, Supreme Court on Wednesday asked Election Commission not to stop adding names in the voter list by the Oct 30 deadline and told it to continue distributing and receiving enumeration forms, and Forms 6 (new voters), 7 (for deletion) and 8 (for those who shifted from one constituency to another).A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also questioned EC on why voters whose names were there on earlier electoral rolls but were deleted from the draft rolls were asked to file Form 6, which is meant for enrolment of first-time voters.
Without passing any order, the bench said, “We will examine the issue after two weeks. The effort should be to reduce the 43 lakh (who have been deleted from draft rolls). One suggestion — publish the list of those who are deleted and specify the reason for deletion against each name. Request them to contact the nearest BLO and fill Form 8. You can give them enumeration forms. Tell them that they are welcome to fill either Form 6 or 8.”
How can you insist on Form 6 for person who was voter earlier: SC
During the proceedings on a PIL filed by activist Anjali Bhardwaj, the bench heard advocate Prashant Bhushan’s complaints against EC for insisting on filling Form 6 by those whose names got excluded and, thereby, compelling them to give a false declaration that they were first-time voters.
The bench said, “Right to vote is a vital right. If a person has shifted out from Vasant Kunj to Dwarka, or had gone out of station for a month or so and for some other reason could not respond to the EC notice or could not file the claim for inclusion of name, or did not get enumeration form because of change of address, should EC permanently disable him from voting by striking his name off the voter list?“How can you insist on Form 6 for a person who was a voter earlier? If a person has shifted from one constituency to another within Delhi, it is erroneous to ask him/her to fill Form 6. You must allow similarly placed persons, whose names are deleted on the ground of ‘permanently shifted’, to fill Form 8.”Appearing for EC, senior advocate D S Naidu said the commission had conducted over one lakh camps in Delhi to spread awareness among people on how to re-enter their names in the voter list.
“The situation on the ground is very different. Not a single person has come to fill Form 8. The petitioner is creating a scare on paper in the courtroom. Any person can seek inclusion of his/her name in the voter list of a constituency till the date of filing of nominations,” Naidu said, and clarified that no one has been prosecuted for using Form 6 to restore names in voter lists across states.But EC relented to keep the window open for inclusion of names in Delhi as SC insisted that the Oct 30 deadline for filing claims and objections need not be set in stone as elections were not imminent in Delhi to warrant urgent completion of the SIR exercise.

====================================================================================================

Mark Carney isn’t the climate hero Europeans think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Ask European Union leaders what they think of Mark Carney’s climate credentials, and you’ll get a gushing response.
“We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her State of the Union speech last month, where the Canadian prime minister was the guest of honor.
“Canada and the EU are very, very like-minded,” the bloc’s climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, told POLITICO in an interview when asked about his hopes for climate collaboration between the two powers ahead of this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal.
But this rosy view sidesteps a less comfortable reality: Canada is a major fossil fuel producer whose climate ambitions fall far short of Europe’s.
And under Carney, those ambitions are weakening.
Last year, Canada produced more crude oil than any other country outside the big three producers, Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United States. Oil and gas are Canada’s biggest exports by far, and the industry lobby is an influential force in Ottawa.
In his previous life as a central banker, Carney was considered a climate champion. POLITICO even dubbed him an “eco warrior” in 2018. But since taking over as prime minister last year, he has weakened Canada’s climate policies at a rate few predicted, scrapping a national carbon tax and electric vehicle mandate and opening new oil and gas projects.
The list of climate laws Carney has watered down, repealed and canceled makes the EU’s own recent backtracking on green laws look minor. Some environmentalists argue it is comparable to U.S. President Donald Trump’s wholesale dismantling of environmental protections.
“The track the Carney government has taken on climate and environmental regulation has been a decisive move in the direction of the U.S.,” said Tim Gray, executive director of environmental non-profit Environment Defence. Carney, he said, “seems to be all in on fossil fuels.”
Keean Nembhard, a spokesperson for Canada’s Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, told POLITICO the Carney government is “committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero by 2050 by taking a pragmatic and durable approach.”
“This includes building major clean energy projects across the country, driving mass electrification, and making significant investment in the low-carbon economy,” he said.
But Gray argued that Carney’s support for fossil fuels and weakening of environmental standards may complicate Canada’s attempts to forge closer ties with Europe, which has some of the world’s most stringent green laws.
Still, in Europe, Carney’s green image persists.
Last week, Belgian member of the European Parliament Saskia Bricmont gave expression to this faith in Carney’s commitment to climate issues when she called on him to lead a global push to put climate back on the agenda ahead of next month’s U.N. climate summit.
“Mr Carney … relaunch the fight against climate deregulation and for the restoration of biodiversity, and re-mobilize the international community around concrete, coordinated measures,” she said.
Carney’s green aura
Carney’s reputation as a climate champion is well earned. As governor of the Bank of England, he led a push among central bankers to take the economic risks of climate change seriously — memorably captured in his 2015 ‘Tragedy of the Horizon’ speech, in which he warned: “The catastrophic impacts of climate change will be felt beyond the traditional horizons of most actors.”
In 2021, after he’d left the Bank of England, he became a United Nations special envoy on climate action and finance and launched a net-zero financial alliance with some of the world’s biggest banks.
But things changed dramatically when Donald Trump took back the White House, and Carney replaced fellow Liberal Justin Trudeau as Canada’s prime minister in 2025. At the time, Trudeau and his Liberals had been way behind in the polls, battered by Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre’s attacks on his climate policies — in particular an unpopular consumer carbon tax.
Carney’s first act as prime minister was to scrap that tax.
Following his surprise victory in the elections that April, Carney set about promoting Canada as an “energy superpower.” To the dismay of environmental groups, he supported the “Pacific Link,” an oil pipeline costing tens of billions of dollars, designed to carry Alberta crude to Canada’s Pacific coast for export to Asia.
He then pushed for thawing relations with Beijing in January, a not-so-subtle pitch to find a new crude oil client that isn’t the U.S. Germany, rushing to replace its dependence on Russian energy, signed a long-term agreement in July to buy Canadian liquefied natural gas from a proposed port in British Columbia, despite backlash from environmental and indigenous groups.
He also scrapped laws on electric vehicle adoption, dropped plans for an emissions cap on oil and gas companies, watered down an existing industrial carbon price and introduced legislation to weaken environmental permitting rules for big infrastructure projects, which critics dubbed the “bulldoze nature bill.”
A landmark moment, according to Gray, came in November 2025, when Carney signed a memorandum of understanding with the government of Alberta, Canada’s biggest oil-producing province. That document, which promised to turn Canada into a “global energy superpower,” contained a string of promises to promote oil and gas and water down federal climate laws.
So why the dramatic shift?
Carney, who has repeatedly positioned energy sovereignty as a bulwark against Trump’s economic aggression, offered his realpolitik response at an event in the heart of Alberta’s oil patch earlier this month.
“There’s a structural challenge of energy security and the existential challenge of climate change, and these challenges are forcing countries to think differently about where their energy comes from and on who they can rely on to supply it,” Carney said in Fort McMurray, Alberta on Oct. 1.
“Even under any plausible net zero scenario, the IEA [International Energy Agency] forecasts the world will still need tens of millions of barrels of crude a day. So the question is: who will emerge as the world’s trusted suppliers? It should be us. It must be Canada.”
Not black and white
Carney, to be sure, is no Trump. Unlike the U.S. president, he has retained his pro-climate rhetoric and promised to develop the country’s mining of critical minerals essential for the clean energy transition.
In May, he unveiled a national electricity strategy which aims to double Canada’s largely clean electricity grid by 2050 to meet soaring demand. “The path to net zero is electrification,” Carney said then.
In August, he announced C$10 billion in federal support for the Churchill Falls hydroelectric project in Newfoundland and Labrador, saying it will be the largest clean energy project in North America, capable of generating enough electricity to light up the equivalent of Canada’s three largest cities.
Nembhard, Environment Minster Dabrusin’s spokesperson, also pointed to new electricity transmission lines, electric vehicle subsidies and a C$2 billion plan to retrofit homes with heat pumps.
Canadian climate activist Alex Cool-Fergus said she does not think Carney “believes that oil and gas is the future,” but is simply being pragmatic about Canada’s economic reality.
“The electricity strategy that came out in May was incredibly important, and actually gives us a better idea of what his thinking is for the future,” she said.
Trudeau’s approach to climate change was “very much values-based, and it was about doing the right thing,” said Cool-Fergus. “I think that’s hit its limits. Carney’s approach makes more sense for the world of 2025-2026.”
The limits of the partnership
Hoekstra, the EU’s commissioner for climate, said he wants to deepen ties with Canada. “Given all the complications the world is facing, it is imperative to team up more closely with your closest partners,” he said. But he’s realistic about how far that relationship can go.
Hoekstra has ambitions of cementing the EU into a global network of economies with carbon pricing regimes. While he conceded nothing is “off the table,” he acknowledged linking the EU’s Emissions Trading System with Canada’s “quite different” version, which varies from province to province: “You’re talking about a completely different horizon, and that is not something we would attempt in the very short run.”
There are, however, other ways Hoekstra believes the EU and Canada can closely link on environmental issues.
“Doubling down, tripling down on electrification, on solar, on wind, on nuclear, on batteries,” he said, adding “that is one area that I think is potentially very fruitful for my portfolio.”
Another is critical raw materials, a key focus of this week’s summit.
Brussels is exploring ways for the European Investment Bank, the EU’s lending arm, to help finance the mining of Canadian mineral deposits that could supply the bloc with an alternative to Chinese-produced metals, with a framework agreement expected to be signed during the summit. Lithium, copper, nickel, and other key ingredients for electric vehicle batteries and clean energy technologies essential for decarbonizing Europe are abundant but often undeveloped all over Canada.
This week’s summit will also explore investing in infrastructure on Canada’s east coast to liquefy and ship Canadian gas to Europe, a move that could help the EU diversify its supply away from the U.S., which, along with Norway, has become Europe’s dominant supplier since it cut off Russian gas imports following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Many EU member countries will welcome success on these goals. But Gray warns that closer ties with Canada could lead to deeper penetration by the country’s powerful fossil fuel lobby, which he described as a “major, major force.”
“They’ll be spending time trying to make sure the alignment with the EU is in a direction that favors them,” he said.
The EU’s lack of oil and gas resources — and, by extension, the absence of a powerful fossil fuel lobby — has kept climate policy relatively bipartisan in the EU. Could inviting a fossil fuel “superpower” into the fold as an “associate member” change that?
“That would depend very much on what is an ‘associate member,’” Dutch Climate Minister Stientje van Veldhoven-van der Meer said.

Airline groups urge US CDC to reconsider Ebola declaration requirements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Airline groups urge US CDC to reconsider Ebola declaration requirements
- Airlines for America and IATA urged the CDC to rethink new Ebola attestations for all US-bound travellers. They said the Nov 3 deadline is too short and the rules are hard to apply.
- The groups said the plan is “unworkable” and too broad. They questioned why air travel is targeted, while maritime and surface transport are not included.
- The CDC’s rules aim to stop Ebola entry after outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and South Sudan. The virus has killed about 4,700 people in Africa, according to the Africa CDC.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Major American and foreign airlines urged the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to reconsider new rules requiring all US-bound travellers to attest they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the prior 21 days.
The International Air Transport Association and Airlines for America (IATA), in separate previously unreported letters reviewed by Reuters, urged the CDC to reconsider the plan announced last week that takes effect on Nov 3 and is aimed at preventing entry by people exposed to Ebola.
“It is unreasonable for the US government to require all airlines serving the US market to modify their procedures to accommodate the collection of attestations from each individual (passenger and crew) flying to the United States in less than two weeks,” IATA, which represents over 370 member airlines in more than 130 countries, said in the letter dated Oct 27.
The new CDC order requires all US-bound airline passengers and crew members to file digital or paper attestations. The CDC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Airlines for America, which represents United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Delta Air Lines, said in a separate letter to the CDC that the plan was unworkable.
“Changes to check-in systems, digital signatures, station procedures, and training cannot readily be completed in the allotted time,” the group said, calling on the CDC to “reconsider a more proportionate and measured US response”.
Airlines for America said that in 2025, US Customs and Border Protection screened about 130 million air passengers, but fewer than 25,000 of them had a connection to the Democratic Republic of Congo.
IATA also questioned why the plan only applied to air travellers.
“The US government has clearly decided that the risk of the importation of Ebola into the United States is high enough to justify this global process. It is difficult to understand why other modes of transportation – maritime and surface – were not included in this mandate,” IATA said.
The CDC in May adopted rules barring foreign airline passengers who had been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the centre of the 2026 outbreak, in the prior three weeks. The restrictions were extended to US citizens in July.
Airlines for America urged the CDC to exempt crew members, the US military and jumpseat travellers, calling the plan “overly stringent, costly and burdensome to Americans and the US airline industry”.
As part of the Ebola measures, the CDC since earlier in 2026 has barred foreign nationals from the US if they were in Uganda or South Sudan in the prior three weeks.
The Bundibugyo strain of the virus spread undetected for months before the outbreak was declared in May. It kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine.
So far the outbreak is confirmed to have killed about 4,700 people in Africa, according to the Africa CDC. REUTERS

US fiscal pressures to persist regardless of midterm election outcome: Fitch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
01:19:49 UTC
10:19:49 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
 The US is likely to face continued fiscal pressures regardless of the outcome of the upcoming midterm elections, with rising entitlement spending and debt-servicing costs threatening to push government debt higher, Fitch Ratings said Wednesday.
In a report, the credit rating agency warned that Democratic control of one or both chambers of Congress could increase the likelihood of political brinkmanship over the federal debt ceiling and government funding, potentially putting further pressure on the country's already-large fiscal deficit.
However, Fitch said the underlying drivers of the US fiscal outlook would persist regardless of which party controls Congress, pointing to rising entitlement expenditures and debt-servicing costs as key challenges.
Without policy changes, these structural pressures are likely to lead to a further deterioration in the country's debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio, the agency said.
The US federal budget deficit reached nearly $2 trillion, equivalent to 6.1% of GDP, in fiscal 2026, according to Fitch.
The agency forecasts that the general government deficit, which includes the balances of state and local governments, will widen to 7.5% of GDP in 2026 and 7.6% in 2027. State and local government balances account for around 1% of GDP.
Such a deficit would be the highest among sovereigns rated in the 'AA' category, Fitch said.
The agency also warned that the fiscal priorities of both major political parties could add to budgetary pressures unless offset by other measures.
