How the Cinema South Festival has survived and thrived in Sderot for 25 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:28:06 UTC
08:28:06 KST

“First of all, let’s say that everything happening here is already a miracle,” said Reuma Mantzur, director of the Cinema South Festival, which celebrates its 25th edition at the Sderot Cinematheque from November 1-5.
Festival directors tend to speak in superlatives about the events they run, but in the case of the Cinema South Festival, Mantzur’s words make perfect sense. The festival has had to cope with more than two decades of frequent, unexpected bombings by Hamas from the Gaza Strip, as well as the tragedy of the October 7 attack in 2023, which took the lives of more than 50 residents, mostly civilians.
For Mantzur, the festival’s identity is inseparable from the community surrounding Sapir Academic College’s School of Audio and Visual Arts, where it began and which still sponsors and runs it. The festival’s screenings are one expression of a broader commitment to helping filmmakers develop their work and giving them reasons to remain in the South.
Mantzur arrived at Sapir as a student in 2006, when both the festival and the region’s filmmaking community were smaller.
“The festival gradually developed in response to the atmosphere and the reality of our lives,” she said. Collaborations expanded, and the connection with the school became increasingly important.
For students completing their graduation films, the festival’s pitching events and development incubators offer a possible answer to an intimidating question: What comes next?
Desire to create more is growing, Mantzur says
“In recent years, somewhat paradoxically, precisely as life here has become more difficult – perhaps it isn’t paradoxical – there has been a growing desire to create more and more work,” Mantzur said.
Among the initiatives reflecting that commitment is Through a Woman’s Eyes, a development incubator for Bedouin women filmmakers. The program, guided by filmmaker Sigalit Banai, works with partners including the Negev Film Fund. Mantzur also emphasized the involvement of the Rahat community center and the local professionals supporting the directors.
“The directors are Bedouin women, and everyone working around them is local,” she said.
The initiative is continuing, with the next group of films already shot for screening next year. For audiences, these works offer an opportunity to encounter life in the South through the perspectives of people who live there.
That relationship between filmmaking and place also shapes the festival’s ties with Sapir graduates and lecturers. Alongside its graduation film competition, it screens work by alumni who have established careers and teachers who continue creating while training another generation.
“We always look first for the local connection,” Mantzur said.
THE FESTIVAL’S regional emphasis does not mean its program excludes entertainment with a national audience. This year’s opening features the first two episodes of the second season of Bros, the series by Guy Amir and Hanan Savyon, which is broadcast worldwide on Netflix.
Watching television at a movie theater, Mantzur noted, gives viewers a shared experience that differs from watching at home. As smartphones, streaming, and changing habits reshape viewing, festivals must also respond.
But the festival is keeping its focus on its community, and the closing ceremony will launch Negba, a new incubator for young southern filmmakers.
Prior to October 7, the festival managed, against all odds, to attract many high-profile guests. I remember attending it in June 2004 to see its guest of honor, Richard Gere, give a master class. The atmosphere was festive, bordering on frenzy, with a huge crowd outside the cinematheque, mostly women but also men and children, there to greet him. Gere posed for photos and signed autographs graciously.
In those pre-Iron Dome days, Hamas was not yet officially in control of Gaza, but it still often fired missiles on Sderot and the surrounding area. A visit to the city took real courage, because all the bodyguards in the world could not help even the biggest stars if they were at the wrong place at the wrong time.
A missile had hit not all that far from the cinematheque just a few hours before the festival began, and Gere was presented with a piece of the shrapnel by then-mayor Eli Moyal. Gere accepted it and joked about how he would fit it into his luggage.
In subsequent years, the festival’s international guests included master documentary director Albert Maysles and acclaimed director Sergei Loznitsa. This year, Swiss director Thomas Imbach will present two films, Nemesis and The Exposure, and give a master class, in cooperation with the Swiss Embassy.
Bringing overseas guests and building collaborations has become much more difficult, Mantzur said, emphasizing that the obstacles have reinforced the importance of supporting the local creative community. Visitors from elsewhere are very welcome, she stressed. Their presence broadens the celebration and brings new audiences to these stories. But its distinctive quality remains rooted in the people making them.
“Let’s invest in ourselves,” she said.
Asked what distinguishes Cinema South Festival from other Israeli festivals, Mantzur described an institution still examining that question after years when survival itself took precedence. Between the pandemic and the upheaval experienced by the region, there was little room for long-term reflection.
“The focus in recent years has been on simply continuing to exist,” she admitted.
The next stage, she said, will grow from the work itself: how it brings people together and lets them examine their own experiences and put their stories on screen.
“We want to see what is developing in the South during these years, emerging from the South,” she said.
The bond between local filmmakers involves more than geography. It rests on experiences and feelings that people who have lived there recognize in one another.
“It’s a festival that belongs to us and is for us… That is what makes us distinctive – that southern perspective,” she said.
For more information and to see the full program, go to the festival website at www.sapir.ac.il/cinema/csf

Ehud Olmert backs Eisenkot, says Netanyahu is 'on wrong side of history'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:27:56 UTC
08:27:56 KST

Former prime minister Ehud Olmert said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is "on the wrong side of history" ahead of Israel's 2026 elections, in an interview with Al-Arabiya English on Tuesday.
"Whether people voted for Bennett or Eisenkot or Lapid or Golan, the differences are not insignificant, but they are all on the right side of history, while Netanyahu is on the wrong side of history,” Olmert said, referring to opposition leaders.
Olmert endorsed Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar Party, arguing that Eisenkot is better suited to lead the country than his political rivals.
"What I think distinguishes Gadi Eisenkot from all of them is that I think he's more mature, he's more ready. And also, I think, the fact that he's more popular than all of them."
Olmert described the upcoming vote as potentially historic.
“These are certainly perhaps the most consequential elections in the modern history of the Jewish people in the State of Israel,” he said.
He emphasized that Israeli voters are fighting to protect the country's democracy and the standing of the Supreme Court.
Addressing Netanyahu's position in the polls, Olmert predicted a substantial decline in the prime minister's political support.
“It is already reflected in the polls that show Netanyahu is going to lose between one-third and 40% of his present political power, which is absolutely considerable.”
Olmert also criticized Netanyahu's recent social media post, where he shared an AI-generated image depicting a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, two days before Israel's October 27 election.
Accompanying the image, Netanyahu warned that Israel faced an existential threat from Iran and that the country's security depended on the outcome of the 2026 election.
In the interview, Olmert described it as a "sign of desperation and of total loss of the real, genuine ability to judge the political circumstances."
He accused Netanyahu of creating an “atmosphere of panic and hysteria and fear and imminent danger to the very existence of the state of Israel," adding, "This is what dictators are normally doing at a time when they are on the verge of complete destruction politically."
Olmert challenges Netanyahu's claims about Iran
Turning to Iran's nuclear program, Olmert also accused Netanyahu of making false claims about the destruction of Iran's nuclear capabilities.
“He said, ‘We obliterated everything.’ And he even said something which is an outright lie, absolute nonsense, that at the time that we attacked Iran in June of 2025 or in February/March of 2026, they had a few atomic bombs which we have obliterated," Olmert alleged.
The former prime minister continued, "We know that they didn't have atomic bombs. We know that what they had, which is bad enough, is enriched to a level of 60% that is stored somewhere underground in boxes, but they never had a bomb, they never possessed a bomb, and we never destroyed a bomb."
Despite his criticism of Netanyahu, Olmert later on emphasized Israel's military achievements in the Middle East.
“In spite of the surprise and the failures of the defense system on October 7, we still defeated Hezbollah in the north, Hamas in the south, and Iran, which is an empire, a hugely powerful nation.”
Olmert calls for two-state solution, accountability for October 7
On the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Olmert called for Israel to take the risk of advancing a two-state solution, which he described as the “best possible solution for the State of Israel."
He also held Netanyahu responsible for the policies that preceded the Hamas-led October 7 massacre.
“He is the one who developed this strategy. He is the one who refused to negotiate or to deal with the Palestinian Authority and preferred to build up some kind of understanding with Hamas."
Addressing settler violence in the West Bank, Olmert warned that Israeli political and security leaders could face legal consequences if they failed to act.
"I have a message to the leadership of the State of Israel and to the commanders of the Israeli army and the Israeli police: If you will not take care of the Jewish terror in the West Bank, you will be held legally responsible for the crimes which are committed there… possibly also in the International Criminal Court."
Olmert concluded with a message to Israeli voters ahead of the elections, urging them to support political change.
"We have to change, and we can change. And the change will be a step forward for the State of Israel, for the Palestinian people, for the region, and for the Jewish people across the world."
Shir Perets contributed to this report.

Historic Polish synagogue acquired through tender, to be restored after years of neglect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:57:24 UTC
07:57:24 KST

After years of neglect, the historic synagogue in Trzebinia, Poland, has been acquired through an international initiative aimed at restoring it to its original purpose and returning it to the Jewish community.
The plans include the restoration of the building, the establishment of a Jewish museum, and the creation of a hospitality center for visitors to the graves of revered rabbis and Hasidic leaders at the local Jewish cemetery.
The historic synagogue, located in Poland’s Silesian region, was returned to the Jewish people on Tuesday, after years of decay.
The Jewish community of Katowice relinquished its right to reclaim the building, after which the municipality put it up for sale through a tender process.
In response, a group of partners joined forces to prevent the property from being converted into a non-Jewish venue, and to ensure that it would be preserved as a site of Jewish historical significance.
The acquisition of the synagogue was made possible through cooperation among three parties: the Israeli delegation, led by Meir Bulka, known as the “Grave Hunter,” who heads J-NERATIONS, an organization dedicated to preserving Jewish heritage in Europe; Jacek Purski, director of Auschwitz Research Center on Hate, Extremism and Radicalisation; and Marcin Majchrowicz, a businessman and philanthropist committed to preserving Jewish heritage in Poland’s Silesian region.
Community history
The Jewish community in Trzebinia dates back to at least the 1500s, with a more prominent presence from the 1700s onward.
An independent Jewish community was established in the city in 1815, growing to its peak in 1921 when Jews accounted for 23% of Trzebinia's population.
Between the two World Wars, Trzebinia was home to four synagogues, a Talmud Torah, yeshivas, prayer houses, charitable institutions, and aid organizations.
Among the prominent rabbinical figures who served in the city were Rabbi Dov Berish Weidenfeld, known as the Gaon of Tchebinas, as well as Rabbi Ben Zion Halberstam, the second Rebbe of Bobov.
Adjacent to the synagogue is the Jewish cemetery, where rabbis and several spiritual leaders are buried.
However, the Holocaust destroyed the vibrant Jewish community. Many members of the community were deported to concentration camps and ghettos, and numerous residents of the city were murdered at Auschwitz.
The Jewish community’s properties were destroyed, leaving the surviving synagogue as the only remaining testimony to the city's Jewish heritage.
“The synagogue, located just a 40-minute drive from Kraków and now returned to the Jewish people, will soon become another destination for Jews visiting the region,” said Meir Bulka.
“I am deeply moved that we have succeeded in preventing the desecration of Jewish religious heritage and in making a meaningful mark on the history of the Jewish people in Poland."
"This is not merely about saving a synagogue; it is also about taking responsibility for preserving the memory of an entire community.”
Polish synagogue restoration aims to preserve Jewish heritage for future generations
Jacek Purski, director of Auschwitz Research Center on Hate, Extremism and Radicalization said that saving a synagogue is not purely about preserving a building, but about recognizing that Jewish life is "not only part of Poland’s past, but also part of its present and future."
Wherever possible, the partners said they will use historical documentation and archaeological evidence to recreate the site's appearance before the Holocaust.
In the coming days, a foundation will be established in Poland to manage the restoration of the synagogue, and it will be possible to participate through donations and investments.

The 2,000-Nit OLED in Apple’s New MacBook Is a Big Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:54:16 UTC
07:54:16 KST

Laptops with OLED screens aren’t particularly special. They’ve been around for a decade. You can currently buy a touchscreen OLED machine for as little as $700, and even the iPad Pro has had an OLED screen since 2024.
So, why did Apple wait over a decade to release its own touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro? The simple answer for the long wait is that the company wanted to do it “the Apple way.” But in this case, “the Apple way” involves somehow cranking up the display to 2,000 nits, solving both the brightness and glare problems that OLED laptops have always suffered from.
Having seen the thing with my own eyes at a media event today in Los Angeles, I can tell you that this screen is the real deal.
Like No Other OLED
Apple is using a tandem OLED panel, the same layer-stacking technology used in the OLED iPad Pro. The real innovation here, however, is that the panel has been optimized to hit a new peak brightness of 2,000 nits, and that’s a result that matters.
That big number is meaningless on its own, but here’s the context. Nits are the standard measure of screen brightness used across the consumer tech industry. A cheap OLED laptop maxes out around 300 nits. A higher-end OLED laptop might get you up to 1,000 nits of brightness—but only in brighter and more colorful High Dynamic Range content like specific streaming apps, YouTube videos, and games. In other words, the vast majority of the time you’re using an OLED, it’ll feel like a dimmer screen than normal. The iPad Pro can get up to 1,600 nits for HDR content, and 1,000 nits for the less bright, less colorful Standard Dynamic Range content. That’s closer.
But this MacBook Pro’s screen is on an entirely different level. It’s a ground-up redesign of the tandem OLED layer arrangement in the iPad Pro, even down to the manufacturing process. And the result is that it can blast your eyes with 2,000 nits of brightness in both SDR and HDR. That means whether you’re looking at some generic wallpaper, a website, or an HDR-compatible movie, you’ll feel that extra brightness. That’s why, I assume, Apple gave it the name PROLED XDR. In a world where the words “OLED” and “HDR” don’t necessarily indicate how good the experience is, more weighty jargon is needed.
As with all tech, bigger numbers don’t always add up to a noticeable difference for the user. But when it comes to HDR performance, we’ve been waiting a long time for OLED to catch up.
HDR, or High Dynamic Range, serves as a measure of color depth, brightness, and contrast—and in the past, this has always involved a trade-off. An OLED screen can turn each individual pixel any color, and it can turn off individual pixels in the display. This allows OLED to have great color control and unbeatable contrast, since when you turn a pixel off, it renders absolutely black.
But OLEDs couldn’t get super bright, and other screen tech like mini-LED could get much brighter, which is why Apple stuck with mini-LED for years, using it on the MacBook Pro and Studio Display XDR. This technology allowed Apple to have the laptops with the best HDR performance out there.
With the 2026 MacBook Pro, that compromise no longer exists. This OLED screen has both the brightness and contrast in its pocket, and you can see it.
An OLED panel has lots of more benefits over conventional backlighting beyond just contrast. Mini-LED struggles with an effect called blooming, where bright parts of images bleed light to the surrounding area, which is where lots of detail is lost in the image. OLED completely fixes that, giving each pixel a much wider range of control (up to completely turning off). As part of the Apple event I attended, we were shown a selection of HDR images with lots of contrast, a number of which had fields of darkness at the edges that made it look like the image simply disappeared into the bezel. Very pretty. We also watched a darker scene in the show Widow’s Bay in HDR, which was an excellent showcase of the range of detail this screen can show.
The new screen helps this MacBook stay exceedingly light, as well. Much of the savings in weight comes from the OLED design, since the screen uses thinner and lighter materials than screens past. Despite the computer using the same aluminum chassis as the previous MacBook Pro, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs just 3 pounds, which is 12 percent lighter than before.
To put the new screen into context, we were also shown a comparison between Apple’s OLED and the OLED of a high-end competitive Windows laptop. The difference was striking, especially in off-axis viewing. At its worst, there were visible rainbow effects on the Windows machine’s screen.
There’s a catch, though. While Apple’s screen can get up to 2,000 nits, it’s normally capped at 1,000 nits. When the laptop’s built-in adaptive brightness sensor thinks you need a boost, the screen’s brightens increases up to 2,000 nits. So the brightness only hits the high end when you’re outside or working under really harsh lighting conditions. The previous-gen MacBook Pros also did this, but to a lesser degree. With this machine, you’re getting 400 more nits of SDR brightness right out of the box, with the ability to crank it up to twice as much.
Glare is another issue with conventional, low-brightness OLED laptops that the MacBook Pro improves. When deeper blacks are rendered on the screen, it often results in harsher reflections. Sometimes it can get so bad, it feels like you’re looking into a mirror. The brightness alone on the MacBook Pro goes a long way toward overpowering glare and reflections, but Apple is also using what it claims is a “state-of-the-art” anti-reflective coating. Almost every laptop screen uses some kind anti-reflective coating, so one can hope that Apple’s “state-of-the-art” coating is at least on par with those, but I can attest that this is the very best I’ve seen.
The ultimate solution to cutting glare and reflections is still the option for a nano-texture display, where the anti-reflective pattern is actually etched into the screen itself rather than layered on top. That’s available as an upgrade on both the 14-inch and 16-inch models.
Reach Out and Touch It
The other major innovation happening with the MacBook Pro’s screen is the introduction of touch. Like OLED itself, this is a feature we’ve seen on many other laptops for well over a decade. I came in hoping Apple would swing for the fences here, but its use of touch interaction feels much more modest. (Let us quickly forget the failure of the Touch Bar from 2016.)
The implementation itself is impressive. Interacting with elements on the screen feels every bit as fluid as it does on an iPad. The screen also supports many of the familiar trackpad gestures, such as pinch to zoom or a three-fingered swipe to switch Spaces.
The most natural feeling touch optimizations have been lifted directly from iPadOS. If you tap in the top left window controls, they zoom in to let you select more precisely. You can even grab a window and flick it to the side to quickly get into Split View. My favorite optimization is the ability to tap, hold, and slide down to select an item within the Menu Bar. Very clever. And yet, I was still hoping for a stronger commitment on the software side. You can’t use an Apple Pencil on this screen, and nothing in the hardware of the MacBook Pro has been adjusted to make touching the screen feel any more ergonomic.
The bigger issue is with third-party apps, though. While touch-to-click will work on all apps automatically, it’s up to developers to do any more than that. Even the third-party apps we were shown during demos had varying degrees of touch optimization.
The 3D modeling application ZBrush was a good example. While certain aspects were touch-enabled, none of the controls or menus had the useful optimizations that Apple’s first-party apps had. Hopefully this touch option will become more widely adopted, but I can foresee a future in which these fingers-first interactions are mostly forgotten outside of occasionally scrolling down a webpage with your thumb. And let me be clear: All of this is more than what Microsoft has ever done to optimize Windows 11 for touch. (And Microsoft even has Windows 2-in-1 tablets to support!)
With the 2026 MacBook Pro, Apple is doubling down on what’s working well for it: leading the way in high-end hardware. There’s plenty more testing to do on the MacBook Pro in the coming weeks, but this OLED screen already looks like the one the entire industry will be chasing for years to come.

Putin to attend plenary sessions on Day Two of Russia-Africa Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:54:00 UTC
07:54:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will continue to take part in a large-scale series of events as Day Two of the Russia-Africa Summit kicks off on Thursday.
The Russian head of state is scheduled to participate in two plenary sessions, make statements for the press, sign a number of documents and hold a range of bilateral meetings.
In his speech at the first plenary session, Putin will focus on the growing role of Africa and the priorities of Russia’s cooperation with African countries at the United Nations and other leading and regional organizations.
Among other things, the Russian leader will assess the current situation in the system of international relations, including the evolving new world order, based on the principle of multipolarity and equality of all independent countries, Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov announced.
Apart from Putin, the president of the Republic of Burundi, Evariste Ndayishimiye, who also serves as the incumbent chairman of the African Union, other African heads of state and government and the chairperson of the African Union commission will speak at the first plenary session.
The second plenary session will follow in the format of a working lunch.
A package of 33 intergovernmental and interdepartmental documents, memoranda, and commercial contracts will be signed with various countries following the Russia-Africa Summit. It is also planned to adopt three other major documents, namely the summit declaration, a separate declaration on cooperation in the sphere of artificial intelligence and an action plan for the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum for 2027-2029.
The Russian president and his Burundian counterpart will make statements for the press following the signing of the documents and give a detailed account of the 3rd Russia-Africa Summit and discussions held.
The two plenary sessions will be followed by Putin’s talks with the presidents of Madagascar, Zimbabwe and Namibia, Michael Randrianirina, Emmerson Mnangagwa and Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, respectively, and he will also meet with Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, chairman of the Sovereign Council of Sudan.
Other plans include holding bilateral meetings with the Burundian leader and Kenyan President William Ruto.

Scans reveal extent of Steve Smith's neck injury ahead of Test summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:53:11 UTC
07:53:11 KST

Cricket Australia has revealed the result of an MRI scan on Steve Smith's neck injury, which found a "cervical facet joint" injury.
Smith ruled himself out of playing the third and deciding Test against South Africa in Cape Town.
What's next?
Smith is expected to be back for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, kicking off a run of 10 Tests in three months.
Australia expects to have Steve Smith back for the home summer after scans confirmed joint damage to the vice-captain's neck in South Africa.
Australian team officials said Smith had scans on Friday before failing in his bid to play in the third and deciding Test.
Those scans detected an injury to a "cervical facet joint", which connects to the spine and acts to guide and stabilise neck movement.
"Due to this and his limited range of motion, he was unfit to participate in the current Test," Cricket Australia said in a statement.
"Steve will continue to receive treatment and rehabilitation, with a full return to availability anticipated for the upcoming home Test series against New Zealand."
Smith has six weeks to recover for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, which will begin a long run of virtually uninterrupted cricket through to mid-March, with a five-Test tour of India (January 21 to March 3) and the 150th anniversary Test against England at the MCG (March 11-15).
Australia will want Smith available for that stretch of 10 Tests in 14 weeks, just as they had hoped to have him for the return to Cape Town this week.
Even well after Friday's scans on arrival in Cape Town, Australia's coaching staff had been extremely confident Smith would be fit to face South Africa.
The 37-year-old batted in the nets for around 35 minutes on Sunday, two days out from the third Test, before sitting down and stretching his neck.
Loading Twitter content
He then briefly returned to batting, before growing increasingly frustrated and walking out of the nets.
Smith also attempted to bat on Tuesday morning just 90 minutes before the match, then determining he was not able to get his neck right.
"He is huge, one of the greatest batters we have ever had," Cummins said the day before the start of play.
"You don't play 100-odd Test matches without playing Test matches where you're not 100 per cent fit.
"Even though he is probably not going to be 100 per cent, hopefully he can compartmentalise that, like he has done 100 times before with other things, and come out and contribute like he does every week."
The injury means Smith is likely to never play another Test at Newlands, the venue of the ball-tampering scandal in 2018 that cost him the captaincy and a 12-month ban.

Details
Netanyahu's Likud party claimed that widespread violations had occurred during the vote, including voter bribery, threats, violence and the use of prohibited software.

We must do everything possible to avoid another round of elections
The final voting results may still change, as hundreds of thousands of ballots remain uncounted, including the votes of military personnel. The count is expected to be completed by the end of Friday.

Estonia to Build 150 Military Bunkers Near Russian Border for Baltic Defense Line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:28:43 UTC
07:28:43 KST

- Category
- World
Estonia to Build 150 Military Bunkers Near Russian Border for Baltic Defense Line
Estonia’s Defense Minister, Martin Herem, revealed plans to construct roughly 150 military bunkers across the northeastern region of Ida-Viru County.
The construction forms part of the broader Baltic Defense Line initiative, according to ERR on October 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the current layout, 100 of these structures are designated for state-owned territory, while around 50 will stand on municipal or privately held land.
Placing installations on private real estate requires formal agreements with property owners. Government officials are considering various options to resolve property usage, including financial compensation for inconveniences, land leasing, or outright purchasing of the needed parcels.
“But, according to my information, currently there are no large-scale plans for the state to acquire a wider belt,” Herem added.
Estonia’s bunker project aligns with broader regional efforts, following Finland's completion of a major fencing project along its own border with Russia.
Finland completed roughly 200 kilometers of new fencing along selected sections of its border with Russia as part of a broader effort to harden NATO’s eastern frontier. Launched in 2023, the project cost approximately $413 million and featured a tall metal mesh fence equipped with surveillance cameras, lighting, loudspeakers, and an adjacent patrol road for border guards.
Finnish authorities originally initiated the construction to prevent unauthorized crossings, but the initiative ultimately became part of a wider regional push among northern and eastern European nations to fortify their borders facing Russia and Belarus.

Non-profit group leaks data of more than 40,000 homeland security workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:27:01 UTC
07:27:01 KST

Data identifying more than 41,000 employees and contractors for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was released on Wednesday in an unprecedented leak that reveals how the agency is organized. The records, which were made public by the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, reference operation names, surveillance programs and information on undercover initiatives.
DHS did not immediately return a message seeking comment.
The leaked data unveils the names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from various DHS agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
Most of the agents in the leak – more than 21,000 – work for CBP, and about 6,600 work for ICE.
The data also includes job titles, email groups and other details that show which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work.
It was made public at a time when DHS, in turn, has aggressively sought to unmask critics on social media, and obtain records on protestors and journalists – even as it moves to keep its own agents anonymous, defending agents’ rights to hide their identities and faces while conducting enforcement.
In a statement, Emma Best, a Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder, said the hacktivist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight.
The Department of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data, it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”.
The disclosure – which the non-profit data transparency group says draws on information obtained by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.
In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the defense department was hit with a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.
The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.
Best’s statement said Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”
Reuters could not immediately verify the authenticity of the entire data trove but it was able to match personal information of about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs. In other cases, Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.
In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations.

Details
Police confirmed that the case was officially closed two months after the actress's death; she was found unconscious in a rented house on August 16.
Based on the medical examiner's findings and the results of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death was ruled an accident. The Greenville Police Department has concluded its investigation
What the medical examiners established
According to the Greenville County coroner's report, the actress's death was caused by the toxic effects of fentanyl and four other substances. These included 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol, and quetiapine.
During a search of the house, investigators also found blue pills that mimicked prescription medications. Analysis confirmed that they contained fentanyl. In addition, law enforcement found a white powder in a sunglasses case.
According to police reports, on August 16, the actress's boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach called emergency services after finding Panettiere unconscious. Medics determined that she was in cardiac arrest, and at 2:32 p.m. officially confirmed her death.
The actress had previously spoken openly about her struggles with alcohol and opioid addiction. In her 2026 memoir "This Is Me: Reckoning," she recalled that a doctor had warned her of a serious threat to her life if she did not stop drinking alcohol.

The cost of the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to a fresh Pentagon assessment submitted to Congress, intensifying political fallout ahead of pivotal midterm elections as President Donald Trump leaves open the prospect of renewed hostilities.
The figures compiled by US Central Command, valid as of October 16, provide the most comprehensive accounting of expenditure since military offensives began in late February alongside Israel.
The sum reflects a $3.5 billion rise in spending since early September, when total costs stood at approximately $43.6 billion.
The economic strain of the conflict and its impact on domestic energy markets threaten Republican candidates facing voters on Tuesday to determine control of Congress.
Although Trump initially pledged an engagement lasting only weeks, he has flagged potential new strikes post-election while dispatching a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops to the region.
Munitions depletion
The mounting expenditure has sparked sharp resistance on Capitol Hill, where the White House is seeking approval for a $1.5 trillion national defence budget alongside a $95 billion package supporting Middle East operations.
Replacing depleted munitions represents the single largest expenditure, absorbing roughly $29 billion.
Advanced defensive interceptors—principally for Patriot and THAAD batteries—account for the bulk of replenishment costs, with individual Patriot interceptors costing millions of dollars.
Direct operational activity totals $11.9 billion, whilst equipment destruction accounts for $6 billion.
Branch tallies list Air Force costs at $7.6 billion, Army expenses exceeding $2 billion, and Navy expenditure at $1.45 billion.
Official records list 21 American service personnel dead—18 from enemy strikes, aircraft crashes, or drone disposal—and 865 wounded, with the assessment omitting physical structural damage sustained across regional bases.

NEW DELHI: Striking a discordant note among a clutch of petitions challenging the Transgender Amendment Act for denying right to gender self-determination, an all-women NGO Wednesday appealed to the Supreme Court not to confer trans-women, biological males identifying as females, the spectrum of constitutional rights guaranteed to biological women.‘Women’s Declaration International India’ through senior advocate Amit Sibal told a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that “self-professed or socio-cultural gender identity or certificate or document cannot change a person’s biological sex or enable a biological male to access the entire spectrum of rights, protections and entitlements created specifically for biological females.” Differentiating between sex and gender, the petitioner said, “Sex and gender identity are distinct; gender identity concerns a person’s deeply felt internal experience, while sex is the stable immutable biological category on which numerous constitutional and statutory protections for women are premised.”

Should a policewoman conduct physical search of a person with male genitals but perceives himself to be a woman? If a biologically male criminal perceives himself to be a woman, should police be barred from arresting him after sunset?”
Drawing the court’s attention to a recent incident in the US relating to a transgender inmate, who perceives himself to be a woman but impregnated two women inmates, Mehta said several aspects needed to be kept in mind while adjudicating the petitions.A male becoming a trans-woman will violate affirmative measures for women under the Constitution, equal opportunity to women in employment, women’s bodily privacy and personal security in sex-segregated spaces and criminal law safeguards, the petitioner said.

China Developing More On-Orbit Space Weapons: New Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:03:19 UTC
07:03:19 KST

China is expanding the arsenal of counter-space weapons it could use in a potential conflict with the U.S., to include on-orbit systems, according to a new report from the Defense Intelligence Agency.
The DIA released the third edition of its “Challenges to Security in Space” report Oct. 26, following on 2022 and 2019 versions. Among its findings, it noted that China “is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk.”
Specifically, the report repeats previous warnings that China has ground-based laser weapons that can “disrupt, degrade, or destroy” satellites in low-Earth orbit but then goes further in adding that, by the late 2020s, “China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”
Directed energy weapons could include anything from microwaves to high-powered lasers—the most common at this point are lasers that can “dazzle” satellites with electro-optical sensors.
The new report also goes beyond previous versions in stating that the People’s Liberation Army’s electronic warfare jamming systems “include a combination of ground-based and on-orbit systems that enable it to leverage a variety of options during a conflict.” It’s the first time DIA has noted the existence of on-orbit jammers.
DIA also states definitively that Chinese firms are developing electronic jammers for the People’s Liberation Army to target synthetic aperture radar, “including military reconnaissance platforms.” The agency’s 2022 report only said China was “probably” developing such a capability, which may prove pivotal given the Space Force’s push to field hundreds of new targeting satellites to track objects on the ground and in the air.
The new report also notes that the Chinese military “probably intends to deploy additional [anti-satellite] missiles that can destroy satellites in low, medium, and high orbits”—previously, the agency had only said China “probably intends to pursue” such weapons. It highlights recent developments with mysterious Chinese satellites maneuvering within 10 kilometers of other nations’ satellites in geosynchronous orbit.
“These close approaches to foreign spacecraft are largely inconsistent with the stated mission of the satellites, suggesting China may have obfuscated their true mission,” the report states.
Taken together, the DIA’s findings reinforce what then-Chief of Space Operations Gen. B. Chance Saltzman told reporters in 2025: that China is pursuing new capabilities across what he calls the six types of counterspace weapons, three in orbit and three terrestrial:
- Kinetic, destructive weapons;
- Directed energy; and
- Radio frequency energy and jamming.
The new DIA report’s focus on on-orbit weapons follows closely on the Space Force’s own acknowledgement for the first time that it has on-orbit weapons for “space control,” something leaders revealed at this September’s AFA conference.
The report also includes a rare image of China’s experimental space plane, a mysterious system often compared to the Space Force’s X-37B orbital test vehicle. The image, captured by a commercial Maxar satellite, shows the Chinese spacecraft’s shape is not unlike the X-37.
“Spaceplanes are … reusable and feature enhanced maneuverability, making them more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA report states, noting that the Chinese space plane has released, maneuvered around, and rendezvoused with other satellites during its time in orbit.
Besides China, the 2026 report also noted expanded counter-space activities by less advanced adversaries like Iran and North Korea.
Iran in particular has used jammers to disrupt satellite communications and navigation signals around the Strait of Hormuz, according to the report, and during Operation Epic Fury, both the U.S. and Iran “took offensive actions against each others’ space capabilities to degrade and disrupt military actions on both sides.” Pentagon and Space Force officials have claimed they have achieved “space superiority” in the conflict but have not detailed Iran’s efforts in space.
North Korea, meanwhile, managed to successfully launch a reconnaissance satellite into orbit in 2023, and “may also be developing jammers effective against military GPS signals,” according to the report.

brazilian studio rótulo em branco turns oversized nails into sculptural steel tables
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:01:14 UTC
07:01:14 KST

brazilian studio rótulo em branco turns oversized nails into sculptural steel tables
designed by ingrid sani lang, the prego collection reimagines construction nails as stainless-steel side, coffee, and bar tables with interchangeable heads.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
OVERSIZED NAILS BECOME SCULPTURAL FURNITURE
A nail is usually meant to hold things together, not become the center of attention. Brazilian design studio Rótulo em Branco turns that logic on its head with PREGO, a collection of sculptural stainless-steel tables inspired by the familiar construction fastener. Designed by architect Ingrid Sani Lang, the series translates the nail’s recognizable silhouette into three furniture typologies: a side table, a coffee table, and a bar table. Through an exaggerated shift in scale, an ordinary industrial component takes on an entirely different role in the domestic interior.
Founded in 2021 in Blumenau, southern Brazil, Rótulo em Branco approaches furniture as an opportunity to reconsider familiar objects and their functions. With PREGO, the studio explores what happens when an everyday element is removed from its original context and reimagined through proportion, material, and use. Rather than producing a literal oversized replica, the designer adapts the nail’s geometry to create functional surfaces with a sculptural presence. The collection retains the simplicity of its industrial reference while introducing an unexpected relationship between construction hardware and contemporary furniture.
INTERCHANGEABLE NAIL HEADS INTRODUCE PLAYFUL FUNCTIONALITY
Beyond its distinctive silhouette, PREGO incorporates a system of removable and interchangeable nail heads, allowing the tables to accommodate different uses. Two versions are available: a smooth surface designed to hold everyday objects and a sculpted alternative featuring recessed details. The latter can accommodate smaller items and introduce additional functions, including uses associated with incense. Both designs maintain the recognizable shape of the original object while giving the user a choice in how the furniture operates.
The interchangeable components introduce an element of interaction into what might otherwise remain a purely sculptural exercise. Users can switch between the two heads depending on their needs, allowing the same piece to move between different domestic arrangements. This flexibility challenges the idea of furniture as an object with one permanent configuration, while the familiar nail shape adds a small dose of visual irony. After all, the very component normally used to fix things in place becomes the part designed to be removed.
STAINLESS STEEL AND LOCAL PRODUCTION SHAPE PREGO COLLECTION
The collection is manufactured from AISI 304 stainless steel, combining a brushed finish on the main structure with polished surfaces on the nail-shaped elements. This contrast emphasizes the geometry of each piece, allowing the industrial material to take on a more expressive character. All three table typologies are developed and produced in southern Brazil, where Rótulo em Branco works with regional manufacturers. The studio’s involvement throughout fabrication, material selection, and finishing keeps the production process closely connected to its design practice.
PREGO was launched in collaboration with Nowdays, a Brazilian digital platform connected to contemporary internet culture, bringing the collection into a dialogue that extends beyond conventional furniture design. The partnership reflects Rótulo em Branco’s interest in objects that engage with visual culture and challenge familiar domestic conventions. Positioned somewhere between functional furniture and sculpture, the series finds new possibilities in one of construction’s most unassuming components. A nail may be a rather modest starting point, but here it has considerably bigger ambitions.

F-22s, F-15s Rotate in at Kadena to Bolster Pacific Airpower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:37:22 UTC
06:37:22 KST

Squadrons of F-22 Raptors and F-15C Eagles have arrived at Kadena Air Base, Japan, for temporary deployments as the critical Pacific base awaits its permanent F-15EX fighters.
Stars & Stripes reported Oct. 27 that a squadron of F-22s from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, finished arriving Sept. 30. Another squadron of F-15s, from Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base New Orleans, La., also recently arrived, Stripes reported, citing a statement from the 18th Wing at Kadena.
The 18th Wing did not immediately respond to a query from Air & Space Forces Magazine. But independent aircraft trackers and photographs published by the military show those planes arriving at or operating from Kadena recently.
Kadena, located on Okinawa, is the U.S.’s closest air base to Taiwan and strategically vital.
The 18th Wing at Kadena flew squadrons of permanently assigned F-15C/D fighters for years. But those legacy fighters were rapidly aging, and in November 2022, the Air Force started withdrawing them. Those fighters will be replaced with 36 permanently assigned F-15EX Eagle II jets, beginning in fiscal 2027.
Until then, the service is rotating various fighters, including F-35s, F-22s, F-16s, and F-15 variants through Kadena on a temporary basis, to maintain the base’s ability to project airpower if necessary.
The first F-15EXs had been scheduled to arrive by now, but labor disputes and other challenges slowed Boeing’s deliveries and delayed plans. The first F-15EX earmarked for Kadena left Boeing’s St. Louis factory Aug. 28, and flew to Portland, Ore., for final systems integration, software updates, and other technical preparations. After that work is done, the jet will fly to Okinawa.
Photos posted by the 18th Wing on Oct. 27 show the Alaska F-22s at Tsuiki Air Base, Japan, taking part in Exercise Keen Sword 27, which aims to improve how U.S. and Japanese forces work together.
Aircraft trackers have also observed F-15 movements to Kadena in recent weeks.
Aviation enthusiast Aux OSINT on Oct. 24 and 25 posted flight tracker images on social media of KC-46 Pegasus tankers flying Coronet missions with F-15Cs from the 122nd, inbound to Kadena.
A Japan-based aviation photographer who posts online under the handle Okadna35 posted images Oct. 24 of F-15s arriving at Kadena, bearing markings of the New Orleans base’s 159th Fighter Wing, nicknamed the Bayou Militia.

Turkish engineer creates live 3D pixel map of adopted hometown Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:36:45 UTC
06:36:45 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.
The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.
The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.
While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.
Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.
The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.
The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.
Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.
Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.
An observation deck at the top of the EU's tallest building, Varso Tower in Warsaw, has opened to the public.
Located 230m up on the tower's 53rd floor, the attraction offers a 360° panorama of Poland's capital.https://t.co/VeEapOmh4s
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2025
The result is an incredible level of explorable detail, from major landmarks, such as the communist-era Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower, the EU’s tallest building, down to the seating steps and bars along the Vistula River boulevards.
The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves.
A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium.
I turned Warsaw into a flight sim 🛩️
Take off from Chopin, fly through the ring over the Palace of Culture, then land a UFO inside Stadion Narodowy as the roof opens 🛸
Desktop only for now. Can you land it? 👇 pic.twitter.com/DT2fdk1Vem
— Bedirhan (@bedcodes) October 27, 2026
Speaking to Notes from Poland, Yildirim says that he moved to Poland in 2022 to pursue a job in IT before starting his own business. Initially living in Kraków, the country’s second-largest city, he then moved to Warsaw in 2025.
Asked what his own personal favourite places in the city are, Yildirim points to Warsaw’s parks, such as Skaryszewski, Pole Mokotowskie and Łazienki. His favourite neighbourhood is Saska Kępa on the right bank of the Vistula.
The software engineer adds that his project is an example of how AI can be an “amazing tool to do 90% of the job very quickly”. The remaining 10% of human input “is what keeps it from being ‘AI slop'”.
Yildirim says that, without the use of AI, the map of Warsaw he created would have needed an entire team to build over a period of months.

Costa Rica’s mega-prison receives first inmates
President Laura Fernandez inaugurated the $35m mega-prison built to house up to 5,100 inmates near San Jose.
A newly opened maximum-security mega-prison in Costa Rica has received its first batch of inmates. The prison was built with the help of the Salvadoran government on the outskirts of the capital, San Jose, the country’s Justice Ministry announced.
The Costa Rican Justice Ministry shared images on Tuesday of 123 inmates dressed in orange, seated with their heads shaved and bowed and their hands behind their necks.
“Costa Rica is writing a new chapter in its penitentiary history,” Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar said in a statement.
The new prison is called the High-Containment Center Against Organized Crime (CACCO) and constitutes a symbol of a new “tough on crime” approach championed by President Laura Fernandez’s administration. It has a capacity for 5,100 inmates.
The CACCO was built with the help of the Salvadoran government on the outskirts of Costa Rica’s capital, San Jose, at a cost of $35m. Fernandez inaugurated it on October 15.
“CACCO is a monument to national security, a forceful response to organized crime, and a guarantee that the state will exercise its authority without hesitation,” the statement added.
The new facility has a capacity equivalent to 20 percent of the country’s prison population and “will also help reduce overcrowding in the prison system”, according to Aguilar.
Costa Rica, long regarded as one of the safest countries in Latin America, has in recent years experienced a sharp rise in violence linked to drug trafficking and organised crime. It witnessed a record-setting 905 homicides in 2023, followed by 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025.
Authorities attribute most killings to disputes between criminal groups over drug trafficking routes and markets.
Right-wing leaders in other Latin American countries have also sought to replicate the mega-prison model.

Sumy Region Expands Underground Schooling, With 9 New Facilities Under Construction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:34:15 UTC
06:34:15 KST

Ukraine’s northeastern Sumy region is working on expanding its network of underground schools as Russian forces increasingly target civilians, with more than 4,200 Russian guided aerial bombs (KABs) launched during this year alone.
There are currently 13 functional underground schools in Sumy, with nine new facilities still under construction. Cost estimates and site plans had also been completed for another 14 facilities, head of the Sumy Regional Military Administration Oleh Hryhorov told Ukrinform in an exclusive interview on Wednesday, Oct. 28.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The process is ongoing and being scaled up as much as possible,” Hryhorov said, noting that the region was seeking international partners to help fund the construction.
Classrooms increasingly below ground
With the full-scale invasion now in its fifth year, Ukrainian authorities have continued working on giving children as normal a childhood as possible under such conditions.
When the school year began on Sept. 1, many students returned to in-person classes under new wartime rules, including restrictions on large gatherings that could put children at risk.
In the Sumy region, new underground schools are being built mainly in larger cities, where the number of students is highest.
The need is much lower in smaller communities, as some only have a single school, Hryhorov said. Of the region’s 280 schools, 225 have their own shelters. Although most are basic, more than 70 schools have radiation-proof shelters.
Putin Calls Musk a ‘Genius,’ Claims Close Cooperation as Ukraine Faces Starlink Disruptions
According to Hryhorov, such infrastructure allows the region to keep many students in physical classrooms. About 75,000 children are currently enrolled in the region’s schools, with 22 of them operating fully in person.
As most schools in other regions do as well, 193 are operating using a mix of in-person and remote classes.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022, 165 schools have been damaged in the region and 21 destroyed beyond repair, Hryhorov said.
Ukrinform reported that another underground school opened in the city of Sumy in October, able to accommodate up to 500 students.
A region under constant fire
The effort comes as Sumy, located about 20 kilometers from the frontline, (12 miles) continues facing near-daily Russian attacks.
Due to the proximity, Russian forces have increasingly begun relying on fiber-optic FPV drones, which can now reach almost 50 kilometers (31 miles) into the region. By October, more than 6,000 drone strikes of several types were recorded.
Since the beginning of the year, more than 4,200 guided aerial bombs were dropped on the region; about 500 targeted the Sumy community, including 192 that struck the regional capital itself.
The overall number of attacks is roughly the same as in 2025, Hryhorov said, although noting that their focus has changed. While Russian forces mostly struck military positions during the last year, they have concentrated on civilian infrastructure and the region’s residents in 2026.
To protect against drones, more than 450 kilometers (280 miles) of roads have been covered with anti-drone nets.
Hryhorov said each kilometer costs more than Hr. 1 million (roughly $22,000), rising to as much as Hr. 3 million ($66,000) when the work is done by private contractors.
The government has so far allocated Hr. 70 million ($1.5 million) for additional nets in Sumy, while regional authorities and local communities have provided a total of Hr. 1.35 billion ($30 billion) for overall security measures, including the netting.
Mandatory frontline evacuations
Meanwhile, in 213 settlements near the border, evacuations remain mandatory.
According to Hryhorov, more than 57,000 people, including 8,000 children, have already left. However, about 34,000 civilians still remain in the region.
Under mandatory evacuation orders, all children have been evacuated from the frontline communities.
On Oct. 22, regional authorities also extended mandatory evacuation of families with children to the entire Sloviansk community after Russian forces struck the settlements of the Donetsk region 42 times, injuring two boys.
Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s university district on Tuesday, Oct. 27, killing one person and injuring over 10, mostly students.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, Oct. 1, while more than 100 children and over 60 teachers sheltered inside. The Geran-4 drone struck the wall of a stairwell between the school’s second and third floors without detonating.
Although deliberate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are prohibited under international humanitarian law, they remain part of daily life for Ukrainian citizens.

Russia and Tanzania to launch joint space program (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:30:37 UTC
06:30:37 KST

Russia and Tanzania to launch joint space program (VIDEO)
Russia and Tanzania have agreed to launch a joint space program, the Russian space agency Roscosmos has said. Moscow will assist Dodoma in establishing its own national space agency and developing the infrastructure needed for a domestic space industry.
On Wednesday, Roscosmos and Tanzania’s Ministry of Information, Communication and Information Technology signed a framework memorandum on strategic partnership and cooperation on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit. The event has brought delegations from 48 African countries to Moscow this week.
“Tanzania is planning to establish its own space agency, and we are ready to provide our colleagues with expert and methodological support,” Roscosmos Director General Dmitry Bakanov told journalists. The Russian space agency has already stepped up cooperation with Tanzanian specialists in the field, with support from the Russian presidential administration, he added.
According to Bakanov, Dodoma is particularly interested in developing its own spacecraft and launching them into orbit aboard Russian rockets. Roscosmos has confirmed that Russia will launch Tanzania’s first Earth remote-sensing satellite in March 2027.
During the summit, Russian specialists demonstrated to the Tanzanian delegation the country’s capabilities in training cosmonauts and space industry specialists, as well as conducting scientific experiments in space.
The two sides also discussed sharing Earth remote-sensing data and establishing ground stations in Tanzania to receive such data. According to Bakanov, the African nation also plans to increase the number of students studying space-related disciplines at Russian universities.
Under the agreement, Russia will assist Tanzania in developing infrastructure for its space industry, while the two countries will exchange expertise and best practices in training space specialists. They have also agreed to establish joint working groups and develop road maps covering all areas of cooperation.
Moscow has been actively supporting African nations’ space ambitions. Last year, the South African National Space Agency (SANSA) hailed Russia as a key partner in advancing its national space program. Pretoria “has received most of its support from the Russian Federation,” SANSA board chairman Patrick Ndlovu told Sputnik Africa at the time. Earlier that year, SANSA CEO Humbulani Mudau announced South Africa’s support for Russia’s proposal to establish a BRICS Space Council to strengthen space cooperation among member states.
In 2024, Zimbabwe announced plans to build its first spaceport with Russian assistance. The country also said it was in talks with Roscosmos about gaining access to Russia’s cosmonaut training system, among other areas of cooperation.

Eleni Stefania Kalapoda is an ARB-registered architect and urban designer and founder of Embedded Climates. 
On a hillside in Anji, in Zhejiang province, a cluster of umbrella-like canopies steps gently down the slope, following the rows of tea bushes. There is no grand entrance, no plinth, no monumental block of stone. On October 22, at Dutch Design Week in Eindhoven, this project, Anji Hood by RoarcRenew Architects, was named Cultural Space of the Year at the Frame Awards 2026, chosen from more than 1,000 submissions by 100 jurors across 10 panels.

China had 7,046 registered museums at the end of 2024, welcoming 1.49 billion visits that year.
Once a nation has built cultural venues on that scale, the question shifts from how many to what kind. The answers now emerging are quieter, lighter and more deeply rooted than the icons of recent decades.

The Italian Consulate in Karachi celebrates World Pasta Day
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:24:45 CET
06:24:45 KST

The Italian Consulate in Karachi celebrated World Italian Pasta Day today (officially observed on October 25), bringing together local businesspeople, officials, diplomats, and friends of Italy to promote Italian cuisine and strengthen cultural and commercial ties with Pakistan.
                                    
Italian Consul Fabrizio Bielli stated that this was the first time the consulate had organized the event, following the success of the Italian Cuisine Week celebrations in Karachi.
                                    
The initiative aims to “promote pasta as a symbol of Italian identity and culture, as well as the country’s manufacturing excellence, as part of broader efforts to highlight products made in Italy,” the consulate said in a press release.
                                    
Bielli noted that Pakistan “is characterized by a spirit of hospitality that extends to international cuisines, which are reinterpreted through traditional recipes and innovative fusion dishes.”
   The consulate plans to organize additional initiatives to promote Italian culture and gastronomy in Karachi, collaborating with local partners and operators, particularly in the hospitality, restaurant, and food sectors.
                                    
In 2025, Italy produced approximately 4.2 million metric tons of pasta, more than 60% of which was destined for export, according to the press release. World Pasta Day has been celebrated annually on October 25 since 1995, when the first World Pasta Congress was held in Rome. This international initiative is coordinated by the International Pasta Organization, a nonprofit organization founded in Rome in 2006 that brings together pasta industry associations from 18 countries.

Ukraine's military reveals what Russia's war has cost Moscow — in dollars, arms, and lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:20:17 UTC
06:20:17 KST

Ukraine's military reveals what Russia's war has cost Moscow — in dollars, arms, and lives
The General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces published a video on Oct. 28 detailing the costs of Russia's full-scale invasion over the past four-and-a-half years.
The price of the war is measured in money, weapons, and soldiers — as well as lost opportunities to invest in Russia's future.
The military's video comes on the 1,707th day of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.
People
Russia has paid a heavy price in blood for every inch of territory occupied in Ukraine. Since Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff calculates that Russia has lost over 1,580,000 personnel.
The casualties include both killed and injured soldiers.
The sum means that Russia loses nearly a thousand people every day, according to the General Staff. Put another way, a Russian soldier dies every 90 seconds.
"This video is three minutes long," the narrator reads.
read also
Equipment
Moscow has lost over $204 billion in military equipment over the course of the war, the military reports.
This includes 12,448 tanks, 51,674 artillery systems, and 25,609 armored combat vehicles. Ukraine also counts 449 destroyed Russian aircraft, 356 helicopters, 35 vessels, and two submarines.
Russia has also lost over five thousand missiles and over 585,000 drones, the military said.
Money
Russia has spent hundreds of billions of dollars waging a war of choice against Ukraine.
In addition to losing billions in destroyed equipment, the Russian government also pays over $95 million per day in compensation for the dead and wounded.
Russia's oil industry has also taken a severe hit due to international sanctions and Ukraine's long-range strikes against refineries, pipelines, and shadow fleet tankers.
In a single year, from August 2025-2026, the industry's total losses reached $13.5 billion, according to the General Staff.
Every year since the start of the all-out invasion, the war has carved an even greater chunk out of the Russian economy. In 2022, the war in Ukraine accounted for 4% of Russia's GDP. In 2025, that number rose to 7.5%.
From spending $86 billion in 2022, Russia spent $190 billion on the war in 2025 and plans to spend another $186 billion in 2026.
In total, Russia has spent over $700 billion on the war against Ukraine.
"With this money, one could build 10,000 kilometers of modern highways, 1,000 new schools, 200 large hospitals, give a million rubles to every child born since the start of the full-scale invasion, pay double the pension to every pensioner for two years, and invest the rest of the money in science, which would be more than Russia has invested in it in the last 10 years," the video says.
The money would also be enough to fund the complete construction of five modern cities of 8-10 million people.
"But Russia chose war," the narrator says.

Microsoft stock jumps 4% as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:57:21 UTC
05:57:21 KST

Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
- Earnings per share: $4.89 adjusted vs. $4.73 expected
- Revenue: $92.28 billion vs. $90.69 billion expected
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement, with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue.
For Azure, Microsoft's finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts that she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus.
"We still have demand that exceeds supply," she said.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. "Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed," Hood said.
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues.
"In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2," she said. The delays have to do with GPU-as-a-service providers, she said.
Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it's attractive to do so, Hood said.
"We're fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our rates ratings are, and sort of we haven't been able to — we haven't yet, I would say, tapped that," she said. "And then, of course, there's other options."
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers.
Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs, and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
