US Democrats allegedly recruited 'spoiler' candidates to undermine Republican senator in Alaska
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:56:04 UTC
05:56:04 KST

Democratic operatives working with US Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign sought to recruit spoiler candidates to undermine Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's closely contested Senate race, according to a New York Times investigation published Wednesday, which uncovered an extensive operation involving campaign aides, national Democratic officials, and a political consultant operating under a false identity.
The operation, internally dubbed the "ballot composition project," sought to exploit Alaska's unusual election system by recruiting candidates who could draw votes away from the Republican incumbent, including another candidate named Dan Sullivan.
The findings emerged less than a week after the Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska's Senate election results if confusion between the two candidates named Sullivan affects the outcome.
Double Dan Sullivan
According to the Times, the effort began in the summer of 2025, when a Peltola campaign staffer was instructed to search Alaska voter records for individuals sharing the Republican senator's name.
The search eventually led to Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, a small fishing community in southeastern Alaska, who entered the Senate race in May. He has maintained that he decided to run independently.
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) both denied involvement in recruiting candidates.
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race," the campaign told the Times.
The DSCC similarly denied recruiting Sullivan or any other Republican candidate.
Democratic operative allegedly used false identity to recruit candidates
The investigation identified Jerid Kurtz, an Ohio-based Democratic operative, as a central figure in the recruitment effort.
According to former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios, Kurtz was introduced to senior campaign aides by DSCC officials in 2025 and subsequently participated in discussions about potential spoiler candidates.
Rios, who was dismissed during an August campaign shake-up, told the Times that Peltola was not directly involved in the operation but was "definitely aware."
The report described Kurtz traveling throughout Alaska using the name "Zane" while approaching potential candidates in bars, restaurants, and private meetings.
One prospective candidate, Matthew Salisbury of Anchorage, said an individual identifying himself as Zane repeatedly encouraged him to enter the race, offering potential financial support through outside political spending.
After receiving a photograph of Kurtz from the Times, Salisbury identified him as the individual who had approached him.
The operation also allegedly involved efforts to recruit Gerald Heikes, a Republican drywall contractor who ultimately secured a place on the November ballot.
Heikes told the Times that a man from the Midwest had encouraged him to run and promised outside support. He did not identify that individual as Kurtz.
Federal Election Commission records cited by the Times showed that a pro-Peltola super PAC paid approximately $87,000 to Wingspan Strategies, a firm co-owned by Kurtz. The PAC denied hiring or paying Kurtz personally for services.
Kurtz did not respond to the newspaper's requests for comment.
Secret messages reveal discussions about manipulating ballots
Text messages reviewed by the Times indicated that senior Peltola campaign aides and DSCC officials discussed the recruitment operation over several months.
Among those involved in the communications were Anton McParland, Peltola's former chief of staff, and Andrew Piatt, the DSCC's director of campaigns.
In January, McParland raised the possibility of establishing a new right-wing political party to attract conservative voters who might otherwise support the incumbent senator.
"Imagine if there was a MAGA party!" McParland wrote.
"Smart," Piatt replied. "Let's see."
The idea was reportedly abandoned in May.
The investigation also described efforts to persuade Democrat David Leslie to withdraw after he advanced through Alaska's August primary. His departure allowed Heikes to claim the fourth position on the general election ballot.
According to the Times, Kurtz contacted Leslie before his withdrawal and later congratulated him.
The August primary resulted in both candidates named Sullivan advancing alongside Peltola, with the eventual four-person ballot containing three candidates other than the Democrat.
Former campaign manager retracts statements
Rios provided extensive interviews about the alleged operation over two months, according to the Times, but later attempted to withdraw her statements.
The newspaper reported that she contacted its journalists shortly before publication and said she no longer wanted to serve as a source.
The Times said its reporting was corroborated by other interviews and documentary evidence, including text messages and records connected to the campaign.
Rios had reportedly been considering a wrongful termination lawsuit against Peltola's campaign but had not filed one.
The Times also reported that political consultant Jim Lottsfeldt had discussed supporting long-shot candidates through outside spending during a dinner with campaign employees.
Lottsfeldt denied knowledge of the operation and disputed Rios's account.
Justice Department lawsuit adds pressure before election
The revelations come as Alaska's Senate race attracts growing national attention, with Democrats seeking to capture Republican-held Senate seats in the November midterms.
The Justice Department's lawsuit argues that the presence of two candidates named Sullivan could mislead voters and improperly influence the results.
The Republican incumbent appears on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan, identified as the incumbent and a registered Republican, while his namesake appears as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., without a party affiliation.
The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the second Sullivan could remain on the ballot, rejecting attempts to disqualify him.
Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, under which voters can rank candidates by preference, with subsequent preferences counted if no candidate initially secures a majority.
Election law experts have questioned the federal government's legal basis for challenging certification over potential voter confusion.

Inquiry slams culture and command of Australia's SAS during Afghanistan war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:53:39 UTC
05:53:39 KST

Inquiry slams culture and command of Australia's SAS during Afghanistan war
In short:
A secretive inquiry into the culture within Australia's SAS during the war in Afghanistan has been partly made public, years after its completion.
It looked into both systemic cultural problems in the special forces unit, and whether warning signs should have been picked up at higher command levels.
What's next?
It found the chain of command in the SAS had been effectively inverted, and that senior commanders overlooked alarming warning signs like a growing number of enemy casualties.
A long-secret inquiry into the cultural and command failures of Australian special forces operators during the war in Afghanistan has found that an "abandonment of curiosity" within the Australian Defence Force's leadership and an "inversion of authority" within units helped create a culture that allowed alleged war crimes to occur.
The inquiry found deep, systemic cultural problems were rife in the ADF's Special Air Services regiment (SASR), and that the lack of intervention to correct them indicated "an absence of effective leadership at various levels".
The inquiry was commissioned in the wake of the 2020 release of the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force Afghanistan Inquiry, which found "credible evidence" of dozens of unlawful killings.
It sought to investigate the culture within the special forces units deployed to Afghanistan and any causal link to the alleged killings and other wrongdoing, as well as possible indicators that more senior commanders should have picked up on.
The inquiry report was handed to the former chief of the defence force, Mark Binskin, in 2022, but the executive summary was only published online recently.
The full report will not be made public because it contains sensitive evidence from the original Afghanistan inquiry.
The Afghanistan inquiry has been criticised by some for its finding that responsibility for alleged war crimes sat almost entirely at relatively low ranks, amid a sense that more senior ADF officers should have carried more responsibility for the actions of soldiers under their command.
This additional inquiry found an "extreme limitation" in the flow of information from SAS units to higher levels of command at the time in question, which limited what those higher ranks knew.
But it sharply criticised the ADF's higher headquarters for not taking more of an interest in some of what it considers to be clearly alarming information that was crossing its desk, like the growing number of people being killed during operations.
"There was tangible data available for higher headquarters through trends in growing numbers of Enemy Killed in Action," it found.
"This included growth and spikes in these statistics over time, as well as features such as a lack of wounded insurgents [only deaths] and the lack of ADF casualties. By historical standards, elements of this data presented as most unusual.
"Some commanders were alert to this data and rumours that accompanied it while others were not, which may suggest an abandonment of curiosity."
It suggested that the rumours circulating about the actions of the SAS in Afghanistan surely warranted investigation at the time.
"It is extraordinary that no effective action was taken given the gravity of the matters the subject of rumours," it found.
"The issues should have been escalated and effective action taken to investigate the matters or, at the least, look behind them."
Former SAS captain turned Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said he welcomed the release of the report because he believed in "transparency".
"I lived a lot of what I read in that report," he told Radio National Breakfast.
"There's almost 50 findings and a lot of it rings very true to me as a junior officer at the time.
"[The report] confirms there was unlawful conduct, that's not in dispute, but rather than focusing on individuals, it spreads responsibility throughout the chain of command."
'Arrogant', 'bikie gang' culture
The inquiry reserved some of its harshest criticism for the culture that developed within the SAS during the period.
It found a pervasive belief among some SAS operators that they were "exceptional" and, as a result, "ordinary norms and standards no longer apply".
But it places some of the blame on both the government and Special Operations Command for fostering the belief that the SAS was "superior" rather than "specialist", and it criticises the over-deployment of special forces more broadly.
It found a "tendency to arrogance" within the SAS, an "unhealthy imitation" of US special forces units and a belief among some that they were "untouchable".
It also found that operational decision-making was being influenced by "a desire to secure awards and the recognition and acclaim that comes with acts of valour", including "seeking out situations where significant contacts with insurgents was likely, or taking excessive risks for personal gain rather than mission effectiveness".
The inquiry found that the chain of command during the time was effectively inverted, with junior officers "effectively subservient" to non-commissioned officers who would ordinarily be under their command.
It found some junior officers prioritised "mateship" over "leadership", and criticised senior officers for knowingly allowing alcohol to be consumed.
"The creation of a dedicated drinking establishment within [special forces base] Camp Russell, particularly in an Islamic country, when there were clear orders that alcohol was not to be consumed, is striking," it found.
And it found when junior officers did try to challenge that structure, they would find networks of non-commissioned officers undermining them by effectively backgrounding against them.
It described the SAS as extremely homogeneous, with a largely closed culture "described by some as akin to a 'bikie gang'" with a "general intolerance of people who were not considered to be 'like us'".
But it noted that efforts toward cultural reform within the SAS were underway as the inquiry completed its work, and commended that attempt at change.
The findings of the initial Afghanistan inquiry led to the establishment of the Office of the Special Investigator, which investigated alleged war crimes.
Former SAS Corporal and Victoria Cross recipient Ben-Roberts Smith was arrested and charged with war crimes earlier this year, which he intends to contest.
Another former SAS trooper, Oliver Schulz, is also before the courts on war crimes charges, which he is contesting.

Lawsuit seeks to block Trump administration effort to find noncitizen voters
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:52:29 CET
05:52:29 KST

By Tom Hals
WILMINGTON, Delaware, Oct 28 (Reuters) - A Trump administration initiative to deploy hundreds of investigators to hunt for noncitizen voters is illegally intimidating naturalized US citizens and subjecting them to possible disenfranchisement, according to a lawsuit filed by civil rights groups that seeks to end the practice.
The lawsuit filed on Wednesday in California federal court by the American Civil Liberties Union and affiliates also alleges that the administration is demanding state election officials deny ballots to certain voters based on flawed eligibility data, potentially undermining confidence in next week’s midterm elections.
President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party is locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress, has repeatedly asserted that noncitizen voting is widespread in US elections, a claim that has been widely debunked.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that the administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas for records on tens of thousands of voters in at least a dozen states as part of the effort to uncover noncitizen voting.
“The administration can’t keep creating political stunts to sow distrust in our elections and lay the groundwork to question results they don’t like,” said Theresa Lee, an attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project, in a statement.
HOMELAND SECURITY AMONG DEFENDANTS
The lawsuit names as defendants the Department of Homeland Security and Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and US Citizenship and Immigration Services and Director Joseph Edlow. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In August, DHS launched the Unlawful Voter Initiative, which directed US Citizenship and Immigration Services personnel to generate lists of individuals to investigate for possibly voting without being a US citizen, as is legally required.
In the months since, the Justice Department has brought more than 100 cases accusing individuals of noncitizen voting. It has also launched a legal effort to prevent California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters that the administration alleges are noncitizens.
The ACLU lawsuit said the initiative has led to thousands of fully naturalized American citizens being subjected to improper investigations, door-to-door interrogations and potential disenfranchisement.
The groups alleged the initiative violates the Civil Rights Act and laws governing privacy and administrative procedures. The lawsuit seeks to vacate the Unlawful Voter Initiative and asks for the destruction of records that were created and maintained as part of the initiative.
Last week, a federal judge in California placed limits on the Unlawful Voter Initiative in nine states, but the plaintiffs said those restrictions expire at the end of Election Day on November 3, allowing the initiative to be used in future federal elections.
(Reporting by Tom Hals in Wilmington, Delaware; Editing by Rod Nickel)

Bolsonaro lands in Miami with his family after fleeing Brazil: 'He is in a safe location'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:49:25 UTC
05:49:25 KST

Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing candidate who lost Brazil's presidential election this week to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, landed in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil despite a court order prohibiting him from leaving the country.
Bolsonaro arrived in the United States with his wife and two daughters after an escape route that took them through Argentina and Ecuador. AFP and Reuters reported his arrival, with the first footage showing the Brazilian politician stepping off a private jet at Opa-locka Executive Airport near Miami.
AFP footage showed Bolsonaro emerging from the aircraft with his family after its door opened. Reuters cameras also captured the family disembarking from a Gulfstream G400 jet and heading into the airport.
According to a report by NPR, uniformed security personnel escorted the family to a waiting vehicle while holding large umbrellas to shield them from journalists gathered at the scene. Bolsonaro made no statement and did not answer reporters' questions.
His arrival in the United States followed a day of widespread speculation about his whereabouts. According to flight-tracking website FlightAware, the private jet carrying Bolsonaro and his family departed Wednesday morning from Guayaquil, Ecuador, where it had stopped to refuel, and landed in Miami at approximately 9:25 a.m. local time.
The journey began Tuesday evening, when Bolsonaro and his family crossed the land border from Brazil into Argentina before boarding a private plane to Ecuador. Brazilian media also revealed that Bolsonaro used his Italian passport to enter Argentina, even though Brazil's Supreme Court had ordered him to surrender all his passports, including foreign travel documents.
According to Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, his wife, Fernanda, and their two daughters presented Brazilian documents. Argentine authorities confirmed that the family entered the country with valid travel documents and that there was no legal impediment to their entry.
Trump backs Bolsonaro's arrival as tensions with Brazil rise
Bolsonaro's entry into the United States was made possible after the State Department announced that it would grant visas to him and his family. President Donald Trump, a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, expressed support for their arrival.
The move could further strain relations between Washington and Brasília after Lula accused the U.S. administration of cooperating with the Bolsonaro family in an effort to return it to power.
Bolsonaro is expected to break his silence Thursday and publicly address his escape for the first time.
Paulo Figueiredo, a close associate of the Bolsonaro family, announced that the politician would hold a news conference in Miami during the afternoon. According to Figueiredo, Bolsonaro is currently in a "safe location" and is "resting with his family."
Figueiredo claimed that false and contradictory reports about Bolsonaro's whereabouts had circulated in the media in recent hours, some of them attributed to officials in other countries.
Election defeat, corruption investigations and a disputed escape
The younger Bolsonaro, 45, fled Brazil just two days after losing the presidential runoff to Lula, receiving 48.21% of the vote compared with 51.79% for the incumbent left-wing president. He refused to recognize the results and alleged voting irregularities, without presenting evidence to substantiate claims that the outcome had been falsified.
Meanwhile, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports amid ongoing investigations into suspected corruption and money laundering. He failed to comply, and authorities revoked the validity of his passport.
On Wednesday, Brazil's Supreme Court also denied reports that federal police had raided Bolsonaro's mansion in the upscale Lago Sul neighborhood of Brasília.
Despite the travel ban, no arrest warrant had been issued for Bolsonaro when he fled the country. According to Folha de S.Paulo, federal police did not monitor his movements after he left his home in Brasília.
The four family members also did not undergo federal police border checks when leaving Brazil, because Brazilian citizens are not required to complete that procedure when crossing the land border into Argentina.
As recently as Monday, after being ordered to surrender his passports, Bolsonaro declared that he had no intention of leaving Brazil and planned to defend himself against the allegations, which he denies. Now that he has arrived in the United States, it remains unclear how long he intends to stay.
His term in Brazil's Senate is expected to end in February, when he will also lose his parliamentary immunity from prosecution.
Argentina investigates possible assistance in Bolsonaro's escape
Bolsonaro's flight has also sparked controversy in Argentina, where a criminal complaint has been filed demanding an investigation into the circumstances of his passage through the country. 
Lawmaker Marcela Pagano called for authorities to examine whether government officials helped Bolsonaro travel onward despite the restrictions imposed by a Brazilian court. She requested the preservation of security camera footage from the border crossing and airport, passenger manifests and documents related to the chartering of the private jet.
"The Argentine border is not anyone's VIP corridor," she declared.
Meanwhile, Argentine news website Infobae reported, citing government sources, that President Javier Milei's administration helped coordinate the operation that enabled Bolsonaro's departure. According to the report, government officials were involved in examining logistical and legal options in an effort to prevent Argentine authorities from becoming entangled in legal complications.
Following in his father's footsteps
Bolsonaro's escape echoes the actions of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who also left Brazil for the United States after losing to Lula in the 2022 presidential election and refusing to acknowledge the result. The elder Bolsonaro later returned to Brazil, where he was convicted of involvement in an attempted coup and sentenced to 27 years in prison.
Flavio's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, already lives in the United States and said before the election that he would support his brother leaving Brazil if he lost.

NEW DELHI: IT & I&B minister Ashwini Vaishnaw Wednesday said the Digital Personal Data Protection Act does not infringe upon press freedom, amid concerns from news publishers that the law could hinder investigative reporting. He said the Constitution’s guarantee of press freedom remains paramount and secure.TOI has learnt that govt would be open to amending the law to explicitly safeguard journalistic work and would also invite editors and other media professionals to have a detailed discussion on their concerns.“Journalistic freedom is guaranteed by the Constitution of India. That freedom is absolutely available. There is not even an intention to affect journalistic freedom,” Vaishnaw told mediapersons. He was responding to questions over the issue in light of a legal challenge by news publishers to the new law’s potential implications for reporting on matters of public interest.Vaishnaw said the enactment of the new Act had followed a Supreme Court judgement recognising the right to privacy as a fundamental right and was framed after more than a year of consultations involving newspapers, television channels, media representatives, IT industry and other stakeholders.
He added that during the consultation process, govt had explained that the legislation would not undermine press freedom.“It was clearly explained that provisions of the DPDP Act nowhere infringe upon freedom of the press, journalism and freedom of media,” the minister said. He argued that the constitutional guarantee of press freedom could not be overridden by data-protection legislation, distinguishing the misuse of private information from its legitimate use in journalism.
Vaishnaw also said that he would invite all editors and mediapersons to have an open dialogue with govt. “We will be very happy to explain, and if there is any doubt, we will be happy to take on record any suggestion and act if there is a need to.”

Five ways out of Israel's political deadlock, and one that keeps every promise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:45:15 UTC
05:45:15 KST

The inevitable conclusion from the near-final results of the 2026 election is clear: There is no decisive winner, and for a government to be formed after the election for the 26th Knesset, someone will have to break one or more campaign promises.
For now, and probably even after the remaining absentee and special ballots are counted, neither bloc is close to securing the 61 seats needed to form a stable government on its own. Without relying on the Arab parties, which achieved a record 19 seats, the opposition's bloc for change remains far from being able to form a government to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
So, with the emerging results giving Netanyahu's bloc a slight advantage over the bloc for change led by Gadi Eisenkot, is there a way to avoid another election? The answer is yes, but in every such scenario, political players on both sides would have to break several campaign promises.
These are the possible scenarios for forming a government, based on the actual election results that defied pollsters' predictions:
Unity government under Netanyahu
In light of the election results, this has become one of the most plausible scenarios, but also the one that would require the most broken promises across the political spectrum.
Under such an arrangement, Netanyahu could break his pledge to form a government with all the parties in his existing coalition, a promise he repeated several times in recent weeks. On the other side, Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman, the potential partners in such a government, would break their promises to voters not to serve under Netanyahu, whose Likud party finished far ahead of its rivals as the largest party.
ynet reported before the election that this was the scenario President Isaac Herzog had sought from the outset. On Wednesday, Herzog commented for the first time on the emerging results, saying everything possible must be done to avoid another election, another indication of his efforts to bring about a unity government amid the political deadlock.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who made no secret of his willingness to intervene in Israel's election before Oct. 27, could also become involved afterward to help bring about such an arrangement. A unity government could make it easier for him to advance diplomatic initiatives, including expanding the Abraham Accords, the normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab countries.
Unity government with Netanyahu first in a rotation
Given Netanyahu's double victory in the election, both in leading the largest party and in heading the larger political bloc, excluding the Arab parties, it is doubtful he would agree to a power-sharing rotation. Still, the possibility cannot be ruled out entirely.
Under this scenario, the leaders of the change bloc would also break their promises to voters, having pledged not to serve under Netanyahu. Some even argued that Netanyahu was unfit to serve as a minister after the failures of Oct. 7 and therefore should have no place in any government, even one he did not lead.
Netanyahu government with defectors from the change bloc
In this scenario, the politicians breaking their promises would be members of the change bloc who chose to join a Netanyahu-led government.
All the bloc's party leaders, and apparently members of all four parties, promised not to serve under Netanyahu. Most also pledged not to cooperate with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which have traditionally been Netanyahu's natural coalition partners.
Even before the election, ynet reported that if Netanyahu emerged closer to the 61-seat threshold, as now appears to be the case, Likud was counting on the possibility of defections, particularly from Eisenkot's Yashar! party.
As ynet previously revealed, Likud even established a special team tasked with persuading lawmakers from Eisenkot's party to cross over to Netanyahu's bloc after the election.
Temporary minority government or caretaker government led by Eisenkot
Under this scenario, every leader of the change bloc except Yair Golan would break a campaign promise.
Throughout the campaign, Golan said Arab parties were legitimate partners in a future government. Senior figures in his Democrats party reiterated that position Tuesday night, saying political leaders must "show political courage" and form a government with Ra'am, the Islamist-leaning Arab party led by Mansour Abbas.
Eisenkot, too, did not rule out such a move during the election campaign, particularly when asked about Ra'am. However, he faced opposition from his main partners in the bloc, Bennett and Liberman.
All three parties, Yashar!, Beyachad and Yisrael Beytenu, have figures who are firmly opposed to such an arrangement.
Meanwhile, in statements over the past 24 hours, the Arab parties have not ruled out the possibility and have said they would help remove Netanyahu from power.
Netanyahu has already launched a campaign to delegitimize the Arab parties, even claiming they "stole the election in Israel" following their dramatic electoral gains.
Another possibility is that the change bloc, together with the Arab parties, could seek to take control of the Knesset. That would mean replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana and, at a minimum, advancing the establishment of an official state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 massacre.
In such a scenario, the Knesset could be dissolved immediately after those measures are carried out, sending Israel to another election.
Another election
That leads directly to the scenario that appeared most likely before Oct. 27: another election.
If no one breaks the many promises made over the past several months, Israel, once again caught in a political deadlock, could find itself heading back to the polls within a matter of months.
The election results revealed something most polls failed to predict: Likud's enduring support. Although the party lost some ground, it remains by far the largest in the Knesset.
According to most assessments within the political establishment, another election could primarily benefit Netanyahu.
Disillusionment within the change bloc could depress turnout in center-left strongholds and perhaps also among Arab voters, who turned out in unprecedented numbers in this election, effectively fulfilling the familiar political refrain about voters "flocking to the polls in droves."

UN votes to condemn embargo of Cuba despite US lobbying push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:22:16 UTC
05:22:16 KST

UN votes to condemn embargo of Cuba despite US lobbying push
US points to increase in abstentions in General Assembly as evidence that push to isolate Cuba is slowly succeeding.
The United Nations General Assembly has again voted in favour of a resolution condemning the United States’s economic embargo of Cuba despite a push by US officials to peel off support.
The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 countries in favour and 17 opposed, including the US and Israel. Another 25 countries abstained, including countries such as Germany and Italy, that had previously voted in favour. The General Assembly has voted to condemn the embargo annually for more than three decades.
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said in a social media post after the vote that the US was “once again isolated in its attempt to continue strangling the Cuban people”.
“Neither its most insane pretexts nor its pressures nor media circus will prevail over the force of facts and truth,” he added.
The US embargo on Cuba, part of an effort to isolate the country and squeeze its economy that has lasted more than six decades, has been widely condemned on the world stage and linked to worsening hardship on the island.
US President Donald Trump’s administration has implemented a series of additional economic restrictions, including an energy blockade, to further tighten the screws.
That economic campaign has also been accompanied by a US diplomatic push to further isolate Havana, an effort that US officials said is apparent in the uptick in countries that abstained during Wednesday’s vote. Cuban officials accused the US of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions and other penalties if they voted to condemn the embargo.
“I’m satisfied that so many countries now, including major economies like Korea, like Germany and others have shifted their position,” US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told reporters after the vote.
“Diplomacy takes time, but now that we’ve had a tripling of countries that have shifted, we expect that to only continue to grow,” he added.
Tensions between US and Cuban officials exploded on Tuesday during a General Assembly debate with both yelling at the other and engaging in an apparent shoving match.
Waltz said on Wednesday that Richard Tur de la Concepcion, a first secretary at Cuba’s UN mission, would be expelled from the country for “assaulting an American diplomat”.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the US and Cuban missions for comment but has not received a response.

Three media outlets seek full White House access in amended lawsuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:21:03 UTC
05:21:03 KST

Three media outlets that President Donald Trump banned from the White House in September, only to have a federal judge's order restore much of their access, amended their lawsuit Wednesday, seeking to regain full access to serve in a press pool for other reporters in the Oval Office and Air Force One.
The amended civil complaint against Trump says that since the judge ordered the White House to allow MS NOW, CNN and Politico journalists into the White House, the White House has blocked those outlets from performing pool functions they long have conducted.
The press pool routinely serves as a key source of information for the public about what a president does or says. In pool assignments, journalists agree to share with other media outlets information and images they obtain while acting as a pooler.
The amended complaint sets the stage for a court fight over whether a president, because of how he or she feels about how a media outlet covers them, can block access to individual media outlets or reporters from areas of the White House that other journalists have access to.
Ted Boutrous Jr., an attorney for the outlets, in a statement Wednesday said, "Despite two court orders restraining it from implementing the President's unconstitutional ban on CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, the White House has continued to violate the First Amendment and due process by excluding those news organizations from areas such as the Oval Office and Air Force One — the very locations that the President most frequently engages with the press."
"These exclusions, intended to punish and chill coverage of the administration that the President doesn't like, make it harder for the press to cover some of the most important events in the world for the benefit of the American people," Boutrous said.
The amended complaint in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C. says that Trump's original ban and "the White House's continued exclusion of Plaintiffs from certain [areas] are unlawful retaliation for protected First Amendment activity."
Those actions "brazenly" discriminate against the outlets "based on their perceived editorial viewpoint; the White House is expressly excluding CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO because the President dislikes the content of their coverage," the suit says.
Judge Tim Kelly's prior orders restoring access for the outlets did not require the White House to restore those outlets' access to the Oval Office or Air Force One.
The amended complaint notes that since his second term began in January 2025, Trump has held 121 press events aboard Air Force One or on the tarmac outside the presidential plane, and 138 events in the Oval Office, "during which he fielded no fewer than 4,700 questions from reporters."
"To be clear, Plaintiffs do not claim an unrestricted right to enter the Oval Office or travel aboard Air Force One," the new complaint says.
"But once the White House opens those spaces to selected journalists for newsgathering and reporting, the White House may not exclude Plaintiffs because it dislikes their coverage."
Since Trump announced the ban on Sept. 18, "the White House has repeatedly barred CNN from fulfilling its duties as designated television network pooler aboard Air Force One — a role CNN has fulfilled for more than four decades," the amended suit says.
MS NOW has not participated in the secondary TV pool since that date, and the White House has barred Politico "from two scheduled out-of-town print pool assignments aboard Air Force One," the suit says.
"Defendants have offered no official explanation for any of these exclusions," the amended complaint says.
"On information and belief, these exclusions reflect an unstated policy to carry out the President's directive to take his viewpoint-discriminatory and retaliatory ban 'as far as you can,'" the complaint says.
"Indeed, the President has been explicit that he intends to limit access to the Oval Office to news organizations that cover him favorably, declaring hours after this action was filed that 'publications that only write negatively . . . shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," the suit said.
The suit notes that after Kelly issued a preliminary injunction against Trump's ban in mid-October, "the White House issued a statement declaring that what it deems the 'Fake News' has 'no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office.'"
The amended complaint says the limited ban on pool access violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution.
"CNN, MS NOW, POLITICO, and their journalists have liberty and property interests in their press credentials and the access those credentials afford to the White House grounds to report on the President and his administration," the suit says. "That access has long extended to the Oval Office, Air Force One, and other fora that the White House has opened to the press for pool coverage."
"The ban, and Defendants' continued exclusion of Plaintiffs from certain White House press areas, deprives Plaintiffs of those interests without meeting the bare minimum requirements of due process: advance notice based on clear standards and an opportunity to be heard," the suit says.
The suit also said the White House is interfering with CNN's ability to perform its duties as one of five television networks that "staff, equip, and bear the costs associated with the primary television network pool upon which the American public (and the White House itself) relies for real-time television coverage of the President in the Oval Office, aboard Air Force One, and at the many other presidential events that due to size and other constraints simply cannot accommodate all members of the press corps."
Trump, when he announced the ban, said he was "sick" of what he called fiction and lies written about him, his administration, and the United States.
On Sept. 19, a day after he announced the ban, journalists from the three media outlets were denied access to the White House grounds and had their passes taken away when they showed up.
Two days later, the outlets first sued Trump, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Chief of Staff Susan Wiles, and Secret Service Director Sean Curran, seeking to regain access.
District Court Judge Tim Kelly on Sept. 23 issued a temporary restraining order mandating that the White House restore access to the outlets for at least 14 days.
Kelly, whom Trump appointed to the federal bench in 2017, said in his order that the ban appeared to flatly violate two federal appeals court rulings that require advance notice and an opportunity to be heard to journalists whose White House press passes are targeted for revocation.
The White House allowed journalists from the banned outlets in the next day.
On Oct. 13, Kelly issued a preliminary injunction, which indefinitely bars the White House from reinstituting the ban while the outlets' lawsuit continues in his court.
In issuing that injunction, Kelly again cited the appeals court decisions, but also said the outlets were likely to succeed on two First Amendment claims in their civil suit, which alleged retaliation and viewpoint discrimination.
Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

Russia is building a new site for operating attack drones near Millerovo airfield, close to the Ukrainian border, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) said on Oct. 28, citing satellite imagery.
The airfield is located in the village of Dolotinka in Russia's Rostov Oblast, about 20 kilometers (12 miles) east of Ukraine's Luhansk Oblast.
According to HUR, the facility's design indicates it is intended for the preparation and launch of jet-powered attack drones, likely Geran-4 and Geran-5 models and their variants.
"The construction of the facility in the Rostov Region may be part of Russia's preparations to intensify its attacks on Ukrainian territory, particularly during the winter," HUR said.
HUR estimated that once construction is complete, the site could accommodate up to 100 drone launches per day.
The site's actual operational tempo will depend on several factors, including supplies of ready-made drones, the availability of fuel and warheads, the number of trained drone crews, equipment readiness and the missions assigned by Russia, the statement read.

Apple shows pricey touchscreen laptops, a first for the iPhone maker
- Apple launched its first touchscreen MacBooks in Los Angeles, led by CEO John Ternus, ending years of resistance to touch on laptops.
- The new MacBook Pro has an OLED display, starts at US$2,899, and goes on sale on Nov 6. Apple says it is aimed at creators and designers.
- Analysts say Apple faces a crowded market where cheaper touchscreen laptops are common. The move may help Apple reach more buyers, but success is not certain.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – Apple chief executive officer John Ternus unveiled the company’s first touchscreen MacBooks on Oct 28, abandoning a long-held aversion to the technology as it caps a burst of product launches ahead of the holiday shopping season.
Ternus took the stage at an Apple event in Los Angeles and showed a MacBook Pro model with an organic light-emitting diode (OLED) display, playing up the display’s contrast, sharpness and brightness in front of an audience of content creators and creative professionals.
He also said the company would return to a glowing logo on the back of the laptops.
“Look, we love the Mac, and it’s the reason why so many of us found our way to Apple in the first place. And the Mac has never been better, and it’s never been stronger,” Ternus said on Oct 28.
The event is part of a media blitz filled with new product launches following Ternus – a former Apple hardware veteran – taking over as the company’s new CEO.
He launched a folding iPhone, Duo, at Apple’s Silicon Valley headquarters in September and a smart home hub in New York earlier in October.
While those products will test new markets for Apple, the Los Angeles event could rekindle an old question: Should Apple put the touchscreens that it made mainstream in iPhones and iPads in its oldest product line?
Apple executives long resisted the idea, with Steve Jobs saying in 2010 that touchscreens on laptops were “ergonomically terrible” and then-CEO Tim Cook saying in 2012 that such devices would be as pleasing to users as converging a toaster and a refrigerator.
Before becoming Apple’s CEO, Ternus argued that Apple already made a touchscreen computer with its iPad line-up.
But touchscreens have been widely available for more than a decade on Windows devices, and with the iPhone nearing its two-decade anniversary, a new generation of buyers expects screens to respond to touch.
“I believe they were always wrong on pushing back on touch, and this is the long arm of reality setting in,” said Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy.
“Some things are purely inevitable.”
How will customers respond?
A key question for Apple is how customers will respond. The company has seen an uptick in Mac sales, but much of that growth has been among technology enthusiasts and businesses buying the machines to handle AI tasks on-device.
The new MacBook Pro starts at US$2,899 (S$3,700) for the 14-inch model with the M5 Pro chip, while the highest-end configuration starts at US$4,799 for the 16-inch model with the more powerful M5 Max chip. The new 16-inch model is 0.7 pounds lighter than the older, non-touchscreen model.
Apple said on Oct 28 that the new MacBook Pro is available for pre-order starting Oct 28 and would go on sale on Nov 6.
“This is going to be towards creators, towards designers, towards photographers, people that are going to leverage that high fidelity screen, and who many of whom have grown up tapping on screens, editing on tablets, on phones, etc,” said Tom Mainelli, head of IDC’s Device & Consumer Research Group.
To guard against burn-in, a common OLED flaw where images from long-running apps leave permanent marks on the screen, Apple redesigned the chassis to draw warm air away from the display and used the computing power in its M5 chips to keep the screen refreshed.
“You can expect an OLED to last as long as your typical LCD screen. Apple came out of the gate firing in terms of putting together both a very vibrant display and then adding the touch,” Mainelli said.
Still, some analysts questioned how much headway Apple can make in a market dominated by enterprise buyers, where rivals such as Lenovo, HP and Dell offer cheaper devices.
PC makers shipped 33.4 million touchscreen notebooks in 2025, up 22% from a year earlier and 16% of all notebooks shipped, according to IDC. The average selling price for the devices was around US$1,009, much lower than Apple’s products.
The cheapest touchscreen laptop Apple unveiled on Oct 28 also costs more than an entry-level iPhone, MacBook, iPad with accessories, Apple Watch and AirPods combined.
But the expanding line-up of products and prices suggests that the company is chasing budget-conscious buyers without losing its premium customers, in an early sign of how Ternus might broaden its appeal. REUTERS

'There cannot be business as usual with Russia' — Dutch minister urges Europe to step up for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:11:12 UTC
05:11:12 KST

'There cannot be business as usual with Russia' — Dutch minister urges Europe to step up for Ukraine
Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Dutch Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 28, 2026. (Handout / Tetiana Bulhakova)
Ukraine is about to enter another harsh winter as Russian attacks continue crippling critical infrastructure, even before the coldest days set in.
In an attempt to relieve Kyiv, the Dutch government on Oct. 28 outlined a package of non-military aid worth 1.2 billion euros ($1.3 billion), to be disbursed over the next three years and directed toward the country's economic recovery.
The Netherlands will also provide 40 million euros ($45 million) to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund, as well as 55 million euros ($62 million) to fund energy equipment from Dutch companies via the Netherlands Enterprise Agency.
The Kyiv Independent walked through central Kyiv with Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Netherlands' minister for foreign trade, to discuss how Europe can help Ukraine withstand mounting pressure on its energy and water infrastructure amid ongoing Russian attacks.
Sjoerdsma explained the benefits of investing in Ukraine and commented on some countries' willingness to do business with Russia as its full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues.
The minister added that the EU must play a bigger political role in discussing how Russia’s war should end.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
The Kyiv Independent: How is the Netherlands coordinating assistance to Ukraine for the upcoming tough winter?
Sjoerdsma: The support package we are bringing, 1.2 billion euros ($1.3 billion), is mainly aimed at helping Ukrainians protect and restore energy and water facilities, but also at training people to prevent damage to and protect these facilities so they keep running.
We see that the urgency of the upcoming winter is to ensure that cities, whether it's Kyiv or small villages in the east, remain livable. We understand that the Russian strategy is to try to break the spirit of the Ukrainian people, to literally put you in the cold, and we're going to do anything we can to prevent that from happening.
The Kyiv Independent: Regarding the protection of these facilities, what is the Netherlands doing to aid Ukraine?
Sjoerdsma: Obviously, we have to make sure there's protection, and that they cannot be easily destroyed. We try, as best we can, to bring completed equipment, but this obviously cannot always happen, as we sometimes require Ukrainian expertise to help install and maintain it.
We try to make sure it's not just a one-off, but instead a complete, integrated process that helps Ukrainian energy and water facilities.
The Kyiv Independent: What potential do you see in investing in Ukraine during wartime?
Sjoerdsma: If you look at Dutch companies already present in Ukraine, their expertise varies a lot. Some are obviously defense companies that help Ukraine build missiles for military use.
Then there are companies like Philips that help supply essential medical materials. And then, there are many smaller companies helping Ukraine, for example, providing bakers with materials. So anything from a very small scale to a very large scale is already present. It's both a sign of solidarity and a business opportunity.
Kyiv Independent: What do Dutch businesses gain from investing in Ukraine?
Sjoerdsma: We are learning so much from Ukraine, just to give two examples. In the field of defense, the innovative way in which Ukraine's army operates and adjusts, changes material needs, and utilizes drones. These are huge lessons for how we organize our army.
But also, Ukraine's resistance against Russia, its ability to adapt and restore certain facilities, especially critical infrastructure, at such speed and ingenuity, is also crucial to us. If there are any problems with the Dutch electrical network or other facilities, we'll definitely call Kyiv first to ask how you do things.
Additionally, the day after the war ends and reconstruction begins, it's not only our duty to help Ukraine rebuild as soon as possible, but also a huge opportunity for Dutch companies. These can be some of their biggest assignments to date: rebuilding entire hospitals, schools, ports, and whatever else will help Ukraine flourish again.
Kyiv Independent: As some countries are showing willingness to trade and do business with the Kremlin and Russian companies, what is the Netherlands' stance on this matter?
Sjoerdsma: Let me be very clear, this war can end today if Russia decides to stop its aggression against Ukraine. For the Netherlands, this scenario is really quite clear. Looking at the way Russia is treating cities, not just Kyiv, and aiming to erase your cultural heritage, it's clear what Moscow's end goal is, and we cannot allow that to happen.
"There's no talk about Ukraine without Ukraine in the driver's seat of what's happening."
We love doing business with Ukraine and don't see any reason to do business with Russia at this time. So no, there cannot be business as usual with Russia. Our prime minister at the European Council was quite clear about this.
While the Dutch are very robust in their support, we also believe that other European countries really need to step up. And this is not a cliche — your security is our security. To treat it as something Ukraine can do on its own, I think, is ridiculous.
This is a partnership. We are doing what we can, but others need to increase their support, and they need to do so as soon as possible, before winter sets in.
The Kyiv Independent: How can the European Union help prevent the West's future deals with Russia?
Sjoerdsma: Obviously, we do not condone the diesel deal between the U.S. and Russia. We feel it not only legitimizes Russia’s government but also reinforces its position.
I think it's crucial that, since the bulk of Ukraine's assistance comes from the EU, the EU is also a political player.
We must use our political influence to ensure that whenever discussions about a ceasefire or peace agreement take place, Ukraine is at the table. There's no talk about Ukraine without Ukraine in the driver's seat of what's happening.
I think Europe's role is to support Ukraine in its resistance against Russia, but also to make sure you are in a position to determine your own future. We see how Russia is trying to erase your identity and history, and we are determined to prevent that from happening.

Chipotle earnings miss estimates, but same-store sales increase for third straight quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:11:00 UTC
05:11:00 KST

Chipotle Mexican Grill on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results and said its restaurant-level operating margin shrank.
But the burrito chain saw traffic and same-store sales grow during the quarter as low-income consumers spent more, bucking industry trends, and CEO Scott Boatwright projected a strong finish to the year.
Shares of the company rose 7% in extended trading.
"Broader consumer and industry headwinds may continue, but initiatives across our recipe for growth strategy are building and giving us more tools to win in any environment," Boatwright said on the company's earnings conference call. "We are still in the early stages of this work, and it's gaining traction."
Like the broader restaurant industry, Chipotle saw trends soften in early October, although executives said its traffic has returned to growth since then. Boatwright said the company has "high confidence" in its performance for the rest of the fourth quarter.
"We feel very confident that November and December set up very well for us," Boatwright said.
Chief Financial Officer Adam Rymer said the company expects fourth-quarter same-store sales growth of about 2%.
Here's what the company reported for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 27 cents adjusted vs. 29 cents expected
- Revenue: $3.29 billion vs. $3.29 billion expected
Chipotle reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $339.9 million, or 27 cents per share, down from $382.1 million, or 29 cents per share, a year earlier. The company's restaurant-level operating margin fell from 24.5% to 23.3%.
Excluding restaurant asset impairment charges and stock-based compensation, the company earned 27 cents per share.
Net sales rose 9.6% to $3.29 billion, fueled by the chain's new restaurants. During the quarter, Chipotle opened 84 company-owned restaurants and five international locations run by licensees.
In the second half of July, Chipotle said it started to see sales pull back as diners grew concerned about consuming raw lettuce due to cyclospora, although its own supply was never tied to an outbreak. Then in August, the chain disclosed that it had temporarily pulled jalapenos from Minnesota restaurants after learning its supply was potentially linked to a salmonella outbreak.
Still, the chain was able to report same-store sales growth for its third straight quarter, shaking off last year's traffic woes.
Sales at stores open at least 13 months increased 2.1%, lifted by a 1.3% bump in average check.
For the first time this year, low-income consumers during the quarter outperformed the high-income cohort at its restaurants, Boatwright said. And discounts aren't the reason — low-income consumers spent the most in September, when promotions were at their low point during the quarter, he told analysts.
For the full year, Chipotle reiterated its previous forecast that its same-store sales will increase by a low-single-digit percentage.
Looking ahead to 2027, the company is projecting that it will open between 340 and 360 new company-owned locations in the U.S. and Canada and around 15 to 25 international restaurants.

Russia Equips Geran Drones With Magnetometers for Improved Navigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:57:32 UTC
04:57:32 KST

Russia has equipped its Geran strike drones with magnetometers to improve navigation.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s commissioner for sanctions policy, reported this in a Facebook post, but did not specify the type of magnetometer.
The sensors were found in the drones’ tail sections and vertical stabilizers.
Vlasiuk also said specialists were examining the operating parameters of a new electronic jamming system found on the drones.
As is typical, all the new components and electronic modules are based on Western-made parts.
A magnetometer is an instrument used to measure the characteristics of a magnetic field and changes in that field across space. The device detects small variations in the magnetic background as it moves within Earth’s magnetic field or near large metal objects.
In military applications on drones, the sensor serves as an additional navigation aid. It measures the strength and direction of the natural magnetic field, functioning like an electronic compass.
The device’s primary purpose is to enable autonomous navigation when satellite navigation systems are being actively jammed. A magnetometer can help determine a drone’s heading and spatial orientation without relying on GPS or GLONASS signals.
In addition to magnetometers, Russian developers are equipping strike drones with new electronic jamming systems designed to counter Ukrainian electronic warfare measures.
Ukrainian specialists are already examining the operating parameters of the electronic equipment discovered on the drones.
Militarnyi previously reported that Chinese company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology supplies Russia with equipment for Geran and Gerbera drones, including mesh modems that allow the drones to maintain communications and be controlled during flight.
Journalists found that the manufacturer’s products had been shipped to Russia through the companies Atlant-Engineering and LT Global Forwarding. Customs declarations listed the equipment as antennas and remote-control devices.

US and Japan Finalize Agreement for AMRAAM Facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:53:39 UTC
04:53:39 KST

At a high-profile meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines this week, U.S. and Japan leaders finalized an agreement to establish a production facility in Japan for the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, following a massive $20.7 billion Pentagon contract to expand production of the missile over the next seven years.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced the agreement in an Oct. 28 press conference after meeting with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Defense Ministers’ Meeting.
The agreement is the culmination of an effort that began in July 2024 under both men’s predecessors.
“We finally reached an agreement on the establishment of a final assembly and inspection facility in Japan for the AMRAAM air-to-air missile, which is essential for the F-35,” Koizumi said, according to a translation of his remarks. “This is a groundbreaking agreement that will not only ensure the acquisition of equipment needed by both Japan and the United States, but will also strengthen Japan’s defense industry base.”
In a readout of the two leaders’ meeting, the Pentagon did not mention the AMRAAM facility but said Hegseth “welcomed Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense industrial capacity, and both leaders committed to continue close coordination on critical munitions production.”
The location for the facility has not yet been announced.
The approval process took more than two years in part because Japan has severe constitutional restrictions on exporting lethal weapons or even coproducing offensive weaponry with allies, which date back to its peace-focused foreign policy following its devastating losses in World War II.
The AMRAAM also contains classified guidance systems and intellectual property that require key safeguards to prevent leaks of crucial information about the weapon.
U.S. and Japanese officials have said the agreement will diversify the AMRAAM industrial base and build regional stockpiles for both the U.S. and its allies at a time when President Donald Trump, and Hegseth and his leadership team at the Pentagon have urged allies to invest more in their own defenses.
AMRAAM has long been the U.S. military’s main dogfighting weapon—the first missiles were delivered in 1988. The latest variant is the AIM-120D, which features GPS guidance and improved range, lethality, and jam-resistance over its predecessors.
All legacy fighters, as well as fifth-generation fighters such as the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II, can carry the AMRAAM.
In late September, the Pentagon and contractor RTX announced a five-year production contract for AMRAAM with two additional option years valued at up to $20.7 billion. The two sides had previously agreed to a framework agreement in February for AMRAAM and other key munitions.
While the contract award—officially published by the Air Force on Oct. 23—does not specify quantities of missiles, the February framework agreement calls for RTX to increase production “to at least 1,900” per year.
Both the length and size of the new contract are far greater than previous deals. Those usually covered a single year, and demand could whipsaw depending on budgetary pressures or service priorities.
As recently as fiscal 2022, the Air Force budget request called for buying just 186 AMRAAMs and the Navy requested none. Those totals wound up changing through reprogramming requests and congressional adds, but generally speaking, procurement stayed at or below 400 missiles between the services from fiscal 2017 to 2022.
AMRAAM Procurement
Source: Department of Defense Program Acquisition Cost by Weapon System reports. 2026 totals not finalized.
This new award expands the Pentagon’s multiyear procurement authorities, covering Lots 41-47. Those lots include fifth-generation technology in AIM-120D-3 variants, such as modernized processors and software-defined measures for the electronic warfare threat.
The deal is part of a broader effort by President Donald Trump’s administration to secure multiyear deals for munitions and aircraft, aiming to break the stop-and-start funding cycles of the past few decades.
The contract also increases output to other countries, with foreign military sales to 16 international partners for additional procurement pipelines included.
“We are accelerating output to record levels to deliver this critical capability for the U.S. services and more than 40 allied nations,” an RTX spokesman told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
“We have invested heavily over the past several years to expand capacity, modernize manufacturing, and strengthen our supply chain,” the spokesman wrote. “RTX proactively sourced $80 million in test equipment before any award. These investments will ramp annual production over the coming years to at least 1,900 AMRAAM missiles.”
The company is currently delivering previously contracted AMRAAMs, but the new multiyear contract helps avoid delivery interruptions, the spokesman wrote.
AMRAAM production has faced bottlenecks from a variety of issues, including subcontractor component supply chain problems and solid rocket motor production lag times.
“Like many advanced defense systems, AMRAAM relies on complex components that have long lead times,” the spokesman wrote. “Through sustained investment, supplier partnerships, and efforts such as new U.S. rocket motor production lines coming online in 2027, we are building faster than ever before.”

Peltola campaign aides, DSCC officials helped recruit second Dan Sullivan in Alaska race: NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:52:06 UTC
04:52:06 KST

People working with Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee participated in efforts to recruit a man named Daniel J. Sullivan to enter the Alaska Senate contest, in a bid to draw votes away from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, The New York Times reported Wednesday.
The Times — citing interviews, texts and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against Peltola's campaign — reported that "not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader."
"The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory," the newspaper reported.
Peltola's former campaign manager Elisa Rios told the Times that Peltola was not directly involved in the project, but she was "definitely aware," according to the report.
The Times noted Rios last week tried to retract comments she made confirming the effort to recruit spoilers.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC "denied participating in efforts to recruit spoilers to the ballot in Alaska," The Times said.
The newspaper's report noted ballot-stacking tactics are "common in politics and generally considered legal — and have been employed by both parties in Alaska."
The report comes days after the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit allegingthe campaign by the non-incumbent Sullivan was geared toward him acting as a spoiler for the incumbent Sullivan because of voter confusion.
The DOJ has asked a federal judge in Alaska to block certification of any Senate race result "that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
The winner of the election could determine whether Democrats regain a majority in the Senate, or if Republicans retain their current majority.
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the DOJ's lawsuit.
After the Times published its report, Trump demanded that Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan both be removed from Alaska's election ballot.
Trump, in a Truth Social post, claimed the report showed Democrats "illegally" sought out the same-named man "in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election, thereby taking votes away from the REAL Senator, Dan Sullivan."
Peltola's campaign, in a statement to CNBC on The Times article, said, "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Like Mary, our campaign is focused on lowering costs and fixing the rigged system in DC."
A DSCC spokesperson in a statement to CNBC said, "The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan."
"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns – including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson pointed to several examples of Republicans promoting third-party and dark horse candidates in the current election cycle and past ones to increase chances of a GOP candidate winning a race.
Peltola's campaign and DSCC, as well as Alaska's election officials, have asked the judge overseeing the DOJ's lawsuit, Sharon Gleason, to dismiss the suit before Election Day, Nov. 3. The League of Women Voters of Alaska and the advocacy group Common Cause have also sought to intervene in the case to oppose the DOJ's efforts.
Alaska officials said the DOJ "lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate," and that the lawsuit and "requested relief cast a cloud over Alaska's election."
State officials said in a court filing that Alaska's Division of Elections "has taken significant steps to distinguish" between the two Sullivans on the ballot, "so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which."
Gleason on Monday evening fast-tracked the case, increasing the chance she will decide whether to dismiss the case in U.S. District Court in Anchorage before Election Day.
Daniel J. Sullivan prevailed in a legal fight that ended with the Alaska Supreme Court allowing him on the nonpartisan primary ballot over the opposition of state election officials who argued his presence would confuse voters.
He won enough votes in that contest to win a place as one of four candidates on the general election ballot.
On that ballot, his name is spelled out "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." with no other words next to it.
Directly below his name, Sen. Sullivan is listed as Sullivan, Dan. S. with the words "Registered Republican, incumbent" next to his name in parentheses.
Peltola, a former U.S. House member, is the only Democrat on the ballot.
Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, which allows voters to rank candidates by preference. That method could allow voters to rank both Sullivans as choices, allowing a vote for the non-incumbent to be transferred to the incumbent senator if the non-incumbent is eliminated in the first round of counting.
The Times quoted Peltola's former campaign manager Rios, who the newspaper reported was fired in August, as saying, "Alaskan voters need to know" about the effort to recruit others into the race.
"There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions," Rios was quoted as saying.
Rios told The Times last week that she wanted to retract her prior statements.
"As discussed on our call earlier today, I am confirming that I have retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race in connection with any article you may or may not be writing," Rios wrote, according to The Times. "I am not willing to be a source for any story in any capacity."
The newspaper said it told Rios she would be part of its article, and noted her interviews "were consistent with The Times's other reporting."

Alliance response must be credible if Russia uses nuclear weapons, former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:51:00 UTC
04:51:00 KST

Alliance response must be credible if Russia uses nuclear weapons, former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy says
Jim Stokes, a GLOBSEC expert and former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy (2023–2025), made the remarks in an interview with Ukrinform.
“In this hypothetical situation, if Russia uses nuclear weapons, NATO will have to respond... The response must be credible,” Stokes said.
He recalled NATO’s stated readiness to inflict damage far exceeding any potential gains. The response could involve nuclear weapons, conventional weapons, or a combination of both. The decision would be made at a later stage, as it would be unwise to reveal to an adversary where these red lines lie or exactly how a response might be formulated and carried out, the former NATO official emphasized.
Stokes said that in an emergency or during a crisis, the Alliance could make political decisions and implement them very quickly. He added that member states were also capable of acting independently and swiftly. The United States, the United Kingdom, and France could each independently employ their nuclear forces to deter aggression against the Alliance, not just a nuclear attack. Stokes described this as a major advantage for NATO.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and NATO’s designation of Russia as a threat to the Alliance, NATO has been adapting its nuclear deterrence posture, including by modernizing its nuclear forces. Exercises and preparations for a potential NATO nuclear operation demonstrate that the Alliance is capable of carrying one out effectively with its current capabilities and force posture, the former official said.
He noted that NATO aircraft could deliver free-fall nuclear bombs. Some advocate the option of launching missiles from sea-, land-, or air-based platforms. In Stokes’s view, all options should remain on the table.
As previously reported, British and French fighter jets conducted joint exercises over the Mediterranean for the first time in October, involving French nuclear forces and demonstrating deeper defense cooperation between the two countries amid tensions with Russia. In July 2025, the two countries agreed to deepen their cooperation on nuclear deterrence in response to growing threats to Europe and uncertainty over the role of the United States as an ally.

Ukraine Rolls Out Amphibious UGVs to Brave1 Market After 40-Km Combat Mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:49:31 UTC
04:49:31 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Rolls Out Amphibious UGVs to Brave1 Market After 40-Km Combat Mission
Ukraine has added a new category of amphibious unmanned ground vehicles to the Brave1 Market , allowing military units to order robotic systems capable of moving across both land and water, Ukraine’s Defence Ministry reported on October 28.
The ministry stated that three amphibious UGV models are already available on the platform, with additional systems expected to be added later. Military units will eventually be able to order them through Ukraine’s ePoints program .
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The deployment forms part of Ukraine’s growing use of unmanned ground systems for frontline logistics and other high-risk missions. By mid-August, Ukrainian UGVs had completed more than 100,000 missions in place of soldiers since the beginning of 2026.
Amphibious UGVs are designed for frontline logistics in areas where rivers, canals, wetlands, or damaged terrain can block conventional ground routes. The systems retain high mobility on land and can switch within seconds to moving through water, according to Ukraine’s Defence Ministry.
The ministry noted that Brave1 and the Defence Ministry have been developing the amphibious systems market to accelerate their deployment to Ukrainian units. Brave1 launched a dedicated grant program for amphibious UGVs in June 2026, while developers have continued refining the systems using feedback from frontline troops.
The technology has already been tested in combat. Soldiers from the Alter Ego unit of Ukraine’s 93rd Separate Mechanized Brigade recently completed what the ministry described as the world’s first combat logistics mission using an amphibious ground robot.
The vehicle traveled more than 40 kilometers across land and water before successfully delivering food and ammunition to Ukrainian positions.
Ukraine is also expanding unmanned aerial systems into battlefield casualty evacuation. UNITED24 Media previously reported that Ukrainian troops used the StarGate aerial CASEVAC drone to evacuate two seriously wounded soldiers in one week, including one mission covering nearly 60 kilometers round trip despite Russian GPS jamming.
