Israel deadlocked: Do the Arabs hold the key to defeating Netanyahu?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:48:26 UTC
04:48:26 KST

Netanyahu’s Israel deadlocked: Were the elections ‘stolen by the Arabs’?
Israel’s parliamentary elections are over, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been wounded, but not defeated. His battle to form a government and stay in power is just beginning.
The final results of the Israeli election won’t be known until Thursday, when Israel’s Central Election Committee (CEC) finishes tallying so-called ‘double envelope’ ballots cast by soldiers, diplomats living abroad, prisoners, and other voters unable to make it to polling stations on election day.
However, with more than 85% of votes counted as of Wednesday evening, a picture of political deadlock is becoming clearer, and neither Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc, nor the center-left to center-right bloc of his opponents, are on track to win a majority in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset. Either bloc must secure 61 out of 120 Knesset seats to form a government.
What are the results of the Israeli election?
Netanyahu’s Likud remains Israel’s largest political party, and is projected to win 26 seats, down from 32 in 2022.
Yashar, led by Netanyahu’s chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is in second place with 21 seats.
Both politicians lead large and potentially fractious blocs. Together with four far-right and religious parties – Otzma Yehudit, United Torah Judaism, Shas, and Religious Zionism, Netanyahu’s bloc controls 53 seats, ten short of a majority.
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc comprises Yashar, former Prime Ministers’ Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s B’Yachad party, Yair Golan’s Democrats, and Yisrael Beytenu, a right-wing party led by former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman. Together, this bloc controls 48 seats.
What about the Arabs?
Israel’s two main Arab parties, Yousef Jabareen’s Joint List and Mansour Abbas’ Ra’am, have almost doubled their representation in the Knesset. Driven by anger over Netanyahu’s war on Gaza and his appointment of overt Jewish supremacists to cabinet positions, voters in Arab-majority districts turned out in record numbers to award the Joint List and Ra’am 12 and seven seats respectively, up from a combined ten seats in 2022.
With a combined 19 seats, the Arab parties could play the role of kingmakers when coalition talks begin. However, they would likely find few allies within either Jewish-led bloc.
Will Netanyahu work with the Arabs?
Netanyahu has explicitly ruled out cooperation with either Arab party, both of which have condemned his war on Gaza. “It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel and to establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties,” he said after polls closed on Tuesday.
In the run up to the vote, the Israeli prime minister framed the election as a choice between “Me and [US President Donald] Trump, or Eisenkot and Abbas,” and accused his opponents of plotting to recognize a Palestinian state after entering a government with the Arabs.
In a statement on Wednesday, Netanyahu claimed that “the elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties,” and that Likud had uncovered evidence of vote-buying, “threats and violence against polling station members,” and repeat voting in Arab districts. The PM called on police and Israel’s Shin Bet intelligence agency to conduct a “thorough investigation” into his claims.
Eisenkot’s party warned on Tuesday that Netanyahu would attempt to delegitimize the election. “Netanyahu is panicking and has begun making up stories and claiming that the election is being stolen,” Yashar said in a statement. “This is no accident. He is already laying the groundwork to challenge the election results.”
What about the opposition?
Eisenkot, Liberman, and Bennett have all ruled out cooperation with the Arabs, with Eisenkot declaring on election night that he intends to form “a Zionist government.” Democrats leader Yair Golan, on the other hand, has called on the anti-Netanyahu bloc to reach out to Ra’am and the Joint List for the sake of ousting Netanyau. Partnership with the two Arab parties would give the bloc 65 seats – a clear majority.
“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid,” he wrote on social media on Wednesday morning. “We have a majority. We have responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel’s Arab citizens.”
Abbas has said that he is willing to enter government with the anti-Netanyahu bloc, while Jabareen has said that his Joint List lawmakers would “pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government” by refusing to oppose a minority government in exchange for some concessions on Palestine and funding for Arab communities.
Who will form a government in Israel?
Israeli President Isaac Herzog will ultimately decide which political leader stands the best chance of forming a stable government, and task them with forming a coalition. Herzog has called on all parties to enter negotiations “with an open mind.” As the political horse-trading begins, three potential outcomes are laid out below:
Netanyahu wins back the right
Netanyahu could secure a majority by striking a deal with Bennett and Liberman to peel B’Yachad away from the opposition bloc. Both are right-wingers, but both campaigned on ousting Netanyahu and forcing military conscription on Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Haredi communities. In this case,, Netanyahu would likely lose the backing of the two ultra-Orthodox parties in his coalition, United Torah Judaism and Shas.
Swapping these parties for B’Yachad would leave Netanyahu’s bloc even further away from a majority, meaning one side would have to compromise on their core campaign promises to make this arrangement work.
Eisenkot joins the Arabs
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc could quickly secure a majority and form a government, but only if he, Bennett, and Liberman decide that taking power is worth cooperating with, or securing the abstention of, the Arab parties.
Doing so would carry political consequences for everyone involved. At a time when public support for a two-state solution has collapsed and fewer Israelis than ever believe that they “cannot coexist peacefully” with their Palestinian neighbors, Eisenkot, Bennett, and Liberman would risk alienating their right-wing voters.
Likewise, Arab voters could see any partnership with the Israeli-right as a betrayal by the Joint List and Ra’am. Earlier this week, Joint List parliamentary leader Ahmad Tibi alluded to this fear, telling Türkiye’s Anadolu news agency that he does not want his party “to be responsible for incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque, a war in Gaza, the continuation of Jewish terrorism and settlement activity, or house demolitions.”
Entering a government with Eisenkot and the right-wing opposition would make the Joint List “collectively responsible” for these crimes, he explained.
Could a grand Zionist coalition emerge in Israel?
A unity government – in which Netanyahu and Eisenkot rotate the premiership with the support of Bennett and Liberman – may seem like an obvious solution for everyone involved. Likud, Yashar, B’Yachad, and Yisrael Beytenu are all aligned on security matters, and entering a grand coalition would allow Netanyahu to cast off his ultra-Orthodox and far-right partners, while Eisenkot could sever ties with the Democrats and Arabs.
Such an arrangement is not without precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz – a centrist ex-general – reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
However, the Netanyahu/Gantz coalition fell apart in less than a year, at a less polarized time in Israeli politics. This time around, all of Netanyahu’s opponents have focused their campaigns around deposing the prime minister, with Eisenkot accusing him of corruption, incompetence, and ignoring “dozens of warnings” prior to Hamas’ attack on Israel in 2023.
“I unequivocally pledge that I will not serve under Netanyahu in a rotation agreement. Period,” Eisenkot told Radio 103 last week. “If that were to happen, you would see me resign an hour later.” Eisenkot did not explicitly rule out working with Likud, if Netanyahu were to retire.
The alternative for Israel: deadlock and elections
Should none of these arrangements work, Israel could be thrust into another election cycle. Repeat elections and failed coalition talks were a leitmotif in Israeli politics until the October 7 attack and subsequent wars ushered in a period of relative stability: in the four years before 2022, Israel went through five elections.
Herzog has made it clear that he wants to avoid such an outcome. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said on Tuesday. However, unless Israel’s main parties can find some kind of compromise, another election may be inevitable.

Israeli firm turned Starlink traffic into espionage tool across 105 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:31:40 UTC
04:31:40 KST

Israeli firm turned Starlink traffic into espionage tool across 105 countries
Netanyahu loses his majority, Eisenkot cannot win one, and the wars go on
TEHRAN — Recent disclosures from digital defense watchdogs have exposed an obscure Tel Aviv-registered advertising company, Discover-Tech, running aggressive online ad campaigns designed to geolocate and track users of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network across more than 100 countries.
Investigative research by TrendAI, a division of Tokyo-based Trend Micro, revealed that Discover-Tech became the dominant global bidder for ad space displayed to Starlink terminals, according to a Reuters report on Oct. 27.
Operating under the internal threat codenamed "Shadow-Earth-79," the Israeli firm captured an implausibly high share of ad auctions in restricted or conflict-heavy jurisdictions including Syria, Libya, Yemen, South Sudan, and Venezuela.
By harvesting the metadata embedded in real-time bidding requests, Discover-Tech systematically turned routine browser traffic into an active intelligence pipeline.
From ad impressions to silent infiltration
Programmatic ad auctions rely on instant exchanges of telemetry. Every time an advertisement loads on a web page or mobile application, a bid request transmits the user's IP address, device model, software configuration, autonomous system number, and exact location parameters to participating ad networks.
Discover-Tech leveraged this routine infrastructure to build a comprehensive tracking map.
TrendAI concluded that the firm’s bidding behavior reflected a dedicated tracking operation rather than commercial marketing, noting that legitimate Western advertising demand in heavily sanctioned states is virtually non-existent.
On observed Starlink connections, Discover-Tech accounted for nearly 13 percent of winning ad bids worldwide.
The surveillance mechanism went far beyond passive location mapping. Concurrent technical investigations by Canada’s Citizen Lab and ad-security firm Confiant exposed a sophisticated exploitation vector named "AdFection."
Discover-Tech's proprietary ad platform served as a conduit, connecting mainstream advertising exchanges directly to mercenary spyware operators. When a targeted device loaded a background advertisement, Discover-Tech servers screened the incoming telemetry.
High-value targets were served malicious JavaScript that delivered zero-click attack payloads without requiring any user interaction, while ordinary users received empty responses.
Citizen Lab confirmed with high confidence that at least 45 devices belonging to news personnel at Al Jazeera were targeted with Candiru spyware through this ad-driven vector.
Starlink and the military-industrial infrastructure
The focus on Starlink underscores how low-Earth-orbit satellite constellations have become central to Western military strategy and intelligence operations.
SpaceX's Starlink network bypasses land-based telecommunications gateways, routing data through satellite links to circumvent national regulatory frameworks and local internet blocks.
The U.S. Department of "War" and NATO forces have integrated Starlink and its military-grade derivative, Starshield, into frontline combat operations. In Ukraine, the technology provides primary battlefield command architecture, directing artillery, facilitating real-time satellite coordination, and guiding long-range combat drones.
This deep integration into Western military operations makes Starlink terminals prime targets for intelligence agencies.
Intelligence outfits seek to identify, geolocate, and compromise satellite terminals operating inside sensitive sovereign territory.
Israeli-owned firms were already pitching commercial clients on specialized methodologies to map and deanonymize Starlink subscribers by exploiting commercial ad data.
The Discover-Tech operation confirms that these theoretical pitches were already operationalized at a global scale, turning satellite terminals into beacons for military intelligence gathering.
The broader ecosystem of Israeli cyber warfare
Discover-Tech represents the latest evolution of a commercial cyber-arms ecosystem cultivated by the Israeli regime.
For decades, intelligence entities such as Unit 8200 and Mossad have maintained an institutional pipeline into private surveillance vendors, enabling former Israeli operatives to commercialize state-funded hacking techniques.
Discover-Tech’s corporate history shows direct ties to veteran surveillance executives, including past directors associated with Circles, an affiliate of NSO Group, and Senpai Technologies, linked to the Intellexa consortium.
This ecosystem includes a wide network of offensive vendors. NSO Group gained global infamy through its Pegasus software, which infected the phones of diplomats, political opponents, and human rights defenders.
Candiru, operating under various corporate names such as Saito Tech and Integrity Labs, specialized in zero-click desktop compromises. Paragon Solutions markets its Graphite interception software, while Intellexa and Cytrox developed the Predator spyware suite.
Other key players include Cognyte, Cytrox, Cellebrite, and Black Cube, the private intelligence agency staffed by former Israeli operatives specializing in deception and corporate espionage.
These entities routinely establish international shell companies across Europe to bypass nominal export restrictions and maintain access to global markets.
Industry self-censorship and structural vulnerability
Despite the scale of Discover-Tech’s operations, accountability remains hindered by self-censorship within the commercial security sector.
TrendAI initially omitted Discover-Tech’s name from its public report, opting instead for the "Shadow-Earth-79" alias after corporate executives raised legal concerns.
This practice allows offensive operators to evade immediate platform bans and legal scrutiny.
Following the public identification by Citizen Lab and news outlets, major tech platforms including Google, Comcast's Beeswax, Vungle, and Eskimi cut off Discover-Tech’s access, while IAB Europe suspended the firm from its approved vendor list.
Internal inquiries were also launched by a major U.S. technology corporation and an international organization to evaluate potential employee targeting.
These platform removals disrupt specific operational routes, but the underlying vulnerability remains unaddressed.
Discover-Tech operated inside approved industry registries for years, utilizing standard European data privacy frameworks to collect targeting parameters.
As long as commercial advertising exchanges permit real-time data harvesting, state-aligned surveillance contractors will continue to use programmatic ad bidding as an unregulated, low-cost vector for global espionage.

M5.1 earthquake strikes China
                  00:15, 29 October 2026
                
A magnitude 5.1 earthquake hit northwestern China on the evening of October 28, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Kazakhstan National Data Center.
The underground tremors were recorded at 8:40 p.m. Astana time (15:40 GMT), according to data from the Institute of Geophysical Research of Kazakhstan's National Nuclear Center.
The epicenter was located at coordinates 44.39°N latitude and 82.60°E longitude.
The earthquake had an mpv magnitude of 5.1 and an energy class rating of K=11.9.
Earlier, a magnitude 4.7 earthquake struck the border area between Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan on October 28.

Tokayev says Türkiye among Kazakhstan’s five largest trading partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Tokayev says Türkiye among Kazakhstan’s five largest trading partners
The meeting between the Presidents of Kazakhstan and Türkiye continued with the participation of members of the official delegations of the two countries, Qazinform News Agency cites Akorda.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev described the meeting as deeply symbolic, as it was being held on the eve of the Republic Day of Türkiye, and congratulated President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and the brotherly Turkish people on this significant national holiday.
“Under your wise leadership, Türkiye is successfully implementing large-scale reforms. The country is developing dynamically, pursuing political and economic modernization. Türkiye’s position on the international stage continues to grow stronger year by year. You are recognized as one of the world’s most influential leaders. Your principled and resolute political course, as well as your tireless efforts to uphold peace and justice, have earned global recognition. I am confident that the standing of the Turkish people will continue to grow. Kazakhstan unwaveringly supports Türkiye and sincerely rejoices in all the achievements of the brotherly Turkish people,” the President of Kazakhstan said.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev emphasized that he attaches particular importance to expanding cooperation with Türkiye.
“Relations between Kazakhstan and Türkiye have deep historical roots. We are united by our shared history and language, as well as similar traditions. Political interaction between our states rests on a solid foundation of mutual trust and enduring friendship. There are no contradictions or disagreements between us. Our countries consistently support each other both bilaterally and within international organizations. Trade and economic ties continue to expand steadily. Türkiye is one of Kazakhstan’s five largest trading partners. Furthermore, Türkiye ranks among the ten largest investors in our country, having made substantial investments in Kazakhstan’s economy. Many major Turkish companies operate successfully in Kazakhstan. We stand ready to provide comprehensive support to our Turkish partners and create favorable conditions for their businesses,” the Head of State said.
According to Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s state visit to Kazakhstan in May this year was highly productive and resulted in a number of important agreements. The sixth meeting of the High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council between the two countries was held. Major projects were launched in trade and economic cooperation, investment, and cultural and humanitarian affairs. Kazakhstan-Türkiye relations have reached the level of eternal friendship and enhanced strategic partnership.
“The steady development of our bilateral partnership serves our common interests. Tomorrow, we will attend the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States together. The COP31 Climate Summit will be held in Antalya in the near future, and I intend to participate. These events will undoubtedly give fresh impetus to strengthening our bilateral and multifaceted ties,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev noted.
In turn, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan congratulated the Head of State and the brotherly people of Kazakhstan on the recent Republic Day.
The Turkish President noted that a presentation of the book The Phenomenon of a Qurultay, dedicated to the history of Kazakh statehood, had recently been held in Ankara. In addition, the book Nauryz – A Common Heritage of the Turkic World, which comprehensively explores the history and significance of the holiday, has been translated into Kazakh.
“During my visit to Astana in May this year, we signed a number of important documents, including the Declaration on Eternal Friendship and Enhanced Strategic Partnership. We intend to reinforce our cooperation with practical steps at the next meeting of the Strategic Cooperation Council. We aim to increase bilateral trade to 15 billion US dollars and intensify the investment dimension of our relations,” the Turkish president said.
During the talks, the two sides also discussed prospects for cooperation in transport and logistics, energy, artificial intelligence, agriculture, and the defense industry, as well as ways to strengthen cultural and humanitarian ties.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had held restricted-format talks.

92-year-old US judge handling Nicolas Maduro case dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

92-year-old US judge handling Nicolas Maduro case dies
NEW YORK – Alvin Hellerstein, the US judge overseeing the case against deposed Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, has died aged 92, an official confirmed on Oct 28.
As he was one of the oldest US federal judges, questions had been raised about whether he was the right justice to preside over what could be a prolonged trial for Maduro on drug trafficking charges.
Hellerstein’s lengthy career included overseeing the civil cases arising from Al-Qaeda’s Sept 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on New York and Washington, often rejecting deals he saw as unfair to complainants.
His death was confirmed to AFP by an official at the United States District Court, Southern District of New York, where he presided.
A court filing showed the case has been reassigned to Analisa Torres, born in 1959.
Hellerstein also tangled with Donald Trump, rejecting a request by the US President to have his New York hush money case moved to federal court.
In 2025, he blocked the Trump administration from deporting alleged Venezuelan gang members without a court hearing.
In a noteworthy 2015 ruling, Hellerstein ordered the US government to release a trove of photos depicting abuse of detainees in Iraq and Afghanistan.
He also presided over a trial in 2025 in which a jury found that French banking giant BNP Paribas’ work in Sudan had helped prop up the regime of former ruler Omar al-Bashir, awarding US$20.75 million (S$26.5 million) in damages to three plaintiffs from Sudan.
For over a decade, Hellerstein handled the sprawling drug trafficking case linked to Maduro that has already seen the conviction of Venezuela’s former intelligence chief, Hugo Armando Carvajal.
Maduro was seized by US forces in January, in a military raid on his compound in Venezuela.
A graduate of Columbia University law school, Hellerstein served as a lawyer in the US Army from 1957 to 1960 before entering private practice.
He was nominated by then US President Bill Clinton in 1998 to be a district court judge for the Southern District of New York. AFP

Two Syrian Defense Ministry personnel were shot dead Wednesday by unidentified gunmen in Al-Foua, state media reported.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported the deaths in the town in the northeastern countryside of Idlib province in northwestern Syria without providing details about the identities of the victims or the circumstances of the shooting. It did not identify those responsible.
The Defense Ministry previously reported the deaths of soldiers in separate shootings by unidentified assailants in eastern Syria earlier this month.
A soldier was killed Oct. 19 in an attack in Al-Baghouz in the eastern countryside of Deir ez-Zor, the Alikhbaria television channel reported, citing a source in the ministry’s Media and Communication Department.
The ministry announced on Oct. 10 that another soldier had died of wounds sustained when unidentified gunmen opened fire in the town of Buqrus in eastern rural Deir ez-Zor on the evening of Oct. 6, according to the channel.

Costa Rica drops bid to join Pacific trade pact, sacks trade minister
- Costa Rica has withdrawn its bid to join the CPTPP after protests from producer groups, especially farmers, over the secretive deal.
- President Laura Fernandez said trade minister Indiana Trejos was sacked for “lack of transparency” after helping with talks under the previous government.
- Costa Rica had applied in 2022, held over 100 meetings, and was invited in November 2024, but the government now says almost no one knows what the pact entails.
AI generated
SAN JOSE - Costa Rica's government has withdrawn its bid to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a major trans-Pacific trade pact, and dismissed its foreign trade minister, president Laura Fernandez said on Oct 28.
Fernandez said the removal of foreign trade minister Indiana Trejos, who had participated in the negotiations as deputy minister during the previous administration, was due to lack of transparency. The president did not say who is due to replace Trejos.
The decision to scrap the application comes after protests from Costa Rica's producer groups, especially from the agriculture sector.
The CPTPP is a free trade bloc of 12 nations across the Americas, Asia, Oceania and Europe that accounts for nearly 15% of global gross domestic product.
“Although it might seem like an excellent opportunity, its full content was declared secret by the negotiators to the point that almost no one knows what it entails,” Fernandez said in a video posted on social media.
Costa Rica submitted a request to join the CPTPP in 2022 and held more than 100 high-level meetings to build consensus among members. In November 2024 the bloc formally invited the Central American country form part of the CPTPP.
Since then, Costa Rica has reviewed its regulations against the agreement's rules and negotiated market access for goods and services.
The CPTPP went into effect in 2018 as an offshoot of the Trans-Pacific Partnership, following the United States' departure from that proposed trade bloc. REUTERS

Ukraine Develops Armored Evacuation Module for Murakha UGV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:24:53 UTC
04:24:53 KST

Ukrainian company Robotic Complexes is developing a specialized CASEEVAK module for the Murakha unmanned ground vehicle (UGV).
The project is designed to protect wounded military personnel during transport and provide communications and monitoring of their condition, the company told Militarnyi.
Unlike conventional cargo UGVs, the new system features an armored capsule made of 3.5 mm Armox 500T steel with an internal HDPE 1000 lining.
The capsule is equipped with ventilation, heating and lighting systems, as well as a first-aid kit. Side and rear doors allow the wounded to be loaded from any side and provide access to them during evacuation.
A camera with day and night channels and two-way audio communication are installed inside to monitor the occupant’s condition.
The system is controlled through ELRS, LTE, Starlink or fiber-optic communication links. If the capsule is detached from the main platform, it retains two independent communication channels.
The developers are currently working to integrate vital-sign monitoring systems. This will allow medical personnel to receive information about the casualty’s condition while the vehicle is moving.
The platform’s protection is supplemented by passive counter-drone measures, net launchers and electronic warfare systems. An electric powertrain has been installed to reduce the vehicle’s signature.
The platform has two electric motors with a combined torque of 1,600 N·m and a 35 kWh battery pack. Its range is up to 80 km.
Company specialists have already conducted ballistic tests of the armor steel at a distance of 50 meters using various calibers. Development of a slat armor system to protect against FPV drones is also underway.
Militarnyi previously reported that in October 2025, Ukrainian forces began using Murakha-Mini ground drones to support logistics near the front line.
The UGVs help deliver equipment, food and other supplies.

Putin tells African leaders Moscow will not pursue ‘neo-colonialism’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:01:46 UTC
04:01:46 KST

Putin tells African leaders Moscow will not pursue ‘neo-colonialism’
Speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit, Putin frames Russia as an alternative partner to former colonial powers.
President Vladimir Putin has told African leaders visiting Moscow that Russia does not engage in “neo-colonial exploitation” of the continent, unlike former colonial powers.
Speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on Wednesday, Putin said the West is still trying to exploit the continent’s resources and uses debt to hold back development.
“Africa is increasingly asserting itself as one of the key players in the global economy and politics. However, the emergence of a multipolar world is, of course, no easy task; it faces resistance from countries that are not prepared to accept this reality,” Putin told the summit.
Russian-backed government forces in a broad swath of North Africa are fighting armed rebellions as many countries in the region emerge from military coups that have shaken regional security.
Putin criticised “active attempts by Western countries” to drive Africans back into debt and to force them to accept much-needed financial resources on predatory terms, which he said slowed their long-term development.
“Our business does not engage in the predatory, neo-colonial exploitation of natural and human resources, but rather expands the processing of raw materials locally, thereby creating new jobs and generating tax revenue,” said Putin.
Disruptions to agriculture
Putin told delegations from 48 African countries, including 22 represented by their heads of state, that Russia was prepared to expand the geographical reach of agricultural product shipments.
Russia had supplied 13 million metric tonnes of agricultural products to Africa in the first nine months of this year alone, he added.
The remarks come as attacks in the Black Sea continue to disrupt exports of grain from both Russia and Ukraine, while the United States-Israel war on Iran has interrupted global fertiliser supplies.
Putin is due to hold one-on-one talks with individual African leaders who are attending on topics ranging from trade to security, grain supplies and arms deals.
The summit is expected to end with a final declaration on deepening cooperation between Russia and African nations.

Ground crews still excluded from nuclear test medal
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:00:08 GMT
04:00:08 KST

There are no plans to extend the Nuclear Test Medal to personnel of 543 and 27 Squadrons who recovered, washed, decontaminated and maintained aircraft used for nuclear cloud sampling between 1966 and 1980, because they did not deploy from the United Kingdom, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Lord Bourne of Aberystwyth, the Conservative peer, asked what progress has been made on extending eligibility to those personnel, in light of representations from nuclear test veterans involved in intelligence gathering of foreign nations’ atmospheric tests.
Lord Coaker, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Nuclear Test Medal (NTM) eligibility has been broadened to include UK personnel who deployed in support of United States atmospheric nuclear tests, and UK personnel who were deployed from the UK in support of operations to monitor atmospheric nuclear tests conducted by France and China up to 1974 and 1980 respectively.
“Ministry of Defence officials will continue to keep the eligibility criteria under review to ensure that they are as comprehensive and inclusive as they can be given the current boundaries. There are no current plans to expand the criteria to include personnel who did not deploy from the UK in support of either UK or other nations atmospheric testing.
“Any formal proposal for the expansion of the NTM eligibility criteria would need to be endorsed by the Committee on the Grant of Honours, Decorations and Medals (HD Committee) and approved by His Majesty The King.”
Everything turns on deployment, because aircrew flown out to sample the clouds produced by French and Chinese tests qualify, while the people who met those aircraft on return and handled contaminated airframes do not, because they stayed at their home station.
Number 543 Squadron flew the Victor B2(SR) in the strategic reconnaissance role until 1974, and 27 Squadron took on the maritime radar reconnaissance and air sampling task with the Vulcan B2(MRR) thereafter. The Nuclear Test Medal was instituted in 2022 for veterans and civilian staff who took part in Britain’s atmospheric testing programme, after decades of campaigning.

Fed keeps interest rates steady despite 'high inflation' owing to US war on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:00:01 UTC
04:00:01 KST

The US Federal Reserve has held interest rates steady, in line with market expectations, days ahead of crucial midterm elections where surging inflation has been a key issue.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, meanwhile, said on Wednesday that political considerations had no bearing on the central bank’s decision.
"Politics played no role in the decision. I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics. I didn't hear a reference to politics, elections, what's happening in the next week," the Fed official said in a press conference.
The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 to 4.00 percent, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.
"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's two percent goal," the Fed said in a statement announcing its decision.
Two members of the committee, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, calling instead for an immediate 0.25-percentage-point rate hike.
The central bank has missed its long-term two-percent target for inflation for more than five years, with households and businesses battered by sustained price increases.
US war on Iran
US war on Iran, launched in late February, has sent energy prices skyrocketing and fuelled domestic inflation, alongside his wide-ranging tariff policies.
Prices have also been driven by an investment boom in artificial intelligence (AI) technology and the build-out of huge data centres to support it.
The decision comes six days ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party is seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from Trump's Republicans.
President Donald Trump's handling of the economy has been a key issue throughout the campaign, with working-class households across the country struggling to make ends meet despite largely stable overall economic growth.
US consumer inflation came in hotter than expected in September, clocking in at 3.7 percent, edging back towards a three-year high established in May.
Still, key policymakers at the Fed — including Warsh — have signaled that they did not see an urgency to raise rates again immediately.
On Wednesday, the Fed said economic activity in the United States was expanding at a "strong" pace, upgrading its language from the FOMC meeting six weeks prior.

Araghchi briefs cabinet on Tehran security summit, warns of risks to global energy markets
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has briefed the cabinet on the latest diplomatic developments, with a focus on a quadrilateral meeting in Tehran involving Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, emphasizing the need for regional cooperation to safeguard security, prevent escalation and protect national sovereignty.
Araghchi presented his report at Wednesday’s cabinet meeting, chaired by President Masoud Pezeshkian, outlining recent diplomatic consultations on regional and international affairs, including discussions with senior officials from neighboring and regional countries.
The report covered meetings involving a Qatari delegation, as well as consultations with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council; Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defense minister; Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of army staff; and Ibrahim Kalin, head of Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization.
According to the report, participants in the four-way discussions stressed the importance of strengthening regional cooperation, developing joint security mechanisms and preventing the further escalation of tensions and conflicts.
They also warned against the 'Israeli regime’s destabilizing policies,' including efforts to weaken regional states, expand military aggression, undermine governments and draw the United States into regional conflicts.
The senior officials underscored the need for regional countries to remain vigilant against developments that could fuel tensions and to deepen cooperation in defence of their sovereignty, stability and territorial integrity.
Regional ownership of security
In a message posted on Instagram following the Tehran meeting, Araghchi described the talks as a valuable opportunity to advance dialogue on regional peace and security and address shared threats and challenges. He said the agreement to continue consultations represented an important step forward.
Turning dialogue into lasting cooperation, the foreign minister stressed, would require agreement on common principles, confidence-building, mutual respect for national sovereignty and practical commitments.
Iran’s position, he said, was that sustainable regional security must be achieved through the participation of regional countries, without the military presence or interference of powers from outside the region.
“This approach is based on the responsibility of regional countries to determine their own destiny,” Araghchi wrote.
He also emphasized the need to counter the Israeli regime’s acts of aggression and destabilization, describing this as essential to protecting countries’ independence and sovereignty and preventing the spread of war.
Instagram message concluded with Iran’s diplomatic motto: “Our Neighbors, Our Priority.”
Energy diplomacy and Persian Gulf security
Araghchi also highlighted the energy dimension of Iran’s recent diplomatic engagements, saying the country’s energy diplomacy had advanced during the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow, where discussions addressed global gas markets and energy security.
He warned that any military adventurism initiated by Israel in the Persian Gulf could have potentially devastating consequences for international energy markets, making the prospect a serious concern for both gas-producing countries and consumers.
The foreign minister’s remarks underscored the connection between regional stability and global energy security, as well as the importance of diplomatic coordination among regional states in preventing conflicts that could disrupt international markets.

Burç Eruygur, Elena Teslova
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday invited African airlines to launch flights to Russia.
Speaking at the plenary session of the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum in Moscow, Putin said Russia was ready to expand cooperation with African countries across trade, energy, pharmaceuticals, and transport.
"We also offer our African partners comprehensive solutions for building reliable logistics routes that will have a direct impact on the growth of trade and investment," he said. "Naturally, we invite African airlines to begin flights to the Russian Federation."
In addition, Russia could provide services in design, construction, and modernization of railways and roads, sea routes, transport hubs, and equip them with digital management, tracking, and customs declaration systems, he said.
Trade between Russia and Africa could exceed $50 billion in the near future, while Russia was involved in more than 30 prospective energy projects across 16 African countries, Putin added.
"Russian-African trade turnover exceeded $27 billion last year. In 2022, by the way, it was only $18 (billion). That's significant growth. True, of course, even that is not enough. I am convinced that we are capable of increasing this figure at least twofold in the very near future and definitely surpassing the $50 billion mark," he noted.
Russia also plans to localize the production of medicines and vaccines in Africa and establish laboratories and diagnostic centers, he said.
The Russian president described the growing influence of African countries on the international stage as part of a broader shift toward a more equitable multipolar world, in which the voices of the majority are increasingly heard.
Putin said Russia and African nations had jointly helped lay the foundations for a fairer international order.
The Russian leader recalled Moscow’s historical support for African liberation movements, economic development, and the formation of national armed forces.
The Russian president criticized Western efforts to push African countries into a “debt trap,” describing tariff wars and sanctions as “tools of neocolonialism.”
He also called for changes to the functioning of the IMF and the World Bank, saying their work should be reoriented toward the needs of developing economies.
The forum is held amid a two-day Russia-Africa summit, the third such summit since 2019, for which many African leaders arrived in Moscow.
Later Wednesday, Putin also met with leaders of Africa's regional organizations at the Kremlin and visited an exhibition held within the framework of the summit.

Inflation tracker: See how the price of everything has changed
By Simon Elvery, Jessica Riga and Madi Chwasta
Posted , updated 
If it feels like (almost) everything is getting more expensive, that's because it is.
Inflation has jumped, putting Australians on alert for another interest rate rise.
The consumer price index rose by 4.3 per cent in the past year, well above the Reserve Bank of Australia's target of 2 to 3 per cent.
Below, we've tracked prices across all kinds of goods and services, including food, electricity, travel and housing.
- You'll notice an increase in automotive fuel. It's higher than a year ago due to the Iran war and has surged in recent months due to the fuel excise cut being ended on August 2.
- There has been a decent rise in the price of games, toys and hobbies as the escalating cost of computer parts has been passed on to consumers.
- Electricity has also gone up in the past year, linked to the ending of various government subsidies that were introduced to help cover soaring power costs mostly caused by the war in Ukraine.

- The monthly CPI series is relatively new and only available for all categories since April 2024, so the figures displayed when "Since COVID" is selected use quarterly CPI data from the same September 2026 ABS release.

Turkic nations formalize new audit body TURKSAI in Antalya

Turkic nations formalize new audit body TURKSAI in Antalya
The Charter of the newly established Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions of the Member States of the Organization of Turkic States (TURKSAI) has been signed in Antalya, Türkiye, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Kazakhstan's Supreme Audit Chamber.
At the signing ceremony, the Kazakhstan delegation was led by Alikhan Smailov, Chairman of the Supreme Audit Chamber.
The decision to create TURKSAI was adopted in November 2025 in Istanbul at a meeting of supreme audit heads from OTS Member States — Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Türkiye, and Uzbekistan.
The new organization is designed to elevate audit cooperation across the Turkic world to a new level. It will facilitate sharing knowledge and expertise, enhancing audit practices, conducting joint audits, and implementing collaborative research projects
Practical cooperation under the umbrella of TURKSAI is already underway. Prior to the signing, audit professionals from across the region completed a knowledge exchange program on Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It covered the entire SDG audit lifecycle, from topic selection and audit question formulation to drafting recommendations and follow-up monitoring.
Seven auditors from the Supreme Audit Chamber participated in the program. The key takeaways will inform the planning and execution of future SDG audits in Kazakhstan.
Addressing the ceremony, Alikhan Smailov thanked Metin Yener, President of the Turkish Court of Accounts, for warm hospitality and organizing the events. He noted that formalizing the new body was the logical outcome of decisions adopted nearly a year ago in Istanbul.
"Today, we cement our agreements with a foundational document that defines the principles, scope, and operational procedures of TURKSAI," Smailov said. "The organization holds significant potential for practical cooperation. I am confident that signing this charter will serve as a reliable foundation for long-term partnership."
The Chairman of Kazakhstan's Supreme Audit Chamber highlighted that rapidly evolving public finances alongside emerging challenges demand upgraded audit methods and higher standards of public asset management.
"This cooperation, rooted in friendship, trust, solidarity, and the spirit of Turkic brotherhood, will allow our supreme audit institutions to jointly respond to modern challenges and make a meaningful contribution to the development of our states," he emphasized.
Following the ceremony, the delegation heads attended a symposium on the Sustainable Development Goals, focusing on the role of public auditing in advancing SDG targets and leveraging audit outcomes to improve public policy.
As reported earlier, Kazakhstan attaches importance to developing comprehensive cooperation with Türkiye and strengthening ties within the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), with the integration of the Turkic world among the country’s key foreign policy priorities, Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi said in an interview with Anadolu.

How do Israeli election results impact timing of possible new Iran war? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:38:46 UTC
03:38:46 KST

The Israeli election results seem to grant Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a better showing than expected. But they also clearly leave his bloc in the minority with no way to avoid new elections without cutting a deal with Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot.
How do those results impact a possible new conflict with Iran?
In recent weeks, Netanyahu was seriously considering renewing the conflict with Iran.
It seems that a mix of opposition by US President Donald Trump and IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir prevented Netanyahu from doing so, although it is also possible with the hard-to-pin-down prime minister that he just wanted Tehran to think he might attack to deter it from doing anything provocative.
But Zamir’s opposition was only to an attack before Israeli elections were held, and Trump’s opposition was only to an attack before the US midterm elections on November 3.
In fact, Trump has made numerous rumblings about resuming strikes on Iran soon after the US midterm elections, and in his endorsement of Netanyahu, he made reference to wanting Israel involved again as well.
If Eisenkot had won the battle of the blocs over Netanyahu, as forecast by the polls, he might have been able to start to form a government before the US midterm elections.
In such a scenario, it is doubtful that Netanyahu could have ordered a new attack against Iran.
As matters now stand, however, one of Eisenkot’s allies, Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman, will not even start serious talks about forming a government before Friday, when the final vote results are in.
At that point, Liberman must make the excruciating decision of breaking a promise: either making a deal with the Arab parties, making a deal with Netanyahu, or going to a second round of elections.
Even if Liberman moves toward forming a new government, it would just start complex negotiations about what each side would need to do to pave the way to a partnership.
Once there would be agreement on that, there is a whole separate negotiation on who gets what ministries and other jobs.
All of these issues are likely to take more than the four days between Friday and the US midterm elections, given that they usually take weeks or even months.
This means that Netanyahu will likely have the freedom to attack Iran if Trump wants to or would not stop him.
Zamir is in favor of attacking Iran under two conditions: The first has been and remains if Iran was either about to actually strike Israel; and the second was and is if Trump restarted the war first, and Israel had full backing offensively and defensively from the US for engaging in another round of conflict.
Generally, Zamir’s instinct has been that he is ready to strike Iran if it starts recovering its threat capabilities too fast, which it has not yet done, or if such a strike would be part of a well-thought-out and considered strategy to finally push Tehran into making key nuclear concessions to the US.
He was against attacking before the election so as not to undermine Election Day voting by a potential Iranian ballistic-missile counterstrike and to avoid the cloud of impropriety that an attack leading into the election might have been carried out to help Netanyahu’s chances.
Netanyahu's main obstacle would be Trump
Post-election, there is no reason to bar an attack, although Zamir also is not rushing toward an attack, given that he does not view Tehran as having gotten much closer to any growing substantial nuclear or ballistic-missile threat.
To be sure, both issues remain threats, but both have been put off by some period of years due to US-Israeli airstrikes in June 2025 and early 2026.
This means that Netanyahu’s main obstacle would be Trump.
Trump did not want to attack leading into the midterms because the Iran war is already dragging him and the Republic Party down in the polls. But post-midterms, and with him unable to run for a third term, he will be unrestrained and could follow his whim to hit Iran again.
Why might he still not?
His top advisers have been and are mostly against a return to war, and while some think a few days of war might loosen Iran up some, others think Iran’s refusal to crack since February has shown a few more intense days will not sway them either.
So, he may have little to gain, and some of his advisers have also warned that Tehran has shown it is willing to keep firing after a US ceasefire, meaning the conflict might last longer than a few days even if Trump wants to stop.
This could lead Trump to walk away from the price tag of another round and continue his long-term attempt to slowly wear down Iran economically.
In fact, this series of Trump’s dizzying switches from economic pressure to a sudden threat to go to war, to backing down back into economic pressure, happened in August, earlier in October, and at other times.
These inconsistent switches probably have also undermined the viability of his threat in the eyes of the Iranians.
Another possibility is that the Iranians finally get scared by his latest threat of force and offer a real deal on the nuclear issue. That would surely lead to a delay of an Iran attack.
But if Trump ultimately favors attacking, it could not come at a better time for Netanyahu.
If Netanyahu is involved with attacking Iran – as he holds a Jewish majority in the vote count, while Eisenkot and his camp are trying to rally together – a return to a focus on war with Iran would place the nation’s focus where Netanyahu prefers it.
Will Eisenkot and company find it harder to cut a deal with the Arab parties while Israelis have ballistic missiles raining down on them?
Might they feel more ready to cut a deal with Netanyahu if Iran has pushed out the October 7 massacre and haredim (ultra-Orthodox) serving in the IDF as the focus of the national conversation?
None of this means that Israel attacking Iran may not be justified on its own. Until Tehran makes new nuclear concessions, such an attack could be justified in theory, based on the idea of getting it to make those concessions.
And anytime the US offers to assist with cleaning house, many Israelis would say that Israel should not miss the chance to jump on board – as opposed to having to fight Iran solo at some later date.
Still, as long as Zamir is in no rush to strike Iran, Netanyahu would need to justify the attack with more than vague statements about Iran making new progress toward threatening Israel.
It is hard for him to both claim he succeeded at removing the nuclear and ballistic-missile threat in one sentence, and to then demand a new strike now, because time is running out.
How Netanyahu explains a third round of conflict, if it happens during coalition negotiations, will be crucial to the success of any attack and its legitimacy among the wider Israeli public.

US campaign to cripple Iran's economy risks falling short without global partners, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:38:17 UTC
03:38:17 KST

The United States’ Operation Economic Outcast, designed to sever the economic lifelines sustaining the Iranian regime, is falling short of its full potential without greater coordination with international partners, according to a new assessment published earlier this week by two experts from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
According to Michael Jacobson, the Mark and Wayne Levy Senior Fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, and Matthew Levitt, the Fromer-Wexler Senior Fellow and director of the institute’s Reinhard Program on Counterterrorism and Intelligence, closer coordination with allies on sanctions would strengthen Washington’s efforts to undermine the Iranian regime alongside the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Criticizing Washington for relying on targeted, limited diplomatic efforts to address Iran-linked terrorism, they argued that the results achieved so far have demonstrated the value of a more international approach.
On October 12, the US and 29 other governments issued a statement accusing Iran of orchestrating plots to destroy US air assets at RAF Fairford in the UK, following a similar statement a week earlier in which the US and eight countries in the Western Hemisphere condemned Iran’s terrorist and malign activities in the region.
In June, the US State Department and more than 20 other governments also accused Iran of being behind a series of attacks in Europe, North America, and Australia.
Jacobson and Levitt said some governments had initially been hesitant to condemn Iranian plots, including those on their own soil, because of concerns about Iranian retaliation and the fate of their nationals wrongfully detained in Iranian prisons, but they eventually did so with American support.
US sanctions against Iran-backed groups require stronger enforcement capabilities, experts warn
Washington’s efforts had also helped multiple countries in Central and South America designate or sanction the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Hezbollah, and Hamas in recent years, they wrote, adding that such measures carry symbolic weight while giving governments additional tools to counter the groups’ activities.
They cautioned that designations and sanctions must be backed by the material capabilities, skills, and knowledge needed to address the complex Iranian threat, including its sophisticated financial schemes, if they are to translate into meaningful action against the regime.
The Trump administration could use foreign assistance funding to advance these efforts, Jacobson and Levitt wrote, adding that Congress has already allocated almost $300 million to the State Department this fiscal year to strengthen partners’ counterterrorism capabilities.
Although the State Department has publicly committed some of that funding to addressing cartel and gang threats in Central America, similar support could also help countries counter Iran’s malign activities, they said.
US experts urge funding to disrupt Iranian smuggling and terror financing networks
The funding could be directed toward programs to train and equip Syrian border-security authorities to intercept Iranian and Hezbollah smuggling operations, including bulk cash transfers; help Yemeni Coast Guard officials detect and disrupt Houthi weapons and procurement networks; and improve Iraqi financial institutions’ ability to identify illicit Iranian financing schemes, Jacobson and Levitt wrote.
Other initiatives could strengthen efforts by authorities in West Africa and South America to uncover and prosecute Hezbollah’s illicit financial networks, they added.

The US goods trade deficit widened 2.1% month-on-month in September to $134.9 billion, marking its highest level since March 2025, the Commerce Department reported on Wednesday. 
The figure exceeded market expectations for a $130.4 billion gap and followed a $132.1 billion deficit recorded in August.

Wholesale inventories climbed 0.6% on a monthly basis in September to $1.01 trillion, the data showed.
Retail inventories also edged up 0.3% month-on-month to $885.3 billion during the same period.

Pathways to power: What happens next after Israel's election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:29:45 UTC
03:29:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Pathways to power: What happens next after Israel's election?
Almost 24 hours after the polls closed, it has become clear that Israel's high-stakes election has ended in a stalemate.
Neither of the two opposing blocs has enough seats to form a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, with Netanyahu's far-right coalition leading with 53 seats to the opposition bloc's 48.
The final tally won't be known until Friday, when the hundreds of thousands of "double envelope" votes are counted, and the official result won't be published until next week.
But with almost 90% of the votes now in, the two blocs' options are becoming clearer. Though Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot have both staked a claim to victory, they will both face an uphill struggle if they are to form the country's 38th government.
Here are three potential paths ahead following yesterday's inconclusive vote.
Netanyahu remains in power
Despite seeing his bloc shrink compared to the 2022 election, Netanyahu's Likud is poised to remain the largest party in the Knesset and his bloc closer to a majority than the opposition.
With 86% of the vote now in, the Likud-far-right-Haredi alliance is eight seats short of a majority, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc requires another 13.
That doesn't necessarily mean Netanyahu has the upper hand.
His options for coalition-building are as narrow as Eisenkot's, and hinge on being able to break his rival's alliance and bring some of the opposition to the other side of the aisle.
Addressing supporters, Netanyahu claimed his coalition had won a "decisive majority" and called for the formation of a "national right-wing government" - a statement that was interpreted in some quarters as an overture to the right-wing members of Eisenkot's coalition.
Avigdor Lieberman's ultranationalist Yisrael Beiteinu and the pro-settler Naftali Bennett align with Netanyahu on key issues, including ensuring Jewish supremacy at home, annexing much of the occupied West Bank, and maintaining a permanent war footing abroad.
But defection is likely to remain a distant prospect. Both have staked out staunchly anti-Netanyahu positions on the campaign trail and have ruled out entering any form of government with him.
They are also firmly opposed to ultra-Orthodox Jews' exemption from military service, which would likely continue under a new Netanyahu government. This is particularly true for the aggressively secular Lieberman, who is dead against working with Haredi parties Shas and United Torah Judaism.
There has also been speculation about whether Netanyahu could try to form a unity government with Eisenkot in a last-ditch bid to remain in power.
President Isaac Herzog - who will soon decide which of the leaders stands the best chance of forming a government - has voiced support for a unity government, though both leaders have until now flatly rejected the idea.
To get Eisenkot on board, Netanyahu could ditch his far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies, though this is unlikely to be enough to convince the Yashar leader to serve in government led by a man he has so sharply criticised.
Since the polls closed, Eisenkot has not tempered his language about the incumbent prime minister, accusing him of "division and incitement" and maintaining a "culture of lies".
Netanyahu ousted by an Arab-backed government
Eisenkot's coalition is currently on course to win 48 seats in the Knesset, five fewer than Netanyahu and 13 shy of an overall majority.
This means that his path to government runs directly through the Arab parties, which are poised to win a record number of seats and hold the balance of power.
Between them, the conservative Ra'am and the leftist/nationalist Joint List are projected to win 19 seats, meaning Eisenkot will not be able to form an administration without their support.
Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas has indicated he would be willing to enter government with the former general, in a repeat of his agreement with Naftali Bennett in 2021.
The problem for Eisenkot is that the math is not likely to add up, even after bringing Ra'am inside the tent. With the Islamist party on course to get seven seats in the Knesset, an alliance would still leave him six seats short of a majority.
That leaves the possibility of cooperating with the Joint List, which has offered to support a minority government led by Eisenkot, should it agree to several conditions, including committing to establishing a Palestinian state.
The group's leader, Yousef Jabareen, appealed to the opposition to start talks, saying it is offering a clear path to ousting Netanyahu and the far-right from power.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," he told Israeli media on Wednesday.
He articulated the choice facing Eisenkot and his partners in stark terms: "It is either continued racism, continued exclusion and continued supremacy, or genuine Jewish-Arab partnership."
Ahmad Tibi, who leads Ta'al, one of the three parties in the Joint List, said the key question coming out of the election is whether the opposition will be "brave enough" to break the taboo of working with Arab parties in order to block Netanyahu's return.
While both Palestinian-led groups clearly want to work with the Jewish-Israeli opposition, it is far less clear whether the feeling is mutual. For most of them, it is likely to be quite the opposite.
Aside from Yair Golan's centrist Democrats, the instincts of most of the opposition will be to refuse working with Arab parties and avoid reckoning with the new Palestinian agency expressed at the ballot box. Even if Eisenkot were to accept the Joint List's support, getting his hawkish partners on board would be a big ask.
Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh – who was banned from running in the election – said that racism among Jewish-Israeli leaders would block Arab parties from helping to unseat the current far-right government.
“When someone who is a candidate to be a prime minister says he does not want to sit with 20% of the population … this is racism," he told The New Arab.
Another election
If both sides fail to form a government, Israelis would be forced to return to the polls for another election.
The second vote would need to be held within 90 days of the Knesset being dissolved, keeping Netanyahu and his cabinet in power in a caretaker capacity.
A new election, coming after potentially weeks of coalition talks, would push the country into a protracted period of uncertainty, with no guarantees that a new vote would resolve the deadlock.
It would recall the years of instability between 2019 and 2022, when four separate elections were held. The gridlock was brought to an end four years ago when Netanyahu entered government with the extreme-right.
President Herzog on Wednesday appealed to political leaders to do everything they can to avoid a rerun of the election and urged them to "keep an open mind" in coalition discussions.
Netanyahu may calculate that a fresh election is his best option, especially with US president Donald Trump threatening to resume the war on Iran following the 3 November midterms.
Matthew Hoare is a journalist at The New Arab

To commemorate the eighth centenary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi, the Italian Embassy in Croatia organized the conference “The Relevance of St. Francis: From Coexistence to Communion and Fraternity’ in Zagreb, in collaboration with the Croatian Catholic University, which hosted the event, and with the Apostolic Nunciature. The conference was followed by a concert by the Ensemble Micrologus-Giullari di Dio, organized by the Italian Cultural Institute, which offered a musical journey dedicated to the Canticle of the Creatures and the ancient melodies of the Italian lauda tradition. The conference proceedings were opened by the Italian Ambassador to Croatia, Paolo Trichilo; by Monsignor Marco Malizia, Ecclesiastical Advisor to the Vice President of the Council of Ministers and Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, the Honorable Antonio Tajani, by the Apostolic Nuncio, Monsignor Leopoldo Girelli, and by the Rector of the Catholic University of Croatia, Prof. Željko Tanjić. Prof. Fra Lorenzo Turchi of the Pontifical Antonianum University in Rome served as the keynote speaker, engaging in a discussion with two Croatian professors from the universities of Split and Zagreb—both members of the Franciscan Order— on the Christian experience of St. Francis and how it can offer criteria for discernment in understanding certain dynamics of the present. The event drew a large audience and was attended by several civil and religious authorities, including Cardinal Emeritus of Zagreb Josip Bozanić, Ivan Mašina, Advisor to the Croatian Minister of Foreign Affairs; and, representing the Ministry of Culture, Šime Jerčić, Director General of the Office of the Commission for Relations with Religious Communities. In his opening remarks, Ambassador Trichilo highlighted the attention given to St. Francis by Italian institutions and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as evidenced by the establishment of the national holiday on October 4 and the organization of dedicated events by the diplomatic corps. St. Francis, the Ambassador emphasized, is a pivotal historical figure for Italian, European, and universal spirituality and culture. His message continues to be a source of inspiration that prompts us to reflect on the future and offers spiritual and ethical guidance for navigating the modern world. He then highlighted how the initiative takes on particular significance in Croatia, given the country’s Catholic tradition. Bishop Malizia conveyed greetings from Minister Tajani, expressing the minister’s satisfaction that the diplomatic network had accepted the invitation to promote initiatives on St. Francis and to focus on a spiritual and human witness capable of speaking to peoples, cultures, and traditions, and to contribute to the promotion of dialogue, peace, and fraternity. He also noted that Italy considers intercultural and interreligious dialogue an essential component of its international vision, emphasizing the important role played by cultural institutions, religious communities, and diplomacy—all united by the responsibility to safeguard peace through mutual understanding, respect, and cooperation. Bishop Malizia then expressed his appreciation for the conference, which represents not only a tribute to St. Francis but also a concrete opportunity to rediscover what unites us and to promote a culture of listening, solidarity, and peace.

Google announced its latest artificial intelligence (AI) model, Gemini 4 Carbon, on Wednesday, claiming significant gains in coding, autonomous agent tasks and cybersecurity defense.  
Unveiled just two weeks after the launch of its Gemini 4 Argon model, the company described Carbon in a blog post as its strongest frontier model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.
Google attributed the rapid release timeline to its researchers and AI models "working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster."  
The company claimed that Gemini 4 Carbon ranks first on the updated version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 59.

Addressing safety and alignment, Google claimed that internal testing showed Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately half compared to Argon, stating methodological caveats directly rather than fabricating missing evidence.
The company also claimed the model retrieves relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to users when facing ambiguity, while reducing task overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% during multi-step workflows.
Google said Gemini 4 Carbon will first become available to cybersecurity defenders this week before rolling out more broadly to developers, businesses and consumers.
The company plans to offer introductory pricing of $2 per 1 million input tokens and $10 per 1 million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted by 95%, before standard pricing rises to $4 per 1 million input tokens and $20 per 1 million output tokens.

TMoCA exhibition to explore how ‘Iran’ is presented and conceptualized in artworks

Unknown Publisher

TMoCA exhibition to explore how ‘Iran’ is presented and conceptualized in artworks
TEHRAN – The exhibition “In Search of Iran: In the Collection of the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art” will open on Saturday afternoon at the museum.
It explores how “Iran” is presented and conceptualized through the lens of various artists among the works kept in the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art (TMoCA), Mehr reported.
The exhibition addresses the national significance of the TMoCA collection within the history of contemporary Iranian art by examining the diverse ways artists experience and interpret “Iran.”
The exhibition statement reads: “We do not ask which work is ‘more Iranian’; rather, we ask how Iran has been the subject of seeing and representation, and how it persists within the modes of seeing and creating. The inquiry into Iranian identity in this exhibition begins with the distinct experiences of artists—experiences that are sometimes explicitly the subject of the work, and sometimes manifest in the style of expression and construction. Belonging to Iran can be accompanied by the memory of a place, daily life, migration, or a sense of loss, taking on different forms in the works of each artist”.
“The exhibition ‘In Search of Iran’ invites the viewer to re-examine their own conception of Iran when encountering these works. In these pieces, soil sometimes becomes the very material of the work, writing turns into a way of seeing, and objects preserve the traces of life and human memory. The presence of familiar symbols does not predetermine the meaning of the work, nor does their absence necessarily signify a disconnection from the Iranian experience”.
“The seven sections of the exhibition, each guided by a specific question, offer parallel paths for the viewer to interpret the works. These paths do not follow a chronological sequence of art history; instead, the visual and conceptual connections between the pieces allow for a confrontation with diverse interpretations. In this view, no single landscape, face, or motif serves as the sole representative of the Iranian experience."
The exhibition will feature over one hundred works from the Iranian Modern Art collection, including pieces by artists such as Sohrab Sepehri, Parviz Tanavoli, Parviz Kalantari, Hossein Zenderoudi, Farah Osouli, Reza Mafi, Mohammad Ehsaei, Bahman Mohassess, and others. It will be open to the public from Sunday, through mid-December.
Established in 1977, the museum has more than 4,000 items that include 19th- and 20th-century world-class Iranian, European, and American paintings, prints, drawings, and sculptures. Being the biggest collection of Western art in the Eastern world, it includes works from almost all artistic periods and movements.
The museum was designed by Iranian architect Kamran Diba, who employed elements from traditional Persian architecture. The building itself can be regarded as an example of contemporary art, in the style of an underground Guggenheim Museum.
Most of the museum area is located underground, with a circular walkway that spirals downwards, with galleries branching outwards. Western sculptures by artists such as Ernst, Giacometti, Magritte, and Moore can be found in the museum's gardens.
