Water tariffs will be reviewed under new rules: will Ukrainians’ bills decrease?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:09:47 EET
03:09:47 KST

Water tariffs will be reviewed under new rules: will Ukrainians’ bills decrease?
Kyiv • UNN
Tariffs will be set by local authorities, while the NEURC will remotely verify their calculations. There will be no automatic reduction in bills.
Ukraine is introducing a new mechanism for monitoring tariffs for centralized water supply and wastewater services. On October 27, the National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission (NEURC) approved a procedure for reviewing decisions on the cost of these services. The regulator will analyze whether the tariffs were calculated correctly and whether the expenses included in consumers’ bills are substantiated.
UNN examined who is now responsible for setting them, how the monitoring will work, and what consumers who doubt the fairness of the charges can do.
Who sets water tariffs in Ukraine
In March 2026, the division of powers in the field of centralized water supply and wastewater services changed in Ukraine. Law No. 4777-IX, which entered into force on March 11, transferred tariff-setting powers to local self-government bodies. Where they have the relevant powers, decisions may be adopted by military administrations of settlements. In turn, the licensing of water utilities and oversight of compliance with licensing conditions were transferred to authorized local state administrations. The NEURC retained responsibility for developing tariff-setting methodologies and verifying the correctness of tariff decisions.
As we can see, the new mechanism does not return to the regulator the right to directly determine the cost of water in each city. Local authorities will continue to adopt tariff decisions, while the NEURC may verify whether a decision complies with legislation and approved methodologies.
Water prices in Ukraine are set by local authorities — Shmyhal21.08.26, 12:55 • 3382 views
How inspections of water supply tariffs will be carried out
The NEURC reported that inspections will be scheduled and unscheduled. Both types of oversight will be conducted remotely: officials will not visit enterprises or local authorities. The basis will be the tariff calculations, documents, and explanations used when the relevant decisions were adopted.
Scheduled inspections will be conducted according to an annual plan published on the NEURC website. Unscheduled inspections may be carried out, in particular, if monitoring reveals inconsistencies in the documents, questionable figures, or grounds for examining a sharp tariff increase.
The oversight process will begin with a request to the body that set the tariff. It must provide the decision, the tariff structure, the water utility’s calculations, and supporting materials. The draft procedure stipulated at least ten working days to respond to a request and no more than twenty working days for the inspection after the documents were received. If the necessary information is insufficient, the deadlines will be suspended in accordance with the procedure.
In addition, the regulator will compare the approved tariff with the calculation data. The result will be a written conclusion. It will serve as the basis for replacing the tariff, but it will not automatically cancel it on the day the document is issued.
What will be examined in the cost of water
The water supply tariff covers the costs of extracting, treating, and delivering water to consumers. The wastewater tariff concerns the collection, transportation, and treatment of wastewater. They are calculated separately, although the vast majority of Ukrainians see a single item on their bills covering payment for water supply and wastewater services.
During the oversight process, authorized officials will verify whether the calculations comply with the established methodology, whether there are sufficient documents to substantiate the expenses, and whether the tariff approval procedure was followed. Particular attention will be paid to the cost of electricity for pumps and treatment facilities, labor costs, network repairs, the purchase of materials, and other economically justified components.
Investment expenses, planned service volumes, and the consideration of the results of previous inspections are separate issues. For example, if an enterprise included certain modernization expenses, it is necessary to determine whether their inclusion in the tariff meets the established requirements.
What will happen if the regulator finds violations
Based on the inspections, the NEURC will draw up conclusions. If the calculations are incorrect or the expenses are unsubstantiated, the conclusion will indicate the violations identified and recommendations for remedying them. They may be taken into account when reviewing, adjusting, or setting tariffs in the future. Once approved, the results must be published on the regulator’s website.
At the same time, local authorities have the right to express their objections to the conclusion.
When discussing the regulator’s recommendations, one more important point should be understood. The NEURC’s conclusions will not mean the automatic cancellation of a tariff or the return of money for services already paid for. A subsequent decision to change the price must be made by the authorized body in accordance with the procedure established by law. The new procedure itself does not establish a separate mechanism for compensating the public for overpayments.
Will water bills become lower, and how can they be challenged?
For household consumers, the new measure will provide an opportunity for additional oversight. If an inspection identifies inflated or incorrectly accounted-for expenses and the local authorities subsequently adjust the tariff, this may affect future charges. However, the regulator does not promise an overall reduction in tariffs.
Consumers should first check the current tariff decision on the website of the city or town council or the service provider. After that, they should determine the date the tariff was introduced, the separate costs of water supply and wastewater services, the consumer category, and whether the bill includes other charges not directly related to the price per cubic meter.
If there are doubts about the calculations, a written request may be submitted to the body that approved the tariff, asking it to provide the decision and an accessible justification. If there are indications of a violation, an appeal may be submitted to the NEURC, including through the "Citizens’ Appeals" section on the regulator’s official website or by writing to [email protected].
The application should indicate the locality, the name of the water utility, the details of the tariff decision, and the specific facts that raise doubts, attaching any available documents.
When the new rules will take effect
The NEURC approved the procedure on October 27, 2026. The text of the resolution prepared for the meeting states that it will enter into force on the day after its official publication on the regulator’s website.
It should also be emphasized that the mechanism is designed to operate during martial law and for twelve months after its termination or repeal. It is connected with the temporary redistribution of powers between the NEURC and local authorities.
Will NEURC oversight make water tariffs for households fairer?
The new inspections make it possible to compare local authorities’ decisions with economic calculations and make identified violations public. However, the effectiveness of the system will nevertheless depend on how fully the authorities provide information and whether they take the regulator’s recommendations into account.
As a reminder
Earlier, UNN reported that Ukrainians and businesses are being offered the option of paying to change their electricity consumption schedule. For example, they could shift the operation of appliances from peak-demand hours to another time. To participate, it will be necessary to conclude an agreement with an aggregator—a company that represents consumers in the energy market.

Constitutional Court rules on conditional early release of life prisoners for military service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:07:40 EET
03:07:40 KST

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine (CCU) on October 28 ruled that provisions of the Criminal Code, which do not provide for the possibility of conditional early release for contract military service for individuals serving life sentences, are constitutional, the CCU's communications department said.
"On October 28, 2026, the Second Senate, at a plenary session, considered the case based on a constitutional complaint filed by Anatoliy Oleksandrovych Luzhynetsky and adopted Decision No. 13-r(II)/2026," according to a statement from the CCU Communications Department, which was received by Interfax-Ukraine on Wednesday.
It is reported that, after reviewing the case, the court concluded that the mechanism for conditional early release from serving a sentence for the purpose of performing military service, established by Article 81-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, is temporary in nature (applicable during mobilization and/or martial law), and its application entails specific consequences due to the possession and use of weapons and military equipment.
Thus, in the court's view, "the conscription of individuals who have committed violent (intentional murder of two or more persons) and other particularly serious criminal offenses entails additional risks to military discipline, subordination, the proper execution of combat missions, as well as the lives and health of other military personnel and civilians."
"In light of the foregoing, the Court has found the provisions of the first part of Article 811 of the Code to be consistent with the Constitution of Ukraine, in that they do not provide for the possibility of applying conditional early release from serving a sentence for the purpose of performing military service under a contract to persons who are serving a sentence of life imprisonment, and exclude the possibility of applying such release to persons convicted of the intentional murder of two or more persons," the court said in its announcement.
The decision and its summary will be published on the court's official website on October 29, 2026.

New city project for Ukraine's reconstruction to be presented at Davos, URC2027 in Tallinn
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:07:09 EET
03:07:09 KST

Ukraine's Alternative Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Vladyslav Rashkovan, Presidential Advisor on Reconstruction and Investment Attraction Oksana Markarova, and Executive Director of the New City innovative urban initiative Viktoria Trotska are working on a new city project as part of preparations for Ukraine's recovery.
"For now, I'm mostly providing inspiration, while Oksana Markarova and Viktoria Trotska are already developing the new city project and plan to present the initiative at the World Economic Forum in Davos and at the URC in Tallinn – and perhaps even display a physical model of the city," Rashkovan said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok on October 12-18.
According to him, following the example of the construction of the city of Slavutych in 1986-1988, the new city project envisages various districts – conventionally Italian, French, German, Eastern, and others: an international team of German, Italian, French, and Japanese architects is working on the city's design, with weekly coordination meetings.
"So far, they're all working for free. To professionalize the project and anchor it to a specific territory, funding from international organizations is needed. The European Commission likes this idea as a showcase project, since Europe also lacks modern experience in building such new cities," Rashkovan said.
He added that over the next year, with the support of international partners, he wants to prepare a kind of blueprint – a book on the principles of building new cities after the war.
"It doesn't matter whether we're talking about a new city or the reconstruction of districts in Kharkiv, Odesa, Kyiv, or Trostianets. What's important is to establish these principles. Such a resource could be useful not only for Ukraine but also for Syria, Lebanon, and other countries that have suffered war damage. It will also be of interest to European partners, who also need to undertake significant construction projects," Ukraine's representative to the IMF said.
He said that since reconstruction takes place at the local level, the idea of building new cities seems promising, as 95% of what exists at the state level is already present at the local level.
According to Rashkovan, at the city level, for example, it is possible to implement green, distributed energy systems and inclusivity, put digital democracy tools into practice, and lay the technological foundation from the ground up for the city's effective functioning: rational use of water and electricity, waste management, and transportation organization.
"We would also like to create a self-sufficient city that will not require additional funding from Kyiv, that will itself create jobs and become a magnet for talent and business, serving as a model of deregulation and a favorable investment climate," Ukraine's representative to the IMF said.
According to him, as part of this project, there is ongoing collaboration with Jenny Roe, former former Director of the Center for Design & Health in the School of Architecture, University of Virginia – who is the author of the book "Restorative Cities" about cities capable of helping people heal – as well as with Finnish and Korean experts on the concept of a two-tier safe city, since Finland leads the Shelter Coalition and has one of the best track records in this field.
Rashkovan is optimistic about the prospects for implementing such a project: it must be supported by the government, but 80-85% of it will be financed by private capital, investments, commercial loans, private equity funds, and so on.
Read the full second part of the interview with Vladyslav Rashkovan, Ukraine's Alternative Executive Director at the IMF, on Interfax-Ukraine website at https://interfax.com.ua/news/interview/1227277.html.

Gokhan Ergocun
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The US Federal Reserve kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at a range of 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday as policymakers weighed elevated inflation against strong economic growth.
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the decision in a 10-2 vote to support the central bank's dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices, the Fed said in a statement.
Policymakers Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented, preferring to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at the meeting.
"Inflation remains elevated," the committee said, pledging that it "will deliver price stability."
"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal," it added.
The central bank noted that US economic activity is expanding at a strong pace, supported by resilient domestic spending, strong productivity growth and robust capital investment despite elevated uncertainty linked partly to geopolitical developments.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce and the unemployment rate has changed little, the Fed said, adding that it is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Expert: Russia must accept reality of NATO’s 32 member countries
Jim Stokes, a senior expert with GLOBSEC’s “Future of Security” program and former director of nuclear policy at NATO (2023–2025), said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Russia will therefore have to accept the reality: NATO now has 32 members. Russia can continue talking about this, and NATO can simply respond: “Noted. We are not going to change,” Stokes said in response to a question about whether the Alliance would be willing to agree to the Kremlin’s demands to roll back its military presence to pre-1997 levels.
According to the expert, this seems “absolutely impossible.” He was referring to the new members—Finland and Sweden—not to mention the 16 countries that joined after the end of the Cold War.
“They are not going to agree to leave the Alliance, and the other Allies are not going to agree simply to let them go. That has never happened in NATO’s 77-year history,” Stokes noted.
However, he acknowledged that another question is whether NATO will ever allow new allies to join. Such a decision is made by consensus among all 32 countries, Stokes reminded.
At the same time, the expert emphasized that the main problem right now is that this Russian war is shaping the perception of the threat, and it is precisely because of this war that Finland and Sweden decided to join the Alliance rather than remain mere partners.
“Much of the responsibility therefore lies with Russia. It can blame NATO for expanding closer to Russian borders, and I understand that it is unhappy about it. But Russia had no problem with this in the late 1990s and early 2000s. It turned the issue into a political one, and now it will have to come to terms with it,” Stokes concluded.
As reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine expects a trilateral format of negotiations involving Ukrainian, American, and Russian representatives in November, and that Europe must be involved in the diplomatic process and participate in decisions regarding the end of the war.

Iranian foreign minister says Tehran in talks with mediators to implement 7-day plan with US
Unknown

2026-10-28
17:51:53 UTC
02:51:53 KST

Sahin Demir
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Iran is in contact with mediators to review proposals to implement a seven-day plan with the US.
Araghchi wrote on US social media company X that Tehran continues to give diplomacy a chance despite tensions with Washington.
“While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed,” he said. “We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week.”
Iran’s seven-day plan, presented to Washington through Qatari mediators in September, proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming negotiations with the US within a week if Washington meets Tehran’s conditions.
The US would take agreed steps during the first five days, including ending hostilities, lifting its naval blockade on Iranian ports, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
On the sixth day, Iran would reopen the strait to normal commercial shipping, while negotiations between Tehran and Washington toward a comprehensive agreement would resume on the seventh day.
The proposed measures remain subject to agreement.
On Oct. 8, Araghchi said Tehran was reviewing Washington’s response to the proposal, with messages continuing to be exchanged through mediators.
The latest remarks come amid diplomatic efforts to maintain a fragile ceasefire between Iran and the US following months of military confrontation.
The two countries signed the Islamabad Memorandum on June 18 following negotiations mediated by Pakistan and Oman.
That agreement addressed several disputed issues, including maritime security in the strait, sanctions relief and the withdrawal of US naval restrictions.
Oman, Pakistan and Qatar have maintained diplomatic contacts aimed at resolving differences between Tehran and Washington.

Apple unveiled the MacBook Pro with a touch-sensitive OLED display
Kyiv • UNN
The new MacBook Pro features a touch-sensitive OLED display, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, and up to 24 hours of battery life. Sales begin on November 6.
Apple unveiled a new MacBook Pro with a touch OLED display, M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, and support for Dynamic Island. The laptop features a display with a refresh rate of up to 120 Hz, up to 24 hours of battery life, and the ability to connect up to four external displays. Preorders are already available, and sales will begin on November 6. The Verge reports, writes UNN.
Details
The presentation took place on Wednesday during the “Pro and tell” event. The new MacBook Pro is equipped with a PROLED XDR display featuring a tandem OLED structure. It supports peak SDR brightness of up to 2,000 nits and has a contrast ratio of 10,000,000:1.
The screen features Dynamic Island, which can display Live Activities—interactive notifications similar to those available on the iPhone. In addition, Apple has brought back the illuminated logo on the laptop lid.
According to the company, the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel rather than placed on top of it. This design is intended to reduce latency when interacting with the screen.
Touch controls can be used to scroll through web pages, zoom in on photos, test apps for iOS and iPadOS, and work with software musical instruments. Apple also said that its apps are optimized for touch input, while an updated API will allow third-party developers to add touch support to their own applications.
The laptop is available in two sizes. The 14-inch model weighs approximately 1.36 kg, while the 16-inch model weighs 1.81 kg. The displays’ actual diagonals are 14.2 and 16.3 inches, respectively. Both models are thinner thanks to a redesigned construction.
According to Apple, the MacBook Pro provides up to 24 hours of battery life. The ports include MagSafe 3, a headphone jack, an SD card reader, HDMI, and three Thunderbolt 5 ports. The laptop supports connecting up to three external displays simultaneously, while the M5 Max version supports up to four.
Apple also highlights a six-speaker audio system that, according to the company, delivers 50% deeper bass and clear sound. In addition, the device features a newly designed hinge for improved stability.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch model starts at $3,399. Preorders can be placed now, and official sales are scheduled to begin on November 6.
Apple did not support the idea of touchscreens in laptops for a long time. In 2016, the company began equipping the MacBook Pro with a Touch Bar instead of traditional function keys. However, in 2021 it brought back physical keys, and in 2023 it completely discontinued the Touch Bar.

Europe must finally hold Russia accountable for hybrid attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:50:35 UTC
02:50:35 KST

Europe must finally hold Russia accountable for hybrid attacks
A soldier patrols outside the building hosting the NATO summit of heads of state and government in The Hague, Netherlands, on June 24, 2025. (John Thys/AFP via Getty Images)
Marek Zenisek
Czech politician and academic
Europe has already learned to better recognize hybrid threats, which is definitely a good thing, but recognition alone is not enough and doesn't serve as sufficient deterrence.
European officials have grown accustomed to scenarios where a cyberattack disrupts public services and critical infrastructure, drones appear over sensitive sites, and a flood of misinformation on social media exploits societal uncertainty.
European governments then investigate, share information, release statements, and sometimes announce new security measures until another incident elsewhere grabs the headlines again.
This approach is obviously not enough. Up until today, it appears that Russia is pretty confident that the cost of these hybrid attacks is a bargain — it costs little, and consequences look spectacular in Russian intelligence reports.
And this is exactly where Europe still has a problem. Resilience and deterrence are not the same thing. Europe must become a harder and, above all, much more expensive target for Russia.
Europeans must ensure that deterrence is a priority, as resilience is an unlikely tool to actually change the cost of a Russian attack.
Let's stop treating every incident as an isolated case and add them all up
A single attack may seem too small to justify a major response.
We've seen it many times.
In July 2024, an incendiary package caught fire at Leipzig airport on July 20, followed by similar incidents in Poland and the U.K. over the next two days.
German security authorities did not issue a wider warning to the aviation and logistics sectors until Aug. 28, more than five weeks after the first incident.
The subsequent investigation established links between the incidents and a broader Russian sabotage campaign. The response eventually came, but the delay illustrates the advantage Russia gains when individual incidents are treated separately rather than as parts of a broader campaign.
Determining responsibility can take weeks, and governments may differ in their assessment of the available evidence as well as their opinion on the appropriate reaction. Before responsibility is confirmed, political attention may shift elsewhere, giving Russia a strategic advantage in this gray zone.
This creates an asymmetry that favors the aggressor. Moscow can carry out a long-term campaign while European states deal with individual incidents one by one.
European governments, therefore, need to evaluate individual incidents in a broader context and together.
A cyberattack, sabotage, or an attempt to infiltrate an intelligence network is a full-blown hybrid campaign targeted against European countries.
Repeated operations also consume European resources, reveal weaknesses, create uncertainty, and above all, test how far Europe is willing to go.
So every new investigation shouldn't start from scratch, and instead should take into account what came before it.
Deterrence can't start only after an attack
The central objective of Europe's deterrence strategy should be to change Moscow's calculus and make further aggression an unacceptable gamble. European governments can rise above the Kremlin's dirty tricks by pursuing a constructive, systemic approach that addresses the threat at its roots.
To develop that, European governments should prepare a credible set of possible consequences before another serious incident occurs. Russia doesn't need to know exactly what Europe will do in every situation; strategic ambiguity has its value, but Moscow must believe that Europe will respond and that the consequences will matter.
That's the foundation of credible deterrence.
There's also a broader reason why this is important. If we add up the various forms of pressure Russia has exerted on European countries in recent years, future generations could rightfully ask why Europe tolerated so many things without developing a more systematic response.
It will be especially hard to explain to our children and grandchildren why a group of countries with much greater economic resources than Russia repeatedly allowed Moscow to set the pace of the confrontation.
Europe needs to be much better prepared. European countries should have a set of possible responses ready that can be adapted to specific cases, instead of having to come up with a reaction from scratch after every new attack.
That way, deterrence becomes more than just a statement made after the damage has already been done.
Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent so far?
and it may appear in our Letters section.
Europe needs to change the calculation
Everyone understands that Europe cannot prevent every hostile operation. It can't know where the next test will come from, just like it can't rule out the possibility that Russia or another adversary will take advantage of Europe's openness. It can, however, make such operations more difficult.
Europe can better protect its societies. It can improve the ability of its intelligence and security services to identify hostile networks. It can coordinate accountability better. It can remove unnecessary legal and institutional obstacles. And it can make it clear that repeated aggression will not go unpunished.
The main goal, as mentioned before, has to be to change the adversary's calculation.
Russia must not only ask whether a certain operation can be carried out successfully. It also has to ask how much it will cost if Europe uncovers it and holds Moscow responsible.

Herzog urges Israeli parties to avert fresh election as neither bloc secures majority

Unknown Publisher

02:49:45 KST

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged political parties to make every effort to avoid another election after preliminary results left neither main bloc with a parliamentary majority.
“Everything must be done, especially after yesterday, to avoid repeating another election,” Herzog told reporters on Wednesday in remarks carried by Israeli public broadcaster KAN.
He said he would begin consultations with parliamentary factions next week after receiving the official election results from the Central Elections Committee.
“I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind,” Herzog said.
He said he would listen to each faction, ask questions and hold discussions before deciding which lawmaker to task with forming a government.
Under Israel's basic law governing government formation, the president must consult parliamentary factions and assign a Knesset member the task of forming a government within seven days of the official publication of election results.
The selected lawmaker receives 28 days to form a government, with the possibility of extensions totalling up to 14 additional days.
If the first candidate fails, the president may appoint another lawmaker. At a later stage, at least 61 lawmakers can nominate a candidate to form a government.
Failure to establish a government could ultimately trigger another election.
Although coalitions generally seek support from at least 61 lawmakers, Israeli law allows minority governments to take office if more lawmakers vote in favour than against in a parliamentary confidence vote.
Until a new government wins the Knesset's confidence and takes office, Netanyahu's outgoing government will continue performing its duties.
According to Israeli Channel 12, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset after all regular ballots were counted on Wednesday.
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot was projected to secure 48 seats, while predominantly Arab parties were expected to win 19 seats, the broadcaster reported.
More than 500,000 special ballots remained to be counted.
Neither main bloc has been projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.

Israeli exit polls show deadlock in apparent setback for Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:48:08 UTC
02:48:08 KST

JERUSALEM (Reuters) -- Israel's wartime election was deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, with Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power.
The projections pointed to a setback for Netanyahu's coalition, though the deadlock could allow Israel's longest-serving prime minister to remain in power as caretaker during coalition negotiations.
"The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu's service as Israel's prime minister ... a worthy leader would have accepted the people's nonconfidence and announced today his retirement from politics," Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv.
Turnout was 77.7%, Israel's Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.
Kan 11 and Channel 13 showed the two blocs level, while Channel 12 gave Eisenkot a narrow edge over Netanyahu's Likud-led camp. None gave either side the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Far-right religious parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were projected to take a combined 13 seats within Netanyahu's bloc.
Arab parties outside the two main blocs could hold the balance of power. But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and a former military chief, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to power.
Final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers.
It was the first election since the Hamas-led attack of Oct. 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, called the exit polls a major defeat for Netanyahu's coalition, but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner and much could change as votes were counted.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: "Don't let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home."
Eisenkot, 66, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu's strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically.
He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticizing the prime minister's leadership.
Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hardline approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
Eisenkot says Israel's response -- a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities -- was a failure because Hamas remains in charge.
The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released, on a historic night for turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
"We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here," Faten Gattas, a candidate in the Joint List, said in a speech at the alliance's headquarters in Nazareth. Candidates hoped high Arab turnout would allow them to play a decisive role in blocking Netanyahu's coalition from returning to power.
Voters grappled with the trauma of Israel's deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran that followed.
While Netanyahu was criticized for the country's biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by killing top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
The policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel's international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel's foes.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises. His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years. Eighteen months later, he was back.
He entered the election facing long-standing corruption charges, which he denies, and criticism over intelligence failures that allowed Hamas-led militants to carry out their attack.
Netanyahu campaigned on an endorsement from U.S. President Donald Trump, his ally in the war against Iran.

In Ukraine's Kherson, brief ceasefire brings rare respite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:46:09 UTC
02:46:09 KST

In Ukraine’s Kherson, brief ceasefire brings rare respite
KHERSON, Ukraine, Oct 28 - Years of near-daily Russian drone and artillery attacks have turned the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson into a battered urban landscape where death is never far away.
On Wednesday, however, the residents who remain ventured cautiously into sun-drenched streets after a US-brokered ceasefire around the nearby frontline town of Oleshky put a temporary pause to the aerial threat.
"Honestly, I can't put it into words," kiosk owner Oleksandra Kosenko told Reuters during a visit on Wednesday. "If it stays this way, it would be really wonderful."
Ukraine said on Wednesday that the six-day ceasefire, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, was holding, providing a rare moment of relief in the fifth year of grinding war.
The pause in fighting is aimed at paving the way for humanitarian relief for Oleshky, where residents face acute shortages of food and medicine.
CRITICAL RESPITE
For Kherson, a regional capital across the Dnipro River from Oleshky, the ceasefire - which took effect early on Tuesday - brings a brief window of respite.
Since Ukrainian troops recaptured the city from Russian occupation in November 2022, Moscow's forces stationed on the opposite bank have shelled it regularly and hunted residents with deadly drones, officials say. Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
As the attacks continued, residents fled and businesses closed, making daily life increasingly dangerous.
The city still functions, with buses ferrying people around and shops and cafes serving customers. But the scars of the war are plain to see. Some buildings are in ruins, the pavements are largely empty and anti-drone nets are draped over the main roads.
On Wednesday, residents walked their dogs without glancing toward the sky. Elderly men sipped coffee on a bench without the din of distant explosions.
"Kherson, which was constantly under fire, literally came to life," said Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, on the Telegram messaging app.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
Kosenko, the kiosk owner, said she had seen a near-doubling in the number of clients: around 50 in total. She was relieved to no longer be dashing for cover on the way to work.
ATMOSPHERE OF TENSION
On Tuesday, top Ukrainian officials described the ceasefire as a major de-escalation that could build confidence for future agreements.
Yet beneath the relief, Kosenko and others expressed wariness that fighting could erupt again at any moment. Many residents approached by Reuters declined to speak, appearing tense.
Anti-personnel mines dropped by the Russians still pose a danger even when hostilities are paused.
Battles are also raging elsewhere along the 1,200-km (750 mile) front line, where Russia remains intent on capturing the parts of the eastern Donetsk region still outside its control.
Moscow is also continuing its bombing campaign of Ukrainian cities, which has damaged critical infrastructure including in Kherson.
Locals like Olha Chyupikova, who lived through Russia's occupation of her city, said they had learned to prepare for the worst.
"The Russians have proven that they can't be trusted," said the 52-year-old municipal worker.
"So I think everyone subconsciously feels like there could be some sort of provocation at any moment." REUTERS

The day after: Opposition moves to oust Knesset speaker before Netanyahu forms government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:44:17 UTC
02:44:17 KST

On the Change bloc agenda for the day after: replace Knesset speaker as Eisenkot, Bennett and Liberman discuss alliance
With neither political bloc securing a majority, opposition leaders are exploring a coordinated effort to oust Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana before a new government is formed; the move would require support from Arab parties, raising political concerns as coalition negotiations begin.
Ahead of the inauguration of the 26th Knesset, scheduled for November 10, parties in Israel's change bloc are beginning to prepare for the political and parliamentary maneuvers that will follow the election. Since Wednesday morning, senior figures in Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party, representatives of Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu and members of Naftali Bennett's Beyachad party have been holding talks aimed at coordinating strategic moves against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
At the center of the discussions is the possibility of replacing incumbent Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana of Likud as soon as the new parliament is sworn in, even before a government is formed. The speaker is one of the most influential figures in the Knesset, wielding considerable power over the parliamentary agenda and the advancement of legislation.
Under a 2020 Supreme Court ruling, a demand by 61 Knesset members to hold a vote on electing a new speaker requires the matter to be brought to a vote, even before a government is formed. However, securing a majority for such a move would also require support from lawmakers representing the Arab parties, a politically sensitive issue for the change bloc.
Some figures within the bloc are seeking to distinguish between forming a coalition or government dependent on Arab parties and cooperating with them on specific parliamentary initiatives. Even those who support the proposal recognize the public sensitivity surrounding such cooperation and are weighing its potential impact on support for the bloc.
Netanyahu's associates, meanwhile, intend to work to block the move and challenge its public legitimacy through an extensive political campaign.
Alongside discussions about replacing the Knesset speaker, senior figures in the change bloc are attempting to establish a center-right alliance comprising Bennett, Liberman and Eisenkot's three parties. The goal is to create a coordinated political framework that would allow the three leaders to present a united front against Likud and strengthen their bargaining power in the expected coalition negotiations.
The discussions also include whether to bring Yair Golan's Democrats into the alliance. Some participants oppose the idea because of the party's identification with the left and concerns that its inclusion could make it harder for the three parties to appeal to center-right voters and broaden their support.
Political observers believe Eisenkot could begin exploring the possibility of forming a government together with Bennett and Liberman in the coming days. One option under consideration would see the three parties operate as a single bloc in negotiations with Likud, maximizing their leverage and influencing the composition of the next government. Such an arrangement could also reduce the bargaining power of Otzma Yehudit chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir and potentially weaken the influence of the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Members of Eisenkot's Yashar! list met to discuss the election results reported so far. They thanked the hundreds of thousands of voters, thousands of activists, campaign headquarters officials and grassroots volunteers "who worked over recent months and helped deliver an unprecedented achievement in public support for a new party established only a year ago, attracting large and diverse groups across Israeli society."
The moves under consideration come against the backdrop of the 26th Knesset election results, which have so far failed to give either political bloc a governing majority. According to the latest interim results, with 85.6% of votes counted, Netanyahu's bloc holds 53 seats, the change bloc 48 and the Arab parties 19.
Likud is the largest party with 26 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar! with 21. The Joint List and Bennett and Yair Lapid's Beyachad each hold 12 seats, while the Democrats have eight. Yisrael Beytenu, Ra'am, United Torah Judaism, Shas and Otzma Yehudit each have seven seats, while the Religious Zionism-Identity list has six.
The picture remains incomplete, however. The counting of double-envelope ballots, estimated at between 430,000 and 480,000, has not yet been completed and could alter the distribution of Knesset seats.
With neither bloc holding the 61-seat majority required to form a government, the Arab parties are in a pivotal position regarding any attempt to replace the Knesset speaker, as well as potential scenarios for forming the next coalition.
Amid the emerging political deadlock, President Isaac Herzog called on the parties Wednesday to approach consultations at the President's Residence with an open mind and do everything possible to avoid another election.
Herzog said he expects to receive the official results next week, after which he will begin consultations with parliamentary factions before deciding which candidate to task with forming the next government.

He did not name the countries allegedly involved.
“What is happening is not a civil war or a struggle for power, but a comprehensive war aimed at destroying Sudan, plundering its resources and changing its demographic composition,” Kabroun said.
The Sudanese army and the RSF have been fighting since April 2023, when disagreements over the integration of military forces escalated into war.

He said Sudan was seeking to join a maritime coalition established to ensure collective protection of the Red Sea.
“Sudan cannot remain outside efforts to secure the Red Sea, which represents a strategic depth for the country,” he said.
Kabroun noted that Sudan has a coastline stretching approximately 800 kilometers (497 miles) along the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia announced the establishment of a maritime coalition on July 30, 2026, to protect navigation, trade and energy supplies in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and Bab al-Mandab Strait.
On Aug. 13, the Saudi Defense Ministry announced that 15 countries signed the coalition’s founding declaration, while 13 had completed their national procedures to join.
Kabroun also said Sudan was surrounded by African countries facing multiple security challenges, including the proliferation of weapons, smuggling, human trafficking and the presence of rebel movements.
He said these cross-border threats directly affected Sudan’s security.

Explainer-What’s at stake for Trump in Israel’s deadlocked election?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:27:20 CET
02:27:20 KST

By Matt Spetalnick
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - With Israel’s election yielding no clear winner, President Donald Trump could face prolonged uncertainty over who will lead Washington’s closest Middle East ally as he confronts challenges from Iran and Gaza across the region.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc secured the most seats in Israel’s parliament but still lost its parliamentary majority on Tuesday despite Trump having endorsed him against a rival alliance of parties led by hawkish former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
While Netanyahu seemed in a stronger position, neither side was projected to have an outright path to form a new government after Israel’s first election since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The stage appeared to be set for a period of painstaking coalition bargaining – or possibly another election – while Netanyahu remains in power in a caretaker capacity.
The outcome will have implications for US-Israeli relations, which have been dominated by the joint fight against Iran, stalled Gaza peace efforts and signs of eroding US public support for Israel.
The uncertainty comes at a sensitive moment for Trump, when he and Netanyahu have threatened to join in another round of attacks against Iran.
“Israeli politics can be messy,” said Aaron David Miller, a former Middle East adviser in Democratic and Republican administrations. From the US perspective, he said, “it would be good to get some clarity, but that’s easier said than done.”
WHICH OUTCOME WOULD TRUMP PREFER?
Netanyahu – a consummate political survivor who has had a close but sometimes turbulent relationship with Trump dating back decades – may have survived again. He is the longest-serving Israeli prime minister and the only one the US president has ever worked with.
Eisenkot, who projected an image as a political outsider and security-minded former general during the campaign, has seen his governing chances dimmed but not extinguished. He is not known to have ever met Trump.
Some analysts say creation of a broad unity government keeping Netanyahu in power might serve Trump’s interest in a politically stable Israeli partner. But neither side has shown a willingness to take that path.
Asked whether he was going to get involved in an effort to form a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump told Axios on Wednesday he hadn’t thought about it, adding: “I will take a look.”
WHAT DOES THE ELECTION MEAN FOR THE WAR WITH IRAN?
Topping the list is how Trump might engage with Israel in the war against Iran, which has rocked the Middle East. The eight-month-old conflict has disrupted global energy supplies, pushed up US gasoline prices and driven down his approval ratings, imperiling his Republicans’ control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump, in his October 18 endorsement, insisted he wanted Netanyahu to remain in power to help him soon “finish the job” against Iran. The president said overnight that Netanyahu, who outperformed pre-election polls, had done “very well” and that his backing had boosted the Israeli leader.
Trump has repeatedly signaled that the US and Israel could restart attacks on Iran after the midterms, with some critics, including in Israel, suggesting Netanyahu might see it as a way to bolster his political standing as caretaker prime minister.
Jonathan Panikoff, a former deputy US national intelligence officer on the Middle East, said any future Israeli leadership would likely be on the same page as Trump if he decides to escalate from the current stalemate with Israel’s regional arch-foe.
“It’s hard to imagine any real daylight between them on that point,” said Panikoff, now at the Atlantic Council think tank in Washington.
Where Netanyahu and many Israelis have sometimes differed with Trump is when he has offered concessions in now-stalled negotiations with the Islamic Republic.
WHAT ARE THE IMPLICATIONS FOR GAZA PEACE EFFORTS?
No matter how Israel’s next government shapes up, there is little reason to believe there will be any sweeping shift in tough policies toward the Palestinians.
This doesn’t bode well for breaking the diplomatic deadlock between Israel and Hamas and fully implementing Trump’s Gaza peace plan following the war there. Israel, in response to the militants’ deadly cross-border attack, leveled much of the enclave and killed tens of thousands of Palestinians.
Administration officials have privately expressed frustration over what they see as intransigence by Netanyahu, who has insisted that Hamas must first disarm.
Eisenkot, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, stressed his military credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically during the election campaign. He has vowed to break with Netanyahu’s far-right coalition allies, but not with the hawkish approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack.
Like Netanyahu, Eisenkot opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas’ military wing must be destroyed.
But he has pledged to prevent violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, which Netanyahu’s government has been accused of tolerating. Settler attacks have drawn criticism in recent weeks from US officials worried the territory could become another Middle East flashpoint.
WHAT ABOUT ISRAEL’S GROWING ISOLATION?
Even as Israel’s political climate is expected to remain unsettled for some time, Trump may have to contend with what opinion polls project could be the Democrats’ takeover of one or both chambers of Congress in the midterms.
That could mean increased pressure from Democrats, whose support for Israel plunged over its conduct in the Gaza war, to curb billions of dollars in US aid and weapons supplies.
Some members of Trump’s MAGA base have also become increasingly critical of Israel, accusing it of having misled Trump – who campaigned for a second term on a promise to avoid foreign military interventions – into believing Iran could easily be defeated.
Trump, in an interview with Axios in June, cautioned Netanyahu about Israel’s deepening international isolation, and most analysts say the trend may be irreversible, even with a new government.
(Reporting By Matt Spetalnick; Editing by Don Durfee and Howard Goller)

"Many of those fleeing are women and children. While some are staying with relatives and host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations like schools and churches," Mohammed-Cole said.
She emphasized that food is the most urgent priority, along with safe drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation, and healthcare.
The UNHCR has deployed an emergency team to Moyale and is collaborating closely with Kenya's Department of Refugee Services, county authorities, and partners, including UN agencies and the Kenya Red Cross Society, to support the local response.
Mohammed-Cole added that the UNHCR is mobilizing emergency relief supplies, including essential household items and temporary shelters, to assist nearly 12,000 people, with plans to scale up operations as needs increase.
The agency is also supporting ongoing assessments to evaluate protection and humanitarian requirements. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: Australian curator hails meaningful homecoming of repatriated Chinese cultural relics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
01:27:06 CST
02:27:06 KST

Carol Cains, a senior curator at the National Gallery of Australia (NGA), receives an interview with Xinhua in Canberra, Australia, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Chu Chen/Xinhua)
CANBERRA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- "One part of me will be sorry to see them go, but most of me is very, very happy that they're going home," said Carol Cains, a senior curator at the National Gallery of Australia (NGA), on Wednesday, referring to the two Chinese cultural relics returned by Australia to China.
The NGA handed over the heads of a military official statue and a civil official statue to China's National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA) in Canberra on Wednesday. Both relics date back to the Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127).
A DECADE OF PROVENANCE RESEARCH
According to Cains, the two relics went into the museum's collection through donation in 1995. But the museum didn't investigate their provenance at the time. In 2015, one of the museum's volunteer guides, Janet Smith, noticed a 1991 book by Anne Paladin that investigated the sculptural figures along "the spirit roads" around the imperial mausoleum in China. The book contains photographs of works that seemed very similar to the two sculptural heads. That's when Cains and her coworkers began investigating the background of the two pieces.
In 2025, NGA received notification through the Chinese Embassy in Australia in Canberra that the NCHA, working with China's Ministry of Public Security and cultural heritage and public security authorities in China's Henan Province, had submitted a memorandum and supporting evidence, formally requesting the return of the two relics.
"We found that the style and the features of our heads here in the national collection match those of the twin pairs of some of the heads that were still intact on the mausoleum," she said. "At that point, we were finally able to pinpoint the place of origin of the sculptures here in the collection, the date of their creation, and their cultural significance in an absolutely firm and incontrovertible way."
That was when they started discussions in depth to try and really move towards repatriation, she said.
"The heads were no longer suitable to be held within the national collection at the gallery, because they didn't belong to us," she noted.
CULTURAL AND ARTISTIC SIGNIFICANCE
As a senior curator who has long studied Asian and Pacific art, Cains said that now that she really understands their context, she can "understand their significance."
"Initially, I appreciate them artistically because of the fineness of their carving plus their size. They're very impressive. The thought of them attached to their original figures is just so overwhelming as an artistic creation," she said.
Cains said the two works must have been extremely artistically impressive and culturally important, because they're part of the whole Chinese respect for ancestors and the structure of Chinese society.
Noting the fact that the two heads were part of pairs, she said there was an identical pair across the "spirit road" to them, adding that hopefully they can be reunited one day.
COOPERATION BEYOND REPATRIATION
Cains said it is a great opportunity for her and her coworkers to collaborate with their peers at the NCHA as well as the Chinese Embassy in Australia to make sure that the relics can be returned to their rightful owner, adding that she is glad to see the process is "very efficient and quick."
Calling the UNESCO 1970 Convention on the means of prohibiting and preventing the illicit import, export and transfer of ownership of cultural property "an evolutionary process," she said it has formed an ethical framework for collecting and shaping the way the art market works.
"The whole ethical framework is now part of an institutional transformation that is happening internationally, where cultural institutions like galleries and museums are working from a kind of colonial acquisition and ownership model towards a much more collaborative, ethical and culturally sensitive model where we seek to learn from each other rather than just impose a framework," she said.
Cains said, as a curator, she is just a temporary steward of the works. "The way forward in the future for sharing cultural antiquities and sharing culture is through loans, mutually agreed loans, because that's a great way to exchange works of art and inform each other about our cultures."
It is a very rewarding process, she noted. ■

The right-wing lawmaker left after receiving a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports in connection with a money-laundering investigation, in which he denies wrongdoing.
Below is a timeline of the events. All times are Brasilia time (GMT-3).

• World leaders quickly recognize Lula’s victory, but US President Donald Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei initially remain silent

WEDNESDAY — ARRIVAL IN THE UNITED STATES

====================================================================================================

Trump expands hunt for noncitizen voters with broad subpoena campaign before midterms
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:27:02 CET
02:27:02 KST

By Peter Eisler, Ned Parker, Mike Spector and Tom Hals
Oct 28 - The Trump administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas demanding records on tens of thousands of voters in at least 13 states, part of an escalating effort ahead of next week’s midterm elections to uncover evidence of unlawful voting by people who aren’t US citizens.
Most of the subpoenas documented by Reuters were issued to state and local election officials in the past three months, though some date to the start of the year. Many were previously unreported, revealing a federal effort to identify potential noncitizen voters that is broader than publicly known. It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in US federal elections. Legal experts say the records could be used to contest results in close midterm races, despite scant evidence that voting by noncitizens is widespread.
Reuters identified the subpoenas through public-records requests and interviews with local and state officials. Many were issued in Democratic strongholds, including Minneapolis, Philadelphia, Los Angeles and other California cities. But they also reach into Republican-leaning states with competitive races, including Texas, Kansas and Georgia.
At least 49 of the subpoenas were issued under the authority of grand juries, indicating they are tied to criminal investigations and making them generally harder to challenge in court than administrative subpoenas issued directly by federal agencies.
The White House says noncitizen voting is a significant problem that warrants the sweeping federal effort to identify and prosecute such cases, including through the deployment of hundreds of federal law enforcement agents. It has vowed to keep the effort a top priority. “The Trump administration is sending a clear message that anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to Reuters. “Only Americans should be electing America’s leaders.”
Multiple studies and a Reuters analysis have found that noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare.
The subpoenas are one piece of an expansive campaign targeting noncitizen voting. Armed Homeland Security agents have questioned residents in several states about their immigration status and voting, while the Justice Department has sued 30 states that refused to provide voter rolls containing sensitive personal information such as driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. A federal judge largely halted Homeland Security’s field operations in nine states on October 21, and courts have ruled against the Justice Department in every voter-roll case so far. Many of those cases remain under appeal.
The subpoenas issued by the Justice Department and Homeland Security offer another way to obtain the same voter information, which legal experts say could figure in disputes over midterm election results. Elections are administered primarily by the states, with the federal government playing a limited role. Under most state laws, only losing candidates or voters can challenge election results, but the Justice Department could still take legal action to delay or block certification of winners.
Heavily Democratic California offers a glimpse of how such a fight could unfold. Its congressional seats could decide who controls the US House of Representatives. The Justice Department alleged this month that more than 20,000 “likely” noncitizens in California had received mail ballots and demanded any ballots cast by them not be counted until their citizenship was verified. California officials refused and called the list unreliable, saying a review of 200 registrations found nearly 40% appeared to be US-born.
The Justice Department declined to confirm or deny its use of subpoenas in noncitizen voter investigations, but said it “will enforce the law wherever the evidence leads.” The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to questions.
Some election officials and lawyers told Reuters the noncitizen voting investigations could bolster a false narrative that American elections are vulnerable to widespread fraud. In a closely divided country, Trump and his allies could use those claims to attack the legitimacy of narrow defeats, particularly in tightly contested races, they said.
The subpoenas issued by the administration are “clearly a distraction” for local and state election officials, said Paul Charlton, a former US attorney for Arizona in the Republican administration of George W. Bush. “In my time as a federal prosecutor, we prosecuted people who shouldn’t have voted, but it was so infrequent as to never even come close to altering the outcome of an election.”
Since Trump returned to office, prosecutors have accused at least 147 people of illegally voting under a federal “voting by aliens” statute, including 102 since the start of September, according to a Reuters analysis of court filings and federal records. The cases – most of which remain unresolved – amount to fewer than one for every million people who voted in 2024.
The investigations are “setting up” post-election challenges that, while legally weak, could sow chaos, said Ben Berwick, a former Justice Department attorney who served in the Obama and Trump administrations and now leads the election law and litigation team at Protect Democracy, an advocacy group. Trump-aligned candidates who lose could argue that suspected noncitizen votes made it impossible to determine the rightful winner and seek to have ballots or even the election result thrown out, Berwick said.
The stakes are high. Democrats need to gain four Senate seats and five House seats to take control of Congress. Winning either chamber would give them power to launch investigations into the Trump administration and Trump family business dealings.
A BROADENING SEARCH
The subpoenas identified by Reuters varied widely in scope, from records on individual voters to demands for entire local voter rolls containing tens of thousands of names. None of the jurisdictions contacted said they were resisting the subpoenas.
In the US, subpoenas are legally binding orders requiring recipients to testify or produce documents or other evidence.
In Minnesota, a traditionally Democratic state with an unexpectedly competitive US Senate race, the Trump administration issued subpoenas for voting records on dozens of people in the Minneapolis-area counties of Anoka and Hennepin, where the administration has carried out a major federal immigration crackdown. To date, the Justice Department has charged at least eight people from the two counties with voting as noncitizens. All the cases are ongoing and no one has been convicted.
In California, the Justice Department has issued at least 17 subpoenas to governments in Democratic-leaning jurisdictions, including Los Angeles and San Diego counties. The state is home to at least two districts with competitive US House races and is typically slow to count ballots, with final results sometimes taking weeks.
Some voting experts said the Trump administration and its allies could use the period before California finishes counting ballots to amplify allegations of noncitizen voting and challenge the legitimacy of close races. Reuters also identified previously unreported subpoenas seeking voter records that were issued to Marin County and Fresno County. Fresno lies within California’s 22nd Congressional District, a closely watched midterm battleground.
In Philadelphia, a Democratic stronghold, local officials confirmed receiving at least four subpoenas for voting records. In reliably Democratic Massachusetts, one of the states where federal courts blocked the administration’s voter roll demands, a Trump-backed US attorney has targeted at least eight cities and towns with grand jury subpoenas, six of them not previously reported, Reuters found.
At least three of the Massachusetts subpoenas required officials to provide a list of all registered voters, including names, addresses, party affiliations, birth dates, voting status and voter identification numbers. An accompanying letter, obtained from one city through a public records request, urged recipients “not to disclose the existence of this subpoena or the fact of your compliance therewith, to anyone,” but said the request for secrecy was not mandatory.
In Lynn, Massachusetts, a city with a large Hispanic population, federal prosecutors subpoenaed records for 25 to 30 people. “Up until now, they’ve found one instance of someone voting in an election that shouldn’t have been voting,” James Lamanna, the city’s clerk and election chief, told Reuters. “This doesn’t reach the level of something serious and pervasive that it would jeopardize the integrity of an election.”
Other states where subpoenas have been issued include Arizona, Washington, New York, Connecticut, Utah and Michigan.
CLAIMS UNDER SCRUTINY
Trump has repeatedly portrayed noncitizen voting as a grave threat to election integrity. The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank that has raised similar concerns for years, argues that weak verification procedures create opportunities for illegal voting and that voter fraud could affect the outcome of a close election.
Voting-rights groups counter that repeated reviews have found no evidence of noncitizen voting on a scale that has changed an election outcome. Thousands of noncitizens have been mistakenly registered to vote because of clerical errors or software glitches, often while obtaining driver’s licenses, but state and local officials say only a small fraction actually cast ballots.
In a nationally televised address in July, Trump said his administration had identified more than 275,000 noncitizen voters, which the White House said were in four Democratic-leaning states. State officials disputed those assertions. In Nevada, federal officials initially claimed to have identified nearly 16,000 potential noncitizens on the voter rolls before revising the figure to fewer than 200. Nevada officials later concluded those remaining individuals were all citizens.
Federal prosecutors are continuing to report suspected new cases. In Washington state this week, they said they had identified more than 400 noncitizens who appear to be registered to vote. They asked state election officials to set aside any current ballots from those individuals until their citizenship could be verified. The Washington secretary of state’s office told Reuters it has received about 60 federal subpoenas in recent weeks seeking information on individual voters.
The administration has also intensified its enforcement efforts. On October 19, the Justice Department said it had charged 28 people in California, all legal permanent residents, with voting as noncitizens or making false statements on voting or naturalization paperwork. California election officials have called the campaign a politically motivated distraction, noting that the cases uncovered so far amount to a tiny fraction of the state’s more than 23 million registered voters.
The administration has also threatened legal consequences for election officials who resist its demands. California officials objected after federal authorities threatened to prosecute election officials who did not act on the list of 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters. Acting US Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, who spearheaded the administration’s claims in California, acknowledged last week that the list could include US citizens.
“We’re not perfect,” he said.
(Peter Eisler reported from Washington. Ned Parker and Mike Spector reported from New York. Tom Hals reported from Wilmington, Delaware. Additional reporting by Nate Raymond, Linda So and Indiana University’s Arnolt Center for Investigative Journalism students, Emerson Elledge, Mary Demarco, Katherine Maners, and Kristen Dickey. Editing by Jason Szep)
