====================================================================================================

The Inside Story of Why Apple Finally Brought a Touch Display to the Mac
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:15:16 UTC
02:15:16 KST

It’s a bright day in Cupertino. Apple’s new CEO strolls to an outdoor seating area within the company’s otherworldly ring-shaped headquarters and pulls up a chair. An employee notes the angle and asks if he minds the sun. John Ternus doesn’t mind at all.
Nearly two months into his tenure, he’s been busy. While the tech world buzzes about AI agents and the upcoming IPO of a company reporting spectacular losses, Ternus’ leadership of a ridiculously profitable firm has so far been defined by a sequence of significant launches—the long-awaited foldable iPhone, a household device that can control digital appliances, new Mac Minis, and AirPods. Intentionally or not, all that activity sends a message that, even as AI dominates the public imagination, hardware products still rule.
Ternus doesn’t endorse that take, but he doesn’t object when I suggest it. “We’ve been working on these products for quite some time,” he says. “It feels like everyone here is just kind of riding high right now, enjoying it.”
I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.
Ternus beams. “Who knew?”
We are referring to the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display that Apple is releasing today at an event in Los Angeles. It’s got a mighty M5 Pro or M5 Max chip and a show-stopping tandem OLED screen. (A tandem screen has multiple light-emitting layers, producing more dramatic contrasts.) But its most conspicuous feature is one that’s been deeply woven into iPhones, iPads, and even Apple Watches for years but not Apple’s laptops: a touch display. After years of resistance, a Mac screen has finally gone digital. As in fingers.
This turnaround is a big deal to Apple fans. Ternus shrugs off the drama. “The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”
Ternus and Apple want to make sure that the Mac faithful don’t panic that the 42-year-old franchise is losing its identity to Apple’s gangbusters mobile products. “We needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”
Apple has a long history of refusing to implement certain desirable features, only to pivot when it feels the time is right. Steve Jobs once proclaimed iPods would never do video, until they did. He also once said “no one’s going to buy” a jumbo-size phone—and then Apple released a supersized iPhone 6. Then there was that time Jobs declared styluses inappropriate for tablets. Now the Apple Pencil works with iPads and the brand-new Duo.
The 2026 MacBook Pro instantly qualifies as the canonical example of this switcheroo. Apple executives had been on record regarding touch on PCs as a misbegotten idea. Never mind that just about every PC maker not headquartered in Cupertino has implemented touch on their laptops. And customers of Microsoft, Dell, Acer, Lenovo, and HP have snapped them up. Clearly, people wanted touch on their laptop displays. Even toddlers knew it—put some rug rats in front of a computer and their little arms shoot straight to the screen in futile attempts to swipe and scroll as they do on their iPads. People were baffled why Apple—the pioneer in touch displays since the iPhone—was so steadfast in its rejection.
In 2015, while doing a story about a new iMac, I pressed Phil Schiller, then the senior vice president of worldwide product marketing, on this very question. Usually, top Apple executives field such queries with cryptic remarks. In this case, Schiller began a filibuster. “I’m going to get a little bit philosophical,” he said, then launched into what I later described as the Grand Unified Theory of Apple Hardware.
He explained that every Apple hardware product—the Watch, iPad, iMac, MacBook—is basically a computer and a piece of glass. Each one has a specific function. And each one has an interface appropriate to the hardware. Multitouch is fine for products like the iPhone, he said—but not the Macintosh. He provided two reasons: ergonomics and the software interface.
“From the ergonomic standpoint, we have studied this pretty extensively, and we believe that on a desktop scenario, where you have a fixed keyboard, having to reach up to do touch interfaces is uncomfortable,” he told me.
As for the interface, Schiller argued that Apple’s two main operating systems were built on different design principles. The iPhone and iPad’s iOS was multitouch from the get-go, and didn’t use macOS conventions that require precision, such as cursors and tiny boxes to close windows. “These two worlds are different on purpose, and that’s a good thing—we can optimize around the best experience for each of those and not try to mesh them together into a least-common-denominator experience,” he told me.
A year later, when Apple introduced a MacBook Pro with the ill-fated “touch bar”—a dynamic strip of virtual function keys above the keyboard’s top row—Schiller doubled down on the view that touch should never find its way into a Mac display. He said that such a move would mean totally redesigning the menu bar for fingers, and that would clash with the experience of pointer devices like a touchpad or mouse. “You can’t optimize for both,” he said.
To double-check this assumption, Apple conducted user tests with touchscreens on Mac. “What the heck, we could be wrong,” Schiller told me then. “We’ve absolutely come away with the belief that it isn’t the right thing to do. Our instincts were correct.”
When I met with Apple executives Johny Srouji and Greg Joswiak this week to discuss the touchscreen MacBook Pro, you bet I invoked Schiller’s list of concerns. (Apple’s reps chose not to make Schiller, who now holds the title of “Apple Fellow,” available for an interview. In fact, they laughed when I asked.) It wasn’t only Schiller drawing a red line. In 2021, Ternus told journalist Joanna Stern, “The Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven’t really felt a reason to change that.”
“Ten years is a very, very long time,” says Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer. “Many things have changed, whether it's the display technology, the custom silicon, et cetera.” Eventually, he told me, the confluence of chips, display tech, and software architecture “met our bar.” “I like my engineers to be gated by physics, not imagination or timelines,” he says.
Joswiak, who holds Schiller’s old title of SVP of worldwide marketing, concedes that touch was overdue, at least for users with sophisticated needs. Its pro customers—engineers, scientists, software developers, and media creators—were impatient with Apple for its failure to let them interact directly with the screen. “Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone,” Joswiak says. “So this is something that they’re natural with. There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.”
Between the lines, Srouji and Joswiak seem to consider their competitors’ touchscreen implementations shabby and lazy. The Apple ethos, as every one of its executives will happily explain to anyone who asks, is an expectation of quality that’s sky-high. “If you’re working on something easy, you’re wasting your time,” says Srouji, who has been at Apple since 2008 and has pretty much driven its innovation by spearheading the company’s charge to custom-build silicon.
“The easy things, I want to outsource,” he continues. “So the custom silicon is hard. The touch is hard. The display is hard. Everything we build is hard.” This swaggering philosophy dates from the Steve Jobs days and, in 2026, stands in contrast to the endgame of the ascendant AI industry, which hopes to turn over the toughest parts of industrial production to superintelligent entities.
Srouji presents Mac touch as a suite of innovations, starting with that screen that Ternus described as the Mac’s best ever. It also involves custom silicon and a rearchitected thermal system to prevent the display from feeling hot when people pinch, stretch, and swipe on it. Srouji contends that current touchscreen laptops suffer from “wobble” when fingers make contact with the display; to minimize this effect, Apple has redesigned the hinge on the MacBook Pro screen to stabilize it.
When I get a demo of the 16-inch version (as with previous Pros, it’s also available in a 14-inch version), I see what they mean about the display. It’s noticeably dense and bright, and the obsidian blacks are the deepest I’ve seen on a computer screen. In part because the OLED screen doesn’t require backlighting, this MacBook weighs less than its predecessor.
As a pair of Apple managers take the MacBook through its paces, I see how Apple has addressed some of Schiller’s decade-old concerns, like having to redesign the menu bar for fingers. While it looks the same, when you move a finger over a menu item, it expands to allow you to select your choice with precision. Some of the objects on the screen, like the traffic-light buttons that close or hide windows, also get bigger when you touch them.
They show me how the touch tech can handle precision tasks, like color grading in the video editing software DaVinci Resolve, or tweaking a soundtrack on Logic Pro, Apple’s high-end audio workstation. One innovation, not just for pros, is a new gesture to pull down the “Dynamic Island,” that black oval hosting ongoing tasks that has made its way to Mac from iPhone. An expanded version floats on the screen like a widget, enabling easy access to Siri responses and Spotlight search.
But what about greasy fingers messing up the screen? I was told that the new display has an anti-reflective outer coating that will require no more cleaning than your normal non-interactive screen.
Apple clearly hopes that the MacBook Pro launch puts an exclamation point on the burst of product announcements that Apple customers are still absorbing. For the foldable Duo, some customers are impatiently waiting for delivery dates that stretch into January. (Lines were long at Apple stores last Friday, when the device went on sale, and Joswiak personally greeted those who queued up at Apple’s Fifth Avenue store in New York City.)
I ask Srouji whether Apple is making a statement with its armada of new products, maybe as a way to say that in a year dominated by AI obsession, Apple is still here. He responds much as his new boss did, contending that Apple is simply sticking to its game plan. “We’re here to build the most amazing products in the world, and we want to ship them when we believe it’s ready and complete,” says Srouji. “That’s the statement we’re making. I think everyone knows we’re here.”
While longtime users will be happy to hear that a Macintosh now has a touchscreen, those with limited budgets will be disappointed. Apple’s current stance—that touch-on-a-Mac display is most appropriate to the “pro” crowd—rationalizes an astronomical price tag: The new MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. Financial analyst Neil Cybart, who got an early MacBook Pro briefing, thinks that serious professionals will pay up. “People are in search of value, and that means going for products that leverage technology to improve what they’re doing,” he says.
When I ask Ternus about the timeline, or even the possibility, of seeing touch displays on less exorbitantly priced MacBook Airs and iMacs, he shakes his head. “You’ve been doing this a long time,” he says. “You know I will never tell you anything about our future.”
I don’t know why I bothered to ask. If Ternus said that touch would never happen on a MacBook Air, who would believe him? I’d be back at The Ring a year later, hearing that Apple had finally figured out a way to do it right.
Let us know what you think about this article. Submit a letter to the editor at [email protected].

The UN World Food Program (WFP) chief Luke Lindberg said Wednesday that the hunger situation in the Gaza Strip is "unacceptable" as he pledged to defend his staff against attacks. 
Speaking at a news conference at UN headquarters in New York, Lindberg said that "there is a very serious need" in Gaza, citing funding cuts as a major constraint on the agency's work. 
Asked how he would address Israeli troops firing on WFP convoys, given his White House connections, Lindberg said staff security is "the number one concern for me." 
"I will absolutely stand up for our employees, no matter where on Earth they are located," he said. 
He added that "if anywhere in the world there are people attacking humanitarians, I will absolutely do what I can to protect them from violence against them and their families." 
Outlining his priorities, Lindberg said: "First and foremost, it is protecting and empowering our staff members. Humanitarians have been killed all over the world in the past two years, at unprecedented levels, and it’s unacceptable." 
"Over 700 people in the last few years have been killed trying to save other people’s lives, and nobody should lose their life trying to save somebody else’s," he added. 
Asked about the WFP's partnership with the US, which backed his candidacy, Lindberg said the "United States plays a critical role. It is the largest funder for the World Food Program." 
"When I was nominated for this role by the United States, President (Donald) Trump personally called me," he said. "I have a great relationship with many members of the Trump administration." 
Lindberg stressed the need for broader donor support. "There is no one nation, no one entity that can do this alone. We have to do it together," he added.

France expects next UN chief to reform, strengthen organization: Foreign minister

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Wednesday that France expects the next UN chief to reform and strengthen the world body.
“What we expect from a future secretary-general is that he can reform the United Nations to strengthen it, and certainly not discredit it in order to better bury it,” Barrot told the French Senate.
Barrot said France would not accept efforts by major powers to weaken or paralyze the UN, which he described as an organization founded to serve peace, development and human rights.
He said international cooperation and multilateralism were essential to protecting people from threats including war, AI, climate change and pandemics.
France, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, was making efforts to reform the organization and make it more legitimate and representative, he said.
Barrot also cited a French initiative to limit the use of veto powers by permanent Security Council members, saying it aimed to help protect civilians in Sudan, Ukraine, the Gaza Strip and Iran when they are targeted.

German police arrest two suspected of planning sabotage attacks for Russia, Spiegel says
Oct 28 - Police have arrested two Belarusian nationals suspected of planning sabotage attacks in southern Germany, the Munich General Prosecutor's Office said on Wednesday, with Der Spiegel magazine reporting they were working on behalf of Russia.
The suspects allegedly planned to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area, the prosecutor's office told Reuters.

Romanian organized crime prosecutors have said they are seeking the extradition of the two suspects apprehended in Germany and one Ukrainian detained in Poland who were all suspected of involvement in the arson case. REUTERS

Israeli opposition seeks Arab party talks to oust Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:10:04 UTC
02:10:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli opposition seeks talks with Arab parties to oust Netanyahu
Israel's opposition has approached Arab parties to discuss cooperation on forming a new government, following an election in which high turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel helped deny Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a parliamentary majority.
Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Arab Movement for Change and a member of the Knesset, revealed that opposition parties had contacted Arab political leaders to coordinate efforts to replace the current Knesset speaker and explore future cooperation.
Tibi said Arab parties were not seeking ministerial portfolios in the next government but intended to use their parliamentary strength to end Netanyahu's rule.
He credited the surge in Palestinian voter turnout with preventing Netanyahu from securing the majority needed to form a government, opening the door to an alternative that could end the far-right coalition's grip on power.
The Joint List would support an opposition-backed candidate to replace the Knesset speaker, Tibi said, while condemning politicians who refuse to cooperate with Arab parties.
"Whoever insists on not forming alliances with Arab parties will lose power," he said, describing attempts to portray Arab votes as illegitimate as racist.
Arab parties offer Eisenkot parliamentary support
According to Israeli public broadcaster Kan, Tibi confirmed that the Joint List was negotiating with the opposition's "change camp" to facilitate the formation of a new government without formally joining the coalition.
"I want to do everything I can in the Knesset to pave the way for the announcement of a government," he said. "We will probably not be an integral part of this government, but there are other arrangements and possibilities."
Sources familiar with the discussions said the Joint List had offered opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot a parliamentary "safety net", similar to the arrangement under which Arab lawmakers supported Yitzhak Rabin's government in 1992.
Such an arrangement could allow Arab parties to support a government from outside the coalition without accepting ministerial positions.
The sources said contacts with Eisenkot's camp had continued over recent days and remained ongoing.
Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen also called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to remove Netanyahu from power.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government must engage in dialogue with us and pave the way for the change that the public in Israel is seeking," Jabareen told Israeli media.
Netanyahu incites against Arab voters
The developments follow an election campaign in which Netanyahu repeatedly warned supporters about rising turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu shared photographs and videos focusing on Arab lawmaker Ahmad Tibi and high turnout in Arab communities.
In one post on X, Netanyahu shared an image purportedly showing voters outside a polling station in Rahat, a predominantly Arab city in southern Israel.
"This is what is happening today in Rahat. You cannot stay at home; go out immediately and vote Likud. We are fighting for our homeland," he wrote.
Meanwhile, Democrats leader Yair Golan suggested that Arab parties should be included in opposition efforts to form a new government.
"Every member of the Knesset elected through the legal process is a legitimate part of our political system," Golan said.
However, far-right Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman rejected cooperation with Arab parties, instead calling for a rebellion within Likud against Netanyahu.
Lieberman accused Netanyahu of destroying the nationalist camp, saying the prime minister had behaved "like the head of a criminal organisation".

Sudan war and inflation leave families struggling to survive in Khartoum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:09:05 UTC
02:09:05 KST

Sudan war and inflation leave families struggling to survive in Khartoum
Soaring food prices and shrinking incomes force families in Sudan’s capital to borrow money and skip meals.
Khartoum, Sudan – Rasha Abdelaziz Musa works every day for seven hours selling tea. But by the time she finishes for the day at 10pm, she’s still unsure if she has enough to feed her four children.
Musa, 39, is doing her best, but her earnings are increasingly no longer enough to cover soaring food prices in the Sudanese capital.
Her husband, a member of the Sudanese military, has spent more than eight months on the front lines of the country’s war, in which the military has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since 2023. Musa has not heard from him for months, and he has sent no money.
In his absence, Musa has been left to provide for their children, who attend kindergarten, primary and secondary school.
Musa told Al Jazeera that feeding her family costs about 40,000 Sudanese pounds per day ($4 at the parallel-market exchange rate) before accounting for rent, household essentials and other expenses.
Some of the family staples are ful medames, a dish of stewed fava beans, or lentils. When lentils are too expensive, Musa serves taamiya, or falafel, sandwiches.
Prices regularly change, and Musa often ends the day in debt to the traders she gets her food from.
Large families struggle
Musa is not alone in struggling to cover her family’s daily expenses.
Ahmed Youssef, 61, supports a family of 12 through his work in a butcher’s shop and as an occasional intermediary in livestock sales. He can earn 90,000 to 140,000 pounds ($9 to $14) when a deal succeeds, but that income is irregular.
He told Al Jazeera that his household spends more than 100,000 Sudanese pounds ($10) daily and his income is no longer enough to support the family.
“One income is no longer enough to cover the family’s needs, and sometimes my older children have to work to help meet expenses,” Youssef told Al Jazeera.
Ali Fadil supports a family of 10. Without a permanent job, he goes to the market each morning to look for work. Some days, the 57-year-old earns enough to buy food, but on other days, he finds no work at all. And yet his daily expenses still reach about 70,000 pounds ($7), with rising prices adding to the financial pressure he faces.
“Sometimes I skip meals so I can pay for school fees or medical costs,” he said. “I also borrow money to meet other obligations.”
Food prices rise as Sudanese pound weakens
A survey of four local markets in the Khartoum State area by Al Jazeera last week found that prices for several essential foods had risen sharply within days, making it increasingly difficult for families to plan their spending.
A kilogramme (2.2.lb) of sugar cost about 10,000 pounds ($1), up from 9,000 pounds ($0.90) two days earlier. A litre (1 quart) of cooking oil rose to 25,000 pounds ($2.50) from 20,000 pounds ($2) while a loaf of bread costs 500 pounds ($0.05), compared with 300 pounds ($0.03) a week earlier.
Lentils cost about 10,000 pounds ($1) per kilogramme, up from 8,000 pounds ($0.80), and rice was priced at 13,000 pounds ($1.30) per kilogramme, up from 10,000 pounds ($1). Powdered milk reached 70,000 pounds ($7) per kilogramme, up from 60,000 ($6) two days earlier.
The Sudanese pound has also continued to weaken. According to exchange rates monitored by Al Jazeera, $1 was trading at 10,050 Sudanese pounds on the parallel market on Friday, compared with 9,500 the previous day.
Food inflation adds to pressure on households
Official figures offer further evidence of the rising cost of living, particularly in Khartoum and other urban areas.
According to Sudan’s Central Bureau of Statistics, prices across the country were 28 percent higher in September than a year earlier, up from 26 percent in August. Prices rose by 7.5 percent in September alone, more than double the increase recorded the previous month.
Food prices have risen even faster. Across Sudan, food and beverages cost nearly 37 percent more in September than a year earlier, up from an annual increase of about 21 percent in August. In September alone, food prices jumped by more than 17 percent.
The situation was particularly severe in Khartoum State, where prices were nearly 60 percent higher than a year earlier. Prices rose by more than 15 percent in September alone, following an increase of nearly 9 percent in August.
That sharp increase comes as the capital region struggles to recover from widespread destruction caused by the war. Although displaced residents have begun returning and businesses are gradually reopening since the military recaptured the state from the RSF last year, damaged infrastructure and rising transport costs continue to constrain the availability of goods.
The return of residents has also increased demand for essential supplies, further driving up prices. In September, fuel shortages hit the capital as consumption rose faster than supplies could be replenished.
Urban areas have generally been hit harder than rural communities. Food prices in towns and cities were 55 percent higher than a year earlier, up from about 40 percent in August. Overall, prices in urban areas rose by 40 percent over the past year, compared with about 21 percent in rural areas.
The war is the main driver of these increases, disrupting livelihoods and supply chains. According to the World Bank, Sudan’s economy shrank by an estimated 29 percent in 2023 and a further 14 percent in 2024 as the war devastated businesses, disrupted agricultural production and eliminated jobs.
The conflict has also forced millions of people from their homes with nearly 8.9 million people still internally displaced as of April, according to the International Organization for Migration.
War destroys livelihoods
Journalist and economic affairs specialist Khalid Teks said Sudan’s economic deterioration began long before the war. Falling oil production after South Sudan’s secession in 2011 worsened conditions as did the depreciation of the pound, cash shortages, international isolation, political conflict and corruption in the years preceding the removal of President Omar al-Bashir in 2019.
Teks said political instability during the power transition undermined Sudan’s economic performance, and deep reforms were not implemented before war broke out in 2023. The conflict devastated infrastructure and productive sectors, depleted savings and disrupted economic activity. The climate has also been a factor. Strong agricultural production in 2024 was followed by concern over limited rainfall this year and possible food shortages after the harvest begins in November.
Teks told Al Jazeera that families increasingly deplete their savings and sell their possessions to cover everyday expenses.
He also pointed to disruptions to remittance channels, which many Sudanese households rely on for financial support.
Teks called for easier humanitarian access, an end to the war, direct support for vulnerable households and low-interest loans for small businesses and craft enterprises.
“The government needs to provide direct support through dedicated funds and the Zakat Chamber, facilitate humanitarian organisations and offer affordable loans for small businesses and vocational activities,” Teks said. “This could help reopen markets and workshops and expand microfinance.

soon to open on copenhagen’s paper island
Kengo Kuma & Associates‘ KAI Water Culture House is set to open on December 5th, 2026, on Copenhagen‘s Papirøen (Paper Island). Bringing ten swimming pools to the city’s harborfront, the 5,800-square-meter spa introduces a new place for swimming and bathing along a waterfront that has gradually shifted from industrial use toward public recreation.
The building is recognizable at once by its five irregular brick towers, which rise above a continuous band of glass at ground level. Their sloping walls form a clustered silhouette along the quay, with spaces between the volumes opening toward the sky. From the harbor, the heavy masonry appears to hover over the transparent base. This lends the building an unusual sense of lightness, even with its monolithic presence.
five brick towers shaped around the water below
The towers in Copenhagen take their forms from the swimming pools beneath them, with each volume responding to its interior layout. Approximately 300,000 handmade bricks cover the angular surfaces, their varying gray tones relating to the city’s surrounding harbor architecture. The masonry is laid in a stepped pattern that gives the sloping walls a textured finish, particularly where the surfaces catch the changing daylight.
Across the brick facades, 403 windows of different sizes create small openings toward the city. Some bring daylight deep into the bathing areas, while others frame views across the harbor. Inside, the walls rise above the water at steep angles, creating tall bathing chambers where the enclosed architecture feels almost geological. The architects led by Kengo Kuma shape the building’s tallest volume, known as the Culture Tower, to house spaces for cultural activities and community gatherings.
an outdoor swimming pool sits between the towers
Perhaps the most unusual part of KAI is its Valley Pool, an open-air swimming basin positioned on the first floor between the five brick towers. Here, visitors can swim surrounded by the textured masonry, with the sky visible directly overhead. The arrangement creates a sheltered bathing space that remains exposed to Copenhagen’s changing weather, allowing swimmers to experience rain and even snowfall from the water.
On the same level, a heated outdoor onsen overlooks Copenhagen Harbour, drawing on Japanese bathing traditions while taking advantage of the waterfront setting. Both outdoor pools are designed for year-round use, supported by a ground-source heat pump system connected to ten boreholes extending 250 meters below ground. The architecture makes these contrasting experiences possible within the same building, moving between enclosed brick interiors and pools open to the elements.
from indoor swimming to the harbor
At ground level, KAI contains a 25-meter fitness pool alongside a teaching pool and three smaller pools for children. Upstairs, warmer bathing areas are joined by a cold plunge pool, while saunas and a steam bath provide additional facilities. The transparent lower level opens views toward the surrounding waterfront, connecting the swimming spaces visually with the harbor beyond.
Outside, a timber boardwalk will lead to designated harbor swimming and dipping areas overlooking the Royal Danish Playhouse and Opera Park. These public bathing facilities are expected to open in early 2027, following the building’s December inauguration. The project itself began with a city-led ideas competition in 2015, when Copenhagen residents submitted 160 proposals for the future of Paper Island, most of them calling for a public swimming facility.
Kengo Kuma & Associates won the subsequent architectural competition in 2017, working with Cornelius Vöge Atelier for Architecture during the early design stages and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects through detailed design and construction. Nearly a decade later, the project brings that original public request to the harbor’s edge.
project info:
project: KAI Water Culture House
location: Papirøen (Paper Island), Copenhagen, Denmark
lead architect: Kengo Kuma & Associates
early design collaboration: Cornelius Vöge Atelier for Architecture
executive architect: Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects
client: Paper Island Water Culture House Foundation
main contractor: MT Højgaard
area: 5,800 sqm
opening date: December 5th, 2026

Canada-EU summit: What do both sides want, and what’s at stake?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:54:51 UTC
01:54:51 KST

Canada-EU summit: What do both sides want, and what’s at stake?
The EU has proposed to make Canada its first associate member amid tensions over US tariffs.
Canada is set to host a summit with the European Union to bolster bilateral strategic and economic ties as its relations with its southern neighbour, the United States, are in sharp decline.
The summit is scheduled for October 29 to 30 in Canada’s French-speaking city of Montreal, and is expected to focus on closer cooperation on trade, technology, defence, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, research and financial services.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the move.
What is the summit, and why is it happening now?
This will be the 21st Canada-EU summit and is expected to build on the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force in 2017. It eliminates duties on up to 99 percent of all imported goods between the two sides, according to the European Council.
“In Montreal, we will take our partnership to the next level by launching our ‘Alliance for the Future’ to deepen our political, economic and institutional ties even further,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, who will be attending the summit along with Carney and von der Leyen. They are expected to issue a joint statement.
The deepening Canada-EU alignment seems fuelled by US President Donald Trump’s policies, which imposed hefty tariffs on both Canadian and European exports to the US and pushed Canada to look for ways to reduce its economic dependence on the US. Before Trump’s tariffs whipsawed relations, Canada sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to the US.
In August, trade talks between Ottawa and Washington, DC, broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
What do Canada and Europe want from each other?
Both sides are seeking opportunities that will open more options beyond the world’s largest economy.
“The opportunity is clear. The EU brings market power, research depth, and manufacturing strength. Canada brings abundant energy, critical minerals, world-class capabilities in space, artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum, and one of the world’s strongest banking systems,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
The summit will give the two sides a chance to turn these “complementary strengths into concrete benefits for our peoples,” the statement added.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a think tank in Ottawa, Canada, sees benefits and challenges.
“These fields could be beneficial for both sides, and we are likely to see specific announcements during the summit on these sectors,” she told Al Jazeera.
“The main challenge is how quickly the political momentum can turn into specific deals and projects to deliver specific economic results,” she added.
The EU describes Canada as “the only non-European country” taking part in Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s 150 billion-euro ($167bn) loan programme that supports and expedites defence procurement by EU member states.
The EU concluded its agreement with Canada, allowing it to participate under SAFE, in February, and it gives Canadian firms preferential access and treatment in defence procurements financed by the SAFE Instrument.
Could Canada become an associate member of the EU?
Last month, von der Leyen proposed that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member, suggesting a deeper relationship spanning trade, technology, defence and economic security.
Carney later welcomed the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.
However, the term “associate member” does not currently exist in EU treaties or its standard enlargement framework, according to the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), a Brussels-based think tank.
“The term does not actually matter; what is important is the practical deepening of the relationship and the actual results, no matter what the final term is,” Nadjibulla said.
Is it an anti-American alliance?
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said in her address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg last month, which Carney attended, making him the first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address.
Nadjibulla agrees.
“I do not see that as an anti-US coalition. It is rather about diversification of economic and defence partnerships and building resilience for Canada. It is a continuation of Canadian Prime Minister Carney’s policies to create opportunities. A deeper alliance with Europe is essential to this agenda,” she said.
“President Trump will likely not appreciate this, but it is about Canada having more choices in an unpredictable world,” she added.
Bob Rae, former premier of Ontario and Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2020 to 2025, told Al Jazeera that “President Trump does not control our policy. We have been having long and productive relations with the Europeans for hundreds of years, but Trump chose to treat Canada in a way that does not respect our sovereignty”.
He added that “engaging in conversations with the EU is perfectly normal and is not directed at the US”.
Trump has threatened the European Union with new tariffs over its proposal to make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member”, suggesting the move could be considered hostile to the US.
“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, in September.
Trump dismissed the prospect of Canada joining the EU as “laughable” and called the US’s northern neighbour a “terrible trade partner”.

Italy approves 2027 budget bill with newborn fund, energy cost measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:52:18 UTC
01:52:18 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's Cabinet approved the country's 2027 budget bill on Wednesday, including a fund for newborns and measures to reduce electricity and gas costs for households and businesses, local media reported.
The budget provides for a state contribution of €100 ($116) annually for each newborn from 2027 until the child turns 18, according to government sources, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
The contribution will be paid into a pension savings fund.
The measure was proposed by Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti.
The Cabinet also approved a decree aimed at reducing electricity and gas costs for households and businesses.
The measure sets a price cap of €58.9 ($68.5) per megawatt-hour, with an application period of 12 to 18 months.
Other measures on the Cabinet's agenda included a legislative decree to reform the craft sector and another to reorganize regulations governing outdoor seating areas.
The budget bill is part of the government's planned €23.5 billion package of measures for 2027, according to the draft budgetary plan previously submitted to the European Commission and the Italian parliament.

Reservists Party's last shot at Knesset: military ballots could upend election results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:51:33 UTC
01:51:33 KST

As the hours pass, it appears that the only party still below the electoral threshold with a possible path into the Knesset is the joint Reservists-Economic Party list led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha.
With 85.6% of votes counted, nearly 128,000 ballots have been cast for the list, which runs under the Hebrew ballot letters "די" (Dalet-Yod). That means the party needs approximately 57,500 additional votes to cross the electoral threshold, estimated at around 185,000 votes.
The chances of the two candidates crossing the threshold are slim, but difficult to assess precisely. While Hendel and Zelekha have so far received only about 2.6% of the general vote, their support could be higher among the double-envelope ballots, which include votes cast by soldiers and other eligible voters outside their regular polling stations.
One reason is that Zionist parties traditionally receive stronger support in these ballots. Another is Hendel's direct appeal to military reservists.
In a ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth poll of reservists published on August 21, Hendel, who was then allied with Hili Tropper, received support equivalent to nine Knesset seats, representing more than 5% of respondents. Although that survey offers little indication of his current standing, it may suggest that the support Hendel sought to cultivate among reservists does exist.
Another ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth survey, published on October 9 among first-time voters ages 18 to 22, gave Hendel and Zelekha six seats, equivalent to 3.68% of the vote. Because this demographic is also relevant to the double-envelope count, the findings provide another indication that the list could receive a higher share of the remaining votes.
If Hendel and Zelekha secure approximately 12% of the votes still outstanding, they are expected to cross the electoral threshold. That remains a significant hurdle given their relatively weak performance among the general electorate, but the possibility cannot be ruled out entirely. All television exit polls had projected that their joint list would fail to enter the Knesset.
If the Reservists-Economic Party manages to overcome the odds and cross the threshold, the parties currently positioned to lose seats, based on the count of 93% of regular polling stations and before the double-envelope ballots are counted, are Shas, Beyachad, the Joint List and Yashar!.
Politically, that would reduce Eisenkot's bloc to 46 seats and leave Netanyahu's bloc with 52. The Arab parties would hold 18 seats, although that figure could also decline as the double-envelope ballots are counted.
Hendel and Zelekha have deliberately avoided aligning themselves with either political bloc. The Reservists Party chairman told ynet Tuesday that he wanted a Zionist government, one that would depend on neither ultra-Orthodox nor Arab parties. He also said he did not want Netanyahu to remain prime minister.
During the election campaign, Hendel said he would support whichever bloc won the largest number of Zionist votes. Because he does not consider the ultra-Orthodox parties Zionist, that position could lead him to recommend Eisenkot to form the next government. In any event, without support from the Arab parties, such a recommendation would have limited practical significance.
Conversely, if Hendel and Zelekha join Netanyahu, he would need just five additional seats to reach a 61-member Knesset majority. That would likely trigger intense efforts to persuade lawmakers from the change bloc to defect. The change bloc, however, could still rely on the Arab parties to defeat the government.
Hendel said Tuesday evening that he was waiting for the double-envelope ballots to be counted. "By the end of the week, we'll know the results from the IDF polling stations," he said. "We saw incredible momentum. Let's see the actual results. In any case, we fought very, very hard, and we are fighters who work hard. We will fulfill our ambitions for the State of Israel and the Jewish people. Nobody here is giving up."

US sways more countries to oppose UN resolution condemning its Cuba embargo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:51:19 UTC
01:51:19 KST

Cuba wins UN vote against US embargo with weakest backing in 30 years
- The UN General Assembly passed a resolution calling for an end to the US embargo on Cuba, with 130 votes for, 17 against and 25 abstentions.
- Support for Cuba was the weakest in 30 years, as US pressure, sanctions and an oil blockade added to the island’s economic crisis.
- The vote followed a heated UN row, with Cuban and US officials trading insults and accusing each other of lies, coercion and corruption.
AI generated
NEW YORK - The UN General Assembly on Oct 28 adopted a new resolution calling for an end to the US embargo against Cuba, although support for the communist-ruled island fell to its lowest level in three decades.
Nearly every year since 1992 similar resolutions have been put to a vote and passed, but support for the measure in 2026 was markedly lower.
The resolution, which has called for lifting the economic, trade and financial embargo against the island, received 130 votes in favour, with 17 against and 25 abstentions.
It was the lowest level of support since 1995.
The debate for 2026, however, is taking place amid a major new pressure campaign by Washington against Cuba, including an oil blockade and broad sanctions that have severely crippled Cuba’s economy.
In recent weeks, Havana accused Washington of mounting a diplomatic offensive to pressure countries into withdrawing their support for the Cuban resolution.
“The world has once again spoken out overwhelmingly against the blockade, even despite the most blatant pressure and blackmail from the US to change the course of this vote,” Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel said in a celebratory post on X on Oct 28, later adding that the US engages in “gangster-like coercion.”
Speaking in New York, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez accused Washington of seeking to “determine the nation’s destiny” and “seize” its wealth.
In the minutes before the vote, US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz denied that Cuba was under a blockade and said “the plight of the Cuban people is exclusively the fault of this corrupt communist regime.”
“The reality is, today as we speak, there is no ring of US Navy warships around Cuba. Their ports are open. In recent months, data shows that shipments have arrived,” from around the world, he added.
The vote came a day after a dramatic shouting match on the floor of the UN General Assembly that at one point saw Rodriguez approach Waltz and shout, “You are a liar!” as Waltz shouted for him to back away.
Amid the interruptions, the chair briefly suspended the session and instructed both countries’ representatives to return to their places.
In his speech arguing against the resolution on Oct 27, Waltz held up pictures of Cuban leaders past and present, including Diaz-Canel, wearing luxury watches, prompting the Cuban delegation to repeatedly smack their desk in protest and interrupt.
Waltz later held up a satellite images and detailed luxury estates, boats and holidays that he claimed the Castro family and Cuban officials enjoy.
“The regime can never find enough fuel for Cuban ambulances. They can never find enough fuel for Cuban buses. But when the Castro family, the elites that are sitting at that table, want to go yachting, suddenly, it’s no problem.” Waltz said.
Speaking on Fox News on Oct 28 after the vote, Waltz said that the previous day’s debate, “got a little spicy.” AFP

How US midterms could fracture bipartisan support for Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:51:02 UTC
01:51:02 KST

Breadcrumb
How US midterms could fracture bipartisan support for Israel
Washington, DC - Across the United States, many candidates who support Palestinian human rights are set to score wins in the country's midterm elections in November, reflecting a big shift in US public opinion on Israel amid the war on Gaza.
The House of Representatives will likely see an influx of progressive Democrats critical of Israel who won primaries against pro-Israel opponents.
And two Senate candidates - Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine - who have accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza are locked in close races that could see them clinch seats in the upper chamber of Congress.
Abdelhalim Abdelrahman, communication director for American Muslims for Palestine (AMP), says US voters are starting to make the connection between foreign and domestic policy.
Progressive candidates have "done an excellent job exploring the intersection between the genocide in Gaza and Israel's broader destabilising conduct in the Middle East with the affordability crisis in America", Abdelrahman told The New Arab.
Since the start of the war on Gaza, the US government has provided Israel with more than $21 billion in military aid at a time when Americans are struggling with skyrocketing inflation.
The war on Iran, which the US launched jointly with Israel, put further strain on the cost of living and pushed energy prices to record highs.
"Every single day Americans are waking up to videos and pictures of the Israeli government bombing civilian infrastructure, killing Palestinian children, spreading crimes across the Middle East," Abdelrahman said.
"Meanwhile, the average American cannot afford rent. The average American has seen their wages stagnate. This funding of the Israeli government has cost the American people tons of money."
Dwindling support for Israel
Public opinion in the US has been turning against Israel for years, polls show - a trend that was accelerated by the well-documented Israeli atrocities in Gaza over the past three years.
A Pew Research Center survey in July suggested that 63 percent of US adults have unfavourable views of the Israeli government.
"The American people have come to their own conclusions that it's a great moral hazard to this country to have a government that wilfully ignores the will of the American people," said Abdelrahman.
"Now more Americans sympathise with Palestinians. Now more Americans are calling for arms embargoes and sanctions on Israel."
During the primary season, pro-Palestine progressives won House races in districts from New York to California through Michigan and Colorado.
In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani's victory last year ushered in what appears to be a new era of progressive politics in the largest city in the US. Candidates backed by the mayor won three major House contests, ousting two staunchly pro-Israel incumbent Democrats.
Darializa Avila Chevalier - who participated in the encampment against the war on Gaza at Columbia University - defeated Adriano Espaillat.
Brad Lander, an Israel critic, won his primary against Congressman Daniel Goldman, who has been one of the most uncompromising pro-Israel Democrats.
Separately, Mamdani-backed state legislator Claire Valdez won the contest for an open US House seat.
All three are running in safe Democratic seats; they are all but certain to win in the general elections on 3 November.
In Pennsylvania, State Representative Chris Rabb, a vocal opponent of Israeli policies, also won the primary in a safe Democratic district. In Colorado, progressive candidate Melat Kiros beat incumbent Diana DeGette.
Several similar storylines played out across the country, setting the stage for the most pro-Palestine Congress in US history that will take office next year to chisel a sizable gap in the near-unanimous bipartisan support that Israel has enjoyed on Capitol Hill for decades.
AIPAC 'is on its heels'
These victories came despite tens of billions of dollars spent by pro-Israel groups - spearheaded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) - to defeat candidates who support Palestinian rights.
Usamah Andrabi, spokesperson for Justice Democrats, a leading left-wing group that backed many of the pro-Palestine candidates that won this year, said overcoming AIPAC's spending took years of organising and building awareness about the role of the pro-Israel lobby group.
In 2024, AIPAC spent record amounts of money in primaries and successfully toppled two Justice Democrats-backed incumbents - House members Cori Bush and Jamal Bowman.
Andrabi said it took multiple election cycles to turn AIPAC's endorsement into "a toxic kiss of death" for Democratic campaigns.
"We suffered some really terrible losses, but this lobby is on its heels," Andrabi said.
AIPAC has been trying to conceal its spending on behalf of candidates by funnelling money to subsidiaries with generic-sounding names, known as shell PACs - a tactic that Andrabi said shows the unpopularity of the pro-Israel group.
Andrabi told The New Arab that the rise of numerous progressive candidates across the country was a product of the anger of Democratic voters after President Donald Trump won in 2024.
"Democratic voters woke up in 2025 realising that the Democratic establishment was wholly unfit and unprepared to defend our communities against Republican extremism and fascism," he said.
Andrabi added that while Gaza may not have been a top priority for all voters, support for Israel featured heavily in many contests because candidates were able to draw a line between foreign wars and domestic issues.
"It's not that every single district and every single voter in this country, the most important issue on their mind is, 'How do we end the genocide in Gaza?' But our candidates were connecting the dots, like Darializa did, who led with the slogan of 'babies, not bombs,'" Andrabi said.
"Why are we spending billions of dollars bombing hospitals and schools and killing babies abroad when the same government is defunding our schools and our jobs and our hospitals at home, and we can't afford to put a roof over our head or food on the table?"
The progressive newcomers will increase the number of legislators in Washington who are willing to push for a break from unconditional support for Israel in US policy. However, the contingency remains a minority within the Democratic caucus.
But Andrabi said the progressive bloc will have a "monumental impact" in the next Congress by highlighting where the Democratic base stands.
As Democratic voters sour on Israel, some lawmakers who have avoided criticising the US ally throughout their years-long careers have backed measures to hold the Israeli government accountable for its abuses over the past year.
Last month, 46 out of 47 Democrats in the Senate voted for a bill to compel the State Department to investigate increasing Israeli violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killing of US citizens.
Abdelrahman, of AMP, said he hopes the next Congress upholds Washington's own laws prohibiting aid to human rights abusers.
"Previous administrations and previous iterations of the American Congress have sidestepped justice and accountability for the sake of protecting Israel, and what we hope to see is that the status quo is broken," he said.
Ali Harb is a journalist based in Washington, DC. His work focuses on US foreign policy, elections, and Arab American communities

Arsenal on Tuesday suffered one of the most humiliating defeats in their history as the Premier League champions were stunned by fourth-tier minnows Fleetwood Town in an EFL League Cup penalty shoot-out.
Mikel Arteta’s side crashed out 5-3 on penalties in an incredible fourth round upset after the tie finished 1-1 in normal time.
Arsenal’s Bruno Guimaraes’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch in the shoot-out and Conor Haughey scored Fleetwood’s winner.
Photo: Reuters
Aaron Loupalo-Bi’s first-half goal had put Fleetwood ahead before Viktor Gyokeres equalized after the interval.
Arsenal’s 16-year-old rising star Max Dowman was sent off for violent conduct in the closing stages.
Arteta paid the price for prioritizing Sunday’s Premier League trip to Liverpool as his decision to make nine changes backfired spectacularly.
No one would have predicted Arsenal’s embarrassment regardless of Arteta’s selection gamble.
They had moved level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City after a 2-0 victory over Everton on Saturday, but instead of extending their run of 11 wins from their 13 previous games, Arsenal returned to north London red-faced after a loss that ranks among the darkest days in the club’s glittering history.
The Gunners boss conceded Arsenal could have no complaints, admitting it was a painful moment in his reign.
“First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through the next round. The manner that they have done it, and for us a very sad day,” Arteta said.
“There is nothing to criticize the players for their attitude, their application,” he said. “The determination, you could see that was there from the start, even with 10 men, but we conceded a really poor goal to start with that gave them some momentum.”
Fleetwood made a mockery of the 84 places between the clubs in the English soccer system with a defiant display that stopped Arsenal establishing any momentum.
Their refusal to be overawed by Arsenal’s star power was a tribute to Fleetwood boss Matt Lawlor, who won the tactical battle with Arteta by sitting deep and attacking on the counter.
“I just can’t believe it. The biggest night in the club’s history in terms of opposition coming to town and we’ve managed to beat the champions,” Lawlor said.
“We’re not stupid enough and not egotistical enough that you think we’re going to outplay the best team in the country and the most organized team in the country,” he said. “So we had to ride our luck, we had to deny space, we had to deny options for them, and I think we did that really, really well in terms of the majority of the game.”

FIRST TIME LUCKY: Milwaukee’s first World Series game in 44 years, Misiorowski helped the Brewers to a 3-2 victory against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday’s opener Jacob Misiorowski stepped on the mound for a World Series debut like no other. “I had so much adrenaline built up,” he said. Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:41:58 UTC
01:41:58 KST

The Ministry of Environment and the National Taipei University of Technology yesterday signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on smart urban forest governance, with a demonstration site set up near the university.
Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) said trees are part of climate resilience infrastructure and require scientific methods to develop.
The cooperation between the ministry and the university focuses on smart energy saving and climate resilience governance, and is expected to set an example for smart urban forest governance, he said.
Photo: Wu Po-hsuan, Taipei Times
It can be divided into four main aspects: using scientific data, and light detection and ranging technology for sustainable governance; promoting circular reuse of critical process waste from semiconductor manufacturing; adopting in-depth energy saving powered by artificial intelligence; and developing climate resilience professionals through interdisciplinary exchanges, Peng said.
The key to urban forest governance lies in respect for life and cultural foundation, he said.
A simulation driven by a digital twin system would be introduced to demonstrate the benefits of lower temperatures for urban pedestrians, Peng said.
University president Jen Yi-jun (任貽均) said the school has long been dedicated to microclimate monitoring, environmental engineering, smart power grid and research on energy conservation in air-conditioning systems.
The university would use scientific research capabilities, and capitalize on its alumni and experience in revitalizing Chienkuo Brewery (建國啤酒廠) — a historical heritage building in Taipei — to develop the demonstration site, he said.
Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠) said his ministry would help include the city’s Air Force Command Headquarters National Cultural Base in the demonstration site for urban forest development.
Each tree carries the history, cultures and memories of locals, he said, adding that the urban forest project is expected to restore trees and cultures.
Meanwhile, a recent rise in the number of trees removed across Taipei has sparked public outrage and raised questions about the city government.
Asked about the issue, Peng said he protested the felling of old camphor trees when he was young.
The environment ministry’s proposed specialized urban forestry act would treat urban trees as vital public infrastructure and living entities, he said.
Public notification would be required before their removal, and treatment for diseased trees would be mandatory instead of immediately felling trees, Peng said, adding that it aimed to curb arbitrary tree felling nationwide.

India has vowed “swift action” after a cheetah was shot dead, the first such killing since the country began reintroducing the animals in 2022, the Indian government said yesterday.
The Indian Ministry of Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change said that it had ordered a “high-level team for an on-ground investigation” into the shooting of the 19-month-old male, treating the incident with “utmost gravity.”
The India-born cheetah — whose mother was among those introduced to India from Botswana, Namibia and South Africa as part of efforts to restore the planet’s fastest land animal — was shot as it prowled in forests outside a protected national park.
Photo: Reuters
Asiatic cheetahs were declared extinct in India in 1952. The critically endangered subspecies, once found across the Middle East, Central Asia and India, now survives in very small numbers in Iran.
Their African cousins were first reintroduced in September 2022 to India, to the Kuno National Park, 300km south of New Delhi.
The wounded cheetah was picked up on Sunday in forests in Madhya Pradesh state, outside Kuno’s boundaries, and taken for veterinary care.
“During the surgery, five firearm pellets were recovered from its body,” the ministry said.
Despite efforts, the cheetah died on Tuesday, it said.
“Medical examinations corroborated multiple internal injuries associated with the recovered firearm pellets,” it added.
The high-profile project, championed by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has been dogged by criticism over the deaths of several of the cats.
However, experts in animal reintroductions say they often result in more than 50 percent mortality, especially in the initial phases.
The National Tiger Conservation Authority, which oversees the cheetah project, said that survival rates and hunting successes are “comparable to other international cheetah reintroduction efforts, with recorded wild prey kills confirming successful adaptation to the Indian landscape.”
The total cheetah population in the wild in India is about 60, including about 40 Indian-born cheetahs.

Lee has returned to Taiwan and is working at the ministry’s Taipei headquarters, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry’s comments came after local media reported earlier yesterday that the Cabinet had approved its recommendation to recall Lee to Taipei, and that he began working at the Department of Treaty and Legal Affairs on Monday.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
Lee’s removal from his post in Geneva followed a determination by an ad hoc investigative team formed by the ministry that he had engaged in workplace bullying.
According to the team’s findings, released on Oct. 7, Lee was found to have frequently “shouted and yelled” during meetings and repeatedly criticized or obstructed some of his subordinates in the office.
The team concluded that Lee had abused his position of power, exceeded the necessary and reasonable scope of his duties, and continuously created a hostile work environment through threats, offenses, insults or other means, thereby harming the physical and mental health of office staff who filed complaints.
Lee was also accused of misusing public resources for personal purposes in late July.
The ministry did not say if those allegations were being investigated.

Asked about the incident during a legislative session yesterday, Department of East Asian and Pacific Affairs Director-General Michael Lin (林昭宏) said he and Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Baushuan Ger (葛葆萱) had informed Hsu that, as an ambassador, he was expected to wear formal attire and maintain a solemn demeanor when addressing attendees and hosting the National Day celebrations.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) told the same session that the ministry had managed to “avert a major controversy.”
Lin said that the ministry had recalled Hsu to clarify the incident and held reviews to ensure that a similar incident would not happen again, adding that Taiwan had remained in close contact with the Marshall Islands government over the incident.
“It was purely the personal behavior of the ambassador — and the Marshall Islands, once apprised of the situation, expressed full support for how Taiwan handled the matter,” he said.
The incident would not affect bilateral ties, Lin added.
Hsu took up the ambassadorial post in December last year.
The Taiwanese embassy in the Marshall Islands is currently headed by its second-in-command, minister Hank Liu (劉漢清), the ministry said.

Runners swap streets for malls in Singapore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

The pounding of shoes echoed through a Singapore shopping mall as runners desperate to train take refuge from choking haze.
Smoke from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia has sent air quality in the city-state plummeting to its worst levels in more than a decade in the past few weeks, canceling outdoor activities.
Those seeking exercise, including runners training for international events, have found an unconventional alternative: air-conditioned shopping malls.
Photo: AFP
On Saturday, more than 80 runners turned the corridors of the Marina Square shopping center into makeshift running tracks, clocking laps past storefronts on two floors before shops opened for business.
There are strict rules.
“No sprinting, no overtaking, no shouting or yelling,” Eugene Beh, 52, founder of Singapore Runners Club, told about 60 members before their run.
Spitting and wiping sweat on the floor are also banned.
Beh said they had to cancel several runs outdoors because of the haze, blown in by the wind from forest and peatland fires in Borneo and Sumatra.
Angeline Zeng, 57, who works in banking, completed 10 loops at the mall, or about 10km.
With a half-marathon in Taipei in less than a week and a full marathon in December, Zeng needs to clock as much mileage as she can.
As treadmills at her neighborhood gym are often full, she and her fellow runners were excited when they heard about the mall runs.
“We were like, wow, we didn’t expect that at all,” she said.
“I love it because the air-con makes you feel like you’re running overseas where there’s cold temperatures, so it’s really great,” Zeng added.
However, circling inside the mall becomes “boring” after a while, she said.
“Maybe for shorter runs this is OK, but if you need to do long runs, maybe not so suitable,” she said.
Singapore Runners Club member Doris Tan, 42, said she thought running indoors would be a bit suffocating.
“I didn’t expect it to be so cool ... but if you have to ask me, I still prefer outdoors,” she said.
Paul Wong, a 54-year-old retiree from a club called X-Run, completed 21 loops inside the mall, or about 21km.
With just more than a month until the Singapore International Marathon — which many other fellow runners are also training for — Wong would have to run up to 80km per week, but the haze has forced him indoors.
“For the last two weeks I’ve been running close to 100km on the treadmill. The longest I’ve run is 28km for two-and-a-half hours; it’s very mental,” Wong said.
“The mall run is definitely better because the treadmill feels like a hamster run. You just keep repeating the routine,” he said.
Eddie Chang, lead coach for X-Run, said they had to present a carefully laid-out plan to get approval from the mall for the runs.
They had to consider factors like walkway width, tight corners and holding the run early in the morning before the shops open.
“The biggest challenge for outdoor training is the weather. Humidity is very high, plus the haze now, the impact is doubled and tripled, so it’s very hard to manage,” Chang said. “By converting to indoors, you definitely reduce all the impact from the outdoor experience and continue running.”
The air quality improved this week, but yesterday, Singapore remained one of the 20 most polluted major cities in the world, according to Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir.
The two running clubs are likely to extend the mall runs if poor air quality persists, and plan to ask more malls to open their doors to them.
“I believe there will be opportunities. This is something new in the sports scene,” Beh said. “Hopefully, with the permission of building management, this can spread out to other sports groups.”

China’s BRI crisis in South Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

China Merchants Port Holdings, a state-owned Chinese port operator, withdrew from a proposed US$392 million joint venture to develop a logistics hub in Sri Lanka’s Port of Colombo this month, renewing questions about the viability of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in South Asia. The development recalls the controversy surrounding Hambantota port, which Sri Lanka leased to a Chinese company for 99 years in 2017 amid mounting financial pressures.
However, the difficulties extend beyond Sri Lanka in South Asia and point to a common problem: the gap between the BRI’s promise of economic transformation and the conditions required to realize it. Pakistan provides the clearest illustration of this dilemma. The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) was designed to connect China’s Xinjiang region with Pakistan’s Arabian Sea coast through transport infrastructure, energy projects and the strategic Port of Gwadar. However, persistent economic instability, energy-sector liabilities and financing difficulties have complicated its implementation.
Security poses an additional obstacle. Attacks on Chinese nationals and projects, particularly in Balochistan, have increased the costs and risks of protecting Chinese investments. The broader lesson is that infrastructure investment does not automatically generate sufficient revenue to service debt or produce sustainable development. Although Pakistan remains strategically important to Beijing, close political relations have proved insufficient to guarantee the economic success of major infrastructure commitments.
Bangladesh illustrates the importance of domestic political change. Chinese investment has supported infrastructure and industrial development, making Beijing an important economic partner. However, the removal of Sheikh Hasina’s government in August 2024 created a new political environment for Dhaka’s external relationships. The implications for China’s position should not be overstated: Political change does not automatically mean that a country would abandon existing investments or partnerships. Nevertheless, it demonstrates that agreements reached under one government do not guarantee continuity of strategic priorities under its successors.
Bangladesh’s challenge is to retain the economic benefits of Chinese investment while diversifying its external partnerships and preserving diplomatic autonomy. Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s trip to Japan on Monday has added a new dimension to the evolving Bangladesh-China ties. For Beijing, the lesson is that access to political elites and strong relations with an incumbent government cannot substitute for broader political legitimacy or guarantee that its long-term interests would remain unaffected by domestic transitions.
Nepal reveals a different limitation: the difficulty of translating geographical proximity into practical connectivity. Its engagement with the BRI reflects an ambition to diversify transport and trade links beyond traditional routes through India. However, difficult Himalayan terrain, high infrastructure costs, financing questions and the practical challenges of cross-border transport have complicated this ambition. Nepal’s dependence on transit access through India also limits the extent to which Chinese connectivity projects can transform its economic geography in the short term.
Therefore the central challenge is not simply whether Nepal and China can reach political agreements, but whether those commitments can produce commercially viable, financially sustainable and operationally viable infrastructure. Announced projects and signed agreements should not be confused with completed transport links or economically productive connectivity. Nepal demonstrates that geography, costs and implementation capacity can constrain the strategic value of infrastructure even when political intentions are aligned.
The Maldives highlights the interaction between infrastructure investment, domestic politics and regional strategic competition. Chinese-backed infrastructure and closer diplomatic relations have become part of the country’s wider debate over foreign influence, economic dependence and national sovereignty. Changes in domestic political priorities can alter the emphasis of the Maldives’ external partnerships without necessarily producing a complete break with Beijing.
As a small island state situated in a strategically important part of the Indian Ocean, the Maldives must balance economic opportunities with the need to preserve its decisionmaking autonomy and maintain relations with competing regional powers, particularly India and China. Chinese investment can generate commercial opportunities and diplomatic access, but neither guarantees an uncontested sphere of influence. The Maldivian experience underlines the importance of local political choices in determining the durability of Beijing’s regional partnerships.
These cases reveal the limits of treating the BRI as a uniform model of regional development. Pakistan illustrates the interaction of economic vulnerability and insecurity; Sri Lanka highlights financial exposure and questions of commercial viability; Bangladesh demonstrates the significance of political transitions; Nepal exposes geographical and implementation constraints; and the Maldives shows how domestic politics and strategic balancing shape the influence that China can exercise. These differences matter as much as the similarities. They suggest that the BRI’s outcomes depend not only on the resources China commits, but also on recipient countries’ economic conditions, institutional capacities and political choices.
India’s opposition adds another dimension to Beijing’s difficulties. New Delhi rejects the CPEC because it traverses territories claimed by India and remains concerned about China’s expanding presence in its neighborhood and the Indian Ocean. India has sought to strengthen regional connectivity and economic partnerships, including through the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, announced in 2023. The BRI’s predicament in South Asia is best understood, hence, as a crisis of conversion: the difficulty of translating infrastructure investment into sustainable development and durable geopolitical influence. China remains a major regional actor, and not all of its projects have failed.
Moreover, the future of the BRI would depend less on the scale of Beijing’s commitments than on the value those commitments ultimately deliver.
Sumit Kumar is a Ministry of Foreign Affairs visiting fellow at National Chengchi University and an assistant professor in Delhi University’s Department of Political Science.

In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Milwaukee was three outs from its first World Series title in a game that stretched well past midnight yesterday when Junior Caminero started the bottom of the 12th inning with a grounder to third. Thousands of Brewers fans who trekked to Tropicana Field to witness the long-awaited moment started to cheer.
Not so fast.
Third baseman Joey Ortiz bounced the throw, and the ball glanced off first baseman Jake Bauers’ mitt for an error.
Photo: AP
One of the most stunning rallies in World Series history started to unfold.
Liam Hicks, Jonny DeLuca, Chandler Simpson and pinch-hitter Ben Williamson followed with consecutive singles in a 15-pitch span against rookie Shane Drohan, and the Tampa Bay Rays staved off elimination with a 4-3 win that forced Game 5.
“Sometimes the game tests you. Sometimes the game makes you want to dig deep,” Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. “It’s all part of the journey, all part of the experience, and that’s part of our story.”
Milwaukee rookie Cooper Pratt hit a tiebreaking home run off Ian Seymour in the top of the 12th for a 3-2 lead, sending the Brewers sprinting out of the dugout in excitement as they sensed completing the first Series sweep since 2012.
Milwaukee’s bullpen, led by seven outs from Aaron Ashby, had combined for seven straight scoreless innings, before Caminero reached against Antonio Senzatela.
Ortiz grimaced.
“I’ve got to make that play,” he said. “Just no excuse about it.”
Caminero appeared to hurt his left foot, but stayed in the game.
Brewers manager Pat Murphy brought in Drohan, a 27-year-old left-hander who had not pitched since a one-inning start in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Oct. 15.
With Pratt shifted toward second for the left-handed batter, Hicks hit an opposite-field grounder through the vacated shortstop hole and into left field as Caminero slid headfirst into third.
“For just regular D, that’s right at Coop,” Drohan said of the defensive alignment.
Pinch-runner Cedric Mullins replaced Caminero before DeLuca, who had made sparkling catches to deny Yelich in the third and William Contreras in the fourth, hit a grounder past the mound as Drohan tried in vain to make a behind-the-back snag. The ball bounced into center as Mullins tied the score at three.
Nick Fortes ran at second for the slower Hicks. After missing a bunt attempt and pulling back another while taking a called strike, Simpson lined a single into center, loading the bases.
Sal Frelick moved in from left to form a five-man infield, with three defenders on the left side and everyone playing in.
Williamson, who had been 1 for 15 in the post-season, batted for Victor Mesa Jr.
“It’s what you dream of as a player to be in that spot,” Williamson said.
On the game’s 367th pitch, he hit a chopper that kicked up chalk from the foul line 2m from home plate. The ball bounded high over Bauers and onto the grass in short right field. Fortes sprinted across the plate with the winning run, then headed toward first to join his jumping teammates in foul territory.
“That was totally what I told him to do,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said, drawing laughs.
Drohan walked off, his head bowed.
