The mid-terms and democracy, a new national park, and political hamburgers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

The mid-terms and democracy, a new national park, and political hamburgers
Welcome to our press review of events in the United States. Every Wednesday we look at how the Swiss media have reported and reacted to three major stories in the US – in politics, finance and science.
Whenever I visit the United States, I always look forward to meals in diners and burger bars – a tasty, messy burger is tough to find in Switzerland, and if you do manage to find one, it could well cost more than CHF30 ($35). But are the days of cheap(er) US burgers over? With supply of beef low and demand as high as ever, prices are going up – with potential political consequences.
Help us improve the press review
As a reader of our weekly press review, your feedback is important to us. Please take two minutes to answer a short survey and help us improve our journalism. This survey is anonymous and all data is confidential.
👉 [Take the surveyExternal link]
Ahead of next week’s mid-term elections, American democracy is suffering a historic setback under Donald Trump, according to the Tribune de Genève.
How is American democracy faring in the run-up to the mid-terms on November 3? “Very badly,” the Tribune de Genève wrote on Tuesday, citing several independent research institutes. “According to V-Dem’s flagship report on democracy, the US has recorded its sharpest decline in history this year. Its score has fallen back to 1965 levels – a time when Martin Luther King Jr was marching in the streets and voting rights for minorities had only just been established.”
A particular problem is the lack of effective checks on the executive by Congress and the judiciary. “During Donald Trump’s second term, power has become concentrated in the hands of the president, who is increasingly governing by executive order,” the Geneva newspaper wrote. “The Republican-dominated Congress offers him little resistance. It has largely ceded its oversight and budgetary powers to the administration. The Supreme Court, too, often rules in favour of the president.”
Beyond this weakening of the checks and balances, the Tribune de Genève said Trump was exacerbating the drift towards autocracy through numerous other measures, such as attacks on the rule of law, a purge of the administration, and attacks on freedom of expression, including a crackdown on protests.
“As a result, an increasing number of Americans believe that their democracy is no longer a good model for other countries,” it wrote. “According to polls by the Pew Research Center, 69% say they are dissatisfied with the way democracy works in their country. Many have lost confidence in their political leaders.”
This frustration with the state of democracy and its institutions is currently fuelling mobilisation, according to the Tribune de Genève. “Forecasts predict a high turnout on November 3, which is likely to benefit the Democrats in particular. Nearly one in two Americans explicitly regard their vote as a vote against Trump.”
The newspaper concluded that, traditionally, mid-term elections serve as a referendum on the incumbent president, but political scientists see the upcoming election as a decisive turning point for the future of American democracy. “These elections will show whether moderate political forces are regaining influence or whether the dismantling of democratic structures is continuing and may become impossible to halt.”
“Americans can barely afford their hamburgers anymore” was the concerning headline in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ), which went on a road trip around Wyoming to explain why burgers have become political.
“Even on this overcast day in Torrington, a small town of 6,000 residents, near-record prices are being fetched once again,” the NZZ wrote from a cattle auction. “Light calves weighing up to 300kg are particularly sought after. A high-quality young Angus steer, hand-castrated and fully vaccinated, can bring in $2,500 (CHF2,050). But basically everything’s selling well.”
It’s clear why prices are high: cattle stocks are at a historic low. The drought, in particular, has taken its toll, the NZZ said, explaining that herds in the US have not been this small for almost 80 years.
“But the shortage of cattle isn’t just driving up prices; for Americans, it strikes at the very core of daily life. The nation needs meat. Fast food. After all, the hamburger is practically a staple food in this country. The culinary embodiment of the American Dream: while in 19th-century Europe meat was a privilege of the upper classes, cattle farming was booming in the US. For just a few cents, a burger soon filled every worker’s stomach. But today, by no means can everyone afford it so easily.”
As a result, burgers have become a political issue. Ahead of the mid-term elections on November 3, affordability is the dominant issue. “Most of the talk centres on petrol prices, which are a cause for concern among voters. But at least some Republicans are willing to give the president a pass on that issue – if the war in Iran is having an impact at the petrol pump, it is, after all, directed against a tyrannical regime which, in their view, also threatens the US, the ‘Great Satan’. When it comes to the Big Mac, however, that’s where their understanding ends.”
Donald Trump knows this, the NZZ explained, which is why he has relaxed the import regulations on beef, signing an executive order temporarily suspending tariffs on so-called lean beef trimmings – the stuff used to make minced beef – for certain quantities. In other words, cheap lean beef from Brazil, for example, is intended to drive down prices.
The measure, which Trump decided on in August, is valid for 90 days. “In other words, pretty much until the mid-term elections are over. The calculation is obvious. Whether it will work is another matter.”
A new national park has been created in the United States – so why are conservationists not happy?
Last week Chiricahua Park in southeastern Arizona became the 64th protected area in the US to be designated a national park. But, as Le Temps reported on Thursday, the announcement has drawn mostly criticism from the environmentalist community, which condemns it as a public relations exercise divorced from the realities on the ground.
“This new status will showcase one of Arizona’s gems, enabling us to welcome more visitors and boost the local economy,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. “This is a victory for all those who have campaigned to protect this place so that our children and grandchildren can enjoy it,” said Arizona’s Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in a rare show of bipartisan support.
The United States now has a 64th national park, “but the champagne is remaining in the fridge for conservationists”, Le Temps wrote. There are two reasons for this, it explained. First, nothing’s really changed. “Covering 49km2, Chiricahua National Park is the fourth-smallest in the country. Its designation as a national park has not been accompanied by an expansion of its area; the level of nature conservation protection previously afforded to the area remains the same, and no additional funding has been allocated for its management – despite the expected influx of more tourists. It’s therefore not a significant environmental breakthrough.”
Second, Trump-era policies remain in place. Christina Hazard, legal director of the National Parks Conservation Association, an independent organisation dedicated to protecting national parks, said that for these sites to be properly maintained, “the new US national park needs the National Park Service’s (NPS) staffing levels and funding to be restored”. Le Temps pointed out that since Donald Trump’s return to the White House, thousands of NPS staff have lost their jobs and, across the country, infrastructure is suffering while the administration prioritises projects such as the controversial refurbishment of a public golf course in Washington, D.C. or, still in the capital, the botched project involving the Reflecting Pool (see previous press review).
“Arizona’s national parks are on the brink of collapse, but instead of investing limited resources in visitor safety and other park needs, Secretary Burgum is overseeing the refurbishment of the president’s projects in Washington,” said the National Association of American Park Rangers. “It’s inexcusable that he is touting the creation of a new national park while refusing to look after the sites his department has been responsible for managing for over a century.”

Dua Lipa's literary takeover at London Literature Festival 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:59:30 UTC
00:59:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Dua Lipa is making reading cool again at this year's London Literature Festival
Pop star, activist, skincare entrepreneur and founder of an editorial platform (among her many ventures), Dua Lipa has long championed manifestation, from writing down her goals and using her song Training Season to manifest her ideal partner to mapping out major career milestones, including headlining Glastonbury.
Now, she is turning her attention to literature, taking on the role of curator for this year's 19th London Literature Festival at the Southbank Centre, one of London's leading arts and cultural venues, and cementing her status as a literary goddess of our time.
The festival brings together established literary names and emerging writers for conversations, readings, and events that explore the stories and ideas shaping our lives.
Generously supported by Bukhman Philanthropies, this year’s edition also coincides with the Southbank Centre’s 75th anniversary.
Running until 1 November, the festival has already offered plenty to get stuck into. From conversations with literary icons to poetry confronting the realities of our time and powerful personal testimony, The New Arab looks at some of the standout moments and ideas that have stayed with us so far.
Literary icons, intimate conversations and the power of poetry
For one day only, Dua made an appearance at the festival, taking to the stage alongside some of the most celebrated names in literature.
First up was British novelist Zadie Smith, whose debut novel, White Teeth, was published when she was just 24 and went on to become one of the most celebrated novels of the new millennium.
The programme also featured American singer and writer Patti Smith, who discussed her memoir, Bread of Angels. She spoke about her family and early interest in art, recalling how seeing a Picasso painting at the age of 12 and leaving the church after being told there was no place for art helped shape the independent spirit that has remained a defining part of her life and work.
Dua also welcomed Mustafa Ahmed, known as Mustafa the Poet, to the stage to discuss Nour, a project created with WePresent that brings together poetry, photography, interviews and visual art. Made freely available in 2025, the project explores themes of faith, love, grief and everyday rituals.
During the conversation, Dua revealed that Mustafa officiated her wedding to Callum Turner and wrote a poem for the couple. She described the gesture as meaningful and dedicated Noor Hindi’s Ode to Friendship to him.
Their discussion also touched on friendship and the importance of allowing the people we love the freedom to change and grow.
Special guest readings from poets Victoria Chang and Safia Elhillo added to the programme’s celebration of poetry.
A celebration of British Somali poetry
The focus on poetry continued beyond Dua’s appearance with A Celebration of British Somali Poetry, which brought together five poets to explore identity, migration and belonging. Among them was Samatar Elmi, who shared The Genocide Will Not Be Televised, a poem that combines historical references with raw, contemporary outrage.
Samatar recited the poem, which includes the lines: “The genocide will not be televised. The genocide will not be brought to you by Newsnight, Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. Piers Morgan will not ask if you condemn Hamas twice a day and thrice on Sundays. There will be no need to learn that if you place a gun to a parrot’s head, it squawks: ‘Israel has a right to defend itself,’ ‘Israel has a right to defend itself,’ in [a hundred and sixteen] languages, because the genocide will not be televised.”
Nadia Murad on survival and reclaiming her life
From poetry confronting the reporting of violence, the festival moved to personal testimony.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Nadia Murad sat down with BBC journalist Lyse Doucet to discuss surviving Islamic State group (IS) captivity in Iraq, becoming a leading voice for survivors of sexual violence and reclaiming her life beyond her past.
As Nadia put it, "Survival isn’t the same as finding peace. It’s an ongoing negotiation with memory." She also reflected on the expectations she faced early in her activism, when people pressured her to put her work before her own hopes of building a new life. "Are you supposed to suppress the part of myself that loved makeup and hair?" she asked.
Nadia also spoke about her mother, who was killed by IS, and the price women have to pay during violence and conflict.
Reflecting on how public conversations often focus on the numbers of soldiers and men killed, she said: "You know, the world focuses so much on how many soldiers are recovering or how many men were killed. It’s always about the numbers and the destruction.
"But there is always a specific price that women pay. My mother was killed because she was a woman, and they felt she was a threat to them. They thought that if she survived, she would rebuild that house or build a new one and bring the family together."
To end, Nadia reflected on how she met her now-husband, Abid Shamdeen, who was working as her translator at the time.
Describing him as the "love of her life, who gives me hope every day," she also shared a touching story from her latest book, I Choose My Beginning: A Story of Courage and Activism.
When Abid asked if there was one thing she wanted to do for herself, Nadia admitted that she felt self-conscious about her teeth. He never judged her for it. Instead, he eventually told her, "Nadia, I found you an orthodontist." Before she knew it, she had braces, "like a teenager."
Ta-Nehisi Coates and Tareq Baconi on Palestine and freedom
The festival also turned to questions of freedom and justice, as authors Ta-Nehisi Coates and Tareq Baconi joined journalist Nesrine Malik to discuss Palestine, decolonisation and their books, The Message and What Now: On Palestine, Freedom, and Our Global Future.
Tareq argued: "People who have and continue to colonise Palestine, there is no way in which the ‘us’ and the ‘them’, this colonial relationship, can coexist. Zionism means Palestinian extermination, so if we are committed to Palestinian life, we have to confront Zionism for what it is: this racist ideology that has no place in our world."
Ta-Nehisi, meanwhile, discussed how American slavery's need for expansion ultimately contributed to its own undoing, suggesting that oppressive systems can be driven by an insatiable appetite for more land and control.
He also pointed to Zionism's emphasis on maintaining a Jewish demographic majority as evidence of its exclusionary character, arguing that such a "project" cannot be separated from questions of racism.
Rama Duwaji brings the festival theme to the screen
Beyond the festival’s live events, a campaign film featuring words by Dua and animation by Syrian artist Rama Duwaji brings this year’s theme, Read the World Differently, to life on the Piccadilly Lights billboard and at the Southbank Centre.
One standout piece of writing on screen was an excerpt from Sufiyaan Salam’s Merky Books New Writers’ Prize-winning debut novel, Wimmy Road Boyz, which was also featured on Dua’s Service95 platform. The story follows three British-Pakistani friends on a chaotic night drive down Manchester’s Curry Mile.
A book swap for readers
For festivalgoers looking to take a little literary inspiration home, the festival’s book swap offers the chance to exchange books and leave recommendations for fellow readers.
It is a simple way to keep the conversation going beyond the stage, with each book offering the chance to discover a new favourite or see a familiar story in a new light.
And if there is one thing Dua’s own love life suggests, it is that a shared love of books can be a pretty good conversation starter.
The singer and Callum reportedly first bonded at a party in Los Angeles after discovering they were both reading Hernán Díaz’s Trust, having each just finished the first chapter when Callum joked, "So we’re on the same page."
The London Literature Festival runs until 1 November 2026, with events still to come
Zainab Mehdi is a British-Iraqi journalist and Associate Features Editor at The New Arab. She holds a BSc in Modern History and International Relations from the University of Essex and an MA in Near and Middle Eastern Studies from SOAS
Follow her on Instagram: @zaiamehdi_/@zainabmehdiwrites_

Former US officials who resigned over Gaza urge 2028 presidential candidates to reject architects of Biden-era policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:59:27 UTC
00:59:27 KST

Rabia İclal Turan
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
A group of former US government officials who resigned because of Washington’s policy in the Gaza Strip has urged candidates seeking the 2028 presidential nomination to pledge not to appoint officials they said enabled Israel's genocide in the enclave.
“Senior Biden Administration officials who were architects of the Gaza policy are now actively white-washing their own roles in enabling genocide,” Gaza Resignees said in a statement signed by 12 former officials.
“They violated U.S. and international law by providing U.S. weapons while Israel indiscriminately and disproportionately attacked civilians and civilian infrastructure, and as Israel arbitrarily blocked humanitarian assistance to Gaza,” it said.
The signatories include former State Department officials Josh Paul, Annelle Sheline and Stacy Gilbert, former diplomats Hala Rharrit and Mike Casey, former White House official Anna Del Castillo and former USAID senior adviser Alexander Smith. Also among them are former Army officer and Defense Intelligence Agency official Harrison Mann, former Air Force Maj. Riley Livermore, former Navy Lt. Cmdr. Hani Z. Nofal and former political appointees Tariq Habash of the Education Department and Lily Greenberg Call of the Interior Department.
“Not even two years since the end of their disastrous time in office, many of these same officials appear to be pursuing a path back into the halls of power,” they said.
“The most basic level of accountability, the most minimal level of consequences, is to ensure that those who have wreaked so much harm from within the highest levels of our Government cannot return to it,” according to the statement.
The group said that “Gaza has become a litmus test for the credibility of American politicians and the viability, in particular, of Democratic candidates.”
The pledge asks candidates to acknowledge US “complicity” in Israel's genocide in Gaza. It also asks them to exclude any past or present political appointee who was “an architect, leader, defender, or key enabler” of the policy.
In a video released with the statement, the former officials took turns reading the call over images of former Secretary of State Antony Blinken, who now sits on the board of directors of the Center for American Progress, a Washington think tank.
“We have watched as elite institutions have welcomed these officials,” said Mann, as the video showed former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk, who is now with venture capital firm Lux Capital and a CNN commentator. It also showed former National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan and former USAID Administrator Samantha Power, who both joined Harvard Kennedy School after leaving office.
“We have watched as these officials have tried to launder their bloody reputations,” Paul said, with Rharrit adding, “and prepare to re-enter the halls of power.”
“And we say, enough,” the former officials said in the video. “Enough with the culture of impunity in Washington. Enough with policies that break our laws and defy our values.”
“They have blood on their hands,” they added.
Top Biden administration officials at that time acknowledged civilian suffering in Gaza but defended Israel’s right to defend itself following the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack.
US-made weapons were photographed several times in Israeli strikes in Gaza, although US authorities have declined to confirm this.
Since October 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, mostly women and children, and wounded over 175,000, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. It has also caused widespread destruction affecting around 90% of the territory’s civilian infrastructure.
More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in the Gaza Strip since an October 2025 ceasefire went into effect.

Elena Dudum's Palestinian memoir confronts identity and erasure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:57:55 UTC
00:57:55 KST

Breadcrumb
They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful: Elena Dudum's memoir asks what it means to inherit a homeland
At its core, every coming-of-age memoir asks: How do I convince the world that I exist? However, Elena Dudum’s memoir They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful (Atria/One Signal) complicates this simple idea by asking: How do I prove my existence when the world is committed to destroying the evidence?
Unlike traditional coming-of-age memoir that simply deals with the trials of childhood, adolescence, and young adulthood, this memoir is dedicated to the process of coming into consciousness in the face of outright denial.
A Palestinian Christian raised in San Francisco, in some ways Elena’s upbringing follows the prototypical footprint for any diasporic Arab American — her grandparents came to America and built lives.
However, the particulars of her story stand out — her Palestinian-born grandparents married American-born Arabs, and contrary to post 9/11 American popular conception, she is not Muslim.
Instead, she was heavily involved in her Palestinian Christian community as a child. She moved through adolescence and young adulthood in proximity to privilege, privately educated and rubbing elbows with San Francisco's elite.
However, the truth is that although she was in the right rooms, people viewed her differently.
A third grader in 2001, she pulled her teacher aside: "I told Miss Crane that my cousin and I would not share where our family was from… We would tell people we were from Guatemala."
The fact of their origins, uttered in hushed tones. Disguised and distorted, for fear that true disclosure would mutate into misunderstood hatred.
Whether it was classmates' parents, a friend's boyfriend at the bar, or even the college administration, Elena Dudum constantly had to push against the idea of her identity rather than its reality.
A scene that stands out: Her own sense of self, punctured as an eight-year-old, when a friend's father driving her asks, "Where’s your family from again?" This inspired a grown man to ask a child whether or not she supports Israel. The first of a lifetime of questions ended with the resolute thought, "You guys anti-Semitic or something?"
From a young age, she is forced to understand that her identity is immediately challenged. Her family, a threat.
But she didn't understand this alone. Her father, forever frenzied with the need to educate his children, through private education and lectures on the way to school, armed them with the phrase: "You would be attributing to me a prejudice to which I do not subscribe."
A legacy of proof
This memoir, of course, follows the coming-of-age canon by having a parent to push against, but what I admire most is that this father-daughter relationship is unsentimental and deeply unresolved.
Are family dynamics ever truly resolved? So many memoirs pretend they can be. But Elena does not stray from truth: the difficulty of her father, and the identity of being Palestinian.
From childhood to adulthood, her father's lecturing is consistent. But his command and ferocity deplete her (and him) over time, her willingness to listen as a child arms her for the revelations she finds on her own as an adult.
How do you not lose your mind when trying to prove something you know exists? Elena writes, "Now he scours the web for one-hundred-year-old magazines about Palestine: LIFE, National Geographic, even The Illustrated London News, the world’s first graphic weekly news magazine. For years, he would reference these mysterious documents but show them to nobody. ‘I have proof,’ he would say, ‘that Palestine exists.’"
He has the archive. The difficulty lies in his inability to trust, even when his own daughter tries to access what he has hoarded as precious truth.
The lack of sentimentality comes down to this fact: this book is about inheriting a mission, whether she wanted to or not.
Each chapter starts with an epigraph from her father's archive: A quote from a 1946 issue of Life Magazine, describing the beauty, bounty, and existence of Palestine.
As much as he tries to keep her from it — growing belligerent and paranoid at the request — the epigraphs nod to one simple fact: she has inherited his mission, his collection.
She doesn't want to inherit this mission; her very existence forces her to.
Refusing to be erased
Elena’s memoir looks hard at who gets cast as actor and who as victim in narratives of atrocity, and how American institutions and everyday language shape that framing.
Her writing is clear and cogent: it points to the syntax and grammar of oppression, as well as the deliberate silence it produces.
What I find most palpable in this text is the question of how language can erase, displacing blame and reframing crime as power.
But it's not simply syntax and grammar; it's a lifetime series of silences. She takes her reader through her experience as an undergraduate at Barnard and a graduate student at Columbia, both institutions I also attended.
However, I did not embody the very identity that those institutions deny, villainise, and deliberately silence. She takes us through her discussions with the president of Barnard after their banner was removed from Barnard Hall after one single day (which I witnessed firsthand).
Elena goes against her father's advice, fearing for her safety. She speaks up, but to no avail: "I resented him for instilling a fear in me just as much as he instilled a fire."
As a graduate student at Columbia, Elena audits a course called The Creation of Israel. After sitting in class, agitated by the rage she witnessed her father embody, she can’t help but push back on every claim backed by studied evidence and stats, and the professor ultimately asks her not to participate.
But Elena knows better. Her family’s orange grove, remembered by her grandfather, whom she calls Siddi. She imagines Siddi as a child, sitting in a tree with ripe fruit in his palm.
The gold jewellery on her wrist, all her Taita carried away with her during the Nakba. In her genome, through generational word of mouth: she remembers. Her family’s name, engraved above a doorway in Palestine. Her family’s history, still standing in Ramallah.
When asking her father the very question she grapples with most: "When did I know I was Palestinian?" Her father replies, "‘It’s not because I’m Palestinian that I’m like this,’ he says. I can’t see him, but I know he’s shaking his head. ‘It’s just who I am."'
Ultimately, Elena’s personal narrative is the counter-archive: her life, testimony. She braids memoir with archival fragments; the form itself treats family memory as resistance. She knows the rage, the denial, the sheer fight, foisted upon her and her father: "Here I am, Palestinian in your wake."
Those who witness her and her memoir in entirety hold her rage and pick up the mantle. She is no longer alone in the fight for posterity, for truth. No one can ignore this memoir, or the power of rage-inducing truth.
Paulina Pinsky is a Los Angeles-based writer, author, writing coach, educator, podcaster and performer. She is the co-author of the teen guide to consent, It Doesn’t Have to Be Awkward: Dealing with Relationships, Consent, and Other Hard-to-Talk-About Stuff
Follow her on Instagram: @paulina_pinsky

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the embassy expressed deep regret over persistent negative approaches toward Iran, including repeated allegations of Iranian interference in Kuwait’s internal affairs.
It said such baseless accusations against Iranian nationals violated the principle of good neighborliness and international law.
The statement said that, amid the dangerous consequences of US and Israeli military aggression against Iran, regional countries should pursue responsible and prudent policies to prevent further escalation of tensions imposed on the region.
Kuwait’s State Security and Terrorism Crimes Court sentenced three defendants to death over alleged espionage for Lebanon’s Hezbollah and plans to assassinate senior figures and officials. Eight others received five-year prison terms.

UK Chancellor pledges 3% GDP on defence spending by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:56:25 UTC
00:56:25 KST

Breadcrumb
UK Chancellor pledges 3% GDP on defence spending by 2030, plans to meet NATO targets by 2035
The UK will increase defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, Chancellor John Healey has announced in the Autumn budget on Wednesday.
The Chancellor said this was part of the UK's plan to meet NATO's defence spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035.
US President Donald Trump has pressured European members of NATO to spend least 3.5% of GDP on core defence requirements after several members of the military alliance failed to meet the previous defence spending target of 2% of GDP.
As well as spending on military forces, NATO counts spending on police forces who are trained in military tactics, and can be deployed abroad as part of military operations, as defence expenditure.
Healey said he will set out the details on how he will meet the defence targets next year.
He also announced an increase in private investment in defence.
Healey previously served as Defence Secretary in Kier Starmer's Cabinet, before resigning in June over the former Prime Minister's defence investment plan, which he said "falls well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time."
Healey's resignation is widely considered one of the key factors behind the end of Starmer's premiership earlier this year.
In 2025, while Defence Secretary, Healey said the UK is in "in a new era of threat," citing the previous US-Israeli war on Iran, and Russia's war on Ukraine.
"As the threat grows, Britain must step up," he said in the same speech in Parliament.
In his budget announcement on Wednesday, he repeatedly cited the war in the Middle East as a leading cause of the UK's high cost of living, especially due to rising energy costs.
"These are the global economic storms we face'" Healey said, "we must choose the course we steer through them."
Healey also announced a £100 winter energy payment for millions of households in the lowest council tax bands.
The Chancellor also announced an extension of the five pence cut to fuel duty until July 2027.
Duty for motor fuels was temporarily cut in 2022 after fuel costs spiked following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Healey announced that the measures to ease energy bills will be funded by a temporary 3% increase in taxes for banks. The rise will be on top of the 25% corporate tax rate they currently pay.
Healey also announced an end to gas standing charges from next year in a bid to help households with energy prices which rose after the US and Israel's February invasion of Iran.
Currently, households pay a fixed yearly fee on top of their household gas bill, regardless of their usage. Scrapping the standing charge will shift that payment onto the unit rates.
That means around 60% household that use less gas will save money, while those that use the most gas will see their bills increase.
The move will not cost the Government any money. Rather, it will shift some of the burden for energy bills from lower income households to those on higher incomes.

Real Madrid issues apology to China over Mbappe’s Mao remarks
Spanish football club seeks to quell anger after its initial response was rejected by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV Sports
2-MIN READ2-MIN

Real Madrid has issued an apology to China over Kylian Mbappe’s controversial remarks about the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong, after the Spanish football club’s initial response failed to quell anger in China.
In a statement published on its website on Wednesday, the club apologised to the Chinese people for “any discomfort” caused by the French footballer’s remarks, a day after Mbappe issued his own public apology.
The apology came after Chinese state broadcaster CCTV Sports rejected Real Madrid’s initial explanation as inadequate, suspending broadcasts of La Liga matches and removing programmes and advertisements featuring Mbappe while demanding apologies from both the club and the player.

Across China: Love born of language exchange blossoms into children's reading room in Xinjiang

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:40:37 CST
00:40:37 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- In a downtown reading room in Urumqi, capital city of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, children sit in a circle around Steven Dahlke, a 45-year-old German teacher.
He holds up a picture book and imitates the sounds of its animal characters. Beside him, his wife Gulayim Akim offers gentle prompts. The room is filled with laughter, amid the rustle of pages and children's eager voices.
This is no ordinary reading room. Opened in 2024 by Dahlke and Akim, it is a bilingual picture-book space where local children are introduced to languages through stories, games and patient encouragement. It is the latest chapter in a cross-border love story that has begun with language itself.
Dahlke comes from Rostock, Germany, and has lived and worked in China for many years. Fifteen years ago, an international language exchange program connected him with Akim, a young woman from Xinjiang. Language built a bridge between them and affection later followed. The couple married in 2015 and have since formed a warm cross-cultural family.
Four years ago, the family settled in Urumqi. While raising their son Jacob, the couple noticed his remarkable ability to absorb languages. Using picture books, stories and everyday conversation, they taught him Chinese, English and German. The boy's language skills improved rapidly.
"I wanted to share this experience with other parents and children," Akim said.
That desire led to the opening of the reading room in 2024. Drawing on years of university teaching experience, the couple carefully selected picture books and designed interactive games to make language learning enjoyable. They emphasize encouragement and patient companionship, aiming to spark children's initiative rather than pressure them.
"We found that when children are having fun, they easily take the initiative to learn," Dahlke said. "In the reading room, children learn together, and that makes it more enjoyable."
Their approach has gradually won recognition among local families. Outside the reading room, the couple also volunteer in the community and organize public reading activities during holidays, encouraging young people to fall in love with reading and language learning.
Dahlke said the community has been kind to them, and they hope to give back in whatever way they can.
For Dahlke, Urumqi's growth is visible almost every year. "In the past, the airport was very small. Now there is a modern international airport with routes to many countries," he noted.
The neighborhood where the family lives was under construction a decade ago. Today, it is surrounded by large parks and a cultural center.
"You can truly feel how this city has grown from a small western city into a big one," Dahlke said. He especially likes the nearby parks and often takes his son to the newly opened cultural venues.
Dahlke has traveled to other Chinese cities such as Shanghai, Beijing, Xi'an and Chongqing, and likes both the modern energy of metropolises and the deep cultural roots of historic cities. But what makes him feel most at ease is the life his family has built here.
Looking ahead, they are full of hope. "Language is an important bond that connects the world, links people and builds friendship. We met, got to know each other, and committed to each other through cross-border language exchange, and we hope to pass on the beauty and warmth that transcends borders," they said. ■

Explainer: What happens next after Israel's inconclusive election?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:40:12 CST
00:40:12 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Counting of votes in Israel's parliamentary election continued on Wednesday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, both claiming a mandate to lead the country, despite neither appearing to have secured the majority needed to form a government.
Israel now faces political uncertainty, with analysts pointing to several possible scenarios, including prolonged coalition negotiations, a unity government or another round of elections, while Arab parties could hold the key to breaking the deadlock.
WHAT DO THE RESULTS SHOW?
With about 85 percent of the votes counted, Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc was projected to win 53 seats in the 120-seat parliament, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition bloc. The Arab-majority parties -- the Joint List, a coalition alliance of three parties, and the Muslim Ra'am party -- were projected to win a combined 19 seats.
The figures could still change, with votes cast under special voting arrangements yet to be counted, including those cast by soldiers, diplomats abroad and hospital patients. Final official results are expected by Nov. 4, according to a timetable issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee.
Israel's proportional electoral system adds to the uncertainty. Parties must win at least 3.25 percent of the national vote to enter parliament, meaning minor shifts in voting margins could significantly alter the distribution of seats.
WHO WILL FORM THE NEXT GOVERNMENT?
Securing the most seats does not automatically give a party leader the right to form a government.
Following the publication of official results, President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of elected parties before assigning the mandate to the lawmaker he deems most likely to assemble a viable majority -- not necessarily the leader of the largest party or bloc.
The designated candidate will have 28 days to negotiate a coalition, with a possible extension of up to 14 days. If he fails, the president can assign another lawmaker to try to assemble a government.
Should that secondary attempt also collapse, a parliamentary majority can request a final opportunity to put forward a third candidate.
If all coalition attempts prove unsuccessful, parliament will automatically dissolve, forcing Israel into another election and extending the political stalemate for months.
In the interim, Netanyahu and his outgoing cabinet would remain in office as a caretaker government until a new government is formed.
On Wednesday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog said that every effort must be made to avoid another round of elections.
COULD ARAB PARTIES DECIDE WHO BECOMES PRIME MINISTER?
To avoid such a costly deadlock, attention has turned to whether Israel's Arab-majority parties, projected to control 19 seats, could hold the balance of power in the next parliament.
Both Ra'am and Joint List have expressed willingness to help Eisenkot's "change bloc" replace Netanyahu. Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas said Tuesday night that his party wanted to join a coalition led by the bloc. On Wednesday, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said the alliance was "ready and prepared to pave the way" for replacing Netanyahu's government through an unprecedented political partnership with Eisenkot's bloc.
"Change can only come through Jewish-Arab partnership, a genuine and equal partnership," Jabareen said in a post on social media platform X.
However, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have rejected forming a government dependent on Arab parties. Eisenkot has repeatedly ruled out including them in his coalition or relying on their parliamentary support from outside it.
Despite this stance, divergent views remain within Eisenkot's alliance, as Yair Golan, leader of The Democrats within the "change bloc", on Wednesday urged his allies to abandon their refusal to cooperate with Arab parties.
One possible outcome could be a minority government supported by Arab lawmakers from outside the coalition, an arrangement that would require Eisenkot to reverse his election pledge against partnering with Arab parties.
Such reversals are not unprecedented in Israeli politics, where coalition negotiations have often forced party leaders to compromise on campaign promises. ■

Swiss AI is forging a different path from US and Chinese giants

Swiss AI is forging a different path from US and Chinese giants
Swiss start-up Giotto is taking a gamble by launching a sovereign artificial intelligence (AI) operating system for the general public.
This marks an unprecedented Swiss push into a global market overwhelmingly dominated by United States and Chinese giants, such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Switzerland is now seeking to showcase its own strengths.
In the global race for generative AI, the American and Chinese trailblazers are taking the lion’s share. However, some Swiss players are hoping to play the role of spoiler. Giotto has already rolled out its tool to large companies such as Groupe Mutuel, RUAG and SAP, and is now targeting the general public.
Another notable success story is Apertus. The large language model, developed in Switzerland, has surpassed six million downloads in a year, overtaking French rival Mistral. This unexpected success is a reward for taking a novel approach.
More
Switzerland’s open AI model could help guard the web – or empower its attackers
“There are two benchmarks: performance and the trust people have in the model. We’re trying to build trust through complete transparency,” Martin Jaggi, professor of machine learning at the Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne EPFL, told Swiss public broadcaster RTS.
This open approach is reassuring at a time when the capabilities of AI sometimes frighten the general public. According to a Politico survey, two in three Americans believe there is a risk that AI could destroy humanity.
Data sovereignty
But a Swiss AI is also a guarantee of sovereignty at a time when international tensions are flaring up again.
“Without a model like Apertus, we have no control over the future of AI in this country,” said Antoine Bosselut, co-founder of Apertus. With systems such as ChatGPT or Claude, developers could decide overnight to cut off access to Switzerland, he added, or they could decide that all data transmitted should go directly to the US government. And it’s the same with Chinese models.
More
Switzerland’s uphill climb to AI sovereignty
This view is shared by Aldo Podestà, co-founder of Giotto, who believes that AI is a fundamental technology that Switzerland must master. He compares control of AI to that of electricity. In his view, a country that lacks the necessary expertise in this field would be unable to maintain its level of development.
He also believes that Switzerland has the necessary expertise to carve out a place for itself in AI. In particular, he cites the research teams at Swiss universities.
To compete with American and Chinese companies, Giotto does not want to rely solely on speed. The company intends to develop high-performance models that consume little energy. “We must focus on efficiency,” said Podestà.
More
Why China’s approach to AI intrigues Switzerland
Investor reluctance
Nevertheless, Switzerland suffers from investor reluctance, according to Charles-Henry Monchau, head of investments at SYZ Bank. “There is a bottleneck: access to capital,” he said. “Generally speaking, Swiss start-ups manage to raise their initial few million. The problem lies in raising the hundreds of millions needed for subsequent development.”
“Unfortunately, the best minds are leaving Switzerland, or companies are being bought out by larger foreign firms.”
Unable to compete financially on generalist, mass-market models, Switzerland’s salvation could lie in specialisation – in other words, AI dedicated to specific tasks.
Just like the watchmaking industry, Switzerland will struggle to compete with major foreign players on entry-level products. But it could become a benchmark for high-performance niche products.

====================================================================================================

Landmark study finds three in four NFL players die with CTE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:25:30 UTC
00:25:30 KST

American football can be brutal. Scientists have long known that the hits, tackles and other collisions that are central to the sport come with health risks, but what these impacts do to the brain has been less clear. What we do know is that many footballers have died with brains that have shown evidence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a disease associated with symptoms such as mood swings and dementia. But because a diagnosis requires that investigators look for damage in a person’s brain after they die, it’s unclear just how common CTE is among current or former athletes.
But now, in a study published in JAMA Network Open, an analysis of medical records from thousands of deceased former NFL players—including hundreds who donated their brains to science—estimates that about 75 percent of these players likely died with CTE.
“No other environmental or occupational exposure ever studied is known to have increased dementia risk at death by that amount,” says Yorghos Tripodis, senior author of the paper and a professor of biostatistics at Boston University.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The study is based on records of 2,362 former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 and played in the league for an average of five years. Among those who donated their brains—almost 400 players—a stunning 93.5 percent had CTE. Signs of CTE in the brain can include atrophy, or tissue wasting, as well as clusters of tau protein—a symptom that is also linked to Alzheimer’s disease.
The high incidence of CTE in those donors may reflect the sample itself: people who donate their brains to science tend to have more severe behavioral symptoms, Tripodis says. That could skew the dataset, potentially making CTE rates appear artificially high.
To better estimate how common CTE might have been across all 2,362 former players in the study, Tripodis and his colleagues analyzed the medical records of donors and nondonors. The team found that people with cognitive symptoms were about five times more likely to donate their brain. Given that, the researchers recalculated their incidence estimate to find that some three in four football players in the study likely had CTE.
For comparison, among the general population, fewer than 1 percent of brains in community-based brain banks show signs of CTE, Tripodis says.
The study only includes NFL players who had died, and it remains difficult, if not impossible, to diagnose CTE in living players. It is hard to say what the risk to NFL players today is, Tripodis says. The NFL has also taken steps to mitigate the risk of head injuries.
The records may also be incomplete or imprecise. For instance, symptoms of CTE such as dementia may not be listed on death records, Tripodis says. And even if dementia is listed, it can have other—even multiple—causes.
This study is “the best attempt so far to correct for selection bias in CTE brain bank data,” says Russell Lonser, a professor in neurological surgery at the Ohio State University, who was not involved in the study. But “it is an estimate from a model and should be read that way.”
"Without similar men who never played contact sports, we can’t tell how much of the pathology or dementia comes from football,” Lonser says. “The 75 percent includes any CTE pathology, even early changes that may never have caused symptoms.”
To better understand how football increases the risks of CTE, Lonser says, you’d need to study players, with and without symptoms, over time, along with conducting brain analyses and including a comparison group of people who had no exposure to head impacts. “Until that work is done, we won’t know how common CTE really is or what, specifically, it means for players.”
Still, Tripodis hopes the findings will prove useful for families who have been affected by CTE and will inform current and future players of the risks involved in the sport.
“CTE is a preventable disease. We find, in study after study, that the more blows to the head over your lifetime, the higher the risk of CTE,” Tripodis says. “If you reduce exposure to repetitive head impacts, then you reduce the risk of CTE.”

====================================================================================================

The Evolution of Taiwan’s Military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:25:00 UTC
00:25:00 KST

The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Eric Setzekorn – historian and author of “On the Brink: A Military History of Taiwan” (Naval Institute Press 2026) with over two dozen academic articles published in Parameters, the Journal of American-East Asian Relations, and the Journal of Military and Strategic Studies – is the 532nd in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.” The views expressed in this publication are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the official policy or position of the Department of Defense or the U.S. government.
Identify the main milestones in the history of Taiwan’s military.
Since 1949, Taiwan’s military has undergone tremendous changes, but two pivotal moments are especially notable.
The 1958 Taiwan Strait Crisis demonstrated that a coherent and well-trained military in Taiwan was increasingly capable of a wide range of sophisticated operations. The poorly organized and equipped soldiers of 1949 would likely have been swept aside by PLA forces if there had been an invasion of Taiwan, but by the end of the 1950s Taiwan’s military had over a dozen well-trained divisions, hundreds of jet fighters, and professional officers.
The enactment of a National Defense Act in 2002 was the culmination of a profound transformation during the 1990s from one-party KMT dominance into a non-partisan, civilian-led defense structure that reflected Taiwan’s democratic culture. The 2002 National Defense Act stipulated that the defense minister must be a civilian and required regular reports on military policies and combat readiness to the Legislative Yuan. The act also provided specific guidance regarding the political status of military personnel, noting, “The ROC Armed Forces shall remain neutral from individual, regional and party affiliations in accordance with the Act.”
Explain how and why the institutional identity of Taiwan’s military moved away from a “party-army” conception.
After 1949, and well into the 1990s, Taiwan’s military was integrated into the KMT political party as a core element of the party’s authoritarian rule over Taiwan. During his nearly half-century as the leader of the KMT, Chiang Kai-shek kept close control over the military through stifling surveillance, required party membership for military officers, and incorporated KMT propaganda into military training. These political linkages meant that military roles often spilled over into numerous domestic functions, such as policing during the period of martial law from 1949 to 1987, often referred to as the White Terror.
Beginning in the 1980s, and continuing into the 2000s, the military has become an apolitical institution that reflected the cultural sophistication and vibrant democracy of Taiwan. Despite this steady evolution, the legacies of Taiwan’s authoritarian past continue to influence the relationship between Taiwan’s military and society.
How did Taiwan’s military become more adaptable after the rise of Xi Jinping and China’s increasingly aggressive posture toward Taiwan?
Taiwan’s adaptation to the rise of Xi Jinping and increasing PLA aggressive behavior has taken two primary forms: increasing civil-military unity, and an operational shift in military planning.
Since 2020, there has been a significant increase in the negative attitudes of Taiwanese towards China, and this has led to increased public support for additional military spending and an extension of military service requirements. Public opinion polling conducted after the visit of U.S. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi in August 2022, and subsequent Chinese exercises, revealed that 85 percent of respondents favored extending compulsory military service. Public concern is also reflected in steady increases to defense budget after 2016, with military spending more than tripling from 2016 to 2027.
During Tsai Ing-wen’s first term (2016-2020), her administration promoted what became known as the Overall Defense Concept (ODC). The ODC emphasized what many Taiwanese and American defense analysts label “asymmetric warfare.” Supporters of the ODC argued that acquisitions should focus on fielding smaller, less expensive defense systems. For Taiwan’s Navy, for example, the ODC approach stressed fielding of smaller vessels, such as stealthy corvettes armed with short-range anti-ship missiles, and naval mines, rather than conventional surface ships such as frigates and destroyers.
Describe two plausible scenarios for a potential Taiwan Strait conflict.
The massive expansion of the PLA Navy, with associated increases in air force and army capabilities, has enabled Chinese political leaders and PLA military planners to envision multiple scenarios for military action against Taiwan.
A sudden Chinese attack on one of Taiwan’s outlying islands would force Taiwan’s military to respond in areas that would strain air and naval support. Taiping Island is 930 miles (1,500 km) from Taiwan’s main port of Kaohsiung, making it far outside the range of any Taiwanese combat aircraft. Taiwan faces a similar situation on Pratas Island, which is roughly 250 miles (415 km) southwest of Kaohsiung, and only 150 miles from the Chinese coast.
In a blockade scenario, powerful PLA naval surface forces, likely including an aircraft carrier, could close shipping lanes near Taiwan. Submarines would provide Taiwan with a potent force to challenge PLA naval deployments and defend sea lanes of communication (SLOC).
In December 2014, the Taiwan began a program to develop an Indigenous Defense Submarine (IDS), and in April 2018, the United States approved the export licenses needed for U.S. companies to sell naval technology to Taiwan for the submarine program. Construction of the first submarine, the Hai Kun, began in 2020, and by mid-2023 it was launched for testing and certification. In total, Taiwan plans to build eight IDS submarines by the mid-2030s.
Looking ahead, assess key factors that will likely shape the future development of Taiwan’s military and their impact on Taiwan-U.S. relations.
In the past 50 years, American support to Taiwan has often been measured in terms of arms sales, but Taiwan’s domestic arms industry has become increasingly sophisticated and efficient. In particular, the development of a wide range of anti-ship missiles and drones has decreased dependence on the United States and made Taiwan’s military more capable. For vital naval systems, Taiwan’s National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST), and Taiwan International Shipbuilding (CSBC) have become the primary suppliers of mines, missiles, drones, and warships for Taiwan.
A second significant development is the shift from a primarily bilateral U.S.-Taiwan security relationship to a possible trilateral U.S.-Taiwan-Japan security relationship. Japan is heavily reliant on sea lanes that pass through both the South China Sea and Taiwan for roughly 90 percent of its energy imports and 40 percent of its maritime trade. Japanese political leaders have begun adjusting expectations about Japanese involvement in a Taiwan conflict. In November 2021, [former Prime Minister] Abe Shinzo made remarks that any contingency related to Taiwan would be an emergency for Japan and for the U.S.-Japan security alliance, and current Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has stated that a Taiwan conflict would be “a survival-threatening situation” for Japan.

EU to boost refining capacity as energy crisis drives up fuel prices, commissioner says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:21:16 UTC
00:21:16 KST

Aysu Biçer
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The EU will work to increase domestic refining capacity and boost fuel production as geopolitical tensions drive up energy prices, European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said Wednesday.
“Once again, due to geopolitical turbulence, Europe faces another energy crisis,” Jorgensen told a press conference in Brussels.
He said crude oil and petroleum product prices had increased significantly worldwide, putting pressure on European households and businesses.
“Fuel bills in the EU are skyrocketing,” he said, adding that the global diesel market is expected to remain tight well into 2027, keeping prices high.
Jorgensen said European refineries had played a vital role in ensuring security of supply, including jet fuel, despite challenging market conditions.
He noted that around a quarter of EU refineries had shut down over the past two decades, reducing domestic refining capacity by around 10%, while divestments had accelerated across Europe.
“But this crisis is a wake-up call: We need to counter this trend and ensure that we have adequate and flexible refining capacity in Europe. Today and for the future,” he said.
Jorgensen stressed that refining capacity was not only a matter of economic competitiveness but also of security, highlighting the need for reliable and affordable fuel supplies for citizens, businesses and defense.
The Commission will continue technical discussions with the sector and reconvene early next year to assess progress, he said.
“We will work to increase outputs from refining assets in Europe. The industry has made some suggestions that we need to assess,” he added.
Jorgensen said the EU would also examine the long-term future of the refining sector as the bloc pursues decarbonization, with a focus on expanding the production of biofuels and e-fuels.
“The production of renewable liquid fuels has already compensated some of the reduction in Europe’s refinery capacity. The potential is significant,” he said.

British far-right activist Tommy Robinson has been found guilty of harassing two journalists following a trial at a London court, according to media reports Wednesday.
Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, 43, faced two charges of harassment causing fear of violence against two men over incidents in 2024.
He was accused of harassment causing fear of violence against Andrew Young, an investigative reporter, and Jacob Dirnhuber, an editor at the Daily Mail and MailOnline.
He was convicted by a jury majority of 10 to two following a trial at Southwark Crown Court in London, the BBC reported.
Robinson pleaded not guilty to the charges at a hearing at Westminster Magistrates’ Court in 2025.  
Posts, messages
The charges related to two counts of harassment causing fear of violence against the journalists through US social media company X between Aug. 5-7, 2024.
They also involved an alleged phone call on Aug. 5, 2024. He was accused of telling Young in the call that he would go to his house, adding: “I’m coming to get you.”
In one of the direct messages he was accused of sending Dirnhuber on X on the same day, he allegedly said: “I’ll be knocking at your door.”
On Aug. 6, Yaxley-Lennon allegedly posted: “Got ya @Jdirnhuber this is Jacob, he likes to locate and endanger families.”
“Jacob and the rest of the Daily Mail journalists who were involved in endangering my children have today been located.”
He continued: “I look forward to hearing on camera your justification for doxxing my children’s location. I got all three of you tagged and bagged in one day.”
Later that day, he was also accused of messaging Dirnhuber to say: “I’ll bring my questions to all your doors.”
Robinson has a long criminal record, with convictions for multiple assaults, mortgage fraud, faking a passport, stalking, contempt of court and various public order offenses. He served five prison terms between 2005 and 2025.
He also co-founded the English Defense League, a far-right, anti-Islam group, and served as its leader from 2009 to 2013.

Caretaker role could limit Netanyahu but not rule out war with Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:16:31 UTC
00:16:31 KST

Caretaker role could limit Israel’s Netanyahu, but not when it comes to waging war on Iran
- Benjamin Netanyahu is likely to face more limits as caretaker prime minister after Israel’s Oct 27 election, as no bloc is projected to win a majority.
- Experts say a caretaker government still has broad powers, and security issues are a key exception to restraint.
- Analysts warn Netanyahu could legally choose war with Iran, while President Isaac Herzog will later consult leaders and name a government candidate.
AI generated
JERUSALEM - Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to face more constraints as Israel’s caretaker prime minister after the Oct 27 election, but experts say his government could still retain significant powers including when it comes to waging war on Iran.
Neither Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition nor an opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is projected by Israeli media to win a majority in the country’s 120-seat legislature.
Eisenkot has acknowledged the prime minister was still in office as a caretaker, but issued a warning that Netanyahu might use security for political ends.
Netanyahu’s office has previously rejected accusations he is using the Iran conflict for political gain. His office did not immediately return a request for comment on Oct 28.
“If you look at the letter of the law, a caretaker government has the same authority, has the same powers as a regular government,” said Guy Lurie, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, adding however that a caretaker government “has a duty of restraint” and more limited discretion to act in some areas.
A caretaker government faces limitations when it comes to issues such as appointments, but has leeway to act in matters where there is a public interest, analysts say.
“In general, security issues are the clearest exception to this duty of restraint,” said Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, noting that Israel’s supreme court has previously held that a caretaker government must avoid far-reaching decisions unless they are justified by a pressing necessity.
“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset convenes and before its committees are formed,” Asher said, adding that “a caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran”.
After the final tally is in, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog is expected to consult party leaders and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government, with the nominee then getting up to 42 days to establish a government. REUTERS

Cop says sorry to Fakir's family, police for saying 'if he croaks we'll have fun'
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:15:36 CET
00:15:36 KST

One of the two police officers who
restrained 42-year-old coked-up and mentally ill Moroccan
Abderrahim Fakir in Bologna on July 19 before he died in their
hands on Wednesday apologised to the man's family and to the
police force for saying, as recorded by his bodycam, "if he
croaks we'll have fun".
                                    
"I want to apologize to Abderrahim Fakir's family and to my
corps for the unacceptable comments I made," he told ANSA.
                                    
The two officers are facing manslaughter charges in the case.
                                    
The other police officers who restrained Fakir allegedly said
"what do I care (if he dies)", as recorded on one of their body
cams, the prosecutors who have charged them with manslaughter
said Tuesday.
                                    
The death was due to extreme agitation, the high dose of cocaine
he had assumed, and his prone position, experts for the
prosecution against the two police officers charged with
manslaughter said Tuesday.
                                    
The cause of Fakir's death, the experts said, is "attributable
to acute respiratory failure in an individual suffering from
acute cocaine intoxication (as a chronic user) and severe heart
disease."
Factors contributing to the death—which was "hypoxic in
nature"—included psychomotor agitation and hyperthermia
(resulting from acute cocaine intoxication), as well as the
prone position. This is the conclusion reached by the
consultants for the Bologna public prosecutors regarding the
case. Furthermore, the analysis "revealed extensive traumatic
injuries—specifically contusions"—which "played no role in
causing the death."
Fakir died after being pinned to the ground face down.
                                    
His family's lawyer has said the case was like that of Riccardo
Magherini, a 39-year-old man who died while being arrested by
Carabinieri police in Florence in 2014.
                                    
Italy was condemned to pay damages by the European Court of
Human Rights over Magherini's case earlier this year.
                                    
The Bologna prosecution experts further said that they had
identified issues regarding the timeliness and effectiveness of
the medical response but that even with a proper intervention,
the chance of Fakir surviving would have been around 15%.
                                    
"Ultimately, shortcomings can be identified in the conduct of
both the first responders and the medical personnel who arrived
subsequently; their actions did not adhere to emergency medical
protocols, neither in terms of timeliness nor in the
effectiveness of the procedures performed," they said.
                                    
"However, even had there been a timely and correctly executed
intervention, Abderrahim's chances of survival would have been
approximately 15%," the experts further noted.

Minister Sjoerdsma announces new support package during visit to Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:57:48 UTC
23:57:48 KST

The Dutch government will provide Ukraine with a package of non-military support worth €1.2 billion over the coming 3 years. The package will address the country’s most urgent needs and contribute to recovery and reconstruction, and improve opportunities for Dutch companies in Ukraine, especially in areas where they can offer expertise.
The bulk of the package is aimed at the energy and water sectors. Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation Sjoerd Sjoerdsma made this announcement during his visit to Kyiv on Wednesday. ‘Ukraine is under heavy fire and facing a tough winter’, he said. ‘It is essential for the security of us all that we continue to support Ukraine and its people to withstand this war. That is why the government has decided on this new package.’
The Netherlands will make a contribution of €40 million to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund before the end of this year, to support the most urgent replacement and repairs to the energy system. Russian air strikes are increasingly targeting Ukraine’s energy and water infrastructure and have caused extensive damage and destruction. Dutch support will make it possible to repair damaged installations, stockpile emergency supplies and train specialist personnel for the energy and water sectors. The Netherlands will also provide € 55 million for in-kind energy support, enabling the delivery of energy equipment from Dutch companies to Ukrainian partners via the Netherlands Enterprise Agency.
Mr Sjoerdsma is visiting Kyiv together with the president of the Confederation of Netherlands Industry and Employers (VNO-NCW), Coen van Oostrom. They will talk with Ukrainian officials and Dutch businesses active in Ukraine about strengthening business relations, forging collaborations and removing obstacles.
The new package increases the government’s private sector support, enabling Dutch companies to play a bigger role in recovery and reconstruction and secure a better position in the Ukrainian market. For instance, €136 million will go toward initiatives including the Ukraine Partnership Facility. Additionally, the government is enlarging the coverage of the existing export credit insurance in order to reduce risks for businesses aiming to export to Ukraine, with an additional €19.5 million available, on top of the existing €60 million facility.
Foreign trade minister Sjoerdsma: ‘Support for recovery and reconstruction can’t wait for a ceasefire. Ukraine needs our help right now: military support, but also social and economic assistance. However successful you are on the battlefield, it's also essential that energy systems, hospitals and food production keep ticking over. This is not possible without the involvement of the private sector. That’s why it’s good to be here today with VNO-NCW. The companies that get involved now will help shape the partnerships, supply chains and opportunities of the future.’
VNO-NCW president Coen van Oostrom: ‘It’s impressive to see how Ukraine is keeping its economy running under very difficult circumstances. But reconstruction will be a huge job, and Dutch companies can play an important role in it. In this, we'll need to work closely with the Ukrainian government and remove obstacles for businesses. That’s what I'll be talking about today.’
Mr Sjoerdsma and Ukraine’s Minister of Economy and Environment Oleksandr Kravchenko will sign a declaration of intent on the Netherlands’ contribution to President Zelenskyy’s Industrial Ramstein initiative (€10 million). Its focus is on repairing and modernising the production capacity of Ukrainian businesses by facilitating the delivery of machines, equipment and other goods from other countries, including the Netherlands.
In addition, through the United Nations Development Programme, the Netherlands continues to support efforts to locate and return abducted Ukrainian children. Finally, the package also includes support in the areas of housing, humanitarian assistance, healthcare, mental health and psychosocial support, demining, democracy and the rule of law, and the restoration of cultural heritage.
With the package, the government is providing more details about how it will spend the amounts it had already pledged for the coming three years, namely €878 million in non-military support set out in the coalition agreement and an additional €327 million announced on Budget Day. A large part of this support is channeled through the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the World Bank, and the European Investment Bank (EIB)

Unknown Publisher

23:55:34 KST

Two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on this morning, leaving dozens dead and prompting a major emergency response.
At least 64 people were killed, according to the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, Reuters reported.
Authorities were continuing to search the damaged trains for victims.
The collision occurred around 9 a.m. near Urda, a town in Toledo province.
Images from the scene showed derailed carriages, including at least one that had fallen down a railway embankment. Several carriages were severely damaged, with wreckage scattered across the area.
An unnamed source briefed on the accident told Reuters that one train had stopped near Toledo because of a signal failure when another train struck it.
According to local authorities, one train was carrying 397 passengers and the other 147.
“We heard a violent noise, a completely enormous bump that lasted for ten seconds,” a passenger named Miguel told Spanish radio station COPE, according to Reuters.
“Through the window we could see a destroyed train. I imagine it was the other one.”
Emergency services deployed firefighters, helicopters and mobile intensive care units. Health Minister Mónica García urged people to donate blood.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez expressed shock at the accident and offered condolences to victims’ families. He also cleared his Wednesday schedule.
The opposition People’s Party (PP) canceled its campaign events ahead of Spain’s November 29 parliamentary election.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “Europe mourns” alongside the victims’ families.
The collision follows another high-speed rail accident in January, when 46 people died and more than 120 were injured near Adamuz in Andalusia.
Both accidents occurred on the Madrid-Seville route.

Copenhagen Airport says tighter security checks and staffing shortfalls contributed to long queues

Unknown Publisher

An order from the Danish Transport Authority led to additional baggage checks from October 8. Some passengers missed flights, and SAS reported rebooking 352 travelers.
Copenhagen Airport introduced additional security checks following an order from the Danish Transport Authority and underestimated staffing needs on some days in October, the airport said Wednesday after long queues caused passengers to miss flights.
The airport received the order on October 6 and introduced the measures two days later. The changes meant more passengers had their baggage checked manually, it said in a press release.
The airport did not explain why the authority issued the order or give details of its requirements.
There were periods of long waits on October 8, October 22 and October 23, the airport said. Passengers also faced waits of up to an hour early on Saturday, October 24.
Danish media have reported lengthy queues, particularly over the past five days, with some passengers reaching their flights too late to depart as booked.
The airport acknowledged that it had underestimated staffing needs on some days during October. It said “it is naturally not satisfactory” that some passengers had had “a bad experience”.
SAS said on October 23 that it had rebooked 352 passengers because of the long waits. Passengers were also urged to arrive earlier than usual and allow extra time for security.
Norwegian also offered affected customers rebooking.
Police announce stop-and-search zone for Copenhagen derby
Copenhagen Police will introduce a stop-and-search zone around Parken on Sunday, 8 November, when FC Copenhagen face Brøndby IF in a match classified as high risk.
The zone will be in force from 06:00 to 20:00 across parts of Østerbro, including Trianglen, Blegdamsvej, Jagtvej, Østerbrogade, Svanemøllen Station and Strandboulevarden.
Within the zone, police can stop and search people without suspecting them of a criminal offence. The measure is intended to prevent unrest surrounding the derby.
Police Inspector Peter Dahl said officers hoped for a festive and peaceful day, but would be deployed in large numbers given the fixture’s history.
“We will also be present in large numbers so that we can intervene if there should be signs of unrest brewing,” he said.
Police have also instructed FC Copenhagen to keep Brøndby supporters inside Parken for up to an hour after the final whistle. The aim is to separate the two groups of fans and prevent confrontations after the match.
Copenhagen Police warned that penalties for certain offences committed in connection with a football match can be increased by up to 50 percent. These include offences involving drugs, weapons and fireworks.
PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Frederiksen declined to comment further when asked about the matter later that day at Amalienborg in Copenhagen.
